units.la: EN quibus illi celebris liber hic blanditur mentis: En quales titulos pagina prima geri:.
units.tr: Behold the titles with which this famous book flatters the mind; see what kind of titles the first page bears.

units.la: Exilium, tormenta, cruces & verbera, flammas, Præcisus linguas, sulphura, vincla, famem.
units.tr: Exile, torments, crosses and scourgings, flames, severed tongues, brimstone, chains, hunger.

units.la: Quaeque tyrannorum rabies immanis & exlex Infanda in solos cogitat usque pios.
units.tr: And whatever the savage, lawless rage of tyrants devises, unspeakable, always against the pious alone.

units.la: Qualia si videat Stygÿs revocatus ab umbris, Ingemat, & pallens horreat ipse Nero.
units.tr: If Nero were recalled from the Stygian shades and saw such things, he would groan and, pale, shudder himself.

units.la: Detque manus victas: & se contenderit istis Cedere, qui reliquos vicerit, Antiochus.
units.tr: He would give up his hands in defeat, and Antiochus, who surpassed all the others, would confess that he must yield to these.

units.la: Talis[?] fonte[?] liber, quemnam Speciosus inescet, Indice vel solo qui nocuisse potest?
units.tr: What handsome man would be lured by a book of this kind, from such a source, one who could do harm by its title alone?

units.la: Ergo Stultitiae damnabitur, hunc tibi, Lector, Qui magnis librum sumptibus exhibuit?
units.tr: Will he therefore be condemned as a fool, reader, the one who offered you this book at great expense?

units.la: Immo satis prudens perse prouidit, ut ambo, Et pius atque pijs hostis, habere velint.
units.tr: Nay, rather, he foresaw wisely enough that both the pious and the enemies of the pious would want to have it.

units.la: Hoc pius in speculo, paria ad certamina quando, Si quando veniet, quos imitetur habet.
units.tr: In this mirror the pious man has those whom he may imitate when equal contests come, if ever they do.

units.la: Unde petenda fiet, longis constantia vinclis, Blanditias spernens, Iudicis atque minas: Unde etiam medijs mens imperterrita flammis, Imploransque Deum libera lingua suum.
units.tr: From here constancy is to be sought under long chains, scorning the flatteries and threats of the judge; from here too the mind is undaunted amid the flames, and the free tongue calls on its God.

units.la: Denique tela, quibus mundus superatur, & Orci Triste triumphati corruit imperium: Præsertim memori Christum quum mente revoluet Ista tulisse Ducem signa sequenda suis.
units.tr: Finally, here are the weapons by which the world is overcome, and the sad empire of Orcus has fallen, once triumphed over; especially when, with a mindful spirit, one recalls that Christ, the leader, bore these signs to be followed by his own.

units.la: Impius hic contra, sævi monumenta furoris Spectabit lætus non moritura sui.
units.tr: The impious man, on the other hand, will look gladly upon the monuments of his savage fury, which will not die.

units.la: Quippe patris Stygÿ vestigia nota prementem, Sese æquasse decus, vel superasse sciet.
units.tr: For he will know, treading the well-known footsteps of his Stygian father, that he has equalled or surpassed that glory.

units.la: Ergo pium ut celebrem crudelia funera reddunt, Sic illi felicitas[?] nomina clara dabit.
units.tr: Therefore, as cruel deaths make the pious famous, so will such fortune give him illustrious names.

units.tr: To the pious and truly Christian reader

units.la: IOANNES CRISPINVS GRATIAM & pacem à Deo Patre per IESVM CHRISTVM.
units.tr: JOHN CRISPIN, grace and peace from God the Father through Jesus Christ.

units.la: ETSI prioribus illis Martyrum editis à me voluminibus, Christiane Lector, satisfecisse videri poteramus desiderio & labori nostro; quoniam quæ in eo genere suscipienda tum essent, ea nos omnia sincerè iudicio nostro, alieno feliciter executi, Reipublicæ Christianæ plurimum ad gratiam & gratulationem attulissemus: tamen quum ante nos nemo nostrorum hominum operi tam raro & inusitato non modò manum admolitus esset, verùm de re generibus adeò varia, partibus infinita cogitare ne venisset ei quidem in mentem; catera fere nos omnia, quæ multa magnáque videbantur, seposuimus libenter, dum hoc etiam erga te postremo munere perfungimur. Excitabat nos veritas ac varietas, multitudóque in omni genere exemplorum eorum hominum, qui superiorum illorum quos attigimus, vel æquarent in re gerenda virtutem atque constantiam; vel fortem & conditionem splendore domestico suo, & omnium ingenuarum artium cognitione superarent (cuius generis ad nos ex utraque Germania & Gallia nonnulli, è Britannia & Hispania plerique peruenerunt) imprimis autem cum vastorum & impotentium hodie quorundam hominum perfidiosa cum immanitate coniuncta peruersitas & insania; quos partim ipsos nihilo meliores effectos horum editione monimentorum, partim inusitata rabie crudeliter ad sanctissimis quibusque viris, planéque [illegible, ~9 letters] periculum inferendum quotidie progredi videamus. Nam quid de Cardinale isto Lotharingo dicemus, o Lector, qui inveterato quodam, & in omnes bonos ac pios concepto crudeliter odio, Senatoris innocentissimi, integerrimi, sanctissimi, Annae Burgi vitam & animam quatuor ipsos menses nefariè persequutus, iniquissimo iudicio martyrem circumventum ipse damnarit; damnatum non solum extinxerit incendio, sed plane etiam mortuum in invidia flammam apud Optimates ac populum seditiosis concionibus adducere tentarit? Sed non faciam ut dum veteratorem illum Galeritam exequor, desiderium interim amplissimi fortissimiq; Senatoris tibi commoveam: quinimo quicquid attigi, eo maximè consilio feci, ut iis quas initio posui, causis intelligeres, me quidem & voluminum illorum reliquias voluisse persequi libenter; & iisdem characteribus eorum omnium qui imposterum illustri quopiam testimonio fidei suae Christi veritatem obsignaturi prodibunt, memoriam usurpaturum esse diligenter. Quorum hominum ad interitum voluntarium pro D. N. Iesu Christi Euangelio quotidie proficiscentium si qua omnino usquam memoria custodita descriptáve aut elogia, aut apophthegmata, aut huius denique generis documenta vestigiaq; giáque rerum præclarissimè ab ijsdem gestarum existere tibi constabit, Lector, hac tu, qua es in omnes beneuolentia, qua in populum reuera Christianum pietate, conquisita diligenter, exscriptáque fideliter, huc ad nos (quod quidem Ecclesiæ commodo fieri putes) officiosè benignéque perferenda velim cures. Quod ipsum vt maiore etiam à te studio petam, cum alia multa sanè faciunt; tum amor ille perpetuus atque singularis, quo Ecclesiam suam complexus Christus, talibus illam atque tot exemplis illustriorem in dies singulos efficere contendit, vt haud sciam an huic operi rediuiuo quotidie magis atque magis, tam longè latéque diffuso, quisquam omnino idoneam assiduitatis ac diligentiæ magnitudinem afferre possit. Quo de genere toto, simul etiam de maximis clarissimisque Dei opt. max. erga Ciuitatem, ex qua tot Pugiles summo Reipub. Christianæ splendore prodierunt, beneficijs, poteram quidem effundi latius; id nisi Ioannes Tagautius, vir ille sanè literis perpolitus, rerumq; varietate atque vsu ipso iam perdoctus, sed (quod quidé est hodie caput) & moribus optimus, & religione Christianus, cumulatissimè præstitisset. Scripsit enim Protrepticon carmé ad S.P.Q. Geneuens. quo carmine situm oppidi præterea describit, vt intelligere æqui & iniqui possint minimè vulgarem esse prærogatiuam, quam voluntatis suæ Deus Geneuæ dederit; siue vitæ huius humanæ cursum, siue futuræ illius quietem & diuturnitatem libeat æstimare. Adiunxit itemq; & Votiuum in gratiam & vsum Electorum omnium, qui tum exauthorati Euangelicam veritatem suo sanguine gloriosissimè consignauerunt; tum merentes adhuc imperatore Christo, pari (si res tulerit) constantia in pulverem & aciem prodituri sunt. quod ipsum & ad breuitatem mihi est aptius, & ad reliqua quaedam quae suo loco & tempore tibi sumus exhibituri, prouidentius. Vale Christiane Lector; & dum reliquorum seriem expectas, his ad gloriam tu Domini, & salutem tuam frui perge. Geneuae, V. Calend. Martij. M. D. LX.
units.tr: Although, Christian reader, I might have seemed to have satisfied my own desire and labour with those earlier volumes of martyrs published by me, since in that kind I had sincerely carried out, by my own judgment and happily through others, everything that needed to be undertaken, and had brought very great grace and joy to the Christian commonwealth; nevertheless, since none of our people before me had not only laid a hand to a work so rare and unusual, but had not even thought of a subject so varied in kinds and infinite in parts, I have willingly set aside nearly everything else, which seemed many and great, while I also discharge this last duty to you. What stirred me on was the truth and variety, and the great number of examples in every kind of those men who either equalled the virtue and constancy of those earlier martyrs I have touched on in their conduct, or surpassed them in rank and station, in domestic distinction and in knowledge of all the liberal arts (of this kind some have come to us from both Germanies and from France, and most from Britain and Spain); and above all the treacherous perversity and madness, joined with savagery, of certain vast and unrestrained men today; whom we see daily advancing, some of them not at all made better by the publication of these records, others cruelly raging with unusual fury against the most holy men, and plainly bringing danger upon them [illegible]. For what shall we say, Reader, of that Lorraine Cardinal, who, with a long-standing hatred conceived cruelly against all good and pious people, wickedly pursued for four whole months the life and soul of the most innocent, upright and holy senator Anne Burg, and himself condemned him, a martyr, caught in a most unjust judgment; and having condemned him, not only put him to death by fire but, even when he was dead, tried to bring a flame of hatred against him among the nobles and the people by seditious sermons? But I will not, while I pursue that old trickster Galerita, stir up in you longing for the most distinguished and brave senator in the meantime. Rather, whatever I have touched upon, I have done with this especially in view: that you should understand, from the reasons I set out at the beginning, that I have been willing to pursue gladly the remnants of those volumes too, and that I will diligently keep in memory, with the same marks, all who henceforth will come forth to seal the truth of Christ with some notable testimony of their faith. If any memory anywhere has been kept or written down of those men who daily go to voluntary death for the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, or any eulogies, or sayings, or in short documents and traces of this kind and of the most distinguished deeds accomplished by them, it will be clear to you, Reader. I wish you, with that benevolence you show to all and that piety towards the true Christian people, to take care to seek these out diligently, copy them faithfully, and carry them to us, dutifully and kindly, as you think would be for the good of the Church. I ask this of you with still greater zeal, since many other things certainly urge it; above all that perpetual and singular love with which Christ embraced his Church and strives to make her more illustrious day by day with such examples, so that I do not know whether anyone at all can bring to this work, which is being revived day by day more and more and spread so widely, a fitting measure of constancy and diligence. On this whole subject, and at the same time on the greatest and most famous benefits of God, most good and most great, towards the city from which so many champions have come forth to the highest splendour of the Christian commonwealth, I could indeed have spoken more widely; but John Tagaut has done this most fully, a man indeed polished in letters and already very learned in the variety and practice of affairs, but (which is now the chief thing) most excellent in character and Christian in religion. For he has written a Protrepticon, a poem addressed to the Senate and People of Geneva, in which he also describes the situation of the town, so that the fair and the unfair may understand that the privilege which God has given to Geneva by his will is by no means common, whether one chooses to weigh the course of this human life or the rest and long duration of that future life. He has also added a Votive poem for the favour and use of all the Elect, who, though deprived of their station, gloriously sealed the Evangelical truth with their blood; and who, still serving under Christ the Emperor, will, if circumstances require, come forth into dust and battle with equal constancy. This is both more suitable to me for brevity, and more prudent for certain other matters which we shall set before you in their own place and time. Farewell, Christian Reader; and while you await the series of the rest, go on enjoying these things to the glory of the Lord and to your own salvation. Geneva, 25 February 1560.

units.la: SANCTE audi: sancto facilis precor annue voto Magne opifex, cuius non enarrabile nomen, Et caelum, ac miseri confusa potentia regni Lucifugum, & mundi bruta haec elementa tremiscunt:
units.tr: Holy one, hear: favour my prayer, which is easy for the holy to grant. Great Maker, whose name cannot be spoken, and heaven, and the troubled power of the wretched kingdom, the light-shunning ones, and these dumb elements of the world tremble.

units.la: Quem Natura tremit venerans, vltróque fatetur Te Regem Authorémque suum, qui numine comples Omnia; Regem, vno quo iudice stántque cadúntque Res hominum, morbo iaceant, seu luce fruantur; Seu bellum pacémue feras, & gaudia vitæ.
units.tr: Nature trembles to reverence you, and freely confesses you as her King and Author, who fill all things with your divine power; King, by whose sole judgment the affairs of men stand and fall, whether they lie sick or enjoy the light, whether you bring war or peace, and the joys of life.

units.la: Tu vero Alme, sacri arcano qui luminis imbre Cuncta foues, feruas & alis, solidáque serenas Lætitia, & castus renouas mortalia corda, Illucesce meæ totúsque illabere menti Irradians, & luce tuâ sua nubila differ.
units.tr: But you, gentle one, who with the secret shower of sacred light cherish, keep and nourish all things, and calm solid joy, and renew mortal hearts in chastity: shine on me, pour yourself wholly into my mind, illuminating it, and scatter its clouds with your light.

units.la: Hauriat ex te illos precor, ô precor hauriat ignes, Viuificos ignes tenebrosa: agè discute noctem, Et præluce intus, ne pes me lubricus imas Auferat in tenebras, & desolata nocentum Antra, bonúsque tuo æternùm me lumine deduc.
units.tr: Let them draw in from you, I pray, O let them draw in the life-giving fires. Dispel the dark night, shine within, lest my slippery foot carry me down into the lowest shadows and the deserted caves of the guilty; and good one, lead me forever by your light.

units.la: Alme faue, & sanctis præsens allabere cœptis: Munere Sancte tuo, mihi casta Poetica mentem Excitet immersam tenebris, dubiúmque mone me Quid sequar: & quæcunque mihi se tramite cæco Ostendet via difficilis, me numine firma Præsenti, dum Sancte nouos tibi molior orsus, Dum iuuat Aonio Latias de vertice Musas Sacra per, & sacros longè deducere saltus.
units.tr: Gentle one, be favourable, and come present to my holy undertakings. By your holy gift, let chaste Poetry rouse my mind, sunk in shadows, and warn me, in my doubt, what to follow; and whatever difficult way shows itself to me by a blind track, strengthen me with your present power, Holy one, while I begin new work for you, while it pleases me to lead the Latin Muses from the Aonian summit through sacred and holy glades far away.

units.la: Nam quid enim:ecce nouos in me sacer impetus ignes Præcipitat, spirántque nouum noua pectora numen. En nuper fandi indocilis, iam pectore magnos Concipio sensus: prior illa euanuit omnis Impietas, & vita olim iuuenilibus annis
units.tr: For what then? Behold, the holy impulse hurls new fires into me, and new breasts breathe a new divinity. Lo, lately untaught in speech, I now conceive great feelings in my breast. All that former impiety has vanished, and the life once spent in youthful years

units.la: Degener, & Musæ studium pellacis inane. Me caligo nocens, tenebrisque horrentibus umbræ Deseruere, tui primos ad luminis ortus. Terra vale, pennis liquidum supra æthera longe Auferor: en ventos pedibus & nubila calco. Sat noctisque umbrisque datum est, pudet isse tot annos Cæcum per tenebras, lucémque hausisse malignam Pœnitet, heu! ægramque animam dolor iste perurit.
units.tr: degenerate, and the empty study of the deceitful Muses. Harmful darkness and the horrid shadows have left me at the first rising of your light. Farewell, earth: on wings I am carried far above the liquid air; lo, I tread on the winds and clouds. Enough has been given to night and its shadows. I am ashamed to have wandered so many years through blind darkness, and I repent having drunk in the malignant light; alas, that grief burns my sick soul.

units.la: En igitur quà Religio caput extulit umbris, Me juvet antiqui Musas super ardua Juræ Sistere: jamque novum hic Helicona, hic quærere laurus Hic alias edico, alias templa horrida rupes: Meque sequi moneo dumos per & aspera saxa: Vos ô vos casti Vates, sanctique Poetæ, Quà via secta recens, & quô vix ulla priorum Me trepidum incertumque viæ vestigia ducant; Hæc via nunc tentanda, mihi Vigor igneus ille Quà se aperit, Vigor omnipotens, qui lumine casto Exhaurit mentes hominum, puráque relinquit. Quà mihi sedat lux oculis clarissima, cæli Munere, me procul ô sævis Pater eripe terris Quæ passim innocuo justorum sanguine inundant; Et quæ te contra flammas & in arma feruntur. Crudelis patriæ jam longa oblivia potem, Nec mihi chara trahant alio natalia mentem, Dum sacra mi plenis evoluere carmina fusis Est animus, medioque oculos jam tollere cælo. Ac jam Pæonias paulum intermittere Musas Cura sit, & docto scriptas in pulvere formas, Formásque radiósque & pictum in pariete mundum.
units.tr: Lo, therefore, where Religion has raised her head out of the shadows, let it please me to set the Muses above the steep heights of old Jura. Now here I seek a new Helicon, here laurels; here I command other things, and elsewhere other temples among the horrid rocks. I bid myself follow through thickets and over rough stones. You, O you chaste bards and holy poets, where the path is newly cut, and where scarcely any of the old tracks lead me, trembling and uncertain of the way: this way must now be tried, where that fiery vigour opens itself to me, the almighty vigour which with chaste light drains men's minds and leaves them pure. Where the brightest light calms my eyes by the gift of heaven, Father, snatch me far from the cruel lands which everywhere flood with the innocent blood of the just, and which are borne against you in flames and arms. Long now I shall not drink the oblivion of my cruel fatherland, nor let my birthplace drag my mind elsewhere, while my spirit is set on pouring out sacred songs in full flow, and on lifting my eyes now to mid-heaven. And now let it be a care to let the Paeonian Muses pause a little, and the forms written in learned dust, and forms and rays, and the world painted on the wall.

units.la: Ergo pij Vates huc jam revocantor, & esto Hac iter in cælum, pia quà modo semita feruet Cursu alacri: hoc agite, hoc nobis via calle secanda: Nam mihi mendaces quid nunc accedere lucos,
units.tr: Therefore the holy bards are now called back here; let this be the way to heaven, where the holy path now glows with eager course. Here let us act; by this track we must cut our way. For what now is it to me to approach deceitful groves,

units.la: Quid iuga Parnasi,quid lauriferam Hippocrenen? Nil canimus mortale,nihil mecum ipse profanum Mente[?] agito; Me, me, cælesti Spiritus aura HIEROPOLIN ducit,tot tempestatibus astam[?], Tot monstris, tot turbinibus, rerumque procellis, Tótque inter gladios,toties extrema gementem, Iámque solo velut excisam,iam-iámque labantem, Ni placeat Dextræ miseram fulcire potenti. Téque tuámque urbem Latio, Christe optime, cornu Iam canere incipio, & populos vulgare per omnes: Atque adeò Lucem magni trans ultima claustra Iam late fusam Oceani,gelidáque sub Arcto. Nam quicquid contra obstiterit furiosa tyrannis Pontificum Regúmque Sacerdotúmque Senatus: Lucem illam,Nomenque tuum,Rex maxime,gentes In gelidis vstisque plagis,tibi sede parata Excipient (verum dederis modò cernere lumen) Et fingi faciles æquis sub legibus olim, Barbariem,morésque feros,victúmque nefandum Mutabunt illi in melius,meliora sequuti: Exemplóque meo casto tibi carmine laudes Expedient,nati forsan melioribus annis. Ergo agè quò pietas quò ducunt vota sequamur.
units.tr: What the ridges of Parnassus, what laurel-bearing Hippocrene? I sing nothing mortal, and in my mind I turn over nothing profane. Me, me, the breath of the heavenly Spirit leads to Hieropolis, I who have been tossed by so many tempests, so many monsters, so many whirlwinds and storms of affairs, and among so many swords, groaning so often at the brink, now almost cut down to the ground, now sinking again and again, unless it pleases the powerful right hand to prop up my wretched self. And now I begin to sing of you and your city, Christ most good, to Latium, and to spread it among all peoples; indeed, of the Light now widely poured out beyond the farthest bars of the great Ocean, and under the icy Bear. For whatever the furious tyranny of the Pontiffs, of Kings and of the Senate of Priests may oppose, those nations in icy and scorched regions will receive that Light and your name, greatest King, with a seat prepared for you (if only you grant them to see the light). Once formed as easy men under fair laws, they will change their barbarism, wild customs and unspeakable food for the better, following better things. By my example they will spread your praises in chaste song, perhaps born in better years. Therefore come, let us follow where piety and vows lead.

units.la: Hîc ubi perpetuus cano se tollit in auras Iura supercilio, & gelidum super aera pulsat Altis abietibus,cælóque minantibus ornis: Qua maturatæ breviora crepuscula noctis Contrahit,& lucis fugientes occupat horas: (Tam densis altè piceis solémque diémque Summouet, horrentíque Larix supereminet umbra:) Non procul Austrum inter spectans Solémque cadentem, Ripa exesa fremit,quam verberat Arua sonoris Præcipitatus aquis,& circum multa coronat Populus,& circum Tamarix & Rhamnus obumbrant: Quas inter fervet, secúmque laborat iniquo Inclusus spatio, ac pontem indignatus, arenæ Conuoluit moles & lubrica saxa fragosus.
units.tr: Here, where the perpetual Jura raises itself into the air with its brow, and strikes the cold sky above with lofty firs and mountain ashes threatening the heavens, where it shortens the twilights of the ripening night and seizes the fleeing hours of light (so thickly, with pitch-pines, it keeps off the sun and day, and the bristling larch rises above in shadow): not far off, looking between the south wind and the setting sun, an eroded bank roars, which the Arve beats, plunging with sounding waters, and around it a poplar crowns much, and tamarisk and buckthorn cast their shade. Between these it seethes and labours with itself, enclosed in an unfair space, and, disdaining the bridge, the rugged mass rolls sand and slippery rocks.

units.la: Ponte sub hoc quantum bis térue superuolet agri Tortum hastile manu: medio clarissima campo Vrbs quaquâ-versum se se venientibus offert Primum humilis, formosa tamen: mox crescere visa Comminus; en facies iam se tota explicat vrbis. Ceu rosa purpureis quam matutinus Eois Sol afflat, paulatim obelisco promit hianti Mucronem exiguum, tenuis quem purpura pingit: Mox vero ecce nouum calathi rutilantis honorem Explicat, & medio rosa punica ridet in horto.
units.tr: Under this bridge, as far as one may fly twice or thrice over the field with a hurled, twisted spear, in the middle of the clear plain the city presents itself from every side to those who come: at first low, yet lovely; soon it seems to grow nearer; lo, now the whole face of the city unfolds. As a rose, which the morning sun breathes upon in the Eastern dawn, gradually thrusts forth from its gaping calyx a small point, which the thin purple paints; then lo, it unfolds the new honour of a glowing cup, and the pomegranate rose laughs in the middle of the garden.

units.la: Talis ad Allobrogum sedet vrbs confinia campi, Quâ Scythicum Boreas mare verrit acerbus & vrens, Lemmano bene tuta lacu, quo pulchrior ullus Vix fuerit, stratis & eat qui lenius undis: Purior Electro, vitrcóque[?] simillimus amni, Nunc viridi lætus facie, nunc æquore glauco Exultans, nunc cæruleus sua littora lambit: Sed furit interdum fluctuque sonante tumescit, Quum Deus aut Eurum aut humentes excitat Austros. Quin & quum rapidis strident Aquilonibus aurae, Et densa Omnipotens tristes nive conspuit agros, Fluctibus iratis sua littora pulsat & vrbem Spumeus insurgens. viridi super æquore dicas Velleribus niueis certatim atque ordine longo Subsultare greges: tanto ferus impete canos Undarum volvit cumulos, longúmque fragosis Se sulcis furiatus agit, transfversa dehiscens! Sed tamen haud illo fuerit piscosior alter, Non vel Benacus, non vel Lucrinus, & ille Addua, quem celeri fugiens præteermeat unda. Siue lacum spectes seu pinguia culta, vel hortos,
units.tr: Such is the city that sits at the borders of the Allobroges' plain, where the harsh and burning North wind sweeps the Scythian sea, well guarded by Lake Lemán, than which scarcely any is more beautiful, and which flows more gently with its calm waves: purer than amber, and most like a glassy river, now joyful in its green face, now exulting in its glaucous surface, now blue, it laps its shores. But at times it rages and swells with sounding waves, when God rouses either the East wind or the damp South winds. Moreover, when the breezes hiss with rapid North winds, and the Almighty spits thick snow over the sad fields, it strikes its shores and the city with angry waves, foaming as it rises. Over the green surface you might say flocks of snow-white fleece leap in long order, each vying with the other: so fiercely, with such force, it rolls its hoary heaps of waves, and, furious, gaping across its course, drives itself along in long broken furrows. Yet no other lake is more fishy than it, not Benacus, nor Lucrinus, nor that Adda which flows past, swiftly fleeing. Whether you look at the lake, or at the rich cultivated fields, or the gardens,

units.la: Seu fontes lucósue & prata sonantia riuis: Sunt hic quae pascunt oculos, animúmque quietum Et mentes penitus caelesti ex igne renatas: Ac victum grauido læta ubere rura beatum Sufficiunt. Tun' hic poscas armenta per alti Pascua Iurai aut pingues in vallibus haedos, Lanigerósue greges, & amantes salsa capellas? An potius teneros iam pingui abdomine lactes Uberibus densis mater quos bruta saginat Fellantes? torua-ne bouis per gramina fœtus Iam grandeis, queis nata nouam modo cornua Lunam Nunc primùm, audaci referunt in fronte, proteruis? Aut etiam pingues læta inter pabula fœtas, Tenta saporato gestantes ubera lactè, Quo premitur pinguis vicinæ caseus urbi? An memorem grauidas fruges, vinetáque plenis Quæ passim fœcunda gemunt onerata racemis; Aut altis referam coniunctas vitibus ulmos? Aut etiam largo fœtu nemus omne grauescens? An Veris tot delicias fructúsque salubres? Muneráque arboribus quæ seris diuite felix Prouentu coquit Autumnus? fœtásne Iuglandes? Aruáne quæ grauibus gaudent inculta Volemis, Hybernámque Pyrum & Mâlos sua pomaferentes, Seráque pétiolis breuibus pendentia poma? (Unde suum Gallis nomen traxisse feruntur) In lœuore aspro maculosæ corticis illa Gratum parte rubent, hac fuluo picta metallo Lutea non magno compressa volumine surgunt Interpuncta croco, & lætum spirantia odorem.
units.tr: or springs and groves, and meadows resounding with streams: here are things that feed the eyes and a quiet mind, and minds reborn from heavenly fire; and the happy fields, blessed with fertile udders, supply abundant food. Would you here seek herds through the high pastures of Jura, or fat kids in the valleys, or woolly flocks, and goats fond of salt? Or would you rather suckle tender young whom the mother beasts fatten with dense udders, now plump in the belly? Or the calves through the meadows, now grown big, whose birth has only just given them new horns in their bold brows, wanton? Or even the fat, pregnant cows amid joyful pastures, carrying udders full of savoury milk, from which the rich cheese of the neighbouring city is pressed? Shall I mention the heavy grain, and the vines that everywhere groan fruitful, laden with full clusters; or shall I tell of the elms joined to the high vines? Or the whole grove growing heavy with abundant fruit? The delights of spring and its healthy fruits? And the gifts that Autumn, rich in late yield, ripens on the trees? Walnuts, fruitful? Fields where wild plums delight, and winter pears, and apples bearing their fruit, and late apples hanging on short stalks (from which they are said to have drawn their name among the Gauls)? On the rough skin of the spotted rind, some are red on one side, and on the other painted with tawny gold, yellow, not large in bulk, dotted with saffron, and breathing a pleasant odour.

units.la: Iurae diuitias referam, & tot commoda vitæ Quæ vel in incultis, vel rupibus in desertis Luxuriant: nempe hic effundit rustica parcis Copia ruricolis pleno sua munera cornu.
units.tr: I will tell of the riches of the Jura, and of the many comforts of life that flourish even in uncultivated places and on barren rocks. Here rustic plenty pours out its gifts from a full horn upon the country folk who live sparingly.

units.la: Sed vero quia vita patrum me simplice cultu In primis capit, & dulci succendit amore, Hoc Voto pia Musa bonos venerabere agrestes, Tantisper dum longe alios tibi molior orsus. En plectrum & citharam paulum quoque rustica poscunt Ipsa sibi & nostri montes. Hic ergo, priorum Quem non parca olim contenta fidelibus aruis, Nec patiens operum delectat vita per agros, Haud ignara sitim sedare sonante fluento, Suetaque decussis ieiunia soluere cornis: Non hic lautitias urbis Salmontica vina: Sed nec multiplici mensas sub lance gementes Hic poscat, nimiaque dapes roget arte paratas.
units.tr: But since the life of the fathers, in its simple manner, first captures me and kindles me with sweet love, pious Muse, you shall honour these good rustics with this vow, for as long as I am preparing to begin on quite different matters for you. Behold, the lyre and the cithara, and our own mountains, ask for a little rustic verse. Here, then, is one whom the thrifty life of former times delights, the life that was content with faithful fields and does not shrink from labour, roaming the countryside. He does not fail to know how to quench his thirst at the sounding stream, and is accustomed to break his fasts with cornel-berries shaken from the tree. Here there are no city luxuries, no Salmontic wines. Nor does he call for tables groaning under many dishes, or ask for feasts prepared with excessive art.

units.la: At tibi quem capiunt agrorum cultus & horti: Quem montes quem rura iuuant, rurisque suppellex Lutea, delitias agri expectare salubres Hic liceat; vescos fructus, olerumque feraces Areolas, centum excipiant quae Pythagoreos. Hic pernas sale duratas, sapidoque rubentes Fumo, quae media duris sunt salgama Bruma Monticolis, hic cocta cado tibi defruta aheno: Cymbiaque hic pingui spumantia flumine lactis, Et vivos latices (nite mage dura picatis Horna cadis, neu te capiant hortensia vina Quae tibi proventu det fertilis vbere malus) Atque super viridi lachrymosa coagula iunco, Quum tellus sitiens languentibus aestuat herbis, Expectare iuuet. Nos hic agreste paratu (Sed quem mundities, sed quem sua gratia condit) Frugales epulis mensas oneramus inemptis, Quales campus alit. Quicunque huc ergo palato Solicito accedes, nostro expectabis in orbe Non plura his, imo potius queis rustica patrum Vita placet, vernis agri purisque volentes Delitijs, facie cælíque lacúsque fruuntor, Et Iuræ aspectu, Rhodaníque liquentibus vndis.
units.tr: But for you, whom the cultivation of fields and gardens attracts, whom the mountains and the countryside delight, and the yellow furnishings of rural life, it is permitted to look forward here to the healthy delights of the land: fruits fit for eating, and fertile little beds of vegetables, enough to satisfy a hundred Pythagoreans. Here are hams hardened with salt and reddened by savoury smoke, which are the salted meat of mountain folk through the harsh middle of winter; here is defrutum boiled down for you in a bronze pot; here are bowls foaming with rich milk, and fresh juices. (Shine rather, hard casks of hornwood smeared with pitch, lest the garden wines of the fruitful apple tree, which yields abundantly, capture you.) And, moreover, weeping curds on green rushes, when the thirsty earth glows with languid grass, it will please you to look forward to. We here, with rustic preparation (yet one seasoned by neatness, and by its own charm), load frugal tables with unbought fare, such as the plain produces. Whoever, therefore, comes here with a discerning palate will look for nothing more in our world than these things. Rather, those for whom the rustic life of the fathers pleases, who wish for the spring and the pure delights of the fields, may enjoy the face of the sky and the lakes, the view of the Jura, and the flowing waves of the Rhone.

units.la: Quid dicam vrticas labris vbi coxit ahenis Rusticus, & densum expressit radicibus humorem Inuergensque sero pingui, iam cogit, & infert Lactea fiscellis informans liba sub vmbra: Hinc tibi caseoli, quorum sapor omnibus vnus Præstiterit, nobisque seri de nomine dicti.
units.tr: What shall I say of the nettles, which the countryman boils in bronze pots, pressing from the roots a thick juice, and then pouring in whey, now curdles and brings forth in the shade milk-white cakes shaped in little baskets: hence for you little cheeses, whose flavour surpasses all others, and which are named after the whey (serum) for us.

units.la: Sed quid pingue illud veluti nubecula, multram [?] Quod superintexit, lactíque supernatat vdo, Et quod in angusta crebris dum tunditur olla Ictibus, in crassum quanto mage vapulat, exit: Ac tandem longo solidum fit verbere corpus? Per medios æstus, nostris hæ scilicet illæ Hic montis sunt deliciæ, queis Loton Vlyssis, Queis nec prætulerit Batauo sub iudice quisquam Condita suberibus natiuis Attica mella.
units.tr: But what is that fat, like a little cloud, which covers the top and floats upon the moist milk, and which, when it is beaten in a narrow pot with frequent blows, comes out thicker the more it is thrashed, and at last with long beating becomes a solid mass? Through the middle heats, these, to be sure, are the delights of this mountain, which no one under a Batavian judge would prefer to the Lotus of Ulysses, or to Attic honey stored in its native hives.

units.la: Haud leuia hæc vrbis sunt ornamenta beatæ (Exteriora licet) largo Pater optimus imbre Quæ fundit; rebusque suos hic ditat opimis. Herbarum quoque terra ferax, succique potentis Innumeras circùm doctis alit vsibus aptas, Et quas vel medici non agnouére priores. Assuetæ fluuio volucres ripisque sonoris, Seu quæ rura colunt, vrbésque aut aspera montis, Sedibus hic errant varijs circúmque supráque. Quæ verò hic habitant, quas non doƈto ordine solers Digeris & multo lustras apprimà labore Textor in antiquis consummatissime chartis?
units.tr: These are no small ornaments of the blessed city, though external ones, which the best Father pours out in a generous rain, and with which he enriches his people. The land is also fertile in herbs, and nourishes around it countless juices of potent strength, fit for learned uses, some of which earlier physicians did not know. The birds accustomed to the river and its echoing banks, whether they haunt the fields, the cities, or the rough mountains, wander here in various seats, round about and above. But what of those things which the skilful weaver of ancient pages, most accomplished in his craft, arranges in orderly fashion and surveys with great labour?

units.la: Quid cælum aeriæque plagæ, ventíque salubres? Purior hic cæli campos habet æthra patentes, Prospeƈtúmque loci grato quoque terminat arcu Iura, vbi nox fugiens séque & sua sydera condit. Quà verò lux alma diem mortalibus affert,
units.tr: What of the sky, the airy regions, and the healthy winds? Here the air has purer sky over the open fields, and the prospect of the place is bounded by a pleasing arc of the Jura, where the fleeing night hides itself and its stars. But where kindly light brings the day to mortals,

units.la: Continuæ rupis viridis sinus imminet urbi, (Rupis quam patrio dicunt sermone Saleuam) Nec procul inde licet surgentes vertice cano Prospicere, & medijs insertas nubibus Alpes.
units.tr: the hollow of a continuous green cliff overhangs the city (a rock which they call Saleva in the native tongue). Nor is it far from there that one may look out upon the snowy peaks rising high, and the Alps set among the clouds.

units.la: Parte alia Rhodanus qua iam defertur in Austrum Egr[?]ditúrque Lacu (tacitus namque influit amnis Lemmanúmque secat) mediam praeterfluit urbem: Sed vero in geminas medius quam separat urbes Paruus adhuc, viridíque fluens pellucidus unda.
units.tr: On the other side, where the Rhone now runs southward and issues from the lake (for the river flows in quietly and cuts through the Lake of Geneva), it flows past the middle of the city. Yet in the midst, which separates the twin cities, it is still small, flowing clear with green water.

units.la: Vrbs ea dives agri, dives fluviòque lacúque Et populis, gaudens plebeio animosa Senatu, Leges æqua suas, libertatémque tuetur: Vnáque tantum alias inter caput exerit urbes Allobrogum, quàm nubiferis minor Alpibus esse Iura potest. veteres appellauere GENEVAM. Nomen adhuc seruat populis tot, & undique circum Iniusum, ac tantis odiosum regibus, olim Quod tenebris immersa, Dei modò munere magno Aspectet lucem, & pura modò luce fruatur.
units.tr: That city is rich in its fields, rich in its river and lake, and in its people, who take pleasure in their plebeian senate and are spirited. It keeps its laws just and its liberty secure. It alone lifts its head above the other cities of the Allobroges, as far as the cloud-bearing Alps allow the Jura to be lower. The ancients called it GENEVA. It still keeps that name, hated by so many peoples and everywhere around, unbearable, and odious to such great kings: a city that once lay immersed in shadows, and now, by the great gift of God, looks upon the light and enjoys a pure light.

units.la: Ac veluti quum se diversis partibus agri Effudere greges, & malis gramina tondent Securi, huc illuc per pascua læta vagantes: Si fidus pecoris custos acerrimus Umber, Non procul insidias meditantes vidit ab alto Aggere forte lupos, inter dumeta latentes: Haud mora, latratu rapido citat ecce magistrum, Horrendúmque micans, & fèlle & dentibus ardet, Ac circum, pecus omne vagum cursu alite lustrat Increpitans: nunc has nunc illas stringit & urget Et morsu compellit agens, caudaque flagello Cogit aberrantes ultro citróque capellas.
units.tr: And just as when flocks, having spread out from different parts of the field, wander here and there through the pleasant pastures, tearing at the grass with their jaws, unconcerned; if the faithful and most keen sheepdog Umber, from a high mound, sees by chance wolves lurking in the thickets, not far off, plotting an ambush, without delay he rushes to bark and alert his master. Bristling and flashing with gall and teeth, he circles the whole straying herd, swiftly running, rebuking them: now he drives this one, now that one, with a bite, and with his tail like a whip he forces the wandering goats to and fro.

units.la: In densum coijsse gregem tum protinus omnes Aspicias, iunctásque simul trepido agmine ferri Ad socios, caulasque metu trepidare silentes.
units.tr: Then at once you would see them all crowd into a dense flock, pressed together in a trembling throng, rushing to their companions, and the silent folds trembling with fear.

units.la: Haud aliter si quando pios (quum sedibus errant, Securi rerum, varijs) Deus hostibus vrget, Hostibus infandis furias nil praeter, & ignem Qui spirent, Christi populum temerare cruentis Ausi omnes diri manibus, quíque omnia turbent: Huc videas plebem inualidam, puerósque senésque, Tot cunas etiam infantum, matrésque viróque Conflucre, & longè crudeles linquere terras.
units.tr: Not otherwise, when at times God presses his pious people, who wander in various places, secure and unconcerned with affairs, by enemies: enemies who breathe nothing but furies and fire, the unspeakable men who have dared to defile the people of Christ with bloody hands, and who throw everything into confusion. Here you would see the feeble folk, boys and old men, so many infant cradles too, mothers and husbands, gathering together and leaving their distant cruel lands.

units.la: Ecce pijs ferunt profugis deserta locorum, Et nemora & montes praerupta & confraga rupium. Heu adeò ingentem terris ex omnibus vndam Huc gentis profugae vomit infelix Europa! En sese huc trepidi per tot discrimina vitae, Mortali, vnanimes, haud sub pastore receptant: Crescit & his demùm praeclara Geneua colonis, Surgit vt exiguo de fonte ingentibus Isler Auctus aquis, aut fluminibus centum Albula dives.
units.tr: Behold, they seek out for the pious fugitives the deserted places, the groves and steep mountains and the broken crags of rocks. Alas, unhappy Europe vomits from all lands here so vast a wave of a fleeing race! Behold, trembling, through so many dangers of life, they take refuge here together, in mortal fear, without any leader. Dear Geneva grows for these colonists, as the Isar rises from a small spring and swells with mighty waters, or as the Albula, rich with a hundred streams, does.

units.la: Haec quanquam munita armis, & ponte quaterno Et muro duplici, fossáque & turribus altis: Hanc Cerui Pluteíque licet multo aggere vallent: Se tamen vna Deo propugnatore tuetur Contra tot gladios, hostésque inter rita perstans.
units.tr: Though it is fortified with arms, with a fourfold bridge, a double wall, a ditch, and high towers, and though palisades and mantlets guard it with a great rampart: yet it protects itself, with God alone as its defender, against so many swords, standing firm amid its enemies.

units.la: Sic gracilis, geminú sed què mare verberat, Isthmos Nunc salis Ionij furias eludit inanes, Nunc rabiem superi frangit maris; impete magno Irrumpat licet, & magno se turbine voluat. Quin, & vtrumq; simul quum perfurit, altáq; feruet Tempestas vtriusque maris, mugitáque planctu Littora raucisono quatit, horrendúmque sonoris Fluctibus: ille suo contrà se robore firmans Immotus, mundi instar habet, pelagíque furorem Despicit; & terram mordet securus vtramque.
units.tr: Thus the slender isthmus, which the sea beats on both sides, now eludes the empty fury of the Ionian sea, and now breaks the rage of the upper sea. It may be struck with a great onslaught, and roll itself in a great whirlwind. Indeed, when the storm of both seas rages together and boils high, and the shore, struck with roaring blows, groans, and the sea terrifies with its sounding waves, it stands firm in its own strength against them, immovable, like the world itself, and it despises the fury of the sea, and bites securely into the land on both sides.

units.la: Ergo Deus nimium indigno Regúmq; Ducúmq; Seruitio exemptam, diraéque tyrannide noxis,
units.tr: Therefore God, having freed it from a most unworthy servitude to kings and leaders, and from the harmful tyranny of the dire

units.la: Non expectato seruauit numine, fractamTantis turbinibus rerum, tantisque procellis, Et bonus asseruit nutantem extrema Geneuam, Inter mille neces inter discrimina mille.
units.tr: did not preserve it by a power it had not looked for, though it was broken amid such whirlwinds of affairs and such storms. Good God upheld Geneva, tottering at the very edge, amid a thousand deaths and a thousand dangers.

units.la: Quo magis haud meritum agnoscat magnumque fauoremNuminis & tanto æternas pro munere gratesPersoluat rediuiua, memor gratissima tantiMuneris, & puros seruet sanctissima ritus.
units.tr: So much the more ought it to acknowledge the undeserved and great favour of the divine power, and render eternal thanks for so great a gift, mindful of this most welcome gift, reborn, and keep its pure rites most holy.

units.la: Nec tantum sat erat miseram de faucibus hostisEripere, immeritóque iugo, & crudelibus armis, Imperióq; Ducum, multos quos mœsta per annosPertulit, & duras domini gens libera leges: Nisi simul ad lucem Deus, & meliora vocassetE' nocte & tenebris quibus ante sepulta iacebat.
units.tr: Nor was it enough to snatch the wretched city from the jaws of the enemy, from an undeserved yoke and cruel arms, and from the rule of leaders, which the free people endured sadly through many years under the hard laws of a lord, unless God had at the same time called it to the light and to better things, out of the night and the darkness in which it had lain buried before.

units.la: Sed mihi nec prima testes ab origine casusSit memorare labor, hæc nostrum ad tempora carmēChriste voca, & trepidū deduc per singula Vatem, Si modò si liceat causas aperire latentesFunestíque odij, & subitos de nocte tumultus( Vnius studio excitos) quibus inclyta nuperArsit, quæ, sine te, iam-iam inclinata rucbatVrbs tua, quam seruas inter tot bella metúsque.
units.tr: But let it not be my labour to recount the witnesses from the very beginning of events. Christ, call these matters down to our own times, and lead the trembling poet through each particular, if it be permitted to reveal the hidden causes, the deadly hatred, and the sudden tumults in the night, stirred up by the zeal of one man, by which the famous city recently blazed. Without you, that city, which you preserve amid so many wars and fears, was already leaning and about to fall.

units.la: Quo feror? & quo me sanctæ rapit impetus iræ?Hac ô Musa tenus: tanto nam gurgite rerumAncipitem incertúmque viæ, prius ærea linguaEt vox deficiant, quàm prima exordia libem. Sunt longæ ambages, longa est iniuria, longiExorsus, quos ipse olim si vita superfit, Aut alij forsan post me venientibus annisExpedient, populíque canent tot gesta futuris:Interea me parua sequi, me stringere littusNunc iuuet; hoc pelago fragilem committere lembūNil opus est, tutus potius ferar amne secundo.
units.tr: Where am I being carried? To what does the rush of holy wrath bear me? Thus far, O Muse. For in such a whirlpool of affairs, uncertain and double-edged in its course, my bronze tongue and voice would fail before I could even taste the first beginnings. The digressions are long, the wrong is long, and the starting point is longer. Either I myself, if life remains to me, or others in the years after me will set these out and sing the deeds to future peoples. Meanwhile it pleases me now to follow lesser matters and keep to the shore. There is no need to entrust a fragile skiff to this sea; I would rather be carried safely on a favourable river.

units.la: Macte igitur, tu macte igitur seruata Geneua:
units.tr: Blessed then, yes, blessed, saved Geneva!

units.la: Surrige te, & puros serua purissima ritus. Te Deus erexit populis insigne theatrum, In quo religio, pietas, rectumque fidesque, Et puri mores, amor & reverentia casti Floreat instaurata: tuum quo nomen in oras Extremas eat, & casti te carmine Vates Æterno celebrent. Ergo rediviva Geneva Illecebris ne dede animum, neu desidè[?] luxu Ocia corrumpant, famæ florentis & illum Splendorem obscurent, quo tu clarissima fulges: Nec vitijs lucem, tibi quam semel attulit ultrò Indulgens Pater, heu, prudens scelerum obrue cæno. Ah precor ah melior sedeat sententia menti Ut solet, & nullis unquam terrebere monstris.
units.tr: Rise up, and keep your rites most pure, most pure. God has raised you as a notable theatre before the peoples, in which religion, piety, righteousness and faith, and pure morals, and love and reverence for chastity, may flourish, restored. Let your name go to the farthest shores, and let poets celebrate you in lasting song. Therefore, reborn Geneva, do not give your mind to allurements, nor let idle luxury corrupt your leisure, nor let it obscure that splendour of a flourishing reputation by which you shine most brightly. Do not, alas, overwhelm with the mire of sins the light which the Father, indulgent and wise, freely brought to you once. Ah, I pray, let a better judgement sit in your mind, as it usually does, and may you never be terrified by any monsters.

units.la: Nî facias sperato Dei miseranda furorem Protinus, & cunctis subitos de partibus hostes, Qui male grati animi ferro te & vindice flamma Arguerint coram indocales, teque omnia cogent Sæva pati, & diris servitum Regibus ire. Omnia sperato contraria, si semel ausis Excussisse Deum, & leges temerare sacratas. Quò maiore Deus te libertate beauit Largus opum, quibus te cumulatam servat & auget, Hoc magè funestam spera lachrymosa[?] ruinam, Si semel à Christo defeceris: ecce Geneva In præceps funesta rues, miseranda Geneva.
units.tr: Unless you do, the wrath of God, which you should hope for, will at once fall upon you, and hostile enemies from every quarter, who, having shown a poor sense of gratitude, will reprove you with the sword and avenging flame, and will force you to endure all cruel things and to go into servitude to harsh kings. Hope that everything will turn out contrary to what you wish, if once you have shaken off God and profaned his sacred laws. The greater the liberty with which God has blessed you, the rich giver of wealth, with which he keeps you and increases you, the more hope for a grievous and mournful ruin, if you once fall away from Christ. Behold, Geneva, you will rush headlong to a deadly fall, pitiable Geneva.

units.la: Si Deus haud Urbíque suæ Templóque pepercit Iratus; totiesque sui tam dira tulerunt Supplicia, & meritas soluerunt sanguine pœnas; Græcia si & Nili populus, gentesque profanæ: Qua nostrum precor ille manu crimenque nefasque Arguerit vindex? quo te precor arguet ore?
units.tr: If God, in anger, has not spared his own city and temple, and so often they have borne such dire punishments and paid the penalties they deserved with blood; if Greece, and the people of the Nile, and the profane nations did so; by whose hand, I ask, will the avenger prove our crime and wickedness? With what mouth, I ask, will he accuse you?

units.la: Non sua terribilis vindictæ fulmina durus Præcipitat, pœnamque statim de fontibus Ultor
units.tr: The stern one does not hurl the terrible thunderbolts of his own vengeance,

units.la: Sumit: quin potius certo Pater ordine fontes Castigat patiens, & vellit sedulus aurem. At deploratis prorsum iam rebus, & omni Maturo scelerum Autumno, ferus omnia falce Demetit irata, gentémque & nomina delet.
units.tr: Nor does the avenger take up punishment at once from its sources. Rather, the Father, with a settled order, patiently chastises the fountains and diligently tugs the ear. But when affairs are now utterly despaired of, and the ripe autumn of crimes is full, the wrathful one reaps everything with a savage sickle, and blots out the race and its names.

units.la: His agedùm monitis, maior prudentia surgat Iam tibi, quinetiam vigilum tibi cura tuorum Cautior accedat, studiúmque fidésque Senatûs. Heu, spe�To Das quæ regna modò & quas obruit vrbes Impia nox, lucis faciem mentita beatæ, Tot grauidas licet imperiis, belloque potentes, Florentes vrbes opibus? Circumspice porrò Quàm magnas sterilis passim occulit herba ruinas, Et desolatos sterilis rubus occupat agros. Aspice tot claros populos, tot regna, tot vrbes Argolicas, Rhodon, aut Delphos, ditémue Corinthum, Aut Ephesum, & magnas olim, nunc rudera Athenas! Quò vetus, heu, Babylon, Tyrus, & Nilotica Memphis?
units.tr: With these warnings now at hand, let greater prudence rise up in you. Let a more cautious care of your watchful people, and the zeal and faithfulness of the Senate, come to you. Alas, what kingdoms and what cities the impious night has now overwhelmed, pretending the face of blessed light, though they were heavy with empires and powerful in war, cities flourishing in wealth! Look around further, how great are the ruins that barren grass hides everywhere, and how the barren bramble occupies the deserted fields. Look at so many famous peoples, so many kingdoms, so many Argive cities, Rhodes, or Delphi, or rich Corinth, or Ephesus, and Athens, great once and now a heap of ruins! Where, alas, are old Babylon, Tyre, and Memphis of the Nile?

units.la: At tu quam tanto Deus est dignatus honore, Cui sauet, ac vultu placidus blanditur amico; Viue diu, mea viue diu, multósque per annos Sis felix, oculisque ferat te turba piorum, Ceu Libani cedrum, aut palmam quæ flumina propter Luxurians, socias felix supereminest omnes Vertice frondoso, cupidumque superba quotannis Agricolam, fructu ditat fœcunda beato. Viue diu, mea viue diu, longósque per annos Sis felix: Fueris patrio gratissima cælo, Si semper vigil ac docilis mandata capessas Illius æterni Vnigenæ, qui sanguine sacro Nos bonus in cælum reuocans mala nostra piauit, Quíque omnes Erebi quas pertulit hostia, Diras Elustans, nobis & Mortem & Tartara vicit.
units.tr: But you, how great an honour God has deigned to bestow upon you, whom he favours and caresses with a kindly and friendly face! Live long, my city, live long, and for many years may you be happy, and may the crowd of the pious gaze upon you, like the cedar of Lebanon, or like the palm that, flourishing beside the rivers, rises happily above all its companions with its leafy crown, and, fruitful, enriches the proud farmer, who longs for it, with its blessed yield each year. Live long, my city, live long, and for many years may you be happy. You will be most pleasing to the heavenly fatherland, if you always watch and readily take up the commands of that eternal Only-begotten, who, with his holy blood, calling us back to heaven as a good one, has atoned for our evils, and who, washing away the dire sacrifices of all the hell that he endured, has conquered death and the underworld for us.

units.la: Masta ergo, tibi mille astant tibi mille ministri
units.tr: Blessed then, a thousand ministers stand by you.

units.la: Cælicolæ, tibi mille acies per inane paratis Curribus igniuomis circunstant curribus omnes Ardenti in nymbo: romphæísque micantibus ardent, Te circum mille Aligeri super ardua Jurae: Quales ille olim uidit stupefactus apertis Prospiciens oculis cani latera ardua montis Cingere, & innumeros lucere ardentibus armis.
units.tr: Heavenly dwellers, a thousand armies are prepared for you through the void; all of them surround you with fiery chariots, in a glowing cloud, and they burn with gleaming swords. A thousand winged ones stand about you on the lofty Jura, such as he once saw, astonished, when with eyes open wide he looked upon the lofty flanks of a white mountain being encircled, and countless ones shining with blazing arms.

units.la: Hæc tibi Hieropolis uigilat custodia pernox: Haud tibi mortales hac in statione locauit Excubias Pater omnipotens. Mactè ergo Geneua, Interea semper tu seruantissima iusti, Tu cæli monitus, tu Religionis amorem Obserua, & cultus nunquam dedisce receptos: Ac nunquam Deus hinc aberit, Deus optimus ille, Qui nullo Patrum merito gentísue, rebellem Abrâmi populum, sæuis tot cladibus olim Ereptum, ferreóque iugo, tristique profanæ Seruitio Ægypti, seruauit munere magno Rebus in extremis. Ille est, idem ille Geneua Qui te seruauit toties: totiesque cadenti, Quum nec libertas nec spes erat ulla salutis, Adfuit, & dextrâ placuit fulcire potenti.
units.tr: This watch of Hieropolis keeps vigil over you through the night. The almighty Father has not appointed mortal sentries for you at this post. Blessed then, Geneva, and meanwhile always most watchful over what is right, observe the warnings of heaven, the love of religion, and never unlearn the worship once received. Nor will God, that best of gods, ever depart from here, who, by no merit of the Fathers or of any race, once saved the rebellious people of Abraham, snatched from so many cruel disasters, from the iron yoke and the grievous servitude of profane Egypt, and saved them at the last extremity by a great gift. He is the one, the same, Geneva, who has saved you so many times, and when you were falling, when there was no freedom and no hope of salvation, he was present, and was pleased to prop you up with his mighty right hand.

units.la: Jam mihi Fortunam celebrent mendacia Graiûm, Fortunásque Jouésque, deûm tot nomina uana:
units.tr: Now let the lies of the Greeks celebrate Fortune for me, and Fortune and Jove, the many empty names of gods.

units.la: Fortunæ non illud opus; sed sancta potestas Illius, ingenti qui tot uasta æquora palma Continet, & cælum digitis premit omne duobus, Qui circumfuso librauit in aere Terram, Quique suas intra metas maria alta coercet Arduus, & Verbo retinet solidata potenti, Cælumque, & gelidi mediam liquidi aeris oram, Humida qui gelidæ Lunæ mouet incrementa, Qui Solem regit, & terris immittit adustis Opportunum imbrem, quum sicco languida cælo
units.tr: That is not the work of Fortune, but the holy power of him who holds the vast seas in his mighty palm and presses the whole sky with two fingers, who balanced the earth in the surrounding air, and who, lofty, restrains the deep seas within their own bounds and holds the solid earth by his powerful word, and the heavens, and the middle region of the cold, clear air; who moves the moist increase of the cold moon, who rules the sun, and sends on the scorched lands a timely rain, when the earth, parched under the dry sky, gapes, alas, and when the thirsty meadows wither with their scorched growth, and the dry crop wastes away in its sickly stalks.

units.la: Terra hiat, ambustis, heu, quum sitientia marcent Prata comis, ægrisque macet seges arida culmis. Nam Pater è cælo miserans incommoda nostra, Protinus accersit nubes, dextráque capaci Exprimit & vitam reddit morientibus herbis.
units.tr: For the Father, pitying our troubles from heaven, at once summons the clouds, and with his capacious right hand squeezes them out and gives life back to the dying herbs.

units.la: Hic magnus naturæ Opifex, cui fulmina parent, Ventíque & nymborum præcipites cataractæ: Hinc euersa metit tercti fata grandine creber Africus, hinc mæstos fructus carbunculat ardens Euronotus, miseras vites hinc frigidus imber Sole nouo nimius sterili rubigine tentat. Putribus hinc Zephyris urenti cuspide voluox[?] Pampíneas frondes intorquet, & enecat uvas Nascentes uvas & adhuc in flore latentes.
units.tr: Here is the great Maker of nature, to whom thunderbolts and winds and headlong cataracts of rain are subject. Hence the south-west wind, often overturning, reaps the fallen crops with hail; hence the burning south-east wind blights the sad fruits; hence the cold rain, too much after the new sun, attacks the poor vines with barren rust. Hence the rotten west winds, with their burning point, twist the vine leaves and kill the grapes, the grapes that are still budding and still hidden in flower.

units.la: Iam mihi nunc igitur madidos venerare Lyæos, Panáque, Robigúmq; deum, Cererémque, Iouémque Iunonísque niues, & quicquid cæca vetustas Mentita est: Procul hinc Vates procul ite profani: Auditisne Deum, ô miseri, vocemque tonantis Horrendam Vocem quæ vasto in nubis inani Mugitus ciet horrificos, clangitque tremendum? Hæc Vox quæ medijs olim metuenda tenebris Increpitans, largo signauit fulgure Sinam. Quæ piceásque ornósque & cani immania Iuræ Fragmina præcipitat, longæuáque robora circùm Deiciens, latéque casas campósque iacentes Obruit, & subito fordas conquassat abortu! Ferrea Vox hæc illa Dei, quæ sicubi fractas Hìc illic celeri percurrit lumine nubes, Intortámque facem Stridens agit ignea glauco Sulphure & insanum rapido vomit impete fulmen, Quæ tibi mens Epicure? malus timor unde repente. Téque tuúmq; gregem, miser, occupat, urget & urit Intus agens, subigítque Deum. scelerate, fateri:
units.tr: Now then, venerate for me the moist Bacchus, and Pan, and the god Robigo, and Ceres, and Jove, and the snows of Juno, and whatever blind antiquity has invented. Far from here, poets; far away, you profane ones! Do you hear God, O wretched ones, the voice of the thunderer, the dreadful voice which, in the vast emptiness of the clouds, raises horrifying bellowings and terribly clangs? This voice, once to be feared in the midst of darkness, which, thundering, marked out Sinai with a broad flash of lightning, which hurls down the pitch-pines and mountain ashes and the huge fragments of snowy Jura, and, scattering the long-lived oaks round about, overwhelms the cottages and the lying fields, and shakes the dregs with a sudden onset! This iron voice is that of God, which, wherever it runs through broken clouds with a swift light here and there, and, hissing, drives the twisted torch with a glaucous, fiery sulphur, and spews forth a raging thunderbolt with rapid force. What mind is yours, Epicurean? Whence this sudden wicked fear, which seizes you and your flock, wretch, and urges and burns you within, and compels you, villain, to confess God?

units.la: Et nos ista nihil tantâ formidine terrent? Terrent ista quidem; non vt trepidemus ad omnes Ventorum Zephyros, & inania murmura syluæ: Mente sed intrepida niuoso in nubis hiatu Cernimus audimúsque Deum sua fulmina dextrâ Vibrantem indocili, quæ nos sed & omnia nostra Arcanis regit imperiis, ille optimus Author, Ille est, ille Opifer, rerum causa vna bonarum Qui parma omnipotente, suos nunc protegit hostem Contra, nunc inopem miserans de puluere tollit, Et nunc imbellem præsenti numine firmat, Pastorémque armat funda in crudele duellum Impare congressu, diri contra ora gigantis. Mille igitur quanuis pestes nostisque profunda Emissi fratres, furiarúmque agmina iam-iam Irruerint, luráNque [?] sua de sede reuellant: Aut etiam feruente Noto per nubila vestæ Terribiles, diros, iubar exitiale, Cometas Accendant, cælíue malus color aera mœstum Insiciat, quum Luna rubens læuo horrida vultu It tristis, Solémque suo lugubris opacat Oppositu, vel & ipsa sua sub noste laborat Tristius, illa quidem nobis aut bella famémue Aut morbos minitans: etiam mille vndique mortes Ingruerint, & nos his tempestatibus actos Diluuio scelerum ingenti circunsonet Orcus Conniuente Deo: quid formidamus inertes Propterca, cæli immemores Dominíque potentis: Quum nullus pereat nostro de vertice crinis, Labátur nullæ quando sine numine frondes ! Masti ergo virtute, animus & pectore forti Speremus mente intrepidi, vel morte sub ipsa. Iámque vbi nulla salus superat, via nulla nec vllus Exitus, & vix vlla spei breuis vmbra fugacis,
units.tr: And do these things terrify us not at all, despite such great dread? They do terrify, but not so that we tremble at every breeze of the winds and the empty murmurs of the woods. With an undaunted mind we see and hear God in the snowy gap of the clouds, brandishing his lightnings with an unteachable right hand. He rules us and all our affairs by secret commands. That best Author, he is the Maker, the one cause of all good things, who with his almighty shield now protects his own against the enemy, now pities the needy and lifts him from the dust, and now strengthens the unwarlike with his present power. He arms the shepherd with a sling for a cruel duel, an unequal encounter against the face of the dreadful giant. Therefore, though a thousand plagues should rush upon us, and the brothers loosed from the deep pit, and troops of Furies, and tear the lurid ones from their seat; or though comets, terrible and dire, deadly torches, should kindle through the clouds under a fervent South wind; or though a baleful colour in the sky should stain the sorrowful air, when the reddened moon goes sadly with a grim, left-turned face and, gloomy in her opposition, darkens the sun, or when the night itself labours more gloomily still, threatening us with wars, famine, or diseases; even though a thousand deaths press in from every side, and Orcus roars around us, driven as we are by these storms into a great flood of sins while God winks, why then do we, sluggish and forgetful of heaven and of the mighty Lord, fear? Since not a hair falls from our head, nor does a leaf fall without his will. Therefore let us hope with strength of courage and a brave heart, with an undaunted mind, even under death itself. And now, when no safety remains, no way, and no exit, and scarcely any brief shadow of fleeting hope,

units.la: Constantem inconcussa tamen fiducia mentemErigat, atque oculos caelo teneamus apertos, Docti nusquam humanis confidere rebus. Nos & nostra videt Deus, aeternumque videbit: Omnia constanti librata examine pensatProvidus, & recte nil non agit optimus Author.
units.tr: Yet unshaken confidence should raise up a steadfast mind, and let us keep our eyes open toward heaven, taught never to trust in human affairs. God sees us and our affairs, and will see them forever. Providently he weighs all things on a steady balance, and the best Author does nothing that is not right.

units.la: His Deus exercet nos artibus, hinc nova nobisPectora format agens, & casibus urit acerbisNe Fidei languens intus fit inutilis ardor, Neu malesuada pios falsa sub imagine rectiSopiat in tenebris miserae fiducia pacis. Sic his saepe suos percellit & implicat olimMonstris Omnipotens, & nos examine duroPertentans, aperit circum mille undique mortes: Quo sibi nos reddat, quo nos super ardua caeliInuitos trahat, atque sui succendat amore,Doctos nusquam humanis confidere rebus; Sed Patris arbitrium cupidos vocemque sequentes. Ista pias adeo formant certamina mentes.
units.tr: By these arts God exercises us. Hence, driving us, he shapes new hearts within us and burns us with bitter trials, lest the languishing ardour of our faith become useless within us, or lest ill-counselling false confidence lull pious hearts into the shadows of a wretched peace under a false image of rest. So the Almighty often strikes down and entangles his own with such trials, and once with monsters, and testing us with a hard trial, he opens a thousand deaths on every side, so that he may restore us to himself, and draw us unwilling above the steep heights of heaven, and kindle us with love of himself, taught never to trust in human affairs, but to follow the Father's will and voice with eager hearts. Such trials thus form pious minds.

units.la: His Deus exercet nos artibus, hinc nova nobisPectora fingit agens: adeo nos degener intusMens facile immemores caeli, immemoresque bonorum( Quelis nos Omnipotens ad se trahit & vocat ultro)Reddiderit, miseros simul ac liquidissima caeliTempestas, vultu ridens illuxit amico.
units.tr: By these arts God exercises us; driving us, he fashions new hearts within us. So readily has our degenerate mind made us forgetful of heaven and of good things (such as the Almighty draws us to himself and freely calls us to), as soon as the clearest weather of heaven shone upon us wretches, smiling with a friendly face.

units.la: Sed variis ubi turbinibus caelique flagellisNos Pater explorans funesta per omnia duxit,Et doces perferre videt nos aspera quaevis: Protinus exoluit facilis, laetosque reponitSecuro tutoque loco, damnumque rependitMunificus Pater, & reficit nos vbere pleno.
units.tr: But when, testing us with various whirlwinds and lashes from heaven, the Father has led us through all sorts of deadly things, and sees that we are learning to bear whatever is harsh, he at once loosens his hold easily and restores us, glad, to a safe and secure place. The bountiful Father makes good our loss and refreshes us with a full udder.

units.la: Sed tamen interdum totis velut irruat ardensIrae fulminibus, simulans iam-iam obruit, & iamFerri praecipites sub tartara caeca videmur. At vero si nos merito pede verset, & acri (onduplicans læua, crebris premit ictibus vrgens, Et taciti patimur non duro à Patre moneri; En medica miserans dextra leuat impiger vltrò Attonitos, medico siccans data vulnera succo. Nouit enim quàm sint mortali in corpore vires Exiguæ, fragilique bonus scit parcere cannæ: Sed neque languentem lychni premit inuidus ignem Absumpto humore, & iam-iam moriente luterna.
units.tr: Yet at times he rushes upon us as if with all the fiery bolts of his wrath, pretending to crush us at once, and we seem already to be hurled headlong into the blind depths of hell. But indeed, if he turns us with a foot deserving it, and with a keen hand doubling the blows, presses us with frequent strikes, and we suffer in silence to be corrected by a Father who is not harsh, lo, his healing right hand, pitying us, lifts us up, astonished, readily and of its own accord, drying our wounds with a healing juice. For he knows how small the strength is in a mortal body, and the good one knows how to spare a fragile reed. But neither does he, grudging, crush the flame of a failing lamp, once its moisture is used up, and a lantern already dying.

units.la: VOTVM
units.tr: A VOW

units.la: Deo optimo max. Seruatori consecratum.
units.tr: Consecrated to God, the best and greatest, the Saviour.

units.la: Ic est ille Deus, quem tu execranda tot annos Persequeris Babylon, inter mala gaudia mensæ Crudelis, iustóque dapes, heu, sanguine tinctas. Sãcte[?] quid expectas? non tu qui Legibus arctis (Quas silice in gemina digito omnipotente notabas, Quum te fulminibus crebris in monte tonantem Cernuus audiret Vates, & Legifer idem Ifacidum) prohibes tibi duci in marmore vultus, Et cudi visenda nouis simulacra figuris Siue hominum, siue alituum, pecudúmue: nec vlla Monstra coli pateris nant æquore qualia in alto, Totus & integros vni tibi poscis honores? Et tamen hæc tacitus spectas, securáque culpæ Pectora nostra facis, tua tu dum fulmina differs. Aspicis vt Babylon pacem tot poscat ab aris Impia, & interea caeco ruat acta furore Inscelera, inque nefas non enarrabile castis? En secura tui vetitos transcribit honores In laruas hominum & mortalia corpora vecors. Aspicis vt spoliet te Maiestate verenda Et titulis, dum nescio quos sibi cônit & ornat, Mentiturque deos, sociúmque tibi agmina iungit, Teque amens crusti concludit in orbe nefandi Quod rerum ignari, & miserum quod vulgus adoret!
units.tr: This is that God whom you, Babylon, have pursued with execration for so many years, cruel amid the wicked pleasures of your table, feasting on dainties, alas, stained with blood. Holy one, what do you wait for? Are you not the one who, by the strict Laws which he marked on two stone tablets with his almighty finger, when the prophet and lawgiver of the sons of Israel heard him bending low while he thundered on the mountain with frequent lightnings, forbids you to have faces drawn in marble, or forms of strange new shapes cast, whether of men, birds, or beasts, nor do you allow monsters such as swim in the deep sea to be worshipped, and demand for yourself alone entire and undivided honours? And yet you look on these things in silence, and make our hearts secure in their guilt, while you hold back your lightnings. You see how impious Babylon asks for peace from so many altars, and meanwhile, driven headlong by blind fury, rushes into crimes and into a wickedness that cannot be told, pure in their sight! See, the mad woman hands over your forbidden honours, unrestrained, to the masks of men and to mortal bodies! You see how she strips you of your revered majesty and of your titles, while she adorns and assigns them to I know not whom, lies about the gods, joins whole hosts as companions to you, and in her madness shuts you up in the orbit of her accursed crust, which the ignorant herd and the wretched crowd adore!

units.la: Aspicis hæc, & ferre potes scelera ista nefasque? Iræ tum patiens potes hæc tolerare tot annos? Quin potius terras iterum Pater obrue terras Diluvio, & penitus nunc rerum elementa laborent; Corruat & fractus jam nunc compage soluta Orbis, jamque nihil, nedum chaos omnia fiant: Aut cadat horrendo mundi cinefacta fragore Crudelis Babylon, terræ communis Erynnis Contemptrixque tui, & tantorum causa malorum Invadens miseras Veri sub imagine gentes, Parca boni, scelerum atque alienæ prodiga vitæ. Jam Romam furor ille tuus, Romaéque tribunal Sacrilegum, furor ille tuus nunc sulphuris imbre Corripiat, qualem mare prodigiale Sodomes Infandæ spirat, dirique bitumínis ater Gurges, & atra palus flammis infamibus undans. Quo quondam fœcunda loco, diti ubere tellus Proventus dabat ingentes frugumque merique, Nunc tantum infamis lacus, illuviéque nefanda Heu, squallens regio, & misero terra horrida vultu.
units.tr: You see these things, and can you bear such crimes and such wickedness? Can you, patient in your wrath, endure these things for so many years? Rather, Father, overwhelm the earth again with a flood, and let the elements of the world now be utterly shaken; let the world, its frame loosed and broken, now fall, and let all things become nothing, much less chaos! Or let cruel Babylon, the common Fury of the earth and despiser of you, and the cause of so many evils, who attacks wretched nations under the appearance of the Truth, the Fate that destroys good things and the lavish source of wickedness and of a foreign life, fall reduced to ashes with a dreadful crash of the world! Now let that wrath of yours seize Rome, and the sacrilegious tribunal of Rome, with a shower of sulphur such as the sea of Sodom breathes out, that accursed sea, and the black whirlpool of dire pitch, and the dark marsh seething with infamous flames. The place where once the fruitful earth, with its rich soil, gave abundant harvests of grain and wine, is now nothing but an infamous lake, a squalid region and a land horrid in its wretched aspect, defiled by unspeakable filth!

units.la: Te dira, heu, Babylon nondum rapit ignea cæli Tempestas, nec adhuc tristes haurire tenebræ Et caligo nocens, terræque immanis hiatus? Non Erebi fratres, nondum te tartara pœnis Exercent scelerata, hominumque Deique flagellum? Te super Omnipotens ægrum nunquámne furore Terribilis pluet incumbens, penitúsque recidet?
units.tr: Alas, dreadful Babylon, does the fiery storm of heaven not yet seize you, nor the sad darkness and the harmful gloom, nor the vast gaping of the earth? Do the brothers of Erebus, do the cursed depths of Tartarus not yet torment you with punishments, you scourge of men and of God? Will the Almighty, terrible, never rain down his fury upon you where you lie sick, and cut you down utterly?

units.la: Sed quid ego? non sic Deus omnia protinus igne Corripit, aut fontes lachrymoso protinus orco Plectit, sed justum expectat (ne accersite) tempus, Quô scelus in cumulum crescat, molisque nefandæ Incrementum ingens, ac jam se ferre laboret: Et iam nutanti sub pondere sponte fatiscat, Seque sui tandem penitus, penitúsque ruina Obruat, & sceleris scelus hauriat alta vorago.
units.tr: But why do I speak thus? God does not at once consume all things with fire, nor does he at once strike the springs with a tearful hell, but he waits for the just time (do not hasten it), in which the crime may grow to its height, and the immense increment of that accursed mass may labour to bear itself up. And then, as it totters beneath its own weight, it will of its own accord collapse, and crush itself utterly by its own ruin, and the deep abyss will swallow crime upon crime.

units.la: Vos igitur quos tanta tenet fiducia vitæ Et scelerum, rebus nunc indulgetæ caducis, Ite: sed ista olim constabunt gaudia magno. Mox aderit tempus, quum iam quas mente secatis Spes interdictas, & inania vota per auras Discerpent venti, fastúmque animósque feroces Molliet una dies, tandémque dolere docebit.
units.tr: You, then, whom so great a confidence in life and in your crimes holds, who now indulge in fleeting things, go on! But those joys will one day cost you dearly. Soon the time will come when the hopes you have cut out in your mind, forbidden and empty vows, the winds will scatter through the air; and a single day will soften your pride and your fierce spirits, and at last it will teach you to grieve.

units.la: Ergo age Roma tuos age; fac pia Roma Cynædos Securos scelerum, satia te sanguine iusto Dum licet, & nullum tibi fac iam crimen inausum. Exulta fidens quantumlibet, omnia tenta Infamis Babylon: terræ commune lupanar Roma (Lupæ nam cur author tuus vbera frustra Suxisset?) meritam quæ te obuoluere tenebræ? O si te quis iam manet exitus ante videres! Nam tibi mox gemitum & lachrymas miserósque vlulatus, Vltrices furias, & ineluctabile fatum Attulerit iam summa dies, tibi sera gementi Ride age terrarúmque nefas crimenque Sodome Impia: quod si nunc cæli te languida claudo Securam vindicta gradu sequitúrue premitue Ingenti, nec adhuc ferri trabe frangit auaros Pontifices, miserúmque istum infamémque Dialem Quem nimium heu nimium funesta Lutetia novit, Hoc mage terribilem spera scelerata ruinam. Sera pedes lanæ instar habet vindicta, sed acres Ingeminans ictus, & ferrea brachia quassans Per populos; pede prosubigit calcátque tiaras Pontificum Regúmque, magistratusque superbos, Aeratis quondam audaces qui frontibus audent Insultare Deo & lentum irridere furorem Numinis, & cornu cælum pulsare feroci.
units.tr: Come then, Rome, drive on your catamites; make, pious Rome, your minions secure in their crimes; glut yourself with just blood while you may, and let there be no crime left for you that you have not dared. Exult in your confidence as much as you like; try everything, infamous Babylon, common brothel of the earth, Rome (for why did your author suck her teats in vain from the she-wolf?), whom the darkness that you deserve has wrapped round! Oh, if only you could now see the outcome that awaits you! For soon the highest day will bring you groaning and tears and wretched howling, avenging furies, and an inescapable fate, too late for you as you lament. Laugh on, then, you impious nefarious thing, the crime of Sodom and the shame of the earth! But if now the slow step of heaven follows you, securely, to take vengeance, and presses hard upon you, and has not yet broken with the iron beam the greedy Pontiffs, and that wretched and infamous Dial whom, alas, too deadly Lutetia knows only too well, hope for a ruin all the more terrible for your wickedness. Vengeance has feet like wool, slow, but it deals fierce blows, shaking its iron arms through the peoples; with its foot it tramples down and treads upon the tiaras of Pontiffs and Kings, and the proud magistrates, who once with brazen brows dared to insult God and to mock his slow wrath, and to strike heaven with a fierce horn.

units.la: Sic vbi Vulturnus, furiosáque verbera Cori Procumbunt pelago(quum matutinus Orion Occidit)ecce ater rapido furit impete fluctus, Et vanum exultans præceps vehit agmen aquarum, Arduus, & longo rupem se murmure contra Impatiens agit; at medijs, elusus, in vndis Frangitur examinis scopuloque refusus in æquor, Dilabens perit ille furor, saxóque latranti Languidus immoritur, vanáque obmurmurat ira.
