units.tr: So when the south-east wind, and the raging lashes of the north-west, crash upon the sea (when the morning star Orion sets), behold, the dark wave rages with swift impetus, and exulting in vain it carries headlong a host of waters, high, and in long murmuring it drives itself impatiently against the rock; but, thwarted in the midst of the waves, it is broken on the shoals and poured back upon the sea, and that fury, falling away, perishes, and, weakened, dies against the barking rock, and its vain anger mutters in vain.

units.la: Ergo Deus populos metuendáque nomina Reges Tum demum edomitos, en tandem pulueris instar Comminuit, spargítque manu, nec iam amplius vsquam Apparent: veluti quum verrit Circius agros, Pulueream in ventos cernis vanescere nubem.
units.tr: So God, at last, crushes the peoples and the fearsome names of Kings, once tamed, and as if they were dust he scatters them with his hand, and they appear nowhere any more: as when the northwest wind sweeps the fields, you see the dusty cloud vanish into the winds.

units.la: Hic tandem miseros ridet securus ab alto Mortales Deus: hic victis ex hostibus vltor Dat ventis spolia, & currum comitantur ouantes Victoris DOMINI, circum ventíque niuésque Fulguráque & nymbi tempestatésque sonorae. Ipse triumphatos spectans longo ordine Reges In ventos abiisse: Viden' ait, impie tandem Quid possit Deus? hæc vobis sunt præmia Reges Debita; sic hominum vanis conatibus obsto, Irridens: mihi non opus est maioribus armis. Non ego qui ranis, paruísque volantibus olim Ægypti potui tot debellare tyrannos Quos populi gentisque meæ ludibria feci? Ille ego qui subito nuper contuiuia [?]luctu Turbaui & Regum ludens furiosa repressi Consilia? & decreta vnus Regum irrita feci. Iste vbi nunc, fama totum qui compleat orbem Terribilis, mediáque volet Cataphractus arena Purpureis inuectus equis? agat ipse triumphum.
units.tr: Here at last God, from on high, laughs at wretched mortals, secure. Here, avenging himself upon his conquered enemies, he gives spoils to the winds, and the triumphant chariot of the Victor, the LORD, is accompanied round about by winds and snows, lightnings and storms and sounding tempests. Looking on the triumphed-over Kings, in long order, as they went off into the winds, he himself says: See, impious ones, at last what God can do? These are the rewards due to you, Kings; thus I stand against the vain attempts of men, laughing: I have no need of greater arms. Was it not I who once, with frogs and small flying things, was able to overcome so many tyrants of Egypt, and made them a mockery to my people and nation? Was I not the one who lately, suddenly, disturbed the feasts with mourning, and, mocking the mad plans of Kings, restrained them? Was I not the one alone who made the decrees of Kings void? Where is he now, that terrible one whose fame fills the whole world, who would ride in armour on purple horses through the middle of the arena? Let him himself triumph.

units.la: Iam sine me; pacem is[?] longos dum quaerit in annos, Ecce meo iussu, mediam ferit ardua frontem Lancea, quae medio stridens stetit acta cerebro. Turbantur procerum cunei, turba inscia mussat: Sed dum nullus adest, galeae qui vincula soluat, Semianimem qui tollat equo, qui vulnus olivo Abluat; exhibeo[?] haec populis spectacula Regum.
units.tr: Now let him go without me; while he seeks peace for long years, behold, by my command a lance, steep, strikes his middle forehead, and, hissing, sticks fixed in the middle of his brain. The ranks of the nobles are thrown into confusion, the crowd, unaware, murmurs; but since no one is there to loosen the straps of his helmet, to lift him half-dead from his horse, or to wash his wound with oil, I display these spectacles of Kings to the peoples.

units.la: Ergo agite ô miseri, & quisquis mea iussa, meósque Spreuerit, ille meum sic sentiat ille furorem, Et Ius Fásque meum poenis, invitus, honoret. Sic eat aeternum, & Legi sua pondera funto.
units.tr: Come then, you wretches, and whoever has despised my commands and my laws, let him feel my wrath in this way, and let him, unwilling, honour my right and my justice with punishments. Let it go on forever, and let my weights be laid upon the Law.

units.la: Sic ait, & dictis dedit immutabile pondus Omnipotens. I frende[?] igitur scelerate, Deúmque Crudelem miser appella, duraéque Tyrannum Legis, & insontes feralibus obrue bustis Tabescens crudeli odio, teque ipse perure Carnifici malus invidia: votique nefandi Impatiens, animo tecum indignante labora Impie: disce tuas prudens cumulare ruinas; Nil intentatum scelerique dolisque relinque. Sed quod agis, votis intactum optaveris olim, Et nolles voluisse, modo quae laetus obibas.
units.tr: So speaks the Almighty, and he gives his words an unchangeable weight. Go on then, wicked one, rage, and call God cruel, and the Law a hard tyrant, and, wasting away with cruel hatred, overwhelm the innocent with deadly tombs, and burn yourself up, you wicked one, with the envy of an executioner; impatient of your impious vow, labour with an indignant mind, impious one: learn, wisely, to heap up your own ruins; leave nothing untried by crime and by tricks. But what you do, you would have wished long ago to have been left untouched by your vows, and you would not have wished to have wished for what you joyfully were undertaking.

units.la: Mira Dei prob[?] consilia, incomprensaque virtus! Hic Maiestatem DOMINI, inscrutabile numen Iam tacitus tandem & supplex Epicurus adoret: Mirandum: sua persequitur Deus hoste ministro Consilia, exequiturque volens quaecunque volebat: Sic tamen ut si quod vitium suat[?], illud ab hoste Fluxerit, & generis lapsa semel indole nostri Sponte sua: nec enim vitii Deus author in ullo est. Caetera semper agit, Deus est qui caetera solus Molitur; nullus vero labor urget agentem, Tranquillus placida secum sed mente quiescit. Et quanvis tot facta hominum tot denique motus,
units.tr: Wonderful are the counsels of God, and his power is beyond comprehension! Here let Epicurus at last, silent and suppliant, adore the Majesty of the LORD, the inscrutable divinity: it is to be wondered at. God pursues his own counsels through a hostile minister, and carries out willingly whatever he willed; yet so that if any fault arises, it flows from the enemy, and from our own nature, once fallen, of its own accord: for God is the author of no fault whatever. He always does the other things; God alone brings about the other things; yet no labour presses upon the one who acts, but he rests tranquil and calm in his own mind. And although he governs and establishes so many deeds of men, and so many motions at last, and the faces and changes of things, nevertheless he always keeps his counsel unchangeable: for that will did not come into his mind for the first time, but from the first origin of things it sat fixed and immovable with the LORD from before.

units.la: Tot regat & statuat rerum faciésque vicesque, Consilium semper tamen immutabile seruat: Nam neque tum primùm mentem subit illa voluntas Aeternā mentem, sed rerum in origine prima, Sic DOMINO antè quidem fixum immotúmque sedebat.
units.tr: Though he rules and orders the faces and changes of all things, he always keeps his counsel unchanging. For that will did not first come into his eternal mind at some point; from the first origin of things it had already stood fixed and unmoved before the Lord.

units.la: O mira ô nullí satis enarrabilis vnquam Prob Natura Dei, modò si Natura vocanda est! Hìc maiestatem DOMINI, inscrutabile numen Jam tacitus tandem & supplex Epicurus adoret. Hìc stupeat Natura, Deum mirata potẽtem, Immensum, æternum, mentisque indagine nulla Deprensum, hìc stupeat veterum sapientia Graiùm, Ac quicunque negant, secum semel omnia certò Decreuisse Deum, nec res curare caducas, Sint fragili cannæ similes licet; Omnia curat Prouida Mens: Nam quid cæli pulcherrimus ordo, Quid cælum, quid Sol radiis vibrantibus ardens Aureus, immensus? quid pleno argentea Phœbe Lumine? quid nitidus vesper? quid cætera mundi Lumináque Stellæque? quid & pulcherrima rerum Si tecum mundi Artificem, si luminis illum Immẽsi Oceanum reputes, Mentémque beatam Lucis inaccessis habitat quæ sedibus ingens; Maxima, inexhausta perfundens omnia luce, Quam nullis hominum verbis effarier vnquam Hìc poteris; captúmque adeò supereminet omnem? Omnia fumus erunt, indignáque Principe tanto Si vel ad exiguam diuni luminis vmbram Protuleris, penitusque illato lumine jam-jam Tabescent liquefacta, niuis vel grandinis instar. Ergo nec illa Deus curauerit? Et tamen omnes Hìc DOMINO imperium tribuunt, sedémque tonanti.
units.tr: O marvellous nature of God, never sufficiently to be told, if indeed it may be called nature! Here let Epicurus, now silent and at last suppliant, worship the majesty of the Lord, the inscrutable divinity. Here let nature stand amazed, wondering at the power of God, immense and eternal, caught by no search of the mind; here let the wisdom of the ancient Greeks stand amazed, and whoever deny that God once and for all decided all things together and does not care for frail things, though they be like fragile reeds. A provident Mind cares for all things. For what of the most beautiful order of heaven, what of the sky, what of the Sun burning with quivering rays, golden and immense? What of silvery Phoebe with her full light? What of the bright evening star? What of the rest of the lights and stars of the world? And what of the most beautiful things of creation, if you consider the Maker of the world, that immense ocean of light, and the blessed Mind that dwells in vast light inaccessible, pouring its light over all things, which no human words can ever express, and which far surpasses all that can be grasped? All things would be smoke, unworthy of so great a Prince, if you brought them even to a small shadow of divine light; and as soon as that light penetrated them, they would melt away like snow or hail. Would God then not care for them? Yet all men here ascribe dominion to the Lord, and the throne to the Thunderer.

units.la: Ille ergo est qui cuncta mouens, & cuncta potenti Mota supercilio amplestens, amplexa gubernat:
units.tr: He therefore is the one who, moving all things, and embracing all things moved by his mighty brow, embraces and governs them.

units.la: Omniáque arcano præeuntibus ordine causis (Quas posuit, revocátque volens iterúmq; reponit) Ante-videns secum statuit, moderatur & urget.
units.tr: And with all causes going before in a hidden order (which he has set in place, and willing recalls and again puts back), foreseeing them within himself, he decides, regulates and drives them.

units.la: Ter quater infelix iam nunc Epicure quid hæres, Agnoscis-ne Deum infelix, Mentémque potentem? Discite degeneres animæ, disce impia turba Iam tandem esse aliquid sine origine, temporis exors, Immensum æternúmque à quo emersere creata Omnia: surrige te, & mentis procul excute noctem. Discite degeneres animæ, disce impia turba Esse Deum, arcano qui temperat omnia motu. Nam quæ obstet vis ulla Deo, quando omnia possit, Omniáque Omnipotens quæ vult molimine nullo Perficiat; rerúmque adeò causa una, Voluntas Ipsíus sua sit? Quanquam tamen ille secundas Substernit causas etiam, noxæque dolíque Et sceleris, quò iam culpa sit liber ab omni. Nam, probé sacrilegæ mentes, Authórne malorum Et scelerum hortator fuerit Deus? Optimus ille Mundi opifex hominúmque sator: licet omnia secum Decernat fieríque velit, noxiisque ministri Consilia ipsius peragant nil tale volentes? Denique quicquid agant, tacita Deus omnia mente Præuidit prius, & secum longè ante futura Constituit; prudénsque suo mox tempore promit Singula. Nec tamen est quòd, ter sclerate Lucreti In culpam hinc traxisse Deum possísue putésue. Sed totam subeunt vltrò, facilésque sequuntur Corrupti mores hominum, scelerúmque tenaces Sponte sua, veteri quanquam hortatore Colubro.
units.tr: Thrice-four times wretched Epicurus, why do you still hesitate now? Do you acknowledge God, unhappy man, and the powerful Mind? Learn, degenerate souls, learn, impious crowd, that at last there is something without origin, free from time, immense and eternal, from which all created things have emerged. Rise up, and drive the night far from your mind. Learn, degenerate souls, learn, impious crowd, that there is a God who governs all things by a hidden motion. For what force could oppose God, since he can do all things, and whatever the Almighty wills he brings about with no effort; and since the one cause of things is his own will? Yet although he also lays down secondary causes, even of harm and deceit and crime, the guilt is free of all blame. For, truly sacrilegious minds, would God be the author and instigator of evils and crimes? That best Maker of the world and Begetter of men: although he decrees all things and wills them to happen, will the ministers of harm carry out his counsels while not willing any such thing? In short, whatever they do, God foresaw all things beforehand in his silent mind, and long before determined them with himself; and wisely he brings forth each thing in its own time. Yet there is no reason, thrice-accursed Lucretius, why you should either have drawn God into blame from this or be able to think it. Rather, the corrupt morals of men willingly undertake the whole of it and readily follow it, and are tenacious of their crimes of their own accord, although the old Serpent is their instigator.

units.la: Sic Lunæ obiectu media quum luce repentè Sol latet, & cælum subitis contexitur umbris: Hæc regio nil noctis habet, tota illa tenebris Obruitur, medióque die noua sydera cœli.
units.tr: Thus when the Sun is suddenly hidden in mid-daylight by the Moon's interposition, and the sky is covered with sudden shadows: that region has no night, yet the whole area is overwhelmed with darkness, and new stars appear in the middle of the day.

units.la: Miratur, mundíque putat venisse ruinam, Nec tamen interea quicquam de lumine Solis Decedit, vultúmue nigra ferrugine tinxit. Non astri hoc vitium, non astri hæc culpa, nec vlla Luminis inuidia est; nam lumine semper eodem Irradiat Solis rutilo globus igneus orbe.
units.tr: He is amazed and thinks the ruin of the world has come; yet meanwhile nothing departs from the light of the Sun, nor has it stained its face with black rust. This fault is not the star's, this blame is not the star's, nor is there any envy in the light; for the fiery globe always shines with the same light in its ruddy orb.

units.la: Obscænæ si noctis aues ad lumina Solis Caligant, nitidiue iubar genitabile Solis Propterea incusent, lucémque diémque perosæ; An hebetes oculos potius, vitiúmque videndi?
units.tr: If the obscene birds of night are dazzled by the light of the Sun, should they therefore accuse the Sun's life-giving bright radiance, hating light and day? Or rather should they blame their own dull eyes and the defect of their sight?

units.la: Iam nunc ergo queri quid possit & audeat vllus? Nam (miseri) exitium nobis accersimus vltro Degeneres, sequimúrque nefas vltro omne volentes. Quòd si aliquos Deus exitio & crudelibus vmbris Destinat, ante quidem quam Sol aut Terra fuissent: Haud tamen in culpa est si quid male gesseris olim: Nec Deus hunc finem spectat, sed Nominis ergò Ille sui, vitæ quos vult educit in auras, Qui iusto tandem interitu meritáque ruina Exortem illustrent Patris omnipotentis honorem.
units.tr: Now then, what can anyone complain of, or dare to? For we wretches bring destruction upon ourselves of our own accord, degenerate as we are, and we willingly follow every wickedness. But if God destines some to destruction and cruel shadows, even before the Sun or the Earth existed, he is nevertheless not to blame if someone has behaved badly. Nor does God look to this end; rather, for the sake of his own Name he brings into the air of life those whom he wills, so that at last, by a just death and deserved ruin, they may illustrate the honour of the blameless almighty Father.

units.la: Nam qui ex vllius damno mala gaudia captet Rex Deus? atque suæ tantùm, non consulat æquus Gloriæ, & æternos quenquam det lætus in ignes?
units.tr: For would God, the King, take wicked joy in anyone's loss? Would he, being just, consider only his own glory, and gladly give anyone to eternal fires?

units.la: En quo nunc igitur gens præcipitata sub vmbras Ausa olim immane nefas in sedibus altis Ore Deum incuset? quid vero deinde querantur Mortales miseri, qui vita & crimine dudum Sint meriti æternæ Chaos irremeabile noctis?
units.tr: Lo, to what shadows, then, has that people fallen headlong, which once dared an immense crime in its high seats? With its own mouth let it accuse God! And what then do wretched mortals complain of, who by their life and crime have long deserved the irretrievable Chaos of eternal night?

units.la: Hic quid habes Babylon? quid habes impure Cynæde Quod possis æquo Domini obiecisse potentis Iudicio? meritámne vides, his te, impia Roma, Vt Deus obuoluat tenebris, quibus ante profanam Obruit AEgyptum? merito tibi maximus Vltor Eripuit mentem, & prorsum sine luce relictam
units.tr: What do you have to say here, Babylon? What do you have, impure harlot, that you could object to the just judgement of the mighty Lord? Do you see that you deserve it, impious Rome, that God should wrap you in shadows, as he once overwhelmed profane Egypt? Rightly has the greatest Avenger snatched away your mind and left it utterly without light,

units.la: In scelera, inque nefas & inelubtabile cænumPermisit ruere, & cæco indulgere furori.
units.tr: to rush into crimes and wickedness and the inescapable mire, and has allowed it to indulge in blind madness.

units.la: Væ tibi væ Babylon cælo & mortalibus ipsisInuisa, heu, toties meritas quæ sanguine pœnasPestę, fame, flamma, cæli terræque ruinisPersoluis recidiua, piį Vatúmque PatrúmqueSanguinis, heu, nimium sitiens scelerata, sed vmbrasLegis, & infandos obseruans sedula ritus!
units.tr: Woe to you, woe, Babylon, hated by heaven and by mortals themselves! You who repay with plague, famine, flame, and the ruins of heaven and earth punishments deserved so often, thirsting, alas, too much, for the blood of the pious and of the prophets and Fathers, wicked woman, yet you watch shadows and diligently observe unspeakable rites!

units.la: Impia proh Meretrix quæ mœchos ebria RegesSanguine spumanti patera temetóque furentiSollicitas, miserósque malo furiata venenoDementas populos, spectas hæc funera, spectas?Tot tristes tabulas, tot sancta cadauera cernis, Bellua, nec te animi tandem crux vlla perurit? Tun' sicco spectare potes tot funera vultu? Ilicet hæc sunt illa, hæc sunt præclara SenatusPurpurei ornamenta; hæc sunt decora inclyta Romæ: En illa hæc sedis sunt firmamenta nefandæ,Hæc pietas, hæc religio tot ficta per annos!
units.tr: Impious harlot, alas, who, drunk, stir up adulterous kings and peoples raging with poison, with foaming blood from your cup and maddened with wine, do you watch these funerals, do you watch them? You see so many sad tablets, so many holy corpses; beast, does no pang of conscience finally burn you? Can you look upon so many deaths with a dry face? Behold, these are those famous ornaments of the purple Senate, these are the glorious decorations of Rome! Look, these are the supports of that accursed seat, this piety, this religion, feigned for so many years!

units.la: Aspicis hos tumulos atque hæc monimenta piorumQui nitidi tormenta inter flammásque relucent, Aut quos mille dolis, vna nec morte necasti? Vltrices illi ad pœnas aliquando reposcentTéque tuósque deos. Satis ô Stola sanguine iustoEbria: iam veniet tempus iam-iámque propinquat, Quum magno, sed vero frustra, optaueris emptosInsontes illos: nec enim sine vindice iustusIllorum tibi sanguis erit, quos candida vestitNunc Stola, quòd CHRISTI calice & crudele dolorumSympullum, int repidi, venis sitientibus, vltròEbiberint, medióque rogos subiere volentes, Victricésque ardenti animas sub fasce dedére: Quæ simul-ac terras auidæ, moribundáque membraLiquère, anteuolant Zephyros plaudentibus alis,
units.tr: Do you see these tombs and these monuments of the pious, who shine bright amid torments and flames, or whom you killed by a thousand tricks and one death? Avenging ones will one day demand them from you, and you and your gods. Enough, O Stole drunk with righteous blood! The time will come, indeed it is now at hand, when you will wish, vainly though greatly, that those innocents had been bought off; for their blood will not be without an avenger for you, those whom the white robe now... they who drank with thirsty veins the bitter cup of Christ and his cruel pain, and of their own will went up to the pyres, and surrendered their victorious souls under the burning load. As soon as they left the greedy earth and dying limbs, they fly before the Zephyrs on clapping wings,

units.la: Vt leuis in Naphtham sulco volat alite flamma; Séque choris alacres tandem felicibus addunt: Et tandem felix Studijs concordibus ævum Lætæ agitant duce cum CHRISTO, viuáque fruuntur Luce Dei, coràmque illum immensumque tuuntur[?] Luminis æterni fontem, vitæque beatæ Diuitias, pedibúsque polos & sydera calcant.
units.tr: As a light flame flies swiftly along a trail of naphtha, so they at last join themselves, joyful, to the blessed choirs; and at last, happy in harmonious study, they spend their life, rejoicing, with Christ as their leader, and enjoy the living light of God, and gaze upon him, the immense fountain of eternal light and the riches of blessed life, and tread the poles and stars beneath their feet.

units.la: At vero nocti sempérque silentibus umbris Iam mersos & densa olim caligine condi, Atque adeo illorum cineres, famámque profundis Obduca[?] tenebris, & ferro & carcere dudum Rebare[?] extinctam flammisque voracibus haustam.
units.tr: But you, who thought that they were long ago sunk in night and ever silent shadows, and buried in dense darkness, and that their ashes and their fame, covered by deep shadows, had been extinguished by sword and prison and swallowed by devouring flames.

units.la: Sed cælo visum est aliter; namque incubat istis Fama ingens tumulis, quæ sese ex ossibus ultrix Protulit innocuæ gentis, latéque per omnes Vulgavit populos, ingenti maxima plausu Egregias animas, nolit velit ægra tyrannis Roma tua, & cineri dat splendida nomina muto.
units.tr: But heaven has decided otherwise; for a great Fame broods over those tombs, which, as an avenger, has risen from the bones of the innocent nation and has spread far and wide among all peoples, with great applause, the outstanding souls. Whether your sick tyranny, Rome, wills it or not, it gives splendid names to the mute ashes.

units.la: Ergo agedum illustres animæ, vos posthuma fama E[?] nocte & tenebris, ad vitæ & luminis auras Ecce tubæ revocat sonitu officiosa potenti Emerentis[?] sanctéque pio certamine functas. Vos Pater amplexu non dedignatus amico, Arbitrio[?] fati exemptas Regumque furori In cælum Pater omnipotens excepit ouantes.
units.tr: Come then, illustrious souls: posthumous fame calls you from night and shadows to the breezes of life and light. Behold, the dutiful trumpet with its powerful sound summons you, who have earned it and finished the holy struggle in pious contest. You whom the Father did not disdain to embrace in friendly embrace, freed from the judgement of fate and the fury of kings, the almighty Father has received into heaven, rejoicing.

units.la: Quare agitè & sacris etiamnum accentibus omnes Inumerum[?], densæ toto date carmina cælo; Cælo ubi perpetuas alas chorus haurit anhelans Delicias, paræque bibunt noua gaudia mentes: Gaudia nil humile, aut fluxum spirantia porrò, Gaudia parta piis atque obseruantibus æqui. Vestra sed hæc olim memores exempla sequuti Sic cælum repetant gratíque pùque[?] nepotes, Qui dederint vltro durae sua nomina CHRISTI
units.tr: Come then, all of you, and with sacred accents still, give songs to the whole thick heaven: heaven, where the breathing chorus drinks in perpetual joys with unwearied wings, and the prepared minds drink new delights. These joys breathe nothing lowly or fleeting, but are joys won by the pious and by those who keep the right. Let grateful and dutiful grandchildren, remembering your examples, follow them and so seek heaven again, those who of their own accord gave their names to hard Christ-service.

units.la: Militiæ, sancta cum maiestate malorumTot læti gladios & tot crudelia passi.
units.tr: Who, with holy majesty amid the evils of warfare, joyfully endured so many swords and so many cruel sufferings.

units.la: HÆC vobis mage marmoribus vel mole superba Pyramidum, longos perduratura per annos Sancta piis incisa notis monimenta parauit Hieropolis; vobis etiam Crispinus amico Iusta facit voto & latio bonus ore parentat. Quod si ego nil aliud potero, vos carmine saltem Prosequar, & Siticen memorabo funera plausu Vestra pio, & vestras comitabor carmine flammas.
units.tr: Hieropolis has prepared this monument for you, carved with sacred marks, to last for long years, more lasting than marble or the proud mass of pyramids. For you also, Crispinus, as a friend, performs the due vow, and with a good Latin voice gives you funeral honours. But if I can do nothing else, at least I will accompany you with song, and I will record in verse your funerals, with pious applause for your Siticen, and I will attend your flames with verse.

units.la: Ergo, Liber, populos procul ex Oriente remotos, Qua patet orbe olim Romana potentia victo, Ad Tanain ad Cimmerios atque vltima Ponti, Aureus a lura peragra viridique Lemanno.
units.tr: Go then, Book, to the peoples far off in the remote East, wherever the Roman power once spread over the conquered world: to the Tanais, to the Cimmerians and the farthest parts of Pontus. Golden book, wander from the Jura to green Lake Leman.

units.la: Sauromatas, i, vise, doce, gelidósque Polonos, Quos modo cælesti renouatos Spiritus aura Progenuit miserans, longáque a nocte reduxit.
units.tr: Go, visit the Sarmatians and teach the icy Poles, whom the breath of heaven, in pity, has lately brought forth renewed, and has led back out of long night.

units.la: Orchadas, & Scotiæ plenis pete littora velis: Hic nuper lux illa Dei, verbúmque Salutis Sacrum illud nostræ manifesto lumine coram Explicuit sese, hic sedes tutíque receptus Sanctis Europæ exulibus profugísque parantur.
units.tr: Seek the Orkneys and the shores of Scotland with full sails. There that light of God, and the sacred word of salvation, lately unfolded itself openly before our eyes in clear light; there a dwelling and a safe refuge are being prepared for the holy exiles and fugitives of Europe.

units.la: Vise anni Solísque vias, vbi nostra Canopum Gens videt, & nostris contraria sydera cernit Admirans, longè Europa Calpéque relictis A tergo, Ammericam propter, quà languidus annū Exiguum vertens, gelido sub sydere nobis Sol hyemem facit & currit breuioribus horis: Quà patet inque sinum pandit se diuite luco Bresilia; infelix supra execratáque tellus Cannibalum, Paranas infrà Lepetísque sonanti Murmure gemmarum & squammis crepitantibus auri In mare præcipites, iunêto simul agmine currunt.
units.tr: Go, visit the courses of the year and the sun, where that nation sees Canopus and, wondering, sees stars opposed to ours, far away, with Europe and Calpe left behind. Near America, where the sun, turning the small year languidly, makes winter for us under a cold star and runs through shorter hours; where Brazil spreads out and opens itself into a bay with rich groves; the unhappy land above, and the accursed land of the cannibals; below, the Paraná and the Lepetis, with the murmur of jewels and the clattering scales of gold, rush headlong together into the sea in one joined column.

units.la: I, Liber, & reduces iterum solare Britannos,
units.tr: Go, Book, and comfort once again the Britons who have returned

units.la: Post longa exilia & laqueos cinerésque suorum; Quos inter pietate grauis venerandus honora Canicie, dextram medios qui lætus in ignes Coniecit, nostro fulget memorabilis ævo Crammerus; pete culta, Liber, quæ Sequana lambit, Quæ Ligeris secat & Rhodanus, rapidúsque Garunna.
units.tr: After long exiles, and the snares and ashes of their own people; among whom, a grave and venerable man, honoured for his pious grey hair, who joyfully cast his right hand into the midst of the fire, Cranmer shines, memorable in our age. Seek the cultivated lands that the Seine laps, that the Loire and the Rhône cut through, and the swift Garonne.

units.la: I, Liber, & veteres mœrens invise tot urbes Quà Rhenus fluit: auriferis quà dives arenis Turbidus Oceanum leni Tagus agmine pulsat: Et te Roma legat caput imperiúmque malorum.
units.tr: Go, Book, and sorrowing, visit those many ancient cities where the Rhine flows; where the rich Tagus, turbid with its golden sands, beats the Ocean with its gentle column. And let Rome read you, the head and seat of evils.

units.la: Tu vero tu CHRISTE fave, cursúmque secunda, Cælestíque patrocinio mendacia contra Et vulgi rabiem, præsens monimenta tuorum Incisa his tabulis iam ter rediviva tucre, Queis latè circùm tua lux & gloria crescant.
units.tr: But you, Christ, favour and prosper the course, and by your heavenly patronage defend your people's monuments against the lies and the rage of the crowd. Preserve these records of your own, carved on these tablets, now twice reborn, so that your light and glory may grow far and wide around them.

units.la: Hæc ego, dum dulces licet intermittere curas, Montibus in nostris cælo sub teste canebam. Quo ter felicem me tempore chara tenebat Hieropolis, ducente Deo, purgata nefandis Monstrorum tot conciliis, tectáque suorum Invidia; instantes lachrymans dum plango ruinas Labentis patriæ, luctúsque & fata meorum: Et dum quisque bonus, penitus rerum ordine verso, Omnia iam pessum ruere infelice ruina Conqueritur, Puerique adeo, lachrymabile Regnum.
units.tr: These things I sang, while the sweet cares allowed me to put them aside, in our mountains, under heaven as witness. At that time, thrice happy, dear Hieropolis held me, God leading, cleansed of the wicked councils of so many monsters and of the envy that had roofed over its own people. While I wept over the approaching ruins of my falling country, and the mourning and fates of my people; and while every good man, with the order of things utterly turned round, complains that all things are now rushing to ruin in unhappy collapse, and indeed a boyish kingdom, a kingdom to be wept over.

units.la: QVI veram ac simplicem Christiana Religionis doctrinam ex ipsis Apostolorum temporibus reuocatam, ac repetitam, insolentia atque novitatis insimulant, unde tandem hi Martyres hodie prodeant, miraturos esse minime dubitamus: quum iidem, à multis iam annis huiusmodi Athletarum amissa memoria, vel potius iam intermissa videri possit. Quibus ut respondeamus, sic habeant: ut de illis ipsi nihil nec audiverint nec audire profecto voluerint, non idcirco haud amissam illorum, haud intermissam videri oportere memoriam. Nam ut istis demus, statis temporum interuallis prostratam ac iacentem quodammodo suisse Christi Ecclesiam; extinctam certe fuisse prorsus sine scelere pronuntiare non possumus. Quod quidem ex eo intelligi potest, quoniam alio tempore plures, alio vero pauciores, nunquam certe nulli Martyres extiterunt: nimirum vlli qui sic Christiana doctrina testes ac praecones extiterint, ut eam suo sanguine obsignare non dubitarent. At vero quum Ecclesiam ipsam aliquandiu iacentem inquam, & quodammodo sopitam Christus longè ampliorem & illustriorem, centum circiter, aut eo amplius, annis ipse renocarit, maiorem etiam qui pro causa sua defensionem pugnarent numerum excitauit. Nam, Vt penè extinctum cinerem si sulphure tangas, Viuet & ex minimo maximus ignis erit. Itaque quum Christus suo sulphure, feruore nempe Spiritus sui, Fidelium animos propè congelatos excitat & attingit; magnum quendam ardorem in eis concipi certum est, qui erumpens flammeolas suas longè latéque diffundat necesse est. Quòd si quis urgeat, cur quum ab ipsis doctrina Christiana velut incunabulis Martyres semper extitisse teneamus; eorum historiam repetitam altius ad nostrum hoc usque tempus serie perpetua deductam protulerimus: is illud demum intelligat, non minus verum quàm esse vulgatum, ut quicquid differtur, id non auferri. tametsi quidem ad priorem historiam Martyrum editionem, tantam accessionem attulimus, ut Reipublica de nobis expectationi fœnerato persoluisse videri debeamus.
units.tr: WE do not doubt that those who charge the true and simple doctrine of the Christian religion, recalled and restored from the very times of the Apostles, with novelty and arrogance, will be astonished why these martyrs now come forth at last; since the memory of such athletes may seem to have been lost for many years, or rather already to have lapsed. To answer them, let this be said. Even if they themselves have heard nothing of these men, and certainly did not wish to hear, it does not follow that their memory ought to seem lost or intermitted. For even granting that the Church of Christ lay prostrate and, as it were, asleep through set intervals of time, we cannot pronounce that it was utterly extinguished without wickedness. This can be understood from the fact that at one time there were more martyrs, at another fewer, but never none at all: there were always some who were witnesses and heralds of Christian doctrine, so much so that they did not hesitate to seal it with their blood. But when Christ, I say, revived the Church, which for some time lay low and was in a manner dormant, far wider and more illustrious, about a hundred years or a little more ago, he also raised up a greater number who fought in defence of their cause. For, as when you touch almost extinct ashes with sulphur, they live again, and from the smallest spark the greatest fire comes forth, so when Christ with his sulphur, namely the fervour of his Spirit, touches and kindles the minds of the faithful, almost frozen, it is certain that some great ardour is conceived in them, which must break out and spread its little flames far and wide. But if anyone presses why, since we hold that from the very cradle of Christian doctrine there have always been martyrs, we have brought forth their history, traced back further and carried in unbroken sequence down to our own time, let him understand at last that it is no less true than commonly held that whatever is deferred is not taken away. Although, indeed, to the earlier edition of the history of the martyrs we have made so great an addition that we ought to seem to have repaid to the Commonwealth, with interest, what it expected of us.

units.la: ¶ Erunt fortasse Critici, qui Inscriptionem aliam aliquam quàm aut Actorum aut Actionum desyderent (quam tamen Inscriptionem, & in priore-olim editione, & in hac posteriore sequuti sumus) quoniam nomen illud augustum, singulari quodam ac proprio quorumdam minimè malorum hominum prœiudicio solis Apostolis attributum, rerum publicè gestarum publicam & popularem memoriam potius, quàm privatæ rei ratione aliquam contineat. Quibus Criticis ut aliquid dare, & interim instituti nostri rationem etiam habere videremur, Actiones libenter, quæ quibusq; vel rebus vel personis accommodari possunt, inscribere maluimus.
units.tr: ¶ There will perhaps be critics who would prefer some other title than "Acts" or "Actions" (which title we have followed both in the earlier edition and in this later one), since that august name, which by a peculiar and proper prejudice of certain not wholly bad men is attributed to the Apostles alone, contains rather the public and popular memory of public affairs than an account of a private matter. To give something to these critics, and at the same time to seem to keep regard for our own plan, we have preferred to entitle these "Actions", which can be fitted to whatever things or persons.

units.la: Acta eorum per quos Euangelii doctrina in lucem cognitionemque Ecclesiæ, densissimis tenebris occupatæ, à Deo revocari ac restitui cœpit.
units.tr: The acts of those through whom the teaching of the Gospel began, by God's will, to be recalled and restored to light and to the knowledge of the Church, which had been held in the thickest darkness.

units.la: Ioannes Vvicless.
units.tr: John Wycliffe.

units.la: ETsi hæc misera & diuturna conditio professióque fuerit eorum, qui Christiani sunt appellati, ut ipsum nudum Christi nomen tantummodo habuerint, summaque ingratitudine se vera salutarique doctrina priuauerint: nulla tamen tanta hominum ingratitudo & impietas unquam potuit ita bonitatem Dei superare, quin is semper aliquod piorum semen conseruarit, ex quo Ecclesia propagari, amissamque religionem recuperare ac retinere posset. Et quanvis nullus fuit orbis angulus, qui non densissimis ac teterrimis ignorantiæ tenebris oppressus extiterit: tamen Deus semper ad illuminandā atque illustrandam veritatem, aliquas scintillas conseruauit ac suscitauit, pro ea temporis ratione quam opportunam suæque iustitiæ ac nostræ saluti accommodatam iudicauit. Quum autem multa & certa & clara sunt signa, & illustria testimonia, quæ hanc Euangelij doctrinam, his temporibus renouatam ac restitutam declarant puram esse Dei veritatem, in qua sit saluberrimus animorum pastus, ad vitam alens sempiternam: tum vero illud minimè obscurum aut dubium, quod multi Martyres ac testes eius non dubitant pro ea confirmanda tuendaque sanguinem suum usque etiam ultimam guttam profundere: atque ita declarare quanta sit misericordia eius, qui nos perditos ac iacentes in horrendis mortis tenebris, ad hanc salutarem Euangelij lucem, suæque voluntatis agnitionem revocarit. Hanc autem veritatem Dei esse, illud maximè demonstrat, quod nulla fuit ætas, in qua Satan omni odio furiosissimo hanc Euangelij doctrinam persequutus non fuerit, & conatus eam omni vifua opprimere atque extinguere. Sed cùm inimicus tam potens ac sœuus, tantóque odio inflammatus, nunquam quod est conatus essecerit, vt aut cursum sanctissimæ doctrinæ impediendo, aut ortum eius prohibendo, eam plane aboleret (in summis enim difficultatibus admirabiliter semper fuit conseruata, & per manus tradita) mirum nemini videri debet, si hominibus piis eam cognoscentibus, tantam certitudinem & fiduciam afferat, vt eius authoritatem dignitatémque toti mundo, atque etiam propriæ vitæ anteponant, grauissimóque eius testimonio confirmati, ad beatam atque æternam vitam toto animo contendant. Quód si Satan eius doctrinæ author esset, non eam tanto oppugnaret odio, neque ad eam abolendam, omnem rabiem suam conferret, Nam hoc modo persequens profligánsque quod suum esset, contra seipsum, vt ait Christus, bellum inferret. Sed quocunque infesto impetu conatúque Satan in eam veritatem feratur, virtute tamen atque ope Filij Dei, furorem eius reprimentis, semper salua permansit Ecclesia. quæ necessario eius ministerio seruata fuit, quæ optimos ac fidelissimos Pastores ac Doctores, ad eam administrandam reseruatos & diuinitus vocatos habuit. Quanuis autem à primis illis temporibus, quibus Euangelium in orbem fuit promulgatum, Ecclesia aliquos semper ministros Verbi habuerit, à quibus veritas Dei & religionis puritas, contra vim mundi ac Satanæ fortiter fuerit defensa & propugnata, tamen humanissimis Lectoribus non ingratum fore arbitramur, si initium huius historiæ à Ioanne wicleuo Anglo ducamus, eámque vsque ad præclara nostræ memoriæ exempla persequamur: ex quibus intelligi poterit quod Christus Dominus affirmauit, ne ipsas quidem vires ac potestates inferorum, aduersum fidem & inuictam Dei veritatem ita valituras, vt eam opprimant aut deleant. Nam eo quidem tempore, quo Deus hunc virum bonum atque integrum Ecclesiæ ministrum excitauit, omnia tyrannis occupauerat, impiáque & scelerata dominatio rectorum Ecclesiasticorum, Ecclesiam ipsam oppresserat, vt nec veritati, nec cuiusquam pij Deúmque metuentis libertati vllus plane locus esset, ne exigua quidem puræ doctrinæ aut Ecclesiæ forma appareret. Hæc autem miseranda Ecclesiæ oppressio ac deformatio, fuit anno à natali Christi die M. C C C. L X X I I. Quo quidem tempore Reges ac Principes Christiani, ut suum in religionem amplificandam ornandamque animum atque studium declararent, in eam unam cogitationem curamque incumbebant, ut lignum crucis Hierosolymitanæ, in Ecclesiam Christianam deferendum curarent. quasi vero tota religionis sanctitas eo in ligno consisteret: aut alia esset crux nulla, nisi ea quæ Hierosolymis asseruari diceretur. Sed tunc Deus singulari bonitate ac misericordia voluit mundum, humanis traditionibus atque impiis superstitionibus oppressum immortuumque excitare, atque ad hanc gratissimam veritatis lucem revocare: idque fideli & opportuna opera Ioannis wicleui. qui cum Oxoniæ in celeberrima Angliæ urbe, diu Theologiam professus esset, videretque doctrina Dei multis inquinamentis eorum qui Papam sequuntur, defœdatam & plane corruptam, continere se non potuit, quin in tanta rerum omnium confusione ingemisceret, veritatisque ita corruptæ ac deformatæ, & Ecclesiæ afflictæ atque oppressæ opem, pro sua in eam charitate, aliquam afferret. Sed in tantis Ecclesiasticorum opibus, confirmatisque atque inveteratis pravis opinionibus, perspiciebat se neque hæc tanta religionis inquinamenta sine summa hominum offensione commouere, neque ea errorum superstitionumque vitia, quæ infixa diu & penitus insederant, ex animis hominum posse facile convellere.
units.tr: However miserable and long-lasting the condition and profession of those who have been called Christians may have been, so that they retained only the bare name of Christ and, through the greatest ingratitude, deprived themselves of true and saving doctrine, yet no human ingratitude or impiety has ever been able to overcome the goodness of God so completely that he has not always preserved some seed of the godly, from which the Church could be propagated and could recover and keep the religion it had lost. And although there was no corner of the world that was not oppressed by the thickest and most hideous darkness of ignorance, God always kept some sparks alive and kindled them to illuminate and make the truth shine, in the way that, according to the circumstances of the time, he judged opportune and suited to his justice and to our salvation. Now there are many firm and clear signs and illustrious testimonies which show that this doctrine of the Gospel, renewed and restored in these times, is the pure truth of God, in which lies the most wholesome nourishment of souls, feeding them to eternal life. Nor is it at all obscure or doubtful that many martyrs and witnesses of it do not hesitate to pour out their blood, even to the last drop, in confirming and defending it; and so they show how great is the mercy of him who has called us, lost and lying in the horrid darkness of death, back to this saving light of the Gospel and to the knowledge of his will. That this truth is of God is shown above all by the fact that there has been no age in which Satan, with the most furious hatred, has not pursued this doctrine of the Gospel and tried to crush and extinguish it by every means. But since that enemy, so powerful and savage and inflamed with such hatred, has never succeeded in what he attempted, either by hindering the course of this most holy doctrine or by preventing its rise, so as to abolish it utterly (for in the greatest difficulties it has always been wonderfully preserved and handed down from hand to hand), no one should be surprised if it brings such certainty and confidence to the pious who know it, that they set its authority and dignity above the whole world and even above their own lives, and, confirmed by its weightiest testimony, strive with all their soul toward blessed and eternal life. And if Satan were the author of this doctrine, he would not assail it with such hatred, nor would he direct all his rage to abolishing it. For by persecuting and destroying what was his own in this way, he would, as Christ says, make war against himself. But whatever hostile assault and attack Satan makes upon that truth, the Church has always remained safe by the power and help of the Son of God, who restrains his fury. The Church, which was necessarily preserved by his ministry, has always had the best and most faithful ministers and teachers, reserved for administering it and divinely called to it. Although from those first times, when the Gospel was published throughout the world, the Church always had some ministers of the Word, by whom the truth of God and the purity of religion were bravely defended and maintained against the power of the world and of Satan, yet we think it will not be unwelcome to the most gentle readers if we begin the history of this period with the Englishman John Wycliffe and follow it down to the notable examples of our own memory; from these it can be understood how Christ our Lord affirmed that not even the powers and forces of the underworld will prevail against the faith and the unconquered truth of God so as to suppress or destroy them. For at that time, when God raised up this good and upright man as a minister of the Church, tyranny had taken over everything, and the impious and wicked rule of the church leaders had so oppressed the Church itself that there was no place at all for the truth, or for the freedom of any pious man who feared God, and not even a small form of pure doctrine or of the Church was visible. This pitiable oppression and deformation of the Church occurred in the year of Christ's birth 1372. At that time Christian kings and princes, to show their zeal and eagerness in extending and adorning religion, devoted all their thought and care to one thing: seeing to it that the wood of the Cross of Jerusalem was brought into the Christian Church, as if the whole holiness of religion consisted in that wood, or as if there were no other cross except the one said to be preserved at Jerusalem. But then God, in his singular goodness and mercy, wished to rouse the world, oppressed and dead under human traditions and impious superstitions, and to recall it to this most welcome light of truth; and he did this through the faithful and timely work of John Wycliffe. He had long taught theology at Oxford, a famous city in England, and, seeing the doctrine of God defiled and utterly corrupted by the many pollutions of those who follow the Pope, he could not restrain himself from groaning over such a confusion of all things, and from bringing, out of his love for the Church, some help to the truth so corrupted and deformed and to the afflicted and oppressed Church. But, given the great wealth of the churchmen and the established and long-rooted false opinions, he saw that he could neither stir up such great pollutions of religion without great offence to men, nor easily tear out of men's minds those vices of error and superstition which had long been fixed and deeply rooted there.

units.la: Itaque usum est ei non incommodum, si ad emendationem tot & tantorum errorum vitiorumque, mox statim & aperte, sed paulatim, & quasi aliud agens, accederet. Ac primum quid efficere posset contra adversarios veritatis, in paruis rebus magis ad philosophiam quam ad Theologiam pertinentibus, experiri voluit: de quibus cum illis disputauit, ut hac ratione aditum sibi ad res maiores faceret. Inter alios fuit monachus ordinis Carmelitani Ioannes Reninghamus, quo cum huiusmodi concertatiunculas suscepit & agitauit. Ab his paruis initiis ad maiora grauioraque progressus, de Sacramento altaris, ut tum loquebantur, cum illis disputauit: qua in disputatione acerrimos aduersarios habuit, affirmans publicè in scholis, sibi nihil aliud esse propositum, quàm ut idololatriam, quæ in Ecclesia, hac quidem in parte maximam vim habebat, tolleret, verumque usum Sacramenti, & purum Dei cultum demonstraret. Sed hic summa occurrebat difficultas, quòd hoc vlcus tági cōtrestarique nō poterat sine maxima mũdi offesione ac dolore.
units.tr: And so it was not inappropriate for him to approach the correction of so many and so great errors and vices not immediately or openly, but gradually, and as if he were doing something else. First he wished to test what he could accomplish against the adversaries of the truth in minor matters that pertain more to philosophy than to theology; in these he disputed with them, so that in this way he might make his way to greater matters. Among others there was John Reynolds, a Carmelite monk, with whom he undertook and carried on such small contests. Advancing from these small beginnings to greater and weightier matters, he disputed with them about the sacrament of the altar, as they then called it; in this dispute he had very fierce opponents. He declared publicly in the schools that his only aim was to remove idolatry, which at that point held very great power in the Church, and to show the true use of the sacrament and the pure worship of God. But here there was a great difficulty, because this sore could not be touched and handled without the greatest offence and pain to the world.

units.la: Monachi,imprimisque Franciscani, furore quoda ferebantur, pergraviter acerbeque ferentes,sublata Missa sibi pabulum ventris eripi, Jeque ad famem vocari. ita pro ventre,quem vnum habet deum,quasi pro focis atque aris acerrime dimicabant. Episcopi vero huius controuersiæ cognitionem ac disceptationem ad suum iudicium arbitriumque deferri postulabant. verum hoc cum assequi non possent, ad parata Papæ fulmina tandem confugerunt. Nam hoc quidem postremum est impietatis perfugium, quum impudentes monachorum sacerdotúmque clamores insanæque vociferationes non satis proficiunt, ad hanc potestatem & vim tyrannicam accedere, ab eaque arma ad oppugnandam atque opprimendam veritatem ac fidem libertatémque piorum capere.
units.tr: The monks, and above all the Franciscans, were carried away by a certain fury, taking it very grievously and bitterly that, with the Mass abolished, the food of their belly was being snatched from them and they were being called to starvation; so for their belly, which they alone regard as their god, they fought most fiercely, as if for their hearths and altars. The bishops, indeed, demanded that the examination and debate of this controversy be referred to their own judgment and decision. But when they could not obtain this, at last they fled to the Pope's ready thunderbolts. For this is the last refuge of impiety: when the shameless shouting and frantic outcries of the monks and priests do not sufficiently prevail, they add this power and tyrannical force, and from it take up arms to attack and crush the truth and the faith and the freedom of the pious.

units.la: Hic vir impetum tot tantorúmque inimicorum solus sustinuit, nulla alia munitus defensione, quàm authoritate veritatéque Scripturarum sanctarum, in quibus firmamenta & arma fidei constituta habebat. Ut autem doctrina sua plus roboris adversus adversarios obtineret, authoritatem veterum Ecclesiæ doctorum proponebat, sed in iis tantùm modo, in quibus cum sanctis Scripturis plane consentire videbantur, demonstrans ac testificans, nullam aliam esse veritatem, quàm eam quæ in literis diuinis contineretur. cæteros verò Legum ac Decretorum ecclesiasticorum Doctores & fabricatores omnino repudiabat, neque eos testes veritatis, sed hostes atque euersores esse iudicabat. Constanter asseverabat, in Sacramento corporis & sanguinis Christi, accidentia sine subiecto non inesse, id est, candorem formámque panis rotundá sine ipsa pane nullo modo esse: sed contra illa transsubstantiatione (quam sacerdotes non minùs absurdam quàm impiam commenti fuerunt) panem esse panem, & vinum suam naturam non mutare: sed eam quam habet ante Sacramentum substantiam, in ipso etiam Sacramento retinere. Argumenta autem quibus id probabat, nos alium in locum magis commodum reseruabimus.
units.tr: This man alone withstood the assault of so many and such great enemies, protected by no other defence than the authority and truth of the holy Scriptures, in which he held the foundations and weapons of faith to be laid. But so that his doctrine might gain more strength against its adversaries, he put forward the authority of the ancient teachers of the Church, yet only in those passages where they seemed to agree fully with the holy Scriptures, showing and declaring that there is no truth other than that which is contained in the divine writings. The other doctors and makers of the laws and decrees of the Church he utterly rejected, judging them not witnesses of the truth but enemies and subverters of it. He constantly asserted that in the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ the accidents do not exist without a subject; that is, the whiteness and round shape of the bread cannot in any way exist without the bread itself. Rather, contrary to that transubstantiation (which the priests devised as absurd as it is impious), the bread remains bread and the wine does not change its nature, but keeps in the sacrament itself the substance it had before the sacrament. The arguments by which he proved this we shall reserve for another, more suitable place.

units.la: Ipsa quidem veritas wicleuo magnam odii offensionem conciliavit apud eos præsertim, qui maximas Ecclesiæ opes obtinebant. tametsi quandiu Edouardus Rex vixit, satis constat wicleuum studio, fauore auxilióque hominum adversus mimicos non plane fuisse desitutum : nisi quod vltimo eius Regis anno, Papae instinctu ab Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi comprehensus fuit : & cum adessent dux Lancastriae Henricusque Perseus, silentium ei impositum. veruntamen dum nonnullorum potentissimorum Principum studium beneuolentiamque recuperasset, silentio non diuturno vsus est. Interea Richardus Edouardi filius, mortuo patre regnum excepit, anno M.CCCLXXVII. Tum vero Gregorius Romanus pontifex nunquam destitit per literas, per regni Episcopos, per bullas suas nouum Regem solicitare, eiusque animum per se generosum & humanum, aduersus wicleuum eiusque doctrinae studiosos incitare.
units.tr: Truth itself brought Wycliffe great hostility, especially from those who held the greatest wealth of the Church. Yet while King Edward lived, it is well established that Wycliffe was not wholly deprived of support: he had the zeal, favour and help of men against his enemies. Only in the last year of that King's reign, at the instigation of the Pope, was he arrested by the Archbishop of Canterbury, and when the Duke of Lancaster and Henry Percy were present, he was ordered to be silent. Nevertheless, having recovered the goodwill and support of some of the most powerful princes, he did not keep silent for long. Meanwhile Richard, son of Edward, succeeded to the kingdom when his father died, in the year 1377. Then indeed Gregory, the Roman pontiff, never ceased, by letters, through the bishops of the kingdom and by his own bulls, to urge the new King and to stir up his mind, naturally generous and humane, against Wycliffe and those who studied his doctrine.

units.la: Et extat quidem Epistola reperta, quam Papa Gregorius ad Regem Richardum misit: eam huic nos historiae intexuimus, hoc exemplo.
units.tr: There survives a letter, discovered since, which Pope Gregory sent to King Richard. We have inserted it into this history, in the following form.

units.la: C[?]arissimo in Christo filio, Richardo Regi Angliae illustri, Sal. &c. Regnum Angliae, quod Altissimus tuae supponit potestati, gloriosum nempe potentia & abundantia facultatem, sed gloriosius pietate fidei & sacrae paginae claritate choruscu, consueuit viros producere diuinarum Scripturarum recta scientia praeditos, maturitate graues, deuotione feruentes, & catholicae fidei defensores, qui non solum proprios praeceptis salutaribus instituebant, dirigebantque in Diuinorum semitam mandatorum, &c. Sed cum ingenti cordis amaritudine, plurimorum fide dignorum suggestione percepimus, Ioannem wicleff rectorem ecclesiae de Lutterwort, Lincolniensis dioecesis, sacrae paginae professorem (vtinam non magistrum errorum) in illam nefandam & abominabilem prorupisse dementiam, quod nonnullas propositiones conclusiones plenas erroribus, & manifestam haeresim continentes, quae statum totius ecclesiae subuertere & eneruare nituntur: quarumque aliquae, licet quibusdam mutatis terminis, sentire videntur per uersas opiniones & doctrinam indoctam damnatae memoriae Marsilij de Padua & Ioannis de Gauduno, quorum liber per felicis recordationis Ioannem Papam XXII, praedecessorem nostrum reprobatus extitit & damnatus, &c. Cum itaque uenerabiles fratres nostri, Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis, & Episcopus Londinensis, a nobis mandatum acceperunt, præfatum Ioannem authoritate nostra capiendi, & carceribus mancipandi, eiusque confessionem ad nos transmittendi, si in profecutione huius negotij noscantur fauore & auxilio tuo indigere, maiestatem tuam (quemadmodû & tui progenitores inclyti catholicæ fidei, cuius in hac parte res agitur, semper confucuerunt esse & præcipui zelatores) requirimus, & deprecamur attente, quatenus ob reuerentiam Dei, dictæ fidei & Apostolicæ sedis & nostrum intuitum, digneris præfatis Archiepiscopo & Episcopo, aliisque qui huiusmodi negotium prosequuntur, in ipsa profecutione, tui fauoris & auxilij patrocinium exhibere. Proinde præter humanæ laudis præconium, Diuinæ retributionis præmium, nostram & dictæ sedis gratiam & beneuolentiam adepturus ampliorem. Datum Romæ apud S. Mariam maiorem, II. Calend. Iunij, Anno pontificatus nostri VII, M. CCC. LXXVIII.
units.tr: To our most beloved son in Christ, Richard, illustrious King of England, greeting, etc. The kingdom of England, which the Most High has placed under your power, is glorious for its strength and abundance of resources, but more glorious for its piety, its faith and its bright knowledge of the sacred page. It has been accustomed to produce men endowed with a sound knowledge of the divine Scriptures, grave in maturity, fervent in devotion, and defenders of the Catholic faith, who not only instruct their own people with salutary precepts and direct them into the path of the divine commandments, etc. But we have learned, with great bitterness of heart, from the reports of many trustworthy men, that John Wycliffe, rector of the church of Lutterworth in the diocese of Lincoln, professor of sacred theology (would that he were not a teacher of error), has broken out into that wicked and abominable madness of putting forward certain propositions and conclusions full of errors and manifest heresy, which strive to overthrow and enfeeble the state of the whole Church. Some of these, although with certain words changed, seem to agree with the perverse opinions and unlearned doctrine of the men of blessed memory, Marsilius of Padua and John of Gaudun, whose book was rejected and condemned by our predecessor, Pope John XXII, of happy memory, etc. Therefore, since our venerable brothers, the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of London, have received from us a command to seize the aforesaid John by our authority, to commit him to prison, and to send his confession to us, if in the prosecution of this business they are found to need your favour and help, we require and earnestly beseech your majesty (as your illustrious ancestors, who in this matter defend the Catholic faith, which is at stake, have always been accustomed to be, and its chief champions) that for the reverence of God, of the said faith, of the Apostolic See and of ourselves, you deign to extend the protection of your favour and help to the aforesaid Archbishop and Bishop, and to others who pursue this business, in the very prosecution of it. In return you will obtain, besides the praise of men, the reward of divine recompense and a greater favour and goodwill from us and from the said See. Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, on the second day before the Kalends of June, in the seventh year of our pontificate, 1378.

units.la: Hæc sunt argumentorum rationumque firmamenta, quibus Pontifices Romani tuentur fidemChristiana, quibus etiam mundo conantur persuadere Vsluládos[?] esse eos quos hæreticos appellant: id est, eos qui ipsorum barbaram immanemque tyrannidem nullo modo ferre possunt: quam crudelissimè exercent non in corpora solum, sed etiam præcipuè in animas, quas Christus Dominus tanto sanguinis sui pretio redemit.
units.tr: These are the props of argument and reason by which the Roman pontiffs defend the Christian faith, and by which they try to persuade the world that the Lollards are those whom they call heretics, that is, those who cannot in any way bear their barbarous and monstrous tyranny, which they exercise most cruelly not only upon bodies but chiefly upon souls, which Christ the Lord redeemed with so great a price of his blood.

units.la: Sed ad institutâ de wicleuo narrationem redeamus. Is crudelissimis illorum interdictis minisque coactus est aliquandiu obmutescere: sed ita tamen, vt præclara pietas ac veritas, quæ antea exarserat, postea eo silê tio compressa, maiore vi eruperit, vehementiusque hominum studia accenderit. Itaque nactus hominum veritati fauentium opportuna tum studia tum auxilia, iterum pia dogmata proposuit ac protulit. Neque aduersarij hac in re sibi defuerunt: sed ijdem animis studiisque conspirantes, omnes suas vires renouarunt, confirmarunt, eoque contulerunt, vt hanc purißimâ lucem extinguerent, quæ tu primum radios in mundû horrendis ignorationis tenebris occupatum, mittere incipiebat. Neque vero hîc Papa dormiebat: sed omnia potius & tetabat & agebat: vt ad scuitiam & crudelitatem eorum animos acueret atque incitaret, qui per se ad eius nutum & arbitrium maximopere erant accommodati, per literas ac bullas eos ad omnem offensionem exacerbans, qui sua sponte veram salutis doctrinam oderant. Inter eas sunt quædā exempla literarum eius, quæ proferri possent: quæ quidem nihil aliud continent, quam comminationes barbaras, immania tyrannicaque interdicta, atque verba homine plane indigna, eoque digna potius, cuius Vicarius cum sit, etiam illius sævitiam malitiamque imitatur, id est, Satana, cuius ab ore atrociora & crudeliora quam hæc sunt, prodire non possent. Itaque monachi ac sacerdotes quidam, quasi titiones inferorum, cum harum literarum acerbitate incitati, tum etiam crudelitate venerandi Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis, tum vero suo ipsorum furore incitati, prædare cum suis Episcopis testificabantur, se, nec si de vita quidem ipsorum ageretur, velle susceptam causam deponere aut negligere, sed eam cum omni iustitiæ acerbitate persequi. Huiusmodi autem testificatio palam à bonis illis viris Ecclesiam amantibus, maxima cum audacia adhibebatur, antequam concilium ipsorum provinciale cogeretur. Hæc autem animi fortis & constantis in optima causa declaratio, & magnifica pronuntiatio, omni laude digna fuisset, si intellexissent quæ esset causæ æquitas & veritas, eamque cum integra animi conscientia defendissent.
units.tr: But let us return to the narrative about Wycliffe. Compelled by their most cruel prohibitions and threats, he was for some time forced to be silent. Yet in such a way that the excellent piety and truth which had previously blazed forth, though then checked by that silence, broke out again with greater force and kindled men's zeal more vehemently. Thus, having found opportune zeal and help from men who favoured the truth, he again proposed and set forth his godly doctrines. Nor were his adversaries lacking in this matter; rather, united in mind and purpose, they renewed, strengthened and directed all their forces to extinguish this most pure light, which had begun to send its rays into a world occupied by the horrible darkness of ignorance. Nor indeed did the Pope here sleep; rather he attempted and did everything, to sharpen and incite the minds of those men to savagery and cruelty, who of themselves were most ready at his nod and will, goading them by letters and bulls to every kind of hostility, those who of their own accord hated the true doctrine of salvation. Among these there are some examples of his letters which could be produced, and these contain nothing but barbarous threats, monstrous and tyrannical prohibitions, and words wholly unworthy of a man, and therefore more fitting to him whose vicar he is, for he imitates the savagery and malice of Satan, from whose mouth nothing more atrocious or cruel could come. And so certain monks and priests, like firebrands of hell, roused both by the bitterness of these letters and by the cruelty of the venerable Archbishop of Canterbury, and also by their own fury, declared with their bishops that they would not, even if their own lives were at stake, give up or neglect the cause they had undertaken, but would pursue it with all the harshness of justice. Such a declaration was openly made with the greatest boldness, in the presence of those good men who loved the Church, before their provincial council was convened. Yet this declaration of a brave and steadfast mind in a good cause, and this proud pronouncement, would have deserved all praise, had they understood what the fairness and truth of the cause were, and had they defended it with a clear conscience.

units.la: Sed Deus, qui vanas cogitationes consiliaque hominum paruo etiam momento sæpe evertit sua tum virtute tum bonitate, istorum motus atque impetus facile comprensit. Nam cum dies iudicii venisset, Ludouicus quidam Clyfordus, unus ex aulicis proceribus, Episcopos adiit, eosque gravissime monuit, ne ullam iuridicialem sententiam in wicleuum pronuntiarent. Ita eorum audacia & superbia, quemadmodum monumentis proditum est, subito concidit, ut ne verbum quidem, quod ad eam prohibitionem responderent, habuerint: sic omnes erant consternati. Illud præterea accidit, quod cum Episcopi vnà cum wicleuo, Lambeti in sacellum Archiepiscopi convenissent, cives Londinenses libere audacterque eo ingressi sunt: eoque conventu nonnihil perturbato, pro wicleuo verba fecerunt, cum summa testificatione suæ in illum voluntatis. Quare huiusmodi piorum hominum studiis adiutus & confirmatus, quum causam & rationem suæ doctrinæ testificans omnibus demonstrasset, ac bonis prudentibusque approbasset, facile inimicorum suorum insidiis, difficultatibus, periculisque est liberatus.
units.tr: But God, who often overturns the vain thoughts and counsels of men, even in a small moment, by his power and goodness, easily checked their movements and assaults. For when the day of judgment had come, a certain Ludovic Clifford, one of the courtly nobles, approached the bishops and most severely warned them not to pronounce any judicial sentence against Wycliffe. Thus their audacity and pride, as is recorded in the chronicles, suddenly collapsed, so that they had not even a word to answer that prohibition; so completely were they all dismayed. Moreover, it also happened that when the bishops had assembled with Wycliffe at Lambeth, in the chapel of the Archbishop, the citizens of London entered freely and boldly, and, the assembly being somewhat disturbed, they spoke on behalf of Wycliffe, with a strong declaration of their goodwill towards him. Therefore, aided and strengthened by the zeal of such godly men, when he had set forth the cause and reasoning of his doctrine to everyone, and had won the approval of good and prudent men, he was easily freed from the snares, difficulties and dangers of his enemies.

units.la: Testificatio autem eius & confessio haec fuit. In principio profestor publice, &c.
units.tr: His declaration and confession was as follows. In the beginning I profess publicly, etc.

units.la: Longum esset conclusiones, quas cum ea testificatione coniunxit ac proposuit, hic referre: satis erit nonnullas hoc loco ponere, ex quibus caeterarum omnium vis, totiusque doctrinae eius summa aequitas & veritas facile intelligi poterit.
units.tr: It would be long to set out here the conclusions which he attached to and proposed with that declaration; it will be enough to put down a few at this point, from which the force of all the rest, and the great fairness and truth of his whole doctrine, can easily be understood.

units.la: Aliquae conclusiones Ioannis wicleui, Lambeti in conuentu Episcoporum propositae, anno M. CCCLXXVII.
units.tr: Some conclusions of John Wycliffe, proposed at Lambeth before a meeting of the bishops, in the year 1377.

units.la: 1 Si[?] aliqua à Principibus ac Regibus donatio ministris Ecclesiae facta fuerit, in ea tacita intelligenda & obseruanda est conditio, vt Deus honoretur, Ecclesia aedificetur. Nisi haec conditio conseruetur, Principes iure possunt ac debent id omne auferre quod in eos contulerunt: quaecunque vis excommunicationis contra fulminare videatur.
units.tr: 1. If any donation has been made to the ministers of the Church by princes and kings, a tacit condition is to be understood and observed in it: that God be honoured and the Church built up. Unless this condition is kept, the princes may and ought in law to take back everything they bestowed on them, whatever force of excommunication may seem to be hurled against them.

units.la: 2 Quòd si ad retinendas hoc modo, aut occupandas possessiones & opes, hæc Papæ fulmina suam vim haberent, totus Clerus ex genere hominum auarissimorum conflatus, omnes mundi opes ac facultates ad se traheret.
units.tr: 2. But if these thunderbolts of the Pope had their force for keeping or seizing possessions and wealth in this way, the whole clergy, made up of the most covetous men, would draw to themselves all the riches and resources of the world.

units.la: 3 Papa iure ac legitimè potest redargui reprehendíque ab iis quos in subiectione ac potestate sua habet: atque ad Ecclesiæ vtilitatem, tam à Laicis quàm à Cleris accusari.
units.tr: 3. The Pope can be rightly and lawfully rebuked and reproved by those whom he holds under his subjection and power, and for the good of the Church he can be accused both by laymen and by clergy.

units.la: 4 Nam quantumuis magnus dominus sit Papa, debet tamen ita sentire atque existimare, caeterorum se, etiam minimorum, fratrem esse.
units.tr: However great a lord the Pope may be, he ought nevertheless to think and judge that he is a brother to all the others, even the least of them.

units.la: 5 Is quemadmodum caeteri peccare potest: atque ita fraterne & admonere & corrigi debet, aliorumque correctiones fraterne ac modeste audire. Imprimis vero si in eo aliqua est pertinacia, qua haeresim aut errore praui Ecclesiaeque perniciosum tueatur, tum quidem in eo non est metuenda reprehensio & accusatio vt periculum euitetur. Ita enim Paulus non est veritus Petrum palam reprehendere.
units.tr: He can sin as others do, and so he ought to be admonished and corrected in a brotherly way, and he ought to hear the corrections of others in a brotherly and modest spirit. Above all, if he is obstinate in holding to heresy or to some perverse error harmful to the Church, then there is no reason to fear rebuke and accusation in his case, lest some danger be avoided. For Paul did not hesitate to rebuke Peter openly.

units.la: Aliae sunt multae eius conclusiones, quibus Cleri Papalis vitia, abusus peccataque ostendebat: atque etiam quàm iniustè maximorum prouentuum redituumque possessiones occuparent. Ego autem satis intelligere non possum, qui factum fuerit vt Episcopi wicleuum post hanc demonstrationem confessionemque doctrinae quietum sine vlla molestia dimiserunt. Fortasse, quasunt in bonis rebus negligentia & insatia, eius conclusiones non legerunt, aut si legerunt, intelligere non potuerunt. Paulo post Gregorius Pontifex e vita decessit. Cuius quidem mors wicleuo, ad ea quae iam suscepcerat agebatque, percommoda accidit. Statim post eius mortem suscepta est summa acerbaque contentio inter duos Pontifices, quorum alter in Gallia, alter Romae creatus fuit. Hoc autem hostile dissidium triginta fere annos inter eos fuit, bellaque suscepta grauia & maxima hominum multitudo propter duorum ne bulonum ambitionem intercipit. Eodem tempore in Anglia grauis & periculosus belli motus extitit, triennio inter plebem & nobiles excitatus, qui regnum illud vehementer perturbauit. Ea in seditione Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis, Simon de Sudburia nominatus, a rusticis hominibus comprehensus, capite truncatus est. Huic in eo Ecclesiae munere atque honore successit Guilielmus Courtnæus, qui omnem curam, studium, operam suam in id unum contulit, vt piis ac fidelibus hominibus bellum faceret, cosque omnibus iniuriis ac molestiis deuexaret. Interea numerus eorum qui causam doctrinamque wideui sectabantur, in dies augebatur singulos, donec Guilielmus quidam Bertonus, Oxoniensis Vniuersitatis (vt vocant) Cancellarius, ad eos comprimendos insurrexit. Hic octo Doctores ex monachorum ordine, quatuorque ex alio professionis genere conuocauit, atque alios quosdam suarum partium homines adhibuit, quorum omnium ex sententia & authoritate huiusmodi literae conscriptae fuerunt, ac publico Vniuersitatis sigillo obsignatae, quibus grauissimis cum nunis studiosi ac literati eius academiae homines a disciplina wicleuiana arcebatur. Adeo vt nisi wicleuus & ij omnes qui eius causam adiuuabant, resipiscerent, post tertiam & publicam praecisamque admonitionem coniiceren-tur in cacerem, grauissimoque excommunicationis genere afficerentur ac notarentur. Itaque wicleuus quum praeclara interdicta accepisset, etsi nihil animaduertebat in his esse quod magnopere pertimesceret dum videretur, tamen relicto Papa totoque illius presbyterio, ad authoritatē atque amplitudinem Regis prouocauit. Sed dux Lancastriae interueniens, hominem monuit ne quid tale attentaret: sed potius se cognitioni censuraeque sui Iudicis ordinarij submitteret. Quare cùm in bis angustiis difficultatibusque versaretur, confessionem iterum doctrinae suae offerre coactus est, in qua quidem huiusmodi moderatione usus est, ut aequiores paulo adversarios & placatiores habuerit. Anno sequenti, qui fuit M.CCC. LXXXII. Guilielmus Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis iterum concilium Londini adhibendum curavit, in quo wicleuus adesse iussus est.
units.tr: There are many other conclusions of his, by which he exposed the faults, abuses and sins of the Papal clergy, and also how unjustly they had seized the possessions that yielded the greatest revenues and incomes. But I cannot sufficiently understand how it came about that the bishops let Wycliffe go quietly and without any trouble after this demonstration and confession of his doctrine. Perhaps, being careless and lazy in good matters, they did not read his conclusions, or if they read them, they could not understand them. Shortly afterwards Pope Gregory died. His death came very opportunely for Wycliffe, as regards what he had already undertaken and was pursuing. Immediately after his death a great and bitter contest arose between two popes, one created in Gaul, the other at Rome. This hostile dissension lasted between them for almost thirty years, and it brought on grave wars and drew a very great multitude of men into destruction on account of the ambition of the two. At the same time a grave and dangerous outbreak of war arose in England, stirred up for three years between the common people and the nobles, which greatly disturbed that kingdom. In that uprising the Archbishop of Canterbury, named Simon of Sudbury, was seized by country folk and beheaded. He was succeeded in that office and honour of the Church by William Courtenay, who devoted all his care, zeal and effort to one thing: to wage war on pious and faithful men and to harass them with every kind of injury and vexation. Meanwhile the number of those who followed the cause and teaching of Wycliffe grew day by day, until a certain William Barton, Chancellor of the University of Oxford (as it is called), rose up to suppress them. He summoned eight doctors from the monastic orders and four from another profession, and brought in some others of his party, and by their opinion and authority letters of this kind were drawn up and sealed with the public seal of the University, by which the studious and learned men of that academy were kept away from Wycliffe's teaching under the gravest penalties. So that unless Wycliffe and all who supported his cause repented, after a third, public and final admonition they would be thrown into prison and struck with the most severe kind of excommunication and branded. Therefore Wycliffe, having received these splendid prohibitions, although he saw nothing in them that he should greatly fear, nevertheless, leaving the Pope and his whole presbytery, appealed to the authority and power of the King. But the Duke of Lancaster intervened and warned the man not to attempt anything of the sort, but rather to submit himself to the examination and censure of his ordinary judge. Therefore, while he was in these straits and difficulties, he was forced to offer again a confession of his doctrine, in which he used such moderation that he had somewhat fairer and more placable opponents. In the following year, which was 1382, William, Archbishop of Canterbury, again arranged for a council to be held at London, in which Wycliffe was ordered to attend.

units.la: Hoc quidem loco minime silentio praetereundum est quod tunc diuinitus euenit. Nam cum ipse Archiepiscopus caeterique eius suffragatores ac fautores, in his etiam doctores Theologiae, Legumque ac Decretorum professores, cum maxima monachorum ac sacerdotum turba Londini in claustris Dominicanorum conuenissent, ut hora post prandium secunda de libris wicleui omnibusque eius opinionibus deliberarent, ingens & terroris plenus terrae motus in universo Angliae regno factus est. Episcopi eo terrore quasi sinistro quodam omine attoniti & consternati, censebant ut causa suscepta supersederent: sed Archiepiscopus, huius totius belli dux, multo audacior quam prudentior, id quod acciderat aliam in partem interpretatus est, atque suos in proposita re susceptaque sententia vehementius obfirmaut[?].
units.tr: It must by no means be passed over in silence here what then happened by divine providence. For when the Archbishop himself and the others who supported and favoured him, including teachers of theology and professors of laws and decrees, together with a great crowd of monks and priests, had gathered at London in the cloister of the Dominicans, to deliberate at the second hour after dinner about the books of Wycliffe and all his opinions, a huge earthquake, full of terror, struck the whole kingdom of England. The bishops, stunned and dismayed by that terror as if by some ominous sign, thought they should abandon the cause they had undertaken; but the Archbishop, leader of this whole war, much bolder than wise, interpreted what had happened in the other direction, and strengthened his men more vehemently in the matter they had taken up and the opinion they had adopted.

units.la: Hi omnes cum wicleui conclusiones discussissent, non ex authoritate diuinorum oraculorum, sed ex libidine acerbissimorum odiorum tandem pronuntiarunt, quasdam earum esse plane haereticas, alias mixtas ex utroque genere, quae non minus erroris contineret quam veritatis, quas semierroneas appellabant: nonnullas vero irreligiosas, & cum offendiculo coniunctas, & quae parum disciplinam curiae Romanae ac Pontificiae redolerent. Rursus Archiepiscopus venerabiles Doctores & Magistros nostros conuocauit, in illudque concilium, Riggæu Cācellariū[?] una cum procuratoribus Vniuersitatis Ioanne Huntemano & Gualtero Dascho, & altero quodam qui M. Bryt-wellus dicebatur, in quos omnes certas suspiciones sectae ac disciplinae wicleuianae criminose conferebat. Primum illi tergiuersando, excusando, verbaque ambigue interpretando elabi conabantur.
