Deinde cum haec illis subterfugia nihil prodessent, aperte quid sentirent confiteri coacti sunt, cum huiusmodi tamen testificatione, quod eas conclusiones, ut verba quidem sonant, haereticas erroneasque esse inuiti concederent. Cancellarius positis in terra flexisque genibus orauit veniā, atque cā per Episcopum winton. deprecatorem impetrauit : ea tamen conditione, vt domum suam reuersus, quum diligenter inquisuisset, os omnium eorum observaret quos wideuo, Herfordo, Repyngtono, Astono, Bednamóque adesse ac fauere comperisset : eodémque tempore conclusiones wideui antea condenatas in summo templo vniuerso populo recitaret. Cæteros etiam quoscunque reperisset fautores eius sectæ, ad abnegationem aut ipsorum purgationem cogeret.
units.tr: When all of them had examined Wycliffe's conclusions, they at last pronounced, not from the authority of the divine oracles but from the lust of most bitter hatreds, that some of them were plainly heretical, others mixed from both kinds, which contained no less error than truth, and these they called semi-erroneous; and some were irreligious and offensive, and smelt little of the discipline of the Roman and Papal court. Again the Archbishop summoned our venerable doctors and masters, and in that council he charged Rygg the Chancellor, together with the proctors of the University, John Huntingdon and Walter Daskh, and another named Master Brytwell, with certain suspicions of Wycliffe's sect and teaching, falsely attributing them to all of them. At first they tried to slip away by evasion, excuse, and ambiguous interpretation of their words. Then, when these subterfuges availed them nothing, they were compelled to confess openly what they thought, yet with this declaration: that they reluctantly conceded that those conclusions, as the words sound, were heretical and erroneous. The Chancellor, kneeling on the ground with bent knees, begged pardon, and obtained it through the Bishop of Winchester as intercessor; on this condition, however, that on returning home he should make a careful inquiry and watch the mouths of all those he found to be adherents of Wycliffe, Hereford, Repyngton, Aston and Bedeman, and at the same time read aloud before the whole people in the high church the conclusions of Wycliffe previously condemned. He was also to compel to recantation, or to self-purgation, any other supporters of that sect he could find.

units.la: Ac cùm Cancellarius respondisset se id nō ausurum facere in tanto proposito sibi vitæ periculo: Quid, inquit Archiepiscopus, Oxoniensis ciuitas huiusmodi fautoribus adeóne est referta, vt nullus in ea locus catholicæ veritati reperiatur ? Postero die, quum res ad consilium relata fuisset, consiliarij regij Cancellario iniunxerunt, vt quod mandatum erat ab Archiepiscopo, exequeretur. Is tunc hoc cum mandato domum suam reuersus est. Tunc inter partes summa dissidia & odia exerceri augeríque cœperunt. Imprimis vero monachi, vt tantorum motuum authores, in maximam inuidiā atque odij offensionem vocabantur. Ex eorum numero fuit quidam monachus Cistertiensis, Henricus Crompeius theologiæ studiosus, qui ab Episcopo in crimen hæreseos vocatus est. Nam cùm eo tempore Lolardos appellarent eos qui recte ac pie de religione sentiret, ab actibus, vt loquuntur, per Cancellarium suspensus est. erat enim primum tantummodo studij sui gradū consequutus, qui Bacalaureis deferri solet. Itaque is statim Londinum profectus, apud Archiepiscopum totúmque Regis consilium, de ignominia iniuriáque graviter conquestus est : quæ fuit causa vt Cancellarius Riggæus cum procuratoribus iterum accerseretur, ídque cùm Regis nomine tum vero totius consilij sententia atque authoritate. Sed eius rei totius Archiepiscopus præcipuus erat author & instigator. Tunc denuò Cancellario mandatum est, vt hærcticos conquirendos persequendósque curaret. itaque Philippus Repyngtonus & Nicolaus Herfordus ea de re clàm à Cancellario certiores factì, illico ad Ioannē Lancastriæ ducem confugerunt. A quo repulsi, ad iudicium censurámque Archiepiscopi reiecti fuerunt. sed de his postea aliquid memorabimus. De wideuo autem quid factum fuerit incertum est : nisi quòd ex waldeno, qui haec literis prodidit, intelligere possumus, illum in exilium missum fuisse, posteaſque in parochiam suam reuersum, cuius erat Pastor, in Domino vltimum diem suum obiisse, anno M.CCC.LXXXVII, mense Decembri iam desinente. Anno post ipsius mortem XLI, eiusdem ossa iussu Pontificis effossa fuerunt, igneque vstulata, atque in cinerem redacta in aquam coniecta sunt. Qua in re videntur Episcopi id metuisse, quod Pharisaei ipsorum parentes, ante in Christo Domino metuerant, ne reuiuisceret. at Christus in suis nō moritur, sed viuit, viuetque perpetuo, quanuis ista suam saeuitiam & crudelitatem non in viuos solum, verum etiam in mortuos exercerent. Porro wicleuus complura scripserat opuscula, quae Oxoniae in ignem coniecta, concremata fuerunt anno M.CCCCX, praesente Abbate Salopiae, Vniuersitatis Cancellario. Magnopere optandum esset, vt nos hodie eos libros ſaluos haberemus: sed tamen nullus tantus furor inimicorum facere potuit, quin aliquos Ecclesiae suae Deus conseruarit, eaque re suam curam beneuolentiamque in eam declarauerit, cum serui ipsius ac ministri, fideles homines, non in sua solum vita Ecclesiae seruiant, verum etiam post mortem: memoria videlicet ipsorum & doctrina fidelissimis literis tradita & conseruata. Inter caetera eius scripta, extat Epistola ad Vrbanū Pontificem, missa anno M.CCC.LXXXIIII, quae breuem & piam (vt tum ea ferebant tempora) fidei eius confessionem complectitur.
units.tr: When the Chancellor replied that he would not dare to do this in so great a danger to his life, the Archbishop said: "What, is the city of Oxford so full of such supporters that there is no place in it for Catholic truth?" The next day, when the matter had been referred to the council, the royal councillors ordered the Chancellor to carry out what the Archbishop had commanded. He then returned home with this command. Then great discord and hatred began to break out and grow between the parties. Above all the monks, as the authors of such great disturbances, were brought into the greatest odium and hostility. Among them was a certain Cistercian monk, Henry Crompe, a student of theology, who was summoned by the Bishop on a charge of heresy. For at that time they called Lollards those who thought rightly and piously about religion; he was suspended from his acts, as they say, by the Chancellor, for he had attained only the first step of his studies, which is usually granted to Bachelors. So he at once set out for London and complained bitterly to the Archbishop and the whole king's council about the disgrace and injury. This was the reason why Chancellor Rygg with the proctors was summoned again, both in the king's name and by the authority and decision of the whole council. But the Archbishop was the chief author and instigator of the whole affair. Then again the Chancellor was ordered to take care to search out and pursue heretics. And so Philip Repyngton and Nicholas Hereford, secretly warned of this by the Chancellor, at once fled to John, Duke of Lancaster. Repulsed by him, they were handed back to the judgment and censure of the Archbishop. But we will say something about these matters later. As for what became of Wycliffe, it is uncertain; except that from Walden, who published these things in writing, we can understand that he was sent into exile, and afterwards, having returned to his parish, of which he was minister, he died in the Lord on his last day, in the year 1387, as December was drawing to its close. Forty-one years after his death, by order of the Pope, his bones were dug up, burned with fire, reduced to ash, and thrown into water. In this matter the bishops seem to have feared what the Pharisees, their forebears, had feared before in the case of the Lord Christ, lest he should rise again. But Christ does not die in his own people; he lives, and will live forever, although these men directed their cruelty and savagery not only against the living but also against the dead. Moreover Wycliffe had written many small works, which were thrown into the fire at Oxford and burned in the year 1410, in the presence of the Abbot of Shrewsbury, the Chancellor of the University. It would be greatly to be wished that we had those books safe today; but nevertheless no such great fury of enemies could prevent God from preserving some for his Church, and by this he declared his care and goodwill towards her, since his servants and ministers, faithful men, serve the Church not only during their lives but also after death, namely through their memory and teaching handed down and preserved in most faithful writings. Among his other writings there exists a letter to Pope Urban, sent in 1384, which contains a brief and pious (as the times then reckoned) confession of his faith.

units.la: Neque vero cognitione indignum videtur, quod idem wicleuus Richardo secundo Angliae Regi, anno regni eius primo respondit, cum is ab illo quaesuisset quodnam esset Regis ius, & quae Pontificis Romani potestas. Responsio autem extat scripta in historia Ioannis Foxi Angli, qui ea quae ad wicleuum pertinent diligentissime collegit. Ex qua responsione facile intelligi potest, quemadmodum iura Principum ac Regum sunt tuenda aduersus libidinem eorum qui sui immemores ossicij, contra verbum Dei omnia volunt occupare, atque ita impium dominatum confirmare. Caeterum cum ille multos in vita sua aduersarios inimicosque habuerit, ex omnibus tamen nullos est expertus acriores atque acerbiores, quam monachos ac sacerdotes, & eos qui in Ecclesia regnum ac dominatum occuparunt. Hoc autem propterea commemoratur, vt intelligatur veritatem facilem habitura locum accessúmque ad homines, nisi ambitio inexplebilisque auaritia horum Pharisaeorum, aditum ei intercluderet. Idem tamen amicos nonnullos habuit, quorum fidem & benevolentiam erga se, egregiumque & constans in causam suscepram studium expertus est, non modo ex infimo hominum ordine, sed ex eo genere quod in aula apud Regem plurimum gratia authoritateque valeret. Ex eorum numero atque etiam ex equestri ordine hi referuntur, Ioannes Clavvoius, Ludovicus Clyffordus, Richardus Sturius, Thomas Latimerus, Guilielmus Neuillus, Ioannes Montacutus, qui cunctas in Ecclesia sua imagines est demolitus. His etiam accedebat Comes Salburiensis, in cuius morte hoc attente accuratéque fuit animaduersum & grauiter notatum, quód auricularem confessionem Papisticúmque deum in ipso pane inclusum & oblatum, indignius repudiare visus sit. Neque vero Ioannes de Northamptonia praetor Londinensis praetereundus est, qui monitu instinctúque wicleui, in impudicos scortatores atque adulteros grauiter animaduertebat, vt non solum eos qui flagitiose aliquid comiserant, ignominia afficeret, verum etiam caeteris hac vtens seueritate, sublatáque omni impunitate, flagitiorum materia & licentiam tolleret. In eundem numerum est ascribendus Ioannes Cobhamus, qui aperte ingenuéque est confessus, se nunquam peccatum ex animo ante odisse, quàm doctrina wicleui imbutus atque instítutus cognouit quantopere peccatum sit detestandum. atque hi quidem summa authoritate dignitateque praestabant. Ex communi autem multitudine hominum infimáque conditione permulti erant, qui illius doctrinam disciplinámque amplexi, omni studio propugnabant ac defendebant: sed insigne studium Oxoniensium extitit, ex quibus tamen nullus Ecclesiasticorum tyrannorum oppressionem crudelitatémque euasit. Aut enim ignominia turpiter affecti fuerunt, aut igne crudeliter vstulati.
units.tr: Nor does it seem unworthy of notice that this same Wycliffe, in the first year of the reign of Richard II, King of England, answered the King when he asked him what the right of the king was and what power the Roman Pontiff had. This answer is written down in the history of John Foxe the Englishman, who gathered very carefully what concerns Wycliffe. From that answer it can easily be understood how the rights of princes and kings must be defended against the lust of those who, forgetful of their duty, want to seize everything against the Word of God and so establish an impious lordship. Moreover, although he had many adversaries and enemies in his life, he found none fiercer or more bitter than the monks and priests, and those who had seized rule and dominion in the Church. This is mentioned for this reason: that it may be understood that the truth would have found an easy place and access among men, had not the ambition and insatiable greed of these Pharisees blocked its way. Yet he also had some friends, whose faith and goodwill towards him, and whose outstanding and steadfast zeal for the cause he had taken up, he experienced, not only from the lowest rank of men but also from that class which held the greatest favour and authority at court with the King. Among their number, and also from the equestrian order, are reckoned John Clanvowe, Lord Ludovic Clifford, Richard Sturry, Thomas Latimer, William Neville, and John Montagu, who tore down all the images in his church. To these was also added the Earl of Salisbury, at whose death it was attentively and carefully noted and gravely remarked that he seemed to have rejected more contemptuously auricular confession and the Papist god enclosed and offered in the bread. Nor must John of Northampton, the mayor of London, be passed over, who at Wycliffe's admonition and urging severely punished shameless fornicators and adulterers, so that not only did he disgrace those who had committed some shameful offence, but also, using this severity with the rest and removing all impunity, he took away the occasion and licence for vice. To the same number must be assigned John Oldcastle, who openly and frankly confessed that he had never truly hated sin in his heart until, instructed and trained in Wycliffe's teaching, he learned how greatly sin is to be detested. These men, indeed, excelled in the highest authority and dignity. From the common multitude and lowest condition of men there were very many who, embracing his teaching and discipline, defended and maintained it with every zeal. But the zeal of the Oxford men was especially notable, yet none of them escaped the oppression and cruelty of the ecclesiastical tyrants. For they were either shamefully disgraced or cruelly burned.

units.la: De Herfordo autem & Repyngtono quaedá supra memorata fuerunt. nunc hic locus postulat, vt repetitam de his historiam ea breuitate complectamur ac persequamur, quam & temporis & huius libri ratio requirit. Herfordus igitur cùm diu fauisset wicleuo, eiúsque causam & doctrinam optimo & constantissimo studio sectatus esset, in suspicionem eius amicitiæ ab inimicis venire cœpit, & cum is apertius liberiusque quædam in suis concionibus profiteretur, quæ ad defensionem wiclevi pertinebant, Carmelitæ cæterorumque ordinum monachi animo exacerbati, multas ei hæreses intentarunt, ex ipsius concionibus excerptas, atque certam in formam per Notarios redactas. Fuit quidam cucullio ac nebulo Carmelita, Petrus Stokyfeus, cuius præcipuè opera id factum est, ut sunt homines improbi, eáque vitæ monasticæ disciplina ita pravi, ut ad huiusmodi odiorum, dissidiorum, motuúmque incendia excitanda & augenda nati esse videantur: in cæteris homines inertes, ignavi, inepti, ac plane inutiles. Evenit autem anno M. C C C. L X X X I I, ut Nicolao Herfordo in cœmiterio Frides-widæ, in ipso Ascensionis festo die ad populum esset concionandum. Hic iterum nova certamina in Herfordum excitantur, criminaque intentantur, quòd is wiclevum, ut virum bonum, fidelem, piùmque defendisset. Dies etiam corporis Christi, ut vocant, advenerat: quo die Repyngtoni concio summis fidelium studijs expectabatur. Hic canonicus erat Licestrefis, eò iam progressus in theologia, ut ad primos doctoratus gradus provectus esset, reliqua eius studij insignia ornamentaque expectans.Quo quidem tempore concionem ad Braclefes quandam habuit, propter quam in grauem Pharisæorum suspicionē offensionémque incurrerat.Sed cùm summa esset ingenij suavitate, morúmque atque orationis comitate & moderatione, animos hominum sibi infensos ita vel vicit vel mitigavit, ut summa illa insignia docthoratus, honorésque propositos, cùm maxima omnium approbatione adeptus fuerit. Cùm verò id quod voluerat ac vehementer expectarat, consecutus fuisset, in suscepta huiusmodi persona fabulâ acturus[?] tali actione non indignam, tandem prodijt, ac bene cœlatû dissimulatúmque ingenium prodidit, testificans se wiclevum defensurum in iis quidem omnibus quæ ad rationem morum pertinerent. : in doctrina verò & quæstione quæ de Sacramento haberetur, ne verbum quidem ullum fasturum[?], quò ad Deus Ecclesiasticorum animos illuminasset. tamen monachi ac sacerdotes egerunt cū Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi, ut eo ipso die & hora qua concio habenda erat, conclusiones wiclevi privatim antea condemnatæ, in publico conventu consessúque totius Vniver [?]sitatis proponeretur, summaque infamia notarentur. Astutè quidem & callidè: si tamen ulla esset hominum calliditas & prudentia, quae aliquid aduersus consilium Domini valeret. Ut breui dicam, negotium datum est Petro Stokysco, qui unus monachorum erat primarius miles, & quasi signifer, in cuius animo non minus erat audaciae, quàm in fronte atque ore impudentiae: simulque datae sunt literae ad Cancellarium, ut is pro sua authoritate potestateque, monacho impudentissimo atque audacissimo in publicandis conclusionibus adesset. Cancellarius eo tempore erat Robertus Riggæus, qui occulte quidè, sed tamen studiosè omnia agebat, quibus Euangelium in aliquam Ecclesiae cognitionem ac suam possessionem venire posset. Itaque is acceptis Archiepiscopi literis, simulque intellecto Carmelitae consilio, non minus perniciosō Ecclesiae quàm improbo, maiorem in modum est animo in fraterculum commotus, atque exacerbatus pergrauiter, de eo ciúsque similibus conquerens, merito quidem & iure optimo, ut quos omnem Vniuersitatis statum perturbare, omniaque tum studia tum etiam privilegia labefactare diceret, affirmans nec quidem ipsos Episcopos, neque Archiepiscopum, ne in causa quidem haeresis ac religionis potestatem ullam habiturum. Postremò, capto cum procuratoribus ac ceteris consilio, aperte nec dissimulanter testificatus est, se Carmelitae nullo modo ea in re affuturum. Quid opus est longa oratione? Repyngtonus ad concionandum suggestum conscendit: ubi inter alia hoc acerbius exceptum notatúmque, quòd affirmasset, pro Regibus ac Principibus similibus preces prius adhibendas esse, quàm pro Pontifice atque Episcopis: eósque iis in hoc genere commendationis atque precationis esse praeferendos. Deinde quòd Dux Lancastriae singulari esset in hanc causam studio ac voluntate, vellétque suam in clientelam tutelámque eos recipere, quos ab ea disciplina non alienos habere animos intellexisset. Dixit praeterea quaedam alia, quae ad wicleui laudem ac defensionem pertinebant.
units.tr: Something has been said above about Hereford and Repingdon. Now this place requires that we take up and pursue the history of these men again, with that brevity which both the time and the plan of this book demand. Hereford, then, having for a long time favoured Wycliffe, and having followed his cause and doctrine with the best and most constant zeal, began to fall under suspicion of this friendship by his enemies. And when he professed some things more openly and freely in his sermons which pertained to the defence of Wycliffe, the Carmelites and the monks of the other orders, provoked in spirit, brought many charges of heresy against him, extracted from his sermons and reduced into a set form by notaries. There was a certain hooded rogue and scoundrel, a Carmelite named Peter Stokes, by whose work above all this was done. Such men are wicked, and so corrupt in that discipline of monastic life, that they seem born to kindle and increase the fires of such hatreds, quarrels, and disturbances, while in other respects they are idle, lazy, inept, and altogether useless. It happened, in the year 1382, that Nicholas Hereford was to preach to the people in the churchyard of St Frideswide's, on the very feast day of the Ascension. Here again new contests were stirred up against Hereford, and charges were brought against him because he had defended Wycliffe as a good, faithful, and pious man. The day of what they call the feast of Corpus Christi had also arrived, on which day Repingdon's sermon was awaited with the highest eagerness by the faithful. He was a canon of Leicester, and had by then advanced so far in theology that he had reached the first degrees of doctorate, looking forward to the other distinctions and honours of his study. At that time he gave a sermon at Braclefes, on account of which he had incurred a grave suspicion and offence among the Pharisees. But since he had the greatest gentleness of nature, and courtesy and moderation of manner and speech, he so either conquered or softened the hostile minds of men that he obtained, with the greatest approval of all, those highest distinctions of the doctorate and the honours set before him. When, however, he had obtained what he had wished for and eagerly awaited, he finally came forward, about to act a part, in the character he had taken up, and with a performance not unworthy of it, and he revealed a nature well concealed and dissembled, declaring that he would defend Wycliffe in all those matters which pertained to the conduct of life, but that in doctrine and in the question which was raised concerning the Sacrament he would not utter a single word, until God should have enlightened the minds of the churchmen. Nevertheless the monks and priests dealt with the Archbishop of Canterbury, so that on that very day and at the hour when the sermon was to be given, the conclusions of Wycliffe, previously condemned in private, should be put forward in a public assembly and session of the whole University, and that they might be marked with the greatest infamy. This was done craftily and cunningly, but if there were any human cunning or prudence able to prevail against the counsel of the Lord. To put it briefly, the business was committed to Peter Stokes, who was the chief soldier of the monks and, as it were, their standard-bearer, a man in whose mind there was no less audacity than impudence in his brow and face. At the same time letters were sent to the Chancellor, so that he, by his authority and power, should attend upon this most impudent and audacious monk in publishing the conclusions. The Chancellor at that time was Robert Rygge, who, though secretly, yet zealously, did everything by which the Gospel might come into some recognition and possession of the Church. Accordingly he, having received the Archbishop's letters, and at the same time understanding the Carmelite's plan, no less harmful to the Church than wicked, was moved and provoked in his mind far more against the little friar, and complained very gravely about him and men like him, and rightly and with the best justice, as men who, he said, troubled the whole state of the University and weakened all its studies and privileges alike, affirming that not even the bishops themselves, nor the Archbishop, would have any power in a case of heresy or religion. Finally, having taken counsel with the proctors and the others, he openly and without dissimulation declared that he would in no way assist the Carmelite in this matter. Why need I say more at length? Repingdon mounted the platform to preach. There, among other things, this was taken very bitterly and noted: that he had said that prayers should be offered first for kings and princes, and similarly, before the Pope and bishops, and that these should be preferred to them in this kind of commendation and supplication. Next, because the Duke of Lancaster had a singular zeal and goodwill for this cause, and wished to take into his clientage and protection those whom he understood to have minds not alien to that discipline. He said besides certain other things which pertained to the praise and defence of Wycliffe.

units.la: Hac habita concione, Repyng-tonus se in templū Fridef-widae recepit, amicis quibusdam stipatus, quos inimici sub vestibus armatos esse suspicabantur & criminabantur. Carmelita, miles strenuus, verbera metuens non ausus est prodire: seque intra templi asylum continuit. Cancellarius & Repyngtonus dimissa cocione, placide ac quiete sine ullo tumultu se domum suam receperunt. Permulti in tota Universitate ea concione maximopere laetati sunt. Interea Carmelita, homo turbulentus ac seditiosus, quiescere non poterat: sed illico quae erant gesta singula Archiepiscopo diligenter accurateque exposuit, sua pericula exaggerans commemorauit, opem ac fidem Archiepiscopi implorauit: nihil denique praetermisit, quod ad animum illius Praesulis per se satis accensum, magis adhuc inflammandum pertinere videretur. Triduo post, Carmelita quū id quod voluisset impetrasset, prodiit quasi quidam gladiator, minas & hæreses intentans: proposuit venire in scholas, probareque Papam atque Episcopos in precibus ad Deum adhibendis commendatiores potioresque quam Principes ac Reges esse oportere. Sed dum hæc ageret, summa cum irrisione, acceptis literis Londinū ad Archiepiscopum suum profectus est. Nec mora interposita sequitur Cancellarius cū Bryt-wello, purgaturus se aduersus ea crimina, quæ sciebat monachum ad Archiepiscopum aut iam detulisse aut delaturū esse. ibi cum essent interrogati de conclusionibus damnatis, victi consenserunt, iureque codemnatas fuisse responderunt. Cancellarius vero accusatus de contemptu literarum quæ ad ipsum missæ fuerant, cum nihil haberet quod ad defensionem afferre posset, ita destitutus & abiectus genua in terra posuit, veniamque supplex postulavit. eam quemadmodum impetrarant, superuacaneum esse hic referre.
units.tr: After the sermon had been given, Repingdon withdrew into the church of St Frideswide, surrounded by certain friends, whom his enemies suspected and accused of being armed under their clothes. The Carmelite, a valiant soldier, fearing blows, did not dare come forth, and kept himself within the sanctuary of the church. The Chancellor and Repingdon, the sermon being ended, withdrew peacefully and quietly to their homes without any tumult. Very many throughout the whole University rejoiced greatly at that sermon. Meanwhile the Carmelite, a turbulent and seditious man, could not keep quiet: but at once he set out before the Archbishop, carefully and accurately, each thing that had been done, magnified his own dangers, recounted them, and implored the Archbishop's help and protection. In short he omitted nothing which seemed likely to inflame still further the mind of that prelate, already sufficiently fired. Three days later, the Carmelite, having obtained what he had wished, came forth like a certain gladiator, threatening and bringing charges of heresy: he proposed to come into the schools and to prove that the Pope and bishops ought to be more commended and more powerful in the prayers offered to God than princes and kings. But while he was doing this, to the great derision of all, he set out for London with letters to his Archbishop. Without delay the Chancellor followed with Brytwell, to clear himself of those charges which he knew the monk had either already laid or was about to lay before the Archbishop. There, when they were questioned about the condemned conclusions, they, being overcome, agreed and answered that they had been justly condemned. But the Chancellor, accused of contempt of the letters which had been sent to him, having nothing that he could bring in his defence, so abandoned and cast down, placed his knees on the ground and humbly begged pardon. How he obtained it, as it was granted, it is superfluous to relate here.

units.la: Herfordus & Repyngtonus sine ulla dilatione ilico excommunicati, ad Ducem Lancastriæ, ut ad præsidiū salutisque perfugium se contulerunt. Tum ibi ministri Pontificis, serpentes ad calcancum Christi persequendum venenati semperque parati, præsto fuerunt ut omne misericordiæ perfugium tollerent. Quibus quidem Dux initio satis se difficilem, atque ab eorum postulatione alienum auersumque præbuit. Postea vero victus Pontificiorum importunitate, eos destituit qui ad ipsius fidem atque opem confugissent. qui in carcere coniecti multas & graues molestias sunt perpessi: ac deinde carcere emissi ac liberati, ad honores etiā ecclesiasticos euecti, varietatem animi atque iudicii Euangelio indigna declararunt. Nos autem hæc de his tribus commemorare voluimus: non ut constantiam eorum ac firmitudinem in fide offenderemus, sed potius vt omnibus demōstraremus quàm inexplebilis & crudelis cupiditas fundēdi innocentis sanguinis iampridē solet esse in co hominū genere, qui veritatē nullo Ecclesiæ loco cōsistere pati possunt. Sed, vt ait Livius, veritas laborare potest, opprimi tamen nunquam poterit. Quantumuis affligatur hominum iniuria & iniquitate, victrix tamen virtute eius qui ipsius aut hoc est, omnia hominum mendacia, difficultates periculaque superabit. Non facile fieri potest vt colligatur omnia Mapy-[?] rū exempla, actaque eorū qui in omnibus prope mundi regionibus sanguine suo profuderunt vt veritatem tuerentur, neque ea amplecterentur quae iniustè ab hominibus & auaris & ambitiosis in Ecclesia sunt constituta, & violeter Christianis impositā. Quidam eorum fraudulēter circumuenti fuerunt, alij coniecti in carcerem, alij torti publicè & excruciati, permulti in carceribus extincti sunt faméque necati, aut alio quodā mortis genere affecti, intra occultos parietes interierunt. Quis verò vlla oratione complecti posset infinitum prope numerum eorum, qui supplicia publicè constituta sunt perpessi: & aut varietatem atque acerbitatem tormentorum, aut crudelitatem ac sævitiam tyrannorum carnificūmque scribendo aut dicendo assequi? In hac tamen tanta tormentorum magnitudine, multitudine ac varietate, istud quidem vere dici potest, omnes prope Papas, qui Romæ dominatum occuparunt, eodem animi odiúque furore in fideles atque innocentes seruos Dei affectos incitatósque fuisse. Eadem fuit ratio eorum omnium & persequendi & condemnandi, extinguendiqué eos qui ad ipsorum impietatem ac libidinem se accommodare noluerunt. Neque verò id mirum videri debet, quum vno spiritu impulsi atque innatati [?], in Christum membráque eius & Euangelium semper conspirauerint, atque omnem animi immicissimi infestissimiqué impetum contulerint. Is autem spiritus est Diaboli, qui iam inde ab initio mundi homicida & pater mendacij, furiosus gloriæ Dei inimicus, omnis author iniquitatis, dolorum ac fraudum fabricator, effectórque omnis abominationis atque impietatis extitit.
units.tr: Herford and Repyngton were at once excommunicated without any delay, and they took refuge with the Duke of Lancaster, seeking protection and a place of safety. Then the ministers of the Pope, venomous serpents always ready to attack the heel of Christ, were present there to remove every refuge of mercy. At first the Duke showed himself quite unwilling to grant their request and turned away from it. Afterwards, however, he was overcome by the importunity of the Papists and abandoned those who had fled to his trust and help. They were thrown into prison and suffered many grave hardships. Later they were released from prison and raised even to ecclesiastical honours, and by this they showed a change of mind and of judgement unworthy of the Gospel. We have wished to mention these three men here, not to give offence to their constancy and firmness in the faith, but rather to show everyone how insatiable and cruel is the lust for shedding innocent blood, which has long been typical of that class of men who cannot bear the truth to stand in any place in the Church. But, as Livy says, truth may be oppressed, yet it can never be crushed. However much it is afflicted by the injustice and iniquity of men, it will still prevail through the power of him who is the truth itself, and it will overcome all the lies, difficulties and dangers of men. It is not easy to gather all the examples of the martyrs and the acts of those who in almost every region of the world poured out their blood to defend the truth, and who would not embrace those things which were unjustly imposed on the Christians in the Church by greedy and ambitious men. Some of them were craftily entrapped, others thrown into prison, others publicly tortured and racked, very many died in prisons, starved to death, or were put to some other kind of death and perished behind closed walls. Who could in any speech embrace the almost infinite number of those who suffered punishments publicly ordained, or could by writing or speaking convey the variety and bitterness of the torments, or the cruelty and savagery of the tyrants and executioners? Yet amid this great magnitude, multitude and variety of torments, this much can truly be said: almost all the Popes who seized dominion at Rome were stirred and incited with the same mind, hatred and frenzy against the faithful and innocent servants of God. The method of all of them, both of persecuting and condemning, and of extinguishing those who would not accommodate themselves to their impiety and lust, was one and the same. Nor ought this to seem strange, since they have always conspired against Christ, his members and the Gospel, moved by one spirit, and have directed every impulse of a most hostile and most savage mind against them. And this spirit is the spirit of the Devil, who from the beginning of the world has been a murderer and the father of lies, a furious enemy of the glory of God, the author of all iniquity, the fabricator of sorrows and frauds, and the producer of every abomination and impiety.

units.la: Paulò post in hoc libro proditum literis reperietur, cætum & quadraginta homines Narbonæ crudeliter cruciatos fuisse, qui malucrunt vim ignis constanter perpeti, quàm ea amplecti, quæ à Romanis Pontifificibus professa, & præter omnem veritatem verbi Dei tradita, cis credenda obseruandaque offerebantur. Illud etiam extat scriptum in quibusdam aliis monumentis, anno M. CC. X. Lutetiæ Parisiorum vgintiquatuor Matyres ac testes, eadem de causa supplicio affectos extinctosque fuisse. Deinde anno sequenti, quadringentos homines eadem in urbe crematos atque vstulatos, præclarum fidei suæ in Christü, ac veræ pietatis testimonium dedisse. Alios vero octoginta extitisse, quibus ob eandem causam religionis, & constantem confessionem, caput amputatum fuit.
units.tr: Shortly after, it will be found recorded in writing in this book that a hundred and forty men were cruelly tortured at Narbonne, who preferred to endure the force of fire constantly rather than embrace those things which were professed by the Roman Pontiffs and handed down beyond all truth of the Word of God, and which were offered to them to be believed and observed. It is also written in certain other records that in the year 1210, twenty-four martyrs and witnesses were put to death and killed at Paris for the same cause. Then in the following year, four hundred men were burned and consumed by fire in the same city, giving a notable testimony of their faith in Christ and of true piety. Others, eighty in number, had their heads cut off for the same cause of religion and for their steadfast confession.

units.la: Ex eo piorū ac fidelium numero, Principem Armerici suspensū[?] fuisse laqueoque suffocatum: Dominam vero Castri, lapidibus obrutam.
units.tr: From that number of pious and faithful people, a Prince of Armerici was hanged and suffocated by a noose, and a lady of the castle was crushed under stones.

units.la: Beghardus in crime[?] hæresis vocatus, Erphurdiæ in Germania crematus fuit, anno M. C C. X V I I I. Quatuor annis post, Oxoniæ in Anglia, Diaconus quidam idem ignis supplicium & tormetum passus est. Cantipratensis historicus author est, in Cameracensi regione Dominicanos quoque huiusmodi vim ignis cruciatuque in eos explicuisse, quos in suspicione hæresis vocauerat. Quod si memoria ætasque remotior & antiquior est repeteda[?], cognoscetur anno M. C. L X X X X I I. multos in Gallia propter eandem suspicionem combustos fuisse, quorum quidam Publicani, alij Cathari, aliqui Paterini, alij aliorum nominum infamia notabantur, atque in summam hominum inuidiam & offensionem adducebantur. Nec multum wicleui tempora præcessit Richardus Dominicanus, quem Heidelbergæ prauæ impiæque opinionis damnatu, certissimi scriptores tradiderunt, anno M. C C C. X X X. Iidem etiam authores sunt, Ioanne in Anglia regnante, Albigenses vsitatum ignis supplicium perpessos esse. Ioannes Bacon memorat anno M. C C C. V I. Eremitam quendam ab eodem hominum genere appetitum vexatumque fuisse, quod in publicis concionibus affirmaret, Sacramenta quæ tum vsurpabantur in Ecclesia, nō esse ea quæ à Christo instituta fuissent.
units.tr: A Beghard, accused of heresy, was burned at Erfurt in Germany in the year 1218. Four years later, at Oxford in England, a certain deacon suffered the same punishment and torment of fire. The historian Thomas of Cantimpré is the authority that in the region of Cambrai the Dominicans also inflicted this kind of force of fire and torment on those whom they had accused of suspicion of heresy. And if the memory of a more remote and older age is to be recalled, it will be found that in the year 1182 many were burned in France for the same suspicion, some of whom were marked with the infamy of the Publicans, others of the Cathars, some of the Patarines, others with the infamy of other names, and they were brought into great hatred and offence among men. Not long before the time of Wycliffe, Richard the Dominican, whom certain most reliable writers report was condemned at Heidelberg for a depraved and impious opinion, in the year 1330. The same authors also state that under King John in England, the Albigenses suffered the customary punishment of fire. John Bacon records that in the year 1306 a certain hermit was attacked and harassed by the same class of men, because he affirmed in public sermons that the sacraments which were then used in the Church were not those which had been instituted by Christ.

units.la: Sed vt ad tepora wicleui redeamus, nō aliena huic historiæ videtur esse memoria Ioannis Aston Oxoniensis, hominis eleganter eruditi, qui in causa & doctrina Sacramenti ab Archiepiscopo Catuariensi, vt hæreticus condemnatus, atque in carcerem coiectus est, ibique inclusus interijsse[?] dicitur.
units.tr: But to return to the times of Wycliffe, the memory of John Aston of Oxford, a man elegantly learned, does not seem foreign to this history. He was condemned as a heretic by the Archbishop of Canterbury in the cause and doctrine of the sacrament, and was cast into prison, and is said to have died there, shut up.

units.la: Ab eo anno M. CCCC. omnes persecutiones, quae jandiu viget in Ecclesia, principium duxerunt, praecipuamque vim maximarum oppressionum & confusionum acceperunt. Anno sequenti, qui fuit M. CCCCI, & XIII. post mortem wicleui, eo tempore quo Henricus IIII. in Anglia regnabat, Lodini in summa curia factum est edictum, quo omnes ij comprehenderentur qui disciplinam wicleui sectarentur, aut aliquo studio fauoreque prosequerentur. Eos autem vulgo Lolardos appellabant. Quod si qui eius doctrinā obstinatius amplexi, retinuissent, ut hi primū Episcopis, deinde Iudicibus civilibus traderētur, morteque afficerentur. Eodem anno quidā sacerdos, quod edicto non paruissēt, comprehensus fuit, & in circo Smithfildensi in frequentissimo hominum coentu ustulatus. Sed historia quæ mox sequitur, inprimis digna videtur quæ memoretur, & ab omnibus cognoscatur. Nam anno M. CCCCX. fuit quidā laici ordinis opifex, qui gravissimū ignis supplicium admirabili constantia est perpessus. Is hanc fidei sententiā tuebatur, Corpus Christi, quod in Ecclesia Cœnaque offertur, ratione magis Sacramenti signique admonitorij ibi esse, quam ulla loci circumscriptione, aut ratione naturalis corporis. Neque vero unquam à suscepta opinione, vel potius certissima cognitione ac persuasione in eius animo facta Divinitus, ullis minis aut blanditijs abduci unquam potuit: sed constanter genus mortis ac supplicij acerbissimum perferre maluit, quam turpiter deserere patrocinium veritatis, testimoniumque ei suum denegare. Hoc modo permanens in sua sententia, Magistratui, quem brachium vocant seculare, per Episcopos traditus fuit. Sententia condemnationis ipsius pronuntiata, ut dolio inclusus, lento igne paulatim cremaretur, in forum suburbanum deductus est: neque ea supplicij acerbitate territus animum unquam abiecit, sed infractu adversus omnes terrores retinuit. Aderat filius regis Henrici natu primus, eius supplicij tā tristis & acerbi spectator, qui maiore permotus misericordia quam Episcopi qui illum crudelissime persequebantur, propius accessit, monuitque humaniter ut suæ rationem vitæ haberet, atque opiniones illas deponeret: nihil denique prætermisit, quo animum eius nō minaciter acerbeque infringere, sed humaniter ac blandè posset inflectere atque ad aliquam opinionis veritatem traducere, ut vitam illi conseruaret. Sed strenuus miles Jesu Christi, omnes blanditias atque illecebras principis humanissimi fortiter repulit, huiusmodique hominũ periculosas tentationes superauit, paratus quiduis potius perpeti, quàm in eam delabi impietatem, ut aliquid à veritate alienum contra conscientiam suâ confiteretur. Itaque intruditur in dolium. quem ita indusum simulatque flãma ignis omni ex parte dolii cœpit inuadere, horrendum miserandumque in modum exclamabat. Hoc tam horribili clamore commotus Regis filius, ad hominem ita miserabiliter afflictu cruciatumque iterum accessit, ut si posset, eum ad aliquam suipsius misericordiam atque vitam revocaret. Jussit ignis materiam semoveri subito, flammamque accensam opprimi atque extingui. atque ita propius accedens, miserum consolatur hominem, promittens illi incolumitatẽ vitæ, si ipsius consilia monitaque audire vellet: atque etiam liberaliter adiumxit, se Regio ex proventu tantum pecuniæ ei curaturum, quantum ad victum quotidianum in reliquum vitæ tempus satis esset.Rursum egregius hic miles domini nostri Jesu Christi, eam summâ Principis oblatam liberalitatem est aspernatus, gratiam & authoritatem summi sui Regis ac Principis domini nostri Jesu Christi omnibus huius præsentis vitæ beneficiis præferens: neque vero minus ardens in animo Dei amore, quàm externo ignis ardore eius corpus inuadente & consumente. Tum princeps cùm videret illum in suâ opinione obfirmatum, jussit eũ iterum dolio imponi & includi, sine ulla spe gratiæ veni æque amplius recuperandæ. Sed quemadmodum nulla præmia & commoda eius animũ in amore Christi confirmatum inflectere potuerunt, atque ad fallacem huius vitæ amorem conuertere, ita nec ulla tormenta & corporis cruciamenta infregerunt ac deterruerunt, quominus id quod verissimum esse sentiebat, omni studio periculo vitæ tueretur. Ita verum est quod ait divus Paulus, nullam esse affectionum ac tentationum tantam magnitudinem, nullam vim potestatemque cœlestem, terrestrem, infernalem, quæ fideles electosque Dei ab amore & charitate Christi possit divellere.
units.tr: From that year, 1400, all the persecutions which have long flourished in the Church took their beginning, and they received the chief force of the greatest oppressions and confusions. In the following year, which was 1401, and the thirteenth after the death of Wycliffe, at the time when Henry IV reigned in England, an edict was issued at London in the highest court, by which all those were to be seized who followed the teaching of Wycliffe or favoured and supported it in any way. They were commonly called Lollards. And if any who embraced his doctrine more obstinately should persist in it, they were first to be handed over to the bishops and then to the civil judges, and put to death. In the same year a certain priest, because he had not obeyed the edict, was seized and burned in Smithfield, in the crowded gathering of men. But the history that follows soon is especially worthy to be recorded and known by all. For in the year 1410 there was a certain craftsman of the lay order, who endured the most grievous punishment of fire with admirable constancy. He maintained this confession of faith: that the body of Christ, which is offered in the Church and at the Supper, is there rather by way of the sacrament and a sign which admonishes, than by any circumscription of place or by the manner of a natural body. Nor could he ever be drawn away by threats or flatteries from the opinion he had taken up, or rather from the most certain knowledge and persuasion divinely made in his mind; but he preferred steadfastly to endure the most bitter kind of death and punishment rather than shamefully desert the defence of the truth and deny his testimony to it. Remaining in this opinion, he was handed over by the bishops to the magistrate, whom they call the secular arm. When the sentence of condemnation had been pronounced against him, that he should be put inside a barrel and slowly burned by a gentle fire, he was led to the suburban field; and terrified by neither the bitterness of the punishment, he never gave up his spirit, but held firm against all terrors. The eldest son of King Henry was present, a witness to this so sad and bitter punishment, who, moved by greater pity than the bishops who most cruelly persecuted him, drew nearer and kindly advised him to take care of his life and to abandon those opinions. In short, he left nothing undone by which he might bend his mind, not harshly and bitterly, but gently and softly, and lead it to some acknowledgement of the truth of the opinion, so as to preserve his life. But the valiant soldier of Jesus Christ bravely repulsed all the flatteries and allurements of the most gracious prince, and overcame such perilous temptations of men, being ready to suffer anything rather than fall into that impiety of confessing something contrary to the truth and against his conscience. So he was put into the barrel. As soon as the flame of fire began to attack the barrel on every side, he cried out in a dreadful and pitiful manner. Moved by this most horrible cry, the king's son drew near again to the man so miserably afflicted and tormented, that if he could, he might call him back to some mercy towards himself and to life. He ordered the fuel of the fire to be suddenly removed and the kindled flame to be smothered and put out. And so, coming closer, he comforted the wretched man, promising him the safety of his life if he would be willing to hear his counsels and admonitions; and he also generously added that he would provide from the royal revenue as much money for him as would be enough for his daily food for the rest of his life. Again this outstanding soldier of our Lord Jesus Christ scorned the generosity offered by the prince, placing the grace and authority of his supreme King and Prince, our Lord Jesus Christ, above all the benefits of this present life; and no less ardent in his mind with the love of God than the external heat of the fire attacking and consuming his body. Then the prince, seeing him fixed firmly in his opinion, ordered him to be put back into the barrel and shut up, without any hope of recovering grace or favour any more. But just as no rewards or advantages could bend his mind, confirmed in the love of Christ, and turn it to the deceitful love of this life, so neither did any torments or bodily tortures break him or deter him from defending with all zeal, even at the peril of his life, what he judged to be most true. Thus it is true what the divine Paul says, that there is no magnitude of affections and temptations, no heavenly, earthly or infernal power, which can tear the faithful and the elect of God from the love and charity of Christ.

units.la: Papa omnesque eius administri putabant se effecisse, ut illa exigua veritatis scintilla, quam Deus in Anglia per Joannem wicleuum accenderat, planè effet oppressa atque extincta: sed prouidentia diuina rem contrariam in partem rationémque deduxit, atque opinionem impiorum hominum maximopere fefellit. Nam primam illam atque exiguam Euangelij lucem ita excitauit & auxit, vt co ex regno postea in totum terrarum orbem diffuderit: atque ita mundum teterrimis tenebris oppressum, hoc tam salutaris cognitionis lumine accenso illustrarit.Res autem hac ratione acta est: Quidā erat scholasticus in Oxoniensi Vniuersitate, ex nobili Bohemiæ familia, nomine Piscis-putris appellatus. Is libros wicleui inscriptos De Vniuersalibus, casu quodam natus est, quibus adeo est delectatus, vt eorū descripta exempla secū in patriā reuertens, quasi pretiosissimū thesaurum deportarit. hos autem libros duntaxat cōmodauit Bohemis, studiosis hominibus, alienis tunc à Germanis, quòd hi scholæ academiaeque Pragensi cum maximo Bohemorum dolore præerant. Ex omnibus scholasticis studiosisque hominibus, qui in ea Vniuersitate tunc florebant, Joannes quidam summa erat existimatione, tametsi loco obscuro natus esset, ex quodam pago qui Hus, id est Anser, dicebatur, à quo cognomen ille accepit. Hic igitur Joannes Hus,cum esset acri acutóque ingenio summáque facundia, doctrinam wicleui omni studio complexus, ita cœpit Germanos in disputationibus agitare ac vexare, vt, qui principatum quendam & dominatum in ea academia obtinebant, victi pudore locum facilè concesserint: cum præsertim ij qui erant ex ipso Bohemiæ regno, à rege wenceslao impetrassent, vt Vniuersitas Pragensis ad formam rationémque Parisiensis instituerctur ac regeretur.
units.tr: The Pope and all his ministers thought they had so completely suppressed and extinguished that small spark of truth which God had kindled in England through John Wycliffe. But divine providence turned the matter the other way and confounded the opinion of impious men to the greatest degree. For it so stirred up and increased that first small light of the Gospel that it afterwards spread from that kingdom through the whole circuit of the earth, and so, with this light of saving knowledge kindled, it illuminated a world oppressed by the darkest shadows. The matter happened in this way. There was a scholar at the University of Oxford, of a noble Bohemian family, called Piscis-putris. By some chance he obtained the books of Wycliffe entitled On Universals, with which he was so delighted that, returning to his homeland with copies of them, he carried them back as if they were a most precious treasure. He lent these books only to Bohemian students, who were then estranged from the Germans, because the Germans presided over the school and university of Prague to the great grief of the Bohemians. Among all the scholars and students who then flourished in that university, there was a certain John, held in the highest esteem, although he was born in an obscure place, in a village called Hus, that is, Goose, from which he took his surname. This John Hus, since he had a keen and sharp intellect and great eloquence, embraced the doctrine of Wycliffe with all zeal, and began to harass and vex the Germans in disputations, so that those who held a certain leadership and dominion in that university, beaten and ashamed, easily yielded their place. This was especially so because those who came from the kingdom of Bohemia itself had obtained from King Wenceslaus that the University of Prague should be established and governed on the model and plan of the University of Paris.

units.la: Ea autem res Germanos à gubernatione rectioneque studiorum demouit. Itaque ea rerum commutatione offensi Germani, cum se mutuo iureiurando obstrinxissent, plures duobus millibus uno eodémque die Praga discesserunt, & Lipsiam, quæ urbs est Misniæ, à Praga trium dierum itinere remota, sedem studiorum suorum domiciliúmque transtulerunt. Bohemi autem postea gymnasii disciplinam pro suo judicio atque arbitrio constituerunt & gubernarunt: ex quibus Joannes Hus omnibus facilè præstabat, cùm doctrina & eloquentia tum verò vitæ sanctitate atque honestate commendatus. qui quidem hanc non mediocrem adeptus existimationem atque authoritatem, cœpit in lucem proferre quod de veritate animo suo pie sentiebat. Fuit quidā ciuis Pragenfis, qui templum præclarum magnificumque extruxerat, nomine S. Matthæi Mathiæque nuncupatum, quod Beth-lehem appellabat. In eo etiam prouentus reliquit, ad alendos tuendosque duos concionatores necessarios, vt hi lingua vernacula apud populum diebus tum festis tum etiam cæteris concionarentur.
units.tr: This matter removed the Germans from the governance and direction of the studies. Therefore, offended by this change of affairs, the Germans bound themselves together by oath, and more than two thousand of them left Prague on one and the same day, and transferred the seat of their studies and their dwelling to Leipzig, a city of Meissen, three days' journey from Prague. The Bohemians afterwards arranged and governed the discipline of the school according to their own judgment and will. Among them John Hus easily surpassed all others, being commended as much for his learning and eloquence as for the holiness and integrity of his life. Having gained no small esteem and authority, he began to bring to light what he piously thought in his mind about the truth. There was a citizen of Prague who had built a splendid and magnificent church, called by the name of Saint Matthew and Matthias, which he named Bethlehem. He also left in it an endowment for maintaining and supporting two preachers, who were needed to preach to the people in the vernacular language on both festal days and other days.

units.la: Ioannes Hus vnus ex duobus delectus fuit, qui cum maximum animaduerteret populi in doctrinam suam studium, cœpit apertè prositeri, quid de libris wicleui sentiret ac iudicaret, plane affirmans in his omnem veritatem contineri: illud etiam sæpe significans, sc post obitum suum nihil magis cupere, quàm animum suum ad eum locum in quo iam wicleuus quiete beata frueretur, peruenire: tam certum de illius viri tum doctrina tum vita iudicium faciebat, atque testimonium ei apud omnes dabat. Omnes prope scholasticos sequebantur Ioannem Hus, multique alij homines non paruæ existimationis, quibus cum etiam maxima pars nobilitatis coniuncta erat: quæ fuit causa, vt Papa & ij qui Constantiæ congregati concilium habebant, eum euocauerint per Sigismundum Imperatorem, cuius interposita fide, quemadmodum postea cognoscetur, euocatus fuit.
units.tr: John Hus was one of the two chosen. When he perceived the great eagerness of the people for his teaching, he began to profess openly what he thought and judged about the books of Wycliffe, plainly affirming that all truth was contained in them. He also often declared that after his death he desired nothing more than to come to the place where Wycliffe now enjoyed blessed rest. So certain was his judgment of that man's doctrine and life, and so did he bear witness to him before everyone. Almost all the scholars followed John Hus, and many other men of no small standing, with whom also the greater part of the nobility was joined. This was the reason why the Pope and those gathered at Constance for a council summoned him through the Emperor Sigismund, under whose guaranteed faith, as will be shown later, he was summoned.

units.la: Ioannes Hus.
units.tr: John Hus.

units.la: Historiam & causam Ioannis Hus, in iudicio & foro Ecclesiasticorum versatam, quoniam omnia vt sunt acta diligenter complectitur, eo modo quo fuit scripta, cum his nostris coniunximus, neque aliquid immutare voluimus, vt melius Lectores cognoscant ea singula quæ in concilio Constantiensi acta & gesta fuerunt.
units.tr: We have joined to our own text the history and cause of John Hus, as it was handled in the court and forum of the ecclesiastics, since it sets out everything fully as it was actually done; we have not wished to alter anything, so that readers may better learn each detail of what was done and transacted at the Council of Constance.

units.la: Oannes Hus, quum officio concionatoris fungeretur Pragæ in templo Beth-lehem, ac Christi Euangelium potius quàm humanas Pontificum traditiones docere instituisset, suborti sunt nonnulli, qui eum ad Ioannem eius nominis XXIII. Pontificem Romanum, tanquam hæreticum detulerunt. Pontifex ipse rem omnem Cardinali de Columna commisit: qui audita accusatione diem dixit Joanni Hus, qua in curia Romana sisteretur. Quo facto, wenceslaus Romanorum & Bohemiæ Rex, flagitante etiam id primùm conjuge sua Sophia, deinde universa nobilitate Bohemiæ, quibus accesserunt preces totius urbis & universitatis Pragensis, legatos suos Romam misit, qui peterent à Pontifice ut hoc judicio Joannem Hus liberaret: invidiosè enim per quosdam malevolos accusatum esse, neque posse cum propter insidias sine periculo Romam proficisci.
units.tr: John Hus, while he held the office of preacher at Prague in the church of Bethlehem, had begun to teach the Gospel of Christ rather than human traditions of the Pontiffs. Some men arose who denounced him to John XXIII, the Roman Pontiff, as a heretic. The Pontiff himself committed the whole matter to Cardinal de Columna, who, having heard the accusation, appointed a day for John Hus to appear before the Roman court. Thereupon Wenceslaus, King of the Romans and of Bohemia, at the urging first of his wife Sophia, then of the whole nobility of Bohemia, and also of the prayers of the entire city and university of Prague, sent envoys to Rome to ask the Pontiff to free John Hus from this trial, since he had been accused spitefully by certain ill-wishers, and could not travel to Rome without danger because of plots against him.

units.la: Ipse quoque Joannes Hus, ante diem sibi constitutum missis legitimis & idoneis procuratoribus in curiam Romanam, firmissimis rationibus innocentiam suam probavit, qua fretus existimavit se facilè consecuturum, ne coràm adesse propter periculum ad dictum sibi diem cogeretur. Sed cùm Cardinalis de Columna cuius unius judicio & dijudicatione res tota permissa erat, nullam defensionem admittere vellet, procuratores Joannis Hus ad ipsum summum Pontificem provocarunt. Quanquam ne hoc quidem ultimum refugium tantùm apud Cardinalem de Columna valuit, quin Joannem Hus, cùm Romam ad diem sibi constitutum non venisset, tanquam contumacem hæreticum, publicè excommunicatum pronuntiaret.
units.tr: John Hus himself, before the day appointed for him, sent lawful and suitable proctors to the Roman court, and by very firm arguments proved his innocence. Relying on this, he thought he would easily obtain that he not be compelled to appear in person on the day set, because of the danger. But since Cardinal de Columna, to whose judgment and decision the whole affair had been entrusted alone, was unwilling to admit any defence, the proctors of John Hus appealed to the Supreme Pontiff himself. Yet even this last refuge availed so little with Cardinal de Columna that, because John Hus had not come to Rome on the appointed day, he pronounced him publicly excommunicated as a contumacious heretic.

units.la: Sed tamen cùm procuratores ad summum Pontificem provocassent, dati sunt eis alii judices, Cardinalis Aquileianus & Cardinalis Venetus cum aliis quibusdam. Qui cùm in sesquiannum usque rem extraxissent, tandem ad Cardinalis de Columna sententiam redierunt: eáque confirmata mandarunt procuratoribus Joannis Hus ut à defensione desisterent: neque enim se amplius hoc passuros esse. Itaque cùm procuratores instare non desinerent, quidam ex eis in carcerem conjecti, graviter multati sunt: reliqui infecta re in Bohemiam redierunt.
units.tr: Nevertheless, when the proctors had appealed to the Supreme Pontiff, other judges were given to them: the Cardinal of Aquileia and the Cardinal of Venice, with some others. When they had dragged the matter out for nearly a year and a half, they at last returned to the sentence of Cardinal de Columna; and, having confirmed it, they ordered the proctors of John Hus to desist from the defence, since they would not allow this any longer. So when the proctors did not cease to press the matter, some of them were thrown into prison and heavily punished, and the rest returned to Bohemia with the business undone.

units.la: Cùm itaque Constantiensis synodus, Pontificis Romani & Sigis-mundi Romanorum & Hungariæ Regis, & aliorum Regum communi consensu indicta essèt, datum est à Romanorum & Hungariæ Rege negotium nobilibus quibusdam viris Bohemis, qui Joannem Hus Constantiam adducerent, ut & se & totum regnum Bohemiæ liberaret ab ea infamia in quam propter falsæ & hæreticæ doctrinæ suspicionem incidisset. Quod ut tuto facere posset, missae sunt ei per eosdem Nobiles literae, nomine et mandato ipsius Regis et Latinae et Germanicae scriptae, quibus publica fides continebatur. Exemplum earum subscripsimus.
units.tr: Therefore, when the Council of Constance had been called by common consent of the Roman Pontiff, Sigismund, King of the Romans and of Hungary, and other kings, the King of the Romans and Hungary entrusted the task to certain noblemen of Bohemia to bring John Hus to Constance, so that he might free both himself and the whole kingdom of Bohemia from the infamy into which he had fallen through suspicion of false and heretical doctrine. That he might do this safely, letters were sent to him through the same noblemen, written in Latin and German in the name and by the command of the King himself, containing a public guarantee. We have subjoined a copy of them.

units.la: SIGISMUNDUS DEI GRATIA ROMANOrum Rex semper Augustus, & Hungariae, Dalmatiae, Croatiae, &c. Rex, universis & singulis Principibus ecclesiasticis & secularibus, Ducibus & Marchionibus, Comitibus, Baronibus, Nobilibus, Proceribus, Militaribus, Militibus, Clientibus, Capitaneis, Potestatibus, Gubernatoribus, Praesidibus, Publicanis, Officialibus, quibuscumque civitatum, oppidorum, villarum, & locorum communitatibus, ac Rectoribus eorundem, caeterisque nostris & sacri Imperii subditis & fidelibus, ad quos praesentes literae pervenerint, Gratiam regiam & omne bonum.
units.tr: SIGISMUND, BY THE GRACE OF GOD King of the Romans, ever Augustus, and King of Hungary, Dalmatia, Croatia, etc., to all and each of the ecclesiastical and secular princes, dukes and marquises, counts, barons, nobles, lords, military men, soldiers, clients, captains, magistrates, governors, presidents, tax-collectors, officials, and to whatever communities of cities, towns, villages and places, and their rulers, and to our other subjects and faithful of the holy Empire, to whom these present letters shall come: royal favour and every good.

units.la: Venerabiles, illustres, nobiles et fideles dilecti, honorabilem Magistrum Joannem Hus, sacrae theologiae B.accalaureū et artium Magistrum, praesentium ostensorem, de regno Bohemiae ad Concilium gene-rale in civitate Constantiensi celebrandum in proximo, transeunte, quem etiam in nostram et sacri Imperii protectionem recepimus et tutelam, vobis omnibus et vestrum cuilibet pleno recommendamus affectu, desiderantes quatenus ipsum cum ad vos pervenerit, grate suscipere, favorabiliter tractare, atque in his quae ad celeritatem et securitatem itineris ipsius pertinent, tam per terram quam per aquam, promotivam sibi velitis et debeatis ostendere voluntatem, nec non ipsum cum famulis, equis et aliis rebus suis singulis, per quoscunque passus, portus, pontes, terras, dominia, iurisdictiones, civitates, oppida, castra, villas, et quaelibet alia loca vestra, sine ulla solutione tributi, telonii, aut alio quouis solutionis onere, omnique prorsus impedimento remoto, transire, stare, morari et redire libere permittatis sibique et suis, cum opus fuerit, de securo et saluo velitis et debeatis providere conductu, ad honorem et reverentiam nostrae maiestatis. Datum Spirae, Anno Domini M.CCCC.XIIII, die Octobris XVIII, Regnorum nostrorum Hungariae, &c. anno XXXIII, Romanorum vero V.
units.tr: Venerable, illustrious, noble and faithful beloved ones: we commend most heartily to all of you and to each of you the honourable Master John Hus, Bachelor of Sacred Theology and Master of Arts, bearer of these presents, who is travelling from the kingdom of Bohemia to the general council to be held shortly in the city of Constance, whom we have also received into our protection and guardianship and that of the holy Empire. We desire that, when he comes to you, you receive him graciously, treat him kindly, and show him your favourable goodwill in all that pertains to the speed and safety of his journey, both by land and by water; and that you allow him, with his servants, horses and all his other belongings, to pass through, stay, linger and return freely through any passes, harbours, bridges, lands, dominions, jurisdictions, cities, towns, castles, villages and any other places of yours, without any payment of toll, tax or any other burden of payment, every impediment being wholly removed; and that you be willing and bound to provide for him and his people, when need arises, with a safe and secure escort, for the honour and reverence of our majesty. Given at Speyer, in the year of the Lord 1414, on the 18th day of October, in the 33rd year of our reign in Hungary, etc., and the 5th of our reign as King of the Romans.

units.la: Quamobrem Joannes Hus, cum sua sponte tum patrocinio et tutela Imperatoris Romani fretus, Constantiam iter instituit. Sed priusquam Praga exiret, publice significavit literis Latine, Germanice et Bohemice scriptis, et foribus templorum passim affixis, de sua prosessione[?] Estione[?], vt si cui suspecta eius doctrina esset, hoc coram domino Conrado Archiepiscopo Pragensi: aut, si malit, in synodo generali proponat. ibi se doctrinæ & fidei suæ rationem redditurum.
units.tr: Therefore John Hus, relying both on his own accord and on the protection and guardianship of the Roman Emperor, set out on the journey to Constance. But before he left Prague, he made public, by letters written in Latin, German and Bohemian, and posted in various places on the doors of churches, a statement of his profession of faith, so that if anyone suspected his doctrine, he might bring it before the lord Conrad, Archbishop of Prague, or, if he preferred, propose it in the general council; there he would give an account of his doctrine and faith.

units.la: Eodem etiam tempore misit Ioannes Hus ad Nicolaum episcopum Nazaretensem, inquisitorem hæreticæ prauitatis, in ciuitate & diœcesi Pragensi, à sede Romana constitutum, cumque rogauit si quid in eo erroris comperisset, vt publicè significaret. sed idem Episcopus respondit se multa sæpius cum Ioanne Hus communicasse, neque vnquam cognouisse quicquam in eo indignum viro pio & fideli. idque suum de Ioanne Hus testimonium comprobauit suis ipsius literis, anno M.CCCC.XIIII[?]. die penultima mensis Augusti.
units.tr: At the same time John Hus also sent to Nicholas, Bishop of Nazareth, inquisitor of heretical depravity in the city and diocese of Prague, appointed by the Roman See, and asked him to make public whatever error he had found in him. But the same bishop replied that he had often communicated with John Hus on many matters, and had never known anything in him unworthy of a godly and faithful man; and he confirmed this his testimony about John Hus by his own letter, dated the penultimate day of August, in the year 1414.

units.la: Idibus Octobris eiusdem anni Ioannes Hus, comitantibus eum nobilibus dominis Wenceslao de Duba & Ioanne de Chlum, relicta Praga, iter Constantiam versus est ingressus. In ipsis ciuitatibus quas transibat, præsertim si quæ fuerant alicuius nominis, publicis literis suam præsentiam significauit, his propemodū verbis, Ioannes Hus iam pergit Constantiam, ad ostendendam ibi fidem quam hactenus tenuit, & nunc tenet, & vsque ad mortem præstante Christo domino tenebit.
units.tr: On the Ides of October of the same year, John Hus, accompanied by the noblemen Wenceslaus of Duba and John of Chlum, left Prague and entered upon the journey toward Constance. In each city through which he passed, especially those of some note, he announced his presence by public letters, in words roughly like these: "John Hus is now proceeding to Constance, to show there the faith which he has held hitherto, and now holds, and, with Christ the Lord's help, will hold until death."

units.la: & sicut antea per totum regnum Bohemiæ notum fecit suas intimationes & literas volens in conuentu generali curiæ archiepiscopalis Pragensis de sua fide rationem reddere, & ante exitum suum cuilibet aliquid sibi obiicienti satisfacere, ita & in hac solenni Imperialique ciuitate notificat, si vult aliquis errorem vel hæresim aliquam imponere, vt se ad concilium præpararet.
units.tr: And just as before, throughout the whole kingdom of Bohemia, he had made known his announcements and letters, wishing at a general assembly of the archiepiscopal court of Prague to give an account of his faith, and before his departure to satisfy anyone who objected anything to him, so now too in this solemn and imperial city he gives notice that if anyone wishes to impose any error or heresy upon him, he should prepare himself for the council.

units.la: In omnibus verò ciuitatibus, maximè verò cùm in Germaniam venisset, ingens ad eum multitudo confluxit, ab ipsis verò hospitibus per omnes Germaniæ ciuitates, à ciui-bus, & nonnunquam ab ipsis etiam parochis, summa humanitate & liberalitate acceptus est, adeò vt ipse Ioannes Hus in quadam epistola fateatur se nusquam maiores inimicitias quàm in Bohemia expertum esse. Ac si fama (vt fit) de eius aduentu præcurrerat, omnes viæ resertæ erant iis qui Ioannem Hus videre cupiebant, eique gratulari, imprimis verò Noribergæ, vbi mercatores qui præcesserant, de aduen-tu eius ipsos ciues feceran t certiores. In eadem vrbe, cùm parochi plèrique secretum cum eo colloquium postularent, respondit se malle publicè coram omnibus suam sententiam patefacere, neque enim se quicquam velle occultum habere. Ab hora igitur prandij coram ipsis sacerdotibus & senatoribus, plurimisque aliis civibus usque ad noctem magna cum admiratione omnium locutus est, solo Carthusiano quodam doctore, & parocho diui Sebaldi improbante.
units.tr: In every city, but especially when he came into Germany, a huge crowd gathered to him; and from the hosts themselves, and from the citizens throughout all the cities of Germany, and sometimes even from the parish priests, he was received with the greatest kindness and generosity, so much so that John Hus himself, in a certain letter, confesses that he had nowhere experienced greater enmities than in Bohemia. And if (as happens) the report of his coming had run ahead, all the roads were thronged with those who wished to see John Hus and congratulate him, especially at Nuremberg, where merchants who had gone ahead had informed the citizens themselves of his arrival. In that city, when many of the parish priests asked for a private conference with him, he replied that he preferred to set out his opinion publicly before everyone, for he did not wish to have anything hidden. So from the hour of dinner until night he spoke, before the priests and senators and very many other citizens, to great admiration of all, with only one Carthusian doctor and the parish priest of St. Sebald disapproving.

units.la: Die vigesima, ex quo ab urbe Pragensi discesserat, hoc est tertia die mensis Nouembris Constantiam venicus[?], ad viduam quandam optimam matronam, in vico sancti Galli diuertit. Postridie eius diei dominus Ioannes de Chlum & dominus Henricus Latzembog, ad Pontificem Romanum ingressi, primum indicarunt ei praesentiam Ioannis Hus, quem ipsi sub fide publica Romanorum Hungariæque Regis, Constantia ad generale concilium adduxissent. Rogabant deinde ut per ipsum quoque, ipsius Regis Romani gratia, Ioannes Hus absque omni periculo atque impedimento Constantiae esse posset. Quibus tum[?] Pontifex respondit, etiamsi Ioannes Hus fratrem sibi germanum occidisset, tamen se nullo modo commissurum, quantum in ipso situm crit, ut aliqua ei fiat iniuria, quandiu Constantiae esset.
units.tr: On the twentieth day after he had left the city of Prague, that is, on the third day of November, he came to Constance and lodged at the house of a certain excellent widow in St. Gall Street. The next day Lord John de Chlum and Lord Henry Latzembog went in to the Roman Pontiff. First they informed him of John Hus's presence, since they had brought him to Constance for the general council under the public safe-conduct of the Roman and Hungarian King. They then asked that, for the sake of the King of the Romans, John Hus might be allowed to stay in Constance without any danger or hindrance. To this the Pope replied that even if John Hus had killed his own brother, he would in no way, so far as lay in him, allow any injury to be done to him while he remained in Constance.

units.la: Interea summus ipsius Husij aduersarius, Magister Stephanus Paletz Bohemus, Constantiam venit, cuius socius Stanislaus, nempe de Znoima, vixdū fines Bohemiæ egressus, ex apostematis dolore mortuus est. Paletz igitur quamprimum Constantiam venisset, adiunxit se Michaeli de Causis, primo Ioannis Hus & acerrimo accusatore. Ac ne hoc omittam, Paletz ipse inde ab adolescentia sua familiarissime usus erat ipsius Ioannis Husij consuetudine. Sed cum bulla quædam Ioannis XXIII. pontificis Romani Pragam allata esset contra Ladislaum Apuliæ Regem, restitit ei bullæ Ioannes Hus, quod videret eam iniquam esse. Paletz vero, quanquam in conuiuio quodam, audiente Ioanne Hus, palam confessus esset bullam æquitati contrariam esse, tamen quia Pontifici Romano erat obnoxius propter quædam eius benefi-cia, defendit eā bullam contra Ioannem Hus. hæc fuit causa discordiæ inter eos. Alter vero ille Michael de Causis, fuerat olim parochus in noua Praga, sed ipse prædæ, nouum quoddam aucupij genus sibi excogitarat. Prae se tulerat enim se consilium reperisse, quo aurifodinæ quæ perierant, restaurari possent. Rex igitur Wenceslaus ingentem ei summam pecuniæ in manus dat, ut quod polliceretur efficeret. Ille vero bonus vir, cum paucos dies laborasset, nec quicquam efficeret, re desperata, clam se cum reliqua pecunia, ex Bohemia in Romanam curiam, dignissimus hoc nido, subduxit. His moribus, facile ab aduersarijs Ioannis Hus, pecunia se corrupi passus est, ut eis suam operam, id quod strenuè fecit, collocaret.
units.tr: Meanwhile Hus's chief adversary, Master Stephen Paletz, a Bohemian, came to Constance. His companion Stanislaus, of Znaim, died of a festering abscess just after leaving the borders of Bohemia. As soon as Paletz arrived in Constance, he attached himself to Michael de Causis, the first of Hus's accusers and his most bitter one. Nor should I leave this out: Paletz himself had been on very intimate terms with John Hus since his youth. But when a bull of Pope John XXIII against Ladislaus, King of Apulia, was brought to Prague, John Hus opposed the bull, because he saw that it was unjust. Paletz, although at a banquet, in Hus's hearing, had openly admitted that the bull was contrary to equity, nevertheless, being beholden to the Roman Pontiff for certain favours, defended that bull against John Hus. This was the cause of the quarrel between them. As for the other, Michael de Causis, he had once been parish priest in New Prague, but, greedy for plunder, he had devised a new kind of fowling for himself. For he gave out that he had discovered a plan by which the gold mines that had failed could be restored. So King Wenceslaus put a huge sum of money into his hands, so that he might carry out what he promised. But that fine fellow, after labouring a few days and achieving nothing, despairing of the business, slipped away secretly with the remaining money from Bohemia to the Roman Curia, a place most worthy of such a nest. With such a character, he easily let himself be bought with money by Hus's adversaries, to put his services at their disposal, which he did with great energy.

units.la: Idem igitur Paletz & Michael de Causis, communi opera certos articulos contra Ioannem Hus conscripserunt, quos dicebant se ex scriptis eius excerpsisse. eos huc illuc obnixè curstando, Cardinalibus, Episcopis, monachis, & alijs huius farinæ hominibus ostendebat: isque adhuc esse longè graviora, quæ Ioannes Hus contra sanctissimas constitutiones Papæ atque ecclesiæ admisisset, quæ si opus sit, in concilio ipso se proposituros esse iactitabant. His facibus incenderunt spontè inratatos[?] homines, ut de comprehendendo viro sanctissimo Ioanne Hus omnes consilia conferrent.
units.tr: Paletz and Michael de Causis therefore, by joint effort, drew up certain articles against John Hus, which they said they had extracted from his writings. They ran hither and thither eagerly showing them to cardinals, bishops, monks and other men of that stamp, and they boasted that there were far graver things, which John Hus had committed against the most holy constitutions of the Pope and the Church, and that if need be they would set these forth in the council itself. By these torches they inflamed men who were already irritated of their own accord, so that they all conferred together on plans for seizing the most holy man, John Hus.

units.la: Cùm igitur Ioannes Hus ad sextum & vigesimum usque diem Constantiæ fuisset (cum interea privatis amicorum colloquijs, legendóque ac scribendo aliquid, tempus illud fefellisset) octavo demum & vigesimo die, Cardinales, qui tunc erant Constantiæ, instante Paletz cum Michaele de Causis, duos ex Episcopis, Augustanum & Viridetinum[?], Consulem præterea civitatis Constantiæ, & equitem quendam, in diversorium Ioannis Hus, sub ipsam horam prandij miserunt, qui dicerent ei, se ex mandato Papæ & Cardinalium missos esse, ut, quod ipse etiam sæpenumero optasset, ad perhibendum coram eis doctrinæ suæ testimonium veniret, se iam ad audiendum paratos esse. Tum Ioannes Hus, Non veni, inquit, huc eo consilio, ut seorsim coram Papa & Cardinalibus causam meam agerem (id enim nunquam desideraui) sed in universa synodi congregatione comparere volui: atque tum pro mea defensione, quæ Deus mihi largitus fuerit, quacunque de re interrogatus fuero, sine ulla dubitatione aperte respondere. itaque non recuso (quandoquidem id à me postulatis) etiam ad ipsos Cardinales quamprimum venire: à quibus etiamsi male accipiar, confido tamen domino meo Iesu Christo, fore ut mori malim[?] pro eius gloria, quàm ipsam veritatem ex sacris Scripturis mihi cognitam negare. Itaque cùm instarent Episcopi, nihil crudele præse ferentes (quanquam in illis ipsis & proximis aliquot ædibus, clam satis multos milites armatos in præsidio collocassent) Ioannes Hus ascenso parvo quodam equo, quem secum habebat, cum domino Ioanne de Chlum episcopos in curiam Papæ & Cardinalium est secutus. Quo quum venisset, & Cardinales ipsos salutasset, Multa inquiunt illi, audiuimus de te, magister Ioannes, quæ si vera sunt, nullo modo tolerari possunt. aiunt enim quòd maximos quosque errores & manifestissimos contra doctrinam veræ Ecclesiæ docueris, ac per totum regnum Bohemiæ iampridem sparseris. itaque huc te ad nos vocari mandauimus, ut rem quomodo se haberet, cognoscemus.
units.tr: When John Hus had been at Constance until the twenty-sixth day (during which time he had passed the period with private conversations with friends, and with some reading and writing), at last, on the twenty-eighth day, the cardinals then at Constance, at the urging of Paletz and Michael de Causis, sent two of the bishops, those of Augsburg and Verden, together with the consul of the city of Constance and a certain knight, to Hus's lodging, just at the hour of dinner.
