They were to tell him that they had been sent by the command of the Pope and the cardinals, so that he might come to bear witness to his teaching before them, which he himself had often desired; they were now ready to hear him. Then John Hus said: "I did not come here with the intention of pleading my case privately before the Pope and the cardinals, for I never wished for that. But I wished to appear before the whole assembly of the synod, and there, when questioned on any matter, to answer openly, with whatever defence God may grant me. So I do not refuse (since you ask this of me) to come to the cardinals themselves as soon as possible. Even if I am ill received by them, I trust in my Lord Jesus Christ that I would rather die for his glory than deny the truth known to me from the holy Scriptures." So, when the bishops pressed him, showing nothing cruel in their manner (although in those very houses and in some neighbouring ones they had secretly stationed quite a number of armed soldiers as a guard), John Hus mounted a small horse which he had with him, and followed the bishops with Lord John de Chlum to the court of the Pope and the cardinals. When he arrived there and had greeted the cardinals, they said: "We have heard many things about you, Master John, which, if true, cannot be tolerated in any way. For they say that you have taught the greatest and most manifest errors against the doctrine of the true Church, and have long been spreading them throughout the whole kingdom of Bohemia. Therefore we have ordered you to be summoned here to us, so that we may learn how the matter stands."

units.la: Tum Ioan.Hus, Sciant, inquit, paternitates vestræ, me ita affectum esse, mori ut malim, quàm vnius alicuius erroris, nedum multorum eorumque maximorum, ut diatis, mihi conscius esse. ac propterea veni tanto libentius ad concilium generale, quod hîc constitutum est, quia paratus sum, si quid in me erroris esse probatum fuerit, ex animo eius emendationem accipere. Ibi Cardinales, Placet nobis quæ dicis. Quod cùm dixissent, abierunt: & Ioannem Hus cum D. Ioanne Chlum sub custodia armatorum reliquerunt: ac tum subornarunt quendam veteratorem ordinis Minorum qui molestis & rixosis quæstionibus Hussum tantisper detineret dum rursus ipsi in curiam Papæ conuenirent deliberaturi quid de Ioanne Hus faciendum esset. Paletz autem & Michael de Caussis, vna cum aliis quos sibi coniunxerant, omnibus modis instabant ne dimitteretur, & iudicium fiducia, sæpe furiosorum hominum more gestientes illudebant Ioanni Hus his verbis, Iam te habemus in nostra potestate, vnde non exibis donec persoluueris extremum quadratem. Sub noctem[?] missus est Præfectus[?] curiæ Romanæ, ut Domino Ioanni de Chlum diceret, licere ei iam ut in diuersorium suum reuerteretur. nam de Ioanne Hus aliter constitutum esse. quod cùm audisset Dominus Ioannes de Chlum, vehementer indignatus, quòd virum optimum fictis & simulatis verbis in insidias præcipitassent, dictu factum, in ipsius Papæ conspectum prouolauit, obtestans eum, meminisset eorum quæ antea etiam domino Henrico Latzembog promiserat, & ne pu-blicæ fidei authoritatem adeò temerè violaret. Papa negabat ex suo mandato mādato quicquam eiusmodi contra Ioannem Hus susceptum esse. Tum seorsim ad dominum Chlum, Quid est quod mihi hoc imputatis, quum scatis me in istorum ( Cardinalium, videlicet, & Episcoporum ) potestate esse ? Meo quidem iudicio, quum Papa Ioānes id metueret quod postea illi accidit: ne dignitate sua priuaretur voluit sibi hoc officio tradendi Christi Herodianos Episcopos & Cardinales demereri. Itaque dominus Ioannes de Chlum tristis inde discessit, frustra per multos inde dies publice & priuatim de Papae iniuria coquestus, quod contra suam & Regis Romani fidem, virum optimum Ioannem Hus per insidias cepisset: qui postea in Cantoris Constantiensis ecclesiae domum ductus per satellites in octauum usque diem ibi sub custodia fuit. inde in monasterium Praedicatorum ad Rhenum perductus, & caceri eius monasterij, magnae latrinae proximo, mandatus est. in quo cum aliquantisper delituisset, incidit ex loci iniuria in grauissimam febrim & ventris constipationem, adeo ut de vita eius desperatum esset. Ac ne forte in ipso carcere vulgari genere mortis periret, misit Pontifex Romanus aliquot ex medicis, qui eum curarent.
units.tr: Then John Hus said: "Let your reverences know that I am so disposed that I would rather die than be conscious of any single error, let alone many, and those the greatest, as you say. For this reason I have come all the more willingly to the general council that is convened here, because I am ready, if any error in me is proved, to receive its correction with a sincere heart." The cardinals replied: "What you say pleases us." When they had said this, they departed, and left John Hus with Lord John de Chlum under the guard of armed men. Then they suborned a certain crafty friar of the Franciscan order, who was to keep Hus occupied with troublesome and quarrelsome questions, until they themselves met again in the Pope's court to deliberate what should be done with John Hus. Paletz and Michael de Causis, together with the others they had joined to themselves, urged by every means that he not be released, and, in the manner of frenzied men, boasting in their confidence and their judgment, they mocked John Hus with these words: "Now we have you in our power; you will not get out until you have paid the last farthing." Toward nightfall the prefect of the Roman court was sent to tell Lord John de Chlum that he might now return to his lodging, for it had been decided otherwise about John Hus. When Lord John de Chlum heard this, he was greatly indignant that they had thrown such a good man into a trap by false and deceitful words. No sooner said than done, he rushed into the presence of the Pope himself, urging him to remember what he had earlier promised to Lord Henry Latzembog, and not to violate so rashly the authority of public faith. The Pope denied that anything of the kind had been undertaken against John Hus by his order. Then, aside, to Lord Chlum, he said: "Why do you charge me with this, since you know that I am in the power of these men (that is, the cardinals and bishops)?" In my judgment, since Pope John feared what later befell him, namely that he would be deprived of his dignity, he wished to win the favour of the Herodian bishops and cardinals by handing over Christ. So Lord John de Chlum left sorrowfully, and for many days afterwards publicly and privately complained in vain of the Pope's wrong, that he had seized a very good man, John Hus, by treachery, contrary to his own and the King of the Romans' faith. Hus was afterwards taken to the house of the cantor of the church of Constance and kept under guard there by soldiers until the eighth day. Thence he was led to the Dominican monastery by the Rhine, and was ordered to be placed in a cell of that monastery, next to a great latrine. While he lay hidden there for some time, the unhealthy place brought on a very severe fever and constipation, so that his life was despaired of. And lest perhaps he should die in the prison by some common kind of death, the Roman Pontiff sent some physicians to attend him.

units.la: Medio infirmitatis eius tempore, accusatores ipsi vehementer apud primates concilij institere pro Ioannis Hus condemnatione, & articulos subscriptos Pontifici Romano obtulerunt.
units.tr: In the middle of his illness, the accusers themselves pressed hard with the leading men of the council for the condemnation of John Hus, and presented the articles they had signed to the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Articuli primi omnium exhibiti Papae Ioanni XXIII. per Mi- chaelem de Causis, pro condemnatione Ioannis Hus, cum primùm incarceratus fuisset.
units.tr: The first articles of all, presented to Pope John XXIII through Michael de Causis, for the condemnation of John Hus, as soon as he had first been imprisoned.

units.la: IN primis, errat circa sacramenta ecclesiae, & signanter corporis Christi: nam publice ad populum praedicauit, id ministrandum populo sub vtraque specie, scilicet corporis & sanguinis. patet iste articulus, quia iam Pragae ipsius discipuli ministrat illud sub vtraque specie.
units.tr: First of all, he errs concerning the sacraments of the Church, and especially the body of Christ: for he preached publicly to the people that it ought to be administered to the people under both kinds, that is, of body and blood. This article is clear, because already at Prague his disciples administer it under both kinds.

units.la: Item à plerisque asseritur, quòd in scholis & in templo docuit, vel ad minimum quòd ipse teneat, quòd post verba consecrationis in altari prolata, in sacramento altaris remaneat panis materialis. Iste articulus scietur ex ipsius examine.
units.tr: Likewise, it is asserted by many that he taught in the schools and in the church, or at least that he holds, that after the words of consecration have been spoken at the altar, the material bread remains in the sacrament of the altar. This article will be known from his examination.

units.la: Secundò, errat circa ministros ecclesiae, quia dicit, quòd non possunt conficere nec ministrare sacramenta, quando sunt in mortali peccato. Iste articulus similiter scietur ex ipsius examinatione. Veruntamē ex scriptis eius de Ecclesia poterit elici, quæ hic habentur. Si negauerit, deputentur ad hoc Magistri in theologia, & alij qui videant eius scripta de Ecclesia.
units.tr: Secondly, he errs concerning the ministers of the Church, because he says that they cannot consecrate or administer the sacraments when they are in mortal sin. This article likewise will be known from his examination. Nevertheless, what is held here may be drawn out from his writings on the Church. If he denies it, let teachers of theology be appointed for this, and others who may examine his writings on the Church.

units.la: Tertiò, errat circa Ecclesiam: primò quòd non admittit, quòd ecclesia significet Papam, Cardinales, Archiepiscopos, Episcopos & clerum eis subditum. & dicit illam significationem extortam à Scholasticis, & nullatenus esse tenendam. Patet ille error manifestè ex tractatu suo dicto De ecclesia.
units.tr: Thirdly, he errs concerning the Church. First, he does not admit that the word "church" signifies the Pope, the cardinals, the archbishops, the bishops and the clergy subject to them. He says that this meaning was wrested by the Schoolmen and is in no way to be held. That error is plain from his treatise called On the Church.

units.la: Item errat circa Ecclesiam, quia dicit quòd Ecclesia non debeat habere temporales possessiones, imò quòd domini temporales impunè possint ea ecclesijs & clericis auferre. Patet ille error, quia propter doctrinam & inductionem suam, multæ ecclesiæ in regno Bohemiæ & ciuitate Pragensi iam de facto sunt quamplurimis bonis temporalibus spoliatæ.
units.tr: Likewise he errs concerning the Church, because he says that the Church ought not to have temporal possessions, and indeed that secular lords may with impunity take these away from churches and clergy. That error is evident, because on account of his teaching and his incitement, many churches in the kingdom of Bohemia and in the city of Prague have already in fact been stripped of very many temporal goods.

units.la: Dicit etiam quòd Constantinus & alij Principes seculares errauerunt, ecclesias & monasteria dotando. iste articulus patet ex immediatè precedenti.
units.tr: He also says that Constantine and other secular princes erred in endowing churches and monasteries. This article is plain from the one immediately preceding.

units.la: Quartò, circa Ecclesiam errat, quòd omnes presbyteros paris dicit esse potestatis. & ideo reseruationes casuum Papalium & Episcopalium, ordinationem & clericorum consecrationem, dicit propter cupiditatem vel ambitionem superiorum adinuentas. Aliqualiter patet iste articulus ex prædictis, sed ex interrogatione & examine melius poterit apparere. Post hos & alios eodem recidentes articulos Papæ exhibitos, pleraque subdidit Michael ille de Causis in hanc sententiam:
units.tr: Fourthly, he errs concerning the Church, in that he says that all presbyters are of equal power. And therefore he says that the reservations of Papal and episcopal cases, the ordination of clergy and their consecration, were devised on account of the greed or ambition of superiors. This article is in part plain from what has been said, but it will appear more clearly from the questioning and examination. After these and other articles of the same kind were presented to the Pope, that Michael de Causis added many more to the following effect:

units.la: Vt prædictus Ioannes Hus vestitus vestimentis ouium, & intrinsecus lupus rapax, ex fructibus suis magis cognoscatur, ad informandam paternitatem vestram dico, quòd primùm habens propositum errores seminandi, sicut postea fecit, sciens se habere resistentiam & contradictionem à Teutonicis magistris in vniuersitate Pragensi, pro eo quòd possent contra ipsum & partem suam concludere, quia tres habebant voces, ipse verò & pars sua solùm vnam, machinatus est vt Teuto-nici solùm vnam haberent vocem, & ipse & pars eius tres, idque per brachium seculare. Quod cùm viderent Teutonici, priusquàm renunciaret iuri suo, quod habebat in vocibus, aut periclitaretur in personis, quod tunc erat eis proximum, ut salvarent personas suas, concorditer elegerunt Praga recedere. & per hoc desolatum est id solenne studium Pragense, quod multos magnos viros in diversis facultatibus procreavit. Ecce primus fructus, quod divisit illam sanctam universitatem, quia non colliguntur uvae de spinis, nec de tribulis ficus.
units.tr: That the aforesaid Jan Hus, clothed in sheep's clothing but inwardly a ravening wolf, may be better known by his fruits, I say, in order to inform your Paternity, that at first, having the purpose of sowing errors, as he afterwards did, and knowing that he would meet resistance and opposition from the German masters in the University of Prague, because they could draw conclusions against him and his party, since they had three votes and he and his party only one, he schemed that the Germans should have only one vote and he and his party three, and this by the secular arm. When the Germans saw this, before they gave up the right they had in the votes, or were endangered in their persons, which then was near to them, so that they might save their persons, they unanimously chose to leave Prague. And by this that famous study at Prague, which had produced many great men in various faculties, was laid waste. Behold the first fruit: he has divided that holy university, for grapes are not gathered from thorns, nor figs from thistles.

units.la: Item, postea orta quaestione inter magistros theologie de universitate Pragensi super XLV. articulis Ioannis Wicleff, & facta convocatione, cum conclusissent omnes alii magistri theologiae de natione Bohemorum, quia Teutonici iam recesserant, quod quilibet dictorum articulorum aut esset haereticus, aut scandalosus, aut erroneus: solus ille posuit conclusionem contradictoriam, quod nullus illorum articulorum esset aut haereticus, aut scandalosus, aut erroneus: sicut postea in scholis Pragae publice disputavit, tenuit & docuit. Per quod satis videtur articulos ipsius Wicleff asserere non solum in Anglia, sed ab ecclesia condemnatos, qui ab Antichristi haereticis sunt positi.
units.tr: Again, after a question had arisen among the masters of theology at the University of Prague concerning the forty-five articles of John Wycliffe, and a meeting had been called, all the other masters of theology of the Bohemian nation concluded (for the Germans had by then withdrawn) that each of the said articles was either heretical, or scandalous, or erroneous; he alone put forward the contrary conclusion, that none of those articles was heretical, scandalous, or erroneous, as he afterwards publicly argued, maintained and taught in the schools at Prague. From this it seems sufficiently clear that he asserts the articles of Wycliffe not only in England, but also that they have been condemned by the Church, having been laid down by the heretics of Antichrist.

units.la: Subdidit in finem accusationis,
units.tr: He added at the end of the accusation,

units.la: Habet etiam pro se generaliter omnes haereticos, qui omnes non curant censuram ecclesiasticam, & oderunt Romanae ecclesiae authoritatem: imo detestantur & vilipendunt: quod multo magis fiet, nisi cum effectu & viriliter resistatur. nā si qualitercunque evadet de concilio, dicet ipse & fautores sui, quod iusta sit doctrina sua, & auctoritate sacri universalis concilij approbata, & quod omnes adversarii sui sint iniqui & mali: & maiora mala faciet quam unquam aliquis haereticus fecit a tempore Constantini magni.
units.tr: Moreover, he has on his side, in general, all heretics, who all disregard ecclesiastical censure, and hate, indeed detest and despise, the authority of the Roman Church; and this will happen much more, unless he is resisted effectively and with manly courage. For if by any means he escapes from the council, he and his supporters will say that his doctrine is sound and approved by the authority of the holy universal council, and that all his adversaries are unjust and wicked; and he will do greater evils than any heretic has done since the time of Constantine the Great.

units.la: Propterea, sancte Pater, attendite vobis & universo gregi, in quo vos Spiritus sanctus posuit regere Ecclesiam Christi, quam acquisivit sanguine suo: & dum novus est morbus succurrite, tam quod ad illum qui sic turbat & inficit Ecclesiam Dei quam quod ad occasiones, quibus illi facere praesumpsit & potuit, scilicet praelati abutuntur censuris ecclesiae, & quod tam ipsi praelati quam ipsorum subditi non servant ordinem sibi a Deo & ecclesia institutum, propter quod fit, cum ipsi per abrupta gradiuntur, quod grex in praecipitium cadit.
units.tr: Therefore, holy Father, take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, over which the Holy Spirit has placed you to rule the Church of Christ, which he purchased with his own blood. And while the disease is new, come to the rescue, both as regards him who so disturbs and infects the Church of God, and as regards the occasions by which he has presumed and been able to act: namely, that prelates abuse the censures of the Church, and that both the prelates themselves and their subjects do not keep the order instituted for them by God and the Church. On account of this, when they go forward by headlong ways, the flock falls into the precipice.

units.la: Deputentur igitur per dominum nostrum & sacrum istud concilium, ad hoc commissarij, qui praesentibus eis qui noverunt factum, interrogent & examinent dictum Hus, super præscriptis & aliis. Deputentur etiam certi Doctores & magistri ut videant libros eius, quos scripsit, quorum aliqui hic habentur: ut ab istis erroribus ecclesia mature possit repurgari.
units.tr: Let commissioners therefore be appointed by our lord and by this holy council for this purpose, who, in the presence of those who know the facts, shall question and examine the said Hus concerning the aforesaid matters and others. Let certain doctors and masters also be appointed to examine his books which he has written, some of which are held here, so that the Church may in time be purged of these errors.

units.la: Dati[?] itaque sunt eis commissarii seu iudices, patriarcha Constantinopolitanus, episcopus Castellae, & episcopus à Libus. qui ipsam accusationem & testimonia producta quorundam sacrificulorum Pragensium, & iuramentis confirmata audiebant, quæ postea Ioanni Hus in carcere, cum dolores febris maximi essent, sunt recitata. Contra ea vero, cum Ioannes Hus peteret sibi advocatum aliquem defendendi sui causa concedi, constanter est recusatum. hoc enim præter cætera, iuris Pontificii authoritate prohibitum esse, Ne quis ei qui de aliqua hæresi suspectus esset, patrocinaretur. Quod sane perfacile fieri potuisset. tota enim fuit vanitas, testimoniorum præsertim, ut nulla accurata confutatione opus fuerit, si modo non iidem iudices & actores fuissent. Testimonia ipsa recitassem hoc loco, nisi scirem ea ciusmodi esse, quæ pius lector sine magno tædio legere non posset. Quanquam postea quædam exponenda erunt, cum ad ipsius iudicii processum ventum fuerit.
units.tr: Commissioners or judges were therefore given to them: the patriarch of Constantinople, the bishop of Castile, and the bishop of Lib. These men heard the accusation and the testimonies produced by certain Prague priests, confirmed by oaths, which were afterwards read out to Jan Hus in prison, while the pains of his fever were very great. Against these things, when Jan Hus asked that some advocate be granted him to defend his cause, it was constantly refused. For, among other things, it was forbidden by the authority of Papal law that anyone should defend one who was suspected of any heresy. This could certainly have been done very easily, for the whole thing was emptiness, especially the testimonies, so that no careful refutation would have been needed, were it not that the same men were both judges and accusers. I would set out the testimonies here, were I not aware that they are of such a kind that a devout reader could not read them without great weariness. Nevertheless, some of them will have to be explained later, when we come to the course of his trial itself.

units.la: Postquam Hus ex morbo nonnihil convaluisset, oblati sunt ei in carcere, mandato trium illorum iudicum, quos dixi, articuli satis multi, quos aiebant ex eius libello De ecclesia excerptos esse. quorum alii consecti ab ipso Paletz[?], alii mutilati erant. horum quoque mentionem in ipsius iudicii historiam differam: ac prius alia quæ interea gesta sunt, exponam. In ipso carcere monasterii fratrum Minorum, usque ad diem Mercurii proximum ante festum palmarum, Ioannes Hus sub certis custodibus detentus est, atque interea libellos quosdam, temporis fallendi causa, conscripsit, scilicet, de Decalogo, de Dilectione & cognitione Dei, de Matrimonio, de Pænitentia, de Tribus hostibus hominis, de Oratione Dominica, de Cœna Domini, &c.
units.tr: After Hus had recovered somewhat from his illness, there were brought to him in prison, by the order of those three judges I have mentioned, quite a number of articles, which they said had been excerpted from his book On the Church. Some of them were distorted by Palec, others were mutilated. I shall also defer mention of these to the history of his trial, and first I shall set out what was done in the meantime. In the prison of the convent of the Friars Minor, Jan Hus was kept under certain guards until the Wednesday before Palm Sunday, and in the meantime he wrote certain little books, to pass the time: namely, On the Decalogue, On the Love and Knowledge of God, On Marriage, On Repentance, On the Three Enemies of Man, On the Lord's Prayer, On the Lord's Supper, and so on.

units.la: Eo die Romanus Pontifex Ioannes XXIII. clàm mutatis vestibus Constantia se subduxit, iudicium metuens quo post fugam ob ingentia crimina, dignitate Pontificali est privatus. hæc causa fuit Ioannis Hus iterum in alium carcerem transferendi. ministri enim Papæ, qui carceri Hus assiterant, cognita domini fuga, traditis claubus carceris ipsi regi Sigismundo & Cardinalibus, confestim sunt eū secuti. Ex sententia vero Concilij, Ioannes Hus in episcopi Constantiesis potestatem traditus est. is per suos satellites armatos curauit eum non procul à Constantia trans Rhenum in arcem quandam deportari, vbi in turri eiusdem arcis interdiu copedibus vinctus incedere poterat, noctu vero compedibus ferreis iuxta lectum parieti est alligatus.
units.tr: On that day Pope John XXIII slipped away from Constance in disguise, fearing the judgment that was to strip him of the papal dignity after his flight on account of his enormous crimes. This was the reason John Hus was moved again, to another prison. For the ministers of the Pope who had been guarding Hus in prison, when they learned of their master's flight, handed over the keys of the prison to King Sigismund himself and the Cardinals, and at once went after him. By the decision of the Council, John Hus was handed over to the power of the bishop of Constance. He, through his armed satellites, arranged for Hus to be carried not far from Constance, across the Rhine, into a certain castle. In the tower of that castle, Hus could walk about by day with his feet shackled, but at night he was fastened by iron fetters to the wall beside his bed.

units.la: Interea nobiles viri Bohemicæ nationis & Polonicæ, eniti summo studio non desinebant pro eius liberatione, vt & ipsius Ioannis Hus saluti, & suæ totiusque regni famæ consulerent, quæ iam per nequissimos quosque homines non mediocriter erat labefactata: adeo vt quicunque ostenderent se Constantiæ Ioannem Hus non odisse, omnibus, etiam infimæ conditionis hominibus, risui atque ludibrio essent. Itaque communi consilio habito, statuerunt suam petitionem scripto ad commune concilium, vel saltem quatuor nationum, Germanicæ, Italicæ, Gallicæ, & Anglicæ deputatis declarare. Huiusmodi autem literas supplices pro liberatione Ioannis Hus missas concilio Constantiensi obtulerunt decimaquarta die Maij, anni M. CCCCXV. Quibus quidem recitatis, episcopus Luthomislensis statim surrexit, sentiens postrema parte earum literarum se in eam criminis inuidiam vocari, quasi per ipsum, regnum Bohemiæ ita infame redditum esset.
units.tr: Meanwhile the noblemen of Bohemia and Poland never ceased to strive with the greatest zeal for his release, both to look after the safety of John Hus himself and to protect the reputation of their own kingdom as a whole, which by now had been not a little damaged by the most wicked men. So much so that anyone who showed that they did not hate John Hus at Constance became a laughingstock and a figure of mockery to everyone, even to people of the lowest rank. So, having taken common counsel, they resolved to set out their petition in writing to the common council, or at least to the deputies of the four nations: German, Italian, French and English. They presented these humble letters for the release of John Hus to the Council of Constance on the fourteenth day of May, in the year 1415. When they had been read out, the bishop of Leitomischl at once stood up, feeling that by the last part of the letters he was being drawn into the odium of that crime, as if the kingdom of Bohemia had been made so infamous through him.

units.la: Ordinati igitur à concilio, constituerunt diem decimam septimam Maij, ad quam iterum adessent domini Bohemi, vt audirent & ipsius concilij responsionem, & seorsim præterea Luthomislensis episcopi excusationem. id quod postea factum est. Nam decimaseptima die Maij, iterum conuenerunt: vbi primum quidam Episcopus, totius concilij nomine, memoriter Bohemis respondit. Ipse quoque Luthomislensis episcopus, ad ea quæ à nobilibus Bohemis erant scripta, ita respondit ac purgauit[?], vt defensionem cū[?] graui Ioannis Hus aliorumque, qui cū[?] sequebatur, accusatione coniunxerit. Cuius orationem ac responsionem nobiles Bohemi pridie Pentecostes confutarunt, fidemque publicam tuti itineris ab Imperatore datam, & causam Ioannis Hus cum fama & existimatione regni coniunctam demonstrarunt.
units.tr: Therefore, having been ordered by the council, they appointed the seventeenth day of May, on which the Bohemian lords should again be present, to hear both the council's response and, separately, the bishop of Leitomischl's excuse. This was afterwards done. For on the seventeenth of May they gathered again, and first a certain bishop, in the name of the whole council, replied to the Bohemians from memory. The bishop of Leitomischl himself also answered the things the Bohemian nobles had written, and cleared himself in such a way that he joined his defence with a grave accusation of John Hus and of the others who followed him. The Bohemian nobles refuted his speech and reply on the day before Pentecost. They also showed the safe-conduct granted by the Emperor, and demonstrated that the cause of John Hus was bound up with the reputation and esteem of the kingdom.

units.la: Præterea propositum est in eodem concilio, publicum totius vniuersitatis Pragensis testimonium, de literis quas Ioannes Hus ad Ioannē XXII. Papam misit, anno M.CCCC XI. die prima mensis Septembris, de sua fide, innocentia, voluntate ad omnem obedientiam obseruantiamque rectam et piam paratissima. quas et a notariis publicis describi, et publico Universitatis sigillo, authoritateque doctorum ac magistrorum consignari postulauerunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, it was proposed in the same council that a public testimony of the whole University of Prague be obtained concerning the letters which John Hus sent to John XXII the Pope on the first day of September 1411, about his faith, his innocence, and his readiness for all right obedience and observance. They asked that these letters be copied out by public notaries and sealed with the public seal of the University, and attested by the authority of the doctors and masters.

units.la: Cum vero ad oblata scripta nihil responsi acciperent per aliquot dies, ipsi nobiles Bohemi statuerunt ultimo die Maij denuo ipsius concilij primatibus supplicare et petere, ut Joanni Hus a carcere liberato. publica defensio concederetur. simul etiam obtulerunt testimonium Nicolai episcopi Nazarethensis, de Joanne Hus: in quo et iniquissimae inimicorum calumniae, et ipsius vitae doctrinaeque moderatissimae rationes fuerunt declaratae. ·
units.tr: When, however, they received no response to the writings they had submitted for several days, the same Bohemian nobles resolved to petition again, on the last day of May, the leading men of the council itself, and to ask that John Hus, freed from prison, be granted a public hearing. At the same time they also presented the testimony of Nicholas, bishop of Nazareth, concerning John Hus, in which both the most unjust calumnies of his enemies and the reasons for his most moderate life and teaching were declared.

units.la: Postremo his prolatis authoritatibus ac testimoniis, de innocentia modestiaque Joannis Hus, supplicitèr iidem nobiles rogauerunt, ut ipse Hus carcere liberatus, ac vinculis solutus, in custodiam liberiorem atque humaniorem quorundam Episcoporum traderetur, in qua et commodius examinari, et mitius ac benignius tractari atque recreari posset. Qua in re, ad euitandum omnem malae custodiae metum et dubitationem, vades sponsoresque certissimos pro ipso Joanne Hus, usque ad exitum causae institutae, asseruandos obtulerunt. Ac ne quis eos iniquam rem postulasse criminari posset, a concilio petierunt ut postulatio ipsorum, summae aequitatis plena, a notario publico perscriberetur.
units.tr: Finally, with these authorities and testimonies produced concerning the innocence and modesty of John Hus, the same nobles humbly asked that Hus himself be released from prison and unshackled, and handed over to the custody of certain bishops, a freer and more humane custody, in which he could be examined more conveniently and treated more mildly and kindly, and refreshed. In this matter, to remove all fear and doubt of harsh custody, they offered most certain sureties and guarantors for John Hus, to be kept until the end of the case begun. And lest anyone accuse them of asking something unjust, they asked the council that their request, full of the highest fairness, be written out by a public notary.

units.la: Perlecto corum scripto coram deputatis quatuor nationum, patriarcha Antiochenus omnium nomine respondit ad singula capita ipsius scriptis, sed breuissimè. Primum, quod ad protestationem Joannis Hus attineret, fuerintne vera ac firma, an non, in ipsius causae processu palam futurum. Deinde, quia dicant aduersarios Joannis Hus nonnulla peruerse ex eius libris excerpsisse, id quoque in exitu causae manifestum futurum. quod si Joannes Hus iniuste accusatus esse decernatur, tunc fore ut aduersarii in perpetuam incidat ignominiam. Sed de fideiussoribus, etiam si mille dentur, tamen fieri non posse, salua conscientia deputatorum concilij, ut recipiantur in causa eius viri, cui nullo modo fides habenda esset. hoc tamen se facturos, ut ad quintum Iunij. Iunij, Ioannes Hus iterum Constantiam aduchatur, & habeat coram ipso concilio liberam dicendi potestatem, eumque pie & benigne audituros esse. Sed rei & actionis totius euentus longe contrarium huic promissioni c[?]stendit.
units.tr: When their writing had been read out before the deputies of the four nations, the patriarch of Antioch replied on behalf of all to each of its points, but very briefly. First, as far as the protestation of John Hus was concerned, whether its contents were true and firm or not would be made plain in the course of the trial of his case. Next, since they said that the adversaries of John Hus had perversely extracted some things from his books, this too would become manifest at the outcome of the case. But if John Hus were decreed to have been unjustly accused, then his adversaries would fall into lasting disgrace. As for sureties, even if a thousand were given, it could not be done, consistent with the conscience of the deputies of the council, to admit in his case a man in whom no faith whatever should be placed. Nevertheless they would do this: that on the fifth of June John Hus would be brought back to Constance and have free opportunity to speak before the council itself, and that they would hear him kindly and benevolently. But the outcome of the affair and of the whole proceeding showed something far contrary to this promise.

units.la: Eodem die iidem nobiles libellum supplicem scriptum concilioque oblatum, etiam regi Sigismundo obtulerunt, vt eius summam aequitatem cognoscerent, simul etiam ei & fidem publicam ab ipso datam reuocarunt in memoriam: & causam Ioannis Hus susceptam, & cum existimatione regni Bohemiæ dignitatéque coiunctam, summo studio commendarunt. Supplicationis verò ipsa verba huc inserenda duximus, vt ex actis publicis plenior historia elucescat.
units.tr: On the same day the same nobles also presented the written petition, which they had delivered to the council, to King Sigismund, so that he might recognise its highest fairness. At the same time they recalled to his memory the public safe-conduct given by him, and they commended with the greatest zeal the cause of John Hus, which had been taken up and was bound up with the reputation and dignity of the kingdom of Bohemia. We have thought it right to insert the actual words of the supplication here, so that a fuller history may emerge from the public records.

units.la: Serenissime Princeps & domine gratiosissime, Serenitati vestrae significamus, quòd nos vnanimi consensu & pari voto concordes, hanc nostram inferius descriptam, rationabilem, iustam & exauditione dignam petitionem reucredissimis[?] in Christo Patribus & Dominis quatuor nationum deputatis, totíque sacro Constantiensi Concilio duximus porrigendam.
units.tr: Most serene Prince and most gracious lord, we make known to Your Serenity that we, united in unanimous consent and equal vote, have resolved to present this our petition, described below, which is reasonable, just and worthy of a hearing, to the most reverend Fathers and lords in Christ, the deputies of the four nations, and to the whole holy Council of Constance.

units.la: Fauore itaque & intuitu rationabilium & iustarum petitionum dictis dominis porrectarum vestrae supplicamus Regiae maiestati, quatenus amore iustitiæ, & famæ præclari regni Bohemiæ, cuius absque dubio hæres & dominus successurus fore dignoscimini, & vestri salui conductus libertati prouidentes, erga dictos reuerendissimos Patres & dominos velitis interponere partes vestras, vt nos in hac iusta petitione nostra, ipsis, vt præfertur, oblata, vclint[?] effectualiter audire. Ne autem minimâ honoris & famæ præclari regni Bohemiæ, & nostri pariter obtrectatores nobis in posterum possint detrahere, prætendentes nos illicita & inordinata à reuerendissimis dominis postulasse: ideo ab eis petiuimus, quatenus nostræ schedulæ tenorem velint decernere manu publica authenticandum.
units.tr: Therefore, favouring and having regard to the reasonable and just petitions presented to the said lords, we humbly ask your royal Majesty that, for the love of justice and for the fame of the illustrious kingdom of Bohemia, of which you are without doubt recognised as the heir and future lord, and providing for the freedom of your safe-conduct, you would be pleased to interpose your good offices with the said most reverend Fathers and lords, so that they may be willing to hear effectually our just petition, offered to them as stated. And lest our detractors, both of the honour and fame of the illustrious kingdom of Bohemia and of ourselves, should in future belittle us, pretending that we have asked the most reverend lords for unlawful and disorderly things, we have therefore asked them to be willing to have the tenor of our schedule authenticated by a public hand.

units.la: Quid verò ipse Rex ad ea respondcrit, non satis constat. sed ex ipsa actione & iudicio facile apparet, virum bonum improbitate Cardinalium & Episcoporum, in eam sententiam persuasum esse, vt fideipublicæ Hussio datæ renuntiaret. neque enim posse, [?]cui haereticus sit declaratus, secundum pontificij iuris sanctionęs, aut fide publica, aut ulla re alia defensionem præstari. Sed ex ipsis Joannis Hus epistolis, facilè de sententia[?] Regis judicari poterit. nunc in historia pergamus.
units.tr: What the King himself replied to these things is not sufficiently clear. But from the very action and judgment it is easily apparent that the good man, through the wickedness of the Cardinals and bishops, was persuaded to renounce the public faith given to Hus. For according to the sanctions of papal law, no defence can be granted, either by public faith or by any other thing, to one who has been declared a heretic. But from the letters of John Hus himself the King's opinion can easily be judged. Now let us go on with the history.

units.la: Dquintum igitur Junij, quum ingens multitudo Cardinalium, Episcoporum, & quicunque fere tum ex ordine ecclesiastico Constantiæ erant, in monasterium Fratrum minorum, ut antea, convenisset: mandatum est ut priusquam Joannes Hus adduceretur, in eius absentia testimonia & articuli, de eius libris calumniosè excerpti, recitarentur. quos articulos, & quid postea Joannes Hus responderit, commemorabo. Eos cum Petrus de Mladonye-witz notarius, qui tum forte adderat, Joanni Hus benevolentia coniunctus, intellexisset ab ipsis Episcopis & Cardinalibus iam decretum esse, ut in absentia Joannis Hus condemnarentur, properans ad dominum Wenceslaum de Duba & Joannem de Chlum, rem omnem exposuit. Hi continuò ad regem Sigismundum haec detulerunt. qui, ut rem cognovit, misit dominum Ludovicum comitem Palatinum ab Heidelberga, & dominum Fridericum Burgravium Norimbergensem, ut in causa Joannis Hus praefecti concilij nihil decernerent, priusquam ipsum, & quidem æquo animo, audiuissent, & quoscunque in eo articulos erroneos deprehendissent, ad se mitterent. se enim daturum operam, ut à viris doctis & bonis examinarentur.
units.tr: On the fifth of June, when a huge crowd of Cardinals, bishops, and practically all others of the ecclesiastical order then at Constance had gathered in the monastery of the Friars Minor, as before, it was ordered that before John Hus was brought in, the testimonies and articles, calumniously extracted from his books, should be read out in his absence. I will recount those articles, and what John Hus replied afterwards. When Peter of Mladonowitz, a notary who happened to be present at that time and was bound to John Hus by goodwill, had learned from the bishops and Cardinals themselves that it had already been decided that Hus would be condemned in his absence, he hurried to Lord Wenceslaus of Duba and John of Chlum and laid out the whole matter. These at once carried it to King Sigismund. When he learned of it, he sent Lord Ludwig, Count Palatine from Heidelberg, and Lord Frederick, Burgrave of Nuremberg, so that the prefects of the council should decide nothing in the cause of John Hus until they had heard him, and heard him with an open mind, and so that they should send to him any erroneous articles they had found. For he would take care that these were examined by learned and good men.

units.la: Ex Regis itaque voluntate, sententia praefectorum concilij usque dum præsens esset Joannes Hus suspensa est. Interea vero Wenceslaus de Duba & Joannes de Chlum, ipsis Principibus à Rege in concilium prædictum missis, certos quosdam libellos Joannis Hus, ex quibus contra eum articuli quidam, ut sæpe iam dictum est, excerpti erant, tradiderunt, ut ipsis præfectis concilij præsentarent, ea quidem lege, ut cum vellent, ab eis repeterent. idque eo consilio factum est, ut tanto facilius adversarij coargui possent, qui mala fide sententias ex libris Joannis Hus collegerant. Traditis libris Concilio ipsi, & eodem adducto Joanne Hus, Principes, qui à Rege missi erant, abierunt. Deinde ipsi libelli cum ostensi essent Joanni Hus, is publicè in eo consessu Episcoporum confessus est, se eius authorem esse, & paratum, si quid incesset erroris, emendare.
units.tr: By the king's will, the prefects of the council suspended their judgement until John Hus should be present. Meanwhile Wenceslaus of Duba and John of Chlum, whom the king had sent to the council together with the princes, handed over to the prefects certain small books of John Hus, from which some of the articles against him had been excerpted, as has often been said. They were to be presented to the prefects on the understanding that they could be demanded back whenever the council wished. This was done so that his opponents, who had collected the opinions from John Hus's books in bad faith, could be refuted all the more easily. When the books had been handed to the council and John Hus had been brought in, the princes who had been sent by the king departed. Then, when the books were shown to John Hus, he openly confessed before that assembly of bishops that he was their author, and said he was ready to correct whatever error might be found in them.

units.la: Hic vero indignum facinus accidit. nam cum unus duntaxat articulus, & pauca quaedā testimonia in eum prolata essent, & ipse respondere conaretur, tota eum simul multitudo undique clamoribus ita obruit, nullum ut omnino verbum facere posset. tanta erat confusio & perturbatio, ut immanium aliquot beluarum tumultum non hominum dixisses. Si quando tantum a vociferationibus remissum esset, ut paululum quiddam Ioannes Hus loqui posset, aut ex Scripturae, aut ex sanctorum doctorum sententia, continuo audiuit, ea nihil ad rem facere. hinc aliorum conuicia in eum, aliorum vero ludibria certatim sequebantur. Victus igitur vociferationum immanitate quum se loquendo nihil omnino proficere videret, tacere tandem decreuit. Ibi vero omnis multitudo aduersantium, putabat se palmarium repperisse & uno ore omnes, Tacet iam, inquiunt, tacet. satis id quidem signi est, eum istis erroribus suis assentiri. Quid multa? eo tandem res redijt, ut propter inordinatam confusionem totius Iudicij, quidam moderatores senatum dimitti censerent, & rem in aliud tempus differri. Ex istorum itaque consilio senatus dimissus, & iudicium in perendianum diem iterum est constitutum.
units.tr: Here an unworthy outrage took place. For when only one article and a few testimonies had been brought against him, and he tried to answer, the whole crowd at once overwhelmed him with shouts from every side, so that he could not get out a single word. The confusion and uproar were so great that you would have said it was the noise of some huge beasts rather than of men. Whenever the shouting eased enough for John Hus to say a little, whether from Scripture or from the opinions of the holy teachers, he was at once told that it had nothing to do with the matter. Hence insults from some and mockery from others followed eagerly, one after another. Overcome, then, by the savagery of the shouting, and seeing that by speaking he achieved nothing at all, he finally decided to be silent. Then the whole multitude of his opponents, thinking they had won the day, cried with one voice: "He is silent now, he is silent. That is surely a sign that he agrees with these errors of his." What more is there to say? The matter came to this: because of the disorderly confusion of the whole trial, some of the presiding men thought the assembly should be dismissed and the business postponed. On their advice the senate was dismissed, and the trial was again set for the day after tomorrow.

units.la: Eo igitur die qui erat vi i. Iunii, horam circiter septimam, cum paulo ante admirandae solis eclipsis visa esset, iterum in refectorium fratrum Minorum, iidem qui antea, convenerunt, & Ioannem Hus magna turba armatorum militum cinctum, coram eis sisti mandarunt. Eodem venit etiam Imperator Sigismundus, quem Wenceslaus de Duba, & dominus Ioannes de Chlū, & Petrus notarius, amici Ioannis Hus, secuti sunt, ut exitum negotij viderent. qui sane quum eo venissent, audierunt tandem praelegi accusationem Michaelis de Caussis in haec verba, Ioannes Hus in sacello Beth-lehem & in aliis locis civitatis Pragensis, ad populum docuit multos errores, partim ex libris wicleff partim a se confictos, eosque summa animi pertinacia defendit. Primum, quod post consecrationem & pronuntiationem verborum in coena Domini, manet panis materialis. idque probatum est testimonijs Ioannis Protiwae, parochi Pragensis ad S. Clementem, Ioannis Pecklo, praedicatoris Pragensis ad sanctum Egidium, Benesij praedicatoris in arce Pragensi, Andreae Brodae canonica Pragensis, & aliorum quo rundam sacrificulorum. Ad hoc respondit Ioannes Hus, sanctè aduransans, se id nunquam dixisse. caeterum hoc se fateri, cum archiepiscopus Pragensis omnino prohibuisset vti illo termino, Panis, tunc se hoc edictum Episcopi non potuisse probare, quia Christus ipse VI. cap. Ioannis vndecies se nominauerit Panem Angelorum, qui de caelo descendisset, vt toti mundo vitâ daret, &c. Cardinalis Cameracensis & plerique alij sophisticis argumentis impetebant Ioanne Hus, praesertim vero Angli, inter quos quidam erat nomine Stokes, sophista acerrimus. Alij vero intentabant varias aduersus eum accusationes, leues quidem & pueriles, vt tum ferebant tempora. Repetitus etiam est in accusatione seques articulus: Condemnatio XLV. articulorum wicleff, per doctores facta est irrationabilis & iniqua, & causa per eos allegata est ficta, videlicet quod nullus ex iis est catholicus, sed quilibet eorum aut est haereticus, aut erroneus, aut scandalosus. Responsio: In meo libello ita scripsi, Condemnati sunt articuli XLV. ex hac causa, quod nullus ex illis articulis habitus est catholicus: sed quilibet eorum aut haereticus, aut erroneus, aut scandalosus iudicatus est. O doctor, vbi probatio? causam fingis quam non probas, &c. vt latius in Tractatu. Tum Cardinalis Cameracensis, Tu dixisti, Ioannes Hus, te nolle vllum errorem wicleff defendere, & iam patet ex libris tuis, quod eius articulos defendisti publicè. Hus respodit, Reuerende pater, idem dico quod antea, quod neque Ioannis wicleff, neque alicuius alterius errores volo defendere: sed quia videbatur mihi contra conscientiam ad condemnationem eorum simpliciter consentire, nulla habita Scriptura de oppositu, ideo ad illorum condemnationem nolui consentire.
units.tr: On that day, which was the 7th of June, at about the seventh hour, shortly after a remarkable eclipse of the sun had been seen, the same men as before gathered again in the refectory of the Franciscan friars, and ordered John Hus, surrounded by a great crowd of armed soldiers, to be brought before them. Emperor Sigismund also came there, followed by Wenceslaus of Duba, Lord John of Chlum and Peter the notary, friends of John Hus, so that they might see how the affair ended. When they had arrived, they heard the accusation of Michael de Causis read out at last, in these words: "John Hus, in the chapel of Bethlehem and in other places in the city of Prague, taught the people many errors, some taken from the books of Wycliffe and some invented by himself, and he defended them with the greatest obstinacy of mind. First, that after the consecration and the pronouncing of the words in the Lord's Supper, the material bread remains. This has been proved by the testimonies of John Protiwa, parish priest of St Clement's in Prague, John Peckel, preacher at St Giles' in Prague, Benesch, preacher in the Prague citadel, Andrew Broda, canon of Prague, and of others some priests. To this John Hus replied, solemnly affirming that he had never said it. He admitted, however, that when the archbishop of Prague had altogether forbidden the use of the term "bread", he had not been able to approve that bishop's edict, because Christ himself, in John chapter 6, eleven times called himself the Bread of the angels, who came down from heaven to give life to the whole world, and so on. The Cardinal of Cambrai and many others attacked John Hus with sophistical arguments, especially the Englishmen, among whom was one named Stokes, a most keen sophist. Others brought various accusations against him, light and childish, as the times then allowed. In the accusation the following article was also repeated: "The condemnation of the forty-five articles of Wycliffe by the doctors was unreasonable and unjust, and the cause alleged by them was false, namely that none of them is Catholic, but each is either heretical, erroneous or scandalous." Answer: "In my little book I wrote this: the forty-five articles were condemned for this reason, that none of those articles was held to be Catholic, but each was judged heretical, erroneous or scandalous." "O doctor, where is the proof? You feign a cause which you do not prove," and so on, as more fully in the Treatise. Then the Cardinal of Cambrai said: "You said, John Hus, that you did not wish to defend any error of Wycliffe, and now it is clear from your books that you have publicly defended his articles." Hus replied: "Reverend father, I say the same as before: I do not wish to defend the errors of John Wycliffe or of anyone else. But because it seemed to me against my conscience simply to consent to their condemnation, with no Scripture opposed to them, therefore I did not want to consent to their condemnation."

units.la: Alij praeterea articuli numero triginta nouem, qui ex alio quodam libello contra Stanislaum de Znoima excerpti esse dicebantur, etiam Ioanni Hus propositi fuerunt, eiusdem propemodum argumenti cum superioribus, quibus idem Hus ementitum Pontificis Romani primatum contra aduersarios oppugnauit.
units.tr: Thirty-nine other articles, which were said to have been excerpted from another little book against Stanislaus of Znoima, were also put to John Hus. They were of nearly the same subject as the earlier ones, and in them the same Hus attacked, against his opponents, the false primacy of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Conclusionibus quoque & propositionibus quotidie nouis diuexabant Ioannem Hus aduersarij, quas confingebant, nunc addendo aliqua, nunc subtrahendo, nunc integram propositionem falsè ascribendo: quod etiam ipsi commissarij, praesente ipso Hus confessi sunt. Postremò etiam articuli à Parisiensibus authore Gersone, aduersus eundem Ioannem Hus compositi fuerunt, numero nouendecim: de quibus ipse in epistolis tantopere conqueritur, quod nō habuerit spatium ad eos respondendi.
units.tr: Day by day, too, his adversaries harassed John Hus with new conclusions and propositions, which they made up: now adding some things, now leaving others out, now falsely ascribing whole propositions to him. The commissioners themselves admitted this in Hus's presence. Finally, articles were also drawn up against the same John Hus by the Parisians, with Gerson as their author, numbering nineteen. About these he complains so bitterly in his letters, because he had no time to answer them.

units.la: Titulus horum articulorum huiusmodi erat: Articuli contenti formaliter aut elicitiuē in tractatu Ioannis Hus Pragensis, quē intitulauit De Ecclesia, sequentes errores Ioānis widess[?]in hac parte, &c. Quibus nouendecim articulis, pro omni ratione hoc addebant, suis suffragijs Magistri illi Parisienses, quod hic ascribere visum est his verbis: Asseriimus articulos prefatos notorie esse hæreticos: & vt tales iudicialiter condemnados, & ne ceteros inficiat, diligentissime cum doctrinis suis scandalosissimis extirpandos. Etsi enim videntur habere zelum contra vitia Prælatorū & clericorum, nimis (proh dolor) abundantium, non tamen secundum scientiam. Zelus itaque discretus ea peccata quae videt in domo Dei se nō posse tollere, tollerat & gemit. Non possunt autem per vitia & errores bene tolli vitia, quia non in Beelzebub eiiciūtur dæmonia, sed in digito Dei, qui est Spiritus sanctus, volēs vt in corrigendo modus adhibeatur prudentiæ, iuxta illud, Quis, quid, vbi, cur, attedas, & quomodo, quādo. Prælati & Principes obligātur sub pœnis iuris grauibus & expressis, vigilāter se habere aduersus errores prædictos & similes, & suos assertores. Attendatur quòd error cui non resistitur, approbatur, nec caret scrupulo sociatis occultæ, qui manifesto facinori desinit obuiare. Sub correctione hæc doctrinaliter posita sunt in transitu. Ioannes de Gerson Cancellarius Parisien. indignus.
units.tr: The title of these articles was of this kind: "Articles contained formally or by inference in the treatise of John Hus of Prague, which he entitled On the Church, the following errors of John Wycliffe in this respect, etc." To these nineteen articles those Parisian masters added, as their full justification by their votes, the following statement, which it seems worth setting down here in these words: "We assert that the aforesaid articles are notoriously heretical, and that they should be judicially condemned as such and most diligently rooted out, together with their most scandalous doctrines, lest they infect the rest. For although they seem to have zeal against the vices of prelates and clergy, which are (alas!) too abundant, yet it is not according to knowledge. A discreet zeal therefore bears and groans over those sins which it sees it cannot remove from the house of God. But vices cannot be well removed by errors and heresies, for demons are not cast out by Beelzebub but by the finger of God, which is the Holy Spirit, and he wishes prudence to be applied in correcting, according to that saying: consider who, what, where, why, how and when. Prelates and princes are bound under heavy and express penalties of law to be watchful against the aforesaid errors and similar ones, and against their asserters. Note that an error which is not resisted is approved, and that a secret accomplice who ceases to oppose a manifest crime is not free of blame. These things are set down in passing, by way of teaching, subject to correction. John Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, unworthy."

units.la: His expositis, ex quibus facile intelligi potest, Ioannem Hus non accusatum quòd aliquid contra articulos fidei, sed quia contra Antichristi regnū pro gloria Christi & Ecclesiæ restauratione strenuè docuerit. Redeo ad historiā. Quū ergo nouē illi & triginta primi articuli, quos supra recitaui, omnes perlecti essent, vnà cū testimonijs, Cardinalis Cameracensis Ioānem Hus compellās, Audisti, inquit, quanta sit atrocitas criminum, eorūmque plurimorum, quæ contra te allata sunt. iam tuum est officium, cogitare quid sis facturus. Duæ tibi viæ à concilio proponuntur, quarum alteram te ingredi necesse est. primùm vt te ipsius concilij iudicio & sententiæ supplex subiicias: & quicquid hùc communi sententia decretum fuerit, illud æquo animo vt feras. quod si feceris, nos propter ipsius clementissimi Imperatoris hic præsentis, & fratris eius regis Bohemiæ honorem, & tuæ salutis causa, ea quæ debemus pietate & humanitate tecum sumus acturi. Sed si adhuc aliquos ex ijs articulis, qui nobis propositi sunt, defendere cogitas, & amplius te audiri postulas, eius rei potestatem tibi non negabimus. Verum cogitabis hic tantos esse viros, & tam illuminatos, cōsque tam firmas & validas rationes contra tuos articulos habere, ut verear ne hoc cum magno tuo incommodo & periculo facturus sis, si amplius eos tueri velis. hæc ego monendi tui causa, non iudicis more loquor. Hanc Cameracensis orationem, alij subsequentes idem pro se quisque Ioannem Hus hortati sunt. Quibus tu submisso vultu respondit, Reuerendissimi patres, iam sæpe dixi me libere huc venisse, non ut obstinatè quicquam defenderem, sed si qua in re minus rectè sentirem, æquo animo paterer me doceri. rogo igitur, ut sit mihi locus amplius sententiam meam declarandi. cuius nisi certas & efficaces rationes attulero, libenter in vestram informationem, ita ut postulatis, concedam.
units.tr: Having set out these matters, from which it can easily be understood that John Hus was accused not because he taught anything against the articles of faith, but because he vigorously taught against the kingdom of Antichrist, for the glory of Christ and the restoration of the Church. I return to the story. When those first thirty-nine articles, which I have recited above, had all been read out together with the testimonies, the Cardinal of Cambrai addressed John Hus: "You have heard how atrocious the crimes are, and how many of them have been brought against you. It is now your duty to consider what you are going to do. Two courses are offered to you by the council, and you must take one of them. First, that you submit humbly to the judgement and sentence of the council, and bear calmly whatever is decreed here by common consent. If you do this, we shall deal with you in the kindness and humanity we owe, out of honour for the most merciful Emperor present here and his brother the King of Bohemia, and for the sake of your salvation. But if you still intend to defend some of the articles that have been put to you, and you ask to be heard further, we will not deny you the power to do so. Yet consider that here are men so great and so enlightened, with such firm and strong arguments against your articles, that I fear you would do this with great loss and danger to yourself if you wish to defend them any further. I speak these words to warn you, not in the manner of a judge." After this speech of the Cardinal of Cambrai, the others who followed each exhorted John Hus in the same way on their own account. To them he replied with lowered countenance: "Most reverend fathers, I have often said already that I came here freely, not to defend anything obstinately, but that if I think somewhat wrongly about any matter, I am willing to be taught with an even mind. I ask, therefore, that I may have room to declare my opinion more fully. Unless I bring certain and effective reasons for it, I will willingly give way to your instruction, as you demand."

units.la: Hic magna voce quidam, Videte quàm callidè loquatur. informationem dicit, non correctionem aut definitionem. Imò, verò ut vultis sive informationem, sive correctionem, aut definitionem. testor enim Deum me nihil nisi ex animo loqui. Tum Cameracensis, Quando igitur informationi & gratiæ ipsius concilij te subijcis, hoc à doctoribus fere sexaginta, quorum aliqui iam hinc abierunt, & tamen in eorum locum Parisienses successerunt, decretum, etiā à toto cōcilio, ne vno quidem contradicente, approbatum est. primum, ut supplici animo te in ijs articulis, qui contra te allati sunt, errasse confitearis: deinde, ut iureiurando promittas, nihil istorum te amplius sentire aut docere velle. Postremo, ut publicè omnes illos articulos recantes. In quâ sententiam cum multi alij multa dixissent, tandem Ioannes Hus, Iterum dico, inquit, me paratum esse ad informationem concilij, sed illud tamen per eum, qui omnium nostrum Deus est, vos rogo atq; obsecro, ne per vos cogar ad id quod conscientia mea repugnante, & sine æternæ damnationis periculo facere non possum, ut omnibus articulis contra me propositis iuramento renunciem. memini enim me in Catholico legere, Abiurare, est errori prius tento renuntiare. Cum igitur multi articuli mei esse dicantur tur,quos ut sentirem aut docerem nunquam mihi in mente venit: quo-modo possum eis per iuramentum renuntiare? Cæterum, quod ad illos articulos attinet, qui vere mei sunt, si quis me aliter docere poterit, libenter hoc faciam, quod postulatis. Tum Imperator, Quid ni, inquit, sine periculo posses omnibus istis renuntiare, quæ etiam falso dicis contra te à testibus propositá esse? Equidem omnes errores abiurare non dubito, neque hinc sequitur continuo, me aliquem errorem professum esse. Ad quem Hus, Imperator clementissime, aliud significat vocabulum abiurandi, quam tua maiestas hic usa est. Et Cardinalis Florentinus inquit, Dabitur tibi, Ioannes Hus, scripta abiurandi forma, satis lenis et tolerabilis, tunc facile inibis consilium, velisne id an non facere. Tum iterum Imperator, verba Cardinalis Cameracensis repetens, Audisti duas vias tibi propositas esse. primum, ut, illis erroribus tuis iam condemnatis palam renunties, et iudicio concilij subscribas. Pro qua re vicissim eius gratia experieris. Sin pergis defendere tuas opiniones, concilium facile habebit, quod secundum leges suas de te decernat. Cui Ioannes Hus respondit, Ego nihil recuso, quicquid ab ipso concilio de me decretum fuerit, Imperator clementissime. Id tantum excipio, ne Deum et conscientiam meam offendam, et dicam me illos errores professum esse, quos nunquam mihi in mentem venit profiteri. Obsecro autem, ut si fieri potest, vobis concedentibus habeam potestatem amplius animi mei sententiam declarandi, ut de iis, quæ mihi obiecta sunt, maxime de officijs ecclesiasticis, quantum satis est, respondere possim. Sed cum alij, tum Imperator eandem ei, quam antea, cantilenam occinere coeperunt. AEtatem habes, inquit Imperator, facile potuisti intelligere, quæ et heri et hodie ad te dixi. nos testimonijs, quæ fide dignissima sunt, credere cogimur. Quod si Scriptura dicit, quod in ore duorum vel trium stet omne verbum, quanto magis in tantorum virorum quam plurimis testimonijs? Tu igitur, si sapis, accipies à concilio pœnitentiam corde contrito, et manifestis erroribus renuntiabis, et iuramento promittes te contra eos deinceps perpetuo et sentire et docere velle. Sin minus, sunt leges secundum quas à concilio iudicaberis. Hunc Imperatoris sermonem excepit quidam Episcopus Polonus iam decrepitæ ætatis, his verbis, Apertæ sunt leges de hæreticis, quæ pœna affici debeant. Ioannes Hus constanter perseverabat, adeo ut pertinacem eum esse inclamarent. Quidam vero bene saginatus sacerdos, acclamans, dixit ad praefectos concilij, Nullo modo ad revocationem admitti debet: scripsit enim ad amicos suos, se etiamsi lingua iuret, mentem tamen iniuratam retinere velle. non est itaque ei habenda fides. Ad hanc calumniam iterum respondit se nullius erroris sibi conscium esse. Tum Paletz, Quorsum haec protestatio, qua dicis te nullum errorem wicleffi defendere, cum tamen id facias? Haec cum dixisset, protulit in testimonium nouem articulos Ioan. wicleffi, quibus publice perlectis, addidit haec verba, Hos cum ego & magister Stanislaus praefecte Ernesto Austriae duce Pragae contra eos praedicaremus, pertinaciter non in concionibus solum, verumetiā editis libris defendit. Quos nisi tu hic exhibueris, nos faciemus. Idē cōfirmabat Imperator. Cui Ioannes Hus, Facile, inquit, patior, ut nō solum illi, verumetiā alij mei libri proferatur.
units.tr: Here someone shouted loudly, "See how cleverly he speaks! He says 'information,' not 'correction' or 'definition.'" Hus replied: "Indeed, but as you wish, whether information, correction, or definition. For I call God to witness that I speak nothing except from my heart." Then the Cardinal of Cambrai said: "Since you therefore submit yourself to the information and grace of this council, the doctors, nearly sixty of them, some of whom have already left here, though Parisians have taken their place, have approved a decree, with not one dissenting voice from the whole council. First, that you confess with a humble spirit that you have erred in those articles which have been brought against you. Next, that you promise on oath that you no longer wish to hold or teach any of them. Last, that you publicly recant all those articles." When many others had spoken to this effect, at last John Hus said: "I say again that I am ready to accept the information of the council. But I beg and implore you, by Him who is God of us all, not to force me to do what my conscience forbids and what I cannot do without peril of eternal damnation: to renounce on oath all the articles brought against me. For I remember reading in the Catholicon: 'To abjure is first to renounce an error one has held.' Since many of the articles are said to be mine, which I never once thought of holding or teaching, how can I renounce them by oath? As for those articles which are truly mine, if anyone can teach me otherwise, I will gladly do what you ask." Then the Emperor said: "Why not? Could you not renounce all these things without danger, even those which you say are falsely brought against you by the witnesses? Indeed, I do not doubt that you can abjure all errors, nor does it follow at once that you have professed any error." To this Hus replied: "Most merciful Emperor, the word 'abjure' means something other than what your majesty has used here." And the Cardinal of Florence said: "A written form of abjuration will be given to you, John Hus, quite mild and tolerable. Then you will easily decide whether you are willing to do it or not." Then the Emperor again, repeating the words of the Cardinal of Cambrai: "You have heard that two ways are offered to you. First, that you publicly renounce those errors of yours, now condemned, and subscribe to the judgement of the council. For this, in return, you will experience its favour. But if you persist in defending your opinions, the council will easily have grounds to decide against you according to its laws." John Hus answered: "Most merciful Emperor, I refuse nothing that the council itself decides about me. I make only this exception: that I not offend God and my conscience, and that I not say I have professed those errors which never came into my mind to profess. I beg, moreover, that if it can be done, and with your leave, I may have the opportunity to declare my opinion more fully, so that I can answer, as far as is sufficient, concerning the charges brought against me, especially those about ecclesiastical offices." But the others, and the Emperor too, began to sing the same old tune to him again. "You are of an age," said the Emperor, "you could easily understand what I said to you yesterday and today. We are forced to believe the testimonies, which are most worthy of trust. Now if Scripture says that every word stands on the mouth of two or three witnesses, how much more on the very many testimonies of such great men! So then, if you are wise, you will accept from the council penance with a contrite heart, renounce your manifest errors, and promise on oath that you wish henceforth to hold and teach nothing contrary to them. If not, there are laws by which the council will judge you." To this speech of the Emperor a certain Polish bishop, now of decrepit age, responded with these words: "The laws concerning heretics, and the punishments they ought to suffer, are plain." John Hus persevered steadfastly, so that they cried out that he was obstinate. But a certain well-fed priest, shouting, said to the officers of the council: "He must by no means be admitted to recantation, for he has written to his friends that, even if he swears with his tongue, he wishes to keep his mind unsworn. Therefore he is not to be trusted." To this slander Hus again replied that he was conscious of no error. Then Paletz said: "Why this protest, by which you say that you defend no error of Wycliffe, when yet you do so?" Having said this, he produced nine articles of John Wycliffe as evidence, and after they had been read publicly, he added these words: "When I and Master Stanislaus were preaching against these articles at Prague, before Duke Ernest of Austria, he defended them obstinately, not only in sermons but also in published books. If you do not produce these books here, we will do so." The Emperor confirmed this. To him John Hus said: "I gladly allow that not only those books but also my other books be brought forward."

units.la: Ita vero tu omnes certatim ei molesti erant, ut jam viribus fere deficeret. nā & nocte[?] præteritam, dolore dentiū totam insomne duxerat.
units.tr: They were all so eager to harass him that he was almost worn out in strength; for during the previous night he had spent the whole time sleepless with toothache.

units.la: Lecta est in concilio etiam haec accusatio, quod videlicet tres Pragae obtruncati fuerint ob ea causam, quod ob Ioannis Husij doctrinā, in literas pontificias contumeliosi fuissent, eósque ipsos per eundem Hus cum pompa scholasticorum elatos, & publica concione in sanctorum numerum relatos esse. Et Naso ille, cuius etiam aliquot testimonia audita in hac causa fuerunt, eadem affirmabat, & se tum praesentem fuisse dicebat, cum rex Bohemiae mandasset blasphemos ultimo supplicio affici. Tum Hus, Utrumque hoc falsum est, & Regem hoc mandasse, & cadauera a me ad sepulturam cum aliqua pompa elata fuisse: cum ego ne adfuerim quidem. itaque & Regi & mihi iniuriā facitis. Paletz hoc argumento confirmabat Nafonis sententiam (tradebant enim operas mutuas) Regis edicto cautum fuit, ne quis bullae pontificiae contradiceret. illi tres contradixerunt bullae pontificiae. ergo virtute edicti regij fuerunt decollati. quid vero de iis senserit Io. Hus, ex eius libro de Ecclesia satis apparet, in quo haec sunt eius verba, Legerunt credo Prophetā Danicle, ubi scribitur, Et ruet gladio & flamma, & captiuitate dicru[?], & associabuntur eis multi fraudulenter. Et postea, Hoc implebitur in illis tribus laicis, qui non consentientes, imo co tradicentes Antichristi mendaciis, ceruices suas exposuerunt, &c. His lectis, mutuò se intuetes omnes, admirabundi aliquandiu tacuerunt. addiderant enim Paletz & Naso, Ioanne Hus publica concione populū adeò incendisse aduersus Magistratu, ut magna multitudo ciuiū palàm se opponeret, & eodem modo ut tres illi, morte contemneret, ita ut ægrè etiam ipsius Regis authoritate tandem sedata fuerit.
units.tr: In the council there was also read this accusation: that three men were beheaded at Prague for the reason that, because of the teaching of John Hus, they had been insulting towards the papal letters, and that the same Hus had carried their bodies to burial with a procession of scholars and had had them enrolled among the saints by a public sermon. And that Nasus, whose testimonies too were heard in this case, affirmed the same, and said that he himself was present when the King of Bohemia ordered the blasphemers to be put to death by the supreme penalty. Then Hus said: "Both of these things are false: that the King ordered this, and that the bodies were carried by me to burial with any pomp. I was not even present. Therefore you do wrong both to the King and to me." Paletz confirmed Nasus's statement with this argument (for they were rendering mutual services): "By a royal edict it was provided that no one should contradict the papal bull. Those three contradicted the papal bull. Therefore by virtue of the royal edict they were beheaded." What John Hus thought of these men is sufficiently clear from his book On the Church, in which are these words of his: "They have read, I believe, the prophet Daniel, where it is written: 'And they shall fall by the sword and by flame, and by captivity and spoil, and many shall join themselves to them deceitfully.' And afterwards: 'This will be fulfilled in those three laymen, who, not consenting but actually contradicting the lies of Antichrist, offered up their necks,' etc." When these passages had been read, all looked at one another and, astonished, were silent for some time. For Paletz and Nasus had added that John Hus had so inflamed the people by a public sermon against the magistrate that a great crowd of citizens openly opposed it, and in the same manner as those three, they despised death, so that the matter was calmed only with difficulty, even by the authority of the King himself.

units.la: Hac accusatione profequuti sunt Angli, exhibitis cocilio literis Scholæ Oxoniensis nomine, quibus quidè perlectis, ad tépus silentiū fuit, quod sanè abrupit Paletz, veluti meditata oratione insurgès, Deū testor, inquit, coràm Imperatoria maiestate, & reuerendissimis patribus, Cardinalibus, Episcopis, &c. me in hac accusatione Ioannis Hus, non aliquo erga eum odio aut malevolètia vsu esse, sed ut iuramèto meo satisfacerem, quod præstiti cum insignibus doctoralibus ornarer, me om errorū ad vtilitatem sacræ & catholicæ ecclesiæ acrè aduersariū fore. Hac oratione assensu profequutus est Michael de Causis. At ego, dixit Hus, cælesti Iudici hæc oia commedo, qui iustè vtriusq; partis causam iudicabit. Tu Cardinalis Cameracensis, Nō possum, inquit, satis mirari & pietatem & humanitatē domini Paletz, qua vsus est in ponendis articulis cōtra Ioanne Hus. profectò multò atrociora sunt in libris ipsius, vt audiuimus. Hæc cùm dixisset, iussit episcopus Rigesis, cuius fidei Hus cõmissus erat, vt in carcere sub præsidio reduceretur. eū sequutus D. de Chlu magnopere animū ipsius confirmauit. dici enim nõ potest, quantū recepit animi, vni' istius viri breuissimo colloquio, cū ī tāta acerbitate odiorū, ab aliisferè omnib' iā se desertū esse videret.
units.tr: The English pursued this accusation, presenting to the council letters in the name of the University of Oxford. When these had been read, there was silence for a time, which Paletz broke, rising as if with a prepared speech: "I call God to witness, before the Imperial Majesty and the most reverend fathers, Cardinals, Bishops, etc., that in this accusation of John Hus I have not acted out of any hatred or ill will towards him, but in order to satisfy my oath, which I swore when I was adorned with the doctoral insignia: that I would be a fierce adversary of every error, for the good of the holy and catholic Church." Michael de Causis followed this speech with his assent. But I, said Hus, commit all these things to the heavenly Judge, who will justly judge the cause of both parties. You, Cardinal of Cambrai, said: "I cannot sufficiently marvel at both the piety and the humanity which Master Paletz has shown in setting forth the articles against John Hus. Certainly, as we have heard, things far more atrocious are in his books." When he had said this, the Bishop of Riga, to whose faith Hus had been committed, ordered him to be taken back to prison under guard. Lord de Chlum followed him and greatly strengthened his spirit. For it cannot be said how much courage he gained from the very brief conversation with this one man, when he saw himself deserted by almost all the others amid such bitter hatred.

units.la: Postea quàm Hus abductus esset, cœpit Imperator in hac sententia præfectos cõcilij adhortari. Multa, cáq; grauissima in Ioanne Hus crimina audiuistis, nõ solùm firmis testimonijs probata, verumetiā ab ipso confessa, ex quibus singula, meo iudicio, mortis supplicio digna essent. nisi igitur recantet illa omnia, censeo vt ignis supplicio afficiatur. sin fecerit imperata, consulo nihilominus vt ei prædicandi & docendi officio, & ipso etiam regno Bohemiæ interdicatur. nequaquam enim committet, si iterum admittatur ad docendum, maximè verò in regno Bohemiæ, quin illorum, quos ibi habet, gratia & fauore fretus, ad ingenium redeat, & præter hos errores, nouos etiam in vulgus spargat. Censeo itaque articulos ipsius condemnatos, fratri meo regi Bohemiae, deinde in Poloniam & alias provincias, in quibus animi hominum eius doctrina sunt imbuti, mittendos esse cum huiusmodi mandato, ut quicunque ita sentire perrexerint, utriusque potestatis communi auxilio puniantur. Ita demum huic malo subueniri poterit, si rami vna cum ipsa radice funditus euellantur. Episcopi vero & alij Praelati, qui de extirpanda hac haeresi nunc laborant, ipsis Regibus & principibus, in quorum ditionibus sunt, totius cocilij[?] suffragijs commendentur. Postremo, si qui hic Constantiae reperiuntur Ioannis Hus familiares, illi quoque ea qua debent seueritate coerceatur.
units.tr: After Hus had been led away, the Emperor began to urge the presidents of the council toward this verdict. You have heard many and very grave charges against John Hus, proved not only by firm testimony but also confessed by himself, and in my judgement each of them deserves the penalty of death. Unless he recants all of them, I propose that he be punished by fire. If, however, he does what is commanded, I still advise that he be forbidden the office of preaching and teaching, and be barred from the kingdom of Bohemia itself. For if he is ever admitted to teach again, he will certainly not refrain, especially in the kingdom of Bohemia, from returning to his former ways, relying on the favour and support of those he has there, and from spreading new errors among the people alongside these old ones. I therefore propose that his condemned articles be sent to my brother, the king of Bohemia, and then into Poland and other provinces where men's minds have been steeped in his teaching, with an order that whoever persists in thinking this way be punished by the joint assistance of both powers. Only in this way can this evil be remedied, if the branches are torn out root and all. As for the bishops and other prelates who are now labouring to root out this heresy, let them be commended, by the votes of the whole council, to the kings and princes in whose lands they are. Finally, if any of John Hus's close associates are found here at Constance, let them too be restrained with the severity they deserve.

units.la: In primis vero discipulus eius Hieronymus. Illum profecto discipulum, acclamarunt alij, punito magistro speramus illico mitiorem fore. Haec cum dixissent, ex refectorio ubi convenerant, abierunt.
units.tr: But above all his disciple Jerome. Some of them shouted, "That disciple! We hope that once the master is punished he will soon become milder." When they had said this, they left the dining hall where they had gathered.

units.la: Eodem autem anno, quinto die Iunij, Sigismundus imperator, antea Ioannem Husiũ variis modis ad concilium illud perducere conatus, partim fide publica data, partim priuatis literis suis tutum fore pollicitus: haud ignarus tamen quid iam tum de eo concilium statuisset: misit clarissimos Barones, D. Ioannem Chlumensem, D. Wenceslaum Dubensem, & simul quatuor Episcopos ad Husiũ, qui apud Fraciscanos vinctus tenebatur: vt quid haberet animi, certo cognoscerent: vellet ne pertinaciter ea capita afferere quae testes obijcicbat, an mutare sententiam, & cum abiuratione suae doctrinae iuxta concilij decretum, diuersa prorsus scribere & docere:
units.tr: In the same year, on the fifth day of June, the Emperor Sigismund, who had earlier tried in various ways to bring John Hus to that council, promising him safe conduct, partly by a public pledge and partly by his private letters, yet well aware of what the council had already decided about him, sent the distinguished barons, Sir John of Chlum and Sir Wenceslaus of Duba, together with four bishops, to Hus, who was held in chains at the Franciscans' house.
