Come now, preachers who proclaim that the Pope is an earthly god, who can sell sacred things, as the lawyers say; that he is the head of the whole holy Church, governing it very well; that he is the heart of the Church, quickening it spiritually; that he is the fount from which all virtue and goodness flows; that he is the sun of the holy Church; that he is the safest refuge to which every Christian must flee, answer these things. Behold that head now cut off by the sword, now the earthly god bound, now his sins openly declared, now that fount dried up, the sun darkened, the heart pulled out and cast aside, lest anyone flee to it. The council condemned that head also for this crime, that he sold indulgences, bishoprics, and other things of that kind. But they condemned him by a judgment in which many had been buyers of such things from him, and in turn, by selling them to others, had carried on the trade. John, bishop of Litomyšl, was present there; he twice tried to buy the bishopric of Prague, but others got ahead of him. O lost men! Why did they not first cast the beam out of their own eye, since their law says: whoever has obtained any dignity with silver, let him be deprived of it? Therefore, seller and buyer, and whoever interposed himself in that contract, be openly condemned. Thus Saint Peter condemned Simon and made him anathema, when he wanted to buy the power of the Holy Spirit. These men have made the seller anathema and condemned him, but the buyers themselves and the approvers of this contract are without danger. What of the fact that they carry on this trade in their own homes? For at Constance one bishop buys and another sells. The Pope, however, who approved the deed, received gifts from both. So it is, as you know, also in Bohemia. I wish God had said in that council, "Whoever among you is without sin, let him pronounce sentence against Pope John." Undoubtedly one after another would have gone out. Why, before his fall, did they bend the knee before him, kiss his feet, and call him most holy, when they saw that he was a heretic, a murderer, a lost sinner, all of which they have now openly made plain about him? Why did the cardinals choose him as Pope, when they knew he had killed his holy father? Why did they allow him to trade in sacred matters even when he already held the office of Pope? For indeed they are his counsellors, so that they may advise him rightly. Are they not equally guilty of these crimes as he is? Since they bore some of these vices in him and were partakers in some of them, why, before he fled from Constance, did no one dare to object to him, but all feared him as a most holy father? When, however, the secular power, with God permitting or willing it, had seized him, they first conspired that he should in no way be freed from death. Now certainly the malice, abomination and filthiness of Antichrist has been revealed in the Pope and in the others of his company. Now the faithful servants of God can understand what the words of the Saviour mean, who says, "When you see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by Daniel," etc. "Let him who can grasp it, grasp it." Surely the greatest abomination is pride, avarice and simony in a desert place, that is, in a dignity deserted by goodness, humility and the other virtues, as we now clearly see in those who are set up in some magistracy or dignity. O how welcome it would be, if time allowed, to lay open the wickedness now known to me, so that the faithful servants of God could guard against it! But I trust in God that he will send after me men more vigorous than I, and there are already some who will better expose the malice of Antichrist, and will give up their souls to death for the truth of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will give both to you and to me the joy of eternal life. Letter written on the day of Saint John the Baptist, in prison, in fetters, in that meditation: that Saint John was beheaded in the chains of a prison for the word of God.

units.la: Recenset terriculamenta somniorum, quibus varie affectus est, etiamsi euentus probauerit omnia somnia vera fuisse[?].
units.tr: He recounts the terrifying dreams by which he was variously troubled, even though the outcome proved that all the dreams were true.

units.la: Dominus vobiscum. Consilium Domini diligo super aurum & topazium. Unde spero de misericordia Jesu Christi, quod dabit mihi spiritum suum, ad standum in veritate. Oretis Dominum: nam spiritus promptus est, caro autem infirma. Dominus omnipotens sit merces aeterna dominorum meorum, qui constanter, firmiter & fideliter stant pro iustitia, quibus dabit dominus Deus in regno Bohemiae cognoscere veritatem, quam, ut sequantur, necesse est cos redire in Bohemiam, postponendo vanam gloriam, & sequendo regem, non mortale, miserum, sed Regem gloriae, qui dat vitam aeternam. O quam grata fuit manus porrectio domini Joannis! qui non est verecundatus mihi misero manum porrigere, tam abiecto haeretico & inferrato, & quasi ab omnibus inclamato. Jam forte non multa loquar vobiscum: idea salutetis tempore quo videbitis omnes fideles Bohemos.
units.tr: The Lord be with you. I love the counsel of the Lord more than gold and topaz. So I hope, from the mercy of Jesus Christ, that he will give me his Spirit, to stand firm in the truth. Pray to the Lord, for the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. May the almighty Lord be the eternal reward of my lords, who stand constantly, firmly and faithfully for righteousness, and to whom the Lord God will give in the kingdom of Bohemia to know the truth. In order to follow it, they must return to Bohemia, setting aside empty glory and following the King, not a mortal and wretched one, but the King of glory, who gives eternal life. O how welcome was the outstretched hand of Master John, who was not ashamed to reach out his hand to me, a wretch, so abject a heretic, and cried out against by almost everyone! Perhaps I shall not say much more to you now; therefore greet all the faithful Bohemians for me, at the time when you see them.

units.la: Palecz venit ad me in carcerem, eius salutatio in maxima mea infirmitate, fuit ista coram commissariis. Quod non surrexit periculosior haereticus a natiuitate Christi, quam widef[?] & ego. Item dixit, quòd omnes qui meum sermonem visitauerunt, sunt infecti ista hæresi: Substantia panis materialis remanet in Sacramento altaris. Cui dixi, O Magister, quàm graviter me salutasti, & quàm graviter peccas! Ecce moriar, vel forte comburendo comburar, quid ergo muneris dabitur tibi in Bohemia? Istud forte non debui scribere, ne videar ipsum male odisse. Semper habui in corde meo, Nolite cōfidere in Principibus, &c. & iterum, Maledictus homo, qui confidit in homine, & ponit carnem brachium suum.
units.tr: Palecz came to me in prison. His greeting, while I was in great weakness, was this, spoken in the presence of the commissioners: that no more dangerous heretic had arisen since the birth of Christ than Widef[?] and I. He also said that all who have visited my sermon are infected with this heresy: the substance of material bread remains in the sacrament of the altar. To which I replied: "O Master, how gravely you greet me, and how gravely you sin! Behold, I shall die, or perhaps be burned in the fire; what reward, then, will be given you in Bohemia? Perhaps I ought not to have written this, lest I seem to hate him badly. I have always held in my heart: 'Put no trust in princes,' etc., and again, 'Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm.'"

units.la: Sciatis pro certo, quòd magnam pugnam habui cum somniis, ne ad ipsa exclamarem. Nam euasionem Papæ antea somniaveram. & post narrationem dominus Ioannes statim in nocte dixit, Vobis Papa redibit. Deinde etiam captiuitatem magistri Hieronymi, licet non in forma. Omnes carcerationes quò ducar, & qualiter patuerunt, licet non in forma. Serpentes multi sæpius apparuerunt, habetes capita etiā in cauda, sed nullus potuit me mordere: & multa alia. Ista scribo, non quòd me æstimem Prophetam, aut me extollam, sed ad dicendum vobis, quòd habui tentationes in corpore & in mente, & maximum timorem, ne transgrederer mandatum domini Iesu Christi. Iam recogito verbum magistri Hieronymi, qui dixit, Si venero ad concilium, æstimo quòd non reuertar. Ad me etiam dixit quidam bonus sartor, Andreas Polonus, valedicendo mihi, Deus sit tecum: vix enim, sicut mihi videtur, redibis incolumis, charissime & constantissime in veritate domine Ioannes: det tibi Rex, non Hungariæ, sed cælestis, omnia bona, pro tua fideli & diligenti, quam à te didici, doctrina.
units.tr: Know for certain that I have had a great struggle with dreams, lest I cry out to them. For I had earlier dreamed of the Pope's escape, and after I told it, Master John said at once that night, "The Pope will return to you." Then also the captivity of Master Jerome, though not in the same form; all the imprisonments to which I am led, and how they were opened, though not in the same form. Many serpents have often appeared to me, having heads even in their tails, but none could bite me; and many other things. I write these things not because I think myself a prophet, or to exalt myself, but to tell you that I have had temptations in body and mind, and the greatest fear lest I transgress the command of the Lord Jesus Christ. I now recall the word of Master Jerome, who said, "If I come to the council, I think I shall not return." A certain good tailor, Andrew the Pole, also said to me when bidding me farewell: "God be with you; for scarcely, as it seems to me, will you return unharmed, most dear and most constant in the truth, Master John. May the King, not of Hungary but the heavenly King, give you all good things, for your faithful and diligent teaching, which I learned from you."

units.la: O sancte Deus, quàm late potentiam & crudelitatem extendit Antichristus! Sed spero quòd abbreuiabitur potentia sua, & amplius denudabitur iniquitas eius in fideli populo. Deus omnipotens confirmabit corda suorum fidelium, quos elegit ante mundi constitutionem, vt accipiant immarcescibilem gloriæ coronam. Et furat quantum velit Antichristus, tamen non prævalebit contra Christum, qui illum interficiet spiritu oris sui, vt ait Apostolus, & tunc liberabitur creatura à seruitute corruptionis, in libertatem gloriæ filiorum Dei, ait Apostolus, subdens, Nosipsi intra nos gemimus, adoptionem filiorum Dei expectantes, redemptionem corporis nostri. Valde me consolatur illud verbum Saluatoris nostri, Beati eritis cum vos oderint homines & cum separauerint vos, & exprobrauerint, & ciecerint nomen vestrum tanquam malum, propter Filium hominis. Gaudete & exultate: ecce enim merces vestra est multa in cælis. Ioannes Hus in spe seruus Iesu Christi: à cuius spe nunquam potuit me diabolus separare, nec separabit etiamsi sum in vinculis & carcere, stas in præsentis vitæ litore, expectans in crastino diram morte, quæ ut spero purgabit mea peccata per Christum filium Dei vivi, Amen.
units.tr: O holy God, how widely Antichrist extends his power and cruelty! But I hope that his power will be shortened, and that his iniquity will be laid more bare among the faithful people. Almighty God will strengthen the hearts of his faithful, whom he chose before the foundation of the world, that they may receive the unfading crown of glory. And however much Antichrist may rage, he will not prevail against Christ, who will slay him with the breath of his mouth, as the Apostle says. Then the creature will be freed from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God, says the Apostle, adding: "We ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption of the sons of God, the redemption of our body." That word of our Saviour greatly comforts me: "Blessed are you when men hate you, and separate you, and revile you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of Man's sake. Rejoice and be glad, for behold, your reward is great in heaven." John Hus, a servant of Jesus Christ in hope, from whose hope the devil has never been able to separate me, nor will he separate me, even though I am in chains and prison, standing on the shore of the present life, awaiting a dreadful death tomorrow, which, as I hope, will purge my sins through Christ, the Son of the living God. Amen.

units.la: Hieronymus de Praga.
units.tr: Jerome of Prague.

units.la: Vemadmodū ratio vitæ ac studiorū, doctrinæque piæ, Ioannem Hus & Hieronymum de Praga summa familiaritate coniunxerat, ita sanctissima sociatas[?] mortis pro Euangelio subeundæ, eos communi fidei confessione copulauit: neque vlla tanta afflictionis magnitudo eos vnquam ab ea causæ optimæ iustissimæque coniunctione disiungere potuit. Possemus quidem hoc loco commemorare vitā antecedentem Hieronymi de Praga, nati in ea ciuitatis Pragensis parte quæ Noua dicitur: eius optima studia, mores, naturam, si res ipsa postularet, sed ratio ordoque huius libri instituti, eam commemorationem potius requirit, qua singularis eorū constantia cognoscatur, qui Martyres à Deo vocati, præclarum eius veritati testimonium dederūt, eāmq; vsq; ad extremū vitæ spiritū nō minus libere, quā pie, defenderunt.
units.tr: Just as the bond of study, of pious learning and of doctrine had joined John Hus and Jerome of Prague in closest friendship, so the most holy fellowship of undergoing death for the Gospel joined them in a common confession of faith; and no affliction, however great, was ever able to separate them from that most excellent and just union in the cause. We could indeed here recall the earlier life of Jerome of Prague, born in that part of the city of Prague called the New Town, and his excellent studies, character and nature, if the matter itself required it. But the plan and order of this book calls rather for that account by which the remarkable steadfastness of those is made known who, called by God as martyrs, gave a notable testimony to his truth and defended it, to the last breath of life, no less freely than piously.

units.la: Anno itaque à Christo nato, M.CCCCXV. vehementer anxius Hieronymus de Praga, quod patria audiret ab hostibus & domesticis & vicinis, multis falsisque premi calumniis, Ioāne quoq; Husiū à cocilio indignis modis vexari, venit summa cū animi alacritate Constantiā quarto Aprilis die. Ibi cū sibi struri insidias intellexit, postridie Iberlingam se recepit, ciuitatem Imperij, quæ ab vrbe distat non amplius vno miliari. Idque faciebat ne se sciens ac prudēs in periculum proiicere videretur. Inde literas ad Sigismundum Imperatorem, reliquosque Bohemiæ proceres, qui tum erat Constantiæ, scripsit: quibus petebat a Rege totoque concilio, ut ab ipsis fide data publica, quam Salui conductu vocant, liceret in vrbem ire: ac se, modò daretur audientia, respondere paratum esse, ad quascunque criminum prolationes. Verùm Imperator quòd sibi suas literas Hußio datas multu molestiæ exhibuisse diceret, id facturum negauit: collegium verò sacerdotum, se facturos illi quidem potestatem veniendi, etiam dato diplomate, affirmabat, sed recedendi, non item. His ad Hieronymū relatis, misit cōplures epistolas, Latinè, Bohemicè, & Germanicè scriptas, quas dclubrorum monasteriorumque valuis, atque Cardinalium ædibus affigi curauit. In his se declarabat Constantiā proptissimo venturū esse animo, propter certos tam patriæ quàm suæ doctrinæ detractatores, vt si qui ibi aliquam aduersus eum erroris aut hæreseos actione haberent, illi nomina sua vt prodcret rogabat: se præsto fore vt ipsis satisfaceret. Quòd si criminis alicuius conuinceretur, quod minimè verebatur[?], doceri, ita vt par est, & demonstrari errore cupiebat, modò fide publica ab ipsis accepta tutus esse posset. sin autem, quin culpa vacaret, per vim aut dolum ibi detineretur, notam omnibus postmodò fore illius concilij iniquitatè, quòd contra omnia diuina & humana iura, ipsum indicta causa condemnaret. Cæterùm quādo ne hac quidem ratione, quod volebat exprimeret ab Imperatore: impetratis saltè à Bohemiæ proceribus, qui tum ibi aderat, literis ipsorum sigillo obsignatis, quibus testabatur innocentia Hieronymi, & quæ admodùm in animo habuisset aduersarijs satisfaciendi de calumnijs. cū ijs, inquā, acceptis ipse in Bohemia reuerti statueret: in via per insidias ceperunt eum officiales Ducis Ioannes, filij Clementis: ac Sultzbrachium ad eundem ducem reduxerunt, vbi detentus tantisper fuit, dum ab Imperatore totóque concilio accerferetur: mox verò acceptis dux Ioannes ab Imperatore & concilio literis, vinctum Hieronymum Constantiā remisit, quem ibi excepit alter Clementis filius, cui Ludouico erat nomen, isque ad maiorem contumeliam catenis constrictum post se deduci curauit (ipse enim veluti triumphās præibat) ad cœnobium Minoritarum, quò principes sacerdotum & reliqua Pharisæorum sex confluxerant. Postquā verò ad Minoritas ventum est, & Hieronymus coram Episcopis constitit catenatus, lecta sunt ei scripta, diuersis nuper locis affixa, quibus ipse in ius vocatus erat, ob suas epistolas, quas passim ante, valuis apponi curarat: ibi quidā Episcopus ipsum copellās: Cur, inquit, fugisti, & in ius vocatò non venisti?
units.tr: In the year of Christ's birth 1415, Jerome of Prague, deeply anxious because he heard from home, from enemies, household members and neighbours alike, that he was being crushed by many false calumnies, and that John Hus too was being harassed by the council in unworthy ways, came to Constance on the fourth day of April with great cheerfulness of spirit. There, when he understood that snares were being laid for him, the next day he withdrew to Überlingen, an imperial city not more than one mile from Constance. He did this so that he would not seem to be knowingly and deliberately throwing himself into danger. From there he wrote letters to Emperor Sigismund and to the other nobles of Bohemia who were then at Constance. In them he asked the King and the whole council that, by a public pledge of faith, which they call a safe-conduct, given by themselves, he might be allowed to go into the city; and he said that he was ready to answer any charges brought against him, provided a hearing were granted. But the Emperor, saying that his own letter given to Hus had caused him much trouble, refused to do this. The college of priests, however, affirmed that they would indeed give him the power of coming, even with a written pass, but not of leaving. When these things were reported to Jerome, he sent several letters, written in Latin, Bohemian and German, which he had fixed to the doors of churches, monasteries and the houses of cardinals. In these he declared that he would come to Constance most willingly, on account of certain detractors both of his country and of his teaching; so that if any of them had some charge of error or heresy against him, he asked them to bring forward their names, and he would be present to give them satisfaction. But if he were convicted of any crime, which he did not at all fear, he wished to be taught and shown his error as is fitting, provided he could be safe under the public faith received from them. But if, on the other hand, he were detained there by force or trickery, though he was not at fault, he said it would afterwards be known to all how unjust that council was, condemning him unheard, contrary to all divine and human law. Moreover, since he could not extract what he wanted even in this way from the Emperor, he obtained at least letters from the Bohemian nobles who were then present there, sealed with their seal, by which they attested the innocence of Jerome and his intention to satisfy his adversaries concerning the calumnies. With these letters, I say, received, he resolved to return to Bohemia. On the way, officials of Duke John, son of Clement, seized him by ambush and led him back to the same duke at Sultzbach, where he was held until he should be summoned by the Emperor and the whole council. Soon, however, Duke John, having received letters from the Emperor and the council, sent Jerome back to Constance in chains. There another son of Clement, named Louis, received him, and to add to the insult had him led behind him, bound in chains (for he himself went ahead as if in triumph), to the monastery of the Minorites, where the chief priests and the rest of the Pharisees had gathered. But when they came to the Minorites, and Jerome stood chained before the bishops, there were read to him the writings, recently posted in various places, by which he had been summoned to judgment on account of his letters, which he had earlier had fixed to the doors everywhere. There a certain bishop addressed him: "Why did you flee, and not come when you were summoned to judgment?"

units.la: Tum ille: Quando nec ab Imperatore, nec a vobis extorquere potui fide publica, quemadmodū Baronum ad me scripta testatur: atque etiam hic mihi infestissimos esse hostes sensi[?], cedere visum fuit, ne temere solus, & non vocatus tantum discrimen subijsse viderer. Sed si mihi aliquid de vestra citatione significatum fuisset: proculdubio me haud piguisset vel e Bohemia Constantiam proficisci.
units.tr: Then he replied: "Since I could extract a public pledge of faith neither from the Emperor nor from you, as the letters of the barons to me attest, and since I have perceived here that my enemies are most hostile, it seemed best to withdraw, lest I seem to have rashly undertaken such danger alone and without being summoned. But if anything had been made known to me about your summons, I would undoubtedly not have minded setting out for Constance even from Bohemia."

units.la: His dictis magna sacerdotum turba cōtra pium virū cōcitata, testimonia producūt, & crimina clamore summo (ut eorū est mos) obiectant[?]. Eo autem tumultu sedato, Doctor quidam senior Cancellarius Parisiensis dicere coepit (is erat Gerson) Hieronyme cum Parisiis ageres, divinam quandam eloquetiam tibi arrogas, universam ibi turbabas Academiam, multis falsis conclusionibus in vulgus sparsis. Cui Hieronymus vicissim modestè admodum respondit: Venerande Magister, quo tempore Parisiis in publicis Gymnasiis orationes habebam, & de thematis, ex more magistrorum, firmis rationibus disserebam, nulla tum erat huius criminis mentio, quod tu intendis: quinimo in catalogum Magistrorum scholae Parisiensis relatus sum, & quod tum temporis astruebam, id etiamnum in hac frequenti coctione repetere non grauabor: & si quod erratum inueneritis, libens corrigam, & saniori doctrinae aequissimo animo auscultabo.
units.tr: With these words a great crowd of priests was stirred up against the pious man; they produce witnesses and, with the greatest clamour (as is their custom), bring their charges. When that tumult had been calmed, a certain senior doctor, the Chancellor of Paris, began to speak (it was Gerson): "Jerome, when you were at Paris you claimed for yourself a kind of divine eloquence; you threw the whole university there into confusion, spreading many false conclusions among the common people." To this Jerome replied in turn, very modestly: "Venerable master, at the time when I gave speeches in the public schools at Paris and disputed on set themes, with firm arguments, in the manner of masters, there was then no mention of this charge which you now bring. Indeed I was enrolled in the catalogue of the masters of the Paris school, and what I then maintained, I will not hesitate to repeat even in this crowded assembly. And if you find any error, I will gladly correct it and listen with the greatest equanimity to saner doctrine."

units.la: Adhuc Hieronymo loquente, alter nescio quis terrae filius (magister videtur fuisse Coloniensis) surrexit, & ad eum dixit: Tua oratio, meliuscule[?] culè, quam Coloniae quondam habuisti, multis erroribus scatebat, qui nondum ex hominum memoria effluxerunt. Agedum, inquit Hieronymus, vel unum quaeso errore palam profer. At ille attonitus quodammodo, Nunc non recordor (ait) cæterum post paulo contra te producetur. Et continuo surgens tertius Heidelbergensis, hoc modo sua accusatione instituit: Cū apud nos viueres, varias blasphemias praesertim de sancta Triade sparsisti, vbi & scutū pinxeras sanctā Trinitatē aquae, nisi & glaciei coparas. Ad hæc verba sic respondit Hieronymus, quaecunque ibi dixi, scripsi siue pinxi, eadē nunc etiā, si vultis, dicā, scribā & pingam: & si quae deprehensa fuerit falsitas, supplex retracta-bo, & meliori sententiae cedam. Interea ij qui circumstabant, exclamauerunt: Exurite, exurite hominem: Quod audiens Hieronymus sic sic est locutus, Quòd si meus interitus adeò insedit cordi & mea mors vobis placet: fiat voluntas Dei. Archiepiscopus verò Salisburgensis, Neutiquàm, ait, Hieronyme. Scriptum enim est, Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed vt convertatur & viuat.
units.tr: While Jerome was still speaking, another unknown son of the earth (he seems to have been a master from Cologne) rose and said to him: "Your speech, which you once gave at Cologne, was full of many errors, which have not yet passed out of men's memory." "Come on," said Jerome, "I ask you, bring forward just one error openly." But he, somewhat astonished, said: "I do not recall it now; however, it will be produced against you afterwards." At once a third man, from Heidelberg, rose and began his accusation in this way: "When you lived among us, you spread various blasphemies, especially about the holy Trinity, when you had even painted a shield with the holy Trinity as water, if not also as ice." To these words Jerome replied thus: "Whatever I there said, wrote or painted, the same I will now say, write and paint again, if you wish; and if any falsehood is detected, I will humbly retract it and yield to a better opinion." Meanwhile those standing around shouted: "Burn him, burn the man!" Hearing this, Jerome spoke thus: "If my death lies so deeply in your heart, and my death pleases you, let the will of God be done." But the Archbishop of Salzburg said: "By no means, Jerome. For it is written: I do not desire the death of a sinner, but that he be converted and live."

units.la: Tandem sine aliquo calumniarum & tumultu facto aduersus Hieronymum, traditur ipse lictoribus urbis: caeteri se domum suam quisque contulerunt. Lictores cum in certas quasdam aedes duxerunt, quò accurrens quidam de familia Hussij Petrus Notarius, per fenestram ei est locutus, Mi praeceptor, inquies, bono & firmo animo sis, nec dubites veritatis causa morte intrepidus subire: de qua multa liber olim sapienter disputasti. Cui Hieronymus, Mi frater, ait, gratias tibi ago, quòd me innuisseris, méque morte non pertimescere scito, de qua cùm multis verbis quondam disseruerim, nunc re ipsa experiri opus est quid possit. Hoc sermone ad fenestram conversi custodes, Petrum cum minis abegerunt. Hieronymum verò arreptum in turrim quandam ad coemiterium S. Pauli, coiecerunt, manibus vinctis, & pedibus prealto carcere conclusis, vt considere non posset, sed capite tantum pendulus terram attingere: atque ita cùm plures dies excruciabatur, pane solo & aqua vitâ trahens. Sed jam ex tantis cruciatibus grani quoque morbo confectus, petebat sibi dari confessorem, Sperans mitius secum actum iri, quia se ritibus ipsorum accomodaret. Quae spes aliquandiu illum lactauit: nam remissiore deinceps usus est custodia, in qua annum mansit, exceptis diebus septem.
units.tr: At last, without any further calumny or tumult against Jerome, he was handed over to the city's lictors; each of the others went home to his own house. When the lictors led him to certain houses, a certain Peter the notary, of Hus's household, ran up and spoke to him through a window: "My teacher, be of good and firm heart, and do not doubt that you will undergo death fearlessly for the sake of the truth, about which you once wisely disputed at length." Jerome replied: "My brother, I thank you that you have encouraged me, and know that I do not dread death, about which I once disputed at length in many words; now it is necessary to experience in fact what it can do." At these words the guards turned towards the window and drove Peter away with threats. They seized Jerome and threw him into a certain tower by the cemetery of St Paul, his hands bound and his feet shut in a deep prison, so that he could not sit but hung down by his head alone, touching the ground. So, while he was tortured for many days, living on bread alone and water, and now worn out by such torments and by a grave illness, he asked that a confessor be given him, hoping that he would be treated more gently if he accommodated himself to their rites. This hope buoyed him for some time, for afterwards he was kept under a more relaxed custody, in which he remained for a year, except for seven days.

units.la: Interea Ioannes Hussius à tyrannis illis iniustè condemnatus, coburitur octauo à feriis Petri & Pauli die: ac circiter festum nativitatis Mariae Virginis eodem anno, Hieronymum diuturnis vinculis confectum ad se evocari iussérunt, eiq; multis minis propositis persuadere conati sunt vt decederet à sententia, & condemnationi Ioannis Hussij iure, vt aicebat[?], cobusti subscriberet. Ibi ille per infirmitatem lapsus, partim horrore supplicij, partim spe euadedi[?] ex ipsorum crudelissimis manib°, formulâ aburationis sibi datâ ex scripto publicè recitauit: addidit praeterea in gratiam illorum, Hussiu[?] iure igni absumptu. Quo quidem facto non cuadebat[?], sed ad eãdem turrim deductus, minùs seuerè quàm ātea tractabatur.
units.tr: Meanwhile John Hus, unjustly condemned by those tyrants, was burned on the eighth day after the feast of Saints Peter and Paul. Around the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary that same year, they ordered Jerome, worn down by his long imprisonment, to be summoned before them. With many threats held over him, they tried to persuade him to abandon his opinion and to subscribe to the condemnation of John Hus, who, as they said, had been rightly burned. There, weakened by infirmity, partly by the horror of punishment and partly by hope of escaping from their most cruel hands, he publicly read aloud from a written text the form of recantation given to him. He added, moreover, to win their favour, that Hus had been rightly consumed by fire. By this act he did not escape, but was led back to the same tower and treated less harshly than before.

units.la: Iam verò sequenti anno M.CCCC. XVI. accesserunt novi hostes Carmelitæ ex Bohemia, qui novas accusationes habebant aduersus Hieronymum. Horum advetu gavisi, pestilentissimi nebulones Michael de causis & magister Paletz apostatae, pergut[?] urgere causa adversus Hieronymum, quem ipsi certis indiciis collegerant non ex animo renuntiasse suae doctrinae, sed id tantum formidine poenae fecisse, atque spe liberationis: instat apud Cardinales, qui in eo concilio iudiciis præsidebant, ut reu ad crimina a prioribus diversa respondere cogat. Verum illi perspecta inimicorum malitia, & iniuria, qua miserum hominem afficerent, sedulo de eo liberando egerunt. Hostes contra summa ope contendebant, ne quo modo illi parceretur, clamantes indignum facinus patrocinari tam scelerato haeretico: atque prae caeteris egregius Doctor, Naso dictus, Cardinales his ipsissimis verbis compellavit:
units.tr: In the following year, 1416, new enemies arrived from Bohemia, the Carmelites, who brought fresh accusations against Jerome. Rejoicing at their arrival, the most pestilent scoundrels, Michael de Causis and Master Paletz, an apostate, went on pressing the case against Jerome. They had gathered from certain signs that he had not renounced his teaching from the heart, but had done so only from fear of punishment and in hope of release. They pressed the cardinals, who presided over the judgment in that council, to compel the accused to answer to charges different from the earlier ones. But the cardinals, seeing the malice of the enemies and the injustice they were inflicting on the wretched man, zealously worked for his deliverance. The enemies, on the other hand, strove with all their might that he should be spared in no way, crying out that it was an outrage to defend so wicked a heretic. And above all the distinguished teacher, called Naso, addressed the cardinals in these very words:

units.la: Miranur de vobis patres reverendissimi, quod vestrae paternitates pro tali pessimo haeretico intercedunt, propter quem nos in Bohemia cum toto clero multa mala passi sumus, & vestrae paternitates patientur. Et timeo quod forsitan ab illis haereticis vel a Rege Bohemiae munera accepistis. Cardinales autem, huius ac ceterorum furiosis clamoribus labefactati, causam Hieronymi deserunt, & se iudicandi officio abdicarunt: in quorum locum, impulsu malevolorum, & veritatis infestissimorum hostium, quos modo nominavi, instinctu, successerunt Patriarcha titulo tenus Constantinopolitanus, & quidam doctor Teutonicus: qui iudices nuper pium virum Ioannem Hus mortis damnaverat.
units.tr: "We, most reverend fathers, are amazed at you, that your paternities intercede for such a wicked heretic, on whose account we in Bohemia, with the whole clergy, have suffered many evils, and your paternities will suffer them too. And I fear that perhaps you have received gifts from those heretics, or from the King of Bohemia." The cardinals, however, shaken by the furious outcries of this man and the others, abandoned Jerome's cause and renounced their office of judging. In their place, at the instigation of the malicious and of the most hostile enemies of the truth just named, there succeeded the Patriarch, bearing only the title of Constantinople, and a certain Teutonic teacher. These were the judges who had lately condemned the pious man John Hus to death.

units.la: At Hieronymus hos novos iudices repudiabat, coram quibus in vinculis ne verbum quidē privatim eloqui volebat: sed subinde cupiebat sibi fieri potestatem publice in frequenti concione animi sui sententiam explicandi. in quo praesides & seniores concilii facile ipsi assenserunt, rati Hieronymum palinodiam paulo ante factam iteraturum, atque magis confirmaturum. Itaque anno eodem XXV. die Maij, qui erat dies Sabbathi ante Ascensionem, Hieronymus ad amplissimum templum ducitur palam audiendus, ubi centum & septem accusationis capita lecta sunt, de quibus etiam testibus cuistum[?] clamabant, atque adeo condemnatum. Attamen reo defendendi sese copia, qua petierat, facta est. Hic Hieronymus, mirum bone Deus, quanta animi solertia & alacritate, ac si nullos cruciatus diuturnae custodiae sensisset, a diluculo usque ad meridiem, plus minus quadraginta articulos refellebat: quorum autem sibi non erat conscius, quæque à falsis testibus ementita agnouit crimina, simplici negatione se se purgans prætermisit. Cæterùm quoniam eo die non posset absoluere suam causam propter horā meridianam, reiectus est in diem martis, quo quidem die summo mane ad eundem locum ductus, ad reliqua accusationis capita non minori constantia & ingenij dexteritate respondit, & commodè supra modum criminationes in ipsos aduersarios retorsit, adeò vt oratione qua ipsorum testimonia eleuabat, pudefacti, turpissimè obmutuerint.
units.tr: But Jerome rejected these new judges, and though in chains he would not utter so much as a word before them in private. He kept asking, however, that he be given the opportunity to explain his mind publicly before a full assembly. In this the presidents and elders of the council readily agreed, thinking that Jerome would repeat and confirm more firmly the recantation he had made a little before. So on the twenty-fifth day of May in that same year, which was the Saturday before the Ascension, Jerome was led to the very large church to be heard openly. There a hundred and seven heads of accusation were read out, which they cried were proved by witnesses, and on which he was therefore condemned. Nevertheless, the accused was granted the opportunity to defend himself, which he had asked for. Here Jerome, good God, with what skill and eagerness of mind, as if he had felt no torment of his long imprisonment, from dawn until midday refuted some forty articles. Those of which he was not conscious, and those crimes which he recognised as having been lied about by false witnesses, he passed over, clearing himself by a simple denial. But since on that day he could not finish his defence because of the midday hour, he was put off until Tuesday. On that day, very early in the morning, he was led to the same place, and he answered the remaining articles of accusation with no less steadfastness and skill in argument. He also turned the charges back against the adversaries with remarkable effect, so that by his speech, in which he exposed their testimonies, they were put to shame and fell silent in disgrace.

units.la: In hoc quoque consessu, mirùm quanta disserendi solertia de variis Philosophorũ disciplinis, & diuinis scriptis cum summa auditorũ admiratione ad pomeridianũ vsque tempus dixerit: demonstrabat enim quemadmodum omnibus seculis odiosa mundo fuisset veritas, idque probabat virorum sapientũ exemplis, nec non Prophetarum & Apostolorum & post eos martyrum, qui omnes veritatis causa tanquam seditiosi & publicæ tranquillitatis perturbatores aut in Deum blasphemi, iniuriâ condemnati, variis supplicior̃ generibus affecti fuere. Tũ oratione ad suum negotium reflexa: nonnulla de vitæ suæ cursu dicere cœpit, perstringens obiter quæ in Germaniæ, Galliæ & Bohemiæ Academiis celeberrimis gesserat, casus etiam & labores enarras quos in diuersis profectionibus passus erat, neque id silentio præteribat, quo pacto regnante wenceslao, ipse cum reliquis suæ gentis magistris, in administrando Pragæ gymnasio, expulsis Germanis, qui Bohemis inuidebant, primas obtinuisset. Adhæc venit ad laudes Iohânis Hussij quæ[?] sibi à paruulo cognitum aiebat, nec tamen in eo vnquam vel libidinis, vel ebrietatis vitia perspexisse, sed summũ semper honestatis & temperantiæ studium, ardentem veritatis amorem, vt qui fideliter & piè synceram doctrinam, in qua diligenter versatus erat, docuisset. Proinde huius & Ioannis wicleffi conciones, quibus illi insolentiam, malitiam, scortationes, & auaritiâ sacerdotum (his enim hoc genus hominum scatebat) insectati fuerant, valdè probare: nec latum quidem vngue (vt aiunt) ab his discessurum. Quod autem ad symbolũ fidei attinet, ea omnia se credere affirmabat & afferere cum sancta Ecclesia catholica, hæreses omnes detestari. Postremò hoc adiecit, ex omnibus peccatis, quibus hactenus maiestatem diuinam offenderat, nullo tantùm suam conscientiam premi & gravari, atque eo, quod in execranda & pestifera cathedra admiserat, ubi infirmitate lapsus & horrore mortis retractare coactus, condemnationi Ioannis Hussij subscripsit, multaque in gratiam adversariorum contra tam pii viri doctrina locutus est: quare se in eodem suggestu, dei beneficio constitutum, iam tanti sceleris poenitere, & irritam habere suam subscriptionem, quoniam bonus ille vir summa iniuria raptus esset ad supplicium. Hactenus Hieronymus.
units.tr: In this assembly too, it was remarkable with what skill in argument, and with great admiration from his hearers, he spoke on the various schools of the philosophers and on the divine writings until the afternoon. For he showed how truth had in every age been hateful to the world, and proved this by the examples of wise men, and of the prophets and apostles, and after them of the martyrs, all of whom, for the sake of the truth, were condemned unjustly as seditious men and disturbers of public peace, or as blasphemers against God, and were subjected to various kinds of punishment. Then, turning his speech back to his own affair, he began to tell something of the course of his life, touching in passing on what he had done in the most famous academies of Germany, France and Bohemia. He also recounted the dangers and labours he had endured in his various journeys. Nor did he pass over in silence how, in the reign of Wenceslas, he himself, with the other masters of his nation, had gained the first place in running the Prague gymnasium, after the Germans, who envied the Bohemians, had been expelled. Moreover, he came to praise John Hus, whom he said he had known from boyhood, and in whom he had never seen any vice of lust or drunkenness, but always the highest zeal for honesty and temperance and an ardent love of truth, since he had faithfully and piously taught the sincere doctrine in which he had diligently been engaged. Therefore he greatly approved the sermons of this man and of John Wycliffe, in which they had attacked the arrogance, malice, fornication and avarice of the priests (for this sort of men abounded), and he said that he would not depart a hair's breadth (as they say) from them. As for the creed, he affirmed and asserted that he believed all those articles together with the holy catholic Church, and that he detested all heresies. Finally he added that, of all the sins by which he had hitherto offended the divine majesty, none weighed so heavily on his conscience as the act he had committed in that accursed and pestilent pulpit. There, overcome by infirmity and the horror of death, and compelled to retract, he had subscribed to the condemnation of John Hus and had said much in favour of the adversaries against the teaching of so pious a man. Wherefore he said that, now set in that same pulpit by God's kindness, he repents of so great a crime and holds his subscription void, since that good man had been dragged to his punishment by the greatest injustice. Thus far Jerome.

units.la: Priore huius orationis parte mirifice auditores commouit, ut homine liberari omnes percuperent, tanta ille dicendi suavitate animos eorum cepit, atque in suam sententiam pertraxit. Sed epilogo, ubi multa de laudibus Ioannis wiclef, & Hus inferebat exacerbati, dixerunt quod iam se ipse condemnaverit. Itaque statim in carcere rapitur, ubi crudelissime, manibus pedibusque & media corporis sui parte catenis constrictus iacuit: donec die Sabbati post Ascensionem, magna armatorum militum cinctus caterva, ad idem templum ducitur. Hic enim eo die frequens erat sacerdotum & monachorum confessus, ad serendā adversus Hieronymum sententiam: ac primo hortatur ut in priori illa revocatione perstet, wiclefi & Hussij doctrinam aperte contemnat. Contra ille sine metu fortique pectore multis in eum ordine invectus: Testor, inquit, Dominum Deum meum, & vos omnes, nihil me hæreticum sentire. Atqui omnes fidei articulos & credo & assero, quemadmodum sancta Ecclesia catholica facit. Caeterum sententiae vestrae, qua factos[?] illos & Christianos, spiritu vertiginis actos[?], damnastis[?], quod vitam vestram perditissimam & verbis detexerat & in suis libris, aptis coloribus depinxerat, neutiquam accedo. Quamvis enim nulla ob rem aliam mihi a vobis certum supplicium decretum esse sciam: nihil tamen contra conscientiam adversus eos proferā, quos recte de flagitiis vestris & traditionibus pravis scripsisse, & locutos esse non ignoro.
units.tr: The first part of this speech stirred the hearers wonderfully, so that all of them desired the man to be freed; with such sweetness of speech he captured their minds and drew them to his view. But in the closing part, where he brought in much in praise of John Wycliffe and Hus, his enemies, enraged, said that he had now condemned himself. So he was at once seized and dragged back to prison, where he lay most cruelly bound, with his hands, feet and the middle of his body fastened in chains. Then, on the Saturday after the Ascension, he was led to the same church, surrounded by a large band of armed soldiers. For on that day a crowd of priests and monks had gathered to pronounce sentence against Jerome. First they urged him to persist in his earlier recantation and openly to despise the teaching of Wycliffe and Hus. He, without fear and with a brave heart, having at length railed against them in order, said: "I call the Lord my God and you all to witness that I hold no heretical opinion. Indeed, I both believe and assert all the articles of faith, as the holy catholic Church does. But I by no means assent to your sentence, by which you condemned those men, who were Christians, as driven by a spirit of giddiness, because they had exposed your most depraved life in their words and had painted it in their books in fitting colours. Although I know that you have decreed no other certain punishment for me, I will nevertheless bring nothing against my conscience against those whom I know to have written rightly about your crimes and your corrupt traditions, and to have spoken rightly."

units.la: Haec postquam intrepide palam confessus esset, tandem Episcopus Londensis conscendens suggestum, concionem, ad ferendam adversus Hieronymum mortis sententiam, concauit[?]. Hoc autem themate suae concionis sumpto ex Marco: Corrupit Christus infidelitatem eorum, & duritiam cordis. Quemadmodum, inquit, nuper sacrū istud concilium, pessimorum haereticorum wiclefi & Hussij vltimum est infidelitatem, doctrinam eorum reiiciens, vt errorum plenam, haeresi infectam, sanctae Ecclesiae perniciosam: ita in Hieronymum eorum sectatorem, hominem durae ceruicis, arrogantem, & in sua malitia pertinacem, animaduertat, vt caeteris exemplo sit, ne tale quid vnquam audeant. Si vero qui posthac emerserint eius sectae homines, tum omnibus promiscue datur authoritas contra eos dicendi testimonium, quamuis infamia etiam notatis, ganeonibus, latronibus, scortatoribꝰ, meretricibus, denique pessimi quique testes audientur, & si opus fuerit diris etiam tormentis ab ipsis confessio extorquebitur, & mox e medio tollentur, neque vllus erit veniae locus, nisi cedant & palinodiam canant.
units.tr: When he had openly and boldly confessed these things, at last the Bishop of London mounted the platform and delivered a sermon to pronounce the sentence of death against Jerome. He took as the theme of his sermon this text from Mark: "Christ rebuked their unbelief and the hardness of their heart." "Just as," he said, "this holy council recently condemned the unbelief of the most wicked heretics Wycliffe and Hus, rejecting their doctrine as full of errors, infected with heresy, and pernicious to holy Church, so it now passes judgment on Jerome, their follower, a man of stiff neck, arrogant and obstinate in his malice, so that it may be an example to others, lest they ever dare anything of the sort. And if men of this sect should emerge hereafter, then testimony against them will be permitted to all without distinction, even to those marked with infamy: debauchees, robbers, whoremongers, prostitutes. In short, the worst sort of people will be heard as witnesses, and if necessary, confession will be extorted from them even with dreadful torments, and they will soon be removed from the midst. There will be no room for pardon unless they recant and sing the palinode."

units.la: Tui vero Hieronyme, quis misereatur? quadoquidem reuocatione quam antea euomuisti[?], jam canis[?] in morem resorbere non es veritus, neq; id fecisti sine offendiculo & summo sacri huius cōcilij dedecore. Quapropter quaecunque condemnationis sententia de te feretur ab hoc cōcilio, iusta & te digna erit.
units.tr: But for you, Jerome, who will have mercy? Since by the recantation you formerly vomited forth, you were not ashamed to lick it up again like a dog, and you did this not without offence and great dishonour to this sacred council. Therefore whatever sentence of condemnation is passed against you by this council will be just and worthy of you.

units.la: Absoluta huius Episcopi concione, Hieronymus iterum non minus sapieti quam forti & praesenti animo aperte ostendere coepit summam sibi fieri iniuriam, nullus se criminis, quod errore, haeresimue saperet, vel cū fide Christiana pugnaret, reū esse: nisi forte peccatum, inquit, ducatis maximum, quia impios sacerdotes, & perditae vitae sacrificos reprehendi: male sane me habuit, quod suo munere abuteretur, nec vita ipsorum cū professione & officio congrueret. Nunc si solis testibus innixi, me quoque nō audiatis: testor Deū & homines, vos iniquos esse iudices, qui in me solum inuidetia ductii sæuiatis. Hac oratione audita, quidā aduersariorum submonebant, vt iamque iterum retractaret, alioqui de ipso actu esse. Is vero morte propinqua cernens, sic contra eos libere est locutus & vaticinatus. Vos statuistis nunc me innocēte ad poenam rapere: at ego post meum obitū vestris conscientijs aculeos & scrupulos relinquo, atque appello ad celsissimū simul & aequissimū iudicē Deum omnipotentem, vt coram eo, centum annis elapsis, respondeatis mihi. Illi autē hac voce risu exceperunt, ac statui iusserunt[?] sententiam cōtra eū multis verbis perscriptam, recitariq; cuius haec summa erat.
units.tr: When this bishop's sermon was ended, Jerome again, with no less wisdom than courage and presence of mind, began to show openly that a great wrong was being done to him. He said he was not guilty of any crime that smelt of error or heresy or fought against the Christian faith, "unless you count it a very great sin that I rebuked impious priests and sacrificers of a wicked life. It indeed went badly with me that they abused their office and that their life did not agree with their profession and calling. Now, if you rely only on witnesses and will not hear me too, I call God and men to witness that you are unjust judges, who rage against me alone, driven by envy." When this speech was heard, some of his opponents urged him to retract again, otherwise it would be all over for him. But he, seeing death near, spoke freely against them and prophesied: "You have now decided to drag me to punishment though I am innocent. But after my death I leave stings and goads in your consciences, and I appeal to God almighty, the most high and most just judge, that when a hundred years have passed you answer to me before him." They received this with laughter and ordered that a sentence written out at length against him be read aloud, the substance of which was this.

units.la: Sacrū Constantiense concilium, Hieronymū Pragensem ob eius errores, temerarios ausus[?], atque pertinaciam: & maximè, quòd priorem retractationem violauit cum magno sacri concilij probro, jam hunc tanquam ramum putridum & marcidum ab radice exscindit, & damnat ut haereticum execrandum & maledictum: tradítque eum magistratui politico, ut de eo dignum impietate ipsius sumat supplicium.
units.tr: The Sacred Council of Constance, on account of Jerome of Prague's errors, rash attempts and obstinacy, and especially because he violated his earlier recantation to the great shame of the sacred council, now cuts him off like a rotten and withered branch from the root, condemns him as an execrable and accursed heretic, and hands him over to the civil magistrate, that he may exact from him a punishment worthy of his impiety.

units.la: Lata itaque in hanc fere rationem sententia: Ecce Hieronymo corona chartacea affertur, depictis circumcirca cacodaemonibus decora: quam simulatque vidit abiecto suo pileo, in turbam sacerdotum, capiti suo imposuit, dicens, Dominus meus Iesus Christus, pro me misero moriturus, spineam coronam in capite suo gestabat, longe quidem graviorem: ego quoque vicissim ipsius gratiae & amoris nomine cum hac libens in ignem accedam. His dictis mox a litoribus teplo[?] educitur & inter eundum, fidem catholicam, ut vulgò in templo catari solet, defixis in cælum oculis, magna voce lætus canebat: & deinceps alios hymnos donec extra portam venit ad eum locum, in quo nuper Ioannes Hus trucidatus fuerat.
units.tr: The sentence was pronounced in roughly this manner. A paper crown, decorated with devils painted all around, is brought to Jerome. As soon as he saw it, he took off his cap and, before the crowd of priests, put the crown on his head, saying: "My Lord Jesus Christ, who was to die for me a wretch, wore a crown of thorns on his head, a much heavier one indeed; I too, in turn, for the sake of his grace and love, gladly go into the fire with this." After these words he was at once led out by the lictors, and as he went he joyfully sang aloud, with his eyes fixed on heaven, the Catholic faith, as is customarily sung in church, and then other hymns, until he came outside the gate to the place where John Hus had recently been put to death.

units.la: Ibi ad stipitem ad quem exurendus erat, in genua procidens, diu tacitè secum orabat: carnifices deinde erectu[?] vestibus exuunt, atque sordido in humeros iniecto linteo, cum staret ad palum catenis deligatus: pyram undique stramin ibus mista construunt. Interea Hieronymus sublata rursus voce hymnū paschalem cecinit:
units.tr: There, at the stake to which he was to be burned, he knelt down and for a long time prayed silently to himself. Then the executioners stripped him of his clothes and, throwing a dirty linen cloth over his shoulders, bound him with chains to the stake while he stood. They built the pyre on all sides with mixed straw. Meanwhile Jerome, raising his voice again, sang the Easter hymn:

units.la: Salue festa dies, toto venerabilis ævo,Qua Deus infernum vicit, & astra tenet, &c.
units.tr: Hail, festal day, venerable through all ages, on which God conquered hell and holds the stars, etc.

units.la: Absoluto hoc hymno, iterum fidem catholicam carmine professus, circunstantem turbam, teutonico idiomate sic allocutus est: Scitote charissimi viri, me non aliter credere quàm modò cecini, neque de fidei nostrae symbolo sentire ut Christianum decet: nunc autem morti addictus sum, quòd huic sacerdotum concilio in condemnando Huffio[?] non consenserim, qui (ut de vitae integritate, & morum suauitate quam in eo viro ab incunabulis perspexi, nihil dicā) fidus diuinae Legis & Euangelij Iesu Christi concionator extitit.
units.tr: When this hymn was finished, again professing the Catholic faith in song, he addressed the surrounding crowd in the German language: "Know, dearest men, that I believe no otherwise than I have just sung, nor do I think about the creed of our faith otherwise than a Christian should. But now I am condemned to death because I did not consent to this council of priests in condemning Huss, who (not to speak of the integrity of his life and the sweetness of his morals, which I have observed in that man from his cradle) was a faithful preacher of the divine law and of the Gospel of Jesus Christ."

units.la: Postquam verò à calce vsque ad verticem vndique lignis sepserant, veste ipsius in rogum iniectâ, facestruem accendunt carnifices. Tum ipse altissimè hæc cecinit: In manus tuas Domine, commendo spiritum meum. Adhæc flamma præpeditus, sic postremò Bohemicè vociferatus est: Domine Deus, pater omnipotens, miserere mei, & remitte mihi peccata mea: tu enim nosti me tuae veritatis amatorem fuisse. Tandem igne obrutus, visus est motis labiis apud se orare, dum expiraret. Interea lectus cum reliqua ipsius supellectili ex carcere apportatur, omnibusq; rebus igne cū cōpenitus [?] cōsumptis, cineres in Rhenum proiecti sunt. Sic eruditus iuxta ac pius vir à Pontificia factione, propter nomen Iesu Christi, in pulverem est redactus:
units.tr: After they had piled wood on him on all sides from his feet to his head, and thrown his garment onto the pile, the executioners set fire to the pyre. Then he sang aloud: "Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit." Still hindered by the flame, at last he cried out in Bohemian: "Lord God, almighty Father, have mercy on me and forgive me my sins, for you know that I have been a lover of your truth." Finally, overwhelmed by the fire, he seemed, with lips moving, to pray to himself as he expired. Meanwhile his bed, with the rest of his household goods, was brought from the prison, and when everything had been completely consumed by the fire, the ashes were thrown into the Rhine. Thus this learned and pious man was reduced to dust by the Papist faction, on account of the name of Jesus Christ:

units.la: S- ubsequuta sunt hæc morte Ioannis Hus & Hierony- mi Pragensis.
units.tr: The events that followed the death of John Hus and Jerome of Prague.

units.la: POsteaquàm nuntium in Bohemiam allatum est, de crudelitate eo-rum, qui Constantiæ Ioannem Hus & Hieronymum Pragensem acerbissima morte multauerant, ij qui eos duos viros amauerant, eorumque opera & disciplina aliquem verbi Dei gustum perceperat, à Wenceslao Bohemiæ rege impetrarunt, vt haberent certa templa, in quibus libere & verbū Dei annūtiari, & sacramēta administrari possent. Deinde ad detestandam eam rem, eo in concilio actam, contra omnem rationem, ius gentium, æquitatem, à barbaris etiam nationibus populisque semper conseruatam, tum verò ad memoriam singularis fidei ac virtutis Ioannis Hus perpetuandam, monetam argeteam curauerunt conficiendam, quam nomine illius inscriptam, Hussiticam nominauerunt: cuius in ora undique hæc verba incisa fuerunt, Post centum annos vos Deo & mihi respondebitis: quibus quidem verbis vsus Ioannes Hus, certissimum Dei iudicium iis denuntiauit, à quibus iniusta morte afficeretur, vnumquenque eorum ad certum definitumque vitæ spatium reuocans: vel potius in spiritu propheticæ prædicens eam rerum commutationem, quæ centum post eius mortem annis, in ecclesia est consecuta. Vir quidem beatissimæ memoriæ Martinus Lutherus, cuius opera Deus Euangelium ecclesiæ restituit, ea verba Hus accommodat ad illud tempus, quo ipse impias Papæ indulgentias aggressus est, qui fuit ānus M. D.XVII. centesimus prope ab eo, quo Ioan. Hus Constantiæ crematus est, qui fuit M.CCCC.XVI.
units.tr: After news reached Bohemia of the cruelty of those who at Constance had put John Hus and Jerome of Prague to a most bitter death, those who had loved these two men, and through whose work and teaching some taste of the Word of God had been received, obtained from Wenceslaus, king of Bohemia, that they might have certain churches in which the Word of God could be preached freely and the sacraments administered. Then, to denounce that deed, done at that council against all reason, the law of nations, and justice, which even barbarous nations and peoples have always observed, and to perpetuate the memory of the singular faith and virtue of John Hus, they had a silver coin struck, named the Hussite after him. Around its rim these words were engraved: "After a hundred years you will answer to God and to me." By these words John Hus, as it were, announced to those by whom he was to be unjustly put to death the certain judgment of God, calling each of them to a fixed and definite span of life; or rather, speaking prophetically in the Spirit, he foretold that change of affairs which followed in the Church a hundred years after his death. The most blessed Martin Luther, through whose work God restored the gospel to the Church, applies those words of Hus to the time when he himself attacked the impious indulgences of the Pope, which was the year 1517, nearly a hundred years after John Hus was burned at Constance, in 1416.

units.la: Itaque idem Lutherus aliud eiusdem vaticinium commemorat de ansere, id est, Hus, qui lingua Bohemorum anserem significat: quem illi quidem tum torrerent, sed non cygnum, qui venturus post ipsum, vstulatione illorum effugeret. Quibus verbis, quũ genus mortis suæ, tum etiam exitum Lutheri quietum, atque ab illorum sœuitia tutũ, videtur significasse.
units.tr: Therefore the same Luther recalls another prophecy of Hus concerning a goose, for "Hus" means "goose" in the Bohemian language: they were roasting him then, but the swan, who would come after him, would escape their scorching. By these words he seems to have signified both the manner of his own death and Luther's peaceful departure, safe from their savagery.

units.la: GVILIELMVS TAYLER.
units.tr: WILLIAM TAYLER.

units.la: Post mortem Ioannis Hus & Hieronymi Pragensis, acerrima in Anglia persecutio aduersus pios ac fideles Dei ministros fuit excitata. Homines non vulgari authoritate & fide, diligenter quasdam historias collegerunt, quas nos in hoc libro intexuimus, vt intelligatur, si memoria omnium eorum, qui Martyres ac testes Christi fuerunt, diligeter fuisset conseruata & literis mandata, nullam fuisse vnquam ætatem, in qua maximus non extiterit numerus eorum, qui veritatè Dei suæ vitæ anteposuerunt. Ex eorum numero fuit quidam literatus, magisterio artium ornatus, Guilielmus Taylerus Anglus, doctrinæ Euangelicæ perstudiosus. Causam autem summi odij ac furoris aduersus eum incitati, attulit liber quidam, quem is contra inuocationem Sanctorum defunctorum scripserat. Itaque Londini ob illud scriptum combustus fuit, anno M.CCCC.XXII, summáque constantia illud ignis supplicium perpessus.
units.tr: After the death of John Hus and Jerome of Prague, a most bitter persecution was stirred up in England against the pious and faithful ministers of God. Men of no common authority and good faith have diligently gathered certain accounts, which we have woven into this book, so that it may be understood that, if the memory of all those who were martyrs and witnesses of Christ had been diligently preserved and committed to writing, there would never have been any age in which the number of those who preferred the truth of God to their own lives was not very great. Among them was a learned man, graced with the degree of master of arts, William Tayler, an Englishman, most zealous for the evangelical doctrine. The cause of the great hatred and fury stirred up against him was a book he had written against the invocation of the departed saints. Accordingly he was burned at London on account of that writing in the year 1422, and he endured the fire's punishment with the greatest constancy.

units.la: GVILIELMVS VVIGET.
units.tr: WILLIAM WIGET.

units.la: GVilielmus wigetus, cùm in legendis wiclefi concionibus diligenter versatus fuisset, institutum vitæ suæ commutauit, eiusque inquinamenta cognoscens, opinum reliquit proventum, quem ex sacerdotio capiebat. Ex sententia & voluntate Dei puellam, Ioannam nominatam, in matrimonium duxit. Qua vitæ societate nunquam impeditus fuit, quo minus incumberet in opus institutum ac susceptum, vt & studeret diligenter, & tum publicè tum priuatim homines in vera Dei agnitione ac pietate institueret, omnémq; suam cogitationè, studium, operam, in communem aliorum vtilitatem, salutémque conferret. Itaque captus in vrbe Noruicensi, cùm triginta articuli ei propositi obiectíque fuissent, crudelissimè eo in oppido combustus fuit, Guilielmo episcopo cum persequente, mense Septembri, anno M. CCCC. XXVIII. Eius autem vxor, sanctum mariti exemplum sequens, quantum quidem poterat, homines in timore Dei instituebat: quam ob causam maximis molestiis iniuriisque ab episcopo affecta & afflicta fuit.
units.tr: William Wiget, having diligently studied the sermons of Wycliffe, changed the course of his life. Recognising its defilements, he left behind the rich income he drew from the priesthood. By the judgment and will of God he married a girl named Joan. Life in this partnership never hindered him from devoting himself to the work he had undertaken and taken up: to study diligently, and to instruct people, both publicly and privately, in the true knowledge and piety of God, and to direct all his thought, zeal and effort to the common benefit and salvation of others. Accordingly, when he was seized in the city of Norwich, and thirty articles had been put to him and brought against him, he was most cruelly burned in that town, Bishop William persecuting him, in September 1428. His wife, following her husband's holy example, instructed people in the fear of God as far as she could; for this cause she was greatly harassed and afflicted with harsh treatment by the bishop.

units.la: RICHARDUS HOUENDENUS.
units.tr: RICHARD HOUENDEN.

units.la: A[?]nno[?] M.CCCC.XXX. post inaugurationem regis Hēricī[?] sexti, fuit quidā lanae carminandae ac pectendae artifex, Richardus Houendenus nominatus, ciuis Londinensis, qui nullis rationibus, quibus ab aliis tentatus ac sollicitatus est, unquam a Christiana veritatis confessione abduci potuit. Itaque magistratus eius urbis ac iudices, eum ut haereticum condemnauerunt, ac prope turrem Londinensem ustulandum curauerunt.
units.tr: In the year 1430, after the coronation of King Henry VI, there was a certain craftsman who carded and combed wool, named Richard Houenden, a citizen of London, who could by no arguments, with which others tried and pressed him, ever be drawn away from the Christian confession of the truth. Accordingly the magistrates and judges of that city condemned him as a heretic and had him burned near the Tower of London.

units.la: THOMAS BUGLUS.
units.tr: THOMAS BUGLE.

units.la: Thomas Buglus natione quoq; Anglus, & vicarius parœciæ Mauendensis, ab inimicis veritatis in crimen haeresis, ac pravae opinionis vocatus est, anno M. CCCC. XXXI. Is circa tempus medium quadragesimæ, de gradu ac ordine sacerdotij motus, & mox crematus fuit.
units.tr: Thomas Bugle, also an Englishman, and vicar of the parish of Mauendensis, was accused by the enemies of the truth of the crime of heresy and of a depraved opinion, in the year 1431. Around the middle of Lent he was deprived of his rank and order of priesthood, and soon afterwards burned.

units.la: PAULUS CRAUS.
units.tr: PAULUS CRAUS.

units.la: E[?]odem etiam anno M. CCCC.XXI. Paulus Craus, propè oppidum sancti Andreæ, per quendam Episcopum, qui Hericus dicebatur, captus est, & ab eodem in manum Magistratus civilis traditus, ut in ignem coniiceretur. Causa autem eius supplicii haec fuit, quòd impias Papistarum opiniones de eucharistia, de invocatione Sanctorum, qui mortui sunt, de auriculari confessione, aliisque rebus nefarie ab illis in Ecclesiam introductis, libere & constanter repellebat.
units.tr: In the same year, 1421, Paulus Craus was seized near the town of St Andrews by a certain bishop called Hericus, and handed over by him to the civil magistrate to be thrown into the fire. The cause of his punishment was that he freely and steadfastly rejected the impious opinions of the Papists concerning the Eucharist, the invocation of the saints who have died, auricular confession, and other things wickedly introduced into the Church by them.

units.la: THOMAS RHEDONENSIS.
units.tr: THOMAS RHEDONENSIS.

units.la: Thomas Rhedonensis, monachus ex eorum instituto, qui Carmelitae appellantur, natione Gallus, in Italiam cum legatis Venetorum profectus est. qui quidem etsi ex illo impuro atque impio mendicantium esset ordine, tamen in ea vitæ professione, cognitionem veritatis non mediocrem habebat. Quod autem Galliam relinqueret, vt se conferret in Italiam, causa eum illa impulit, quod sperabat se illic aliquos homines pios, Deumque metuentes reperturum, quibuscum posset sanctè atque honestè viuere. Hanc vero spem suam ea ratione confirmabat, quod vbi homines profitebantur omnem sanctitatem, ibi etiā omnia virtutum genera vigere floreréque deberent.
units.tr: Thomas of Rennes, a monk of the order called the Carmelites, a Frenchman by birth, set out for Italy with the envoys of the Venetians. Although he belonged to that impure and impious order of mendicants, he nonetheless had no small knowledge of the truth within his profession of life. What drove him to leave France and betake himself to Italy was this: he hoped to find there some pious men who feared God, with whom he could live holily and honourably. He strengthened this hope by reasoning that where men professed every kind of holiness, every kind of virtue ought also to flourish.

units.la: Itaque ea religionis ac pietatis lumina ante oculos sibi proponens, Romam est profectus, cum ea optima spe, quod multis sanctissimorum hominum exemplis, quibus eam vrbem abundare arbitrabatur, rationem pie modestèque viuendi disceret. Sed res in contrariam vitæ rationem plane instituta, eius opinionem atque spem longè fefellit. Nam pro sanctitate, hypocrisin, id est, affectam pietatis speciem, sanctitatemque fucosam ea in vrbe offendit: pro gratiis spiritualibus ac cœlestibus, magnificos apparatus fastúsque: pro puro Dei timore, summum eius contemptum, in omni libidinis intemperantia impudentiáque effusum: pro sana salutarique doctrina, superstitiones, otium, abominationes: pro mansuetudine Apostolica, inhumanitatem & huiusmodi tyrannidem, quæ omnem Barbarorum immanitatem superaret: ita vt non modò id quod quis ignoraret, discere non liceret, sed ne id quidem docere quod sciret. Imprimis vero & vehementer cum offendit ambitio superbiáque intolerabilis, quam perspiciebat in iis, in quibus summa modestia relucere debebat. Itaque his tot vitiis flagitiisque offensus, eos publicè admonere in concionibus constituit, atque ad aliam vitæ magis Christianæ rationem reuocare: quanquam eos infanabiles & plane deploratos, qui nec libris Wiclefi, nec recenti Ioannis Hussij, Hieronymique sanguine, eos quodammodo admonente, nec tot piorum hominum Deumque timentium, non solum emendassent mores suos, verumetiam in omni malitia atque impietate obfirmati, deteriores atque impudentiores effecissent. His tamen tot ac tantis vitijs, difficultatibus, periculis, Thomas non est impeditus neque territus, quo minus, id quod proposuerat agere, personam præceptoris, monitoris, obiurgatorisque susciperet, quoniam ex illorum disciplina & schola omnium vitiorum, errorum, flagitiorumque plenissima, nihil discere poterat, quod cum doctrina Dei & sua conscientia non pugnaret. Itaque cum ad sanam doctrinam, summam vitæ integritatem, modestiam, sanctitatem adiunxisset, acriter vehementérque in mores hominum vitiosos inuehi cœpit, nemini parcere, imprimis vero Cardinalium scelera & flagitia, summa cum libertate insectari. Hac autem orationis veritate atque acerbitate magnopere offensi reucrendi homines, statim ad suam confugerunt consuetudinem, vt ea cõfingerent hæresis crimina, quibus monitorem suum cricunuenirent atque opprimerent. Nam quemadmodum suis quæque animalia armis instructa sunt, quibus ad iustam defensionem sui vtuntur, ita istæ bestiæ, alioqui semper otiosæ, crimina, calumnias, mendacia in ore, quasi arma in manu parata, habent, cum in periculum ventris ignauissimi à seruis Dei fidelibus se vocari arbitrantur. Ad hæc malitiam atq; impudentiam, adiungunt etiam armorum vim, vt hoc modo nõ solum vocem cuiusquam in ecclesia, sed ne spiritum quidem liberum esse patiantur. Itaq; vt essent sui similes, Thomă Romæ iisdem artibus rationibúsque circunuenerunt, quibus antea Constantiæ Ioanne Hus, atq; Hieronymũ Pragensem oppresserat. Namq; eum comprehenderunt, suspicionibus criminibúsq; obruerunt, importunis perturbarunt quæstionibus, articulos fidei ei proposuerunt. denique accusatum hæreseos, conuictum & condemnatũ, de gradu sacerdotali ordinéq; primũ demouerunt: deinde summo vsitatóq; ignis supplicio affecerunt. Hæc est iustitia, mansuetudo, integritas eorũ, qui se Apostolorum successores esse dicunt, quorum corda, maleuolentia, acerbitate inuidiáque infecta sunt, linguæ fallaces, omniáque doli, periurij, mendacij plena: manus vero cruentæ eorum sanguine, quorum iustam & sanctam libertatem, nullo modo ferre possunt. Sed articuli, quos conflarunt aduersus Thomam, & quorũ nomine eũ cremandũ curauerunt, hi sunt.
units.tr: Therefore, setting before his eyes these lights of religion and piety, he went to Rome, with the very good hope that he would learn a manner of living devoutly and modestly from the many examples of the most holy men with which he thought that city abounded. But things planned on a wholly contrary way of life far disappointed his expectation and hope. For instead of holiness he found hypocrisy in that city, that is, a feigned appearance of piety and a counterfeit sanctity; instead of spiritual and heavenly graces, magnificent displays and pomp; instead of pure fear of God, the utmost contempt for him, poured out in every intemperance of lust and shamelessness; instead of sound and wholesome doctrine, superstitions, idleness and abominations; instead of apostolic gentleness, inhumanity and a tyranny of that kind which would surpass all the savagery of barbarians. So much so that not only was it not permitted to learn what one did not know, but not even to teach what one did know. Above all, he was most vehemently offended by the intolerable ambition and pride that he saw in those in whom the greatest modesty ought to shine. Therefore, offended by these many vices and crimes, he resolved to admonish them publicly in sermons and to call them back to a more Christian way of life. Yet they were incurable and utterly hopeless, those who, though the books of Wycliffe, the recent blood of John Hus and Jerome, which in a sense admonished them, and the many pious men who feared God, had not only failed to amend their morals, but, hardened in all malice and impiety, had made themselves worse and more shameless. Nevertheless, Thomas was not hindered or frightened by these so many and great vices, difficulties and dangers from undertaking what he had proposed, namely to assume the role of teacher, admonisher and rebuker, since from their discipline and school, which was full of every vice, error and crime, he could learn nothing that did not conflict with the doctrine of God and his own conscience. So, having joined sound doctrine to the highest integrity of life, modesty and holiness, he began to inveigh sharply and vehemently against the vicious morals of men, sparing no one, and above all to attack with the greatest freedom the wickedness and crimes of the cardinals. But the reverend men, greatly offended by this truthfulness and bitterness of speech, at once fell back on their accustomed practice, to invent charges of heresy by which they might entrap and crush their critic. For just as every animal is equipped with its own weapons, which it uses for its just defence, so these beasts, otherwise always idle, keep accusations, calumnies and lies ready on their tongues, as weapons ready in hand, whenever they think that their worthless bellies are in danger of being called out by the faithful servants of God. To these they add the force of arms, malice and shamelessness, so that in this way they allow no one's voice, nor even his spirit, to be free in the Church. Therefore, to be true to themselves, they besieged Thomas at Rome with the same arts and devices with which they had previously oppressed John Hus at Constance and Jerome of Prague. For they seized him, overwhelmed him with suspicions and accusations, troubled him with importunate questions, and proposed to him articles of faith. Finally, having accused him of heresy, convicted and condemned him, they first removed him from his priestly rank and order, and then subjected him to the usual extreme punishment of fire. This is the justice, gentleness and integrity of those who say they are the successors of the Apostles, whose hearts are infected with ill will, bitterness and envy, whose tongues are deceitful, and who are full of every guile, perjury and lying; whose hands are bloody with the blood of those whose just and holy liberty they cannot bear in any way. But the articles which they drew up against Thomas, and in whose name they took care that he should be burned, are these.

units.la: Ecclesia reformatione opus habet, eáque affligetur ac reformabitur.
units.tr: The Church needs reformation, and it will be afflicted and reformed.

units.la: Quòd his nouissimis temporibus infideles ad Christum Iesum conuertentur.
units.tr: That in these latest times infidels will be converted to Christ Jesus.

units.la: Roma abominationibus referta est.
units.tr: Rome is filled with abominations.

units.la: Excommunicatio Papæ, quæ non potest esse nisi iniqua, nõ est metucenda:& qui eam non obseruant, non peccant.
units.tr: The excommunication of the Pope, which cannot be anything but unjust, is not to be feared: and those who do not observe it do not sin.

units.la: Ita Eugenius, qui tum erat pontifex, Thomam accersitum, in carcerem includendum curauit: vbi summas tormentorum acerbitates perpessus est. Post ea cruciamenta, ad iudicem, vt manfuetissimus agnus in maximum luporum rabidissimorum ac sæuissimorum cœtum, adductus est. Itaq; cum homo non minus modestus quàm pius malitiæ bestiarum immanissimarum resistere non posset, primũ ignominiam, vel potius summam gloriam commutati ordinis sacerdotalis, deinde acerbâ ignis pœnam sustinuit.
units.tr: Thus Eugenius, who was then pope, had Thomas summoned and shut up in prison, where he suffered the utmost bitterness of torments. After those tortures he was brought before the judge, like a most gentle lamb led into the greatest gathering of the most rabid and savage wolves. And so, since the man, no less modest than pious, could not resist the malice of most savage beasts, he first endured the disgrace, or rather the highest glory, of having his priestly order changed, and then the bitter punishment of fire.

units.la: RENAVDVS PECOLZ.
units.tr: REGINALD PECOCK.

units.la: Historia Renaudi Pecolz, episcopi Cicestrensis, ob pietatē ac profesionem Euāgelii à pseudepiscopis afflicti ac vexati, atque in carcere tandem necati.
units.tr: The history of Reginald Pecock, bishop of Chichester, harassed and vexed by the false bishops on account of his piety and his profession of the Gospel, and at last done to death in prison.

units.la: Quod scripsit Paulus, Deum velle saluos omnes homines fieri, deducique ad agnitionem veritatis, id hoc tempore videmus bonitate eius admirabili re præstari. Nam ex omni hominum genere atque ordine, Deus ad cognitionem sui vocauit, & vocat quotidie, etiam ex iis qui desperati plane atque à sancta eius vocatione maximè omnium abalienati esse videbantur. Hoc in numero sunt monachi, sacerdotes, Episcopi, quorum rationem vitæ considerare non possumus, quin simul bonitatem ac veritatem Dei, eorum tenebras illuminantis admiremur atque omni laude & benevolentia prosequamur. Episcoporum quidem huiusmodi est difficultas & raritas, vt cum extat aliquod exemplum misericordiæ Dei, in vnum eorum aliquem collatæ, beneficii eius singulare, in primisque memorabile esse videatur. Quo in genere Renaudꝰ Pecolzus Anglus, episcopus Cicestrensis, merito ponendus est: qui cum puram Euangelij doctrinam cognouisset, eam tamen palàm statim profiteri, apertèque testificari noluit: sed hominum existimationem, periculum terroremque veritus, aliquandiu cognitæ veritatis professionem occultauit. Sed is nō diu in obscuro occultóque illo pietatis studio latere potuit, nec cæterorum Episcoporū ac sacerdotum suspiciones euitare, tot notas, oculos, coniecturas suspiciosas illi habent, vt nulla sit, aut tā infima hominū cōditio, aut tā summa dignitatis amplitudo, quam illi cogitatione, animo, potestate sua non comprehendat, tyrannidiq; sue subijciat. Comprehensus igitur ab his Pecolzꝰ Labetum deductus est: vbi in frequentissimo aduersariorum conuentu consessuque, Thomas archiepiscopus Cantuariensis praesidebat. nam eò maximus doctorum, atque Episcoporum numerus confluxerat. Eo etiam in consilio dux Buckyngamiae adesse voluit, episcopo Roffensi ac Lincolniensi comitatus. Tum vero inter multos alios articulos, hunc Pecolzo proposuerunt, An substantia panis maneret in sacramento. Quibus quidè ille commodè verèq; respondit, planéq; satisfecisset, si æquos nactus fuisset iudices, quibus aliqua ratione satisfieri potuisset. Is tamen vt causam & vitam suam tueretur, omnibus quibus poterat rationibus, sententiam suam propugnabat. Aduersarij vero atque inimici, vt factus apparatúsque suos tueretur, contrà omnibus conatibus ac viribus eũ oppugnabat. Atq; vt nihil illis plane deesset, quod aut ad dominatum suum tuendum, aut ad opprimendum Episcopum pertinere videretur, vndiq; & sophistas peracutos, & oratores excellentes, & philosophos ac theologos in huiusmodi quaestionibus ac disputationibus versatos atq; exercitatos conuocarunt. neq; verò homines legum & canonum peritissimos praetermiserunt.
