units.tr: What Paul wrote, that God wills all men to be saved and brought to the knowledge of the truth, we see at this time being done wonderfully by his goodness. For from every kind and rank of men God has called, and calls daily, to the knowledge of himself, even from those who seemed utterly hopeless and most of all estranged from his holy calling. Among these are monks, priests and bishops; when we consider the manner of life of such men, we cannot but at the same time marvel at, and praise with all goodwill, the goodness and truth of God, who illumines their darkness. Indeed, among bishops such a thing is so difficult and rare that when some example of the mercy of God shown to one of them is found, it seems a singular benefit and, above all, a memorable one. In this class Reginald Pecock, the Englishman, bishop of Chichester, rightly deserves a place. When he had come to know the pure doctrine of the Gospel, he was nevertheless unwilling to profess it openly at once and to bear witness to it plainly; fearing men's opinion, danger and terror, he hid his profession of the truth he had come to know for some time. But he could not long lie hidden in that obscure and secret zeal for piety, nor escape the suspicions of the other bishops and priests: they had so many marks, eyes and suspicious conjectures against him that no condition of men, however lowly, and no height of dignity, however great, was beyond their grasp in thought, mind and power, or beyond subjection to their tyranny. Pecock, therefore, was seized by them and led to Lambeth, where Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, presided over a very crowded assembly and gathering of his opponents; for the greatest number of teachers and bishops had flocked there. In this council the Duke of Buckingham also wished to be present, accompanied by the bishops of Rochester and Lincoln. Then indeed, among many other articles, they put this one to Pecock: whether the substance of bread remains in the sacrament. To these he answered fittingly and truthfully, and would have fully satisfied them, had he found fair judges by whom some satisfaction could have been given. Yet, to defend his cause and his life, he maintained his opinion by every argument he could. His adversaries and enemies, however, to protect their handiwork and apparatus, assailed him with every effort and every strength. And so that nothing might be lacking to them that seemed to pertain either to upholding their domination or to crushing the bishop, they summoned from every side keen-witted sophists, excellent orators, and philosophers and theologians practised and trained in such questions and disputations. Nor did they overlook men most skilled in the laws and canons.

units.la: Sed primum non incommodum illis est visum, vt priuato familiarique colloquio cũ illo ageretur: in quo nihil plane est praetermissum, quod aut blandam vitae ac dignitatis retinendae atque etiam augedae spem, aut horrendam mortis infamiaeque comminationẽ habere videretur. Quibus quidem rebus Episcopus variè tentatus atq; agitatus, in eam sententiã & voluntatẽ adductus est, vt palàm apud populum, quae professus fuerat, se retracturum esse promitteret. In hac tamen veritate animi atque iudicij, quam promiserat, exitus ipse satis ostendit, cum quod pie sentiebat, populo etiam aperte declarasse. Nã cùm aduersariorum voluntati, vel potius libidini, non satisfecissset, in carcerem reductus est, ibíque mortuus, non sine graui coniectura necis, ab inimicis iniustissimè allatae.
units.tr: But first it seemed not inappropriate to them that he should be dealt with in a private and familiar conversation, in which nothing at all was left out that seemed to hold out either a flattering hope of keeping his life and dignity, or even of increasing them, or a dreadful threat of death and infamy. Pecock, variously tempted and harassed by these things, was brought to such a frame of mind and will that he promised publicly before the people that he would retract what he had professed. Yet the outcome itself showed well enough, in the sincerity of mind and judgment which he had promised, that he had openly declared to the people also what he held in piety. For since he had not satisfied the will, or rather the lust, of his adversaries, he was led back into prison, and there he died, not without a strong suspicion of murder, inflicted most unjustly by his enemies.

units.la: NOBILIS CANDIENSIS.
units.tr: THE NOBLE OF CANDIA.

units.la: De quodam Candiensi, illustri nato genere, Euangeliique nomine combusto.
units.tr: Concerning a certain Candiot, born of an illustrious family, who was burned for the name of the Gospel.

units.la: F Aventinus historicus est author, quendam vxoris ducis Candiae propinquum, nomine Euangelij, ea in insula accusatum fuisse, & à Petro Thomasio, qui in Candia Pontificis Romani legatus erat, hæresefeωs condemnatum, conftater pœnam ignis perpessum esse: cum ceteri, qui in eadem fuissent causa, quod erant professi, renuntiasset, anno M. CCCC. XC.
units.tr: Aventinus, the historian, is the authority that a certain kinsman of the wife of the duke of Candia, by the name of Evangelius, was accused of heresy on that island, and was condemned by Peter Thomas, who was legate of the Roman Pontiff in Candia; and that he certainly suffered the penalty of fire, while the others who were in the same case, and had professed the same things, he had made to recant, in the year 1490.

units.la: Idem scribit, eundem legatum offa cuiusdam mortui, post morte hærefeωs accusati, effodienda atque exhumanda curauisse.
units.tr: The same writer records that the same legate had the bones of a certain dead man, who had been accused of heresy after his death, dug up and exhumed.

units.la: MATER DOMINAE YONG.
units.tr: The Mother of Mistress Yong.

units.la: D testimonium Euangelij illustrandum maximopere pertinet, quòd nullus sexus est prætermissus, quem Deus ad martyrium non vocauerit. Exempla multa præclaraque sunt hodie fidelissimarum fœminarum, quæ cum viris in hanc Euangelij communionem ac societatem veniunt: vt cum eis multa grauia & opprobria & tormenta patiantur. Sed olim in Anglia insignis & commemorabilis exempli fuit lestissima fœmina, dominæ Yongæ mater, quæ propter religionem virili constantia virtuteque cremata est, anno M.CCCC.XC.
units.tr: The testimony of the Gospel is greatly illuminated by the fact that no sex has been passed over whom God has not called to martyrdom. Today there are many and notable examples of most faithful women who, together with men, enter into this fellowship and partnership in the Gospel, and who therefore suffer many grievous things, reproaches and torments along with them. But long ago in England there was a remarkable and memorable example in the most excellent woman, the mother of Mistress Yong, who was burned for her religion with manly constancy and courage in the year 1490.

units.la: ROGERIVS DVLE.
units.tr: Rogerius Dulus

units.la: ROgerius Dulus, homo nobili genere ortus & professione militari, pro vetitate defendenda & propugnanda in Anglia suspensus atque strangulatus fuit, anno M.CCCC.XC.
units.tr: Rogerius Dulus, a man of noble birth and military profession, was hanged and strangled in England in 1490 for defending and upholding the truth.

units.la: EX eo tempore verbum Dei maximum accepit incrementum, fructusque admirabiles protulit. Nam Spiritus sanctus animos tum eorum qui doctrinam Euangelij annunciabant, tum etiam eorū qui audiebant, ita feliciter tetigit, vt numerus fidelium ac piorum in dies singulos vehementer augeretur. Huiusmodi autem virtus constantiaque diuinitus eis dabatur, vt quidā ex illis molestias & ærumnas carcerū, suma cum voluntate susciperent ac subirent: alij amissione bonorum æquo ferret animo: multi vero ne mortem quidem, eámque acerbā, pertimescerent. Ex quo facile intelligi potest, ac vere dici, persecutiones ecclesiæ Christianæ per Apostolos natæ, repetitas renouatásque suisse, Christūmque dominum eam operum admirabilem virtutem, quam primis illis temporibus exhibuit, his nostris quoque nouissimis exhibuisse ac declarasse, cum tantam gratiam in mundū protulit atque effudit, tandiu summa ingratitudine hominum obscurata & prope delectam. Eam Dominus obsignare voluit morte testiū fidelium, qui pro defendenda Dei veritate, sanguinem suum profuderunt, praeclare Iesum Christum imitati, qui coram Pontio Pilato, pro eadem cōfirmanda & obsignanda, testimonium non minus salutare quam graue dedit. Etsi haec mors Sanctorum pro Euāngelio suscepta, iudicio mundi ignominiosa sit & detestanda, apud Deum tamen eā gratiam & honorem habet, quem Spiritus sanctus in quodam Psalmo declarauit.
units.tr: From that time the Word of God received very great increase and produced remarkable fruit. For the Holy Spirit so happily touched the minds both of those who announced the doctrine of the Gospel and of those who heard it, that the number of the faithful and the pious grew greatly from day to day. Moreover, such virtue and constancy were given to them by God that some of them undertook and endured the troubles and hardships of prisons with the greatest willingness, others bore the loss of their goods with an equal mind, and many did not fear even death, and a bitter death at that. From this it can easily be understood, and truly said, that the persecutions of the Christian Church, which began with the Apostles, were repeated and renewed, and that Christ the Lord, who displayed the admirable power of his works in those first times, has displayed and revealed the same in these our most recent times too, when he has brought forth and poured out so great a grace into the world, a grace long obscured and almost destroyed by the great ingratitude of men. The Lord wished to seal it by the death of faithful witnesses, who poured out their blood to defend the truth of God, following the splendid example of Jesus Christ, who before Pontius Pilate gave a testimony, to confirm and seal the same truth, no less saving than it was grave. And although this death of the saints undertaken for the Gospel is shameful and to be detested in the judgment of the world, nevertheless before God it has that grace and honour which the Holy Spirit declared in a certain Psalm.

units.la: HENRICVS SVPPHEN,ab Diethmar.
units.tr: Henricus Supphenus of Diethmar

units.la: INter caeteros fuit Henricus Supphenus, vir praestanti virtute, qui in vrbe Diethmar, pro confitenda & tuenda Euangelij veritate grauissimo supplicio affectus, neque vlla aduersariorum crudelitate ac doloris acerbitate passus est sibi eripi eam fidei confessionem, quam Christus dominus ab eo postulabat. Is itaque anno M.D.XXII. Meldorffo cum contumelia expulsus est, propter Euangelium, quod ea in vrbe vsque ad annum M.D.XXIIII. praedicauerat. nam ob eam causam, Curio Meldorffensis, & cum eo aliqui fideles homines eum vocauerant, vt parum ipsis Dei verbum annunciaret, eosque liberaret grauissima Antichristi seruitute, qua oppressi tenebantur.
units.tr: Among others there was Henricus Supphenus, a man of outstanding virtue, who in the city of Diethmar was subjected to the most grievous punishment for confessing and defending the truth of the Gospel, and who, despite the cruelty and bitter pain inflicted by his adversaries, did not allow that confession of faith, which Christ the Lord required of him, to be taken from him. He was therefore expelled from Meldorf with disgrace in 1522, on account of the Gospel, which he had preached in that city until 1524. For it was for this reason that Curio of Meldorf, together with some other faithful men, had summoned him, so that he might proclaim the Word of God to them and free them from the most grievous slavery of Antichrist under which they were held oppressed.

units.la: Eo autem venit Supphenus ad aduentum Domini, vt vocant: quem Curio ipse, aliique fideles magna cum laetitia exceperunt. Is concionabatur bis diebus singulis, cum maximo fidei fructu, & piorum consolatione. Itaque cum is ita integrè ac diligenter in eo munere versaretur, Dominicani grauiter offensi, & maximo in eum odio affecti fuerunt, multaque & grauia aduersus eum machinati, tandem cum quadraginta & octo regionis Diethmarensis gubernatoribus consilium coeperunt, vt virum pium & fidelem Christi ministrum comprehenderet & sine vlla mora cremarent, antequam incolae ipsius regionis intelligere aliquid possent. Imprimis autem Franciscanus hoc consilium gratum, & magnopere iucundum accidit. Interea dum haec malitiosè ab illis parantur, quingenti rustici, coacti ad dimidium miliare ab vrbe Meldorffi, conuenerunt, atque omnes viarum aditus occuparunt, ne quis ad vrbem nuncium consilij ipsorum adferre posset. Populus id quidem tum invitus agebat. quia tamen duces, ac totius eius negotij gubernatores, graue tum fortunarum omnium, tum etiam vitæ periculum comminantes, id iubebant, eorum imperium recusare ac detrectare non audebant. Atque ut animum eis maiorem adderent, curauerunt, ut ante suum in vrbem aduentum, tria dolia ceruisiæ Hamelburgensis biberent.
units.tr: Supphenus came there at what they call the coming of the Lord, and Curio himself and other faithful people received him with great joy. He preached twice on each day, with the greatest fruit for faith and the consolation of the pious. And while he discharged that office so faithfully and diligently, the Dominicans were gravely offended and were filled with the greatest hatred against him, and they plotted many grievous things against him. At last they began to plan with the forty-eight governors of the region of Dithmarsch that they would seize this pious man and faithful minister of Christ and burn him without any delay, before the inhabitants of that region could learn anything. The Franciscan in particular found this plan agreeable and very pleasing. Meanwhile, while these things were being maliciously prepared by them, five hundred peasants, summoned to a place half a mile from the city of Meldorf, gathered and occupied all the approaches to the roads, so that no one could bring news of their plan to the city. The people, indeed, did this then unwillingly; yet since their leaders, and the managers of the whole affair, threatened them with grave danger both to all their property and to their lives, and ordered it, they did not dare to refuse or resist their command. And so that they might add greater spirit to them, they arranged that before their arrival in the city they should drink three casks of Hamburg beer.

units.la: Ita postremo Meldorffum cum copijs armatis circiter mediam noctem peruenerunt, quibus Dominicani, ut in tenebris noctis eis praelucerent, tedas ac faces antea paratas atque adornatas, illis attulerunt. Cum igitur venissent in vrbem, ilico cum magno impetu ac vi in domum curionis irruerunt: & ut est consuetudo istorum latronum ac praedonum, cum huiusmodi furore agitantur, totam domum compilarunt ac diripuerunt, vasa, lectos, lintea, vtensilia omnia domestica, vestes etiam, quibus quotidie induebatur, aurum, argentumque eius abstulerunt. Neque vero praedonibus his satis fuit, latrocinium huiusmodi in bonis fortunisque illius exercere: sed ab ea praeda & rapina, ad vim corpori eius cum omni petulantia & saevitia inferendam, se converterunt. Alius petulanter illum caedebat, alius sica pungebat & gladio: omnes vero ut occiderctur, maximis clamoribus iubebant.
units.tr: Thus at last they came to Meldorf with armed forces about midnight, and the Dominicans brought to them torches and flares, prepared and made ready beforehand, so that they might give light to them in the darkness of night. When they had come into the city, they at once rushed with great force and violence into the curate's house, and, as is the custom of those robbers and plunderers when they are driven by such fury, they pillaged and plundered the whole house, and carried off his vessels, beds, linen, all household utensils, even the clothes he wore every day, and his gold and silver. Nor was it enough for these plunderers to carry out such robbery upon his goods and property; but from that plunder and rapine they turned to inflicting violence on his body with every wantonness and savagery. One wantonly beat him, another stabbed him with a dagger and a sword; and all of them shouted with the loudest cries that he should be killed.

units.la: Quidam etiam ex illis, hominem pium ex lecto nudum comprehenderunt, eumque ita in plateas vrbis protraxerunt, ut per lutum incederet. Alij vero idem egerunt in Henricum, quem nudum ex lecto arripuerunt, eum caedentes atque impellentes, manibus illius ad dorsum arctissimè colligatis, pedibus nudis super glaciem ita inambulare cogebant, ut pedes eius rigore frigoris laesi, sanguinem emitterent. Ita eum inhumaniter tractantes, usque ad domum cuiusdam sacerdotis pertraxerunt, atque ei in ima cauea positum, asservandum tradiderunt.
units.tr: Some of them also seized the pious man, naked, from his bed and dragged him in this state through the streets of the city, so that he had to walk through the mud. Others did the same to Henry: they snatched him naked from his bed, beating and pushing him, bound his hands very tightly behind his back, and forced him to walk barefoot over the ice, so that his feet, injured by the bitter cold, poured out blood. Treating him in this inhuman way, they dragged him as far as the house of a certain priest, and handed him over to be kept, placed in the lowest dungeon.

units.la: Postridie mane illi carnifices in forum conuenerunt, ut quid de Henrico agendum esset, ipsi inter se statuerent. Neque interea desinebant, maxima vociferatione eum ad supplicium ignis vocare. Ne longior fit oratio, vir pius atque innocens Supphenus[?], causa indicta & maudita fuit condenatus, ut igni cremaretur, ab iis qui eius & iudices & tortores constituti erant. Qua ex re monachi in primis maxima voluptatem acceperunt: eósque iudices ac gubernatores reipublicæ maximopere laudauerunt, quòd iustitiam tum colerent, tuerentur & conseruarent. Tum vero eum comprehensum, & manibus, collo, pedibusque vinctum & constrictum, eum in locum adduxerunt, vbi erat supplicio afficiendus. Ibi sententia fuit pronuntiata à quodam præfecto, id est, eo qui maleficijs in regione aliqua, aut prohibendis, aut cùm sunt commissa, puniendis, præpositus est: à quo hæc sententia nummis numeratis empta fuit. Ea autem continebat, impium hominem Henricum, contra fidem Christianam matremque Dei concionatum fuisse: & ob eam causam se illum ex authoritate reuerendissimi episcopi Bremensis, domini sui obseruandissimi, illum condemnare, vt viuus combureretur. Sententia pronuntiata, improbi homines eum in plateam protraxerunt, in qua magna struES lignorum facta erat, vt in ea viuus cremaretur, pedibus eum appetentes, vexantésque, neque vllum iniuriarum & contumeliarum genus prætermittentes, quod ab illis excogitari aut adhiberi poterat. Quidam ex illis sica in summa capitis parte eum percussit: alius hallebarda eandem corporis partem violauit. Denique vnusquisque certatim propius ad illum accedebat, vt eum caederet. Atque in hac quidem tanta sæuitia & crudelitate, ad populum magnis clamoribus vociferabantur: Deum à se ea in re stare, insolenter affirmantes. Sed quum omnem darent operam, vt ignem accenderent, non tamen id poterat: atque ita incerti quid agerent, fustibus & hallebardis eum cædere non desistebant, omniáque & tormenta & opprobria adhibere, quæ ab illorum petulantia proficisci poterant. Atque huiusmodi quasi quædam prolusio ante supplicium, duas prope horas facta fuit. Interea vir pius erat constitutus coram hominibus temulentis, furiosè in eum debacchantibus, suósque in Deum oculos habens conuersos & intentos, eius opem implorabat. Postea eum in valida quadam scala ligauerunt, in qua cùm verus Iesu Christi seruus confessionem fidei suæ edere cœpit, quidam ex rusticis eum in os percussit, cum huiusmodi verborum petulantia, quæ illum prius vstulandum esse dicebat, deinde quantum vellet murmurarent. Alius etiam pectus eius pede prosit, collùmque eius in vnojcalæ gradu alligauit cù vi tanta, vt sanguis per os & nares efflueret: quem videret nullis adhibitis tormentis doloribusque mori posse, eum suffocare conabatur. Postremo ita alligatum in scala, cum hallebardis elatum ad paratam struem lignorum detulerunt. Nam tum quidem in ea regione nullus erat, qui in eo supplicij genere exequendo expertus esset. Una ex hallebardis, quibus scala cum eo nixa ferebatur, delapsa, ita in hominem incidit, ut eum medium perfoderit. Ita, in paratam lignorum congeriem iniectus fuit. Sed quum scala in latus eius inclinasset, quidam celeriter accurrens, securi militari tot ictus pectori eius inflixit, ut confectus expiraret. Mortui corpus ardentibus carbonibus ustulaverunt, propterea quod nulla ratione efficere unquam potuerunt, ut ignis in parata lignorum struc accenderetur. Atque hic quidem illius viri ac servi Christi exitus fuit, opinione mundi calamitosus atque horrendus, sed Spiritus iudicio gloriosus ac perbeatus.
units.tr: The next morning those executioners gathered in the market-place to decide among themselves what was to be done about Henry. Meanwhile they did not cease to call loudly for him to be taken to the punishment of fire. To keep the account short: the pious and innocent man Supphenus, his case having not been heard and his trial not held, was condemned to be burned with fire, by those who had been appointed both his judges and his torturers. At this the monks in particular took the greatest delight, and they greatly praised those judges and governors of the commonwealth, because they cherished, upheld and preserved justice. Then indeed they seized him, bound his hands, neck and feet, and led him to the place where he was to be executed. There sentence was pronounced by a certain prefect, that is, the man set over a district to prevent crimes or to punish them when committed; this sentence was bought for counted coins. It stated that the impious man Henry had preached against the Christian faith and the mother of God, and that for this reason, by the authority of the most reverend bishop of Bremen, his very respected lord, they condemned him to be burned alive. When the sentence had been pronounced, the wicked men dragged him into the square, where a great pile of wood had been made in which he was to be burned alive, and they kicked and tormented him, leaving out no kind of insult or abuse that they could think of or inflict. One of them struck him with a sword on the top of the head; another wounded the same part of his body with a halberd. At last each of them pressed forward to strike him, one after another. And in the midst of this great savagery and cruelty they shouted loudly to the people, insolently declaring that God was on their side in this matter. But although they made every effort to light the fire, they could not do so; and so, uncertain what to do, they did not stop beating him with clubs and halberds, and applying every torment and disgrace that the wantonness of those men could produce. This kind of prelude before the execution lasted almost two hours. Meanwhile the pious man stood before drunken men raging furiously against him, keeping his eyes turned and fixed upon God, and implored his help. Afterwards they tied him to a strong ladder; and when the true servant of Jesus Christ began to make a confession of his faith while tied to it, one of the peasants struck him in the mouth, with insolent words saying that he should first be burned and then they would mutter as much as they liked. Another pressed his chest with his foot and bound his neck to a rung of the ladder with such force that blood flowed out through his mouth and nostrils; seeing that he could die without any torments or pains, he tried to choke him. Finally, having tied him thus to the ladder, they carried him aloft on halberds to the prepared pile of wood. For at that time there was no one in that region who had experience in carrying out that kind of punishment. One of the halberds by which the ladder with him upon it was being carried slipped, and fell upon the man so that it pierced him through the middle. Thus he was thrown onto the prepared heap of wood. But when the ladder had tilted onto his side, a certain man ran up quickly and struck his chest with many blows of a military axe, until he expired exhausted. They burned the dead body with glowing coals, because in no way could they ever manage to make the fire catch in the prepared pile of wood. And this was the end of that man and servant of Christ: calamitous and dreadful in the opinion of the world, but glorious and most blessed in the judgment of the Spirit.

units.la: Eodem autem tempore multi homines pij Deúmque metuentes, propter testimonium Evangelij coniecti fuerunt in profluentem Rheni, aliorumque fluminum, in quibus corpora eorum submersa, postea inventa fuerunt. Inter cæteros fuit quidam Magister Georgius, qui Halæ concionabatur, quem quia Cœnam utraque in specie exhibebat, latrones quidam & sicarij, à monachis parati ac subornati, invaserunt, & fœdum in modum prope oppidum Aschemburgum trucidarunt. Quoniam autem summa Dei gratia ad agnitionem ipsius vocati fuimus, sine maximo scelere atque impietate reticere ac dissimulare non possumus eorum confessionem, qui virtute Spiritus sancti impulsi suo testimonio, quum gloriam Dei, tum Ecclesiæ salutem tueri voluerunt, eaque in re plurimum, gratia Dei, profuerunt.
units.tr: At the same time many pious men who feared God were thrown, on account of their testimony to the Gospel, into the flowing Rhine and other rivers, and their drowned bodies were found afterwards. Among the rest was a certain Master Georgius, who preached at Halle. Because he administered the Supper in both kinds, some robbers and assassins, readied and suborned by monks, attacked him and foully slaughtered him near the town of Aschemburg. Since by the highest grace of God we have been called to the knowledge of him, we cannot, without the greatest wickedness and impiety, keep silent about or dissemble the confession of those who, impelled by the power of the Holy Spirit, wished by their testimony to defend both the glory of God and the salvation of the Church, and who in this matter, by the grace of God, have been of very great benefit.

units.la: Diversi Martyres tum in Germania, tum in Austria & aliis locis pro Evan- gelio morti traditi.
units.tr: Various martyrs put to death for the Gospel, both in Germany and in Austria and in other places.

units.la: Fuit prætera alius, Ioannes nominatus, qui eadem in urbe Diethmar, pro Christi nomine, non solum maxima opprobria, verumetiam mortem constanter pertulit. Ita hi duo boni ac pii homines, verique testes, qui ad cognoscendam veritatem, quasi duo accensa lumina diuinitus adhibebantur, in suavem Deo odorem, sacrificium confessionis, sanguine suo commendatum, obtulerunt. Neque in hoc Martyrū numero prætereundus est Gaspar Tamberus, qui pro testimonio Euangelij, Viennæ in Austria crematus est. Quo etiam in loco, Georgius quidam librarius, acerbissimam editæ confessionis pœnam igne sustinuit. Præterea Pragæ in Bohemia, alius fuit combustus, quòd genus vitæ monasticæ impium, infamémque cælibatum reliquisset, atque ad honestam & Deo probatam coniugij societatem se contulisset. Certum autem est, eos quos memoravimus, & alios, qui pro Christi nomine moriuntur, aliam ob causam hæc tormenta perpeti, quàm fures, sicarios, latrones, aliósque facinorosos homines, qui iustas maleficiorum suorum pœnas luunt. Iustitia, æquitas, & veritas, fideles Christianósq; homines, ad hæc ferenda, pro gloria Dei salutéque hominum adducit. Sed mundus, qua est ingratitudine atque impietate, claudit oculos, ne hanc Dei tam excellentem vocationem, ac fidei in Martyribus cõfessionem intueatur: &, quod est grauius, arbitratur se sacrificium præ-stare Deo, si in fideles Christi seruos tantam crudelitatem exerceat. Hæc tamen hominum infidelitas, veritatem Dei nunquam abolere poterit, neque pios homines priuare ea iustitiæ corona, quæ in cælo parata est ijs omnibus, qui causam veritatis, & gloriam Christi fortiter tutati fuerint: qui quidem exemplo Mosis, cum populo Dei malùt affligi, atque in omni paupertate ignominiáque versari, quàm frui ijs commodis, honoribus & gaudijs, quæ cũ impijs ac superbis hominibus in hac vita consequi possent.
units.tr: There was also another, named John, who in the same city of Diethmar endured constantly, for the name of Christ, not only the greatest reproaches but also death. So these two good and pious men, true witnesses, who were divinely given as two kindled lights for the recognition of the truth, offered to God a sweet-smelling sacrifice of confession, commended by their blood. Nor is Gaspar Tamberus to be passed over in this number of martyrs; he was burned at Vienna in Austria for the testimony of the Gospel. In the same place a certain bookseller, Georgius, underwent the most bitter punishment of fire for the confession he had published. Besides, at Prague in Bohemia another was burned, because he had left the impious monastic way of life and its infamous celibacy, and had betaken himself to the honourable partnership of marriage, which is approved by God. It is certain, however, that those we have mentioned, and others who die for the name of Christ, suffer these torments for a different reason than thieves, assassins, robbers and other criminals, who pay the just penalties for their wrongdoing. Justice, equity and truth lead faithful Christians to bear these things for the glory of God and the salvation of men. But the world, in its ingratitude and impiety, closes its eyes so that it does not look upon this most excellent calling of God and the confession of faith in the martyrs; and, what is worse, it thinks it offers a sacrifice to God if it exercises such cruelty against the faithful servants of Christ. Yet this unbelief of men can never abolish the truth of God, nor deprive pious men of that crown of righteousness which is laid up in heaven for all who have bravely defended the cause of truth and the glory of Christ. Indeed, following the example of Moses, they chose rather to be afflicted with the people of God and to live in all poverty and disgrace, than to enjoy those advantages, honours and joys which they could obtain in this life along with impious and proud men.

units.la: HENRIC. VOES & IOAN. ESCH.
units.tr: Henry Voes and John Esch.

units.la: A[?]nno M.D.XXIII. Bruxellis in Brabantia, duo iuuenes cremati fuerunt, quorū alter Hericus Voesus, viginti & quatuor natus annos, alter Ioannes Eschus vocabatur, vterque monachus ordinis Augustiani. Hi mense Iulio insequente post editam Euangelij Christi confessionem, primùm de gradu ordinéque sacerdotij expuncti suerunt, monasticisq; vestimentis spoliati, idq; instigatione inquisitoris fidei Egmondani eos persequentis, atq; authoritate theologorū Louaniensium: quòd illos ab opinione & sententia nunquā revocare potuissent. Tū lætantes, gratias Deo patri cælesti agere cœperunt, quòd se illo falsa & abominando sacerdotij genere atq; ordine solutos & liberatos, in alium meliorem cooptaret sacerdotum ordine, in quo etiam seipsos in sacrificium odoris suavissimi offerret. Scriptum eis est datum, quod recitarent, ac palam omni populo declararet, quid de religione sentirent ac crederent. Summum erroris crimen, quod eis obiectum est: hoc erat, quòd in unum Deum credendum esset, quoniam homo vanus & mendax in omnibus suis verbis atque operibus, & ipse falleretur & alios falleret: eam ob causam non esse fiduciam in ullo homine ponendam. Cùm autem ducerentur ad supplicium, laeti hilaresque accedebant, cum huiusmodi testificatione perpetua, quòd pro gloria Christi, & doctrina Euangelij Apostolorumque, ut Christiani morerentur, non ut haeretici gentilesque increduli, & quòd ecclesia Filij Dei sanctam crederent, affirmantes illum diem, quo ita morerentur, eum esse diem, quem tanto opere optassent. Cùm autem venissent ad locum, in quo ustulandi erant, denudati, satis diu ibi cum indusio steterunt, palum ad quem excurendi erant, animo magno amplectentes, nec solum patienter: sed etiam lubenter atque hilariter feretes omnes molestias & contumelias, quae ab aduersarijs in ipsos proficiscebatur: Psalmis & canticis Dei gloriam celebrabant, formulamque symboli ab Apostolis relicti, testem fidei suae ac confessionis pronuntiabant. Quidam ex doctoribus, qui ibi aderant, videns animi laetitiam & hilaritatem Henrici, cum monuit, ne ita inepte ac stulte gloriaretur, Absit, inquit ille: mihi gloriari, nisi in cruce Domini mei Iesu Christi. Alius, cùm eum quoque monuisset, ut Deum ante oculos haberet, Ego vero, inquit ille, in meo animo vere habeo ac fero. Alter vero eorum, cùm ignis pedibus eius subijceretur, flammas huiusmodi, quasi rosas suaves spargi sibi videri dixit. Postremo fumus & flamma, cùm iam altius vultum inuasisset, eos suffocauit. Dixerat inter alia Henricus, contra ius Diuinum esse, quod clerici ac sacerdotes, potestate magistratus civilis, ciusque iurisdictione à Deo constituta soluti essent. nam Episcopos quidem nullam potestatem habere aliam, quam verbi Dei fideliter integreque annuntiandi, ac pascendi ea doctrina oues Christi in Ecclesia.
units.tr: In the year 1523 at Brussels in Brabant two young men were burned, one called Henry Voes, twenty-four years old, the other John Esch; both were monks of the Augustinian order. In the following July, after they had confessed the Gospel of Christ, they were first stripped of the rank and office of the priesthood and deprived of their monastic garments. This was done at the instigation of the inquisitor of the faith, Egmondanus, who was persecuting them, and by the authority of the theologians of Louvain, because they could not be called back from their opinion and judgment. Then, rejoicing, they began to give thanks to God the heavenly Father that he had freed them from that false and abominable kind and order of priesthood, and had chosen them into another, better order of priests, in which they might offer themselves as a sacrifice of most sweet savour. A written statement was given to them, which they were to read out and openly declare to all the people, setting out what they thought and believed about religion. The chief charge of error laid against them was this: that one must believe in one God, since a man is vain and a liar in all his words and works, and both deceives himself and deceives others; for that reason no trust is to be placed in any man. When they were led to execution they went gladly and cheerfully, with this continual testimony: that they were dying for the glory of Christ and the doctrine of the Gospel and the Apostles, and that they were dying as Christians, not as heretics, pagans or unbelievers, and that they believed the Church to be the holy Church of the Son of God. They affirmed that the day on which they so died was the day they had longed for so greatly. When they came to the place where they were to be burned, they were stripped and stood there for quite a while in their shirts, embracing the stake to which they were to be fastened with great courage. They bore not only patiently but also willingly and cheerfully all the troubles and insults directed at them by their adversaries. They celebrated God's glory with psalms and canticles, and recited the formula of the creed left by the Apostles as the witness of their faith and confession. One of the teachers who were present there, seeing Henry's cheerfulness and joy, admonished him not to boast so foolishly and stupidly. "Far be it from me," he replied, "to glory except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ." Another, when he too had admonished him to keep God before his eyes, said, "Indeed, I truly have him in my mind and bear him there." Another of them, when the fire was set at his feet, said that the flames seemed to him to be scattered like sweet roses. Finally smoke and flame, having risen higher to his face, suffocated them. Among other things Henry had said that it was against divine law that clergy and priests should be released from the power of the civil magistrate and its jurisdiction, which God has established; for bishops have no other power than to announce the Word of God faithfully and sincerely, and to feed the sheep of Christ in the Church with that doctrine.

units.la: IOANNES CASTELLANVS.
units.tr: John Castellanus.

units.la: Anno M.D.XXIIII. M. Ioannes Castellanus Tornacensis, doctorque theologus, professus est institutum eorum, qui Eremitae diui Augustini appellantur: postea vocatus ad cognitionem Dei, verus doctor ac praeco Euangelii eius extitit. Is cum in Gallia Euangelium annunciasset, eo in loco qui Barle Duc dicitur, apud Vitriacum oppidum in Partesi regione, Cabilloni in Campania, atque in Lotharingia in vrbe Vicensi, sede episcopi Metensis: postquam etiam in ipsa vrbe Meti, aliqua doctrinae Euangelicae fundamenta posuisset, discedens inde, a ministris Cardinalis Lotharingi Gorsae captus fuit. quo ex oppido deinde ad castellum Nommenium per eosdem Cardinalis administros traductus fuit. Hoc autem ita factum est, non sine magna offensione perturbationeque Metensium, qui graviter indigneque ferentes, ministrum suum ac virum pium, ita captum in ea arce detineri, quosdam certos homines Cardinali subditos comprehenderunt, eosque diu apud se captiuos in custodia habuerunt. Itaque Abbas sancti Antonij Viennensis, Theodorus Caumontius nominatus, vicarius Cardinalis, in omnibus tum spiritualibus, tum corporalibus, in episcopatu Metensi, Tullensi, ac Verdunensi, cum literis ac mandato Pontificis Romani Metim venit, consulesque vrbis & magistratus senatoresque monitos atque placatos, in eam sententiam voluntatemque adduxit, vt captiuos Cardinali subditos dimiserint. Ioannes autem Castellanus fuit in custodia habitus, & crudeliter tractatus in arce Nōmeniensi, a quarto die Maij, vsque ad XII. Ianuarij, anno supra notato M. D. XXIIII. in omnibus quae ab eo quaesita fuerunt, causam doctrinamque filij Dei Iesu Christi, constantissimè tutat° est. Quae fuit causa, vt a castello Nommenio, in vrbem arcemque Vicensem deductus fuerit, summa cum constantia in confessione propositae doctrinae perseuerans, ita vt aduersarij ad eam sententiae formam sint progressi, qua illum a gradu ordinéque sacerdotali, pristinam eius vnctionem eradentes, demouerent, vt cum sacra solutum professione, in manum saecularem ac potestatem traderent.
units.tr: In the year 1524, Master John Castellanus of Tournai, doctor of theology, professed the order of those called the Hermits of St Augustine. Afterwards, called to the knowledge of God, he became a true teacher and herald of the Gospel. When he had preached the Gospel in France, in the place called Bar-le-Duc, at the town of Vitry in the region of Partois, at Châlons in Champagne, and in Lorraine in the city of Vic, the seat of the bishop of Metz, and had also laid some foundations of the evangelical doctrine in the city of Metz itself, he left there and was captured at Gorze by the servants of Cardinal of Lorraine. From that town he was then taken to the castle of Nomeny by the same servants of the Cardinal. This was done not without great offence and disturbance to the people of Metz, who took it heavily and indignantly that their minister and a pious man should be held prisoner in that fortress in this way. They seized certain men subject to the Cardinal and kept them for a long time captive in their custody. So Theodore Caumont, abbot of St Antony of Vienne, who was vicar of the Cardinal in all spiritual and temporal affairs in the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun, came to Metz with letters and a mandate of the Roman Pontiff, and brought the consuls, magistrates and senators of the city, having warned and appeased them, to such an opinion and will that they released the captives subject to the Cardinal. John Castellanus, however, was held in custody and cruelly treated in the castle of Nomeny, from the fourth day of May until the twelfth of January in the year noted above, 1524. In all the questions put to him he most constantly defended the cause and doctrine of the Son of God, Jesus Christ. This was the reason why he was led from the castle of Nomeny into the city and fortress of Vic, persevering with great constancy in the confession of the doctrine he had professed, so that his adversaries proceeded to that form of sentence by which they would remove him from the rank and order of the priesthood, erasing his former anointing, and hand him over, deprived of his sacred office, to the secular arm and power.

units.la: Quoniam forma sententiae pronuntiatae, ratioque tota degradationis,vt vocant,notabilis est,non indigna visa est,qua huic loco inter xeremus ad demonstrandas horribiles blasphemias,cum stolida & plane belluina subtilitate coniunctas maximorum mysteriorum, quae continentur in ea formula degradationis, qua inimici veritatis, adversus sanctos homines & filios Dei uti solent: ex qua omnes, etiam ij qui omnium maxime ignari sunt & imperiti, quasi manibus palpare poterunt horrendam caecitatem, qua huiusmodi cornutae bestiae percussae fuerunt.
units.tr: Since the form of the sentence pronounced, and the whole manner of what they call degradation, is remarkable, it seemed worth setting it down here, among other things, to demonstrate the horrible blasphemies joined with a foolish and plainly brutish subtlety concerning the greatest mysteries, which are contained in that formula of degradation that the enemies of the truth are accustomed to use against holy men and sons of God. From it, all people, even those who are most ignorant and inexperienced, will be able to feel, as it were with their hands, the dreadful blindness by which such horned beasts have been struck.

units.la: Forma sententiae in causa Ioannis Castellani pronuntiatae, & ratio ac via degradati- onis, ex eo iudicio ad verbum translata.
units.tr: The form of the sentence pronounced in the case of John Castellanus, and the manner and course of the degradation, translated word for word from that judgment.

units.la: Cognita causa tua cum inquisitione informata & instructa accusatoria ratione, contra te, Ioannes Castellane, sacerdotem ac religiosum ex fratribus eremitis S. Augustini: intellectaque pariter confessione tua, quam tua sponte ac voluntate falsam erroneamque doctrinam defendens edidisti: perspectis etiam piis admonitionibus, atque amantissimis exhortationibus, quibus ad te in urbe Metensi usi sumus, quibus tu instar aspidis serpetis, auris omni surditate affectas, atque ad omnem audiendam veritatem clausas, nunquam adhibere voluisti: cognitis responsis tuis, quae tu iuratus ad interrogata nostra, non semel sed saepius repetiisti, in quibus quidem arte diabolica inductus, non solum reticuisti atque occultasti veritatem, verum exemplo Cain confessione tuorum peccatorum & maleficiorum suppressisti: auditis postremo testimoniis eorum, qui maximo numero contra te ea dixerunt: quorum genera, personae, crimina contra te delata, caeteraque omnia non indigna iuris cognitione ac disceptatione, diligenter collata & considerata fuerunt: post, inquam, haec omnia cognita & perspecta, venerabilis magister Nicolaus Sauinus, in theologia doctor ac fidei exquisitor nobis adsistens, causam iam tuam instituit, ac plene perfecteque informauit. Accedit hic confessus communicato consilio cum multis hominibus literatis, magistris doctoribus, inscientia utriusque iuris, tum Diuini, tum humani praestantissimis, imprimisque cum iis, qui in causa nomen suum subscripserunt ac subsignarunt. Nam ex iis quae in causa continentur, nobis evidenter apparuit, & nunc etiam apparet, te, Ioannes Castellanc[?], saepius diversisque in locis divulgasse, & quasi dogmata quædam tradidisse, ac prædicasse multas propositiones erroneas & falsas, hæresisque Lutheranæ plenissimas, planè fidei catholicæ & veritati Euangelicæ, sedique Apostolicæ derogantes ac repugnantes. Itaq; cùm ita miserè, vt apostata defeceris, à tergóque respexeris, satis convictus es, te non eam fidem præstitisse Deo, quam debebas, sed ei mentitum fuisse. Etiam per sacras iuris canonici regulas est constitutum, æquum esse, vt qui mortiferis linguæ venenatæ telis Diuinas scripturas peruertut [?], atque animos moresque fidelium inficiut [?], atque corrumpunt, grauissimis supplicijs afficiantur, vt cæteri metu pœnarum in officio contineantur, omnes Christiana lætentur concordia, exemplàque huiusmodi tum seueritatis, tum bonitatis, propositá intucantur.His de causis & aliis, quæ ex ipsa causa colliguntur, de authoritate Apostolica, ac reuerendi Cardinalis domini, qua hac in parte vtimur, hac nostra sententia, quam pro tribunali sedentes decernimus, atque in his scriptis pronunciamus, Deum ante oculos solùm habetes, atque illud rectè considerantes, quòd qua mesura alijs mesi fuerimus, eadem remetietur nobis: nos igitur dicimus, pronunciamus, declaramus, atque etiam sententialiter ac definitiuè iudicamus, te Iohannem Castellanum propter merita tua fuisse excommunicatum, & esse nunc maxima excommunicatione, simulque etiam reum læsæ maiestatis diuinæ, criminosum atque aduersariu fidei catholicæ, Euangelicæque veritatis, præterea hæreticum manifestum, sectatorem ac participem impiæ crudelitatis Martini Lutheri, hominis turbulenti, à quo veteres hæreses, & iam antea condemnatæ suscitantur. Quam ob rem te omni honore sacerdotali, omnibus ordinibus, etiam tonsura, vestituque religioso, atque etiam ecclesiastico beneficio tuo, si vllum habes, omnique priuilegio dericali [?] iudicamus deiectum priuatumque fuisse: qucmadmodum etiam nunc deijcimus ac priuamus, & vt membrum putridum, à communione fidelium segregamus: atq; ita priuatum ac segregatum, iudicamus actualiter degradandum esse, vt ita deformatum spoliatumque, curiae seculari relinquamus: committentes hanc degradationem actualémque sententiæ nostræ executionem, huic reuerendo Domino & episcopo præsenti, propter authoritates mandatáque supra memorata. Hac sententia ita pronunciata,perfectáque concione, quæ de fide catholica eorum haberi solet, episcopus Nicopolensis, cuius paulo ante mētio facta est, civitatis Metensis suffraganeus pro tribunali sedens, cū authoritate ac potestate pontificia, cū clero, nobilibus, ac populo, degradationem Ioannis Castellani ita coepit peragere. Primum enim Castellanus iam degradandus, per officiarios eius episcopi omnibus sacerdotalibus vestimentis indutus fuit: deinde ex sacello per sacerdotes ad eam rem constitutos, cum omni sacerdotali apparatu ornatúque deductus, manibus iunctis flexisque genibus coram Episcopo est collocatus. Illico officiarij calicem cū vino & aquā, præterea patenam hostiamque ei in manu tradiderunt. Quæ omnia Episcopus degradator, de manibus eius cum huiusmodi verbis abstulit, Nos auferimus, aut iubemus auferri tibi potestatem sacrificij Deo offerendi, Mis-sæque tam pro mortuis quam pro vivis celebrandæ. Deinde Episcopus sacros utriusque manus digitos lamina vitrea erasit, dicens, Nos hac rasura potestatem sacrificandi, consecrandi benedicendique tibi auferimus, quam tu ex unctione manuum, pollicisque accepisti.
units.tr: Your case, John Castellanus, priest and religious of the order of the Hermits of St Augustine, having been learned through an inquiry, informed and instructed by an accusatory process against you; your confession also having been understood, which you made by your own free will and consent, defending a false and erroneous doctrine; the pious admonitions and most loving exhortations also having been weighed, with which we dealt with you in the city of Metz, though you, like a serpent, stopped your ears with every deafness and would never allow yourself to listen to any truth; your answers having been examined, which you repeated under oath to our questions, not once but many times, in which indeed, led by the devilish art, you not only kept silent about and hid the truth, but like Cain suppressed the confession of your sins and crimes; and finally the testimonies of those who spoke against you in greatest number having been heard, whose kinds, persons, and charges brought against you, and all the other matters not unworthy of legal examination and debate, having been carefully compared and considered; after, I say, all these things were learned and perceived, the venerable master Nicholas Savin, doctor of theology and examiner of the faith, assisting us, has now instituted your case and fully and perfectly informed it. Here is added the confession, made after shared counsel with many learned men, master doctors, most excellent in the knowledge of both laws, divine and human, and especially with those who subscribed and signed their names to the case. For from what is contained in the case, it has clearly appeared to us, and now also appears, that you, John Castellane, have on many occasions and in various places spread abroad, and as it were handed down and preached, many erroneous and false propositions, most full of Lutheran heresy, plainly derogating from and opposing the Catholic faith, the evangelical truth, and the Apostolic See. Therefore, since you have so wretchedly revolted like an apostate and looked back, you are sufficiently convicted of not having given to God the faith you owed, but of having been false to him. It is also established by the sacred rules of canon law that it is fitting that those who pervert the divine Scriptures with the deadly darts of a venomous tongue, and infect and corrupt the minds and morals of the faithful, be visited with the gravest punishments, so that others may be kept in their duty by fear of penalties, and all may rejoice in Christian concord, and look upon examples of such severity and such goodness set forth. For these reasons and others which are gathered from the case itself, by the Apostolic authority and that of the reverend lord Cardinal, which we use in this matter, by this our sentence, which we decree sitting on the tribunal and pronounce in these writings, having God alone before our eyes, and rightly considering that with whatever measure we have measured to others, it will be measured back to us; we therefore say, pronounce, declare, and also judge by sentence and definitively, that you, John Castellanus, on account of your deserts, have been excommunicated, and are now under the greatest excommunication, and at the same time guilty of injured divine majesty, criminal and adversary of the Catholic faith and of evangelical truth, moreover a manifest heretic, follower and participant in the impious cruelty of Martin Luther, a turbulent man, from whom old heresies, long since condemned, are revived. Wherefore we judge that you have been deprived and stripped of all sacerdotal honour, of all orders, even of the tonsure and religious garb, and also of your ecclesiastical benefice, if you have any, and of every clerical privilege; just as we now also depose and deprive you, and as a rotten member we cut you off from the communion of the faithful; and so deprived and cut off, we judge that you are to be actually degraded, so that, thus deformed and stripped, we may leave you to the secular court, committing this degradation and the actual execution of our sentence to this reverend lord and bishop present, on account of the authorities and mandates mentioned above. This sentence having thus been pronounced, and the customary sermon on the Catholic faith of these men having been completed, the bishop of Nicopolis, whose mention was made a little before, suffragan of the city of Metz, sitting on the tribunal with papal authority and power, with the clergy, nobles and people present, began to carry out the degradation of John Castellanus in this way. First, Castellanus, now to be degraded, was clothed by the officials of the bishop in all the sacerdotal vestments; then he was led out of the chapel by priests appointed for that purpose, with all the sacerdotal equipment and adornment, and placed before the bishop with his hands joined and knees bent. Immediately the officials handed him a chalice with wine and water, and also a paten and host in his hand. The bishop who was degrading him took all these from his hands with these words: We take away from you, or order to be taken away from you, the power of offering sacrifice to God, and of celebrating the Mass both for the dead and for the living. Then the bishop scraped the sacred digits of both hands with a piece of glass, saying: By this scraping we take from you the power of sacrificing, consecrating and blessing, which you received from the anointing of your hands and thumbs.

units.la: Deinde summo illo indumento atque ornamento, quod cāsula appellant, à tergo cum caputio detrasto[?], eum exuit, his utens verbis, Nos iure optimo exuimus te veste sacerdotali, quæ charitatem significat. nam tu eam quidem atque omnem innocentiam exuisti.· Postea stolam ei detrahens, dixit, Tu turpiter abiecisti & post tergum reiecisti signum Domini nostri, qui hac stola repræsentatur. Quamobrem eam tibi auferimus inhabilemque reddimus, ad ullum officium sacerdotale exercendum, aut aliam rem, quæ ad sacerdotium pertineat. Sed reliqua eius generis nugamenta cognosci possunt ex eorum libris, quibus ineptissima tota hæc disciplina continetur. Eorum quidem nunc gustum nos hic dare voluimus, ut omnes homines intelligant, quam scelerata audacia Papistæ sua execranda mysteria peragant & quam impune verbis sacræ Scripturæ abutantur.
units.tr: Then, from his back, they stripped off that highest garment and ornament, which they call the chasuble, together with the hood, and he put on his vestments, using these words: "We rightly strip you of the sacerdotal vestment, which signifies charity; for you have indeed cast off both this and all innocence." Afterwards, taking the stole from him, he said: "You have shamefully abandoned it and thrown behind your back the sign of our Lord, who is represented by this stole. Wherefore we take it from you and render you unfit to exercise any sacerdotal office, or anything else that pertains to the priesthood." The rest of this sort of trifling can be learned from their books, in which this whole most absurd discipline is contained. We have wished to give only a taste of it here, so that all men may understand with what wicked audacity the Papists carry out their execrable mysteries, and with what impunity they abuse the words of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Perfecta degradatione, procurator fiscalis curiæ civitatisque Metensis, ab Actuario seu notario causæ postulavit, ut ad perpetuam rei memoriam, unum aut etiam plura instrumenta peractæ degradationis conscriberentur. Tum ministri Episcopi Ioannem Castellanum vestitu habituque clericali exuerunt, eumque amictu seculari induerunt. hoc autem propterea ita fit, quoniam is qui loco gradúque sacerdotali est demotus, potestati magistratus civilis est tradendus, secundum constitutiones Papæ Innocentij tertij, qui ea in re sacram unctionem, sanctissimumque sacerdotij religionem violari noluit. Episcopus igitur degradator non ulterius progressus, hoc modo locutus est, Nos pronuntiamus ut curia secularis, te ita degradatum spoliatumque omni ordine ac privilegio clericali, in sua cura suscipiat. Id autem cum factū effet, idem Episcopus usitato more, specie quadam officij simulationeq; humanitatis se pro eo deprecatorem apud iudicem præbes, Domine iudex (inquit) nos te omni quo possumus studio rogamus, cum propter Deũ, tũ etiam propter dona pietatis ac misericordiæ nostrasque preces, ne in hunc miserum atque infelicem hominem aliquid mali constituas, quod ad mortem, aut mutilatione corporis eius pertineat. His ita actis, magistratus secularis urbis Vicensis, confirmans sententiam ante pronuntiatam, condemnauit Ioannem Castellanum, ut vivus cremaretur. Quam quidem pœnam tanta constantia atque animi magnitudine sustinuit, ut non solum ignari homines maximo numero ad cognitionem veritatis conversi fuerint, verumetiam cæteri, qui non pauci aliquem pietatis gustum sensumque habebant, hoc genere mortis tam prætiosæ, in oblata gratia Dei confirmati maximam utilitatem perceperint.
units.tr: When the degradation was complete, the fiscal procurator of the court and city of Metz asked the notary or clerk of the case that one or more instruments of the completed degradation be drawn up, for the perpetual memory of the matter. Then the ministers of the bishop stripped John Castellanus of clerical dress and bearing, and clothed him in secular garb. This is done in this way because the man who has been deposed from sacerdotal rank and position is to be handed over to the civil magistrate, according to the constitutions of Pope Innocent III, who was unwilling that the holy anointing and the sacred dignity of the priesthood should be violated in this matter. The bishop who performed the degradation therefore went no further, but spoke in this manner: "We pronounce that the secular court should take you, thus degraded and stripped of every clerical order and privilege, into its own care." When this had been done, the same bishop, in the customary manner, putting on a certain show of office and a pretence of humanity, presented himself as a intercessor on his behalf before the judge: "Lord judge," he said, "we ask you with all the zeal we can, both for God's sake and for the gifts of piety and mercy, and at our prayers, not to decree anything evil against this wretched and unhappy man that would concern his death or the mutilation of his body." With these things done, the secular magistrate of the city of Vic, confirming the sentence pronounced before, condemned John Castellanus to be burned alive. He bore this punishment with such constancy and greatness of spirit that not only did a very great number of ignorant men turn to the knowledge of the truth, but also the others, of whom not a few had some taste and feeling of piety, were confirmed by this so precious kind of death, and received the greatest benefit from the grace of God offered to them.

units.la: IOANNES CLERIC
units.tr: John Clerc

units.la: IOannes Clericus Meldensis, frater fuit natu maior Petri Clerici, eius qui cum quatuordecim (quorum memoria postea in hoc libro reperictur conseruata) supplicio affectus est. Is Ioannes in urbe Meldensi captus est, anno M. D. XIII. quod schedulam affixerat valvis summi templi eius urbis, contra indulgentias a Papa missas, in qua scripserat eum esse Antichristum. Quamobrem eo quidem tempore fuit condemnatus, ut tribus diebus certo spatio intermissis, verberibus caederetur, atque impressa in fronte nota ignominiosè afficeretur. Eius autem mater, mulier verè Christiana, tametsi maritum haberet adversarium, quum videret filium virgis verberari, atque ea nota compungi ac deformari, animum ei addidit, & in hanc vocem exclamauit, Vivat Christus, eiusque insignia. Postea Ioannes ea poena ignominiaque affectus, Rosoium in Briam profectus est, inde Metim in Lotharingiam: quo in loco aliquandiu est commoratus, artificio utens lanae carminandae ac pectendae. Is pridie eius diei, quo cultus quorundam idolorum exiguo in sacello extra urbem celebrandus erat, permotus eo Dei studio quod exitus postea rectissimum sanctissimumque esse declarauit, urbe egressus, venit cum in locum, eaque simulachra fregit, quae postero die homines superstitiosi adoraturi erant. Itaque canonici, sacerdotes, ac monachi, cum eo omnem populum solenni processionis pompa conduxissent, omniaque simulachra fracta aut mutilata offendissent, totam civitatem concitarunt ad authorem eius facinoris quaerendum, qui non multo post repertus est. Nam praeter sinistram opinionem, quam de eo iam susceptam habebant, visus fuerat a quibusdam ab eodem loco revertens in urbem in ipso diei crepusculo. Itaque comprehensus factum statim confessus, coram populo rationem cur id fecisset, reddidit, cum tanta populi offensione ac furore, ut ad gravissimum mortis supplicium mox poscereretur. Causa eius informata, postquam puram filij Dei Iesu Christi doctrinam, tum perpaucis in ea urbe cognitam, constanter asseruit, ad locum extremo supplicio constitutum ductus est, in eoque atrox atque horribile genus mortis perpessus. na primum manus dextra ei amputata fuit. deinde nasus forcipibus tenacissimis avulsus, duoque eius brachia cum mamma utraque eodem instrumento dilaniata fuerunt. Nemo sane erat in eo tam atroci spectaculo, qui non commoveretur attonitus: praesertim cum videret eximiam virtutem, invictamque constantiam, qua Deus hunc Martyrem muniverat & roboraverat. qui quidem in maximis atque acerbissimis tormentis, pronuntiauit illos versus Psalmi 115, Simulachra eorum sunt argentum & aurum, opus manuum hominum. Reliquum autem vitae, quod in eius corpore tam crudeliter affecto supererat, paulo post igni consumptum fuit.
units.tr: John Clerc of Meaux was the elder brother of Peter Clerc, who was put to death with fourteen others (whose memory is preserved later in this book). John was arrested in the city of Meaux in 1513, because he had posted a placard on the doors of the principal church of that city, against the indulgences sent out by the Pope, in which he had written that the Pope was Antichrist. For this he was condemned at that time to be flogged on three days, at set intervals, and to be branded disgracefully on the forehead. His mother, a truly Christian woman, although her husband was an opponent, when she saw her son being beaten with rods and his forehead pierced and disfigured with that brand, encouraged him and cried out, "Long live Christ and his marks!" Afterwards John, having suffered that punishment and disgrace, went to Rosoy in Brie and from there to Metz in Lorraine, where he stayed for some time, earning his living by carding and combing wool. On the day before a certain idol cult was to be celebrated in a small chapel outside the city, he was moved by a zeal for God, which his later end showed to have been most upright and holy. Leaving the city, he came to that place and broke the images which superstitious people were to worship the next day. So the canons, priests and monks, leading all the people with them in a solemn procession, found all the images broken or mutilated, and they stirred up the whole city to seek the author of this deed. He was found not long after. For apart from the bad reputation he already had, some people had seen him returning to the city from that place at dusk. So he was seized, and at once confessed the deed, and gave his reasons for doing it before the people. The people were so offended and enraged that they immediately demanded the most severe penalty of death. His cause was taken up, after he steadfastly asserted the pure doctrine of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, which was then known to very few in that city. He was led to the place of execution and suffered there a savage and horrible kind of death. First his right hand was cut off; then his nose was torn away with the most tenacious pincers, and both his arms, together with the flesh of each breast, were torn to pieces with the same instrument. Certainly no one present at so atrocious a spectacle was not moved and astonished, especially when they saw the remarkable courage and unconquered constancy with which God had fortified and strengthened this martyr. In the greatest and most bitter torments he pronounced those verses of Psalm 115: "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands." The rest of his life, which remained in his body so cruelly mutilated, was consumed by fire shortly afterwards.

units.la: M. NICOLAUS ANTVERPIANUS.
units.tr: M. Nicolaus of Antwerp.

units.la: Circiter annum M.D.XXIIII. Antuerpiæ (quod est celeberrimū emporiū in ducatu Brabatino) atque in locis finitimis, magnus erat numerus hominū omnis generis, qui tū primum aliquē verbi Dei gustū capiebant. Eo tempore quidam Parochus fuit Melzae, qui locus ab Antuerpia duo prope milliaria abest. is ad suas conciones tantam hominum multitudinem undique attrahebat, ut sæpius in patentibus locis campisque concionari cogeretur. Cum autem libere annuntiabat verbum Dei, tum non obscurè ac timidè falsas & impias hominū doctrinas arguebat. In quadam vero novissima concione sua audiente populo iucundè ac graviter & seipsum & alios sacrificulos accusauit, ac loquens de Missa, dixit, Nos quidem Iuda proditore sumus deteriores, atque improbiores. is enim Christum dominum vendidit & tradidit: nos vero cum vobis vendimus, nec tamen tradimus. Non multo post tempore, sacerdotes ac monachi, hoc felici Euangelij successu offensi, metuentes ne præda de manibus ac faucibus extorqueretur, mandatum ab aulâ Brabantica contra hunc Pastorem & quēdam Augustinensem, qui tum etiam Antuerpiæ magno populi cōcursu concionabatur, impetrarunt. Illud vero mandatum potestatem dabat vi auferendi summum corporis indumentum (ut vestem aut pallium) ijs qui in huiusmodi eorum conuentibus atque concionibus deprehensi essent. Qui vero eos cōcionatores comprehendissent, ijs præmium triginta Caroleorum aureorum eodem edicto propositum fuit & constitutum. Hoc tamen edictum Imperatoris Caroli V. nomine promulgatu, impedire non potuit quo minus postea populus quadam die Dominica ad audiendum Dei verbum conuenirent eu in locum, vbi scaphæ atq; naues subducuntur ac conficiuntur. In eo conuentu ac cœtu aderat quidā iuuenis, Nicolaus nominatus, in doctrina verbi Dei apprimè institutus. qui cum videret Augustinensem illũ, cuius conciotā auidè expectabatur, non venire: dixit minimè æquum esse eā multitudinem ita congregatam, famelicā sine vllo pastu verbi Dei discedere. Itaq; nauē quæ litori erat proxima, vnde melius audiri posset, afcedit[?], & multo plura ex syncerae pietatis doctrina eis annutiauit ac declarauit, quàm vnquà antea audierant. Exposuit ea concione illam ab omnibus Euangelistis descriptã de quinq; panibus & duobus piscibus parabolā: ostendit q; Dominũ nõ aliquot hominũ millia diuina sua doctrina nunc pascere: verùetiā per totũ mundũ spargendā doctrinā hāc,
units.tr: About the year 1524, at Antwerp (which is a most famous trading centre in the duchy of Brabant) and in the neighbouring places, there was a great number of people of every kind who at that time first began to taste something of the Word of God. At that time there was a parish priest at Melzen, a place about two miles from Antwerp. He drew such a multitude of people from every side to his sermons that he was often forced to preach in open places and fields. When he preached the Word of God freely, he also openly and boldly refuted the false and impious doctrines of men. In one of his last sermons, with the people listening gladly and seriously, he accused both himself and the other little priests, and speaking of the Mass he said: "We are indeed worse and more wicked than Judas the traitor. For he sold and betrayed the Lord Christ; but we sell him to you, though we do not betray him." Not long after, the priests and monks, offended by this happy success of the Gospel, and fearing that their prey would be wrested from their hands and jaws, obtained from the court of Brabant an order against this minister and against a certain Augustinian who was then also preaching at Antwerp to large crowds. That order gave power to strip off the outer garment of the body (such as a coat or cloak) from those who were found at such assemblies and sermons. Those who arrested the preachers were promised a reward of thirty gold Carolus coins, set out in the same edict. Yet this edict, issued in the name of the Emperor Charles V, could not prevent the people from gathering one Sunday to hear the Word of God in the place where boats and ships are hauled up and built. In that gathering there was a young man named Nicolaus, thoroughly trained in the doctrine of God's Word. When he saw that the Augustinian, whose sermon they were eagerly awaiting, was not coming, he said it was by no means right for that crowd, so assembled, to depart hungry without any feeding on the Word of God. So he went up into a ship that lay nearest the shore, where he could be heard better, and proclaimed and explained to them far more of the doctrine of pure piety than they had ever heard before. In that sermon he expounded the parable of the five loaves and two fishes, described by all the Evangelists, and showed that the Lord now feeds many thousands of people with his divine teaching, and that this teaching is to be spread throughout the whole world and to feed an infinite multitude of men.

units.la: Quid differat sacrificulus a Iuda. exque ea infinitam hominum turbam alendam esse. Post concionem, duo serui cuiusdam lanij saepe praemij, cum detulerunt atque in potestate magistratus tradiderunt. Is vero Nicolaus posteaquam pura Euangelij doctrinam constanter defendisset, postero die, qui fuit dies Lunae, sacco infutus, propter metum populi, subito in profluentem coiectus est, iuxta cranam vulgo portus Antuerpiensis, eo ipso anno M.D.XXIIII.
units.tr: What a little priest differs from Judas. After the sermon, two servants of a certain butcher, eager for the reward, informed on him and handed him over to the power of the magistrate. Nicolaus, after he had steadfastly defended the pure doctrine of the Gospel, was sewn into a sack on the following day, which was a Monday, and, for fear of the people, was suddenly thrown into the flowing river near the crane, commonly called the harbour of Antwerp, in the same year, 1524.

units.la: Ex tribus historiis quas OEcolampadius scripsisse dicitur, nos eam huic libro Martyrum intexuimus, quae causam & rationem propriam eius, qui propter Euangelii testimonium mortuus describitur, habere videbatur.
units.tr: Of the three histories which OEcolampadius is said to have written, we have woven this one into this book of Martyrs, because it seemed to have its own cause and reason, being the account of a man who died for the testimony of the Gospel.

units.la: N. PASTOR BRISGOIVS.
units.tr: No. Pastor of Breisgau

units.la: IN quodam Brisgoiae pago, pastor erat vigilans, ac homo in diuinis literis eruditus, sanctimonia vitae clarus, humanitate & comitate insignis, pastoris officio multos annos egregie functus. In synodis compresbyterorum doctrina excellebat, ac etiam episcopo Constantiensi gratus, authoritateque valens apud omnes, quibuscum negotij aliquid habebat, amans pacis, tragoedias inter fratres ortas mira prudetia sopiebat, ad mutuam charitatem inuitans: honestatem vitae & morum emendationem in omnibus conuentibus, quibus praeerat, summe extollebat: seipsum saepe exempli gratia, quum lites subnatae erant, adducebat. Hic quum Euangelij Christi sermo purior in lucem diuulgaretur, adiectis vbique ex patribus scholiis, coepit mira auiditate Euangelicos libros euoluere, deuorareque, quos iam olim etiam legerat, sed nullo intellectu, nulla attentione verborum & sententiarum. Iudicio & intelligentia accedente ex continua lectione, homo senex, apud seipsum coepit cogitare, in quantis tenebris, in quantis erroribus totum sacerdotale genus inuolutum iam longo tempore fuisset. Deum immortalem, dicebat, quis vnquam cogitasset, tam doctos, tam sanctos viros, tot annis ita potuisse a scopo verae doctrinae aberrare, tot erroribus implicari Scripturam sacram, situ & squalore humanae creationis ac aliuae obductam conspurcatamque, & a paucissimis cognitam? Se enim id Euangelium, ordine quo scriptum est, nunquam credidisse veritatem esse, quum multa de cruce, de persecutione, de turpissima morte in eo continerentur, & sacerdotibus omnia quam felicissime succedercnt[?] cederent, nemoque contra eos sine damno maximo causam iustam agere, aut publica vitia emendare ausus fuisset. Iam autem palam Euangelium vim suam exercere, crucem in foribus esse, adversarios verbi insanire, impios caput tollere, ac ad omnia facinora in pios designanda, audacissimos. Episcopos, quorum erat Verbi potentiam asserere, crudeliores esse, quam ullos unquam tyrannos. Se igitur omnem dubitationem, cum praesens seculum consideret, abiecisse, iam manibus tenere, oculis videre Christum vera praedixisse, quum tot Sanctorum corpora quotidie virgis caedantur, in exilium proscribantur, lanientur nō dicendis poenis, igne tradantur comburenda, aquis suffocentur, laqueo suspendantur. Quis enim enumeret poenas, quas pij homines hoc anno, apud eos qui se dicunt Christianos pertulerunt ob Christi liberam confessionem? Quinetiam cum tumultus rusticus, nō dicendo furore eruperet, sursumque & deorsum omnia ferrentur, pius pastor (nam hoc temporis nemo audebat contra Euangelij praedicationem mutire) ne perpetuo scortationis peccato inficeretur, duxit famulam, quam domi habebat, in uxorem, ex qua etiam liberos procrearat. Insania rusticorum augmentum quotidie & vires sumebat. Coenobia & sacerdotum domos, diligentissime invisebant: quicquid eduli invetum, hoc mox devorabant. Quod absumere non poterant, hoc perdebat, aut secum aucebant. Cohors quaedam illorum etiam in illius pij pastoris aedes sese ingessit. Nullum enim discrimen habebant inter pium sacerdotem & impium: & quae inveniebant, aut absumebant, aut furto auferebant: quod illis libitum erat, instar bestiarum insanientium agebant. Abitum parantibus, non potuit pastor fidelis a lachrymis temperare & eos hac admonitione prosequi, Heus, inquit, boni viri, futuram calamitatem, exitiumque incuitabile[?] vobis denuntio. Quid sibi volunt hi tumultus, atque haec turba? Nullam aequitatem, nullam iustitiam servatis? quid agitis? quem consultorem habetis? ad quem finem respicitis? rapitis quicquid sese offert, more latronum. Annon in mente venit omnia tandem, quae iam rapitis, destruitis, evertitis, restituenda esse vestro maximo malo? Quae seditio unquam felicem habuit exitum? quae & pios & honestos involuit viros, ut fortunis omnibus & ipsa vita periclitetur. Euangelium praetexitis, & nihil Euangelij habetis neque in ore neque in corde. Satanæ est Euangelium, quod omnia turbat, per fas & nefas proximo sua rapit & destruit. sed Christi Euangelium docet bene omnibus facere, seditionem fugere, periuria vitare. Dico vobis, Deum iustum iudicem hoc vestro facto offenditis, ad iracundia prouocatis, qui malum impunitum non sinet. Videte & perspicite, qua defensione sitis usuri: intelligetis absq; dubio, hoc quod dixi de vobis fatendum esse. Contra secundam Mosis tabulam strenue pergitis, quæ quidem proximi curam describit, ad quà quisque Christianus obligatur. Scriptum est in Euangelio, quod in ore vestro natat, Quod tibi non vis, alteri ne feceris. Offenditis insuper mirum in modum totam nobilitatem, magistratum vestrum legitimum, cui iuramento obstricti estis, quorūmque servi. Clades imminet: perfidia enim Deus punire solet. Annon sæpe audistis à me, fidem iuramenti esse solvendam? vinculū enim est totius humanæ societatis. & legitima iuramēta violare semper fuit nefas apud omnes homines sobrios, etiam apud ipsos Gentiles. Iosue iuramentum præstitū Gabaonitis seruauit, licet dolo hoc esset obtentum. Saul hoc fœdus iuramento sancitum inter Ifraelem & Gabaonitas, postea. rupit, dissolutique fœderis & violati iuramenti pœnas dedit, fame & filiorum suorum nece. Perpendite, obsecro per Christum Iesum, quid agatis, qualem inuidiam super caput vestrum consletis[?]. Nō est parua res, sed capitalis, seditionem mouere, excitare alios, turbare reipublicæ tranquillum statum. Non quiescent nobiles vestri, quos deturbare è suis possessionibus conamini, plus æquo crudeles erga innocentes, censu vestro lacunæ rei familiaris explebunt, & in tributis imperandis tantum oneris vobis imponent, ut etiam liberi vestri satis pecuniarum dare non possint, ob delistum[?] vestrum: quod faciliime intelligi re ipsa poterit. postquam furor semel conceptus, extinctus fuerit, alius alii prodet. Hæc ipso loquete mœsto vultu, inermis coram illis stans, abierunt nebulones, vocantes sene delirum & stolidum. Unus ex iis nequitia præstantior, dixit, Iam sæpe à vobis per Missarum nundinationes, per purgatorij terrorem, per exequias defunctorum, decepti sumus spoliatique etiam iterum repetimus profusam pecuniam. tace itaque sacrificule, sat bonorum adhuc habes. Christus pauper fuit, nō habes quo caput suum reclinaret: adhuc multa habes. aut totam domum tuam evacuabimus, incendemusque.
units.tr: In a certain village of Breisgau there was a vigilant pastor, a man learned in the divine writings, distinguished for the holiness of his life, outstanding for his courtesy and affability, who had discharged the duties of a pastor admirably for many years. In the synods of the presbyters he excelled in doctrine. He was also pleasing to the bishop of Constance, and carried authority with all those with whom he had any dealings. He loved peace, and with remarkable prudence he calmed the quarrels that arose between brothers, inviting them to mutual charity. In all the assemblies over which he presided he greatly commended honesty of life and the amendment of morals, and whenever disputes had arisen he often held himself up as an example. When the purer preaching of the Gospel of Christ began to be spread abroad, with the scholia of the Fathers added everywhere, he began with remarkable eagerness to pore over and devour the evangelical books, which he had read long before but without any understanding, without attention to the words and meanings. With judgment and understanding coming from continual reading, the old man began to reflect within himself into what darkness, into what errors, the whole priestly class had been enveloped for so long. "Immortal God," he said, "who would ever have thought that such learned and holy men could for so many years have strayed so far from the goal of true doctrine, and that Holy Scripture could be entangled in so many errors, covered and defiled by the filth and squalor of human invention, and known to very few? For he had never believed that this Gospel, in the order in which it is written, was true, since it contained so much about the cross, persecution and the most shameful death, while everything turned out most happily for the priests, and no one had dared to plead a just cause against them without great loss, or to correct public vices. Now, however, the Gospel plainly exercises its power: the cross is at the doors, the adversaries of the Word rage, the impious raise their heads and are most audacious in devising every crime against the godly. The bishops, whose duty it was to uphold the power of the Word, are more cruel than any tyrants ever were. Therefore, looking at the present age, he had cast off all doubt. He now holds in his hands and sees with his eyes that Christ foretold the truth, since so many bodies of saints are daily beaten with rods, banished into exile, torn with punishments not to be named, handed over to be burned, drowned in waters, hanged on the noose. For who could count the punishments which pious men have endured this year, at the hands of those who call themselves Christians, for their free confession of Christ? Moreover, when the rustic uprising broke out with a fury not to be named, and everything was tossed up and down, the godly pastor (for at that time no one dared to murmur against the preaching of the Gospel), so that he might not be stained by the perpetual sin of fornication, took as his wife the maidservant he kept at home, by whom he had also begotten children. The madness of the peasants daily gained strength and power. They most diligently visited the monasteries and the houses of the priests, and whatever food they found they at once devoured; what they could not consume they destroyed, or carried off with them. A band of them also forced its way into the house of that godly pastor. They made no distinction between the pious priest and the impious, and whatever they found they either consumed or stole; whatever pleased them, they did like raging beasts.
