As they prepared to leave, the faithful pastor could not refrain from tears, and sent them off with this admonition: "Hey, good men, I announce to you a coming calamity and an inescapable ruin. What do these tumults and this mob mean? Do you keep no fairness, no justice? What are you doing? Whom do you have as your counsellor? To what end do you look? You plunder whatever presents itself, like robbers. Has it not come into your minds that all that you now seize, destroy and overturn will at last have to be restored, to your own greatest harm? What sedition ever had a happy outcome? It entangles both pious and honest men, so that fortunes and life itself are endangered. You pretend the Gospel, and yet you have nothing of the Gospel either in your mouth or in your heart. It is the Gospel of Satan that throws everything into confusion, and by right or wrong seizes and destroys what belongs to one's neighbour. But the Gospel of Christ teaches us to do good to all, to flee sedition, and to avoid perjury. I tell you, by this deed you offend God, the just judge, and provoke him to anger, for he will not leave evil unpunished. See and consider what defence you will use; you will undoubtedly understand that what I have said of you must be confessed. You press on vigorously against the second table of Moses, which describes the care of one's neighbour, to which every Christian is bound. It is written in the Gospel, which floats on your lips: 'What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.' Furthermore, you offend in a remarkable way the whole nobility, your lawful magistrate, to whom you are bound by oath and whose servants you are. Ruin hangs over you, for God is wont to punish perfidy. Have you not often heard from me that the faith of an oath must be kept? For it is the bond of all human society, and to violate lawful oaths has always been an impiety among all sober men, even among the Gentiles themselves. Joshua kept the oath sworn to the Gibeonites, although it had been obtained by deceit. Saul later broke the covenant sworn between Israel and the Gibeonites, and paid the penalty for dissolving the covenant and violating the oath, by famine and by the slaughter of his sons. Consider well, I beg you through Christ Jesus, what you are doing and what hatred you are bringing upon your own heads. It is no small matter but a capital one to stir up sedition, to rouse others, and to disturb the peaceful state of the commonwealth. Your nobles, whom you try to drive from their possessions, will not be quiet; they are more cruel than is right towards the innocent, and they will fill the gaps in their household finances from your wealth. In levying taxes they will impose on you so great a burden that your children too will not be able to pay enough money, on account of your crime, which can very easily be understood from the facts themselves. Once the fury has been conceived and then extinguished, one will betray another." Speaking these words with a sorrowful countenance, standing unarmed before them, the scoundrels went away, calling the old man mad and foolish. One of them, more wicked than the rest, said: "Often by you, through the selling of Masses, through the terror of purgatory, through funerals, we have been deceived and despoiled, and now we demand back the money lavished on you. So be quiet, little priest; you still have enough goods. Christ was poor, and had nowhere to lay his head; you still have many things. Either we will empty your whole house, or we will set it on fire."

units.la: Sedato partim rustico tumultu, & agricolis in gratiam (abiectis videlicet armis) assumptis: quum multi ex coryphæis seditionis caperentur passim in agris, sine delectu, sine misericordia: etiam pius hic pastor, nihil tale timens, ob Euangelij liberam praedicationem, quod multos pessime habebat, noctu a militibus in hoc ordinatis, crudelissime captus est. qui eum reuinctis in tergum manibus, constrictisque pedibus magno fune, præsente uxore & liberis, equo abduxerunt: & scōmata in captiuum iaciebant, nihilque crudelitatis omittebant. Tales tyrannos habet seculum nostrum, tales administros, quibus accensus est animus aduersus electos Dei. Strepitu audito (nox enim pavore addit) fit concursus maximus, non virorum, sed mulierculorum: quidnam sibi hic clamor & ploratus, & equorum multitudo velit, summè expectantium. Viri latitabant in tutis locis, ne deprehenderentur. permulti non solum agros, vineas, prata, uxores & liberos, sed etiā sedes suas patrias, istorum hominum iniurijs exagitati, reliquerant. Abite, inquiunt milites, & securè somnum capite. nihil periculi hic vobis imminet: cum sacerdote nobis res est. viros adducite vestros, si domi sunt, & cum illis colloquium habituri sumus. eorum interest noctu vigilare, pagum armis custodire, ab incursionibus latronum & prædonum defendere.
units.tr: When the rustic tumult was partly quelled, and the peasants taken back into favour (their arms, of course, having been laid aside), while many of the leaders of the sedition were seized everywhere in the fields, without discrimination and without mercy, this godly pastor too was most cruelly seized at night by soldiers appointed for this purpose. He had nothing of the kind to fear, since he was preaching the Gospel freely, although many bitterly hated him for it. They led him away on a horse, his hands bound behind his back and his feet tied with a great rope, in the presence of his wife and children; they threw jeers at the captive and omitted no cruelty. Such tyrants our age has, and such agents, by whom the spirit is inflamed against the elect of God. When the noise was heard (for night adds to fear) there was a great gathering, not of men but of women, most anxious to know what this shouting and weeping and multitude of horses meant. The men were hiding in safe places, lest they be caught. Very many, harassed by the injuries of these men, had left behind not only their fields, vineyards, meadows, wives and children, but also their native homes. "Go away," said the soldiers, "and sleep safely. No danger threatens you here; our business is with the priest. Bring your men, if they are at home, and we shall have a conference with them. It is in their interest to keep watch at night, guard the village with arms, and defend it from the attacks of robbers and plunderers."

units.la: Verum post longum carceris tetri squalorem, post quaestiones crudeles & non dicendas, tam in pudendis, quam in aliis corporis partibus, morti tandem est adiudicatus. Quid facinoris impegerunt huic tam insigni viro? nempe, quod uxorem duxerat, non publicè coram ecclesia, sed domi suæ, paucis præsentibus: Dei scilicet iussum sequens, ne a regno Dei propter scortationem excluderetur, iuxta dictum Pauli. Eam, inquam, ob causam, aqua submergendum ac suffocandum existimarunt. Neque enim vllam seditionis aut sceleris notam impingere potuerunt, tametsi diligentissimè illius conciones, vitam & mores per quosdam maleuolos homines expiscati sint. Quum autem abduceretur per tortorem ad locum supplicij, placidè omnibus, qui eum consolandi gratia compellabant, respondebat. Verum cum sacrificuli quidam & monachi cum eū morte luctante, oratione interna Deum orante, ac jām paradisum cogitate, obtunderet suis nænijs, quibus eū a sano verborū Christi intellectu auocare studebat, eos non semel rogabat, vt silerent, se Christo Iesu domino caeli & terrae sua peccata quotidie confessum esse, absolutione accepisse, & se hac in re dubitare minime. Christo saluatori meo, inquit dulci voce, victima hodie ero grata. nihil designaui, quod Domino hac in re, propter quam damnatus sum, displiceat: quietâ conscientiâ Dominus dedit. videat hi qui innocentes sanguine sitiunt & effundunt, quid incœptent, quæ offendat, cuius est vere iudicare corda hominum: quia dicit, Mihi vindictam & ego vlciscar. Pellem hanc ossibus vix haerentem, breui alias abiecturus eram (macilento enim erat corpore) Noui me mortalem, vermem, corruptibilem, & in hoc natum. Etiam olim diem extremum exoptaui, petúque[?] dissolui & esse cum Christo, cruce dignus ob varia peccata, quæ in Dominum commisi immanissima. & Christus meus saluator crucem sustulit, in cruce mortuus est. Volo igitur & ego gloriari in cruce domini nostri Iesu Christi. Hanc nebulones quidam cygnæam cantionem ferre non poterant. Carnifici itaque annuerunt, vt senem deturbaret e loco, in quo sedebat constrictus, paratusque ad lanienam. In aquis diu se mouit, adeo vt sanguinolentus fieret fluuiolus. Indicium fuit, quod iusti sanguis hoc die effusus esset. Omnes qui aderant, viso hoc spectaculo, mœsti apud se, quidnam sibi sanguineus iste aquae rubor velit, admirantur. Stupidi adstant attractis crebris singultibus: domum reuertuntur tacito corde, considerantes ea quæ acta essent: licet nemo quicquam diceret, ob metum qui illis incussus, eo quod omnia tyrannorum more exercerentur cum rusticanis hominibus. O crudelia pectora! o perfidum factum! Hæc ab illo hausi, qui suis oculis vidit hoc horrendum spectaculum.
units.tr: But after a long stay in the foul squalor of the prison, after cruel interrogations, too shameful to describe, both on his private parts and on other parts of his body, he was at last condemned to death. What crime did they charge this distinguished man with? Namely, that he had taken a wife, not publicly before the Church, but in his own home with a few people present, following the command of God, so that he would not be excluded from the kingdom of God on account of fornication, according to the saying of Paul. For that reason, I say, they decided he should be drowned and suffocated in water. Indeed, they could fix no mark of sedition or crime on him, although they had most diligently sifted through his sermons, his life and his conduct by means of certain malicious men. When he was led by the executioner to the place of punishment, he answered calmly all who came to comfort him. But when certain priests and monks, while he struggled with death, prayed inwardly to God, and was already thinking of paradise, pestered him with their trifles, by which they tried to draw him away from the sound understanding of the words of Christ, he asked them more than once to be silent: he said that he had confessed his sins daily to Christ Jesus, the Lord of heaven and earth, had received absolution, and had no doubt at all about this. "To Christ my Saviour," he said in a sweet voice, "I shall be a welcome victim today. I have done nothing that displeases the Lord in this matter, for which I am condemned; the Lord has given me a quiet conscience. Let those who thirst for and pour out innocent blood see what they are undertaking, and whom they offend; it belongs to him alone to judge truly the hearts of men, for he says, 'Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.' This skin, barely clinging to my bones, I was soon going to cast off in any case, for my body is wasted. I know that I am mortal, a worm, corruptible, and born for this. Long ago I too desired the last day, and longed to be loosed and to be with Christ, though I deserve the cross for my various and most monstrous sins committed against the Lord. But my Christ, my Saviour, took up the cross and died on the cross. I too therefore wish to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Some scoundrels could not bear this swan-song. So they nodded to the executioner to thrust the old man from the place where he sat bound and ready for slaughter. He thrashed about in the water for a long time, so that the little stream became bloody. It was a sign that the blood of a righteous man had been shed that day. All who were present, seeing this spectacle, were saddened and wondered in themselves what this bloody redness of the water might mean. They stood stunned, drawn in by frequent sobs, and went home with silent hearts, pondering what had been done; although no one said anything, for fear that had been struck into them, since these things were being carried out in the manner of tyrants upon country folk. O cruel hearts! O treacherous deed! I have drawn these things from him who saw this horrible spectacle with his own eyes.

units.la: Hæc de insigni Christi martyre, ab ipso Ioanne Occolampadio memoriæ & scriptis mandata feruntur: quæ his inseruimus.
units.tr: These things about the notable martyrdom of Christ are reported as committed to memory and writing by Johannes Oecolampadius himself; we have inserted them here.

units.la: VVOLFGANGVS SCHVCH GERMANVS.
units.tr: WOLFGANG SCHUCH, A GERMAN.

units.la: INter eos, qui tunc temporis in Germania cognitionem Euagelij habuerant, in primis non immeritò numerandus est wolfgangus Scuchus Germanus. qui cum venisset in oppidū Lotharingiae, nomine S. Hippoliti appellatum, pastorq; ecclesiæ receptus fuisset, in primis ei curæ fuit, ut superstitiones, & idolomanias, quæ iam altè in animis populi radices egerant, funditus eucleret. Exigui itaque temporis spatio & quadragesimæ obseruationem, imagines atque idola, ipsam denique Missæ abominationem aboleuit. id quod non admodum fuit difficile: quoniam populum ibi reperit ad disciplinam Euangelij, obedientiamque accommodatum & paratum, & qui statim singulari quadam opinione ac voluntate in ipsum wolfgangum affectus est. Rumor autem defectionis à doctrina Papali factæ, aduersarijs veritatis facile dedit materiam falsæ & iniquæ criminationis apud Antonium Lotharingiæ ducem, quasi populus vellet omnem Principum & superiorum, authoritatem ac potestatem repudiare: ita ut iniustissima calumnia ad eam offensionem atque indignationem Principem impulerit, ut ipsam urbem flamma ac ferro se vastaturum esse minaretur. Quòd periculum, cum optimus ac fidelissimus pastor intellexisset, ad ducem Lotharingiæ scripsit epistolam, in qua sui officij ratione reddit, & falsis premi calumniis populum demonstrat, quaque is erga Principe esset voluntate, & obedientia aperte declarat. Scripta autem fuit in hanc sententiam.
units.tr: Among those who at that time had come to know the Gospel in Germany, Wolfgang Schuch, a German, deserves in the first place to be counted, and not undeservedly. When he had come to the town in Lorraine called by the name of St Hippolytus, and had been received as minister of the church there, his first concern was to root out thoroughly the superstitions and idolatries which had already struck deep roots in the minds of the people. Within a short space of time he abolished the observance of Lent, the images and idols, and finally the abomination of the Mass itself. This was not very difficult, since he found the people there suited to and ready for the discipline and obedience of the Gospel, and they at once came to feel a singular affection and loyalty towards Wolfgang himself. But the rumour of a defection from Papal doctrine readily gave the adversaries of the truth material for a false and unjust accusation before Antoine, Duke of Lorraine, as if the people wished to repudiate all authority and power of princes and superiors. So the most unjust calumny stirred the prince to such offence and indignation that he threatened to lay the city waste with fire and sword. When the best and most faithful minister learned of this danger, he wrote a letter to the Duke of Lorraine, in which he gives an account of his office, shows that the people are oppressed by false calumnies, and openly declares their goodwill and obedience towards the prince. It was written to this effect.

units.la: Illustrissimo Principi D. Domino Antonio Lothoringiæ Duci. &c, Domino suo Clementissimo V Volfgangus Scuch, mini- ster Christi felicitatem per Iesum Christum optat.
units.tr: To the most illustrious Prince, Lord Antoine, Duke of Lorraine, etc., his most clement Lord: Wolfgang Schuch, minister of Christ, wishes felicity through Jesus Christ.

units.la: Posteaquam ad hanc tuam S. Hippoliti ciuitatem, clementissime Princeps, Deo disponente peruéni: repperi turbam, velut oues errantes absque pastore, vagabundam, multis errorum superstitionumque abominationibus miserabiliter perditam: cœpi mox iuxta ministerium à Domino mihi commissum in viam reuocare errantes, hortari prioris vitæ pœnitentiam. nam esse in propinquo regnum Dei, comminari securim ad arboris radicem positam, haud longè abesse ut præscindatur, qua sterili inuenta in ignem coniici: tempus esse quo Dominus angelis suis, id est verbi sui nuncijs missis, colligat omnia scandala è Regno suo, Matthæi 13. Cœpi, inquam, mox ut boni agricolæ est, euellere quidquid spinarum atque errorum cōtra Dominum, ciúsque verbum succreuerat, demoliri, dissipare ac destruere omnem altitudinem, machinam ac munitionem aduersus scientiam Dei erectam: plantare arbores, fruſtum suum in tempore suo reddere non tardantes: edificare domicilium non transitorium & terrestre, sed aeternum in caelis, superaedificatum fundamento Apostolorum & Prophetarum, ipso summo angulari lapide Christo Iesu, in quo omnis structura coagmentata, crescit in templum sanctum Domino, in quo nos omnes coaedificari oportet in tabernaculum Dei in Spiritu sancto. & ut apertius loquar, Missus sum ad tuae Clementiae populum, praedicare Euangelium Dei, quod ante promiserat per Prophetas suos in scripturis sanctis de Filio suo, qui factus est ei ex semine Dauid secundum carnem. Virtus enim Dei est ad salutem omni credenti, in quo Dei iustitia revelatur ex fide in fidem. Sicut scriptum est, Iustus autem ex fide vivit. Iustitia Dei (qua coram Deo iusti reputamur) per fidem est Iesu Christi in omnes & super omnes qui credunt in eum. Gratis nanque per gratiam ipsius iustificamur per fidem, in sanguine ipsius, sine operibus Legis. Iustificati per fidem, pacem habemus ad Deum per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Ipse enim factus nobis a Deo, sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio, ut non glorietur fapiens in sapientia sua, fortis in fortitudine sua, dives in divitiis suis, sed qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Haec fides in Iesum Christum pro nobis mortuum, filios Dei nos facit: haeredes Dei, coheredes Christi. Ob hanc in nobis instaurandam, unigenitus Dei filius, e sinu Patris ad nos emissus. Sic enim Deus dilexit mundum ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Non enim misit Deus Filium suum in mundum ut iudicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus per eum. Qui credit in eum non iudicatur, qui autem non credit, iam iudicatus est. Porro quid aliud uspiam docuit Christus, quam ut in eum credentes salvi fiant? Quaerentibus enim turbis quid facientes operarentur opera Dei.
units.tr: Since, by God's disposing, I have come to this your city of St. Hippolyte, most clement Prince, I found a crowd like sheep wandering without a shepherd, roaming and wretchedly lost in many abominations of errors and superstitions. Immediately, in accordance with the ministry committed to me by the Lord, I began to call the wanderers back to the way and to exhort them to repent of their former life. For the kingdom of God is at hand; the axe is laid to the root of the tree and is not far from being cut down, and the barren tree, once found, is cast into the fire; and it is the time when the Lord, by sending his angels, that is, the messengers of his Word, gathers all offences out of his kingdom (Matthew 13). I began, I say, just as a good farmer does, to pull up whatever thorns and errors had grown up against the Lord and his Word, to pull down, scatter and destroy every height, engine and fortification raised against the knowledge of God; to plant trees, not delaying to render their fruit in its season; to build a dwelling that is not temporal and earthly but eternal in the heavens, built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, fitted together, grows into a holy temple to the Lord, in whom we all must be built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit. And to speak more plainly: I have been sent to your Clemency's people to preach the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh. For it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, in which the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written: "The just shall live by faith." The righteousness of God (by which we are reckoned righteous before God) is through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe in him. For we are justified freely by his grace, through faith, in his blood, without the works of the Law. Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. For he was made unto us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, so that the wise man does not glory in his wisdom, the strong in his strength, the rich in his riches, but he who glories, let him glory in the Lord. This faith in Jesus Christ, who died for us, makes us sons of God, heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ. It was for the restoring of this faith in us that the only-begotten Son of God was sent to us from the bosom of the Father. For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through him might be saved. He who believes in him is not condemned; but he who does not believe is already condemned. Moreover, what else did Christ teach anywhere, except that those who believe in him should be saved? For when the crowds asked him, "What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?"

units.la: Respondit, Hoc est opus Dei ut credatis in eum quem misit ille. Hic clamat dicens, Si quis sitit veniat ad me & bibat. Qui credit in me (sicut dicit Scriptura) flumina de ventre eius fluent aquae vivae. Ad hac fidę nemo venit nisi caelestis Patris tractu: ut ne quis se fallat, quasi proprijs hac viribus paraturus: gratia (ait Paulus) estis salvati per fidem & , hoc no ex vobis, Dei enim donum est, no ex operibus, ut ne quis glorietur. Nec alia aut minor virtus est hanc in nobis creare, quam qua Christus ex mortuis suscitatus & ad patris dextra in caelestibus est collocatus. Haec no otiosa quaedam ac stertens in anima hominis qualitas est, ut finxerunt quidam, sed spiritu Dei in cordibus nostris effuso, efficax & operosa quaedam virtus, plena operibus bonis, & ijs non a nobis aut nostra prudentia excogitatis, sed a Deo electis & mandatis. haec sunt charitatis non fictae opera: sic ait Apostolus, In Christo Iesu neque circuncisio aliquid valet neque praeputium, sed fides quae per charitatem operatur: haec sola veros a falsis Christianis discernunt. ait enim Salvator, In hoc cognoscent omnes quia discipuli mei estis, si dilectionem habueritis ad invicem, & quid aliud mandat tot dulcissimis verbis toto sermone ultima Coena facto? De his solis in dic novissimo exiget rationem dicens, Esurivi & dedistis mihi quo vescerer & c. splendentem vero operum quae ipsi facimus laruam reicit Dominus, cum ait: Quis haec petijt a vobis?
units.tr: He answered: "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." Here he cries out, saying: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me (as the Scripture says), out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." No one comes to this faith except by the drawing of the heavenly Father; lest anyone deceive himself, as if he could prepare it by his own powers: "By grace (says Paul) you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast." Nor is there any other or lesser power to create this faith in us than that by which Christ was raised from the dead and set at the right hand of the Father in the heavens. It is not some idle quality lying dormant in the soul of man, as some have imagined, but, with the Spirit of God poured out in our hearts, an effective and active power, full of good works, and those not devised by us or by our own prudence, but chosen and commanded by God. These are the works of unfeigned charity. So the Apostle says: "In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith which works through charity." This alone distinguishes true Christians from false ones. For the Saviour says: "By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another." And what else does he command with so many sweet words throughout the whole discourse at the last Supper? Of these alone he will require an account on the last day, saying: "I was hungry and you gave me food to eat," etc. But the Lord rejects the shining mask of the works we ourselves do, when he says: "Who required these things at your hands?"

units.la: Prosequitur deinceps Schucus eadem epistola ad Principem Antonium pluribus hunc de vera fide, quam boni fructus sequuntur, sermonem: commendat & verbi Dei authoritatem quod a Christo ciusque Apostolis acceptum, se quoque sine fuco concionatum fatetur. Principi ante oculos ponit, atque eleganti seruorum Dei, ac mercenariorum Papae antithesi facta, se aduersariorum impudentissimis imposturis inductu fuisse ut contra eos loqueretur, atque in eos inueheretur qui nihil praeter traditiones humanas praedicaret, & vetris[?] causa, non quae Christi, sed sua quaereret. Deinde refellit calumnias aduersariorum qui eum cum toto populo S. Hippoliti iugum obedictiae[?], quae magistratui debetur, excutere velle obiectabant: idque validis argumentis e Scriptura petitis facit. non esse cur tale quid de se aut suis Princeps cogitet, cum illa moneat passim, omni potestati a Deo constitutae parendum: Caesari dandum quod sit Caesaris. Postremo supplicat Duci, cumque per Deum obtestatur, ut ipsum audiat, admonens eum (zelo, quo vir erat, ardenti atque prophetico spiritu) sui officii, quia in causa salutis, inquit, [illegible, ~10 letters] cum quibusuis sit agẽdum. a Deo enim omne principatus stabiliri: proinde illius, utpote supremi Regis, habendam praecipue rationem, ne quid temere aut credat aut iudicet. Atque ita humilem suam conditionem agnoscens, excusat se, quod hanc epistolam humili quoque stylo scriptam, de materia quae per se satis est ornata, ipsius Maiestati obtulerit. Tandem summam & perpetuam optans Principi felicitatem finem epistolae imponit.
units.tr: In the same letter, Schuch goes on to speak at greater length to Prince Antoine about this true faith, which good fruits follow, and he commends the authority of God's Word, which he received from Christ and his Apostles, confessing that he too has preached it without pretence. He sets before the Prince, by an elegant antithesis between the servants of God and the hirelings of the Pope, that he was led by the most shameless impostures of his adversaries to speak against them and to attack those who preached nothing but human traditions and sought, for the sake of their belly, not what is Christ's but their own. Then he refutes the slanders of his opponents, who alleged that he and the whole people of St. Hippolyte wished to throw off the yoke of obedience owed to the magistrate, and he does this with strong arguments drawn from Scripture. There is no reason for the Prince to think any such thing of him or his people, since Scripture everywhere warns that every power ordained by God must be obeyed: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's." Finally he begs the Duke, and calls God to witness, that he would hear him, reminding him (with the zeal and fervent prophetic spirit that he possessed) of his duty, since in the matter of salvation, he says, [illegible] must be dealt with by anyone. For all principality is established by God; therefore the Prince should have regard above all to him, as the supreme King, so that he neither believes nor judges anything rashly. And so, acknowledging his own humble condition, he excuses himself for having offered this letter, written in a humble style too, on a matter which of itself is well enough adorned, to his Majesty. At last, wishing the Prince lasting and perpetual felicity, he brings the letter to a close.

units.la: Quum vero wolfgangus nihil hac epistola effecisset, vel quod intercepta fuisset, vel potius quod improbae calumniae, quas contra ipsum excogitarant Romani Antichristi asseclae, plus apud Principem valerent (qui in ea sententia manebat de vastanda penitus urbe S. Hippoliti:) ipsemet sua sponte se Nanceium metropolim Lotharingiae, in qua Dux praecipuam habebat sedem, contulit, tum ut fidei confessione ac doctrinae rationem palam ederet, tum etiam ut cives S. Hippoliti tanto periculo liberaret, atque in se omne odium totumque onus deriuaret. Eo cum primum pervenisset, protinus in carcerem durum ac graueolentem, pro more regionis, detrusus, inhumanissimorumque hominum custodiae traditus fuit, quorum ipse linguam non noverat. Id tamen viri constantiam non fregit, sed in vinculis per annum mansit, neque ullis interea minis aut precibus, aut uxoris, liberorumque quos habebat sex vel septem, commiseratione a sententia deduci potuit. Ductus autem subinde ad Franciscanorum coenobium, ut fidem suam profiteretur, summa ingenij dexteritate, quotquot adversus eum disputabant, confutauit.
units.tr: But since Wolfgang had achieved nothing by this letter, either because it was intercepted or rather because the wicked calumnies which the followers of the Roman Antichrist had devised against him carried more weight with the Prince (who remained of the opinion that the city of St. Hippolyte should be utterly laid waste), he himself of his own accord went to Nancy, the metropolis of Lorraine, where the Duke had his principal seat, partly so that he might openly give an account of his confession of faith and doctrine, and partly so that he might free the citizens of St. Hippolyte from so great a danger and draw all hatred and the whole burden upon himself. As soon as he arrived there, he was at once thrust, according to the custom of the region, into a harsh and foul-smelling prison and handed over to the custody of most inhumane men, whose language he did not know. Yet this did not break the man's constancy; he remained in chains for a year, and neither by any threats or entreaties, nor by the pity of his wife and of his six or seven children, whom he had, could he be turned from his opinion. Then, being led from time to time to the Franciscan convent so that he might profess his faith, he refuted, with great skill and ability, all who disputed against him.

units.la: Tum temporis quidam monachus, nomine Bonaventura, Provincialis, homo tam ipso ultu & vetre[?] horridus atque deformis, quam in summa ignoratia omnis etiam civilitatis atque honestatis contemptor, magnae erat authoritatis in aula Lotharingae, quae sane iam a multis annis & noverca & hostis virtutis extitit. Ille (inquam) homo perfrictae frontis, praecipuas Confessoris partes apud Ducem Antonium tum obtinebat, a quo etiam amabatur, quod ei liberam omnis libidinis ac voluptatis licentiam faceret. Trux autem ista bellua nihil magis persuadere Principi conabatur, quam ut doctos omnes ab aula, suisque regionibus eiiceret, neque quenquam fineret qui plus consueto sapere vellet. Haec enim erat summa doctrinae quam habebat, Satis esse ad salutem scire, Pater noster, & Aue Maria: hàncque adeò inculcauerat Principis animo, vt ipse Dux Antonius, melioribus annis natus, non erubesceret eandem suis aulicis in familiaribus colloquijs commendare & sæpius repetere. Hoc igitur monstro hominis præsidè, interrogabatur de sua fide Scuchus: neque quicquam in disputando aliud eructabat, præterquam, Tu hæretice, Iuda, Beelzubub. at bonus Scuchus ad iniurias nequicquam respondebat, sed potentia verbi diuini quasi fulmine, ita lusciosos eorum oculos perstringebat, vt prorsus attoniti aut ringentes discederent. Tandem ægre ferentes non sine arbitris & se auditos & coniuctos[?], ne nihil fecisse viderentur, Biblia ipsius Scuchi, quæ marginalibus notationibus referta erant, veluti mordicus arripientes in suo monasterio combusserunt. Quum vero postrema haberetur disputatio, Antonius dux mutato nonnihil, vt minus agnosceretur, habitu, interfuisse dicitur: qui tametsi minimè intelligeret ipsius wolfgangi sermonem, qui Latinus erat, videns tamen hominis intrepidam constantiam, discedens è disputatione, censuit exurendum esse, quandoquidem ecclesiam (sicilli videbatur) & sacramentum Missæ negaret. Paulò itaque post condemnatus fuit, vt vivus igni supplicio afficeretur: audita illa sentētia, orsus est Psalmum CXXII. Lætatus sum in his quæ dicta sunt mihi, in domum Domini ibimus. &c, Dum vero ad supplicium duceretur, prætcribat cœnobiū Franciscanorum, qui pro foribus expectabant. Cyclops autem ille Bonauentura exclamans, dixit Scucho, Heus Hæretice, exhibe honorem Deo, ipsiusque matri, & sanctis eius, ostendens ei idola, quæ istiusmodi ferarum lustris in vestibulo præponi solent. Scuchus vero illi respondit, Hypocrita, paries dealbate, perdet te Dominus, teque tuasque fallacias & imposturas[?] palam faciet. Cum iam ad locum supplicij peruenisset, primum ipsius libri conburebantur, & rogabatur ipse num vellet sibi mutigari pœnam. negauit velle se. addebat enim, Deum sibi semper affuisse, proinde ne tunc quidem defuturum, cum eo maximè omnium opus haberet: oratione sua his verbis concludens, Mādetur executioni sententia. Deinceps incipies canere Psal. LI. subiut locu[?] fascibus & lignis undiq; septu[?], prosecutusq; est cunde[?] Psalmu, donec fumo flamaq; præfocatus, obyt 19 die Aug. M.D.XXV. Præclara autem virtus atque constantia, magnaque eruditio sancti istius hominis, multas pias animas refecit atque aedificauit: veritatis vero hostes, contra, mirum in modum attonitos reddidit. Etenim continuo post, subitanea morte correptus est Commendator S.Antonij Viennensis, qui fuerat ecclesiasticus, ut vocant, iudex eiusdem Schuci. Affecta quoque ipsius Abbas Clariloci, suffraganeo Metefis, in illa populari aggratulatione ob aduentū Ducissae Christianae Danicae in vrbe Nacciesem, repentino timore ob fragore bombardarū percussus expirasse dicitur: quemadmodū viri fide pleni haec ita euenisse luculento testimonio declararunt.
units.tr: At that time there was a certain monk named Bonaventura, a Provincial, a man as hideous and deformed in his very face and bearing as he was a despiser of all decency and courtesy through his great ignorance. He held great authority at the court of Lorraine, which for many years had been both a stepmother and an enemy to virtue. This man (I say) of brazen forehead then held the chief position of confessor to Duke Antoine, by whom he was also loved, because he granted him free licence for every lust and pleasure. That savage beast tried to persuade the Prince of nothing more than to drive all learned men from the court and from his lands, and to allow no one who wished to be wiser than usual. For this was the sum of the learning he possessed: that it was enough for salvation to know the Our Father and the Hail Mary. He had so impressed this on the Prince's mind that Duke Antoine himself, though no longer young, was not ashamed to commend the same in familiar talks with his courtiers and to repeat it often. Therefore Scuch was questioned about his faith before this monstrous man who presided, and in the disputation he belched out nothing but, "You heretic, Judas, Beelzebub!" But good Scuch answered these insults in vain. Yet with the power of the divine word, as with a thunderbolt, he struck their blinking eyes, so that they left completely astonished or gnashing their teeth. At last, bearing it badly, and not without witnesses who had heard and been present, lest they seem to have done nothing, they seized Scuch's Bibles, which were full of marginal notes, and burned them in their monastery, as if tearing them with their teeth. When the last disputation was held, Duke Antoine, having changed his dress somewhat so as to be less recognised, is said to have been present. Although he hardly understood Scuch's speech, which was in Latin, yet seeing the man's fearless constancy, as he left the disputation he judged that Scuch should be burned, since (as it seemed to him) he denied the Church and the sacrament of the Mass. Soon afterwards he was condemned to be burned alive. On hearing the sentence he began Psalm 122: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the Lord." As he was led to his punishment he passed the Franciscan monastery, whose friars waited before its doors. But that Cyclops Bonaventura cried out, "Hey, heretic, give honour to God and to his mother and his saints!", showing him the idols which are usually set up in the vestibule of such wild beasts' dens. Scuch answered him: "Hypocrite, whitewashed wall! The Lord will destroy you, and will openly expose your deceits and impostures." When he had reached the place of execution, first his books were burned, and he was asked whether he wished his punishment to be mitigated. He said no. For, he added, God had always been with him, and so would not fail him now, when he needed him most of all. He concluded his speech with these words: "Let the sentence be carried out." Then he began to sing Psalm 51. He was placed at the stake, surrounded on all sides by faggots and wood, and he went through the psalm to the end, until, choked by smoke and flame, he died on 19 August 1525. The remarkable virtue, constancy and great learning of this holy man refreshed and built up many pious souls, but it struck the enemies of truth with astonishment in a marvellous way. For soon afterwards the commander of St Antony of Vienne, who had been the ecclesiastical judge, as they call him, of this same Scuch, was struck down by sudden death. Also the Abbot of Clairlieu, suffragan of Metz, is said to have died of sudden fright, struck by the thunder of the cannon during the popular rejoicing at the arrival of the Christian Duchess of Denmark in the city of Nancy. Men full of faith have clearly declared by this plain testimony that these things happened just as they did.

units.la: IACOBVS PAVANE.
units.tr: JAMES PAVANE.

units.la: Briçonnetus ille episcopus Meldensis, initio quidem in sua Dioecesi scholam aperuerat Euangelio, ac fouebat pios omnes & doctos viros: inter quos fuit Iacobus Pauaneus patria Bolonicensis, quae ad oceanum Britannicum spectat, qui propter doctrinam Euangelij Christi captus, in carcerem coniectus est, anno M. D. XXIIII. Eo captiuitatis tempore, cum a quibusdam hominibus in fide Christiana dubijs ac frigidis solicitatus fuisset, eo tandem adductus est, ut quae ante pie professus erat, indigne abnegarct, cum ea ignominia, quam Emendationem honorariam vocant. Ex his fidei subornatoribus atque euerforibus, fuit quidam doctor Martialis, qui poenitentiarius Parisiensis mortuus est: qui cum Pauanco disputans, dicebat, Erras Iacobe: neq; enim profundum maris, sed tantum summa aquarum & vndarum superficiem aspexisti. immuere voles profundum illud Theologiae pelagus nondum vidisse aut expertum esse. Haec vox, Erras Iacobe, adhuc in communi apud Meldenses sermone versatur, atque ab eo tempore pro proverbio vsurpata & iactata fuit.
units.tr: Briçonnet, that bishop of Meaux, had at first opened a school of the Gospel in his diocese, and he cherished all the pious and learned men. Among them was James Pavane, a native of Boulogne, which faces the British Ocean. Taken on account of the teaching of the Gospel of Christ, he was thrown into prison in the year 1524. During his captivity, when he was pressed by certain men who were doubtful and lukewarm in the Christian faith, he was at last brought to shamefully renounce what he had before piously professed, with that disgrace which they call honourable amendment. Among these subverters and overthrowers of the faith was a certain teacher, Martial, penitentiary of Paris, who has since died. He, disputing with Pavane, said, "You are wrong, James. For you have looked not at the depths of the sea, but only at the surface of the waters and the waves. Perhaps you will want to admit that you have not yet seen or experienced that deep sea of theology." That phrase, "You are wrong, James," is still in common use among the people of Meaux, and from that time it has been used and bandied about as a proverb.

units.la: Is igitur Pauaneus in sua fide perturbatus, a pioque animi proposito abductus ab eo hominum genere, ut vitam conseruaret suam, ea emendationem quam vocant honorariam (infame videlicet & Christiano homine indignam veritatis abiuratione) passus est, solemni pompa & aggratulatione aduersariorum, postridie Natalis Christi, Anno M. D. XXIIII. Qua quidem ex re tanto postea dolore ac poenitentia Pauaneus affectus fuit, ut ad conspectum amicorum, qui eum in carcere carcere(ad quem per sententiam illam superiorem damnatus erat)inuisebant, non nisi gemere ac detestari miseram illam conditionem redemptæ tam fœda abiuratione vitæ, visus sit. Ad mortem itaque tanti dedecoris reparatrice devoto animo ferebatur: ab eóq; tēpore & verbis & scriptis purā religionis Christianæ fidē profiteri nō desistit. in primis verò illam doctrinam de Cœna Domini, quæ tum temporis nova plerisque atque inaudita videbatur. Post illam itaque carceris detentionem, anno sequenti M.D.XXV. condemnationis optatam sententiam accepit, ac vivus crematus est Lutetiæ in eo celebri loco, qui à Greva nomen habet, cum summa alacritate atque animi constantia.
units.tr: Pavane, therefore, troubled in his faith and drawn from his pious purpose by that kind of men, in order to preserve his life underwent that so-called honourable amendment (that is, an infamous renunciation of the truth, unworthy of a Christian man), with solemn pomp and the rejoicing of his adversaries, on the day after Christmas in the year 1524. Yet Pavane was afterwards so affected with grief and repentance over this act that when friends visited him in prison (to which he had been condemned by that earlier sentence), he seemed to do nothing but groan and detest his wretched condition, a life bought back by so foul an abjuration. He therefore met death with a devoted mind, as the means of repairing so great a dishonour. From that time, in word and writing, he did not cease to profess the pure religion of the Christian faith, and especially that doctrine of the Lord's Supper which at that time seemed new and unheard of to most people. After that detention in prison, then, in the following year, 1525, he received the longed-for sentence of condemnation and was burned alive at Paris, in that famous place which takes its name from the Grève, with great eagerness and constancy of spirit.

units.la: Acta Georgii Carpentarii Emeringensis, qui vstulatus fuit pro tu- endo Euangelio Monychi Bauariæ.
units.tr: The Acts of Georg Carpentarius of Emmering, who was burned for defending the Gospel at Munich in Bavaria.

units.la: Omplures viri primarij in Germania extiterunt qui instinctu inflatúque diuino, non modò maximè illustrem atque insignem reddiderunt Euangelij veritatem, sed etiam effuso sanguine suo, veluti chirographo quodam, confirmarunt & obsignarunt. In quorum ordine Georgius Carpentarius Emeringensis prætereundus non est, propterea quòd admirabili virtute & constantia in defensione Euangelij suscepta permansit. Cum enim anno Domini M.D. XXVII, Monychi Bauariæ, veritatis Euangelicæ nomine in carcere coniectus esset, nullis unquam minis, nullo barbaro atq; immani terrore, nulla denique vi tormentorum abduci potuit à vera doctrina: adeò vt iudices nihil efficere valentes, capitis hominem innocentissimum damnarint. Ita q; eiusdem anni die Februarij 8, post latam mortis sententiam duo carnifices cum in carcere, quæ Falcoturris appellatur, cōprehenderunt, vt ad locum supplicio destinatum ducerent. Et ecce Franciscani aliquot monachi sese obtruserunt, qui cupiebant Georgium in itinere proficiscentem ad supplicium comitari atque instruere & erudire suo usitato more. At uero rogauit, ne in ea re elaborarent, sed se in claustra sua reciperent, quando eorum doctrina & institutione nihil ei prorsus opus esset.Carnifices igitur cum perduxerunt usque ad gradus aedis publicae, ubi causae suae quatuor capita confessa & defensa publice fuerunt recitata. Primum autem fuit, quod non crederet sacrificum posse homini peccata remittere in confessione auriculari. Alterum quod non adduceretur ut crederet hominem posse Deum caelo euocare. Tertium, quod non persuaderetur Deum inclusum esse in pane, quem sacerdos consecrat & versat multis modis in altari. Quartum uero fuit, quod non crederet Baptismum aquae per se posse hominem facere beatum. Aduersarii contra etiam atque etiam urgebant & instabant ut istam opinionem reuocaret: uerum in sua sententia constantissime perstitit. Tum accessit ad eum ludimagister quidam eius urbis, his cum uerbis alloquens, Mi Georgi, nunquid horres & reformidas mortem quae tibi mox obeunda est? Si nunc liber esses, numnam summa uoluntate & egregia animi alacritate redires domum ad uxorem & liberos? Cui ille, Si iudices a se me dimitterent, ad quos quaeso libentius me reciperem quam ad uxorem & carissimos filios? Te igitur reuocato, inquit ludimagister, & in libertatem uindicaberis. Ad quae Georgius, Uxor quidem & liberi chariores mihi sunt quam ut ullo pretio, aut uel suo prouentu Dux Bauariae redimere queat, sed tamen libenti animo pro summo meo erga Deum amore eos relinquo. Cum uero ipse iam ad supplicium duceretur, ludimagister rursum est eum allocutus in medio foro, in hanc fere sententiam, Mi Georgi, crede sacramentum altaris, nec tantum ipsum esse signum affirma. Fateor, ait ille, sacramentum hoc esse signum & tesseram corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi, qui pro nostrorum peccatorum expiatione mortem crucis ultro pertulit. Ludimagister haud ita multo post addidit, Georgi, quid cogitas, dum tu nihili facis Baptismum, quo tamen ablutum fuisse Iesum Christum in Iordane non ignoras? Ad id ille, ut par erat, respondit, ostenditque quis fuit Baptismi finis in Iordane, & quam necesse fuit pro hominum salute comparanda Christum mori in cruce, quæ quidem res salutis nostræ scopus est. Ille ipse ergo Christus, inquit Georgius, seruator meus est, in cuius fidem me totum trado, atque eum hodie clara cōfessione celebrabo in omnium conspectu. Interea Magister Conradus Sceitther, vicarius & ecclesiastes primarij templi, ad illū accessit & dixit, Mi Georgi, nisi fidem adhibere vis sacramento, saltem tuam spem in Deo collocato, & palàm dicito, Nihil quidem de causæ meæ æquitate & bonitate dubito, sed tamen si forte peccarem, me erroris & insciitiæ maximè pœniteret. Ad quæ Georgius, Deus nequaquam permittat ut in errore verser. Cui ludimagister, Ne scis festinantior: delige tibi quendam bonum virum nempe Magistrum Conradum aut alterum quenpiam, cui animi sensum indices & sententiam tuam aperias: non ut ad aurem eius confitearis, sed ex re & tempore consilium capias. Ille respondit se id nequaquam commissurum, quippe qui ea re non egeret. Postea aliquantò, quum Magister Conradus clara voce orationem Dominicam recitare cœpisset, Pater noster qui es in cælis: interiecit Georgius: Mi Deus, reuera Pater noster es, neque vllus alius est, vehementer cupio hodie tecum habitare. Magister Conradus incœpta persequebatur, Sanctificetur nomen tuum: tum intermiscuit Georgius, Mi Deus, quàm exiguè & frigidè nomen tuum sanctificatur. Conradus progrediebatur longius, Veniat regnum tuum. Ad cum orationis locum Georgius addidit, Equidem spero me hodie in illud magno gaudio intraturum. Conradus orationem prosequebatur, Fiat voluntas tua sicut in cælo, etiam in terra: Georgius dixit, Præsto hic sum, mi Pater, ut tua voluntas fiat, non autem mea. Conradus orare perrexit, Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie. Georgius ad id ita respondit, Iesus Christus verus & cælestis panis, sit mihi hodie in cibum. Conradus progrediebatur, Et remitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Georgius ad hunc ferè modum locutus est, Ego omnibus tum amicis, tum inimicis quicquid in me designarunt ex animo remitto & condono. Conradus orandi finem fecit dicens, Et ne nos inducas in tentationem, sed libera nos à malo. Georgius interposuit, Deus bone, proculdubio tu me hodie liberaturus es: reposui enim spem meam in te solo. Tum postea Conradus symbolum fidei recitare aggressus est, Credo in Deum patrem omnipotentem: cui mox addidit Georgius, Etsi hostes omnibus viribus conati sunt me abs te longissimè disiungere, ego tamē in te uno spem omnem meam positam habeo, non autem in ullis rebus creatis. Ita fere G. respondebat ad singula capita: quæ si commemorare pergeremus, longior esset sermo. His vero peractis Ludimagister eum nominatim compellavit dicens, Credisne corde tam asseveranter in Deum Dominum tuum, quàm alacriter ore profiteris? Cui Georgius, Mihi quidem res admodum difficilis & ardua esset, crudelem mortem tam acri præsentíque animo perserre, nisi quod ore profiteor, ex animi mei quodam intimo sensu prodiret. Ego sanè longè ante certum habebam quid mihi ferendum esset pro Christo, si modò afflictionum eius socius ac particeps esse vellem. O Deus! ubi est hominis thesaurus repositus, ibi quoque illius animum esse oportet. Tum M. Conradus ei dixit: Credisne Georgi, necesse esse pro te mortuo preces concipi: quod si credis, spondeo me celebraturum Missæ sacrificium tua causa. Cui Georgius, tàtisper dum animus hoc corpore, tanquam ergastulo concluditur, precamur ut mihi Deus patientiam, veram animi deiectionem & Christianam fidem largiatur: quibus quidem virtutibus munitus & instructus supplicium mortis mihi constitutum præsenti animo ferre queam. Postea vero quàm animus a societate & contagione corporis separatus fuerit, tum mihi nihil opus erit precationibus. Iam vero cùm a carnifice constantissimus martyr ad scalam alligaretur, pleraque doctrinæ Christianæ capita populo spectanti exponebat. Tum nonnulli pij & Christiani fratres, qui illi tristi spectaculo forte aderant, cum rogarunt ut simul atque in ignem coniectus esset, signum aliquod daret suæ firmæ & constantis fidei: quibus ille respondit, Hoc signum fidei meæ in Iesum Christum certissimum vobis esto: quòd usque dum os aperire aut certè hiscere licebit, Deum laudibus celebrare & Seruatoris nostri nomë profiteri nunquam intermittam. Perspice quæso, Lector, quà incredibili constantia paratus fuit hic nobilis Christi martyr ad acerbissimam mortem subeundam. vix enim unquam par animi virtus audita est aut perspecta. Etenim in eo semper idem vultus fuit, neque vlla mentis & sensuum facta est mutatio. Perrexit igitur in ignem hilari animo & prompto: dumque testis ille tam patiens atque tam fortis ad lanienam duceretur, dixit in medio vrbis, Hodie Dei nomen palam in ore atque oculis omnium profitebor. Quod revera strenue praestitit iam extentus & ad scalam alligatus. Nam cum duo carnifices sacculum puluere tormentario plenum circa collum alligarent, ita locutus est, Sit hoc in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti. Cum autem duo illi carnifices eum scalae astrictum & alligatum attollerent in sublime, circunstantem ibi fratrem quendam valere iussit, petita ab eo exporrecta fronte cuiusdam errati venia. Porro simulac in flammas a carnificibus cōtrusus est, sublata voce exclamauit, Iesu, Iesu. Deinde carnifex eum crudelissimè versauit. Tandem demum post repetitum clara voce Iesu nomen, ita vitam felici fine conclusit.
units.tr: Many leading men arose in Germany who, moved and inspired by God, not only made the truth of the Gospel most notable and remarkable, but also, by shedding their blood, confirmed and sealed it as with a kind of signed deed. Among these, Georg Carpentarius of Emmering must not be passed over, because he persevered in the defence of the Gospel with remarkable courage and steadfastness. When, in the year of the Lord 1527, he had been thrown into prison at Munich in Bavaria on account of the evangelical truth, he could never be drawn away from the true doctrine by any threats, any savage and monstrous terror, or finally by any force of torture. So the judges, unable to achieve anything, condemned this most innocent man to death. Accordingly, on 8 February of that same year, after the sentence of death had been pronounced, two executioners seized him in the prison called the Falcon Tower, to lead him to the place of execution. And behold, several Franciscan friars thrust themselves forward, wishing to accompany Georg on his journey to the execution and to instruct and teach him in their customary manner. But he asked them not to trouble themselves over this, but to return to their cloisters, since he had no need at all of their teaching and instruction. The executioners therefore led him as far as the steps of the public building, where the four articles of his cause, which he had confessed and defended, were read out publicly. The first was that he did not believe a priest could forgive a man's sins in auricular confession. The second was that he could not be brought to believe that a man can call God down from heaven. The third was that he could not be persuaded that God is enclosed in the bread which the priest consecrates and handles in many ways at the altar. The fourth was that he did not believe that water baptism of itself can make a man blessed. His opponents pressed and urged him again and again to retract this opinion, but he persisted most steadfastly in his view. Then a certain schoolmaster of that town approached him and addressed him in these words: My Georg, do you shudder and dread the death that is soon to be undergone by you? If you were now free, would you return home to your wife and children with the greatest willingness and eager spirit? To this he replied: If the judges were to release me, to whom, I ask, would I more gladly return than to my wife and my dearest sons? Then, if you retract, said the schoolmaster, you will be vindicated and set at liberty. To this Georg answered: My wife and children are dearer to me than the Duke of Bavaria could buy back for any price, or even for his own revenue; yet nonetheless I leave them with a willing spirit, out of my great love for God. But when he was now being led to the execution, the schoolmaster again addressed him in the middle of the marketplace, to this effect: My Georg, believe in the sacrament of the altar, and do not affirm that it is merely a sign. I confess, he replied, that this sacrament is a sign and token of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, who of his own accord endured the death of the cross for the expiation of our sins. Not long afterwards the schoolmaster added: Georg, what are you thinking, that you make nothing of baptism, by which you know Jesus Christ was washed in the Jordan? To this he replied, as was fitting, and he showed what the purpose of Christ's baptism in the Jordan was, and how necessary it was for Christ to die on the cross to obtain the salvation of men, which is indeed the aim of our salvation. That same Christ, said Georg, is my Saviour, into whose faith I entrust myself entirely, and today I will celebrate him with a clear confession in the sight of all. Meanwhile Master Conrad Sceitther, the vicar and preacher of the principal church, came up to him and said: My Georg, if you are unwilling to place your faith in the sacrament, at least place your hope in God, and say openly: I do indeed have no doubt about the fairness and goodness of my cause, but if perhaps I were in error, I would be most deeply sorry for my mistake and ignorance. To this Georg said: God will by no means permit me to remain in error. The schoolmaster replied: Do not be too hasty. Choose for yourself some good man, namely Master Conrad or some other, to whom you may reveal the feeling of your mind and open your opinion, not so that you may confess into his ear, but so that you may take counsel from the matter and the occasion. He answered that he would by no means do this, since he had no need of it. Some time later, when Master Conrad had begun to recite the Lord's Prayer in a clear voice, "Our Father, who art in heaven," Georg interjected: My God, you are truly our Father, and there is no other; I earnestly desire to dwell with you today. Master Conrad went on with what he had begun: "Hallowed be thy name." Then Georg broke in: My God, how meagrely and coldly your name is hallowed. Conrad went further: "Thy kingdom come." At this point of the prayer Georg added: Indeed I hope that today I shall enter into that kingdom with great joy. Conrad continued: "Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven." Georg said: Here I stand, my Father, that your will may be done, and not mine. Conrad went on praying: "Give us this day our daily bread." To this Georg replied: May Jesus Christ, the true and heavenly bread, be my food today. Conrad proceeded: "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Georg spoke more or less in this manner: I freely forgive and pardon all, both friends and enemies, whatever they have plotted against me. Conrad brought the prayer to an end, saying: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil." Georg interposed: Good God, without doubt you are going to deliver me today, for I have placed my hope in you alone. Then Conrad began to recite the Apostles' Creed: "I believe in God the Father almighty." To this Georg at once added: Although my enemies have striven with all their might to separate me far from you, yet I have all my hope placed in you alone, and not in any created things. Georg answered in much the same way to each article; if we were to go on recounting them, the account would be too long. When these things were done, the schoolmaster addressed him by name and said: Do you believe in your heart as firmly in the Lord your God as you eagerly profess with your mouth? To this Georg replied: For me, indeed, it would be a very difficult and arduous thing to endure a cruel death with such a keen and present spirit, unless what I profess with my mouth came from the innermost feeling of my mind. Indeed, I had long since clearly known what I must endure for Christ, if I wished to be a sharer and partaker in his sufferings. O God! Where a man's treasure is stored, there his heart must also be. Then Master Conrad said to him: Do you believe, Georg, that prayers must be offered for the dead? If you believe this, I promise that I will celebrate the sacrifice of the Mass for your sake. To this Georg replied: As long as the soul is shut up in this body as in a prison, we pray that God will grant me patience, true humility of spirit, and Christian faith; armed and equipped with these virtues I shall be able to bear with a steadfast spirit the death penalty appointed for me. But after the soul has been separated from the company and contagion of the body, I shall have no need of prayers. Now when the most steadfast martyr was being bound to the ladder by the executioner, he set forth most of the heads of Christian doctrine to the watching people. Then some pious and Christian brothers who happened to be present at that sad spectacle asked him to give some sign of his firm and constant faith as soon as he was thrown into the fire. To them he replied: Let this be a most certain sign of my faith in Jesus Christ to you: as long as I am allowed to open my mouth, or at least to gape, I will never cease to praise God and to confess the name of our Saviour. Consider, I beg you, reader, with what incredible constancy this noble martyr of Christ was prepared to undergo the most bitter death; for scarcely ever has such strength of spirit been heard of or observed. Indeed, his countenance remained always the same, and there was no change at all in his mind or senses. So he went into the fire with a cheerful and ready spirit; and while that witness, so patient and so brave, was being led to the slaughter, he said in the middle of the town: Today I will openly profess the name of God in the mouths and before the eyes of all. This he truly carried out bravely, even as he was stretched out and bound to the ladder. For when the two executioners were fastening a little sack full of gunpowder about his neck, he spoke thus: Let this be in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Then, as the two executioners were raising him, fastened and bound to the ladder, high into the air, he bade a brother who was standing nearby farewell, asking his forgiveness for some offence, with his forehead held out to him. Moreover, as soon as he was thrust by the executioners into the flames, he cried out aloud: Jesus, Jesus. Then the executioner turned him cruelly over. At length, after repeating the name of Jesus in a clear voice, he brought his life to a happy end.

units.la: LEONHARDVS KEYSER, Germanus
units.tr: LEONHARD KEYSER, a German

units.la: NEque obliuioni mandanda aut silentio praetereunda est constatia Leōhardi Caesaris cognominati, ex Bauariae ducatu, qui propter testimonii Euangelio datum combustus fuit. Is Cæsar, erat ex Raubo oppido quatuor milliaribus à Passawo, illustri genere ac domo natus. Quo tempore wittenbergae literis optimisque disciplinis operā dabat, certior factus à fratribus, de patris valetudine, vt si eū vellet vnquam viuū videre, quamprimum reuerteretur, ilico se in patriā domumque suam pio patris ac fratrum videndi desiderio recepit. Sed simulatq; cō[?] is venit, Passawiensis episcopi, qui Euagelij studiosos summo odio insectabatur, mandato captus est. Qua in re non incōmodum erit hoc loco exponere articulos fidei, quos libere confessus est, & propter quos ab inimicis inhumaniter extinctus, sanguine suo testimonium doctrinae Filij Dei debitum ac redditum obsignauit. Primum asseruit nos sola fide saluos fieri. deinde ipsa opera esse fructus fidei. Missam non esse oblationem aut sacrificium, neque prodesse viuis, multō minus mortuis. Postremō tria genera confessionis affirmabat, vnum & praecipuum fidei, nobis quidem quotidie[?] perpetuōque necessarium, alterum charitatis, quod ad proximum ofsensum alienatumque reconciliandum adhibere oporteat, de quo genere Matth.XV III.[?] à Christo domino praeceptum. tertium ad graves ac prudentes viros ministrosque Ecclesiae referri, à quibus in magnis ac perplexis conscientiae vitaeque rationibus, consilium saepe petendum & accipiendum est.Itaque quoniam haec omnia erant adversaria bullae Leonis X. Papae Rom. atque edicto decretoque Imperatoris facto Wormaciae, sententia fuit pronuntiata, ut pius vir Leonhardus Caesar, degradatus, in manum & potestatem civilis magistratus traderetur. A quo quidem acceptus ac tonsus, indutusque diploide, pileumque in capite habens diffectu, carnifici civitatis traditus est. Porro cum extra urbem duceretur, eum in locum, ubi morte multandus erat, libere & constanter Germanico sermone loqui coepit, nunc in hanc, nunc in illam partem caput convertens. Ita autem dicebat, O Domine Iesu, patere mecum, sustenta me, da mihi robur. Tum ligna iam parata erant, ut accenderentur, cum ille magna voce exclamare coepit, O Domine Iesu, ego sum tuus, conserva me. Hoc autem dicebat, cum iam igne accensum sub pedibus haberet, atque etiam vim eius, non in pedibus solum, sed etiam in manibus & capite, acerbissimo cum dolore sentiret. Et quoniam ignis non ita erat magnus, ut corpus eius ató[?] possset absumere, carnifex pertica bisulca illud tantummodo femiustulatum attraxit, ac super ligna undique impositum. Deinde perforato corpore, pertica illam traiecit: atque ita illud reposuit in igne, & omnino exussit. Hic exitus Caesaris, pii hominis, pro causa & doctrina filii Dei Iesu Christi morientis, decimo sexto die Augusti, anno M. D.XXVII.
units.tr: The constancy of Leonhard Caesar, surnamed [Keyser], of the duchy of Bavaria, who was burned for the testimony he gave to the Gospel, must not be consigned to oblivion or passed over in silence. This Caesar was born of an illustrious family and house in the town of Raubo, four miles from Passau. While he was devoting himself to letters and the best studies at Wittenberg, he was informed by his brothers that his father was ill, and that if he ever wished to see him alive he should return as quickly as possible. Moved by a devout desire to see his father and brothers, he at once went back to his homeland and his house. But as soon as he arrived, he was seized by order of the bishop of Passau, who pursued the friends of the Gospel with the greatest hatred. In this matter it will not be out of place to set out here the articles of faith which he freely confessed, and on account of which he was cruelly put to death by his enemies, sealing with his blood the testimony owed and rendered to the doctrine of the Son of God. First, he asserted that we are saved by faith alone. Second, that good works are the fruits of faith. That the Mass is not an oblation or a sacrifice, and that it profits neither the living, much less the dead. Lastly, he affirmed three kinds of confession: one, the chief confession of faith, which is necessary for us every day and without ceasing; a second, of charity, which ought to be used to reconcile an offended and estranged neighbour, a kind of confession commanded by Christ the Lord in Matthew 18; and a third, which is referred to grave and prudent men and ministers of the Church, from whom counsel is often to be sought and received in great and perplexing matters of conscience and of life. Since all these things were opposed to the bull of Leo X, Pope of Rome, and to the edict and decree issued by the Emperor at Worms, sentence was pronounced that the godly man Leonhard Caesar, having been degraded, should be handed over into the hand and power of the civil magistrate. Received by the magistrate, shaved, and dressed in a double-folded gown, with a cap on his head, he was given over to the executioner of the city. As he was led outside the city to the place where he was to be punished with death, he began to speak freely and steadfastly in German, turning his head now this way, now that. And he spoke thus: "O Lord Jesus, stay with me, sustain me, give me strength." Then the wood was already prepared to be lit, when he began to cry out with a loud voice: "O Lord Jesus, I am yours, keep me." He said this while already having the fire lit beneath his feet, and while he felt its force, with most bitter pain, not only in his feet but also in his hands and head. And since the fire was not so large that it could consume his body entirely, the executioner, with a forked pole, dragged out only the half-burnt body and placed it again upon the wood, which had been piled up on all sides. Then, with the body pierced through, he thrust the pole through it, and so put it back into the fire and utterly burned it up. This was the end of Caesar, a godly man, for the cause and doctrine of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, dying on the sixteenth day of August, in the year 1527.

units.la: Magister Hericꝰ (hoc enim nomine notior erat quam cognomine) natione Flander, cum institutum ordinis Augustinianis diu sequutus ac professus fuisset, postea abiecto eo vitae genere, meliorque suscepto, captus fuit propter verbum Dei in civitate Cortracensi oppido Flandriae, habitu indutus mercatorio, atque inde Tornacum deductus. Qua in urbe cum septem menses in profundo ac tetro carceris loco adservatus fuisset, tandem ei oblata est conditio, per quendam M. Baltazarem à Cordis, qui tum erat Officialis Episcopi Tornacesis[?], vt si vellet confiteri eā quā vxorē duxerat, esse meretricē suam, vita ei conseruaretur. Hoc autem ille vt diceret, nunquam potuit adduci: sed in ea fidei confessione, quam initio coram eis fecerat, constanter perstitit: ita vt ab aduersarijs pristino illo turpis sacerdotij gradu atque ordine deiectus aut erasus, cum summa animi laetitia & gratiarum actione canere coeperit, Te Deum laudamus, te Dominum confitemur: caeterosque versus eius Cantici, qui Ambrosio & Augustino vulgo tribuitur. Postea fuit condemnatus, vt viuus cremaretur: quod supplicium admirabili virtute & animi magnitudine pertulit, circiter mensem Maium, anno M.D. XXVIII.
units.tr: Magister Heric (for he was better known by this name than by his surname), a Fleming by birth, had long followed the rule of the Augustinian order and had professed it; afterwards he abandoned that way of life and embraced a better one. He was arrested for the word of God in the town of Courtrai in Flanders, dressed in merchant's clothing, and was led from there to Tournai. When he had been kept for seven months in a deep and foul prison cell, a condition was at last offered him through a certain Master Balthasar à Cordis, who was then official of the bishop of Tournai: if he would confess that the woman he had married was his whore, his life would be spared. He could never be brought to say this; but he stood firm in the confession of faith he had first made before them. So his adversaries stripped him of his former rank and order of the filthy priesthood, scraping away his tonsure, and he began to sing with great joy of mind and thanksgiving, "We praise thee, O God; we acknowledge thee to be the Lord," and the remaining verses of that canticle, which is commonly attributed to Ambrose and Augustine. Afterwards he was condemned to be burned alive, a punishment he endured with remarkable courage and greatness of spirit, about the month of May, in the year 1528.

units.la: DIONYSIVS DE RIEVX.
units.tr: Dionysius de Rieux.

units.la: Dionysius ab Ricux, fuit vnus ex iis qui primi pro pura Euangelij Christi doctrina, Meldis mortem magno animo pertulerunt. Is inter primos in Gallia palàm asseruit, Missam certissimam esse abnegationem mortis & passionis Iesu Christi: à qua Missae opinione Bricomentus[?] episcopus Meldensis, de quo supra mentio est habita, modis omnibus abducere voluit, promittens se eum liberaturum, cíque pensionem annuam atque alia commoda daturum. Cui ille fortiter semper restitit, & graviter obiurgans, dixit, Itane, domine, in eam animi mollitiem ignauiamque delapsus es, vt me nunc quidem ad huiusmodi abnegationem Dei mei, renunciationémq;que inducas? Hic autè pius vir sententiam illam Iesu Christi, Qui me negauerit coram hominibus, & c. vehementer in animo suo infixam habebat, ita vt eam saepe cum pondere & gravitate eius vsurparet ac repeteret, atque etiam ad mentionem eius perhorresceret. Is igitur damnatus, vt viuus comburetur, crate ad supplicium tractus fuit, perpetuò loquens, ac populum exhortans, vt ad suscipiendam veram vitae salutisque doctrinam converteretur. Eius manibus crux lignea fuit illigata, quam excussit magna vi, abiecitque in quendam locum, qui aquas fluentes recipiebat: atque eo quidem die valde pluerat, ita vt crux vna cum aqua auferretur. Quae res sacerdotes ac monachos ita vehementer irritauit, vt ab contumelijs iniuriisque ei inferendis, continere se non possent. Itaque is viuus fuit vstulatus, summa voluntate ac voluptate inimicorum veritatis, id est, cum lento magnoque tormento ac dolore. Nam ter in sublime fuit sublatus, ignem sub se habens exiguum, perpetuo usque ad ultimum spiritum vitae, Deum invocans. Hunc vitae finem, vir probus & Deum timens habuit, tertio die Iulij, anno M. D. XXVIII.
units.tr: Dionysius ab Ricux was one of the first to endure death at Meaux with a brave spirit for the pure doctrine of the Gospel of Christ. Among the first in France he openly maintained that the Mass is a most certain denial of the death and passion of Jesus Christ. From this opinion Briconnet, bishop of Meaux, of whom mention was made above, wished to turn him by every means, promising that he would set him free and give him an annual pension and other advantages. To this he always resisted firmly, and rebuking him severely said, Have you, sir, fallen into such softness and cowardice that you now urge me toward such a denial and renunciation of my God? This godly man kept deeply fixed in his mind that saying of Jesus Christ, Whoever shall deny me before men, etc., so that he often used and repeated it with great weight and seriousness, and even shuddered at the mention of it. Condemned therefore to be burned alive, he was dragged to the execution on a hurdle, speaking continually and exhorting the people to turn to the acceptance of the true doctrine of life and salvation. A wooden cross had been tied to his hands. He shook it off with great force and threw it into a place that received flowing water; and indeed on that day it had rained heavily, so that the cross was carried away with the water. This so violently provoked the priests and monks that they could not restrain themselves from insults and injuries to be inflicted upon him. So he was burned alive, to the great will and delight of the enemies of the truth, that is, with a slow and great torment and pain. For three times he was lifted up on high, with a small fire beneath him, invoking God continually until his last breath. This end of life the upright man, who feared God, met on the third day of July, in the year 1528.

units.la: PETRUS FLYSTEDEN ET ADOLPHUS CLAREBACH, Germani.
units.tr: Peter Flystede and Adolph Clarebach, Germans.

units.la: Anno M. D. XXVIII, Petrus Flystedius & Adolphus Clarebachus homines literis perpoliti & praeclara eruditione atque doctrina ornati, Coloniae ad Rhenum sitae vincti tenebatur, quod de Cœna Domini caeterisque religionis Christianæ capitibus à Pontificijs dissentirent. Senatusquidè urbis potest iure suo cotrudere in carcere, sed damnandi aut absoluendi potestas est penes Archiepiscopum: adeò ut contingere queat, ut qui in locum & vicem Archiepiscopi substitutus sit, emittat è cacere eum & in integrum restituat, qui capitis damnatus fuerit à senatu. Illi igitur duo in custodia inclusi fuerunt plus sesquianno. tandem vero anni eiusdem mense Septembri ad igne damnati sunt iniquissimo iudicio senatus & vicarij Archiepiscopi: quorum sententiam, carnifices postea ad extremum usque sunt executi cum acerbissimo plurimorum dolore & commiseratione. Tantae crudelitatis causa. in Theologastros Colonienses transferebatur, qui in suis publicis concionibus vociferabantur, oportere placare ac lenire iram Dei, qui tum novo & inusitato morbi genere, Germaniam affligebat. Etenim praeter famem quae saeuiebat, insolens quidam morbus sudoris nomine appellatus sic grassabatur, ut qui eo exitiali sudore opprimeretur, intra quatuor & viginti horarum spatium morerentur. Cuius quidè rei causa hominũ numerus prope infinitus morte interceptus interiit ante inventũ remedium. Vulgus morbũ Anglicũ appellabat quòd anno M. CCCC .LXXXVI, hac impura lue afflictata fuisset Anglia. Deinde vero ut Deus omnia sua flagella in Germaniam semel explicaret, potentissimus ille Turcarũ rex Solymanus. (Vayvoda ex parte aliqua Hugariæ regè, & Hieronymo à Lasco Polono instigantibus) obsessam tenebat Viennam Austriæ. Porrò cũ duo illi illi sanctißimi homines ad morte ducerētur, suæ fidei ratione omnibus publicè reddebant, seque mutuò cohortabantur & incitabant præclaris verbi diuini testimonijs ad tolerantiam: adeò ut omnes qui aspectabant admiratione obstupefacti, utriusque constantem vultum motumque corporis intuerentur: præsertim vero Adolphi, qui adolescens erat egregia forma, doctrina atque optimarum artium studijs maximè eruditus.
units.tr: In the year 1528, Peter Flystede and Adolph Clarebach, men polished in letters and adorned with outstanding learning and doctrine, were held bound at Cologne, a city on the Rhine, because they dissented from the Papists concerning the Lord's Supper and other heads of the Christian religion. The senate of the city indeed may by its own right throw men into prison, but the power to condemn or acquit lies with the Archbishop; so it can happen that one who has been substituted in the place and stead of the Archbishop releases from prison and restores to full standing a man whom the senate has condemned to death. Those two were therefore kept in custody for more than a year and a half. At last, however, in the month of September of that year, they were condemned to the fire by the most iniquitous judgment of the senate and the Archbishop's deputy; the executioners afterwards carried out this sentence to the end, to the bitter grief and pity of very many. The cause of such cruelty was laid upon the Cologne theologasters, who in their public sermons cried out that it was necessary to appease and soothe the anger of God, who was then afflicting Germany with a new and unusual kind of disease. For besides the famine which was raging, a strange disease called the sweating sickness was spreading, so that those overcome by that deadly sweat died within twenty-four hours. Because of this, an almost countless number of people were cut off by death and perished before a remedy was found. The common people called it the English disease, because England had been afflicted by this foul plague in the year 1486. Then, so that God might unfold all his scourges upon Germany at once, that most powerful king of the Turks, Suleiman (with the Vayvoda, king in part of Hungary, and Jerome à Lasco the Pole instigating), was holding Vienna in Austria under siege. Moreover, when those two most holy men were being led to death, they openly gave an account of their faith to everyone, and mutually encouraged and urged each other to endurance with excellent testimonies of the divine Word; so that all who watched were stunned with admiration and gazed at the steadfast face and bodily bearing of both, especially of Adolph, who was young, of remarkable appearance, and most learned in literature and the studies of the liberal arts.

units.la: LUDOVICUS BERQUINUS.
units.tr: Louis Berquin.

units.la: Ludouicus du Berquin, nobili Berquinorum apud Arthesienses familia ortus, ea Arthesiae parte quae ab oppido S. Audomari denominatur, adscitus in aulam Francisci I. Galliarum Regis, in eorum numerum qui aulae Regis nobiles censentur, cooptatus fuit eo tempore cum adhuc suprema potestas Arthesiae & Flandriae ad regem Galliae pertinebat. Annos natus plus minus quadraginta caelibem vitam egerat, ea morum integritate ut ne suspicio quidem ulla impudicitiae (quod rarum est in homine aulico) aduersus eum, dum vixit, exorta fuerit: mirè benignus in amicos & egenos. Antequam Dominus illum ad cognitionem Euangelij vocasset, constitutionum ac rituum papisticorum, nempe praescriptorum ieiuniorum, dierum sacrorum, ciborum, Missarum, concionum, quemadmodum ab incunte aetate edoctus fuerat, obseruantissimus fuit: alienissimus verò ab omni fuco, ingenio aperto ac libero: quod iniuriam nec cuiquam facere vellet, neque etiam a quoquam perpeti posset. A doctrina Lutheri quae tunc in Gallia coeperat increbrescere ita abhorrebat ut qui maximè. Nihilominus tamen, ut erat vir ingenuè doctus, oderat grauissimè insulsos illos & morosos Sorbonicos theologos ac monachos. in hos etiam aliquando palàm debacchabatur: nec stomachum suum dissimulare poterat. Fuerat illi sermonis conflictatio cum quodam primi nominis inter Theologos Parisienses doctore Gulielmo videlicet à Quercu. Ex eo sanè odio coepit vir pius propius applicare animum ad studium verae pietatis: neque defuit Dominus qui multis modis ac medijs solet suos ad Christi Filij vnigeniti cognitionem trahere. Ab eo tempore nullum intermittebat tempus, quod aut lectioni aut scriptioni aut vertendis in linguam Gallicam piis libellis, non impertiret. Ex iis qui fere sparsi erant, decerptæ sunt ab inimicis sententiæ, quæ Theologi ad suam cognitionem & censuram pertinere existimabant. Huius fere generis erant illæ sententiæ, In concionibus non recte Virginem Mariam invocari pro Spiritu sancto. Non recte vocari Thesaurariam gratiæ. Item in Salutatione illa vespertina quæ illi exhibetur, contra omnem veritatem Spem & Vitam nostram vocari, quum ea omnino ad Christum pertineant.
