units.tr: Louis du Berquin, born into the noble Berquin family among the Artesians, in that part of Artois which takes its name from the town of St Omer, was received into the court of Francis I, King of France, and enrolled among those nobles who are counted as the king's courtiers, at a time when supreme power over Artois and Flanders still belonged to the king of France. About forty years old, he had lived a celibate life with such integrity of conduct that no suspicion of immodesty (rare in a courtier) was ever raised against him while he lived; he was remarkably kind to friends and the needy. Before the Lord called him to the knowledge of the Gospel, he was most observant of the constitutions and rites of the Papists, namely the prescribed fasts, holy days, foods, Masses and sermons, as he had been taught from early youth; but he was utterly averse to all pretence, of an open and frank disposition, because he would not do injury to anyone, nor could he endure it from anyone. He abhorred the doctrine of Luther, which had then begun to spread in France, as much as anyone. Nevertheless, since he was a man of frank learning, he hated most bitterly those foolish and peevish Sorbonne theologians and monks. Sometimes he openly raged against them, nor could he hide his indignation. He had a verbal clash with a certain doctor of the first rank among the Parisian theologians, William à Quercu (du Chêne). From that hatred the godly man began to apply his mind more closely to the study of true piety, and the Lord did not fail to draw his own to the knowledge of his only-begotten Son by many means and occasions. From that time he let no time pass that he did not devote to reading, writing, or translating pious little books into French. From those that were widely scattered, his enemies picked out sentences which the theologians thought belonged to their own judgment and censure. Of this kind were these sentences: that in sermons the Virgin Mary is not rightly invoked in place of the Holy Spirit; that she is not rightly called the Treasurer of grace; likewise that in that evening salutation addressed to her she is called, contrary to all truth, our Hope and Life, since these belong entirely to Christ.

units.la: Ob huiusmodi sententias à Theologis annotatas herefeos reus delatus est, ac in carcerem coniectus. Iudices qui ingenium hominis noverant, parui momenti eas conclusiones existimaverunt, absolverūntque Berquinum. Qui detulerant, vulgo iactabant eum elapsum fauore Regis: ipse vero prædicabat se iure atque æquitate causæ victorem, adeo ut ferio de iis triumphum apparaāret. Interea alios etiam libellos vertit, inter quos etiam Enchiridion militis Christiani Erasmi Gallicè emisit, additis plerisque atque intermixtis, quæ propius ad veritatis Evangelicæ lucē pertinebāt. Erasmus ille, qui se suo more [illegible, ~10 letters] semper ostendit, acriter expostulauit cum eo per literas quod non prudenter ageret, eiusmodi grauem vtrique conflans inuidiam nullo, ut dicebat, fructu pietatis: proinde suā causam sic ageret, ne Erasmum admiscerēt[?]. Interea Natalis Bedda Sorbonicus doctor & ipsius assedæ, collectis multò pluribus articulis aduersus Berquinum, curarunt eum rursus pertrahendum in carcerem. Beddæ se adiunxerant Prior Cartusianorum & Prior Celestinorum urbis Parisiensis ac nonnulli alii ut multitudine obruerent hominis constantiam. Cohors illa Beddaica adeo præiudicijs Berquinum grauarat, ut nihil in causa superesse videretur, nisi ut exustis libellis ac honoraria emendatione facta reciperet præscriptam à Magistris illis satisfactionem, aut si id recusaret, iret ad ignem. Berquinus ne in vno quidē illis cessit: & sane actum erat tum de ipso, nisi quidam è Senatu consultiores, perspicientes rem calidis Monachorum ac Beddaicorum odiis geri, responderent se totā causam à capite usq; ad calce denuò velle cognoscere. idque non sine fremitu illorum qui iam eum morti adiudicaverant, adiudicave-rant. rant . Id quidem fauore Ludouicæ matris Francisci regis, quæ tunc regni habenas moderabatur, procuratum fuisse plerique existimauerunt. Dum hæc aguntur Rex ex vinculis Hispanicis commodùm reucrsus, admonitus fuit Berquinum inter monachos & Theologastros periclitari. itaque per literas denunciauit senatui Parisiensi, ne quid temere pateretur fieri in persona sui Berquini: se breui adfuturum, ac diligetius velle de toto negocio cognoscere. Aliquanto post exemptus è carcere, seruatus est in aula satis commodè, attamen sub custodia. Tandem suae libertati redditus est, quo posset facilius suae causae consulere. Mirum dictu quantum fiduciae tum conceperit animo Berquinus. non enim solùm promittebat sibi absolutionem, verumetiam victoriam & quidem speciosam. Aiebat victoriā esse in manibus, sed malle serius aliquanto finiri causam, quo magnificentius de ijs triumpharet. Iam itaque mutatis viribus sacram illam facultatem, Theologos videlicet & Monachos reos peragebat impietatis. dicebat enim se arcana quædam deprehendisse in eorum actis. Pleriq; eū amici hortabantur, sineret crabrones, extricaret se ab ea causa quàm quiret minimò, vel prætextu Regiæ alicui[?] legationis aliquò proficisceretur, vel in Germaniam iret, dum causa hæc tempore euanesceret. Cogitaret etiam atque etiam qualis excetra esset Bedda, acerrimus ipsius aduersarius, quòtque capitibus venenum efflaret. Expenderet cum immortali ho-ste rem esse, Facultas enim non moritur. Facultatis phalanges non conquicturas donec ei exitium procurassent. Principum ac magnatū fauores esse temporarios, ac delatorum artibus facile in diuersum trahi illorum affectus. Denique, vt nihil eorum accidat, Reges etiam ipsos vel delassari talium improbitate, vel etiam metu nonnunquàm cogi vt cedant. Tot modis deterrentes amici, tantum abest vt Berquinum ab incœpto abstraherent, vt potius animum adderent. ingenium enim ipsius quiddam habebat cum palma commune: nanque aduersus deterrentem tollebat animos. Pergebat itaque in causa aduersus Theologos ac Monachos, maximè verò in Beddam, impetrauitq; à rege Francisco literas ad Theologicam facultātē, vt duodecim articulos, qui in Beddæ libris videretur habere manifesta impietate, atq; adeò blasphemiā, aut damnaret omnium suffragijs aut sacrarum scripturarum testimoniis comprobarent. Haec Berquino polliceri certam victoriam videbantur, sed progressus causae demonstrauit irritamenta haec tantum fuisse ad acuendam magis ac magis insanam aduersariorum rabiem. Frigida enim sunt, ut plurimum edicta aut diplomata Regia, praesertim in causis eorum qui se pro veritate opponunt. Sic itaque excitati crabrones, omni malarum artium genere instructissimi nunquam conquieuerunt, donec Berquino procurassent exitium. Iudicibus duodecim a summo Parlamenti Parisiensis Senatu lectis, tandem delegata fuit tota causae cognitio & suprema in ea pronunciandi authoritas. Quum instaret dies, Berquinus carceri traditus est. Sententia ab iis Iudicibus arcto lata est, ut exustis Berquini libellis & abiuratis articulis perpetuo carcere inclusus vitam degeret: re tamen tota arbitrio Regis reseruata. Is audita praeter expectationem hac sententia, Regem appellauit. Iudices illi delegati indigne ferentes appellandi verbum, Si non recipis, inquiunt, hanc sententiam, efficiemus ne posthac quoquam appelles. Magnus ille Gulielmus Budaeus tunc supplicum libellorum in Curia magister, unus erat e Iudicum illorum numero. Is pro ea benevolentia qua omnes humanitatis studiosos complectebatur, hunc quoque Berquinum amabat: ac paulo antequam grauior sententia mortis in eum ferretur, multis hortatus est, ut a vesanis illis erroribus recipisceret, & palinodiam praescriptam non grauatim amplecteretur, consuleret vitae, ac melioribus studijs se seruaret: neue suo (quod aiunt) indicio sibi exitium accerseret: quod quidem affirmabat ex sententia Iudicum omnino decretum, nisi priori illi tam aequabili setetiae[?] mox acquiesceret. Hac grauui monitione, atque obtestatione tanti viri eo adductus est Berquin[?], ut polliceretur se ea facturum quae ille multis suaserat. Domum reuersus Budaeus, praesagire illi coepit animus non praestiturum ea Berquinum, quae se facturum receperat: Noui enim, aiebat, hominis ingenium, imponet illi sua fiducia atque ingenuitas. Haec cū antemeridianis horis acta fuisset, pomeridianis Berquinus eadem confirmabat quae prius. Itaque Iudices non multo post sententiam alium tulerunt, nempe ut laqueo praefocatus, cremaretur in loco celebri Lutetiæ , Greua appellato.Huius posterioris sententiæ exequendæ occasionem omnem captabant aduersarij: quum primùm semotius rex Franciscus excurreret, quæ sanè mox ut cupiebant oblata est.nam Rex Blesiacum petebat, quum ad supplicij locum deductus est Berquinus, qui adeò præsenti animo tum maximè visus fuit, ut nec vultu, nec vllo corporis gestu dederit vllum perturbati animi specimen: ne tum quidem, cùm carnifex in egressu carceris, truculenta voce crimen ac supplicium pronunciaret. Quum ad plateam Greuensem ventum est, verba fecit ad populum, sed vix quisquâ potuit aliquid percipere. tātus erat satellitum fremitus, tā magna corū, qui à Sorbonicis mercede conducti dicebantur, vociferatio dedita opera exacatata[?] fuit. Sic animos omnium in illum excitarant Monachi ac Sorbonici, qui nusquàm non adsunt, ut etiā pueros initio causæ munusculis illexerint ut vicatim diceret, Berquinum hæreticū esse. Quū itaque ad palum præfocaretur, vix vnus aut alter è turba acclamauit nomen Iesu , quod parricidis tamen ac sacrilegis apud eos acclamari solet.Hoc itaque graue mortis supplicium admiranda animi constantia perpessus est vir insignis, mense Maio, Anno M.D.XXIX.
units.tr: For such opinions, noted by the theologians, he was accused of heresy and thrown into prison. The judges, who knew the man's character, thought these propositions were of little importance and acquitted Berquin. Those who had brought the charge loudly claimed that he had escaped through the king's favour. But he himself declared that by the justice and fairness of his cause he was the victor, so much so that he was preparing to triumph over them straight away. Meanwhile he also translated other little books, among which he published in French Erasmus's Enchiridion of the Christian Soldier, adding and inserting many passages that bore more directly on the light of the Gospel truth. Erasmus, who always showed himself as he was, sharply remonstrated with him by letter for not acting prudently, since he was bringing on both of them a serious odium with no fruit of piety, as he put it. He should therefore conduct his own cause in such a way that they did not mix in Erasmus. Meanwhile Noël Bédier, doctor of the Sorbonne and his follower, having gathered many more articles against Berquin, saw to it that he was again dragged off to prison. The Prior of the Carthusians and the Prior of the Celestines of the city of Paris joined Bédier, and several others too, so as to overwhelm the man's steadfastness by their numbers. That Bedda-led band had so burdened Berquin with prejudices that nothing seemed left in the case except that, after his books were burned and an honourable retraction made, he should accept the satisfaction prescribed by those masters, or, if he refused, go to the fire. Berquin did not yield to them even in one point. And indeed it would have been over for him then, had not some of the more prudent members of the Senate, perceiving that the matter was being driven by the heated hatreds of the monks and the Beddists, declared that they wished to examine the whole case again from head to foot. This was done not without the fury of those who had already adjudged him to death. Most people thought this was brought about through the favour of Louise, mother of King Francis, who then governed the reins of the kingdom. While these things were going on, the king returned from his Spanish captivity, and he was warned that Berquin was in peril among the monks and the little theologians. So he wrote to the Parisian Senate that nothing was to be rashly done to Berquin's person: he would soon be present and wished to inquire into the whole business more carefully. Some time later Berquin was released from prison and kept at court fairly comfortably, though under guard. At last he was restored to liberty, so that he could better attend to his cause. It is wonderful to say how much confidence Berquin then conceived. For he not only promised himself an acquittal but even a splendid victory. He said the victory was in his hands, but he preferred the case to be finished somewhat later, so that he might triumph over his opponents more magnificently. Now, with his strength renewed, he pressed the case against that sacred faculty, namely the theologians and the monks, accusing them of impiety. For he said he had detected certain secrets in their acts. Many of his friends urged him to let the hornets be, and to extricate himself from that cause as quickly as he could, either by some pretext of a royal embassy setting off somewhere, or by going to Germany, until the matter faded away in time. They also urged him to consider again and again what a viper Bedda was, his most bitter adversary, and with how many heads he spewed out poison. He should weigh that he had to do with an immortal enemy: the Faculty does not die. The phalanxes of the Faculty would not rest until they had procured his ruin. The favours of princes and great men were temporary, and by the arts of informers their feelings could easily be turned the other way. Finally, whatever happened, even kings themselves might be wearied by the wickedness of such men, or sometimes be forced by fear to give way. His friends, dissuading him in so many ways, were so far from drawing Berquin away from his undertaking that they rather spurred him on. For his temper had something in common with the palm tree: he lifted up his spirits against the one who tried to deter him. So he went on with his cause against the theologians and the monks, and above all against Bedda, and he obtained from King Francis letters to the theological faculty, ordering that they either condemn, by the votes of all, the twelve articles which seemed to contain manifest impiety, and indeed blasphemy, in Bedda's books, or else approve them by the testimonies of Holy Scripture. These letters seemed to promise Berquin a certain victory, but the course of the cause showed that these were only incitements to sharpen ever more the mad rage of his opponents. For royal edicts and letters patent are for the most part cold, especially in the causes of those who set themselves against the truth. So the hornets were roused, fully equipped with every kind of wicked art, and they never rested until they had procured Berquin's destruction. When twelve judges had been chosen from the chief Senate of the Parisian Parlement, the whole examination of the case and the supreme authority of pronouncing judgment in it was at last committed to them. When the day approached, Berquin was handed over to prison. The sentence was pronounced by those judges with severity, that after his books were burned and his articles abjured he should live out his life shut up in perpetual prison, the whole matter however being reserved to the king's pleasure. Berquin, hearing this sentence contrary to his expectation, appealed to the king. The judges who had been appointed, taking it ill that the word "appeal" should be used, said: "If you do not accept this sentence, we will make sure that you never appeal to anyone again." The great Guillaume Budé, then master of petitions in the Court, was one of those judges. Because of that kindness with which he embraced all lovers of humane learning, he also loved this Berquin; and shortly before the heavier sentence of death was pronounced against him, he urged him earnestly to turn back from those mad errors, and not to hesitate to embrace the prescribed recantation, to look to his life and to preserve himself for better studies, and not to bring about his own destruction by his own confession, as they say. He affirmed that the judges had certainly decreed this, unless he quickly agreed to that first and so moderate sentence. Moved by this grave warning and by the entreaty of so great a man, Berquin was brought to promise that he would do what Budé had urged on him at length. Budé, on returning home, began to have a presentiment that Berquin would not keep what he had undertaken to do. "I know the man's temper," he said; "his own confidence and frankness will undo him." When this had been done in the morning hours, in the afternoon Berquin reaffirmed what he had said before. So the judges, not long after, pronounced another sentence, namely that he should be strangled with a noose and burned in the famous place of Paris called the Place de Grève. The opponents seized every opportunity of carrying out this later sentence, as soon as King Francis should be far away; and indeed this opportunity was soon offered as they wished. For the king was heading to Blois when Berquin was led to the place of execution. He appeared so composed at that time that neither by his countenance nor by any gesture of his body did he show any sign of a troubled mind, not even when the executioner, on leaving the prison, announced in a savage voice his crime and punishment. When they came to the Place de Grève, he addressed the people, but hardly anyone could make out anything he said. So great was the roar of the guards, and so great the deliberate shouting of those who were said to have been hired for pay by the Sorbonnists. Thus the monks and the Sorbonnists, who are present everywhere, had stirred up the minds of all against him; they had even enticed boys, at the beginning of the affair, with little gifts, to go about the streets saying that Berquin was a heretic. So when he was being strangled at the stake, scarcely one or two in the crowd shouted the name of Jesus, although among those people that name is usually shouted by parricides and sacrilegious men. Thus this remarkable man, of notable character, underwent this grave punishment of death with admirable steadfastness of mind, in the month of May, in the year 1529.

units.la: Hanc pleniorem de Berquino historiam, ab iis accepimus, qui totius causæ a-ctionem probè cognitam habuerunt, & illi interfuerunt: tum etiam ex Erasmi epistolis nonnulla, quæ ad rem ut gesta est pertinere videbantur, desumpsimus.
units.tr: I have taken this fuller account of Berquin from those who knew the whole course of the case well and were present at it. I have also drawn some material from the letters of Erasmus, insofar as they seemed to bear on the matter as it actually happened.

units.la: MARTINVS GONIN.
units.tr: Martin Gonin.

units.la: Martinus Goninus, natus fuit in exigua valle regionis Pedemō-tanæ, Angiuena[?] nominata: cuius vallis incolæ, iam à multis annis, abusus impios traditionum humanarū probè cognitos habuerūt. Is cùm venisset ad eum coetum, qui cōmuni Valdenses appellantur, ministerium ab illis delatum accepit. Valdenses autem etsi boni erant homines, cumprimis Deum metuetes, summóque verbi Dei studio affecti: tamen luce Euangelij tum apud Germanos, tum etiā apud Heluetios & Sabaudos exorta, cognouerunt multa desiderari in suis ecclesiis, quæ ad veram religionem ac pietatem pertinerent: pleraque etiam ignoratione, ac temporum culpa iandiu recepta retineri, quæ à pura Euangelij doctrina Ecclesiæque disciplina abhorrerent. Itaque cum Martinum cum Ioanne Gerardo, qui postea typographiam, summa cum laude ac utilitate Ecclesiae, Genevae aliquot annos exercuit, in Sabaudiam miserunt ad Guilelmum Farellum, qui tum in ea patria Euangelium annunciabat, ab eo rogantes, ut curam etiam suscipéret[?] reformandarum atque instituendarum suarum ecclesiarum, cum earum quae citra Alpes in Delphinatu, in Provincia Gallica, ac in Pedemontio haberentur, tum etiam illarum, quae in Italia, in Calabria, Apuliaque aliquem pietatis cultum ac timorem Dei retinerent. Quod negotium Martinus sibi commissum, cum diligenter ac fideliter curasset, reditu itérque suum instituit, mense Aprili, anno M.D.XXXVI, ut ad vallem Angruenam, suos parentes amicosque visendi causa prosicisceretur. Eo in itinere dominus Champolionensis, Georgius Martinus appellatus, comprehendit eum in montibus ducatus Chansauri in Delphinatu, speculatorem esse suspicatus. Inde ductus est ad Portam Troinam, quo in loco carcer est urbis Grationopolis: ibique a magistratu eius Parlamenti examinatus. Sed cum in eo nulla deprehenderetur suspicio eius criminis, censuerunt ut salvus & incolumnis dimitteretur. Cum autem carcere egrederetur, Georgius Borelus custos carceris, eum perscrutans, deprehendit quasdam scriptas literas, quas Guilelmus Farellus & Antonius Saunerius, aliique ministri ecclesiae Geneuensis, ad Pedemontanos pios homines ac verbi Dei studiosos mittebant. Tum custos carceris eum redire iussit, atque in infima & obscura fossa inclusum, per duos dies detinuit. Tertio die procurator regius cum aliis quibusdam viris eius summae curiae, ad eum venit, eumque speculatorem esse arguit, cum literas secum adferret. Tum Martinus, Legite, inquit, eas, & cognoscetis de rebus bellicis non esse scriptas, nec ad principum negotia ullo modo pertinere: sed tantummodo complecti[?] pia quaedam monita atque praecepta, quibus vita in timore Dei instituatur. Tum alii, cuias is esset, rogaverunt: atque ex literis, quas dicebant eum habere, Lutheranum esse vehementius arguebant. Ego, inquit Martinus, sum ex valle Angruena Pedemontana: hoc quidem tempore Genevae agens, artem typographicam exerceo. Nec sane Lutheranus sum, nec vellem quidem esse cum non Lutherus pro me, sed Christus Iesus sit mortuus, cuius nomine censeor, Christianúsque appellor, & pro quo & cum quo, ego tum vivere tum mori paratus sum. Interrogatus ab illis, quis Genevae concionaretur, Guilelmum Farellum & Petrum Viretum respondit. Tum procurator, eos duos sectae Lutheranae principes esse affirmavit. Cui Martinus comiter contradicens, Pace tua, inquit, illi minime sunt ij, quos tu arbitraris, sed fideles sunt servi Dei, a quibus, sicut Apostoli fecerunt, pura verbi Dei doctrina annuntiatur. Ain tu, inquit procurator, ea omnia, quae nos tenemus tradita a matre nostra sancta ecclesia Romana, Missam, purgatorium, indulgentias, bona opera, & cetera huiusmodi, falsa esse? Martinus respondit, eam ecclesiam esse malignorum, a diabolo ortam & propagatam, cuius Papa, verus Antichristus, caput esset. Sed ita, inquit, eveniet, quemadmodum apud Matthæum scriptum est, Ut omnis plantatio, quam non plantaverit Pater caelestis, evellatur. Tum procurator ex eo quaesiit, quando id futurum esset. Tum, inquit Martinus, cum filius perditionis, qui in sanctuario Dei sedet, revelatus fuerit, quemadmodum Divus Paulus admonuit. Sed date mihi Biblia, & ego ostendam vobis. Satis quidem est hodie, inquit procurator: cras tibi doctores adducentur, qui aliter tibi respondebunt, Bibliaque & Missale adferent. Postridie igitur magna turba monachorum, Franciscanorum, Dominicanorum, sacerdotum, cum aliquot eius Parlamenti consiliariis, ad eum in carcerem convenit. Tum procurator, & fidei inquisitor, eum hoc modo interrogarunt, Age, visne aliquid amplius dicere praeter ea quae dixisti? Ego, inquit ille, nescio quid ex me velitis quaerere. Tum inquisitor, ut omnium audacissimus, cum interrogare ita coepit: In quem tu credis? Ego, inquit Martinus, credo in Deum patrem per Christum Iesum, sicut continetur in symbolo Apostolorum, nec aliam fidem habeo. Inquisitor ex eo iterum quaesiit, quo modo ipse oraret Dominum, Eo, inquit ille, quo Salvator noster nos orare docuit ac voluit: Pater noster, qui es in caelis. Inquisitor ira commotus, interrogando instare coepit, Dicis ergo suffragia nostrae matris sanctae ecclesiae, nihil plane prodesse? Vos quidem, inquit ille, ita statuitis & affirmatis. Sed haec inventa sunt humana & diabolica, quae cum suo capite atque authore Papa corruent, quemadmodum in Apocalypsi scriptum est XVII, & XVIII, capitibus. quæ quidem lecta eadem hora, & à Martino exposita fuerunt. Tum vero monachi ac sacerdotes eo furore permoti atque agitati fuerunt, ut mensam pugnis percutientes, ac pileos in terram suos proiicientes dixerint, nihil amplius quærendum ac percontandum ab eo esse, qui hæreticus damnatus esset. Si Prophetæ, inquit Martinus, & Christus Iesus saluator meus, Apostolique sunt hæretici, ego quoq; unà cum his esse volo. neque enim ullam aliam doctrinam, quam eorum teneo, nec tenere volo. Ita quatuor diebus continuis, quatuorque aut quinque dierum singulorum horis, de capitibus religionis, atque abusibus ecclesiæ Romanæ disputarunt. Postremo Martinus Missale ab illis petijt, ut eis ostenderet insignem abusum in eo Canone, qui ita incipit, Te igitur: cùm Christum iterum in carne sua ossibusque[?], buccella panis inclusum, pro peccatis tum viuorum tū mortuorū offerunt. quod quidè, inquit, ridiculum plane, atque à veritate pietatéque in Christum dominum, maximopere alienum. Etenim summus ille saluator Christus Iesus, in sancta sanctorum semel est ingressus, seipsumque semel in cruce ita obtulit pro peccatis nostris, ut purissimo sanguine effuso & Patri oblato, omnes sordes ac maculas vitiorum peccatorumque nostrorum plane eluerit, nósque ita expurgauerit. Nunc quidem contra verbum Dei sacrificium illud renouare, atque ita repetere, non superuacaneum solum est, sed etiā impium, cùm hoc modo vis illius sacrificij aboleatur. Tū rursus monachi ac cæteri qui eis adhærebant, magis insanire cœperunt ac furere, terrā pedibus, mensam manibus ferientes, pugnisque pileos prehendentes suos, dicebant hominem esse hæreticū diabolumque habere, quòd Missam nollet credere. Itaque mandatum est custodi, ut eum reduceret in carcerem, atque in turri quadam arctissime inclusum perdiligenter asseruaret. Cùm ij qui conuenerant, vellent abire, inquisitor eis consilium dedit, quoniam homo extraneus minimeq; in Gallia notus esset, commodissimum esse, si in profluentem proiceretur, ne populus eum loquentem audiret. periculum enim esse, ne ille gratia sermonis sui, homi-nes deteriores quàm ipse esset efficeret, si eū audire possent. quare summum eius prouinciæ magistratum & consilium ea de re consideraturum deraturū. Bidno[?] post xxvi. die Aprilis, anno M.D.XXXVI. hora nona, Suppræfectus vrbis, quē Castellanū vocāt, cū carnifice reliquoque satellitio venit in carcerē cum Martinus quiesceret, vt eum comprehenderet. Quibus ille dicere cœpit, Quónam vos itis, amici? equidem intelligo ac perspicio quid vos agere statueritis, quòd me vultis proicere in profluentem, ne vllus ex populo me videat. sed Deus omnium inspector vos facillimè aspiciet. Ego quidē iam eo, vt cum eo perpetuò viuam, quem rogo vt eam vobis cognitione impertiat, vt hoc vestrum iniquissimum consilium & factum cognoscatis. Eamus igitur in nomine Domini: quoniā ei quidem ita placet. Hæc cum essent dicta surrexit, seque à carnifice ligari passus est, vt ad supplicium duceretur.
units.tr: Martin Gonin was born in a small valley of the Piedmontese region called Angrogna. For many years the inhabitants of that valley had been well acquainted with the impious abuses of human traditions. When he came to that group which is commonly called the Waldenses, he was entrusted with their ministry. The Waldenses, though they were good people, who feared God above all and were deeply devoted to the Word of God, nevertheless, when the light of the Gospel rose among the Germans and also among the Swiss and the Savoyards, recognised that many things were lacking in their churches that pertained to true religion and piety. Many other things, retained for a long time through ignorance and the fault of the age, were at odds with the pure doctrine of the Gospel and the discipline of the Church. So they sent Martin, together with John Gerard, who later ran a printing press at Geneva for some years to the great praise and benefit of the Church, into Savoy to Guillaume Farel, who was then proclaiming the Gospel in that country. They asked him to take up also the task of reforming and organising their churches, both those which lay on this side of the Alps, in the Dauphiné, in the Gallic province, and in Piedmont, and also those in Italy, in Calabria and Apulia, which still kept some form of piety and fear of God. Martin carefully and faithfully carried out this commission, and in April of the year 1536 he set out on his return journey, intending to visit his parents and friends in the valley of Angrogna. On that journey, Georges Martin, lord of Champollon, arrested him in the mountains of the duchy of Chanssaur in the Dauphiné, suspecting him to be a spy. He was led to the Porte Troina, where the prison of the city of Grenoble is, and there he was examined by the magistrates of that Parlement. But since no trace of that charge could be found against him, they decided that he should be released safe and unharmed. However, as he was leaving the prison, Georges Borel, the gaoler, searched him and found some letters that Guillaume Farel, Antoine Saunier and other ministers of the Church of Geneva were sending to the pious Piedmontese who loved the Word of God. Then the gaoler ordered him back and kept him for two days shut up in a deep and dark pit. On the third day the king's procurator came to him with certain other men of that high court and accused him of being a spy, since he carried letters with him. Then Martin said: "Read them, and you will see that they are not written about matters of war, nor do they in any way concern the affairs of princes. They contain only certain pious admonitions and precepts by which life is ordered in the fear of God." Then the others asked whose man he was, and from the letters, which they said he had, they argued vehemently that he was a Lutheran. "I," said Martin, "am from the valley of Angrogna in Piedmont. At present I am working at Geneva and practise the printing trade. Nor am I in fact a Lutheran, nor would I wish to be one, since it was not Luther but Christ Jesus who died for me, and it is from him that I am named and called a Christian, and for whom and with whom I am ready to live and to die." Asked by them who preached at Geneva, he answered: Guillaume Farel and Pierre Viret. Then the procurator declared that these two were leaders of the Lutheran sect. Martin politely contradicted him: "With all respect, they are by no means the men you think, but faithful servants of God, by whom the pure doctrine of the Word of God is proclaimed, as the Apostles did." "Do you say," said the procurator, "that all those things which we hold, handed down by our mother, the holy Roman Church (the Mass, purgatory, indulgences, good works and the like), are false?" Martin replied that that church was of evil men, begotten and propagated by the devil, whose head was the Pope, the true Antichrist. "But it will happen," he said, "as is written in Matthew: Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up." Then the procurator asked him when this would happen. "When," said Martin, "the son of perdition, who sits in the sanctuary of God, shall be revealed, as the divine Paul warned. But give me the Bibles and I will show you." "It is enough for today," said the procurator. "Tomorrow teachers will be brought to you who will answer you otherwise, and they will bring the Bible and the Missal." So the next day a great crowd of monks, Franciscans and Dominicans, priests, together with several councillors of that Parlement, came to him in the prison. Then the procurator and the inquisitor of the faith questioned him in this way: "Come, do you wish to say anything more besides what you have said?" "I do not know," he replied, "what you want to ask of me." Then the inquisitor, the boldest of them all, began to question him thus: "In whom do you believe?" "I believe," said Martin, "in God the Father through Jesus Christ, as it is contained in the Apostles' Creed, and I have no other faith." The inquisitor asked him again how he prayed to the Lord. "In the way," he answered, "that our Saviour taught us and wished us to pray: Our Father, who art in heaven." The inquisitor, roused to anger, began to press him with questions: "So you say that the intercessions of our mother, the holy Church, are of no benefit at all?" "You," said he, "so decide and affirm. But these are human and devilish inventions, which will fall together with their head and author, the Pope, as is written in chapters 17 and 18 of the Apocalypse." These chapters were read that same hour and expounded by Martin. Then the monks and priests were so stirred and agitated with fury that, striking the table with their fists and throwing their caps on the ground, they said that nothing more was to be asked or inquired of one who had been condemned as a heretic. "If the prophets," said Martin, "and Christ Jesus my Saviour, and the Apostles are heretics, then I too wish to be with them together, for I hold, and wish to hold, no other doctrine than theirs." So for four days in a row, and for four or five hours each day, they disputed about the chief points of religion and the abuses of the Roman Church. At last Martin asked them for the Missal, so that he could show them the notable abuse in that Canon which begins: "Te igitur." Christ again in his flesh and bones, enclosed in a morsel of bread, they offer for the sins both of the living and of the dead. This, he said, was downright ridiculous and utterly remote from the truth and from piety towards Christ the Lord. For that supreme Saviour, Christ Jesus, entered once into the holy of holies, and offered himself once on the cross for our sins, so that, his most pure blood having been shed and offered to the Father, he completely washed away all the stains and blemishes of our vices and sins, and thus cleansed us. To renew that sacrifice now, against the Word of God, and so to repeat it, is not only superfluous but also impious, since in this way the power of that sacrifice is annulled. Then again the monks and the others who adhered to them began to rage and fume even more, stamping their feet on the ground, striking the table with their hands, and seizing their caps with their fists. They said the man was a heretic and had the devil in him, because he refused to believe in the Mass. So the gaoler was ordered to take him back to prison and to keep him most closely guarded, shut up in a certain tower. When those who had gathered wished to leave, the inquisitor advised them that, since the man was a stranger and little known in Gaul, it would be most convenient to throw him into the river, so that the people should not hear him speak. For there was a danger that, by the charm of his speech, he might make men worse than he himself was, if they were able to hear him. Therefore the chief magistrate and council of that province would consider the matter. On the 26th day of April, in the year 1536, at the ninth hour, the deputy governor of the city, whom they call the Castellan, came with the executioner and the rest of the guards into the prison, while Martin was resting, to seize him. He began to speak to them: "Where are you going, friends? I understand and see well what you have decided to do, since you wish to cast me into the river, so that no one of the people may see me. But God, the overseer of all, will very easily see you. For my part, I am now ready to live forever with him, whom I beg to grant you the knowledge of him, so that you may recognise this most unjust counsel and deed of yours. Let us go then in the name of the Lord, since this indeed pleases him." When these words were spoken he rose, and allowed himself to be bound by the executioner, so that he might be led to his punishment.

units.la: IOANNES FRITHVS ET ANDREAS HEVVETVS, Angli.
units.tr: JOHN FRITH AND ANDREW HEWET, Englishmen.

units.la: Ex[?] iis, quæ superiori libro diximus, wicleui temporibus, si quis recensere vellet quot Christi martyres Anglia dederit, magnum opus conficeret, etiamsi obiter tantum recensendis eorum nominibus insisteret, adeo profuerunt patriæ wicleui viri optimi exilia, carceres, denique etiam combusta ossa anno M.cccc.xxviii. qui fuerat ab eius morte quadragesimus primus, Martino V. pontifice Rom. ac Senensi concilio iubente. Nos tamen, ut cœpimus, eos potissimum huic catalogo ascribendos duximus, quorum monimenta extant, quorumque minimè obscura fama est. Occurrit itaque hac anni serie notandus Ioannes Frithus Londini natus, iuuenis ingenio magnus & Latinè & Græcè insigniter doctus. Hunc ut testatur Balæus centuria octaua Scriptorum Britanniæ, Cardinalis Eboracensis Thomas Wolsius, ob raras ingenij dotes à collegio Regio, quod est Cantabrigiæ, ad suum nouum in urbe Oxoniensi collegium pellexerat, ut esset set ei ornamento, in eoque disciplinas profitercetur[?] liberales. Quam sane provinciam iuvenili illa ætate, summa cum laude & omnium admiratione obiit.
units.tr: Of those we have mentioned in the previous book, from the time of Wycliffe, anyone who wished to list how many martyrs of Christ England has produced would undertake a great work, even if he only touched briefly on their names. So greatly did the exiles, the prisons, and finally even the burning of the bones of that excellent man Wycliffe benefit his country, in the year 1428, the forty-first after his death, under Pope Martin V and by order of the Council of Siena. Nevertheless, as we began, we have thought fit to assign to this catalogue chiefly those whose records survive and whose fame is by no means obscure. Thus in this sequence of years there occurs John Frith, born in London, a young man of great talent, notably learned in Latin and Greek. As Bale testifies in the eighth century of his Writers of Britain, Cardinal Thomas Wolsey of York, on account of his rare gifts, had enticed him from the King's College at Cambridge to his new college in the city of Oxford, so that he might be an ornament to it and teach the liberal disciplines there. Indeed, he discharged this office in that youthful age with the highest praise and the admiration of all.

units.la: Hunc postmodum Gulielmus Tyndalus illius ætatis mirificus Evangelij præco, de quo mox suo loco (uti martyrij coronam accepit dicturi sumus) ad se advocans, hortabatur ut adversus Iudaicas ineptias & Papisticas superstitiones, Christum Iesum doceret atque in ministerij partem succederet. paruit vocanti Frithus: unaque promovit Evangelij negotium adversus impuram illam meretricis Romæ doctrinam, ac fermentum plusquam Pharisaicum. Iohannes Frischerus episcopus Roffensis & Thomas Morus, duo fulmina belli Papalis, quorum hebetes oculi quum ad tantam Evangelij lucem caligarent, nec quicquam vana eorum coaxatio proficeret: non desinebant tamen eam persequi, atque omnem authoritatem ad opprimendos veros Christi servos interponere. Dixerat postremo hic Frithus, Transubstantiatione in sacris literis nō inveniri, sed novum fuisse Papæ decretum ex Sathanæ officina deprōptum. itē, Post mortem nullum restare Purgatorij locū. ac multa alia ex ipsa veritatis luce petita constanter asseverabat. Itaque non defuerunt graves Evangelij hostes qui exitium huic sancto martyri procurarent. Atque in carcerem coniectus quum ea ex sacris literis invicta constantia tueretur[?], tandem à Londinensi, Lincolniensi ac wintoniensi pseudoepiscopis, qui cum duobus illis conspiraverant, damnatus fuit. Constans itaque hic Christi Martyr cum socio Andrea Heveto, Londini in foro ferrario crematus est die XXII. Iulij, M.D.XXXIII. qui illi ætatis erat annus XXVI. Multa adhuc extant eo scripta, quæ pestilens[?] prorsus Christianum & spirant & referunt.
units.tr: Afterwards William Tyndale, that wonderful herald of the Gospel of his age (of whom we shall speak in its proper place, when we come to his crown of martyrdom), summoned him and urged him to teach Christ Jesus against Jewish follies and Papist superstitions, and to succeed to a share of the ministry. Frith obeyed the summons, and together they advanced the cause of the Gospel against that impure doctrine of the harlot of Rome and its leaven, more than Pharisaical. John Fisher, bishop of Rochester, and Thomas More, the two thunderbolts of the Papal war, whose dull eyes grew dim before so great a light of the Gospel, and whose vain croaking availed nothing, nevertheless did not cease to persecute it, and brought all their authority to bear in order to crush the true servants of Christ. Finally, this Frith had said that transubstantiation is not found in the sacred letters, but was a new decree of the Pope drawn from Satan's workshop; likewise, that after death there is no remaining place of Purgatory; and he constantly affirmed many other things drawn from the very light of truth. Therefore there was no lack of grave enemies of the Gospel who procured the destruction of this holy martyr. Thrown into prison, he defended these things from Scripture with unconquered constancy, and at last he was condemned by the pseudo-bishops of London, Lincoln and Winchester, who had conspired with those two. So this steadfast martyr of Christ, together with his companion Andrew Hewet, was burned at Smithfield in London on the 22nd of July, 1533, in the twenty-sixth year of his age. Many of his writings survive, which breathe and express a thoroughly Christian spirit.

units.la: ALEXANDER CANUS, alioqui vulgò Laurentius Cruceus appellatus.
units.tr: ALEXANDER CANUS, otherwise commonly called Laurentius Cruceus.

units.la: Quanta vis sit misericordiæ Dei in electos suos vel hinc liquet, quòd extremis illis temporibus quibus vix respirare cœperat Evangelium, Alexandrum hunc ex lustrorum monachalium faucibus ereptum, & cœlesti quodam instinctu concitatum, Evangelicæ veritatis suæ gravissimum testem esse voluerit. Quod eò quidè videri possit illustrius, quoniā & monachus fuit: & in ruinis illis primoribus Christianæ Reipublicæ iacuit: & in eam incidit tempestatem, quæ non modò verbi Dei prædicandi, sed ne cogitatione percipiendi quidem animum, facultatem quidem certè darer. Et tamen in hac ipsa vel acerbitate rerum, vel iniquitate temporum quàm & animosè depugnarit, & iustū ex inimicorum dolore triumphū victor retulerit, ex ipso
units.tr: How great the power of God's mercy towards his elect is can be seen from this: in those last times, when the Gospel had barely begun to draw breath, he snatched this Alexander from the jaws of a monastic brothel, stirred him by a certain heavenly impulse, and willed him to be a most weighty witness of his evangelical truth. This can appear all the more remarkable because he had been a monk, lay among the ruins of the leading men of the Christian commonwealth, and fell into a storm that gave the mind not only the power to preach the Word of God but not even the chance to think about it. Yet in this very harshness of affairs and iniquity of the times, how bravely he fought, and how, as victor, he carried off a just triumph from the grief of his enemies, may be seen from the following account.

units.la: Memorabile[?] nobis exemplum Alexander Canus Avrincensis, constantiae suae reliquit. Is enim eiurata Dominicalium familia, in qua annos aliquot antea vixerat, locum quaeres ubi profligata superstitione regnare coepisset Evangelium, eoque nomine ad Allobroges profectus, & annos aliquot in comitatu Neocomensi comoratus, venit Geneva, quo in loco Gulielmus Farellus cum aliis nonnullis fidelibus Dei ministris Evangelium vere profiteri coeperat, maximo motu ac tumultu Canonicorum, Presbyterorum & Monachorum qui tum ibi summa rerum omnium potestate gerebant. Quorum omnium insectatione commotus potissimum Alexander, urbe cedere, coque modo saluti suae consulere cogitat. Itaque profectus per Segusianos in Gallia, venit Castilione Ducatus Borboniorum oppido, indeque Matisconu, tandem Lugdunu. quibus omnibus locis iter faciens, Evangelij doctrinam spargebat animo maximo: eoque tanto, ut neq; rem ullam suam, neq; sane vitam respicere videretur. Lugduni quidem fideles omnes qui tum aderant, hortatus saepe fertur maxima contentione animi atq; verborum, Christianisq; Cerealibus ac item postridie concione habuisse frequentibus auditoribus quibusdam aurificibus, qui Lugduni tum habitantes ei negotio non interessent tantum, sed etiam homini praesto semper exisferent. Vix autem ibi diutius egerat, cum Praefecti iudiciorum, illius ecclesiae facti certiores ipsum comprehendunt; comprehensum e vestigio post morte multandum censent. provocat Alexander: Lutetia adducitur: saepius ad quaestione abripitur impetu tanto, ut effracto demum crure altero exclamaret, o Deus! postquam istorum animi misericordia moveri nequeunt, at respexeris ipse me Deus misericors. Nec desunt qui testentur gemebunda ac lamentabili voce dixisse quoq; illum, Num quis Gamaliel tandem, qui mitigandae tantae crudelitatis atq; saevitiae locum apud istos quaerat? Sane tanta tamq; excellente sanctissimi viri in omni genere patientia & aequabilitate animi quum praesentes omnes admirabantur; tum quidem unus propter eximiam eius eruditione & authoritate valde gratiosus, Nu, inquit, sat hactenus in miserum hunc saevitum est? nu cruciatum istorum plus satis adhibitum? Ego quidem ipse non video quid ex eo praeterea expectare, quorsum pergere debeatis. Horum honore verborum quievit tormentum; quod idcirco fuerat iteratum saepius, ut indices exprimerentur. Decuria tota Parifieri[?]sis admirabili viri perseuerantia stupens atq; comota, martyrisque conturbandi locum undique & occasionem captans, sisti iudicio iubet: praesentem iudicat praeter morem atque legem, qua (ut nunc quidem est) cauebatur, reos omnes quibus mortis supplicium irrogaretur, ad phylacistam reijci oportere. Alexander autem audita de se palam dicta sententia, maiorem adhuc quam unquam antea, fortitudinem animi praese ferre videbatur. Breuiter, infulis omnibus sacerdotalibus ritu Papistico Alexander exauguratur: silentium facit. Verebatur numirum ne si multus esset in sermone, quemadmodum ei fuerat indictum, lingua sibi praecideretur. Execrata linguarum exputandarum inuentio hoc primum anno inuchi & in consuetudinem induci coeperat. Ac etsi ne verbum ille quidem, tamen & gestu & vultu; & interiecta plerunque subrisione facile quam parum ceremonias huiuscemodi penderet, populo declarabat. Sannionis habitu vestitus exclamat, Prob tuam, o Deus, fidem! mihine maiorem honorem haberi potuisse, quam insigne mihi hodie deferri ei simile, quod quondam apud Herodem Filius tuus unicus accepit? Ad locum igitur supplicio delectum, Malbertinam arcam, plaustro delatus, populum ad Christum agnoscendum, & ad poenitentiam hortatur. circunstantium Dominicanorum tricis encestus, Quid? mene, inquit, eo adigere, ut ipsum eiurem Christum, scelesti, vultis? Facessite impostores. Postea ad Ioannem Morinum Comitiorum quaesitorem conuersus, petiit ut sibi cum populo pauca quaedam agere liceret. Morinus id velle quidem se, dicere; quod ipsum tamen ex N. Molini Basilicae praecentoris ac choragi (aderat enim) sententia fieri posset. Molinus, id ipsum velle se quoque: at obsecrare, iam satis ut haberet tam multis catenus egisse. Illud autem eo subijciebat Molinus, quoniam ex quo plaustrum conscenderat Alexander, nunquam fere populum erudire, & ut se colligeret aliquando comonere desiisset; eoque ventum esset, ut etiam existeret, qui quidem illum iniquissimo iudicio perfusum & oppressum affirmaret. Antequam igitur ad patibulum raperetur impetrata libere loquendi facultate, concionem habuit bene longam, sed vibratem, sed eruditam, sapientissimisq; sententijs, & gravibus verbis ornatā atq; perpolitā: qua cocione vir constans & sapies fidei suae totius, ac imprimis Coenae Domini nostri Iesu Christi, rationem exposuit tanto studio, tanta contentione, vt plerique qui tum forte ibi aderant, ipsumque alias audiuerant tonantem, nunquam illum neque tam eleganter, neque sane feliciter sibi visum esse dicere faterentur. Porro qui sermonem exceptum literarum monimentis mandauerunt, illi quidem hanc seriem eius perpetuationémque tradiderunt.
units.tr: Alexander Canus of Avranches left us a memorable example of his constancy. For having renounced the Dominican family, in which he had lived some years before, he sought a place where, with superstition overthrown, the Gospel had begun to reign. For this purpose he went to the Allobroges, and after spending some years in the county of Neuchâtel, he came to Geneva, where William Farel, with some other faithful ministers of God, had begun to profess the Gospel openly, to the great agitation and uproar of the canons, priests and monks who then held the highest power in all things there. Moved above all by the persecution of all of these, Alexander decided to leave the city and so to look to his own safety. Setting out through the Segusians in Gaul, he came to Châtillon, a town in the Duchy of Bourbon, and from there to Mâcon, and at last to Lyon. In all these places, as he travelled, he spread the teaching of the Gospel with the greatest zeal, and with such intensity that he seemed to have no regard for his property or indeed for his life. At Lyon, it is said, he often exhorted all the faithful who were then present with the greatest vehemence of mind and word, and on the following day, on a Christian feast, he preached a sermon to a large audience, including some goldsmiths who were living in Lyon at that time, who not only took part in that business but also always attended the man. But he had scarcely stayed there longer when the prefects of the courts, having been informed by that church, seized him; once seized, they judged that he should be condemned to death without delay. Alexander appealed. He was led to Lyon, and was dragged before the judges so often, with such violence, that at last, with one leg broken, he cried out, "O God! Since the minds of these men cannot be moved to mercy, at least look upon me, merciful God." There are also those who testify that he said in a groaning and lamentable voice, "Is there no Gamaliel at last, who might find a place among these men to soften such great cruelty and savagery?" Indeed, while all those present marvelled at the very great and excellent patience and evenness of mind of this most holy man in every respect, one man, very influential because of his outstanding learning and authority, said, "Well, has enough not already been done to this wretched man? Has not enough torture already been applied? For my part I cannot see what more you can expect from him, or where you ought to go on." At the honour of these words the torment ceased; it had been repeated many times for this reason, to force out the names of his accomplices. The whole bench of the Parisian court, astonished and moved by the wonderful perseverance of the man, and seeking on all sides an occasion to unsettle the martyr, ordered him brought before the court; contrary to custom and law, which (as it then stood) provided that all the accused who were to be punished with death should be sent to the prison, they pronounced judgment on him in his presence. Alexander, having heard the sentence pronounced against him openly, seemed to show even greater fortitude of mind than ever before. In short, Alexander was stripped of all his priestly insignia according to the Papistical rite. He made silence. For he feared that if he spoke at length, as he had been ordered, his tongue would be cut out. The accursed invention of tongue-clipping had begun to be introduced and brought into custom that very year. And although he said not a word, yet by his gesture and countenance, and often by an interposed smile, he made clear to the people how little he valued ceremonies of this kind. Dressed in the garb of a mocker, he cried out, "Thanks be to you, O God, for your faith! Could I have been given a greater honour than the insignia now handed to me, like those which your only Son once received before Herod?" Then, carried in a cart to the place of execution chosen for him, the Malbertine square, he exhorted the people to acknowledge Christ and to repentance. Surrounded by the trickery of the Dominicans standing about, he said, "What? Do you wish to drive me to deny Christ himself, you wicked men? Begone, impostors!" Afterwards he turned to John Morin, the president of the assembly, and asked that he might be allowed to say a few things to the people. Morin said that he wished this himself, but that it could be done only with the consent of N. Molin, the precentor and choirmaster of the basilica (for he was present). Molin said that he too wished it, but begged that he should be content, since he had already spoken so long to so many. Molin added that since Alexander had mounted the cart he had hardly ever instructed the people, and had ceased to compose himself at any time; and so it had come to the point that some even affirmed that he had been overwhelmed and crushed by a most unjust judgment. Before he was dragged to the gallows, therefore, having obtained freedom to speak, he gave a long sermon, yet a lively one and learned, adorned and polished with very wise sayings and weighty words; in this sermon the man, constant and wise, set out with such zeal and such energy the whole account of his faith, and above all of the Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, that most of those who happened to be there, and who had heard him at other times thundering, confessed that they had never seen him speak so eloquently, nor indeed so successfully. Moreover, those who committed his speech to the written record have handed down this sequence and continuity of it.

units.la: Clarissimi viri, leCtiss.[?] q. fœminæ, qui quæq; omnes in hunc locū conuenistis vt supplicium misere damnati hominis spectaretis, intelligite iuste id effectum quidem, si communes hominum offensiones consideremus; at si legem & consuetudinem hominum, inde maxime profectum esse, quòd cum de multis ad salutem hominum pertinentibus rebus, tum vero de cœna Domini nonnihil attulerim asseruerímque præter popularem hominum opinionem.
units.tr: Most distinguished men, most learned women, and all of you who have gathered in this place to watch the execution of this wretched condemned man, understand that this was done justly, if we consider the common offences of men; but if we consider the law and custom of men, it arose chiefly from the fact that I have said something, and asserted something beyond the popular opinion of men, not only about many matters that pertain to the salvation of men, but especially about the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Quam Cœnam, inquam, Dominus noster Iesus Christus instituit pridie quàm pro salute mortalibus restituenda ad mortem (& quidè crucis) proficisceretur, vt eosdem vniuersos Deo Patri reconciliatos, arrogandos in filios eius, suosque coheredes instituendos, & natalibus quasi restituendos curaret. Id quod est ipse morte propria cumulatissimè sine dubitatione consecutus. Cuius rei contemplatione & memoria sempiterna Cœnam instituit: Apostolosque docuit, hæc quotiescunque facerent, in sui commemorationem esse fasturos. Atque hoc illud est quod ipse quoque vult Paulus, Quotiescunque manducabitis panem hunc, & calicem bibetis, mortem Domini annuntiabitis donec veniat. Hoc autem dicebat Christus, panem distribuens: vultque vt accipientes illum panem, tanquam monimentum & signum mortis suæ, mortem eandem suam annuntiemus, & in eadem charitate vniuersi voluntateque viuamus.
units.tr: This Supper, I say, our Lord Jesus Christ instituted on the day before he set out to death (and indeed the death of the cross) in order to restore salvation to mortals, so that he might bring all of them back into favour with God the Father, adopt them as his sons, make them his co-heirs, and restore them, as it were, to their birthright. This he himself obtained most fully, without doubt, by his own death. With the contemplation and the everlasting remembrance of this thing he instituted the Supper, and taught the apostles that whenever they did this, they would do it in remembrance of him. And this is what Paul himself means: "As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." Christ said this while distributing the bread; and he wills that those who receive that bread, as a memorial and sign of his death, should proclaim that same death of his, and live in the same charity and will, all of us together.

units.la: Itaque probare nos ipsi debemus, antequam ad mensam illam sanctissimam accedamus: nepe fidem integram & perennem habere debemus, próq; nobis Christū mortuū esse ducere. Nàaliter, sumptum indignè tantū panē in condemnationem nostrā conuerteremus, vt inquit idem Paulus: sic enim ille, Probet seipsum homo: & sic de pane illo edat, & de calice bibat.
units.tr: Therefore we ourselves must examine ourselves before we approach that most holy table: namely, we must have a whole and abiding faith, and hold that Christ died for us. Otherwise, if we eat that bread unworthily, we would turn it into our own condemnation, as the same Paul says: "For let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup."

units.la: Quæ omnia cùm ita mihi nota putarem, vt de isdem meo iure quodam mihi viderer aliquid posse pronuntiare, sanè tenui, panem illum exhibitum nobis esse tanquam signum ac symbolum mortis Domini nostri Iesu Christi : non autem in illo veram Christi personam atque corpus existere putaui. Reliquas res, de quibus accusor, ad ipsius Dei optimi max. iudicium defero. quem unum, obsecro, precemur ut mentibus omnium Christianorum lumina sua præferat, ut & verbum eius pure perspicueque nuntietur, & Spiritu sancto suo Ecclesia illustretur. iacuit enim perdiu nobis ipse Iesus Christus. Ad extremum autem, ô viri, peto etiam atque etiam à vobis ea charitate, cuius in Christo vinculo coniuncti sumus, Deum oretis ut sicut eius Filius Iesus Christus pro me mortuus est: ita etiam ego pari pro illo constantia mori hic hodie possim. mox, Eamus, inquit. Itaque orandi munere perfunctus, sublatis in cælum oculis, medioque rogo existens, Rogemus, inquit, Christum ut nostri misereri, & ad finem usque perseuerantem animum meum suscipere dignetur. O Redemptor, miserere mei: lactū deniq; vitæ diem extremum morte confecit.
units.tr: Although I thought all these matters were so well known to me that I seemed entitled to pronounce on them, I certainly held that the bread given to us is a sign and symbol of the death of our Lord Jesus Christ, and I did not believe that the true person and body of Christ is present in it. I leave the remaining charges against me to the judgment of God himself, the best and greatest, whom alone we should beseech to hold up his light before the minds of all Christians, so that his Word may be preached purely and clearly, and the Church may be illumined by his Holy Spirit. For Jesus Christ himself has lain hidden from us for a long time. Finally, men, I ask you again and again, by that charity with which we are bound together in Christ, to pray to God that, just as his Son Jesus Christ died for me, I too may be able to die here today for him with equal constancy. Then he said, "Let us go." Having finished the duty of prayer, with his eyes raised to heaven, and standing in the midst, he said, "Let us ask Christ to deign to have mercy on us and to receive my spirit, which perseveres to the end. O Redeemer, have mercy on me." At last he brought the final day of his life to an end by death.

units.la: Porrò senatus consulto constitutum erat ut erumpente sensim igne, sicut initio posuimus, exureretur. Ac cum & reflaret ventus, & martyre ipso trochlea suspenso, disiectus ignis huc illuc euanescere potius, quam ferri sublime rapiq; videretur, lictor fune succiso, cōfossum harpagimbus, & fascibus virgultorum oppressum interemit, spectantium hominum maximo luctu & fletu, martyris longe sane magis innocentiam, quam ullam aut humanitatem, aut affectum animi leuiorem aliquem innuente. Quibus omnibus ita confectis rebus, erant, vel monachi, qui dicerent, Si hic salvus non esset, neminem salvum fore mortalem. Alii vero discedentes percutiebant pectus, dicebántque grauem illi factam iniuriam, qui totus in Dei solius commemoratione fuisset. Alii denique, legi sustinendæ suæ pertinaciter immortuum: mirúmque sibi videri, istiusmodi viros quotidie passim, dum legis illius suæ conscientiam ipsi vitæ, nedū rebus omnibus humanis anteponunt, adeò fideliter, adeò constanter ad ignē ruere voluntarium. Atque hæ quidem erant una de re singulorū hominum variæ discrepantésque sententiæ.
units.tr: The sentence of the senate was that he should be burned slowly, as the fire spread gradually, as we said at the beginning. But since the wind was blowing hard, and the martyr was hanging suspended from a pulley, the fire, scattered this way and that, seemed to vanish rather than to rise up and seize him. So the executioner cut the rope, and, having pierced him with hooks and crushed him under bundles of brushwood, killed him, to the great grief and weeping of the onlookers, who showed far more admiration for the martyr's innocence than any kindness or lighter feeling of pity. When all this was over, some monks said that if this man were not saved, no mortal would be saved. Others, leaving, beat their breasts and said that a grave wrong had been done to a man who had been wholly devoted to the remembrance of God alone. Still others declared that he had died stubbornly in defence of his law, and it seemed strange to them that men of this kind, who put the conscience of their law before their very lives and all human affairs, should so faithfully and constantly rush into the fire of their own accord, and that this happened almost every day. These were the various and conflicting opinions of individual men about one and the same matter.

units.la: Atnus publice Lutetiæ affixorum Programmatum & Inscriptorum nominatus.
units.tr: The year in which the placards and notices were publicly posted at Paris is named.

units.la: Quo tempore, concionante ferè tum primùm fidelissimo Doctore Martino Luthero, prodeuntéque sensim in lucem & aciem Euangelio, præstigiæ Papistarum detegi cœperunt, erupit impetu maximo Sathan, irrupitque diu quidem atque multum in gregem Domini nostri Iesu Christi passim, sed anno potissimùm millesimo supra quingētos triginta quatuor Lutetię Parisiorū. Vnde quoque programatū& Inscriptorum annus in Gallia est prouerbiali quasi genere dicēdi nominatus. Eorū autem qui tum cæterorum omnium amplissimè fideliss.q.vitam vouissent, aliquando tandem inuentā plānè,& in lucem hic nunc primum(vt quidē voluimus) edita historiā damus.
units.tr: At that time, when the most faithful teacher Martin Luther was first preaching, and the Gospel was gradually coming into the light and into the field of battle, the tricks of the Papists began to be uncovered. Satan broke out with the greatest violence and for a long time attacked the flock of our Lord Jesus Christ in many places, but especially in the year one thousand five hundred and thirty-four, at Paris. From this event the year of the placards and notices is named in France, in a kind of proverbial way of speaking. Now we give the history of those who at that time had vowed their lives most fully and most faithfully to the cause of all, a history at last discovered, and here now first brought into the light, as we had wished.

units.la: NNI 1534. tempus cum ad varios rerum & ancipites euentus plerisque in locis,tum Lutetiæ maximè insigne & fatale fuit. Nam cum Gerardus Russus Margaritæ Francisci Galliæ Regis sororis, Reginæ Nauarræ auspicio,& Couraldus,& Berthaudus, alii que clariss. viri quidam itademum Euangelij veritatem enuntiarent, vt tum primum illuxisse Lutetiæ verbum Domini videretur; Euangelij perduelles Sorbonistæ quum horum hominum splendorem in dicendo,& concurrentis illò populi celebritate & frequentiā animad uerterent, expugnauerunt vt illis suggestus interdiceretur,grauis simo dolore eorum qui ex huiusmodi concionibus plurimūm se consecutos esse arbitrabantur.Illi tanta iniuria Reipub. commoti Christi anæ,concionem in priuatam & domesticam docendi rationem æquali fere successu professúque conuerterunt. quod ipsum quoque per tæsi hostes iurati veritatis,rursum obtinuerunt,vt de concionibus in terdistū etiam ad domesticam Euangelij profitendi & in præccepta di gerendi consuetudinem indista graui multa pertinere putaretur. Quo nomine Gerardus ipse comprehensus, Couraldus in custodiam pontificiam traditus fuit.Porro fideles destituti concionibus, desecti doctoribus,in lustu & squalore versabantur.Vnde impetu quodam animi præcipiti commoti magis quàm vsi cogitatione nōnulli,operæ pretium cēsuerunt esse,rem ad Allobroges deferre;idque sequi potis simum, quod optimum interea factu putarent. Itaque Feretum quen dam famulum tum pharmacopolæ Francisci Regis, ad eam expeditionem deligunt,delestum expediunt:qui Neocomum profestus sub id fere tempus cum Gulielmus Farellus Euangelium populariter auspicato Geneuæ profiteri cœpisset, programata quædam in Missæ deliria,& rituum huiusmodi papisticorum ludibria charasterib° excudi curauit.Quibus inscriptionibus Lutetiam deportatis,dedustisque in deliberationem proferrine eas,an omnino comprini oporteret, Cou raldus ipse quidem minimè proferri censebat oportere. hinc enim & motum maximum populi fore;& huius totius facinoris inuidiam in odium atque caput fidelium hominum redundaturam esse. Ad extre- mum num autem placuit optimis quidem illis & studiosis hominibus, at feruidioribus, vsque rerum minus quàm illa tempora postularent eruditis, vt non modo perferrentur, sed etiam compitatim affigerentur. Erat ea programmata libellique illi stylo confecti vibrante quodam & incitato: inque potissimum detestabilem illam bestiam, Missam inquā, turbinem & funus sacrosanctæ Cœnæ Domini nostri Iesu Christi, impetu rapidissimo ferebatur. Spargūtur igitur in vulgus partim illi libelli momento Lutetiæ mense Octo. partim, etiam per compita passim, ac in ipso ostio Basilicani cubiculi affiguntur. Quod cum Franciscus Rex intellexisset, iram oculis & ore vomens, vel eos qui tenuissimam aliquam in suspicionem incidissent, nulla cuiusquam habita ratione, comprehendi iussit: cuius edictum tanta rerum omnium consecuta fuit perturbatio, vt maiorem patrum nostrorum memoria fuisse constaret nullam. Suppræfectus Comitiorum Morinus huc illuc concursans in domos atque gymnasia penetrat ac perrumpit: neque, dum nemini parcit omnino, personarum rationem habet neque locorū. In hac rerum conuersione summa cum plerique luctuosè comprehenduntur, in flammámque conjiciuntur, tũ Simon quidam aurifex, idémque Regi à sacello, ipsi Regi propter singularem eius canendi artem vocisque suauitatem vehementer sanè charus & dilectus. At eorum omnium qui illo tempore constantissimè fortissimèque pugnantes pro Domini nostri Iesu Christi dignitate decubuerunt, hi nimirum sunt:
units.tr: The year 1534 was remarkable and fateful for various and dangerous events in many places, but especially at Paris. For when Gerard Roussel, under the patronage of Margaret, sister of King Francis of France and Queen of Navarre, and Courault, and Berthaud, and other very distinguished men, began to proclaim the truth of the Gospel, so that the Word of the Lord seemed to have dawned at Paris for the first time, the Sorbonnists, enemies of the Gospel, noticing the brilliance of these men in preaching and the crowds of people flocking to them, succeeded in having the pulpits forbidden to them, to the great grief of those who thought they had gained a great deal from such sermons. Moved by such an injury to the commonwealth of Christians, they turned the sermon into private and domestic teaching, with almost equal success and with the same profession. The sworn enemies of the truth again managed to have this also forbidden, so that even the domestic profession and practice of the Gospel's precepts, apart from public sermons, was thought to carry heavy penalties. On this account Gerard himself was seized, and Courault was handed over to papal custody. Meanwhile the faithful, deprived of sermons and of teachers, lived in mourning and squalor. Hence some men, moved by a hasty impulse of mind more than by careful thought, judged it worthwhile to carry the matter to the Allobroges, and to pursue this above all, since they thought it the best course for the moment. So they chose and prepared for that errand a certain servant named Feret, then of the apothecary of King Francis, who set out for Neuchâtel. About that time William Farel had begun to preach the Gospel publicly at Geneva, and Feret had some placards against the absurdities of the Mass and the mockery of such papal rites printed in letters. When these notices had been brought to Paris, and the question was raised whether they should be put forward at all or altogether suppressed, Courault himself was clearly of the opinion that they should not be put forward. For this, he said, would stir up great unrest among the people, and the odium of this whole crime would fall back on the faithful and make them hated. In the end, however, those excellent but zealous men, too zealous for the times, who were less learned than those times required, decided not only that the placards should be circulated, but that they should be posted up at every crossroads. These placards and little books were written in a vehement and inflamed style, and were aimed especially at that detestable beast, the Mass, I mean, the whirlwind and the death of the most sacred Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, with the most rapid force. So some of these little books were scattered among the people at Paris in the month of October, and others were posted up everywhere at crossroads and even on the very door of the king's bedchamber. When Francis the King learned of this, pouring out wrath from his eyes and mouth, he ordered that anyone who had fallen under even the slightest suspicion be seized without any regard for the person. The result of his edict was such a disturbance of all things that it is established that our fathers' memory knew nothing like it. The deputy prefect Morin, running hither and thither, broke into and forced his way through houses and colleges, sparing no one at all, and having no regard for persons or places. In this upheaval many were seized in mourning, and were thrown into the flames. Among them was Simon, a goldsmith, also one of the king's chapel singers, very dear to the king himself for his singular skill in singing and the sweetness of his voice. But of all those who at that time fell fighting most constantly and bravely for the dignity of our Lord Jesus Christ, these, to be sure, are the most notable:

units.la: BARTHELOTVS MILONVS quidem in primis; qui vt erat, ita Paralyticus appellabatur, iuuenis summa membrorum omnium debilitate, exceptā lingua & brachiis, captus atque oppressus, tanto spiritus feruore & pietatis studio amoréque accensus fuit, vt nullum tempus instituendi ac monendi vnumquenque, & amplificandi gloriam Dei prætermittētem, viuum in platea Greuensi, paruo lentóque igni crudeliter vstulandum curauerunt.
units.tr: Barthélemy Milon first of all, who, because of his condition, was called the Paralytic, a young man, captured and overcome by an extreme weakness of all his limbs except the tongue and arms, was so inflamed with a fervour of spirit and zeal for piety and love that, never letting slip any opportunity of instructing and admonishing each person and of magnifying the glory of God, they cruelly ordered him to be burned alive in the Place de Grève over a small and slow fire.

units.la: IOANNES à BVRGO mercator Parisiensis, cuius domus Insigne equi nigri habebat, propter eandem causam religionis restituendæ, in eadem vrbe apud Hallas, viuus comburitur.
units.tr: John of Bourgo, a Parisian merchant, whose house had the sign of the black horse, was burned alive in the same city, at Les Halles, for the same cause of restoring religion.

units.la: NICOLAVS VALLETONVS, Quæstor ærarius apud Nannetes Brittonum, incadem causa Euangelij ac religionis deprehensus, ad crucem du Tiroir eandem poenam perpessus est, & viuus ibidem Lutetiæ crematus.
units.tr: Nicolas Valleton, treasurer of the revenue at Nantes in Brittany, was arrested for the same cause of the Gospel and of religion, suffered the same punishment at the Croix-du-Tiroir, and was likewise burned alive there at Paris.

units.la: HENRICVS CVBERONENSIS
units.tr: HENRY OF CUBERON

units.la: eandem in poenam fuit vocatus, faber cæmentarius, cui etiam lingua fuit perforata, & ad alteram genam clauo ferreo alligata.
units.tr: He was summoned to the same punishment: a mason, whose tongue was also pierced and fastened with an iron nail to his other cheek.

units.la: STEPHANI quoq; FORGEI
units.tr: STEPHEN FORGEI, ALSO

units.la: non minus etiam beata atque summa cum benevolentia & charitate laudeque Dei vsurpanda est memoria. Is natione Tornacensis erat: ac Lutetiæ agens, mercaturam que summa cum existimatione exercés, in eadem temporis invidia offensionémq; adductus, in cœmeterio S. Ioa. eadé ignis flammas perpessus morte sua testimonium Euangelij, maxima cum pietate, constantia, animiq; æquitate obsignauit.
units.tr: His memory is to be recalled no less blessedly, and with the highest goodwill, charity and praise of God. He was a native of Tournai. While living at Paris and carrying on trade with the highest esteem, he was brought into the same hatred and offence of the times. In the cemetery of St John, he suffered the same fire and flames, and by his death sealed his testimony to the Gospel with the greatest piety, constancy and equanimity of mind.

units.la: N. QVOQVILLARDVS Vesontinus.
units.tr: N. QUOQUILLARDUS OF BESANÇON

units.la: Ex Sontione in comitatu Burgundiæ fuit quidam, Quoquillardus nominatus, qui confessione piæ doctrinæ præclarè edita, primùm de gradu sacerdotali iuridicialiter erasus, deinde ad supplicium adductus mortem in ea vrbe æquo magnóque animo pertulit, atque eo testimonio Euangelii gloriæ Dei illustrauit, anno eodé M. D.XXXIIII.
units.tr: There was a certain man from Sontion in the county of Burgundy, named Quoquillardus. Having openly published a confession of pious doctrine, he was first struck from the clerical rank by legal sentence, and then led to execution. In that city he endured death with an even and great courage, and by that testimony he illustrated the glory of God in the Gospel, in the year 1534.

units.la: Atrebatenses tres pro Euangelio passi.
units.tr: Three Arras men who suffered for the Gospel.

units.la: Nni[?] eiusdem mense Aprili in vrbe Atrebatensi, capitis damnati pro eadem Euangelij doctrina & causa religionis, mortis supplicio affecti fuerunt, Nicolaus Scriba cognominatus, in quodam Arthesiæ loco natus, non procul à pago Paso in Arthesia. Item Ioan.à Pisis, ipse Atrebas, atque Stephanus Burletus, sartor vestiarius natus Beuricí viculo in diœcesi Tornacensi.
units.tr: In the same month of April, in the city of Arras, three men condemned to death for the same doctrine of the Gospel and cause of religion were put to death: Nicolas Scriba, so surnamed, born in a place in Artois not far from the village of Pas in Artois; likewise John of Pisis, himself from Arras; and Stephen Burlet, a tailor, born in the village of Beuvry in the diocese of Tournai.

units.la: MARIA BECAVDELLA
units.tr: MARIA BECAUDELLA

units.la: Aria Becaudella, cognomento Gaborita, Effaris nata in Pictonibus, ex ditione comitis Fontenani, in vrbe Rochella apud quendam patremfamilias, cui seruiebat, in pietate religionéq; Christiana fuit instituta. deinde Effaros profecta, vt ibi commoraretur cum Franciscanum quendam, verbum Dei non pure integréque annuntiantem audiuisset, certissimis Scripturæ testimonijs cum redarguit atque admonuit. Quare commotus Franciscanus, egit vt illa pluribus quam decem testibus adhibitis, eadem verba repeteret. quæ qui dem illa minimè negauit: sed in pura & sancta fidei suae ac veritatis confessione constanter perseuerauit grauissimū Dei iudicū ei denuntians. Itaq; Fontenani condemnata vt igni cremaretur, eáque sententia authoritate summae curiae Parisiensis confirmata, morte eam eximia quadam magnitudine animi potius virilis quàm muliebris pertulit.
units.tr: Maria Becaudella, surnamed Gaborita, born at Effaris in Poitou, in the lordship of the count of Fontenay, was brought up in piety and the Christian religion at La Rochelle, in the household of a certain head of a family whom she served. Then she went to Effaris to live there. When she heard a Franciscan announcing the Word of God not purely or entirely, she refuted and admonished him with the most certain testimonies of Scripture. Stirred by this, the Franciscan brought it about that she, with more than ten witnesses called in, should repeat the same words. She did not deny them, but she constantly persevered in the pure and holy confession of her faith and of the truth, warning them of the most grievous judgment of God. Therefore she was condemned at Fontenay to be burned by fire. That sentence, confirmed by the authority of the supreme court of Paris, she endured in death with a remarkable greatness of mind, more manly than womanly.

units.la: PETRVS GAVDET.
units.tr: PETER GAUDET

units.la: Petrus Gaudetus è Valligalien si pago, non longè à S. Clodoueo propè Lutetiam ortus, postquam institutum ordinémque eorum professus esset qui equites Rhodienses appellantur, Geneuam in ecclesiam Dei cum vxore sua se contulit, anno M.D.XXXIIII. Post annum circiter dimidium, quidam eius auunculus eques Rhodiensis, commendator Compesiarum, acerrimus Euangelij inimicus, quum eum Gencua dolosè ac fraudulenter euocasset, XXIII. Iunij, pridie eius dici qui S. Ioanni sacer celebratur, comprehendendum curauit per homines proditores, qui in arce Peneia partes episcopi Geneuensis, ex ea vrbe tum eiecti, tuebantur. Quum autem ea in arce quinque dies cum grauissimis tormentis & cruciatibus inclusus fuisset, semper causam Euangelij fortiter constantérque defendens, postea lento igni saepius repetito adeò crudeliter vstulatus est, vt ex igni eductus at-que in eundem reductus ac remissus fuerit. Atque in hoc quidem tam atroci ac horribili supplicij ac tormenti genere, Deum sine vlla intermissione inuocauit, ipsóque secundo die spiritum reddidit, anno M.D. XXXIIII.
units.tr: Peter Gaudet, born in the village of Valligalien, not far from St Cloud near Paris, after he had professed the rule and order of those called Knights of Rhodes, went with his wife to the church of God at Geneva in 1534. About half a year later, a certain uncle of his, a Knight of Rhodes and commander of Compesières, a most bitter enemy of the Gospel, deceitfully and fraudulently summoned him from Geneva. On 23 June, the day before the feast day consecrated to St John, he had him seized through treacherous men who held the side of the bishop of Geneva in the castle of Peney, from which that city had then been expelled. When he had been kept in that castle for five days with the most severe tortures and torments, always defending the cause of the Gospel bravely and steadfastly, he was afterwards burned so cruelly with a slow fire, often repeated, that he was drawn out of the fire, put back in, and let down again. In this kind of atrocious and horrible punishment and torment he called upon God without any pause, and on the second day he gave up his spirit, in 1534.

units.la: IOANNES CORNON.
units.tr: JOHN CORNON

units.la: Anno M.D.XXXV. mense Maio, Matiscone Euangelij nomine fuit captus, atque in carcerem inclusus Ioannes Cornonus, ex ipsa regione Matisconensi, homo colonus, agris colendis deditus, in ipsa verbi Dei doctrina valde piè institutus, ac bene exercitatus: quanuis nullas sciret literas.
