Quapropter date operam, ut vos veros Iesu Christi milites exhibeatis, neq; animo molliore, magisque ignauo sitis, quàm ii qui militant sub auspiciis terreni alicuius Imperatoris: qui quidem semel scripti, sacramentóque obstricti, nulla in re sibi parcunt, quae ad gloriam Imperatoris ipsorum pertinere videatur. Nullae sunt fossae tam profundae, aut muri tam alti, aut bombardae tam horrendae, nulla acies[?] inimicorum optimo ordine instructa & parata, quam illi non contemnant, idque ob eam causam, ut suo satisfaciant officio, quod iureiurando sacramentóque obstricti promiserunt. Vos autem diabolo & mundo renuntiastis, ascripti in numerum eorum militum, qui nomen suum Christo dederunt. Nunc ergo nihil vos impediat, quò minus strenuos ac fortes milites, seruósque fideles Regi vestro ostendatis & praestetis. Is cum Angelis suis è superiore loco vos intuetur, & libenter certamen vestrum spectat. quòd si vos non satis fortes estis, paratus est descendere, ut vobis opem ferat, quemadmodum Diuo Stephano caelis apertis adfuit. Nam quòd ipse perpessus est, cum versaretur in huiusmodi certamine ac dimicatione, eò est passus, ut vos nunc victores aduersus omnes inimicos reddat, quemadmodum is suos admonuit, In mundo afflictione habebitis: sed in me confidite. nam ego vici mundum. Et sicut ait eius Discipulus, Haec est victoria, quae mundum vincit, fides vestra. Quod si aliqua est res vobis proxima, valdeque coniuncta, quae officium vestrum impediat, abiicite eam, atque excindite, etiamsi vester oculus, manus, aut pes esset. Quibus corporis membris intelligit eos, qui non minus sunt nobis chari ac pretiosi, quam oculus, nec minus utiles, quam manus, nec minus necessarij, quam pes. Atq; hoc ita esse ipse Dux satis ostendit, cum milites suos ita admonuit, Qui diligit patrem aut matrem plusquam me, non est me dignus: & qui uxorem, aut suos liberos plusquam me diligit, non est me dignus. Denique qui nō renuntiat iis omnibus, quae habet, propter me, is me dignus non est. Atque haec quidem, fratres, maiori hominum parti gravia alienaque videntur: vobis vero, ut ego existimo, non ita, qui Christum amplexi estis passum, & tormentis summisque cruciatibus affectum & afflictum, antequam in gloriam suam ingressus sit: atque eum didicistis crucifixum, ut una cum eo, sicut vera ipsius membra crucifigamini. Vos etiam in schola eius didicistis, oportere in primis ut discipulus abneget semetipsum, & eius crucem tollat, eumque sequatur. Qui metu horum malorum offensus, retrocedet, dissimulabitque cum mundo, existimans se sine cruce ferenda posse esse Christi discipulum (nō ego ita hoc dico, sed ipse Magister) seipsum perdit. Dicit enim Dominus, Qui diligit vitā suā in hoc mundo, is in seculo venturo eam perdet: & qui perdit eam in hoc mundo, is eam conservat in vitam aeternam. Hoc autem optime cognovit D. Paulus, verus Iesu Christi Apostolus, cum fratres eum rogarent, ne Hierosolymam proficisceretur, Ego, inquit, vitam meā nō ita pretiosam & charam habeo. Is etiam ad Philippenses dicit, se omnia huius mundi ponere a tergo, atq; ad res spirituales ac caelestes extendere, ut praemiū vitae aeternae apprehendat. Atque haec quidem in re falso & calumniose accusamur, quasi authores nostri mali, qui dies nostros breviores efficiamus. Nec enim is qui iussu imperatoris aliquo profectus est, ut voluntatem eius exequatur, si incurrens in hostes, ab iis occidatur aut vulneretur, author erit mali sui, aut propriae reus mortis: sed contra, ut fidelis servus fortisque laudabitur, qui vitae suae parcere noluerit, ut voluntas Imperatoris nperatoris fui & mandatum præstaretur: ita nobis quoque evenit. Etenim ij sunt inimici Christi, qui nullo modo ferre possunt, ut honorem eius tueamur, & voluntatem cōpleamus. Itaque nos ita tractat, affligunt, vexant, nostrósque dies & annos breviores efficiunt. Et ita quidem nobiscum agunt, quoniam ad ipsorum idololatriam, superstitionem, blasphemiam, ad omnem in potu cibóque intemperantiam atq; impudicitiam, aliáque eorū unaleficia[?] & flagitia, à Rege nostro prohibita, conformare & accōmodare nos non volumus. Vehementer nos derunt, quòd testemur opera eorum esse mala, damnatáque à Deo, tam ea quæ videntur ipsis esse optima & præstantissima. Ea enim non solum sunt introducta[?] sine verbo Dei, sed maxima ex parte contra ipsum verbum Dei instituta, cū maxima Iesu Christi eiusque mortis contumelia. Vos intelligitis fratres, quæ dicam opera: & propterea eos persequūtur. Isti sunt Sancti, qui ab aliis nolunt attingi, verentes e aliorū tactu maculētur, aut polluantur. Isti sunt montes, qui simultque attacti sunt, subitum ignem, sanguinémque evomunt, in filios Dei magnis clamoribus vociferantes. Et quemadmodum supra demonstravi, nihil in nos faciunt aut dicunt, quod in fideles servos Dei, qui os præcesserunt, antea factum non fuerit. Quid ego dico in servos?
units.tr: My brothers, I think it good to share with you the joy I take in the afflictions that have befallen us, so that you too may give thanks to the Lord with me and rejoice together with me in my chains and sufferings. For these are the fruits of the teaching we have learned, if indeed we have learned and come to know Jesus Christ crucified. Let none of us therefore fail or lose heart. Let him persevere in the course he has begun for a little while longer, and he who is to come will come and will not delay: "But my just one shall live by faith; but if he draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him," says the Lord. We must therefore take care on this point, for you know that those will be saved who persevere to the end, and that even those who strive in a race or a contest receive no crown unless they have competed lawfully. Therefore take pains to show yourselves true soldiers of Jesus Christ, and do not be of a softer and more cowardly spirit than those who serve under some earthly commander. These men, once enlisted and bound by oath, spare themselves in nothing that seems to pertain to the glory of their commander. No ditches are so deep, no walls so high, no cannons so terrible, no enemy battle line drawn up in the best order and ready, that they do not despise them, and this for the sake of discharging the duty they have promised under oath and sacrament. You, however, have renounced the devil and the world, and have been enrolled among those soldiers who have given their name to Christ. Therefore let nothing now hinder you from showing and proving yourselves vigorous and brave soldiers and faithful servants to your King. He looks upon your struggle from a higher place, with his Angels, and watches your fight gladly. But if you are not strong enough, he is ready to come down and bring you help, as he stood by holy Stephen with the heavens opened. For what he himself suffered while he was engaged in such a struggle and battle, he suffered so that he might now make you victors over all your enemies, just as he admonished his own: "In the world you will have affliction, but trust in me, for I have overcome the world." And as his disciple says: "This is the victory that overcomes the world, your faith." But if there is any thing close to you and very closely joined to you that hinders your duty, cast it away and cut it off, even if it were your eye, hand, or foot. By these members of the body he means those who are no less dear and precious to us than the eye, no less useful than the hand, and no less necessary than the foot. That the Leader himself shows this to be so is clear from how he admonished his soldiers: "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves wife or children more than me is not worthy of me. Finally, he who does not renounce all that he has for my sake is not worthy of me." Now these things, brothers, seem grievous and strange to most people, but to you, as I judge, it is not so, since you have embraced Christ, who suffered, was afflicted with torments and the most severe cruelties before he entered into his glory, and whom you have learned as crucified, so that together with him you may be crucified as his true members. You have also learned in his school that the disciple must first deny himself, take up his cross, and follow him. The one who, offended by fear of these evils, draws back and dissembles with the world, thinking he can be Christ's disciple without bearing the cross (I do not say this, but the Master himself), loses himself. For the Lord says: "He who loves his life in this world will lose it in the world to come, and he who loses it in this world will keep it unto eternal life." Paul, the true Apostle of Jesus Christ, understood this very well, when the brothers begged him not to go up to Jerusalem: "I do not hold my life so precious and dear," he said. He also says to the Philippians that he puts all the things of this world behind him and stretches out to spiritual and heavenly things, so that he may lay hold of the reward of eternal life. Yet in this matter we are falsely and calumniously accused, as if we were the authors of evil, who shorten their days. For he who has set out at an emperor's command to carry out his will, if he runs into enemies and is killed or wounded by them, will not be the author of his own harm or guilty of his own death, but on the contrary will be praised as a faithful and brave servant, if he has not spared his life so that the will and command of his Emperor might be carried out. So it has happened to us as well. For those are the enemies of Christ who cannot in any way bear that we should uphold his honour and fulfil his will. Thus they treat us, afflict and harass us, and shorten our days and years. And they deal with us in this way because we do not want to conform and adapt ourselves to their idolatry, superstition, blasphemy, to every intemperance in drink and food and impurity, and their other wicked and shameful deeds, which are forbidden by our King. They rage vehemently against us because we testify that their works are evil and condemned by God, even those which seem to them the best and most excellent. For these have been introduced not only without the Word of God, but for the most part were instituted directly against the Word of God itself, to the greatest insult to Jesus Christ and his death. You understand, brothers, what works I mean, and therefore they persecute us. They are the saints who will not be touched by others, fearing to be stained or polluted by the touch of others. They are the mountains which, as soon as they are touched, belch forth sudden fire and blood, shouting with great clamours against the sons of God. And as I showed above, they do nothing to us or say anything against us that was not done before against the faithful servants of God who went before us. Why do I say servants?

units.la: nō vero in ipsum Magistrum & Dominum gloriæ, Dei Filium, quē ini potorem & edacem, Samaritanum, incantatorem, daemoniacum, seductorem vocauerunt. quem quidem sacerdotes in manus Romanorum tradiderunt, à quibus colaphis cæsus, cōsputus, irrisus, à [?]mo capite usque ad pedes flagellatus fuit, corona spinea cerebrum eius perfodiente redimitus: postremò cōdēnatus mortis, omnium quæ tu[?]ssent, turpissimæ atque teterrimæ: ea autem erat mors crucis detestanda. Atque ut eum maiore dedecore ignominiaque afficerent [?]edium inter duos latrones, quasi magistrum eorum ducémq; suspenderunt. Atque his quidem tantis contumeliis, & iniurijs eum affecerunt, qui eorum cæcis lumen oculorum restituerat, surdisque sensum audiendi, qui leprosos eorum plane mundauerat, mortuos ad vitam revocauerat:denique omnia beneficiorum genera in ipsos contulerat. Ut tamen pro refereda his tam præclaris operib° ac beneficijs gratia, [?]idemus quàm malè illū tractauerint, quánq; gratiā ei reddiderint: qui quidem ut erat iustus coram hominibus, ita etiam coram ipso Deo fuit. Is tamen, qui lignum fuit viride, haec omnia tam acerba indignaq; pertulit: nos vero qui lignum aridum sumus, ad exardescendum & coflagrandū apti atque opportuni, quid expectare possumus aut debemus? An arbitramur nos in paradisum ituros sine ulla incomodorum perpessione? Ne fallamus nosipsos, Per multas afflictiones nobis eò veniendum est. Nos scimus duas tantummodo vias esse, neque aliam esse tertiam. Altera earum est arcta & angusta, quae difficiles & asperos aditus habet: sed in eius exitu vita aeterna reperitur. Altera est lata atque spatiosa, quae quidem commoda amoenaque videtur, nulla habens incommoda & pericula: sed in exitu ac fine eius sunt dolores, nam ad damnationem ducit aeternam. Prioris viae haec sunt incommoda & mala: paupertas, afflictio, infamia, bonorum huius mundi indigentia ac inopia, pessime tractari ab unoquoque, in exilium mitti, in carcerem coniici, igne cremari, in aquam submergi, truncari capite, bestiis immanibus obici, aliaque multa & grauia tormenta atque opprobria perpeti. Sed omnes huiusmodi calamitates, non sunt condignae ea gloria, quae filijs Dei est revelanda. Sed quemadmodum testatur Apostolus, II. Corinthior. IIII. cap. ingens pondus admirabilis gloriae nobis pariunt, cum earum acerbitas in hac vita sit breuis & momentanea. Propter autem has propositas molestias & aerumnas, perpauci istam viam ingrediuntur, in eaque insistunt: sed omnes prope eam [?]aucersantur, maluntque illam amplam viam ingredi, quam exiguam istam semitam. Itaque nos in hac, Fratres, insistemus, eamque tenebimus, quàtumuis ardua esse videatur, cum praesertim optimum certissimumque instituti itineris ducem habeamus Iesum Christum, qui omnia huius itineris incommoda, molestias, & pericula peruasit: quo duce nostro ac directore in eiusmodi periculis perire nullo modo possumus. Nā quēadmodum dicit Apostolus, unus ex iis qui ab eo diriguntur, ego plane mihi habeo persuasum, quod nec Angeli, nec principatus, nec potestates, nec vita, nec mors, nec altitudo ulla aut profunditas, neque praesentia, neque futura, impedient nos, quo minus hac via transeamus, atque eò, quò vocati sumus, cōtendamus. Eritne ulla afflictio, quae nostrum animum debilitet? an angustia, fames, nuditas, aut etiam gladius? Nos [?]os vero nihil horum malorum formidabimus, cũ huiusmodi directorem habeamus, cuius à dilectione atque admirabili amore, nunquã avelli aut abstrahi poterimus. Nostræ quidem carni ac sensui aliquâdo videtur, nos ab eo destitutos esse & desertos: sed non ita est. Dicit enim, Ego non te desero nec derelinquo: & alio loco, Ego tecum sum in afflictione: invoca me & ego exaudiam te, atque eripiam. An vero, fratres, existimatis, nisi Dominus nobiscum esset, nos posse ea ferre, vel ferri ac tolerari à nobis vult? non certè. Nam inimici nostri sunt multò fortiores ac potentiores, quàm nos simus: quorum unus eorum [?]itas virium habet, ut possit nos in perpetuum perdere. Summa est potesta diaboli, qui princeps est & caput nostrorum inimicorum, cuius potentiam & malitiam satis sunt experti primi parentes nostri, cũ primo eius impetu deiecti corruerunt. Hic est, fratres mei, qui ceteros impellit & contra nos incitat. Toto igitur studio animóque enitatur, ut huic inimico resistamus, altera manu clypeum fidei tenentes, altera verò verbi Dei gladium. Quòd si indignamur aut irascimur, nostram in istum indignatione atque iram conferamus. Mundus quidè est fortis & robustus, ut & caro nostra. Sed si primus hostis fuerit nobis superatus, cæteri non multum nobis nocere poterunt. Nam etsi caro sit nobis permolesta, aduersaria atque inimica, eam tamen spiritus, diaboli victor, paulatim subiget, & in suam potestatem rediget. Hæc sunt, fratres charissimi, quæ nos in nostris afflictionibus oportet cogitare ac facere. Si quispiam alius expers harum afflictionum in [?]ubus vos versamini, de huiusmodi rebus scriberet, possetis merito [?]licere, eũ facilè & sine ulla sua molestia de his loqui, eúmque, qui domi [?]uæ quietus ageret, posse hæc facilè laudare: sed si ista ei toleranda essent, aliter loquuturum. De me verò, fratres, credo vos nihil tale dicturos aut cogitaturos, qui unà vobiscum harum afflictionum sunt particeps, eandem bibens potionem, quæ nobis à Domino exhibetur. Ac quod ad me quidem attinet, quotidie atque in dies singulos nihil aliud expecto, quàm grauem & atrocem mortem. Quid dixi mortem atrocem? falsus sum, cùm eam ita nominaui. cognosco enim eã nihil aliud esse, quàm optimam Patris mei voluntatem, qui cà vult vitam corporalè finire, atque cum spirituali & immortali commutare: cuius quidem beneficij nomine ac magnitudine, magnopere ei deuinctus sum & obligatus. Vos autem orate omnes, pro mea, inquam, salute orate Dominum, ut mihi eam constantiam praestet, qua in confessione sanctissimi verbi eius permaneam, quoad me in quietum locum, id est, sanctum suum regnum recolligat & recipiat. Ego pro meo officio, idem salutis vestrae causa sum facturus. Gratia Domini nostri, sit cum omnibus vobis, Amen.
units.tr: But not against the Master and Lord of glory himself, the Son of God, whom they called a glutton and drunkard, a Samaritan, a sorcerer, a demoniac, and a seducer. The priests handed him over into the hands of the Romans, by whom he was struck with blows, spat upon, mocked, and scourged from head to foot, and crowned with a crown of thorns that pierced his brain. Finally he was condemned to death, the most shameful and most hideous of all kinds of death, namely the detestable death of the cross. And to load him with still greater dishonour and disgrace, they hanged him in the middle between two robbers, as if he were their master and leader. With such great insults and injuries they treated him, who had restored sight to their blind, hearing and understanding to their deaf, who had thoroughly cleansed their lepers and raised their dead to life, in short, who had conferred every kind of benefit upon them. Yet consider how badly they treated him, and how they repaid him for these so excellent works and benefits. He, indeed, was just before men, and so also before God himself. Yet he, who was a green tree, endured all these things, so bitter and undeserved. But we, who are dry wood, fit and ready to flare up and burn, what can we expect or ought we to expect? Do we think we shall enter paradise without suffering any hardship? Let us not deceive ourselves: through many afflictions we must come there. We know there are only two ways, and no third. One of them is narrow and strait, with difficult and rough approaches, but at its end eternal life is found. The other is broad and spacious, which seems pleasant and agreeable, with no discomforts or dangers; but at its exit and end are sorrows, for it leads to eternal damnation. These are the discomforts and evils of the former way: poverty, affliction, infamy, lack and want of the goods of this world, being treated very badly by everyone, being sent into exile, thrown into prison, burned with fire, drowned in water, beheaded, exposed to savage beasts, and enduring many other grievous torments and reproaches. But all such calamities are not worthy of the glory which is to be revealed to the sons of God. As the Apostle testifies in 2 Corinthians 4, they produce for us an exceeding and eternal weight of admirable glory, since their bitterness in this life is brief and momentary. Because of these troubles and hardships set before us, very few enter upon that way and persist in it; nearly all shun it and would rather enter that broad way than this narrow path. Therefore we, brethren, will keep to this way and hold to it, however steep it may seem, especially since we have as the best and most certain leader of our chosen journey Jesus Christ, who has borne all the discomforts, troubles, and dangers of this journey. Under his leadership and direction we can in no way perish in such dangers. For as the Apostle says, one of those who are directed by him: I am fully persuaded that neither angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor life, nor death, nor any height or depth, nor things present, nor things to come, will prevent us from passing along this way and striving toward where we are called. Will there be any affliction that weakens our spirit? Or distress, hunger, nakedness, or even the sword? We however will fear none of these evils, since we have such a director, from whose love and admirable affection we can never be torn away or dragged off. To our flesh and senses it sometimes seems that we are forsaken and deserted by him, but it is not so. For he says, I will not leave you nor forsake you; and in another place, I am with you in affliction: call upon me and I will hear you and rescue you. But do you think, brethren, that we could bear these things, or that he wills them to be borne by us, unless the Lord were with us? Certainly not. For our enemies are much stronger and more powerful than we are; one of them has such a store of strength that he could destroy us forever. The power of the devil is supreme; he is the prince and head of our enemies, whose power and malice our first parents have sufficiently experienced, when at his first assault they were cast down and fell. This is he, my brethren, who drives on the others and stirs them up against us. Let us therefore strive with all our zeal and mind to resist this enemy, holding the shield of faith in one hand and the sword of the Word of God in the other. But if we are indignant or angry, let us direct that indignation and anger against him. The world is indeed strong and robust, as is our flesh. But if the first enemy has been overcome, the others will not be able to harm us much. For although the flesh is very troublesome to us, adversarial and hostile, the spirit, the conqueror of the devil, will gradually subdue it and bring it under its power. These are the things, dearest brethren, which we ought to think upon and do in our afflictions. If someone free from these afflictions, who lives among you, were to write about such matters, you might rightly allow that he speaks of them easily and without any trouble to himself, and that one who lives quietly at home can easily praise them; but if these things were to be endured by him, he would speak otherwise. As for me, brethren, I believe that you, who share these afflictions with me and drink the same cup which is offered to us by the Lord, will say and think nothing of the kind. As for me, day by day and from one day to the next, I expect nothing but a grievous and cruel death. What did I say, a cruel death? I was wrong to call it so. For I know it is nothing other than the best will of my Father, who wills to end this bodily life and exchange it for a spiritual and immortal one; for this benefit, in its name and greatness, I am greatly bound and obliged to him. But do you all pray for me, I say, pray to the Lord for my salvation, that he may grant me that constancy by which I may remain in the confession of his most holy Word, until he gathers me in and receives me into a quiet place, that is, his holy kingdom. For my part, I shall do the same for the sake of your salvation. The grace of our Lord be with you all. Amen.

units.la: Alia eiusdem epistola, ad vxorem scripta.
units.tr: Another letter of the same man, written to his wife.

units.la: IEsus Christus tibi salutem impertiat. Mea charissima soror, scias me in Domino nostro maximopere laetatum, cum ex iis literis, quas optimus pater tuus simul & me, tuo nomine ad me scripsit, intellexi te in Deo laetari & gaudere, non in captiuitate, quam certo scio tibi grauem esse: sed quod habuisti maritum a Deo tibi datum & electu, ut pro nomine ipsius, Euangelioque filij eius Iesu Christi pateretur. Itaque te rogo, ut maiorem adhuc in eo laetitiam capias: ampliorémque, quam hactenus fecisti, huius beneficij & honoris laudem tribuas. Nam nunc quidem pro sua gratia vult in me effici ac praestari, quod tu scis a me diu saepeque desideratum atque expetitum, ut pro Euangelio ipsius, ad Ecclesiae aedificationem ac salutem electorum morerer. Id quod faciet his diebus, me malis liberans omnibus, ut in regnum suum recipiat. Ac propter meam quidem mortem ne despondeas animum, atque ut desolatam ac destitutam te affliges: sed in ipso Domino potius vigorem animi recolligas: persuasa plane de eius providentia, amore, curaque paterna, quam post meum ex hac vita discessum, de te ancilla sua suscipiet. Itaque ostende te in eo unam[?] spem omnem ac fiduciam tuam locauisse.Genus autem mortis, ut ego arbitror, est id, quo ante me defuncti sunt ij, qui Christo eiusque doctrinae constans ac fidele testimonium dederunt, id est, ut viuus igni absque vlla misericordia comburar: ac tandiu quidem ignis ardere debet, quoad omnia redigantur in cinerem, qui deinde in profluentem conijciendus est. Neque vero hoc ad te scribo, quod hanc supplicij acerbitate magnopere pertimescam & exhorresco. Nam quemadmodum scio eam diem ad mortem corporis mihi praestitutam esse, ita etiam certo scio, quod mihi magnum mortis contemptum adfert, eandem diem pertinere[?] ad vitam spiritus,qui cum Christo,sponso suo sine corporis dissolutione plenè regnare non potest. Quandiu enim in hoc versamur corpore,à Domino longè absumus & peregrinamur. Lætare igitur, charissima soror,in Domino, atque omni tempore viduitatis tuæ in co‑ spera, & sanctissimis precibus aliisque piis operibus dedita,Deum integrè & caste colas,sicut officium est viduæ, quæ Domino modis omnibus placere vult.Caue vero in primis, ne ex illarum sis numero viduarum,quas Paulus ad Timotheum discipulum suum scribens,dicit esse otiosas & vagas,sursum ac deorsum per domos alienas cursitantes:neque otiosas modò, verumetiam nugatorias ac ineptas,loquentes ea quæ non oportet.Cùm autem tempus venerit,Dominus prospiciet ac iunget tibi maritum alium,qui tui curâ habebit,cui tu obedies, quem reuereberis,cóque honore afficies,quem viro mulier modesta ac pia debet,quod ego ,te , charissima soror,facturam spero in Domino & confido. Atque hæc quidem ad te volui scribere , quemadmodum officium est eius,qui debet te instituere atque docere.Quòd si coràm tecum loqui nô possum,per literas tantùm hoc quidem tempore, quo vocor à Domino , meum tibi officium hac in parte præstare debeo.Tu habes patrem tuum,apud quem scripsisti mihi te nunc esse ac viuere. sine eius consilio nihil suscipias & agas,sed eo in omnibus negotijs tuis vtere . caue eum vlla in re offendas nec matrem tuam. Tu fratrem tuum reuereberis,sororésq; tuas,vt poteris,in Domino instituès . Hæc autem moneo in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi.Si qui ex fratribus meis ad te veniat,te rogo,propter me eos omni cum suauitate excipias , atq; ita tuum erga me amorem ostendas.Reliquum est vt Marguarita sororem nostram tibi commendem,cui has dedi literas, quas tibi redderet. Ea mihi declarauit constituisse se istuc ad vos recipere , reliquúmque vitæ suæ tempus, Deo piè colendo atque honorando dedicare. Tu ei quantum poteris, aderis,eámque toti ecclesiæ Iesu Christi commendabis. Mihi quidem perdigna videtur esse, quam tu & omnes fideles subleuent & adiuuent.Nam ea multorum afflictiones studio & officio leuauit suo , in primis verò meas , in quibus sæpe ad me venit , & facultatibus suis me adiuuit ac recreauit.Domin°misericordiâ ei impertiat. Saluta ecclesiam meo nomine,præcipuè verò tuos parentes, atque meos.Gratia Domini nostri sit cum tuo spiritu, Amen. Tornaci, XVII. Februar. M.D.XLV. Existimabam heri me vltimo martyrio defuncturum, ego hora semper expecto.
units.tr: Jesus Christ grant you salvation. My dearest sister, know that I have rejoiced greatly in our Lord, since I learned from the letter your excellent father wrote to me in your name that you rejoice and take delight in God, not in your captivity, which I know full well is a heavy burden for you, but because you have a husband given to you by God and chosen for you, to suffer for his name and for the Gospel of his Son Jesus Christ. So I ask you to take still greater joy in this and to give more praise than you have so far for this blessing and honour. For now, by his grace, he wishes to bring about and grant in me what you know I have long and often desired and sought, namely that I should die for his Gospel, for the building up of the Church and the salvation of the elect. He will do this in these days, freeing me from all evils so that he may receive me into his kingdom. Do not lose heart at my death, nor grieve as one left desolate and forsaken; rather, gather your spirit's strength in the Lord himself, being fully persuaded of his providence, love and fatherly care, which he will extend to you, his handmaid, after I have departed from this life. So show that you have placed all your hope and trust in him. The kind of death, as I think, is that by which those have died before me who gave a steadfast and faithful witness to Christ and his doctrine: that is, I shall be burned alive in the fire without any mercy, and the fire must burn so long until everything is reduced to ashes, which then must be cast into the running stream. I write this to you not because I dread and shudder at the bitterness of this punishment. For just as I know that the day of my bodily death has been appointed for me, so too I know for certain that this same day brings me to the life of the spirit, which cannot fully reign with Christ, its bridegroom, without the dissolution of the body. For as long as we dwell in this body, we are far away from the Lord and live as pilgrims. So rejoice, dearest sister, in the Lord, and in all the time of your widowhood, devote yourself to hope and to most holy prayers and other pious works, and worship God wholeheartedly and chastely, as is the duty of a widow who wishes to please the Lord in every way. But above all take care not to be among those widows whom Paul, writing to his disciple Timothy, says are idle and wandering, running up and down from house to house, and not only idle but also gossiping and foolish, speaking things that they ought not. When the time comes, the Lord will provide and join you to another husband, who will care for you, whom you will obey and revere, and whom you will honour with that respect which a modest and pious wife owes her husband, as I hope and trust in the Lord that you, dearest sister, will do. And these things I have wished to write to you, as is the duty of one who ought to instruct and teach you. But if I cannot speak with you face to face, and at this time, when I am called by the Lord, I must perform my duty to you in this part by letter alone. You have your father, with whom you wrote to me that you are now staying and living. Undertake and do nothing without his counsel, but use his advice in all your affairs. Take care not to offend him in any matter, nor your mother. You will show reverence to your brother, and, as you are able, instruct your sisters in the Lord. I give this admonition in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. If any of my brothers come to you, I ask you to receive them with all kindness for my sake, and so show your love for me. It remains for me to commend to you our sister Margaret, to whom I have given this letter to deliver to you. She has told me that she has decided to come to you there, and to dedicate the rest of her life to devoutly honouring and worshipping God. Help her as much as you can and commend her to the whole Church of Jesus Christ. She seems to me most worthy that you and all the faithful should relieve and assist her. For she has eased the afflictions of many by her zeal and service, and above all mine, when she often came to me and helped and refreshed me with her resources. May the Lord grant her his mercy. Greet the Church in my name, and especially your parents and mine. The grace of our Lord be with your spirit, Amen. Tournai, 17 February 1545. I thought yesterday that I would die by my final martyrdom; I always await the hour.

units.la: Tuus fidelis maritus PETRVS BRVLIVS.
units.tr: Your faithful husband, PETER BRULIUS.

units.la: Hæc ferme sunt monimenta quæ in carcere à Brulio scripta extare voluit Dominus, ad nostram totiusque Ecclesiæ suæ consolationem. Brulius tandem post quatuor fere mensium detentionem sententia à commissarijs Imperatoris (qui tum erat Bruxellis) lata, condemnatus fuit vt vivus igne cremaretur in amplissimo illo theatro quod apud magnum forum extructum erat, in quo paulò ante exustus fuerat Miocius: & Mariona viua defossa, vt mox dicetur. Cùm verò ad supplicium duceretur, pauca quædam ad Tornacensem populum verba fecit, omnia à Domino prospera illis exoptàs: maximè verò incrementa fidei Christianæ abiectis hominum impijs traditionibus & commentis. Multi aderant monachi & sacerdotes qui non desierunt clamoribus obstrepere etiam Brulio precanti Deum, dum flamma eum in sublime eductum corriperet. Quam quidem pœnam summa cum animi constantia & magnitudine justinuit die lunæ XVII.Februa.qui Papistis sextus tum erat à festo cinerum, quos e culina sumptos initio quadragesimæ fronti illinunt. Acta sunt hæc anno à natali Christi supto M D.XLV.
units.tr: These are nearly all the records that the Lord wished to be written by Brulius in prison, for our consolation and that of his whole Church. Brulius at last, after nearly four months' detention, was condemned by sentence passed by the commissioners of the Emperor (who was then at Brussels), to be burned alive in that large theatre which had been built in the great marketplace, where Miocius had been burned a little before, and Mariona was buried alive, as will be told shortly. When he was being led to punishment, he spoke a few words to the people of Tournai, wishing them every blessing from the Lord, and above all the growth of the Christian faith, with the false traditions and inventions of men cast aside. Many monks and priests were present, who did not cease to drown out with their shouts even Brulius as he prayed to God, while the flames seized him and lifted him aloft. He endured this punishment with great firmness and courage on Monday, 17 February, which by the Papists' reckoning was the sixth day after Ash Wednesday, when they smear their foreheads with ashes taken from the kitchen at the beginning of Lent. These things were done in the year from the birth of Christ 1545.

units.la: PETRVS Cognomine MIOCE,
units.tr: PETER, surnamed MIOCE,

units.la: Tornaci exustus paulò ante Petri Brulii martyrium.
units.tr: Burnt at Tournai shortly before the martyrdom of Peter Brulius.

units.la: ON immerito Spiritus Domini per os prophetæ Isaiæ exclamat, Admodum pulchros esse pedes promulgantis pacem, annū ciantis bona, qui prædicat salutem: ac dicit Sioni, Deus tuus regnat. Videmus enim in ijs locis ad quæ missi sunt Euangelij præcones, fructus quoque cultura dignos extare, & quotidie eorum prædicatione uberiores dari. Sanè quidem aduentus Petri Brulij, de quo modo egimus, ad inferioris Germaniæ urbes, quibus nunc rex Hispanus imperat mirum dictu quantum profuerit, apud eos potissimum qui iam ad recipiendum cœlestis doctrinæ semen excultos[?] habebant animos. At quato maior horum erat numerus, tanto etiam grauior sequuta est in ijsdem regionibus persecutio, post quam in vincula coniectus esset Brulius. quæ quidem vt semper fuit index, & veluti lapis Lydus, quo idcles[?] ab hypocritis facilè internosci possent: sic etiam ea persecutio veros verbi Diuini auditores discreuit ab ijs qui nescio qua leuitate, ut nouarum rerum, vt ipsi censent, auiditate, Euangelij doctrinam ad tempus arripuerat. Inter eos itaque qui tunc captiui tenebatur, erat quidam Petrus, cognomine notior, Miocius scilicet, qui texendo assimi latu sericum in ea vrbe sibi victu parabat. Hic sanè antequam ad veritatis cognitionem pertractus esset, vita omnibus peccatis ac vitiis delibutam degebat, sed postquam Euangelij luce à Deo donatus suit, ita protinus immutatus est, ut vitae integritate ac zelo Spiritus reliquos ea in vrbe superaret: quod quidem cum in carcere, tum verò etiam in morte, quam obijt crudelissimam, satis demonstrauit. Prima coitione ab aduersarijs rogatus, fuissetne vnus auditorum Germanici illius concionatoris (sic enim vulgò Tornaci Petrum Brulium, qui tum captiuus detinebatur, appellabant) liberè respondit, Vnum se fuisse, magnóque in doctrina ab eo annunciata progressus fecisse. Quid, inquiunt aduersarij, vísne eam tueri? Volo, inquit, quoniam consentit cum veteri ac nouo Testamento. Post primam hanc percontationem, protinus demissus est in profundissimam fossam magnae turris castri Tornacensis, quod undiq; aquis cingitur. Locus in quo inclusus fuit, refertus erat bufonibus atque aliis impuris bestijs, propter profunditatem atq; vliginē fossae, nec in eam alij demittuntur nisi qui breui morte multandi censentur. Magistratus autem vt metum incuteret Miocio, cōstantiámque quam in eo singularem perspiciebat, labefactaret, mandauit vt illic detineretur quoúsq; demissus loqueritur, aut palinodiam caneret. proinde in hac fossa mansit à mense Nouembri donec mortis aduersus eum lata est sententia. Interea loci senatus, assumptis secum monachis, saepius cum examinarunt, hac tantum ratione vt illum à recta via atque fide deducerent. venit etiam Franciscanus, cuius ante mentionem fecimus, doctor Hasardus, cum alijs suae nequitiae fautoribus, vt contra eum disputarent: sed nulla res cum mente solida concussit. quinimo, quodā die ab istis valde lacessitus: Miror, inquit, domini mei, vos nunc adeo mihi infensos esse, vt etiam ad necem poscatis: nemo tamen vestrum mihi adhuc improbo & vitā inhonestā palam agenti, vel verbum quidem faciebat. Quo audito, qui aderant taciti alii alios intuebantur. Hasardus autem omnium impudentissimus, ei dixit, Anno videris tibi nunc esse magis impius q[?] dudum? Tuo quidem iudicio, inquit Miocius. Sed magistratui qui adest, loquor, non tibi Cucullate, ne erres: tacuisse tu profecto debueras ut honori tuo consuleres, aliis vero loquendi vices dedisse. Quo verbo impudens illud monachi os facile obturavit. Ad haec ipse Senatus, ut certam iudicij formam pertractaret, interrogavit eum de pluribus articulis, ac maxime de Missa & Sacramentis, praecipiens ei ut compendiaria cognitione responderet. Miocius autem gaudens se de fide sua interrogari, orsus est edere confessionem, singulos eius articulos certis Scripturae testimonijs probans atque confirmans. Adversarij vero lippientibus oculis non ferentes lumen veritatis: Non, inquiunt, habemus opus tuis concionibus: sed fatedo aut inficiando responde: Domine mei, inquit ille, non hic de homicidio aut furto est quaestio: verum in hoc totius causae versatur cardo, ut sciamus vestrane an mea melior sit sententia: quae res nec summatim nec breviter demonstrari potest. Ac quum iam iterū coepisset loqui, semper ab iis interruptus est sermo. Quibus ille tum dixit, Si me loquentem audire non vultis, remittite quaeso, in eam carceris foveam in qua bufones habeo sodales, qui mihi nec clamore nec fremitu quicquam impedimento sunt, si quando aut Psalmis Deum laudo aut precibus eius opem imploro: Vos autem creaturae rationis capaces cum sitis, formatae ad imaginem Dei, non potestis ferre ullam de ipsius Verbo mentionem coram vobis haberi. putatisne me fabulas incepturae, aut nugas agere, ut vestri Monachi solent? erratis sane, si id creditis. pura enim Dei veritate annuncio. Haec quidem hominis constantia auditorum animos non mediocriter commovit, ac varie quidem affecit: etenim quibusdam consolationem, plerisq; vero summam offensionem, ad stridorem usque dentium, attulit.
units.tr: RIGHTLY does the Spirit of the Lord cry out through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah, "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good tidings, who publishes peace, who announces good things, who proclaims salvation, and says to Zion, Your God reigns." For we see that in the places to which the heralds of the Gospel are sent, fruit worthy of cultivation also appears, and daily yields more abundantly through their preaching. Certainly the arrival of Peter Brulius, of whom we have just spoken, in the cities of Lower Germany, which are now ruled by the King of Spain, has been wonderfully helpful, especially among those whose minds were already prepared to receive the seed of heavenly doctrine. But the greater their number, the more severe was the persecution that followed in the same regions after Brulius was thrown into chains. This persecution, as it has always been, is a sign and, like the touchstone of Lydia, by which the genuine can easily be distinguished from hypocrites. So this persecution separated the true hearers of God's Word from those who, with I know not what fickleness and eagerness for novelties, as they themselves think, had for a time embraced the doctrine of the Gospel. Among those then held captive was a certain Peter, better known by his surname, Miocius, who earned his living by weaving silk in that city. Indeed, before he was brought to the knowledge of the truth, he lived a life steeped in every sin and vice; but after God gave him the light of the Gospel, he was so immediately changed that in integrity of life and zeal of the Spirit he surpassed the rest in that city. He showed this plainly both in prison and in his death, which was most cruel. At the first questioning, the adversaries asked him whether he had been one of the hearers of that German preacher (for so they commonly called Peter Brulius, who was then held captive at Tournai). He answered freely that he had been one, and had made great progress in the doctrine announced by him. "What," said the adversaries, "do you wish to defend it?" "I do," he said, "since it agrees with the Old and New Testament." After this first questioning, he was at once lowered into the deepest pit of the great tower of the castle of Tournai, which is surrounded on all sides by water. The place where he was shut up was full of toads and other foul beasts; because of the depth and foulness of the pit, no one is lowered into it except those judged to be punished with a quick death. The magistrate, however, wishing to strike fear into Miocius and to weaken the constancy which he saw in him in a singular degree, ordered that he be kept there until he should speak out or sing a recantation. So he remained in this pit from November until the sentence of death was passed against him. Meanwhile the council, taking monks along with them, examined him many times, with the sole aim of leading him away from the right way and from the faith. The Franciscan mentioned earlier, Doctor Hasardus, came too, with others who favoured his wickedness, to dispute against him; but nothing shook his solid mind. Indeed, one day, when they had provoked him sharply, he said, "I marvel, my lords, that you are now so hostile to me that you even ask for my death; yet none of you said a word to me when I openly lived a wicked and dishonest life." On hearing this, those present looked silently at one another. But Hasardus, the most shameless of all, said to him, "Do you now think yourself more impious than before?" "In your judgment, perhaps," said Miocius. "But I am speaking to the magistrate who is present, not to you, cowled one, lest you go astray. You should certainly have kept silent to consult your own honour, and given others the chance to speak." With these words he easily stopped that shameless monk's mouth. Then the council itself, in order to proceed with a definite form of judgment, questioned him on several articles, above all on the Mass and the sacraments, ordering him to answer briefly. Miocius, rejoicing that he was being asked about his faith, began to set out a confession, proving and confirming each of its articles with certain testimonies of Scripture. But the adversaries, with bleary eyes that could not bear the light of truth, said, "We have no need of your sermons; answer with a yes or a no." "My lords," he replied, "this is not a question of murder or theft. Rather, the hinge of the whole case turns on whether your opinion or mine is the better, and this cannot be shown in summary or in brief." When he began to speak again, they always interrupted him. Then he said to them, "If you do not wish to hear me speak, please send me back into that pit of the prison, where I have the toads as my companions. They are no hindrance to me, with their croaking or hissing, when I praise God with psalms or implore his help with prayers. But you, though you are creatures capable of reason, formed in the image of God, cannot bear that any mention of his Word be made before you. Do you think I am about to tell fables or talk nonsense, as your monks usually do? You are certainly wrong if you believe that, for I announce the pure truth of God." This constancy of the man moved the minds of his hearers not a little, and affected them in different ways: for it brought consolation to some, but great offence, even to the gnashing of teeth, to most.

units.la: Eodem tempore in vinculis ibidem erat quidam nominatus Bergibanus, qui eximia à Deo dona receperat, & tantos in Scripturae intelligentia progressus fecerat, ut ante Petri Brulij in eam urbem adventum, subinde in fidelium conventibus interpretem ageret. Quàmprimum Brulius comprehensus fuit, quaerebatur in primis ut unus ex coryphaeis Bergibanus: qui quidem domi suae inventus non est, aut quòd inde egressus esset, aut ꝑ se aliquò abscondi curasset. Ex quo deinceps tantum concepit animo dolorem, vt se in manus satellitū vltro tradere deliberaret, eandem cum reliquis captiuis causam defendere cupiēs. Amici ipsius, qui in eo singularem vitæ integritatem cum summa eruditione coniunctam semper perspexerant, admodum mirabantur, cùm viderent hominem ea voluntate ferri, vt se parato exitio obijceret, nec verò aliud ei ob oculos ponere poterant, nisi vt etiam atque etiam cõsideraret, ne Deum temere tentasse argui possit. Nulla autem res illum ab instituto dimouere potuit: non vxoris lachrymæ, non parentum aut propinquorū preces, nec totius deniq; familiæ, quæ adducebatur, conspectus, quicq; efficere apud ipsum valuit, quominus re familiari constituta atque confecta, extremo suis dicto vale, post triduum sponte se ad custodiam conferret. Præsidium itaque castri, eo viso, rogauit quónam pergeret: Magistratus, inquit ille, me quæsiuit, venio vt sciam quid me velit. proinde ad Præfectum castri ductus, fassus est ibi, se malè fecisse, quum se absconderet à Domino vocatus ad eandē cū Brulio aliisque captiuis causam defendendam. Præfectus verò valde perculsus erat, audiens hunc hominem tanta animi tranquillitate, acsine metu facti sui reddere rationem coram vniuerso castri præsidio: & sanè dolebat istum eò venire, sed quum cerneret adeò confidentem, iussit in carcerem abduci. Initiò quidem admodum se constantem præbuit: sed vbi Imperatoris commissarij incusissent ei horrorem carceris, & mortis quam ei ferendam minabantur crudelissimam: cœpit hic homo sensim vacillare, atq; ita paulatim à veritate deficere, in gratiam pseudoprophetarum & monachorum, qui illi euadendi spem fecerant. In[?] summa, tandem Bergibanus, vt ex-tremum beneficium acciperet, quale carnifices omnes & tyranni dare solent, nempe quò mitius secum ageretur, commutato tantùm ignis supplicio cum capitis præcisione, in omnibus libidini professorū veritatis hostium obscuebatur. Quæ res, vt gesta erat, postquam populo nota fuit, plurimis certè summam admirationem attulit. Aduersarij ex istius incommodo sua comparabant commoda, & sedulò de ipso triumphabant: atque ob id historiam pluribus prosecuti sumus, quia exemplo Bergibani, Miocum quoque terreri posse sperabāt. Nā in postremis percontationibus, cum nihil suis caullis apud Miocium proficerent: hoc saltem illi obiectabat, dicentes, En socius tuus Bergibanus, qui multo te eruditior est, omnia reuocauit: visne tu plus illo sapere? Respondit Miocius, se non iurasse in verba ullius hominis: aliud longe sibi ante oculos positum habere exemplum, Iesu Christi scilicet saluatoris sui. De Bergibano, inquit, si vera sunt quae dicatis, perfidus merito & proditor haberetur, ac satis declararet se Dominum tentasse, cum sponte sua in manus vestras venit. Equidem, si Deus aliquam cadendi obtulisset occasionem, haud sane praetermisissem. quare dum me habetis, agite de hoc corpore quod collibuerit, in anima vero nulla penes vos est potestas. Iudices magis quam antea obstupefacti, sine ulla mora sententiam de ipso tulerunt, quae paucis post diebus illi pronunciata fuit, ut videlicet vivus igne cremaretur in amplissimo theatro, quod in magno foro extructum erat. Dum ad locum supplicii duceretur, graui vinctus catena, monebat populum ne crederet sacrificis & monachis, sed Euangelium filii Dei unice amplecteretur. Ibi sacrifici cum monachis mirifice fremuerunt, quod tam impio, ut aiebat, loquendi copia daretur. Inter hos fremitus & clamores ipse clara voce Psalmos canere coepit. Quum iam ad palum deligatus esset, facculo tormentarii pulueris pleno ad pectus ipsius appenso, qui quidem puluis igne accensus cum magno sonitu dedisset, sacrifici & monachi qui aderant, populo persuadere conabantur, animam esse Miocii, quam diaboli secum auferrent. Miocius autem in media flamma perpetuo oculos in caelum defixos habebat: qua tandem flamma praefocatus, fidelem Deo spiritum reddidit.
units.tr: At that same time there was in the same prison a certain man named Bergibanus, who had received remarkable gifts from God and had made such progress in understanding Scripture that, before Peter Brulius came to that city, he would often act as interpreter at the meetings of the faithful. As soon as Brulius was seized, Bergibanus was sought first of all as one of the leaders; but he was not found at home, either because he had left it or because he had taken care to hide somewhere. From then on he was so grieved in mind that he resolved to hand himself over to the soldiers of his own accord, wishing to defend the same cause as the other captives. His friends, who had always seen in him a singular integrity of life joined with great learning, were greatly astonished to see the man carried along by such a will as to expose himself to certain destruction. They could set before his eyes nothing except that he should consider again and again, lest he be charged with rashly tempting God. But nothing could move him from his purpose: neither his wife's tears, nor the entreaties of his parents and kinsfolk, nor even the sight of his whole household, which was brought to him. Nothing that had any power with him prevailed to keep him from going of his own accord into custody, once his family affairs were settled and finished, after a last farewell of three days. So the garrison of the castle, seeing him, asked where he was going. "The magistrate," he said, "has sought me; I am coming so that I may learn what he wants of me." Led to the prefect of the castle, he confessed there that he had done wrong in hiding when the Lord had called him to defend the same cause as Brulius. The prefect was greatly disturbed to hear this man, with such calm of mind and without fear, give an account of his action before the whole garrison of the castle. He grieved that the man had come there, but seeing him so confident, he ordered him to be led off to prison. At first he showed himself very steadfast; but when the Emperor's commissioners set before him the horror of the prison and the most cruel death they threatened he must endure, he began gradually to waver, and so little by little to fall away from the truth, into favour with the false prophets and monks, who had held out to him the hope of escape. In short, at last Bergibanus, to receive that final favour which executioners and tyrants are wont to give, namely that he be treated more gently, the fire being exchanged for beheading, was given over to the lust of the enemies of the professors of the truth in all things. When this, as it happened, became known to the people, it certainly caused great astonishment to many. The adversaries turned his misfortune to their own advantage and eagerly triumphed over him. We have therefore related the story at some length, because they hoped that Miocius too could be frightened by Bergibanus's example. For in the last examinations, when they gained nothing from Miocius by their tricks, they at least threw this at him, saying, "See, your companion Bergibanus, who is far more learned than you, has taken back everything: do you want to be wiser than he?" Miocius replied that he had not sworn allegiance to the words of any man; he had before his eyes a quite different example, namely that of Jesus Christ, his Saviour. "As for Bergibanus," he said, "if what you say is true, he would rightly be held a faithless man and a traitor, and would plainly show that he had tempted the Lord when he came of his own accord into your hands. Indeed, had God offered me any chance of falling away, I would certainly not have let it pass. So long as you have me, deal with this body as you please; but over the soul you have no power." The judges, more astonished than before, passed sentence on him without delay. It was pronounced a few days later: namely, that he should be burnt alive in the great theatre built in the main square. As he was led to the place of execution, bound with a heavy chain, he warned the people not to believe the priests and monks, but to embrace the Gospel of the Son of God alone. There the priests and monks raged wonderfully, because such freedom of speech, as they said, was granted to so impious a man. Amid these murmurs and cries he himself began to sing psalms in a clear voice. When he was already bound to the stake, a bag full of gunpowder was hung at his breast; it was set alight and gave a loud report. The priests and monks who were present tried to persuade the people that it was Miocius's soul which the devils were carrying off with them. But Miocius kept his eyes fixed constantly on heaven in the midst of the flames; at last, overcome by the fire, he gave up his faithful spirit to God.

units.la: MARIONA, UXOR ADRIANI SARTO- ris in urbe Tornacensi.
units.tr: MARIONA, WIFE OF ADRIAN THE TAILOR, in the city of Tournai.

units.la: Igente adhuc persecutione illa contra fideles, quae eo tempore Tornaci, propter Petrum Brulium, ut diximus, exorta erat maxima, quidam etiam, cui Adrianus erat nomen, qui in ea urbe artem farciendi vestes profitebatur, cum Mariona uxore sua, in vincula coniecti fuerunt. Causa autem cur apprehenderentur una eademque in utroque fuit, Euangelicae scilicet veritatis ergo: exitus tamen in antin ambobus longè diuersus extitit. Adrianꝰ enim veritate, quã debuerat virili cōstātia, nō defendit, sed turpissimè ab ea defecit, ac sententiam præ nimia mollitie renocare coactus, verè Cyclopis beneficium à Iudicibus accepit, vt capitis saltem supplicio plecteretur: idque nō ita diu post, quàm in carcerem detrusus fuisset. Contrà verò, Mariona ipsius vxor, masculâ præstans virtute fœmina, constanter semper in sententia permanebat, & magnum profecto fidelibus, qui tum Tornaci erant, exemplum constantiæ exhibuit. Tyranni autem quãtumuis truculenti, neque minis, neque sæuitia, neque vllo denique terrore mortis crudelissimæ, mulierem hanc ab officio non solùm abducere non potuerunt, sed ne quatefacere quidem eximiam eius fidem. Atque ei quum proponerent mariti exemplum, quem pœnitentia ductum omnia abiurasse dicebant: nullam illa verbis aduersariorum fidem dans, tota in hoc vt inuictæ veritati, inuictum quoque ederet testimonium, Iudicibus abundè declarauit, se nequaquam ipsorum truculetia perterritam fuisse, nec eo quidè mortis genere, quod illi subèundum minabantur, nisi[?] mutaret opinionem. Iudices itaque quum nihil suis minis proficerent, sententiam aduersus illam pertulerunt, vt viua videlicet in terram defoderetur. (id nanque mortis ac supplicij genus, in Flandria ac vicinis regionibus, fere vsitatum est in fœminas Christianas & fideles.) Ipsa igitur ad locum supplicij quum duceretur, ad theatrum scilicet, quod Tornaci in magno foro (vt supra dictu est) extructum erat: nunquam desistit populum ad veritatis studium hortari, & precari Deum pro iis qui adhuc in densissimis ignorantiæ tenebris versabantur. Præteriens in itinere turrim, quæ vrbis Specula dicitur, in qua maritus eius detentus fuerat, illic adhuc eum sedere putàs, sublata voce clamauit, Vale mi Adriane, aliis mihi nuptiis hic dictus est dies. Conscenso iam theatro, vt vidit terræ aggerem & cistam in modum sepulchri concauam, traiectis vtrinque clathris ferreis, quibus imponi solet mulier quæcunque id genus supplicij subire cogitur: Mariona, inquam, tam crudelis apparatus spectaculo nequicquam perculsa fuit: quinimo alacri prorsus ac virili animo eos qui circunstabant ipsam in theatro, sic allocuta est, Huncine mihi parasitis pastillum? alludens ad formam cistæ in qua trucidanda erat, & artocreatis confectionem. In hunc itaque modū defossa, obiit fidelis in Christo virago.
units.tr: The persecution against the faithful, which had arisen at Tournai at that time over Pierre Brully, as we have said, was still very great. At that time a certain man named Adrian, who practised the trade of mending clothes in that city, was thrown into prison together with his wife Mariona. They were both seized for one and the same cause, namely for the sake of the truth of the Gospel. Their outcome, however, was very different. Adrian did not defend the truth with the manly constancy he should have shown, but shamefully abandoned it. Out of excessive weakness he was compelled to recant his opinion, and so from the judges he received what was really a Cyclops' kindness: he was to be punished only by beheading. This happened not long after he had been thrust into prison. Mariona, his wife, on the other hand, a woman who excelled in manly virtue, remained steadfast in her opinion throughout, and she gave a great example of constancy to the faithful who were then at Tournai. The tyrants, however savage they were, could neither by threats, nor by cruelty, nor by any terror of the most cruel death, lead this woman away from her duty. They could not even shake her remarkable faith. When they set before her the example of her husband, who they said had been moved to repentance and had renounced everything, she gave no credence at all to the words of her adversaries. Rather, by her whole conduct she bore an unconquered witness to an unconquered truth, and she made clear to the judges that she was in no way frightened by their savagery, nor even by the kind of death they threatened her with unless she changed her opinion. Since their threats achieved nothing, the judges pronounced sentence against her: she was to be buried alive in the earth. (This kind of death and punishment was almost customary in Flanders and the neighbouring regions for Christian women who were faithful.) So as she was led to the place of punishment, namely the scaffold that had been built in the great square at Tournai (as was said above), she never ceased to exhort the people to seek the truth and to pray to God for those who were still living in the thickest darkness of ignorance. As she passed on the way the tower called the Specula, in which her husband had been held, supposing that he was still sitting there, she raised her voice and cried out: "Farewell, my Adrian; this day has been appointed for me for another wedding." When she had mounted the scaffold and saw the mound of earth and the chest hollowed out like a tomb, with iron bars fixed across it on both sides, in which any woman forced to undergo this kind of punishment is usually placed, Mariona, I say, was in no way dismayed by so cruel a preparation. Rather, with a thoroughly cheerful and manly spirit she addressed those who stood around her on the scaffold, saying: "Is this little cake for me, for the parasites?" alluding to the shape of the chest in which she was to be slain, and to the confection of pastry. In this manner she was buried, and the faithful woman, a heroine in Christ, died.

units.la: IACOBVS CHOBARDVS, Lotharingus.
units.tr: James Chobardus, of Lorraine.

units.la: IN vrbe S. Michaelis in ducatu Bari apud Lotharingos, permulti fideles capti fuerunt, quidā etiam profugi, quoniā conuentus summo cū pietatis fructu inter se habuerāt, in quib° libros sacrae Scripturae exponebāt. In eorū numero fuit vir pius & doctus qui scholae ci°vrbis praeerat, Iacob° cognomine Chobardus, natus in pago vrbi S. Michaelis admodum propinquo, Mescrigna nominato. Is sanè de sacramentis cum sacerdotibus Papae qui in ea vrbe erant, in disputationē venit. Illi vt sunt ϑεὸς τὰ ἀξίωμα attētiores, in eam partem acceperunt eā disputationem, quasi Missa nec mortuis nec viuis quicquā prodesset atq; inseruiret. Itaque accusatus ab illis, atq; in carcerem coniectus quatuordecim aut quindecim hebdomadibus, sententiā suā rationibus authoritatibúsq; Scripturae constanter tutatus est. Cum autem multi eū hortarētur, vt quae professus fuerat, retraetaret, & cū caeteris vinctis honoraria poenae irrogatione acciperet: tantū abest, vt in eā sententiam fuerit adductus, vt maiore spiritus ardore accensus vltro confessionem fidei suae amplissimam scripserit, quam matri suae ad iudice perferendam dedit, admonens illam, ne ea in manus alterius cuiusquā deveniret. Fœmina simplex, ignorans quid secum ferret, confessionē iudici reddidit: quam quidem ille furore quodam incitatus, detulit ad Francisci Lotharingiae ducem: cuius sententia & authoritate Chobardus statim fuit condemnatus, vt viuus igni cremaretur. Iudex autē nulla rei delatae quaestione aut animadversione amplius habita, sententiā à Duce pronuntiatā executioni mādauit. Cum ad supplicii Chobardus iā duceretur, populū, qui eū circūstabat, monere ac docere coepit: sed iudex inferior, qui in ea vrbe Praepositus dicitur, ei silētiū imperauit, testificās eos qui adessent, melius quàm ipsum mādata Dei doctrinámq; tenere. quòd nisi taceret, se lingua excisa silētiū ei impositurū minat° est. Quamobrē Chobard° nihil postea loquutus est, nisi quòd saepe Deū inuocans implorānsq; illa verba repetebat, Deus mi, miserere mei: Deus mi, miserere testis tui ac martyris. Deinde sine vllo corporis motu quietus & mansuctus, instar mitissimi agni, viuus est ex-ustus stus[?].cuius in morte,quidā etiā ex magistratibus homine doctū,peri-[illegible, ~3 letters]umque linguarū conquesti fuerūt & summa probitate atque innocentia praeditum,ita extinctū fuisse. Itaque edicto magistratus cautum[?] fuit, ut non nisi pro haeretico haberetur & diceretur.
units.tr: In the town of St Michel in the duchy of Bar, among the Lotharingians, many of the faithful were arrested, and some fled, because they had held meetings among themselves with great fruit of piety, at which they expounded the books of Holy Scripture. Among their number was a godly and learned man who was master of the town school, James Chobardus by surname, born in the village of Mescrigna, very near the town of St Michel. He entered into a disputation about the sacraments with the priests of the Pope who were in that town. Being very attentive to their dignity [ϑεὸς τὰ ἀξίωμα], they took the disputation in the sense that the Mass profited and served neither the dead nor the living. Accused by them and thrown into prison for fourteen or fifteen weeks, he steadfastly defended his opinion with the reasons and authority of Scripture. When many urged him to retract what he had professed, and to accept with the other prisoners the honorary penalty imposed, he was so far from being brought to that view that, kindled with a greater ardour of spirit, he of his own accord wrote a full confession of his faith and gave it to his mother to carry to the judge, warning her that it must not fall into the hands of anyone else. The simple woman, not knowing what she carried, handed the confession to the judge. He, incited by a kind of frenzy, carried it to Francis, Duke of Lorraine. By the duke's sentence and authority Chobardus was at once condemned to be burned alive. The judge, without any further inquiry into the matter reported or any examination of it, ordered the sentence pronounced by the duke to be carried out. As Chobardus was being led to the execution, he began to admonish and teach the people standing around him. But the lower judge, who in that town is called the Provost, imposed silence on him, testifying that those present knew the commands and doctrine of God better than he did; and he threatened that, unless he held his tongue, he would have his tongue cut out to silence him. Therefore Chobardus said nothing more afterwards, except that he often called upon God and kept repeating those words: "My God, have mercy on me; my God, have mercy on your witness and martyr." Then, without any movement of his body, quiet and gentle like a most meek lamb, he was burned alive. At his death, some of the magistrates complained that a learned man, endowed with the highest uprightness and innocence, had been put to death in this way. Accordingly, by an edict of the magistracy it was provided that he should not be regarded or called anything but a heretic.

units.la: AYMONDVS à VIA.
units.tr: Aymond à Via.

units.la: Circiter annū M.D.XLI. mense Decemb. decretum fuit à summo Burdigalesi Senatu ac Parlameto, ut cōprehenderetur Aymodus à Via, qui docebat & concionabatur Evangelium Iesu Christi in urbe S. Fidei in Agennesi tractu: idq; accusatione Parochi eiusdem loci, atq; aliorum sacerdotum quos sibi Parochus in causa habebat socios, dicentes prædicatione illius multum de ipsorum quæstu decedere.
units.tr: About the year 1541, in the month of December, the supreme Senate and Parliament of Bordeaux decreed that Aymond à Via should be arrested; he taught and preached the Gospel of Jesus Christ in the town of St Foy in the district of Agen. This was on the accusation of the parish priest of the same place, and of other priests whom the parish priest had as allies in the cause, who said that by his preaching their gain was much diminished.

units.la: De hoc autem Senatusconsulto certior factus fuit Aymondus, tribus ante diebus quam apparitor ad exequendum venirét, atque à pluribus incitatus ut periculum fuga declinaret. Id vero ut faceret nunquam induci potuit: sed his fere apud suos verbis usus est, Malo equidem me nunquam fuisse natum, quam hoc facinus committere. neque enim boni Pastoris est fugere imminente periculo, ut ait Dominus: verum illius est manere, ne dissipetur oves. Gratiā autem à Domino accepi prædicandi vobis ipsius Evangelium: quòd si nunc propter vnicam tentationem abirem, æstimarer concionatus fuisse fabulas, somnia, aut alia Deo contraria, quum vos in offendiculo relinquerem. Quapropter vos rogo ne mihi amplius de hac re verba faciatis. nam scio quæ concionatus sum vera esse, pro quibus sustinendis, Deo iuvante, neque corpori neque animæ parcam: atqui cum D. Paulo dicam, Non solum paratus sum pro Christo ligari in urbe Burdigalensi, sed etiam mori. Quæ hominis constantia, cæteris silentium imposuit.
units.tr: Aymond was informed of this decree three days before the officer came to carry it out, and many urged him to avoid the danger by flight. But he could never be induced to do this; he answered more or less in these words to his people: "I would indeed rather never have been born than commit this crime. For it is not the part of a good shepherd to flee when danger threatens, as the Lord says; rather it is his part to remain, lest the sheep be scattered. But I have received from the Lord the grace of preaching to you his Gospel; if now, because of a single temptation, I went away, I would be judged to have preached fables, dreams, or other things contrary to God, since I would be leaving you in a stumbling-block. Therefore I ask you not to say any more to me about this matter. For I know that what I have preached is true, and for its defence, with God's help, I will spare neither body nor soul. Indeed, I may say with St Paul: I am ready not only to be bound in the city of Bordeaux, but also to die for Christ." This constancy of the man silenced the others.

units.la: Accessit itaque apparitor ut sententia exequeretur, qui tribus diebus in urbe mansit. Interea Aymodus tres conciones habuit, in quibus summa atq; ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν[?] omnium superiorum præcedentium sermonum, singulari quadam memoria repetebat, dicens se ad eos tuendos mille vitas, si tot haberet, non dubitaturum abijcere. Quæ oratio cum zelo divino atq; innocentia coniuncta, vehementer populi animos commouit, adeò ut plerique dicerent, Quid? hic causa est quòd ludos, & vinarias tabernas reliquerimus, quódque multi improbi homines ad meliorē vitā se conuerterint ! Proinde multitudo in Apparitorem irruit, ut hominem liberarent. id quod Aymondus nequaquam permisit, his verbis multitudinem compellans, Sinite quaeso, fratres atque amici mei, ne meum martyrium impediatis. voluntas enim Dei est eiusmodi, ut pro illo patiar, cui nequaquam repugnandum est.
units.tr: The officer therefore came to carry out the sentence, and he stayed in the town for three days. In the meantime Aymond gave three sermons, in which, with a remarkable memory, he recited the whole summary and recapitulation [ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν] of all his earlier sermons, saying that he would not hesitate to lay down a thousand lives, if he had so many, to defend them. This speech, joined with divine zeal and innocence, greatly stirred the people's minds, so that many said: "What? Is this the reason we have given up our games and our wine-taverns, and that many wicked men have been converted to a better life?" Accordingly the crowd rushed upon the officer to free the man. Aymond by no means allowed this, addressing the crowd with these words: "Please, my brothers and friends, do not hinder my martyrdom. For it is the will of God that I suffer for him, to whom we must in no way oppose ourselves."

units.la: Tum consules dimisso Apparitore, statuerunt eum capere, atque Burdigalam deducere. quo quidem tribus post diebus magno comitatus satellitio ductus fuit. Burdigalae autem plures adversus eum producti sunt testes, fere omnes sacrifici praeter dominum Riveracum, hominem (ut uno verbo dicam) verè φιλόχριστον[?], ciusdemque famulum quos habebat hostes capitales. etenim Riveracus ille iactarat saepius, aut mille coronatis aureis sibi negotium conflaret, aut cum breui comburendum curaret. Ac etiamsi Aymondus iustissimas adversus illos testes refutationes in promptu haberet, Regij tamen delegati Iudices ad eas proponendas admittere noluerunt: sed solas sacrificorum accusationes audiuerunt. Atqui omnes isti testes contra eum nihil aliud afferebant, quàm quod sinistrè de Purgatorio sentire diceret, quippe qui semper ipsis asseruisset, purgationem nostram solùm esse per sanguinem Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Then the consuls dismissed the officer and decided to seize him and bring him to Bordeaux. Three days later he was led there with a large escort of soldiers. At Bordeaux several witnesses were produced against him, almost all of them priests, except Lord Riveracus, a man (to put it in one word) a true lover of Christ [φιλόχριστον], and his servant, who were his chief enemies. For that Riveracus had often boasted that either he would make a profit of a thousand gold crowns for himself, or he would arrange for Aymond to be burned before long. And although Aymond had most just refutations of those witnesses ready at hand, the royal commissioned judges were unwilling to admit them to be put forward; they heard only the accusations of the priests. Yet all these witnesses brought against him nothing else than that he said things unfavourable about Purgatory, since he had always asserted to them that our purgation is only through the blood of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Proponebat item Aymondus à Via, quemadmodum primus & secundus Praeses reiiciendi in ea causa bono iure forent: quia primus praeses, dum lis (quae illi cum Parocho S. Fidei intercesserat) adhuc suspensa maneret, curasset ut causam generalis Procurator Regius susciperet, & parochiatus beneficium à Parocho ad quendam é filijs suis transfiret. Atque ea ratione duo illi praesides merito ab hoc iudicio removendi erant, quùm & inter se cōsobrini essent, & adversariorum tuerentur partes. nam de reditibus illius parochiatus agebatur. Quanvis autem, antequam decretum venisset, abundè ipsis perspecta erat hominis innocentia: tamè & se purgare, vel ut in foro loquuntur, iustificare, & obiectiones suas probare iussº est. id quod ille fecit, adhibitis octoginta plus minus testibus, ijsque gravibus quidem: quos tamen alij admittere noluerunt, sed suspectos sibi eos aequè atque ipsum dicebant, eiusdè enim esse sectae homines: tametsi in eos nunquam inquisitum fuisset.
units.tr: Aymond à Via also argued that the first and second presidents could rightly be rejected in that case: for the first president, while the lawsuit which he had with the parish priest of St Foy was still pending, had arranged for the king's general procurator to take up the cause, and had transferred the benefit of the parish from the parish priest to one of his sons. And so those two presidents ought rightly to have been removed from this judgment, since they were cousins to each other and were defending the side of his adversaries; for the income of that parish was at issue. However, although the innocence of the man had been fully apparent to them before the decree was issued, he was nonetheless ordered to clear himself, or, as they say in the courts, to justify himself, and to prove his objections. He did this, bringing forward some eighty witnesses, or thereabouts, and those of weight; but others refused to admit them, saying that these witnesses were suspect to them just as he himself was, for they were men of the same sect; although no inquiry had ever been made into them.

units.la: Octo autem vel circiter nouem mẽsibus in carcere multas ærumnas pertulit, quibus ille tamẽ fide ac spe fultus minimè succubuit. Sed cum interea illi denunciaretur ignis supplicium breui subeundum: nuncios istos tam firmo animo excepit, ut etiam inimicos ipsos attonitos redderet: quia semper idem erat vultus color, atq; in ore verba Pauli habebat, Cupio separari à corpore, & esse cum Iesu, Christus mihi lucrum est siue viuam siue moriar. verum una hæc res me male habet, quod diutius mihi aliis prodesse non liceat docendo, atque talentum à Deo mihi traditum, cum fratribus communicando: quódque ea non apertius ac plenius exposuerim, quorum mihi Dominus vberiorem notitiam dederat. Attamen si placet eidem me nunc ad se vocare, voluntas eius fiat, non autem quod desidero. Praeterea vitam ante actam multis lachrymis deplorabat, dicens se male vixisse, non iuxta cognitionem quam à Deo acceperat. Idque praeter cetera maxime dolebat: quanuis eius vita, si homines tantum spectemus, irreprehensibilis fuisset: adeo ut aduersarij & accusatores, vitae ipsius sanctimoniam praedicare cogerentur. tanta erat huius viri integritas atq; simplicitas. Ex quo primo coprehensum fuisse diximus, menses fere nouem ad primum & vigesimum diem Augusti in carcere mansit, eo quidem die acceptis Iudicum delegatorum literis, perrexerunt agere de ipsius condemnatione, posthabitis iustificationibus, ut ipsi dicunt, atque aliis causis recusationum, quas ille aduersus eosdem Iudices protulerat: qui quàprimum captus esset, nondum causa cognita ac perspecta, praeiudicijs cum onerarat, passim dicentes ignis supplicio adiudicandum esse. Denique negocium ita subito in camera Iudicum delegatorum confectum referri coepit, ut statim à prandio Aymondus maioribus copedibus constringeretur. Quod quidem ille videns, praesagium sibi atq; mortis nuncium esse aiebat: minus tamen laborare, quod omnia pro Christo libens pateretur. Obsecrabat etiam eos qui illum inuisebant, ne quid celarent eorum quae de ipso dicerentur. nam si, inquit, is essem cui caro dominaretur, merito reticendi quicquam esset occasio. ast meã fidem nec mors nec cruciatus nec persecutiones unquam concutient: constans permanebo in eo qui me confirmat, Iesu Christo.
units.tr: For eight or about nine months he endured many hardships in prison, yet, supported by faith and hope, he by no means gave way. But while in the meantime the sentence of fire was announced to him, to be undergone shortly, he received these messengers with so firm a spirit that he even astonished his enemies themselves; for his colour and expression never changed, and he had on his lips the words of Paul: "I desire to depart from the body and to be with Jesus; for Christ is my gain, whether I live or die." Yet one thing troubles me greatly, that I may no longer be permitted to profit others by teaching, and to share with the brethren the talent given me by God; and that I have not set forth more openly and fully those things of which the Lord had given me a fuller knowledge. Nevertheless, if it pleases him to call me now to himself, let his will be done, and not what I desire." Moreover, he lamented with many tears the life he had lived before, saying that he had lived badly, not according to the knowledge he had received from God. And this above all else grieved him greatly: although, if we look only at men, his life had been irreproachable, so much so that his adversaries and accusers were compelled to proclaim the holiness of his life. Such was the integrity and simplicity of this man. From the time when, as we said, he was first arrested, he remained in prison for about nine months, until the twenty-first day of August. On that day, having received the letters of the commissioned judges, they proceeded to deal with his condemnation, setting aside, as they call it, the justifications and the other grounds of objection which he had brought forward against those same judges; for they had burdened him with prejudgments from the very moment he was taken, not having yet heard and examined the case, saying everywhere that he must be adjudged to the punishment of fire. Finally the business began to be concluded so suddenly in the chamber of the commissioned judges that right after lunch Aymond was bound with heavier fetters. When he saw this, he said it was a presage and a message of death for him; yet he was less troubled, because he was willing to suffer all things for Christ. He also begged those who visited him not to hide from him anything that was being said about him; "for," he said, "if I were one whom the flesh ruled, there would be good reason for silence. But neither death, nor torments, nor persecutions will ever shake my faith: I shall remain steadfast in him who strengthens me, Jesus Christ."

units.la: Die aut Mercurij proximo, crudelissimum in modū tormētis examinatº fuit, non de sua causa, nam ita illi mors certa erat constituta, sed ut quos haberet socios declararet. ibi tu primarius praeses barba illū prehendes, Dic inquit, homo nefarie, dic: condemnatus enim es, restat modo ut tuos cognoscamus socios. Quosnam, inquit ille, socios quaeritis? equidem alios non habeo socios, quam qui sciunt ac faciunt voluūtatem Dei Patris mei: sive ij nobiles, mercatores, agricolae, sive alterius ordinis homines sint. Atque his diris cruciatibus, vir alioqui tenui valetudine, ad horas duas vel tres exercitus fuit, ubi se his verbis consolatus est, Corpus quidem hoc morietur, spiritus vero viuet: Regnum autem Dei manebit in aeternum.
units.tr: On Monday or Wednesday following, he was examined under the most cruel torments. This was not about his cause, for his death had already been decided, but so that he would name his fellow believers. There the chief president seized him by the beard: "Speak, wicked man, speak! You are condemned, so it only remains for us to learn who your associates are." "Which associates do you ask about?" he replied. "I have no associates except those who know and do the will of my Father, whether they are nobles, merchants, farmers, or men of any other rank." Under these dreadful tortures, though he was otherwise of weak health, he was stretched for two or three hours. There he comforted himself with these words: "This body will indeed die, but the spirit will live, and the kingdom of God will remain forever."
