units.la: Porro inter haec tormenta passus est animi deliquium: quumque ad se rediret: Domine, Domine, ait, cur me reliquisti. Secundus praeses tu ad eum: Inprobe Lutherane, tu es qui dereliquisti Deum. Rursus Aymondus, Hei mihi, domine, inquit, ecquid me tantum cruciatis? Domine, ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciant. Tum idem Praeses, Ecce, inquit, ipsum nefarium, qui pro nobis orat. Caeterum ne unius quidem nomen ab eo extorquere potuerunt, ita ille omnia patieter & constanter perferebat, inquiens, Putabam equidem plus apud homines clementiae reperire: proinde Dominum oro, ut in ipso misericordiam inveniam. Postea vero in arctissimum carcerem (quae turris Baronum vocatur) detrusus est in diem Sabbathi: quo quidem die, circiter horam octava mane pronuntiata est ei sententia ut ustularetur. Quod sane illum nō magis perculit, quam alias cum idem illi nunciaretur, sed Deum magnopere laudabat, quod ipsum eo beneficio dignatus esset, ut hora mortis illi significaretur. Protinus itaque missum est ad C.A.I.M. qui ipsius confessionem exciperent. At ille ipsos repudiauit, cupiens sibi dari quendam sui ordinis, Parochum nempe S. Christophori: monachis vero in hanc rationem locutus est: Abite hinc omnes, ego confitebor Domino peccata mea. videtis me satis perturbatum ab hominibus, vultis adhuc adducere perturbationes? alij habuerut corpus, vultis & vos auferre animam? abite hinc, obsecro. Deinde accesserunt consiliarius de Longa, & consiliarius Chassagneus, qui ipsum volebant consolari: sed fides atque constantia huius tanta erat, ut ipsemet eos consolaretur. Quum autem videret interdictum esse Parocho Sancti Christophori, ne suam confessionem audiret: assumpsit Carmelitam quendam, monachorum minimum, quem, caeteris abire iussis, retinuit, atque remotis arbitris longo satis tempore una fuerunt, adeo ut cum ipsum monachum ad veritatem converterit. Ad haec allato ei prandio, accersi iussit custodem carceris, cum uxore & filia eiusdem, quibus dixit: Obtinui à Deo complementum desideriorum meorum: nam plus minus octo anni elapsi sunt, ex quo Deus, prosua bonitate, mihi suae voluntatis notitiam largitus est: sed repente venit in mentem mori Burdigalae pro ipsius Verbo: quod nunc verè completum cerno.
units.tr: Amid these torments he fainted, and when he came to himself he cried, "Lord, Lord, why have you forsaken me?" The second president said to him, "Wicked Lutheran, you are the one who forsook God." Again Aymond cried out, "Alas, Lord, why do you torment me so? Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." Then the same president said, "Look, there is the wicked man who prays for us!" Yet they could not extract from him the name of a single person, so calmly and steadfastly did he endure everything, saying, "I did indeed think I would find more mercy among men; therefore I pray the Lord that I may find mercy in him." Afterwards he was thrown into a very narrow prison, called the Tower of the Barons, until the Sabbath day. On that day, about eight o'clock in the morning, the sentence was pronounced that he be burned. This did not dismay him any more than when it had been announced to him on other occasions. Rather, he greatly praised God, who had deigned to grant him this favour, that the hour of his death was revealed to him. Immediately a message was sent to the C.A.I.M. to hear his confession. But he rejected them, wishing that someone of his own order be sent, namely the parish priest of St Christopher. To the monks he spoke thus: "Go away, all of you; I will confess my sins to the Lord. You see that I am disturbed enough by men; do you want to add further disturbances? Others have had my body; do you want to take my soul as well? Go away, I beg you." Then the councillors de Longa and Chassagneus came in, wanting to console him, but his faith and constancy were so great that he himself consoled them. When he saw that the parish priest of St Christopher was forbidden to hear his confession, he took a certain Carmelite, the least of the monks, and, having dismissed the others, kept him. With the witnesses removed, they were together for a fairly long time, so that he converted the monk himself to the truth. Then, when lunch had been brought in, he ordered the jailer's wife and daughter to be called, and said to them: "I have obtained from God the fulfilment of my desires. For it is now some eight years since God, by his goodness, granted me knowledge of his will; but suddenly it came into my mind to die at Bordeaux for his Word, which I now see truly fulfilled."

units.la: Ad horam autem primam à prandio, venerunt in carcerem primus & secundus praeses, Chassagneus, Longa, & plures alij consiliarij. Hic tum M. Aymondus sermonem habere coepit de Coena, hanc suam fidem dicens: Quod scilicet, quotiescunque Christiani in vera unitate ac concordia conveniunt, docentes eandem omnes doctrinam, atque in fide non ficta & spe certa sumunt panem, revera corporis & sanguinis Christi participes fiant: ibique in eam sententiam citavit locum Pauli I.Corint. XI, summa profecto cum gratia Scripturam exponens. Ac dum ipsis loqueretur, semel alta voce exclamavit: Verba quae vobis loquor, Spiritus sunt & vita. Tandem subiecit, Haec mea est fides, Domini mei, de qua nunc accusor: sed in primis, omnibus notum esse volo quid de Coena sentiam, Omnes nempe Christianos communicare corpori & sanguini Iesu Christi, quicunque fide recipiunt panem & vinum oblatum in Coena: iterumque varios Scripturae locos in quibus Coenae fit mentio, produxit. Sed plenius de singulis differere volentis sermonem interrupit secundus praeses: Audi, inquiens, oportet nobis aperias tua de Purgatorio opinione. Ad hoc ille, Recte mones, inquit, dicā quod setio[?], nosti in scriptura synonyma esse haec verba, Purgare, Mundare, & Lauare. Habes apud Isa. Dolores nostros ac languores ipse tulit, revera factus est nostra salus & purgatio. Dico equidem nisi expurgati fuerimus quasi aurum in fornace, nunquam introibimus Paradisum. Tum secundus praeses, Videte, inquit, quemadmodum Lutherani isti circuitione utatur. Id minimè rogamus: sed dic an aliquis sit locus ubi animae post corporis separationem purgentur, quãdo in vita nõ egerunt debitam pœnitentiā. Cui ille respondit, Eheu mi domine, sine me. scis enim certò quod in turba & perturbatione dicitur haud posse intelligi. dico jam tibi, Iesum Christum sua morte pro omnibus peccatis nostris satisfecisse, nosq; in eius sanguine lotos esse, ut est in sacris literis: Ipse lavit vos in sanguine suo, redempti estis non auro, sed sanguine Christi. Non legisti epistolas D. Pauli, in quibus toties inculcatur, nos per sanguinem Iesu Christi mundos esse à peccatis? Epistolae illae, respondit secundus praeses, pueris ipsis notae sunt. Quid pueris? inquit Aymondus, vereor ne tu vix eas legeris. Tum quida monachus, Magister Aymonde inquit, uno verbo ipsis satisfeceris, si dixeris locum quendam esse in quo animae quae ex hoc corpore migrarunt, purgentur. Hoc inquit ille, tibi dicendum relinquo. Ecquid vultis me damnari, & dicere quod nesciam. Ibi denuò idem secundus praeses illum aggressus est, Ades, inquit, nonne tu jam moriturus speras adire Purgatorium? & qui moritur in peccato veniali, rectàne introibit Paradisum? Ad haec ille respondit, tantà se habere in Deo suo fiduciam, ut eo die in Paradisum iturum esse certò consideret. Rogauit alter, ubinam esset Paradisus. Ibi, inquit ille, est, ubi Dei maiestas & gloria residet. Canones, inquit primus praeses, faciunt mentionem, ut canon, Animae defunctorum, & alij: atque in tuis concionibus maximè semper commendabas pauperes. Ad quae respondit, se verbum Dei concionatum fuisse, Canones vero non didicisse. Excepit mox praefes, Credisne in Ecclesiam? Respondit ille, se credere verum esse, quod Ecclesia regenerata per sanguinem Christi, fundata in eadem verbo, statuisset. Quaenam ea esset Ecclesia, interrogabat praeses. Cui ille, graeca vox est Ecclesia, quae latinis significat Congregationem sive Conventum. Equidem dico, ut promisit Christus: Quotiescunque fideles congregantur ad honorem Dei, religionisque Christianae propagationem, vere inter eos esse sanctum Spiritum. Ad hoc secundus praefes intulit, Sequitur igitur ea ratione plures esse ecclesias: ac si conuenirent rustici, fore ecclesiam. Non est quicquam, inquit ille, absurdi, plures haberi inter Christianos, coetus. sic enim loquitur D. Paulus, Omnibus ecclesiis quae sunt in Galatia: tamen omnes illi coetus unica constituunt Ecclesiam. Tum consiliarius de Longa, Ecclesia, inquit, in quan. quam credis, an non ea est, quam vocat nostrum Credo, Sanctam ec-clesiã? Ad hoc ille, Confiteor sane, atq; de ea loquor. Ibi secundus praeses interrogauit, quisnam esset eius Ecclesiae caput. Iesus Christus, respondit Aymondus. Non autem Papa? subdit praeses. Non, inquit. Quid igitur? Minister, si vir bonus est: quemadmodum & Episcopi ministri sunt, ut testatur caput quartum prioris Epist. ad Corinth. Sic nos existimet homo, ut ministros & dispensatores arcanorum Dei. Rogatus autem an crederet Papae, dixit nescire se quisnā ille esset. Iterum rogatus, anne is esset successor Petri. Si, inquit, similis est Petro, fundatus super veram Petram Iesum Christum, credo opera ipsius atque statuta optima esse. Hic praeses, Miseret me tui, inquit, quia miser hono exitio devotus es. Quid? exitio devotus ais, inquit Aymondus, & semel atque iterum repetens ea verba, exclamavit, O qualem mihi ste affert consolationem! at ego contra spero videre hodie Deum meum, ac Patrem meum: & quis me separabit a charitate Dei? an gladius, an fames, an nuditas? non, nihil me ab ea divellet: sed me omnium vestrum valde miseret. his dictis illi egressi sunt, Aymondus cum monachis solus relictus est. Non ita multo post exiuit ipse ad supplicij locum ducendus: atque in egressu canere coepit Psal. In exitu Israel de Aegypto. substitit vero ante custodiam Palatinam, ad captiuos respiciens, & clamans, Fratres mei, sperate in Iesum Christum, ponite in eo spem vestram, nec vos quicquam percellat. Locutus sum de vobis cum secundo Praeside, ostendens ei miserias quas toleratis propter procrastinationes iudiciorum: qui mihi promisit se vos breui expediturum: fratres mei, vobis iam vale-dico. Abeo ad Deum, qui & meus & vester est communis Pater. precamini illum mecum, ut sua me gratia dignetur. Domina custos, gratias tibi ago pro tuis in me officijs, tibique commendo miseros captiuos, ut te ipsis mitem exhibeas. Ibi conscendit rhedam, atque egrediens Palatium orsus est istud: Caeci sunt & duces caecorum, aures habent, & non audient: oculos habent, & non videbunt, atque ita Psalmum absoluit usque ad S. Andreae, ubi illum iucitabant ut veniam peteret a Deo, Virgine Maria, atque Iustitia. Implorabat quidem veniam a Deo, ipsiusque iusti-tia: sed Mariam nulla in re se offendisse dicebat: atq; in quo nulla esset offensa , nullam quoque veniam requiri. Inde ductus fuit ad S. Legiæ , totóque itinere non desistit concionari populo , seipsum confirmans , atque exultans quòd pro Christo moriturus esset , qui pro ipso horrendos mortis dolores perpessus erat. Tum quidam satellitum, Perge, Perge, inquit aurigæ: concionum plus satis habemus. Ad hoc Aymondus dixit, Qui ex Deo est, libenter audit sermones de Deo.
units.tr: At about one o'clock after lunch, the first and second presidents, Chassagneus, Longa and several other councillors came into the prison. Then Master Aymond began to speak about the Supper, stating his faith thus: "Whenever Christians come together in true unity and concord, all teaching the same doctrine, and in sincere faith and certain hope take the bread, they truly become partakers of the body and blood of Christ." In support of this he cited 1 Corinthians 11, expounding the Scripture with great grace. While he was speaking to them, he once cried out in a loud voice: "The words that I speak to you are spirit and life." Finally he added: "This is my faith, my lords, for which I am now accused. But above all I wish everyone to know what I think about the Supper: that all Christians who receive in faith the bread and wine offered in the Supper communicate in the body and blood of Jesus Christ." And he went on to bring forward various passages of Scripture in which the Supper is mentioned. But when he wished to discuss each point more fully, the second president interrupted him: "Listen," he said, "you must explain to us your opinion about Purgatory." To this he replied: "You are right to remind me. You know that in Scripture these words are synonyms: to purge, to cleanse, and to wash. You have in Isaiah, 'He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; he was wounded for our transgressions,' and truly he became our salvation and purging. I say indeed that unless we are purged like gold in the furnace, we will never enter Paradise." Then the second president said: "See how these Lutherans use circumlocution. We are not asking that. But tell us whether there is any place where souls are purged after separation from the body, when in life they have not performed due repentance." He answered him: "Alas, my lord, leave me alone; for you know surely that what is said in a tumult and confusion cannot be understood. I tell you now that Jesus Christ, by his death, has satisfied for all our sins, and that we have been washed in his blood, as is said in the sacred writings: 'He washed us in his own blood; you were redeemed not with gold but with the blood of Christ.' Have you not read the epistles of St Paul, in which it is so often repeated that we are cleansed from sins through the blood of Jesus Christ?" "Those epistles," replied the second president, "are known even to children." "To children?" said Aymond. "I fear you have hardly read them." Then a certain monk said: "Master Aymond, you would satisfy them with a single word if you said that there is a place where the souls that have departed from this body are purged." "That," said he, "I leave for you to say. Do you want me to be condemned and to say what I do not know?" Then the same second president attacked him again: "Come now, do you not hope, since you are about to die, to go to Purgatory? And he who dies in venial sin, will he enter Paradise straightaway?" To this he replied that he had such trust in his God that he was certain he would go to Paradise that very day. Another asked where Paradise was. "It is there," he said, "where the majesty and glory of God dwell." The first president said: "The canons make mention of the canon 'Souls of the departed,' and others; and in your sermons you always most highly commended the poor." To which he replied that he had preached the Word of God, but had not learned the canons. Then the president went on: "Do you believe in the Church?" He answered that he believed it true that the Church, regenerated by the blood of Christ and founded on the same Word, had decreed these things. "What Church is that?" asked the president. He replied: "The word 'Church' is Greek, and in Latin it means a congregation or assembly. I say, as Christ promised: whenever the faithful gather to honour God and to propagate the Christian religion, the Holy Spirit is truly among them." To this the second president added: "It follows, then, on that reasoning, that there are many churches: if country folk were to gather, there would be a church." "There is nothing absurd," he replied, "in there being several assemblies among Christians. For St Paul speaks thus: 'To the churches that are in Galatia'; yet all those assemblies make up one Church." Then the councillor de Longa said: "The Church in which you believe, is it not the one that our Creed calls 'the holy Church'?" To this he replied: "I certainly confess it, and it is of that Church that I speak." Then the second president asked who was the head of that Church. "Jesus Christ," answered Aymond. "Not the Pope, then?" said the president. "No," he said. "What then? The minister, if he is a good man; just as bishops too are ministers, as the fourth chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians testifies: 'Let a man so account of us as of the ministers and stewards of the mysteries of God.'" Asked whether he believed in the Pope, he said he did not know who that man was. Asked again whether he was the successor of Peter: "If he is like Peter, founded on the true Rock, Jesus Christ, I believe that his works and his best statutes are good." Then the president said: "I pity you, because you are devoted to a wretched ruin." "Devoted to ruin, you say?" replied Aymond, and repeating those words once and again he exclaimed: "Oh, what a consolation you bring me! But I, on the contrary, hope to see my God and my Father this very day. And who shall separate me from the love of God? Shall tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness? No, nothing shall tear me from it; but I pity all of you greatly." With these words they went out, and Aymond was left alone with the monks. Not long afterwards he himself came out, to be led to the place of execution, and as he went out he began to sing Psalm 114, "When Israel went out of Egypt." He stopped in front of the Palatine prison, looked at the captives and cried out: "My brothers, hope in Jesus Christ, put your hope in him, and let nothing dismay you. I have spoken about you with the second president, showing him the miseries you endure because of the delays in your trials; and he has promised me that he will soon settle your case. My brothers, I now bid you farewell. I go to God, who is both my Father and yours. Pray to him with me that he will deign to show me his grace. Mistress jailer, I thank you for your kindnesses to me, and I commend to you the wretched captives, that you may show yourself gentle to them." Then he climbed into the cart, and as he left the palace he began to recite that psalm: "They have eyes and see not; they have ears and hear not"; and he finished the psalm as far as St Andrew's, where they urged him to ask pardon of God, the Virgin Mary and Justice. He indeed implored pardon of God and his justice, but said that he had given no offence to Mary in any way, and that where there was no offence there was no pardon to be sought. He was then led to St Leger's, and all along the journey he did not cease preaching to the people, strengthening himself and rejoicing that he was about to die for Christ, who had suffered dreadful pains of death for him. Then one of the guards said: "Go on, go on, driver; we have more than enough of sermons." To this Aymond replied: "He who is of God gladly hears words about God."

units.la: Quum autem praeteriret quandam effigiem Divae Virginis, hominum turba non sine contumeliis in eum vociferabatur, quia imaginem non salutasset: & quia unicum Iesum Christum assiduè invocaret, non autem Virginem Mariam. Quo viso ille vocem extulit, Precor te Domine Deus, ne unquam permittas, ut quenquam praeter te solum, ad auxilium implorem. In ipso supplicij iam loco, cùm vellet condemnationis suæ rationem explanare, non licuit per satellites, sed ferè à tortore in terram detrusus fuit: descendens autem de rheda, Domini mei, inquit, morior pro Euangelio Iesu Christi, & verbo eius: ac plenius dicere volens, orsus est hoc pacto: Christiane, audi me: Quod ut impedirent apparitores, magnos excitarunt tumultus, cum huiusmodi clamoribus, Tolle, tolle, ne quid loquatur. Quid, inquit ille, an non per vos licebit mihi declarare populo, me non ut haereticum sed Christianum mori? Minime, clamabant cæteri. Ehen, quid ni? Ac tum locutus est submissa voce ad aurem parui illius Carmelitæ, quæ ante converterat. Carnifex dein arreptum iussit conscendere scalas: Hic ille clamare cœpit: Domine, ad auxiliandum mihi festina, & ne-quid tarda: opus manuum tuarum ne despicias. Ignosce istis, quia nesciunt quid agant. fratres mei, Domini scholastici, obsecro vos ut Euangelio operam detis: solum enim verbum Dei manet in æternū. Discite notitiam voluntatis Dei. ne timeatis eos penes quos tantum est potestas in corpus, non autem in animam. Postremò dixit, Caro hæc mirificè cum Spiritu luctatur, sed eam continuò abiciam. Domine, in manus tuas commendo animam meam: Domini mei orate Deum pro me. ac subinde iterabat hanc precationem: Domine Deus meus, in manus tuas commendo animam meam. Tandem carnifex eum in scalis quassabat ut præfocaretur: atq; ita vir pius expirauit, corpus autem postmodò igne consumptum fuit.
units.tr: As he was passing a certain image of the blessed Virgin, a crowd of men shouted abuse at him, because he had not greeted the image, and because he invoked only the one Jesus Christ and not the Virgin Mary. Seeing this, he raised his voice: "I beseech you, Lord God, never to permit me to implore the help of anyone besides yourself alone." At the place of execution itself, when he wished to explain the reason for his condemnation, the guards would not allow it, and he was thrown down to the ground, almost by the torturer, as he got down from the cart. "My lords," he said, "I die for the Gospel of Jesus Christ and his word." And wishing to speak more fully, he began thus: "Christians, hear me." At this the officers, to stop him, raised a great uproar with cries of "Take him away, take him away, let him not say a word." "What," he said, "will you not let me declare to the people that I die not as a heretic but as a Christian?" "No indeed," the others shouted. "Oh, why not?" Then he spoke in a low voice into the ear of a certain little Carmelite, who had earlier converted him. Next the executioner ordered him to climb the ladder. There he began to cry out: "Lord, hasten to help me, and do not delay; do not despise the work of your hands. Forgive these men, for they do not know what they are doing. My brothers, my lords, the scholars, I beg you to devote yourselves to the Gospel, for the word of God alone remains for ever. Learn the knowledge of the will of God. Do not fear those who have power over the body only and not over the soul. Finally he said: "This flesh struggles wonderfully against the Spirit, but I will cast it off at once. Lord, into your hands I commend my soul. My lords, pray to God for me." And again and again he repeated this prayer: "Lord my God, into your hands I commend my soul." At last the executioner shook him on the ladder so that he would be choked; and so the godly man breathed his last, and his body was afterwards consumed by fire.

units.la: MARTINVS HOEVRBLOC, Gandauus.
units.tr: MARTIN HOEVRBLOC, of Ghent.

units.la: GAndauū Flandriæ metropolis, vrbs amplißima, inter alia quæ accepit bonitatis diuinæ testimonia, maximum hoc merito numerandum est, quòd plurimos verè Christianos & pios homines habuerit, qui rectam salutis viam, Iesum Christum scilicet, docere omnino conati sunt. Illa verò, ut pleraque omnes faciunt, nō modò nullam ex eo gratiam habuit, sed veritati pertinacißimè semper restitit, ut quos placidè excipere debuerat, crudelem in modum trucidarit. Quod cùm multis constet exemplis, tum supplicium de Martino Hœurbloccio piscium mercatore, religionis ac iustitiæ prætextu sumptū octauo die Maij. M.D.XLV, turpissimam illius urbis ingratitudinem, atque insignem crudelitatem satis & super testatur. Nam quum ille in tenebris adhuc manens, omnis generis voluptatibus indulgeret, libidinum atque aliorum peccatorum, quorum ibi effrænis ad perniciem est licentia, particeps esset: obseruantißimus interea traditionum atque decretorum Antichristi, omnibus quidem gratus erat, ac pacificè & sine inuidia viuebat, sub imperio nimirum fortis illius & armati principis degens. Verùm Dominus ille fortior miseri istius hominis misertus, à tyrannide Satanæ eum liberauit, eiusque oculos cœno illo barbarico oppletos, aperuit. id verò opera primùm & concione cuiusdam Parochi, qui nonnulla subinde ex purioris doctrinæ fontibus hausta, cōcionibꝰ suis intexebat, populoque gelidè satis ac trepidè ministrabat. Martinus quidem ex iis fructum faciebat, & quicquid boni dicebat, tam avidè arripiebat ut ab illo immutatus fuerit, ac deinceps ab improborum consuetudine recedens, sese ad meliorem vitam converterit: pauperum domos tam noctu quàm interdiu frequentabat, consolando & reipsos iuuās, nec sibi nec facultatibus parcens quo ægroto aut inopi subueniret. Dominus autem in hoc homine mirificè suam gratiam extulit, opusque suum prosecutus est. nam ex quo cor illius, virtute Spiritus sui in quadam concione iam dicti Parochi tetigit, domum ille reuersus res suas omnes compositi, summo studio, quippe ingentem sitim iustitiæ explere cupiens, inuestigauit piæ ac sanæ doctrinæ homines, à quibus amplius in pietate erudiri posset. Ac quo melius instituetur[?] urbe egressus, per tres menses vicina loca circumijt, in quibus viros pios atq; fideles degere intellexerat. Postquam vero Gandauum redijt multò quàm antea in verae religionis doctrina instructior: summam admirationem ciuibus attulit tam subita ac noua in hoc homine vitae mutatio. Pauci admodum nouae creaturae effectorem agnoscentes Christū, gloriam ei debitam exhibuerunt: maxima vero hominum pars, vt fit, diuinum istud opus calumniantes, quod à Spiritu Dei profectu erat, errori atque seditioni attribuebant. Tum etiam Satanae administri & reliqui qui Antichristi insignia gerunt, ac praesertim stigmatici illi Franciscani, quibus re salua & incolumi Martinus, adhuc idololatra cum esset, profuerat, videntes tam opimam praedam velut e faucibus ipsorum ereptam, conspirarunt aduersus ipsum, eo quod cum illorum superstitionibus & idolomanijs communicare nollet, sed acriter eas reprehenderet. deinde quod fideles in vinculis audacter adiret, & consolarctur[?], eosdemque ad supplicium quum ducerentur, pijs admonitionibus prosequeretur, neque cessaret usque ad locum poenae destinatum consolari, atque verbo Dei eos confirmare: idque publice atque in oculis omnium. Monitus autem per Parochum vt ad sacramentum altaris sumendum veniret: respondit se velle sumere sacramenta Domini nostri Iesu Christi, idque omnes ecclesias habere pro sanctis, vbi pure verbum Dei annunciatur. quare, inquit Parocho, si tibi placet (vt istiusmodi ecclesiae ministrum decet, & pium pastorem) administrare sacramentum ex mandato Christi, gratissimū mihi feceris, & libentissimè accedā. Id autem se nec posse nec audere respondit Parochus: verum multis apud eum precibus instabat, vt contentus consueto more, cum caeteris ad altare accederet. His itaque rebus compertis, & ad Antichristi assectas qui Martino assiduè infidiabantur, delatis, tandem comprehensus & in carcerem coniectus fuit: paulóque post iam in vinculis interrogatus fuit per Ludices, quinam essent suae sectae, eosque vt nominaret precabus minisque incitabant. Respondit ipse, quód ea ratione illos in odium & graue periculum vocare sibi videretur. id quod non putaret licere vllo modo per secundam Legis tabulâ. proinde graues tormentorum cruciatus perpeti malle, quàm illorum nomina prodere: Attamen si vestrum aliquis, inquit, me hac in re aduersus prioris tabulae praecepta peccare, [?]er Scripturam ostendere possit, nō recusò equidē Dei honorem præponere fratrū meorum commoditatibus: paratus facere quicquid nobis in ea præscriptum est, seruatis suo quibusque ordine rebus. Interrogatus dein à monachis quid de sacramento altaris sentiret. respondit merum esse Deum panaceum, si ex decreto Papæ administretur. Protinus excæperunt ipsi, Non igitur credis corpus Iesu Christi esse in manibus sacerdotis, quum Missam celebrat?Cùm autem Martinus ad hæc dudum taceret, nec tamen cucullati illi asini, molesti esse desinerent, incitando eum ut loqueretur: dixit, Christum tam malè ab ipsis tractatum, ut in manus eorum redire nolit amplius. Tum isti nebulones(toti in hoc ut serui Dei omnibus iniquitatibus exerceant, molestiam molestia cumulent, atque afflictionem afflictioni addant: quod contrà Dominus vertit in suorum consolationē, quando iis spiritum prudentiæ largitur, quò aduersariis resistant, eosque attonitos reddant) prosecuti sunt priorem de sacramento altaris quæstionem. Quandoquidem, inquiunt, ais nudum esse sacramentum, cur tanti facis, illud sub utraque specie recipere? Ad hæc ille: Elementa quidem per se nuda remanere, panem scilicet panem, ac vinum, vinum: sed si ex præcepto Iesu Christi exhiberentur, elementa tum sibi esse in sacrosancta signa magni illius mysterij, quod nobiscum communicauit summus ille animarum Pastor, Iesus Christus. Quòd autem exhibitionem sub utraque specie tanti faceret, id icàrco se urgere, quia neminem putaret mortalium tam arrogantem vel temerarium esse debere, qui ulla ratione Christi institutionem immutaret, atque ad eâ aliquid adderet, aut ex ea demeret quicquam: quoniam ipse Deus & verus homo, satis fuisset sapiens ad prævidendum incommoda, quæ acuti Ecclesiæ istorum doctores postmodò effinxerant. Tandem vir pius, post multas habitas magna tormentorum vi quæstiones, ut homines suæ opinionis accusaret, nec quicquam extorquerent carnifices, octauo, ut suprà posuimus, die Maij, deductus est ad confessum consiliariorum Flandriæ, qui in ea urbe suam sedem habent, in Castellum quod Comitis appellatur: ibique quòd sæpe munero[?] clandestinos, propter metum Pharisæorum, conuentus & piorum cætus adiisset: quódque sinistrè[?] de maiestate sacramenti sentiret: purgatorium Papæ, & preculas pro defunctis prorsus reijceret, atq; subinde de errore admonitus non desisteret, neque mutare animum unquam voluisset: his de causis lata est aduersus Martinum sententia, vt ductus ad forum, quod vocat Pharaelidis, viuꝰ in eo combureretur, atq; in cinere corpꝰ redigeretur, cum amissione omnium facultatum. Cumq; iam in theatro staret alligandus ad palū, monachis cinctus, quidam Franciscanus ad illum dixit, Martine, nisi conuertaris modò, ex hoc igne transfibis ad ignem æternum. Cui ille modestè admodum, Non est, inquit, tuum iudicare. Importuna autem hæc monachi ad Martinum oratio, tantam populo offensionem attulit, vt postmodò carmina ad ignominiam istiusmodi rasorum composita, vulgò per plateas decantata fuerint. Hœurbloccius itaque crudelem hanc & probrosam apud homines morte, pretiosam verò & gloriosam in conspectu Filij Dei & Angelorum, mirabili constantia pertulit, ad confusionem hostium veritatis, & confirmationem Ecclesiæ Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui è cineribus suorum martyrum (quicquid Satan & ministri eius machinentur) tanquàm è bona semente, frugem ac messem vberrimam producit.
units.tr: Ghent, the metropolis of Flanders and a very large city, has received many tokens of divine goodness, and among the greatest of these must be counted that it has had many truly Christian and godly men who strove above all to teach the right way of salvation, namely Jesus Christ. But the city, as most places do, not only got no benefit from this but always stubbornly resisted the truth, and it slaughtered in a cruel manner those whom it ought to have received gently. This is established by many examples, and the execution of Martin Hoeurbloc, a fish merchant, carried out under the pretext of religion and justice on 8 May 1545, bears witness more than enough to that city's shameful ingratitude and remarkable cruelty. For while he was still living in darkness, he indulged in every kind of pleasure and took part in the lusts and other sins, for which there is unrestrained licence there to the city's ruin. Meanwhile he was most observant of the traditions and decrees of Antichrist, and he was indeed liked by everyone and lived peaceably and without envy, under the rule, of course, of that strong and armed prince, Satan. But that stronger Lord took pity on this wretched man, freed him from the tyranny of Satan, and opened his eyes, which were filled with that barbarous mire. This was first done through the work and sermon of a certain parish priest, who from time to time wove into his sermons some things drawn from the purer springs of doctrine, but who ministered to the people in a rather cold and timid way. Martin indeed profited from these things, and he seized on whatever good he heard so eagerly that he was transformed by it, and afterwards, turning away from the company of the wicked, he converted himself to a better life. He visited the houses of the poor by night as well as by day, comforting them and helping them in person, sparing neither himself nor his goods to assist the sick or needy. The Lord, moreover, wonderfully displayed his grace in this man and carried his work forward. For from the time that his heart was touched by the power of his Spirit in a sermon of the aforesaid parish priest, he returned home, settled all his affairs with the greatest zeal, and, desiring to satisfy his great thirst for righteousness, sought out men of pure and sound doctrine from whom he could be further instructed in godliness. And so that he might be better taught, he left the city and for three months travelled round the neighbouring places, where he had learned that godly and faithful men dwelt. When he returned to Ghent, he was far better instructed in the doctrine of the true religion than before, and this sudden and new change in the man brought the citizens great astonishment. Only a very few, recognising Christ as the author of the new creation, gave him the glory due to him; but the greater part of the people, as usually happens, slandered this divine work, which had proceeded from the Spirit of God, and ascribed it to error and sedition. Then also the servants of Satan and the rest who bear the marks of Antichrist, and especially those stigmatic Franciscans, to whom Martin, while he was still an idolater, had been useful in keeping their rewards safe and sound, seeing such a rich prey snatched, as it were, from their jaws, conspired against him, because he refused to share in their superstitions and idolatries but sharply rebuked them. Further, because he boldly visited the faithful in their chains and comforted them, and when they were led to execution he accompanied them with godly exhortations, and did not cease to console them and strengthen them with the Word of God right up to the place of punishment, and that publicly and in the sight of all. Admonished through the parish priest to come to receive the sacrament of the altar, he replied that he wished to receive the sacraments of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that he regarded as holy all churches where the Word of God is purely proclaimed. Therefore, he said to the priest, if it pleased him (as a minister of such a church and a godly pastor should) to administer the sacrament by the command of Christ, he would do me a great kindness and I would come most willingly. The priest answered that he neither could nor dared to do so; yet he pressed him with many entreaties to be content with the customary practice and approach the altar with the others. When these things had been discovered and reported to the followers of Antichrist, who were constantly lying in wait for Martin, he was at last seized and thrown into prison. Shortly afterwards, while he was already in chains, the judges questioned him as to who the members of his sect were, and they urged him with entreaties and threats to name them. He replied that by doing so he would seem to himself to be bringing them into hatred and grave danger, which he did not think was permitted in any way by the second table of the Law. Therefore he preferred to endure the severest tortures rather than betray their names. Nevertheless, he said, if any of you can show from Scripture that I sin in this matter against the precepts of the first table, I do not refuse to put the honour of God before the advantage of my brothers, and I am ready to do whatever is prescribed for us in it, each thing being kept in its proper order. Then, questioned by the monks as to what he thought of the sacrament of the altar, he replied that it was a mere panacea if it was administered by the decree of the Pope. Immediately they retorted: "Do you not therefore believe that the body of Jesus Christ is in the hands of the priest when he celebrates Mass?" Martin, who had been silent for a while in answer to this, but since those hooded donkeys would not stop pestering him, urging him to speak, said that Christ had been treated so badly by them that he no longer wished to return into their hands. Then those scoundrels (wholly intent on this, that, as servants of God, they might exercise every kind of wickedness, heap trouble upon trouble and add affliction to affliction, which the Lord on the contrary turns to the comfort of his people, when he gives them the spirit of prudence to resist their adversaries and make them astonished) pursued the earlier question about the sacrament of the altar. "Since," they said, "you say that the sacrament is a bare thing, why do you make so much of receiving it under both kinds?" To this he replied: the elements, indeed, remain bare in themselves, bread as bread and wine as wine; but when they are presented according to the precept of Jesus Christ, then they are for us the holy signs of that great mystery which that supreme Shepherd of souls, Jesus Christ, has shared with us. As for his insisting so much on the administration under both kinds, he pressed the point because he thought no mortal ought to be so arrogant or rash as to change in any way the institution of Christ, or add anything to it or take anything away from it, since God himself and true man was wise enough to foresee the inconveniences which the clever teachers of that Church later invented. At last, after many examinations under great force of torture, in which the executioners could extract nothing to accuse him of being a member of their opinion, the godly man was led, on 8 May as we have said above, before the council of the Flemish counsellors, who have their seat in that city, in the castle called the Count's Castle. There he was condemned for having often gone to secret meetings and gatherings of the godly out of fear of the Pharisees, for thinking ill of the majesty of the sacrament, for utterly rejecting the Pope's purgatory and prayers for the dead, and for not giving up these errors even when often admonited, nor ever being willing to change his mind. For these reasons sentence was passed against Martin that he should be taken to the forum which they call the Friday Market, and there be burned alive, his body reduced to ashes, and that he should lose all his goods. And when he stood on the scaffold, about to be tied to the stake, surrounded by monks, a certain Franciscan said to him: "Martin, unless you are converted now, from this fire you will pass to the eternal fire." To him Martin replied very modestly: "It is not yours to judge." But this unseemly speech of the monk to Martin caused such offence to the people that afterwards songs composed to shame such shavelings were sung commonly through the streets. Thus Hoeurbloc endured with wonderful constancy a death cruel and shameful in the eyes of men, but precious and glorious in the sight of the Son of God and of the angels, to the confusion of the enemies of the truth and the strengthening of the Church of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, from the ashes of his martyrs (whatever Satan and his ministers may plot), produces a most abundant crop and harvest, as from good seed.

units.la: IOANNES DE BVCK ipsiúsque vxor, & NICOLAVS VAN POVLE.
units.tr: ## JOHN DE BUCK and his wife, and NICHOLAS VAN POULE.

units.la: Ostridie autem, qui dies erat non° Maij, ibidem capite obtruncati suerunt, Gandaui videlicet, eiusdem Consilij Flandriæ sententia, Ioannes de Buck professione Sartor, & alter quidam nominatus Nicolaus van Poule. Vxor item iam dicti Nicolai de Buck, viua in terra defossa fuit, ob easdem causas, quas in sententia pij Martyris Hœurbloccij recitauimus. Atq; omnes isti præsentissimo animo morte obierunt. Deo autem immortali honos & gloria tribuatur, à quo solo virtus hæc admirabilis proficiscitur.
units.tr: On the following day, which was the Nones of May, they were beheaded in the same place at Ghent, by sentence of the same Council of Flanders: John de Buck, by trade a tailor, and another man named Nicholas van Poule. The wife of the aforesaid Nicholas de Buck was likewise buried alive for the same causes which we recited in the sentence of the godly martyr Hoeurbloc. And all of them died with the most steadfast courage. Let honour and glory be given to the immortal God, from whom alone this admirable virtue proceeds.

units.la: Liber tertius Actionum MARTYRVM.
units.tr: Liber tertius Actionum MARTYRVM.

units.la: Historia excidii Merindolii, Cabrierae, vicinorumque locorum.
units.tr: Historia excidii Merindolii, Cabrierae, vicinorumque locorum.

units.la: QVOD[?] priore huius historiae Martyrum cõfectione atque editione, daturos nos diximus pleniorẽ ac perfectiorẽ de Merindolii ac Cabrierae, vicinorumq; locorum excidio historiam, id nos iam vtcunque praestare voluimus. Itaque tertius hic Actionum liber non immeritò ab iis sumet exordium, qui in Provincia Gallica, ea loca incoluerunt in quibus non duo aut tres memorandi & cognoscendi sunt ob Euangelium morte multati, sed populus certus, & maximus numerus vtriusq; sexus hominum, atq; etiam puerorum & infantium, qui omnes malorum acerbitates omniáque genera mortis pertulerunt. Ea verò tantū attingenus quae ad cognitionem institutionemq; fidelium pertinere videbuntur.
units.tr: Since in the earlier compilation and publication of this history of the Martyrs we said that we would give a fuller and more complete history of the destruction of Merindol and Cabrières and the neighbouring places, we have now endeavoured to supply it, in whatever manner we could. This third book of the Acts therefore rightly takes its beginning from those who dwelt in those places in the Gallic Province, where not two or three men are to be remembered and known as put to death for the Gospel, but a whole people and a very great number of men and women of both sexes, and even of boys and infants, who all suffered the bitterness of evils and every kind of death. We shall touch only on those things which seem to pertain to the knowledge and instruction of the faithful.

units.la: Qui altius horum hominum genus repetunt, aiunt à CC. fermè annis è Pedemontio in Provincia profectos, vt ibi habitaret, & multa loca inculta ac deserta emphyteusis titulo ac perpetuae locationis nomine accepisse: quae ab illis diligentissimè exculta, maximā frumēti, vini, olei amygdalarū, aliarúmque frugum ac fructuū copiam protulerunt: in re etiā pecuaria, greges & armenta bona & copiosa habuisse: priusquàm autē illi eò se contulissent, locum Merindolii inhabitabilem deser-tum atque sterilem planè fuisse.
units.tr: Those who trace the origin of this people further back say that about two hundred years ago they set out from Piedmont into the Province to live there, and that they received many uncultivated and deserted lands under the title of emphyteusis, that is, by a perpetual lease. These lands they cultivated with great diligence and brought forth a very great abundance of wheat, wine, oil, almonds and other crops and fruits; they also had good and plentiful flocks and herds in livestock. Before they went there, however, the place of Merindol had been plainly uninhabitable, deserted and barren.

units.la: Sed boni homines, Deum timentes, in quibus Deus semper exiguum aliquod pietatis semen conseruare voluit, quanuis dissipati, atque ab hominum societate segregati, cum bestijs in terris desertis vitam degere coacti fuerunt: quas tamen Domini benedictione & labore improbo fertiles reddiderunt. Interea tamen mundus eos maximè detestans, ita exhorruit, in eósque omnia probrorum & criminum genera congesit, vt indigni planè quos terra sustineret, viderentur. Varijs autem nominibus sunt appellati, pro varietate regionum ac locorum, quae incoluerunt. Nam in regione Lugdunensi, Pauperes de Lugduno vocati fuerunt: in extremis Sarmatiae Liuoniæque partibus, Lolardi sunt nominati: in Flandria & Arthesia, à loco deserto, ac lupis expositio, Turrelupini appellati: in Delphinatu fumo cōteptu Chagnardi dicti, quasi apricarij, quod in locis apricis sine domibus tectisq; desiderent. Appellatio vero waldensium maxime omnium peruulgata illis remansit, donec nomen Lutheranorum prolatum, quod inuidia, odio, infamiaq; cetera omnia opprobria superauit. Sed in his tātis calūnijs & criminibus, reliquus populus, qui ad pedē Alpiū, & qui Merindolij, Cabrieraeque degit, ita pie, ac modeste semper vixit, vt in eorum tota consuetudine ac vitae ratione, timor Dei maxime cluxerit, summa fides & iustitia perspecta fuerit.In exigua cognitionis luce, quam Dominus eis dederat, in eam vnam curam incumbebant, vt id quod habebant, magis quotidie accenderent, nullis rebus aut facultatibus suis parcētes, siue libri Scripturae sacrae parādi[?] essent, siue homines optimo ingenio praediti, in doctrina pietatis instituendi, siue huc illucq; mittēdi[?], etiā vsq; ad extremas mūdi partes, vbi aliquē lucis salutaris radiū exortū esse audiuerat.Nā anno M.D.XXX, cum intellexissent, in quibusdam Germanorum atq; Heluetiorum ciuitatibus Euangelium annūtiari, ad eas duos ex suis miserūt, Georgiū Maurclū[?], Fresmeriae[?] natū in Delphinatu, qui apud eos concionatoris munus obibat, homine pium, & quem in scholis erudiendum informandumque curauerant, & Petrum Latonum Borgundum, vt de fidei pietatisque doctrina cum fidelibus ac prudentibus ecclesiarum ministris communicarent, eorumque formam rationemque totam in colendo Deo cognoscerent, ac priuatim eorum sententiam exquirerent de quibusdam rebus, quae tum ipsis nonnullam dubitationem adferebant. Quum itaque hi duo abunde omnia communicassent cum primarijs in Ecclesia Dei viris, videlicet Basileae cum OEcolampadio, Argentinae cum Bucero & Capitone, Bernae cum Berktoldo Hallero, ac per Borgundiam reditū instituissent, Petrus Latomus Diuione captus, in carcerem coniectus est: Georgius vero solus Merindolium est reuersus, cum libris & literis ac mandatis, quae ab ecclesijs Germanorum adferebat.Eò autem cum venisset, omnia legationis suae capita exposuit, eisque declarauit publice, in quot & quantis erroribus versarentur, in quos veteres ipsorum ministri, quos Barbas eorum idiomate, id est, Auunculos vocabant, eos coniecissent, atque à recta pietatis via abduxissent. Hæc populus cum accepisset, tanto studio ecclesiæ emendandæ commotus fuit, ut ex sociis quos in Apulia & Calabria habebant, natu grandiores, & usu rerum graviores peritioresque accersiverint, ut cum his de emendatione correctioneque ecclesiæ consilium caperent. Res autem ita fuit tractata atque agitata, ut usque ad Aquas Sextias, quæ urbs curialis est totius Provinciæ, peruenerit, aurèsque Episcoporum, sacerdotum, monachorum, qui sunt in Provincia, vehementer commouerit. Inter cæteros prodijt quidam monachus ex ordine Dominicanorum, Ioannes de Roma appellatus, homo ad sævitiam & crudelitatem natura disciplináque implicatus, qui ab Episcopis, legatóque Aucnionensi inquisitionis venia postulata adversus eos qui sectæ waldensis & Lutheranæ nomine suspecti essent, ex eo tempore nunquam desitit fideles homines vexare & affligere omnibus tormentis, quæ ad summam doloris acerbitatem excogitare atque exquirere poterat. E multis ab eo exquisitis tormentis, hoc unum fuit singulare, eique imprimis usitatum. implebat ocreas adipe ferucscente[?], quas tibiis eorum aptabat, quos scamno alligatos & supinos interrogabat: eo modo ut tibiæ eorum super exiguum ignem subiectum dependerent. Primi quos hoc tormenti genere cruciauit, fuerunt Michelotus Serra Cabrierensis, Marrus appellatus, & Guilelmus[?] Melius, & multi post illos alij, quos postremò grauissima atque acerbissima morte multabat. Itaque Franciscus rex Galliæ de eius monachi singulari atque inaudita crudelitate certior factus, ad supremam Provinciæ curiam seu parlamentum literas misit, quibus iubebat illum quàm diligentissimè comprehendi, causaque eius informata & cognita cum ita condemnari, ut ipse quamprimùm de illius condemnatione certior fieret. Hic Ioannes de Roma, intellecto per fautores periculo suo, Auenionem se recepit, ut frueretur ea præda & rapina quam insignis latro in bonis fortunisque Merindolensium fecerat. Verùm præter spem suam ipse prædo à domesticis fuit expoliatus, qui ei opima illa spolia, latrocinio parta, eripuerunt. Paulò itaque post incidit in morbum ita grauem & acerbum, ut nulla adhibita fomenta aliquam doloris leuationem afferre possent. nullus erat, qui ob fœtorem qui ab ipsius corpore manabat, prope eum cõsistere posset:ne ipsi sodales Dominicani ferre poterant, imò ne ipse quidē iam ferre poterat teterrimum illum odorem, qui è carne corporis exulcerata, ac vermibus scaturiente exhalabat. Dolore eum cruciante ac premente, sæpe ita exclamavit, Quis me liberabit aut occidet? neque enim voluntas necis sibi consciscendæ deerat, sed vis & facultas. Itaque in his tantis cruciatibus doloribúsque corporis, atque in summa horrendáque animi desperatione, homo impius & sœuus, qui alios crudelissimè necauerat vitam suam miserrimè finiuit. Vix etiam inventus quisquam est, qui eum vellet attingere, vt mandaret sepulturæ, nisi monachus cius ordinis è Novitiorū gradu, qui pro optimo sepulturæ iure atque honore, correptum & ligatū pedibus cadauer in foueam ad id paratam pertraxit. Post mortem huius nefandæ belluæ, episcopus Sextiensis persecutionem excepit & continuavit, vtens ad eam opera Peironeti officialis sui, multósque in carcerem coniiciendos curauit, quorum nonnulli, magnitudine tormentorum ac dolorum, veritatem abiurarunt: alij vero qui firmiores & constantiores inuenirentur, postea quam hæresis damnati essent, in manus tradebātur ordinarij iudicis, qui tunc erat Mciranus[?], homo in hoc crudelitatis genere nobilitatus, qui sine vlla causæ informatione & cognitione, cos quos Officialis hæreticos pronūciauerat, vltimo mortis supplicio assicicebat. Is non multo post tempore, recepit mercedem suæ iniustitiæ ac sœuitiæ meritam, quemadmodum postea videbimus. Porrò post obitum Cuisineti, optimi præsidis, parlamentum Sextiense complures fideles morte multauit, quandiu Dominus Reuesti, in ea summa curia locum primi præsidis obtinuit. qui quidem ea iurisdictione ac potestate abdicatus, Reuestum domum suam se recepit: ubi ea vi morbi & sœuitia correptus atque agitatus fuit, propter quam vxor ipsius, cæterique propius accedere ad eum non audebant. Ita rabie ac furore mortuus, dignas suæ iniquitatis & crudelitatis pœnas dedit. Eius officium & munus in ea iurisdictione, magister Bartholomæus Chassaneus excepit. Quo præside, anno à mortalibus salute restituta millesimo quingentesimo quadragesimo, Procuratore generali Regio in suprema Senatus curia, postulante, dicta fuit ad sistendum iudicio dies Andreæ Maynardo, Ioanni Cambrio, Francisco Maynardo, Ioanni Bonio, Antonio Palenco, Guilielmo Armantio, Michaeli Maynardo, Ioanni Palenco, Mondono Brumerollo, Facio Bernardo, Merindolij pagi ciuibus, ut quibusdam rebus de quibus in eos inquiri cœptum esset, respondere possent, ad statum ut tempus vadimonium obirent. Ac omnes quidem ad diem præstitutum ut vadimonium obirent Aquas Sextias profecti sunt: egerúntque cū doctissimis quibusque patronis, ut haberetur forensi ritu deliberatio, videretúrque quêadmodum ipsos se gerere, quomodo negotium administrari oporteret. Quibus patroni procuratoresque responderunt, minimè sibi licitum esse cuiquam ipsorum copiam consilij sui facere, quos à religione desciuisse, atque in impietatis Lutheranæ suspicionem incidisse cognouissent: tametsi quidem patronorum unus aliquis appellatos seorsum universos ac semotis arbitris admonuit diligenter, non debere eos omnino in Senatum venire, nisi forte sensim igni concremari, igni, inquam, [?]straminco, idque ipsum indicta causa, studerent ac cuperent. [?]sic cum ab eodem Senatu cautum atque constitutum esse. Hac oratione perculsi Merindolienses vehementer obstupuerunt, maximè verò cùm plerosque viros bonos torqueri tam inhumaniter, ac cruciari suis oculis ipsi vidissent: nullam ob aliam causam damnatos, depressósque ad supplicium, quàm quòd sermones habuissent Lutheranos, animaduersos à Theologis doctoribus, eósque ad extremum usque tutati essent: cùm hi quidem sermones omnes & cum verissima essent coniuncti pietate, & locupletissimo Scripturarum testimonio confirmati. Itaque cùm patroni illius oratione, tum co spectaculo perterriti Merindolienses, vadimonium deseruerunt, eóque nomine factum postea Senatusconsultum est, inde semper Merindoliense Senatusconsultum appellatum: de quo maxima diuturnáque suit Lutetiæ in Senatu, interposita scilicet à procuratore Regio prouocatione, contentio. Hoc Senatusconsulto non modò Merindolienses ij, quos appellatos à Senatu docuimus, tanquam delati conuictique imminutæ humanæ diuinæque maiestatis, flammæ, quam primùm comprehendi possent, adiudicati, eorumque proscriptæ possessiones fisco addictæ : verumetia omnes quicunque Merindolium ipsum (quo in loco fuisse octoginta circiter urbana prædia feruntur) tum viri tum mulieres incolerent ac inhabitarent, ne paruulis quidem exceptis infantibus, eidem incendio traditi damnatique fuerunt. Eodem Senatus consulto decretum, ut omnia, quæ tum illic essent, ædificia deturbarentur: vicus totus excanderetur: omnes ad unum ab eo vico lapides, tam olivæ, quam alius generis arbores (ut ea deserta vagaque colonia, habitationis in posterum occasio præcideretur) radicitus interlucarentur ac intercidentur. Ac senatus consultum quidem illud omnibus hominibꝰ adeo mirabile visum fuit, nullus ut esset in Provincia tota locus, quo non in loco de eo aliqua semper à patronis ac literatis hominibus excitaretur maxima contentione disputatio. Nec deerant qui mirari se, profiteri publicè non vererentur, Senatum illum in tantam insaniam incidere potuisse, decretum ut tale faceret, tam perspicuè iniquum, tam ab omni non modò civili iure & ratione, sed etiam æquabili vitæ statu ipso, communique sensu humanitatis alienum. Violato prætereà solenni iureiurando illo, quod in omni Curia suprema ab hominibus muneris alicuius forensis publici functionem petentibus fieri consuevet: Iuste se videlicet æquabiliterque, ex præscripto divinæ Legis, popularium que regni constitutionum esse iudicaturos, eóque iudicaturos modo, ut suis sententiis Deo quidem ipsi plurimum ad honorem deferretur, ius suum unicuique conservaretur ac tribueretur. Alij contrà, qui decretum illud æquum affirmarent, in omni Lutherana causa neminem teneri iudicem iuris ac rationi locum dare, Legum aut constitutionum ratione habere, dicebat: Iudices, utram in partem Statuerent ferréntque sententiam, errore duci non posse: nimirum id agentes, ut qui Lutheranorum nomine suspecti essent opprimerentur. Excipiebant patroni, cæterique non indocti viri, ex eo quod hi iam in sermonem intulissent, facilè consequi, Iudices huius ætatis eandem usurpare planè rationem in prosequendis iudicijs Christianis eis, qui vulgò Lutherani postulentur, quam olim Sacrificos, Scribas, Pharisæos in insectando, condemnandóque D.nostro Iesu Christo, sequutos Euangelium testatur. Atque eo sanè modo illius decreti fama momento percrebrescebat: neque usquam aut convetus fiebat ull° aut celebrabatur convivium, ubi de eo non agitaretur ultrò citróque certatio. Quinctiam duodecimo circiter die postea quàm interpositū decretū illud fuit, splendidissimum convivium in ea urbe apparatum aiunt: eóque acceptum Bartholomæum Chassanæum præsidem, complurésque tū Senatores, tum alios viros clarissimos, summaque apud populum authoritatis: Archiepiscopum etiam Arelatensem, ipsúmque Aquensem Episcopum: denique fœminas urbe tota nobiliores: atque unam quandam ex eis, quæ nuntio rumore populari scortum Episcopi Sextiensis vulgò tenerétur. Hæc ipsa, vixdum cum esset accubitum his verbis Præsidem adorta, sic ait: Domine præses, num senatusconsultum illud quod in Merindolienses istos Lutheranos superioribus diebus factum est, executioni mandandum jubere vis? Ad hæc, conniuens, nihil omnino præses. Mox nobilis vir quidam petere cœpit, Ecquod tandem senatusconsulto in Merindolienses factum esset. Illa verò eodem quo factum esset modo à capite progrediendo ad calcem memoriter ac jucundè recitauit nihil oblita, haud secus atq; si memoriam ipsius longè ante recordari cœpisset. Audiebatur interim à convivis summa cum attentione & silentio, dum sermocinationi suæ finem atque modū statuit. Ac tum quidem Dominus Alencius, vir & pietate insignis, & in literis minimè contemnendus homo: Didicisti, inquit, aut hanc ab aliquo fabulâ, qui rem in illud vellet adductam jam esse discrimen: aut decretū hujusmodi ab aliquo miliebri senatulo factū & profectum est. Bona verba domine Alenci, inquit senator Senensis: non id, non id inquam, commentitium est, quod audiuisti, sed plane decretum Senatus. Nec verò tibi crebrius est utendum eadē libertate dissolutionéque verborum, nisi Provinciæ quoque Curiā concilium senatúmque fœminarum appellari mauis oportere. Alencius tum ipse locum excusationi quærere, déque suâ perpetua erga viros illos voluntate polliceri: profiteri palàm nihil se quicquam velle dicere unde ullius supremæ Curiæ dignitati detractum esse videri posset: adduci tamen omnino non posse, verum id ut esse quod mulier illa commemorauisset, arbitraretur: decreto nempe Senatus (qui quidem in Provincia haberi cœptus sit) totam Merindoliorum nationem: fœminarum, proh dolor! impotentiam: miserè vagientes in cunis infantes, hos inquam vniuersos gladio crudeliter adiudicatos: vici[?] totius ædificia omnia, ne qua eius in posterum memoriæ vis existeret, ruinis & incendio: culpa præsertim ac vitio duodecim nescio quorum hominum, quos in Senatu præsto non fuisse, vadimoniumque deseruisse constaret. Nec ipse quoque, inquit D.Belloiocius, persuaderi mihi facile patior, tale decretum, tam alienum à ratione, tam expers omnis humanitatis, tam impie Turcicum, tã Geticum crudeliter ex Curia profisci potuisse: præsertim cum quantum ego de Merindolis, quos iam olim me nosse memini permultos, iudicare sane possum, nihil in cis esse mihi videatur non cum integritate vitæ singulari, naturæq; bonitate quadam maximè coniunctum. Eximercetque hunc nobis, si videretur, scrupulum omnium optimè D.præses. scitum est enim, muliebri testimonio stari semper, ac fidem haberi non oportere. Mulier interea quæ Senatusconsultum aperuisset, expectandum sibi minimè putauit dum à præside responsum auferretur, sed conuersa quamprimum ad Episcopū Aquensem, Mirarer, inquit, nisi prosiluisset hic aliquis, qui sceleratorum illorum statim causam defensionemque suscipéret[?]. Sublatisque oculis in cælum, ac mulicbris iracundiæ tumore feruida: Vtinã, inquit, omnes qui sunt in prouincia Lutherani, ipsa denique tota Gallia, cornua in frontispicio gererent: non deessent vbique cornuti. Cui dominus Belloiocius extemporè, Vtinam scorta sacerdotum omnia loquerentur ea vocis articulatione, qua anseres. tum illa, Non est, ô Belloioci, sic obloquendum tandem matri nostræ Sanctæ Ecclesiæ: nullus vnquam canis crucifixo oblatrasse reperitur, qui non idem in rabiem actus aliquando sit. Aquensis tunc Episcopus arridere statim cœpit, leuiterque mulieris humerum percutiens, ac petens dicere: Per ordines sacrosanctos meos, gratissimum mihi fecisti, mea lux. Illa te perstrinxit eleganter, ô domine Belloioci, retincto[?], quæso, id quod ab illa tibi prælectu[?] fideliter ac præceptum est. Non moror, inquit Belloiocius ira paulò concitus magis, vestrum vtriusque gymnasiu:[?] nihil enim à vobis ambobus quod honestum quidem sit, assequi[?] possum. Itaque licet Episcopos vt plurimum atque sacerdotes flagitiosos, adulteros, cæcos, idololatras, raptores fallaces, latrones, depeculatores,
units.tr: But good men, fearing God, in whom God has always willed to preserve some small seed of piety, though they were scattered and cut off from human society, were forced to live among the beasts in deserted lands. Yet by the Lord's blessing and their unrelenting labour they made these lands fruitful. Meanwhile the world, detesting them most of all, was so horrified that it heaped upon them every kind of disgrace and accusation, so that they seemed utterly unworthy of being endured by the earth. They were called by various names, according to the diversity of the regions and places they inhabited. In the region of Lyons they were called the Poor Men of Lyons. In the farthest parts of Sarmatia and Livonia they were named Lollards. In Flanders and Artois, from the deserted place and the wolves to which they were exposed, they were called Turrelupins. In Dauphiné, under the scorn of smoke, they were called Chagnards, as if "sunbathers," because they remain in sunny places without houses or roofs. The name Waldenses, however, the most widely spread of all, remained with them, until the name Lutherans came into use, which surpassed all other reproaches in envy, hatred and infamy. But amid all these slanders and accusations, the rest of the people, who dwell at the foot of the Alps and who live at Merindol and Cabrières, always lived so piously and modestly that in their whole manner of life and conduct the fear of God shone out above all, and the greatest faith and justice were seen in them. In the small light of knowledge which the Lord had given them, they applied themselves to this one care: to kindle daily more and more what they had, sparing no resources or means of their own, whether it was a matter of procuring books of holy Scripture, or of training men of excellent talent in the teaching of piety, or of sending them here and there, even to the furthest parts of the world, wherever they had heard that some ray of saving light had risen. For in the year 1530, when they learned that the Gospel was being proclaimed in certain cities of Germany and Switzerland, they sent two of their own to them: Georges Maurel, born at Fresnières in Dauphiné, who served among them as a preacher, a pious man whom they had arranged to be educated and trained in schools, and Pierre Latomus of Burgundy, so that they might confer about the doctrine of faith and piety with the faithful and prudent ministers of the churches, learn their whole form and manner of worshipping God, and privately seek their opinion on certain matters which were then causing them some doubt. When these two had fully conferred on everything with the leading men in the Church of God, namely at Basel with Oecolampadius, at Strasbourg with Bucer and Capito, and at Bern with Berthold Haller, and had begun their return journey through Burgundy, Pierre Latomus was seized at Dijon and thrown into prison. Georges, however, returned alone to Merindol, bringing books, letters and instructions from the churches of Germany. When he got there he set out all the heads of his mission and declared publicly how many and how great were the errors in which they were living, into which their old ministers, whom they called Barbes in their own language, that is "uncles," had cast them and drawn them away from the right way of piety. When the people heard this, they were so moved by eagerness to reform the Church that they sent for the older men among their associates in Apulia and Calabria, men more experienced and weightier in affairs, to take counsel with them about the amendment and correction of the Church. The matter was so handled and pursued that it reached as far as Aix, which is the seat of the courts of the whole province, and it greatly stirred the ears of the bishops, priests and monks who are in the province. Among the rest there came forward a certain monk of the Dominican order, called John of Rome, a man by nature and training given over to savagery and cruelty, who, having sought from the bishops and the legate of Avignon a licence of inquisition against those who were suspected of the Waldensian and Lutheran sect, from that time never ceased to harass and afflict the faithful with every torment that he could devise and invent for the utmost bitterness of pain. Of the many torments he devised, this one was singular and was especially his favourite. He filled leggings with seething fat, which he fitted onto the shins of those whom he had bound to a bench and laid on their backs, and he questioned them in such a way that their shins hung over a small fire set below. The first whom he tortured with this kind of torment were Michel Serre of Cabrières, called Marre, and Guillaume Mello, and many others after them, whom at last he punished with the most grievous and cruel death. King Francis of France, having been informed of the singular and unheard-of cruelty of this monk, therefore sent a letter to the supreme court of the province, or parlement, ordering that he be seized as carefully as possible, and that, once his case had been looked into and examined, he be condemned, so that the king might be informed of his condemnation as soon as possible. John of Rome, learning through his supporters of his danger, withdrew to Avignon, so that he might enjoy the booty and plunder which this notorious robber had made of the goods and fortunes of the people of Merindol. But, contrary to his hope, this plunderer was himself stripped by his own household, who snatched away those rich spoils, won by theft. Soon afterwards he fell into a disease so grave and bitter that no remedies applied could bring him any relief. There was no one who could stand near him because of the stench that flowed from his body; even his fellow Dominicans could not bear it, nor indeed could he himself bear that most foul odour which breathed out from his flesh, ulcerated and swarming with worms. Tormented and oppressed by pain, he often cried out, "Who will free me or kill me?" For the will to take his own life was not lacking in him, but the power and the means were. So in these great torments and bodily pains, and in the extreme and dreadful despair of his mind, this impious and savage man, who had cruelly put so many to death, ended his life most wretchedly. Hardly anyone was found who would touch him so as to bury him, except a monk of his own order, of the rank of novices, who, for the best right and honour of burial, dragged the corpse, seized and bound by the feet, into a pit made ready for it. After the death of this unspeakable beast, the bishop of Sisteron took up and continued the persecution, using the services of Peironet, his officer, and he had many thrown into prison. Some of them, through the magnitude of the torments and pains, abjured the truth; but those who were found firmer and more constant, after they had been condemned as heretics, were handed over to the ordinary judge, who was then Mécran, a man made famous in this kind of cruelty, who, without any inquiry or examination of the case, put to the final penalty of death those whom the officer had pronounced heretics. He, not long after, received the reward of his injustice and cruelty that he deserved, as we shall see later. Moreover, after the death of Cuisinet, the excellent president, the parlement of Sisteron put many of the faithful to death, for as long as Lord Revest held the place of first president in that high court. He, indeed, having been deprived of that jurisdiction and power, withdrew to his own house at Revest, where he was seized and harassed by such violence of disease and savagery that his wife and the others did not dare to come near him. Dying thus in rage and fury, he paid the penalties due to his iniquity and cruelty. Master Barthélemy Chassanée took over his office and duty in that jurisdiction. Under him as president, in the year of salvation 1540, at the request of the royal Procurator-General in the supreme court of the Senate, a day was set for appearing before the judgement for Andrew Maynard, John Cambrio, Francis Maynard, John Bon, Antoine Palenc, Guillaume Armand, Michel Maynard, John Palenc, Mondon Brumerol, and Fache Bernard, citizens of the village of Merindol, so that they might answer about certain matters concerning which an inquiry had begun against them, and might undergo their bail at the appointed time. And indeed all of them set out for Aix to undergo their bail on the set day, and they consulted with the most learned advocates, so that a deliberation might be held in the forensic manner, and so that it might be seen how they ought to conduct themselves and how the matter ought to be managed. The advocates and attorneys answered them that it was in no way lawful for anyone to give them counsel, since they had learned that these men had departed from the religion and had fallen under suspicion of Lutheran impiety; although one of the advocates, taking them all aside and away from the hearers, warned them carefully that they ought by no means to come into the Senate, unless perhaps they were eager and wished to be burned slowly by fire, by fire, I say, of straw, and that without any case having been stated. Thus it was decided and settled by the same Senate. Dismayed by this speech, the people of Merindol were greatly astonished, most of all because they had seen with their own eyes many good men tortured so inhumanly and racked, condemned and brought down to punishment for no other reason than that they had preached Lutheran doctrines, which had been noticed by the theologian doctors, and that they had defended these doctrines to the very end, since these teachings were all joined with the truest piety and confirmed by the richest testimony of the Scriptures. So, terrified both by that speech of the advocates and by that spectacle, the people of Merindol abandoned their bail, and for this reason a decree of the Senate was afterwards made, which has always since been called the Merindol decree; about it there was for a long time a great dispute in the Senate at Paris, the royal procurator having lodged an appeal. By this decree those Merindolites whom we have shown were summoned by the Senate, as having been accused and convicted of diminishing divine and human majesty, were adjudged to the flames as soon as they could be seized, and their confiscated possessions were forfeited to the treasury. Moreover, all who lived and dwelt in Merindol itself (where there were said to be about eighty urban estates), men and women alike, not even infants excepted, were given over to the same fire and condemned. By the same decree it was ordered that all the buildings which then stood there should be pulled down, that the whole village should be levelled, and that all the stones from that village, and the olive trees as well as trees of every other kind, should be cut down and uprooted to the ground, so that the opportunity of habitation in the future might be cut off from that deserted and wandering colony. Indeed that decree seemed so astonishing to all men that there was no place in the whole province where some great dispute about it was not constantly stirred up with great contention by advocates and learned men. Nor were there lacking those who wondered and did not hesitate to declare publicly that the Senate could have fallen into such madness as to make a decree of this kind, so plainly unjust, so alien not only to all civil law and reason, but even to the equable order of life itself and to the common sense of humanity. Moreover, that solemn oath was violated which is customarily taken in every supreme court by men who seek the discharge of any public judicial office: namely, that they would judge justly and evenly, according to the precept of the divine Law and the constitutions of the realm, and would judge in such a way that by their sentences the greatest honour would be rendered to God himself, and each man's right would be preserved and assigned to him. Others, on the contrary, who affirmed that that decree was fair, said that in every Lutheran cause no judge was bound to give any place to law or reason, or to take account of statutes or constitutions; judges, they said, could not be led into error whichever way they decided and gave sentence, plainly intending that those who were suspected of the name of Lutheran should be crushed. The advocates and the other not unlearned men objected that from what these men had now brought into the discussion, it was easy to infer that the judges of this age were using exactly the same method in prosecuting Christian trials against those who are commonly accused of being Lutherans, as the Gospel bears witness that the priests, scribes and Pharisees once followed in harassing and condemning our Lord Jesus Christ. And in this way indeed the report of that decree spread through the city in a moment: no assembly met anywhere, and no feast was celebrated, where it was not debated back and forth. Moreover, about twelve days after that decree had been issued, they say a most splendid banquet was prepared in that city, and to it were invited President Barthélemy Chassanée, several senators as well as other men most distinguished and of the highest authority with the people, the Archbishop of Arles, the Bishop of Aix himself, and finally the noblest women of the whole city, and one of them who was commonly kept, as a rumour among the people reported, as the mistress of the Bishop of Sisteron. This woman, scarcely having taken her place at table, addressed the president with these words: "Lord President, do you wish that decree which was made a few days ago against those Lutheran Merindolites to be carried into execution?" To this the president made no reply at all, merely winking. Presently a certain noble man began to ask what decree had at last been made against the people of Merindol. She then recited it from beginning to end, exactly as it had been made, fluently and cheerfully, leaving nothing out, as though she had begun to recall it long before. Meanwhile she was heard by the guests with great attention and silence until she set an end and limit to her talk. Then Lord Alençon, a man distinguished both for piety and not at all contemptible in learning, said: "You have learned this from some fable-teller, who wanted to bring the matter into peril; or a decree of this sort has been made and issued by some thousand-fold little senate." "Mind your words, Lord Alençon," said the Senator of Sisteron. "It is not, I say, not something invented, what you have heard, but plainly the decree of the Senate. Nor should you use again so freely this same liberty and looseness of words, unless you prefer that the court of the province also be called a council and a senate of women." Alençon then himself sought an excuse, and promised about his constant goodwill towards those men; he declared openly that he would say nothing that could seem to detract from the dignity of any supreme court; yet he could by no means be induced to believe that what that woman had mentioned was true: that by a decree of the Senate (which, indeed, had begun to be kept in the province) the whole nation of Merindol, women, alas! helpless, and infants wretchedly crying in their cradles, were all, I say, cruelly adjudged to the sword; that all the buildings of the whole village were to be destroyed by ruin and fire, so that no trace of it might remain in the future; and this through the fault and vice, it was agreed, of twelve men I know not who, who were shown not to have been present in the Senate and to have abandoned their bail. "Nor, too," said Lord Belloiocius, "do I easily allow myself to be persuaded that such a decree, so alien to reason, so devoid of all humanity, so impiously Turkish, so cruelly Gothic, could have come forth from a court. Especially since, so far as I can truly judge about the people of Merindol, whom I remember having known for many years, I see nothing in them that is not most closely joined with unusual integrity of life and a certain goodness of nature. And the most excellent Lord President could remove this scruple for us, if it seemed good to him. For it is well known that one should never rely on the testimony of a woman, and that she should not be believed." Meanwhile the woman who had revealed the decree did not think she had to wait until the president gave an answer, but, turning at once to the Bishop of Aix, said: "I would be surprised if some one did not leap up to take up the defence and cause of those wretches at once." And raising her eyes to heaven, and burning with the swelling of womanly anger: "Would that all who are Lutherans in the province, indeed all France, bore horns on their foreheads: there would be no lack of horned ones everywhere." To her Lord Belloiocius replied on the spur of the moment: "Would that all the mistresses of the priests spoke with that articulation of voice which geese use." Then she said: "No, O Belloiocius, you must not speak so against our mother, Holy Church. No dog is ever found that barked at the crucified one who did not himself at some time go mad in the same way." The Bishop of Aix then at once began to smile, and gently striking the woman's shoulder, and asking her to speak: "By my most sacred orders, you have done me a most welcome favour, my light. She has smartly struck you down, O Lord Belloiocius, I beg you, retracting what she has faithfully taught you from that reading." "I will not delay," said Belloiocius, somewhat more stirred by anger, "your gymnasium of both of you: for I can gain nothing honourable from either of you. And so, although I would call bishops for the most part, and priests shameless, adulterers, blind, idolaters, deceivers, robbers, pilferers, impostors, I would not think I was saying anything foreign to the matter, or making any reproach against the Catholic Church at all; I would confess that I was pursuing a most hostile and most troublesome troop and flock of wolves, dogs, pigs and brutes of that kind; nor would I think I need fear their rage on that account, unless perhaps…

units.la: tores, ores,impostores appellarem,nihil alienum me dicere, aut omnino cōitium Ecclesiæ catholicæ facere arbitrarer: insectari me quidem infestissimum ac importunissimum luporum, canum, porcorum, eiusfemque generis brutorum animantium quoddam agmen & gregem onfiterer: nec vero propterea rabiem mihi pertimescendam putaem, nisi forte in rabiem impetu quodam animi ferimur eo tempore, quo testimonium veritatis amplectimur atque consectamur. Ac tu Episcopus impotenter & furiose, Male tu locutus es, o domine Bellooci, loco ac tempore redditurus rationem eorum omnium, quæ tu multa de viris Ecclesiasticis intulisti. Vellem profecto, inquit Belloocius, primo quoque die istud accidere, neque molestiam ad eam quam tu putas, temporis aliquid mihi prorogari. reciperem enim me plura longe vitia sacerdotum, graviores Episcoporum noxas in lucem editurum, quam ea sint adhuc quas attulimus. Supersedeamus, inquit præses Chassanæus, hoc toto genere disputandi, o Belloiocisque vestigijs, quæ maiores nostri fixerunt, insistamus. Cui Beloiocius, Nescio me filium esse sacerdotis, beneficium ut illud huic hominum genere debeam, uti scelera quibus affines sunt, mihi tuenda eximium hoc tempore. Veros autem Ecclesiæ pastores ac ministros, eruditione, vitæque confirmatione præstabiles in honorem adducendos esse facile, minimeque contumeliarum aculeis compungendos statuo. Verùm, heus tu domine Arelatensis, túque rursum o Aquensis, cùm Dominus noster Iesus Christus Hierosolymæ sacerdotes, hypocritas, cæcos, latrones, impostores esse diceret, hisque nominibus illos honestaret, vobisne contumeliosus ergaeos ac maledicus extitisse videatur? Minimè, inquiunt. Nec ipse quoque, cùm Episcopos istos atque sacerdotes isto modo sum executus, eis iniuriam obtulisse videri debeo. Sic enim ad eorum sceleratissimæ vitæ commemorationem obstupesco horrècque totus, uti ne mediam quidem partem earum rerum quas de nebulonibus illis intellexi, audeam in lucem apertumque proferre. Itaque si ad comprimendam meretricis alicuius improbæ loquacitatem veritati subscribo, non video quæ tandem ex eo sacerdotum animis afferri iure possit offensio.
