Obsecro missa isthæc facianus, inquit Senator Senensis, meminerimúsque eo consilio conuenisse nos in hunc locum, non vt ipsi nos aegritudini dederemus, sed vt perfuncti necessarijs occupationibus, ad animi remissionem ludumque descederemus. Itaque pro ea qua te complector beneuolentia, Domine Belloioci, non pigebit admonere te trium praeceptorum, quae si quemadmodum quidem ego spero, tu tenueris, & te summum a nobis accepisse beneficium, & tuis omnibus rebus optime consultum esse iudicabis. Primum illud est, ne quos acceperis esse Lutheranos, eos vlla re vnquam aut omnino consilio aut verbo iuues. Secundum ne mulieres in eo quod illis collibuisse, in deliciisque fuisse sententias, tibi censendas vnquam palam, atque reprehendedas putes. Tertium, ne quid in vitae genere sacerdotum, quantumuis imbuto sceleribus, quantumuis Christianae profes​sioni contrario, non solum animaduersione dignum tu, sed ne tantum quidem nefas animo concipiendum esse arbitrere: scitum est enim, Nolite tangere Christos meos. Cui D.Belloiocius ita respondit: Quòd ad primum attinet, ego nec vllos noui Lutheranos, neque quid Lutheranismus sit intelligo: nisi forte Lutheranos cos[?] esse definitus, qui doctrinam Euangelicam publicè profiteantur. Nec vero Senatusconsultum illud vnquam, quod in absentes, indictaque causa, maximè fœminas & pueros, ipsos etiam vixdum in hanc humanae vitae lucem editos infantes, factum ita sit, vt populum illum vniuersum immanissimè trucidandum exurendumque censuerint, æquabile ac legitimum esse meo iudicio potest. Ne quid hic de vlla Galliae totius Curia suprema commemorem, de qua sic Statuo, nullam vt inueniri posse profecto quae decretum eiusmodi fixum ac ratum sit habitura, facilè mihi persuadeam. Quod autem mulieres reprehendi non putauisti oportere, sane si cunde resciuero consanguineam vllam meam adeò transuersam atque fractam, vt omissa rei bene gerendae occasione vitium inferri sibi à sacerdote aut clerico quem vocant, (Cardinalis ille sit, aut Episcopus) idque quod antiquissimo loco ducere debeat, sibi turpiter eripi permiserit, non dignabor reprehensione mulierem: sed aut euulso certè, aut illi praeciso naso, testatum apud animos omnium relinquam quid egerit. Postremò, quòd in vitam irruere sacerdotum, alienum quoque à viri prudentis officio esse voluisti, non impedio quominus eadem omnes impunitate & licentia viuant, qua velint: ea tamen lege, dum meam mihi libertatem ipsi concedant, atque ita posthac in domum meā venire desinant. Certum est enim, ibi si quos offendero, detonsum eis sic, rasúmque iri coronam sacerdotalem, minimè postea laborandum eis ut sit, unde porrectum ad humeros capitis amictum invenire possint. In eandem fere cum Senatore sententiam & præses Chassanæus ratiocina-tus dicitur. Cæterum egregia illa Aquensis Episcopi amica, quam iam altercationis initium introduxisse ostendimus, Nondum mihi placebo, inquit, donec verbum adhuc unum cum domino Belloiocio secero: Arbitraris ô Belloioci, tot Cardinales & Episcopos, Abbates & sacerdotes cæterosq; sacrosanctos viros, ecclesiasticæ religionis alumnos ac ministros, qui in hominum illustrium quotidie domibꝰ, regūq; ipsorū ac principum palatiis maxima familiaritate versantur, omnes hoc animo illò proficisci, ut & mereri pessimè de principibus, & in Dei optimi maximi offensionem incurrere possint? Equidem si semper istius ordinis sententiam tueri vis, necab opinione unquam, obfirmatóque isto animo facere discessionem, non dubitem te vocare (si Deo placet) ex iure manu confertum, accusaréque plane lædæ & humanæ & divinæ maiestatis. Suntque hoc in cœtu viri minimè sanè veriturí, instituti tui rationem à te aliquando reposcere. Vixdum eo sermone consumpto, stomachabundus Belloioci ac feruens[?], Abi, inquit, ô Herodias, scortum impurissimum atque impudentissimum. siccine tandem hiscere te, hoc hominum conventu decet? Intelligerene potuisti quid esset humana divinaque lædā maiestas? Non deberes satisfactum tibi iam esse ducere, neque tanto convitio sanguinem humanum effundi curare? His verbis perturbatior aliquanto mulier, concertandi finem factura videbatur: iamque factum omnes qui aderant existimabant: incumbebant in eā curā, uti nulla mora interposita ad facetias urbanitatémque, converso sermone ab istiusmodi contentione discederetur. At mulier impatiens contumeliæ (ut interpretabatur) superioris, qua sibi sanguinem innocentium obiectum meminerat, omnium interrupto sermone vociferans ait, Si perinde vir ipsa essem, atque fœminâ natura esse voluit, experirer ego mehercule duello tecum, Belloioci, iuréque vindicarem extremo, neque eam esse me quam tu tuis verbis esse voluisti, neque cupidam vllo modo respergendi sanguinis innocentium. Quod vt ita quidem fit, impiorum ne tu sanguinem illorum, sceleratorumq; Merindoliorum, innocentium hominum sanguinem interpretaris? Desidero profecto, meaque omnia in hanc rem vna polliceri ac conferre non desino, vt peruerfissimæ nationis illius statu conuulso, omnes ad vnum illi nebulones eorumque subscriptores de medio tollantur: idque videre aliquando vt possem, eorumque cum corporibus extinctam plane memoriam intelligere, quantum gratia, quantum subsidiis amicorum efficere licuit, denique quoad efferre se mea vires, facultates effundere potuerunt, tantum artificio, labore, diligentia mihi perpetuo conandum existimaui. Internecione igitur & clade Lutheranorum, ô Belloioci, sanguinis innocentis effusionem appellari placet. eia[?] perge videlicet vt instituisti: ego vero, fremat omnes licet, honoris mei salua dignitate, próq; eo iure quod ego libenter matri nostræ S.Ecclesiæ debeo, quoties interdiu atq; noctu aut ad sacerdotes exire aut domos Episcoporum celebrare mihi licebit, nō prætermittā: at eos vicissim ipsa recipiam in domū omnes familiariter, cū eis initura ratione quemadmodū istos Lutheranos vniuersos ad cædē & vastitatem deducere possimus. Belloiocius mulieris garrulitate fastidiens, supersedit. erat enim nemo, qui non eā jam nunc in contemptionē adduceret, ac audiendi satietate defessus effet. Interquiescere tu omnes occeperat, cum ecce nobilis quidā adolescens ioco illa adortus, dicere statim cœpit, Necessarium est, ô domina, nefarios illos ac perditos homines in offensa esse vehementer apud te, quibus tu tam graviter infensa profectò fis. At illa, Equidē omni asseueratione confirmare possum, ex miseris illis ac profligatis hominibus esse plane neminem, quē ego nouerim, quē viderim: longeque libentius in cacodæmones ipsos decem, quam in illorum vnicū incurrerim. nam sic est eorum sermo vitiosus, fœlices vt existimē atq; cum eis agi præclarè, qui nunquā de eo quicquā intelligere potuerunt. mèque nō mediocriter errasse fateri debeo, atq; meæ culpæ imprudentiæ præstare, quòd D.Aquensem Episcopum semel aliquādo conspicata perturbatū & anxium eo modo, vt cibi ac potionis vsum amisisse videretur, vix precibus ac minis ab illo tādē expressi causam ægritudinis ac perturbationis sue. quā intellexi fuisse hāc, Regnare videlicet hodie passim genus quoddam hominum haereticorum, nostram matrem S. Ecclesiam petulatissimis maledictorū notis inurentium. Hac sopita concertatione, deductaque tandem ad otium, magna postea consecuta perturbatio atque contentio, terroresque non contemnendi propositi verborum. de quibus hactenus. Longiores enim sunt, quam ut historiæ positæ angustiis, includi possint. Interea præses Chassanæus, & senatores simul ac nobiles illinc digressi diversis itineribus proficiscuntur.
units.tr: plunderers, impostors. I would think I was saying nothing out of place, nor that I was in any way disturbing the fellowship of the catholic Church, if I called them so. I would confess that I am assailing a most hostile and troublesome pack of wolves, dogs, swine, and other brute beasts of that sort. Nor, for that reason, should I think I must fear their rage, unless perhaps we are carried into rage by some impulse of the mind at the very time when we embrace and pursue the testimony of truth. And you, Bishop, speak intemperately and furiously. "You have spoken badly, Lord Belloiocius, and you will give an account, in the proper place and time, of all the things you have brought forward about churchmen." "Indeed I would wish," said Belloiocius, "that this came about on the very first day, and that some time were not granted me, which you think is a nuisance. For I would bring to light far more of the faults of priests and the graver crimes of bishops than those we have so far produced. Let us set aside," said President Chassanaeus, "this whole kind of disputation, and, Belloiocius, let us follow the footsteps our elders have set down." To this Belloiocius replied: "I do not know that I am the son of a priest, so that I should owe this favour to that class of men, to defend the crimes that belong to them at a time such as this, which is remarkable. But I hold that true ministers and pastors of the Church, distinguished for learning and for the steadfastness of their lives, should easily be held in honour, and should by no means be stung with the barbs of insult. But tell me, Lord Archbishop of Arles, and you too, Bishop of Aix: when our Lord Jesus Christ said that the priests of Jerusalem were hypocrites, blind men, thieves, and impostors, and so honoured them with these names, does he seem to you to have been insulting and abusive towards them?" "By no means," they replied. "Nor, when I have dealt with those bishops and priests in this way, should I seem to have done them any wrong. For I am so struck and horror-stricken at the recollection of their most wicked lives that I dare not bring into the light even the half of what I have learned about those scoundrels. So if, to check the chatter of some wicked whore, I give my assent to the truth, I do not see what offence can rightly be taken by the minds of the priests. I beg you, let us drop these matters," said the Senator of Sens, "and let us remember that we came to this place with the purpose not of giving ourselves over to vexation, but of setting aside our necessary business and going down to relaxation and play. So, for the affection with which I embrace you, Lord Belloiocius, I will not hesitate to remind you of three precepts. If, as I hope, you keep them, you will judge both that you have received the greatest kindness from us and that all your affairs have been very well looked after. The first is this: whomever you have found to be Lutherans, you must never help them in any matter, whether by counsel or by word. The second: do not think that you should ever openly censure or rebuke women for the opinions they have fancied and made their delight. The third: do not think that anything in the manner of life of priests, however steeped in crimes and however contrary to the Christian profession, is not only worthy of punishment but is even such a sin that it should not be entertained in the mind. For it is well said: Touch not my anointed ones [Nolite tangere Christos meos]." To this Lord Belloiocius replied as follows: "As to the first, I do not know any Lutherans, nor do I understand what Lutheranism is, unless perhaps those are to be called Lutherans who openly profess the evangelical doctrine. Nor can I in my judgement regard as fair and lawful that decree of the Senate, which was made against absent persons, without a hearing of their case, and especially against women and boys, and even infants scarcely brought into this light of human life, so that they judged that whole people should be most savagely slaughtered and burned. I shall not here mention anything of the supreme court of all Gaul, concerning which I hold this view: I am quite persuaded that no such decree could be found that would be fixed and valid. As for your judgement that women should not be reproved: indeed, if I were to learn that any kinswoman of mine was so perverse and so broken that, neglecting the opportunity of acting well, she allowed a priest or clergyman, as they are called (whether he be a cardinal or a bishop), to inflict upon her a wrong, and to snatch from her shamefully what she ought to hold most dear, I would not deign to reprove the woman, but I would leave it witnessed in the minds of all what she had done, by tearing off her nose or cutting it off. Finally, as to your wish that it is also foreign to the duty of a prudent man to rush into the lives of priests, I do not hinder them from living, all of them, in the same impunity and licence as they wish, on this condition only: that they grant me my own freedom, and so from now on cease to come into my house. For it is certain that if I find any of them there, they will be shaved and their priestly crown will be shorn, and they will not afterwards have to trouble themselves about where to find a cloak to hang over their shoulders." The President Chassanaeus is also reported to have reasoned to much the same effect as the Senator. But that notable friend of the Bishop of Aix, whom we have shown to have begun the quarrel, said: "I am not yet satisfied, until I have said one more word to Lord Belloiocius. Do you think, Belloiocius, that so many cardinals and bishops, abbots and priests, and the other most sacred men, the nurslings and ministers of the ecclesiastical religion, who every day move in the houses of illustrious men and in the palaces of their kings and princes with the greatest familiarity, all go there with the intent of deserving very badly of princes and of incurring the displeasure of God, the best and greatest? Indeed, if you always wish to uphold the opinion of that order, and do not, from that settled and fixed mind, make a withdrawal, I would not hesitate to summon you (if it pleases God) by the law of arms, and to accuse you plainly of treason against both human and divine majesty. And there are men in this assembly who will by no means be afraid to demand from you, at some time, an account of your conduct." Scarcely had he finished his speech, when Belloiocius, angry and seething, cried out: "Begone, Herodias, most impure and most shameless whore! Does it befit you at all to open your mouth in this company of men? Could you understand what the majesty of man and of God is? Ought you not to consider yourself already satisfied, and do not take care that human blood be spilt by such abuse?" The woman, somewhat more disturbed by these words, seemed about to bring the quarrel to an end, and all who were present thought it was already done. They set themselves to the task, so that without delay the conversation could be turned to jests and pleasantries, and the dispute abandoned. But the woman, impatient of the insult (as she construed it) of the earlier speech, in which she recalled that the blood of the innocent had been thrown at her, broke into everyone's talk, crying out: "If I were a man, as nature meant women to be, I would by heaven fight a duel with you, Belloiocius, and I would avenge the wrong to the last drop, and I would show that I am not the woman you have wished to make me out to be in your words, nor in any way eager to spill the blood of the innocent. But since it is so, do you interpret as the blood of innocent men the blood of those impious and wicked Merindolians? I certainly desire, and I do not cease to promise and to devote all my resources to this one end, that once the state of that most perverse nation has been overthrown, all those scoundrels and their supporters, without exception, be removed from the midst. And I have thought it my perpetual duty to strive with art, labour and diligence, so far as I might be able to see this some day, and to understand that their memory has been utterly extinguished along with their bodies, using whatever favour and whatever help of friends I could command, and, finally, as far as my strength could bear, and my means could pour themselves out. So, Belloiocius, you are pleased to call the destruction and slaughter of the Lutherans an effusion of innocent blood. Well then, go on as you have begun. As for me, let them all rage, I will not fail, with my honour safe and with that right which I gladly owe to our mother, holy Church, as often as by day or by night I shall be permitted to go out to the priests or to celebrate in the houses of the bishops. And in turn they will receive me into their houses, all of them, on familiar terms, and we shall consider with them how we can lead all these Lutherans to slaughter and destruction." Belloiocius, disgusted by the woman's chatter, let the matter drop. For there was no one who did not now hold her in contempt, and who was not weary from having listened to her too long. They had all begun to rest, when behold, a certain noble young man, attacking her in jest, at once began to say: "It is necessary, lady, that those wicked and lost men should be very greatly in your displeasure, since you are so bitterly hostile to them." But she replied: "I can assure you with every affirmation that among those wretched and abandoned men there is no one, so far as I know, whom I have met or seen. And I would far more willingly run into ten demons than into one of them. For their talk is so vicious that they think themselves happy, and that things go splendidly for them, who could never understand anything about this. And I must confess that I was not a little mistaken, and that it is my own fault and my imprudence, that once, when I saw the Lord Bishop of Aix disturbed and anxious in such a way that he seemed to have lost the use of food and drink, I at last drew from him, with difficulty, by prayers and threats, the cause of his sickness and disturbance. And I understood it to be this: that there reigns everywhere today a certain kind of heretical men, who brand our mother, holy Church, with the most insolent marks of abuse. When this quarrel was quieted and at last brought to rest, there followed a great disturbance and contention, and terrors of no small consequence in the words spoken. Concerning these things, so far. For they are too long to be contained within the narrow limits of this history. Meanwhile President Chassanaeus, and the senators and nobles, withdrawn from there, set out by different roads."

units.la: Ex eo tempore Archiepiscopus Arelatensis, Episcopus Aquensis, Abbates nonnulli ac Priores, Præpositus Aquens.[?] cum quibusdam senioribus Canonicis, non prius conquiescendum sibi putauerunt, quam in locum aliquem vniuersi conuenirent, vbi de rebus quæ acciderant, deliberationem habere possent. Quo in conuentu constitutum fuit, vt vnusquisque eorum pro re nata & suscepta, Merindolien. Senatus cos.[?] memoriam charissimam atque commendatissimam haberet: persequereturque diligenter omnes vias, quibus illud ad extremum deduci posset: compararet nouas insectationum faces, eásque ipsas viuidiores atq; torrentiores, quam eæ fuissent quas Ioannes de Roma Dominicanus de quo antea diximus, excitasset. Alioqui enim agitur, inquiunt, status ac dignitas omnium nostrum: nemoque reperietur, cuius in reprehensionem atque ludibrium non incurramus. Atqui leuis ac momentanea res sit, si præter Merindolios, eiusque generis idiotas ac rusticos nemo nobis insultaret, non etiam essent qui fere perniciem Reipublicæ nostræ molirentur: sed præter ordinem est, emergere quotidie non paucos Theologos doctores virosque religiosos, nonnullos etiam senatores ac patronos, aliosque reconditioris eruditionis ac ingenij monimentis præstantes viros, denique bonam partem (si dici licet) illustrioris nobilitatis, sed eius quoque nobilitatis quæ altissimo loco sita sit in omnium hominum conspectu, ac Europæ totius oculis, à quibus omnibus despicatui duci paulatim incipiamus, minimeque veri Ecclesiæ pastores existimemur: vt nisi diligenter occurrimus & caucemus, non modo vt omnium sacerdotiorum quæ nos ampla ac lauta possidemus, naufragium faciam[?], ipsique proscribamur: verum etiam ne suis orba parietibus atque pastoribus Ecclesia, ad tristes miserabilesq; casus postea properatura sit, periculi esse profecto videatur. Quamobrem in diligentia & celeritate posita sunt omnia hoc tepore. Hac habita inter ipsos oratione. Archiepiscopus Arelatensis. Hispanicæ calliditatis nondū oblitus, retulit in ea sententia: Aduersus nobilitate nihil temere suscipiedum, sed applaudendum omnino. illam enim omnium Ecclesiasticorum esse propugnaculum ac præsidium. Quòd quamuis nemini dubium esset plærósque nobiles existere, qui pessimè de eis & loquerētur & existimaret: nec ipsi quoque dubium haberent illos ex eorum hominum esse genere, qui noui Euangelistæ vulgò dicerentur. cauendum esse tamen ne eorum animos cōtrouersiarum anfractibus aut delationibus exulceraret: sed plus iam satis immutatos, largitionibus recolligere potius ac retinere studeret: hoc artificio potissimum, eorum se patrocinio, quasi quodam vallo, tutos ac munitos fore. certum enim esse, si quid aduersus nobilitatis authoritate splendoremque molirentur, ciuium iudices causarum eius cognitione ad se reuocaturos, nullumque se hac in re compendiu facturos ipsos, quæadmodum quidem clarissimis antea monimentis & exemplis probatum atque consignatum sit. Eleganter id quidem & recte, inquit, Aquensis Episcopus: at ipse medicinam afferam non vulgarem qua morbus iste sanari facile posse videatur. Profundenda sunt omnia, amici tentandi omnes, in eo denique cogitationes omnes nostræ figendæ ac locandæ, vt tanta Merindoliorum & rusticorum cædes efficiatur, nemo posthac vt sit, quantumuis affinitate ac sanguine regio, qui ad male de nobis, aut Ecclesiastica viuendi consuetudine loquendum, vel os ipsum aperire audeat. Idque vt minori negotio consequamur, antiquissimum esse videtur Auenionem concedere: qua in vrbe reperire liceat Abbates & Episcopos complures, aliosque in Reipublicæ luce amplissimos viros, non dubituros se nobiscum ad nostræ matris Ecclesiæ maiestatem tuendam sustinendamque coniungere. Hoc consilium cum omnes approbauissent, Arelatensis Archiepiscopus, Episcopus ipse Aquensis, cæterique coniuratores nihil prius habuerunt, quam vt reiectis omnibus rebus, Auenione quamprimum proficiscerentur. Quo cum venissent, Episcopos ipsos celeriter, virosque totius illius ciuitatis opibus & gratia florentissimos atque potentissimos, vt mature de negotio deliberaretur, vnum aliquè in locum cogere constituerunt. Orandiqué prouincia Aquensis sortitus Episcopus, traditionū paternarum acerrimus propugnator, in hanc rationem exorsus dicitur: Nō ignoratis, ô patres fratresq; charis.aduersa maxime tempestate ventorum iactari Iesu Christi nauiculam: procellasq; concitatas, in illam eo impetu ferri, ut strangulata propemodu, parum absit quin obruise se fluctuum inundatione resorberiqué patiatur. Ipse turbo ab Aquilone proficiscitur, quem eundem maximus motus rerum omnium perturbatióque consequitur. torrentes undique procurrunt ac profluunt, summaque iactura venti, ac prope naufragio nostrarum omnium rerum passim reflant, inque domicilium nostrum sæviunt. Nam oblationes feviantur[?], peregrinationes & devotiones refrigerantur, charitas apud nos otio fere congelauit, quodque pessime nobis cedet, authoritatis nostrae magnitudo non mediocriter infecti, iurisdictio prævaricari, rei ecclesiasticæ sanctiones infirmari perfringiq; cœperunt. At ipsi hoc potissimum loco constituti, populorū regnorumq; ditionibus præfecti quodamodo ac prærogati sumus, ut etiā abrogare ac dissoluere omnia, ac perrumpere soli possemus. Quamobrem serio quæso expergefiamus, inq; possessionis nostræ iure consistamus, ut Lutheranorum familiam totam: Lutheranorum, inquam, illorū vulpium, vineã D. nō decussantium sed subuertentium: Balenarū, filij Dei nauiculam non constitutam sed submergetium funditꝰ, ex hominum omni memoria deleamus. Incepimus quidē certē iam non inauspicato meo iudicio, atq; ut in Lutheranos illos impios Merindolios, Senatuscōs.borrendum ingēs, tandiu Præsidū ac Senatorum pectoribus inclusum, aliquando tandem erūpere, forasq; ꝓiceretur, maximo Reip.bono perfecimus: eóque rem plane deduximus, nihil ut[?] cogitādum hodie nobis sit, nisi ut cōcinnatiam operis reliquias fortiter diligéterq; psequamur[?]. Quapropter, ô viri, laboremus, efficiamus, occurramus, ne quod interim rebus præclarè gestis impedimentum inferatur, denique caueamus ne, si in tam pio christianóque faciundo sacrificio pecuniæ parcimus, aurum nostrum & argentum extremo illo diuini iudicij die nos perstringere suo testimonio possit. Ego quidem pro mea parte polliceor, in meq; recipio, me cum maturum erit, cētum homines armatos rebus omnibus diligenter instructos Reip.curaturum, cisque stipendium, quoad exitiū & internecionem perditis illis nebulonibꝰ intulerint, propria pecunia numeraturū.
units.tr: From that time the Archbishop of Arles, the Bishop of Aix, several abbots and priors, the provost of Aix, and some senior canons felt they could not rest until they had all gathered in one place to deliberate on what had happened. At this meeting it was agreed that each of them, as the occasion and the business required, should keep the Merindol senate's case in dear and special remembrance, should pursue diligently every way by which it might finally be brought to ruin, and should prepare fresh torches of persecution, livelier and fiercer than those which John of Rome, the Dominican of whom we spoke earlier, had kindled. Otherwise, they said, the standing and dignity of all of us is at stake, and there will be no one whom we do not expose to reproach and ridicule. And yet it would be a small and passing matter if, apart from the Merindolians and that kind of common and rustic folk, no one insulted us; but it is outrageous that there are not a few theologians, doctors, religious men, some senators and patrons, and other men distinguished by the monuments of a more refined learning and talent, and finally a good part (if it may be said) of the more illustrious nobility, and of that nobility which stands in the highest place in the sight of all men and under the eyes of all Europe, who are gradually beginning to despise us and who think we are by no means the true ministers of the Church. Unless we meet and guard against this carefully, not only will all the rich and lavish benefices we possess be wrecked, and we ourselves proscribed, but it will surely seem a danger that the Church, bereft of its walls and ministers, will hasten on to sad and wretched disasters. Therefore everything at this time depends on diligence and speed.' After this speech among themselves, the Archbishop of Arles, not yet forgetting his Spanish cunning, gave his opinion: nothing should be undertaken rashly against the nobility, but it should be wholly courted, for it is the bulwark and protection of all churchmen. Although no one doubted that many nobles existed who spoke and thought very badly of them, and they themselves did not doubt that those nobles belonged to the sort of men commonly called the new evangelists, nevertheless care must be taken not to exasperate their minds with the twists of controversy or with accusations; rather, they should strive to win them back and keep them, now already sufficiently changed, by largesse. By this artifice above all, they would be safe and fortified under the nobles' patronage as if behind a rampart. For it was certain that if they plotted anything against the authority and splendour of the nobility, the judges of the citizens would call the case to their own cognizance, and they themselves would gain nothing by it, as indeed has been proved and recorded by very clear earlier monuments and examples. "Elegantly and rightly said," replied the Bishop of Aix, "but I will offer a remedy that is not commonplace, by which that disease may seem easily cured. Everything must be overturned, all friends tried, and all our thoughts fixed and directed to this end: that such a slaughter of the Merindolians and rustics be made that henceforth no one, however great his kinship or royal blood, would dare to open his mouth to speak ill of us or of our ecclesiastical manner of life. And so that we may achieve this with less trouble, it seems most urgent to go to Avignon, where we may find several abbots and bishops, and other most distinguished men in the light of the Commonwealth, who will not hesitate to join us in defending and sustaining the majesty of our mother the Church." When all had approved this plan, the Archbishop of Arles, the Bishop of Aix himself, and the other conspirators made it their first business, all other matters set aside, to set out for Avignon as quickly as possible. When they had arrived there, they resolved to gather together as soon as possible the bishops themselves, and the most powerful and influential men of that whole city, wealthy and flourishing in favour, so that the business might be deliberated upon without delay in one place. The bishop who had been allotted the praying for the province of Aix, a most fierce champion of ancestral traditions, is reported to have begun in this manner: "You are not unaware, O fathers and dear brethren, that the little ship of Jesus Christ is tossed by a most adverse storm of winds, and that stirred-up tempests are driven against it with such violence that it is almost strangled, and it is but a little short of being overwhelmed and swallowed by the flood of the waves. The storm itself rises from the North, and with it comes the greatest upheaval and confusion of all things. Torrents rush and flow from every side, and with the greatest loss, and almost the shipwreck, of all our affairs, the winds blow everywhere and rage against our dwelling. For offerings are cut short, pilgrimages and devotions grow cold, charity among us has nearly frozen with idleness, and, what will turn out very badly for us, the greatness of our authority has begun to be considerably tainted, our jurisdiction to be violated, and the sanctions of ecclesiastical affairs to be weakened and broken. Yet we, placed in this highest position and set over the dominions of peoples and kingdoms, have been as it were preferred and privileged, so that we alone might be able to abrogate, dissolve, and break through everything. Therefore, I earnestly beg you, let us wake up and stand firm in the right of our possession, so that we may wipe out from all human memory the whole family of the Lutherans: the Lutherans, I say, those foxes that do not cut down but overturn the vineyard of the Lord; the Balaams, who do not lay down but sink the ship of the Son of God. Certainly we have already begun, and in my not unfavourable judgement we have brought it about, for the greatest good of the Commonwealth, that that dreadful and huge thing, long shut up in the breasts of the presidents and senators against those impious Lutheran Merindolians, has at last burst forth and been thrown out, and we have so brought the matter to a head that nothing remains for us to consider today except to pursue the remaining scraps of the work bravely and diligently. Therefore, O men, let us labour, let us accomplish, let us prevent, lest in the meantime any hindrance be thrown in the way of things so well done; finally, let us take care lest, if we spare money in making this so pious and Christian sacrifice, our gold and silver may at that last day of divine judgement accuse us by their testimony. For my part, I promise and undertake that, when the time is ripe, I will provide for the Commonwealth a hundred armed men, carefully equipped with everything, and I will pay them from my own money as wages until they have brought destruction and extermination upon those wretched scoundrels.

units.la: Hæc oratio cum vehementer multitudini placuisset, Basinetus Domi-nicanus, D. theologus, referre sic instituit: Consilij magni rem esse, itaque in ea versari religiose, neque temere quicquam efficere oportere. Si enim iniuria miseros illos ac ærumnosos homines morte multet, eaque facinoris atrocitas ad Regem Principesque perveniat, periculum esse ne in ipsos idem statuatur, quod in Sacerdotes Baal memini religionis antiquitas. Cogi se nunc demum ingenuè fateri (quod ipsi tamè confessionis vice dictu existimēt) eorum qui hæreseos accusati sæpe sint, plerásque causas atque lites à se leuiusculè professò subsignatas: Deũ tamẽ qui nos intueatur, omniũ nostrum corda scrutetur, obtestari posse, vt primum subsignationũ suarũ tristes euentũ ipse viderit, se videlicet suiqué similibus doctoribus referentibus, ciuiũ iudicum sententia capitis damnatos eos, quos ipsi hæreticos pronunciassent, impeditum conscientia requiescere ex eo tempore non potuisse. Perturbationis illi’ animi fui causam hanc esse, quòd paucis abhinc mensibus Scripturarũ desiderio cupidior, eas propius inspicere cœpisset, ex quibus coperisset maximã parte eorũ propositorũ, quæ tuerétur ij qui Lutheran vocaretur, adeò consentaneam & affinè Euangelio, vt ipse quidè in posterũ ei reclamare non posset, nisi forte de industria Dei opt.ma præceptiones impiè petere, atque hostiliter insectari vellet. De tamē, quod S.nostræ matris ecclesiæ, S.patris nostri Papæ, ac ordinis commodo facere potuerit, doctorum Theologorũ opinionibus hactenus adstipulatum: idque tũ ignoratione, tum ne quid alienum ab Episcoporũ, Vicariorũq; generaliũ voluntate ac libidine quærere videretur. Iã vero cõmutandam plane illa totam vitæ ratione, deligendúq; aliud hac in re quoddã artificij genus sibi videri. Satis esse, eos qui fuerint in ecclesiasticis, pontificisqué constitutionibus perstringédis intéperatiores, pecunia exilióue mulctare. De cæteris ita constituere vt qui blasphemi, hæreticiq; pertinaces Scripturarũ testimonijs aperte conuicti deprehendentur, ad morte profectò illi quemadmodũ criminis ipsius ratio postulabit, aut perpetuos certè carceres mittatur. Petere autè se tandem ab illis, vt suam opinione æqui boníq; cófulerent. Hastenus Basinetus: cuius admonitio cũ omnũ animos vehementer, tum Aquef. Episcopi magna cũ admurmuratione præcipuè concitauit. Itaq; Episcopo, O homo paruæ fidei, quare du-
units.tr: When this speech had greatly pleased the crowd, Basinetus the Dominican, a doctor of theology, undertook to speak in this way: "It is a matter of great counsel, and one must proceed in it with due care and not do anything rashly. For if we punish those wretched and unhappy men with death unjustly, and the atrocity of such a crime reaches the King and the princes, there is a danger that the same may be decreed against us as was decreed, as antiquity records, against the priests of Baal. I must now frankly confess what those who have often been accused of heresy, and many causes and suits which I myself have too lightly signed, have, as it were, taken as a confession (though they think them said in the manner of a confession): God, who looks upon us and searches the hearts of all of us, can bear witness that, when I saw the sad outcome of those signings, and when, as I and similar doctors reported, the sentence of the civil judges condemned to death those whom we had pronounced heretics, my conscience could not rest from that time on. The cause of this disturbance of my mind is this: a few months ago, being more eager for the desire of the Scriptures, I began to look into them more closely, and from them I discovered that the greater part of those propositions which the so-called Lutherans maintain is so consonant and akin to the Gospel that I myself could not afterwards contradict it, unless perhaps I were willing to wickedly seek to pervert the most excellent precepts of God and assail them with hostility. Yet, as far as I could do so for the benefit of our holy mother the Church, of our holy father the Pope, and of our order, I have so far agreed with the opinions of the learned theologians, both from ignorance and so as not to seem to seek anything foreign to the will and pleasure of the bishops and general vicars. Now, indeed, that whole plan of life must be plainly changed, and some other kind of artifice must, in my view, be chosen in this matter. It is enough to punish with money or exile those who have been too intemperate in denouncing ecclesiastical and papal constitutions. As for the rest, let them decide that those who are blasphemers and obstinate heretics, plainly convicted by the testimonies of Scripture, shall be sent to death, as the nature of their crime demands, or at least to perpetual prisons. Finally, I ask of you that you consider what is in accordance with fairness and goodness in my opinion." So far Basinetus. His admonition greatly stirred the minds of all, and above all it aroused the Bishop of Aix to great murmuring. Therefore, to the Bishop, "O man of little faith, why did you

units.la: quare dubitauisti? Ha ha magister.n. adeon' te recte fecisse poenitet? Dicitasti quaedam hic tu palam fasciculos sulphuratos haud dubie resipientia. Interesse ne tibi videtur aliquid inter haereses & blasphemias quae in Scripturas afferuntur, & opiniones matri nostrae S. ecclesiae, ipsiq; diuo P. nostro D. Papae, in terra Deo verissimo contrarias? tu magister es in Israel, & isthaec ignoras? Tu Archiepiscopus Arelatensis, Magister noster, inquit, tibi ne videtur de Iesu Christi nauicula disputari posse rectius à quoquam quàm est à D. Aquef. episcopo disputatii? Sane, inquit Basinetus, Episcopi reuerendissimi concio expressit elegantissime mores, vitaeq; conditionem hominum Ecclesiasticorum: fuitq; reprehendendis etiam mortalium huius aetatis vitijs & haeresibus accommodatissima. Itaque cum primum de Iesu Christi nauicula fieri mentione intellexi, tum demiq; reuocare coepi memoria sacrificatoris illi maximi Hierusalē, Sacerdotū, Doctorum legis, Scribarū, Pharisaeorū, qui constituti pastores in Ecclesia Dei, aliquo certe tempore ad gubernaculū illius nauiculae sederunt: at postquā legem Dei repudiantes, hominū constitutionē nb°i[?] seruire voluerunt, iratus ipse hypocritas illos operosos omnibus rebus euertedos cauit: tu vero misertus hominum qui ad ouium similitudinem destituti pastore vagabatur, demisit sedulos piscatores, vt homines expiscarentur: in messem suam operarios, in vineā institutores culturesq;: quae omnia consecuta maturitate legitimos aetatis fructus afferet. Secundo loco, D. episcopi orationē audiēs, succurrit statim 4.cap.1.ad Timoth. Emergēt, inquit, extremis temporibus defciscetes à fide, spiritus immundos & diaboli dogmata sectates: subijciq; statim Paulus signa quaedam quibus illi cognosci possunt. In eandē quoq; ratione & D. noster Iesus, ait Matthaei 7, Pseudoprophetas, qui veniunt ad nos induti vestibus ouium, intrinsecus aut lupi rapaces, ex fructibus cognitu iri. Ex his duobus, aliisq; similibus plerisque locis intelligere proclive est, quinā demum ij sint, qui Christi nauicula euertere, ac machinis omnibus perfidiose deprimere conetur. Ii videlicet omnino, qui illa caeno & luto, aquisque putredine tabescentibus perfundunt: qui Christo, aquae viuae fonti limpido atque perpetuo, vt puteos interusos ac hiantes sibi defoderent, nuntium remittere non dubitauerunt. Ii certè, qui se terrae sal esse (saporis habentes nihil) vulgò iactitant, qui se Pastores appellitant, cum nihil minus ipsi sint quàm certè pastores, huiusq; cognomenti profectò longissimi temporis praescriptione ius amiserint. Non enim pastum legitimum quibus impertiuntur: non ipsum verbi divini panem discindunt atque distribuunt. Ac si tati mysterij piaculum efferre plane licet, nunquid eiusdem hodie miraculi prodigiúque sit, Episcopum nos unum aliquem concionantem audire, ac asinum pegaseo traiectu per aera volitantem conspicere? Nunquid à Deo diris omni-bꝰ defixos eos ac devotos intelligimꝰ, qui se claves regni caelorum habere gloriantes, nec ingrediuntur ipsi, nec eos qui veniunt ingredi patiuntur? Innotescent illi suis sanè fru-ctibus, abiurauerunt enim & fidem, & iudicium, & misericordiam, neq; in illis praeter vestimentorum ac lineorum superficiem, speciosum est quicquam ac candidum: intrinsecus autem luxuria ac mulierositate delibuta omnia. Extrinsecus nitidi quidem illi plus satis, in recessu vero rapinis & ingluuie sordidi supramodum ac vitiosi. Nempe sepulchra sunt dealbata quaedam, quae splendorem atque venustatem præse ferentia, intrinsecus obscoenitate turpitudineque deformata diffluunt. Innotescet, inquam, suis fructibus illi lupi rapaces, qui praetextu longissimarum orationum, superstites sugunt ipsos ac mortuos. Itaq; quando progressi eo sumus ut coccedendum veritati sit, meque magistrum in Israel ipsi dicitis, Scripturarum testimonijs asserere non verebor, magnum illum gubernatorem Papā, ipsosq; vectores ac remiges Episcopos, similesq; nauiculatores, qui ut scaphas confecederent, Iesu Christi naviculam impudentissimè deseruerunt, piratas, pseudoprophetas, impostores, non Ecclesiae Christianae pastores existere. Vix absoluerat Basinetus sermonem institutum suum, cum universa multitudo circumfundi statim, editoq; murmure in illum invchi[?] coepit. At Episcopus quidem Aquef.[?] inclamans atq; vociferans, Exi foras, inquit, apostata scelerate: nec enim dignus es, qui nobiscum hic sis. Dispereunt incendio quotidie quamplurimi, sed eodem tu incedio dignior. Itaque videmus nullum hominum genus passim in fide constatius, in fide ferentius canonicis doctoribus: estq; primo quoque Generali concilio futurum operæpretium, edicto publico sanciri, ne quis præter Canonicos doctores viros religioni manum admoveat, ab istis enim monachis nebulonibus omnia peffundatum, omnia conuulsum iri. Mendici tum reliqui doctores audacter illum incusare, expostularéque cum eo cœperunt de iniuria, qua ordinem universum homo concitus adficeret, non sine maximo utrinque motu ac tumultu: eóque tanto, ut tum quidem de negotioconsici minimè potuerit. A prædio universi illi venerandi Præsules concilium habuerunt, Medicis reiectis minimeque convocatis ac monachis, nisi si quis inter eos Abbas existeret: tandemque interposito iureiurando conspiraverunt daturos se quàprimum operam ut Merindoliense Senatusconsultum expediretur: pollicitique sunt ad unum omnes, certum se numerum armatorum hominum singulos effecturos, ac pro parte, quantum quidem ad Merindolium evertendum satis esset, stipendium esse soluturos. Mandaverunt Aquensi Episcopo, Præpositoque canonicorum, ut rem sumptibus communibus persequerentur: omniqué artificio præsidi atque senatoribus persuaderent, metu minimè premenda Senatusconsulti quod ipsi fecerint expeditione: sed imperterritis animis, adhibito tubarum cantu, prolatis signis, conductis in rem præsentem machinis ac tormentis, in aciem quasi pdeundum. Hac ita conflata constitutaque conspiratione, Aquensis episcopus Avenione statim Aquas Sextias, mandatum effecturus perfectione molicbatur. Interea tamen cum rogatus ut lautissimo cuidam conuivio, quod postridie domi Rivièsis Episcopi parabatur, interesse vellet, expectat.
units.tr: "Why did you doubt? Ha, ha, master! Does it really grieve you to have acted rightly? You openly said here some things, sulphurous bundles of papers, undoubtedly savouring of heresy. Does there seem to you to be any difference between the heresies and blasphemies that are brought against the Scriptures and the opinions that are contrary, on earth, to our mother, the holy Church, and to our divine father, Lord Pope, the true God? You are a teacher in Israel, and do you not know these things? You, Archbishop of Arles, our master," he said, "does it seem to you that the boat of Jesus Christ could be discussed more rightly by anyone than by the Lord Bishop of Aix?" "Indeed," said Basinet, "the most reverend Bishop's sermon has expressed most elegantly the manners and the condition of life of churchmen, and it was most fitting for reproving the vices and heresies of men of this age. So when I first understood that mention had been made of the boat of Jesus Christ, I began to recall the memory of those great high priests of Jerusalem, the priests, teachers of the law, scribes and Pharisees, who, appointed as ministers in the Church of God, at some time sat at the helm of that boat; but after they rejected the law of God and wished to serve human constitutions, Christ himself, angry, promised to overthrow those hypocritical workers in every way. But you, having pity on men who were wandering like sheep without a shepherd, sent diligent fishers to catch men, workers into his harvest, planters and cultivators into his vineyard; all of which, when maturity has come, will yield the lawful fruits of their age. In the second place, on hearing the Lord Bishop's oration, I at once recalled 1 Timothy 4: 'Some shall depart from the faith in the latter times, giving heed to seducing spirits and doctrines of devils'; and Paul at once adds certain signs by which they can be recognised. In the same way also our Lord Jesus says in Matthew 7 that false prophets, who come to us dressed in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves, will be known by their fruits. From these two passages, and from many similar ones, it is easy to understand who they are that try to overturn the boat of Christ and to sink it treacherously by every kind of device. These are surely those who drench it with mud and filth, and with waters rotting in putrefaction; who did not hesitate to send word to Christ, the living water, clear and everlasting, that they would dig for themselves broken and gaping cisterns. Those certainly are they who commonly boast that they are the salt of the earth, though they have no savour; who call themselves pastors, though they are in no way pastors, and by the long prescription of time have certainly lost the right to that name. For they do not break and distribute the lawful pasture to those to whom it is due, nor the bread of the divine word itself. And if it is lawful to bring forth the guilt of so great a mystery, is it not a miracle and portent of the same kind today that we hear some bishop preaching and see an ass flying through the air by a Pegasus-like flight? Do we not understand that those men are fixed and devoted by God to all curses, who glory that they hold the keys of the kingdom of heaven, yet neither enter in themselves nor allow those who would come to enter? They will surely be made known by their own fruits, for they have renounced faith, judgement and mercy, and in them there is nothing fair or pure except the surface of their vestments and linen; but within, all is anointed with luxury and lust. Outwardly they are shining, more than enough; but inwardly, in the recesses, they are filthy and exceedingly vicious with plunder and gluttony. Indeed they are like whitewashed tombs, which, bearing splendour and beauty, within are deformed and fall apart with obscenity and foulness. They will be made known, I say, by their fruits, those ravening wolves who, under the pretext of very long prayers, devour the living and the dead. Therefore, since we have come so far that you must yield to the truth, and you yourselves call me a teacher in Israel, I will not hesitate to assert from the testimonies of Scripture that the great pilot the Pope, and the rowers and oarsmen, the Bishops, and similar boatmen, who, in order to fill their skiffs, shamelessly deserted the boat of Jesus Christ, are pirates, false prophets and impostors, and not pastors of the Christian Church." Basinet had scarcely finished the speech he had planned when the whole crowd at once surged around him and, raising a murmur, began to attack him. But the Bishop of Aix, shouting and crying out, said, "Get out, wicked apostate! For you are not worthy to be here with us. Very many perish daily in the fire, but you are more worthy of that same fire. And so we see that no class of men is more constant in the faith, or more steadfast in the faith, than the canonical teachers; and it would be worth while at the first general council to enact by public edict that no one except canonical teachers should lay hand to religion; for by these monkish scoundrels everything will be ruined and everything overthrown." Then the remaining teachers, the mendicants, began boldly to accuse him and to protest to him about the injury which that excited man had done to the whole order, not without great commotion and tumult on both sides, and to such an extent that nothing could be settled about the business. After lunch all those venerable prelates held a council, with the mendicants rejected and not summoned, nor the monks, unless some Abbot among them was present; and at last, having sworn an oath, they agreed that they would see to it as soon as possible that the decree of the Senate concerning Merindol was carried into effect. They all promised, each one, that they would supply a certain number of armed men, and each would pay a share of the cost, as much as would be enough to overthrow Merindol. They ordered the Bishop of Aix and the provost of the canons to pursue the matter at common expense, and by every artifice to persuade the governor and the senators that they must not be deterred by the senate's decree from carrying out what they had decided, but, with spirits undaunted, with trumpets sounding, standards raised, and machines and artillery brought up for the present business, they should advance as if into battle. With this conspiracy thus formed and settled, the Bishop of Aix at once set about carrying out the order, moving from Avignon to Aix-en-Provence. In the meantime, however, when he was asked to attend a most lavish banquet which was being prepared the next day at the house of the Bishop of Rivière, he waited.

units.la: Eodem conuivio & mulieres Avenionenses eæ, quæ cæteras pulchritudine, existimationeque omnes antecellere ferebantur, ad reficiendas ex tot quotidianis Ecclesiasticis laboribus præsulum istorum humanitate & conscientia, accipiuntur. Confecto prandio, ductis choreis, alea ludendi reperto fine, qualia mensas Episcoporum vulgò subsequuntur, reverendissimi viri cœnam expectantes, in ambulatione veniendum sibi putaverunt.
units.tr: To the same banquet were also admitted the women of Avignon, who were said to surpass all others in beauty and reputation, so that the prelates might be refreshed after so many daily ecclesiastical labours by their courtesy and their conscience. When the lunch was finished, dances were led, gambling came to an end, and such things as commonly follow the tables of bishops took place; the most reverend men, awaiting supper, thought they should go out for a walk.

units.la: Itaque transeuntes via Mensularia, ducentesque sub axillis singuli domicellas, quas vocant: conspicati quendam imaginum inhonestissimarum venditorem, cuius scripturæ vim præse ferentis, qua animi ad libidinem incendi facile posset, ad illum universi confluxerunt. Coemptæ omnes ab Episcopis imagines, ac plures quoque, si fuisset: tametsi quidem erat ea multitudine, ut nulli legitimum onus hominum opinione perficere posse videretur.
units.tr: So, passing along the Mensularia street, each leading under the arm one of those young women, as they are called, they caught sight of a seller of most indecent pictures, whose inscription carried a force by which the mind could easily be kindled to lust, and they all flocked to him. The bishops bought up all the pictures, and more too, had there been more; though there were so many that no one would seem able to carry out the burden of them to men's satisfaction.

units.la: Quòd si quid aut ænigmate obscurius, aut difficultate subtilius ea pictura contineretur, totum ab eruditis ingeniosisque præsulibus in promptu, iucundéque deridebatur. Erat in eadem via etiam librarius quidam peregrinus, facturus auctione Bibliorum, quorundam Latinorum, Gallicorū, quorum ipse numerū aliquē venditioni iam expositum habebat, libros aūt præterea multos, quæ præsules intuentes, mirati sunt, ab eoq; petiuerunt, qua audacia fretus eas mercès tali in vrbe venales proposuisset. nū talium auctione librorū interdicta meminisset. quibus librarius, Nūquid ꝯ vos, inquit, Biblia saltē in tanto beneficij loco ponitis, tamque bona & excellētia putatis, quam illas imagines & picturas, quas ad harū domicellarum voluptate cōparasti? Vix postremū librarij verbum absoluerat, cum episcopus Aquensis eodem vestigio intonuit, Abiuro paradisi partē meā totā, nisi Lutheranus iste sit. Heus, heus, inquit, cōprehendatur. Mox abreptus in carcerem cōtumeliosissimè deductus fuit. nā cohors quædā ganeonum ac latrunculorū, quæ præsules pximè cōsequebatur, vt illis gratificaretur, vociferari statim cœpit, In Lutheranum, in Lutheranum, ad ignem, ad ignem. Mox vnus ei pugnum impingebat, alter capillis abreptum præcipitē fere in terra dabat, tertius ei barbā auellebat: adeo vt totus cruore maderet miser, antequam in carcerem pductus esset.Postridie adductus in iudicium præsentibus Episcopis, in hanc rationem interrogatus fuisse dicitur: Vcnaliāne proposuisti hæc Biblia, atque hæc Testamenta Gallica? Feci, inquit. Nesciebas in toto Christianorū orbe phibitum, ne Biblia excuderetur aut vēderetur alia lingua, quam Latina? Sciebā oīo aliud, inquit, quì Imperatoris priuilegio Gallicè cōuersos Bibliorū codices permultos à me distractos esse meminerā: nec Imperatoris priuilegio solum, sed & Regis ipsius, Lugdunēsib. typis excusos: nullū se locum inter Christianos audiuisse, nullam esse hodie regionem scire dicebat, in qua nō idiomate populari Scriptura loqui cœpisset. num qui Auenione cōmorarentur, soli essēt ex vniuersa Christianorum ratione, apud quos Patris cœlestis instrumētum odio inuidiāq; premeretur. cur impedirent, quominus authentica monumenta literarū, quibus assertio diuina cōtineretur, vtiq; pferrentur ac illustrarentur. idne interdicere ac tegere niterentur, quod Christus ipse detegendum, pferendūmque mandaret. nescirent permisisse Christum Apostolis omni linguarum loqui varietate, vt omni creaturæ nuntiaretur & innotesceret Euangelium. quin libros atque picturas, quibus omne genus obscœnitatis ac flagitij ad parendum libidini, Deūmq; negligēdū cōprehēderetur, interdicerent. licerēt. Quæ tàm arrogantia, quod fastidiū intolerabiliꝰ fit, quàm Dei opt.max. scripturas, quibꝰ animi paulò magis tenebris obductis, ad veritatis lucē adduci: vagi dispersiq;, ab errore ad viā salutis æquabile traduci possint, interdicto publico prohiberi? Quæ sæuitia, quæ crudelitas miseris animabꝰ ea quibus alūtur, quibꝰ educātur eripere? Atqui reduituros de eo ratione reuerendos præsules qui suauibꝰ rebꝰ amaritudinē, amaris dulcedinē suauitatēq; tribuant, qui deprauatissimorū librorū picturarūq; voluptatem aucupētur: quæ sunt spiritus atq; veritatis facilè cōtemnant. Ac tu quidem Episcopi furore impotenter impio disrumpebantur, crepitúq; dentium interuallato minimè verebantur animū suum ipsa maleuolētia ieiunum & inanem insani ꝑdere Iudicibus.
units.tr: And if anything in that picture was more obscure in riddle or more subtle in difficulty, it was readily and gleefully mocked in its entirety by the learned and clever prelates. In the same street there was also a foreign bookseller, who was about to hold an auction of Bibles, some Latin and some French, of which he already had a number set out for sale, and many other books besides. The prelates, looking at these, were amazed, and asked him by what boldness he had put such wares up for sale in such a city, and whether he had not remembered that the auction of such books was forbidden. To which the bookseller replied, "Do you then at least put the Bibles in so favoured a place, and think them as good and excellent as those pictures and images which you have bought for the pleasure of these young women?" Hardly had the bookseller finished his last word, when the Bishop of Aix at once thundered, "I renounce my whole share of paradise, unless this fellow is a Lutheran! Hey, hey," he said, "let him be seized!" Straightway he was dragged off to prison and led away with the greatest insults. For a band of gluttons and cutthroats, who followed the prelates closely, began at once to shout, to please them: "The Lutheran! The Lutheran! To the fire! To the fire!" Soon one struck him with his fist, another seized him by the hair and threw him almost headlong to the ground, a third tore at his beard; so that the wretched man was soaked in blood before he was led into prison. The next day he was brought before the judgement with the bishops present, and is said to have been questioned in this manner: "Did you offer these Bibles and these French Testaments for sale? I did," he said. "Did you not know that throughout the whole Christian world it is forbidden for the Bibles to be printed or sold in any language other than Latin?" I knew quite otherwise, he said, since I remembered that I had sold very many copies of the Bible translated into French, by the privilege of the Emperor, and not only by the privilege of the Emperor but also of the King himself, printed at Lyon; he said he had never heard of any place among Christians, and knew of no region today in which Scripture had not begun to be spoken in the popular language. Were those who lived at Avignon, out of the whole body of Christians, the only ones before whom the instrument of the heavenly Father was to be burdened with hatred and envy? Why should they hinder authentic monuments of letters, which contain the divine assertion, from being brought forth and made clear? Were they trying to forbid and conceal what Christ himself had commanded to be uncovered and brought forth? Did they not know that Christ had allowed the Apostles to speak in every variety of tongues, so that the Gospel might be proclaimed and made known to every creature? Let them rather forbid the books and pictures in which every kind of obscenity and wickedness, serving lust and neglecting God, is contained; that would be permitted. What arrogance, what disdain more intolerable is it, to forbid by public edict the Scriptures of God Most High, by which minds somewhat darkened may be led to the light of truth, and the wandering and scattered may be brought from error to the way of salvation? What cruelty, to snatch from wretched souls that by which they are nourished and brought up? Yet the reverend prelates will have to give account of this, who ascribe bitterness to sweet things and sweetness to bitter, who hunt after the pleasure of most depraved books and pictures, and readily despise what belongs to the Spirit and to truth. And the bishop, indeed, was torn in impotent and impious fury, grinding his teeth at intervals, and not at all afraid to betray to the judges his own mind, empty and hungry with sheer malice, and mad.

units.la: Qui cùm furoris impetu illius ferre non possent, conclamarunt omnes una voce, Quid opus illum interrogari pluribus? mittendus rectà in ignem est, ne quid ipsi de illo verbosius. Laberius iudex, aliique nonnulli qui iudicii illud exercebant, in eandem cum Episcopis sententiam adduci non poterant. intelligebat enim minimè iusta satis habere se causam rei condemnandi, minimēque ex æquo & bono satis hac in re versari posse. Itaq; censebant irrogari solum ei mulctam honorariam, ipsumque Præsules eos à quibus in iudicium vocatus esset, veros esse Ecclesiæ pastores, agnoscere profiteríque oportere. At librarius id se salua conscientiæ suæ religione, facere non posse ostendit, quādo flagitiosas ab illis sustineri picturas atque libros, verbū Dei haberi pro derelicto conspiceret: eáque se de causa sacrificos illos potius quosdam Bacchi ac Veneris, quàm Ecclesiæ catholicæ pastores esse existimare, quamobrem ilico posteà adiudicatus igni fuit, ac eodem ipso die morte mulctatus. Gestabat autem in signum causæ condemnationis, Bibliorum codices duos: vnum à gutture porrectum ad stomachum, alterum à ceruice spectantem ad humeros. At in his asperitatibus rerum, vitióque temporum, ei solatium dabat Diuini verbi commemoratio, quam fixam in corde, in ore promptissimam habebat. Nec verò cessabat in ipso itineris cursu, eóque loco ac tempore, quo ad supplicium raperetur miser, populum hortari ac monere vt Scripturas perlustraret ac euolueret: cuius oratione, plerique permoti, veritatis, quam oppugnabant studium accuratissimè postea persecuti putantur. Miscebatur interim populo motus ac seditio suboscura quædam, cùm quòd eius viri mors iniquissimo iudicio pronunciata videretur, tum verò quòd sacrosanctos utriusque testamenti libros ignominia quodammodò notari cœptos magna pars hominum existimaret. Quod cùm Episcopi animaduerterent, timoréque proposito populo facilius imperare possent, prodamandum præconis voce in vrbe quidē, comitatúe Ve-nissiæ toto curauerunt, vt quicunque libros haberent vllos Gallicos, mentione aliquâ omnino Iesu Christi faciētes, eos ipsi libros asportarent, manibúsque subijcerent eorū, qui delegati nominatim ad hanc rem essent: aliter si facerent, atque penes eos hi libri reperirentur, fore vt morte quoque ipsi plecterentur. Comparatis igitur à D. præsulibus, atque compositis ad Christianorum infestatione omnibus rebus, Aquēs. Episcopus Senat. Merindioliese persecuturus ex vrbe profiscitur. Aquas Sextias vbi peruenit, accurrit quamprimùm ad præsidē Chassanæum, huic molitionem quam Auenione fecerint, ostendit: mirificè de præsulum eorum qui quidē in Prouincia, Auenionéque sint, omniū erga ipsum voluntate pollicetur, siquidem Senatusconf. quòd factum iam sit, nec non ad opus tandem deductum iri plane speretur, extrema persequi velit. Obiectis eo modo magnis ab Episcopo, ac infinitis propè pollicitationum molibus, Chassanæus præses respondit, rem neque parui negotij esse, neque mediocris deliberationis atque consilij: itaque quòd decretum ipsi tale fecissent, eo consilio factum potius, vt Lutheranis, quorum multitudinem augeri quotidie intelligebant, metus incuteretur, quàm vt reuera id efficeretur quod ipsius decreti capitibus cōtinebatur. Tum Episcopus, Video inquit, nobiles eos qui aderant nobiscum nuper in conuiuio, facultate dicēdi sua cōsecutos apud te plurimum saltem iniecisse tibi scrupulum. Cui præses, Merindoliense decretum nondum plane definitiuæ est sententiæ, vt quemadmodum res est ita loquamur: deinde Regni constitutiones eius executione absque pluribus litium instrumetis minimè patiuntur. Mox Episcopus, Si qua te lex, aut constitutio impedit, indemnitatē ipsi vobis, culpæque præstationē pollicemur. Præses vero, At impium, effundi sic sanguine humanum. Merindoliensium quidem sanguis, ait Episcopus, nobis ipsis nostrisque successoribus adscribatur. Rursum Præses, Non dubito quin si eo progredimur, Rex tantam suorum hominum calamitatem indignissimè laturus sit. Si Rex impetu primo commonebitur, habemus unde Principis animum tęporis decursu molliamus. Accedit omnium Cardinalium, maximè verò Turnonij studium ac voluntas: quę cum nostræ causæ defensionem vltrò suscepturum facilè mihi persuadeo, tum nihil ei gratius, quàm Lutheranorum interimendorum occasionem accidere posse certò scio. Quare ne dubitemus, quin eius si consilio præsidioue hac in re egebimus, eo nos vti facilè commodéque possimus. nam quis Lutheranorum oppugnandorum artifex atque princeps cum reuerendissimo Cardinale Turnonio comparādus? His omnibus, ac alijs huiusmodi rationibus argumentandi Episcopus Aquensis Præsidibus senatoribúsque persuasit senatusconsulti Merindolienses executionem. Vnde haud ita post multò delectus tota Prouincia haberi cœpti: imperatores constituti: equitum peditúmque maxima multitudo sublatis signis Aquarum ex vrbe paulatim egressa, procedere, Merindoliúmq; perpetuis itineribus proficisci cœpit. Quibus de rebus Merindoliesęs[?] facti certiores, collachrymari, seque cau-samque suam Deo summis precibus commendare: hoc vnum perfugii sibi reliquum esse ducere, vt tanquam oues ad carnificinam adductę, sic ipsi se hostium explendę crudelitati præpararent. Itaque in squalore acsitu miseri mortales, pater videlicet cum filio suo, filia cum matre, vxor cum viro versabantur, quum repentino motu nuntiatur, adem retrocessisse: & quorsum tandem res euaderet, intelligere neminem. cognitum tamen fuisse postea, dominum Alencium, hominē in Theologia, ciuilíque iure versatum, adductum iustitiæ quodam ardore cum Chassanæo præside audaciter locutum: Aduersus Merindolienses minimè viribus & armis, indicta causa, nec innocentium à nocentibus facta distinctione, contra communem fori consuetudinem dimicare oportere: optare vehementer eum vti præses sui cuiusdam consilij recordetur, quod ille ei libro consignarit, quem Catalogum gloriæ mundi, inscriptum reliquerit, quo in loco persecutus fuit litis contestatione facta à præfectis iurisdictioni Episcopi Heduensis aduersus mures. Nam cum in iurisdictione fere tota Leussensi murium numerus infinitus erupisset, totius illius regionis frumenta corrodentium, statutum fuit, uti res ea Officiali Heduesi significaretur, murésquequi tantam patriæ vastitatem intulissent, excommunicarentur. Itaque audita Procuratoris fisci postulatione, decreuit Officialis antequam ad excommunicationem procederetur, ex iustitiæ formula monitione opus esse. cauitque ea de causa ut Heduesi in vrbe publice facta proclamatione ipsi mures ad tertium posteà diem citarentur: Quod in iudicio sisterent, processum iri aduersus eos, &c. Tribus illis elapsis diebus, fisci Procurator ipse sistit: aduersus mures, quod idem ipsi non fecissent, vadimonij desertionem obtinet: eáque fretus postulat ut ad excommunicationem procederetur. Iterum ex æquo cautum, ut quoniam murium tantæ multitudinis existimatio atque salus illo iudicio disceptaretur, seque ipsi exclusos exceptione queri possent, curaretur eis aliquis, patrocinio cuius eorum causa sustineretur. Itaque Chassanæum præsidem eam causam totam egisse, patronum tum Regium apud Heduos: superiorémque citationem irritam variis nominibus esse disse [?]. Decretum propterea secundam citationem quam de suggestu pronuntiari oporteret. Qua re perfecta, Procurator idem fisci sistit, quemadmodum initio fecerat. at Chassanæum ipsum, sistendi tempus muribus præstitutum breuius esse docuisse, quàm rei tantæ magnitudo postularet: tot præterea feles in villis excubias agetes, ut mures abesse non immeritò cogerentur: itaque nullum esse contumaciæ locum. Quare non temerè muribus inferendam litem, sed ea de re totæ consulendas Scripturas, ex præscripto quarum intelligeretur, quemadmodum ipsos se gerere oporteret. Adductos autem ex Scripturis ab eodem Chassanæo complures locos, ut ipse quoq; in illo suo libro memoriæ proditum reliquisset. Atque eo patrocinio quidem, quod alioqui parui momenti videretur, magnam eum laudem fuisse consecutum: persecutum enim illum iuris infractus omnes, quos Iudices criminalibus in causis ex officio sequi maximè teneantur. Iam verò, cum qui cæteros ipse docuerit, num eodem illo suo libro velit esse prudentior: quo libro oppressus conscientia convictusque teneatur, siquidem ulterius progrediatur, miserósque Merindolienses, qua cæperit inhumanitate, sibi persequendos arbitretur? Nam quid habebant miseri, quare Christiani viri non sint? num æquitatis fructum & idem officium ipsi mercantur, quod olim aliquando in causa murium, præses conseruándum existimasset? Hac oratione vehementer illum fuisse perculsum, exercitúmque, qui iam tribus à Meridolio[?] circiter milliaribus abesset, regredi iussisse. Quod cùm Merindolienses intellexissent, Deo quidem primum gratias egerunt: consolatione se inuicem sustentantes: hortantes, Dei timorem semper ob oculos statuendum, cuius præceptis obtemperare, voluntati parere debeant subijciétes se prouidétiæ suæ, expectantésque fructum beatorù ac fœlicium, Salutis scilicet æternæque vitæ possessionem: sibi proponentes exéplum D.nostri Iesu Christi, filij Dei, qui quidem afflictionibus multis & angustijs in gloriam suam ingressus sit. Hoc modo se Merindolienses ad omnia parabant genera tormentorum & cruciatuum, quæ accidere potuissent, erátque semper huiusmodi responsum illorum ijs, qui aut vicem ipsorum commiseratione persequebantur, aut qui perniciem eis occultè molicebantur. Manabat autem ea fama quotidie latius, cùm propter Senatusconsultum ipsum, quódque non defuissent qui illius executionem aggredi non dubitauisset: tum vero propter Merindoliensiû animi fortitudinem singulare, atque constantiam: adeò vt pauci essent in Gallia, paulò magis curiosi nouarum rerum, quorum ad aures ea fama non peruenisset. Nec vero tam leuis hæc causa visa fuit, quin perlata quoque fuerit ad Franciscum Regem haud ita diu ante eius obitum, Regem, inquam, excellentissimo ingenio, iudicio grauissimo sanè præditum: qui Guilielmo Bellaio Langeio, Proregi Thaurini, vrbe Pedemontana, significandum statim curauit, vt quo statu Merindoliensium res essent, maxima diligentia sciscitaretur. Itaque Lãgeius expediuit in Prouincia homines duos, probitate insignes illos, integritate ac fide præstátes: quibus mandauit vt exéplum Senatusconsult. Merindoliensis ad se deportarent, acsimul de omnibus rebus quæ postea consecutæ essent, inquirerent: intelligerent denique qua vita, quibus moribus Merindolienses tum ipsi, tum alij quibus in Prouincia negotium exhiberetur, instituti essent. Quæ cum omnia diligentissimè fidelissimèque curauissent, exemplum senatusconsulti, rerúmque omnium quas postea consecutas intellexissent, ad Langeium detulerút. Commemorauerunt iniquitates, exactiones, oppressiones, furta, rapinas, tyrannides, crudelitates, quibus singulis fere diebus Iudices Ecclesiastici, civilesque aduersus eosdem Merindolienses abuti consuevissent. Quòd autem ad ipsorum vitam morésque pertineret, retulerunt ex caeterorum Provincialium testimonio & sententia, eos operis laboribusque maximè deditos: ducentisque ab hinc annis ex regione Pedemontana profectos, in Provinciae partem illam commigrasse, quæ vacuam hominum consuetudine iniuriâ bellorum, planéque desertam, emphyteutico nomine tenere posteà, possidereque coepissent. Eamque terram ex eo tempore tantis corporis laboribus, sudoribusque subegisse, eo artificio coluisse, ut consecuta fœcunditatem, frumento, vino, oleo, melle, amygdalis, pecudibus, armentis abundaret: ex quibus rebus maximarum fructuum commoditatum ad Provinciam totam, aliasque regiones quotidie peruenirent. Quinetiam antequam ibi consedissent, Merindolium nunquam pluris annuis quibusque censibus, quàm quatuor aureis conducî solitum: cùm ante urbis ipsius vastitatem quotannis supra trecentos quinquaginta, dissolutis aliarum omnium rerum oneribus, à domino loci conducerétur. Tantundem & de Lormarino aliisque permultis Provinciae locis vulgò dicitur, qui tot latrociniis antequam eos hi viri celebrauissent, infestabantur, ut summo periculo illac transferretur. Affirmabat etiam Provinciales, Merindolienses ipsos cæterosque ad quos illa calamitosa pestis, tempestásque peruasisset, amatores maximè pacis & tranquillitatis: morum suauitate confirmationeque singulari, nec non æquabilitate vitæ quadam ac perpetuatione præditos: dictorum conuentorumque veritate & constantia commendabiles: nomina, si qua fecissent, aut expungere omnino si tum quidem possent, aut certè transferre, eos verò qui in ære essent ipsorum, nunquam in ius educere suetos: atque hac de causa potissimum & ornatos honoribus, & amoris vinculo singulari cum vicinia coniunctos. Si mansuetudinem ac humanitatem quis desideret: & eleemosynarum beneficio viatorum difficultatibus commodantes, & suorum egestatem, quatenus illi necessitate premerentur, quantumque in his situm esset, humaniter ac pie sustentantes: Internosci quidem solitos eos, ab aliisque distingui his nominibus, quòd temerè nunquam ad iusiurandum adigi, aut omnino proferendum Diaboli vocabulum eorum ulli ulli posset: quòd nunquā ad sermonē adduci obscœnū ac vitiosum: quin quoties alicubi versaretur, ubi aut lasciva alicuius cōmemoratione, aut blasphemiarū aliquo genere Deū offēdi ab hominib⁹ arbitraretur, illinc tōfestim se submoueret. Verum quidē esse (quemadmodum ijdem Provinciales ostenderent) cùm aut ad nundinas ad negotiādum, aut in urbes animi gratia proficiscerentur, vix unquam eos in templis conspiciri: aut si conspicerentur quidem, tamen Deum orātes, obversas habere perpetuò cervices ab imaginibus, quibus nec cereos offerrent, nec osculi pedibus figerent: reliquias Sanctorum aut Sanctarum adorare planè nunquam, ac ne dignari obtutu quidem: si peregrè profecti in cruces aliquas ligneas inciderent, illis quoque nunquam honorem exhibere consuevisse. Testabatur deinde Sacerdotes suo loco, eos nullas unquam sibi aut Missas, aut Libera me, aut De profundis iniungere: aqua lustrali nunquam se respergere: quòd siquando in illos ab aliquo mitteretur, gratias ei nihilo magis agere: imò animadverti facilè, fastidiri ab eis genus hoc totum conspersionum irrorationumque, tantum abesse ut eo nomine debere se quicquam existimarent. Suscipere verò peregrinationes, Sanctis vota nuncupare, peccatorum remissiones ære proposito comparare, quanvis obolo redimi potuissent, horum omnium nihil efficere. Porrò cùm tonaret, cùm coruscaret, nunquam se signo crucis inaugurare: tātum ex imo suspirates, oculos in cælū alios attollere, quosdam flexis genibus orare, signumcrucis aut lustralem aquam minime requirere. Denique pro luminaribus, pro confratrum sodalitio, pro refectione templorum, pro superstitibus ac mortuis nihil in pelum iniicere, nullas oblationes offerre. harum rerum expensas nullas faciebant, sed facultates in subsidium afflictorum ac pauperum seruabant. Atque hæc sunt omnia, quæ de Merindoliensium, aliorumque eandem cum illis vitæ rationem insequentium planè, moribus ac ritibus à superioribus legatis missis ad G. Langæum perlata fuere fideliter: deque Senatusconsulto, eisque rebus quæ postea consecutæ dicebantur, singulatim quoque ei relata fuerunt. De quibus rebus Franciscus Rex Langæi literis factus certior, ex optimi Principis officio expedienda diplomata curavit, quibus non solum eos qui defertovadimonio capitis damnati fuissent, verumetiam omnes quorum in tam populari causa eadem videretur esse defensio, ab omni impostorum iniuria sartos ac tectos iusset esse: Senatuique Provinciæ mandauit, ac nominatim etiam iniunxit, caueret etiam atque etiam diligenter, ne quid Merindolien-sium Respublica detrimenti caperet: neue in eodem negotij genere, tantam in posterum vim acerbitatis vsurparet, quantam superioribus temporibus fecisse diceretur. Quod si quis reperiretur, quem post legitimum inquirendi munus atque tempus ignorantia hallucinatum, aut cacodaemonis alicuius astu circumuentum, à vera religionis Christianæ professione declinasse constaret, huius animus ex informatione diuini verbi, ac vtriusque Testamenti locorum inductione recolligeretur: eoque modo sensim adhibito verbi gladio, vir is in Ecclesiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi restitui curaretur. Sic enim sibi placere, vt qui haereseos insimulati, eo, quo dictum est, modo conuincerentur, errorem, quo duci cœperant, abiurare cogantur. Ad extremum vero interdixit Princeps omnibus cuiusuis ordinis hominibus, ne quid aduersus Merindolienses ipsos, eorumque subscriptores alia via molirentur: sed abrogatis omnibus iudicum condemnationibus atque sententijs, ijs etiam ergastula soluerent, quos in vinculis sectæ Lutheranæ nomine suspectos retinerent. Ea diplomata temporis interuallo quodam obsignata delituerunt: tandemque Aquas Sextias perlata quum essent, petitum fuit à captiuis, num diplomatum eorum (quorum exemplum aureo proposito ipsis exhiberetur) iure vti vellent. Hac ratione miseri homines carceribus emissi fuerunt, deductis sumptibus, factaque fide iudicio se sistendi, quoties Curia mandaret. Scriba interim, cæterique pragmatici sibi inuicem diplomatum illorum nomine gratulabantur, quod eorum beneficio magnam se pecuniæ vim conflare quotidie viderent, sperarentque quinque circiter millia exemplorum exaratum à se iri oportere: quem numerum totidem nummi aurei adæquaturi aliquando putarentur. Cæterum Merindolienses primum quidem cum Regis voluntatem esse cognouerunt, vti diplomata ea in omnibus oppidis ac pagis totius Provinciæ, publice pronunciarentur. Itaque supplicem libellum summo Senatui obtulerunt, quo eorum diplomatum promulgationem ex Regij mandati sententia postulabant: quorum item exemplum petierunt: simulac ostenderunt, Regis ipsius animum eo minimè pertinere, ut omnes quos odium aduersariorum in Lutheranæ doctrinæ suspicionem vocaret, singuli diplomatum eorum exemplum accipere cogerentur. eam enim exigendi rationem iniquam & novam, minimeque ab eis, qui se homines esse meminissent, sanè ferendam. Valuit libellus: neminem videlicet ad exēplum accipiendum cogi posse: si qui tamen requireret, quinque saltē asibus auferret: si qui plus soluissent, reliquum ex edicto reciperet. Constitutum ab eodem Senatu quoque, ut infra tres à promulgatione diplomatum menses, universi qui tum quidem in Lutheranorum suspicionem venissent, cuiuscunque essent ipsi sexus, quamcunque etiam ætatem degerent, sive in urbibus sive ruri agerent, iudicio se sisterent. Huic sententiæ vehementer ab utroque Syndico Merindolensi reclamatum fuit, libellúsque supplex secundò propositus, quo continebatur, rem maximæ molis ac laboris esse, sumptus propemodum infiniti, ut viri, fœminæ, pueri, qui partim Merindolii, partim ruri commorarentur, in Senatum venire necesse haberent. Orare Curiam, id ut per procuratorem efficere sibi liceret: exceptis iis aduersum quos Procurator regius ipse concluderet, quorúmque potissimum exceptione defideraret: hos enim viros promittere vadimonium oportere. Acquieuit Senatus.itaque octavo postea die incolæ Merindolii duo venerunt in Senatum tum suo, tum omnium nomine Merindolensium, quorum ipsi nomen & cognomen in procuratione sua diligenter expressum atque consignatum secum deportarent: postulantes, ut seruato iudiciorum forensium more, hæreses quarum nomine suspecti haberentur, in medium adducerentur: his enim se promptissimè verissimèque in tempore ac loco satisfacturos. Quod si quid à fidei Euangelicæ synceritate, officióque virorum Christianorum alienum asseruisse conuincerentur, expeditos sese ac paratos universos canere palinodiam (ut est in proverbio) abiurarēque omnia quæ quidem ex præscripto verbi Domini Dei nostri hæreses esse constaret. genus enim hoc disceptationis totum ad illud unum, tanquam ad certam normam, esse dirigendum: tametsi co scelerisfese progressos minime profecto arbitrentur. Omnino tamen obire vadimonium cos, ut quibus de rebus accusarentur, quarumque hæresium insimularentur intelligere posset. Porro Senatus cum neque diplomatum Regiorum sententiam percepisset, neque Principis ipsius metem considerasset, multo vero minus eorum, quæ se facturos Merindolienses Procuratores spoponderant, rationem habuisset, decreuit ut qui errores suos abiuraturi essent, beneficio Principis uti quidem illi possent: reliqui vero qui manerent in sententia, eodem supplicio quo hæreseos convicti afficerentur, nulla amplius informatione habita. Quod decretum cum Merindolienses contra ius ac rationem factum animaduertissent, miserunt Procuratores suos Aquas Sextias, ut eorum nomine supplicem libellum Senatui subiicerent in hanc ratione:
units.tr: When they could not bear the force of his outburst, they all cried out with one voice: "Why need we question him further? He must be sent straight to the fire, lest he say anything more of his own wordiness." Laberius, the judge, and some others who sat in judgment could not be brought into agreement with the bishops. They realised that they had not sufficient just cause for condemning the accused, and that they could not in this matter act with enough fairness and goodness. They therefore thought that he should be fined only a token sum, and that the bishops who had summoned him should be acknowledged and declared to be the true ministers of the Church. But the bookseller showed that he could not do this without betraying his conscience, since he saw that the shameful pictures and books were upheld by those men, and that the Word of God was treated as abandoned. For this reason he judged those priests to be ministers of Bacchus and Venus rather than of the catholic Church. He was therefore at once condemned to the fire and put to death that same day.
