As a sign of the cause of his condemnation, he carried two codices of the Bible: one hung from his throat down to his stomach, the other from his neck, facing towards his shoulders. Yet amid these bitter circumstances and the evil of the times, the remembrance of the divine Word gave him comfort, which he kept fixed in his heart and had most ready on his lips. Nor did he cease, even in the course of the journey itself, and at the very time and place where the wretch was being dragged to punishment, to urge and warn the people to go through and read the Scriptures diligently. By his speech many were moved, and it is thought that they afterwards pursued with great care the truth which the bishops were attacking. Meanwhile a certain obscure stir and sedition arose among the people, partly because the man's death seemed to have been pronounced by a most unjust sentence, and partly because a great part of the people thought that the most holy books of both Testaments had begun to be branded with disgrace. When the bishops noticed this, and saw that they could more easily command the people by inspiring fear, they took care that, by proclamation of a herald, both in the city and throughout the county of Venaissin, whoever possessed any French books that made any mention whatever of Jesus Christ should bring those books themselves and hand them over to those who had been named and appointed for this task. Otherwise, if they did not do so and such books were found in their possession, they would also be punished with death. Therefore, when the lords bishops had arranged everything for the harassment of Christians, the bishop of Aix, intending to pursue the Merindolians, set out from the city. When he came to Aix-en-Provence, he hurried at once to the president Chassanée and showed him the plot that had been hatched at Avignon. He promised, with wonderful assurance, the goodwill of all those bishops who were in Provence and at Avignon towards the president himself, provided he were willing to pursue the matter to the utmost, since the decree of the senate had now been passed and it was plainly hoped that it would at last be carried into effect. The bishop heaped upon him many great and almost endless promises, but President Chassanée replied that the matter was of no small business and not of ordinary deliberation and counsel. He said that the decree had been made by them with the intention of striking fear into the Lutherans, whose numbers they knew were increasing daily, rather than of really carrying out what was contained in the articles of that decree. Then the bishop said: "I see that the noblemen who were with us lately at dinner, having obtained the opportunity of speaking, have at least put a great scruple into your mind." The president answered: "The decree of Merindol has not yet been made fully final, so that I may speak as the matter stands. Moreover, the constitutions of the kingdom do not allow its execution without many instruments of legal process." Presently the bishop said: "If any law or constitution hinders you, we promise you indemnity and that the blame will be borne by us." But the president said: "Yet it is an impious thing to shed human blood in this way." "Let the blood of the Merindolians," said the bishop, "be charged to us ourselves and to our successors." Again the president: "I do not doubt that if we go so far, the King will take very badly so great a calamity to his subjects. If the King is warned at the first onset, we have means by which over time we may soften the prince's mind. Moreover, there is the zeal and goodwill of all the cardinals, and above all of Turnon. While I easily persuade myself that he will readily undertake the defence of our cause, I know for certain that nothing would be more welcome to him than an opportunity of slaughtering the Lutherans. Let us not doubt, therefore, that if we need his counsel or help in this matter, we can use it easily and conveniently. For who is a craftsman and leader in attacking the Lutherans comparable to the most reverend Cardinal Turnon?" By all these and similar arguments the bishop of Aix persuaded the presidents and senators to carry out the decree against the Merindolians. Hence, not long afterwards, a levy was begun throughout the whole province; commanders were appointed; and a very large multitude of horsemen and foot soldiers, with standards raised, gradually left Aix and began to advance and march towards Merindol by continuous marches. The Merindolians, informed of these matters, wept together and commended themselves and their cause to God with the most earnest prayers. They considered that the only refuge left to them was to prepare themselves, like sheep led to the slaughter, for the cruelty of their enemies. And so, miserable mortals, living in squalor and distress, father with son, daughter with mother, wife with husband, they were suddenly told that the army had withdrawn; but nobody understood how the matter would finally turn out. It was afterwards learned, however, that Lord Alençon, a man versed in theology and civil law, moved by a certain zeal for justice, had spoken boldly with President Chassanée: that against the Merindolians one ought not to fight with forces and arms, without a hearing and without distinguishing the innocent from the guilty, contrary to the common custom of the courts; that he earnestly wished the president would recall a certain counsel of his, which he had set down in that book which he left behind entitled "The Catalogue of the Glory of the World," in the place where he described the joining of issue made by the officers of the jurisdiction of the bishop of Autun against the mice. For when in almost the whole jurisdiction of Leuse the number of mice had broken out in infinite multitude, gnawing the grain of the whole region, it was decided that the matter should be signified to the official of Autun, and that the mice who had inflicted such devastation on the country should be excommunicated. So, having heard the request of the prosecutor of the treasury, the official decided that, before proceeding to excommunication, a warning was needed according to the form of justice. He therefore provided that, after public proclamation had been made in the city of Autun, the mice themselves should be summoned on the third day afterwards, to appear in court; that otherwise proceedings would be taken against them, and so on. When those three days had passed, the prosecutor of the treasury himself appeared; against the mice, because they had not done the same, he obtained a judgment of default for failing to appear, and relying on this he asked that they should proceed to excommunication. Again it was provided, on equal terms, that since the estimation and safety of so great a multitude of mice was being disputed in that court, and they could complain that they had been shut out by an exception, someone should be appointed for them by whose advocacy their cause could be defended. Accordingly, President Chassanée had conducted that whole cause, the royal advocate at that time among the Autunians being his patron; and the earlier summons was declared void on various grounds. Therefore a decree was issued that a second summons should be proclaimed from the pulpit. When this was done, the same prosecutor of the treasury appeared, as he had done at the beginning. But Chassanée himself showed that the time granted to the mice for appearing was shorter than the greatness of so great a matter demanded; moreover, so many cats were keeping watch in the farmhouses that the mice could not reasonably be blamed for being absent; and so there was no ground for contumacy. Therefore the suit should not be brought lightly against the mice, but in this matter all the Scriptures should be consulted, from whose prescript it might be understood how they ought to conduct themselves. Chassanée also adduced from the Scriptures several passages, as he himself had recorded in that book of his. And by that advocacy, which otherwise seemed of little importance, he had gained great praise: for he had pursued all the rules of law which judges are especially bound to follow in criminal cases of their own office. But now, since he who taught the others, will he wish to be wiser in that same book of his, by which, if he proceeds further, he is held convicted and overcome in conscience? Does he think that the wretched Merindolians are to be persecuted by him with the same cruelty with which he began? For what did those wretches have that would make them not Christian men? Do they earn for themselves the fruit of equity and the same duty which the president once thought should be preserved in the case of the mice? By this speech he was greatly struck, and he ordered the army, which was then about three miles from Merindol, to turn back. When the Merindolians learned this, they first gave thanks to God, sustaining one another with consolation, exhorting one another that the fear of God should always be set before their eyes, that they should obey His precepts and submit their will to His providence, looking for the fruit of the blessed and happy, namely the possession of salvation and eternal life; and setting before themselves the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, who entered into His glory through many afflictions and straits. In this way the Merindolians prepared themselves for every kind of torment and torture that could befall them, and their reply was always of this sort to those who either pitied them and persecuted them, or who secretly plotted their destruction. Moreover, this report spread more widely every day, both on account of the decree of the senate itself, and because there were not lacking those who did not hesitate to undertake its execution, and also on account of the singular courage and constancy of the Merindolians. So much so that there were few in France, even those a little more eager for new things, whose ears this report had not reached. Nor did this cause seem so trivial that it was not also carried to King Francis, not long before his death, the King, I say, endowed with most excellent wit and very grave judgment. He at once took care to inform Guillaume Bellay de Langey, the lieutenant-general at Turin in Piedmont, that he should make the most diligent inquiry into the state of the affairs of the Merindolians. Accordingly Langey sent into Provence two men, notable for their uprightness, distinguished for their integrity and good faith, whom he commissioned to bring back to him a copy of the decree of the senate of Merindol, and at the same time to inquire into all the matters that had followed afterwards; in short, to learn by what manner of life and by what morals the Merindolians, both they themselves and others with whom they had dealings in the province, were trained. When they had carefully and faithfully attended to all these things, they brought to Langey the copy of the decree of the senate, together with an account of all the things they had learned had followed afterwards. They recounted the injustices, exactions, oppressions, thefts, robberies, tyrannies and cruelties with which ecclesiastical and civil judges were accustomed to abuse the same Merindolians almost every day. As for their life and morals, they reported, on the testimony and judgment of the other provincials, that they were devoted above all to work and toil; and that about two hundred years before, they had come from the region of Piedmont and migrated to that part of the province which, empty of human habitation through the injury of wars and wholly deserted, they had afterwards begun to hold and possess under an emphyteutic lease. From that time on, by such great labours and sweat of the body, they had brought that land under cultivation, and tilled it with such skill that, having gained fertility, it abounded in wheat, wine, oil, honey, almonds and livestock and herds; and from these things the greatest advantages of produce came every day to the whole province and to other regions. Moreover, before they had settled there, Merindol had never been let for more than four gold coins a year, whereas before the devastation of the town it had been let every year by the lord of the place for more than three hundred and fifty, the burdens of all other charges being removed. The same is commonly said of Lourmarin and very many other places in Provence, which had been so infested by robberies before these men had cultivated them that one could pass that way only at great peril. The provincials also affirmed that the Merindolians themselves, and the others whom that calamitous plague and storm had reached, were especially lovers of peace and tranquillity; that they were endowed with a sweetness of manners, a singular steadfastness, and an evenness and constancy of life; that they were commendable for the truthfulness and firmness of their agreements and promises; that if they had ever incurred any names, they either wiped them out altogether if they could at that time, or at least transferred them; and that those who were in their debt they had never been accustomed to bring into court. For this reason they were especially honoured and bound by a singular bond of affection to their neighbours. If anyone seeks gentleness and kindness: they lent to travellers in difficulty by the benefit of alms, and they humanely and piously sustained the poverty of their own people, so far as they were pressed by need and so far as lay in their power. They were commonly known, and distinguished from others by these names, because they were never rashly brought to swear an oath, nor could anyone ever bring them to utter the devil's name at all; because they could never be drawn into obscene and vicious talk; and because whenever they were anywhere where they thought God was offended by men, either by some wanton mention or by some kind of blasphemy, they at once withdrew from there. It was true, as the same provincials showed, that when they went to fairs to trade, or to towns for their own pleasure, they were hardly ever seen in churches; or if they were seen there, yet while praying to God they kept their necks always turned away from the images, to which they neither offered candles nor fixed kisses on the feet; that they never at all adored relics of saints, male or female, nor even deigned to look at them; and that if, when travelling abroad, they came upon any wooden crosses, they were accustomed never to show honour to those either. They further testified, in their proper place, that the priests never enjoined on them any masses, or the "Libera me," or the "De profundis"; that they never sprinkled themselves with holy water; and that if anyone ever sent such things to them, they did not thank him any the more for it. Indeed, it was easy to observe that all this kind of sprinklings and asperges was loathed by them, so far were they from thinking themselves obliged to give any thanks for it. But to undertake pilgrimages, to make vows to the saints, to buy remissions of sins for a price set out in money—though they might have been redeemed for a halfpenny—these things they did none of. Further, when it thundered or lightened, they never used to make the sign of the cross; they only sighed deeply from the bottom of the heart, some lifted their eyes to heaven, some prayed on bended knees, and they sought neither the sign of the cross nor holy water. Finally, for lamps, for the fellowship of brotherhoods, for the repair of churches, for the living and the dead, they cast nothing into the chest and offered no oblations. They did not incur these expenses, but kept their means as help for the afflicted and the poor. And these are all the things which, concerning the manners and rites of the Merindolians, and of others who followed the same way of life with them, were faithfully reported to Langey by the men sent from the officials above: and concerning the decree of the senate, and the things that were said to have followed afterwards, they were also related to him in detail. Informed of these matters by Langey's letters, King Francis, in keeping with the duty of a most excellent prince, took care to issue documents by which he ordered that not only those who had been condemned to death for defaulting on a summons, but also all those whose defence in so public a cause was the same, should be kept safe and sheltered from every injury of the impostors. He also charged the senate of the province, and expressly enjoined on it, that it should take the greatest and most careful heed that the commonwealth should suffer no harm to the Merindolians, and that in future it should not use in this kind of business such great violence of harshness as it was said to have used in earlier times. And if anyone were found who, after the lawful time and office of inquiry, had been led astray by ignorance, or deceived by the cunning of some evil spirit, and was known to have turned aside from the true profession of the Christian religion, his mind should be recalled by instruction from the divine Word and by the citation of passages of both Testaments; and in this way, by the gradual use of the sword of the Word, care should be taken to restore that man to the Church of our Lord Jesus Christ. For it pleased him that those accused of heresy, if they were convicted in the manner described, should be compelled to abjure the error into which they had begun to be led. Finally, the prince forbade all men of whatever rank to devise anything else against the Merindolians themselves or their supporters; but, having annulled all the condemnations and sentences of the judges, they should also open the prisons for those whom they held in chains on suspicion of the Lutheran sect. These documents were kept hidden for a certain interval of time, and at length, when they were brought to Aix, the captives were asked whether they wished to avail themselves of those documents (of which a copy was shown them under the golden seal). In this way the wretched men were released from prison, the costs being deducted, and on giving surety that they would present themselves for trial whenever the court commanded. Meanwhile the clerk and the other officials congratulated one another on account of those documents, because by their benefit they saw that they were gathering a large sum of money every day, and they hoped that some five thousand copies would have to be written out by them; a number which, they thought, would one day be equalled by the same number of gold coins. But the Merindolians, when they first learned that it was the King's will that those documents should be publicly proclaimed in all the towns and villages of the whole province, presented a humble petition to the high senate, asking that those documents be promulgated in accordance with the royal command; they also asked for a copy of them. At the same time they showed that it was by no means the King's intention that all those whom the hatred of their adversaries had brought under suspicion of the Lutheran doctrine should be compelled each to take a copy of those documents. For that method of exacting payment was unjust and new, and by no means to be endured by those who remembered that they were men. The petition prevailed: no one, it appears, could be compelled to take a copy; yet if anyone should demand one, he should pay only five asses; and if they paid more, they should receive the balance back according to the edict. It was also decreed by the same senate that, within three months of the promulgation of the documents, all who at that time had fallen under suspicion of Lutheranism, of whatever sex they were, whatever age they had reached, whether they lived in towns or in the countryside, should present themselves for trial. Against this sentence both syndics of Merindol protested vehemently, and a second humble petition was put forward, in which it was stated that the matter was of the greatest magnitude and labour; that the expense would be almost infinite if men, women and children who lived partly at Merindol and partly in the countryside had to come before the senate; and they begged the court to allow this to be done through a procurator, except for those against whom the royal procurator himself might conclude, and whose exception he particularly desired: for these men ought to give surety for appearance. The senate assented. Therefore, eight days later, two inhabitants of Merindol came before the senate, both in their own name and in the name of all the Merindolians, and they brought with them the names and surnames of their procuration, carefully written out and sealed. They asked that, in accordance with the customary practice of the courts, the heresies on account of which they were suspected should be brought forward, for they would most readily and truthfully satisfy the court in the proper time and place. And if they were convicted of having asserted anything foreign to the sincerity of the evangelical faith and to the duty of Christian men, they declared that they were ready and prepared, one and all, to sing a palinode (as the proverb has it) and to abjure all those things which were plainly shown to be heresies according to the prescript of the Word of the Lord our God. For this whole kind of dispute, they said, ought to be directed to that one thing as to a certain rule; although they did not believe that they had gone so far in wickedness. Nevertheless, they were prepared to appear, so that they might understand of what things they were accused and of what heresies they were charged. But the senate, having neither heard the sense of the royal documents nor considered the mind of the prince himself, and much less having taken account of what the Merindolian procurators had promised, decreed that those who were willing to abjure their errors might indeed avail themselves of the prince's benefit; but the rest, who remained in their opinion, should be punished with the same penalty as those convicted of heresy, no further inquiry being held. When the Merindolians perceived that this decree had been made contrary to law and reason, they sent their procurators to Aix, so that in their name they might lay before the senate a humble petition in the following form:

units.la: Supplicant Franciscus Chay, & Gulielmus Armantius tum suo tum incolarum Merindolii nomine: quod cum ex Regiorum diplomatu promulgationis sententia, postulati hæreseos, aut omnino secta Lutheranæ nomine suspecti, iudicio sistere teneantur infrà menses tres post eandem promulgationem, ipsi quidem procuratorio nomine ut & Regis voluntati obtemperarent, & diplomatum eius sententiam maximiduxisse viderentur, munere suo legitimè perfuncti sint: tamè Senatus neglecta diplomatum mente & sententia, neglecto Merindolien sium iure, quod cum diplomate Regis prorsus conuenicbat (qui æquitate vere Regia consilium attulerat, quo Merindolienses aut affines culpæ, aut ab eadem liberi dignoscerétur.) Senatus, inquâ, ipse tamen decretum fecit alienissimum ab omni eo iure, planéque diplomatum Regiorum æquitati contrarium, neminem videlicet diplomatum ipsorum beneficio uti posse, præter eos, qui se statim hæreticos esse profiteantur. Itaque postulare eos, ut decreti superioris sententia reuocetur: simulac legitimis inquisitionibus ostendatur, quænam demùm hæreses eæ sint, propter quas ipsi in iudicium hoc tempore vocentur. Idè eos hoc libello polliceri, quod illo superiori fecerint: quòd si in tanta æquitate causæ eos Senatus iure destitutos esse patiatur, profitentur ex diplomatum sententia, querelam suam ad Regem ipsum se delaturos, probaturósque propriæ vitæ periculo, quicquid adversus eos statuatur, id nonab ullo religionis studio, sed ab ambitione aut aritiaque proficisci: eóque maximè pertinere vti facultatum, quas maximo labore temporisque diuturnitate consecuti putentur, iacturam iniquissimo iudicio facere possint. Id enim ex omnibus litium instrumentis quæ quidem aduersus eos scripta sint, esse perspicuum: quorum instrumentorum exemplum ipsi petant, nec non huius libelli supplicis, & formula qua par sit, vt Regi eiusque consilio fidem facere possint contemptionis & despicientiæ, in quam adducta diplomata sint ipsius, quibus ratio maximè contineretur qua causæ propositæ veritas cognosci posset. Eámque veritatem plerosque Senatores iudicio niti confundere, quòd falsis delationibus obtinuerint, vti bonorum quæ ab optima parte Merindolienfium hominum possideantur, ad eos, aut ipsorum consanguineos proscriptio perveniat: idque ipsum indicta causa, ciuili saltem & æquabili: sicut negari minimè profecto possit. Quinetiā affirmare postulates ipsos optimo iure liberéq; posse, non habituros quosdam ex Senatoribus, eorumque consanguineos unde victum vitamque colerent, si bona non essent miserorum accusatorum, quorum in possessionem olim irruperint. eóque consilio miseros homines quocunque artificio possunt, accusare, calumniari, appetere ignominia contendunt, vt eos aut evertant omnibus rebus, aut certè in exilium proficisci cogāt: sic enim fore, vti bona libere pacificéque teneant, quorum possessionem vsurparint. Quamobrem postulant etiam atque etiam, vt Senatus miserabilis ipsorum causæ rationem habeat, eisque ius ex præscripto diplomatum Regis constituat: cuius optimi Principis voluntas ea mandatumque sit vt ipso iure primùm adhibitis inquisitionum formulis omnibus liqueat, quinam denum errores hæresesque sint, propter quas in iudicium miseri rei deferantur. Deinde Euangelica propositá veritate commonentur: conuicti abiurare teneantur: denique eo ordine conseruato, quasi postliminio quodam, Ecclesiæ restituatur. Senatus tū censuit, vt libellus patrono procuratorique Regio communicaretur, ipsíque postulantes octauo postea die sese sisterrent, vt quid hac de re tota decerneretur, intelligi posset. Audito patrono procuratoréque Regio, exhibitóq; postulatibus exemplo instrumentorum litis libellíque supplicis, eodem ipso die Chassanæus præses ac Senatores delecti quidam, procuratórq; Regius postulates seorsum allocuti, oftedere cœperunt, nihil opus esse inquirere in errores quos tueantur: neminem enim esse nescium, alienà eos ducere solitos vitam ab ecclesiæ constitutionibus, nihilóque fere plus Sanctissimi Patri, diuo Papæ, quam cuilibet homini populari deferre. quàobrem eos in errore aperte versari, extra controuersiam esse: abiuràdique occasionem minimè differre oportere: quòd si faciant, vitam eos in omni quiete tranquillitateque liberè propagaturos. His Postulantes responderunt, quod etsi literarum ne tenuissimam quidem particulam vnquam attigissent, tamen si Præsidi Senatoribúsque videretur, se libenter fidei suæ capitúq; ac locorum quos ipse Præses obiecisset, ratione esse reddituros: idq; se nulla mora interposita, omnique sublata dissimulatione optimè verissimèque facturos. Tum Præses atq; Senatores, Eius rei provinciam à Senatu minimè sibi tributam esse: longè verò sibi videri præstatius, vt scriptum conficerent, quo vitæ suæ genus totum, doctrinæq; rationem quam accepissent à maioribus, diligenter exequeretur: auferrentq; à Merindoliensibus omnibus procuratorium libellum, quo eandem illos vitæ rationem perpetuò secutos esse nominatim intelligeretur. Postulantes id se curaturos, perfecturósq; responderunt. profectíque Merindolii, omnia quæ gessisset, quæ Chassanæus præses Senatoresq; constituisset, ordine recitauerunt: protulerunt etiam libelli supplicis exemplum à Scriba subsignatum. itaq; magna Merindoliensium admiratio consecuta, quod nunquam hactenus vllum instrumentorum litis exemplum auferre ab illo Senatu potuissent: quin fuerat etiam interdictum, ne quis aut Scriba, aut tabellio, vllius foresès administri instrumentum vllius litis illorum accipere describereue tentaret. Quo nomine Regijs quoq; diplomatibus cautum eis fuit: quibus mandabatur vt omnium litis instrumentorum exempla, quæ Merindoliensés postularet, eis quàprimum expediretur, vt si quid inesset in illis vitij ad culpæ præstatione Senatus ipse cogi posset. Regis igitur diplomata postulates obtinuerunt, à Scriba Curiæ, sicut initiò diximus, subsignata: necnò ab eadem Curia mandatum, quo Tabellionibus omnibus iniungebatur, ne litis instrumeta Merindoliensium accipere, describéq; dubitaret: quicquid Senatus cõ[?]f.aliter ante cautum fuisset, quod in hoc genere Senatus ipse revocauisset. Itaq; repetè Merindoliensés tabellionē quēpiam ex oppido quod vulgò Malemort appellatur, acciuerunt: quē admonuerunt se ex Præsidis Senatorúq; sententia libere profiteri constituisse doctrinæ institutione quā hausisset à pueris, cultúmq; religionis eius quàm à Maioribus quasi per manus accepissent, ab hinc anno post Christi incarnationē millesimo ducētesimo, quemadmodū ex omni memoria ætatū ac temporum à veteribus intellexerint. Quare tabellio quidem cum & diplomata Regis & Curiæ simul alligatum mandatum inspexisset, nihil veritus hominum inuidentiam, facile eorum fidei capita omnia atque confessionem scripturæ suæ monumetis commendauit: fuitq; paulo post ipsa confessio ab ipsorum ꝓcuratoribus delata in Curiā: simulac libellus supplex, quo capita quædam eodem fere pertinetia continebatur. Iis omnibus rebus ex Senatº præscripto diligentissimè confectis, non defuerunt qui confessionis eorum illustriorē commemorationem desiderarent. Itaq; Merindoliēses[?] existimates operæpretiū fore requirētibus omnib° fidei suæ reddere rationē: reputates præterea, quicunque Christū Euangeliquæ[?] veritate & amplitudine abiurauerint coram hominibus, eos ab eodē Christo coram Patre cælesti & Angelis abnegatū iri: deniq; memoria tenctes maiores eorū in Bohemia in capitis adductos periculū idē ipsos aliquādo fecisse, suæque fidei confessionem ad Vladislaū Hugariæ & Bohemiæ Regē, à quo premebatur, misisse: hæc inquā, omnia cogitates secū Merindolienses, vberiore fidei suæ declarationem Cardinali Sadoleto, consulibus Auenionensibus, Episcopo Cabaglionensi curauerunt: necnon omnibus hominibus, qui publicè priuatimue illud ab eis efflagitauerunt. Quin etiam Franciscus olim Rex, Merindoliēsium vitæ rationem nosse voluit: cuius in conspectu Regio ipsorum confessio publicè per Castellanum eius Anagnosten recitata fuit. qua ad verbum fere perlecta tota, Rex ipse petere cœpit, ecquid in illa confessione de qua & audiuisset antea permulta, & nunc ipso exitu cognouisset, desiderandum videretur. At conticuere qui aderāt omnes, neque quisquam prosiluit qui in illam quicquam auderet adducere. Confessio autem fuit eiusmodi.
units.tr: Franciscus Chay and Gulielmus Armantius make this supplication in their own name and in the name of the inhabitants of Merindol. When, by the sentence of the royal decree, they were bound to appear before the court within three months of its promulgation, having been accused of heresy or of suspicion of the Lutheran sect altogether, they did so. They discharged their duty as procurators lawfully, and they showed that they were obeying the King's will and had greatly esteemed the sentence of his decree. Yet the Senate neglected the intent and sentence of the decrees, and neglected the right of the Merindolians, which agreed entirely with the King's decree. The King, with truly royal equity, had provided that the Merindolians should be distinguished either as guilty or as free of the charge. The Senate, I say, nevertheless made a decree wholly alien to all such right, and plainly contrary to the equity of the royal decrees: namely, that no one may enjoy the benefit of those decrees except those who at once profess themselves heretics. They therefore ask that the sentence of the earlier decree be revoked, as soon as it is shown by lawful inquiries what the heresies are, on account of which they are now summoned to judgment. They promise in this petition what they did in the earlier one. But if, in so fair a cause, the Senate allows them to be deprived of justice, they declare that, according to the sentence of the decrees, they will carry their complaint to the King himself, and that they will prove, at the peril of their own lives, that whatever is decided against them proceeds not from any zeal for religion but from ambition or greed; and that this is especially aimed at, so that they may be made to suffer the loss, by most unjust judgment, of the property which they are thought to have acquired with the greatest labour and over a long time. This, they say, is plain from all the records of the suits that have been written against them. They ask for copies of these records, and also of this supplication, and for the form in which they may be able to make it clear to the King and his council that the decrees have been brought into contempt and disregard, and which contain above all the reasoning by which the truth of the case put forward could be known. They say that many of the senators strive to obscure this truth in the court, because by false accusations they have obtained that the property possessed by the best part of the Merindolian people should pass by forfeiture to themselves or their kinsmen; and this, they say, cannot by any means be denied, even though the case has not been heard, at least in a civil and even-handed way. Indeed, they ask leave to assert, with the best right and in freedom, that certain senators and their kinsmen would not have the means to maintain their living and their lives, if the goods of the wretched accusers, into whose possession they have long ago forced their way, were not theirs. With this purpose they strive, by whatever trick they can, to accuse, slander and seek to disgrace the wretched people, so that they either ruin them in every respect or at least compel them to go into exile; for in that way, they think, the goods whose possession they have usurped will be held freely and peaceably. Wherefore they ask again and again that the Senate take pity on their case and grant them justice according to the prescription of the King's decrees. Let it be the will and command of that most excellent Prince that, first by the law itself and with all the forms of inquiry applied, it be made clear what errors and heresies they are, on account of which the wretched defendants are brought to judgment. Then let them be admonished by the proposed truth of the Gospel; let those convicted be bound to abjure; and at last, the order being kept, let them be restored to the Church as by a kind of return of rights. The Senate then decided that the petition be communicated to the royal advocate and procurator, and that the petitioners present themselves eight days later, so that it might be understood what was decreed on the whole matter. When the advocate and the royal procurator had been heard, and a copy of the records of the suit and of the supplication had been shown to the petitioners, on that same day the president Chassanaeus, certain chosen senators and the royal procurator spoke with the petitioners apart and began to point out that there was no need to inquire into the errors which they maintained. For everyone knows, they said, that they were accustomed to live a life estranged from the constitutions of the Church, and that they paid to the most holy Father, the divine Pope, scarcely more honour than to any common man. Therefore it was beyond dispute that they were plainly persisting in error, and they ought not to delay the opportunity of abjuring; if they did so, they would be able to pass their lives freely in all quiet and tranquillity. To this the petitioners replied that, although they had never touched even the smallest part of the letters, nevertheless, if it seemed good to the president and senators, they would gladly give an account of their faith, of the chapters, and of the places which the president himself had objected; and that they would do this at once, without delay and without any concealment, and would do it most well and most truly. Then the president and senators said that this matter had not been assigned to them by the Senate at all; rather, it seemed to them far better that they should draw up a writing which would set out fully the whole manner of their life and the account of doctrine which they had received from their forefathers; and that they should take from all the Merindolians a written petition by which it would be clearly understood that they had always followed the same manner of life. The petitioners replied that they would see to this and bring it about. Going to Merindol, they related in order everything that had been done, and all that the president Chassanaeus and the senators had laid down; they also produced a copy of the supplication, signed by the clerk. Thereupon the Merindolians were greatly amazed, because until then they had never been able to obtain from that Senate any copy of the records of the suit; indeed, it had been forbidden that any clerk or notary, or any servant of any court whatever, should attempt to receive or copy any record of their suits. For this reason the royal decrees also provided for them, ordering that copies of all the records of the suit, which the Merindolians asked for, should be dispatched to them as quickly as possible, so that if there were any defect in them, the Senate itself could be compelled to answer for the fault. The petitioners therefore obtained the royal decrees, signed, as we said at the beginning, by the clerk of the court; and also from the same court a mandate by which all notaries were enjoined not to dare to receive or copy the records of the suits of the Merindolians, whatever the Senate had previously provided on this matter, since the Senate itself had revoked it in this kind of case. And so the Merindolians again summoned a notary from a town commonly called Malemort. They told him that, by the sentence of the president and senators, they had resolved to profess freely the doctrine in which they had been instructed from boyhood, and the worship of religion which they had received from their forefathers, as it were by hand, from the year one thousand two hundred after the incarnation of Christ, as they had understood from the memory of the old men of every age and time. Wherefore the notary, having examined both the royal decrees and the mandate of the court attached together, feared nothing from the hatred of men, and readily committed to the records of his writing all the heads of their faith and their confession. Soon afterwards that confession was brought into court by their procurators, together with a supplication which contained certain chapters pertaining more or less to the same matter. When all these things had been most diligently drawn up according to the Senate's prescription, there were not lacking those who wanted a fuller account of their confession. Accordingly the Merindolians, judging it worth while to give a reason for their faith to all who asked, and considering also that whoever renounces Christ and the truth of the Gospel before men will be renounced by the same Christ before the heavenly Father and the angels, and remembering that their forefathers in Bohemia, brought into peril of their lives, had once done the same and had sent the confession of their faith to Vladislaus, King of Hungary and Bohemia, by whom they were oppressed; all these things, I say, weighing them in their minds, the Merindolians took care to send a fuller declaration of their faith to Cardinal Sadoletus, to the consuls of Avignon, to the Bishop of Cavaillon, and likewise to all men who, publicly or privately, demanded it of them. Indeed, King Francis of old also wished to know the manner of life of the Merindolians; and in his royal presence their confession was read aloud publicly by his Castellan, acting as reader. When the whole had been read through almost word for word, the King himself began to ask whether anything seemed to be lacking in that confession, which he had heard much about before and now at the end had come to know. But all who were present fell silent, and no one stood up who dared to bring forward anything against it. The confession was of the following kind.

units.la: Redimus & confitemur vniuersi, sanctam Scripturam inclusam veteri nouóq; Testamēto, diuino afflatu plane instinctúq; cælitus infusam: neque humana aliqua voluntate demersam in has terras, sed ab ore sanctissimorum hominum Spiritus sancti beneficio impulsúque profectam. Ipsúmque Deum ex omni memoria vetustatis Prophetarum suorum ore loquutum: verùm extremis hisce temporibus loquutum profectò per vnicum Filium suum, cui præstandam modis omnibus attentionem imperauerit: pereundum ei vt sit qui docilitatem & attentionem illi minimè præstiterit. Itaque qui ex Deo est, facilè eius sermonem audit & auscultat: qui sermo formula quædam sola, certa, perfectáque est ipsius veritatis, vitaque rectè instituendæ, vtilis ad omnem eruditionem, ad omnem animaduersionem, ad reprehensionem, ad iustitiæ informationem, vt qui ex Deo est, ad integritatem operum paratus sit. Hinc consequitur, Scripturæ sanctæ volumina satis esse fusa ampláque ad restituendam salutem hominibus: ad verum Dei cultum illustrandum: ad depellendum errorem eorum qui oppugnant veritatem: ad hæreses & vitia, deprauatósque hominum censendos atque corrigendos mores. His de causis sanctæ Scripturæ scientiam auro & gemmis longè magis expetendam esse: eiúsque disciplina omne hominum genus ad præceptorum omnium obseruationem erudiri, ad eius lectionem assuefieri oportere. Nec verò quicquam esse tentandum extra cancellos verbi Dei, cui nec adiungendum aliquid, nec detrahendum omnino sit: ne qua Dei animaduersio in nos, aut impostoria noxa maximo hominum incommodo consequatur.
units.tr: We all acknowledge and confess that holy Scripture, contained in the Old and New Testaments, was plainly breathed into by divine inspiration and infused from heaven: it did not come into these lands by any human will, but proceeded from the mouths of the most holy men by the benefit and impulse of the Holy Spirit. God himself spoke through the mouths of his Prophets throughout all ancient times, but in these last days he has truly spoken through his only Son, to whom he has commanded that attention be paid in every way, so that whoever fails to show him docility and attention shall perish. Therefore whoever is of God readily hears and heeds his word. This word is the sole, certain and perfect formula of truth itself and of rightly ordering life, useful for every instruction, every admonition, for reproof, for correction in righteousness, so that the one who is of God may be ready for every good work. It follows that the volumes of holy Scripture are full and ample enough to restore salvation to men, to set forth the true worship of God, to drive away the error of those who attack the truth, and to censure and correct heresies, vices and corrupt morals. For these reasons the knowledge of holy Scripture is to be desired far more than gold and gems, and every kind of men ought to be trained by its discipline to observe all its precepts and be accustomed to reading it. Nor should anything be attempted beyond the bounds of the Word of God, to which nothing is to be added and from which nothing is to be taken away at all, lest some punishment of God fall upon us, or an impious harm, to the greatest injury of men.

units.la: Ex eiusdem Scripturæ disciplina confitemur, & credimus in vnum Deum, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, tribus distinctum personis, sed eadem vna, spirituali, æquabili, perpetua, nullum neque principium, neque diuinitatis exitum habente essentia præditum: qui maxima potentia sua, infinitáque bonitate creat omnia, eáque vegetet, tueatur, & conseruet.
units.tr: From the same teaching of Scripture we confess and believe in one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, distinguished in three persons, yet one and the same spiritual, equal, perpetual essence, having neither beginning nor end of deity, who by his great power and infinite goodness creates all things, and sustains, protects and preserves them.

units.la: Et quanquam maiestas eius est plané tanta, vt eam in hac humanæ vitæ luce, cogitatione nullo modo consequi possimus (quicunque enim eam inuestigare supra sortem humanæ conditionis, ad ipsámque perrumpere conabitur, gloria eius opprimetur) tamen inanis præstantissimarum rerum testimoniis & insignibus relicta non est. Inuisibiles enim Dei actiones, eiúsque virtus & diuinitas immortalis, oculis animi facilè subijciuntur cùm ex orbis vniuersi constitutione, ex harmonia & quasi concentu, conseruatione denique omnium rerum quas admirabili, & incomprehensibili consilio suo & sapientia creauit, considerantur. Illustratur quoque eadem Dei potentia iudiciis suis iustis & æquabilibus, supplicijs hominum perniciosorum, præsidio liberationeque eorum omnium, qui ipsum amore venerationeque complectuntur. Quod ipsum eiusdem verbo facile declaratur, vbi peccantium hominum diluuij tempore supplicium animaduersioque, Noah autem eiusque familiæ totius conseruatio describitur. Declaratur item Sodomæ subuersione, & ereptione Lothi: postremò, vastitate submersioneque Pharaonis & Aegyptiorum, & contrà liberatione Israelitarum: aliisque compluribus historiarum monumentis & exemplis, quibus homines instituti Dominum Deum æternum, Regum Regem ac Principem agnoscere confiteríque debent. Ac testimonia quidem hæc omnia cùm ad præcidendam hominibus excusationis occasionem si minus Deum cognouerint, nec in gloria qua par est, ipsum quoque posuerint, optima locupletissimaque sunt: tùm prolixius adhuc ac familiarius nobiscum agens, exprimere se mortalibus in persona Filij sui voluit: quemadmodum nos in his quæ sequuntur, pie veréque confitemur.
units.tr: And although his majesty is so great that we can in no way attain to it in this light of human life, or grasp it by thought (for whoever tries to investigate it beyond the lot of human condition and to break into it will be overwhelmed by its glory), yet he has not left himself without witness in the testimonies and marks of most excellent things. For the invisible actions of God, his power and his immortal divinity, are readily brought before the eyes of the mind when we consider the constitution of the whole world, its harmony and, as it were, its concord, and finally the preservation of all the things that he created by his wonderful and incomprehensible counsel and wisdom. The same power of God is also made manifest by his just and equitable judgments: by the punishment of wicked men, and by the deliverance and protection of all those who embrace him with love and reverence. This is plainly declared in his Word, where the punishment and vengeance upon sinful men at the time of the flood are described, but also the preservation of Noah and his whole family. It is likewise declared by the overthrow of Sodom and the rescue of Lot; finally, by the destruction and drowning of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and on the contrary by the deliverance of the Israelites; and by many other monuments and examples of history, by which men who are instructed ought to acknowledge and confess the Lord God eternal, the King of kings and Prince. All these testimonies are excellent and most abundant, to cut off from men every occasion of excuse, if they have not known God, nor given him the glory due to him. Yet he has wished to reveal himself to mortals in the person of his Son, dealing with us still more fully and more familiarly; and in what follows we piously and truly confess this.

units.la: Certum habemus, Dei Filium in hunc mundum venisse, & humanæ carnis inuolucro tegi voluisse: qua in re una Christianæ religionis mysterium est constitutum, eoque nomine spem nostram totā & fidem in Iesu Christo, filio Dei, Domino nostro, Deo admirabili, authori æternæ vitæ, solo saluatore, iustificatore, sanctificatore, solo interprete, & patrono generis humani, solo Sacrificatore, cui successore non sit opus: cumque verè Deum, ac verè hominem existere.
units.tr: We hold it certain that the Son of God came into this world and willed to be covered with the envelope of human flesh; in this one thing the mystery of the Christian religion is established. Therefore we place our whole hope and faith in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, our Lord, the wonderful God, the author of eternal life, the sole saviour, justifier, sanctifier, the sole interpreter and patron of the human race, the sole Priest, to whom no successor is needed; and we acknowledge that he truly exists as God and truly as man.

units.la: Credimus atque confitemur Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum conceptum esse ex Spiritu sancto, opere virili in totum detracto sublatoque, quemadmodum Angelus ante conceptionem ipse nunciauit, idque consilio potissimum, vti Sanctus integerque nasceretur, cuius procreationem ab omni labe deformationeque vacuam esse necessarium esset.
units.tr: We believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit, with the male act wholly removed and set aside, just as the Angel announced before the conception; and this was done chiefly by design, so that he might be born holy and blameless, since it was necessary that his procreation be free from every stain and deformity.

units.la: Credimus & confitemur Iesum Christum omni detracta corruptione ex virgine Maria natū in Bethleē ciuitate (ex Michaea Propheta) corpusque sumpsisse ad nostri plane similitudinē, excepto peccato, cui obnoxius esse minimè potuit: Angelorum autem naturam noluisse suscipere, sed seminis Abrahami, quod testimonio Prophetarum omnium prædictum fuit, ut in peccatorum humanorum expiationem & sacrificium offerretur.
units.tr: We believe and confess that Jesus Christ, with all corruption removed, was born of the Virgin Mary in the city of Bethlehem (according to the Prophet Micah), and took a body wholly like ours, except for sin, to which he could in no way be subject. He did not, however, wish to take on the nature of angels, but the seed of Abraham, which was foretold by the testimony of all the Prophets, so that he might be offered as a sacrifice for the expiation of human sins.

units.la: Credimus & confitemur Iesum Christum sub Pontio Pilato passum, crucifixum, mortuum, sepultum pro peccatis nostris. Illum enim unum Agnum verè Paschalem esse, in victimam oblatum, ut nos ex Diaboli faucibus eriperet, quemadmodum adumbratum id fuit per serpentem Aeneum in deserto erectum: quoniam qui in Christum crucifixum aciem oculorum direxisset, omni morbo levaretur, maledictioni, ac morti eriperetur: passionéque sua iis qui in eum crederent salutem & vitam restitueret.
units.tr: We believe and confess that Jesus Christ suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried for our sins. For he alone is the true Paschal Lamb, offered as a victim so that he might snatch us from the jaws of the Devil, just as this was foreshadowed by the bronze serpent raised up in the desert: for whoever directed the gaze of his eyes to Christ crucified would be relieved of every disease, rescued from curse and death, and by his passion would restore salvation and life to those who believe in him.

units.la: Credimus & confitemur descendisse illum ad inferos: non tantùm enim corporea morte defunctus est Christus, verùm etiam oportuit eum cum inferorum copiis æternæque mortis horrore quasi consertis manibus luctari.
units.tr: We believe and confess that he descended into hell. For Christ did not only die a bodily death, but it was also necessary that he wrestle with the hosts of the underworld and the horror of eternal death, as if with hands locked together.

units.la: Credimus & confitemur Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum tertio postea die suscitatum à mortuis, ad iustificationem nostram, verissimumque testimonium salutis & consecutionis æternæ vitæ eorum qui libenter in Christo fideliterque moriuntur.
units.tr: We believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, raised from the dead on the third day afterwards, for our justification, and as the most true witness of salvation and of the attainment of eternal life for those who gladly and faithfully die in Christ.

units.la: Credimus, & confitemur Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum quadraginta post resurrectionem suam diebus in cælum ascendisse, corporeámque præsentiam suam ex his inferioribus locis submouisse, quemadmodum prædixerat discipulis suis Ioā.16. & sicut Angeli quoque testati sunt.
units.tr: We believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ ascended into heaven forty days after his resurrection, and withdrew his bodily presence from these lower places, just as he had foretold to his disciples in John 16, and as the Angels also testified.

units.la: Credimus, & confitemur, sedere illum ad dexteram Dei Patris omnipotentis: in omnia quæ sunt in terra & in cælo imperium habentem, constitutum Dominum omnibus ditionibus ac dominationibus: hostes suos nostrosque duxisse captivos in triumphum: eisque exinanitis omnibus rebus, populum suum diuitiis omnibus & opibus auxisse: ingressum etiam in Sanctuarium, humano artificio minimè factum atque constitutum, ubi patronus & mediator generis humani perpetuò consistit & apparet.
units.tr: We believe and confess that he sits at the right hand of God the Father Almighty, having dominion over all things in heaven and on earth, appointed Lord over all powers and dominions; that he led his enemies and ours captive in triumph; and that, having emptied them of all things, he enriched his people with all riches and resources; and that he entered the Sanctuary, which was not made or established by human craft, where as the patron and mediator of the human race he constantly abides and appears.

units.la: Credimus, Iesum Christum iudicatum venturum super stites ac mortuos semel aliquando extremo ipso iudicij die, qui quidem soli Deo perspectus exploratusque sit: Venturum, inquam, eum in Regia sua maiestate, Angelorum comitatu septum, ad iudicium orbis vniuersi constituendum atque pronunciandum.
units.tr: We believe that Jesus Christ will come to judge the living and the dead once, at last, on the final day of judgment, a day known only to God. I say he will come in his royal majesty, surrounded by a company of Angels, to establish and pronounce judgment upon the whole world.

units.la: Credimus in Spiritum sanctum, tertiam eiusdem cum Patre & Filio diuinae essentiae personam, ex eodem Patre Filioque manantem, vtriusque eorum aequalem, depulsorem molestiarum omnium, consolatorem vnicum humani generis: cuius instinctu sancti Patriarchae, omnes Prophetae Apostolique Domini nostri Iesu Christi loquuti sunt: per quem sancta Ecclesia omni tempore constituta & gubernata fuit. Hic est doctor syncerus, cuius afflatu omnes Christiani veritatis cognitionem habent: hic Spiritus in ipsis habitat, regenerans eos in vitam nouam, veterem hominem in iis mortificans, cosdemque viuificans ad omne opus bonum, in afflictionibus consolans, confirmans in aerumnis, qui suis adest in rebus aduersis, testificans eos esse filios Dei per adoptionem, caelestis haereditatis cum Iesu Christo participes.
units.tr: We believe in the Holy Spirit, the third person of the divine essence, together with the Father and the Son, proceeding from the same Father and the Son, equal to both of them, the driver away of all troubles, the sole comforter of the human race. By his impulse the holy Patriarchs, all the Prophets and Apostles spoke of our Lord Jesus Christ; through him the holy Church has been established and governed at all times. He is the sincere teacher, by whose inspiration all Christians have the knowledge of the truth; this Spirit dwells in them, regenerating them into a new life, mortifying the old man in them, and quickening them to every good work; comforting them in afflictions, strengthening them in hardships, and standing by his own in adversity; testifying that they are sons of God by adoption and partakers with Jesus Christ of the heavenly inheritance.

units.la: Credimus ac confitemur sanctam Ecclesiam catholicam, quae est congregatio & coetus omnium vere credentium, fidelium, & electorum Dei qui fuerunt a principio mundi, & erunt vsque ad finem: cuius quidem Ecclesiae Iesus Christus est caput, concilians eam sibi per suum Spiritum, eamque sceptro verbi sui regens, vna eademque voluntate ac spiritu eam coniungens vinculo fidei & charitatis. Omnia itaque Ecclesiae membra coniuncta, vnum Deum, & caput vnum ac mediatorem Iesum Christum agnoscunt, vnam fidem ac legem habent, vnus iis est Baptismus, & eadem mensa spiritualis, in qua idem cibus ac potus spiritualis proponitur. Pro hac Ecclesia Christus seipsum tradidit vt eam sanctificaret, mundans lauacro aquae in verbo: vt sisteret ea sibi gloriosam Ecclesiam, non habentem maculam aut rugam, aut quicquam tale: sed vt esset sancta & irreprehensibilis. Sola corporis, carnis & ossium ipsius membra in sancta censentur Ecclesia: exulat hinc superbi Pharaones, pertinaces Pharisaei, & Simones magi. nullum est membrum putridum, corruptum, aut alioqui infectum: nec in ea locum habent Iudae similes, Caino, aut malo Diviti: recipiuntur in eam tantum oues & agni: putidi vero ac foetidi haedi remouetur & excluduntur. Atque hæc differentia est inter Ecclesiam quæ aliàs capitur pro congregatione bonorum & malorum, & Ecclesiam quam nos credimus, quæ sancta vocatur, sanguine Agni illius immaculati mundata atque sanctificata, extra quam non est salus. Quare in eam qui sunt verè Christiani convenire debent, nam eadem Ecclesia est communio sanctorum, qui omnes sunt membra capitis sui Jesu Christi: ita coadunati, ut simul coram visuri sint conspectum Dei. Hæc est egregia fraternitas, in quam cooptati & conscripti sunt quicunque verè sunt fideles, vocati à Deo ad communionem Filii sui Jesu Christi.
units.tr: We believe and confess the holy catholic Church, which is the gathering and assembly of all who truly believe, the faithful and the elect of God, who have been from the beginning of the world and will be until the end. Jesus Christ is the head of this Church, winning it to himself through his Spirit, ruling it with the sceptre of his Word, and joining it together in one and the same will and spirit, with the bond of faith and love. Therefore all the members of the Church, joined together, acknowledge one God and one head and mediator, Jesus Christ; they have one faith and law; they have one baptism, and one spiritual table, at which the same spiritual food and drink is set forth. For this Church Christ gave himself up, so that he might sanctify it, cleansing it by the washing of water in the Word, and that he might present to himself a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but holy and blameless. Only the members of his body, flesh and bones, are counted in the holy Church: proud Pharaohs, stubborn Pharisees and Simon the magician are excluded from it. No member is rotten, corrupt or otherwise infected; nor do those like Judas, Cain or the wicked rich man have a place in it: only sheep and lambs are received into it, while stinking and foul goats are removed and shut out. This is the difference between the Church, which is otherwise taken to mean the gathering of good and bad together, and the Church which we believe, which is called holy, cleansed and sanctified by the blood of that spotless Lamb, outside which there is no salvation. Therefore those who are truly Christians ought to assemble in it, for this same Church is the communion of saints, who are all members of their head Jesus Christ, so joined together that they shall see the face of God together. This is the excellent fellowship, into which are enrolled and registered all who are truly faithful, called by God to communion with his Son Jesus Christ.

units.la: Credimus & confitemur remissionem peccatorum gratuitam, à misericordia & mera bonitate Domini nostri Christi professam, qui mortuus est semel pro peccatis nostris, justus ille pro injustis, qui tulit peccata nostra in corpore suo ad crucem: qui est Agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi. Is est Jesus Christus ille justus, qui noster est advocatus apud Deum: ipse est pretium reconciliationis nostræ: fidelis & justus ut nobis omnem iniquitatem condonet, sanguis eius delet chirographū quo obligati eramus , & mundat conscientias nostras ab operibus mortuis, ut serviamus Deo vivo, qui solus peccata condonat, & abolet iniquitates hominum, ut convertantur à vita mala, & deponant iniquitatem quæ in manibus ipsorum est, ut tristitiam habeant, quæ est secundum Deum, quæ gignit certam pœnitentiam ad salutem. cuius rei exempla habemus, Davidem, S. Petrum, filium prodigum, Peccatricem illam, ac plures alios Judæos. Ut non est inter homines qui macula careat, & se justum præbere possit natus ex muliere: ita nec est quisquam per se innoxius coram Deo. Quæ stellæ non sint mundæ in conspectu eius: quanto minus homo in sua putredine, & filii hominis, qui nihil est quàm vermis? Omnes facti sumus velut immundi, & justitiæ nostræ quasi pan-nus mulieris menstrualis, &c. proinde singuli gratia Dei per Christum oblata opus habent, qui solus pro fidelibus satisfecit, quibus peccata non imputantur, quemadmodum incredulis atque reprobis.
units.tr: We believe and confess the forgiveness of sins to be free, professed from the mercy and pure goodness of our Lord Christ, who died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, who bore our sins in his own body on the cross. He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. This is Jesus Christ, the just one, who is our advocate with God. He himself is the price of our reconciliation, faithful and just, so that he forgives us all our iniquity. His blood blots out the handwriting by which we were bound, and cleanses our consciences from dead works, so that we may serve the living God, who alone forgives sins and abolishes the iniquities of men, so that they may turn from an evil life and put away the iniquity that is in their hands, and so that they may have the sorrow that is according to God, which produces a sure repentance unto salvation. We have examples of this in David, St Peter, the prodigal son, the sinful woman, and many other Jews. As there is no one among men who is free from stain, and no one born of a woman can show himself just, so no one is innocent of himself before God. The stars are not pure in his sight; how much less man, in his corruption, and the son of man, who is nothing but a worm? We have all become like the unclean, and our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruous woman, etc. Therefore each of us has need of the grace of God offered through Christ, who alone made satisfaction for the faithful, to whom sins are not imputed, just as they are not imputed to unbelievers and the reprobate.

units.la: Credimus resurrectione carnis benedictorum Dei, ad possidendum regnum cœleste in æternum: maledictorum vero Dei, ad ignem & cruciatum perpetuum, ubi erit ploratus, &c. Credimus item animas esse immortales: fidelium autem ac filiorum Dei animas quâ primum ex hoc corpore migrarunt, ad gloriam cœlestem transfire, in qua Dominus noster Iesus Christus residet. certi enim sumus cum hæc nostræ commorationis in terra domus destructa fuerit, restare habitationem diuinam, ac domum æternam in cœlis, quæ non est facta manibus. Infidelium vero ac reproborum animas, cum è corporibus discedunt, ad inferorum cruciatus se conferunt usque ad diem iudicij & resurrectionis carnis, ut ibi corpore & anima in perpetuum torquentur in gehenna ignis inextincti.
units.tr: We believe in the resurrection of the flesh: of the blessed of God, to possess the heavenly kingdom for ever; but of the cursed of God, to fire and everlasting torment, where there will be weeping, etc. We likewise believe that souls are immortal, and that the souls of the faithful and sons of God, when they first departed from this body went over to heavenly glory, where our Lord Jesus Christ dwells. For we are certain that when the house of our sojourning on earth is destroyed, a divine dwelling remains for us, an eternal house in the heavens, not made with hands. But the souls of unbelievers and the reprobate, when they depart from their bodies, betake themselves to the torments of the underworld, until the day of judgement and the resurrection of the flesh, so that there they may be tormented for ever, body and soul, in gehenna, the fire that is never quenched.

units.la: Credimus vitam æternam, nobis gratia Dei per Christum oblatam, qui verè vita est, ac mortem confecit, ut fideles vitæ æternæ hæredes fiant. nam quotquot in ipsum credunt, & mandata eius seruant, nunquam morientur: neque est ulla condemnatio ijs qui sunt in Iesu Christo, qui non ex carne, sed ex Spiritu ambulant: ij non subcunt reatum, sed transeunt à morte ad vitam. Qui enim credit in Iesum Christum non condemnabitur: qui verò non credit iam condemnatus est. Hæ sunt duæ (quas nobis ob oculos Scriptura ponit) viæ, nec ullam nouam tertiam: quarum altera ampla quidem est & spatiosa, atq; ea ducit ad interitum, quam magna multitudo & frequentia hominum celebrat: altera verò arcta, quæ ducit ad vitam, ac pauci admodum per eam ingrediuntur.
units.tr: We believe in eternal life, offered to us by the grace of God through Christ, who truly is life and has overcome death, so that the faithful may become heirs of eternal life. For whoever believes in him and keeps his commandments shall never die, and there is no condemnation for those who are in Jesus Christ, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. They do not incur guilt, but pass from death to life. For he who believes in Jesus Christ will not be condemned; but he who does not believe is already condemned. These are the two ways (which Scripture sets before our eyes), and there is no new third way. One of them is indeed broad and spacious, and leads to destruction, and a great multitude and crowd of men throngs it; the other is narrow, and leads to life, and very few enter by it.

units.la: Credimus & confitemur, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum abolita Circuncisione instituisse Baptismum, per quem in populi Dei Ecclesiam recipimur, ut Domino consecremur, & segregemur ab alijs omnibus qui varias & diuersas religiones colunt: quæ nota est & signum visibile. Baptismus verò exterior, alium quoque interiorem nobis exhibet, gratia scilicet Dei, quæ cerni his oculis non potest, & beneuolentia qua nos prosequitur propter Iesu Christũ, qui nos suo Spiritu baptisat, lauans, purgans ac mundans animas nostras ab omnibus pollutionibus & iniquitatibus, renouans corda nostra: atque eas explet consolatione, fiducia paternæ ipsius bonitatis, ex veteri nouâ efficiens creaturam, vasa iræ in vasa misericordiæ mutans. idque virtute Dei inuisibili sic in nobis operante. nã Christi sanguis lauacrũ est animarũ nostrarũ, nõ autẽ elementum aquæ. Forma autem baptisadi præscripta est à Iesu Christo, qui dicit: Ite, & docete omnes gẽtes[?], baptizates eas in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti. Ioannes Baptist. Apostoli atque alij ministri Ecclesiæ baptisant, prolato verbo Dei ad sacramentum, ac signum visibile tantum donant: Dominus vero Iesus Christus ἀρχιποίμην[?], solus incrementum dat, & facit ut res signatas percipiamus: gratiis & donis quæ sub visum non cadunt, suos ornat. Quæ sacrifici[?] ad Baptismum addiderunt, præter sacræ Scripturæ authoritatem: ut sunt, aquæ coniuratio, chrisma, sal & sputum, mera sunt hominum commenta. Errant etiam graviter qui pueros Christianorū à Baptismo remouent.
units.tr: We believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, having abolished circumcision, instituted baptism, through which we are received into the Church of the people of God, that we may be consecrated to the Lord and separated from all others who worship various and diverse religions. This is the mark and visible sign. But outward baptism also presents to us an inward baptism, namely the grace of God, which cannot be seen with these eyes, and the goodwill with which he pursues us for the sake of Jesus Christ, who baptizes us with his Spirit, washing, purging and cleansing our souls from all defilements and iniquities, renewing our hearts, and filling them with consolation and confidence in his fatherly goodness, making a new creature out of the old, changing vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy. This is done by the invisible power of God working thus in us. For the blood of Christ is the washing of our souls, not the element of water. The form of baptizing is prescribed by Jesus Christ, who says: Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. John the Baptist, the apostles and other ministers of the Church baptize, by proclaiming the word of God, and they give only the sacrament and visible sign; but the Lord Jesus Christ, the chief shepherd [ἀρχιποίμην], alone gives the increase, and causes us to receive the things signified, and adorns his own with graces and gifts which do not fall under sight. The things which the priests have added to baptism, apart from the authority of Holy Scripture, such as the exorcism of the water, chrism, salt and spittle, are mere inventions of men. Those also grievously err who remove the children of Christians from baptism.

units.la: Credimus & confitemur Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum deinde ordinasse sacramentum Cœnæ, quæ gratiarum est actio, & memoria mortis ac passionis Iesu Christi, in cœtu populi Dei rite celebrata. in quo quidem panis & vinum distribuuntur & sumuntur, ut visibilia signa & monimenta rerum sacrarum: corporis videlicet & sanguinis Iesu Christi suspensi atque in cruce oblati pro peccatorum nostrorum remissione, & generis humani cum Deo reconciliatione. Quisquis credit Iesum Christum tradidisse corpus suum, & profudisse sanguinem ad remissionem peccatorum, ille comedit carne & bibit sanguinem Domini, & utriusq; fit particeps: considerans conuenientiā earū rerū quæ oculis subiiciuntur, & cibi quo corpus istud sustentatur, cū iis rebus quæ non videntur, atq; cibo spirituali. Etenim ut corpus in hac vita pane corroboratur, vinūq; cor hominis recreat: ita etiā corpus Iesu Christi morti traditū, eiusq; sanguis p nobis effusus nutrit, cōfirmat, & reficit animam tristem & afflictam. Cæterum ne quis existimet signum visibile cum re per id significata, quæ est inuisibilis, adeo coniungi aut conglutinari, ut disiungi aut dissolui nequeant, quin unum sine altero esse possit. Nam Iudas signum quidem cœpit, rem vero significatam & fructum non percepit, nec unquam corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi particeps factus est: sed infidelitate sua partem sibi apud Sathanam est consecutus, & membrum Diaboli factus. Probet itaque seipsum homo, an syncera fide & pœnitentia cum charitate Christiana coniuncta, ad hanc sanctam mensam accedat: nam alioqui reus erit corporis & sanguinis Domini, dum mortem Iesu Christi, & consilium Dei pro nihilo ducit, qui non temere sacrosanctum istud sacramentum instituit, sed nos hac ratione excitare ac perducere voluit ad ardentem sui & fratrum nostrorum dilectionem, ut vere efficiamur tepla Dei, ui in nobis habitare dignatur,quemadmodum apud Ioan.testatur Dominus,Siquis me amat,seruabit verbum meu, & Pater meus illũ anabit,& venimus ad eum,atq; cum eo habitabimus. Atqui istud non o modo accipiendum quo nonnulli opinati sunt,verum Christi corpus & naturale, carne & ossa in pane illo Coenae esse ac delitescere, aut in euouerti.nā hæc opinio pugnat cū verbo Dei,& fidei nostrę articulis est contraria, in quib° clare habemus, Christum ascendisse ad caelos, sedere ad dexteram Dei Patris omnipotentis, unde & venturus est ad iudicadū vivos & mortuos. sed Dominus Iesus Christi° sacramento Coenae adest potētia, virtute, atq; praesentia Spiritus sui in cordib° electorum suorum & fidelium. Nullus igitur Christianus carnalem quandā inter Christi & eius electos communitatē atq; unitatē imaginetur, quāuis revera coadunati sint corpori ac sanguinem illius, utpote carnis & ossium eius membra. mysterium enim coniunctionis & communionis Iesu Christi magnum esse norunt fideles,atq; haec ratio copulae cū sit spiritualis, hominis ingenio nec percipi nec intelligi potest. Christiani autē corpora in Domini praesentia non opus habent. Incarnatio eius & passio, ad salutem mortalium prorsus necessariae fuerunt: id quod ipse testatur, dicens, Exiui a Patre, & veni in mundum: rursus relinquo mundum & vado ad Patrē: quare certum est impostores esse qui docet panem Coenae esse ,pprium & reale (ut loquuntur) Christi corpus. Errant etiam qui affirmant,in Coena Christi corpus comedi corporaliter. caro enim comesta nihil prodest: Spiritus est qui vivificat. Fideles igitur vere Iesu Christi carnem edunt,& sanguinem bibunt spiritualiter in ipsorum cordibus. Quapropter sacrilegi merito censendi sunt, qui istud Sacramentum contemnunt: pij vero credunt & confitentur uno ore omnes, Coenam Dominicam publicum esse conventum ad testificandum Iesum Christum panem esse vitae, qui de caelo descendit. In Coena complementum est ac veritas Agni illius & solennitatis Paschae: participatio nempe corporis & sanguinis Christi: memoria mortis & passionis eius: confessio fidei sub symbolis atque insignibus veri Regis: separatio & segregatio ab omnibus sectis : coadunatio in unum corpus: mutua inter Christianos charitatis obligatio, neruus ac vinculum fraternae illius coniunctionis : exemplum ac monimentum posteris: arrhabo misericordiæ Dei: figura Cœnæ æternæ.
units.tr: We believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ afterwards ordained the sacrament of the Supper, which is an act of thanksgiving and a remembrance of the death and passion of Jesus Christ, duly celebrated in the assembly of the people of God. In it bread and wine are distributed and taken as visible signs and memorials of sacred things, namely of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, hung and offered on the cross for the forgiveness of our sins and the reconciliation of mankind with God. Whoever believes that Jesus Christ delivered up his body and shed his blood for the remission of sins, he eats the flesh and drinks the blood of the Lord, and becomes a partaker of both, considering the agreement between those things which are placed before the eyes, and the food by which this body is sustained, with those things which are not seen, and with spiritual food. For just as the body in this life is strengthened by bread, and wine refreshes the heart of man, so also the body of Jesus Christ delivered to death, and his blood poured out for us, nourish, confirm and refresh the sorrowful and afflicted soul. Moreover, let no one think that the visible sign is so joined or cemented to the thing signified, which is invisible, that they cannot be separated or dissolved, so that one could not be without the other. For Judas indeed received the sign, but did not receive the thing signified and its fruit, and never became a partaker of the body and blood of Jesus Christ; but by his unbelief he obtained for himself a share with Satan, and became a member of the devil. Let a man therefore examine himself, whether he approaches this holy table with sincere faith and repentance joined with Christian love; for otherwise he will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, while he counts the death of Jesus Christ and the counsel of God as nothing. God did not institute this most holy sacrament rashly, but wished by this means to stir us up and lead us to a fervent love of himself and of our brethren, so that we may truly become the temple of God, in whom he deigns to dwell, as the Lord testifies in John: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our abode with him. Yet this is not to be understood in the way some have supposed, that the natural body of Christ, flesh and bones, is in that bread of the Supper, and lies hidden there, or is changed into it. For this opinion fights against the word of God and is contrary to the articles of our faith, in which we clearly have that Christ ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty, whence also he will come to judge the living and the dead. But the Lord Jesus Christ is present in the sacrament of the Supper by the power, virtue and presence of his Spirit in the hearts of his elect and faithful. Therefore let no Christian imagine any carnal communion or unity between Christ and his elect, although they are truly joined to his body and blood, as members of his flesh and bones. For the faithful know that the mystery of the union and communion of Jesus Christ is great, and since this bond is spiritual, it can be neither perceived nor understood by human wit. Christians have no need of his body to be present. His incarnation and passion were altogether necessary for the salvation of mortals, as he himself testifies, saying: I came out from the Father, and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father. Therefore it is certain that they are impostors who teach that the bread of the Supper is the proper and real (as they say) body of Christ. Those also err who affirm that in the Supper the body of Christ is eaten corporally; for flesh eaten profits nothing; it is the Spirit that gives life. The faithful therefore truly eat the flesh of Jesus Christ and drink his blood spiritually in their hearts. Wherefore those who despise this sacrament are rightly judged sacrilegious; but the godly all believe and confess with one mouth that the Lord's Supper is a public assembly for testifying that Jesus Christ is the bread of life, which came down from heaven. In the Supper there is the fulfilment and truth of that Lamb and of the solemnity of the Passover: namely the participation in the body and blood of Christ, the remembrance of his death and passion, the confession of faith under the symbols and badges of the true King, separation and segregation from all sects, union into one body, the mutual obligation of charity among Christians, the sinew and bond of that brotherly fellowship, an example and memorial for posterity, a pledge of the mercy of God, and a figure of the eternal Supper.

units.la: Credimus & confitemur syncerum Dei cultum consistere in eo, ut voluntati eius pareamus, atque omnem nostram diligentiam, operam, ac studium conferamus in hoc ut, quoad in nobis erit, eam sequamur.
units.tr: We believe and confess that the pure worship of God consists in obeying his will, and that we should devote all our diligence, effort and zeal to following it, as far as lies in us.

units.la: Regula vero obsequij quod Deo præstandum est, in Præceptis divinæ Legis nobis præscripta est, quibus docemur quid Deo primùm, deinde quid proximis nostris debeamus. Porrò finis præcepti est Deo obedire in vera charitate, ex puro & integro corde, & conscientia bona, & fide non simulata. Hæc denùm est ratio suum Deo honorem tribuendi, qui nec ex nostro ingenio aut hominum traditionibus colí, nec quod cuique bonum & æquum videbitur, sed quod ipse præcepit tantùm fieri vult. nam omnia bona opera, quæ præparauit Deus ut in iis ambulemus, in Mandatis ipsius habemus.
units.tr: The rule of the obedience owed to God is prescribed for us in the precepts of the divine Law, which teach us what we owe first to God and then to our neighbours. The purpose of the precept is to obey God in true love, from a pure and sincere heart, with a good conscience and unfeigned faith. This is the only proper way to give God his honour: he is not to be worshipped according to our own wit or human traditions, nor according to whatever seems good and right to each person, but only as he has commanded. For all the good works which God prepared that we should walk in them, we have in his commandments.

units.la: Confitemur, agnitionem peccati ab ipsa Legis intelligentia proficisci, quæ nostram nobis quasi digito ostendit imbecillitatem, quum nemo sit mortalium qui eam implere valeat.
