Omnes enim homines peccatores sunt: Legis neutiquam observantes: natura filij iræ: iusto Dei iudicio obnoxij, & quouis reatu ac morte æterna digni. Unde sequitur nullum restare aliud remedium quam ut ad gratia Dei & misericordiam veniamus, quæ nobis in solo Christo offertur: sicut scriptum est, Verbum prope est in ore tuo, & in corde tuo: hoc est verbum fidei, quod prædicamus. Quòd si Dominum Iesum ore tuo confessus fueris, & credideris in corde tuo quòd Deus suscitauit illum ex mortuis: salvus eris. corde enim creditur in iustitiam, ore fit confessio in salutem. omnis qui credit in eum non pudefiet. Nam Dei promissiones fide apprehenduntur, quæ certa est cognitio amoris Dei erga nos, in gratuita Dei promissione, quam in Iesu Christo habemus, fundata: deinde per Spiritum sanctum in cordibus nostris confirmata atque obsignata, qua gratis salvi fimus: nec id à nobis, sed dono Dei, non autem operibus, ne quis gloriari possit. Proinde Paulus omnia sibi detrimento esse duxit, nec pluris quam fimū æstimauit, ut sibi Christum lucrifaceret, utq; in Christo inueniretur induti non iustitia Legis, sed fidei, quæ quidem iustitia à Deo est. Præterea idem alibi infert: Nos itaque scientes hominem non ex operibus, sed per fidem iustificari: credimus etiam in Iesum Christum, ut per fidem
units.tr: We confess that the knowledge of sin arises from the very understanding of the Law, which shows us our weakness as if with a finger, since no mortal can fulfil it. For all men are sinners, not keeping the Law at all, children of wrath by nature, liable to God's just judgment, and deserving of every kind of guilt and eternal death. It follows that there is no other remedy left than to come to the grace and mercy of God, which is offered to us in Christ alone. As it is written: "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart; that is, the word of faith which we preach. If you confess the Lord Jesus with your mouth, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." For God's promises are apprehended by faith, which is the certain knowledge of God's love towards us, founded on the free promise of God that we have in Jesus Christ, and then confirmed and sealed in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. By this we are saved freely, and not from ourselves but by the gift of God, not by works, lest anyone should boast. Therefore Paul counted all things loss, and regarded them as dung, so that he might gain Christ, and be found in Christ, not having a righteousness of his own from the Law, but that which is through faith, the righteousness that is from God. Moreover, he infers the same elsewhere: "Knowing therefore that a man is justified not by works but by faith, we also have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the Law."

units.la: Rom. 10. b 8. 9. 10. 11. Verbum prope est in ore tuo; referenced at the line "Verbum propè" in the text. idem in cum,non ex operibus Legis iustificemur. Eadem est doctrina Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui quaerentibus discipulis, ecquis igiur salvus fieret: respondit, apud homines id quidem esse impossibile: apud Deum vero, omnia esse possibilia. Vbi itaque restat gloriatio? prorsus excluditur. Qua tandem lege? Operum-ne? Non: sed per legem fidei, quae reputatur ad iustitiam.
units.tr: Rom. 10. b 8. 9. 10. 11. Verbum prope est in ore tuo; referenced at the line "Verbum propè" in the text. That is, we are justified not by the works of the Law. The teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ is the same: when the disciples asked who then could be saved, he answered that with men this is indeed impossible, but with God all things are possible. Where, then, is boasting? It is utterly excluded. By what law? By the law of works? No, but by the law of faith, which is reckoned to righteousness.

units.la: Confitemur bona opera, quae Deus praeparavit ut in iis ambula-remus, quaeque in verbo eius propositá sunt, fieri debere atque studiose adimpleri: non quidem spe promerendi aliquid apud Deum, aut metu aeterni exitij: sed ex officio atque amore quo communem omnium nostrum Patrem complecti oportet, ut obsequium nostrum ad ipsius gloriam & proximi aedificationem spectet: utque vera ac viva fides, tanquam arbor à bonis fructibus, dignoscatur. Huc tendunt verba Petri, cum ait, Quamobrem, fratres, date operam ut bonis operibus certior reddatur electio vestra, conversationem vestram inter gentes habentes bonam, ut in quo detrahunt de vobis tanquam maleficis, ex bonis operibus vos aestimates, glorificet Deum in die visitationis. Quoniam autem frigidi & pigri ad omne op° bonum impij in hoc se excusant, quod Lex sit impossibilis carni, atque ita ducti falso gaudio, sibi in peccatis placent: certum est quod qui veram fidem habebunt, fructus illius & opera quoque producet: increduli vero mala opera perpetrabunt, necnon hypocritae qui tantum fidem mortuam iactitant, quos Divus Paulus inquit, ore quidem confiteri se Deum nosse, operibus vero negare: quandoquidem abominabiles sunt, infideles & ad omne opus bonum inutiles.
units.tr: We confess that the good works which God prepared that we should walk in them, and which are set forth in his Word, ought to be done and diligently performed: not indeed in the hope of earning anything from God, or from fear of eternal punishment, but out of duty and the love with which we ought to embrace our common Father, so that our obedience may look to his glory and to the edification of our neighbour, and so that true and living faith may be recognised, as a tree is known by its good fruits. To this point the words of Peter tend, when he says: "Wherefore, brethren, labour the more to make your calling and election sure by good works; having your conversation honest among the Gentiles, so that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation." Since the cold and lazy, and the ungodly, excuse themselves in this, that the Law is impossible for the flesh, and so, led by a false joy, they are pleased with their sins, it is certain that those who have true faith will also produce its fruit and works; but unbelievers will commit evil deeds, and so will hypocrites, who boast only of a dead faith, whom the divine Paul says confess with their mouths that they know God, but deny him by their works, since they are abominable, disobedient, and useless for every good work.

units.la: Credimus & confitemur, sobrietatem & continentiam nobis ex praeceptis divinis, in omnibus rebus servandam. Ieiunium quoq; nobis in Scriptura iniunctum est, quod corporis afflictione atque humiliatione constat, non id quidem ut tantummodo caro affligatur, sed ut alacriores, magisque ad precandum idonei reddamur. Unde facile patet, verum ieiunij usum his temporibus negligi, imo prorsus aboleri. quod quidem Isaias reprehendit in Iudaeis, atque ostedit quinam ieiunio abutantur, Nolite, inquit, ieiunare quemadmodum ad hunc usque diem fecistis, &c.
units.tr: We believe and confess that sobriety and self-control must be observed in all things, according to the divine precepts. Fasting too is enjoined on us in Scripture; it consists in the affliction and humbling of the body, not so that the flesh alone may be afflicted, but so that we may be made more alert and better fitted for prayer. From this it is easily seen that the true use of fasting is neglected in these times, indeed altogether abolished. Isaiah rebuked this among the Jews, and showed who abuse fasting: "Do not fast," he says, "as you have done until this day," etc.

units.la: Cōfitemur etiam in veteri quidē Testamento certos cibos fuisse prohibitos, quorū tamē apud Christianos liber māsit vsus per IesumChristum, qui nos plane immunes ac liberos fecit istiusmodi ceremonia atque seruitute Legis. Qua de re omnia munda mundis, contráque impuris & incredulis nihil purum esse potest, quorum mens & conscientia impura est. Atqui [?]scianos Deo gratiores non reddit. nam quod per os intrat, nequaquam hominem inquinat: omnis creatura Dei bona est: proinde nec aspernanda, modò cum gratiarum actione vtamur. Sanctificata enim est verbo Dei & oratione. Sed diligenter nobis videndum est, ne libertatem hanc ad carnis voluptatem traducamus, atque in primis cautio adhibenda, ne corda ingluuie aut ebrietate, aut solicitudinibus & curis huius seculi impediantur, ac penitus obruantur.
units.tr: We confess also that in the Old Testament certain foods were forbidden, yet among Christians their use has been free through Jesus Christ, who has made us altogether immune and free from such ceremonies and the bondage of the Law. For this reason, "all things are pure to the pure," but nothing is pure to the unclean and unbelieving, whose mind and conscience are defiled. Yet certain foods do not make us more pleasing to God; for what enters through the mouth does not defile a man; every creature of God is good, and therefore not to be rejected, provided we use it with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the Word of God and by prayer. But we must take care that we do not turn this liberty to the gratification of the flesh, and above all caution must be used lest our hearts be weighed down by gluttony or drunkenness, or by the cares and anxieties of this age, and utterly overwhelmed.

units.la: Confitemur Reges, Principes, ac magistratus personas esse à Deo constitutas, vt gladium gestent ad bonorum defensionem, atque punitionem facinorosorum. Ideóque iis obedientia debetur non modò propter iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam. Reddendum enim suum cuique tributum, vectigal, honorem & alia pro suo cuique iure persoluenda censemus. Ad Regem in primis obedientia pertinet, vtpote qui cæteris dignitate præstet: ad Duces verò quòd ab illo missi sint. Omnibus denique proceribus ac magistratibus parendum, quòd Deus in hoc ordinauit, vt præmio bonos, sceleratos verò pœna afficiat.
units.tr: We confess that kings, princes and magistrates are persons appointed by God, to bear the sword for the defence of good people and the punishment of evildoers. Therefore obedience is owed to them not only out of fear but also for conscience's sake. We judge that to each person must be rendered his due tribute, tax, honour, and whatever else must be paid according to each one's right. Obedience pertains first of all to the king, as he excels the others in dignity; to the commanders, because they are sent by him. Finally, all nobles and magistrates must be obeyed, because God has ordained this, that he should reward the good and punish the wicked.

units.la: Confitemur ministros & Ecclesiæ pastores, exemplo gregi, & fidelibus esse oportere, in sermone, consuetudine, charitate, fide & castimonia aliis prælucere, concionando Verbum Dei, & perseuerando in syncera doctrina. Contrà verò pastores auari, qui turpis lucri causa sub prætextu nihilominus cultus Dei, falsas doctrinas cŏminiscuntur, istiusmodi mercatores, propolæ, qui suarum rerum aspectum atque eandem rem plus millies vendunt, qui templum Dei prophanant, vt speluncam latronum efficiant: qui pecunia se animas, è Purgatorio vt vocant, redimere posse confirmant, atque accepto precio veniam & peccatorum remissionem promittunt, qui mala opera venditant: tales inquam, impostores sacrilegi, atque idololatræ, de gradu demouendi Regum ac Magistratuum authoritate, aliíque in ipsorum locum substituendi forent. Quanquam hoc tempore plerique se à Princi-pum obedientia non modò subtraxerint, eorúmque iuga plane excusserint: sed etiam ambitione ac tyrânide diabolica totius fere orbis dominatum sibi attribuerint. Principum potétia atq; authoritate usurparint, derelicto proprio officio, quod erat gregé Dei pascere, prouidere ei non inuito, sed alacri & prompto propter Deũ animo: non autè occupare imperium in Clericatũ, quemadmodum satis declarat triplex illa Antichristi corona, regnum etiam Episcoporum atque Abbatum, qui tandem stipendium iniquitatis suæ recipient. Sed cum [illegible, ~9 letters] ille venturus est, qui fideles serui inuenti fuerint, coronam gloriæ incorruptam accipient.
units.tr: We confess that ministers and pastors of the Church ought to be an example to the flock and to the faithful, to shine before others in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity, preaching the Word of God and persevering in pure doctrine. On the contrary, there are greedy pastors, who for the sake of base gain, under the pretext nonetheless of the worship of God, invent false doctrines; such merchants and hucksters, who sell the look of their wares and the same thing a thousand times over, who profane the temple of God so as to make it a den of robbers; who assert that they can redeem souls by money from Purgatory, as they call it, and who, for a price received, promise pardon and remission of sins, who hawk evil works; such impostors, I say, sacrilegious and idolaters, ought to be removed from their rank, and their authority over kings and magistrates, and others, should be replaced in their place. Although at this time most people have not only withdrawn from obedience to princes, but have altogether shaken off their yoke, they have also, by diabolical ambition and tyranny, claimed for themselves dominion over almost the whole world. They have usurped the power and authority of princes, abandoning their own office, which was to feed the flock of God, providing for it not unwillingly but with a ready and eager mind for God's sake, and not seizing dominion over the clergy, as that triple crown of Antichrist sufficiently shows, and also the kingdom of bishops and abbots, who will at last receive the wages of their iniquity. But when that one comes who will come, those faithful servants who are found will receive the incorruptible crown of glory.

units.la: Hæc confessio fidei primùm oblata fuit summæ Curiæ seu Parlamento Prouinciæ, deinde additis aliquot articulis tradita & exposita latius fuit Episcopo Cabellionensi, vt ipsemet petierat. Tũ etiam totidem capitibus descripta & exhibita fuit Cardinali Sadoleto Episcopo Carpentoractensi, ascripta quadam postulatione in hanc sententiam: Incolas Cabrieræ in comitatu Venissæ, officiosè postulare, vt æquo animo reäperet atque perlegeret doćtrinam, in qua patres eorum & ipsi à longa temporũ serie instrućti fuerant: quam quidem iudicabant, cum veteris ac noui Testamenti doćtrina congruere. Ac quoniam Cardinalis ille peritus & studiosus sacrarum literarum habebatur, Cabrierenses ab eo petebant vt notaret propositiones eorum,quæ sibi à doćtrina Dei discrepare viderentur, & si quid esse contrarium veræ religioni probare possit: se non modò non recusare quin ad eius abiurationem adigantur, verumetiam subituros vel capitis vel fortunarum omnium discrimen. Ad hæc si quis esset iudex in comitatu Venissæ qui certa inquisitione affirmare possit, eos souisse doćtrinam impiam, aut aliam religionem coluisse quàm in articulis Confessionis eorum contineretur: rogabant vt is cum ipsis communicaret, seque vicissim æquo animo obtemperaturos pollicebantur.
units.tr: This confession of faith was first presented to the supreme court, or Parliament, of the Province. Then, with some articles added, it was delivered to the Bishop of Cavaillon and explained at greater length, as he himself had asked. It was also set out in the same number of chapters and presented to Cardinal Sadoleto, Bishop of Carpentras, with an added petition to this effect: the inhabitants of Cabrières in the county of Venaissin humbly ask that he would calmly read through and study the doctrine in which their fathers and they themselves had been instructed through a long succession of times, a doctrine they judged to agree with the teaching of the Old and New Testaments. Since that cardinal was regarded as learned and devoted to the sacred letters, the Cabrierans asked him to mark whatever propositions of theirs seemed to differ from the doctrine of God, and to prove, if he could, anything contrary to true religion. They said they would not only not refuse to be forced to abjure it, but would even face the peril of life and all their property. Moreover, if there were any judge in the county of Venaissin who could affirm by certain inquiry that they had harboured impious doctrine, or had cultivated a religion other than what was contained in the articles of their confession, they asked that he communicate it to them, and they promised in turn to submit with equanimity.

units.la: Ad hanc postulationem, Cardinalis Sadoletus respondit epistola manu Secretarij sui scripta, propria verò manu obsignata, atque ipsius sigillo confirmata, quam plures, etiamnum superstites, viri graues legerunt, in hanc fere sententiam:
units.tr: In answer to this petition, Cardinal Sadoleto replied by a letter written in the hand of his secretary but signed with his own hand and confirmed with his seal. Many grave men, some still living, read it, and it was to this effect:

units.la: Postulationem vestram accepi, & confessionis vestrae articulos perlegi: ampla profecto est materia, nec vos de alia doctrina accusari unquam intellexi, nisi quam ipsi confitemini. Certum quidem est leves homines quaedam de vobis sparsisse in vulgus, quae reprehensionem a-crem merebantur. sed ubi accuratius inquisitum est de re ipsa, meras calumnias & falsas criminationes fuisse compertum habuimus. Caeterum in vestris articulis nonnulla verba recte mutari posse videntur, ita tamen ut ne quid vestrae confessioni detrimenti accidat. Praeterea non necesse habebatis (meo quidem iudicio) tam aperte in Pastores ecclesiae invehi. Quod ad me attinet, ego vobis benefieri cupio, contraque malè me profectò haberet, ac vehementer ipse angerer, si, quod aliis de vobis vastandis decretum est, exequerentur. Atque ut quantum vobis faveam certius cognoscatis: ego brevi profecturus sum ad praedium quod habeo prope Cabrieram, eo vobis integrum erit ad me venire: idque sive pauci sive plures numero, absque vestro incommodo aut malo facere poteritis, ibique quod in rem vestram, quodque ad salutem tuendam faciendum censeo, ingenuè exponam.
units.tr: I have received your petition and have read through the articles of your confession. The matter is indeed weighty, nor have I understood that you have ever been accused of any other doctrine than the one you yourselves confess. It is certain that some light men have spread rumours about you among the people which deserved sharp reproof. But when the matter itself was more carefully inquired into, we found them to be mere calumnies and false accusations. Moreover, in your articles some words seem rightly open to change, yet in such a way that nothing is taken from your confession. Besides, in my judgement, you did not need to attack the ministers of the Church so openly. As for me, I wish you well, and I would be truly ill at ease and greatly distressed if what has been decreed by others for your destruction were carried out. So that you may know more certainly how much I favour you: I am shortly going to my estate near Cabrières. There it will be open to you to come to me, whether few or many in number, without inconvenience or harm to yourselves; and there I will frankly set out what I think should be done for your cause and for the preservation of your salvation.

units.la: Eo quidem tempore, anno scilicet M.D.XLII. Vicelegatus Auenionensis, hortatu Cabellionensis Episcopi delectu militum habebat ad destruendam Cabrieram: cumque exercitus ad milliare unum prope Cabrieram accessisset, Cardinalis Sadoletus summa festinatione obviam iuit Vicelegato, eique ostendit postulationem Cabrierensium: & fidei eorum confessionem cum eo communicavit, additis conditionibus, quibus illi se staturos receperant. Quo factum est ut eius rogatu exercitus inde recesserit, nec ulla sane tum Cabrierensibus iniuria illata fuerit. Postea vero Sadoletus Romam iturus, priusquam se viae daret, plures Cabrierensium cum suis villicis quos saebat[?] ex eorum numero esse qui Lutherani appellantur, accersi iussit (nec enim alios in tota ditione sua villicos sibi dari optabat) his, inquam, pollicitus est se ipsorum memorem fore, ac quamprimum Romam peruenisset, totam confessionem, eorumque articulos communicaturum cum Cardinalibus. hacque ratione sperare futurum ut Concilio aliquo melior instituatur reformatio: quae res ad gloriae Dei amplificationem, & ad Christianae concordiae conseruationem perquam foret utilis ac necessaria, nec dubitare quin eodem modo abusus saltem qui nimis sunt crassi & toti omnibus, corrigerentur. Interea etiam monebat eos, ut prudenter egerent: vigilandum ipsis diligenterque ac serio precandum, quoniam hostibus undique cingeretur acerrimis. Hæc autem Sadoleti oratio Cabrierensibus magnæ consolationi fuit, qui huius sedulitate, breui aliquod responsum ad confessionem ipsorum redditum iri sperabat: attamen postquam Roma reuersus esset Cardinalis, intellexerunt eum illic res omnes usque adeo depravatas offendisse, ut nulla inde reformationis ac correctionis spes foret, sed potius crudelis belli apparatus adversus eos qui Ecclesiæ Romanæ ordinationes atque traditiones non sequerentur: facile quidem perspici abusus tam crassos diu durare non posse, cum præsertim multitudo hominum cuiuslibet nationis qui sacræ doctrinæ notitiam sunt consecuti, in tantum numerum excreuerit. Tandem quoque dicebat Thesaurarius Carpentoractensis, qui licet pecuniam suppeditaret ad persoluenda stipendia militibus, quorum delectus habebatur ad euertendam Cabrieram, occulte tamen ipsi opem ferebat: verum non potuit adeo tecte rem gerere, quin ad Vicelegatum delatus fuerit, qui illum festinanter recedere coegit.
units.tr: At that time, namely in the year 1542, the Vice-legate of Avignon, at the urging of the Bishop of Cavaillon, was levying soldiers to destroy Cabrières. When the army had come within a mile of Cabrières, Cardinal Sadoleto hastened with the greatest speed to meet the Vice-legate. He showed him the petition of the Cabrierans and communicated their confession of faith to him, adding the conditions on which they had agreed to stand. As a result, at his request, the army withdrew from there, and no harm was then done to the Cabrierans. Afterwards, however, Sadoleto, before setting out for Rome, ordered several of the Cabrierans to be summoned, together with their farm-managers, those of their number who were called Lutherans (for he did not wish any other farm-managers to be assigned to him in his whole jurisdiction). To these, I say, he promised that he would remember them, and that as soon as he reached Rome he would lay the whole confession and their articles before the Cardinals. By this means he hoped that a better reformation might be instituted through some Council, which would be most useful and necessary for the increase of the glory of God and the preservation of Christian concord; and he did not doubt that in the same way at least those abuses which are too gross and obvious to all would be corrected. Meanwhile he also advised them to act prudently: they must be watchful, and pray diligently and earnestly, since they were surrounded on all sides by most fierce enemies. This speech of Sadoleto was a great comfort to the Cabrierans, who, through his diligence, hoped that a reply to their confession would soon be given. Yet after the Cardinal returned from Rome, they learned that he had found all things there so corrupted that there was no hope of reformation or correction from that quarter; rather, a cruel preparation for war was being made against those who did not follow the ordinances and traditions of the Roman Church. It was easy to see that abuses so gross could not last long, especially since the multitude of men of every nation who had attained knowledge of sacred doctrine had grown to such a number. Finally, too, it was said that the Treasurer of Carpentras, who, though he supplied the money to pay the soldiers whose levy was being held to overthrow Cabrières, nevertheless secretly gave them help, could not manage the affair so discreetly that he was not reported to the Vice-legate, who forced him to leave in haste.

units.la: Episcopus autem Aquensis & Cabellionensis, sedulo instabat ut decretum Merindoliense execution mandaretur. Unde a Senatu ac Parlamento Prouinciæ constitutum fuit secundum Regis diplomata, ut Ioan. Durandius consiliarius Curiæ, cum quodam Secretario & Episcopo Cabellionensi, ac Doctore aliquo Theologiæ, Merindolium ipsum adiret, eiusque incolis errores & hæreses, quas in confessione fidei ipsorum agnoscerint, ostenderent, certisque rationibus falsas eorum opiniones arguerent, conuictos deinde per Verbum Dei, abiurare cogerent suas hæreses: id qui facerent, ipsos omni pœna ac reatu liberarent. Quod si Merindolienses hæreseos conuicti, oblatam abiurationem præstare recusarent: tum eorum omnium quæ gesta fuerint dicam scribi oportere, ut tandem Curia quid agendum sit statuat.
units.tr: The Bishops of Aix and Cavaillon, however, urged insistently that the decree of Mérindol be carried into execution. Accordingly, the Senate and Parliament of the Province resolved, in accordance with the royal letters patent, that Jean Durand, a councillor of the court, together with a certain secretary, the Bishop of Cavaillon, and some doctor of theology, should go to Mérindol itself. There they were to show its inhabitants the errors and heresies which they acknowledged in their confession of faith, and by sound arguments refute their false opinions. Then, when they were convicted through the Word of God, they were to be compelled to abjure their heresies; those who did so were to be freed from all penalty and guilt. But if the Mérindolians, convicted of heresy, refused to make the offered abjuration, then everything that was done was to be written down, so that the court could at last decide what should be done.

units.la: Promulgato hoc decreto, Episcopus Cabellionensis non expectauit diem executioni a Senatu præfixum, sed ipsemet doctore Theologiæ assumpto Merindolium venit, ut eos ad abiurationem adigeret. Qua de re per Merindolienses reprehensus fuit, quod præter authoritate Senatus, negotium susciperet, dicentes id eum non habere in mandatis. Nihilominus haud destitit cos urgere ut abiurarent, idque si facerent, aiebat in tutela sua ac protectione, velut sub alis gallinæ latent pulli, fore tutos, nec amplius ab ullo hostili incursu ipsis metuendum. Merindolij incolæ petierunt, ut ea explanaret quorum abiuratione fieri volebat. Respondit Episcopus, non opus esse ullam instituere disputationem: se solum postulare universalem quandam errorum omnium abiurationem, qualem vel ipsemet facere non admodum grauaretur. Idque etiam ipsos sine ullo suo incommodo facere posse. At Merindolienses negabant se violaturos ulla in re Senatus arestum, aut Regis literas, quibus ille diligenter cauerat declarandos primum errores quorum rei aguntur: ut verbo Dei edocti, Regij diplomatis argumento satisfacere recte possint. alioqui enim simulatione tantum & turpem hypocrisin fore, imo conceptum iuris sibi a Rege præscripti. Itaque quod antea sæpius professi sunt, id etiam nunc confirmant: nempe, si idonea inquisitione habita probentur in aliquo errasse, aut ex verbo Dei hæreseos convincantur, se absque ulla cunctatione abiuraturos esse quicquid in ipsorum confessione reperietur quod cum sacrosancta Dei doctrina non consentiat. contra, si ipsos nullo errore ductos, nullaque hæreseos nota vel macula infectos, constet puram Evangelij doctrinam semper docuisse & coluisse: non esse consentaneum se ad canendam palinodiam errorum, quibus obnoxij non sint, impelli aut ulla vi cogi. Tum Episcopus Cabellionensis mirum in modum excaduit nullam admittens mentionem verbi Dei, quo errores Merindoliensium arguendos Rex & Senatus ipse decreverant, sed tanquam amentia quadam correptus, diris imprecationibus devovebat qui primi hanc rationem excogitassent. Tandē Doctor theologus, qui illuc cum Episcopo venerat, rogabat quinā[?] essent articuli, quos Merindolij incolæ proposuissent (Episcopus enim eos cum Theologo non cōmunicarat) Hic Merindolienses: Episcopus, inquiunt, Cabellionensis eos quidē habet: attamen nobis alterum ad manus est eorum exēplum. Tū Episcopus Cabellionensis tradidit Theologo doctori consessionem integram: vixque eam perlegerat, quū ipse Episcopus inclamaret: Quid quæris testimonia? aut quid disputationibus egemus? omnia hæc sunt hæreseos plena. Cedo, inquiunt Merindolienses, quoniā in loco[?]? Episcopus autem non habebat quod responderet. Doctor vero theologus ostulabat[?] sibi tépus dari, quo articulos istius confessionis exactis exenderet[?]: atque examinaret num a Scriptura dissentanei essent. quocirca Episcopus summo cũ animi dolore illinc re infecta digressus est. Post triduum iussit Episcopus accersi Doctorẽ, ut ex eo cognosceret qua potissimum via uti posset ad demonstrandas haereses quae in illa consessione haberentur. Ad hoc Doctor aiebat, se nunquam ita fuisse attonitum quàm quum articulos expendisset, & diligenter contulisset testimonia sacrarum literarum, quae ad confirmationem eiusdem confessionis adducta in ea fuerant. fatebatur etiam libere, tota se vita tantum in diuinis scriptis nõ profecisse, quã illis octo diebus, quibus Scripturae locos in iis articulis citatos excutere coactus fuerat. Paulò autẽ post Episcopus Cabellionensis, comitatus tantummodò famulis suis, Merindolium venit: ibique pueris grandiusculis simul & paruis ad se vocari iussis, pecunia singulis largitus, blandè praecepit ut orationem Dominicã cũ symbolo Apostolorum Latino idiomate edisserent. Plerique eorum excipiebat, se Latinè quidẽ nosse Pater noster, & Credo: non posse tamen reddere rationẽ eorum quae recitarent nisi suo, id est Gallico idiomate. Quibus tunc Episcopus dixit, non requiri tãtam in ipsis scientiam, satis esse modò ea Latinè tenerent: neque ad salutẽ conducere tam exactam fidei rationem atque intelligentiã: multos Episcopos, Parochos, quin etiam Doctores theologiæ inveniri, quibus satis negotij exhiberet vel tenuis ac rudis expositio orationis Dominicæ, aut symboli Apostolici. Hæc audiens Merindoliensis Præfectus Andreas Maynardus, Quid, quaso inquit, proderit verba non intellecta proferre, & psittaci more recitare Pater noster aut Credo? mentitur certè, & Deum irridet quisquis absque intellectu usurpat haec verba, Credo in Deũ: & quid ipsa valeat ignorat. Intelligisne tu, inquit Episcopus, quidnam valeat Credo in Deum. Cui praefectus, miserũ sanè me deputem, nisi intelligerem: ac tu ordine ratione fidei reddere coepit.
units.tr: When this decree had been published, the Bishop of Cavaillon did not wait for the day fixed for its execution by the Senate. Instead, taking a doctor of theology with him, he himself came to Mérindol to force them to abjure. The Mérindolians rebuked him for this, because, beyond the authority of the Senate, he was undertaking the business, saying that he had no such commission. Nevertheless he did not cease to press them to abjure, and said that if they did so they would be safe under his protection and guardianship, as chicks hide beneath a hen's wings, and would no longer have to fear any hostile attack. The inhabitants of Mérindol asked him to explain exactly what they were to abjure. The Bishop replied that there was no need for any disputation: he only demanded a general abjuration of all errors, such as he himself would not be too reluctant to make, and that they could do this without any inconvenience to themselves. But the Mérindolians replied that they would not violate in any respect the decree of the Senate or the king's letters, in which the king had carefully provided that the errors at issue should first be declared, so that, being instructed by the Word of God, they could properly satisfy the terms of the royal letters patent. Otherwise, they said, it would be mere pretence and foul hypocrisy, indeed a mockery of the right prescribed to them by the king. And so what they had professed many times before, they now confirm again: namely, that if, after a proper inquiry, they were shown to have erred in anything, or were convicted of heresy by the Word of God, they would abjure without any delay whatever was found in their confession that did not agree with the most holy doctrine of God. On the other hand, if it were established that they had been led into no error, and were stained by no mark or blemish of heresy, but had always taught and cultivated the pure doctrine of the Gospel, then it was not fitting for them to be driven, or forced by any violence, to sing a palinode of errors to which they were not liable. Then the Bishop of Cavaillon was strangely upset. Making no mention of the Word of God, by which the king and the Senate themselves had decreed that the errors of the Mérindolians should be refuted, he, as if seized by some madness, cursed with dire imprecations those who first devised this method. At last the doctor of theology who had come there with the Bishop asked what the articles were that the inhabitants of Mérindol had put forward, for the Bishop had not communicated them to the theologian. Here the Mérindolians said: "The Bishop of Cavaillon indeed has them, but we have another copy at hand." Then the Bishop of Cavaillon handed the theologian the whole confession. Scarcely had he read it through when the Bishop himself cried out: "Why do you ask for testimonies? Or why do we need disputations? All these things are full of heresy." "Show us where, then," said the Mérindolians. But the Bishop had nothing to answer. The doctor of theology, however, asked that time be given him in which to work carefully through the articles of that confession and examine whether they were at odds with Scripture. Whereupon the Bishop left the place with great vexation, his business undone. After three days the Bishop ordered the doctor to be summoned, so that he might learn from him by what particular method he could demonstrate the heresies contained in that confession. To this the doctor replied that he had never been so astonished as when he had weighed the articles and carefully compared the testimonies of sacred letters which had been adduced in the confession to support it. He also freely admitted that in his whole life he had made less progress in the divine writings than in those eight days in which he had been compelled to examine the passages of Scripture cited in those articles. Shortly afterwards the Bishop of Cavaillon, accompanied only by his servants, came to Mérindol. Having ordered some boys, both somewhat older and quite small, to be called before him, and giving money to each, he kindly instructed them to recite the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed in Latin. Most of them replied that they indeed knew the Pater noster and the Credo in Latin, but could not give an account of what they recited except in their own language, that is, French. To them the Bishop then said that so great a knowledge was not required of them; it was enough that they held these in Latin. Nor did so exact a grasp and understanding of the faith contribute to salvation; for many bishops, parish priests, and even doctors of theology were to be found for whom even a slight and rough explanation of the Lord's Prayer or the Apostles' Creed would be no small trouble. Hearing this, the prefect of Mérindol, Andreas Maynard, said: "What, I ask, will it profit to utter words not understood, and to recite the Pater noster or the Credo like a parrot? Whoever uses these words without understanding, 'I believe in God,' surely lies and mocks God, and does not know what they are worth." "Do you understand, then," said the Bishop, "what 'I believe in God' is worth?" To which the prefect replied: "I should think myself a wretched man indeed if I did not understand it. Now you, in order, begin to set out the articles of the faith."

units.la: Qua quidem re Episcopus perculsus, ei dixit, Non putassem mehercule Merindolium tantos habere doctores. Quid? inquit Præfectus, etiam infimae sortis homuncio qui Merindolium incolit, rectius multo quam ego fidei capita tibi enarrare poterit: sed periculum fac, ac percontare, anabo, pueros istos, aut istorum aliquem: ut rectene an perperam instituti sint, ipse iudices. Episcopus qui neq; respondendi neq; interrogandi scientiam tenebat, fremitu atq; indignatione pudorem obtegens nihil respondit. Quod facile perspicies alter Syndicus Merindolij cui nomen erat Perronius Regius, Domine, inquit, si vis ut parvulorum aliquis suos interroget sodales, nō ægre id præstabit. Permisit Episcopus. Ibi tu unus e pueris interrogare coepit alios summa gravitate, ac singulari gratia: dixisses plane præceptoris partes illum agere. Alij vero vicissim pueri, quæreti adeo apte & commode respondebat, ut ea res auditoribus non mediocre admiratione afferret. gesta enim fuit hæc res coram multis. inter quos erant etiam religiosi quatuor, qui non ita multo ante à Parisiesi Academia redierat, quorum unus sic Episcopu allocut° est, Necesse est, inquit, ut verum fatear, me sæpius de disputationibus theologicis Sorbonæ interfuisse, nu quatamen ex ijs tantum pfecisse, quatum nunc audiedo istos puerulos fructus percepi. Cui tum quida Gulielmus Armatius dixit, Legistine unquam quod apud Matt. scriptum est de Iesu Christo, Gratias ago tibi Pater, Domine cæli & terræ, quia abscondisti hæc à sapientibus & prudentib. & revelasti ea parvulis: Sane Pater, quoniam beneplacitu tuu est eiusmodi. Omnia hæc verba, atq; responsa, quæ dabat Merindolij incolæ, cunctis summæ admirationi fuere. Episcopus cum hac nō succederet, alia aggressus est via, & conatus est blandis verborum lenociniis Merindoliefes in sua pellicere sententiam. Remotis itaque extraneis, seorsim fassus est perspectu quidem habere minus in ipsis mali esse quam multi arbitrarētur, sed ut persequetibus satisfieret, leui quadā abiuratione opus esse, quam generatim coram ipso præfectus & syndici Merindoliefes communi cuiu nomine facerēt, nullo adhibito actuario aut notario, qui ea scripto exciperet. Ita ipsos amore atq; fauore vel apud hostes cosecuturos esse, nulla iusta infamiæ nota. nam ad Papa tantummodo Curiam que Prouinciale negotiu relatu iri. Quinetiam si qui postmodo factum :illud vitio verterent, aut forsan hoc prætextu molestij ipsis esse velint, sane omnino negari posse quod nec literis nec testibus verè probaretur. Atq; ut rectius hæc transfigeretur, rogabat ut convenirent & inter se deliberaret. Præfectus autē ac syndici, aliique plures ex senioribus vicissim responderunt, iandudū deliberatū ac constitutū sibi esse non ion cōsentire ulli abiurationi, nisi (quæ semper eorū fuit exceptio) ex verbo Dei hæreses arguerentur. mirari quoque admodum se dicebant, quod Episcopus eos adigere vellet ad mentiendum Deo & hominibus. His dictis Episcopus magnis animi perturbationibus agitatus illinc discessit. Paucis vero post diebus Episcopus Aquensis assiduè instabat apud Ioannem Durandium summæ Curiæ in Provincia consiliarium, ut mandatum quod à Senatu habebat persequeretur: de quo mandato & iam ante sæpius & mox etiam dicemus. Durandius itaque incolas Merindolij certiores fecit de die quo illuc cū Episc. Cabellionēsi, eiusdemque comite doctore Theologo, & quodam Scriba veturus esset, ne quis stato die ibi desideraretur. Accurrerat etiam tunc tēporis undiq; viri nobiles & docti, & alii cuiusuis ordinis homines, eo tantum consilio ut huius executionis spectatores essent. Merindoliēses quoq; præmoniti fuerant ne se una oēs sisteret, sed iuxta templū starēt, ut vocati eo ordine ac numero, quo ipsis indicaretur, in medium prodirent. Postquam Durandius consedisset vbi iudicia sua exercere solebat Merindoliēses, iuxtaque illum Episcopus Cabellionēnsis, Theologiæ doctor, & Scriba: accersebatur Andreas Maynardus præfectus: Ienonus Romanus & Michelinus Maynardus syndici: Ioannes Cabrius, cum Ioanne Palenco seniores Merindolij. qui cùm accessissent, vnicuique honore exhibito: Durandius orationem suam ita est exorsus, Non ignoratis, inquit, aresto summæ Curiæ Provincialis, vos cū vxoribus atq; ipsis pueris ad vnū omnes igni & incēdio adiudicatos, domos vero vestras sedibus suis cōuellēdas ac diruēdas, vt pagus omnino inutilis habitationi reddatur, &c. attamē placuit Regi, clementissimo nostro principi, literas mittere per quas rebus vestris cōsuluit, ne summo iure actio gereretur, sed ex decreti sui moderatione: quod tum ibi prælectū fuit. Post multas itaque constitutiones, visum fuit Senatui, ut ab Episcopo Cabellionēsi doctoréque Theologiæ coram me de erroribus admoniti, conuiciisque[?] hæreseos, quâ vos fouere dicimini, doctrinæ falsæ renunciatis[?]: imò publicè ac soleniter abiuretis errores pristinos, prout res ipsa postulat. Quod si feceritis, gratiam à Rege principe nostro in vos collatam consequemini. Quare necesse est ut nunc obedientiam Deo, Regi, & magistratui exhibeatis. Quo dicto, rogauit quidnam illi ad ea quæ proposita erant, responderent. Præfectus autem Andreas
units.tr: Struck by this, the bishop said to him: "Upon my word, I would not have thought Merindol had such learned teachers." "What?" replied the prefect, "even a humble little man of the lowest rank who lives in Merindol can explain the articles of faith to you far better than I can. But put it to the test: question these boys, or any one of them, and judge for yourself whether they have been rightly or wrongly taught." The bishop, who had neither the skill to answer nor to question, covered his embarrassment with growling and indignation and said nothing. Perronius Regius, the other syndic of Merindol, made this plain. "Sir," he said, "if you wish one of the little boys to question his companions, he will not find it difficult." The bishop agreed. One of the boys then began to question the others with great seriousness and remarkable grace; you would have said he was playing the part of a teacher. The others in turn answered his questions so aptly and fittingly that the audience was greatly astonished. The matter was witnessed by many people, among them four friars who had recently returned from the Paris Academy. One of them addressed the bishop: "I must be honest," he said, "I have often attended theological disputations at the Sorbonne, yet I have never gained from them as much profit as I have just now from hearing these little boys." Then a certain William Armatius said to him: "Have you ever read what is written in Matthew about Jesus Christ: 'I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them unto babes. Even so, Father, for so it seemed good in thy sight'?" All the words and answers given by these inhabitants of Merindol caused the greatest wonder to everyone. When the bishop made no headway with this, he tried another way and sought to win the Merindolites over to his opinion with smooth, flattering words. Dismissing the outsiders, he confessed in private that he saw there was less wrong in them than many supposed; but to satisfy their persecutors, some light form of abjuration was needed, which the prefect and the syndics of Merindol should make in the name of the whole community, in front of himself, with no clerk or notary present to put it in writing. In this way, he said, they would win the favour even of their enemies, with no just mark of infamy; for the matter would be referred only to the Pope's Curia at Provence. Moreover, if anyone afterwards found fault with the deed, or perhaps wished to use it as a pretext to harass them, it could certainly be denied, since it could not be truly proved by any document or witness. So that this might be carried out more properly, he asked them to meet and deliberate among themselves. The prefect, the syndics, and many others of the elders in turn replied that they had long since decided and settled that they would agree to no abjuration, except (this had always been their condition) if the heresies were refuted from the Word of God. They also said they marvelled greatly that the bishop wished to force them to lie to God and to men. With these words said, the bishop, shaken by great agitation, left the place. A few days later, the bishop of Aix kept pressing John Durand, a councillor of the supreme Court in Provence, to carry out the mandate he had from the Senate, concerning which we have spoken often before and shall speak again shortly. So Durand informed the inhabitants of Merindol of the day on which he would come there with the bishop of Cavaillon, his companion, a doctor of theology, and a certain clerk, and warned them that no one should be absent from the place on that day. At that time men of rank and learning came running from every quarter, and men of every class, with the sole purpose of being spectators of this execution. The Merindolites too had been warned not to present themselves all together, but to stand beside the church, so that they could come forward into the middle when called, in the order and number that would be indicated to them. After Durand had taken his seat where he was accustomed to exercise his judgments, with the bishop of Cavaillon, doctor of theology, and the clerk beside him, the following were summoned: Andreas Maynardus the prefect; Jenon Romanus and Michael Maynardus, the syndics; and John Cabrius with John Palenc, the elders of Merindol. When they had come forward and been shown due respect, Durand began his address in this way: "You are not ignorant," he said, "that by the decree of the supreme Provincial Court you, together with your wives and children, have all been condemned to fire and burning, and your houses to be torn from their foundations and razed, so that the village is wholly rendered useless for habitation, and so on. Nevertheless, it has pleased the King, our most clement prince, to send letters by which he has provided for your affairs, so that the action should not be conducted by strict law, but by the moderation of his decree, which was read out there. Therefore, after many deliberations, the Senate has thought fit that you be admonished by me, in the presence of the bishop of Cavaillon and the doctor of theology, concerning the errors of the heresy with which you are said to be favoured, and that you renounce false doctrine; indeed, that you publicly and solemnly abjure your former errors, as the matter itself requires. If you do so, you will obtain the grace bestowed upon you by our prince the King. Therefore it is necessary that you now render obedience to God, to the King, and to the magistrate." With these words he asked what they had to answer to what had been set before them. The prefect Andreas

units.la: Maynardus facto signo indicauit syndicis Merindolii ut responderent: syndici contra, id ex Præfecti officio esse significabant. Tum Cosiliarius Durandius ad Præfectum, Tuum est, inquit, primo respondere qui magistratum geris. Præfectus vero, dixit negotium istud ad commune totius pagi pertinere: proinde syndicorum fore primo responsum dare. Sed quoniam, inquit, tibi ita placet, velimus aliquem nobis aduocatum dari, qui, ut mos est forensis, de toto negotio certior factus causam nostram agat. Nam nos homines illiterati sumus & rudiores quam ut pro rei dignitate responsum reddere possimus. Cosiliarius autem dixit se nec scripto nec per aduocatum causam hanc, sed ex ipsorum ore audire velle: haud recusare tamen, modo nullus extraneus det eis consilium, quin inter se deliberarent quid dicturi essent, ac deinde vicissim ipsi dicat. Præfectus conditione accepit, ipseque cum syndicis & senioribus aliquandiu consultatum secessere, nec aliud illorum fuit consilium, quam ut syndici primo, deinde Præfectus, postremo seniores, quod cuique Dei gratia suggereret, eloqueretur: ac quamprimum redierunt. Mirabatur Cosiliarius, quod tam cito deliberassent. Michelinus Maynardus syndicus Merindoliensis, rogans Durandium & Episcopum sibi ignoscerent, ut pote rustico & rerum forensium imperito, si minus eleganter diceret: in hanc rationem respondit, Magnas profecto Deo gratias agere debemus, quod ad alia beneficia quæ in summo discrimine ab illo accepimus, istud etiam dederit maximum, quod Regis animum ita assecit, ut iure nobiscum agi præciperet, omnem vim & violentiam suo diplomate reprimens: qui exemplo Davidis & Solomonis non dedignatus subditorum miserrimos respicere, iis prouidit ut bonum principem decet: quo quidem nomine nos illi summam in Christo felicitate optamus, deinde gratia habemus summo Provinciæ Senatui, quia ius administrarit nobis ex mandato Regis, principis nostri: & tibi quoq; domine Durandi, qui huc cum mandatis Curiæ venisti propterea quod viam nobis monstraris facile, quæ in hoc negotio tenenda sit. Quocirca velim equidem hæreses declarari, de quibus accusor: ac si vllum me sermone in quo Dei maiestatem læserim, vsquam habuisse constet, libens revocabo, & pœnam pro tuo arbitratu non inuitus dabo. Post hunc Ienonus Romanus, vir admodum grandis natu, syndicus Merindoliensis, dixit se sententiæ Collegæ sui accedere, Deoque laude tribuere quòd in extremo ætatis suæ tempore, lætos istos nuncios & audiret & videret quibus allatum erat ut causa religionis ex Sacrarum literarum authoritate transfigeretur. id enim iuris nunquam obtinere potuisse maiores, apud ullos iudices contra persecutores suos. Præfectus autem Maynardus dixit Commissario, Scribam ipsius stultum adolescentulum nihil quàm ridere, nec quicquam eorum quæ dicerentur chartæ mandare. Quod ægre ferens Commissarius, acriter Scribæ obiurgavit, & singulari memoria quæcunque ante dicta fuerant repetes[?] describi iussit: ac postea rogavit, nunquid aliud vellet dicere. Cui Præfectus, Quum mihi potestate facis libere dicendi quod sentio, nulla profecto hic mihi videtur esse iudicij forma, cū nō sit qui accusatoris partes agat, ut nisi probare possit eade[?] quibꝰ nos accusamur, poena afficiatur qua falsos accusatores puniri iubet Scriptura. In eandem rationem locutus est Ioan. Brunerollus Merindolij subpræfectus, postulas exhiberi inquisitiones certas, quibus cōstaret incolas eius loci in errore versari. aut si id non facerent adversarij, ipsi ut innoxij iudicis sententia absolverentur, illi vero molesti esse desisterent, ac deinceps nec capitibus nec fortunis ipsorum manus intentarent. Commissarius autem eo quòd prandij tempus instaret, rem in horam primam pomeridianam reiecit. ibi cum urgerent Merindolienses ijdē qui mane responderant, ut errores & hæreses de quibus accusarentur, in medio ponerent adversarij. Episcopus Cabelliōncsis[?] & theologiæ doctor, rogati per Commissarium si quid contra haberet, aut si articulos ab illis propositos impugnare vellent: Episcopus non ausus aperte loqui, diu multumque in aurem Consiliarij susurravit. quos quidem susurros cum diutius ferre non posset, Consiliarius ad Merindolienses sermonem convertit, Episcopum dicere nihil opus esse inquisitionibus, sed eiusmodi de ipsis undique spargi rumores. Doctor vero theologiæ nullum articuli confessionis, quæ tum recitata fuit, impugnauit, sed pleraq; Latinè cum Commissario loquebatur. Merindolienses qui aderant in iudicio, petebant ut Consiliarius in sua renunciatione, quam processum verbale vocat, accuratè describi curaret tam ipsius Episcopi quàm Doctoris tergiversationes. Promisit Consiliarius nihil se omissurum quod in rem eorum fore existimaret. addebat insuper non necesse esse reliquos Merindolienses vocari, si nihil aliud contra eos afferri vel probari possit. Habes hic summâ eorum quæ in hac disceptatione gesta fuerunt. Quotquot autem audiendæ disputationis sæpe ducti undique concurrerant, mirabantur admodum videntes Episcopum & doctorem Theologum victos plane obmutuisse. Atque ea res multis utilitati fuit, qui exempla confessionis Merindoliensium secum asportantes ad sanioris doctrinæ cogitationem animum appulerunt. præcipuè vero tres illi doctores, qui sæpius Merindolienses ad defectionem à vera fide solicitarat, ut veritatis convicti, pristinis superstitionibus abiectis, syncera amplexi sunt religione, eorum quæ ministerio usus est postea Dominus ad Evangelij sui prædicationem.
units.tr: Maynardus made a sign to the syndics of Merindol to reply; the syndics in turn signified that this was the prefect's duty. Then the councillor Durand said to the prefect: "It is for you, who hold the office of magistrate, to answer first." But the prefect said that this matter concerned the common interest of the whole village, and therefore the syndics should give the first answer. "But since it pleases you," he went on, "we should like an advocate to be assigned to us, who, as is customary in the courts, having been fully informed of the whole affair, may plead our cause. For we are unlettered men and too rough to make a reply worthy of the weight of the matter." The councillor replied that he wished to hear this cause not in writing or through an advocate, but from their own mouths; he would not refuse them, provided no outsider gave them advice, but that they might deliberate among themselves what they were going to say, and then speak in turn. The prefect accepted the condition, and he and the syndics and elders withdrew for a while to consult together; their only plan was that the syndics should speak first, then the prefect, and last the elders, each saying whatever God suggested to him. They returned very quickly. The councillor wondered that they had deliberated so swiftly. Michael Maynardus, syndic of Merindol, begged Durand and the bishop to pardon him, as a rustic and inexperienced in legal affairs, if he spoke less elegantly, and he answered in this manner: "Truly we ought to give great thanks to God, that among the other benefits we have received from him in our utmost peril, he has also given us this greatest one: that he has so moved the heart of the King that he ordered the law to be applied to us, restraining all violence and force by his decree. Following the example of David and Solomon, who did not disdain to regard the most wretched of their subjects, he has provided for them as a good prince should. For this we wish him the highest happiness in Christ; then we give thanks to the highest Senate of the Province, because it has administered justice to us by the King's mandate, our prince; and to you too, Lord Durand, who came here with the mandates of the Court, because you have easily shown us the way we should hold in this business. Wherefore I would indeed wish the heresies of which I am accused to be declared; and if it can be shown that I have ever uttered any word by which I offended the majesty of God, I will gladly retract it and will not be unwilling to pay whatever penalty you think fit." After him Jenon Romanus, a man of great age and syndic of Merindol, said that he agreed with the opinion of his colleague, and gave praise to God that in the last part of his life he had heard and seen these joyful messengers, by whom it had been brought about that the cause of religion should be decided by the authority of the Holy Scriptures. For his ancestors had never been able to obtain such a right before any judges against their persecutors. The prefect Maynardus then said to the commissioner that his clerk was a foolish youth who did nothing but laugh and would not commit to paper anything that was said. The commissioner, taking this badly, sharply rebuked the clerk and ordered him to write down, with careful memory, everything said before, and afterwards asked whether he wished to say anything more. The prefect replied: "Since you give me the freedom to say freely what I think, I can see no proper form of judgment here at all, since there is no one to play the part of accuser; so that unless they can prove the very things with which we are charged, they should be punished with the penalty that Scripture commands for false accusers." John Brunerollus, the sub-prefect of Merindol, spoke in the same vein: he demanded that definite inquiries be produced, by which it might be established that the inhabitants of that place were living in error; or, if the adversaries would not do this, that the Merindolites be absolved as innocent by the sentence of the judge, and that the others cease to harass them and from then on lay no hands on their lives or property. The commissioner, however, since the hour of dinner was approaching, put the matter off until the first hour after noon. Then, when the same Merindolites who had answered in the morning urged that the adversaries should set forth the errors and heresies of which they were accused, the bishop of Cavaillon, doctor of theology, was asked by the commissioner whether he had anything to set against them, or whether he wished to attack the articles they had put forward. The bishop, not daring to speak openly, whispered for a long time into the ear of the councillor. Unable to bear these whisperings any longer, the councillor turned to the Merindolites and said that there was no need for inquiries, but that such rumours about them were spreading on every side. The doctor of theology did not attack any article of the confession that was then read out, but for the most part talked with the commissioner in Latin. The Merindolites who were present at the hearing begged that the councillor have care taken to record accurately, in his report which he calls the verbal process, the shiftings and evasions of both the bishop and the doctor. The councillor promised he would omit nothing that he judged to be to their advantage. Also, he added, it was not necessary for the rest of the Merindolites to be summoned, if nothing else could be brought or proved against them. You have here the sum of what was done in this dispute. Whoever had gathered from all quarters, as often happens, to hear the debate, marvelled greatly when they saw the bishop and the doctor of theology, having been beaten, fall quite silent. And this was of great use to many, who, carrying copies of the Merindolites' confession away with them, turned their minds to the thought of sounder doctrine; and especially those three doctors who had often tried to draw the Merindolites away from the true faith, who, convinced by the truth, cast off their former superstitions and embraced the pure religion. Among these the Lord afterwards made use of them in the ministry for the preaching of his Gospel.

units.la: Post tam varias & graves has forenses conflictationes, tandem Deus grata ocij & requietis vicissitudine, Merindoliensium ac sociorum animos refecit: idque incusso hostibus eorum terrore propter exempla quæ in sceleratos eius populi vexatores adeo luculenta ediderat, non tantum in repentina præsidis Chassanæi morte, verumetiam in plerisque aliis Provincialis Curiæ primariis viris, quorum quidem horrenda mors multos perterrefecit: inprimis vero ea quam Ioanni de Roma impurissimo homini omnes accidisse noverant: quemadmodum antea commemoravimus. Itaque crudelis adversariorum rabies multis interpositis impedimentis aliquandiu repressa fuit: vique atque executio crudelissimæ illius adversus Merindolios latæ sententiæ tantisper interpellata fuit, dum Ioannes Minerius recutiti patris ut ferebatur, soboles, munus primi in ea Curia præsidis obtinuit. Is cùm antea papali magistratu, quem Viguicrum dicunt, Cabellione fungeretur, ex depresso loco ad summas opes & dignitates repente euectus est. nam ad præsidentiæ authoritatem accessit etiam præfecturæ Regiæ dignitas, qua absente domino Griniano ac in Germania legationem agente fungebatur. Is sanè omnes vires opésq; suas eò contulit, ut sanguinolentum illud Curiæ arcstum antea factum, non confirmaret solum, atque ipsa re præstaret: verumetiam ut Sathanæ administer & infestissimus carnifex ad eius crudelitatem permultum adderet: quemadmodum ipsa executione declarauit. Itaque domino Griniano, à Provincia tum absente, egregiº hic præses Minerius, obserobseruatis omnibus rationibus atque occasionibus, quibus posset quod susceperat, perficere: omnes copias Regis (quæ tum è Pedemontio in Provinciam venerant, vela daturæ Massiliæ ad expeditionem belli Anglicani) coegit, easque coniunxit cum eo exercitu quem Papæ legatus Auenione atque in toto Venissæ comitatu contraxerat. Atque ita magnanimus dux, oblitus sui officij, infestis signis progredi coepit, ad excindendum vastandumque Merindolium & Cabrieran, aliaque oppida, & pagos numero viginti duos euertendos ac delendos. Atque vt id facilius efficeret, militibus potestatem fecit diripiendi omnia & incendendi, atque etiam homines, mulieres, infantesque trucidandi. Antequam autem peruenirent Merindolium, incendio atque direptioni dedit oppidum Rupem nominatum, San-Stephanum, Villelaurum, Lormarinum, Mottam, Cabrierettam, San-Martinum, Pipinum, aliaque loca vltra montem Lebronem posita. Eorum autem locorum incolæ, quorum maior pars se Merindolium receperat, cum viderent tantam inimicorum immanitatem, secesserunt in syluam Lauram appellatam, quoad eorum vis & furor, quasi tempestas quædam sæua violentaque illata præteriret. Sed videntes eos magis magisque confirmari, atque ad sese propius accedere, omnes vnum idemque senserunt, atque statuerunt nihil melius esse, quam si coniuges cum liberis relinquerent: viri alio aliquo concederent. Sic enim existimabant ipsis absentibus facilius eas plus misericordiæ apud hostem quātumuis[?] barbarū inueturas. Nulla oratio explicare posset gemitus, dolores animi. Fletus, questusque promiscuos, qui in hoc acerbissimo discessu digressuque editi fuerunt: cum vir à charissima vxore, pater ab iucundissimis liberis, ita abstrahi auellíque cogeretur[?]. Tamen habita concione à Ministris, precibusque vsitatis vespertino tempore adhibitis, viri ea nocte discesserunt, vt maius incommodum ac periculum vitarent. Postero die mane, copiæ pedestres propius accesserunt ad eum locum vbi mulieres à viris relictæ erant, plerique eorum qui in Minerij castris erant, beneuolentia in eos aut misericordia aliqua permoti, ab exercitu præcedentes, eum in locum properarunt, vt eos, qui ibi erant, de infesto hostium aduentu certiores facerent, quos quidem omnes offenderunt, vnanimiter orantes, post confuctam[?] concionem, quæ manè habita fuerat. Porrò ut primùm exercitus eò venit, omnia bona, quæ miseri homines salua ex prioribus rapinis inimicorum ac latrocinijs reseruarant, statim direptioni expo-sita fuerunt: mulieres ac puellæ expoliatæ, quædam violatæ, ac verberibus cæsæ, atque omni cum contumelia petulantiáque tractatæ: aliæ verò venditæ, atque omnibus opprobrijs iniurijsque expositæ. Interea Minerius via, quam vocant, regia Cadeneti, cum equitatu Merindolium contendebat, per mediam Laurensem silvam. Quò quum esset peruentum, præses quendam natus adolescentem, iussit eum alligari ad oleam, globulisque tormentorum missilibus, crudelem in modum à suis confodi & confici. Hoc in supplicio & martyrio, iuuenis oculos semper suos habebat in cælum erectos & intentos, cum maximo clamore piæ inuocationis indice. Vltima eius vox hæc fuisse dicitur, Domine Deus, ipsi quidem homines vitam mihi ærumnosam miseramque eripiunt: sed tu per Iesum filium tuum vitam mihi tribues sempiternam. Merindolium igitur sine vlla repugnantia captum ac direptum fuit & incensum, ac per fossores belli afseclas[?] solo æquatum. Vastato igitur Merindolio, postea vicesima die Aprilis eodem anno, Cabrieram omnibus viribus obsederunt, quam cū vehementer machinis bombardisque oppugnassent, neque possent expugnare: Minerius cum domino ipsius Cabrieræ & Polino earum copiarum duce, interposita fide promiserunt, se curaturos, ut eorum causa in iudicium ciuile, ab omni armorum violentia vocaretur, neque vlla eis vis & iniuria adferretur, si portas oppidi vellet aperire. Ea fide data propugnatores statim portas aperuerunt, Polinúmq; & Dopedâ cum exercitu receperunt. Sed homines non minore perfidia, quàm animi fa-vitia[?] prædi-ti, cùm ingressi in id fuissent, omnem fide fefellerunt ac violarunt. Dopeda quidem viginti quinque ex iis quos delegerat, comprehendi iussit, vinctosque extra urbem in pratum quoddam deduci suburbanum, vbi milites eos crudelissimè omnes cōtrucidarut. Ac ne quid sceleris aut crudelitatis intentatum relinqueret, in sexu quoque muliebri experiri voluit. mulieres etenim quadraginta, quarum quædam erant grauidæ, comprehendi iussit, eásque in horreum includi: deinde quatuor ex angulis ignem subijci. Ac cùm iam flamma inualuisset & horrendum in modum clamores vndique exaudirentur, tantum abSic ut hostis vlla misericordia tactus fuerit, ut etiam mulieres quæ semiustulatæ ab incendio sese proripere conabantur, contis hastisq; militum undique propellerentur, atque in ignem adigerentur. Complures etiam reperti sunt in caueis, qui bini vinculis constricti, in aulam arcis Cabrieresis ducti fuerunt, vbi acerba & indigna cæde, militibus ludibria fuerunt. Postremò ductores lenonum latronúmque Auenionensium temulentô ingressi, & maximum mulierum, infantium, puerorúmque numerum sustulerunt, nullum crudelitatis genus prætermiserunt, nulliq; sexui aut ætati pepercerunt. Reliqui verò, qui eodem tempore aut deinceps, vario mortis genere interierunt, circiter mille numero fuerunt: in quos quidem omnes, sine vllo discrimine ætatis, sexúsque infesta inimicorum lindo grassata est, vel potius summa cum petulantia debacchata. Ad monumentum autem tam præclarae rei gestæ partæq; victoriæ, administri Papæ columnam Cabrieræ erigendam curauerunt, in qua dies & ann. oppidi capti ac direpti, per Ioannem Minerium Dopedæ dominum, Curiæ Prouinciæ primum præsidem, incisis literis notatus fuit, ad memoriam tam fœdæ atq; horrendæ immanitatis, non solum nouæ ac inusitatæ, sed etiam inauditæ. Ex quo sanè poterit ipsa posteritas intelligere quibus rationibus Romanus Antichristi sedem illa impietatis atq; abominationum tueri soleat, qui iam ad eum omnium scelerum cumulum venit, ut omni æquitate, iustitia, veritate posthabita causæ suæ defensionem in armis, terrore atque oppressione constitutam habeat. Interea illi, qui paulò ante è Merindolio secesserat, locisque in circuitu vicinis, per montes ac rupes, in summa inopia & rerum omnium ad victum pertinentium destitutione vagi, aut abditi versabatur: qui quidem ante eam calamitatem importatam, priusquam inimici eò sceleris furorisq; progressi, à præside per homines apud eum aliquam gratiam authoritatemq; habentes contenderant, ut ipsis iter pacatum & tutum daret, quo recipere eò se possent cum uxoribus ac liberis, quo Dominus ipsos vellet conducere, solum indusium habentes, quo carnem suam aliquo modo contegeret. At præses amicis suis ita respondit, Ego, inquit, scio quid mihi agendum sit. Nevnus quidem meas effugiet manus, ego mittam eos in regionem inferorum vt ibi cum diabolis habitet. His aliisq; minacibus atrocibusque utens verbis, quibus duces exercitus præfetes, ad omnem acerbitatem & sæuitiam incitabat, eosdé fortis ille imperator hortabatur vt omnia oppida, domos, locáque aperta, infirma & iam diruta, hostiliter inuaderent, diriperent, vastarent, in quibus ne minima quidem ad resistendum vis aderat. Sed egregius sane vir, qui à iudicio & foro ad bellum atque imperium, toto animi impetu se contulerat, quanta esset sua potentia, vel potius naturæ ferocia & immanitas in hominum innocentium, Deúmque pie colentium imbecillitate inopiaque experiri voluit. nam eadem crudelitas ac vastitas, & ab istis oppidis & pagis in Costam oppidum, quasi tempestas quædam sævissima & calamitosissima delata est. Eius oppidi dominus cuibus antea suaserat vt omnia arma in arcem conferrent, & murum etiam aliqua parte diruerent, vt in eos præsidio destitutos, clementius hostis ageret. Quum vero ipse Costa discessisset, non longè progressus, obuios habuit Minerij milites, recta in vrbem tendentes. nihil tamen primo impetu effecerunt: postero tamen die, incensis circum ædificijs suburbanis, vrbem crudelius oppugnantes, vi ceperunt: plerique enim su-periori nocte, deserta vrbe profugerant delapsi funibus. Capta vrbe ac direpta, post stragem editam excurrunt milites in locum castro proximum, vbi mulieres ac puellas quæ trepidantes eò confugerant promiscuè constuprant: & quum aliquandiu detinuissent, adeò inhumaniter tractarunt, vt eæ quæ gerebant vterum, & natu minores puellæ non multò post extinguerentur.
units.tr: After these many and grave contests in the courts, God at last restored the spirits of the Merindolians and their companions with a welcome change of leisure and rest. He did so by striking terror into their enemies through the examples he had made so plain against the wicked persecutors of his people: not only in the sudden death of President Chassanaeus, but in the deaths of many other leading men of the Provincial Court, whose dreadful end frightened many. Above all, there was the fate of Jean de Roma, a most impure man, which everyone knew had befallen him, as we related earlier. So the cruel rage of the adversaries was for a time held in check by many obstacles, and the execution of that most cruel sentence against the Merindolians was delayed, while Jean Minier, said to be the son of the late father of that name, obtained the office of first president of that Court. Before this, he had held the papal magistracy at Cavaillon, which they call the viguerie, and from a humble position he was suddenly raised to the highest wealth and dignity. For to his authority as president was added the office of royal prefect, which he exercised in the absence of the lord of Grignan, who was then on an embassy in Germany. This man, as president, devoted all his strength and resources to confirming and carrying out in practice that bloody decision the Court had earlier made, and even to adding much to its cruelty as a servant of Satan and the most hostile executioner, as the execution itself showed. So when the lord of Grignan was absent from the province, this distinguished president Minier, having carefully observed every consideration and occasion by which he could accomplish what he had undertaken, gathered all the king's forces, which had then come into Provence from Piedmont, about to set sail from Marseille for the expedition against England, and joined them to the army which the papal legate had raised at Avignon and throughout the whole county of Venaissin. Thus the great-minded commander, forgetting his office, began to advance with hostile standards, to destroy and lay waste Merindol and Cabrières and other towns, and to overthrow and wipe out twenty-two villages. And to make this easier, he gave the soldiers license to plunder and burn everything, and even to slaughter men, women and infants. Before they reached Merindol, however, he gave to fire and pillage the town called La Roque, Saint-Estève, Villelaure, Lourmarin, La Motte, Cabrerolles, Saint-Martin, Pertuis and other places beyond the Mont Lubéron. The inhabitants of these places, most of whom had withdrawn to Merindol, seeing the great savagery of their enemies, retreated into a wood called Lauris, until the force and fury of the enemy had passed over them like some savage and violent storm. But when they saw the enemy gather strength and draw ever nearer, they all agreed with one mind and resolved that nothing was better than for the wives to remain with the children while the husbands went off somewhere else. For they thought that with the men absent the women would more easily find mercy from the enemy, however barbarous. No speech could describe the groans and anguish of mind, the weeping and lamentation shared by all in that most bitter parting, when the husband was forced to be torn away from his dearest wife and the father from his sweetest children. Nevertheless, after the ministers had held a sermon and the usual prayers were said in the evening, the men departed that night so as to avoid greater danger and hardship. The next morning the foot soldiers drew nearer to the place where the women had been left by their husbands. Several of those who were in Minier's camp, moved by some goodwill or pity towards them, ran ahead of the army to that place, so that they might warn those who were there of the hostile approach of the enemy. They found them all, and they begged them earnestly, after the sermon had been finished, which had been held in the morning. Moreover, as soon as the army came there, all the goods which these wretched people had saved from the earlier plunderings and robberies of the enemy were at once exposed to pillage. The women and girls were stripped, some were violated and beaten, and treated with every insult and wantonness; others were sold and exposed to every kind of disgrace and outrage. Meanwhile Minier, by the royal road which they call the Cadenet road, was hastening with his cavalry to Merindol, through the middle of the wood of Lauris. When he had arrived there, the president ordered a certain young man of noble birth to be tied to an olive tree, and to be shot through and killed by his men with musket balls, in a cruel manner. In this torment and martyrdom the young man always kept his eyes raised and fixed on heaven, with a great cry as a sign of his pious invocation. His last words are said to have been these: "Lord God, men indeed take from me a wretched and miserable life, but through Jesus your Son you will give me eternal life." Merindol was therefore taken without any resistance, plundered and burned, and by the sappers and camp followers of war levelled to the ground. So, after Merindol had been laid waste, on the twentieth day of April of the same year, they besieged Cabrières with all their strength; and when they had assaulted it fiercely with engines and bombards and could not take it, Minier, together with the lord of Cabrières and Polin, leader of those troops, gave their pledged word that they would see to it that their cause was brought before a civil court, free from all violence of arms, and that no force or injury would be done to them, if they would open the gates of the town. Trusting this promise, the defenders at once opened the gates and received Polin and Dopède with the army. But these men, no less treacherous than their hearts were prone to evil, once they had entered, broke faith entirely and violated it. Dopède, indeed, ordered twenty-five of those he had selected to be seized, and, bound, led out of the town into a suburban meadow, where the soldiers slaughtered them all most cruelly. And so that he might leave no crime or cruelty untried, he wished to test it on women too. He ordered forty women, some of whom were pregnant, to be seized and shut up in a barn; then fire was set at four corners. And when the flames had already taken hold and cries rose on every side in a dreadful manner, so little was the enemy moved by any pity that women who, half burned, tried to tear themselves away from the fire were pushed back from every side with the poles and spears of the soldiers and driven into the flames. Several were also found in cells, bound two by two, and led into the hall of the castle of Cabrières, where they were made the sport of the soldiers by a bitter and unworthy slaughter. Finally the leaders of the pimps and brigands of Avignon entered drunk and carried off a very great number of women, infants and boys; they left no kind of cruelty untried and spared no sex or age. As for the rest, who in the same time or afterwards perished by various kinds of death, they numbered about a thousand; and upon all of them, without any distinction of age or sex, the hostile rage of their enemies raged, or rather ran wild with the greatest wantonness. Moreover, as a monument of so splendid a deed and of the victory won, the servants of the Pope had a column raised at Cabrières, on which the day and year of the town's capture and plunder, by Jean Minier, lord of Dopède, the first president of the Provincial Court, were marked with inscribed letters, as a memorial of so foul and dreadful a cruelty, not only new and unusual but unheard of. From this posterity itself can well understand by what means the Roman seat of Antichrist is accustomed to defend that seat of impiety and abominations, which has now come to such a heap of crimes that, with all equity, justice and truth set aside, it holds its cause established by arms, terror and oppression. Meanwhile those who had shortly before withdrawn from Merindol, wandering or hiding among the mountains and rocks of the surrounding neighbourhood, were in great want and destitute of everything needed for life. Indeed, before that calamity was brought upon them, and before the enemy had advanced so far in crime and fury, they had sought through men who had some favour and authority with the president that he would give them a peaceful and safe road by which they might withdraw, with their wives and children, wherever the Lord wished to lead them, having nothing but a shirt with which to cover their flesh in some way. But the president answered his friends thus: "I know," he said, "what I must do. None of them shall escape my hands; I will send them to the region of the dead, that they may dwell there with the devils." Using these and other threatening and savage words, by which he urged the commanders of the army and the prefects to every bitterness and cruelty, that brave commander exhorted them to attack, plunder and lay waste all the open towns, houses and places, feeble and already ruined, in which there was not even the smallest force to resist. But this man, an outstanding figure who had turned from the courts and law to war and command with all the impetus of his spirit, wished to try how great his power was, or rather how great the ferocity and savagery of his nature was, against the weakness and helplessness of innocent men who piously worshipped God. For the same cruelty and devastation was carried from these towns and villages like a most savage and calamitous storm onto the town of Costa. The lord of that town had earlier advised its people to bring all their arms into the citadel and to pull down the wall in some part, so that the enemy would deal more mercifully with them, left undefended. But when Costa himself had left, not having gone far, he met the soldiers of Minier, who were heading straight for the town. At first they achieved nothing by their first attack; yet on the next day, after burning the buildings around the suburbs, they assaulted the town more cruelly and took it by force, for most of its people had fled from the deserted town during the previous night, letting themselves down by ropes. When the town had been captured and plundered, after a massacre, the soldiers ran out to a place near the castle, where they indiscriminately violated the women and girls who had fled there in alarm; and having held them for some time, they treated them so inhumanly that those who were pregnant, and the younger girls, were soon put to death.

units.la: Sane impossibile esset omnes acerbos ac luctuosos exitus euentúsque suscepta tam crudelis persecutionis in Merindolios ac socios enarrare, adeò nullum sævitiæ genus prætermissum fuit: ac qui euaserant per q; sylvas & rupes oberrabat, intercepti, vel ad triremes mittebantur, vel confodiebantur: multi qui speluncas ingressi sub rupibus latitabant, alij inedia, alij iniecto igne enecati ac fumo suffocati fuerunt. quæ quidem amplius cognosci possent ex forensibus actis, aduersariisque orationibus in primaria classis Curiæ Parisiensis auditorio, apertis valuis magnaque hominum frequentia habitis, à duobus celeberrimis & frontis prorsus panegyricæ Causidicis, altero quidem cui Aubrio cognomen erat, Minerum præsidem in vincula coniectum accusante: altero vero qui Robert-tus nominabatur, defendente. Hæc vero omnia iussu atque authoritte Henrici II.
