Galliarum Regis ea potissimum gratia Lutetiæ, ve-ti in summo totius regni theatro geri dicebantur, ut patrem Frācium regē, cui successerat, ab ea crudelitatis nota vindicaret, quæ multorum Principum animos offenderat, ut ipse Carolus V. imperator in publicis omnium ordinum Germaniæ comitiis eum perstrinxisse dicatur, quod subditum populum nulla sexus aut ætatis ratione habita integrum vastasset. Hæc vero causa quum quinquaginta plus minus audientiis vltrò citróque habitis peragi non posset, in sinum Palatinum habuit, tandémque Minerius vinculis solutus, in integrum restitutus fuit ea conditione ac fide data Carolo Lotharingo Cardinali, ut novos Christianos (sic enim appellant veritatis Evangelicæ studiosos) tota Provincia expelleret. Reuersus itaque in Provinciam maiora quàm antè crudelitatis specimina dedit: neque prius extrema quæque in homines innocentes tentare destitit quàm morbo correptus horrendas pœnas admirabili Dei iudicio dedit. Etenim insitata per posticā corporis partem sanguinis emissione, ac graui ἰσχυείᾳ[?] paulatim illi inguina computruerunt. Ac quum nullum morbo remedium inueniretur, & iam intestina vermibus arroderetur, accersitus fuit clari nominis Chirurgus natione Gallus, qui Arelate cōmorabatur cognomine La Motte, vir non minus pietate quàm arte insignis, qui quum ἰσχυείας[?] molestia Minerium leuasset, ac iam plurimum authoritatis apud eum conciliasset: antequàm alias putidi cadaueris partes attingeret, ut penitius exquireret morbi causas, petijt ut qui Minerio in cubiculo aderant, paululùm secederent. Illis semotis cœpit pluribus Minerium hortari, iam tempus esse ut ob tam horrenda scelera, maximè verò ob innocentem sanguinem manibus ipsius effusum, veniā à Deo per Christū posceret: eam denùm esse causam insitatæ profusionis sanguinis quem emittebat. Hæc sanè adeò impuram hominis conscientiam pupugerunt, ut morbo graviore molestiā tulerit. Adeste, inclamat, coprehendatur Chirurgus hæreticus. Lamotteus, has monitiones tyranno dictas quauis mercede potiores existimans, protinus Arelatē se recepit. Revocatus tamen precibus ac præsidio ab amicis fide obfirmato Lamotteus ad Minerium redijt, quū iam omnia cōclamata essent, & crudeles ac horrendas voces impuro ore animam agens emitteret.
units.tr: It would be impossible to recount all the bitter and dismal ends that came of that cruel persecution waged against the Merindolians and their companions, since no kind of cruelty was left untried. Those who had escaped wandered through woods and over rocks, and when they were caught they were either sent to the galleys or cut down. Many who had gone into caves and hidden under the cliffs were killed, some by hunger, others by fire lit at the mouth of the cave and smoke suffocation. More could be learned of these things from the court records and the speeches for each side, which were heard in the great chamber of the first class of the Parisian Court, with the doors thrown open and a large crowd present. Two very famous advocates, both utterly given to flattery of the cause, pleaded: Aubry, who prosecuted Minerius, the president of the Merindolians, and was thrown into prison, and Robert, who defended him. All these proceedings were carried out by the order and authority of Henry II, King of France, chiefly so that they could be seen to take place at Paris, the greatest stage of the whole kingdom. The purpose was to clear his father, King Francis, whom he had succeeded, of the stain of cruelty that had offended the minds of many princes. Even Emperor Charles V is said to have rebuked him in a public assembly of all the orders of Germany, because he had laid waste his subjects without any regard to sex or age. Since this case could not be concluded after some fifty hearings held back and forth, it was adjourned to the Palatine bench. At length Minerius was released from his chains and restored to his former standing, on the condition and promise given to Cardinal Charles of Lorraine that he would drive the new Christians (for so they call those who zealously pursue the truth of the Gospel) out of the whole province. Returning to the province, he showed greater cruelty than before, and he did not stop trying every extreme against innocent men until, struck down by disease, he paid horrible penalties by the wonderful judgment of God. For blood was let out through the back part of the body, and by degrees his groin rotted away from a grave strangury [ἰσχυείᾳ]. When no remedy for the disease could be found, and his intestines were already being gnawed by worms, a famous surgeon, a Frenchman named La Motte, who lived at Arles, was summoned. He was distinguished no less for piety than for skill. When he had relieved Minerius of the pain of the strangury, and had already won great authority with him, before he touched the other putrid parts of the corpse, he asked, so that he could search more deeply into the causes of the disease, that those who were present with Minerius in his bedchamber should withdraw a little. When they had gone, he began to urge Minerius at length that it was now time, for such horrible crimes, and above all for the innocent blood shed by his own hands, to ask pardon from God through Christ. This, he said, was the reason for the bleeding that was being drawn. These words so stung the impure conscience of the man that he suffered more grievously from his illness. "Come here!" he cried. "Let the heretic surgeon be seized!" La Motte, judging these admonitions, uttered to a tyrant, to be worth more than any payment, at once retreated to Arles. Yet he was recalled, by the prayers and protection of friends, with his faith confirmed, and he returned to Minerius when everything was already in an uproar, and the dying man was pouring out cruel and horrible cries from his impure mouth.

units.la: Insignis Euangelicæ doctrinæ confessio, & persecutio fidelium apud Meldenses, quo- rum Quatuordecim extremo ignis supplicio affecti fuerunt.
units.tr: A notable confession of the Gospel doctrine, and the persecution of the faithful at Meaux, where fourteen of them were put to death by the extreme punishment of fire.

units.la: INTER multas regni Galliæ urbes, quibus gratia cœlestis per verbum Dei communicata atque impertita fuit, oppidum Meldense primo loco numerandum est, quod in Bria positum ad Matronam fluvium, milliaria decem Lutetia abest. nam perpaucæ reperiuntur civitates sub impio Antichristi dominatu, in quibus veritas verbi Dei tanta fide annunciata, tanto studio ardoreque recepta, tanto aucta incremento, ac subito amplificata, tanta constantia defensa & conservata fuerit. Ratio autem qua Dominus hanc urbem illuminavit, quæ nullo fere alio hominum genere, quam opificum ac mechanicorum frequentatur, huiusmodi est: Guilielmus Briconnetus eius urbis fuit episcopus, homo optimis literis eruditus, ac tum quidem admirabili quodam studio veritatis tum cognoscendæ, tum etiam aliis declarandæ inflammatus. Is initio episcopatus, cum ecclesias dioecesis suæ adiret, atque ut verus pastor, inspectorem ageret, reperit populum cognitione Dei plane destitutum, eumque à Franciscanis cæterisque manticariis mendicis ea solùm doceri, quæ ad cœnobium illorum, ac ventrem explendum pertinerent. Itaque Episcopus eorum imposturis ac fallacis intellectis, sanctissimo animi studio permotus, eis in universa dioecesi sua prædicationem interdixit, atque in eorum locum viros alios vocavit, summa cum vitæ probitate[?], tum etiam pietatis doctrina atque intelligentia probatissimos. In quibus fuit Iacobus Faber Stapulensis, Michael Arandensis, Martialis, Gerardus Rufus. quorum cum fide & diligentia, tum etiam singulari studio feruoreque Episcopi (qui ipse tum veritatem Dei annuntiabat, nulliq; parcebat sumptui, quo libri ad eam rem utiles parari possent) cognitio Euangelii longè lateque cœpit propagari, & præclara huius tanti boni & solatii à Deo profecti fama per totam Galliam diffundi: quibusdam in suavem vitæ odorem, aliis verò contrà in offensionem. Tamen hoc semen Euangelii ea in ecclesia iactum, quotidie magis efflorescebat, atque ad electorum consolationem, salutemque maxinum fructum afferebat, donec Sathan, princeps tenebrarum, & salutaris huius lucis inimicissimus, cum videret ruinam regni sui instare, vsitata sua instauit mancipia, ipsos nempe Franciscanos, qui episcopum Briçonnetum in iudicium & crimen haereseos ad summam Curiam vocauerunt: cum quibus Sorbonici doctores caeteriq; veritatis inimici se facile coniunxerunt. Primum igitur Sathan his vtens instrumentis, facile Episcopi fidem expugnauit, eumque ad defectionem adduxit. deinde caeteros maiore vi aggressus est, quos in fide firmiores & constantiores inuenit. horum quidam fuerunt combusti: quo in numero fuit ille de quo in fine primi libri egimus, Iacobus Pauaneus. qui quidem tanto animi ardore & studio veritatem docere coepit, vt primus Lutetiae crematus fuerit, nomine eius potissimum doctrinae quam de Coena pauci tum cognouerant. Alij verberibus caesi, aut in theatro cum ignominia constituti, aut missi in exilium, atque ipso ex regno profligati. Denique hostes Euangelij nunquam desiterunt, quoad libertas veritatis publicandae erepta, eaque lux & cognitio salutaris, quae paulo ante erat exorta, plane oppressa extinctaque fuerit. Nam Franciscani quidem, cum conciones maximis studijs, ambitiosisque rationibus solitas recuperassent, sua vsitata mendacia coeperunt iterum populo obtrudere. Neque tamen cum omnia maximè quidem conarentur, id sunt assecuti, vt cognitione veritatis in multorum cordibus infixam impressamque euellerent, aut eam plane delerent. Nam pij homines, in quorum animis timor Dei cum illa cognitione insederat, cum viderent veritatem publicis ex locis profligatam, vnà cum libertate Dei pure innocandi, coeperunt conuentus inter se occultos habere, exemplo Prophetarum, qui sub Achab extiterunt, & eorum Christianorum, qui in ecclesia primum nascente, propter horribiles persecutiones huiusmodi loca secreta ad orandum opportuna quaesiuerunt. Ita isti homines Deum reuerentes, vt opportunitas facultasque eis dabatur, modo aliquam in domum, modo in reductam vallem aut speluncam, interdum in dumetis aut syluis conueniebant. Eo in conuentu ac coetu is qui in Scriptura sancta maximè omnium versatus atq; exercitatus videbatur, verbo Dei alios consolabatur, docebat, hortabatur: eoq; munere perfecto, omnes vnanimiter ardentérq; Deum comprecabantur: alentes perpetuò ac fouentes eam spem, quòd ipsa Gallia breui reciperet Euangelium, neque diutius impium ac scelerátum Antichristi dominatum perferret. Postremò, cùm post longam expectationem viderent tantùm abesse ut religio repurgaretur ab inquinamentis, ut fœditas superstitionum atque omnium abominationum à Papa in Ecclesiam introducta, magis in dies magisque augeretur & confirmaretur: plerique eorum qui spiritu erant feruentiore, & qui à primo doctrinæ receptæ tempore, se puros atque impollutos ab omni Missarum idololatria conseruarunt, anno M.D.XLVI. deliberarunt certam inter se piæ ecclesiolæ formam instituere. Ad id autem faciendum, imprimis fuerunt permoti exemplo ecclesiæ Gallicanæ quæ tum Argentinæ præclarè instituta, apud omnes fama religionis celebrabatur, & quam quidam ex ipsis adierant, ac diligenter inspexerant. Præcipui authores totius eius negotij ac moderatores erant, Stephanus Manginus, vir sanè bonus, grandisq; natu, & Petrus Clericus, arte sua ac professione carminarius, sed in sacris literis apprimè exercitatus, eo quidem genere sermonis, qui Gallorum proprius est. Hi cum aliis quibusdam quadraginta aut quinquaginta consilium ceperunt, ministri alicuius ex ipsis eligendi, qui eis verbum Dei annuntiaret, & Sacramenta administraret. Quod quidem ab illis non temere leuiterque factum est: nam cum uno eodémq; animo aliquot dies ieiunijs precibúsque impendissent, Petrus Clericus summo omnium consensu ministerelectus est. qui munus susceptum diligentissimè obire cœpit, eósque in domum Mangini diebus Dominicis festisque colligere. Eo in conuentu exponebat eis Scriptura, pro ea gratia & facultate quæ ei à Deo tributa erat. ibi oēs unà preces atque orationes ad Deum adhibebant, Psalmos canebant & cantica spiritualia. Ibi posteaquam testificati essent se nunquá Papisticis idololatriis adhæsuros, sacrá Cœnà semel aut bis celebrarunt, ut à Christo Domino est instituta. Itaque hæc parua ecclesia, exiguo temporis spatio huiusmodi fecit incrementum, ut trecēti aut quadringēti [?] reperirentur, tum viri tum mulieres ac cuiusq; ætatis homines, qui eò confluebant: nō ex urbe modo, sed etiam ex pagis quinq; aut sex milliaribus in circuitu. quæ fuit causa ut statim detecti atque obseruati, per quosdā homines improbos fuerint. Ea de re admoniti quidē fuerūt ab amicis quibusdam & benevolis hominibus, ut ab insidijs, quae eis parabātur sibi cauerent. verūm hi responderunt Etiā capillos capitis sui numeratos esse, atq; id futurū quod Domino placeret. Octauo igitur die Septembris, anno M.D.XLVI. quae die Papistae natalitijs virginis Mariae celebrandis consecrarunt, hora septima matutina accessit quidā delator ad magistratū, eos coepisse iam congregari. Eo nuntio allato, magistratus eius urbis, & praepositus cū suis satellitibus atque ministris, simul etiā is qui tota in regione latronibus coprehendedis puniendisque praefectus est, magna satellitū caterva stipatus, ad domū ipsius Mangini accesserunt. Petrus Clericus, tum exponebat eo in coetu locū quendā primae epistolae Pauli ad Corinthios. Satellites coenaculū ingressi in quo oēs congregati erāt, aliquādiu quasi attoniti summo cū silentio constiterūt. Tandē Quaesitor rogauit, quid agerēt ibi tot homines, qui suas parœcias non adirent. Id quidē quod ipse vides, inquit Clericus, sed aequo animo expecta, quoad nos ista absoluamus. Tu caeteri e magistratu, Eundū vero, inquiunt, est in carcere. Eamꝰ, inquit ille, si ita Domino visum est. Et simul se ligari cōstringíq; passus est: eadēmq; mānsuetudine caeteri oēs, tum homines tū mulieres, numero sexaginta duo, sunt imitati. In his puella erat, quae propter aetatē intelligere nōdū poterat, quā odij magnitudine veritas verbi Dei premeretur. ea cum se propterea duci ab illis videret vinctam, quod in coetu & conuentu tā sancto honestóque deprehensa esset, dixit magistratui, Si vos me in lupanari deprehendissetis, aut in loco pudendo, nunquā me his vinculis constringendā curassetis. At magistratus impositō ei pro authoritate sua silentio, totā multitudinem in vrbis carcere duci iussit. Res digna admiratione visa est, cū tot homines in vtroq; sexu, à tam paucis summa voluntate ac mansuetudine ducerētur. Nam si aliquā recusandi voluntate declarassent, facile à parentibus & propinquis, qui in ea vrbe erant, liberari potuissent. Sed tantū aberat, vt hi vim aliquā aut rebellionem cogitarent, vt contrà laeti atque hilares, per vicos vrbis irent Psalmos canetes, in quibus praecipuè LXXIX, Deus, venerunt gentes, elatis vocibus canebatur. His in carcerem inclusis, coeptū est anquiri in eorum sabbatha & conuenticula, ita enī inuidiosè ac criminosè sanctissimum eorū coetū appellabat. Inter alia crimina, hoc ipsorū iudicio grauissimum obijcebat, quòd Cœnam Domini facere ausi suissent. Qua in re, quid opus est quaerere, quanto perè ordo monachorum ac sacerdotum hoc vno verbo fuerit offensus & irritatus, quum viderent suam existimationem aboleri, atque authoritatem, quam tandiu támque studiosè inuiolatam coseruassent, delabi in manus imperitorum: optimumque sacrificium, non tam ad memoriam Christi celebrandam, quàm ad culinam ventris colendam tuendámque comparatum, iam in fumum euanescere? Postquam omnia, quae ad causam innocentiámque eorum premendam pertinebant, diligenter essent expiscati, curribus vinctos imposuerunt nullo superiecto stramine, in quo possent aliquo modo quiescere: atque ita fine vlla itineris intermissione ac remissione Lutetiam summa celeritate portandos curauerunt. Ac tametsi plerique eorum iam aetate ac laboribus confecti ipsaque itineris contentione currúsque agitatione fracti essent, non tamen destiterunt in via sese mutuo adhortari atque consolari: ac cum Parisiensem urbem ingressi essent Psalmos canere dum ad Palatinum carcerem peruenirent, quo excepti nouis tormentis miserè diuexati sunt. Ea autem non leuia remissáque extiterunt, sed acerrima maximéque exquisita, praesertim in reos quatuordecim, qui à summa curia Parisiensi capitis damnati fuerunt,sicut satis constat ex ea iudicum sententia, quae deinde Lutetiae ad perpetuam rei memoriam publicata fuit. Id quidem arestum summam iudicij acerbitatem complectitur, praesertim in quatuordecim viros, qui, vt firmissimi in confessione fidei piaeque doctrinae, ita etiam grauissime omnium accusati. Hi autem fuerunt, Petrus Clericus, StephanusManginus, Iacobus Bouchebecus, Ioa. Brisebarr, Henricus Hutinot, Thomas Honoratus, Ioan. Baudouinus, Ioa. Flescbus, Ioan. Piquerius, Petrus Piquerius, Ioa. Mateslonus, Philippus Paruus, Michael Caillous, & Franciscus Clericus, qui omnes fuerunt condemnati, vt crate ad locum supplicij pertracti, viui cremaretur apud magnum forum Meldensè, loco Mangini aedibus propinquo. In reliquos, qui in doctrina pietatis suscepta minus firmi & constantes extiterunt, poena non ita acerba, ex tamen varia constituta fuit, atque in vtrumque sexum peruagata. Nam alij fuerunt caesi virgis atque in exilium missi, alij vero eorum XIIII. quos supra nominauimus, acerbissimae mortis spectatores, summa cum ignominia constituti, in quibus etiam unus sub axillis suspensus, laqueum habens collo ligatum, grauissimum illorum casu intueri iussus est. Mulieres vero quaedam sunt condemnatae, ut supplicium in viros constituerent, ignominiose spectarent. Deniq; ab eadem Curia decretum fuit & constitutum, ut domus ipsius Mangini, in quam illi convenire soliti esse dicebantur, ad sempiternam memoriam tanti sceleris, ut ipsi iudicabant, solo plane aequaretur, eoque in loco sacellum extrueretur, in quo Missa ad cultum maximi illius Papistarum dei quē in sacramento affingunt, institutã singulis diebus Iouis celebraretur: cui proventus necessarij suppeditarentur ex eorum bonis ac fortunis, quibus omnia cum vita crudelissimè eriperent. Haec sunt illa praeclara Areopagitica Curiae Parisiensis monimenta, quae quàm sint iniqua, etiam qui aliquid habet sani iudicij, facile iudicare poterit. Sed videamus quemadmodum haec res ab illis ita decreta & constituta, postmodum administrata fuerit. hac sententia à Cofiliarijs eius camerae pronuntiata, Sathan non contentus innocentum sanguine, videns nihil plane factum esse, quod regno prodesset suo, sed potius se victu & confusum, si hi constantes in confessione susceptae veritatis permanerent, eos omnibus rationibus à propositā sententia abducere, corumq; constantiā inflectere conatus est, cùm nulla vi ea possset infringere. Itaq; omnium malorum author ac fabricator Petrus Lisetus primus tum Curiae praeses reliquis Senatoribus iudicibus persuadere conabatur, ut quatuordecim, qui capitis erant damnati, per monasteria separarentur alij ab aliis, atque ita seorsim singulorum fides & constantia perspiceretur. Sed cum omnia experti viderent infractos esse, neque eos posse ullo modo à suscepta sententia deduci, tandem Aegidio Berthelolo, qui latrunculatoris tum officio fungebatur, Meldas ad supplicium reducendos tradiderunt, quatuordecimque illos seorsim in currum imposuerunt. Vt autem eos omni molestia afficerent, ac priuaret consolatione, duo Sorbonici doctores, Maillardꝰ & Picartꝰ, mulis insidentes, currus eorum obequitabant qui non desinebant odiosissimis latratibus aures illorum obtundere, ut à veritate abducerent: adeo ut Petrus Clericus indignatione commotus Picarto dixerit, Recede à nobis Sathan, neque impedias quo minus memoria recolamus Dei nostri erga nos beneficia. Interea cum hoc iter omnium molestiarum plenum conficeretur, res divinitus accidit plane memoranda, quæ miseros homines, omnibus tum animi tum corporis laboribus affectos & quasi viribus exhaustos erexit & confirmauit. nam cum transirent per sylvam Liurēsem, quæ ab urbe Lutetia tribus milliaribus abest, obviam eis prodiit è pago proximo, qui Couberon appellatur, quidam telæ texendæ artisex, qui currus sequens, eos ad confessionem veritatis retinendam hortari cœpit, Bono, inquiens, & forti sitis animo, fratres mei atq; amici, neque fatigemini, ut testimonium, quod vos debetis Evangelio, constāter detis. Quoniam autem currus summa celeritate ferebantur, ut ab iis qui præcedebat, non facile posset exaudiri, sublata in cœlum manu exclamauit, Fratres, sitis memores eius, qui supra in cœlo est. Tum satellites, cæterique administri, qui Latrunculatorem sequebantur, arbitrati illum esse Lutheranum, nulla inquisitione habita constrinxerunt, atque ita vinctum in currum in quo quatuordecim vincti erant coiciunt. Hæ sunt viæ Domini admirabiles ac nullis cognitæ, nisi iis qui eius voluntatem & prouidentiam experiuntur, quibus ipse infirmitatem suorum in maximis ærumnis consolari solet. nam hic homo eo animi zelo ac recenti ardore divinitus in ipso itinere oblatus non modo eorum vires refecit, sed etiam nova promissionum Dei prædicatione animum reddidit, confirmauit, ac plane instauravit. quod sane quidam ex ipsis cōfessi sunt, inexpectato eius hominis adventu atque occursu, quasi Angeli è cœlo missi novas collegisse vires: & qui mœrore tacebant oppressi, caput tum erigere ac gaudere in Spiritu sancto cœpisse. adeo hic homo mechanicus, prodiens è solitudine sylvestri, eos ad causam Domini nostri Iesu Christi tuendam animauit. Paulò post ad pagum Liurium nominatum pervenerunt, ubi populus ex locis undique propinquis, ad viam qua ducebantur, effusus hominem eum qui se obtulerat, facile agnouit. Quidam etiam ex illis Lutheranum eum esse clamauerunt, suppliciumque ignis magis meritum, quam eos quibus tum additus fuisset, id quod Latrunculatorem atque eius satellites commovit ut arctius eum constringerent. Consimilis[?] huic historia memoratur in primitiva Ecclesia, de quodam Martyre, qui summa voluntate se obtulit ad mortem cum iis, quos ad pœnam mortis duci viderat, & quoniam ille homo incognitus fuisset, Adauctus est appellatū[?], quod numeum sanctissimorum Martyrum testiúmque Iesu Christi adauxisset. Cùm pervenissent Meldas, in carcerem omnes incluserunt: ac tū quærere tormentis extraordinarijs, vt vocant, cœperunt: præsertim in illos XIIII. ad accusandum eos qui eádem doctrinam fouerent, quorum tamen nullus eorum ore accusatus aut nominatus fuit. In ea quæstione, cùm crudelem in modum tortores membra eorum distraherent, ac tantum nō dilacerarent, quidam ex ipsis animo confirmatior, carnificibus clamasse dicitur, hortatúsque fuisse, ne misero corpori parcerent, quòd tantoperè spiritui voluntatique Creatoris sui restitisset.
units.tr: Among the many cities of the kingdom of France to which heavenly grace was imparted and given through the Word of God, the town of Meaux must be counted first. It lies in Brie, on the river Marne, ten miles from Paris. For very few cities are to be found under the impious tyranny of Antichrist in which the truth of God's Word was proclaimed with such faith, received with such zeal and ardour, grown so greatly, and so suddenly spread, and defended and preserved with such constancy. The way in which the Lord enlightened this city, which is inhabited by almost no class of men except workers and craftsmen, was as follows. Guillaume Briçonnet was bishop of that city, a man learned in the best literature, and then inflamed with a remarkable zeal both to know the truth and to make it known to others. At the start of his episcopate, when he visited the churches of his diocese and acted as a true minister and overseer, he found the people utterly without knowledge of God, and taught only those things by the Franciscans and the other begging hucksters that pertained to their monastery and the filling of their bellies. So the bishop, having recognised their deceptions and falsehoods, and moved by a most holy zeal of mind, forbade them to preach in all his diocese, and called in their place other men, most approved both for the uprightness of their life and for the teaching and understanding of piety. Among them were Jacques Lefèvre of Étaples, Michel d'Arande, Martial, and Gérard Roussel. Through the faith and diligence of these men, and through the singular zeal and fervour of the bishop himself, who preached the truth of God and spared no expense to have books useful for this purpose made ready, knowledge of the Gospel began to spread far and wide. The famous report of this great good and comfort, which came from God, was diffused through all France, a sweet fragrance of life to some, and to others, on the contrary, an offence. Yet this seed of the Gospel, sown in that church, flourished more and more every day, and brought the greatest fruit to the consolation and salvation of the elect. until Satan, prince of darkness and the bitterest enemy of this saving light, seeing the ruin of his kingdom at hand, set up his customary instruments, namely the Franciscans themselves, who summoned Bishop Briçonnet to the supreme Court on a charge of heresy. With them the doctors of the Sorbonne and the other enemies of truth readily joined themselves. First, then, Satan, using these instruments, easily overcame the bishop's faith, and brought him to apostasy. Then he attacked the others with greater force, and those whom he found firmer and more constant in the faith. Some of these were burned, among them that Jacques Pavanne of whom we spoke at the end of the first book. He began to teach the truth with such ardour and zeal that he was the first to be burned at Paris, chiefly on account of his teaching about the Lord's Supper, which few then understood. Others were beaten with rods, or set up on the stage with disgrace, or sent into exile and driven out of the kingdom. At last the enemies of the Gospel never ceased until the freedom to publish the truth was snatched away, and that light and saving knowledge which had shortly before arisen was utterly crushed and extinguished. For the Franciscans, having regained their accustomed sermons with the greatest eagerness and ambitious schemes, began again to thrust their usual lies upon the people. Yet although they strove with all their might, they did not succeed in tearing out or wholly destroying the knowledge of the truth that had been fixed and impressed in the hearts of many. For godly men, in whose minds the fear of God had settled along with that knowledge, when they saw the truth driven from public places, together with the liberty of calling purely upon God, began to hold secret meetings among themselves, after the example of the prophets who lived under Ahab, and of those Christians who, when the Church first began, sought out secret places suitable for prayer because of the terrible persecutions. So these men, who feared God, gathered as opportunity and means were given them: now in some house, now in a secluded valley or cave, sometimes in thickets or woods. In that gathering and assembly, the one who seemed most versed and practised in Holy Scripture comforted, taught and exhorted the others with the Word of God. When this duty was done, they all prayed to God together and with fervour, nourishing and cherishing constantly the hope that France itself would soon receive the Gospel again and would no longer endure the impious and wicked tyranny of Antichrist. At last, when after long waiting they saw that religion was so far from being cleansed of its defilements that the foulness of superstitions and of all the abominations introduced into the Church by the Pope was growing and being confirmed more and more every day, most of those who were of a more fervent spirit, and who had kept themselves pure and undefiled from all idolatry of the Mass since the first time the doctrine was received, resolved in the year 1546 to set up among themselves a certain form of a pious little church. They were moved to do this above all by the example of the French church, which was then famously established at Strasbourg and celebrated everywhere for its reputation for religion, and which some of them had visited and examined carefully. The chief authors and leaders of the whole undertaking were Étienne Mangin, a good man and advanced in years, and Pierre Leclerc, by trade a carder of wool, but thoroughly practised in Holy Letters, in that kind of speech which is peculiar to the French. These men, with some forty or fifty others, took counsel to choose one of their own number as minister, to preach the Word of God to them and to administer the sacraments. This was not done rashly or lightly by them. For when they had spent some days in fasting and prayer with one mind, Pierre Leclerc was chosen minister by the unanimous consent of all. He began to discharge this office most diligently, and to gather them on Sundays and feast days in the house of Mangin. In that assembly he expounded Scripture to them, according to the grace and ability which God had given him. There they all together offered prayers and supplications to God, and sang Psalms and spiritual songs. Then, having testified that they would never cling to the Papistical idolatries, they celebrated the holy Supper once or twice, as it was instituted by Christ the Lord. So this little church, in a short space of time, grew to such a size that there were found three or four hundred, men and women and people of every age, who gathered there, not only from the town but also from villages five or six miles around. This was the reason why they were soon detected and watched by certain wicked men. Some friends and well-disposed people warned them of this, and urged them to beware of the snares laid for them. But they answered that the very hairs of their head were numbered, and that whatever pleased the Lord would come to pass. Therefore, on the eighth day of September in the year 1546, the day on which the Papists dedicate the celebration of the Virgin Mary's birthday, at seven in the morning an informer came to the magistrate to say that they had begun to assemble. When this news was brought, the magistrate of that town, and the provost with his attendants and officers, together with the man who had charge of hunting down and punishing robbers throughout that region, attended by a large band of soldiers, went to the house of Mangin himself. Pierre Leclerc was then expounding to that gathering a passage of the first Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians. The soldiers, entering the upper room where they were all gathered, stood for a while as if astonished, in complete silence. At last the examining magistrate asked what so many people were doing there, who did not attend their own parishes. "You see what we are doing," said Leclerc, "but wait calmly until we finish these things." "You others from the magistracy," they said, "you must go to prison." "Let us go," said he, "if it so pleases the Lord." And at the same time he allowed himself to be bound and tied. All the others, men and women, sixty-two in number, followed his example with the same meekness. Among them was a girl who, because of her age, could not yet understand how the truth of God's Word was being pressed down by the great hatred against it. When she saw that she was being led away bound by them because she had been caught in so holy and honourable an assembly, she said to the magistrate, "If you had caught me in a brothel, or in some shameful place, you would never have bothered to bind me with these chains." But the magistrate, imposing silence on her by his authority, ordered the whole multitude to be led into the town prison. It seemed a thing worthy of wonder that so many men and women of both sexes should be led away by so few, with the utmost willingness and meekness. For if they had shown any will to refuse, they could easily have been freed by their parents and relatives, who were in that town. But so far were they from thinking of any violence or rebellion, that on the contrary, joyful and cheerful, they went through the streets of the town singing Psalms, above all Psalm 79, "O God, the nations have come," which they sang with loud voices. When they had been shut up in prison, inquiry began into their "sabbaths" and little conventicles, for that was how they spitefully and maliciously named that most holy assembly of theirs. Among other charges, their judges laid this one as the gravest of all: that they had dared to celebrate the Lord's Supper. There is no need to ask how greatly the order of monks and priests was offended and provoked by this one word, when they saw their reputation being destroyed and their authority, which they had kept so long and so zealously unharmed, slipping into the hands of the unskilled, and their best sacrifice, prepared not so much to celebrate the memory of Christ as to serve and protect the kitchen of their bellies, now vanishing into smoke. When they had carefully sifted everything that pertained to pressing down their cause and their innocence, they had them tied in carts, with no straw laid down on which they could rest in any way. So, with no break or pause on the journey, they arranged for them to be carried with the greatest speed to Paris. And although most of them, worn out by age and labours, were broken by the strain of the journey and the jolting of the carts, they did not cease on the way to exhort and comfort one another. When they had entered the city of Paris they sang Psalms until they reached the Palace prison, where, received with new torments, they were miserably tormented. These were not light or lenient, but most severe and most exquisite, especially against the fourteen accused who were condemned to death by the supreme Parisian court, as is sufficiently clear from the judges' sentence, which was afterwards published at Paris for the perpetual memory of the affair. This decree embraces the great bitterness of the judgment, especially against the fourteen men, who, as the most steadfast in the confession of the faith and the pious doctrine, were also accused most gravely of all. These were Pierre Leclerc, Étienne Mangin, Jacques Bouchebec, Jean Brisebarre, Henri Hutinot, Thomas Honorat, Jean Baudouin, Jean Flesch, Jean Piquery, Pierre Piquery, Jean Mateslon, Philippe Paruus, Michel Caillou, and François Leclerc. All of them were condemned to be dragged on a hurdle to the place of execution, and burned alive in the great marketplace of Meaux, near the house of Mangin. For the rest, who had been less firm and constant in the doctrine of piety they had embraced, a punishment was set, not so harsh, yet varied, and spread through both sexes. For some were beaten with rods and sent into exile; others of the fourteen whom we named above were set up with disgrace as spectators of a most bitter death, and among them one was hanged by the armpits, with a noose tied about his neck, and was ordered to look upon the terrible fate of the others. Certain women were condemned to stand and watch the punishment of the men with shame. Finally, the same Court decreed and ordered that the house of Mangin, to which those men were said to have been accustomed to gather, should be levelled completely with the ground, for an everlasting memorial of so great a crime, as they judged it; and that on that spot a little chapel should be built, in which a Mass for the worship of that great god of the Papists, whom they feign to be in the sacrament, should be celebrated every Thursday. Its necessary revenues were to be supplied from the goods and property of these men, whom they were cruelly stripping of everything along with their lives. These are those famous Areopagite records of the Parisian Court, and anyone with some sound judgment can easily see how unjust they are. But let us see how this business, once so decreed and ordained by them, was afterwards carried out. When this sentence had been pronounced by the councillors of that chamber, Satan, not content with the blood of the innocent, and seeing that nothing had been accomplished that would benefit his kingdom, but rather that he himself would be defeated and confounded if these men remained steadfast in confessing the truth they had embraced, tried by every means to draw them away from the sentence pronounced and to bend their constancy, though he could not break it by any force. So Pierre Lizet, the first president of the Court and the author and maker of all these evils, tried to persuade the other senators and judges that the fourteen who had been condemned to death should be separated, one from another, in different monasteries, so that the faith and constancy of each might be examined apart. But when they saw by trying every means that they were unbroken, and that they could in no way be led away from the sentence they had received, at last they handed them over to Gilles Berthelot, who then held the office of provost of the constabulary, to be brought back to Meaux for execution, and they placed those fourteen separately in carts. And to afflict them with every discomfort, and deprive them of consolation, two doctors of the Sorbonne, Maillard and Picard, riding on mules, rode alongside their carts, and did not cease to deafen their ears with the most hateful barking, to draw them away from the truth. So much so that Pierre Leclerc, moved with indignation, said to Picard, "Get away from us, Satan, and do not hinder us from calling to mind the kindnesses of our God toward us." Meanwhile, as this journey full of every discomfort was being completed, a thing happened by divine providence that is truly worth recording, which lifted up and strengthened those wretched men, who were worn out in body and spirit by every labour and as it were drained of strength. For when they were passing through the wood of Livry, which is three miles from the city of Paris, there came out to meet them from the nearby village called Coubron a certain weaver, who, following the carts, began to exhort them to hold fast to the confession of the truth. "Be of good and brave heart, my brothers and friends," he said, "do not be weary, so that you may steadfastly give the witness that you owe to the Gospel." And since the carts were being driven at great speed, so that he could not easily be heard by those who went in front, he raised his hand to heaven and cried out, "Brothers, be mindful of him who is above in heaven." Then the constables and the other officers who followed the provost, thinking that he was a Lutheran, seized him without any inquiry and threw him, bound, into the cart in which the fourteen were bound. These are the wonderful and hitherto unknown ways of the Lord, known only to those who experience his will and providence, by which he is wont to comfort the weakness of his own in their greatest distresses. For this man, offered by God on the very journey, with such zeal of spirit and fresh ardour, not only refreshed their strength, but also restored, strengthened and wholly renewed their courage by proclaiming again the promises of God. Some of them indeed confessed this, that by the unexpected arrival and meeting of that man, as if an angel sent from heaven, they gathered new strength; and those who had been silent, oppressed with sorrow, began to lift up their heads and rejoice in the Holy Spirit. So much did this humble craftsman, coming forth from the solitude of the woods, encourage them to defend the cause of our Lord Jesus Christ. Shortly afterwards they arrived at the village called Livry, where the people, pouring out from the places all around along the road by which they were being led, easily recognised the man who had offered himself. Some of the crowd even cried out that he was a Lutheran, and deserved the punishment of fire more than those to whom he had been joined, which moved the provost and his men to bind him more tightly. A story similar to this is recorded in the early Church, about a certain martyr who with the greatest willingness offered himself to death together with those whom he saw being led to the penalty of death; and because that man was unknown, he was called Adauctus, since he had increased the number of the most holy martyrs and witnesses of Jesus Christ. When they arrived at Meaux, they shut them all up in prison, and then began to question them with what they call extraordinary tortures, especially the fourteen, in order to make them accuse those who fostered the same doctrine; yet none of them was accused or named by mouth. In this questioning, while the torturers in a cruel manner pulled their limbs apart, and all but tore them to pieces, one of them, stronger in spirit, is said to have called out to the executioners and urged them not to spare the wretched body, since it had so greatly resisted the spirit and will of its Creator.

units.la: Postero die quo erant supplicio afficiendi, disputationem cum iis doctores theologi renouarunt, præcipuè de sacramento Cœnæ Domini. Sed Picartus & cæteri, incerti quid dicerent, plane obmutescebant cùm Clericus quæreret ab eis, in quo fundata esset ipsorum transubstantiatio, & an cùm panem ederent aut vinum biberent, aliquem carnis sanguinisque gustū perciperent.
units.tr: The next day, the day on which they were to be executed, the doctors of theology renewed the disputation with them, chiefly about the sacrament of the Lord's Supper. But Picart and the others, uncertain what to say, fell completely silent when Clerc asked them what their transubstantiation was founded on, and whether, when they ate bread or drank wine, they perceived any taste of flesh or blood.

units.la: Postremo hæc illis conditio oblata est, vt qui vellent in aurem sacerdotis insusurrare, quod illis est peccata cōfiteri, ij aliquid gratiæ obtineret, nec linguæ eis præciderentur.
units.tr: Finally this condition was offered to them: whoever wished to whisper into the priest's ear what for them is the confession of sins would obtain some favour, and their tongues would not be cut out.

units.la: Itaq; ex XIIII. quos supra nominauimus, septē eā conditionē acceperūt, aut quòd id nō magni momenti esse arbitrarentur, aut quòd eo pacto beneficium vocis redimere se posse existimarent. idque maximo dolore cæterorum, qui nullis nec minis nec promissis flecti, à sententiáq; deduci vnquā potuerūt.
units.tr: Thus of the fourteen we named above, seven accepted this condition, either because they judged it to be of no great importance, or because they thought that by this means they could buy back the gift of speech. This caused great grief to the others, who could never be moved from their judgment by threats, promises or any other means.

units.la: Hora autē post meridiē secunda, quæ supplicio dicta erat, cū è carcere educerentur, carnifex linguam primùm à Stephano Mangino postulauit, quam ille præbuit libenter atque exeruit: quā præcisa, sanguinem euomens, loquutus est, ita vt satis intelligeretur, huiusmodi verbis ter precatus, Sit nomen Dei benedictum. mòxque super crate tractus fuit, quemadmodum & Clericus: cæteri verò plaustro impositi deportabantur. quos quidem ij qui non fuerant damnati capitis, proximi pedibus sequebantur vsque ad forum magnum.
units.tr: At the second hour after noon, which had been appointed for the execution, they were led out of the prison. The executioner first demanded the tongue of Étienne Mangin, who offered it willingly and thrust it out. When it had been cut off, spitting blood, he still spoke, so that it was understood well enough, calling on God three times with these words: "Blessed be the name of God." Soon afterwards he was dragged on a hurdle, as was Clerc. The others were carried away on a cart, and those who had not been condemned to death followed close behind on foot as far as the great marketplace.

units.la: Quo in loco quatuordecim patibula forma circulari erecta erant, atque è regione domus Mangini posita. Et aliud patibulum separatum ab alijs ac paulò longius remotum, in quo sub axillis suspendēdus erat adolescens, Michael Piquerius nominatus, quem propter ætatem quò minus cremarent, pudore impediebātur. Tum verò carnifices, eos non secus atque agnos sacrificio destinatos alligarunt. Quoniam autem ij quibus lingua erat præcisa, etiam blæsa voce Dominū invocare non desinebant: cæteri vero qui linguæ beneficio fruebantur Psalmos canebāt. Sacrificuli & monachi qui ibi aderant quasi amentes furoreq; correpti decantare ipsi quoque cœperunt, O salutaris hostia, deinde, Salve regina, aliaque huiusmodi blasphemias, neque ante nefarium hunc & insanum cantum intermiserunt, quam sanctissimæ hostiæ in suavissimum odorem igne consumptæ fuerunt. Porrò sequenti die, qui fuit dies octavus eius mensis, adversarii, quasi rem suam bene gessissent, ac veritatem victam captivamque in triumphum ducerent, magnificam instituerunt pompā in qua panaceum illud suum idolum circumferebant, innumerabilibus tædis cereisque medio die accensis comitatum. Quum autem venissent ad supplicii locum, in quo adhuc ignis ardebat, idolum ibi suum collocarūt. Tum Picartus in medio foro suggestum ascendit obtectum conopeo seu integumento aureo quo splendidius & sine ulla molestia delicati hominis caput obtegeretur. Ibi theologus iste insignis cœpit pro suo more in eos, qui supplicio affecti erant, debacchari, & quod illi usque in profundum inferni damnati essent, Angelumque, si de cælo veniens secus diceret, reiiciendum esse, imo vero Deum ipsum non fore Deum, nisi eos in perpetuum damnaret. Veruntamen uxores eorum qui combusti fuerant, ad eam de maritis existimationem adduci nunquam potuerunt, etiam cum e carcere dimitterentur. Hoc enim responso potius contra pugnabant, quod eo toto vitæ tempore, quo cum illis vixerat, eorum summam integritatem in timore Dei ac vera pietate perspexissent, quæ potius vitæ æternæ comes esse solet. Horum autem hausto sanguine inimici non contenti atque exatiati, omne suum studium & conatum eo contulerunt, ut gregem Domini dissiparent, occiderent, ac plane delerent. Itaque multi ex illis magnitudine & sæuitia eius persecutionis profugi se ad urbes tum propinquas, tum remotas cotulerunt.
units.tr: In that place fourteen gibbets had been set up in a circle, opposite the house of Mangin. A further gibbet stood apart from the others and a little further off, on which the young man named Michel Piquery was to be hanged by the armpits; because of his age they were held back, out of shame, from burning him. Then the executioners bound them, as though they were lambs destined for sacrifice. Those whose tongues had been cut out did not cease to call upon the Lord even with a stammering voice, while the others, who still enjoyed the use of their tongues, sang psalms. The priests and monks who were present there, as if they were mad and seized by fury, also began to chant themselves, first "O saving victim," then "Hail, Queen," and other such blasphemies, and they did not stop this impious and insane singing until those most holy victims had been consumed by fire as a most sweet odour. On the following day, which was the eighth day of that month, the adversaries, as though they had done well and were leading truth conquered and captive in triumph, arranged a magnificent procession, in which they carried about that panacea idol of theirs, attended by countless torches and wax candles lit at midday. When they came to the place of execution, where the fire was still burning, they set their idol down there. Then Picart mounted a platform in the middle of the marketplace, covered with a canopy or golden cover, so that the head of this delicate man might be shaded more splendidly and without any discomfort. There this notable theologian began, as was his custom, to rage against those who had been executed, saying that they were damned to the depths of hell, and that if an angel came down from heaven and said otherwise he should be rejected; indeed God himself would not be God unless he damned them for ever. Yet the wives of those who had been burned could never be brought to share this opinion of their husbands, even when they were released from prison. For they argued rather against that answer, because throughout the whole of their life together they had seen the utmost integrity of their husbands, in the fear of God and true piety, which is wont rather to accompany eternal life. Yet the enemies, not content or sated with this blood, directed all their zeal and effort to scatter the flock of the Lord, to slaughter it and to destroy it utterly. And so many of them, fleeing from the greatness and savagery of that persecution, betook themselves to towns, some near and some far away.

units.la: Quæ Ecclesiæ dispersio ac dissipatio, non sine magno Evangelij incremento facta est. Nam unusquisque suum officium & studium præstabat, ut oblata occasione ad confessionem ac testificationem veritatis uteretur, quæ ac[?] modo Faronus Maginus, vir maximo spiritus ardore, Aureliæ aliisque in locis faciebat: sic Petrꝰ Bopanius vocatus, se gerebat Aubigniaci, qui paulo post Lutetiæ combustus est.
units.tr: This dispersal and scattering of the Church took place not without a great increase of the Gospel. For each one performed his duty and zeal, so that he might use the opportunity offered for confessing and bearing witness to the truth, as Faron Magin, a man of the greatest ardour of spirit, did at Orléans and in other places; so too Pierre Bopain, called to the ministry, conducted himself at Aubigny, and shortly afterwards was burned at Paris.

units.la: Liber quartus Actionum MARTYRVM.
units.tr: The Fourth Book of the Acts of the MARTYRS.

units.la: FRANCISCVS SAN-ROMANVS, HISPANVS.
units.tr: FRANCISCUS SAN-ROMANUS, A SPANIARD.

units.la: Vanquā Hispani præter cæteras Europæ totius gentes, papisticis superstitionibus supra modum addicti fuerint, adeò ut è Basilisci Romanis unus aliquando dixerit, Germaniam atque Angliam se quidē amisisse, Hispaniam velut unicam filiam castā & intactā virginem adhuc retinere: Dominus tamē (qui iā Antichristū spiritu oris sui perdere cœpit) natione etiā istā respexit, suæq; bonitatis ac misericordiæ testimonium locupletes edidit in sanguine Martyrum ibi pro veritate asserenda profuso. Fuit autē inter alios quos in Hispania Christ° habuit Martyres Fraciscus San-rom.natus Burgi oppido in Castilia Hispaniarum,ortus parētibus vitæ honestate claris,sed omni disciplina Hispanica.i.omnis generis idololatria adeò delibutus, ut ipsius conversio maiori admiratione digna esse videatur. Anno M.D.XLV,quidā mercatores Bremenses,cū statô die ad nundinas Antuerpianas nõ venissent persoluturi certam pecuniarum summam,quam mercatoribus Hispanis debedat,visum fuit iis aliquē Bremam Ostlādiæ oppidum mittere, qui nummos à debitorib°. exigeret,nec vero ad obeundum negotium promptior nec magis idoneus quisquam inventus est, quàm Franciscus iste cui mercatores Bremenses noti erant.Is igitur cū altero quodam Hispano,qui idem in mandatis habebat,Bremam proficiscuntur.Bremæ cũm essent, pro more solito templum adeunt eo ipso tempore quo M.Iacobus cocionabatur,qui olim Antuerpiæ Prior Augustinensium fuerat, vir certè pietate & doctrina insignis.quamuis autem San-romanus nō exactè linguā Germanicā teneret,magna tamē animi attētione cocionē auscultauit, curiose scire cupiēs quænā illa esset Germanorum doctrina, à qua tantopere abhorreret Hispani. Dominus autē miris modis istū homine affecit.nec enim solū concionem ipsam intellexit:sed concione absoluta, posthabitis negotiis ob quæ illuc venerat, ad ministrū accurrit:Minister vero benignè illum excepit, domumque suam deduxit, ubi Franciscus concionem ipsius ad verbum memoriter recitauit. Vera narramus, quae etiam homines fide digni ab ipso Bremensi ministro acceperunt. Atqui Franciscus tanto veritatis studio flagrabat, postquam ea in concione primum eam degustauit, ut nec disputandi nec percontandi de ea doctores, quo ampliore cognitionem sibi compararet, finem faceret. Minister vero ardens istud studium subitamque hominis mutationem admiratus, monuit ut modestius paulo atque prudentius se gereret, simulque ei scientiam salutis pedetentim instillauit: quam quidem tam auidè arripuit, quasi diuturnam sitim explere cupiens, ut totum triduum apud Pastorem haesisset, negotium quod cum Bremensibus habebat, socio committens. Ipse interea adeo studiosè diligenterque de pietatis doctrina cum pastore disserebat ut quae illi proponebantur, cuncta memoriae mandaret. In quo Pastor facilè perspexerat, istius conuersionem extraordinaria quadam & inusitata ratione accidisse. Nam quum communis hominum natura sit sensim in cognitione progredi: hic noster exiguo temporis spatio ac momento praecipuos religionis articulos perceperat: quotquot ibi reperit libros Gallicè aut Germanicè scriptos, diligenter perlegit: frequentes etiam sermones habuit cum D. Machabaeo, qui tum ibi erat, a quo se plurima didicisse postea professus est. Interea misit illinc ad Hispanos suos Antverpiam prolixas literas, quibus Deo gratias agebat quod ipsum ad ea loca perduxisset, ubi & cognitionem Christi Saluatoris sui & sacrarum literarum intelligentiam adeptus fuerat: quam certè multis laudibus ad coelum efferrebat. Deplorabat insuper crudelitatem Hispaniarum, & caecitatem suae gentis quae nec oculos ad lucem Euangelii aperire, nec aures praebere Deo cunctos ad poenitentiam vocanti dignaretur. ideoque sibi in animo esse dicebat Antverpiam redire, ut amicis quoque gratiam diuinitus sibi datam impertiretur: deinde Hispaniam cogitare, ut parentes suos, Dei fretus auxilio ad veritatis notitiam, Deique purum cultum pertraheret. Scripsit praeterea unam atque alteram epistolam ad Imperatorem Carolum V. quibus illi Reipublicae Christianae calamitates, Ecclesiaeque miserum statum explanabat: ipsum deinde Caesarem hortabatur ut utriusque rationibus consuleret atque prospiceret: nisi turpiter in-gratus gratus in Deum esse velit, cuius beneficio ipse ea quæ hominum opinione sunt maxima, & monarchiâ cõsecutus erat. officium enim Cæsaris esse tumultus Reip. Christianæ componere: gloriam Dei in omnibus tueri: Hispaniam, aliásque suo imperio subditas regiones, hominum perversis traditionibus depravatas, ex verbo Dei emendare atque corrigere. Confecit ad hæc ibidem Catechismum & nonnullos libellos Hispanicè, in quibus veræ religionis articulos exponebat. Quæ quidem omnia, unius mensis spatio composuit, dum scilicet suarum literarum responsum ab Antuerpiensibus expectabat. Illi vero ex literis re ut accideratperspecta, blandis illi verbis revocarút, dolis scilicet & arte Hispanica instructi, spem ei fecerunt, quæ scripserat, modò quàprimum ipse rediret, facilè & rectè curatum iri. Hac itaque spe ductus San-romanus Antuerpiam revertitur. Hispani interea Antuerpiæ illi insidias struunt, & subdolè monachos subornant, qui istum adeuenientem excipiant, ac de fide interrogent, ut nisi in singulis consentiret, interficiendum curarent, aut in dirum carcerem conijcerent, ubi vivum in terram defossum lenta nece trucidarent. Miser ille, horum omnium ignarus, lætus ipse sua Antuerpiam venit, vixq; urbem ingressus erat, quum illi qui studiosè diem quo veturus esset observabant, & monachi quos subornarat, in hominem ruunt, atque ex equo demissum abducūt in domum cuiusdam mercatoris. Franciscus autem ardore quodam animi inflammatus, quum se præter opinionē ac spem captum videret, magis hoc facto efferbuit. Domum quum venisset ubi detinendus erat, monachi raptim manus & pedes ei loris constrinxerunt: sarcinas eius aperuerūt, in quibus libros quosdam Lutheri, Melanchthonis & Oecolampadij repererunt, & nonnullas etiam imagines ad ignominiam Papæ depictas. Tum monachi oculis ad ipsum conversis, Vere, inquiunt, magnus hic est Lutheranus. Ille non mediocriter commotus negauit se Lutheranum esse, sed doctrinam filij Dei profiteri, quâ hostili animo & capitali odio prosequerentur Papæ administri: contráque se depravatam eorum religionem, ineptias videlicet & nugas quibus sibi adeò placet, prorsus detestari. Intererat his disputationib° aliquot Hispani, qui monachis faucebant: quæ res sanè nebulonibus animum addidit, ut liberius in hunc sæviret, suisque camillis hominem vexaret vehementiùs.
units.tr: Although the Spaniards, more than all the other peoples of Europe, were given over beyond measure to papistical superstitions, so that one of the Roman Basilisks once said that they had indeed lost Germany and England, but kept Spain, like an only daughter, still a chaste and untouched virgin, nevertheless the Lord, who had already begun to destroy Antichrist with the breath of his mouth, looked upon that nation too, and gave a rich testimony of his goodness and mercy in the blood of martyrs shed there in defence of the truth. Among the others whom Christ had as martyrs in Spain was Franciscus San-Romanus, born in the town of Burgos in Castile, of parents distinguished for the honesty of their lives, but so steeped in all Spanish discipline, that is, in every kind of idolatry, that his conversion seems worthy of great wonder. In the year 1545, some Bremen merchants, not having come to the Antwerp fair on the appointed day to pay a certain sum of money that they owed to Spanish merchants, thought it best to send someone to Bremen, a town in East Friesland, to demand the money from the debtors. No one more ready or more suitable for the task was found than this Franciscus, to whom the Bremen merchants were known. He therefore set out for Bremen with another Spaniard who had the same commission. When they were there, they went, as was their custom, to the church at the very time when Master Jacobus was preaching, who had formerly been Prior of the Augustinians at Antwerp, a man certainly distinguished for piety and learning. Although San-Romanus did not understand German exactly, he listened to the sermon with great attention, eager to find out what that doctrine of the Germans was, from which the Spaniards shrank so much. The Lord, however, affected this man in wonderful ways: for he not only understood the sermon itself, but when it was over, setting aside the business for which he had come there, he ran to the minister. The minister received him kindly and led him to his home, where Franciscus recited the minister's sermon from memory, word for word. We relate true things, which trustworthy men also received from the Bremen minister himself. Indeed Franciscus burned with such zeal for the truth, after he first tasted it in that sermon, that he did not stop disputing with and questioning the teachers, so that he might acquire a greater knowledge of it. The minister, admiring this ardent zeal and the man's sudden change, advised him to conduct himself a little more modestly and prudently, and at the same time gradually instilled in him the knowledge of salvation. He seized it so eagerly, as if desiring to quench a long-standing thirst, that he stayed with the pastor for three whole days, entrusting the business he had with the Bremen men to his companion. Meanwhile he discussed the doctrine of piety with the pastor so diligently and eagerly that he committed to memory everything that was put before him. In this the pastor clearly saw that his conversion had come about in an extraordinary and unusual way. For while the common nature of men is to advance gradually in knowledge, this man of ours had grasped the chief articles of religion in a short space of time and in a moment. Whatever books he found there written in French or German he read through carefully. He also had frequent conversations with Master Machabaeus, who was there at the time, and from whom he later confessed he had learned very much. Meanwhile he sent long letters from there to his Spanish friends at Antwerp, in which he gave thanks to God that he had led him to that place, where he had obtained both knowledge of Christ his Saviour and understanding of the sacred letters, and he extolled these with many praises to heaven. He further lamented the cruelty of the Spaniards and the blindness of his own nation, which would not deign to open its eyes to the light of the Gospel, nor to give ears to God calling all to repentance. Therefore, he said, he intended to return to Antwerp, so that he could share the grace divinely given to him with his friends too; and then to think of Spain, so that, relying on God's help, he might draw his parents to the knowledge of the truth and the pure worship of God. He also wrote one or two letters to the Emperor Charles V, in which he explained to him the calamities of the Christian commonwealth and the miserable state of the Church, and urged the Emperor himself to consult and provide for both, unless he wished to be shamefully ungrateful to God, by whose benefit he had obtained both the things that men consider greatest and his monarchy. For it was the emperor's duty to calm the disturbances of the Christian commonwealth, to uphold the glory of God in all things, and to amend and correct Spain and the other regions subject to his rule, which had been corrupted by men's perverse traditions, by the word of God. Meanwhile he composed there a catechism and some small books in Spanish, in which he set out the articles of true religion. He did all this within the space of one month, while he awaited a reply to his letters from the Antwerp men. They, having carefully considered the matter from his letters, called him back with flattering words, being schooled in Spanish trickery and craft, and gave him hope that what he had written would be easily and rightly remedied, provided he returned as soon as possible. Led by this hope, San-Romanus returned to Antwerp. Meanwhile the Spaniards laid snares for him at Antwerp, and secretly suborned monks to meet him as he arrived and question him about his faith, so that, if he did not agree on every point, they would see to it that he was killed, or thrown into a dreadful prison, where they would butcher him by a slow death, buried alive in the earth. That wretched man, ignorant of all this, came joyfully to Antwerp; and hardly had he entered the city when those who had carefully watched for the day on which he would arrive, and the monks whom they had suborned, rushed upon him, pulled him down from his horse, and led him away to the house of a certain merchant. Franciscus, however, inflamed with a certain fervour of spirit, when he saw himself seized beyond his expectation and hope, burned all the more at this. When he came to the house where he was to be held, the monks quickly bound his hands and feet with thongs. They opened his baggage, in which they found some books of Luther, Melanchthon and Oecolampadius, and also some images painted to shame the Pope. Then the monks, turning their eyes upon him, said, "Truly, this man is a great Lutheran!" He, not a little moved, denied that he was a Lutheran, but professed the doctrine of the Son of God, which the Pope's ministers pursued with hostile mind and deadly hatred; on the contrary, he utterly detested their corrupt religion, namely the trifles and nonsense in which they take such delight. Several Spaniards who sided with the monks were present at these disputes, and this gave the scoundrels courage to rage more freely against him and to harass the man more violently with their lackeys.

units.la: Quum a nostra, inquiunt, abhorreas religione, & te Christianum dicas, quaenam est tua religio? quae fides? Ia, inquit, fassus sum me tantummodo Christum eumque crucifixum praedicare. mea fides est ea quam Christi Ecclesia per vniuersum orbem dispersa, omni tempore confessa est, atque instituit. Vos autem corrupistis & plane peruertistis synceraм doctrinam qua nobis Iesus Christus crucifixus proponitur: atque aliud vitae genus abominabile suscepistis, vestraque impietate magnam mundi partem in extremas miserias coniecistis. Sed quo plenior meae fidei constet ratio, Credo in Deum Patrem, qui omnia creauit: Credo in Deum Filium Iesum Christum, qui suo sanguine genus humanum redemit, dum illud e faucibus inferorum & diaboli tyrannide eripiens, in Euangelij libertatem vindicauit: Credo in Deum Spiritum sanctum, qui occulta quadam & diuina virtute credentes sanctificat. Credo propter Filium me gratuito peccatorum omnium remissione potitum: Credo me solius Christi mediatoris beneficio, nullo meo merito, nullaque operum satisfactione, aut Papali indulgentia praemunitum atque praefultum [?], vita aeterna fruiturũ. His dictis, Cucullati sciscitati sunt an crederet Pontificem Romanum, vicarium esse Christi, caput Ecclesiae in terra, qui omnes Ecclesiae thesauros in potestate sua habeat, penes quem sit arbitrium ligandi & soluendi quicquid libitu fuerit, cui etiam nouos articulos facere, & eos quos nunc habemus abolere fas sit. Fraciscus respodit, se nihil eorum credere, sed contra affirmare Papam Antichristum esse, fatum patre diabolo, quippe qui sit inimicus Iesu Christi, sibi vendicans diuinum cultum, quíque oestro patris Sathanae percitus sursum deorsum omnia versat, & sacra prophanis miscet vt fallacias suas tueatur, quibus velut lupus rabie agitatus gregem Christi dissipat, ipsas denique oues Domini dilaniat & devorat. Ac tum primum Hispani reuera blasphemum iudicarunt. nam hactenus in confessione fidei nihil a monachis dissentire videbatur, donec Papae maiestate laederet, Missam & Purgatorium paruipederet, bullas atque indulgentias acriter insectaretur. Monachi porro illum mortis & ignis supplicio terrere coeperunt. Quibus ille respondit, Non equidem dubito mortem subire ad defendendam Dei mei causam, imo id mihi magnae gloriae fore spero quod sanguine meo de testinonium[?] doctrinæ Filij Dei, qui suum pro me misero peccatore sanguinem in cruce profudit. Sed quânam existimatis esse vestram potentiam? non potestis sanè aliud mihi eripere quàm hanc miseram carnem & peccatricem, eámque (si velitis) igni tradere. at ego timere didici cum qui in corpus simul & animam potestatem summam habet. Beatum certè me deputem, si quàm celerrimè vestra tyrannide liberer, vt vestram consuetudinem impuram relinquens, in æternam Dei gloriam & Angelorum societatem recipiar. Hæc verò Francisci intrepida oratio tantum dolorem monachis attulit, vt igni accenso coràm libros ipsius exusserint.
units.tr: Since you shrink from our religion and call yourself a Christian, what is your religion? What is your faith? Yes, he said, I have confessed that I preach only Christ, and him crucified. My faith is that which the Church of Christ, scattered throughout the whole world, has always confessed and taught. But you have corrupted and utterly perverted the pure doctrine by which Jesus Christ crucified is set before us, and have taken up another, abominable way of life, and by your impiety have cast a great part of the world into extreme misery. But so that the account of my faith may be fuller: I believe in God the Father, who created all things. I believe in God the Son, Jesus Christ, who redeemed the human race with his blood, snatching it from the jaws of hell and the tyranny of the devil, and vindicating it into the liberty of the Gospel. I believe in God the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies believers by a certain hidden and divine power. I believe that, on account of the Son, I have obtained the free remission of all my sins. I believe that by the benefit of Christ alone, the mediator, with no merit of my own, no satisfaction of works, and no papal indulgence to protect me and support me, I shall enjoy eternal life. When he had said this, the hooded men asked whether he believed that the Roman Pontiff is the vicar of Christ, the head of the Church on earth, who holds all the treasures of the Church in his power, in whose hands lies the authority to bind and loose whatever he pleases, and to whom it is lawful to make new articles of faith and to abolish those we now have. Franciscus replied that he believed none of these things, but on the contrary affirmed that the Pope is Antichrist, begotten by the father devil, since he is an enemy of Jesus Christ, claiming divine worship for himself, and who, goaded by the gadfly of his father Satan, turns everything upside down and mixes holy things with profane in order to protect his deceits; like a wolf driven by rage, he scatters the flock of Christ and finally tears and devours the very sheep of the Lord. Then for the first time the Spaniards truly judged him a blasphemer. For until then he had seemed to differ from the monks in nothing in his confession of faith, until he began to injure the majesty of the Pope, to belittle the Mass and Purgatory, and to attack bulls and indulgences fiercely. The monks then began to terrify him with the punishments of death and fire. To them he replied: I certainly do not hesitate to undergo death in defence of the cause of my God; indeed I hope it will be a great glory to me that with my blood I bear witness to the doctrine of the Son of God, who shed his blood on the cross for me, a wretched sinner. But what do you think your power is? You certainly cannot take from me anything but this wretched and sinful flesh, and deliver it, if you wish, to the fire. But I have learned to fear him who has supreme power over both body and soul. I should count myself truly blessed if I were freed as quickly as possible from your tyranny, so that, leaving your impure customs, I might be received into the eternal glory of God and the fellowship of the angels. But this fearless speech of Franciscus so grieved the monks that they lit a fire and burned his books before his eyes.

units.la: Ipse videns impuros istos homines ne nouo quidem Testamento parcere, mirum quanta in illos dicta ingesserit. Hispani hisce auditis, hominem mente captum esse rati curarunt in turrim quandam deducendum, quæ Antuerpia sex milliaribus distat, vbi in profundam fossam demissus octo miser cruciabatur mensibus. Interea plures illum viri graues inuisebant, qui hortabantur vt mutaret opinionem, & modestius loqueretur. Respondit Franciscus se nullam sinistram opinionem habere, nec vllam hæresim tueri velle. Tandem Hispani, illum ad saniorem mentem redijsse arbitrati, dimittendum censuerunt: dimissusque fuit circa id tempus quo Imperator comitia Ratisbonæ habebat. Liberatus itaque hac molestia San-romanus viginti plus minus dies Antuerpiæ commoratus est. Inde Louanium prosectus ad quendam amicum & ciuem suum Franciscum Dryandrum, multa cum eo de variis religionis capitibus disseruit: qui vir amicus hunc libere monebat ne temere mercaturæ statum, quem ante susceperat, cum alio vitæ genere commutaret: cum præsertim mercatura honestè & salua conscientia exercere, & prodesse plurimis ea posset.
units.tr: Seeing that these impure men spared not even the New Testament, he (Francis) uttered remarkable things against them. When the Spaniards heard this, they judged the man out of his mind and had him taken to a certain tower about six miles from Antwerp, where, let down into a deep pit, the wretched man suffered for eight months. Meanwhile several serious men visited him and urged him to change his opinion and speak more moderately. Francis replied that he held no unsound opinion and wished to defend no heresy. At last the Spaniards, thinking he had come to his senses, decided he should be released, and he was let go about the time when the Emperor held the diet at Regensburg. Freed from this trouble, San-romanus stayed at Antwerp for some twenty days more or less. From there he went to Louvain to a friend and fellow citizen, Francis Dryander, and discussed with him at length various articles of religion. This friend warned him frankly not to rashly exchange the trade he had previously taken up for another way of life, especially since he could practise commerce honourably, with a clear conscience, and be of great use to many through it.

units.la: Quod ad religionem attinet, sedulò ac seriò hortatus est, ne quid aut diceret vnquàm aut faceret in gratiâ vel fauore hominum, quo quidem Dei gloriam imminui posse sciret: attamen etiam in hoc requiri sanum rectumque iudicium ad normam Verbi diuini conformatum: ne sibi vsu veniret id quod plerisque solet accidere, qui inconsiderato zelo aEli[?], deserentes vocationem propriam, dum ædificare studeant, omnia prorsus destruunt, seque temere in periculum coniiciunt.
units.tr: As for religion, Dryander earnestly and seriously urged him never to say or do anything for the sake of men's favour or goodwill, since he knew that God's glory could thereby be diminished. Yet even in this, he said, a sound and right judgment, shaped by the norm of the divine Word, was required, lest it happen to him what commonly happens to many who, through ill-considered zeal for other people's affairs, abandon their own calling, and while they strive to build up, altogether destroy, and rashly expose themselves to danger.

units.la: San-romanus hanc beneuolam amici monitionem non repugnanter accepit: sed rcie-[?] Ista culpa in monachos quòd primo impetu concitatior paulò fuisset, postmodò se attentius omnia & consideratius acturum promisit. Atqui promisso non stetit. etenim postquam à Dryandro discessisset (ut quidam itineris ei comites narrarunt & exitus ipse comprobauit) è vestigio Ratisbonam profectus est. Quò quum peruenisset, ac tempus Imperatorem conueniendi natus esset, libera oratione ipsum compellauit, ac monuit ut regiones suas falsa religione solueret, ac verum Dei cultum restitueret. Demonstrabat etiam, Principes Germaniæ, qui tum Protestantes dicti sunt, meliorem tueri causam, eorumque de pietate sententiam infinitis partibus rectiorem esse quàm Hispanorum, qui densis ignorantiæ tenebris immersi prorsus ad lumen veritatis cæcutirent. Addebat & alia eodem pertinentia. Imperator patienter quidem ipsum audiuit, & responsum dedit satis placidum, sibi nempe totum negotium cordi esse, idque diligenter curatum iri. Hæc Cæsaris tam lenis responsio non mediocrem Francisco spem attulit: quam licet exempla crudelitatis à Cæsarianis in ea urbe edita facile imminuerant, non tamen animo deiectus est: sed iterum ac tertio Imperatorem adiit, liberè cum illo agens, nec unquam certè asperius vllum à Cæsare responsum accepit. Tandem cum audentior instaret, & iam quartò Cæsarem conuenire vellet, exceptus fuit ab Hispanis, qui (ut sunt impotenti animo) protinus hominem sine vlla causæ disceptatione in Danubium deiecissent, nisi Imperator ipse cauisset ne quatum illi iniuria fieret, atque iuxta leges Imperij iudicandum pronuntiasset. Inclusus itaque in custodiam fuit, donec cum aliis rerum capitalium condemnatis in curru catenis ligatus hac illac non sine suo magno malo circunuectus est, aulam sequens Imperatoris, qui tum in Aphricam contendebat. Vbi in Hispaniam ventum est, confestim ad inquisitores Pintia (quæ vrbs hodie Vallis-oletana dicitur) deportatus est. Ac primum illi Francisco in specum subterraneam abdiderunt, ut ipsum horrore tam diri carceris terrerent. Sæpius quoque illum in publicum produxerunt, vbi palam ipsorum & iniurias & contumelias pati cogebatur. Accesserunt ad hæc mala indocti monachi, qui illi sua importunitate, & qua pollet maximè impudentia assiduè molesti erant, ut si fieri posset, à vera fide deducerent. Sed ille tantis cruciatibus non modò nec victus nec debilitatus fuit, vt contrà multò quàm ante constantior, atque in dies spiritu ferventior euaserit. Nec enim unquam hostibus suis cessit, quin quas illi nugas ad cælum laudibus efferebant, ipse ad inferos usque deprimeret: quæ vero adversarij hæreseos condemnabant, Franciscus vt orthodoxa defenderet. Doctrina autem quam ad extremum usque spiritum palàm atque aperte profitebatur, fuit eiusmodi: nempe, quòd negaret hominem virtute propria vitam æternam consequi, aut bonis operibus salute potiri, aut suo merito iustum aliquem in conspectu Dei stare posse: sed sola Dei misericordia affirmabat salutem mortalibus exhiberi: non ope humana, sed Christi Mediatoris sanguine, quo nos impuros mundauit: cuius denique sacrificio unico & æterno Pater cœlestis nobiscum pacificatus est. Præterea Missæ sacrificium, quo vivis & mortuis ex opere operato, vt loquuntur, remissionem peccatorum acquiri dicunt Papistæ, horrendam abominationem esse dicebat. Consessionem verò auricularem ad enumerandam omnium peccatorum seriem institutam, Satisfactionem, Purgatorium papisticum, Indulgentias, Sanctorum invocationem, Imaginum adorationem, meras in Deum unum esse blasphemias: manifestam quoque profanationem sanguinis Domini nostri Iesu Christi fieri in illis Papæ præstigijs contendebat atque asseuerabat.
units.tr: San-romanus received this kindly admonition of his friend without objection, and promised that, although he had been rather too heated at the first onset against the monks, he would afterwards act everywhere more carefully and considerately. But he did not keep his promise. For after he had left Dryander (as some fellow travellers on the journey reported, and the outcome itself confirmed), he set off at once for Regensburg. When he arrived there, and the time came to meet the Emperor, he addressed him in frank speech and admonished him to free his lands from false religion and restore the true worship of God. He also showed that the princes of Germany, who were then called Protestants, defended the better cause, and that their judgment on piety was infinitely more correct than that of the Spaniards, who, sunk in the thick darkness of ignorance, were utterly blind to the light of truth. He added other things to the same effect. The Emperor indeed heard him patiently and gave a fairly mild reply: namely, that the whole matter lay close to his heart and would be carefully attended to. This gentle answer of the Emperor brought Francis no small hope; and although the examples of cruelty committed by the Imperialists in that city had easily diminished it, he was not cast down in spirit, but approached the Emperor a second and a third time, speaking freely with him, and never certainly received a harsher answer from the Emperor. At last, as he grew bolder and wished to meet the Emperor a fourth time, he was seized by the Spaniards, who (being men of unbridled temper) would at once have thrown the man into the Danube without any hearing of the case, had the Emperor himself not taken care that no wrong be done to him, and declared that he must be judged according to the laws of the Empire. Thus he was put into custody, until, bound in chains in a cart with other men condemned for capital crimes, he was carried hither and thither, not without great suffering of his own, following the Emperor's court, which was then heading for Africa. When they came to Spain, he was at once brought before the Inquisitors at Pintia (which today is called Vallis-oletana). And first they shut Francis up in an underground cell, so as to terrify him with the horror of such a dreadful prison. They also often brought him out in public, where he was forced to suffer openly their insults and abuse. To these evils were added ignorant monks, who harassed him continually with their importunity and with the impudence in which they especially excel, so that, if possible, they might lead him away from the true faith. But he was not only not conquered nor weakened by such torments, but on the contrary became far more steadfast than before, and day by day more fervent in spirit. For he never yielded to his enemies, but on the contrary, whatever trifles they extolled to the heavens with praise, he cast down to the depths, and whatever things the adversaries condemned as heresy, Francis defended as orthodox.
