The doctrine which he openly and plainly professed to his last breath was of this kind: namely, that he denied that a man attains eternal life by his own virtue, or obtains salvation by good works, or can stand as righteous in the sight of God by his own merit; but he affirmed that salvation is offered to mortals by the mercy of God alone, not by human help, but by the blood of Christ the Mediator, by which he cleansed us who were impure; and finally, that the heavenly Father has been reconciled to us through his one and eternal sacrifice. Moreover, he said that the sacrifice of the Mass, by which the Papists say that remission of sins is obtained for the living and the dead ex opere operato, as they put it, was a horrible abomination. He maintained and asserted that auricular confession, instituted for enumerating the whole series of sins, satisfaction, the Papist purgatory, indulgences, the invocation of saints, and the adoration of images were nothing but blasphemies against the one God, and that a manifest profanation of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ was made by those tricks of the Pope.

units.la: Inquisitores autem cùm viderent hominem nulla ratione de gradu, quod aiunt, deiici posse, sententiam ipsi publicè tulerunt, vt vivus pro hæretico obstinato atque in sua opinione obfirmato combureretur. Plures verò qui huic tam tristi spectaculo aderant, testati sunt quemadmodum alij scelerum admissorum rei simul cum ipso in theatrum ad populum producti fuerint, quibus dimissis in ipsum solum ignis supplicium constitutum sit. Hic igitur solus Euangelij causa populo exosus, ad locum supplicij extra urbem ducitur, coronam chartaceam in capite gerens, atris cacodæmonum figuris undique pictam. Portam urbis egressi quum venissent ad quandam ligneam crucem iuxta iter, vt mos est in Papatu, erectam: ibi Franciscũ vt crucè hanc adoraret cogere volebant. Verùm Franciscus nullo pacto induci potuit vt id faceret: quin prompto atque intrepido animo respondit, Christianos non adorare lignum: se verò Christo nomen dedisse, Deiqué opem intus sentire, quem corde suo summa cum reuerentia adoraret. proinde urgebat inquisitores ut pergerent ad locum poenae destinatum. Magnus tum populi clamor ortus est, quod ligneæ cruci nullum exhibuisset honorem, atque ut proclives sunt ad mendacia idololatrae, cruci diuinitatem repente affinxerunt, quod se ab haeretico adorari passa non esset. deinde quasi nescio quod in ea miraculum diuinitus apparuisset, strictis turba gladiis certatim accurrens crucem in frusta iecerunt, adeo ut se quisque beatum iudicaret, qui particulam eius sacri ligni auferret.
units.tr: The Inquisitors, however, seeing that the man could not be moved from his position by any reasoning, as they say, publicly pronounced sentence against him, that he be burned alive as an obstinate heretic, fixed in his opinion. Many who were present at this sad spectacle testified how other men, guilty of crimes, were led out before the people in the theatre together with him, and then, when they were dismissed, the punishment of fire was reserved for him alone. So he, hated by the people for the sake of the Gospel alone, was led outside the city to the place of execution, wearing a paper crown on his head, painted all over with black figures of demons. When they had come out of the city gate to a wooden cross erected beside the road, as is the custom in Papistry, they wished to compel Francis to adore this cross. But Francis could by no means be brought to do so; on the contrary, with a ready and fearless spirit he replied that Christians do not adore wood; he had given his name to Christ, and felt God's help within, whom he adored in his heart with the greatest reverence. Therefore he urged the Inquisitors to proceed to the place appointed for punishment. Then a great clamour of the people arose, because he had shown no honour to the wooden cross; and, as idolaters are prone to lies, they at once attributed divinity to the cross, because it had not suffered itself to be adored by a heretic. Then, as if some miracle had appeared in it by divine power, the crowd, drawing their swords, ran eagerly and broke the cross into pieces, so that each man thought himself blessed who could snatch away a little fragment of that sacred wood.

units.la: Caeterum in ipso supplicij loco Franciscus cum esset, nec desisterent ipsum monachi solicitare ad palinodiam, praesenti animo rogauit eos ut mox sententiam executioni mandarent, ne & tempus perderent, & operam uociferando luderent. Protinus itaque Franciscus in lignorum struem impositò[?] ignis undique accenditur, utque flammam sentire coepit, ceruicem nonnihil crexit, fumo fortasse aut alia re praepeditus. Quo viso inquisitores raptum ab ipsa struc attolli iubent, sperantes ipsum doctrinam quam fuerat professus reuocare velle. Franciscus ita ab igne sublatus, Quaenam, inquit, vos modo dementia cepit, mutedtis[?] ne magno meo bono? Aduersarij tum spe sua frustrati, in mediam flammam iterum coniici iusserunt, a qua dicto citius consumptus fuit.
units.tr: Moreover, when Francis was at the very place of execution, and the monks did not cease to urge him to recant, with a ready mind he asked them to carry out the sentence at once, so that they would not waste time and labour in shouting uselessly. Straightway, therefore, Francis was placed upon the pile of wood, and the fire was lit on all sides. As soon as he began to feel the flame, he raised his neck somewhat, perhaps hindered by the smoke or something else. Seeing this, the Inquisitors ordered him to be snatched from the pile and lifted up, hoping that he would wish to retract the doctrine which he had professed. Thus taken from the fire, Francis said: "What madness has now seized you, that you wish to change this to my great good?" The adversaries, then frustrated in their hope, ordered him to be thrown back into the middle of the flame, and he was consumed sooner than the word was spoken.

units.la: Post mortem autem huius Martyris, inquisitores publicè affirmabant eum inferorum cruciatibus addictum, ac propterea neutiquam fas esse ulli pro eo orare: quinimo haereticos eos censebant qui de eius exitio dubitarent. monachi etiam sequebantur opinionem inquisitorum, dicentes, sanctos patres non posse errare, quia qui secus faceret, directè ut loquuntur, in decreta ecclesiae peccaret, quae rata haberi in caelo perinde atque in terra necesse sit. Fuerunt tamen aliquot satellites & μαπφύλακες[?] Imperatoris, qui Francisci cineres collegerunt. quin legatus ipse Regis Angliae, qui tum aderat, curauit sibi afferri particulam ossium eius quae vere Christi martyrem esse cognouerat. Sed res istorum adeo teste geri non potuit, quin ea ad aures inquisitorum atque ipsius Imperatoris peruenerit, cuius mandato satellites in carcerem inclusi fuerunt: Legatus vero Regis Angliae ad tempus ab aula recedere coactus fuit. Habes historiam, partim ut [illegible, ~4 letters] & oculati testes memoriae tradiderunt, partim ut pii homines ab aliis, qui viderant, accepta fideliter narrarunt.
units.tr: After this martyr's death, the inquisitors publicly declared that he had been consigned to the torments of hell, and that therefore it was in no way right for anyone to pray for him. Indeed, they counted as heretics those who doubted his damnation. The monks also followed the opinion of the inquisitors, saying that the holy Fathers could not err, since whoever thought otherwise would sin directly, as they put it, against the decrees of the Church, which must necessarily be held valid in heaven just as on earth. Nevertheless, some of the Emperor's attendants and bodyguards gathered Francis's ashes. Indeed, the English king's envoy, who was present at that time, took care to have a small piece of his bones brought to him, because he had recognised him as a true martyr of Christ. But these men's actions could not be carried out so secretly that they did not reach the ears of the inquisitors and of the Emperor himself. By his order the attendants were shut up in prison, and the envoy of the King of England was forced to withdraw from the court for a time. You have a history, partly as eyewitnesses and those who saw it have handed it down to memory, and partly as godly men faithfully related what they received from others who had seen it.

units.la: ROCHVS Statuarius apud Hispanos exustus.
units.tr: ROCHVS, a statuary, burned in Spain.

units.la: Rarum & memorabile exemplum inquisitionis Hispanicensis.
units.tr: A rare and memorable example of the Spanish inquisition.

units.la: T [?]inquisitionis Hispanicae horror, ac furor potiꝰ omnibus notior at, egregiū hic ponemus[?] exemplum summae saeuitiae, quam inquitores[?] Hispani exercuerunt in quendam nomine Rochum, natione Brabantum, eximiū in fingĕdis statuis ac signis artificem, hominem pietate & morum integritate insignem. Is quum anno M.D.XLV. in maritima vrbe San-lucar vocata non procul ab Hispali Beticae regionis commoaretur[?], vt primum veritatis notitiam consequutus est, nō amplius statuis ad idolomaniam conficiendis, sed effingendis signis operam dabat.
units.tr: The horror and fury of the Spanish inquisition is better known to all than anything else. Yet here we will set out an outstanding example of the extreme cruelty which the Spanish inquisitors practised against a certain man named Roch, a Brabanter by birth, an eminent craftsman in carving statues and images, a man distinguished by piety and integrity of life. When in the year 1545, he was living in the seaport called San-lucar, not far from Seville in the region of Baetica, as soon as he came to know the truth, he no longer devoted his labour to making statues for idolatry, but to carving other images.

units.la: Retinebat quidem in sua officina D.Mariae imaginem affabrè sculptā velut artis statuariae specimen. Inquisitor quidam Hispanus quum forte officinam Rochi praeteriret, artificium illius statuae suspiciens, quaesiuit quanti venirēt[?] statuario certum pretium diceti[?], Inquisitor vix dimidium obtulit.
units.tr: He did keep in his workshop an image of the Blessed Virgin Mary, skilfully carved, as a specimen of his art of statuary. A certain Spanish inquisitor, passing by Roch's workshop by chance and admiring the craftsmanship of that statue, asked how much it would sell for. When the sculptor named a fixed price, the inquisitor offered barely half of it.

units.la: Quid, inquit Statuarius, quum tantum laboris & temporis in eius imaginis confectione impenderim, si quanti offers[?] venderem, vix aquae interea epotae mihi pretium persoluerētur. Inquisitor verò acrius instabat vt eo oblato pretio suam faceret. Tua erit, inquit, Rochus, siquidem iustam laboris mercedem atque æstimationem dederis, alioquin illam potius confringerem. Cui inquisitor, Eia confringe sodes.
units.tr: "What," said the statuary, "since I have spent so much labour and time on making this image, if I sold it for what you offer, I would scarcely be paid enough to buy water to drink in the meantime." The inquisitor, however, pressed harder, so that he might have it for the price offered. "It will be yours, Roch," he said, "if you give me a just reward and valuation for my labour; otherwise I would rather smash it." To which the inquisitor replied, "Well then, smash it, if you please."

units.la: Protinus alter arreptum fabrile instrumentum in faciem imaginis impegit, quam strictim attingens nonnihil allisit. Inquisitor & caelum & terram indamans tanquam gravissimo scelere admisso iussit mox Rochum abripi atque in carcerem deduci. Quid, vicissim acclamabat ille, an non pro meo arbitratu fingere ac refingere opus mearum manuum possum? haud recte mihi factum videbatur, quid ad vos attinet? Sed nihil haec verba profuerunt: insania etenim correptis carnificibus isthæc dicebantur. Tribus itaque post diebus sententia capitis illi pronunciata fuit, Quia scilicet Divam Virginē laesisset, crimen divinae maiestatis laesae in summa incurrisse, atque ob id ignis supplicio plectendum condemnari & executoribus committi. Ignem itaque subiturus Rochus sublata voce rogauit, an in multitudine quae circumstabat quisquam Flander adesset. Quidam responderunt adesse Flandros, ac duas nauēs Flandricas in portu San-lucareo esse, quæ ventum secundum ad remeandum in Flandriam expectarent. Velim, ait Rochus, rogatum eorum aliquem, vt patri meo qui Antuerpiæ habitat, significet me in hac vrbe exustum esse ob eam causam, quam omnes audistis. Hic deinde præfenti animo Dominum precatus, intrepidè mortem oppetijt, habuitque hunc vitæ exitum vir pius in Hispanienfi terra. Ac ne quis in tam raro ac inaudito crudelitatis Hispanicæ exemplo de fide historiæ dubitet, vir quidam grauis ac spectatæ fidei, natione Hispanus, diligenti inquisitione Antuerpiæ habita, atque indicio eorum qui sunt artis statuariæ parentes Rochi reperit, qui rem totam vt à nobis prædicta est, confirmarunt ac ipsius Rochi patrem paulò post acceptu de tam crudeli morte filij nuncium, dolore interiisse..
units.tr: At once the other seized a metal tool and struck it against the face of the image, touching it lightly yet damaging it somewhat. The inquisitor, appealing to heaven and earth as if a most grievous crime had been committed, ordered Roch to be seized immediately and taken to prison. "What," Roch cried out in reply, "may I not shape and reshape the work of my own hands as I see fit? It did not seem to me that I had done wrong; what is it to you?" But these words did him no good, for they were spoken to executioners blinded by madness. So three days later the sentence of death was pronounced upon him: because he had wounded the Blessed Virgin, he had incurred the guilt of high treason against the divine majesty, and was therefore condemned to the punishment of fire and handed over to the executioners. About to undergo the fire, Roch asked in a raised voice whether any Fleming was present in the crowd standing around. Some replied that Flemings were there, and that two Flemish ships were in the harbour of San-lucar, waiting for a fair wind to sail back to Flanders. "I would like," said Roch, "one of you to ask someone to tell my father, who lives at Antwerp, that I was burned in this town for the reason you have all heard." Then, having commended himself to the Lord with a calm mind, he met death fearlessly, and this godly man ended his life in the Spanish land. And so that no one may doubt the history of so rare and unheard-of an example of Spanish cruelty, a certain serious man of proven faith, a Spaniard by birth, made a careful inquiry at Antwerp and, through information from those who are the parents of the statuary art, found Roch's people. They confirmed the whole matter just as we have related it, and Roch's father, shortly after receiving word of his son's cruel death, died of grief.

units.la: IOANNES DIAZIVS.
units.tr: JOHN DIAZIUS.

units.la: Historia memoranda de morte Ioannis Diazii Hispani quem ipsius frater germanus Alphōfus Diazius, exemplum sequutus primi parricidæ Cain, velut alterum Abelem nefarie interfecit.
units.tr: A memorable account of the death of John Diazius, a Spaniard, whom his own full brother Alphonsus Diazius, imitating the first murderer Cain, wickedly slew as though he were a second Abel.

units.la: IOANNES Diazius, natus in vrbe quæ vulgò Cuença dicitur, quæ est sedes Episcopalis in ea parte vlterioris Hispaniæ sita, quæ finitima est Beticæ regioni, paulò supra fines regni Toletani: cum tredecim totos annos, aut eo amplius Lutetiæ vixisset, Geneuam tandem se contulit, vt eius ecclesiæ statum videret, quam à viro doctissimo Ioanne Caluino, qui officio pastoris in ea ecclesia fungitur, ab inquinamentis idololatriæ paulò ante in Dei ecclesiam inuectæ, sciebat esse repurgatam, suoque pristino, hoc est Apostolico nitori restitutam. Mansit in ea vrbe ad menses aliquot, vt ecclesiæ ac reipublicæ formam consideraret: quo tempore cum ipso Caluino, atque alijs ecclesiæ Geneuensis ministris, suam de singulis Christianæ religionis articulis sententiam communicauit, quorum iudicio Ioannis Diazij doctrinam atque integritatem constat fuisse approbatissimam. Deinde & reliquas bene constitutas in Germania ecclesias videre voluit, in quibus sciebat sonare veram Euangelij vocem, vt regionem perlustraret, mores hominū cognosceret, & cum viris doctis, cum de omni doctrina, tum præcipuè de religione conferret. Prosectus igitur Geneua, Basileam venit, vbi paucis diebus commoratus, postquam fideles Christi ministros, qui scholæ & ecclesiæ isthic præsunt cōuenisset, ac omnes peramanter salutasset, Argetina cogitat, quia in vrbe, quoniam prouectu doctissimorum hominum eam florere arbitrabatur, firmiorem ibi sedem figere constituerat: tantisper sane, donec ad alium vtiliorem locum Dominus ipsum euocasset. Vixit ergo Argentinae partem superioris ætatis vsque ad ipsam [illegible, ~5 letters] brumalem, omnibus interim gratus, qui eum propter insignem integritatem ac virtutem, tanquam verum singuli fratrem complectebatur.
units.tr: John Diazius was born in the city commonly called Cuenca, the episcopal see in that part of Further Spain which borders the region of Baetica, a little north of the boundaries of the kingdom of Toledo. After he had lived at Paris for thirteen full years or more, he finally went to Geneva to see the condition of that church. He knew it had been cleansed by the very learned John Calvin, who serves as minister in that church, from the pollutions of idolatry that had lately been introduced into the Church of God, and restored to its former brightness, that is, its apostolic purity. He stayed in that city for some months to observe the order of the church and the commonwealth. During this time he shared his opinion on each article of the Christian religion with Calvin himself and the other ministers of the Geneva church, and it is well established that by their judgment John Diazius's teaching and integrity were most highly approved. Then he wished to see the other well-ordered churches in Germany, in which he knew the true voice of the Gospel was sounding, so that he might travel through the region, learn the manners of the people, and confer with learned men on every kind of learning, but above all on religion. So he set out from Geneva and came to Basel. After staying there a few days, and having met the faithful ministers of Christ who preside over the school and church there, and greeted them all very warmly, he thought of going to Strasbourg. He had decided to establish a more permanent home there, since he judged that city to be flourishing through the progress of very learned men. He meant this only for the time being, until the Lord should call him to some more useful place. So he lived at Strasbourg for the greater part of his later life, until the very beginning of winter, being welcome to everyone, who embraced him as a true brother for his remarkable integrity and virtue.

units.la: Imprimis autem clarissimo viro, domino Martino Bucero charissimus fuit, cuius ipse consuetudine propter excellentem hominis doctrinam familiariter vtebatur. Denique cum in fine pene superioris anni, colloquium de religione a Cæsarea maiestate indiceretur Ratisbonæ celebrandum, visum est senatui populoque Argentinensi, Ioannem quoque Diazium publico ciuitatis nomine mittere, vt cuius fidem ac integritatem probatam satis atque spectatam haberent, eiusdem quoque opera in hoc publico negotio vterentur. Mittitur ergo Ioannes Diazius Ratisbonam, vna cum domino Bucero, addito insuper publicæ fidei commeatu, ne quisquam eorum qui Pontificiam dignitatem defendunt, ac veritati doctrinæ cælestis aduersantur, temere auderet publica authoritate missum violare.
units.tr: Above all, he was very dear to the most distinguished man, Master Martin Bucer, whose company he enjoyed on close terms because of the man's outstanding learning. Finally, when at the end of almost the previous year a colloquy on religion was announced by His Imperial Majesty to be held at Regensburg, the senate and people of Strasbourg thought fit to send John Diazius as well, in the public name of the city, since they regarded his faith and integrity as proven and tried, and wished to use his services in this public business too. So John Diazius was sent to Regensburg together with Master Bucer, and in addition was given a safe-conduct under public faith, so that none of those who defend the Papal dignity and oppose the truth of heavenly doctrine would presume to harm a man sent with public authority.

units.la: Posteaquàm Ratisbonam ventum est, Diazius conuenit Petrum de Maluenda Hispanū, qui aduersæ partis, videlicet idolomaniæ Pontificis fuit nominatus colloquutor ac defensor. Ille Maluenda cum primum illum vidit, quem aliqui nouerat Lutetiæ familiariter, non secus admiratus est quàm si rem aliquam prodigiosam sibi coram oculis propositam videret. Tandem vbi multis signis declarasset admirationem, quam ex eo inopinato conspectu concepisset, aggreditur hominem, dixitque videri sibi somnium videre, non re ipsa cum præsentem intueri, præsertim in Germania, & quidem in societate Protestantum, qui magis gloriaturi essent si vnum Hispanum in suam sententiam possent pertrahere, quàm si decem millia Germanorum, aut innumeros aliarum gentum homines converterent. Rogat Diazium, quandiu in Germania vixisset: quo consilio in eam regionem venisset: an Buceri doctrinam & aliorum Germanorum approbaret. Respondet placidè ac moderatè Diazius, id quod res erat, se quidem habitasse in Germania sex fermè menses, nec alio consilio eam profectionem suscepisse, quàm vt regionem perlustraret, instauratam religionis doctrinam probè cognosceret, & cum viris doctis suam de religione sententiam conferret. Ad hæc Maluenda, vultu ad superstitiosam quandam admirationem composito, Profectò (inquit) sex menses in Germania, non menses tantùm, sed integri anni, aut certè totidem secula videri possent homini pio: vsquèadeò in Germania viuere miserum est ei, qui vnitatem ecclesiæ Romanæ amat, authoritatémque veretur.
units.tr: When they had arrived at Regensburg, Diazius met Pedro de Maluenda, a Spaniard, who had been named the colloquist and defender of the opposing side, that is, of the idolatry of the Pope. When Maluenda first saw him, whom he had known well at Paris, he was no less astonished than if he were looking at some monstrous thing set before his eyes. At last, having shown by many signs the amazement he had felt at this unexpected sight, he addressed the man and said that he seemed to be dreaming, not seeing him actually present, especially in Germany and in the company of Protestants, who would glory more if they could draw one Spaniard to their opinion than if they converted ten thousand Germans or countless men of other nations. He asked Diazius how long he had lived in Germany, what plan had brought him to that region, and whether he approved the teaching of Bucer and the other Germans. Diazius answered calmly and moderately, and as the truth was, that he had indeed lived in Germany for about six months, and had undertaken the journey for no other purpose than to travel through the region, to learn well the restored doctrine of religion, and to confer his own opinion on religion with learned men. To this Maluenda, composing his face into a kind of superstitious wonder, said: "Truly, six months in Germany, not merely months but whole years, or certainly as many ages, must seem long to a pious man. Living in Germany is wretched indeed for one who loves the unity of the Roman Church and reveres its authority."

units.la: Post hanc primam collocutionem, bis eum conuenit solus Diazius, & multa cum ipso Maluenda de religione contulit. Postremo colloquio rogauit Diazium Maluenda, cuius rei gratia venisset Ratisbonā. Diazius respondit, publico se Argentinensium nomine esse missum, vt hoc publico in colloquio, etiam suas preces cum ecclesiæ Christi precibus coiungeret, & conciliationem articulorum, qui hodie in disceptatione versantur, pro virili promoueret. Frustra, inquit Maluenda, huc venisti. nam in hoc toto colloquio nihil omnino constituetur. quòd si tuam operam ad publicam vtilitatem conferre volebas, ad concilium quod Papa instituit Tridenti, erat tibi proficiscendum: vbi conuenient Catholici præsules, ac in eo celebrando & perficiendo summo studio elaborabunt. Quum igitur audisset Maluendam diserte profitentem, nihil omnino fieri debere in colloquio Ratisbonensi, facilè intellexit omnia Pontificiorum consilia esse fraudulenta, à quibus (incolumi religionis integritate) nulla esset speranda concordia. Proinde valedixit Maluendæ, neque fuit illi animus posthac eum amplius conueniendi.
units.tr: After this first conversation, Diazius met Maluenda alone twice more, and discussed many matters of religion with him. At their last meeting, Maluenda asked Diazius for what purpose he had come to Regensburg. Diazius replied that he had been sent by the public authority of Strasbourg, so that in this public colloquy he might join his prayers to the prayers of Christ's Church, and might promote, as far as he could, the reconciliation of the articles that are today in dispute. "You have come here in vain," said Maluenda, "for nothing at all will be settled in this whole colloquy. But if you wished to contribute your effort to the public good, you should have set out for the council that the Pope has established at Trent, where the Catholic prelates will assemble and labour with the greatest zeal to hold and complete it." When Diazius heard Maluenda openly declare that nothing at all ought to be done at the Regensburg colloquy, he readily understood that all the plans of the Papists were fraudulent, and that from them, while the integrity of religion remained intact, no agreement could be hoped for. Therefore he bade Maluenda farewell, and afterwards had no inclination to meet him again.

units.la: Post id colloquium Diazius non amplius conuenit Maluendam. sed ille exasperatus libertate Diazij, ab eo tempore cœpit insidias struere, fraudes nectere, atque in hoc prorsus incumbere vt hominem innocentissimum perderet. Quod aperta vi aut iustæ causæ prætextu facere non poterat, clandestinis consiliis, & impudenter à se confictis mendaciis, negotium aggreditur. Scripsit literas in aulâ Imperatoris ad monachum Dominicanum, qui ab auribus erat Cæsari, in quibus finificabat esse Ratisbonae Ioannem Diazium Hispanum, quem cùm ipse olim Lutetiae nouisset studiosum catholicae fidei, & obsequentem ecclesiae filium (ecclesiam isti appellant, quam ex Romanis columnis flagitiosorum hominum ipsi fabricarunt) nunc Ratisbonae videret acrem defensorem partium Protestantium, qui se iam inimicum ecclesiae catholicae, Lutheranorum amicum ac propugnatorem publica professione declarârit. Præterea incendit multis etiam falsis delationibus (ut euentus rerum postea ostendit) animum peruersi proditoris alioqui ardentem, atque etiam inflammatum, & propria sua malitia & odio æternæ Dei veritatis, quam neque ipse nouerat, neque audire sustinebat. Urget insuper atque obtestatur, ut tantum malum violento aliquo remedio conetur auertere. futurum enim augurabatur, si crescéret malū quod iam tum in herba esse putabat, ut Hispania tandem aperiret oculos, videret suam miseriam & cæcitatem, videret seruitutem ac tyrannidem, videret ignorationem cum magna superbia & superstitione coniunctam.
units.tr: After that colloquy Diazius did not meet Maluenda again. But Maluenda, exasperated by Diazius's freedom, from that time began to lay snares, to weave deceptions, and to devote himself entirely to ruining this most innocent man. What he could not do by open force or under the pretext of a just cause, he undertook by secret schemes and by lies shamelessly invented by himself. He wrote a letter at the Emperor's court to a Dominican friar who was the Emperor's confessor, in which he asserted that John Diazius, a Spaniard, was at Regensburg. He said that he had once known him at Paris as a zealous adherent of the Catholic faith and an obedient son of the Church (they call it the Church, which those men have built from the Roman pillars of wicked people), but that now at Regensburg he saw him an keen defender of the Protestant party, who had already openly declared himself an enemy of the Catholic Church and a friend and champion of the Lutherans. Besides, he inflamed, with many false accusations (as the outcome of events later showed), the mind of a perverse traitor that was already burning and fired up by his own malice and by hatred of the eternal truth of God, which he neither knew nor could bear to hear. He further urged and entreated that they should try to turn away so great an evil by some violent remedy. For he predicted that if the evil, which he already thought was in its first shoot, were to grow, Spain would at last open its eyes, see its misery and blindness, see its slavery and tyranny, and see its ignorance joined with great pride and superstition.

units.la: Lectis à monacho Confessionario literis, quem ille affectum induerit, quid in ea causa faciendum putarit, affirmare non possumus. Si quid autem licet ex præteritis eius factis æstimare, verisimile est, pro sua consuetudine nihil leue, nihil vulgare ab homine nefario fuisse excogitatum.
units.tr: What mood the confessor was in when he had read the letters, and what he thought should be done in the matter, we cannot affirm. But if one may judge anything from his past deeds, it is likely that, as is his custom, the wicked man devised nothing mild or ordinary.

units.la: Cæterum quum Maluenda expectaret Confessionarium, diutius opinione sua cunctantem, videretque Ioannem Diazium Ratisbonae, qui in officio suo sedulam ac diligentem nauaret operam: non contentus primis literis, secundas etiam, sed multo acerbiores ad Confessionarium scribit. Rem eandem inculcat, acriter contendit atq; obtestatur, ut aliquam inueniat viam, qua hunc hominem, qui ipsorum consilia & actiones aliquando poterit euertere, de medio tollat, priusquam vel ipse vires sumat, vel in negotio iam tū incœpto ulterius progrediatur. Quum forte has literas Maluendae Confessionarius acciperet, aderat Bruxellis legenti quidam Hispanus nomine Marquina, qui in publicis quibusdam negotiis Romæ versabatur, unde paulo ante in aulam Imperatoris venerat. Iste Marquina, qui olim familiariter nouerat Diazium, cum audiret nunc quæ de ipso à Maluenda scriberentur, grauiter ac permolestè tulit amici quem vnicè diligebat, famam & existimationem notari: præsertim hæreseos crimine: quod vt est grauissimum, ita etiam omnibus bonis est (sicut esse debet) odiosissimum. Et quia eum familiariter nouerat, sciebátque hominem esse integerrimæ vitæ ac virtutis approbatissimæ, cœpit eum excusare apud Confessionarium, quàm id facere potuit diligenter. Dicit clarè, non esse adhibendam fidem verbis Maluendæ, qui vel aliquo priuato odio, vel alia quacunque occasione inductus, limites in ea parte veritatis transiliret: credendúmque potius esse publico præstantissimorum hominum testimonio, qui Ioannis Diazij virtutem atque integritatem semper approbarunt. Proinde orabat Confessionarium vt eam rem apud se occultam retineret, suámq; ipse suspenderet sententiam, tantisper sanè, donec aliquid certius audiretur. Fertur dixisse Confessionarius, Si Ioannes Diazius maneat apud hæreticos, dabit ecclesiæ magnum malū: ideóq; modis omnibus prospiciendum est, vt quacunque ratione vel conuertatur, vel tollatur.
units.tr: Meanwhile Maluenda, waiting for the confessor, who delayed longer than he expected, and seeing that John Diazius at Regensburg was diligently and carefully performing his duty, was not content with his first letters, and wrote a second letter to the confessor, much harsher than the first. He pressed the same matter, argued fiercely, and entreated him to find some way of removing from the world this man, who might one day overturn their plans and actions, before he gained strength himself or advanced further in the business already begun. As it happened, while the confessor was reading these letters of Maluenda, a certain Spaniard named Marquina was present at Brussels; he had been engaged in certain public affairs at Rome, from which he had lately come to the Emperor's court. This Marquina, who had known Diazius intimately for some time, when he heard what was being written about him by Maluenda, took it very much amiss, and grievously resented that the reputation and standing of a friend whom he dearly loved were being attacked, especially with the charge of heresy, which is as grave as it is hateful to all good people, as it ought to be. Because he knew the man well, and knew him to be of most upright life and of proven virtue, he began to excuse him to the confessor as carefully as he could. He said plainly that no faith should be given to the words of Maluenda, who, moved either by some private hatred or by some other occasion, overstepped the bounds of truth on this point; rather, credence should be given to the public testimony of the most distinguished men, who had always approved the virtue and integrity of John Diazius. Accordingly he begged the confessor to keep the matter secret and to suspend his judgment, at least for the time being, until something more certain should be heard. The confessor is reported to have said: "If John Diazius remains among the heretics, he will do great harm to the Church; therefore every means must be taken to ensure that he is either converted or removed, by whatever method."

units.la: Paulò post celeri cursu profectus Romam ipse Marquina, rem vniuersam significauit fratri Ioannis, Alphonso Diazio, qui in controuersiis iudicij Rotæ longo tempore in ea vrbe se exercuit, quale inter se cōsilium iniuerint & Marquina & Alphonsus frater Ioannis, nondum plane constat, nec rectè affirmari potest: quanuis ex eo, quod postea sequutum est, non difficulter licebit æstimare. Omnino aliquid magni facinoris iam tum fuit inter eos constitutum, vt scelerata eorum flagitia postea declararunt. Hæc omnia, vt antea gesta sunt, & hic à nobis narrata, ipse Alphonsus Diazius suo fratri ordine, vt dictum est, Neoburgi narrauit.
units.tr: Shortly afterwards Marquina himself set out for Rome at full speed and reported the whole affair to John's brother, Alphonso Diazius, who had for a long time been active in that city in the disputed cases of the Rota. What plan Marquina and Alphonso, John's brother, agreed upon between themselves is not yet fully clear, nor can it be stated with certainty; yet from what followed afterwards it will not be hard to guess. Certainly some great crime was already then being planned between them, as their wicked deeds later revealed. All these things, as they happened before and as we have narrated them here, Alphonso Diazius himself afterwards related to his brother at Neuburg, in the order described.

units.la: Interea temporis Ratisbonense colloquium, satis acriter initio incœptum, abrumpitur, & subitò quasi mutata colloquutorum voluntate in altum silentium conuertitur. Causam huic silentio præbuerunt aduersarij veritatis nouo atque inaudito commento, quod ipsi in suo cerebro vel ad fraudes suas occultandas, vel ad veritatem opprimendam, non minus callidè quàm impiè excogitarunt. Fingunt ab Imperatore missas literas, quibus iubentur vniuersam de religione disputationem clandestinis susurrationibus transfigere. Id autem quò magis[?] ratum ac firmum esset iuxta eorum voluntatem, iubent coln cutores utriusque partis iureiurando adstringi, ne quid eorum quae in colloquio tractarentur, vel suis principibus, vel vlli mortalium significarent. Eam conditionem, quoniam absurda nimis erat, & unquam antehac in libero colloquio vel audita vel propositá, nostri homines accipere noluerunt. quasi vero disputatio de articulis Christianae doctrinae sint Eleusinia sacra, de quibus vel vnum verum coram hominibus proferre nefas esse videatur. Sed ita omnino natura comparatum esse videmus, vt mens sibi male conscia, & lucem vereatur & iudicia bonorum hominum pertimescat.
units.tr: Meanwhile the Colloquy of Regensburg, which had begun quite sharply, was broken off, and suddenly, as if the wills of the speakers had changed, it gave way to deep silence. The adversaries of the truth provided the cause of this silence with a new and unheard-of invention, which they devised no less cunningly than impiously, either to conceal their frauds or to suppress the truth. They feign letters sent by the Emperor, ordering that the whole dispute about religion be carried on through secret whisperings. To make this more firmly settled according to their wishes, they ordered the speakers of each side to be bound by oath not to disclose anything of what was treated in the colloquy, either to their princes or to any mortal. Our men refused to accept that condition, since it was absurd beyond measure and had never before been heard of or proposed in a free colloquy, as if a disputation about the articles of Christian doctrine were the Eleusinian rites, about which it seems wicked to bring forward even one true word before men. But we see that nature is so constituted that a conscience aware of its wrong fears the light and dreads the judgments of good men.

units.la: Suspensis hunc ad modum negotijs colloquij in urbe Ratisbona, propter eam causam quam modo narravimus, profectus est Ioannes Diazius Neoburgum, oppidum illustrissimi principis Ottonis Henrici Palatini, ad ripam Danubij situm, ut praeesset editioni cuiusdam libri doctissimi viri Martini Buceri, qui tum in ea urbe imprimebatur.
units.tr: With the negotiations of the colloquy suspended in the city of Regensburg for the reason we have just described, John Diazius set out for Neuburg, a town of the most illustrious prince Otto Henry, Count Palatine, situated on the bank of the Danube, to oversee the printing of a certain book by the most learned man Martin Bucer, which was then being printed in that town.

units.la: Dum haec aguntur in Germania, non est otiosus Alphonsus frater Ioannis, qui erat Romae. Etenim cum is admonitus esset a Marquina de literis quas Maluenda scripserat ad Caesaris Confessionarium, sine mora in Germaniam profectionem adornauit, ut quibuscunque posset modis fratrem ab instituto verae religionis cursu conaretur revocare. Adducit unâ secum nebulonem quendam sicarium, qui ut postea compertum est, Romae fuerat publicus carnifex: cuius atque tertij cuiusdam sodalitio comitatus, celeri cursu equorum Augustam peruenit. Inde Ratisbonam se contulit unâ cum suo carnifice, ubi fratrem inueniri posse arbitrabatur. Ratisbonae primum conuenit Maluendam apud quem sui pectoris consilia deposuit: a quo vicissim rationem vel decapiendi vel convertendi fratrem postulauit. Quodnam illi consilium dederit Maluenda, nondum plane constat, paulo post fortasse fiet manifestius. Fertur dixisse Hispano cuidam, Utinam veniat illa dies, in quo ego corpus Ioannis Diazij combustum videre possim, ut vel eo supplicio extincto corpore, melius animae consultum videatur. Quod si verum est, ut certe verisimile videtur, satis declarauit Maluenda Sorbonicus doctor ista una, non humana sed plusquam ferina & prorsus diabolica sua voce, se æternæ iræ Dei reum esse, in quem tota culpa istius innocentis sanguinis effusi, tanquam in verum parricidam, transferatur. Illud sine controversia in confesso est, inter se constituisse modis omnibus inquirere, ubi gentium Ioannes Diazius posset reperiri. Mittunt ergo quendam Hispanum, qui in sodalitio Maluendæ habitabat, ipsi non absimilem, ut de Diazio ubinam esset interrogaret ab amico quem præ cæteris id scire, ac eius consilia tenere arbitrabantur. narrat venisse quasdam literas magni momenti ex aula Imperatoris ad Diazium, cuius permagni interesset fideliter eas accipere: ac proinde orabat, ut locus in quo esset indicaretur. Respondit ille amicus non plane constare ubi tum ageret Diazius: & tamen si quid ad eum cuperet perferri, se curaturū summo studio ut fideliter ad ipsius manus perferretur. Abiit Hispanus eo quasi responso contentus: sed paulo post revertitur, narrátque esse in diversorio Coronæ quendam virum nobilem, summum amicum Diazij, qui ad eum literas ex aula Imperatoris ab aliis amicis adferebat, in quibus negotium magni momenti contineretur. proinde ipsius nomine perstudiose amicum Diazij orabat, ne grauaretur vel locū ubi Diazius esset indicare, vel eum in hospitio convenire. Ille ut officium præstaret amico, cuius negotia cupiebat diligeter curata, venit cum Hispano ad diversorium, ut quid omnino esset, quod ad Diazium pertineret, propius cognosceret. Ibi invenit quendam Hispanum, ut ex cultu & vultu licuisset æstimare, hominem non vulgarem, qui eum per fidem atque humanitatem, perque omnia sacra & profana impensissime cœpit orare atque obsecrare, ut locum ubi Diazius esset illi indicaret. esse enim magnum negotium, quod cum eo deberet peragere. Nam & literas à summis eius amicis ex aula Imperatoris ad ipsum adferre, & prætercea res cum eo non vulgares debere transfigere, quæ maximè ad utilitatem Ioannis Diazij pertinerent.
units.tr: While these things were going on in Germany, Alphonso, John's brother, who was at Rome, was not idle. For when he had been warned by Marquina about the letters that Maluenda had written to the Emperor's confessor, he at once prepared to travel to Germany, so that by whatever means he could, he might try to call his brother back from the course of the true religion. He brought with him a certain scoundrel and assassin, who, as was later discovered, had been the public executioner at Rome; accompanied by him and a certain third companion, he came swiftly on horseback to Augsburg. From there he went to Regensburg together with his executioner, where he thought his brother could be found. At Regensburg he first met Maluenda, to whom he disclosed the plans of his heart; in turn he asked from him a method either of killing or of converting his brother. What counsel Maluenda gave him is not yet entirely clear; perhaps it will become plainer a little later. It is reported that he said to a certain Spaniard, "I wish that day would come on which I could see the body of John Diazius burned, so that, with the body destroyed by that punishment, the soul might seem better provided for." If this is true, as it certainly seems likely, Maluenda, the Sorbonne doctor, made clear by this one voice, not human but more than savage and altogether diabolical, that he himself is guilty before the eternal wrath of God, upon whom the whole blame for the shedding of this innocent blood should be laid, as upon a true murderer. It is beyond dispute that they agreed between themselves to inquire by every means where in the world John Diazius could be found. They therefore sent a certain Spaniard, who lived in Maluenda's household and resembled him in some respects, to ask about Diazius's whereabouts from a friend whom they believed knew this above others and held his plans. He said that some letters of great importance had come to Diazius from the Emperor's court, and that it greatly mattered that he receive them faithfully; therefore he begged that the place where Diazius was might be pointed out. That friend replied that it was not altogether certain where Diazius was at that time; yet if anything were wished to be delivered to him, he would take the greatest care that it reach his hands faithfully. The Spaniard went away content with that answer, as it seemed, but a little later he returned and reported that there was at the inn of the Crown a certain noble man, a very close friend of Diazius, who was bringing him letters from the Emperor's court sent by other friends, in which a matter of great importance was contained; therefore, on that man's behalf, he earnestly begged the friend of Diazius not to refuse either to point out the place where Diazius was or to meet him at the inn. That friend, in order to do a service to a friend whose affairs he wished carefully attended to, came with the Spaniard to the inn, so that he might learn more closely what the matter was that concerned Diazius. There he found a certain Spaniard who, judging from his dress and face, was no ordinary man, and who began most urgently to implore and beseech him, by faith and courtesy and by all things sacred and profane, to indicate to him the place where Diazius was. For it was, he said, a great business that he had to transact with him: he was bringing letters from his chief friends at the Emperor's court to him, and moreover had to carry out with him matters of no small importance, which pertained most of all to the advantage of John Diazius.

units.la: Hic vero amicus idem pene huic dedit responsum, quod paulo ante famulo dederat: se non prorsus scire ubi esset Diazius, sed tamen ab aliis id velle percontari, à quibus aliquid certi sperabat posse intelligere. Domum is reversus rem omnem cum domino Bucero, cū domino Brentio & cum reliquis colloquutoribus communicavit, & consilium quod in eo negotio sequi deberet, ab eis postulauit. Variæ ibi fuerunt sententiæ, dum alij locum vbi Diazius esset indicandum censent, alij contrà negant: sed vtrinque rationes satis idoneæ ad confirmationem suæ sententiæ afferebant. Denique valuit ea sententia, vt locus indicaretur, qui alioqui liber & securus erat, ne quid propter ignorationem negotij, quod magni momenti dicebatur, aduersus vtilitatem Diazij imprudenter peccaretur. Interea priuatim scriptis literis admonitus fuit Diazius, vt si quod periculum ab eo homine impendere putaret, prudenter sibi ac tempestiuè caueret. Hoc igitur consilio & voluntate indicauit ille amicus Alphonso (qui nondum patefecerat se fratrem esse Ioannis Diazij) eum esse in ciuitate vicina, quæ vulgò dicitur Neoburgum. Egit illi ingentes gratias pro hoc nuntio, & impensè orauit vt cum eo ad amicum veniret: quam ad rem dicebat se habere equum in promptu, & res omnes necessarias. Respondit ille non esse integrum eo tempore Ratisbona discedere: sed tamen promisit se ad Diazium daturum literas, atque ipsi etiam significaturum quo in loco eum posset inuenire. Scripsit ergo literas ad Diazium quas Alphonso dedit, in quibus nihil aliud, quàm quod sine periculo publicum esse poterat, continebatur. Scripsit verò alias quas priuatim tradidit nuntio publico, qui cum Alphonso proficiscebatur: eúmque admonuit, vt eas literas seorsim ac diligenter custodiret, nec alteri quàm ipsi Ioãni Diazio traderet. In his literis copiosè ad eum perscribebat quicquid cum eo viro illi accidisset, simúlque eum admonebat, vt ab eius insidijs, si quas vellet struere, caueret diligenter. Scripsit etiam per eúdem nuntium dominus Bucerus, scripseruntque & alij amici, qui omnes eum diligentissimè de periculis, quæ accidere poterant, admonebát & quomodo ea posset depellere significabant. Ac vt res tota magis careret suspicione, data sunt nuntio acta in colloquio Ratisbonensi ad Secretarium illustrissimi Principis Ottonis perferenda. Addiderunt seorsim pecunias, vt res à nuntio fidelius curaretur, qui alioqui recepit se totum illud negocium curaturum, non solùm libenter, sed etiam valde diligenter. Hoc negotio ita constituto valere iussis nuntio atque etiam Alphonso: ipse rursus Amico fratris agit gratias ingentes pro eo officio, ac simul gratitudinem & benevolentiam integro ac fideli amico dignam, plusquam officiose promittit. Sed priusquam à se dimitteret amicum fratris, denuò coepit obtestari, perque amicitiae fidem & Christianam charitatem adiurare, si Ioannis Diazij dignitatem & existimationem integram atque illibatam cuperet, ne quid omnino earum rerum, quae inter eos essent constitutae, tum ulli morta-lium, tum vero nominatim Maluendae ullo modo significaret. etenim non dubitare eius animum adversus Diazium esse valde infensum, quòd eius consiliis noluisset obtemperare: ac proinde ad utilitatem Diazij omnino pertinere ut ea res, quam apud eum agere volebat, ignorante Maluenda perficeretur. Quid multis? tanta est usus orationis vehementia, tam serio in hoc incubebat, ut nihil eius rei Maluendae indicaretur, quinetiam fidem faceret, nihil ab eo simulatè geri, sed prorsus ex animo loqui. Sed ô facinus infandum perversi proditoris! Nam vix ab eo digressus erat ille amicus, cum ipse ad nuntium venit, eumque omnibus literis & scriptis spoliavit, seq; ad Maluendam cum eis contulit. ibi postea quam omnia perlegissent, atque inter se consilia, haud dubie Cainica, cepissent: omnes epistolas lacerauit, solum scriptum aliorum, quod Secretario principis Ottonis erat tradendum, retinuit: quod alioqui servaturus non erat, nisi ad parandam & conciliandam eius viri amicitiam id sibi pernecessarium fore putasset. Amicis Ioannis Diazij paulò post fuit significatum, Alphonsum apud Maluendam fuisse: & quæ cum nuntio egisset, ipse postea Ioannes Diazius Neoburgi amicis narravit. Cum autem amici Ioan. Diazij intellexissent hanc tam insignem hominis perfidiam, qui tam accuratè fidem atque integritatem simulabat, in suspicionem venerunt omnes, cum aliquod magnum facinus moliri. Proinde rursus per nuntium proprium, Ioannem Diazium adhortati sunt, ut ab insidiis illius hominis omnino sibi cauceret. Tandem proficiscitur Alphonsus Neoburgum, per quem Maluenda scripsit literas ad Ioannem Diazium, quibus eum hortabatur ut fratri recta monenti obtemperaret. Promisit etiam, si cum in Italiam sequi vellet, & Germaniam cum suis Germanis penitus relinquere, ut qui essent corruptores bonorum ingeniorum (istis enim verbis in suis literis utebatur) se apud Cæsaris Confessionarium curaturum, ut ea mala, quae de ipso prius scripsisset, recens nunc in aliam n aliam sententiam scriptis literis, ab ipso emendarentur, ne in posterum innocenti homini fraudi esse posset quod antea parum considerate fuerat scriptum. Itaque in suis propriis literis simul impietatem infidelitatemque[?] prodebat, & pene diversis verbis suam perfidiam confitebatur. Istis literis Maluendae, ac simul etiam carnifice suo comitatus, pervenit Alphonsus Neoburgum: quem cum frater Ioannes coram videret, cum magna admiratione (sicut est consentaneum) praesentem intuebatur, à quo nullas lōgo tēpore literas acceperat, quemque Romae tunc esse putabat. Percontanti causam tam subitae atque insperatae praesentiae, respondet veras causas, ut antea dictum est, quibus impulsus laboriosam illam profectionem suscepisset. Pietatem in fratrem simulat impius parricida, & latentia in animo scelerata consilia praetextu amoris occultat. Quid hic suspicari poterat vir integerrimus? arbitratur vere fraterno amore permotum fratrem ad se venire: & quanvis multa in eo desiderat, affectum tamen probat, atque eius amorem magna pietate complectitur. Excipit igitur fratrem amantissime, ignorans interim se viperam in sinu fovere, cuius effrenatus furor, paulo post eius sanguinem debebat profundere. Ubi familiarius inter se agere coeperunt, paulatim prodit Alphonsus suae impietatis significationem. narrat eam tantum ob causam laborem illum diuturnum & periculosum suscepisse, ut eum ab instituta vitae ratione ad saniorem professionem, atque (ut isti loquuntur) ad gremium ecclesiae reuocaret. Speciosum ecclesiae nomen praetexit sceleratus parricida, qui in Romana impietate est versatus atque educatus, & quid sit Ecclesia prorsus ignorat. Cōmemorat pericula terribilia, quae si diutius in hoc instituto perfisteret, sequutura videbatur. Objicit illi summorum ordinū execrationes, qui odio Lutherani nominis, supra quam credi facile queat, exarserunt. Ponit ob oculos ingens dehonestamentum totius familiae, privatas miserias, carceres, exilia, proscriptiones, gladios, incendia, & quicquid alioqui periculorum eos plerunque comitatur qui vera sunt Ecclesiae Christi membra, quique puram atque integram Euangelii doctrinam pio & flagranti animi studio amplectuntur. Multa praeterea in hanc & simulem sententiam adducebat, ut constantem alioqui, & firmis Dei promissionibus munitum fratris animum commemoratione periculorum labefactaret.
units.tr: That same friend gave almost the same answer to him as he had earlier given the servant: that he did not really know where Diazius was, but that he wished to ask others, from whom he hoped to learn something certain. Returning home, he reported the whole matter to Master Bucer, Master Brenz, and the other conversation partners, and asked them for advice on what course he should follow in that business. Opinions differed. Some thought the place where Diazius was should be disclosed, while others said no, and each side gave reasons sufficiently sound to support its view. In the end the view prevailed that the place should be disclosed, since Diazius was otherwise free and safe, lest through ignorance of a matter said to be of great importance, something should be done carelessly to the detriment of Diazius. Meanwhile Diazius was warned by private letter that, if he thought any danger threatened him from that man, he should take prudent and timely precautions. Therefore, with this purpose and consent, that friend revealed to Alphonsus (who had not yet disclosed that he was the brother of Johannes Diazius) that Diazius was in the neighbouring city commonly called Neuburg. Alphonsus gave him immense thanks for this news and urgently begged him to come with him to the friend. For this purpose, he said, he had a horse ready and all the necessities. The friend replied that it was not possible for him to leave Regensburg at that time, but he promised to send letters to Diazius and also to tell him the place where he could find him. He therefore wrote a letter to Diazius, which he gave to Alphonsus, containing nothing beyond what could be made public without danger. He wrote, however, other letters, which he entrusted privately to the public courier who was travelling with Alphonsus, and he warned him to keep those letters separate and carefully, and not to hand them to anyone but Johannes Diazius himself. In these letters he set out at length whatever had happened to him with that man, and at the same time warned him to beware carefully of that man's snares, if he should try to lay any. Master Bucer also wrote through the same courier, and other friends wrote too, all of whom warned him most diligently about the dangers that could arise and indicated how they might be avoided. And so that the whole affair might be less open to suspicion, the courier was given the acts of the Regensburg colloquy to deliver to the secretary of the most illustrious Prince Otto. They also added money separately, so that the courier would take more faithful care of the matter; he had undertaken to see to the whole affair, and not only willingly but very diligently. With this business arranged, the courier and Alphonsus were dismissed. He in turn offered the brother's friend immense thanks for that service, and at the same time promised, more than dutifully, a gratitude and goodwill worthy of a sound and faithful friend. But before he let the brother's friend go, he began again to beseech him, and to adjure him by the faith of friendship and Christian charity, that if he wished Johannes Diazius's dignity and reputation to remain whole and unimpaired, he should in no way report to any mortal anything of the arrangements made between them, and least of all to Maluenda. For he did not doubt that Maluenda's mind was very hostile toward Diazius, because Diazius had been unwilling to obey his counsels; and therefore it was altogether in Diazius's interest that the matter he wished to transact with him should be carried out without Maluenda's knowledge. What more? Such was the force of his speech, and so earnestly did he press the point, that nothing of this matter was disclosed to Maluenda; indeed he even gave assurance that nothing was being done by him in pretence, but that he was speaking altogether from the heart. But oh, the unspeakable crime of a perverse traitor! For scarcely had that friend departed when Alphonsus himself came to the courier, stripped him of all letters and writings, and took them to Maluenda. There, after they had read everything through and had devised plans between themselves, no doubt Cain-like, they tore up all the letters. They kept only the other document, which was to be delivered to the secretary of Prince Otto, a thing he would not otherwise have preserved, except that he judged it very necessary for winning and securing the friendship of that man. Shortly afterwards, Diazius's friends were informed that Alphonsus had been with Maluenda, and what he had done with the courier was later related by Johannes Diazius himself to the friends at Neuburg. When Johannes Diazius's friends learned of this so remarkable treachery of a man who had so carefully feigned faithfulness and integrity, all of them came to suspect that he was plotting some great crime. Accordingly, they again, through a special courier, urged Johannes Diazius to beware altogether of that man's snares. At last Alphonsus set out for Neuburg, and through him Maluenda wrote a letter to Johannes Diazius, in which he urged him to obey his brother's sound advice. He also promised that if he wished to follow him into Italy and to leave Germany entirely with its Germans, who were (for so he called them in his letter) corrupters of good minds, he would arrange with the Emperor's confessor that those harmful things which he had previously written about him should now be corrected by him, by a fresh letter in a different sense, so that what had been written rather carelessly before could not in future be a discredit to an innocent man. Thus in his own letter he at the same time betrayed his impiety and unfaithfulness, and in almost contrary words confessed his treachery. With these letters from Maluenda, and accompanied by his own executioner, Alphonsus reached Neuburg. When his brother Johannes saw him in person, he gazed at him with great astonishment, as was fitting, since he had received no letters from him for a long time and believed him to be at Rome. When asked the reason for so sudden and unexpected a presence, he gave the true causes, as was said before, which had moved him to undertake that laborious journey. The impious parricide feigned piety toward his brother and hid his wicked plans in the cloak of affection. What could a man of the greatest integrity suspect here? He supposed that his brother had come to him moved by true fraternal love; and although he found much in him to lament, he nevertheless approved his affection and embraced his love with great devotion. He therefore received his brother most lovingly, ignorant meanwhile that he was nourishing a viper in his bosom, whose unbridled fury was shortly to pour out his blood. When they began to talk more familiarly together, Alphonsus gradually revealed the sign of his impiety. He related that he had undertaken that long and dangerous labour only for this reason: to recall him from the way of life he had adopted to a saner profession and, as they put it, to the bosom of the Church. The wicked parricide, who had been bred and educated in Roman impiety and utterly ignorant of what the Church is, put forward the venerable name of the Church as a pretext. He recounted the terrible dangers which seemed likely to follow if he persisted longer in this course. He set before him the curses of the highest orders, who had blazed with hatred of the Lutheran name beyond what could easily be believed. He placed before his eyes the great disgrace to the whole family, private miseries, prisons, exiles, proscriptions, swords, fires, and whatever other dangers usually accompany those who are true members of Christ's Church and who embrace the pure and whole doctrine of the Gospel with a devout and burning zeal of soul. He brought forward many other arguments to this and a similar effect, so that by recounting dangers he might shake the mind of his brother, which was otherwise steadfast and fortified by God's firm promises.

units.la: Ad has rationes fratris, etsi deplorabat in animo suo Ioannes depravatum Alphonsi iudicium, qui pericula & furores hominum professioni verae doctrinae anteferret, respondit tamen illi blandissime, Nec errore mentis, frater, nec ulla privata cupiditate adductus, sed certo & firmo iudicio eam doctrinam sum amplexus, quam ex fontibus sacrarum literarum (diligenter perquisitis initijs & progressionibus verae religionis) clare agnosco esse verum ac perpetuum consensum Prophetarum & Apostolorum. Hanc igitur doctrinam Dei beneficio apprehensam sine nefario scelere abjicere non possum: neque ulla mundi pericula me ab hoc instituto deterrebunt.
units.tr: Although John Diaz privately deplored Alphonsus's distorted judgment, who put dangers and the rage of men ahead of professing the true doctrine, he answered his brother very kindly to these arguments: "Not from any error of mind, brother, nor driven by any private desire, but by a certain and firm judgment have I embraced that doctrine which I clearly recognise, from the sources of the holy letters (having carefully examined the beginnings and progress of true religion), to be the true and perpetual agreement of the Prophets and the Apostles. Having received this doctrine by God's benefit, I cannot cast it off without wicked crime, and no dangers of the world will turn me from this purpose."

units.la: Considera, quaeso te frater, utrum sit prudentis, momentanea pericula vitare, ut incidat in aeternam condemnationem. atqui nullum profecto aliud est peccatum blasphemiae, quam agnitam veritatem flagitiosè insectari, cuius criminis nec in hoc seculo, nec in sempiternum ulla fiet condonatio. Magni ergo momenti res est, quae me in hoc incepto cursu & in hac professione retinet. Ac ego quidem vehementer optarem, mi frater, ut in voluntate Dei cognoscenda tantum tibi operis ac studij ponendum putares, quantum alioqui solertiae ac sedulitatis in negotijs humanis vel perquisitandis vel expediendis hactenus posuisti. quae tua est ingenij dexteritas, quae immensa est aeterni Patris misericordia, non dubitarem Deum velle thesauros caelestis sapientiae suae tibi patefacere: teque posse, si adesset labor & industria, voluntatem Dei ex divinis literis cognoscere atque illustrare. Vtinam vero eam cognitionem tibi ego, mi frater, vel meo sanguine possem comparare. Nam, ut testatur ipse filius Dei, haec est vere vita aeterna, cognoscere Deum verum, & quem ille misit Iesum Christum.
units.tr: "Consider, I beg you, brother, whether it is the mark of a prudent man to avoid momentary dangers so as to fall into eternal condemnation. Indeed there is surely no other sin of blasphemy than to pursue with wicked hostility the truth once acknowledged, and for this crime there will be no forgiveness in this age or forever. So the matter that keeps me in this course I have begun and in this profession is of great moment. I would earnestly wish, my brother, that you would think you ought to spend in learning the will of God as much labour and zeal as you have hitherto spent in searching out or managing human affairs, in which you are so skilful and diligent. Given your natural cleverness, and given the immense mercy of the eternal Father, I do not doubt that God wishes to open to you the treasures of his heavenly wisdom, and that you can, if there is effort and diligence, know and make clear the will of God from the divine letters. Would that I, my brother, could obtain that knowledge for you even with my own blood! For, as the Son of God himself testifies, this is eternal life: to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent."

units.la: Et profecto illud in primis deplorandum est, tantam esse in re omnium maxima & gravissima hominum negligentiam & impietatem, ut haec oracula Dei (clara aeterni numinis voce de caelo sonante & ad omnes creaturas promulgata) vel otiosè negligant ipsi vel superbè contemnant. Etenim si rem ipsam tecum recta reputes via, quam aliam, amabo te, reperies causam quare nos ab impijs hominibus condemnemur, ac pene quotidie morti tradamur, quàm quod universam spem nostram in Deo vivo, non in ullo homine, non in ullis rebus humanis reposuimus, extra quem nulla est homini speranda salus? Cognosce igitur prius causam nostram, mi frater: quam ubi serio perdidiceris, tu ipse judicabis propter nulla vitæ pericula esse deserendam. Certè quod ad me attinet, itameum[?] animum gratuita Dei misericordia & bonitate confirmaui, ut nulla ratione me ab instituta doctrinæ professione patiar revocari.
units.tr: "And indeed this above all is to be lamented: that in a matter of all others the greatest and most serious there is such negligence and impiety among men that they either idly neglect or proudly despise these oracles of God, which sound out from heaven in the clear voice of the eternal Godhead and are published to all creatures. For if you weigh the matter with yourself in a right way, what other cause, I ask you, will you find why we are condemned by wicked men and handed over to death almost every day, than that we have placed our whole hope in the living God, and not in any man or any human thing, outside whom no salvation is to be hoped for by man? Know, therefore, my brother, our cause first; and when you have learned it in earnest, you yourself will judge that it must not be abandoned for any dangers of life. Certainly, as far as I am concerned, I have so strengthened my mind by the free mercy and goodness of God that I will suffer myself in no way to be called back from the profession of the doctrine I have adopted."

units.la: Cùm videret Alphonsus constantiam fratris, nouum arietem intendit: & quod ab eo periculorum metu extorquere non poterat, proposita praemiorum spe se posse cõsidit impetrare. Dicit se habere singulis annis ex beneficiis ecclesiasticis proventus quingentorum ducatorum: quos omnes in eum cupit transferre, modo ipse Romam una secum profiscatur.
units.tr: When Alphonsus saw his brother's constancy, he tried a new assault; and what he could not extort from him by fear of dangers, he trusted he might obtain by holding out the hope of rewards. He said that he had revenues from ecclesiastical benefices of five hundred ducats a year, all of which he wished to transfer to John, provided that John would set out for Rome together with him.

units.la: Ad hoc respondet Joannes, Non sum tam avidus pecuniae, frater, quam tu fortasse arbitraris. nam si divitiarum aut honorum viam mihi insequendam proposuissem, longè aliter vitæ meæ rationes instituissem. Nunc verò istam qualemcunque cœlestis doctrinæ cognitionem, quam Dominus gratuita sua bonitate in me contulit, pro summo honore habeo: & iste animus, nullius sibi criminis conscius, mihi quouis thesauro pretiosior est.
units.tr: To this John replied: "I am not so greedy for money, brother, as you perhaps think. For if I had proposed to myself the way of riches or honours, I would have ordered my life very differently. But as it is, I hold that knowledge of heavenly doctrine, whatever it may be, which the Lord in his free goodness has bestowed upon me, as the highest honour; and this mind, conscious of no crime, is more precious to me than any treasure."

units.la: Postremò cùm ne hac quidem illi succederet, aliam aggreditur viam, ac extremam vim machinarum & proditionum admonet, quibus fratrem innocentem, candidum atque omnis malitiæ dolique expertem, homo pessimus fraudulenter oppugnet. Pietatem simulat impius homo, ut sanctum virum, qui totus à Deo pendebat, opinione religionis facilius decipiat. Ac tandem ex imo pectore suspiria trahens, ingemiscens & quasi lachrymabundus fratrem aggreditur in hanc sententiam, Video, frater, tantam esse tuam constantiam, fidem atque integritatem in cognoscenda atque retinenda Evangelii doctrina, ut me quoque in tuam sententiam cœperis pertrahere. neque enim sum adeò rudis aut ferox, frater, ut ego vel mirandam atque imitandam tuam istam integritatem non videam & agnoscam, vel ingentem illam utilitatē cupiam impedire, quā ex tua ista doctrina & profes-sione, cùm ad universam ecclesiam Dei, tum præcipuè ad nostros homines spero adhuc posse redundare. Quinetiam toto pectore, quasi coniunctis viribus hoc agamus ambo, atque in hoc potissimum incumbamus, ut vera doctrina de Filio Dei, quam maxime fieri poterit, toto orbe terrarum latissime propagetur, & professio Euangelij etiam in nostris finibus, & apud nostros homines, sicut apud alios orbis nationes, floreat ac promoveatur. Sed ad hoc tantum Dei opus, debe-res, frater, non solum prudenter, sed etiam diligenter dispensare do-num Dei, quod in te prae ceteris nostrae gentis hominibus caelestis bonitas contulit. Etenim dum in Germania manes, & apud illos homines vivis quorum linguam ignoras, quid aliud, quaeso te, facere videris, quam talentum quod a Deo copiose accepisti, humi defossum sine utilitate hominum tenere? Vides in hac regione esse plerosque viros doctos in literis & religione praeclare institutos, qui tua opera non indigent: atque adeo non indigent, ut si recte illorum virtutem novi, illi ipsi tibi authores erunt ut eam doctrinam quam ab ipsis didicisti, ad aedificationem ac reformationem nostrorum hominum, nostraeque patriae utilitatem conferas. Sed quoniam illa in hoc tempore, incredibili tyrannide iacet oppressa, nec in ea tibi habitare esset satis tutum, non desinam tibi esse author atque hortator, ut mecum in Italiam venias. Ex hac professione tantum mihi utilitatis audeo polliceri in promovenda gloria Dei, & illustranda Euangelij doctrina, quantum nunquam tu vel in Germania, vel in alio loco sperare potuisses. Primum igitur Tridentum venimus, ubi multi praesules magnae authoritatis congregati sunt, qui in favorem Euangelicae doctrinae prorsus inclinant: & si te haberent vel stimulatorem vel hortatorem, quod rectissime in animo sentiunt, nec impediti pontificia tyrannide audent evulgare, clara voce profiterentur. Expende nunc apud te quanta hinc utilitas exoritur, ut integrum concilium, alioqui ad tyrannidem impiorum hominum stabiliendam institutum, ad studium inquirendae ac patefaciendae veritatis per te reducatur. Conferes tuam sententiam cum illis viris doctis: & si quid melius quam ipsi tenent, didicisti, habebis illos (quod eorum nomine audeo promittere) attentos ac dociles auditores. Quin & tuam doctrinam alioqui firmam, & expressis Dei testimonijs stabilitatem, puritate vita ie[?] sanctitate, qua semper excelluisti, & reliquas tuas virtutes doctrinamque ipsam exornasti, quamque illi quoque ipsi, qui tibi non omnino bene volunt, in te amant & venerantur, multo magis confirmabis. Deinde veniemus Romam, Neapolim, & in alias civitates Italiae, in quibus magna est cognitio & studium veritatis, ubi erit tibi negotium non cum infimae notae hominibus, sed cum viris principibus, quos in vera doctrina confirmare, & publica pene voce tuam sententiam licebit profiteri.
units.tr: Finally, since he did not succeed even in this, he tried another way, and set before him the utmost force of machinations and treacheries by which the worst of men might fraudulently assail his innocent brother, upright and free of all malice and guile. The wicked man feigns piety, so that he might more easily deceive, by the appearance of religion, a holy man who wholly depended on God. And at last, drawing sighs from the bottom of his heart, groaning and as if weeping, he addressed his brother in this sense: "I see, brother, that your constancy, faith and integrity in knowing and holding fast the doctrine of the Gospel are so great that you have begun to draw me too to your opinion. For I am not so unfeeling or so fierce, brother, that I either fail to see and acknowledge that integrity of yours which is wonderful and worthy of imitation, or that I wish to hinder that great benefit which, I hope it may still redound from your doctrine and profession, both to the whole Church of God and especially to our own people. Moreover, let us both work with all our heart, as if with joined strength, and let us chiefly labour toward this, that the true doctrine concerning the Son of God be spread as widely as possible throughout the whole world, and that the profession of the Gospel flourish and advance in our own borders also, and among our own people, just as among the other nations of the world. But for this work of God, brother, you ought to dispense the gift of God not only prudently but also diligently, the gift which heavenly goodness has bestowed upon you above the other men of our nation. For while you remain in Germany and live among those men whose language you do not know, what, I ask you, do you seem to do but keep hidden in the ground, to no advantage of men, the talent which you have received abundantly from God? You see that in this region there are many learned men, admirably trained in letters and religion, who do not need your work; and indeed they do not need it so much that, if I rightly know their virtue, they themselves will be your advisers to turn the doctrine you learned from them to the edification and reformation of our people and the benefit of our country. But since that country at this time lies oppressed under an incredible tyranny, and it would not be safe enough for you to live there, I will not cease to be your author and encourager that you come with me into Italy. From this profession I dare to promise myself as much usefulness in advancing the glory of God and illustrating the doctrine of the Gospel as you could never have hoped for in Germany or anywhere else. We shall first come to Trent, where many prelates of great authority are assembled, who are wholly inclined toward favour of the Evangelical doctrine; and if they had you as a spur and encourager, they would openly profess what they most rightly think in their hearts, and not dare to publish it, being hindered by papal tyranny. Now consider how much usefulness arises from this, that the whole council, otherwise set up to establish the tyranny of wicked men, may be brought back through you to the zeal of inquiring into and laying open the truth. You will compare your opinion with those learned men; and if you have learned anything better than they hold, you will have them (which I dare promise in their name) as attentive and teachable hearers. Indeed you will strengthen even more their regard for your doctrine, which is otherwise firm and established by express testimonies of God, and for your purity of life and holiness, in which you have always excelled and which you have adorned along with your other virtues and with the doctrine itself; those too who do not altogether wish you well will love and revere you. Then we shall come to Rome, Naples, and other cities of Italy, in which there is great knowledge and zeal for the truth, where you will have business not with men of the lowest rank but with princely men, whom it will be permitted to confirm in true doctrine, and to profess your opinion almost with a public voice.

units.la: Perculsus Ioannes Diazius noua oratione fratris Alphonsi, coepit in animo suo mirabiliter exultare, existimans fratrem Alphonsum ex animo loquutum. Proinde multo blandius illi respondet quam solitus erat, se quidem paratum esse quacunque posset ratione, etiam cum vitae suae dispendio, gloriam Christi promouere. laudabat animum fratris, comprobabat consilia, atque ad ea perficienda, ut ipse volebat, suum quoque suffragium nunquam defuturum promittebat. Caeterum, quoniam erat negotium magni momenti, arduum & periculi plenum, maturo etiam consilio & deliberatione opus esse, ut iudicio bonorum atque prudentium id tandem statueretur, quod magis ad utilitatem reipublicae, ad promouendam gloriam Dei utile ac necessarium videretur. Quare hoc sibi praeter cetera videbatur consultissimum, ut haec tota de-liberatio colloquutoribus, qui erant Ratisbonae, committeretur, quorum arbitrio se totum permittebat. Hoc consilium non omnino displicuit Alphonso, quia fortasse existimabat fungos aut lapides esse, qui de hoc negotio debebant iudicare: nec fieri posse arbitrabatur, ut quisquam Germanorum subtiles eius fraudes ac proditiones intelligeret. Scripsit igitur literas Ioannes Diazius ad collocutores, qui erant Ratisbonae, in quibus aduentum fratris significabat, qui hoc ab eo summo studio postulabat ut ipsum in Italiam sequeretur. Addebat quoque rationes fratris, quibus id fieri omnino debere contendebat. postremo suam etiam voluntatem scripsit, ita in animo suo constituisse, ut in hoc toto negotio nihil aliud facere velit, quam quod ipsi re deliberata faciendum esse iudicarent. Scripsit quoque literas in eandem sententiam ad Bernardinum Ochinum, qui in civitate Augustana Italis Euangelium concionabatur, a quo etiam suum de hac re iudicium postulabat. Denique vbi literae Diazij perlectæ fuerunt Ratisbonæ, omnes colloquutores sunt cōgregati, vt in ea causa singulorum sententiæ audirentur. In hac deliberatione omnes vno ore consenserunt, nullo modo credendum esse falsis fratris rationibus: quem in hoc tantum incubere videbat, vt prætextu pietatis fratre innocentem deciperet. nec defuerunt in eo consessu, qui parricidium, quod facinorosus ille in animo suo conceperat, iam tum prædicerent. Itaque communi omnium sententia ad Diazium scripserunt, & quid omnino de toto illo negotio Fratres vno consensu & sentirent & constituerent, diligenter significarunt. idem quoque Bernardinus literis scriptis indicauit. Iam vero vbi frater Alphonsus videt se vndique exclusum, nec latere sua consilia diutius posse: etsi ingentem animo concepit dolorem, tamen quoniam fratris benevolentiam ad perpetranda facinora quæ destinauerat, sibi permecessariam esse videbat, noluit eum acerbitate verborum lædere, sed potius mærorem animi summo studio dissimulauit. Dicit se quidem æquo animo ferre sententiam illam doctorum hominum, quam propria ipsorum manu videbat consignatam: sed tamen vt aliqua ipsi gratia pro tanto labore reponeretur, impensissimè orabat Ioannem vt saltem Augustam vsque cum eo venire non gravaretur, qua in vrbe extrema quasi sententia totum illud negotium definiretur. Hæc non sine ingenti malitia à nesario parricida dicebantur, qui blandis verbis conabatur innocentem fratrem, in liberum & patentem agrum extra ciuitatem producere, vt in aliquo deserto loco eum interficeret. Omnino id facturus erat Ioannes, nisi Bucerus, qui forte interuenit ante fratris profectionem, ne id fieret prohibuisset. Etenim cum Ratisbonæ nihil ageret colloquutores, Statuerentque domum redire, Bucerus cum Martino Frechtio concionatore Vlmensi, voluerunt Neoburgum venire, vt quod per literas Ioannem Diazium admonuerant, ne videlicet fratri Alphonso crederet, nec eum in Italiam sequeretur, id magis & magis præsentes inculcarent. Conuentum igitur est inter Fratres, vt Alphonsus proficisceretur solus, die XXV. Martij: hoc est triduo postquam amici Neoburgum venissent. Ea res quanquam peracerba erat in animo Alphonsi, simulabat tamen externam lætitiam quantum poterat, vt modis omnibus fidem faceret fratri, se nihil aliud velle aut optare quam quod Ioanni anni, quem se mirifice amare prædicabat, gratum atque optatum ideretur. Pridie ante profectionem, post cœnam, hoc est vigesimo quarto die Martij, quum postridie summo mane esset profecturus, convenit fratrem seorsum, eumque ad constantiam in professione veræ religionis adhortatus est. Promittebat quoque se & sua omnia ad arbitrium Ioannis fore perpetuo paratissima. Quin & nolenti obrusit quatuordecim coronatos, ut emeret novas vestes: quos invitum ac repugnantem pene violenter accipere coegit. Itaque additis ultro citroque plurimis verbis, quæ teneritudinem fraterni pectoris ac verum amorem testarentur, non sine magna vi lachrymarum andem utrinque discessum est cubitum. Postridie summo diluculo, hoc est vigesimoquinto die Martij, paratur currus Neoburgensis, in quo Alphonsus cum suo carnifice Augustam veherentur. Ibi rurius in discessu novæ lachrymæ profunduntur.
