Sed tamen recessit omimo frater Alphonsus, & Ioannes mansit cum amicis Neoburgi[?] pui profecto feriò sibi gratulabantur, quod eo tandem homine essent liberati, quem semper omnes habuerant suspectum. Denique cum Bucerus & Frechtius existimarent iam esse in tuto omnia, voluerunt & ipsi eodem die post prandium proficisci.
units.tr: Ioannes Diazius, astonished by the new speech of his brother Alphonsus, began to rejoice wonderfully in his mind, thinking that Alphonsus had spoken from the heart. Therefore he answered him much more warmly than was his custom, saying that he was indeed ready, by whatever means he could, even at the cost of his own life, to advance the glory of Christ. He praised his brother's spirit, approved his plans, and promised that his own support would never be lacking in carrying them out as Alphonsus wished. However, since it was a matter of great importance, difficult and full of danger, it needed mature counsel and deliberation, so that by the judgment of good and prudent men it might at last be decided what seemed most useful and necessary for the welfare of the commonwealth and the promotion of God's glory. For this reason he thought it wisest above all else that the whole deliberation should be committed to the colloquy members who were at Regensburg, and he entrusted himself wholly to their judgment. This plan did not altogether displease Alphonsus, because perhaps he thought that those who were to judge in this affair were blockheads or stones, and he did not believe that any of the Germans could understand his subtle deceits and betrayals. Therefore Ioannes Diazius wrote a letter to the colloquy members at Regensburg, in which he announced his brother's arrival, and reported that he had most earnestly asked him to follow him into Italy. He also added his brother's reasons, by which he insisted that this ought absolutely to be done. Finally, he wrote that his own will was fixed in his mind, that in this whole matter he wished to do nothing other than what they, after deliberation, judged should be done. He wrote a letter to the same effect to Bernardino Ochino, who was preaching the Gospel to the Italians in the city of Augsburg, and from whom he also asked his judgment on the matter. Then, when Diazius's letter had been read at Regensburg, all the colloquy members assembled, so that the opinion of each might be heard in this case. In this deliberation they all agreed with one voice that the brother's arguments were by no means to be believed, since he seemed to be labouring only to deceive his innocent brother under the pretext of piety. Nor were there lacking in that assembly those who already foretold the parricide that the wicked man had conceived in his mind. Therefore, by the common judgment of all, they wrote to Diazius, and carefully informed him what the brothers had unanimously thought and decided about that whole affair. Bernardino also indicated the same thing in a written letter. But when Brother Alphonsus saw that he was shut out on every side, and that his plans could no longer be hidden, although he felt a great grief in his mind, nevertheless, since he saw that his brother's goodwill was absolutely necessary for carrying out the crimes he had planned, he did not wish to wound him with bitter words, but rather concealed the sorrow of his mind with the greatest care. He said that he indeed bore calmly the judgment of those learned men, which he saw had been sealed by their own hands; yet, so that some favour might be returned to him for so great a labour, he most earnestly begged Ioannes at least not to be reluctant to come with him as far as Augsburg, where the whole affair would be settled as a final verdict. These things were said, not without great malice, by the wicked parricide, who with smooth words tried to lead his innocent brother out of the city into the open countryside, so that he might kill him in some deserted place. Ioannes would certainly have done so, had not Bucer, who happened to intervene before his brother's departure, prevented it. For when the colloquy members at Regensburg accomplished nothing, and resolved to return home, Bucer and Martin Frecht, preacher of Ulm, wished to come to Neuburg, so that they might press more and more upon those present what they had urged on Ioannes Diazius by letter: namely, that he should not trust Brother Alphonsus, nor follow him into Italy. Therefore it was agreed among the brothers that Alphonsus should set out alone on the 25th of March, that is, three days after the friends had come to Neuburg. Although this matter was very bitter in Alphonsus's mind, he nevertheless pretended outward joy as much as he could, so that by every means he might convince his brother that he wished and desired nothing other than what seemed pleasing and welcome to Ioannes, whom he declared he loved wonderfully. On the day before his departure, after supper, that is, on the 24th of March, since he was to set out very early the next morning, he met his brother apart and urged him to constancy in the profession of true religion. He also promised that he and all his possessions would always be most ready at Ioannes's disposal. Indeed, though his brother was unwilling, he pressed fourteen crowns into his hand so that he might buy new clothes, and forced him to take them, though he was unwilling and resisting almost violently. So, after many words had passed back and forth which bore witness to the tenderness of a brotherly heart and true love, they at last parted for bed, not without great flow of tears on both sides. Early the next morning, that is, on the 25th of March, a Neuburg carriage was made ready, in which Alphonsus and his executioner were to be carried to Augsburg. There, again at parting, fresh tears were shed. Yet Brother Alphonsus did in fact depart, and Ioannes remained with his friends at Neuburg, who truly congratulated themselves that they had at last been freed from that man, whom they had always regarded with suspicion. Finally, since Bucer and Frecht thought that everything was now secure, they too decided to set out that same day after lunch.

units.la: Ubi ad portam civitatis venit Alphonsus, non passus est ut auriga urbem intraret, sed coegit cum per mœnia circumire, donec tandem in domum, in qua esse volebat, magno quidem dispendio itineris, sed tamen magis occultè ducereturne: ne videlicet in urbe ab aliquo cognosceretur, qui postea ingens illud facinus impediret, quod in animo suo patrare constituerat. Tandem ubi eum in hospitio suo depositisset auriga, dixit illi Alphonsus, velle se postridie summo mane in Italiam proficisci: sed tamen velle quoque ante profectionem scribere literas ad fratrem, & proinde orabat eum, ut priusquam Neoburgum reverteretur, veniret ad se, apud quem inventurus erat postridie paratas literas. Promisit auriga: & sequenti die summo mane, hoc est vigesimo sexto die Martij, venit ad hospitium Alphonsi sicut antea promiserat, ut literas ab eo ad Ioannem fratrem acciperet. Responsum est aurigæ, Alphonsum esse in lecto: & quia præcedente nocte in longum tempus protraxerat compotationem, altum adhuc dormire. Credidit auriga, & rogatus à domesticis vt intra vnam aut alteram horam reuerteretur, recepit se factu-rum. Sed hæc omnia inter ipsos ignorante auriga de composito gerebantur, vt istiusmodi fraudibus auriga diutius detineretur Augustæ, quo plus esset spatij parricidis ad suum facinus magis impune perpetrandum. Cum igitur auriga secundo rediret ad Alphonsum, dictum est, illum iam esse profectum in Italiam, nec potuisse Augustæ literas scribere: sed tamen promisisse se ex Oeniponte scripturum. Itaque numerata aliqua pecuniola, dimiserunt aurigam platatum, qui plane verum esse credebat quod de Alphonso sibi fuerat narratum. Ac ipse quoque paulo post cum suo socio, qui pridie in eodem curru cum Alphonso venerat Augustam, rursus Neoburgum proficiscuntur. Circa horam eius diei duodecimam pervenerunt in oppidulum Bothmes, quod in medio fere itinere inter Augustam & Neoburgum est positum, & abest fere tribus milliaribus ab utroque. Ibi præter opinionem inuenerunt in diuersorio Alphonsum, qui adhuc erat in mensa, & cum eo assidebant qui cum ipso venerant, suus carnifex & nuntius Augustanus quem secum adducebat ignarum suorum consiliorum: præterea cuius oppidi sacrificulus quidam, & alij conuiuæ. Alphonsus vbi aurigam cum socio vidit, non leuiter fuit perturbatus: quorum opera futurum verebatur, vt quod ipse iam in animo suo patrare proposuerat, vel impediretur, vel perturbaretur. Sed composito ad hilaritatem vultu, orauit aurigam vt ipsi cum sodalitio mensæ assiderent. Quod principio illi, quia multi erant, & domum properabant, facere recusauerunt. Cum vero ille magis instaret, tandem assederunt omnes. Inter prandendum, nouo atque inaudito commento, quod tum primum in mentem venit, auriga aggreditur. Ait sibi præter opinionem oblatum esse negotium magni momenti, de quo fratrem Ioannem ex eo loco deberet facere certiorem. Sed quoniam prius essent quædam, quæ ad hanc rem pertinerent in eo loco perscribenda, in quo illo die manere constituisset, orauit valde officiosè aurigam cum suo socio, ne grauarentur eodem die cum ipsis manere, & quidem suis sumptibus, vt postridie per ipsos videlicet homines notos & fideles ea quæ vellet fratri posset nuntiare. Illi vero etsi libentius ibentius eodem die domum peruenissent, tamen vt gratificarentur Alphonso, qui anxiè hoc postulabat, & permagni eius interesse putabant, manere cum eo illo die voluerunt. Post prandium autem, vbi hoc inter eos fuit constitutum, vtrinque discessum est. Auriga curauit quaedam sua: Alphonsus cum suo carnifice ad alia multò horribiliora negotia se contulerunt. Consultabant inter se rationem & modum, quo in fratre interficiendo vti deberent: & quia longo & vsitato gladio non bene id fieri posse videbant, securim ad hoc facinus perpetrandum accommodatam, in illo oppido emere constituerunt. Sed rursus hîc noua adhibetur cautio. etenim ab artifice qui eas vendebat, emere securim noluerunt, ne hac occasione in aliquam ipsi venirent suspicionem. sed cùm forte fabrum quendam lignarium, securi ligna dolantem vidissent, eum accedunt, & rogant vtrum securim aliam habe-ret vænalem. faber illis propo fuit aliquot, ex quibus vnam elegerunt, quam ad facinus quod instituerant aptissimam esse iudicarunt. Deinde numerata pecunia fabro, qui postea rem omnem prodidit, ipsi domum reuertuntur, in qua praeter hospitem domesticum & nuntium Augustanum, qui cum eis venerat, neminem inuenerunt. Ibi significarunt hospiti, e vestigio sibi esse aliquò proficiscendum, vnde citò erant reuersuri: & quia nolebant suos equos in eo itinere defatigare, iusserunt vt noui, sed celeres & boni, ipsis pararentur. Vbi fuerunt parati equi, conscendit Alphonsus, conscendit carnifex: tertius etiam comitatur nuntius Augustanus, ignarus rerum omnium: sed quia liberaliter illi soluebant, sequebatur quanuis ægrè, parricidas.
units.tr: When Alphonsus came to the city gate, he did not allow the driver to enter the town, but forced him to go around the walls, until at last, at great cost of travel but more secretly, he was taken to the house in which he wished to be; namely, so that in the town he might not be recognised by anyone who would afterwards hinder that huge crime which he had resolved to commit. At last, when the driver had set him down at his lodging, Alphonsus told him that he wished to set out for Italy the next morning very early; but he also wished to write a letter to his brother before his departure, and therefore asked him to come to him before returning to Neuburg, promising that he would find the letter ready the next day. The driver agreed; and on the following morning very early, that is, on the 26th of March, he came to Alphonsus's lodging as he had promised, to receive a letter from him for his brother Ioannes. He was told that Alphonsus was in bed, and because on the previous night he had prolonged the drinking for a long time, he was still sleeping deeply. The driver believed this, and when the servants asked him to return within an hour or two, he agreed to do so. But all these things were arranged in advance between them, without the driver's knowledge, so that by such frauds the driver might be detained longer at Augsburg, and the parricides would have more time to carry out their crime with less risk of discovery. Therefore, when the driver came back to Alphonsus a second time, he was told that he had already set out for Italy and could not write a letter at Augsburg; but that he had promised to write from Innsbruck. So, after some small sum of money had been counted out to him, they dismissed the driver, who fully believed that what had been told him about Alphonsus was true. And a little later he himself, together with his companion who had come to Augsburg the day before in the same carriage with Alphonsus, set out again for Neuburg. Around the twelfth hour of that day they arrived at the little town of Bothmes, which lies roughly midway between Augsburg and Neuburg and is about three miles from each. There, contrary to expectation, they found Alphonsus at the inn, who was still at table, and with him were seated those who had come with him: his executioner, and the Augsburg messenger whom he had brought along, ignorant of his plans; besides these, a certain priest of that town, and other guests. When Alphonsus saw the driver with his companion, he was not a little disturbed; he feared that through them what he had already planned to carry out might either be hindered or thrown into confusion. But, with a cheerful look composed, he begged the driver and his companion to sit down with the company at table. At first they refused, because there were many people and they were hurrying home; but when he insisted more, at last they all sat down. During the meal the driver took up a new and unheard-of pretext, which came into his mind at that moment. He said that a matter of great importance had unexpectedly been put before him, about which he ought to inform Brother Ioannes from that place. But since certain things that pertained to this matter had first to be written down in the place where he had decided to stay that day, he very politely begged the driver and his companion not to mind staying with them that day, and indeed at their own expense, so that the next day, through those men who were known and trusted, he might be able to send to his brother whatever he wished. Although they would more gladly have reached home that same day, nevertheless, to oblige Alphonsus, who was anxiously asking this, and because they thought it was greatly in his interest, they agreed to stay with him that day. After lunch, when this had been settled between them, they parted on both sides. The driver attended to his own affairs; Alphonsus and his executioner turned to other business, much more horrible. They discussed between themselves the method and means by which they should kill their brother; and since they saw that this could not be done well with a long, customary sword, they decided to buy in that town an axe suited to committing this crime. But here again a new precaution was taken. For they did not want to buy an axe from the craftsman who sold them, lest on this occasion they should fall under some suspicion. Instead, when they happened to see a carpenter chopping wood with an axe, they went up to him and asked whether he had another axe for sale. The carpenter offered them several, from which they chose one, which they judged most suitable for the crime they had planned. Then, having paid the money to the carpenter, who afterwards betrayed the whole affair, they went back home, where, apart from the domestic host and the Augsburg messenger who had come with them, they found no one. There they told the host that they had to set out somewhere at once, from which they would return quickly; and because they did not want to tire their horses on that journey, they ordered that new but swift and good horses be got ready for them. When the horses were ready, Alphonsus mounted, the executioner mounted; a third, the Augsburg messenger, ignorant of everything, accompanied them; but since they paid him generously, he followed the parricides, though reluctantly.

units.la: Interea temporis Alphonsus cum suis, postquam equos conscenderunt, intra pauculas horas peruenerunt ad pagum, qui vulgo dicitur Veldkirchen, prope ipsum oppidum Neoburgum situm, ibique illa nocte pernoctarunt. Sequenti die, hoc est XXVII. Martij, antequàm portae aperirentur peruenerunt Neoburgum. & cùm nondum planè diluxisset, ac portae oppidi iam paterent, descenderunt de equis, eósque ad sepem alligatos, in custodia nuntij reliquerunt. Ibi carnifex Alphonsi famulus, accepit veste & pileum nuntij, vt minus in oppido agnosceretur: eóque modo deformatus, ingreditur cum suo domino in oppidum. Carnifex praecedebat, parricida sequebatur. nã sic inter cos convenerat, ut carnificis manu, qui alioqui dexterior erat, facinus perpetraretur: ipse vero parricida præsto adesset suo carnifici, ut si necessitas aliqua postularet, aut parum feliciter negotiu succederet, opem ferret facinoroso nebuloni. semper itaque sequebatur Alphonsus parricida vestigia famuli carnifici. Isto igitur modo deformati ingrediuntur oppidum, & in ædes concionatoris, in quibus Ioan. erat hospitio exceptus, perveniunt. Ibi primum pulsat carnifex, & interrogat fratre concionatoris, qui ianuam aperuit, ubinam esset Ioan. Diazius, ad quem literas ab Alphonso se adferre prædicabat. respodit iuvenis domesticus, qui antea quoque probe noverat hunc famulum & Alphonsum, Ioannem quidem esse adhuc in lecto. sed quid sibi vellet illa nova forma vestitus, aut quid significaret illa vestis mutatio? Carnifex autem ne ibi prodere-tur, coegit ascendere iuvenem, & Ioanni nuntiare, se ibi adesse cum literis fratris. Ubi hoc intellexit Ioannes Diazius, exilit cum magno impetu de lecto avidus agnoscendi quid frater significaret. Ac præ nimia festinatione nullas accepit vestes, præter leuem quandam penulam, qua sola tectus egreditur cubiculum atque hypocaustum, quod e regione cubiculi positum est, ingreditur, in quo venientem famulum exciperet. Ascendit carnifex, a iuvene, quem antea nominavi, deductus: ad ianuam inferiorem, quæ gradus claudebat, mansit Alphonsus, ut ingressum observaret, ne quis ascenderet qui facinus impediret. Cum igitur in hoc statu essent negotia, satis ut apparebat perturbata propter præsentiam iuvenis qui celeritatem facinoris impediebat, missus est iuvenis ad fontem, ut inde adferret poculum aquæ. Digresso igitur ad hunc modum iuvene, carnifex, qui solus cum solo manserat, exhibuit literas fratris, quas ex Augusta missas dicebat: cum alioqui parricida improbus illis esset proximus in gradibus. Ioannes accepit literas, & quoniam vixdum diluxerat, accessit ad fenestram, ut eo lumine paulatim inclarescentis diei facilius legeret, quod in literis continebatur. Sententia autem epistolæ, ut postea amicis compertum est, qui eam legerunt, talis erat, Dicebat sibi esse nuntiatum, cum primum Augustam peervenisset, ipsum esse in magno periculo: ac proinde fraterna pietate motum cum admonere voluisse, ut diligenter sibi caveret ab insidiis Maluendæ confessoris, & similium, qui omnes tanquam inimici Christi proter veræ religionis professionem, eius sanguinem modis omnibus profundere conaretur. Alia etiam quædam in hanc sententiam fraudulenta verba fictitiæ literæ continebant. Tandem cum intentus esset lectioni literarum Ioannes Diazius, carnifex qui a tergo stabat, exeruit securim, quam hactenus sub pallio tectam occultaverat, eámque in dextrum latus capitis circa tempora viri sancti, totam usque ad manubrium inseruit. Et quoniam uno quasi momento fuerant læsa & planè destructa omnia organa sensuum in cerebro, nullam edere vocem potuit vere gloriosus martyr Christi. Deinde, ne corpus iam penè exanimatum sua sponte concideret, suaque ruina strepitum in ædibus excitaret, qua occasione in ipso facinore deprehenderentur parricidæ, carnifex, qui facinus perpetrarat, utraque manu prehendit corpus, ac humi reclinatum, & securim in ipso capite infertam, in medio hypocausto reliquit. Postea ad suum herum parricidam, paulatim gradus descendit, quæ quidem omnia tanta celeritate & silentio gesta sunt, ut nullus interim vel interuenire, vel exaudire rem gestam potuerit. Claudius vero Senarclæus, iuuenis nobili loco apud Sabaudos ortus unà cum Diazio tum cubabat, atque in lecto remanserat: sinistra tamen nescio qua suspicione perculsus statim de lecto exilit, & arreptis vestibus ingredi voluit hypocaustum, ut quid ageret Diazius videret. egressus igitur cubiculum, audit primum calcaria parricidarum, qui erant in ipsis gradibus: & quoniam dubitabat utrum ascenderent an vero descenderent, clausit ianuam gradum, & rectà ingreditur hypocaustum, ut ibi vestes induceret. Cum primum illud ingressus est, & spectaculum quod in ea humi reclinatum iacebat, vidit, totus cohorruit, & præ stupore ceciderunt vestes de manibus, vóxque ipsa faucibus hæsit interclusa. Tandem ubi se recollegit, accessit ad amicum, quem humi prostratum videbat, in cælum conversis oculis, cōplicatis manibus oranti similem. pertenuis restabat in eo vitalis spiritus qui ad unam fermè horam duravit. Interim ipse quando aliquam de Deo mentionem audiebat, se intelligere tenui quodam oculorum indicio præbebat significationem. Claudius vero mox convocauit domesticos omnes, qui adfuerunt tristissimi spectaculi atque horrendi facinoris spectatores. Illi facinus perpetratum inter vicinos diuulgarunt ea celeritate, vt rei gestæ esset per vniuersam platea iam peruagata fama, priusquam parricidæ essent egressi porta ciuitatis. Paulatim quoque res delata est ad magistratum oppidi & ad præfectum arcis, qui nomine illustrissimi principis Ottonis Henrici Palatini locum & gubernationem tenet. Isti quoniam erant viri honestissimi, & in vera religione præclarè instituti, sciebantque Ioannem Diazium propter excellentem virtutem atque pietatem fuisse Christianissimo principi Ottoni charissimum, sine mora constituerunt aliquot equites qui celeri equorum cursu parricidas insequerentur. Itaque post cædem factam vsque ad tempus quo equites insequuti sunt facinorosos, vix semi-horæ spatium est interpositum. Parricidæ qui eos præcedebat, cum audiretur hora septima, iam erat in oppido Bothmes, vbi relictis equis iam prorsus delassatis, suos qui erant pulchrè habiti & requieti, conscenderunt, in quibus celeri cursu Augustam contenderunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile Alphonsus and his companions, once they had mounted their horses, reached within a few hours the village commonly called Veldkirchen, situated near the town of Neuburg itself, and there they spent the night. On the following day, that is 27 March, before the gates were opened, they came to Neuburg. It was not yet fully light, though the town gates were already open, so they dismounted, tied their horses to a hedge and left them in the care of the messenger. There the executioner, Alphonsus's servant, took the messenger's coat and cap, so that he would be less recognised in the town. Thus disguised, he went into the town with his master. The executioner walked in front and the parricide followed behind, for they had agreed that the deed would be done by the executioner's hand, since he was otherwise the more skilful, while the parricide himself would stay close at hand, to bring help to his executioner if some necessity required it or if the business went less well, and so give aid to the wicked ruffian. So Alphonsus the parricide always followed in the footsteps of the servant-executioner. Thus disguised, they entered the town and arrived at the house of the preacher, where John had been received as a guest. There the executioner first knocked and asked the preacher's brother, who opened the door, where John Diazius was, to whom he claimed to be bringing a letter from Alphonsus. The young man who served in the household, who had already known this servant and Alphonsus well, answered that John was indeed still in bed. But what did that new form of dress mean to him, or what did that change of clothing signify? The executioner, however, so that he might not be betrayed there, made the young man go up and announce to John that he was there with a letter from his brother. When John Diazius understood this, he leapt out of bed with great haste, eager to learn what his brother meant. In his excessive hurry he took no clothes except a light cloak, with which alone he covered himself, and went out of his bedroom into the heated room that lay opposite the bedroom, where he was to receive the servant as he came in. The executioner went up, led by the young man mentioned above. Alphonsus remained at the lower door, which closed the stairs, to watch the entrance, so that no one should come up and hinder the deed. While matters stood in this state, and were evidently somewhat disturbed by the presence of the young man, who was hindering the speed of the deed, the young man was sent to the spring to fetch a cup of water. With the young man thus gone, the executioner, who had remained alone with the victim, showed the letter from his brother, which he said had been sent from Augsburg, although the wicked parricide was close by on the stairs. John took the letter and, since it was barely daylight, went to the window so that he could more easily read what was written in the letter by the light of the gradually brightening day. The content of the letter, as was later learned by friends who read it, was as follows: it said that he had been informed that, on first arriving at Augsburg, he himself was in great danger; and therefore, moved by brotherly affection, he had wished to warn him to take careful heed against the plots of the confessor of Maluenda and others like him, who all, as enemies of Christ, were trying in every way to shed his blood on account of his profession of the true religion. The forged letter also contained several other fraudulent words to the same effect. At last, while John Diazius was intent on reading the letter, the executioner who stood behind him drew the axe, which he had hitherto hidden under his cloak, and drove it into the right side of the holy man's head, near the temple, right up to the handle. And since in almost a single moment all the organs of sense in the brain were injured and utterly destroyed, the truly glorious martyr of Christ could utter no sound. Then, lest the body, now almost lifeless, should fall of its own accord and its collapse cause a noise in the house, by which the parricides might be caught in the very deed, the executioner who had committed the crime seized the body with both hands, laid it down on the ground in the middle of the heated room, and left the axe sunk in the head. Afterwards he went down the steps step by step to his master the parricide. All these things were done with such speed and silence that meanwhile no one could either come in or hear what had happened. But Claudius Senarclaeus, a young man of noble family born among the Savoyards, had been lying in the same room with Diazius and had remained in bed. Yet struck by some sinister suspicion, he leapt from the bed at once, and, grabbing his clothes, wanted to enter the heated room to see what Diazius was doing. So he left the bedroom and first heard the spurs of the parricides, who were on the stairs themselves; and since he hesitated whether they were going up or coming down, he shut the door at the top of the stairs and went straight into the heated room to put on his clothes there. As soon as he entered and saw the spectacle lying on the ground there, he shuddered all over, and from sheer astonishment the clothes fell from his hands, and the voice itself stuck in his throat. At last, when he collected himself, he went to his friend whom he saw stretched on the ground, with eyes turned to heaven and hands folded, like one praying. Only a very slight spark of life remained in him, which lasted for nearly an hour. Meanwhile, whenever he heard any mention of God, he gave a faint sign with a slight movement of his eyes that he understood. Claudius then at once summoned all the household, who were present as spectators of this most sorrowful sight and horrible crime. They spread the news of the deed among the neighbours with such speed that, before the parricides had left the city gate, the report of the event had already spread through the whole street. Gradually the matter was also reported to the magistrates of the town and to the commander of the castle, who held the place and government in the name of the most illustrious prince Otto Henry, Count Palatine. These men, since they were most honourable and well instructed in the true religion, and knew that John Diazius, on account of his outstanding virtue and piety, had been most dear to the most Christian prince Otto, without delay appointed several horsemen to pursue the parricides at a swift pace. So between the killing and the time when the horsemen set out after the wrongdoers, scarcely half an hour had passed. The parricide who was going in front, when it was heard to be the seventh hour, was already in the town of Bothmes, where, leaving their horses now quite exhausted, they mounted their own, which were well fed and rested, and in these they hastened to Augsburg at full speed.

units.la: Iam verò equites Neoburgenses, qui parricidas insequebatur, vbi Augustam peruenissent, ibique certò accepissent multò antea vlterius esse progressos, consultare inter se coeperunt de redeundo, quia se assequi posse præcurrentes dissidebat. sed inter eos extitit quidam cæteris ætate minor, cui nomen erat Michaeli Herpffer, qui præ reliquis ingenti zelo permotus, dicit amicis qui secum venerant, Amici, vobis quidem si ita videtur, integrum erit redire domum. Nam quod attinet ad præsens negotium, tantùm meo iudicio vel vnus solus præstare poterit, quantum alioqui magna hominum multitudo. Ego ista curam ad me recipio, ac sanctè vobis promitto me in hoc negotio extrema omnia tentaturum: nec prius cursum intermissurum, si suppetent vires & vita perstabit, quàm parricidas ipsos fuerim assecutus. Et cum hoc dicto denuò conscendit equum, & facinorosos insequitur. cucurrit toto illo die vsque ad noctem, donec peruenit ad oppidum quoddam quatuor milliaribus ab Oeniponte situm, quo in loco intellexit parricidas adesse. Ibi iussit accersiri hospitem, cuius in diuersorio parricidas esse intellexerat. Hospes aduenieni narrauit eos dormire, ac mandasse familiæ, vt antequam hora integra elaberetur, ipsos è somno excitaret. Michael admonuit hospitem, homines esse facinorosos, qui tantum facinus perpetrassent, quantum à memoria hominum post primum parricidium, cidium, nullum extaret: mandauit autem hospiti silentium, deinde vt ps[?] duas integras horas dormire permitteret.
units.tr: Now the Neuburg horsemen who were pursuing the parricides, when they had reached Augsburg and there had learned for certain that the men had gone much further ahead, began to deliberate among themselves about turning back, since they despaired of being able to overtake those who were running ahead. But among them there was one younger than the rest, named Michael Herpffer, who, moved by a great zeal beyond the others, said to the friends who had come with him: "Friends, if it seems so to you, it will be open to you to return home. For as far as the present business is concerned, in my judgement one man alone may accomplish as much as a large crowd otherwise would. I take this care upon myself, and I solemnly promise you that in this business I will attempt every extreme measure, and will not give up the pursuit, if strength holds and life endures, until I have overtaken the parricides themselves." And with these words he mounted his horse again and pursued the wrongdoers. He rode the whole day until nightfall, until he came to a certain town four miles from Innsbruck, where he learned that the parricides were present. There he ordered the host summoned, in whose inn he had learned the parricides were. The host, on his arrival, reported that they were asleep, and had ordered the household that before a full hour had passed they should wake them from sleep. Michael warned the host that these were men who had committed so great a crime that none like it had been known in human memory since the first parricide. He ordered the host to keep silent, and then to let them sleep for two full hours.

units.la: Ipse vero linteis & annis obligauit pedes equorum, ne forte strepitu solearum in plateis excitarentur è somno parricidæ, magnáque celeritate ad OEnipontē contendit, vbi eos aliquot horis anteuertit. Cùm primùm ad ciuitatē peruenit, magistratum admonuit, flagitium parricidarum narrauit, & eius fidem atque auxilium, ne tantum facinus maneret impunitum, implorauit.
units.tr: Michael himself wrapped the horses' hooves in linen and cloth, so that the clatter of their shoes on the streets would not wake the murderers from sleep, and he hurried to Innsbruck with great speed, where he got ahead of them by several hours. As soon as he reached the city, he informed the magistrate of the murderers' crime, told the story, and implored its trust and help, so that so great a crime would not go unpunished.

units.la: Magistratus suum auxilium & diligentiam in hoc sceere puniendo promisit. Admonetur praeterea hospes in diuersorio, vni[?] diuertere cogebantur, vt si quando tales viri ad se venissent, non prius illos abire permitteret, quàm eos adesse magistratui significasset. Paulò post aduenerunt[?] parricidæ, eósque iam aduenisse mox indicauit hospes. Ibi tum aliquot armati equites mittuntur, qui ædes obsederūt, ne quà facinorosi elaberentur, alij pedites ministri publici ædes ingrediuntur[?], vt parricidas comprehenderent: qui cùm viderent se hoc modo circunuentos, inceperunt clamare cælum & terram, testari omnia sacra & prophana, se nobiles esse viros Cæsareæ maiestatis legatos, qui ad peragenda negotia grauissima totiúsque Reipublicæ salutaria ab ipso Imperatore mitterentur. Sed apud eos qui eorum parricidium iam nouerant, & vanissima esse quæ dicerent omnia faciebant, nihil istiusmodi falsi clamores & conficta mendacia valuerunt. Primum itaq; Alphonsum, qui viribus ministrorum non potuit resistere, cöprehenderunt. Carnificem verò, qui viribus & audacia valebat, & ministris publicis audacissimè obsistebat, vix tandem post longam pugnam, necsine aliquot vulneribus comprehendere potuerunt. Tandem vbi ad hunc modum parricidæ fuerunt in carcerem detrusi, Michael qui negotium perdiligenter curauerat, celeri cursu equorum significauit rem gestā Neoburgensibus. Illi vicissim illustrissimo principi Ottoni Henrico Palatino, qui audita captiuitate parricidarum, diserte mandauit, vt in persequenda illa causa in iudicio contra parricidas, nullis sumptibus, nullis laboribus parceretur. Sunt igitur constituti duo viri præstantes, qui è Neoburgo, nomine principis Ottonis OEnipontem proficiscerētur: quorum alter nobilis Thomas Redwitz, alter iuris vtriusq; quop ctor[?], Galielmus vocabatur. Isti duo per celeres equos profecti OEnipontem primo die Aprilis peruenerunt, tanquam actores, ut intenderent parricidij crimen aduersus captiuos, & secum attulerunt pileum nocturnum Diazij, fictitias literas fratris, & securim sanguine sanctissimi martyris Diazij undique respersam, ut si forte parricidae inficiarentur factum, certissimis testimonijs euincere possent. Interim autem concessum Alphonso parricidae fuit, ut scriberet literas ad Cardinales Tridentinum & Augustanum, qui nihil omiserunt, ut a merito supplicio parricidas liberarent.
units.tr: The magistrate promised its help and diligence in punishing this wicked deed. The host at the inn was further warned, since the men were obliged to lodge there, that if such men ever came to his house, he was not to let them leave until he had told the magistrate that they were there. A little later the murderers arrived, and the host soon reported that they had come. Then some armed horsemen were sent, who surrounded the house so that the criminals could not escape, and other public servants, foot soldiers, went into the house to seize the murderers. When the men saw that they were surrounded in this way, they began to cry out to heaven and earth, to call on every sacred and profane witness, saying that they were noblemen and envoys of the Imperial Majesty, sent by the Emperor himself to carry out most weighty business, one that was vital to the whole commonwealth. But these cries and invented lies counted for nothing with those who already knew of the murder and who judged everything they said to be utterly empty. So first they seized Alphonsus, who could not resist the force of the servants. The executioner, who was strong and bold, and who most boldly opposed the public officers, could only be captured at last, after a long struggle and not without several wounds. When the murderers had been thrown into prison in this way, Michael, who had taken great pains over the affair, sent word of what had been done to the men of Neuburg by a swift horse. They in turn informed the most illustrious prince Otto Henry, Count Palatine, who, on hearing of the capture of the murderers, expressly ordered that no expense and no labour be spared in pursuing the case against them in court. Two outstanding men were therefore appointed to set out from Neuburg for Innsbruck in the name of Prince Otto: one was the nobleman Thomas Redwitz, the other, called Wilhelm, a doctor of both laws. These two travelled on fast horses and reached Innsbruck on the first day of April, as prosecutors, to press the charge of murder against the prisoners. They also brought with them Diaz's night cap, a forged letter of his brother, and an axe spattered all over with the blood of the most holy martyr Diaz, so that, if the murderers should deny the deed, they could prove it by the most certain evidence. Meanwhile Alphonsus, the murderer, was allowed to write letters to the Cardinals of Trent and Augsburg, who left nothing undone to save the murderers from their deserved punishment.

units.la: Secundo die Aprilis legati Neoburgenses postularunt ut supplicium de parricidis sumeretur, ab iis qui Regis Ferdinandi nomine praesunt gubernationi OEnipotanae. Hi responderunt, non esse suarum partium capitale supplicium de quoquam sumere: sed mandaturos iudici Suneburgensi, ut is assessores suos sine mora conuocaret, quorum authoritate iudicium erat instituendum. Eodem die à prandio gubernatores OEnipontani curauerunt per duos, quos illi secretarios vocant, denuntiari parricidis aducentum & accusationem legatorum Neoburgensium. Audito nuntio & accusatione, apud istos duos Secretarios uterque parricida factum negauit: sed minister constantius, Alphonsus vero timidius, & mutatione coloris acvultus significationem vulneratae conscientiae clare ostendebat. Supplex tamen orauit, ne quid praepropere de se statuerent. Eodem die inter primam & secundam horam pomeridianam, translati sunt parricidae à publico illo loco supremi iudicij, vbi primum fuerant collocati, ad custodiam ciuitatis OEnipotanae, quo in iudicio breuior sententia sperari posse videbatur.
units.tr: On the second day of April, the envoys from Neuburg demanded that the murderers be punished, from those who presided over the government of Innsbruck in the name of King Ferdinand. They replied that it was not within their power to inflict capital punishment on anyone, but that they would instruct the judge of Sonneburg to summon his assessors without delay, by whose authority the trial was to be held. On the same day, after dinner, the governors of Innsbruck arranged for two men, whom they call secretaries, to inform the murderers of the arrival and the accusation of the envoys from Neuburg. When the messenger and the accusation had been heard, each murderer denied the deed before these two secretaries. But the minister did so more firmly, while Alphonsus did so more timidly, and his change of colour and expression clearly showed the signs of a wounded conscience. Nevertheless, he begged as a suppliant that they should not decide anything rashly about him. On the same day, between one and two o'clock in the afternoon, the murderers were transferred from that public place of the supreme court, where they had first been placed, to the custody of the city of Innsbruck, since a shorter sentence seemed likely to be obtained in that court.

units.la: Sequenti die, qui tertius erat Aprilis, Legati postularunt ut parricidae tormentis subiicerentur. Id verò non solum non est factum, verùm etiā aduocati nomine Regiminis sunt parricidis designati, nobiles viri & iurisconsulti, Vlrichus Schmatzer, & Georgius Hipp, vtriusq; iuris doctores, & Michael Schenck, & Christophorus Grumperger. Reclamabant ad hoc fortiter legati, affirmantes neque humano iure neque Diuino concessum esse, ut in tanto tamque manifesto scelere patronus reo concederetur. Sed haec denoranda[?] fuit legatis iniuria, qui causam iustitiae ac veritatis volebant defendere, ne tantum facinus maneret impunitum, adeò iudicum animos fregerant improborum hominum solicitatio[?]licitationes. Constituto igitur die, rei producti sunt in curiam oppili, ubi legati Neoburgenses eos accusarunt: pileum cum literis & scuri exhibuerunt. Advocati vero detrectantes respondere ad legatorum Neoburgensium accusationem, forum[?] declinarunt exceptione clericatus, petieruntque illos tradi iudicandos eius loci ordinario episcopo Brixiensi, qui est idem Tridentinus, homo ea vitæ dissolutione, ut merito sit creatus Cardinalis. Legati sedulo instabant, petentes iudicium secundum morem eius provinciæ sicut par erat, quia nolebant cam disputationem ingredi de competenti foro & privilegiis clericorum, quibus advocati extrahere illos nitebantur.
units.tr: On the following day, which was the third of April, the envoys demanded that the murderers be put to torture. This was not only not done, but advocates were actually appointed for the murderers in the name of the government: nobles and jurists, Ulrich Schmatzer and Georg Hipp, doctors of both laws, and Michael Schenck and Christoph Grumperger. The envoys protested strongly against this, asserting that neither human nor divine law allowed that, in so great and so manifest a crime, a defender should be granted to the accused. But this injustice was overlooked by the envoys, who wished to defend the cause of justice and truth, lest so great a crime should remain unpunished, so far had the solicitations of wicked men broken the spirit of the judges. When a day had been fixed, the accused were brought into the court of the magistrate, where the envoys from Neuburg accused them and produced the cap, the letters and the axe. But the advocates refused to answer the accusation of the envoys from Neuburg and declined the court on the plea of clerical privilege. They asked that the men be handed over for judgment to the ordinary bishop of that place, the bishop of Brixen, who is the same as the bishop of Trent, a man of such dissolute life that he was rightly made a Cardinal. The envoys urged persistently, asking for a trial according to the custom of that province, as was fitting, because they did not wish to enter into a dispute about the competent court and the privileges of clerics, by which the advocates were trying to remove the men from the court.

units.la: Iudices per interlocutoriam pronuntiarunt, advocatos cum parricidis debere de responsione ad accusationem legatorum inter se constituere, eámque tertio inde die, hoc est, x Aprilis, ad horam septimam ante meridiem in iudicio exhibere. Et sive responderent, sive minus, iudices nihilominus facere debere quod iuris esset de more regionis. Eo die cum rursus in iudicium ventum est, advocati cœperùt urgere exceptionem de clericatu, & tradendis reis ordinario iudici. Legati contra urgebant superius dictam sententiam interlocutoriam. Iudices itaque secundo pronuntiarunt, reos & advocatos citra ullam exceptionem aut ulteriorem dilationem respondere debere ad accusationem legatorum: sed alterum illis terminum designarunt, diem Aprilis xii, & quamvis eo tempore non responderent, debere tamen fieri quod ius & consuetudo provinciæ postularent. Iam vero xii die, qui ultimus terminus ad respondendum in iudicio fuerat constitutus, non solùm nihil actum est ab advocatis reorum, sed ne Legatos quidem Neoburgenses ad agendum iudices admiserunt, contra id quod ipsi de iure ac more regionis ante iudicaverant. Hæc videntes Legati protestati sunt nisi in iudicio maturè & ordine, sicut par erat, procederent, se velle graviter de hac iniuria conqueri suis principibus, non solùm propter sumptus, qui permagni fiebant (nam impensis ipsorum iudices convocabantur, & dum iudicij causa aderant, sustentabantur) sed etiam quòd nulla fieret apud istos parricidas matura inquisitio eorum consiliorum, quæ adversus Evangelij professores Romæ aut in aliis locis capta essent. Audita protestatione horum, Regetes illis responderunt, iudicē habere mandatum, ut postridie,hoc est, decimo tertio Aprilis, in iudicio progrederetur. Is autem iudex paulò post condixit legatis horam sequentis diei duodecimam: ad quam in locum iudicij legati comparuerunt. adeo nullam occasionem prætermittebant, quanvis ludibrio se haberi à iudicibus videbant: qui puerorum more in ista causa pro suo arbitrio ludebant. Hora igitur constituta aderant legati: sed aduocati parricidarum neque aderant, neque inveniri poterant. quos cùm iudex satis diu expectasset, iussit tandem eos voce præconis è curia vocari. cumque nec sic vocati adessent, iudex in causa procedere volebat. Ibi demùm advenerunt advocati, & primùm conquesti sunt graviter de vocatione per præconem factâ. deinde petiuerunt spatium respondendi usque ad horâ tertiam: quod iudex illis permisit. Interim advocati apud consilium regiminis egerunt, ut iudex hora demùm sexta responsum daret: atque, ut aiebat, ex mandato Regentum, legatos debere suam accusationem contra parricidas in iudicio ante propositam, curare vertendam in linguam Latinam & Hispanicam: eóque facto, tum demùm imponendum esse reis ut responderent. quod aperte contrarium erat primæ & secundæ interlocutoriæ sententiæ: maximè autem secundæ, quæ diserte omnem ulteriorem dilationem & exceptionem præciderat. Cùm itaque legati viderent tam indignis modis protrahi iudicium, aliam rursus postulationem exhibuerunt in consilio Regiminis, circa horam octauam sequentis diei, qui Aprilis erat XIIII. in qua de ista ludificatione iudicij, & iniuria quæ suis Principibus & toti causæ fieret, gravissimè querebantur.
units.tr: The judges pronounced by an interlocutory decree that the advocates and the murderers should agree among themselves on an answer to the envoys' accusation, and should present it in court on the third day after that, that is, on the tenth of April, at seven o'clock in the morning. And whether they answered or not, the judges were nonetheless to do what the law and the custom of the region required. On that day, when they came again to court, the advocates began to press their plea about clerical privilege and the handing over of the accused to the ordinary judge. The envoys in turn pressed the aforesaid interlocutory sentence. So the judges pronounced a second time that the accused and their advocates were to answer the envoys' accusation without any further plea or delay, but they set another deadline for them, the twelfth of April, and declared that, even if they did not answer at that time, what the law and custom of the province demanded was to be done. Now on the twelfth day, which had been fixed as the final deadline for answering in court, the advocates of the accused not only did nothing, but the judges did not even admit the envoys from Neuburg to make their case, contrary to what they themselves had previously decided according to the law and custom of the region. Seeing this, the envoys protested that, unless the court proceeded promptly and in proper order, as was fitting, they would complain seriously of this injustice to their princes, not only because of the expenses, which were becoming very great (for the judges were summoned at their expense and maintained while they were present for the trial), but also because no timely inquiry was being made among these murderers into the plans that had been devised against the professors of the Gospel at Rome or in other places. When they had heard this protest, the regents answered them that the judge had orders to proceed in court the following day, that is, on the thirteenth of April. Shortly afterwards the judge arranged with the envoys that they should appear at the twelfth hour of the next day. At the place of the court the envoys came at that hour; so little did they neglect any opportunity, though they saw that the judges were mocking them, playing with the case as children do, following their own whim. So at the appointed hour the envoys were present, but the advocates of the murderers were neither present nor could be found. When the judge had waited a long time for them, he at last ordered them to be summoned from the court by the voice of a herald. And when they still did not come even after being summoned in this way, the judge wished to proceed with the case. Then at last the advocates arrived, and first complained bitterly of the summons made by the herald. Next they asked for time to answer until the third hour, which the judge granted them. Meanwhile the advocates pleaded before the council of government that the judge should give his answer only at the sixth hour, and that, as they said, by order of the regents, the envoys should first have their accusation against the murderers, already presented in court, translated into Latin and Spanish, and only after that was done should the accused be required to answer. This was plainly contrary to the first and second interlocutory sentences, and especially to the second, which had clearly cut off every further delay and plea. Therefore, when the envoys saw the trial being dragged out in such shameful ways, they presented another petition to the council of government, about the eighth hour of the following day, which was the fourteenth of April, in which they complained most gravely of this mockery of the trial, and of the injustice done to their princes and to the whole cause.

units.la: Lecta illa petitione legatorum, consilium Regiminis, hora inter nonam & decimam eius diei, legatos in consilium admiserunt: atque illis præsentibus legerunt scriptum Imperatoris, quod per veredarios eodem die se accepisse affirmabant. Illud autem datum erat in urbe imperiali Dinckelspihel, IIII. Aprilis, in quo mandabat Imperator, ut totum huius parricidij iudicium suspenderetur: de quo ipse cum fratre Romanorum rege in præsentibus comitijs volebat iudicare. Auditis igitur istis literis, alter legatorum Neoburgum rediit, quia nullam spem consequendæ iustitiæ reliquam habebant. Palàm enim quidam pontificiæ impictatis sectatores, præcipuè autem Hispani, in urbe OEnipote diceint, parricidas fecisse quod iustum esset. nam qui haereticum interfiat, eum iam esse à Pontifice absolutum. Scripserunt interea illustrissimi principes, Elector Palatinus & Otto Henricus, ad regentes OEi-pontenses, ut parricidae sub cautione constituerêtur in oppido Neoburgensi, quo in loco perpetratum erat parricidium, aut certè permitterent, ut ipsi illos iudicarent prout iure gentium deceret. At illi sine ulla responsione, scriptum Imperatoris obiecerunt. Communes deinde status Protestantium Ratisbonae ter apud Imperatorem institerunt, ut permitteret ad finem istius iudicij, sicut coeptum erat, peruenieri. Sed nullum ab eo responsum acceperunt. Quae omnia Papae cum suis Cardinalibus accepta ferenda sunt, qui ad defensionem suorum carnificum, totam istam causam instituerunt. quibus etiam debemus responsum datum gubernatoribus Neoburgensibus Ingolstadij, ad libellum supplicem quem ipsi obtulerunt Imperatori, cum hospes eorum esset Neoburgi: in quo reuerenter ab eo postularunt, ut mandaret iudiciibus in O Eniponte, ante quorum tribunal ista causa pendebat, ut iudicium maturarent. Quibus nihil aliud responsum fuit, quàm Imperatorem non habere potestatem mandandi in ea regione quae ad [illegible, ~2 letters]atrem regem Romanorum pertineret: apud quem, si quid esset impetrandum, instare oportereret, cum alioqui paucis ante diebus mandatum esset datum in urbe Dinckelspihel, nomine Imperatoris, de suspendendo iudicio.
units.tr: When the legates' petition had been read, the council of the government admitted the legates to the council between the ninth and tenth hours of that day. In their presence the council read a letter from the Emperor, which the legates affirmed they had received that same day by courier. It had been issued in the imperial city of Dinkelsbühl on 4 April, and in it the Emperor ordered that the whole trial of this parricide be suspended, since he wished to judge the matter himself, together with his brother the King of the Romans, at the present Diet. After hearing this letter, one of the legates returned to Neuburg, because they had no hope of obtaining justice. For some followers of Papist impiety, especially the Spaniards, openly said in the city of Oeniponte that the murderers had done what was just, since whoever kills a heretic has already been absolved by the Pope. Meanwhile the most illustrious princes, the Elector Palatine and Otto Henry, wrote to the rulers of Oeniponte asking that the murderers be placed under security in the town of Neuburg, where the murder had been committed, or at least that they allow the princes themselves to judge them as the law of nations required. But those rulers, without any answer on the point, pointed to the Emperor's letter. Afterwards the common estates of the Protestants at Regensburg pressed the Emperor three times that he would allow the trial to be brought to an end as it had been begun. But they received no answer from him. All of this must be charged to the Pope and his Cardinals, who set up this whole affair in defence of their executioners. We also owe to them the reply given at Ingolstadt by the governors of Neuburg to the supplication that they presented to the Emperor while they were staying as his guests at Neuburg. In it they respectfully asked him to order the judges at Oeniponte, before whose tribunal the case was pending, to hasten the judgment. To them nothing was answered except that the Emperor had no power to give orders in that region, which belonged to his brother the King of the Romans, and that if anything was to be obtained they should press him; yet only a few days earlier an order had been issued at Dinkelsbühl in the Emperor's name to suspend the trial.

units.la: In hoc igitur statu erant negotia parricidarum: cum quibus etiamsi eos Papa absoluat, nõ poterit non agi pessimè. Interea habet fideles exemplum in istis duobus fratribus coram oculis propositum, multis nominibus admirandum, plenum fraudis, crudelitatis, malitiae, impietatis: rursus plenum innocentiae, mansuetudinis, gloriae, grauitatis, constantiae, verae religionis. Denique totum exemplum tale est, cui vix simile vllum in historijs memoriae proditum reperiri queat, praeter exemplum primi fratris parricidae Cain, qui propter eandem verae religionis professionem, innocentissimum fratrem Abelem interfecit, ad. quam imaginem haec ipsa plenè facta atque exculpta videtur.
units.tr: Such, then, was the state of affairs of the murderers. Even if the Pope absolves them, they cannot but be dealt with most severely. Meanwhile the faithful have before their eyes in these two brothers an example that is to be wondered at in many respects, full of fraud, cruelty, malice and impiety, and yet again full of innocence, gentleness, glory, gravity, constancy and true religion. In short, the whole example is such that scarcely any like it can be found recorded in history, except the example of the first murderous brother, Cain, who, for the same profession of true religion, slew his most innocent brother Abel. This present deed seems to be fully formed and modelled on that image.

units.la: Marci XIII.
units.tr: Mark 13.

units.la: Tradet frater fratrem in mortem.
units.tr: Brother shall betray brother to death.

units.la: STEPHANUS POLLIOTUS.
units.tr: STEPHANUS POLLIOTUS.

units.la: TEphanus Polliotus in oppido Saint-dauberuille nat' vicino urbi Caudebek quae in est Neustria armorica quam Normandiam vocant, relicto natali solo in Meldarum oppidum se contulit. Eo in loco diu non desedit quin ab hostibus veritatis Evangelicae acerrime vexaretur, adeo ut discessum adornare & parare, atq; urbe excedere cogeretur. Haud ita multo post recta inde contendit Feram, Tretenesum oppidum, quod a Suessionibus decè millium intervallo abest. ibi porro comprehensus est & Lutetiam deductus, atque in vincula coiectus: in quibus diu multumq; asseruatus in magno squalore & paedore versabatur. Tandem quando in mentem Senatoribus venit, illius amplissimae Curiae decretum factum est quo lingua ei amputaretur, vivusq; cremarctur[?] inaudito & plane novo modo. sarcina enim librorum illius humeris imposita est, cum qua exustus fuit. Cum vero e carceribus Curiae supremae ad supplicium duceretur, antequam lingua praecisa esset, his fere verbis locutus est, Hei Deus bone, mundúsne adhuc in tenebris[?] & densissima veritatis ignoratione iacet? Existimabat enim vir pius, dum tetro carcere inclusus solem hunc non intuitus esset, Christum, verum iustitiae solem homines verbi sui cognitione illuminasse. Hic Stephanus clarissimus Iesu Christi martyr, supplicii mortis atrocissimae patienter, placide & sedate pertulit Lutetiae in platea Maubertina, anno circiter M.D.XLVI.
units.tr: Stephanus Polliotus, born in the town of Saint-Dauberuille near Caudebec, which lies in Neustria Armorica (the region they call Normandy), left his native soil and went to the town of Meaux. He did not stay long there before the enemies of the Gospel of truth harassed him most fiercely, so much so that he was forced to prepare for departure and to leave the city. Not long afterwards he went straight from there to Fère, the town of Tretenes, which is ten thousand paces from Soissons. There he was seized and taken to Paris and thrown into chains. Kept in them for a long time, he lived in great filth and squalor. At last, when it occurred to the senators, a decree of that most distinguished court was made that his tongue should be cut out and that he should be burned alive, in an unheard-of and entirely new manner: a bundle of his books was placed on his shoulders, and he was burned along with it. Indeed, when he was being led from the prisons of the supreme court to execution, before his tongue was cut out, he spoke roughly these words: "Good God, does the world still lie in darkness and in the thickest ignorance of the truth?" For this godly man believed that, since he had been shut up in a foul prison and had not looked upon the sun, Christ, the true sun of righteousness, had illuminated men with the knowledge of his Word. This Stephanus, the most illustrious martyr of Jesus Christ, endured the most atrocious death patiently, calmly and steadily, at the Place Maubert in Paris, in about the year 1546.

units.la: SAINTINUS NIVETUS.
units.tr: SAINTINUS NIVETUS.

units.la: Hic extremum vitae spiritum acerbissima morte profudit Parisiis, aliquanto post Polliotum martyrem.
units.tr: He breathed out his last breath at Paris by a most bitter death, shortly after the martyr Polliot.

units.la: S[?]i quis hisce nostris temporibus unquam extitit qui cultus divi-ni profanationem feruido animo detestatus est, & cui haec vita inucunda fuit propter horrendam Ecclesiae ruinam quae sub crudelissimo Antichristi dominatu conspicitur: si quis praeterea praesenti paratáque voluntate se unquam morti obtulit pro tuenda & defendenda Dei gloria: is certe Saintinus Niuetus Meldensis fuit. Cum enim XIIII. illi insignes Martyres quorum historia supra descripta est libro tertio, Meldis combusti fuere, quaesitus se recepit aliquatisper cum uxoin eas regiones in quibus publicè & summa libertate Euangelium nūntiatur. Animaduertes autem se Mombeliardi inutile esse & ecclesiae[?] tantum onerierat enim membris penè omnibus captus ac debilis, instituit ad certamen reuerti: à quo instituto nullis neque Ministrorum eius loci, neque vxoris suae admonitionibus abstrahi potuit: imò verò vxori respondebat, se commodius & tutius illic agere, quam ob usam ignaui & inertes redderentur: breuiter rursum se periculis expositum cupiebat. Itaque Meldarum in oppidum rediit, atque in nundinis quae ibi ad diem festum S. Martini celebrantur, nonnullas exiguas merces publico foro venales exposuit. Illico agnitus fuit & in carcerem compactus: ipsius denique causa sine mora & confestim instructa & confecta fuit. Nihil enim opus erat inquisitionibus aut testium productionibus. Nam longè plura ipse sponte confitebatur, quàm iudices vel postularent vel audire cuperent. Iam verò cum aliquod doctrinae Christianae caput proponeret, & iudices ei dicerent his verbis, Visne hoc tueri ac defendere? fidenter respondebat, Et vos Iudices, audeatis pernegare quod tam aperte verum est & testatum? Quae quidem responsio imprimis digna est memoria & accurata observatione. Enimvero tantum abest vt sibi gratiam fieri postularet, vt etiam Meldis & Parisiis iudices precibus obsecraret, vt tandem aliquam suarum animarum rationem haberent, & salutis suae curam susciperent, secumque perpenderent quantum sanguinis innoxij iam crudeliter effudissent, quotidie bellum suscipiendo aduersus Iesum Christum ac eius Euangelium. Equidem dubium non est quin eiusmodi grauissimis exhortationibus delicatae Senatorum aures magnopere offenderentur, praesertim verò M. Petri Liseti qui tunc temporis Senatui Parisiensi praesidebat, qui tum Meldis Regis vice ius dicebat, conspicatus illius hominis constantiam supplicibus verbis orauit praesidem vt cum Meldas non remitteret ad supplicium, ne vt dicebat, vir tam peruicax & obstinatus, longè deterior XIIII. illis praedictis clarissimis Martyribus, omnium ciuium fidem pergeret labefactare & corrumpere, hoc est, populum aedificare & veritate ad syncerum Dei cultum informare. Quocirca curauerunt iudices vt praeclarus ille Domini nostri Iesu Christi martyr Lutetiae Parisiorum vitā pro doctrina Euangelica redderet, anno fere M.D.XLVI. qua in morte nullum crudelitatis (quam acerrimi veritatis hostes quotidie aduersus seruos Dei excogitant & exercent) genus praetermissum est.
units.tr: If anyone in these our times has ever arisen who with a fervent spirit detested the profanation of divine worship, and for whom this life was unpleasant because of the dreadful ruin of the Church that is seen under the most cruel dominion of Antichrist; if anyone moreover has ever offered himself to death with a ready and prepared will to defend and maintain the glory of God, that man was certainly Saintin Nivet of Meaux. For when those fourteen famous martyrs, whose history is described above in the third book, were burned at Meaux, he withdrew for a while with his wife to those regions where the gospel is proclaimed publicly and with the greatest freedom. But realising that he was useless at Montbéliard and a burden to the church, for he was crippled and weakened in nearly all his limbs, he resolved to return to the conflict. Neither the admonitions of the ministers of that place nor those of his wife could draw him from this resolve. Indeed he replied to his wife that he was acting more suitably and safely there, than that men would be made lazy and slothful through disuse. In short, he again wished to be exposed to dangers. And so he returned to the town of Meaux, and at the fair held there on the feast of St Martin he put a few small wares up for sale in the public market. He was immediately recognised and thrown into prison. His case was then prepared and concluded at once, without delay, for there was no need of inquiries or the production of witnesses. Indeed he confessed of his own accord far more than the judges either asked or wished to hear. When he put forward some article of Christian doctrine and the judges said to him, "Will you maintain and defend this?", he answered boldly, "And will you judges dare to deny what is so openly true and attested?" That reply is especially worthy of being remembered and carefully noted. Indeed he was so far from seeking any favour for himself that, both at Meaux and at Paris, he even begged the judges with prayers that they would take some account of their souls, look to their salvation, and consider within themselves how much innocent blood they had already cruelly shed, waging war every day against Jesus Christ and his gospel. There is no doubt that the delicate ears of the senators were greatly offended by such grave exhortations, especially those of Master Pierre Lizet, who at that time presided over the Parisian Senate and was then administering justice at Meaux in the king's place. Seeing this man's constancy, Lizet prayed with pleading words to the president that Meaux should not be sent back to execution, lest, as he said, a man so stubborn and obstinate, far worse than those fourteen famous martyrs, should go on to shake and corrupt the faith of all the citizens, that is, to build up the people and form them in the truth for the sincere worship of God. Therefore the judges saw to it that this famous martyr of our Lord Jesus Christ gave up his life for the evangelical doctrine at Paris, in about the year 1546, and in that death no kind of cruelty was omitted, the kinds which the bitterest enemies of the truth daily devise and practise against the servants of God.

units.la: ANNA ASKEW Angliae decu- s.
units.tr: ANNA ASKEW, the glory of England.

units.la: Ntexuit[?] Dominus huic tam fragranti Martyrum coronae virgines & matronas insigni pietate praeditas, ut magnanimitatis atque inuictae constantiae exempla etiam in muliebris sexus imbecillitate ederet. His etenim temporibus ab illa toto orbe diuisa Britannia regnante adhuc Henrico eius nominis VIII. ad hunc testium suae veritatis chorum euocauit Annam Askeuam puellam aetate integra: quae cum generis nobilitate ac morum suauitate summa vitae integritatem coniunxerat. Patrem habebat nobilem ac praestantem virum D. Guilelmum Askeuum ex equestri apud Anglos ordine in ditione Lincolniensi, genere cum primis illustrem. Sane si quis ea quae Eusebius de Blandina memoriae tradidit cum huius Annae actionibus conferat, longe inter se differre intelliget. Nam haec quidem omnem sui sexus infirmitatem superans, mirabilem confessionem edidit ad defendendam Dei veritatem, ipsiusque gloriam: ac refellendam Missatici sacrificii blasphemiam atque idolomaniam. Inuicto quoque animo carceris horrores tulit: aduersariorum contumelias & iniurias fortiter perpessa est. Ac reuera Dominus in iuuenis illius foeminae infirmitate virtutis suae documentum exhibuit.
units.tr: The Lord wove into this most fragrant crown of martyrs virgins and matrons distinguished by remarkable piety, so as to display examples of greatness of spirit and unconquered constancy even in the weakness of the female sex. For in those times, when Britain, cut off from the whole world, was still ruled by Henry VIII, he called to this chorus of witnesses to his truth the girl Anne Askew, still in the bloom of youth, who had joined the nobility of her birth to the greatest sweetness of character and integrity of life. Her father was a noble and distinguished man, Sir William Askew, of the equestrian order among the English in the county of Lincoln, most illustrious by birth. Indeed, if anyone compares what Eusebius handed down in memory of Blandina with the acts of this Anne, he will understand that they differ greatly from one another. For she, surmounting all the weakness of her sex, made a wonderful confession in defence of God's truth and his glory, and in refuting the blasphemy and idolatry of the sacrifice of the Mass. She also bore the horrors of prison with an unconquered spirit, and bravely endured the insults and injuries of her adversaries. And truly the Lord showed in the weakness of this young woman a proof of his power.

units.la: Dum tormentis examinaretur, sanguis ruptis per vim venis passim effluxit, carnifices qui ea his cruciatibus affecerant, iidem erant & iudices: quod nusquam gentium etiam barbarissimarum fieri licitum est. ipsa tamen barbariem illorum & truculentiam plusquam belluinam patientia vicit. Quum ipsi iudices tam immanem quaestionem exercuissent, mulierem ad carcerem deduci curarunt; ipsa tamen in his miseriis non destitit se in Domino oblectare, firmamque spem concipere de eius bonitate, qui illam ad extremum fortem constantemque in asserenda veritatis causa redderet ac conseruaret. Interea dum in vinculis detineretur, literis mandauit quae in prima iudicum percontatione aduersus ipsam dicta aut gesta fuerc. scripsit etiam certamen quod contra hostes veritatis postremum sustinuit: idque praestitit rogatu multorum utriusque sexus fidelium lelium[?] qui illam,quandiu in custodia manebat,inuisebant,atque ut id facęret ad Dei gloriam & Ecclesiae utilitatem,impellebant. sed ipsam, in iis quae scripta reliquit,loquentem potius audianus[?] : quae Ioannes Foxus Anglus e vernaculo latinè,optimè expressit ut sequitur.
units.tr: While she was being examined by torture, her blood flowed everywhere from veins burst by force. The executioners who inflicted these torments were the same as the judges, which is permitted nowhere among the nations, even the most barbarous. Yet she conquered their barbarity and cruelty, which were more than beastly, by her patience. When the judges themselves had carried out so monstrous an interrogation, they had the woman taken back to prison; yet even in these miseries she did not cease to delight herself in the Lord, and to conceive a firm hope in the goodness of him who would keep her and make her at last strong and steadfast in asserting the cause of the truth. Meanwhile, while she was held in chains, she set down in writing what had been said and done against her at her first examination by the judges. She also wrote down the contest she had finally waged against the enemies of the truth, and she did this at the request of many faithful men and women who visited her as long as she remained in custody, and urged her to do so for the glory of God and the benefit of the Church. But let us rather hear her speaking in what she left written, which John Foxe the Englishman rendered excellently into Latin from the vernacular, as follows.

units.la: Prima disquisitio seu examinatio D. Annae Askeuae.
units.tr: The first examination, or inquiry, of Mistress Anne Askew.

units.la: Viri fratres, ac coniunctissimi in Christo commilitones, ut vobis vestris ac flagitationibus respondeam, Anno M. D. XLV. mense Martio,primùm in praetorio ephippiario, vbi adesse iubeor,venit ad me vnus è duodecim cognitoribus, qui quaestionibus exercendis praeerat, Christophorus Darius,rogans num crederem sacramentum, quod alari impendebat, re ac natura corpus esse Domini nostri. huic vicissim respondi,rogans similiter ipse mihi ostenderet,quamobrem beatus Stephanus lapidibus olim caederetur. quod quum ille se nescire diceret: Ita nec ego,inquam,futili quaestiunculae tuae sum responsura. Secundò, fœminae cuiusdam sermone dicebat testatum ac confirmatum esse, quae diceret,ita lectum esse à me alicubi, quemadmodum Deus in manufactis templis non habitaret : produxi illi cap. Act. vii, & xvii,ostendens quid Stephanus & Paulus ea de re reliquissent. Sciscitatur ille, quo pacto huc ego locum accepissem? Non sunt, inquam,margaritae porcis proijciendae,quibus multo magis glandes quercinae convenirent. Petit deinde, quur dicerem malle me versus quinque in bibliis Dei sacris legere,quàm totidem missas audire in templo? Ita quidem à me dictum esse non negaui: haud tamen propterea quòd de epistola ac euangelio[?] minus sentirem bene:sed ob hoc, quòd in illis plurimum sentiam ædificationis,hic verò omnino nihil.Cuius rei Divus Paulus 1.Cor.14 idoneus accedit testis, qui ait,Si incertam vocem det tuba,quis parabit se ad bellum?
units.tr: Brothers, and most closely joined fellow soldiers in Christ, to answer you and your questions: in March of the year 1545, first in the saddlers' court, where I was ordered to appear, one of the twelve examiners who presided over the questioning, Christopher Dare, came to me and asked whether I believed that the sacrament, which was offered at the altar, was in substance and nature the body of our Lord. In reply I asked him in turn to show me why the blessed Stephen was once stoned with stones. When he said he did not know, I said: "Neither will I answer your trifling little question." Secondly, he said that a certain woman's testimony had been confirmed, the woman saying that I had been heard to read somewhere that God does not dwell in temples made with hands. I produced for him Acts 7 and 17, showing what Stephen and Paul had left on that matter. He then asked how I had come by this passage. "Pearls are not to be cast before swine," I said, "and acorns would suit them far better." Next he asked why I said I would rather read five verses of the holy Word of God than hear as many masses in the temple. I did not deny that I had said this, yet not because I thought poorly of the Epistle or the Gospel, but because I found much edification in them, and none at all in the masses. The divine Paul is a fitting witness to this, who says in 1 Cor. 14: "If the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle?"

units.la: Pergens tum ille: Dixisti,inquit,siquidem malus ac impurus sacerdos sacramentum conficeret, Sathanam id esse non Deum. Respondi, nunquam id à me dictum esse: sed hoc affirmasse me, Quisquis esset, aut quacunque vitahuius[?] administer Sacramenti,id nihil derogare meae fidei, nec obstare mihi, quin spiritu nihilominus sumerem corpus & sanguinem Christi. Quinto loco, quid de Confessione sentirem interrogat: Idem prorsus, inquam, quod Divus Jacobus, qui nos mutuò peccata confiteri, ac precari inuicem monet. Post hæc ventum est ad librum quem regium nominant, de quo quid haberem animi requirebat. Respondi, Nihil esse de eo quod iudicarem, quando nondum viderim. Inde à me quærit, an spiritum Dei habercm? Cui rursus, Quòd nisi habeā, inquam, Dei non sum, sed inter abiectos planè numeranda. Tum ille, Sacerdotem adduxisse se, qui me examinaret dicebat. Moxque sacrificus, qui præsto ad manum aderat, sic incipit, Primum quid de sacramento altaris dicam ac sentiam, id scire à me enixè cupere se. At ego silentium excusans, de hac materia ne quid vellet anxiè monere, aut acrius urgere rogito. Neque enim animum esse in hac materia, quoniam papistam esse persensi, pluribus verbis cum eo disceptare. Postremò huc redijt meus percontator, quid de privatis missis, an post hanc vitam animulis corporibus solutis eas solatio fore sentiam? Qua de re respondi, Idololatria ac sacrilegio non carere, si quis eis fidat magis quàm sanguine Domini qui pro nobis mortuus est.
units.tr: He then went on: "You said," he said, "that if a wicked and impure priest were to consecrate the sacrament, it would be Satan and not God." I answered that I had never said this, but that I had affirmed that whoever he was, and whatever his life, the minister of the sacrament did not detract from my faith, nor prevent me from receiving the body and blood of Christ nonetheless in spirit. Fifthly, he asked what I thought of confession. "Exactly what the divine James thinks," I said, "who bids us confess our sins to one another and pray for one another." After this we came to the book which they call the King's book, and he asked what I thought of it. I answered that I had nothing to say about it that I could judge, since I had not yet seen it. Then he asked me whether I had the Spirit of God. To this again I replied: "If I did not have it, I would not be God's, but must be counted among the castaways." Then he said that he had brought a priest to examine me. And straightway the priest, who was at hand, began: first, he earnestly wished to know what I said and thought about the sacrament of the altar. But I excused myself from silence on this subject, and asked him not to anxiously press or urge anything on this matter. For I had no mind to dispute at length on this subject with a papist, since I had perceived him to be one. Finally my questioner came back to ask what I thought of private masses, and whether I believed they would be any comfort to souls, once they were freed from their bodies, after this life. On this I answered that it was not free of idolatry and sacrilege if anyone trusted in them more than in the blood of the Lord, who died for us.

units.la: Postquam hæc ita acta sunt, demum ad summum urbis prætorem (maiorem vocant nostri) me perducunt. Cui tum eadem hæc omnia, eodemque ordine percontanti, eisdem & ego verbis per omnia respondi, quibus sum prius apud eos usa:nisi[?] quod à D. Prætore illud mihi obiectum est, quod tamen ab ipsis ortum, à me nunquam prosectum fuerat. Id autem erat eiusmodi, nempe si mus in librum illud consecratum casu incidens corroderet, an Deum ederet necne? At enim huius ego sententiæ nunquam author fui. Illi verò eiusdemmodi aliquid sunt à me scisciţati[?]: ad quod verbum quidem nullum respondi, tantum ad eam subrisi interrogationem. Aderat ibi tum episcopi Cancellarius, qui me sævis castigabat verbis, quòd quum mulier essem, sacras Dei scripturas recitarem, affirmans interdictum esse à diuo Paulo, ne fœminæ de Scripturis sermocinentur. Ad hoc respondi, Paulinæ mentis nequaquam ita me ignaram esse, ut nesciam quid ad Corinth. scribens præcipiat, cap. xiiii: ubi prohibet ille ne mulieres in ecclesia loquantur, velut in cœtu virorum dogmatistas agentes. Ac illico percontata ab illo rogabam hoc mihi diceret, quot unquam vidisset fœminas in suggestum conscendere cœcionaturas[?]? Idque quum se nunquam vidisse fateretur: Ergo, inquam, noli miseras mulierculas tuo præiudicio oneio onerare, quas lex absoluit. Cumque ijs dominus Praetor me custodiae mandabat, a quo tum depoposci, an recipere dignaretur qui pro me sponderent. Id quum impetrari ab eo non posset, in carcerem illico abripior, vbi ad dies xii. nulli amicorum omnium ad me dabatur aditus. Interea temporis venit ad me sacrificus, qui cum mandatis episcopi missum se ad disquisitionem meam dicebat, ac consilij impartiendi gratia. At ille ad interrogationes quam ad consilia multo proclivior, causam incipit primum percontari, quur in eam venissem custodiam. Ego me ignorare dicebam. Tum ille, dolendum id sibi quidem videri si immerito, praeterque causam ea mihi calamitas imponeretur. Caeterum audisse se aiebat, negari a me altaris sacramentum. Quod dixi, inquam, dixi: interrogata deinde num crimina apud sacerdotem exonerassem? nequaquam, inquam. Tum ille, adducturum se qui confessionem exciperet dicebat. Respondi, modo ex ijs tribus adduceret aliquem, sive doctorem Cromum, sive Gillanum, sive alioqui Huntyngtonum, licere id quidem: quoniam horum maxime mihi spectata esset tum pietas, tum sapientia. non quod vel teipsum vel caeteros contemptui habeam ac fastidio: sed quod perinde notus mihi non sis. Subintulit posthac interrogationem eiusmodi: Si hostia, inquit, humi forte collapsa, a mure aut bestia alia corripiatur, quid ais, bestia illa Deum ne edit nec ne? Cui ego: Quo labore, inquam, aenigma hoc propositi, eodem & ipse tibi solvas licet. Mihi enim non libet hic respondere quicquam, quando tentatum huc te venire videam.
