At enim, inquit, consentaneum non est, & praeter scholarum mores, ut idem simul opponentis & respondentes partes obeat. At ego, inquam, mulier sum, scholarum vestrarum rudis omnino & ignara. Quanto rogor ab eo, an decreuissem in animo, paschate hoc sacra adire synaxim? Alioqui, inquam, indigna sim quae inter Christianos habear. adeoque laetor non parum hunc ipsum diem sic munimere. Sicque discessit meus ille cosiliarius, non sine verborum tandem subblanda quadam coronide. Post haec 23. Martij, venit ad carcerem consobrinus meus Britannus, quaerens num vade aut sponsione interposita possem redimi. Atque inde recta via ad praetorem contendit, petens ab eo ut honestorum hominum & sponsorum satisdatione facta, permitteret e custodia me emancipari.
units.tr: After these things had been done in this way, at last they led me before the chief magistrate of the city, whom our people call the Mayor. There, when he asked me all these same things, in the same order, I answered him word for word as I had before answered them. Except that the Lord Mayor objected to me something which had originated with them, and never proceeded from me: namely, if a mouse, running into that consecrated book by chance, were to gnaw it, would it eat God or not? But I was never the author of this opinion. Yet they asked me questions of this kind: to this I made no reply at all, but only smiled at the question. The Chancellor of the bishop was present there, who harshly rebuked me, saying that since I was a woman I was reciting the sacred Scriptures of God, affirming that the divine Paul forbade women to speak of the Scriptures. To this I replied that I was by no means so ignorant of Paul's mind as not to know what he commands when he writes to the Corinthians, chapter 14, where he forbids women to speak in church, as though they were teaching in an assembly of men. And I immediately asked him to tell me how many women he had ever seen mount the pulpit to preach. When he confessed that he had never seen any, I said: "Then do not burden poor women with your prejudice, whom the law has acquitted." And when they were consigning me to custody, the Lord Mayor, I asked him whether he would deign to accept people who would stand surety for me. When I could not obtain this from him, I was immediately dragged off to prison, where for twelve days no access to me was granted to any of my friends. Meanwhile a priest came to me, who said that he had been sent by the bishop's orders to examine me and to offer advice. But he, being much more inclined to questions than to counsel, began first to ask why I had come into this prison. I said I did not know. Then he said that it grieved him, if undeservedly, and that this calamity was being imposed on me without cause. But he said he had heard that I denied the sacrament of the altar. "What I said, I said," I replied. Then he asked whether I had unburdened my sins to a priest. "Not at all," I said. Then he said he would bring someone to hear my confession. I replied that he might bring one of those three, whether Doctor Crome, or Gilham, or Huntington, for these men I particularly esteemed for both their piety and their wisdom; not that I despised you or the others, or held you in contempt, but because you were not as well known to me. After this he put a question of this kind: "If a host, fallen to the ground by chance, is seized by a mouse or some other beast, what do you say, does that beast eat God or not?" I said: "Propose this riddle with whatever effort you like, you may solve it yourself. For I do not care to answer anything here, since I see that you have come here to test me." "But," he said, "it is not fitting, nor according to the custom of the schools, for the same person to play both the part of the objector and the respondent." "But I," I said, "am a woman, utterly untrained and ignorant of your schools." Then he asked me whether I had decided in my mind to approach the communion at this Easter. "Otherwise," I said, "I would be unworthy to be counted among Christians; and I am not a little glad that this very day is so fortified." And so my counsellor departed, not without some smooth flourish of words at last. After this, on 23 March, my cousin, the Briton, came to the prison, asking whether I could be redeemed by bail or by a surety being given. And from there he went straight to the magistrate, asking him that, on the security of respectable men and sureties, he would permit me to be released from custody.

units.la: Tum ille, non illibenter se quidem dicebat facturum omnia, quo mihi gratificari posset. sed rem eiusmodi esse in qua parum ipsius valeret potestas, nisi spiritualis fori simul accedente calculo. Suadere itaque, ut Cancellarium episcopi Londinensis super ea re compellare vellet. sese enim, ut sine iurisdictione spirituali, carceri me mandare non posset, ita nisi ex eadem authoritate sine spirituali ministro, me nunc eximere nequaquam posse. Dimissus cum hoc responso meus aduocatus, rectà Cancellarium petit, opem in hac re illius implorans. Cui in hunc modum Cancellarius: Causam permagni esse momenti respondit, cui longè inferior eius esset vnius authoritas. nec audere etiam in re tanta, ac tali ius suum interponere: episcopi siquidem proprium hoc munus esse, ac proinde necessario accersendam eius huc consensionem. alioqui nihil esse quod solus ipse sine episcopo posset, audeátue conficere. polliceri id tamen, episcopum eo de negotio conuenturum se obnixè & diligenter. Itaque crastino ad se redire iubet, fusius pleniúsque de illius tunc voluntate auditurum. Breuiter, ad diem ac horam indictam reuersus cognatus meus, vtrumque pariter conuenit episcopum cum cancellario, res denique eò rediit, vt diceret episcopus exituram quidem me ad communicationem, sic enim appellabat: dicítque ei horam diei sequentis tertiam pomeridianam. addítque insuper, adhibiturum se collocationi illi viros maximè eos quibus ipsamet potissimum fauerem: vt omnibus videri posset quàm nullo rigore, nec pro summo suo iure mecum ageret. Ad hoc vero respondit ille, Neminem se scire, cui essem prae caeteris addictior. Imò sunt, inquit episcopus, quos peculiariter sibi prae caeteris eximios habeat, doctorem Cromum, Gillamum, Vuhithedum, & Huntyngtonum. hos enim & doctos agnoscit, & synceri iudicij homines. Praeterea multis verbis instat apud consobrinum hunc meum, vt mihi persuaderet, intimos recessus animi mei atque latebras omnes libere audaceróque apud ipsum exponerem. quod si facerem, fidem obstringit suam, nullo pacto id mihi vel fraudi vel intertrimento fore, nec quicquam euenturum mihi in ea disquisitione captiosum. Quin si quid scrupuli aut erroris esset in quo impingerem, ipse cum suis doctoribus facile discuteret, ac consiliis me imbueret rectioribus.
units.tr: Then he said that he would indeed gladly do everything he could to grant me this favour. But that the matter was of such a kind that his own power was of little weight in it, unless the spiritual court added its vote. He therefore advised that my cousin should approach the Chancellor of the Bishop of London about this matter. For just as he could not commit me to prison without spiritual jurisdiction, so without the same authority, and without a spiritual officer, he could by no means now release me. My advocate, dismissed with this reply, went straight to the Chancellor, imploring his help in this matter. To him the Chancellor replied in this manner: the matter was of very great importance, and his own authority was far inferior to it; nor would he dare to interpose his right in a matter so great and of such a kind; for this function belonged properly to the bishop, and therefore his consent had to be sought there of necessity. Otherwise there was nothing that he alone could presume to arrange without the bishop. He promised, however, that he would speak with the bishop about the business earnestly and diligently. And so he bade my kinsman return to him the next day, when he would hear more fully and completely what the bishop's will was. In short, my cousin returned at the appointed day and hour, and met the bishop together with the Chancellor. The matter at last came to this, that the bishop said I would indeed be brought out to "communication," for so he called it, and he named the next day's third hour in the afternoon. He added moreover that he would bring to that meeting those men whom I most favoured myself, so that it might appear to all how he was dealing with me without any harshness, and not by his full legal right. To this my cousin replied that he knew of no one to whom I was more devoted than to others. "Indeed there are," said the bishop, "whom she has specially singled out above the rest as outstanding: Doctor Crome, Gilham, Wilkinson, and Huntington. For she acknowledges these men as both learned and of sound judgement." Besides, he urged my cousin at length to persuade me to lay open to him freely and boldly the innermost recesses and hiding places of my mind. If I did so, he pledged his word that this would in no way bring me harm or loss, nor would anything hostile to me arise from that inquiry. Indeed, if I was entangled in any doubt or error, he himself, with his own doctors, would easily resolve it and imbue me with sounder counsel.

units.la: Postridie itaque accersita per episcopum hora prima venio, quum tamen tertia esset constituta. Vbi vero adueni, magnum se dolorem capere ex mea hac calamitate dicit, quid autem illud sit, quamobrem ab aduersarijs accusér: ac porro quaecunque in animo haberem liberè ac intrepidè illi vt aperiam sine omni metu monet. neminem esse qui nerotum mihi vllo de verbo faceret, quod intra eius esset parietes lictura: cui rursus: Quoniam, inquam, celsitudo tua horam mihi statuerit tertiam ad quam aduturi sunt mihi aduocati, veniam mihi tantisper flagito abs te dari, quoad illorum expecto aduentum. Quin ergo, inquit, quatuor illos quos ante dixerā, quam primum aduocandos censeo, qui huic intersint auscultationi. Id autem ne faceret rogaui: neque enim opus esse, eos hoc labore fatigari, quum duo illi viri generosi abinde testes essent idonei, quantum ei negotio sufficeret. Post haec episcopus in porticum intus se recipit, vbi aduocatum ad se D. Spilnanum iubet omnibus modis apud me instare, ne quid reticerem, quin palam haberem quaecunque in animo essent. Ac interea archidiaconum id me suum mittit, qui primo mox aduentu accusationis à me causam scire petebat. Id ego ab accusatoribus meis postulandum esse, me prorsus ignorare dicebam. tum ille erepto mihi libro, quem habebam in manu, Hic, inquit, talesque libelli huc te calamitatis perduxerunt. quapropter ab his vehementer vt caueas, moneo. Qui etenim huius libri author fuit in circo Smythsfildiano vstulatus est. Rogo num probè compertum haberet, quod diceret. Maximè vero, inquit, scire enim se librum esse Ioan. Frythi. Vide, inquam, an non te pudet tam temerè iudicium ac sententiam de re praecipitare, quam nescias. sane vero haec tam inconsulta & violenta in iudicando temeritas, ingenium arguit in homine non prudentissimum: simulque explicato libro, ostendebam qualis esset. Atqui putaram, inquit, fuisse alium. nam in eo nihil potuit reprehendere. Denique admonitus à me ne posthac tam praepropere ac inconsultus in iudicando esse velit, nisi re prius diligenter perspecta, de qua censura ferenda sit, reliquit me archidiaconus ac abijt. Inde ad me venit Brytannus agnatus meus, vnà cum D. Hawlo iureconsulto, ac quibusdam aliis. Ibi tum episcopus consobrinum meum anxiè apud me instare monet, vt sensus animi mei omnes illi audacter exponerem:
units.tr: Accordingly, the next day I came at the first hour, summoned by the bishop, although the third hour had been appointed. When I arrived, he said that he was greatly grieved by my misfortune, but he did not say what it was that my adversaries accused me of. He advised me to lay out freely and fearlessly whatever I had in mind, without any fear. No one would make a fuss over any word of mine spoken within his walls. To this I replied: "Since your lordship has appointed the third hour for me, by which my advocates are to come, I beg you to grant me a little time until I await their arrival." "Indeed," he said, "I think those four whom I named before should be summoned as soon as possible to be present at this hearing." I asked him not to do this, since there was no need for them to be wearied by this labour; those two gentlemen were sufficient witnesses for that business. After this the bishop withdrew into the inner porch, where he ordered my advocate, Mr. Spilman, to press me by every means not to keep anything back, but to lay open whatever was in my mind. Meanwhile the archdeacon sent his man to me, who, as soon as he arrived, asked me to tell him the cause of the accusation. I said I was altogether ignorant of what my accusers would demand. Then he snatched from my hand the book I was holding: "Such books as this have brought you to this calamity. Therefore I earnestly advise you to beware of them. For the author of this book was burned in Smithfield." He asked whether I had properly considered what I was saying. "Most certainly," he said, "for I know the book to be by John Frith." I replied: "See whether you are not ashamed to pass judgment so rashly on a matter you do not know. Indeed, this hasty and violent rashness in judging shows a mind not very prudent." At the same time, unfolding the book, I showed him what sort of book it was. "But I thought," he said, "it was another; for I could find nothing in it to reprehend." Finally, having been admonished by me not to be so hasty and ill-advised in judging again, unless he first examined carefully the matter on which judgment was to be passed, the archdeacon left me and went away. Then my kinsman Brytannus came to me, together with Mr. Hawle the lawyer and certain others. There the bishop urged my cousin to press me anxiously to lay open freely all the feelings of my mind to him.

units.la: Ioā. Frythi historiam 1.lib.commemoraui mus.
units.tr: I recalled the history of John Frith in the first book.

units.la: D. Brytannus. D. Hawlus. idémque insuper pluribus verbis me hortatur, ut ea in re consiliis amicorum acquiescerem, sibique in eo quod iubebat obtemperarem. nihil quippe fore periculi. Quod enim mihi esset atque illis supra pollicitus, indubitata fide præstaturum se in eo quod diceret, neminem fore qui molestiam mihi ullam exhiberet de his quæcunque apud se dicturam essem. Ideóque confidenter apud se proferre, quæ laterent in animo iubet. respondeo nihil esse in pectore, quod patefacerem. conscientiam (sit Deo gratia) undique esse sine omni scrupulo tranquillam ac requietam. hicque ille adhibita similitudine: Quemadmodum, inquit, chirurgus peritus ac doctus vulneri malagma adhibere non possit, nisi cuius latebras ipse atque altitudinem prius rite accuratéque explorarit: ita neque ego consilia ægritudini tuæ accommodare potero, nisi conscientiæ mihi morbum prius aperias. Dixi rursus conscientiam meam nulla re mala laborare. sanæ vero ac integræ cuti emplastrum admovere, dementiæ videri. Cogis me ergo, inquit, tuis te verbis premere. dixeras enim, Quisquis ab impuro sacerdote sacramentum perciperet, Sathanam cum nō Christum percipere. Ita, inquam, non dixi. Cæterum illud D. prætor ac quæsitoribus dixisse me fateor, quod & tibi nunc fassura sum. nempe quantumlibet impurus contingat minister, nihil id obstare mihi, quin spiritu & fide corpus Christi & sanguis à me percipiatur. Episcopus: Quidnam, inquit, hoc habet, quod addis in spiritu? quanquam age, nolo te urgere nimium. Scit, inquam, tua dominatio, sine spiritu & fide nulla est sacramenti huius digna ac salutaris perceptio. Post hæc veniebat, quòd dicerem sacramentum quod in loculo inclusum continebatur, panem esse. Nego me unquam dixisse, verum à quæsitoribus super ea[?] re interrogata quid sentirem, postulabam vicissim ab illis, quur lapidatus fuisset Stephanus. quod quum illi se ignorare dicerent, nec mihi[?] illis dicturam quod quærerent, respondi. Obiecit deinde, citatum à me esse locum Scripturæ quendam. Nullum, inquam, omnino, præter illum modo, ubi Apostolus Atheniensibus olim de Deo in templis manufactis non habitante respondit, Act. xvii. Et quo pacto, inquit, tua fides in hac sacramenti materia se habet? Credo, inquam, quod me docet Scriptura Dei sacra. Ecquid si Scriptura corpus esse Christi doceat? Cre-do, inquam [?]), inquam, quicquid jubent sacræ illæ literæ. Episcopus: Quid autem si dicat Scriptura esse corpus Domini? Sequor, inquâ, per omnia Scripturæ docentis authoritatem, huicque aliquandiu immorabatur quætiunculæ, subinde refricans, atque inculcans quò id tandem à me ratione eliceret quod venabatur. At ego semper intra eum circulum continebam, ut quicquid præciperet Euangelicæ Scripturæ canon, id me tota fide secuturam responderim. Ibi tum quærebatur, Cur tam parca verborum essem, adeóque restricta in respondendo? Siquidem donum mihi intelligendi datum esse dicebam, sermonis item: Quid quòd Solomō nobis laudi id vertit, quod tu criminaris, mulierem temperati sermonis & parci donum esse Dei affirmans, Prou. xix. Dixisti porrò ait episcopus, Missa esse idololatria. Ego id inficior à me dictum esse. Cæterùm sciscitantibus nuper prætorianis, num Missas privatas salutares esse post hac vitā animabus à corporibus exolutis existimarē: idololatria diceba nō carere si quis Missis magis fidat quàm sanguine Domini quo redempti sumus. rursusque ille, Quæso, inquit, qualis hæc erat responsio? Etsi, inquâ, non optima fortassis, nec doctissima, at quæ satis tamen illorum digna interrogatis videri poterat. præterea sacerdote quendâ ibi tum adfuisse dicebam, qui eorum omnium quæ coram prætore acta sunt, testis esse potuit. Tum Cancellarius (is enim fuit) ubi hæc audit, Certè verò, inquit, hæc ipsa verba apud me atq; prætore, eâ habuisse memini.
units.tr: Mr. Brytannus. Mr. Hawle. And moreover, in many words he urged me to yield to the counsel of my friends in this matter and to obey him in what he commanded, for there would be no danger. He promised me, and them too, with unfailing good faith, that he would do what he said: no one would give me any trouble over whatever I told him. He therefore bade me confidently bring out what lay hidden in my mind. I answered that there was nothing in my breast to disclose; by God's grace my conscience was on every side tranquil and at rest, without any scruple. Then he used a comparison: "Just as a skilful and learned surgeon cannot apply a plaster to a wound unless he has first properly and carefully examined its depths and extent, so neither can I fit counsel to your sickness unless you first disclose the disease of your conscience to me." I said again that my conscience was troubled by no evil thing. To apply a plaster to healthy and sound skin would seem madness. "You force me, then," he said, "to press you with your own words. For you said that whoever received the sacrament from an impure priest received Satan and not Christ." "Yes," I said, "I did not say that. But I admit that I said to the lord praetor and the examiners what I now tell you as well: however impure the minister who happens to be, nothing prevents the body and blood of Christ from being received by me in spirit and faith." The bishop: "What is this that you add, in spirit? Still, come, I do not want to press you too hard." "Your lordship knows," I said, "that without the spirit and faith there is no worthy and saving reception of this sacrament." After this came the charge that I had said the sacrament which was kept enclosed in the pyx was bread. I denied ever saying this. But when the examiners asked me on that point what I thought, I in turn demanded of them why Stephen was stoned. When they said they did not know, and I would not tell them what they were asking, I answered. He then objected that I had cited a certain passage of Scripture. "None at all," I said, "except that one just now, where the Apostle once answered the Athenians about God not dwelling in temples made with hands, Acts 17." "And how," he said, "does your faith stand on this matter of the sacrament?" "I believe," I said, "what the holy Scripture of God teaches me." "What if Scripture teaches that it is the body of Christ?" "I believe," I said, "whatever those holy letters command." The bishop: "But what if Scripture says it is the body of the Lord?" "I follow," I said, "in all things the authority of Scripture when it teaches." He lingered for a while on this little question, repeatedly rubbing it in and pressing it home, to draw from me by reasoning what he was hunting for. But I always kept within that circle, answering that whatever the canon of the Gospel Scripture commanded, I would follow with my whole faith. Then it was asked why I was so sparing of words and so restrained in answering. I said that a gift of understanding had been given to me, and of speech too. "Moreover, Solomon turned to praise what you criticise, affirming that a woman of measured and sparing speech is a gift of God, Prov. 19." "You said further," said the bishop, "that the Mass is idolatry." I deny that I said this. But when the praetorians lately asked me whether I thought private Masses were beneficial to souls after they had been released from their bodies, I said that whoever trusted in Masses more than in the blood of the Lord by which we were redeemed was not free of idolatry. "Again," he said, "I ask, what was this answer like?" "Though perhaps not the best nor most learned," I said, "yet it could seem worthy enough of the questions put to me." Besides, I said, a certain priest was present there at that time, who could be a witness to everything that was done before the praetor. Then the chancellor (for he was the one) on hearing this said: "Certainly, I remember these very words were spoken before me and the praetor."

units.la: Inter cæteros qui huic interfuerunt quæstioni, erat D. Stādicius cum ciusdem farinæ sacrificulis nonnullis, qui multa ac sæpius interrogando, omni circuibant via sententiam meam de sacramento clarius expisçaturi, quos omnes unico hoc responso semper repuli, ut dicerem, satis de hac re D. episcopo me respondisse: actum, quod aiunt, agere nihil opus esse. Standicius confestim susurrans cum episcopo, rogat ut mihi liceret planius de eo Pauli loco sententiam edicere. respondi, Plane adversari Paulinæ disciplinæ, ut quæ mulier essem, munus ac personam dogmaticæ in Scriptura interpretanda mihi sumerem, in eo præfertim cœtu virorum doctrina tam excellentium.
units.tr: Among the others present at this examination was Mr. Standish with some of the same breed of priests, who, questioning me many times and in many ways, went about by every route to draw out my opinion on the sacrament more clearly. I always repelled all of them with the same one answer: that I had already sufficiently answered the bishop on this matter, and that, as they say, what is done need not be done again. Standish at once whispered with the bishop and asked that I might be allowed to set out my opinion more plainly on that passage of Paul. I replied that it was plainly contrary to Paul's discipline for me, being a woman, to take upon myself the office and role of interpreting doctrine in Scripture, especially in such an assembly of men so excellent in learning.

units.la: Post hæc deinceps ingerente episcopo aliam criminationem, nempe quòd appellata nuper à quodam, num sacramentum paschali illa celebritate sumptura essem, viderer rem habere ludibrio. petebā produci mihi accusatores: hoc tamē ille nec velle nec posse dicebat, verum quum quendam ille cōsilij impartiedi gratia ad me mitteret, primo verbo papistam illum me aiebat nominasse. quod ne negabam quidem. perfenseram etenim talem esse eum quem dixeram, cui tamen ad id quod quærebat ne verbum quidem respondi. Pergens porrò episcopus, acriter me suggillabat, eò quod dicerem aliquando sexaginta fuisse Lincolniæ sacrificos, qui conjuratis consilijs capiti meo periculum struerent. Neque id etiam negaui:sic enim tum mihi per amicos significatum est, Lincolniæ esse qui deuotis animis in me coniurauerant, palàm etiam minantes nescio quid, si aduenissem. Id simulatque intellexi, propero recta via Lincolniam, ibíque commoror ad nonum usque diem, certius quid esset rei exploratura. Interea dum in summo eorum templo sto, lectitans in sacris Biblijs, aduolant nunc bini, nunc terni, nonnunquam & seni, quasi qui interpellaturi viderentur, at ijdem nulla emissa voce, rursum discesserunt. Roganti tum episcopo, an inter eos nullus ibi sermonem mecum habuisset, unum fuisse aiebam inter cæteros, qui demùm paucula mecum verba agitarat. Et quid is tibi tum aiebat? Planè tam exigui erant momenti quæ diceret, ut memoriam eis non intenderim. Tum episcopus: Sunt, inquit, permulti qui Scripturas legunt, vita tamen ac moribus non exprimentes quæ legunt. Equidem vero, inquam, ô reuerende, optarim ut palàm fieret omnibus vitæ meæ ac morum contemplatio: cùm certò sciam, neminem esse qui inhonestæ conditionis maculam vllam mihi possit impingere. Si quem ipse noueris qui possit, rogo plurimum, huc eum coràm adductum velis.
units.tr: After this, the bishop pressed another charge against me: that, having recently been asked by someone whether I was going to receive the sacrament at that Paschal festival, I seemed to make a mockery of the matter. I asked that my accusers be produced before me, but he said he neither wished nor was able to do so. Instead, when a certain man was sent to me to offer advice, I had at once called him a Papist. I did not deny this, for I had perceived that he was the sort of man I had described, though I did not reply a single word to what he was asking. The bishop went on to reproach me sharply for saying that once there were sixty priests at Lincoln who had conspired together to plot against my life. I did not deny this either. For so I was told at the time by friends: there were men at Lincoln who had sworn together against me with devoted hearts, openly threatening I know not what if I should come. As soon as I learned this, I hastened straight to Lincoln and stayed there until the ninth day, so that I might find out more certainly what was happening. Meanwhile, as I stood in their great church, reading the holy Bible, people came up to me now two, now three, sometimes even six at a time, as if they meant to speak to me; but they said nothing and went away again. When the bishop asked whether none of them had spoken with me there, I said that one among the rest had at last exchanged a few words with me. "And what did he say to you then?" he asked. "Truly, what he said was of so little weight that I did not bother to remember it." Then the bishop said: "There are very many who read the Scriptures, yet do not express in their life and conduct what they read." I replied: "Indeed, reverend sir, I would wish that a full view of my life and conduct might be made plain to everyone, since I know for certain that no one can cast upon me any stain of dishonourable condition. If you yourself know of someone who can, I earnestly ask that you bring him here before me.

units.la: Moxque discedens episcopus, dicebat scripto se mandare velle partem eorum nonnullam, quæ respondissem. Quod & fecit. Ego verò singula complecti[?] memoriæ haud quibam, vel quia tam multa essent, vel quia exemplar mihi ad legendum non concedebatur. Quæ autem recordari poteram, in hanc ferè summam tendebant.
units.tr: Immediately afterwards the bishop, as he was leaving, said that he wished to have some part of my answers committed to writing. And he did so. But I could not keep each point in my memory, either because there were so many or because I was not allowed a copy to read. Those things that I could recall tended more or less to this sum.

units.la: Rescriptum episcopi.
units.tr: The bishop's written statement.

units.la: Cire[?], inquit, omnes volo quotquot sunt mortales, fidei meæ hanc firmam certámque esse profesionem, quantumlibet mendax fama secus de me peruagatur. Primùm, quod ego Anna Askena[?] indubitatò credam ac teneam, eos qui synaxin à ministro quocunque aut quantumlibet mlibet impuro percipiant, nihilo minus corpus & sanguinem Christi, re atque substantia ipsa percipere. Credo insuper hoc ipsum sacramentum, post consecrationem, siue sumatur, aut asseruetur, perdurare nihilominus corpus & sanguinem Christi realiter iuxta substantiæ veritatem. Credo denique tum in hoc, tum in cætera omnia ecclesiæ saramenta, iuxta omnes articulos, vbicunque in catholica Christi ecclesia receptos. In cuius rei fidem Anna Askeua nominis mei atq; manus adhibui subscriptionem. Plura in hoc rescripto continebantur, quæ quoniam exemplar peruidere non licuit, singulatim collecti ac memoriæ mãdare non potui. Hæc igitur ordine omnia quũ perlegisset, quæ it num ijs quæ recitasset, assentiri velim. Ego verò in hunc respondeo modou, quantum sacra Dei scriptura permitteret, tãtum ijs me assensuram esse. itaque hoc ipsum simul annecteret cum subscriptione, efflagito. Respondet: Doceri se à me non velle in iis quæ ipse agere scribereque ebeat. Ac continuò inde in aulam conuolat exteriorem, vbi in publica multitudinis frequentia hoc scriptum recitat, compluribus ibi me hortantibus vt manu subscriberem: affirmantibus porrò, præclare etiam necum actum iri si vel sic res posset transfigi. Subinfert ad hæc episcopus: Quod tantum apud se experiar fauoris, non id tam mea causa fieri, quàm amicorum. intelligere autem se, ex illustri ac generosa mertam[?] familia, atque amicos habere conspicuo splendore viros, quibus hoc deberem ferre acceptum beneficium. Ad hæc verba interfatus est Christophorus quidam D. Denei famulus: Atqui, inquit, tuum erat, ô episcope, Dei causa potius quàm hominum hoc ei contulisse beneficium. Consedens deinde episcopus scriptum mihi tradit, mandans vt ei subscriberem. Subscripsi itaque in hanc quidem formulam, Ego Anna Askeua credo omnia quæ in fide ecclesiæ catholicæ continentur. Quod vbi vidit ille, offensus non parum iraque inflammatus in cubiculum intus quantum potest irrumpit. Nec mora consequitur à vestigio dominus Brytannus, deprecans per sacra omnia celsitudinem ipsius, parceret iracundiæ veniámque mihi eius tribueret ignoscentia.
units.tr: "I want all mortal men," he said, "to know that this is the firm and certain profession of my faith, however much a lying rumour may spread otherwise about me. First, that I, Anna Askew, indubitably believe and hold that those who receive the Communion from any minister whatever, however unworthy (however impure) they may be, nonetheless receive the body and blood of Christ, in deed and in the very substance. I further believe that this same sacrament, after consecration, whether it is taken or kept, the body and blood of Christ nonetheless endure really, according to the truth of the substance. Lastly, I believe both in this and in all the other sacraments of the Church, according to all the articles received wherever in the catholic Church of Christ. In witness of this faith, I, Anna Askew, have added my name and the signature of my hand." Several more things were contained in this statement, but since I was not permitted to see the copy, I could not gather them one by one or commit them to memory. When he had read through all of this in order, he asked whether I would agree to what he had recited. I answered that I would assent to these things only so far as the holy Scripture of God allowed. So I asked earnestly that he join this very qualification to the signature. He replied that he did not wish to be taught by me in matters which he himself ought to do and write. And straightway he hurried into the outer hall, where, before a public crowd, he read this writing aloud, while several people there urged me to sign it with my hand, adding that my case would go remarkably well if the matter could be settled in this way. Thereupon the bishop added that he would show me such favour, not so much for my sake as for my friends'; he understood, he said, that I came of an illustrious and noble family and had friends of conspicuous distinction, to whom I ought to credit this kindness. At these words a certain Christopher, servant of Master Denny, interrupted: "Surely, my lord bishop, it was your duty to grant this favour for God's cause rather than for men's." The bishop then sat down and handed me the paper, ordering me to sign it. So I signed it in this form: "I, Anna Askew, believe all things that are contained in the faith of the catholic Church." When he saw this, he was not a little offended and, inflamed with anger, burst as far as he could into the inner chamber. Straightway Lord Britain followed after him, begging by all that is holy that his lordship would spare his anger and grant me pardon through his forgiving clemency.

units.la: Respondet ille, Mulierem quidem esse me, nec animum ipsius quicquam fefellisse. Tum alter: Verum quidem hoc affirmat, ideóque mc vt fœminam æstimare, ne muliebrem sensum meum excellenti sapientia ipsius metiri velit.
units.tr: To this he replied that I was indeed a woman, and that my mind had not deceived him in any way. Then the other said: "It is true that he affirms this; therefore regard him as a woman, and do not wish to measure my womanly sense by your excellent wisdom."

units.la: Post hæc subingressus ad eum doctor wcstonus [?], causam exponit cur adderem illud de ecclesia catholica, eam fuisse quod nescirem eius factam superius fuisse mentionem. Demum vix multa prece ab eo impetratum est, vt redirem denuò nomen meum ac fideiusorum excepturus, quorum alter erat D. Brytannus, alter D. Spihnannus [?], è iuristarum collegio Graio, quod appellant. Hæc vbi perfecta essent, sperabamus mox futurum vt cum hac transactione sponsioneque accepta ilico dimitteremur, iuxta iuris æquitatem. At episcopus id concedere minimè volebat, iterum me relegans in carcerem, in sequentem videlicet diem. Postera deinceps luce in ædem prætorianam vocor. vbi nihil etiam perfectum est, nisi quod scriptum illud duntaxat episcopi vt ante proferebatur: quo perlecto, in custodiam denuò remittor. Iussitque sponsores postridie in æde diui Pauli comparere, quod & factum est. Nec multum abfuit quin & ibi iterum fideiusores meos re frustrata dimisissent, eo quod nomine alterius fœminæ, cuius neque vitam neque causam habebant cognitam, pro ipsorum libidine sese obstringere recusarent. Demum post multa vltro citròque agitata, interposita fideiusorum satisfactione ac fide, qua me producere, si res ita ferret, tenebantur, è custodia restituor in libertatem.
units.tr: After this, Doctor Weston came in to him and explained why I had added that matter about the catholic Church: it was because I did not know that it had been mentioned earlier. At last, after much pleading, I was prevailed upon to return once more to give my name and that of my sureties, one of whom was Master Britain and the other Master Spelman, of the college of lawyers called Gray's Inn. When this was done, we hoped that, with this agreement and bond accepted, we would be released at once, in accordance with the equity of the law. But the bishop was utterly unwilling to concede this, sending me back again to prison, namely until the following day. Early the next morning I was summoned to the praetorian hall, where nothing was finished except that the bishop's written statement was again read out; once it had been read, I was sent back to custody. And he ordered my sureties to appear the next day in St Paul's church, which was done. Nor was it far off that they should once more have dismissed my sureties with nothing achieved, because they refused to bind themselves for the sake of another woman, whose life and cause they did not know, as the bishop pleased. At last, after much back and forth, a surety and pledge was given by which they were bound to produce me if the matter so required, and I was restored from custody to liberty.

units.la: SECUNDA DISQUISITIO ANNAE ASKEVAE.
units.tr: THE SECOND EXAMINATION OF ANNE ASKEW.

units.la: Anna Askeva Amico cuidam.
units.tr: Anne Askew to a certain friend.

units.la: Intelligo (chare in Christo frater) nondum plenè tibi satisfactum esse in causa cœnæ Dominicæ, eò quòd dixerit Apostolis Dominus, Accipite, comedite, Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur. Christus verò in eo exhibendo pane id voluit, externum ob oculos proponere sacramentum, ore quidem sumendum. cuius admonitu in fidem passionis suæ pro populo obeundæ pleniorem perduceremur, ac salutis inde in internas animas nostras propagandæ. Cuius quidem salutis ac incomparabilis beneficij relictus est nobis panis pro monumento ac sacramentali communione: in qua participanda gratos nos illi pro necessaria redemptionis nostræ gratia præberaberemus. Sic enim Dominus ipse sequētibus verbis nos admonet, quiens, Hoc facite in commemorationem mei. additque insuper, Quotiescunque de pane hoc ederitis, aut biberitis de calice, Lucae undecimo: item prioris Corinthior. vndecimo capite. Nam alioqui fieri fortasse posset, vt obliuio nos tantarum rerum caperet, ac ingratitudo etiam sequeretur. retulerit non parum, vt communibus votis liuinam implorem us [?] clementiam, vt veram huius mysterij cognitionem, ac metem Spiritus sancti nostris inserat pectoribus. Litera enim, vt docet beatus Paulus, occidit: Spiritus autem viuificat, posterioris Corinthiorum tertio cap. Perpende etiam atque etiam caput Ioannis octauum, vbi ad fidem omnia referuntur. item epistolae ad Corinthios prioris caput quartum, vbi sub finem capitis reperies, ea quae videntur, temporaria esse: quae autem non videntur, aeterna, &c. Praeterea capite ad Hebraeos tertio, in haec verba leges, quòd Christus non tanquam seruus, sed filius erat in domo sua, quae domus sumus nos, non templorum parietes: si fiduciam & gloriam spei vsque ad finem firmam retineamus. Quapropter sicut dicit Spiritus sanctus, Hodie si vocem eius audieritis, nolite obdurare corda vestra, &c. Psalm 94.
units.tr: I understand, dear brother in Christ, that you are still not fully satisfied about the Lord's Supper, because the Lord said to the Apostles, "Take, eat, this is my body, which is given for you." In giving that bread, Christ meant to set before our eyes an outward sacrament, to be received by the mouth. By its reminder we are to be led more fully into faith in the passion he was to undergo for the people, and so into the spreading of that salvation into our inner souls. Of that salvation and of this incomparable benefit he has left us bread as a memorial and a sacramental communion, in sharing which we show ourselves grateful to him for the grace of our redemption, which is necessary. For the Lord himself admonishes us in these words: "Do this in remembrance of me," and he adds, "As often as you eat this bread, or drink from the cup" (Luke 11; likewise 1 Corinthians 11). Otherwise it might perhaps happen that forgetfulness of such great things would seize us, and ingratitude would follow. It will be of no small help if, with common prayers, I implore the living clemency of God to plant in our hearts a true knowledge of this mystery and the mind of the Holy Spirit. For, as the blessed Paul teaches, "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" (2 Corinthians 3). Consider again and again the eighth chapter of John, where all things are referred to faith. Likewise in the fourth chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, where near the end of the chapter you will find that "the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal," and so on. Further, in the third chapter of Hebrews you will read these words: that Christ, as a son and not as a servant, was over his own house, "which house we are, not the walls of temples, if we hold fast the confidence and the glory of hope firm to the end." Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says, "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts," and so on (Psalm 95).

units.la: De concaptiuis meis, quod postulas, tuo in eo desiderio satisfacere non habeo, quorum examinationi ipsa non interfuerim. Ad meam vero quod attinet, sic res habet: Primùm ante consilium perducta, atque interrogata à D. kymo, respondeo iam satis animi mei sententiam D. Cancellario, quod ad eam rem attinebat, explicatam à me esse, ac teneri. At illi satis id quidem esse denegabant, Regis eam esse voluntatem, vt etiā ipsis quid sentirem in ea re exponerem. Contrà verò id me facturam prorsus negaui. quin si ita Regi videretur, me coràm audire, cupidè lubenterque id facerem. Rursúsque illi minimè id æquum esse dictitant, Regis otium mea causa meíque similium perturbari. Respondeo, Solomonem quondam inter sapientissimos reges merito censeri ab omnibus, qui quum duarum inter se dilitigantium pauperculārum causam audire ac cognoscere non dubitaret: nihil me Regiæ diffidere pietati, quin peraeque [?] & me humiliter & fideliter subiectam illi ancillam sit auditurus. Exquirenti deinde meam de sacramento Eucharistiae opinionem D. Cancellario in haec verba respondeo: Fidem meam ac sententiam hanc esse, quoties in Christiano sin coetu, sacramentum corporis & sanguinis me sumere in passionis Dominicae memoriam, simulque cum gratiis iuxta sacram eam institutionem peractis, fructum quoque salutiferae eius passionis participare. Iubet tum wintoniensis me simpliciter, citraque circuitionem omnem, in alterutram respondere partem. Cum ego, Nouam me recinere cantionem Domini in terra aliena non posse dicebam. Ibi episcopus figurate me atque in parabolis loquutam dicebat. Nempe sic quidem maxime aiebam ei convenire, namque si syncere ipsi quod res esset enunciarem, nequaquam haberet dicenti fidem. Tum ille me Psittacam appellitare. Ego non verba solum illius, sed & quaecunque porro in me strueret, aequo atque etiam lubenti animo perpeti velle dicebam. Ibi vero multis me conuitiis onerant consiliarij, quod ad eorum videlicet interrogata renuerem explicate respondere, quanquam necdum aliquid ego vicissim pro mea defensione propositem. Verum singula hic referre quum tam multa fuerint neque attinet, nec paucis id fieri poterit, quippe horis non minus quinque me detinuerunt. Post demum multam disceptationem a protonotario consilij, inde ad aedes D. Garnishae deduci iubeor. Postridiana luce, pro conventu rursus senatorio, ubi sistor, contendunt a me ac urgent vehementer, ut fidem meam clare de sacramento edisseram: respondeo dictum hac de re quantum a me dici posset. Post deinde sermones aliquot, secedere me seorsum iubent. Nec multo post accedunt ad me D. Lyssius, D. Eßexiensis, & Episcopus wintoniensis, serio solicitéque mecum agentes, ut sacramentum confiterer, carne, sanguine & ossibus corpus esse Christi. Tum ego D. Parro, & D. Lyssio dicebam, turpe dictu, id se mihi suadere, quod ipsorum conscientia aliter habere non ignoraret. Cui tum illi respondentes, cupere se hoc modo aiebant, bene ut sint omnia. Tum wintoniensis, velle se aiebat familiarius mecum agere: Sic, inquam, Iudas quum Christum esset proditurus. Petebat tum episcopus ut seorsum me conueniret, at ego id recusabam. Cur non, inquit ille: Quia, inquam, in ore duorum aut trium stabit omne verbum, ut ait Dominus cap. Matthaei decimo octauo, & Paulus secunda ad Cor. Cor.xiii. Inde cœpit rursum Cancellarius meum de sacramento iudicium rimari, quem ego iterum, quousque in vtramque partem claudicaret rogabam. Illud, inquit, vbinam habes? Tertio, inquam, Reg. xviii. Móxque discedente illo, dixit episcopus me combustum iri. Cui rursus Euolui, inquam, ac renolui Scripturas omnes, nunquam tamen hactenus comperire licuit Christum aut Apostolos quenquam dedisse neci. Age, age, Dominus vos minásque vestras eludet ac eneruabit. Psal. ii. Postquam vero inde concedere me iusserunt, aduenit ad me doctor Coxus, & doctor Robinsonus. In summa inter nos couenire satis non potuit. Móxque illi scriptum quoddá de sacramento concinnabat, horantes vt manu ei subscriberem, quod ego tamen renuebam. Post id die sequente Dominico graviter periculoséque ægrotabá, nihil minus quá de salute sperans. Eáque causa expetebam mihi adduci Latamerum vt conuenirem: minimè tamen concedebatur. Demum in summo ægritudinis periculo in carcerem Neopylum traduci iussa sum, vsque adeò ex infirmitate languens, vt nunquam æque graues in vita dolores sentirem. Dominus te in veri cognitione corroboret. Ora, ora, iterum atque iterum ora.
units.tr: As for my fellow prisoners, about whom you ask, I cannot satisfy your desire in that matter, since I was not present at their examination. As for my own case, it stands thus. First, when I was brought before the council and questioned by Master Kyme, I answered that I had already sufficiently explained and held to my opinion on that matter to the Lord Chancellor. But they denied that this was enough: it was the King's will that I should also set out for them what I thought on the matter. I replied flatly that I would not do so. Indeed, if it seemed good to the King, I said, I would gladly and eagerly be heard in person. Again they kept saying that it was not right that the King's leisure should be disturbed on account of me and people like me. I answered that Solomon was rightly counted among the wisest of kings, for he did not hesitate to hear and examine the case of two poor women quarrelling with each other; I said that I did not distrust the King's piety, and that he would hear me, a humble and faithful handmaid subject to him, no less fairly. Then, when the Lord Chancellor asked for my opinion of the sacrament of the Eucharist, I answered in these words: "My faith and opinion is this: whenever I am in a Christian assembly, I take the sacrament of the body and blood in remembrance of the Lord's passion, and together with the thanksgiving performed according to that holy institution, I also share in the saving fruit of that passion." Then the Bishop of Winchester ordered me to answer plainly, without any circumlocution, one way or the other. When I said that I could not sing the Lord's new song in a strange land, he replied that I spoke figuratively and in parables. Indeed, I said, that was most fitting for him, for if I declared to him sincerely what the matter was, he would by no means believe what I said. Then he called me a parrot. I said that I wished to bear not only his words but whatever else he might contrive against me, with an even and willing mind. Then the councillors heaped many insults on me, because I refused to answer their questions explicitly, although I had not yet put forward anything in my own defence. It would be pointless to report each detail here, since there were so many, and they could not be recounted briefly; for they kept me for no less than five hours. Finally, after a long dispute, I was ordered to be taken from there to the house of Master Garnish. On the following day, the council again sat, and I was brought before it. They insisted and pressed me vehemently to state my faith clearly about the sacrament. I answered that I had said as much on this matter as I could say. After some further talk, they ordered me to withdraw to one side. Soon afterwards Master Lyssius, Master Essexiensis, and the Bishop of Winchester came to me and, seriously and earnestly, urged me to confess that the body of Christ is in flesh, blood, and bones. Then I said to Master Parro and Master Lyssius that it was shameful to say that they were urging me to something which their own consciences knew was not the case. In reply they said they wished things to go well in this way. Then the Bishop of Winchester said he wanted to deal with me more familiarly. "So," I said, "Judas did when he was about to betray Christ." The bishop then asked that he might speak with me alone, but I refused. "Why not?" he said. "Because," I said, "in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand," as the Lord says in Matthew 18, and Paul in 2 Corinthians 13. Then the Chancellor began again to probe my judgment on the sacrament, and I again asked him to show where his own view was lame on either side. "Where do you have that?" he said. "In the third book of Kings, chapter 18," I said. And as he was leaving, the bishop said that I would be burned. To this I replied: "I have gone through and turned over all the Scriptures, yet I have never been able to find that Christ or any of the Apostles put anyone to death. Go on, go on! The Lord will mock you and your threats and weaken them" (Psalm 2). After they ordered me to leave, Doctor Cox and Doctor Robinson came to me. In sum, we could not agree at all. Presently they drew up a written statement about the sacrament and urged me to sign it with my hand, which I nevertheless refused. After that, on the following Sunday, I fell seriously and dangerously ill, hoping for nothing less than recovery. For that reason I asked that Latimer be brought to me so that I might speak with him, but this was by no means granted. At last, in the greatest danger of my sickness, I was ordered to be taken to prison in Newgate, so weak from infirmity that I never felt more severe pains in my life. May the Lord strengthen you in the knowledge of the truth. Pray, pray, again and again pray.

units.la: Exemplar confessionis, quam Anna Askeua in carcere Neopylo scriptam reliquit.
units.tr: Copy of the confession which Anna Askew left, written in the prison of Newgate.

units.la: Lego ac reperio in Scripturis, quemadmodum Christus panem sumpsit, deditque discipulis, dicens: Accipite, manducate, hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangetur: innuens videlicet re quidem ipsa atque substantia verum corpus suum, cuius utique panis ille symbolum existit ac sacramentum. Neque enim dissimili loquutionis genere dicebat se templum destructurum, atque in triduo reædificaturum esse, intelligens sine dubio corpus ipsius proprium, quemadmodum ex Ioa. ii. clarè constat. Vnde in sacramento hoc corporis & sanguinis spectandus est mysticus quidam symbolismus, gratæque commemorationis sacramentum, quo simul & illi coniungimur, & ipsi inter nosmet per mutuam Christianámque communionem. Et si permulti sint, qui syncerum huius sacramenti intellectum minus assequatur, ob velamen quod Moses super faciem ponebat, vt non intenderent filij Israel in claritudinem eius. Exod. xxxiiii. 11, Cor. iii. Quin & idem velamen adhuc manere in cordibus quorundam intelligo. cùm autem conuersi fuerint ad Dominimum, sublato velamine tum videbunt cæci. Liquidò enim constat ex historia Bel, nulli rei materiatæ ac manufactæ inesse divinitatem. Daniel itaque: Ne erres, inquit, ô Rex. Dan. xiiii. quippe excelsus non in manufactis habitabit. Actor. vii, Oh quàm dura cervice populus iste, ut semper resistant spiritui sancto. sicut patres ipsorum sic & ipsi, quia præduro sunt corde:
units.tr: I read and find in the Scriptures that, as Christ took bread and gave it to his disciples, saying, "Take, eat, this is my body, which shall be broken for you" (Matt. 26), he indicated, of course, that in very fact and substance his true body is present, of which that bread is indeed the sign and sacrament. For he did not speak in a different manner when he said that he would destroy the temple and raise it up again in three days, understanding without doubt his own body, as is plainly clear from John 2. Hence in this sacrament of the body and blood we must look for a certain mystical symbolism, a sacrament of grateful remembrance, by which we are joined both to him and to one another through mutual Christian fellowship. And although there are many who fail to grasp the pure meaning of this sacrament, it is because of the veil which Moses put over his face, so that the children of Israel would not look upon the brightness of it (Exod. 34; 2 Cor. 3). Indeed, I understand that the same veil still remains in the hearts of some; but when they turn to the Lord, the veil being taken away, then they will see, who are now blind. For it is clear from the story of Bel that no divinity inheres in any created or man-made thing. So Daniel says: "Do not be deceived, O king" (Dan. 14). For the Most High does not dwell in man-made things. "O how stiff-necked are this people, always resisting the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you, for they are hard of heart" (Acts 7).

units.la: Vestra Anna Askeua, quæ nec opto morte, nec valdè vim eius extimesco, tam læta & alacris, quàm queat esse qui ad cælos tendit, veritas in carcere conjecta est, Luc. xxi. Lex versa est in absynthium, Amos vi: Et judicium conversum est retrorsum, Esa. xlix. Parce Domine, omnè auferiniquitatem, & propitius esto, & reddemus vitulos labiorum nostrorum, nec dicemus ultrà, Dij nostri opera manuum nostrarum, quia in te misericordiam consequetur pupillus. quòd si sic facerent, dicit Dominus, sanarem contritiones eorum & diligerem eos libenterque benefacerem. Ephraim, quid mihi ultrà idola? Quis sapiens & intelligit ista, intelligens & sciet hæc? quia rectæ viæ Domini, & justi ambulabunt in eis, prævaricatores verò corruent in eis. Osea xiiii. Salomon autè (ut ait beatus Stephanus) ædificavit illi domum: sed excelsus non in manufactis habitat, sicut per Prophetam dicit: Cælum mihi sedes est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum: quam domum ædificabitis mihi, dicit Dominus, aut quis locus requietionis meæ est? Act. vii. Christus Dominus ad Samaritanam, Crede, inquit, mihi mulier, quia venit hora, quando neque in monte hoc, neque Hierosolymis adorabitis Patrem. Vos adoratis quod nescitis, nos adoramus quod scimus, quia salus ex Judæis est. Sed ventura est hora, & nunc est, quando veri adoratores adorabunt Patrem in spiritu & veritate, Joan. 4. Operamini, dicit Dominus, cibum non qui perit, sed qui vitam æternam parit, quem Filius hominis dabit vobis. hunc enim consignavit Deus, Joan. 7.
units.tr: I, Anna Askew, who neither wish for death nor greatly fear its power, am as glad and cheerful as anyone can be who is heading for heaven; the truth has been cast into prison (Luke 21). The law has been turned into wormwood (Amos 6), and judgement has been turned backward (Isa. 59). "Spare, O Lord, take away all iniquity, and be merciful, and we will render the calves of our lips, and we will not say again, Our gods are the works of our hands; for in you the fatherless finds mercy" (Hos. 14). "If they should do so," says the Lord, "I would heal their hurts and love them freely and do them good." "Ephraim, what have I more to do with idols? Who is wise and understands these things? Whoever has understanding will know them, for the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them, but transgressors shall fall in them" (Hos. 14). But Solomon, as blessed Stephen says, built him a house; yet the Most High does not dwell in man-made things, as the Prophet says: "Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool; what house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest?" (Acts 7). Christ the Lord said to the Samaritan woman: "Believe me, woman, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor at Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is of the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth" (John 4). "Labour," says the Lord, "not for the food that perishes, but for that which brings forth eternal life, which the Son of man will give you; for God has sealed him" (John 6).

units.la: De judicio necisque sententia contra me lata in prætorio.
units.tr: Concerning the judgement and the sentence of death passed against me in the court.

units.la: Dicebant primùm hæreticam me esse, ac legibus ultimum me manere supplicium, si pergam cas tueri opiniones pertinacius. Ego rursus hæreticam me esse pernegavi, quippe quæ nullius essem hæreticæ doctrinæ conscia: neque verò legibus Dei ullum mihi deberi supplicium fide autem illa & confessione mea, quam dominis & satrapis sectorijs conscripseram, quoniam in ea nihil sit cuius me debeat poenitere, non esse animum permutare quicquam. Tum illi scire à me cupiunt, an corpus Christi atque sanguinem in sacramento negaturus sim. Prorsus negare me respondeo, siquidem filius ille Dei, quem Maria virgine natum omnes confitemur, sublimis nunc in caelo reliquit, inde rursus rediturus è caelis, quemadmodum in caelos subiectus est, Actor. 1. Etsi vero sacramentum hoc sacrosanctum esse, iusque veneratione dignum haud abnuerim, tamen quia vos sacramentorum non contenti limitibus, in tantam excurritis superstitionem, ut quod sacramentum sit, pro Deo etiam habeatis & veneremini: concor propterea panem esse quod vos pro numine colitis. Quóq; magis les adhibeatur verbis, eius rei certum habeat iudicium qui volet. Iuppe[?] si trimestri spatio asservetur, ita mucescit situ ac putore corrumpitur, ut in nihilum tandem trimestris ille deus evanescat. Quae sane res satis pro argumento est, panem esse, sacramentum esse, Deum vero nequaquam. Incipientibus demum de sacrificio accersendo mecum agere, ad excipiendam confessionem, subrisi illico. Quid, inquiunt, an non nium est crimina sacrificio confiteri? Mihi, inquam, sat erit Deo confiteri, de quo nihil addubito quin & audire possit confitentem, & ignoscere velit poenitenti. Tumque lata sententia de nobis iudiciali, capitis aliter condemnamur, citra duodecimviralem omnem inquisitionem, praeter legitimam fori consuetudinem.
units.tr: First they said that I was a heretic, and that by the laws the final punishment awaited me if I continued to defend these opinions more stubbornly. I, in turn, denied that I was a heretic, since I was conscious of holding no heretical doctrine; nor did I owe any punishment under the laws of God. But as for that faith and confession of mine, which I had written out for the lords and the sheriffs, since there is nothing in it which I ought to regret, I had no intention of changing anything. Then they wished to know from me whether I would deny the body and blood of Christ in the sacrament. I answered that I utterly denied it, since that Son of God, whom we all confess born of the Virgin Mary, now remains on high in heaven, from which he will come again, just as he was taken up into heaven (Acts 1). And although I would not deny that this sacrament is holy and worthy of reverence, yet because you, not content with the limits of the sacraments, rush into such great superstition that you even hold and worship as God what is a sacrament, therefore I say that the bread which you worship as a deity is bread. The more it is subjected to words, let whoever wishes have a sure judgement of this matter: for if it is kept for three months, it grows mouldy with age and rots with stench, so that in the end that three-month god vanishes into nothing. This fact is surely enough proof that it is bread and a sacrament, but by no means God. Then, when they began to deal with me about summoning a priest to hear my confession, I laughed at once. "What," they said, "is it not right to confess sins to a priest?" "For me," I said, "it will be enough to confess to God, of whom I have no doubt that he can hear the one who confesses and is willing to forgive the penitent." And so, the sentence of judgement being passed upon us, we are condemned to death, without any inquest by the twelve men, beyond the lawful custom of the court.

units.la: De fide autem & confessione quam Anna haec è Neopylo carcere conscriptam misit senatui, iam ante commemoratum est.
units.tr: Concerning the faith and confession which Anna here sent, written from the prison of Newgate, to the senate, it has already been mentioned.

units.la: Exemplar epistolae quam post latam condemnationis sententiam ad D. Cancellarium miserat sacra Christi martyr Anna Askewa.
units.tr: A copy of the letter which the holy martyr of Christ, Anna Askew, sent to the Lord Chancellor after the sentence of condemnation had been pronounced.

units.la: In Domino rerum omnium conditore, per quem universae subsistunt creaturae salute, ac salutiferae veritatis ipsius agnitionem, Amen. Subrustica[?] haec mihi, nimisq; fortasse molestam compellandi audaciam, quam partim necessario res ipsa imponit, partim fiducia quadam tuae benignitatis adauget, celsitudo tua ignoscat precor. atq; ne multis sublimes occupationes tuas detineā: quod à sublimitate tua rogatu veli eiusmodi est, ut pietas tua pauculas has lineas Regiae maiestati de ratione fidei meae à mé conscriptas exhibere velit. Quas si pro æquitate sua ac fide, ita ut par est, appendat, cumque acerba sententia illa contulerit, quam in me tulerunt iudices, morti me adiudicantes, satis confido maiestatem illius facile intellecturam, causam supplicij mei non æquissimam profecto trutina libratam esse. Caeterum universum hoc quicquid est negotij, summo ac iustissimo omnium rerum æstimatori ac vindici Deo permitto. Itaque ut finiam, opto celsitudinem tuam in Domino valere, qui te cum sanctis suis sospitem custodiat, dirigatq; in omnibus. Amen. Tua in Domino ancilla, Anna Askeua.
units.tr: In the Lord, the creator of all things, through whom all creatures subsist unto salvation, and in the knowledge of his saving truth, Amen. May your Lordship pardon me, I beg you, for these rough lines and for the boldness of addressing you, which may be excessive: partly the matter itself compels me, and partly a certain confidence in your kindness increases it. And that I may not detain you from your weighty occupations: the request I make of your Lordship is of this kind, that your piety would be willing to present these few lines, which I have written myself concerning the reason of my faith, to his royal Majesty. If he weighs them with his own fairness and faith, as is right, and sets them against that harsh sentence which the judges have passed upon me, condemning me to death, I am fully confident that his Majesty will easily understand that the cause of my punishment has certainly not been weighed on the most just scales. For the rest, I commit this whole business, whatever it is, to God, the highest and most just judge and avenger of all things. And so, to finish, I pray that your Lordship may fare well in the Lord, who keep you safe with his saints and direct you in all things. Amen. Your handmaid in the Lord, Anna Askew.

units.la: Exemplar ac ratio fidei ad regiam maiestatem conscriptæ.
units.tr: A copy and account of the faith, written for the royal Majesty.

units.la: Ego Anna Askeua, mentis ac memoriae bene sanae: tametsi panem aduersitatis, & aquâ afflictionis mihi dederit Dominus, non tamen quantum mea promeruerint peccata, percupiam id maiestati tuae innotescere: Quod quum legibus sim capitis condemnata, tanquam maleficia & facinorosa: caelum hic ac terram appello, immerito me ac innocentem moriturum. Quódque initio dixi, idem & postremo nunc repeto, tota voluntate ab omni me haeresi abhorrere, semperque abhorruisse. De Coena autem mystica quod attinet, credo, teneóque quicquid ea in re præscribit Dominus, suóque sacrosancto confirmauit sanguine. Credo praeterea, ac profiteor, non solum in hac re, sed in aliis omnibus, quicquid vel vox ipsius, vel ecclesia catholica dictauit, nobisque ad credendum proposuit. Neque enim animus vnquam fuit a verbo oris ipsius vlla in re, quod sciam, deflectere. Breuiter atque in summa, quicquid os Domini vsquam præscribit, certum est firmo pectoris proposito amplecti atque retinere, pro virili, vel muliebri potius facultate mea. Itaque ne pluribus maiestatem tuam detineam, his verbis voluntatis meae ac literarum finem claudo eruditionis amplioris inopia, Anna Askeua.
units.tr: I, Anna Askew, of sound mind and memory: although the Lord has given me the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet I would very much like your Majesty to know how great my sins have deserved. Since I have been condemned to capital punishment by the laws as a malefactor and criminal, I call heaven and earth here to witness that I am to die innocent and undeserving. And what I said at the beginning, I now repeat at the end: with my whole will I abhor every heresy, and have always abhorred it. As for the mystical Supper, I believe and hold whatever the Lord has prescribed in that matter, and confirmed with his most holy blood. Moreover, I believe and profess, not only in this matter but in all others, whatever his own voice or the catholic Church has dictated and set before us to believe. For my mind has never, so far as I know, turned aside from the word of his mouth in any matter. Briefly and in sum: whatever the mouth of the Lord prescribes anywhere, I am resolved with a firm purpose of heart to embrace and hold, as far as my strength, or rather my woman's strength, allows. And so, that I may not detain your Majesty further, I close the end of my will and of this letter with these words, lacking any greater learning, Anna Askew.

units.la: Quibus tormentis excepta est & excruciata, è carcere Neopylo discedens.
units.tr: With what torments she was racked and tortured, as she was leaving the prison of Newgate.

units.la: Die Martis è carcere in diuersorium corona pensili insigne extrahor, vbi D. Rychæus, & episcopus Lond. ad me veniunt, multis verborum blanditiis me à veri defensione impellentes. sed frustra. Venit postea Nicolaus Shaxtonus, qui in eadem prius cum fuisset opinione resiliuit[?], suadens vt idem suo exemplo facerem. Cui respondi, præstare non natam esse, aliaqueid genus similia. Nec multò post D. Rychæus inde de in arcem Londinensem me transfert, ubi ad tertiam demùm hom[?] commoranti, D. Rychaeus cum altero e senatu regis ad me accurrens, mandat pro mea erga regem fide & obseruantia, ut si quos sciam viros aut foeminas meae factionis alios, apertos facerem. Ego vero prorsus me quenquam scire pernegaui. Tum illi, de domina Ducissa Suffolciae, de Comitissa Sussexiae, de Comitissa Herfordiae, de uxore D. Denei simul & D. Fitzwuiliami spectatae nobilitatis heroinis recontantur. Respondeo, si quam vellem in eas criminationem derivare, probare sane me ubi id fecissem, non posse. At rex, inquiunt, pro imperto nouit, ingentem esse tuae factionis multitudinem, quos si licet, facile proferre ac nominare poteris. Nimirùm, inquam, rex in hac re, quemadmodum in aliis multis rebus fallitur. Porrò ingenti illi studio a me contendere ut palam facerem, quorum maxime beneficio intra carceres fulta, atque in sententia confirmata fuerint. Respondi nullum esse omnino mortalium, cuius instinctu ad eam doctrinae constantiam animatior sim facta & confirmatior. Porrò quod ad victus attinet rationem, eam nullo alio pacto mihi suppetere dicebam, quàm ministerio ancillae, quae per urbis plateas nonnunquam incedens bonorum hominum, meo nomine, auxilia implorabat. Illíque ac famuli eorum pij quidam mittunt ad me quae deferuntur, at nomina eorum prorsus mihi ignota sunt. Imò, inquiunt, ex magnatibus non desunt, qui pecuniam tibi submministrant. At nomina, inquam, prorsus nescio. Atque inter eos, inquiunt, sunt etiam primates foeminae, atque adeò ex primaria nobilitate nonnullae, quae idem faciunt. Venit, inquam, ad me famulari veste quadam dono ferens florenos duos quos ab illustrissima Comitissa Herfordiensi ad me missos dicebat. Itémque alter similiter tunicatus, qui francum nummum sole insignem mihi deferebat dono, ut dicebat, clariss. heroinae D. Deneae. quod an ita fuerit, certum equidem non habeo, nisi duntaxat ex praedicatione ancillae meae. Adhaec insuper addunt illi, fuisse ex summa & senatoria nobilitate, qui in hoc me adanimarent opinionum genere. At ego constanter pernegabam. Postremò, quia confiteri nolebâ quosdam e nobilitate heroas & heroinas in me a pariter fuisse opinione, in nervos me inq; tormenta mittunt, ut sic doloribus a me extorquerent, quod per quaestiones non possent. demum vbi longo iam tempore me in tortorū equuleo habet, nec interim vocem emittere, nec corpus quicquam mouere, aut doloribus vident cedere, irati atque incensi magis D.Cancellarius & D.Rychaeus, ilico exutis togis ipsi tormenta capessunt, tortorum perfunctturi ministerio, tanta asperitate, vt ruptis pene artubus, ab ipsa minimo minus morte abfuerim. Id vbi praesensit arcis praefectus, monet vt me e tormentis exoluerent. exoluta concido statim in vitae deliquium, viribus vndique & membris destituta. Illi tamen adhibitis fomentis, vires tandem ac vitam fugientem redintegrant, ac recolligunt. Post id humi sedens horarum spatio duarum, detinear a Cancellario: qui blandis verborum illecebris hortari me coepit, vt repudiata sententia in illorum decreta concederem. Sed Dominus Deus meus (gratiam habeo aeternae ipsius bonitati) ea me muniuit constantia, vt de euangelicae prosessionis synceritate nihil remittere, idemque porro dabit perseuerandi (vt spero) vires ad finem. His itaque cruciatibus hactenus & tormentis defuncta, ducor posthac in aediculam quandam, atque in lectu collocor. Rursus Cancellarius per nuncium ad me mittit, vt si opinione discederem, re nulla egerem. sin minus facere, futurum vt in carcere iterum, atque inde ad supplicij locum deducta, facibus ac flammis denique torrefierem. Remitto iterum per eundem respondens nuncium, nullam esse tam diram infestamque mortem, quam nō sæpius subire malem, quam semel datam religioni fidem abnegare. Dominus illis aperiat precor caecos mentis oculos, vt veritatem aliquando agnoscant atq; amplectantur, Amen. Bene vale chare in Christo Domino frater, ora.
units.tr: On Tuesday I was taken from the prison to an inn, marked with a hanging crown, where Master Rich and the Bishop of London came to me, trying by many smooth words to drive me away from the defence of the truth. But in vain. Afterwards Nicholas Shaxton came, who had earlier held the same opinion but had gone back on it, urging me to do the same as he had done. I answered him that it was better not to have been born, and other things of that kind. Not long after, Master Rich transferred me from there to the Tower of London, where, as I was staying there until the third hour, Master Rich came running to me with another of the king's council, and ordered me, for the sake of my loyalty and obedience to the king, to make known any men or women of my party whom I knew. But I firmly denied that I knew anyone at all. Then they recounted to me the names of the Duchess of Suffolk, the Countess of Sussex, the Countess of Hereford, the wife of Sir Anthony Denny, and Lady Fitzwilliam, heroines of distinguished rank. I replied that if I wished to lay any accusation against them, I could certainly not prove it once I had done so. But, they said, the king knows for certain that your party is very large, and if you are allowed, you can easily name and point them out. Surely, I said, the king in this matter, as in many others, is deceived. Then they pressed me with great eagerness to make public by whose help above all I had been supported and confirmed in my opinion while in prison. I answered that there was no mortal at all by whose urging I had become more spirited and firmer in that constancy of doctrine. Furthermore, as to the manner of my living, I said that it could be supplied to me in no other way than by the service of a maidservant, who, walking now and then through the streets of the city, begged help from good people in my name. And some pious men and their servants send me what is brought to me, but their names are wholly unknown to me. Indeed, they said, there are not lacking among the great men some who supply you with money. But, I said, I know their names not at all. And among them, they said, there are also women of high rank, and indeed some of the first nobility, who do the same. A man came to me, I said, in a certain servant's coat, bringing as a gift two florins which he said were sent to me by the most illustrious Countess of Hereford. And likewise another, similarly dressed, who brought me a French coin stamped with the sun, as a gift, he said, from the most distinguished heroine, Lady Denny. Whether it was so, I certainly do not know, except from the word of my maidservant. Besides, they added that there were some of the highest senatorial nobility who encouraged me in this kind of opinion. But I constantly denied it. Finally, because I was unwilling to confess that certain heroes and heroines of the nobility had likewise been of my opinion, they sent me to the cords and the torments, so that they might by pains extract from me what they could not by questioning. At last, when for a long time they had me on the rack, and I neither uttered a sound nor moved my body, nor gave way to the pains, the Chancellor and Master Rich, angrier and more inflamed, at once took off their gowns and themselves took up the instruments, undertaking the office of torturers, with such harshness that, my limbs almost broken, I was little short of death. When the lieutenant of the Tower perceived this, he advised that they release me from the torments. Released, I at once collapsed into a swoon of life, deprived of strength on every side and in my limbs. Yet, after applying remedies, they at last restored and gathered my strength and life, which was slipping away. After this, sitting on the ground for the space of two hours, I was detained by the Chancellor, who began with smooth enticements of words to urge me to give up my sentence and yield to their decrees. But my Lord God (I give thanks to his eternal goodness) strengthened me with such constancy that I have not given up anything of the sincerity of the gospel profession, and he will give, as I hope, the strength to persevere to the end. Thus, having been finished with these torments and racks so far, I was afterwards led into a little chamber and laid upon a bed. Again the Chancellor sent a messenger to me, saying that if I departed from my opinion, I would gain nothing by it; but if I did not do so, it would come about that I should be taken back to prison, and from there led to the place of execution, and at last be burned with torches and flames. I sent back by the same messenger the answer that there is no death so dreadful and hostile that I would not rather undergo it many times than once deny the faith given to religion. May the Lord open the blind eyes of their minds, I pray, so that they may at length recognise and embrace the truth, Amen. Farewell, dear brother in Christ the Lord, pray for me.

units.la: Exemplar epistolae, qua literis domini Laffellii[?] concaptiui fui respondet.
units.tr: Copy of a letter in which she replies to the letter of Lord Laffellius[?], her fellow prisoner.

units.la: Charissime in Domino salute. Satis demirari nequeo, quae tandem res ea tibi suspicionem moueat, de pusillanimitate ac vecordia mea, quasi mortis adeo horrore concutiar, quae malorum omnium finis est ac terminus. Etiam atq; etiam in Domino te precor, ne quid huiusmodi in pectus tuum de me altius descendere, aut diutius infidere patiaris. Nihil enim addubito, quin opus suum, quod coepit in me Dominus, idem porro sit perfecturus. Audio nunc aegre habere consilium regis, postquam videt esse palam, quod ob religionem tormentis me in arce dederint. Causantur nunc, id se perterredi causa fecisse: vel quod ipsos facti tandem pudeat, ut[?] [?]cl id verentes potius ne qua res domũ ad aures regis promanet. Itaq; unc edictis[?] cauent, quò rem omnibus tegant modis: verũ enimuero, [?]uod ad me attinet, Dominus ipsis ignoscat precor. Bene vale. Ora.
units.tr: Most beloved in the Lord, greetings. I can hardly wonder what it is that has moved you to suspect me of cowardice and madness, as though I were so shaken by the dread of death, which is the end and limit of all evils. Again and again I beg you in the Lord not to let any such notion sink deeper into your heart or remain there longer on my account. For I have no doubt that the Lord, who has begun his work in me, will also bring it to completion. I hear that the king's council is now troubled, since it has become plain that they tortured me in the prison for the sake of religion. Now they claim they did it only to frighten me, or else they are ashamed of what they did, and they fear above all that the matter will reach the king's ears. So now they take precautions by edicts, to hide the affair from everyone by every means. But as far as I am concerned, I pray the Lord to forgive them. Farewell. Pray. Ora.

units.la: Apologia de falso illi ascripta recantatione.
units.tr: Apology concerning the recantation falsely ascribed to her.

units.la: Perlegi mendax & infame scriptum, quod vice & titulo mecæ re-cantationis per multorum passim manus circumfertur. Ita me amet Dominus, nihil unquam in animum hunc admisi minus, quàm ut veri fide recantando differrerer. Id tamen fateor, in prima disquisitione quæ mihi cũ pisćopo Lodinensi fuit, multa mihi obiecta ab illo de sacramento, ac viipsum[?] à me responsa esse. Qui tamen præter hoc nihil à me aliud extorquere potuit, quàm quòd videlicet in ea re tantũ me credere ac tenere liceb am, quantũ diuini verbi iussit præscriptio: præterea nihil à me aliud exprimi quitũ[?] est. Tũ ille instrumentũ confecit, quod nunc formulis excusum extat in manibus, eique confecto iussit subscribere. Renuebam. Tum duo illi patroni ac sponsores mei, nullo non persuadedi genere instabant acriter ut facerem, rem leviculi esse momenti dictitantes. Post multa, subscripsi tandem, in hanc videlicet sententiam: Ego Anna Askeua, credo assentiorq;, siquidem diuini verbi & Ecclesiæ catholicæ non dissentiat institutio. Ea tu subscriptione offensus non parũ episcopus, me in carcerem iterum ac custodiam mandat: ubi aliquandiu cõmorata, amicorũ operâ vix tandem restituor. Atq; hactenus vera certamq; habes huiusce rei narrationem. De ea verò re in qua potissimũ tibi esse satisfactum postulas, relego te ad cap. Ioa. sextum, quod tibi pro certissimo esse gnomone peruelim, quod sanè ad hanc rem attinet. Bene vale.
units.tr: I have read the lying and infamous writing which is circulated from hand to hand everywhere, under the title of my recantation. As the Lord loves me, I never admitted anything into my mind less than the thought of putting off the faith of the truth by recanting. I do confess this much: in my first examination, which I had with the bishop of Lincoln, many objections were raised against me by him concerning the sacrament, and I gave him answers. Yet beyond this he could extort nothing else from me, except that I might believe and hold in that matter only so far as the prescription of the divine Word commanded; nothing else could be drawn out of me. Then he drew up a document, which now stands in print in the hands of many, and ordered me to sign it once it was drawn up. I refused. Then my two advocates and sponsors, by every kind of persuasion, pressed me hard to do it, insisting that it was a thing of little importance. After much pressure I finally signed, to this effect: "I, Anna Askew, believe and assent, provided that it does not dissent from the teaching of the divine Word and of the catholic Church." Offended by this signature, the bishop, not a little, ordered me back into prison and custody, where, after I had stayed there for some time, I was with difficulty restored by the efforts of friends. So far you have a true and certain account of this matter. As for the point on which you especially demand satisfaction, I refer you to the sixth chapter of John, which I would gladly have you hold as a most certain touchstone for this question. Farewell.

units.la: Oratio ad Deũ, quã Anna Askeua morte cõfessione suæ fidei obsignatura habuit.
units.tr: Prayer to God, which Anna Askew meant to seal with her death and the confession of her faith.

units.la: O Domine, plures habeo inimicos, quàm capitis mei capillos numero. Da tamen clementissime Deus, necubi verborũ lenocinijs victa succumbã. Verũ tu & me pugna, próq; me responde ô Domine.
