Ingressi urbem benigne a fratribus excepti fuere, qui non mediocrem acceperunt consolationem ex piis istius hominis admonitionibus. Ibique cum diebus aliquot mansissent, Tornacum profecti sunt persequentes iter Anglicum: sed in ipso itinere Augustinus cum uxore sua agniti fuerunt atq; e vestigio ad Praefectum urbis delati, qui illos insecutus, cu quatuor milliarib° Tornaco abessent omnes cepit, praeter Augustinum, qui tum nescio quo modo manus istorum evasit, de quo postea dicemus. Satellites autem quum nusquam iste appareret, M. Nicolaum cum duabus mulieribus reduxerunt, qui a Praefecto contumelias in via passi sunt. Interdum quando mensae accumbendum erat, M. Nicolaus Deo gratias agebat, ut fidelibus moris est. Praefectus illi convitia multa faciens, variisque iuramentis in Deum blasphemus dixit, Videamus nunc, improbe haeretice, an te Deus tuus de manu mea eripiet. Nicolaus modeste admodum ei respondit, Quid, quaeso, in te commisit Christus, quod eum tuis blasphemiis in frusta quodammodo seces: desine, quaeso, maledicere: aut si tanto furore ageris in filium Dei, ipsiusque verbum, ut ab iniurijs abstinere non queas: in me iram tuam converte ut me tundendo, illam evomas: longe prosecto mihi gratius ita feceris. Itaque in curru impositi manibus & pedibus vinctis Bergas pervenerunt, ubi in imum Castri carcere catenis constricti includuntur. Dum sic misere detinerentur accessit ad eos Dux Arscotus, multis sacrificis, & Franciscanis comitatus, cum eorum antistite quem Gardianum vocant, doctore Theologo. Ab his M. Nicolaus in medio constitutus & rogatus, cuias esset, quonam tenderet, quae ipsius fides esset: alacri sane animo respondit, exactamque rationem reddidit ad omnia: ut saepius perstricte alioqui Franciscanorum fronti ruborem afferret: atque dum illos turpissimae ignorationis convinceret, uno ore omnes ad veterem illam ac tritam coaxationem consugiebat, Daemonium habet, ad ignem ducatur Lutheranus. Excepit M. Nicolaus, Quid, domini mei, Iudaeo etiam ac Turcae datur pro se loqui: nihil est quod timeatis ne quis vos seducat aut vincat: si veram doctrinam deseditis, & veritas ipsa vestras partes tuetur. Tandem interrogationibus fine imposito, petiit ipse ut sibi liceret confessionem fidei suae describere: quod illi ut in carcere faceret non recusarunt adversarij. Interea dum in custodia esset, extremumque supplicium in dies expectaret, hostibus in mentem venit ut illum rogarent ubinam diuertisset quum Bergas advenisset. Ad hoc ille dixit, se ante id tempus nunquam in ea urbe fuisse. proinde locum nominare non posse: adversari quum ab eo nihil se extorquere posse viderent, adorti sunt Barbaram [?] uxorem ipsius, atque in primis dux Arscotus illa manibus prehendens blandi landis verbis sic est locutus, Barbara, rogo te ut vitam tuam serues. [?]orenti enim adhuc es ætate mulier, si mihi nomines eos apud quos diertisti, efficiam equidem ut hoc carcere soluta & libera dimittaris. Misera autem hæc fœmina blanditiis & pollicitationibus Ducis facile victa, nihil non fecit. quæ res maioris persecutionis aduersus fideles [?]causa fuit, quorum plures in vincula coniecti fuere. Nicolaus autem posteaquam omnia tentassent veritatis hostes, tandem è carcere Ambronensi ad Iudices ductus est qui illum condemnarunt, ut vivus exuretur, atque in cineres, ut ibi ferè solet fieri, corpus redigeretur. Qua sententia pronunciata Nicolaus continuò in Domino exultans dixit, Benedictus sit Dominus Deus noster qui me tanto dignatur afficere beneficio, atque ad eum honoris gradum extollere, ut me adhibeat testẽ in causa charissimi Filij sui. Quo dicto eximio Spiritus ardore Psalmũ canere cœpit, stupetibus satellitibus qui illum à tribunali in quoddam carceris cubiculum ducebat dum adesset hora supplicij in illum constitu-tuti: ibi cum esset, pulverem è vestibus excutiebat & paleas quæ tum cæ adhærebant, manu deijciebat quasi ad ornatum se componeret: atque ijs qui aderant locutus est. Amici, ne miremini cur nunc ita me adornem namq; inuitatus sum ad nuptias & epulas Agni illius immaculati. Interea venit quidam satelles qui suppræfecti urbis nomine interminabatur ne quod verbum ad populum faceret. Ille verò respondit cupere se suppræfecto loqui, quum verò idẽ cõfirmauit, ac nisi pareret, pila ipsi os obstrueretur. Siquidẽ, inquit reus, tu ipse mihi sermone ad populum interdicis, obediam: sed unum vicissim abs te postulo. Eloquere, inquit suppræfectus, quid velis. saltẽ ut dum ad supplicij accedo liceat mihi inuocare Dominum & laudibus nomen eius celebrare inter eundum. quod illi concessum fuit, modò nihil ad populũ diceret. Post horam itaque à meridie secundam venit ad illum magistratus ut sententia executioni mandaretur. Ipse per clivum è Castro descendens, sublatis in cælum oculis ac hilari vultu Dominum invocauit. Plures autem ipsum sequebantur Franciscani vsitata Sathanæ stabella, vt impedirent ipsius preces. Vbi ad locum supplicij ventum est, cernens ingentem populi multitudinem, nulla tum interdicti ratione habita, ad populum conuersus alta voce exclamauit: O Carole, Carole, quousque tandem tibi cor adeo induratum erit? at plura dicere volenti satellitum unus impegit colaphum. Hic iterum Nicolaus, Ha miser populé, inquit, non es dignus cui verbum Dei proponatur. Hæc dicens ad palum deligabatur. Franciscani qui circunstabant, multa ipsi conuitia fecerunt: solitam catilenam subinde, ut sunt vere cuculi, occinentes, quod dæmonium in se haberet. Quibus Nicolaus hoc versu Dauidici Psalmi valedixit, Discedite à me omnes qui operamini iniquitatem, quoniam exaudiuit Dominus vocem fletus mei: ac de-repente stramen accenditur, quum ille defixis in cælum oculis, semel atque iterum vociferatus est, Domine Iesu, Pater æterne, in manus tuas totum me trado atque commendo. atque ita fœliciter ex hoc mundo migrauit pia anima.
units.tr: Today the Lord has left no corner of the earth, however remote, without evidence of his goodness and mercy, since among the nations everywhere he brings forward faithful witnesses to defend his cause, by whom the ignorant are taught, those who have received heavenly knowledge are strengthened, and every man who resists the truth in any way is left without excuse [ἀναπολόγητος] and inexcusable. In the year 1549, a persecution having arisen among the people of Hainault, among others taken and shut up in prison were Master Nicolas, a Frenchman by birth, and his wife Barbara, and Augustine the barber and his wife Mariona, born in a certain village not far from Bergen in Hainault. After they had stayed for some time at Geneva, they withdrew together into Germany, intending to go on to England. When they had come into Hainault, Augustine asked Nicolas, who was not unlearned, to visit the little flock in the city of Bergen and to share generously with the brothers whatever gifts of the Spirit of God he had. He gladly agreed to so fair a request, especially since he knew that in this way the kingdom of the Son of God is spread. Entering the city, they were kindly received by the brothers, who took no small comfort from the pious admonitions of this man. After they had stayed there some days, they set out for Tournai, continuing their journey toward England. But on that very road Augustine and his wife were recognised, and at once were reported to the prefect of the city, who pursued them and, four miles from Tournai, seized all of them except Augustine, who somehow then escaped the hands of these men, of whom we will speak later. But since the officers could nowhere find him, they led back Master Nicolas with the two women, and on the way they suffered insults from the prefect. Sometimes, when it was time to sit at table, Master Nicolas gave thanks to God, as is the custom of the faithful. The prefect, heaping many abuses on him and blaspheming God with various oaths, said: "Let us now see, wicked heretic, whether your God will snatch you from my hand." Nicolas answered him very modestly: "What, I ask, has Christ done to you, that you should cut him to pieces with your blasphemies? Stop cursing, I beg you. Or if you are driven by such fury against the Son of God and his Word that you cannot refrain from insults, turn your anger against me, so that by beating me you may vent it; you will certainly do me a much greater kindness that way." So they were put in a cart, with hands and feet bound, and came to Bergen, where they were shut up in chains in the lowest prison of the castle. While they were held there in this wretched state, the Duke of Arschot came to them, accompanied by many priests and Franciscans, together with their head, whom they call the Guardian, a doctor of theology. Nicolas was placed in the midst of them and asked whose he was, whither he was going, and what his faith was. He answered with a cheerful spirit and gave a full and exact account of everything, so that he often put the Franciscans to shame; and while he convicted them of the most shameful ignorance, they all with one voice fell back on that old and worn-out croaking: "He has a demon; let the Lutheran be led to the fire." Nicolas replied: "What, my lords? Even a Jew or a Turk is allowed to speak for himself. There is nothing for you to fear, lest anyone seduce or overcome you, provided you do not desert the true doctrine, and the truth itself defends your cause." At last, when the questioning had been brought to an end, he himself asked that he be allowed to write out the confession of his faith; the adversaries did not refuse him this, so that he could do it in prison. Meanwhile, while he was in custody and daily expected the final punishment, it came into the minds of his enemies to ask him where he had lodged when he came to Bergen. To this he replied that he had never been in that city before, and so could not name a place. When the adversaries saw that they could extract nothing from him, they turned on his wife Barbara, and above all the Duke of Arschot took her by the hands and spoke to her with flattering words: "Barbara, I beg you to save your life. You are still a woman of young age; if you name for me those with whom you lodged, I will certainly see to it that you are released and set free from this prison." This wretched woman, easily overcome by the Duke's flatteries and promises, did everything they asked. This affair was the cause of a greater persecution against the faithful, of whom many were thrown into chains. But after the enemies of the truth had tried everything, Nicolas was at last led from the prison at Ambron before the judges, who condemned him to be burned alive, his body to be reduced to ashes, as is usually done in that place. When this sentence was pronounced, Nicolas, exulting continually in the Lord, said: "Blessed be the Lord our God, who deigns to bestow such a benefit on me and to raise me to such a degree of honour that he takes me as a witness in the cause of his dearest Son." With these remarkable words, in an ardour of the Spirit, he began to sing a Psalm, while the officers who were leading him from the tribunal to a certain cell of the prison were astonished. There, while the hour of his punishment drew near, he brushed the dust from his clothes and with his hand removed the straws that clung to them, as if he were arranging himself for an adornment; and he spoke to those who were present: "Friends, do not be surprised that I adorn myself thus now, for I have been invited to the wedding and the feast of that spotless Lamb." Meanwhile a certain officer came who, in the name of the under-prefect of the city, threatened that he should say no word to the people. He replied that he wished to speak with the under-prefect; when the officer confirmed this, and said that unless he obeyed, a ball would be stuffed into his mouth: "Since you yourself, as the judge, forbid me to speak to the people in this way, I will obey. But in turn I ask one thing of you." "Say," said the under-prefect, "what you wish." "That, while I go to the punishment, I may be allowed to call upon the Lord and celebrate his name with praises as I go." This was granted him, provided he said nothing to the people. So, after two o'clock in the afternoon, the magistrate came to him so that the sentence might be carried out. He came down the slope from the castle, with his eyes lifted to heaven and a cheerful countenance, calling upon the Lord. Many Franciscans followed him, the usual little stools of Satan, to hinder his prayers. When he came to the place of execution and saw the huge multitude of people, taking no account of the prohibition he turned to the people and cried out in a loud voice: "O Charles, Charles, how long will your heart be so hardened?" But as he was about to say more, one of the officers struck him a blow. Here Nicolas again said: "Ah, wretched people, you are not worthy to have the Word of God set before you." Saying this, he was bound to the stake. The Franciscans standing round heaped many abuses on him, repeatedly singing their usual ditty, as true cuckoos do, that he had a demon in him. Nicolas took leave of them with this verse of the Psalm of David: "Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping." Suddenly the straw was set alight, while he, with his eyes fixed on heaven, cried out again and again: "Lord Jesus, eternal Father, into your hands I entrust and commend my whole self." And so the pious soul happily departed from this world.

units.la: Sequitur mors Marionæ, vxoris Augustini.
units.tr: Here follows the death of Mariona, the wife of Augustine.

units.la: Post hanc executionem, ludices ad causam Marionæ venerunt vxoris Augustini de quo supra, quæ quidem de variis rebus interrogata, ac præsertim quid Geneuæ fieret, quomodo ibi sacramenta administrarentur: vtrum ipsa cœnam Dominicam in ea vrbe celebrasset: confessa est omnia libere, nempe se ibi Cœnæ participem fuisse, affirmans veram Domini nostri institutionem Geneuæ retineri atque seruari. Ad alia quæ percontabantur aduersarij respondit pro modulo fidei atque cognitione quæ illi à Domino tradita erat: adeo vt nec precibus vllis, nec minis à veritatis confessione deduci potuerit. Paucis post diebus causa in iudicijs confecta, constitutum est in illam supplicium quod ferè fidelibus matronis aut puellis, quæ ob causam religionis ijs in locis capiuntur, ferendum est: vt scilicet viua in terram defoderetur. Hæc autem insignis mulier ad istud genus supplicij ducta, eleuans ad cælum oculos prorupit in laudes Domini, eique gratias egit quòd se miseram è defis[?] tenebris eripuisset. In fossam simulac demissa fuit, in genua procumbens Domini opem implorauit, & priusquam prosterneretur à tortore, petiuit sibi dari sudariolum aut linteum quo faciei eius tegi posset. Postquam itaque prostrata esset, faciesque primum sudariolo, ac deinde cum ea reliquæ etiam corporis partes terra cooperta essent, cō-culcauit. ulcauit eam pedibus carnifex:donec sic miserè trucidata Deo accetum reddidit spiritum.
units.tr: After this execution, the judges turned to the case of Mariona, the wife of Augustine mentioned above. She was questioned on various matters, especially what went on at Geneva and how the sacraments were administered there, and whether she herself had celebrated the Lord's Supper in that city. She confessed everything freely: that she had taken part in the Supper there, and affirmed that the true institution of our Lord is kept and observed at Geneva. To the other questions the adversaries put she replied as far as her faith and the knowledge the Lord had given her allowed, so that she could be turned from confessing the truth neither by any prayers nor by threats. A few days later, when the case had been completed in the courts, it was decided that she should suffer the punishment usually inflicted in those places on faithful matrons or girls seized for the sake of religion: namely, that she should be buried alive in the earth. This remarkable woman, led to this kind of punishment, lifted her eyes to heaven and broke out in praise of the Lord, giving thanks that he had rescued her, a wretch, out of thick darkness. As soon as she was lowered into the pit, she knelt and implored the Lord's help, and before she was thrown down by the executioner, she asked that a small cloth or linen be given her with which her face could be covered. Once she was laid down, her face first covered with the cloth and then the rest of her body covered with earth, the executioner trampled her with his feet, until, so cruelly murdered, she gave up her spirit acceptable to God.

units.la: AVGVSTINVS TONSOR.
units.tr: AUGUSTINE THE BARBER.

units.la: Maritus Marionæ istius qui interfectus fuit Bellimonte, quæ urbs sex milliaribus Bergis Hannoniæ distat.
units.tr: This Mariona's husband, who was put to death at Bellimont, a town six miles from Bergen in Hainault.

units.la: Diximus dum Nicolaus cum Mariona caperentur, Augustinum mi-ris modis euasisse, qui sic liberatus ope procul dubio diuina, dedit mercaturae aromatum atq; aliarum rerum minutarum quas per mercatus urbium circumferebat, ut ita sine fraude victus pararet. Quum venisset Bellimontem oppidum Hannoniae, mercesque suas ibi in foro venum proposuisset, agnitus fuit à quibusdam, nomenque ipsius ad magistratum delatū: ipse vero perfentiens insidias, relictis mercibus fuga sibi consulere volebat. Dum hoc pacto fugeret, vidit procul domū in qua iuerterat satellitibus cinctam: ac magis tum quàm antea sibi metuere cepit (erat enim ille homo perpusilli animi, adeò ut ad conspectum vel cursum vnius satellitis totus tremeret atque horreret). Eo itaq; corceptus pauore atque tremore urbem exit, seque in dumum mox proriuit sperās ibi tutò latere posse. Sed iam aderat hora ipsius, Deóq; alier visum fuit. Etenim cum se post dumum[?] abconderet, erant quidam in muris urbis qui illum facile poterant videre, ac quàprimum satellitibus qui insequebatur indicarunt. Proinde cōprehensus ilico deductus fuit Bergas, ut in ea urbe Hannoniae metropolitana, causa ipsius disceptaretur. Ibi rogatus fuit de tota vitæ suæ ac fidei ratione: ipse vero quæstionibus omnibus plenè satisfecit, ostendens aduersarijs fiduciam suam quam in Christo positam habebat, id quod à se constanter præstitum ipse amicis qui eum in carcere iuuisebant, narrauit. In quo sanè mirabile Dei opus ernimus[?], ut qui semper natura timidus extiterat, tandè Diuinæ voluntati se totum tradens, inuicta constantia & patientia aduersariorum minas & truculentiam fortiter contempserit. Re ipsius in Senatu perita[?], lata est de eo sententia ut viuus igni subiiceretur. Octo fere diebus ante sententiæ executionem priusquam Bellimontem reduceretur, antistes Franciscanorum, Gardianum vocant, professus Euangelij hostis[?] longa oratione apud illum egit ut ei inculcaret, nisi renuntiaret doctrinæ, ipsum hæreticū esse, perpetuisq; inferorū cruciatibus destinatū.
units.tr: We said, when Nicolas and Mariona were arrested, that Augustine had escaped by wonderful means. Freed in this way, doubtless by divine help, he took up the trade in spices and other small wares, which he carried round the markets of the towns, so that he might earn his living without fraud. When he came to the town of Bellimont in Hainault and offered his goods for sale in the market, he was recognised by some people, and his name was reported to the magistrate. He, perceiving the plot, left his goods and wanted to save himself by flight. While fleeing, he saw from afar the house where he had lodged surrounded by guards, and he began to fear more than he had before (for he was a man of very timid spirit, so that at the sight or the running of a single guard he would tremble and shake all over). Seized therefore by this fear and trembling, he left the town and soon threw himself into a thicket, hoping that he could lie hidden there safely. But his hour had come, and God had decided otherwise. For as he hid himself behind the thicket, there were some men on the city walls who could easily see him, and they at once pointed him out to the guards who were pursuing him. Accordingly he was seized immediately and taken to Bergen, the metropolitan city of Hainault, so that his case might be heard there. There he was questioned about the whole course of his life and his faith. He fully answered all the questions, showing the adversaries the confidence he placed in Christ, and he later told friends who visited him in prison that he had kept to this steadfastly. In this there was truly a wonderful work of God: he who had always been timid by nature, at last surrendering himself wholly to the divine will, bravely despised the threats and savagery of his adversaries with unconquered constancy and patience. When his case had been heard in the Senate, sentence was passed that he should be burned alive. About eight days before the sentence was carried out, before he was brought back to Bellimont, the head of the Franciscans, whom they call the Guardian, a professed enemy of the gospel, pressed him in a long speech to renounce his teaching, warning him that otherwise he was a heretic and destined to the everlasting torments of hell.

units.la: Augu-stinus vero interea non obmutuit, sed garrulitatem hominis saepe reprehendit, ac sermonem nugatoris coram omnibus qui aderat interrupit, dicens, Proba, quaeso, verbi Dei authoritate quae dicis, ut verbis tuis fides habeatur, multa quidem garris sed nihil probas, in quo satis constat te mendacij doctorem esse, cui nulla sit omnino habenda fides. His dictis Augustinus in diversorium Angelo pensili insigne extrahitur, ut in equum conscendens Bellimontem reduceretur. In eodem loco diverticbat quidam vir nobilis extraneus, qui huic potum obtulit in phiala plena vino, sic hunc affatus, Miserear tui, ac si non dubitas vitam amittere, animae tuae saltem rationem habe. Cui Augustinus hoc pacto respondit, De tua erga me voluntate habeo gratiam: atqui vides quantum mihi animae meae salus curae sit, utpote qui corpus hoc, igni consumi malim quam peccare aliquid contra conscientiam. Haec locutus, atque in equum impositus, Bellimontem ducitur magna satellitum cinctus caterva. Simulac in urbem ingressus esset, in vincula conijcitur. Caeterum, quia tum ibi funus filij ducis Arscoti curabatur, qui interfectus fuerat, multi eo undique venerant viri nobiles & Principes, qui certiores facti de adventu isti captivi, inuisunt hominem & de fide ipsum ac religione interrogat. Ipse vero singulis iucunde respondens satisfecit. Prae ceteris autem Comes Alainius diu multumque cum eo familiariter disseruit. Die praestituto executioni, extra urbem in collem quendam educitur ut ibi immolaretur. Maior pars populi in tantam rabiem adacta est propter hominis constantiam, ut clamarent pedes eius ad caudam equi alligandos esse, atque ita ad locum supplicij pertrahendum. Sed Dominus eam crudelitatem in servum suum exerceri haudquaquam passus est. Cum ad locum supplicij pervenisset, supplex Deum precatus est, ac deinde ad palum alligatus. Nec interea quidem verbum ullum protulit, sed cum iam accenso stramine ignem sensit, coepit Dei laudes praedicare. Postremo in medio ignis clara voce exclamavit: Pater caelestis, in manus tuas animam meam commendo, quam paulo post acceptam reddidit Domino.
units.tr: Augustine, however, did not keep silent in the meantime. He often rebuked the man's chatter and, in front of everyone present, interrupted the nonsense of this babbler, saying: Prove, I beg you, by the authority of God's word what you say, so that your words may be believed. You chatter much but prove nothing, and so it is quite clear that you are a teacher of lies, in whom no faith at all should be placed. With these words spoken, Augustine was taken to the inn that bears the sign of the Hanging Angel, to be put on a horse and led back to Bellimont. In the same inn a certain foreign nobleman was lodging, who offered him a drink in a cup full of wine, and addressed him thus: I pity you. If you are not afraid of losing your life, at least take thought for your soul. To this Augustine replied: I am grateful for your goodwill towards me. But you see how much the salvation of my soul is my concern, since I would rather let this body be consumed by fire than sin in any way against my conscience. Having said this, and set upon a horse, he was led to Bellimont, surrounded by a great band of guards. As soon as he had entered the town he was thrown into chains. Moreover, since the funeral of the son of the Duke of Arschot, who had been killed, was being arranged there at that time, many noblemen and princes came together from everywhere. Having been informed of the arrival of this prisoner, they visited him and questioned him about his faith and religion. He answered each of them cheerfully and to their satisfaction. Above all the rest, Count Alainius talked with him at length and in a friendly way. On the day appointed for his execution, he was led outside the city to a certain hill to be sacrificed there. Most of the people were driven into such a rage by the man's constancy that they shouted that his feet should be tied to the tail of a horse, so that he might be dragged to the place of punishment. But the Lord by no means allowed such cruelty to be inflicted on his servant. When he had come to the place of punishment, he prayed to God as a suppliant, and then was tied to the stake. Meanwhile he did not utter a single word, but when he felt the fire, now kindled with straw, he began to proclaim the praises of God. Finally, in the midst of the flames, he cried out in a clear voice: Heavenly Father, into your hands I commend my soul, which shortly afterwards he gave back to the Lord, having received it.

units.la: LEONARDUS PRATENSIS.
units.tr: LEONARD OF PRÉ.

units.la: Leonardus Pratensis, apud Lemovices natus, homo valde in literis exercitatus, circiter mensem Iulium, anno M.D.XLVII. in oppido Barri, quod est ad Sequanam in Burgundiae ducatu, captus est, proditus à duobus falsis fratribus, qui eum Divione usque ad illud Barri oppidum fuerant comitati. Quum igitur apud Praefectum eius urbis de praecipuis Christianae religionis capitibus copiose respondisset, monachi caeterique homines fictae religionis professores hominem sunt aggressi. à quo convicti falsarum atque impiarum opinionum, vi veritatis expressa confessione, eum Euangelij testem agnoscere & fateri coacti sunt. Hoc tamen non impedivit, quo minus ad supremae Parisiensis curiae cognitionem reiectus fuerit: ac tandem condemnatus, ut vivus igni cremaretur, mense Augusto, anno M.D.XLVII. Nec vero ipse unquam destitit suo testimonio usque ad extremum vitae spiritum, doctrinam Euangelij quoad potuit profiteri ac confirmare.
units.tr: Leonard of Pré, born at Limoges, a man very well trained in letters, was arrested around July 1547 in the town of Bar, on the Seine in the duchy of Burgundy. He had been betrayed by two false brothers who had accompanied him from Dijon as far as that town of Bar. When he had answered fully before the governor of that town on the chief articles of the Christian religion, the monks and the other professors of a feigned religion attacked him. Convicted by him of false and impious opinions, and forced by the power of the truth to confess, they had to acknowledge him as a witness of the Gospel. This did not prevent his being referred to the supreme court of Paris, where at last he was condemned to be burned alive, in August 1547. Yet he himself never ceased to bear witness until his last breath, professing and confirming the doctrine of the Gospel as far as he could.

units.la: APUD LINGONES COMBUSTI ob Euangelium.
units.tr: BURNED AT LANGRES FOR THE GOSPEL.

units.la: Interea gravis persecutio grassabatur apud Lingonenses, adeo ut mense Septembri eiusdem anni, propter verbum Dei plurimi exusti fuerint: inter quos memoria conseruata fuit, nempe Ioannis Taffignon, eiusque uxoris Ioannae Seiournã, Simonis Mareschal cum uxore sua Ioanna Bailli, Guilielmi Michaut, Iacobi Boulereau, & Iacobi Bretenay, qui omnes in ea urbe Lingonensi nati, singulari virtute & constantia qua in confessione fidei praediti fuerunt, multis veritatis studiosis consolationem & laetitiam, inimicis vero offensionem atque indignationem cum admiratione coniunctam attulerunt. Inter caeteros, Ioanna Bailli, Simonis coniunx, in sexu muliebri virtutem plusquam virilem declaravit. Nam cum iam supplicium esset subeundum, ea caeteros, imprimisque maritum suum, magno animo ad patientiam constantiamque Christianam hortabatur. Atque inter alia pie tum ab ea dicta, hoc praeclarè dixisse fertur, Eam coniunctionem vitae atque consuetudinem corporis, qua aliquandiu usi fuissent in coniugio, quaedam quasi sponsalia promissaque habuisse: at nunc Dominum Iesum ipsos vere desponsaturum eo die, quo morte sua fidei testimonium ei praestarent. Quoniam autem ea natu omnium mulierum quae captivae detinebantur, minima erat, idcirco in postremum supplicij locum fuit referuata[?], ut aduersarij praedara[?] quaedam pollicentes, animum eius inflecterent, atque a suscepta sententia deuocarent. Sed ea & caeteri virtute spiritus Dei roborati, in veritate confitenda & testificanda costantes permanserunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile a severe persecution raged among the people of Langres, so that in September of that same year many were burned on account of the word of God. Among them the following are remembered: Jean Taffignon and his wife Jeanne Seiournã, Simon Mareschal with his wife Jeanne Bailli, Guillaume Michaut, Jacques Boulereau, and Jacques Bretenay. All of them were born in that city of Langres, and by the outstanding courage and constancy with which they confessed the faith they brought consolation and joy to many lovers of the truth, but to their enemies offence and indignation mixed with admiration. Among the rest, Jeanne Bailli, Simon's wife, showed a courage more than manly in a woman. For when the execution was at hand, she urged the others, and above all her husband, with great spirit to Christian patience and constancy. Among other pious words she spoke then, she is said to have put it nobly: that the union of life and bodily intimacy which they had enjoyed for some time in marriage was a kind of betrothal and pledge; but now the Lord Jesus would truly wed them, on the day when they gave their testimony to him by their death. Since she was the youngest of all the women who were being held captive, she was reserved for the last place of execution, so that the adversaries, promising her certain favours, might bend her mind and call her back from the sentence she had accepted. But she and the others, strengthened by the Spirit of God, remained steadfast in confessing and bearing witness to the truth.

units.la: Eadem in causa & poena versati fuerunt, Michael Mareschalus & Ioannes Camus, ipsi quoque Lingonenses, Magnus Ioannes Camus Diuionensis, & Ioannes Seraphinus Turonensis, qui omnes eodem prope tempore Lutetiae cremati, constantissima confessione doctrinam Euangelij confirmarunt, ornauerunt, illustrarunt.
units.tr: Michael Mareschal and Jean Camus were in the same cause and suffered the same punishment; they too were of Langres. Great Jean Camus of Dijon and Jean Seraphin of Tours, all of whom were burned at Paris at about the same time, confirmed, adorned and illustrated the doctrine of the Gospel by their most steadfast confession.

units.la: IOANNES ANGLUS.
units.tr: JOHN THE ENGLISHMAN.

units.la: Adeò inualuit persecutio ut a Lingombus[?] vicinos Burgundos eadem de persuaserit, plurimi comprehensi fuerunt, inter quos vir cum doctus tum pius Ioannes cognomento Anglus, in urbe Senonensi causarum patronus, propter Christianam doctrinam, quam sua confessione comprobauerat Lutetiae a summa curia post diuturnam detentionem condemnatus est ut igni uiuus cremaretur: ea vero poena apud eosdem Senones constantissime defunctus est, mense Mart. anno M. D. XLVII.
units.tr: The persecution grew so strong that it persuaded those from Langres to the neighbouring Burgundians that the same course should be taken, and very many were seized. Among them was a man both learned and pious, John, surnamed the Englishman, an advocate in the city of Sens. On account of the Christian doctrine which he had supported by his confession at Paris, he was condemned by the supreme court, after a long imprisonment, to be burned alive. He died this punishment most steadfastly at Sens itself, in March 1547.

units.la: HUBERTUS CHERIET.
units.tr: HUBERT CHERIET.

units.la: HUBERTUS Ioannis Cherieti filius, patria Diuionensis, sartor annos natus circiter XIX. combustus fuit Diuione, mense Maio, anno M.D. XLIX. Is nullis unquam nec mortis terroribus, nec parentum blandis illectamentis[?], quibus illum a pura Christi confessione deuocare conabatur, propositu fidei suae ac testimonii Euangelij deposuit, sed illud morte sua aequissimo animo suscepta, obsignaunt.
units.tr: Hubert, son of Jean Cheriet, a native of Dijon, a tailor about nineteen years old, was burned at Dijon in May 1549. Neither the terrors of death nor the coaxing enticements of his parents, by which they tried to call him away from the pure confession of Christ, ever moved him from the purpose of his faith and his witness to the Gospel. Rather, by the death he embraced with the most equable spirit, he sealed that testimony.

units.la: MICHAEL TORNACENSIS.
units.tr: MICHAEL OF TOURNAI.

units.la: Isdem temporibus Michael cognomine diminutiuo, ut apud illos frequens est, Michelotus dicebatur, natus Froyennae apud Neruios, homo admodum iuuenis, & sartor professione, captus propter consessionem Euangelij, sententia iudicum condemnatus fuit, ut capite truncaretur, si quidem sententiam de religione, quam professus fuerat retractarct: si vero in proposito permaneret uiuus cremaretur. Itaq; cum iudices ex eo quaesiuissent, utrum ex his duobus mortis generibus malet suscipere, summa cum comitate atque hilaritate vultus respondit: Qui eam mihi gratiam impertiet ut patienter pro nomine ipsius moriar, is quoque gratiam mihi largietur ut ignem pro eiusdem honore sine vlla degeneris animi nota perpeti possim. Hanc virilem ea ætate constantiam cum summa omnium admiratione ad extremum vitæ spiritum Deo vires suppeditante retinuit.
units.tr: At the same time Michael, called by the diminutive name which is common among them, Michelot, born at Froyennes in the land of the Nervii, a very young man and by trade a tailor, was seized on account of his confession of the Gospel. By the sentence of the judges he was condemned to be beheaded if he retracted the religion he had professed, but if he persisted in his purpose, to be burned alive. So when the judges asked him which of these two kinds of death he preferred to undergo, he answered with great courtesy and cheerfulness of countenance: He who grants me the grace to die patiently for his name will also grant me the grace to endure fire for his honour without any mark of a degenerate spirit. With this manly constancy, unusual at his age, he held out to the last breath of life, with God supplying the strength, to the amazement of all.

units.la: CLAVDIVS THIERRY.
units.tr: CLAUDIUS THIERRY.

units.la: CLAVDIVS Thierrius, patria Carnutensis, homo iuvenis, arti inserviens pharmacopolæ, cùm Geneva in Gallia rediret, captus est Aureliæ, ubi fidem eam, quam in Ecclesia Dei ex doctrina Evangelij acceperat, maximo pietatis studio testificatus, sententia suit condemnatus, ut vivus combureretur. A qua quidem sententia appellare nunquam animum induxit, sed ut parentum atque amicorum voluntati summæque solicitudini satisfaceret, Lutetiam ad supremam Curiam provocavit. Unde priore sententia decreto eius curiæ confirmata, Aureliam remissus ustulationem corporis sui summa constantia perpessus est eodem anno M.D.XLIX.
units.tr: Claudius Thierry, a native of Chartres, a young man who worked as an apothecary's assistant, was arrested at Orleans while returning to France from Geneva. There, having openly testified with the greatest zeal for godliness to the faith he had received in the Church of God from the teaching of the Gospel, he was condemned to be burned alive. He never made up his mind to appeal against this sentence. Yet, to satisfy his parents and friends, who were deeply anxious for him, he appealed to the supreme court at Paris. The court confirmed the earlier sentence by its decree, and he was sent back to Orleans, where he endured the burning of his body with great constancy in the same year, 1549.

units.la: FANINVS Italus.
units.tr: FANINUS the Italian.

units.la: Memorabilis vita & mors Fanini Itali, Iesu Christi veri martyris.
units.tr: The memorable life and death of Faninus the Italian, a true martyr of Jesus Christ.

units.la: FAninus natus Faventiæ Italiæ oppido, in ea regione, quæ Romaigna vocabulo corrupto appellatur, ex familia ortus Faninorum. Is quidem primis ætatis temporibus nullam doctrinæ salutiferæ cognitionem habuit: sed postea Scripturam sanctam summo studio & diligentia legere cœpit, libris adiutus in linguam vernaculam conversis: propterea quòd Latini sermonis non ita erat peritus, ut eius facultate in sacris literis versari posset: verùm optimè intelligens eam esse virtutem Dei, optimi maximi ut eùm hominibus vult reclari, ad eam cognitionem certo aliquo genere sermonis non utatur, commoditate linguæ patriæ adiutus, diligentem operam ad legendam Scripturam contulit. Post diuturnum autem studium, sentiens in seipso optimũ suavissimumque fructũ, quem ex ea lectione atque meditatione perceperat, statuit pro singulari pietate ac gratitudine, thesaurum tam liberaliter à Deo sibi communicatum, non in seipso occultare, sed aliis communicare atque impertire. Erat enim plane persuasus nullo modo hominibus licere, neque æquum esse, postquam Deus eos semel Spiritu suo illuminauit, atque in agnitione voluntatis suæ instituit, cognitam occultare veritatem qua nihil est ei preciosius, camque quodammodo sepelire. Itaque cœpit paulatim diuersis in locis diuulgare, ac pluribus patefacere hominibus eam cognitionem, quam tum quidem ex Euangelio Domini nostri Iesu Christi adeptus erat. Non quod primum omnibus quid sentiret, publice declararet: sed satis esse arbitrabatur, si initio priuatim aliquem eius gustum dare potuisset. At satellites Pontificis Romani, eiusque administri, cum hoc eius studium intellexissent, omnibus modis operam dederunt, ut Faninus caperetur. Cum esset in carcere, uxor liberique eius & amici eum continuis precibus ita solicitarunt, ut homo victus eorum studiis, patrocinium veritatis suscepturn[?] deposuerit, testimonioque iudicij sui, quod Euangelio dederat, improbato, veniam, & carceris liberationem fit consequutus. Verum simul atque carcere dimissus est, ita animo fuit perturbatus, mentéque assectus, ut desperare plane videretur. Et certè nisi Deus eum sua praebedisset manu, atque eum pro sua misericordia retinuisset, in horribilem desperationem confusionemque prolapsus esset. Sciebat enim se Christi Iesum quem & summo studio amplexus fuerat, & magno cum gaudio spiritus professus, perfidiose indigneque abiecisse, ut cum suis in hac vita remaneret: atque ita charitatem suorum pietati Christo debitæ præstulisse. Conscientia autem eum ita premebat, ut perpetua perfidiæ recordatio, summum & acerbum animo eius cruciatum die noctuque adferret. Itaque grauissimum illud peccatum suum gemere, & peramare deflere cœpit, quod Christum Iesum, Domini gloriæ, ac pro se mortuum, verbum eius prodens, abnegare ausus esset: vitamque ita tristem acerbamque suscepit, ut eum nemo lætum alacremque postea viderit: donec eum animum recepit, quo officium studiumque suum Domino fidelius quam antea fecerat, præstare constituit. Cum igitur animo ita esset confirmatus ac persuasus, ut causam veritatis, quam turpiter deseruerat, omni animi contentione tueretur, abiecto omnium periculorum & malorum metu, cœpit palam dicere, ut illam suam abnegationem ac proditionem præclarissima confessione resarciret, seque tanto magnificentius Deum Christumque Filium eius confessurum, quanto turpius indigniusque antea illum abnegauerat. Itaque hoc spiritus studio summóque ardore inflammatus, omnem illam regionem Romaignam peragrans, singulas vrbes adibat, in quibus publicè puram Euangelij doctrinam tanta vi spiritus & constantia annuntiabat, vt omnes maxima admiratione afficeret. Si verbum Dei quibusdam in oppidis ac locis publicè non erat ita receptum, tum priuatim ad certos homines aliquos accedebat, vt hoc modo experiretur qui essent dociles capacésq; percipiendæ eius doctrinæ, quæ in Euangelio continetur. In quibus quidem docendis atque instituendis quantum poterat, elaborabat, vt eos ad cognitionem voluntatis Dei & salutis viam adduceret. Dicebat autem se in iis instituendis, quibuscum versaretur, huiusmodi ratione vti & ordine, vt primùm ex eorum animis euelleret prauas impiasque opiniones ac errores quibus erant occupati atque persuasi: quo intelligere ac sentire possent eam impietatem in qua erant iandiu confirmati: deinde paulatim eos ad meliorem disciplinæ vitæque rationem adduceret. Atque ita eos erudiebat, vt temporis progressu ad maiorem veritatis cognitionem deduceret. Hoc quidem certè magni æstimabat, cùm ex aliquo loco discederet, si duos aut tres in vera pietatis doctrina informassef: propterea quòd vnusquisque eorum rectè institutus, alios ipse docere atque instituere poterat: cæteri idem si facerent, maximum si delium[?] hominum numerum futurum. Porrò cùm hæc ita gererētur, pius homo Faninus captus est quodam in loco cui Bagnacauallo lingua Italica nomen est, in quo cùm capitis damnatus esset vt igni cremaretur, gaudere cœpit, dicens, horam suam nondum venisse, sed hunc esse tantummodò doctrinæ suæ introitum, vt plus aliis prodesse posset, & in eo quidè verù dixit. nam paulò post Ferrariá deductus est, vbi multi fideles, pijs eius exhortationibus nō mediocrem consolationem acceperunt magisque in timore Dei ac vera pietate ab eo instituti seipsos in propositò gratiæ diuinæ confirmarūt, sed Papa Roman. qui sua semper cogitat veritus huius hominis parrhesiam mandauit vt Faninus arctiore custodia teneretur. Itaque interioribus arcis ergastulis inclusus octodecim menses fuit, ibique grauia tormenta perpessus, graviora etiā passurus, si Dominicani eius vrbis cum apud se habere potuissent. Et quanquam carcerem eius sæpè mutarent, cumque nunc in hunc, nunc in illum locum tetrum atque horribilem includerent: hæc tamen animum metémque ipsius non mutarunt: sed idem qui ante extiterat, constans in ea fide qua Iesum Christum amplexus fuerat permansit. Includebatur aliquando solus in carcere, ab aliis separatus: aliquando cum aliis captiuis coniungebatur. Sed peræque illi erat, propterea quòd utraque in ratione fructum aliquem semper adferebat. nam & alios, quos in consuetudine sua habere poterat, cum exemplo vitæ modestæ, tum optima pietatis doctrina instituebat. Hac verò priuatus vitæ societate, in solitudine constitutus, perpetuò scribebat aliquid, suisque scriptis demonstrabat, quod coram sermone declarare non poterat. Denique inclusus fuit in quodam carcere, vbi erant primarij duces ac principes hominum factiosorum, qui in Italia plerunque partes sectasque facientes, magnorum authores motuum existunt. à quibus pius homo sæpe atque asperè diuexatus est, propterea quòd scelerati homines, qui videbant illum ita loquentem, arbitrabantur aliquem melancholicum humorem, ut vulgò dici solent, in cerebrum eius ascendisse, atque ita mente esse alienata. porrò etiam homines cauti ac prudentes, ossicio monitorum apud eum utebantur, demonstrantes eam opinionem ei esse deponendam, libere cum hominibus viuendum, neque fatigandum animum, sed quiescendum esse quoad de huiusmodi rebus ecclesiasticis aliquid communi concilio decretum esset. Tum Faninus, ut erat homo admodum modestus & summa comitate præditus, primum de solicitudine & cura quam haberent de salute ipsius, gratias egit. deinde eam doctrinam, quam constanter tuebatur, ostendit non esse humorem aut opinionem in suo natum ingenio, sed puram Dei veritatem, in verbo atque Euangelio Iesu Christi reuelatam hominibus, & his maximè temporibus restitutam: se nullo modo constituisse hanc certissimam veritatem abnegare, ut mendacijs hominum adhærescērēt. quod vero ad animam, quæ sanguine filij Dei redempta esset, suauissima frui libertate.
units.tr: Faninus was born at Faenza, a town in Italy, in that region which is called Romagna by a corrupted name, and he came of the family of the Faninis. In his early years he had no knowledge of saving doctrine. Later, however, he began to read Holy Scripture with great zeal and diligence, helped by books translated into the vernacular, since he was not skilled enough in Latin to engage with the sacred writings through that language. Yet he understood very well that it is the power of God, the best and greatest, who wishes to be known by men, and that for this knowledge no particular kind of language is required. Aided by the convenience of his native tongue, he devoted diligent effort to reading Scripture. After long study, perceiving in himself the best and sweetest fruit he had gained from that reading and meditation, he resolved, out of singular piety and gratitude, not to hide in himself the treasure so generously imparted to him by God, but to share and pass it on to others. For he was thoroughly persuaded that it is in no way lawful, nor right, for men, once God has enlightened them by his Spirit and instructed them in the knowledge of his will, to conceal the truth they have come to know, than which nothing is more precious, and in a manner to bury it. And so he began gradually to spread it abroad in various places, and to make known to many people the knowledge which he had then gained from the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. He did not at once declare publicly to everyone what he thought; he judged it enough if at first he could give some taste of it to certain individuals in private. But the henchmen of the Roman Pontiff and his officials, when they had learned of this zeal of his, did everything they could in every way to have Faninus seized. While he was in prison, his wife, his children and his friends beset him with constant entreaties, so that the man, overcome by their efforts, gave up his defence of the truth, and, having disowned the testimony of his judgment which he had given to the Gospel, obtained pardon and release from prison. But as soon as he was let out of prison, he was so disturbed in spirit and so affected in mind that he seemed to be utterly in despair. And indeed, unless God had stretched out his hand to him and held him back by his mercy, he would have fallen into dreadful despair and confusion. For he knew that he had shamefully and unworthily cast off Jesus Christ, whom he had embraced with the utmost zeal and professed with great joy of spirit, so that he might remain in this life with his own people; and thus he had preferred the love of his kin to the devotion owed to Christ. His conscience weighed so heavily on him that the constant memory of his faithlessness brought him a bitter and grievous torment of mind by day and by night. So he began to lament that most grievous sin of his, and to weep bitterly, because he had dared to deny Christ Jesus, the Lord of glory, who died for him, by betraying his word. He took up so sad and bitter a life that afterwards no one saw him cheerful or lively, until he recovered the spirit to resolve to perform his duty and zeal to the Lord more faithfully than before. Therefore, when he was so confirmed and persuaded in his mind that he defended with all the energy of his soul the cause of the truth which he had shamefully deserted, and, casting off all fear of dangers and evils, began to speak openly, he meant to atone for that denial and betrayal by a most splendid confession, and to confess God and his Son Christ so much more magnificently as he had denied him more basely and unworthily before. Inflamed by this zeal of the spirit and with the greatest ardour, he travelled through all that region of Romagna and visited each town, in which he proclaimed the pure doctrine of the Gospel in public with such force of spirit and constancy that he filled everyone with the greatest admiration. If the Word of God was not publicly received in some towns or places, he approached certain individuals in private, so that in this way he might find out who were docile and capable of grasping the doctrine contained in the Gospel. In teaching and instructing these people he laboured as much as he could to lead them to the knowledge of the will of God and the way of salvation. He said that in instructing those with whom he associated he followed this method and order: first he would tear out of their minds the depraved and impious opinions and errors with which they were occupied and convinced, so that they might understand and perceive the impiety in which they had long been confirmed; then he would gradually lead them to a better rule of discipline and life. And so he taught them, so that in the course of time he might lead them to a greater knowledge of the truth. Certainly he set great store by this: when he was leaving any place, if he had formed two or three in the true doctrine of godliness, since each of these, rightly instructed, could himself teach and instruct others, and if the rest did the same, there would be a very large number of faithful people. Meanwhile, while these things were going on, the godly man Faninus was arrested in a place called Bagnacavallo in Italian, where, having been condemned to be burned at the stake, he began to rejoice, saying that his hour had not yet come, but that this was only the entrance to his teaching, so that he could be of more use to others; and in that he spoke truly. For soon afterwards he was taken to Ferrara, where many faithful people, through his godly exhortations, received no small comfort, and, being instructed by him in the fear of God and true godliness, were more firmly established in the purpose of divine grace. But the Roman Pope, who always thinks of how to ward off the frankness of this man, ordered that Faninus be held under closer custody. So he was shut up in the inner dungeons of the citadel for eighteen months, and there, having suffered grievous torments, he would have suffered even worse, had the Dominicans of that city been able to have him in their hands. And although they often changed his prison, sometimes shutting him up in this foul and horrible place, sometimes in that, these things did not change his spirit and mind; rather he remained the same as before, steadfast in that faith by which he had embraced Jesus Christ. Sometimes he was shut up alone in a prison, separated from the others; sometimes he was joined with other captives. But it made no difference to him, because in either situation he always brought some benefit. For he instructed both those whom he could have in his company, both by the example of a modest life and by the best teaching of godliness. Moreover, placed in solitude and deprived of the company of others, he was constantly writing something, and by his writings he showed what he could not declare by speech. Finally he was shut up in a certain prison where there were the chief leaders and princes of factious men, who, making parties and sects in Italy as they often do, become the authors of great disturbances. By these men the godly man was often and harshly harassed, because the wicked men, seeing him speak in such a way, thought that some melancholy humour, as is commonly said, had gone up into his brain and so his mind had become deranged. Moreover, cautious and prudent men also acted as his admonishers, showing that he must abandon that opinion, live freely with people, not wear out his spirit, but keep quiet until something had been decreed about such ecclesiastical matters by a common council. Then Faninus, as he was a most modest man and endowed with the greatest courtesy, first gave thanks for their anxiety and care for his salvation. Then he showed that the doctrine which he steadfastly upheld was not a humour or an opinion born of his own mind, but the pure truth of God, revealed to men in the Word and Gospel of Jesus Christ, and restored especially in these times; that he had in no way resolved to deny this most certain truth in order to cling to the lies of men; and, as for his soul, which had been redeemed by the blood of the Son of God, that it enjoyed the sweetest freedom.

units.la: De concilio vero dicebat se nullam aliam sententiam & authoritatem expectare aut velle, quàm eam quæ in Euangelio declarata ei constaret. nam Christum Iesum, cum illud lætum gratiæ & salutis nuntium attulit, concilium ac decretum huiusmodi annuntiasse, atque morte sua confirmasse, ut nulla confirmatione alia opus esset. Huiusmodi verbis illorum animos ita commouit, ut eos ad rationem vitæ melioris revocarit, ad eámque adduxerit admirationem, ut eum sanctum virum appellarent. Quod cum ille animadvertisset, eos ita confirmauit, Equidem, fratres, scio & agnosco me miserum esse peccatorem: sed fide, qua de gratia Domini nostri Iesu Christi persuasus sum, peccata mihi condonantur: quemadmodum vestra vobis quoque ignoscentur, si Euangelio, in quo certissimum est gratiæ Dei testimonium, firmam fidem habeatis. Erant præterea alij captiui, qui molliori ac lautiori vitæ assueuerant: quibus commutata iam conditio maximum dolorem afferebat. sed eorum dierum consuetudine, quam cum Fanino habuerant, ita fuerunt recreati, ut eam vitæ rationem molestiæ atque acerbitatis plenam, non tam graviter indigneque ferrent, neque liberationem ita vehementer appeterent: sed huiusmodi captiuitatem sibi quodammodo gratularentur, de eaque gloriarentur, per quam in meliorem libertatem, quam unquam antea edocti fuerant, vocati essent. Porro parentes eius, de ipsius statu certiores facti, facile intellexerunt eo illum in discrimine versari, ut de vita eius actum esse videretur. Itaque uxor sororque Fanini, ad carcerem accesserunt. Res erat plane acerba, cum hæ duæ mulieres, quarum altera amore fraterno, altera maiore benevolentiæ & charitatis coniugalis vinculo apud eum plurimum valere poterat, ambæ mœstæ ac mœrentes, cum fletu ac lachrymis eum orarent, obtestarentur, monerent, ut si sui nollet rationem aliquam habere, memoriam certè & benevolentiam curamque erga liberos suos suscipiet & conseruaret. At verò Faninus eis ita respondit, ac tenerrimo naturæ sensui admirabili fidei constantia ita restitit, ut qui videbant & audiebant, admiratione tantæ virtutis atque magnitudinis animi, attoniti viderentur. Dominus, inquit, meus & magister, mihi non mandauit ut ipsum abnegem familiæ causa tuendæ meæ. vobis quidem satis esse debet, quòd propter vos semel in eam perfidiam sum delapsus quam scitis. Quanquā gratia Dei non ita turpiter lapsus fuissem, si hanc tantam cognitionem, quam post illum lapsum mihi dedit, habuissem. Sed, obsecro, domum vos recipite in pace. ego enim plane scio, Deum usque ad hunc diem
units.tr: Concerning the council, he said that he expected and desired no other opinion or authority than what he found declared in the Gospel. For when Christ Jesus brought that joyful message of grace and salvation, he had announced such a council and decree and confirmed it by his death, so that no other confirmation was needed. By such words he so stirred their minds to a better way of life, and brought them to such admiration that they called him a holy man. When he noticed this, he strengthened them thus: "Indeed, brothers, I know and acknowledge that I am a wretched sinner. But my sins are forgiven me by the faith with which I am persuaded of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins will be forgiven you too, if you have firm faith in the Gospel, in which is the most certain testimony of God's grace." There were also other prisoners who had been accustomed to a softer and more comfortable life, and for them the change of circumstances was a great grief. But through the custom of those days, which they had kept with Fanino, they were so refreshed that they no longer bore that manner of life, full of hardship and bitterness, so grievously or indignantly, nor did they so eagerly long for release. Rather, they counted it a kind of blessing and gloried in this captivity, by which they had been called to a better freedom than they had ever known before. Meanwhile his parents, informed of his condition, easily understood that he was in such danger that his life seemed to be at an end. So Fanino's wife and sister went to the prison. It was a truly bitter scene. These two women, one of whom could prevail much by sisterly love and the other by the stronger bond of conjugal affection and charity, both sad and grieving, begged him with weeping and tears, urging and entreating him that, if he would have no regard for himself, he should at least keep in mind and take care of his children and show them affection. But Fanino answered them thus, and with admirable constancy of faith he resisted the tenderest feeling of nature, so that those who saw and heard him were astonished at such virtue and greatness of spirit. "My Lord and master," he said, "has not commanded me to deny him for the sake of protecting my family. It should be enough for you that because of you I once fell into that faithlessness which you know about. Yet I would not have fallen so shamefully, if I had had the knowledge that God has given me since that fall. But I beg you, go home in peace. For I know clearly that God has made use of my work until this day, and now my end is approaching, that I may go from this life to him." Then those women departed with loud wailing and many tears, but he himself remained in that admirable constancy and firmness without any disturbance of mind.

units.la: Note: Carceris asperitas lenior fit aliis Fanini consuetudine.
units.tr: Note: The harshness of the prison becomes milder for others through the custom of Faninus.

units.la: Note: Fanini constantia. opera mea vsum fuisse: nunc finem meum appropinquare, vt ex hac vita me ad eum conferam. Tum mulieres illæ cum magno eiulatu ac multis lachrymis discesserunt. ipse vero sine vlla animi perturbatione in illa sua admirabili constantia firmitateque permansit. Porro Paulo Pontifice mortuo, successor eius Iulius tertius, id temporis Papa creatus, misit literas, quibus iubebat vt Faninus vita priuaretur. Itaque minister quidam magistratus eum convenit, ac significauit ipsum vesperi in communem ducendum esse carcerem, propterea quod capitis damnatus esset. Tum vero Faninus ministrum eum nuntiumque mortis suæ amplexus ac deosculatus, pro allato nuntio huiusmodi tam grato atque exoptato gratias ei egit, ac dixit, Ego vero, mi frater, mortem quam nuntias mihi, æquissimo animo suscipio propter Dominum & saluatorem Iesum Christum, qui vt me a morte redimeret, vitæ non pepercit suæ. Deinde perlongum sermonem habuit de felicitate vitæ sempiternæ, coram iis qui tum ibi aderant. quorum quidam ei dixit, Quo in statu nunc discedens liberos tuos relinquis? quem tutorem & vicarium tui absentis mortuíque instituisti? obsecro te, mi Faninne, vt paruulorum liberorum tuorum recorderis, vxorisque tuæ, quam tanto pere diligis, miserearis. Ego, inquit Faninus, optimum omnium tutorem curatoremque illis reliqui, in cuius quidem certissima & fidelissima custodia tutelaque eos perpetuo fore tibi affirmo. Tum ille quæsiuit quisnam ille foret. Dominus, inquit, Iesus Christus, fidelissimus eorum tutor & conseruator futurus est. Ita digressus ex eo loco, in manum ciuilis magistratus est traditus: cumque in cubiculo quodam inclusus fuisset, compedibus eum constrinxerunt, hancque solam impertierunt gratiam, vt manus solutas liberasque haberet: reliquo vero corpore toto vinctus & constrictus fuit. Interea nullus ex vrbe eum adire poterat, nisi ij qui ex domo & familia Præfecti erant eiusque satellites, aut ij qui apud Præfectum gratia valebant. qui autem potuerunt ad eum accedere, quorum magnus fuit numerus, dicebant eum diabolum habere in corpore: ea etenim vi ipsum loqui vt eum a diabolo occupari oporteret. nam hoc quidem modo profani homines, de veritate Dei contumeliose loqui solent. Verum cum eximiam eius constantiam propius aspexissent, summamque animi æquitatem...
units.tr: Note: Faninus's constancy. My labour has been of use; now my end is drawing near, so that I may betake myself from this life to him. Then those women departed with loud wailing and many tears, but he himself remained in his admirable constancy and firmness, without any disturbance of mind. Then, when Paul the Pope had died, his successor Julius III, who had been created Pope at that time, sent letters ordering that Faninus be deprived of life. Accordingly, a certain minister of the magistrate met him and made known that he was to be taken to the common prison in the evening, because he had been condemned to death. Faninus embraced and kissed the minister, the bearer of his death, and thanked him for bringing such welcome and longed-for news. He said: "Indeed, my brother, I accept with the most equal mind the death you announce to me, for the sake of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, who did not spare his own life so that he might redeem me from death." Then he gave a very long address on the happiness of everlasting life, in the presence of those who were there at the time. One of them said to him: "In what state are you leaving now, and what children are you leaving behind? Whom have you appointed as guardian and deputy in your absence and after your death? I beg you, my dear Faninus, to remember your young children and to have pity on your wife, whom you love so greatly." Faninus replied: "I have left them the best of all guardians and keepers, in whose most certain and faithful custody and protection I assure you they will remain forever." Then the other asked who he was. "The Lord Jesus Christ," he said, "will be their most faithful guardian and preserver." Thus, having departed from that place, he was handed over into the hands of the civil magistrate; and when he had been shut up in a certain chamber, they bound him in fetters, and granted him only this favour, that he might have his hands loose and free; but the rest of his body was bound and fettered. Meanwhile no one from the city could approach him, except those from the household and retinue of the Prefect and his attendants, or those who had influence with the Prefect. Those who were able to come to him, and they were many, said that he had the devil in his body, for he spoke with such force that he must be possessed by the devil; for this is how profane men are accustomed to speak insultingly about the truth of God. But when they had looked more closely at his remarkable constancy and his great equanimity of mind...

units.la: Iulius III. P.P.
units.tr: Julius III, Pope.

units.la: Quis liberorum optimus tutor.
units.tr: Who is the best guardian of the children?

units.la: Faninus arctius constringitur. quitatem atque tranquillitatem aduersus omnem mortis horrorem comparatam viderent, & in ore nihil eum nisi verbum Dei habere, & totum ardore Spiritus cælestis accensum atque inflammatum, coeperunt vt cæteri, oculos in eum suos intendere, aurésque ad eum attentè audiendum adhibere. Mulieres quidem eorum qui erant in magistratu, cùm audirent eum tanta suauitate & gratia loquentem, à fletu ac lachrymis continere se non poterant. quinetiam ipse carnifex, cuius mortis administer, non potuit se à lachrymis temperare. Faninus autem eis dicebat, Fratres mei, Deus quidem vobiscum sit: sed venistisne vos huc, vt mecum vna gaudeatis quòd ex hoc mundo decedens, in cælum ad Deum meum concedo? Deinde sursum oculos attollens suos, tanta vehementia ardoréque precabatur, vt quasi igneus exardescere totus videretur. Tum paulò post animo & vultu ita hilarescebat, vt omnium oculos in se conuerteret, omnésque ad se alliceret, vt etiam ii qui ad eum accedebant vt ipsum confirmarent, consolationem ab eo acciperent. Fuit quidam ex amanuensibus publicis, qui eum monuit, si quod professus erat retractare vellet, consilium Papæ non esse vt ipse moreretur. Cui Faninus tum subridens respondit, si quid haberet falsi aut praui, posse facilè coargui atque conuinci: sed eam vim esse veritatis, vt quamuis laboret aliquando, opprimi tamen nunquam possit. itaque se nullo modo velle ita liberari, vt veritas obscurarctur atque extingueretur. Sed amanuensi illo relicto, quoniam id quod ab eo proponebatur non erat ita magni momenti, cœpit exponere multos sacræ Scripturæ locos: ac quo maiorem authoritatem haberet oratio, Latinum textum proferebat, ac memoriter pronuntiabat. quæ res erat non parua admiratione digna: propterea quòd homines satis sciebant eum in lingua Latina exiguè versatum atque exercitatum esse. is tamen magnum numerum locorum ac testimoniorum adducebat, singulaq; capita ita allegabat, vt in nullo falleretur, vt omnes facilè animaduerterent eum Spiritu Dei regi & gubernari. In his etiam pronuntiauit quosdam versus, quos de iustificatione, de prædestinatione, & aliis quibusdam grauissimis fidei capitibus composuerat. Sed quoniam paulò lætior hilariorq; esse videbatur, exultaréque immoderatius: quidam ex ijs qui ibi aderant, ei dixit, Quid causæ est, quòd tu nunc tantopere lætaris? nam si Christus, cùm mors ei impenderet, præ animi tristitia sanguinem & aquam sudauit, Patrémque orauit cum summo animi angore ne moreretur: quid habes tu, cur hac tanta lætitia efferaris? Et tum Faninus respondit, Dominum Iesum, quanuis nullum vnquam peccatum habuisset: tamen cum nostra causa iudicio Dei vellet satisfacere, omnes nostras infirmitates suscepisse, poenasque omnes luisse ac persoluisse, quæ peccatis nostris debebantur, ita vt cum in horto esset & in cruce suspensus, veros mortis dolores senserit, easque inferorum pœnas, quas nos meriti iure perferre debebamus. Itaque eam causam fuisse cur in horto tanto animi angore affectus afflictúsque fuerit: quoniam in carne nostra mortem nostram infernúmque sentiebat. Ego vero, inquit, qui vera fide{} possideo benedictionem Iesu Christi, ea nunc perfruens, maximopere lætor planè persuasus, quòd moriens in vitam transferor sempiternam & beatam. Cur igitur ego non lætarer, cùm huiusmodi fiduciam atque ipsam habeam? Porrò cùm Faninus hac consolatione perfusus ita loqueretur, ecce tribus horis ante diluculum duxerunt eum in plateam vrbis, ne populus posset adesse, eáque audire, quæ ipse ante mortem dicere consueuerat. Tum vero de more crux ei allata est, quam cum vidisset, Obsecro vos, inquit, ne tantum laboris suscipiatis, an existimatis vos memoriam Domini nostri Iesu Christi in cælo viuentis ac regnantis, hoc fragmento ligneo mihi magis renouaturos ac confirmaturos, quam ego in corde meo infixam habeo? Et simul genibus in terram positis Deum summo animi studio precatus est, verbis maximi ardoris plenissimis, quibus à Deo petebat vt ipse pro sua gratia & misericordia mentes cordaque occæcata miserorum eorum hominum qui ibi aderant, illuminaret. Deinde cum scipsum ad trabem ac funem, qua suspendendus atque strangulandus erat, composuisset ac præparasset, hilaris dixit carnifici, vt quod ei mandatum esset perageret. Ita semper se commendans Domino Iesu Christo, eumque orans vt animam suam reciperet, laqueo vitam finiuit. Circiter vero horam prandij consuetam, in eodem loco quo corpus eius combureretur, plerique dixerunt ipsum vaporem, qui ex corpore eius exhalabat, quasi gratissimum mortis eius odorem, in mentes multorum hominum penetraturum, maioremque vim ad homines adnotdmonendos[?] & consolandos habituru[m], quàm verba illius habuissent. Consuetudo autem in ea regione est, ut ossa & cineres relicti, extra urbe[m] deferantur, sed nec Præfectus, nec inquisitor, nec Episcopus, nec magnus eius vicarius, nec ullus Theologus id negotium suscipere voluit: unusquisque eam curam à se reijciês & conferens in eum qui mortis illius causa fuisset: plane omnes aperte declarabant quid de eo homine sentirent, quem innocentem fatebantur, neque mortem huiusmodi commeruisse. Tandem populus negotium suscepit ut ossa eius ustulata cum cineribus ex platea deportaret.
units.tr: Fanin is bound more tightly. Equanimity and tranquillity against every horror of death were prepared, and when they saw that he had nothing in his mouth but the Word of God, and that he was wholly kindled and inflamed with the ardour of the heavenly Spirit, they began, like the others, to fix their eyes upon him and to give their ears to listen to him attentively. The wives of those in office, when they heard him speaking with such sweetness and grace, could not restrain themselves from weeping and tears. Indeed, the executioner himself, whose assistant in the death he was, could not refrain from tears. Fanin, however, said to them: "My brothers, may God be with you. But have you come here so that you may rejoice with me that I, leaving this world, go to my God in heaven?" Then, lifting up his eyes, he prayed with such vehemence and ardour that he seemed to be entirely aflame like fire. Then a little later he became so cheerful in spirit and countenance that he turned everyone's eyes to himself and drew them all to him, so that even those who came to strengthen him received consolation from him. There was one of the public scribes who warned him that, if he wished to retract what he had professed, it was not the Pope's intention that he should die. To him Fanin replied, smiling, that if there were anything false or wicked in what he held, it could easily be refuted and convicted; but such is the power of truth that, although it may labour at times, it can never be overcome. Therefore he did not wish in any way to be freed in such a manner that the truth would be obscured and extinguished. But when the scribe had been left behind, since what was being put to him was not of great importance, he began to set out many passages of Holy Scripture; and to give his speech greater authority he brought forward the Latin text and recited it from memory. This was no small matter for admiration, since men knew well that he was only slightly practised and trained in the Latin tongue. Yet he cited a great number of places and testimonies, and quoted each chapter so that he made no mistake in any, so that everyone easily perceived that he was ruled and governed by the Spirit of God. Among these he also recited certain verses which he had composed on justification, on predestination, and on other most weighty heads of faith. But because he seemed rather more joyful and cheerful, and exulted too immoderately, one of those present said to him: "What is the cause that you now rejoice so greatly? For if Christ, when death was impending over him, sweated blood and water from sadness of spirit, and prayed to the Father with the greatest anguish of mind that he might not die, what have you to make you carried away by such great gladness?" And then Fanin answered: "The Lord Jesus, although he had never had any sin, yet, because for our cause he wished to satisfy the judgement of God, took upon himself all our infirmities, and paid all the penalties which were owed for our sins, so that when he was in the garden and hung on the cross he felt the true pains of death and those torments of hell which we ought rightly to have borne. That was therefore the reason why he was afflicted with such anguish in the garden: because in our flesh he felt our death and our hell. But I, who possess with true faith the blessing of Jesus Christ, now enjoying it, rejoice exceedingly, being fully persuaded that, in dying, I am transferred into eternal and blessed life. Why then should I not rejoice, since I have such confidence?" While Fanin, bathed in this consolation, was speaking thus, behold, three hours before dawn they led him into the square of the city, so that the people might not be present and hear what he had been accustomed to say before death. Then, as was the custom, a cross was brought to him; and when he saw it he said: "I beg you, do not take so much trouble. Do you think that you will renew and confirm in me the memory of our Lord Jesus Christ, living and reigning in heaven, with this wooden fragment more than I have it fixed in my heart?" And at the same time, placing his knees on the ground, he prayed to God with the greatest earnestness of spirit, with words full of the most ardent feeling, asking that by his grace and mercy God would enlighten the blinded minds and hearts of those wretched men who were present there. Then, when he had set himself and prepared for the beam and the rope by which he was to be hanged and strangled, he cheerfully told the executioner to carry out what had been commanded him. So, always commending himself to the Lord Jesus Christ and praying that he would receive his soul, he ended his life with the noose. About the customary hour of dinner, in the same place where his body was to be burned, many said that the vapour which rose from his body, like a most pleasing odour of his death, would penetrate the minds of many men, and would have greater power to admonish and console them than his words had had.

units.la: Quòd autem ad causas attinet, propter quas fuit ita condemnatus atque hoc supplicio affectus, non est magnopere necesse eas hoc loco referre, quæ ex illius scriptis melius cognosci possunt: in quibus aperte & copiosè exponit ea quæ & à se dicta & ab aduersarijs obiecta fuerunt, & quemadmodum omnia à se dissoluta & refutata fuerint. Is scripsit complures epistolas & multa alia, tum cum in carcere teneretur. Inter alia eius opera, duo sunt libri de Proprietate Dei, & alij duo de Confessione, totidem etiam de Modo ac ratione qua fidelis homo cognosci, atque ab infideli discerni possit. Præterea sunt eiusdem centum homiliæ de maximis & grauissimis fidei capitibus, multaque alia scripta, quæ hic sanctus Martyr Faninus post mortem suam reliquit.
units.tr: As for the causes for which he was condemned and put to this death, it is not greatly necessary to set them out here, since they can be learned better from his writings, in which he clearly and fully explains both what was said by himself and what was objected by his opponents, and how he answered and refuted everything. He wrote many letters and much else while he was held in prison. Among his other works are two books on the Property of God, two others on Confession, and as many on the manner and method by which a faithful man may be known and distinguished from an unbelieving one. There are also his hundred homilies on the greatest and most weighty heads of the faith, and many other writings which the holy martyr Faninus left behind after his death.

units.la: MACAEVS MOREAV.
units.tr: Macaeus Moraeus.

units.la: SEQVENTI anno qui erat post millesimum quingentesimum quinquagesimus, Macaeus Moræus Trecis Campanis (Troia in Campania à Gallis nunc nominatur) combustus fuit, atque in confessione huius piæ salutarisque doctrinæ constantissimus semper permansit.
units.tr: In the following year, which was after 1550, Macaeus Moraeus was burned at Troyes in Champagne (called Troia in Campania by the Gauls today), and he remained most steadfast in the confession of this pious and saving doctrine.

units.la: IO. GODEAV, ET GABRIEL BERAVDIN.
units.tr: John Godeau and Gabriel Beraudin.

units.la: IOANNES Godæus, Chinone Turonensis Galliæ oriun-dus, & Gabriel Beraudinus patria Iuliodunensis, cum Genevæ uterque habitaret, capti fuerunt Chamberiaci, quòd sacerdotem quendam, nomine Dei contumeliosè in sermone abutentem reprehendissent amicéque admonuissent. Godæus cùm doctrinam Evangelij purissimè integerrimèque defendisset, ea in urbe combustus est, mense Aprili, anno M.D.L. Gabriel autem Beraudinus, quanuis initio, horrore tormentorum sensibus percepto, in confitenda veritate nonnihil vacillasset: ea tamen morte quam Ioannes perpessus erat, ita fuit animo confirmatus vt paucis post diebus idem genus mortis constanter sustinuerit: adeo vt aduersarij, cum summam eius constantiam cernerent, ne posset loqui, linguam ei praecidendam curauerint. Is tamen sanctissima quadam vi spiritus praeditus, nunquam loqui desistit, adeo vt satis intelligeretur: Praepositusque qui cum ad vltimum supplicium ducebat, carnificem vehementer accusarit, quasi non bene ei linguam amputasset. Cui ille multis audientibus satis aspere respondit, in sua nonesse potestate vt eum loqui prohiberet. Hi autem duo, multos veritatis ignaros aedificarunt, cum summam fidei constantiam diuinitus datam, ad extremum vsque spiritum declararent ac praestarent. hoc vero exemplum imprimis memorabile est eorum, qui cum in ecclesia Dei Geneuae pie vixissent ac Deum coluissent, egressi postea, doctrinam Euangelij in qua fuerant instituti, grauissimo constantissimoque testimonio & martyrio comprobarunt.
units.tr: John Godeau, a native of Chinon in Touraine, France, and Gabriel Beraudin, of Joinville, lived together at Geneva. Both were arrested at Chambéry because they had rebuked a certain priest who was abusing the name of God in his sermon, and had admonished him in a friendly way. Godeau, having defended the doctrine of the Gospel most purely and uprightly, was burned in that town in the month of April, 1550. Gabriel Beraudin, although at first, struck with horror at the torments he had felt, wavered somewhat in confessing the truth, was nevertheless so strengthened in spirit by the death that John had suffered that a few days later he endured the same kind of death constantly. So much so that his opponents, seeing his great constancy, arranged for his tongue to be cut out, so that he could not speak. Yet he, endowed with a most holy power of the Spirit, never ceased to speak, so that it was well understood. The provost who was leading him to the final punishment bitterly accused the executioner, as if he had not cut out his tongue properly. The executioner answered him fairly sharply, in the hearing of many, that it was not in his power to stop him speaking. These two men built up many who were ignorant of the truth, since they showed and displayed, down to their last breath, a great constancy of faith given them by God. This example is especially memorable of those who, having lived piously and worshipped God in the Church at Geneva, afterwards went out and confirmed by a most grave and steadfast witness and martyrdom the doctrine of the Gospel in which they had been instructed.

units.la: THOMAS SAMPAVLINVS.
units.tr: Thomas Sampaulinus.

units.la: Thomas Sampaulinus, patria Suessionensis, cum anno M.D. XLIX. cum matre, ac fratribus, aliisque multis propinquis se Geneuam ad Deum pure colendum contulisset, reuersus est in Galliam propter quaedam sua negotia, anno M.D. LI. quo in itinere magna in pericula incidit, cum spiritu Dei permotus (quem purissime in ecclesia aluerat) blasphemias ferre non posset, sed libere eas reprehenderet atque alia vitia, quae in eo Galliae regno diuturna iam consuetudine & licentia, veluti ius quoddam obtinuerunt, vt non sine summo piorum periculo reprehendi possint. Deus tamen cum ex omnibus eripuit, & pro sua singulari prouidentia, alium in locum theatrumque celebrius reseruauit, quod ei Lutetiae ad Euangelij doctrinam confitendum, paratum erat & constitutum. Is igitur in eam vrbem cum venisset, atque ibi quasdam merces venderet, ferre non potuit cuiusdam blasphemias, quin cum eum libere redarguisset, comiter etiam pro ea qua praeditus erat humanitate ac naturae suauitate, monuit vt huiusmodi verba contumeliosa, sanctissimo Dei nomine indigna, euitaret. quare offensus ille
units.tr: Thomas Sampaulinus, a native of Soissons, went to Geneva with his mother, his brothers and many other relatives in 1549, in order to worship God purely. In 1551 he returned to France on account of some business of his own. On this journey he fell into great danger.
