Moved by the Spirit of God, whom he had nourished most purely in the Church, he could not bear blasphemies, but freely rebuked them, and also other vices which in that kingdom of France had by long custom and license gained a kind of right, so that they cannot be rebuked without great danger to the godly. Yet God snatched him out of all these, and by his singular providence reserved him for another place and a more famous stage, which had been made ready and set up for him at Paris to confess the doctrine of the Gospel. When he had come to that city and was selling some wares there, he could not endure the blasphemies of a certain man. Having freely rebuked him, he also, with the courtesy and sweetness of nature with which he was endowed, kindly advised him to avoid such abusive words, unworthy of the most holy name of God. Offended by this holy admonition, which is unusual among the Papists, who regard the things of God as nothing, and suspecting that he was a Lutheran (which is the invidious name they give to those who think piously about God), he took care to have him diligently watched and followed as far as the house where he was lodging. When this had been noted and marked, he immediately reported it to John Andreas, a man ennobled by the same cruelty he had shown towards the servants of God, in which he had especially added fuel to those flames. At last Sampaulinus was seized and taken to that court of the crown called the Châtelet in Paris, where his case was investigated and prepared by the councillors of that court, more from his own mouth and confession than from the papers and notes which they had with them. Finally he was condemned by that court to be burned alive. The cause of this sentence was a remarkable constancy in the confession of the faith and of the truth, which was known and clearly seen in him, and which neither threats of torture could ever break, nor promises of the most pleasant and agreeable life, which the judges offered and held out to him, without any disgrace and public correction, if he would be willing to repudiate before them, by his confession, what he had felt and testified.

units.la: le tamsancta admonitione, atque inter Papistas inusitata quibus bonos Dei pro nihilo ducitur, suspicatusque eum esse Lutheranum, (ut invidioso nomine appellant eos, qui pie de Deo sentiunt) eum curavit diligenter observandum, eiusque vestigiis insistendum usque ad domum in quam diverterat. qua notata ac designata, cum statim ad Ioannem Andream detulit, hominem nobilitatum ea crudelitate, quam in servos Dei exercuerat, in qua ad flammas illas excitandas inprimis faces subdidit. Captus denique ac ductus est in eam comitialem curiam, quae Castelletum Lutetiae appellatur: ubi per consiliarios eius curiae, magis ex ore ipsius & confessione, quam ex chartis & commentariis quos secum habebat, causa eius fuit informata atque instructa. Postremo ab ea curia fuit condemnatus ut vivus igni cremaretur: cuius quidem sententiae causa, fuit eximia quaedam illius constantia in confessione fidei ac veritatis cognita atque perspecta: quam neque ullae tormentorum minae ei propositae infringere unquam potuerunt, neque promissiones huius suavissimae incundissimaeque[?] vitae, quam iudices, sine ulla ignominia atque emendatione publica, ei promittebant deferebantque, si, quod senserat ac testatus fuerat, vellet apud ipsos confessione sua improbare.
units.tr: by so holy an admonition, and by language unusual among the Papists, which holds the good people of God as nothing. Suspecting that he was a Lutheran (which is the hateful name they give to those who think piously of God), he took care to have him closely watched, and followed his footsteps as far as the house where he had lodged. Having noted and marked the house, he at once reported it to Jean Andrieu, a man ennobled by the cruelty he had shown to the servants of God, and in whose case he had especially fanned those flames. Finally he was seized and taken before that court of the Châtelet at Paris. There the councillors of the court were informed of his case and briefed on it, drawing more from his own mouth and confession than from the papers and notes he carried with him. At last the court condemned him to be burned alive. The cause of this sentence was a remarkable constancy in confessing the faith and the truth, which was known and clear. Neither threats of torture could ever break it, nor the promises of a most pleasant and agreeable life, which the judges offered and held out to him, without any disgrace or public recantation, if he would by his confession disown before them what he had believed and testified.

units.la: Hoc autem illi cum consuetudine quadam adducti agebant ut eum perderent, ipsique religioni hac iudicii varietate, omnem detraherent authoritatem, tum etiam permoti com-miseratione quadam aetatis, in qua vix annum XVIII egressus esse videbatur. sed singularis Dei bonitas & veritas, quae nullis rebus vinci unquam potest, contra impetus omnes cum infractum inuictumque effecerat. Nam cum quaestio de eo tam vehementer atque acriter, quam de ullo unquam latrone aut sicario homine, habita fuisset, ut socios fideles homines quorum conscius esset, nominaret: Deus tanta animi vi eum confirmavit, ut nullum eam in partem verbum exprimi potuerit: nec ulla mentio facta fuerit eorum quidem, qui maxime ab aduersariis poscebantur. eos vero solum nominavit, qui aduersariorum manum, dominatumque Antichristi effugerant, ac iam in liberis civitatibus degebant. ita Deus Sampaulinum gubernavit, coque robore muniuit, ut suo indicio neminem in periculum adduxerit: nam iudicibus qui instabant, eumque premebant, ita dicebat, Cur me tam atrociter torquetis, ut vobis tot probos homines nominem? quæ utilitas ad vos redibit, cum eo modo eos quo me nunc torquetis, cruciaveritis? sane si referre vestra existimare, eorum nomina quemadmodum & cæterorum, nunc proferrem: sed certo scio vos in eos, si in vestra potestate haberetis, maiore sæuitia atque atrocitate supplicioru, quam in meipsum, usuros esse. Nihilominus tamen tortores illi & carnifices in illa immani crudelitate obfirmati, oia odii sui, sæuitiæ ac furoris instrumenta ad eum iam satis afflictum & prope confectum, magis adhuc cruciandum & lacerandum adhibuerunt atque explicarunt, cum summis tormentis, tum etiam clamoribus eum urgentes prementesque ut socios indicaret: aut se eius corpus in frusta discerpturos. Denique tortorum manus in huiusmodi quæstione exercenda fuerunt fatigatæ. Maillardus vero, egregius doctor & Sorbona dignus, ac plerique eius similes, à curia accersiti ut Thomam converterent, perculsi tanta in iuuene constantia, exclamarunt, vehementius arctiusque torquendum. Homines fide digni audiverunt ex Auberto, qui unus erat e numero urbanorum conquisitorum urbis Parisiensis, qui tu ei quæstioni præerat, homo ad sæuitiam procliuis, tu vero maxime cum de religione ageretur: cum tamen tanta atrocitate ferre non potuisse coactumque fuisse præ lachrymis scorsum recedere: eundem porro dixisse pluribus audientibus, se multis de rebus cum privatis, tum etiam ad disquisitionem Lutheranam pertinentibus loquutum esse: sed eum sibi iuuenem probum integrumque visum fuisse. Cum autem eorum immanissima crudelitas, singulari Thomæ fide, constantia, animique magnitudine ita victa fuisset, tandem fuit ductus ad plateam celeberrimam Malbertina appellata, ut ibi vivus cremaretur, habes in comitatu ad consolationem sua doctore Maillardu, ut eum ab invocatione nominis Dei avocaret, atque ad omnem aliam fallacem spem cogitationemque traduceret. is Thomæ sæpius dixit, se ab ipsa Curia mandatum habere, ut vitam ei offerret, si pristinam fidei confessionem vellet contraria testificatione improbare. ad quod cum alter responderet se millies mori malle, statim in aerem sublatus est: ubi simulatque coepisset populum de gratia Dei & ipsius salute admonere, ignis subiectus exarsit. eum autem cum vehementer sentire coepisset, subito ex o fuit extractus hortatu ipsius Maillardi, qui ei affirmando incolumitatem promittebat, si commutata sententia vellet summam Curiam appellare. hoc autem ille agebat, existimans se de eo triumphaturum, cum horrore mortis ipsum ac sensu tormenti, de sententia deiecisset. Sed Deus verus fidelisque in suis promissis, oculos ei aperuit, vt contemplaretur excellentem ipsius gloriam, ad quam vocatus, toto animi studio ac desiderio aspirabat. Itaque maxima voce eis dixit, Cum ego fuerim in via vt irem ad Deum, remittite me in eam ac me ire sinite. Ita Thomas Sampaulinus, cum fortiter, vt egregius miles Iesu Christi, causam eius & gloriam Dei propugnasset, atque admirabili constantia defendisset, Lutetiæ coronam martyrii est adeptus, XIX. Sept. anno M.D.LI.
units.tr: They were moved to do this partly by a custom of theirs, to destroy him, and partly so that by this variety of judgment they might take all authority away from the religion itself; and they were also moved by some pity for his age, for he seemed hardly to have passed eighteen years. But the singular goodness and truth of God, which can never be overcome by anything, had made him unbroken and unconquered against all their assaults. For when he was questioned about it as vehemently and sharply as any robber or assassin, to name the faithful brethren of whom he was aware, God strengthened him with such force of mind that not a word could be drawn from him on that point, nor was any mention made of those who were especially demanded by the adversaries. He named only those who had escaped the hand of the adversaries and the dominion of Antichrist and were now living in free cities. Thus God guided Sampaulinus and fortified him with such strength that by his testimony he brought no one into danger. For to the judges who pressed him and urged him on, he said: Why do you torment me so savagely, to make me name for you so many upright men? What advantage will come back to you, when you have tortured them in the same way you now torture me? Indeed, if it mattered to you to know their names, as well as those of the others, I would now declare them; but I know for certain that if you had them in your power you would use greater cruelty and a more savage kind of punishment against them than against myself. Nevertheless, those torturers and executioners, hardened in that monstrous cruelty, brought out and applied all the instruments of their hatred, cruelty and fury against him, already sufficiently afflicted and nearly spent, to torment and mangle him further, pressing and urging him to name his companions, with the most severe torments and also with shouts, or else they would tear his body into pieces. At last the hands of the torturers grew weary of carrying out this kind of inquiry. Maillard, an outstanding doctor and worthy of the Sorbonne, and many like him, summoned from the court to convert Thomas, were struck by such constancy in a young man and cried out that he must be tortured more violently and more tightly. Trustworthy men heard this from Aubert, one of the chosen citizens of the city of Paris, who presided over that questioning. He was a man inclined to cruelty, especially when religion was the subject, yet he had been unable to bear such atrocity and had been forced to withdraw aside for tears. The same man further said to several listeners that he had talked with him about many things, both private matters and those pertaining to the Lutheran inquiry, but that the young man had seemed to him upright and blameless. When their most monstrous cruelty had been overcome by Thomas's singular faith, constancy and greatness of spirit, at last he was led to the famous square called Maubert, to be burned alive there, having with him as a comfort Doctor Maillard, whose task was to call him away from invoking the name of God and to turn him to every other deceitful hope and thought. He often told Thomas that he had a commission from the Court itself to offer him his life, if he would disown his former confession of faith by a contrary declaration. When the other replied that he would rather die a thousand times, he was at once lifted up on high; and as soon as he began to admonish the people about the grace of God and his own salvation, the fire beneath him blazed up. But when he began to feel it intensely, he was suddenly drawn out of the fire at the urging of Maillard himself, who promised him safety, provided he would change his view and appeal to the supreme Court. He did this, thinking he would triumph over him, if by the dread of death and the feeling of torment he could bring him down from his sentence. But the true God, faithful in his promises, opened his eyes to behold the excellent glory to which he had been called, and toward which he aspired with all the zeal and longing of his mind. So with a loud voice he said to them: Since I have been on the way to go to God, send me back onto it and let me go. Thus Thomas Sampaulinus, having bravely defended the cause and glory of God as an outstanding soldier of Jesus Christ, and having championed them with admirable constancy, won the crown of martyrdom at Paris, on 19 September 1551.

units.la: CLAVDIVS MONIER.
units.tr: CLAUDIUS MONIER.

units.la: Claudius Monerius, natus in urbe sancti Amandi, Talanda appellata, alio dicta nomine Cathedra, tribus milliaribus ab Ifsiodoro in Aruernia, cum ea in urbe & Claromonte, quæ Gergobia a Cæsare nominata, metropolis est totius Aruerniæ, scholas aperuisset: ac iuventutem imprimis in timore Dei eiusque verbi cognitione instituisset, in suspicionem venit apud eos qui huiusmodi integritatem ac pietatem ferre non possunt. Itaque eum a munere suscepto instituendæ iuventutis removerunt. Postea regionem Aruerniam locaque finitima obiit, docens semper & annuntians verbum Dei, donec gravi persecutione eiectus illinc, eo se contulit ubi & doctrinam Evangelii receptam, & ecclesiam verbo Dei emendatam esse audiverat.
units.tr: Claudius Monerius, born in the town of Saint-Amand, called Talanda and also by another name, Cathedra, three miles from Issoire in Auvergne, opened schools there and in Clermont, which Caesar called Gergovia and which is the metropolis of all Auvergne. He took especial care to bring up the young in the fear of God and in knowledge of his Word. This made him suspect to those who cannot bear such integrity and piety. So they removed him from the office of teaching the young that he had undertaken. Afterwards he travelled through Auvergne and the neighbouring regions, always teaching and proclaiming the Word of God, until a severe persecution drove him out. He then made his way to the place where he had heard that the doctrine of the Gospel had been received and the Church had been reformed by the Word of God.

units.la: Itaque Lausannam est profectus, urbem in ditione Bernensium positam: quæ quoniam non studiis solum religionis ac pietatis, verum etiam omnis doctrinæ elegantis liberalisque florebat, in ea aliquandiu studuit. Inde Lugdunum profectus, aliquorum puerorum curam disciplinamque suscepit: quos in literis sacris ita erudiebat, vt multis hominibus piis cognitus, & in sancta modestaque vitæ consuetudine probatus gratusque extiterit. Erat enim suavi, placido mitique ingenio, quemadmodum complures homines testesque fideles retulerunt: qui omnem eius & vitæ & doctrinæ rationem, ea in urbe cognoverant. quam quidem ipse etiam maxime declaravit ea nota, quæ verae piæque doctrinæ propria sequi solet. Nam cum aliquando in ea urbe ita viuens docensque versatus esset, accidit vt die Dominica, XV. Iulij cum ipse domum cuiusdam amici ac familiaris hominis venisset nunciaturus illi adventum Praefecti urbis, ut periculum vitaret: ac quum amicum extra portas deduxisset, reuersus redijt ad aedes amici, ut uxorem eius & familiam consolaretur. hoc officio amici Christianique hominis perfunctus, in ea domo Praefectus eum quadam suspicione motus comprehendit, ac deinde ad Officialem adduxit, à quo interrogatus de praecipuis Christianae religionis capitibus, receptisque in Papatu superstitionibus ita respondit, ut subito periculo nihil plane territus esse videretur: sed potius paratus ad ea omnia quae homini Christiano Euangelium prositenti proposita, sunt expectanda. Sed in iudicium postridie adductus, ut de pluribus rebus interrogatus fuit, ita de omnibus non minus constanter quàm prudenter commodéque respondit, ac veritati huiusmodi dedit testimonium, in quo summa sacrarum literarum cognitio & pietas cum pari magnitudine animi coniuncta esse videbatur. Cùm autem ab eo vehementissimè flagitaretur, ut eos nominaret, qui eam doctrinam sequerentur, nullius unquam fecit mentionem, nisi eorum qui eò profecti erant ut nullum periculum eis pertimescendum videretur. Sed quandoquidem in carcere cùm detineretur nactus est De beneficio occasionem scribendi exemplar quoddam actionum atque percontationum iudicialium aduersus ipsum habitarum: illud hic inseremus ut ipse in sua ad fideles Lugdunenses epistola loquens audiatur
units.tr: So he went to Lausanne, a city in the territory of Berne, which flourished not only in the study of religion and piety but also in every refined and liberal learning, and he studied there for some time. From there he went to Lyons, where he took on the care and instruction of some boys, whom he taught in the holy Scriptures so well that he became known to many godly people and was approved and valued for his holy and modest way of life. For he had a sweet, calm and gentle disposition, as many men and faithful witnesses have reported, who had come to know his whole manner of life and teaching in that city. He himself showed this most clearly by the mark that true and pious doctrine usually bears. For once, while he was living and teaching in that city in this way, it happened on the Lord's Day, 15 July, that he had come to the house of a certain friend and familiar to warn him of the coming of the provost of the city, so that he might avoid danger. After he had escorted his friend outside the gates, he returned to the friend's house to comfort his wife and household. Having performed this duty of a friend and a Christian, he was arrested in that house by the provost, who was moved by some suspicion, and then brought before the official. Questioned by the official about the chief articles of the Christian religion and the superstitions received under the papacy, he answered in such a way that he seemed in no way frightened by the sudden danger, but rather ready to face all the things that are set before a Christian who professes the Gospel. The next day he was brought to trial, and when questioned on many matters he answered all of them as steadfastly as wisely and aptly, and he bore witness to the truth in such a way that his great knowledge of the sacred letters and his piety appeared joined with an equal greatness of spirit. Yet when he was most vehemently pressed to name those who followed that doctrine, he never named anyone except those who had already gone away, so that no danger seemed to threaten them. But since, while he was held in prison, he found an opportunity to write, he has put in here a copy of the actions and judicial examinations conducted against him, so that he may be heard speaking in his own letter to the faithful of Lyons.

units.la: Claudius Monerius captiuus Iesu Christi, omnibus fratribus pauperibus simul & diuitibus, electis à Deo ad hæreditatem immortalitatis perpetuamque in domo eius habitationem μετὰ ἀντιμισθίας[?]: Gratiam & fiduciam per unigenitum Filium eius.
units.tr: Claudius Monier, prisoner of Jesus Christ, to all the brethren, poor and rich alike, chosen by God to the inheritance of immortality and to an everlasting dwelling in his house, with reward [?]: grace and peace through his only-begotten Son.

units.la: Antea quidem ad vos scripsissem, nisi papyrus aliaque ad scribendum necessaria mihi defuissent. Gratias ago quòd vobis adeò curæ sim ut & certis hominibus & literis ad me missis facile perspexi Dominus in regno suo compenset vestram operam. Non latet vos, non fallor, quo modo comprehensus fuerim: reuersus scilicet in domum amici quem deduxeram: sex aut septem satellites in eam irruunt infesti sanè animis, nec quenquam ibi reperiunt praeter me extraneum. In summa, praeda petita frustrati, me velut suspectum arripiunt: ad Officialem deducor. Is ut primum ingressus essem, rogat ex me, num corpus Iesu Christi in pane esset. respondeo, me adorare Iesum Christum sedentem dentem[?] tem in cælis ad dexteram Patris sui. De purgatorio autem quid ais? Quia, inquam, post mortem nullus est misericordiæ locus, nihil etiam opus est purgatione. nam antequam ex his corporibus migremus, purgatos esse oportet. De Papa vero quid sentis? inquit ille: Episcopum equidem dicerem æque atque alium, modò Diui Petri imitator esset. Sed quia eo die Dominico nempe, pauci habiti erant sermones: pro Stridie ad auditorium ducor, vbi à me studiosè contendebant, vt dicerem si quos in hac vrbe nossem, quibus familiariter visus essem: quod genus vitæ aut quam artem profiterer, fassus sum, siquidem ille quem dixi amicus iam notus erat ipsis pro Lutherano, vt vocant, me ædes illius subinde frequentasse, nec alias insuper quàm ab octo aut nouem diebus diuersorium meum oliua pensili insigne celebrasse: in quo ego diuertercm, quòd in meditullio ciuitatis situm esset, quò facilius illic arte mea scitè scribendi scilicet, quæstum aliquè facerem. illud autem diuersorium minimè ipsis suspectum est. Sequenti die venerunt tria religiosorum genera, ac tum ego accersitus, cùm illi supra modum vrgerent vt nominarem mihi notos homines, vi magna coactus, cupiens vitare duriora tormenta, tandem duos nominaui qui iam à duodecim vt minimum diebus discesserat, alter in Angliam, alter Geneuam: cuius quidem rei mihi testis est Dominus. Nam reuera, fratres mei, nihil meum animum adeo cruciat, quum coram ipsis sto, quàm si quando de vobis aliquid ex me audire volunt. Inter religiosos istos, inquam, varie vexatus fui, hinc inde me pupugerunt aduersarij suis aculeis venenatis. Sed quoniam pluribus Papistarum articulis respondendum erat, Quæsiuit ex me Officialis quid de votis sentirem. dixi tanta voueri haud posse quin multò plura præstari à nobis Lex ipsa requirat. Deinde, an inuocandi essent Sancti, Respondi ipsos precari sine fide nequire, ac proinde frustra quos ipsos obtunderet: Angelos enim à Deo constitutos vt nobis obsequium præstent ex præcepto eius. Tum etiam, annon oporteret recitare Aue Maria ad salutandã Virginem. Quum in hoc mundo, inquam, versaretur, salutatione egebat Angelica, quia salute opus habebat perinde ac cæteri mortales. nunc autem quum plenè beata sit, nulla illi maior optari potest salus. Rogatus præterea an habendæ essent imagines. respondi, Quum ingenium hominum adeò proclive fit ad idololatriam, ac magis semper omnes occupati sumus & intenti iis quae oculis cernimus, quam quae non videmus, Christianis nō proponendas esse eiusmodi imagines. Scitis enim, fratres mei, adorandum esse quod oculis non subiicitur: Deum nempe solum, qui Spiritus est. hunc itaque in Spiritu & veritate adorare oportet. Visus nihil prodest, cor tantummodo ille desiderat. De voto autem religionis, respondi unam nos retinere & servare religionem Christianam. Quod ad horas canonicas attinet, negavi nos certis horis anxie astrictos, sed quoties nos spiritus Dei impelleret, precari: ac tum quidem attentius cum necessitas aliqua urgeret. Ventum est ad oleum illud sacrum, salem, aliaque eius generis nugas, quas aiebam merum esse Marranismum. Hic cum viderem Officialem haesitare in voce Marranismi, declaravi illi quid ea sibi vellet, dicens istiusmodi unguenta & salsamenta, prorsus redolere legem Marranorum, ac superstitionem Iudaicam. Ad extremum percontati sunt num probarem si qui Psalmos Davidicos lingua vernacula canerent publice. Quidni? inquam ego, modo id cum reuerentia[?] fiat: omissis nimirum putidis catilenis, quarum putore atque spurcitie totus aer passim infectus est. Paucis diebus post revocatus fui, ut quid haberem animi cognoscerent. Illi nihil me immutatum offendentes, a percontationibus prorsus abstinuerunt. Tum ego rogavi, quinam essent aduersae partis. Officialis autem subridens, Sunt, inquit, plurimi qui diversas partes tuctur[?]. Excipiebā[?] ego, quod optarem de fide mea interrogari. Iudex vero dixit satius esse ut consessionem meam in scripto exhiberem, quemadmodum Richardus fecerat. His dictis, me recedere iusserunt, se de ea re deliberaturos nec ipse eos deinceps vidi. Spero autem (si Deo placet) me ad vos missurum confessionem meam postquam illam nitidius descripsero. Hactenus de testatione mea. Reliquum est ut nunc in quo statu sint res meae, & quid valeam cognoscatis: meque vobiscum consoler in hac nostra captiuitate. Nostram dico captiuitatem, quandoquidem ut me vestram sic & vos meam sentire oportet. Inter fratres enim omnia communia sunt bona simul & mala.
units.tr: I would have written to you earlier, had I not been without paper and the other things needed for writing. I give thanks that you care for me so much; I have readily perceived this from certain men and from letters sent to me, and I trust that the Lord in his kingdom will repay your labour. You are not unaware, and I am not mistaken, of how I was arrested: I had returned to the house of the friend whom I had escorted out. Six or seven attendants rushed in, certainly hostile in mind, and found no one there but me, a stranger. In short, having failed to find the booty they sought, they seized me as a suspect and led me to the official. As soon as I entered, he asked me whether the body of Jesus Christ is in the bread. I answered that I worship Jesus Christ, sitting in heaven at the right hand of his Father. "And what do you say about purgatory?" I said that after death there is no place for mercy, and so there is no need of purgation either, for we must be purged before we leave these bodies. "And what do you think of the Pope?" he said. I would call him a bishop like any other, provided he were an imitator of the blessed Peter. But since on that Sunday only a few sermons had been given, on the next day I was led to the hearing-room, where they earnestly insisted that I name any people I knew in this city with whom I had been on familiar terms, and what kind of life or trade I followed. I admitted that the friend I mentioned was already known to them as a Lutheran, as they call it, and that I had often visited his house, and that for not more than eight or nine days my lodging, marked by a hanging olive branch, had been in use; I had lodged there because it lay in the middle of the city, so that I could more easily earn something there by my skill in writing. That lodging was not at all suspicious to them. On the following day three kinds of religious men came, and then I was summoned. While they pressed me beyond measure to name for them acquaintances, I was compelled by force, and wishing to avoid harsher torments, I at last named two men who had left at least twelve days before, one for England and one for Geneva. The Lord is my witness to this. For truly, my brethren, nothing so torments my mind when I stand before them as when they want to hear something from me about you. Among those religious men, I say, I was variously harassed; the adversaries stung me on this side and that with their venomous barbs. But since I had to answer many articles of the Papists, the official asked me what I thought about vows. I said that vows cannot be made so great that the law itself does not require far more from us. Next, whether the saints should be invoked: I answered that they cannot pray without faith, and so it is in vain that they were bothering me with them; for the angels were appointed by God to render us service by his command. Then they asked whether one ought not to recite the Ave Maria in greeting the Virgin. I said that while she was in this world she needed an angelic greeting, because she needed salvation just as other mortals did; but now that she is fully blessed, no greater salvation can be wished for her. Asked further whether images should be kept, I answered: since the nature of men is so prone to idolatry, and we are always more occupied and intent on what we see with our eyes than on what we do not see, such images should not be set before Christians. For you know, my brethren, that what is not present to the eyes must be worshipped: namely God alone, who is Spirit. He must therefore be worshipped in Spirit and in truth. Sight profits nothing; the heart alone desires him. As for the religious vow, I answered that we hold and keep one religion, the Christian. As for the canonical hours, I denied that we are anxiously bound to certain hours, but that we should pray whenever the Spirit of God moves us, and more attentively when some necessity presses. They came to that holy oil, salt and other trifles of that kind, which I said were pure Marranism. When I saw the official hesitating over the word Marranism, I explained to him what it meant, saying that such unguents and salted things smell wholly of the law of the Marranos and of Jewish superstition. Finally they asked whether I approved of people singing the Davidic Psalms publicly in the vernacular. Why not? I said, provided it is done with reverence, leaving aside those filthy ditties, whose stench and foulness have spread through the whole air. A few days later I was summoned again, so that they might learn what state of mind I was in. Finding me unchanged, they abstained altogether from questioning. Then I asked who the adverse party were. The official, smiling, said: "There are very many who support the opposing side." I added that I would like to be questioned about my faith. The judge replied that it would be better for me to set forth my confession in writing, as Richard had done. With these words they ordered me to withdraw, saying they would deliberate on the matter; and I did not see them again after that. I hope, however (if it pleases God), to send you my confession once I have written it out more neatly. So far concerning my testimony. It remains now that you should know in what state my affairs are and how I am, and that I may console myself with you in this our captivity. I say our captivity, since you must feel mine as I feel yours; for among the brethren all goods are common, and so are all evils.

units.la: Primùm, amici mei, siquidem Dominus vestris impulsus precibus me patientia fulserit, nolim in domo Regis esse, atque hunc carcerem regis palatio prætulero, ac potiorem duxero. nam ibi si fuero menuens veritatem profitcri, punget me atque intus accusabit conscientia: qui haud mediocris est cruciatus, sed ipsis inferorum tormentis quodammodò gravior. cuius rei mihi testes esse potestis, quicunque inter Babylonios vitam agitis. In ea, inquam, detinemini captivitate, quæ mea nihilo est levior. Corpore quidem liberi estis: sed animæ vestræ non sine gemitu ferunt, non ferendum sanè cuiquam iugum Antichristi. Ac licet corpus meum intra quatuor parietes inclusum sit: spiritus tamen habet quòd se in Domino oblectet: quum is me tanto honore dignatur ut me in societatem Filij sui ad ferendam crucem asciscat. Orandus est præcipuè Dominus, ut quàm illa carni est tristis & amara, spiritui contrà tam iucunda & suavis reddatur, ut quo maiore metu illam antehac subire recusavi, nunc fortiori animo complectar. Eheu, fratres mei, si gustu percipi possit suavitas quæ sub hac cruce latet, nemo à se illam reiceret, sed certatim omnes contenderemus, quò primus quisque eam humeris sustineret. Multi tum inuenirentur Simones Cyrenæi qui crucem portarent. Verùm caro nostra tam delicata est, ut ne extremitate quidem digiti attingere velit. Precemur igitur, precemur, inquam, Omnipotentem, ut nos corroboret Spiritus sua virtute propter Filium suum, ad ineundum certamen pro virili: quo superemus omnes hostes nostros, carnem, mundum cum principe eius Sathana, mortem, ipsos denique inferos. Sed præ cæteris non reperio capitaliorem hostem (quemadmodum sæpe in precibus meis dicebam) quàm proditricem illam Voluntatem nostram quæ perpetua nobis comes est. Ipsa cùm sit domestica & familiaris, aliique omnes externi tantum hostes, plus nobis ab illa metuendum est. Non enim caret dolis, probeque novit insciare[?] hominem. Si quis huic veneficæ indulget & assentatur, eique placere studet: si miser eius maritus Spiritus astutiā & arrogantiam illius dissimulat & tolerat: tota repente domus tumultu ardet, subit diabolus, quo illa velut nitido fidit adultero, à quo tentata facile se patitur opprimi, nec fidem sponso datam rumpere veretur. id multum curat scilicet. Nonne ipsa scelceratis parentibus, filia sceleratior? Quo semel est imbuta recens seruabit odorem Testa diu, necesse est ut ortus sui naturam referat, atque ad ingenium semper redeat improbum, nisi illam Dei gratia couertat, ut patriam, familiam parentes, omnia denique quae possidebat prius, relinquat: atque adeo semet ipsa abneget.Sed quis tanti operis effector existet? Quis nisi Iesus Christus, nouus maritus ac sponsus omnium piarum animarum & voluntatem syncerarum.is eam de-integro immutabit, eamque liberam, obedientum ac placidam dabit.tum demum castus erit lectus, nullis diuulsus querimoniis: nequaquam metuendum erit ne Sathan eius tentet pudicitiam. quandiu fidelis erit Spiritui sancto, procul erunt omnes maligni spiritus. Quapropter,fratres mei,precemur assiduè Patrem caelestem, ut erect in nobis cor mundum, det nobis cor nouum, gubernet semper voluntatem nostram spiritus sui ductu, ne adulter ille Sathan eam suis praestigiis illudat, qui ut illam ad nequitiam abducat, nihil omittit, eamque assumpta boni Angeli forma petit. O terque quaterque felicem D. Paulum, qui probe huius nouerat infidias & quo tati nebulonis calliditas tenderet exploratu habebat. Considerate, quaeso, fratres mei & sorores, an vllus locus segnitiae aut socordiae sit, ac non potius assiduas in specula excubias agere debeamus, cum tam cautos habeamus inimicos, maximeque periculosissimum omnium in nobis ipsis domi certamen. Dicat nunc aliquis nos a cruce liberos, omnique molestia & praelio vacuos. nonne constat in hoc quam vere dixerit Iobus? militia est vita hominis in hoc mundo? Quod quidem bellum perpetuum & funestum iure dici potest, siquidem in eo ad extremum usque vitae spiritum nobis dimicandum sit, nec ulla ante mortem pax aut induciae iniri queant. Adhaec nonne horrenda & ferox pugna est, quando ipsi nosmet petimus & nobis ipsi infestissimi hostes sumus? Atqui si nostri nosmet haud miseret, quis quaeso nos respiciet? Pater nimirum omnis misericordiae, ei si videbitur: qui etiam inimicis suis benefacit, atque iniuria accepta beneficium reddit. faxit is pro sua gratia, ut & nostri & aliorum misericordia tanganur[?]. Agite ergo commilitones mei, ad praelium accingamur, ad arma, inquâ, ad arma. Bono animo esse viri fortes, & audaciter in medium procedite. Nequid timeatis hostes. facile ipsos superabimus: duce enim Christo nihil despeesperandum[?], qui eos omnes pro nobis vicit. Spes itaque victoriae eius obis fit loco galeae. deinde clypeum assumamus qui telorum sufficiat, fidem scilicet vivam, firmam & constantem. Videamus etiam atque etiam ne gladius nobis e manibus elabatur: ensis, inquam, Spiritus sancti utrinque incidens, qui est verbum Dei vivi, quod penetrat corda & animas, cogitationes omnes & voluntates, denique nihil ei resistere potest. cuncta illi patent ac cedunt: illud prosternit inimicos suos, etiamsi ne strictim quidem attingat. Solo verbo, ut ait Paulus, interficiendus est Antichristus. Sed diligenter cavendum ne quis haec arma commutet ferro. nec enim ferrum, lacerti, equitatus, nec aliae humanae vires in militia Christiana adhibendae sunt. relinquamus haec omnia tyrannis atque Rhodiensibus equitibus, qui nihil non arrogant armis, & fustibus inculcare fidem hominibus conantur. Sed videtis quid proficiant & quam feliciter res ipsis succedat. Idem illis impedet quod Templariis, ut vocant, accidit, qui una nocte omnes profligati fuere. Capta iam est Rhodus maximum illorum praesidium & munitissimum propugnaculum. atque ita paulatim amittent quicquid habet reliquum. est enim planta quam non plantavit Pater caelestis, quapropter etiam convelletur. Papa cum fautoribus nequitiae suae nonne robore & potentia humana utuntur, dum nos volunt cogere ut abiuremus Iesum Christum: contraque credamus Antichristo falsamque religionem amplectamur? Vincula, ignes, & alia eorum tormenta recte dici possunt, potentia tenebrarum & vis tyrannica. quae quidem tyrannis, etiamsi omni alio crimine vacarent, satis tamen arguit ipsos māgia esse Antichristi, totumque papatum plantam esse non bonam quae tandem eradicabitur. Turca si cum papistis comparetur plus sane habebit humanitatis. nec enim quemquam cogit ad religionis suae abnegationem: cuius etiam in orationibus nostris immemores esse non debemus.
units.tr: First, my friends, since the Lord, moved by your prayers, has strengthened me with patience, I would not wish to be in the king's house. I have set this prison above the royal palace and judged it the better place. For if I were there and failed to profess the truth, conscience would prick me and accuse me from within. That is no slight torment, indeed in some ways heavier than the torments of hell itself. Of this you can be witnesses, all of you who live your lives among the Babylonians. You are held, I say, in a captivity no lighter than mine. You are free in body, but your souls bear, not without groaning, the yoke of Antichrist, a yoke truly not to be borne by anyone. And although my body is shut within four walls, my spirit still has cause to rejoice in the Lord, since he has deigned to honour me so highly as to take me into fellowship with his Son in bearing the cross. Above all we must pray to the Lord that, as that cross is sad and bitter to the flesh, so it may be made pleasant and sweet to the spirit, so that with the greater courage I now embrace what before I refused to undergo through fear. Alas, my brothers, if the sweetness hidden under this cross could be perceived by taste, no one would cast it from himself; we would all strive eagerly to be first to bear it on our shoulders. Many Simons of Cyrene would then be found to carry the cross. But our flesh is so delicate that it will not even touch it with the tip of a finger. Let us therefore pray, I say, pray to the Almighty, that his Spirit may strengthen us by his power for the sake of his Son, to enter the struggle manfully, so that we may overcome all our enemies: the flesh, the world with its prince Satan, death, and at last hell itself. Yet above all others I find no more deadly enemy (as I often said in my prayers) than that betraying Will of ours which is our constant companion. Since it is domestic and familiar, while all the others are merely external enemies, we have more to fear from it. For it lacks no tricks, and knows well how to deceive a man. If anyone indulges and flatters this sorceress, and strives to please her; if her wretched husband, the Spirit, dissembles and tolerates her cunning and arrogance, the whole house suddenly blazes with tumult. The devil comes in, and she, like a gleaming adulterer, trusts herself to him; tempted by him, she readily lets herself be overcome, nor does she fear to break the faith pledged to her spouse. She cares very much for that, of course. Is not the daughter more wicked than her wicked parents? Whatever a freshly made jar is first steeped in, it keeps the smell for a long time; so she must always return to her original nature and to her wicked disposition, unless the grace of God turns her, so that she leaves her country, family, parents, and in short all she possessed before, and so denies herself. But who will be the author of so great a work? Who but Jesus Christ, the new husband and bridegroom of all pious souls and sincere wills? He will change her anew and make her free, obedient and gentle. Then at last the bed will be chaste, undisturbed by any complaints; there will be no fear that Satan may tempt her chastity. As long as she is faithful to the Holy Spirit, all evil spirits will be far away. Therefore, my brothers, let us constantly pray to the heavenly Father that he may create in us a clean heart, give us a new heart, and always govern our will by the guidance of his Spirit, lest that adulterer Satan mock it with his deceits. To lead it into wickedness he omits nothing, and he seeks it under the assumed form of a good angel. O thrice and four times happy St Paul, who well knew these snares and clearly understood where the cunning of such a scoundrel tended! Consider, I beg you, my brothers and sisters, whether there is any room for sloth or carelessness, and whether we should not rather keep constant watch from the lookout, since we have such cautious enemies, and above all the most dangerous of all contests, the one within ourselves at home. Someone may now say that we are free from the cross, empty of all trouble and battle. Does it not hold true in this matter, how truly Job spoke: is not the life of man on this earth a warfare? This war can rightly be called perpetual and deadly, since in it we must fight until the last breath of life, nor can any peace or truce be entered before death. Moreover, is it not a dreadful and fierce fight, when we attack ourselves and are our own most hostile enemies? Yet if we have no pity on ourselves, who, I ask, will look upon us? The Father of all mercy, surely, if it pleases him, who also does good to his enemies and returns a benefit for an injury received. May he grant, by his grace, that both we and others be touched with mercy. Come then, my fellow soldiers, let us gird ourselves for battle: to arms, I say, to arms! Be of good courage, brave men, and advance boldly into the midst. Let there be no fear of the enemy: we shall easily overcome them, for with Christ as our leader nothing is to be despaired of, since he has conquered them all for us. Therefore the hope of his victory serves us in place of a helmet. Then let us take up the shield, which will suffice against the missiles, namely a living, firm and constant faith. Let us also take care, again and again, that the sword does not slip from our hands: the sword, I say, of the Holy Spirit, cutting on both sides, which is the word of the living God, which penetrates hearts and souls, all thoughts and wills; in short, nothing can resist it. All things lie open to it and yield; it strikes down its enemies even if it does not touch them at all. By the word alone, as Paul says, Antichrist is to be slain. But we must take care that no one exchange these weapons for iron. For neither iron, nor horsemen, nor cavalry, nor other human strength are to be used in Christian warfare. Let us leave all these things to tyrants and to the Knights of Rhodes, who claim everything by arms and try to hammer faith into men with clubs. But see what they gain, and how well things turn out for them. The same will happen to them as happened to the so-called Templars, who were all destroyed in one night. Rhodes, their greatest stronghold and most fortified bulwark, is now taken, and so little by little they will lose whatever remains to them. For it is a plant which the heavenly Father did not plant, and therefore it will be uprooted. Do not the Pope and his supporters in wickedness use human force and power, when they want to compel us to abjure Jesus Christ, and instead to believe Antichrist and embrace a false religion? Chains, fires and their other torments may rightly be called the power of darkness and tyrannical violence. And this tyranny, even if they were free of every other crime, would still sufficiently prove that they are the masters of Antichrist, and that the whole papacy is a plant that is not good and will at last be torn up. If the Turk is compared with the Papists, he surely shows more humanity: he compels no one to renounce his religion. Nor ought we to be forgetful of him even in our prayers.

units.la: Videtis ergo crudelissimos in orbe tyrannos esse eos qui nomen Christiani usurpantes, falso praetextu sanctitatis, vi occupant locum Filij Dei.
units.tr: You see, then, that those who, usurping the name of Christian, occupy by force the place of the Son of God under a false pretext of holiness, are the most cruel tyrants in the world.

units.la: Tempus breui affore manifesta sunt praesagia, quod iam Papae dominatus multum imminuitur, alaeq; ipsi praecidiuntur, dum se exosum reddit Principibus. Utinam Deus regnum Filij sui Iesu Christi instauret, Antichristum vero sede sua pellat. fiet quando illi visum fuerit. nostrum est orare & optare tatam generi humano fœlicitatem. Cæterùm ne cogitemus hæc humanis viribus perficienda. Deus enim, ut ait Paulus, filium illum perditionis spiritu oris sui conficiet. i. virtute Verbi. Quatos anmodò[?] progressus fecerit in variis regnis lenis ille spiritus oris Dei, verbum illud Domini amabile supra modum, absque ullo tumultu, nullâque vi externa, res ipsa passim loquitur. Hoc ipsum divinum Verbum docet, haudquaquam certandum cum inimicis nostris robore corporis aut ferro. Discite à me, ait Iesus Christus, quòd mitis sum & humilis corde.Sanctis igitur armis contenti simus, de quibus supra locuti sumus, fide scilicet & spe quam in Iesu Christo habere debemus, Verbo ipsius tantummodò præfulti. Restat, fratres mei, ut de charitate dicamus, cuius praxis inter homines parum est in usu. Nunc etenim sunt tempora, quibus Christus charitatem plurimorum labefactatum iri prædixit, frustra nomen Christianorum, fidelium & euangelistarum usurpamus, frustra etiam libros Scripturæ euoluimus: frustra Scripturam semper in ore habemus, si charitas friget: nihil aginus, inquam, si illa non excolitur. An fides dare luce potest absque charitate? non secus quàm si lumini nō instilletur[?] olcum[?]. Charitas singularis est nota qua veri discipuli Iesu Christi dignoscuntur. Charitas certissimus est nostræ fidei testis. Charitas de pluribus unum cor & unam animam efficit. Charitas pusillum gregem compellit in unum. Charitas communionem Sanctorum conciliat. Qui charitatis expers est, inquit Ioannes, in morte manet, in tenebris versatur, atque homicida est. Res ipsa tam excellés[?] est, ut Ioannes ipsum Deum charitatem esse scribat. Cùm tanta igitur támque necessaria sit charitas, ut sine ea mortui simus, quantumuis nobis omnia prospere cedant: orandus est assiduè Dominus, ut in nomine dilecti Filij eam in cordibus nostris accendat virtute Spiritus sui, ut toti ardeamus eius amore, zelo gloriæ eius, & desiderio eius videndi: quò tandem præsentes cum eo in æternum mutuo conspectu fruamur, festúmque celebremus perpetuum in perfecta lætitia, hymnos & cantica spiritualia incessanter canentes in honorem & gloriam Dei nostri. Amen. Fratres, ne cœtus vestros celebrare omittatis, etiasi paruo numero congregati: néue usque adeo vestes aut anulos respiciatis. scitis quòd Divus Jacobus eam curam ut inanem reprehendat. Æstimet se quisque minoris quam caeteros. Frequenter invicem invisite, ac praesertim imbecillos animo & corpore: vestrasque domos ita constituite, ut merito ecclesiolae dici possint: atque dum corpus cibo & vino reficitis, sermones habetote sanctos. hac enim ratione familiam totam aedificabitis animaeque pastum simul & corpori praebebitis. Ne mea vos terreat captiuitas quo minus in officio sitis, sed potius meo exemplo firmiores nunc reddamini quam unquam antea. Hic enim sum ut asseram veritatem Dei in me operantis, precibus etiam vestris assiduis adiutus, quibus me plus millies commendo. commendabo itidem me ecclesiis superioribus. Quod ad me attinet, meministis quanta mea desideria vim habeant. Reliquum est, fratres mei, ut Deum orem, quo beneficia quae à vobis in me adhuc in dies proficiscuntur, sua bonitate compenset, quemadmodum iam initio dixi: supplicans vobis coram Domino, ut mihi ignoscatis quòd ea prudentia atque constantia inter vos non egerim qua oportuit. Nam revera probè mihi conscius sum imbecillitatis meae, quòd recesserim quum me progredi opus esset. idque feci prae nimio metu hominum, aliisque infirmitatibus, quas mihi condonet Deus merito Jesu Christi Filii sui obedientissimi, rogo. Ministris honorem exhibete, non velut idolis, sed nuntijs Domini. De me autem ne aliàs soliciti sitis quàm in orationibus vestris. nam & me & mea Deo trado omnia, cui honos, laus, gloria exhibeatur cum gratiarum actione pro omnibus beneficiis in aeternum. Amen. Rogo vos ut hanc epistolam in multorum manus tradendam curetis: non quòd illius dignitas id mereatur, sed ut omnes simul fratres gaudere possint, & pro me Dei opem implorare. Saluto vos & amplector omnes in Jesu Christo. Vester frater Claudius Monerius.
units.tr: The signs that the time is near are already clear: the Pope's domination is greatly diminished, and his wings are being clipped, since he has made himself hateful to princes. Would that God restore the kingdom of his Son Jesus Christ and cast Antichrist from his seat. It will happen when it seems good to him. Our part is to pray and to wish for the fullest happiness of the human race. But let us not think these things are to be accomplished by human strength. For God, as Paul says, will destroy that son of perdition with the Spirit of his mouth, that is, by the power of the Word. What progress the gentle Spirit of God's mouth, that lovely Word of the Lord, has lately made in various kingdoms, without any tumult or external force, the thing itself speaks everywhere. The divine Word itself teaches that we must by no means contend with our enemies by bodily strength or by the sword. "Learn from me," says Jesus Christ, "that I am meek and lowly in heart." Let us therefore be content with the holy arms of which we have spoken above, namely the faith and hope that we ought to have in Jesus Christ, relying on his Word alone. It remains, my brothers, that we speak of love, the practice of which is little in use among men. For these are the times in which Christ foretold that the love of many would grow cold. In vain do we take the name of Christians, of the faithful and of the evangelical, in vain also do we turn over the books of Scripture, in vain do we always have Scripture on our lips, if love grows cold; we accomplish nothing, I say, if it is not cultivated. Can faith give light without love? It is no different from oil not being poured into a lamp. Love is the singular mark by which the true disciples of Jesus Christ are known. Love is the most certain witness of our faith. Love makes one heart and one soul out of many. Love gathers the little flock into one. Love brings about the communion of saints. He who lacks love, says John, remains in death, dwells in darkness, and is a murderer. The thing is so excellent that John writes that God himself is love. Since love is so great and so necessary that without it we are dead, however well all things turn out for us, the Lord must be constantly entreated that in the name of his beloved Son he would kindle it in our hearts by the power of his Spirit, so that we may burn wholly with his love, with zeal for his glory and with desire to see him, so that at last, present with him, we may enjoy the mutual sight of him for ever, and keep a perpetual festival in perfect joy, singing hymns and spiritual songs without ceasing, to the honour and glory of our God. Amen. Brothers, do not neglect to hold your assemblies, even if gathered in small numbers; and do not look so much at clothes or rings, for you know that the blessed James rebukes that care as vain. Let each esteem the others as better than himself. Visit one another often, and especially those weak in mind and body; and arrange your homes so that they may rightly be called little churches. While you refresh the body with food and wine, have holy discourses; for in this way you will build up your whole household and give food to the soul as well as to the body. Let not my captivity frighten you from doing your duty, but rather, by my example, be now firmer than ever before. For I am here to assert the truth of God who works in me, aided also by your constant prayers, by which I commend myself a thousand times over. I will likewise commend myself to the churches above. As for me, you remember how great my desires are. It remains, my brothers, that I pray to God that he, by his goodness, may repay the benefits which day by day still come to me from you, as I said at the beginning, while I beg you before the Lord to forgive me that I have not acted among you with the prudence and constancy that I ought. For I truly am well aware of my weakness, in that I withdrew when I needed to go forward. I did this out of excessive fear of men and other infirmities, which I beg God to pardon for the sake of Jesus Christ, his most obedient Son. Show honour to the ministers, not as to idols, but as to messengers of the Lord. Do not be anxious about me otherwise than in your prayers; for I commit myself and all that is mine to God, to whom honour, praise and glory be given, with thanksgiving for all his benefits, for ever. Amen. I ask you to see that this letter is handed on into the hands of many, not because its worth deserves it, but so that all the brothers together may rejoice and implore God's help for me. I greet you and embrace you all in Jesus Christ. Your brother, Claudius Monerius.

units.la: In carcere vero Lugdunensis Archiepiscopi quandiu fuit, & fideles homines Deumq; timentes literis magnopere in fide vocationéque Christiana confirmavit, & magistratus iudicesque Lugdunenses de ipsorum saevitia & crudelitate in filios Dei, atque intolerabili dominatione graviter admonuit. quæ fuit causa, ut in locis carceris profundioribus atque obscurioribus demissus fuerit: ubi cum maxima corporis molestia & ærumna, usque ad xxvi.diem Octobr. inclusus fuit, patienter constanterque perseveras in ea fidei confessione quam antea præclaram ediderat. Quanquam saepius maxima vi impetuque tentationum moueretur, quibus sathan eius fidem oppugnabat: tum etiam adversarii, qui variis modis ac rationibus eum a proposito avocare conabantur. sed summa Dei benignitas eum semper in puritate fidei eiusque constanti confessione conservavit. Itaque eodem Octobris die, qui fuit dies Lunæ, in maximam plateam summi templi nomine sancti Joannis appellati, deductus est: ibique hæreticus palam declaratus: deinde a vicario Archiepiscopi Lugdunensis motus de eo gradu, quem sacerdotibus & suo clero consecrare consueuerunt: ac ita ea gradus necessitudine solutus, in manum civilis magistratus est traditus. indeque lætus, quod turpissima illa nota liberatus esset, ad alium carcerem Roanam appellatum traductus, in fossamque obscuram missus usque ad diem Sabbathi sequentem fuit, pridie eius diei quem festum omnium Sanctorum appellant & celebrant. Eo autem profesto die sententia pronuntiata, capitis damnatus ut vivus igni cremaretur, in locum, Sacclum appellatum, deductus est, ut ibi expectaret illud tempus quo judices pravi fuissent. Ibi parum piscis & panis vinique allatum est ei ut pranderet. Itaque cum diu flexis genibus Deum oraret, atque aliquantum panis cœpisset sumere, duo Franciscani ad eum accesserunt: qui multis & variis sermonibus cum eo habitis, in quibus ab illo præclare repulsi refutatique fuissent, alio tandem tentationis genere aggressi sunt, crimen edacitatis ei objicientes[?], tempusque illud non edendi esse demonstrantes, sed alia maiora magisque necessaria cogitandi. Quibus ille cum summa mansuetudine lenitateque respondit, se non ventris ac voluptatis causa concedere, sed corporis tantummodo aliquantum confirmandi: ne ipsam, cum sit infirmum, promptitudinem spiritus interturbaret in gravissimo atque asperrimo certamine quod ei statim subeundum esset. Hoc responso tam manueto summæque æquitatis pleno, homines impudentes maximo pudore affecit coram hominibus quibusdam qui eo in loco aderant. Horam circiter secundam, suis exutus vestimentis, curru ad locum supplicio constitutum ductus fuit: cuius constantiam, mansuetudinem, summámque patientiam cum iudices viderent, continere se non poterant quin gemerent: quidam etiam lachrymas, eius innocentiae indices ac testes, emitterent. Nam priusquam inde discederet, petiit ab illis vt sibi liceret Deum orare atque inuocare. Id quod ea conditione ei concessum est, ne contra ipsos vllo modo loqueretur: aut eam sibi poenam esse propositam sciret, vt lingua ei amputaretur. A carcere igitur ductus est vsque ad eum locum, qui a magnitudine terrae congestae, atque ad Rhodanum vsque in amplam & longam plateam complanatae, Territorij nomen habet, iunctis manibus vultúque semper in cælum erecto, aspectúque laeto atque hilari. Porrò cum duceretur per vrbem magna hominum multitudine occurrente aut comitante, quidam obuius ei factus, cum his verbis salutauit, Vale in Christo. Qui statim instinctu duorum Franciscanorum qui ibi aderant, comprehensus est. Cum igitur ad locum supra nominatum demonstratúmque venissset, declarata fidei suae ratione, & oratione Domini Iesu pronuntiata, catena praecinctus est: deinde accenso igne in aerem sublatus: diu priusquam moreretur, flammas eius perpessus est, semper orans atque haec verba iterans, Mi Deus, mi pater: atque ita spiritum Domino reddidit.
units.tr: While he was in the prison of the Archbishop of Lyon, for as long as he remained there, he strengthened faithful men and those who feared God greatly in the faith and Christian calling by letters, and he gravely admonished the magistrates and judges of Lyon about their savagery and cruelty against the sons of God and their intolerable domination. For this reason he was let down into the deeper and darker places of the prison, where he was shut up, with the greatest bodily discomfort and hardship, until the 26th day of October, patiently and constantly persevering in that noble confession of faith which he had earlier published. Although he was often moved by the greatest force and onslaught of temptations, by which Satan attacked his faith, and also by his adversaries, who tried in various ways and by various arguments to call him away from his purpose, the great goodness of God always kept him in the purity of his faith and in its steadfast confession. And so on the same day of October, which was a Monday, he was led into the great square of the cathedral called by the name of Saint John, and there he was publicly declared a heretic; then, by the vicar of the Archbishop of Lyon, he was stripped of the rank which they are accustomed to confer on priests and their clergy; and thus released from the bond of that rank, he was handed over into the hands of the civil magistrate. Glad from there that he was freed from that most shameful mark, he was taken to another prison called Roana, and was put into a dark pit until the following Saturday, the day before the day they call and celebrate as the feast of All Saints. On that feast day sentence was pronounced, and condemned to death, he was to be burned alive, and he was led to a place called Sacclum, so that he might wait there until the time when the wicked judges should be ready. There a little fish and bread and wine were brought to him so that he might dine. And so, while he was praying to God for a long time on bended knees, and had begun to take some bread, two Franciscans approached him. After many and varied discussions with him, in which they were clearly repulsed and refuted by him, they at last attacked him with another kind of temptation, charging him with the sin of gluttony and declaring that this was not a time for eating but for thinking of other, greater and more necessary things. To these men he replied with the greatest gentleness and mildness that he was yielding not for the sake of the belly or pleasure, but only to strengthen his body somewhat, lest, being weak, it should disturb the readiness of the spirit for the most grievous and bitter struggle which he was about to undergo at once. By this answer, so mild and so full of the highest fairness, he put those shameless men to great shame in the presence of certain people who were there at that place. At about the second hour, stripped of his clothes, he was led in a cart to the place set for execution. When the judges saw his constancy, his gentleness and his greatest patience, they could not restrain themselves from groaning, and some even shed tears, witnesses and signs of his innocence. For before he left there, he asked them that he might be allowed to pray and call upon God. This was granted to him on the condition that he should in no way speak against them, or else he would know that the punishment set for him was the cutting out of his tongue. He was led from the prison, therefore, as far as the place which, from the great heap of earth thrown up and levelled out as far as the Rhône into a broad and long square, has the name of Territory; with his hands joined and his face always turned to heaven, and with a joyful and cheerful countenance. Moreover, as he was led through the city, with a great crowd of people meeting or accompanying him, a certain man who came across his path greeted him with these words: "Farewell in Christ." At once, at the instigation of two Franciscans who were present there, this man was seized. So when he had come to the place mentioned above and had been shown it, after he had declared the grounds of his faith and recited the Lord's Prayer, he was bound with a chain; then, the fire being lit, he was lifted up into the air; and before he died, he endured its flames for a long time, always praying and repeating these words: "My God, my Father." And so he gave up his spirit to the Lord.

units.la: GILLOTVS VIVIER, & alii Vallencenis ob verbum Dei exusti.
units.tr: Gillotus Vivier, and others of Valenciennes burned for the Word of God.

units.la: PErsecutionum tempestas, rursus nos ad Hannonnieses[?] revocat. Nam circa illud tempus, multi nomine Euangelij in carcerem coniecti fuerunt, grauémque persecutionem passi in ea inferiore regione Flandrica quae ad Hispanū Regē pertinet, imprimisque Vallencenis Hanoniae vrbe, comite Lalaino acerrimo eius persecutionis authore ac principe. Inter alios isti sunt, quorū memoria est cōseruata: Gillotus Viuierus, natus in pago quē vocānt San-saluatoris tribus milliaribus à Tornaco, homo pānni texēdi artifex: & Michael Faber, ex eodem quoque loco affinis ipsius Gilloti, annos natus XIX, patērque eius Iacobus Faber, annos LX. natus, pater Annae quae Gilloti uxor fuit, quae paulo post propter eandem Euangelij causam in carcerem coniecta est. Eorum autem vnusquisque suscepta Euangelij veritatem constantissime defendit. Iacobus vero Faber cum in summa aetate ad agnitionem veritatis deductus esset, in eius professione ac confessione adeo permansit, vt nullis impeditus aduersariorum quaestionibus cauillisque obiectis, ab ea vllo modo dimoueri potuerit. Si minus aduersariorum argumentis satisfacere aut respondere posset, constanter tamen ad veritatem Euangelij provocabat. Neque vero minus insignis atque admirabilis fuit virtus Annæ Fabrae, Gilloti vxoris, quae praeclarum patris, fratris, maritique exemplum fideique testimonium imitata, eorum quoque supplicium ac martyrium aliquo tempore, puerperio videlicet absoluto, post sequuta est. Nam capitis damnata propter constantem Christi eiusque Euangelij confessionem, eandem ignis poenam mulier virili animo cum summa omnium admiratione sustinuit.
units.tr: The storm of persecution calls us back again to Hainaut. About this time many men were thrown into prison for the sake of the Gospel and suffered severe persecution in that lower region of Flanders which belongs to the King of Spain, and especially in the city of Valenciennes in Hainaut, where Count Lalaing was the most fierce author and leader of the persecution. Among the others, these are the ones whose memory has been preserved: Gillotus Vivier, a weaver of cloth, born in the village called Saint-Sauveur, three miles from Tournai; and Michael Faber, from the same place, a kinsman of Gillotus, nineteen years old; and his father Jacob Faber, sixty years old, the father of Anna, who was Gillotus's wife and who shortly afterwards was thrown into prison for the same cause of the Gospel. Each of them firmly defended the truth of the Gospel that he had embraced. Jacob Faber, though he had been brought to a knowledge of the truth in extreme old age, persisted in his profession and confession so steadfastly that, though his adversaries pressed him with questions and objected their quibbles, he could in no way be turned from it. If he could not satisfy or answer his adversaries' arguments, he nevertheless constantly appealed to the truth of the Gospel. Nor was the virtue of Anna Faber, Gillotus's wife, less remarkable and admirable. She imitated the splendid example of her father, her brother and her husband, and the testimony of their faith, and after some time, once her childbirth was over, she followed them to their punishment and martyrdom. For she was condemned to death for her steadfast confession of Christ and his Gospel, and this woman endured the same penalty of fire with a manly spirit, to the great admiration of all.

units.la: MICHELLA de CAIGNONCLE.
units.tr: Michella de Caignoncle.

units.la: Odem quoque tempore fuit fœmina primaria, Michella de Caignoncle nominata, viduaque relicta à Iacobo Clerico, qui ex eadem vrbe Vallencenensi fuit ex qua Michella eius vxor. Ea autem antequam in manus eorum inciderent qui Euangelium persequuntur, fuerat postulata in coniugium à quodam fideli atque honesto homine, vt eam secum in ecclesiam verbo Dei emendata ac purae religioni restitutam adduceret. Quod quidem illa recusauit, modestissimeque excusauit, non quod in cum hominem amicam non haberet voluntatem: sed quod Spiritu Dei nondum se impulsam eo diceret, vt patriam suam relinqueret: ac contra in propositio gratiae Domini atque eius vocationis confirmatam, vt pura & integra ab omni idolorum atque abominationum pollutione conseruari posset. Quod si in huiusmodi ratione vitae caperetur, Dominum pro sua benignitate & consuetudine, virtutem eam daturum, qua predita confiteri sanctissimum eius nomen posset, id quod etiam summo cum honore Dei & singularis fœminae exemplo præstitit. Nam cum capitis damnata esset, vt cum Gilloto ac cæteris, quorum supra mentio facta est, viua combureretur, ad supplicium ducta cæteros ad constantiam hortabatur, ostendes ipsos iudices à quibus erant condemnati & qui ad illud supplicium constituendum aderant, nō posse aliud habere quam horrenda & perpetua conscientiæ carnificina: cum cùm ipsi qui paterentur, placidissima animi pace summáq; certitudine salutis suae fruerentur. Itaq; Psalmos canens & laudes Domini, animo non solùm æquo, sed etiam lubenti laetóque suum reddidit spiritum ei, cuius nomine poenam mortis propositam sustinebat.
units.tr: At the same time there was also a leading woman, named Michella de Caignoncle, widow of Jacob Clerc, who came from the same city of Valenciennes as did Michella, his wife. Before she fell into the hands of those who persecute the Gospel, she had been asked in marriage by a certain faithful and honest man, who wished to take her with him into a church that had been reformed by the Word of God and restored to pure religion. She refused this, and excused herself very modestly, not because she had no friendly feeling towards the man, but because she said that the Spirit of God had not yet moved her to leave her homeland; rather, she was confirmed in her purpose of the grace of the Lord and his calling, so that she might be kept pure and whole from all pollution of idols and abominations. She said that if she were to be taken up in such a way of life, the Lord, in his kindness and custom, would give her the strength by which she might be enabled to confess his most holy name; and this she also did, to the great honour of God and as a singular example for a woman. For when she was condemned to death, to be burned alive with Gillotus and the others mentioned above, she was led to the punishment and exhorted the rest to constancy, showing that the judges who had condemned them and who were present to decree that punishment could have nothing but a horrible and perpetual torment of conscience, whereas those who suffered enjoyed the most peaceful calm of mind and the greatest certainty of their salvation. And so, singing psalms and praising the Lord, she gave up her spirit with a mind not only equal to the task but even willing and glad, to him in whose name she endured the threatened penalty of death.

units.la: MAVRICIVS SECENAT.
units.tr: Mauricius Secenatus.

units.la: Mauricius Secenatus fuit natus in iis motibus, qui quoniam Provinciae Narbonensi adiacent, Graecè videntur esse appellati Κέ[illegible, ~3 letters]μμοι, Gebenni nunc vulgari Prouincialium lingua appellantur. Proprius tamen eius patriae locus S.Saturnini nominatur, prope montem Coletum in Deza, vnum ex iis montibus qui paulò ante nominati sunt. Is igitur Mauricius cum Nemausi studeret literis, studiáque humanitatis cum pietate coniungeret, in qua eos quos poterat in aedibus priuatis instituebat, captus est anno M.D.LI. atque in arcem eius urbis inclusus, in qua cum à Locumtenente eius curiae quadam arte & summa prudentiae humanae moderatione de sua fide interrogatus fuisset, ita respondit, vt dissimulata veritate quam debebat cōfiteri, incolumitatem vitae adepturus esse videretur. Nā ita solent agere astuti homines vt artificiosè & callidè totam interrogationem moderates, fideles homines à vera Christi confessione abducant. Sed interrogatione à Iudice primario repetita, Mauricius tanto dolore dissimulatae veritatis affectus est, vt eam perfidiam Christiana testificatione corrigendam sibi esse existimauerit. Itaque à primario Iudice interrogatus, ita liberè constantérque respondit, vt ipsius confessionem sententia capitis & poena ignis sit consecuta, quam summa cum laetitia suscepit ac pertulit. Eius autem mors praeclara & beata omnes fideles Prouinciae Narbonensis maximopere in fide Christi ac vera religione confirmauit, XVI. Augusti, postridie eius diei qui Virgini Mariae consecratus in Papatu colitur.
units.tr: Mauricius Secenatus was born in those mountains which, because they lie next to the Province of Narbonne, are called in Greek the Cebennae [Κέ…μμοι], and are now commonly called the Gévaudan in the vernacular of the people of the province. His own homeland, however, is named Saint-Saturnin, near the mountain Coletum in Gévaudan, one of the mountains mentioned a little earlier. This Mauricius, while he was studying literature at Nîmes and joining the study of the humanities with piety, instructing in private houses those whom he could, was seized in the year 1551 and shut up in the citadel of that city. There, when he was questioned about his faith by the lieutenant of the court, he answered with a certain craft and great human prudence, in such a way that, by concealing the truth he ought to have confessed, he seemed to be going to secure the safety of his life. For this is how crafty men are wont to act, skilfully and cunningly steering the whole questioning so as to draw faithful men away from the true confession of Christ. But when the question was repeated by the chief judge, Mauricius was so pained by his concealment of the truth that he judged that this faithlessness had to be corrected by a Christian testimony. So, questioned by the chief judge, he answered so freely and steadfastly that his confession was followed by a sentence of death and the penalty of fire, which he accepted and endured with great joy. His splendid and blessed death greatly strengthened all the faithful of the Province of Narbonne in the faith of Christ and the true religion, on the 16th of August, the day after the day consecrated to the Virgin Mary, which is celebrated in Papistry.

units.la: IOANNES à PVTEO,
units.tr: JOHN OF PUTEO,

units.la: Hic vulgò Medicus appellabatur.
units.tr: Here he was commonly called Medicus, the physician.

units.la: Cetiae in Prouincia Narbonensi, eodē tempore ac mense quodā die Lunae mensis Aug. nomine Euangelij ac religionis crematus est Ioannes, cognomento dictus Medicus, homo literarum omnium imperitus, in ea vrbe artificio vtens eo,quod ad ligna cædenda trastandaque pertinet.Is autem doctrina Euangelij tum imbutus fuit quum Episcopus eius vrbis,rebus quietis ac tranquillus,sine vllo persecutionis periculo,veram pietatis disciplinā nescio quomodo amplexus,eam curarat & Vcetiæ & in tota diœcesi annunciandam, ita vt ab ijs verbi ministris,quos ad concionandum asciuerat,forma quædam & ratio pie pureque docendi conseruarentur.Itaque Medicus cum eorum conciones diligenter atque studiosè frequentaret,in agnitione veritatis fuit institutus.Sed causa cur delatus ad Prætorem vrbis fuerit,atque in carcerem coiectus,hæc fuit.Is puteum habebat cōtrouersum cum alio quodam ciue Vcetiensi, qua in controuersia aduersarius vt causam meliore faceret,confugit ad ea remedia,quibus plerique hodie causæ diffidentes suæ vtijdent[?],vt eos crimine hæreseos consisto[?] obiectóque opprimat quos non possunt iure atque æquitate causæ superare. Hac igitur calumnia vtens,non modò in re priuata & parua aduersarius,sed in religione inimicus,non puteum solum,verum etiam caput proximi ac vicini petere cœpit. Atque vt facilius quæ intentabat testimonijs comprobaret,omnes vinitores,quorum opera Medicus in vinea sua vsus suerat,conduxit,ac quid ille sensisset aut dixisset de religione,exquisiuit atque ad Prætorem detulit.Itaque Medicus causa informata approbatáque ijs testibus,in carcerem coniectus est,in eóque de fide sua interrogatus de cœna Domini,ita respondit homo illiteratus,vt à docto & literato nihil purius dici potuerit. nam & disciplinam eam,in qua fuerat institutus allegauit, ex qua didicerat Christum Dominum in co frusto panis nullo modo esse inclusum,& illud caput fidei suæ protulit, in quo illum ad dexteram Dei Patris sedere confitebatur. Itaque ea sententia à iudicibus est condemnatus, vt strangulatus primum, igne deinde cremaretur. Interea autem cum in sacello quodam asseruaretur,du ad supplicium duceretur,quidam facinorosus,qui ob maleficia sua flagellabatur,per eum locum ducebatur,quem cum vidisset Medicus,causamque cur caederetur intellexisset,statim exclamauit,beatos esse qui propter iustitiam paterentur,& carmen quoddam spirituale in eam sententiam compositum,vsque ad locum supplicio constitutum cecinit
units.tr: At Cetia in the province of Narbonne, at the same time and in the month of August, on a Monday, John, surnamed Medicus, a man wholly unlearned in letters, was burned for the name of the gospel and of religion. In that city he practised the craft of cutting and working wood. He had been imbued with the teaching of the gospel at the time when the bishop of that city, living in peace and quiet without any danger of persecution, had somehow embraced the true discipline of piety and arranged for it to be proclaimed both at Cette and throughout the whole diocese, so that a certain form and method of teaching piously and purely was kept by the ministers of the Word whom he had engaged to preach. Therefore Medicus, attending their sermons diligently and eagerly, was instructed in the knowledge of the truth. But the reason he was denounced to the praetor of the city and thrown into prison was this. He had a dispute over a well with another citizen of Cette. In this quarrel his adversary, to make his cause look better, had recourse to those remedies which many today use when they distrust their cause: he sought to crush those whom he could not overcome by right and equity by charging them with the crime of heresy. Using this calumny, the adversary, an enemy not only in a private and minor matter but also in religion, began to seek not only the well but the head of his neighbour. And so that he might more easily prove by testimony what he was alleging, he hired all the vinedressers whose labour Medicus had used in his vineyard, inquired what he had thought or said about religion, and reported it to the praetor. Therefore the case was laid out and approved by those witnesses, and Medicus was thrown into prison. There, questioned about his faith concerning the Lord's Supper, he answered, unlearned as he was, in such a way that nothing purer could have been said by a learned and literate man. For he cited the teaching in which he had been instructed, from which he had learned that Christ the Lord is in no way enclosed in that piece of bread, and he put forward that article of his faith in which he confessed that Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father. Therefore the judges condemned him to this sentence: that he should be strangled first and then burned with fire. Meanwhile, as he was being kept in a certain chapel and was led to execution, a certain criminal who was being flogged for his crimes was led through that place. When Medicus saw him and understood why he was being flogged, he at once cried out that those are blessed who suffer for righteousness, and he sang a certain spiritual song composed to that effect, right up to the place set for execution.

units.la: Ante vero quàm laqueo præfocaretur, orans Dominum memoriter pronunciauit eam orationem, quæ Geneuæ die Mercurij in precibus solenibus ad Deum haberi solet. Deinde propositam pœnam summa cum æquitate animi & mansuetudine, quasi agnus sustinuit. Huius viri constantia atque integritas tanta fuit, ut plurimos qui ab ipsa veritate alieni erant, ad ipsius cognitionem pertraxerit.
units.tr: Before he was choked by the noose, he prayed to the Lord and recited from memory that prayer which is customarily offered at Geneva on Wednesdays in the solemn prayers. Then he bore the punishment set before him with great equanimity and gentleness, like a lamb. The constancy and integrity of this man were so great that he drew very many who were far from the truth itself to the knowledge of it.

units.la: IOANNES IOERY, & Famulus ipsius.
units.tr: JOHN IOERY, and his servant.

units.la: IOANNES Ioerius natus in quodam pago Sanct-ioerio nominato, tribus milliaribus ab urbe Albigesi, maiore parte ætatis suæ Montalbani educatus fuit.Ex ea urbe Geneuam se contulit ad maiorem pietatis cultum capiendum, atque in ea ecclesia pure Deum invocandum. Ubi cum aliquandiu esset commoratus, mense Iul. anni M. D. LI. atque ætatis suæ XXII. iter in patriam instituit, habens secum itineris comitem quendam adolescentem, qui ei serviebat. Ut autem aliquem professionis suæ fructum & consolationem fidelibus adferrent, secum libros pie de religione scriptos, deferendos acceperunt. quæ fuit causa, ut cum essent Mendæ in Prouincia Narbonensi, capti fuerint & condemnati ut igni cremarentur. Ab ea sententia Ioerius (qui sæpe amicis ac familiaribus dixerat, si Dominus ipsum vocaret ad testificandam veritatem, se maxime cupere Tholosæ testimonium ei suum dare, & morte sua obsignare) appellauit. Itaque Tholosam ad supremam curiam missi fuerunt: ubi Ioerius amplam confessionem fidei suæ edidit, eamque confirmauit authoritate Scripturæ, in qua erat non mediocriter versatus: in omnibusque suis responsis se valdè modestum & temperatum præbuit. Neque vero adolescens seruus, pro ætate & cognitione qua præditus erat, minus gratiæ habebat, eandem fidem professus, quam Ioerius illius herus declarauerat. Quanquam tum propter ætatis infirmitatem, tum etiam ignorantiam earum rerum quæ in controuersia agitari solent, non ita commodè poterat dissoluere ea argumenta, quæ ad aduersarijs obijciebantur. quare cum videret se vehementius premi ab his qui quæstioni exercendæ, causaque informandæ præfecti erant, eos ad Ioerium herum suum & magistrum remittebat, testificans se quidem velle in edita confessione omni ratione permanere.
