Cum autem illi dicerent, ipsum non debere vllam fidem adhibere hero suo, qui haereticus esset ac plane reprobatus: eis respondebat, se cum cognouisse virum bonum & sanctitate vitæ præditum: certumque se esse nihil ab eo præter veritatem, quæ verbo Dei continetur, dixisse. Porrò eo die quo hi duo capitis damnati fuerunt, multi sacerdotes & monachi veniebant in carcerem, vt cum Ioerio disputarent: quibus ille ita placide ac sedate respondebat, quasi solutus vinculis in summa libertate sine vllo periculi terrore esset. Cum autem ducti essent ad locum supplicio constitutum, in plateam S. Georgij appellatam: adolescens postremo interrogatus, ad struem lignorum adductus est, dum Ioerius postremis interrogatis responderet. Ibi complures hypocritæ adolescentem coeperunt solicitare vt virginem Mariam inuocaret, susceptamque sententiam deponeret: atque ita importuni extiterunt vt iuuenis vel imbecillitate quadam ætatis, vel importunitate aduersariorum & molestia motus, illachrymari coeperit. Tum vero Ioerius, qui cum aliis loquebatur, cum conuersus illum ab aduersarijs solicitari animaduertisset, ilico festinauit eo accedere. Et cum eum ita fletem reperisset, Cur, inquit, mi frater, tu fles? an nescis nos nunc quidem accedere ad optimum benignissimumque Deum nostrum, & quam primum fore liberos ac solutos his ærumnis quibus affligimur? Cui adolescens, Ego, inquit, flebam quod mecum non esses. Non est, iuquit, Ioerius tepus quo ploremus, quin potius canamus Domino. Tum coeperunt Psalmum canere. At cum flamma ignis exarsisset, & iam ipsum Ioerij corpus inuasisset, ille quasi sui oblitus, & magis de adolescente quam de se solicitus, se quatu[?] poterat ad postem erigebat, respiciens vt adolescentem confirmaret eique animum adderet. Deinde cum animaduertisset illum iam extinctum, ore aperto flammam ignis hausit, caputque demittens spiritum Deo reddidit.
units.tr: John Ioerius was born in a village called Saint-Ioerius, three miles from the city of Albi, and was brought up for the greater part of his life at Montauban. From that city he went to Geneva to take up a fuller practice of piety and to call upon God purely in that church. When he had stayed there for some time, in July 1551, at the age of twenty-two, he set out on the journey home, taking with him a young man who served him as his travelling companion. In order that they might bring some fruit of their profession and some consolation to the faithful, they took with them books written piously about religion, to be delivered. This was the cause of their arrest: when they were at Mende in the province of Narbonne, they were seized and condemned to be burned with fire. Ioerius appealed from that sentence. (He had often said to his friends and acquaintances that if the Lord called him to bear witness to the truth, he most wished to give his testimony at Toulouse and seal it with his death.) So they were sent to the supreme court at Toulouse. There Ioerius gave a full confession of his faith and confirmed it by the authority of Scripture, in which he was no mean student; and in all his answers he showed himself very modest and restrained. Nor did the young servant, according to his age and the knowledge he possessed, have less grace in professing the same faith that his master Ioerius had declared. Yet, partly because of the weakness of his age and partly because of his ignorance of the matters usually debated in controversy, he could not so readily dissolve the arguments which the adversaries threw at them. Therefore, when he saw himself pressed more vehemently by those who had been placed in charge of the questioning and the conduct of the case, he sent them back to Ioerius, his master and teacher, testifying that he indeed wished to persist in the confession he had made by every means. But when they said that he ought not to place any trust in his master, who was a heretic and utterly reprobate, he answered that he had known him as a good man endowed with holiness of life, and that he was certain Ioerius had said nothing but the truth contained in the Word of God. Moreover, on the day on which these two were condemned to death, many priests and monks came into the prison to dispute with Ioerius. He answered them so calmly and composedly, as if he were freed from his chains, in the greatest liberty and without any fear of danger. When they were led to the place set for execution, in the square called St George's, the young man was questioned last and brought to the pile of wood while Ioerius was answering the final questions. There several hypocrites began to importune the young man to invoke the Virgin Mary and renounce the sentence he had accepted, and they were so insistent that the youth, either from some weakness of age or from the importunity of the adversaries and the distress it caused him, began to weep. Then Ioerius, who was speaking with others, noticed that his young companion was being pressed by the adversaries, and at once hurried to go to him. When he found him weeping, he said, "Why do you weep, my brother? Do you not know that we are now going to our best and most kind God, and that we shall soon be freed from these troubles by which we are afflicted?" To this the young man replied, "I was weeping because you were not with me." "This is not a time to weep," said Ioerius, "but rather to sing to the Lord." Then they began to sing a psalm. But when the flame of the fire had blazed up and had already seized Ioerius' body, he, as if forgetful of himself and more anxious about the young man than about himself, raised himself as far as he could against the post, looking round so that he might strengthen the young man and give him courage. Then, when he saw that the young man was already dead, he drew the flame into his open mouth, and bowing his head, he gave up his spirit to God.

units.la: GODEFRIDVS DE HAMELLE.
units.tr: Godefridus de Hamelle.

units.la: GOdefridus Hamellaeus, natus in vrbe Brabantiæ Niuella nominata, Tornaci vbi agebat, arte vestiu[?] conficiendarum farciendarumque exercens, propter Euangelij doctrinam captus est. Et quoniam ex suis literis quas in carcere scripsit, acta iudicij & confessionem de plurimis & grauissimis rebus ad religionem pertinentibus complexus est, nos existimauimus dignas quæ in Latinum sermonem conuersæ ad om[?]ium cognitionem peruenirent. Nam quantum ex illius epistolis intelligere possumus, videtur vir fuisse cum magnitudine spiritus amoréq; in[?] Christum excellenti, tum etiam studio & cognitione sacrarum lite[?]arū singulari: tametsi nullius alterius linguae facultate, quàm verna-[?]ulae & Gallicae instructus esset. Hanc autem primam epistolam misit [?]d quandā mulierem fidelem, vt eam caeterosque pios hoc fidei suae & [?]ratiae in se Dei testimonio, in doctrina Euangelij suscepta cōfirmaret.
units.tr: Godefridus of Hamelle, born in the Brabant town called Nivelles, was arrested at Tournai, where he lived and earned his living making and trimming garments, on account of the doctrine of the Gospel. Since we have gathered from his letters written in prison the record of his trial and his confession on very many and very weighty matters pertaining to religion, we judged them worth turning into Latin so that they might come to the knowledge of all. For as far as we can gather from his letters, the man seems to have been both of outstanding greatness of spirit and love for Christ, and of singular zeal and knowledge of the holy letters, although he was instructed in no language other than his mother tongue and French. He sent this first letter to a certain faithful woman, so that she might strengthen herself and other godly people in this faith of theirs, and in the testimony of God's grace towards him, in the doctrine of the Gospel which they had received.

units.la: Gratia & misericordia optimi Patris nostri per Iesum Christum Filium eius, salutem tibi impertiatur.
units.tr: May the grace and mercy of our best Father, through Jesus Christ his Son, be imparted to you.

units.la: Ego charissima atque amantissima soror, toto animi studio tibi gra[?]ias ago pro ea memoria & cura, quam tum corporis tum spiritus mei suscepisti. Certè huiusmodi amorem vestrum ita mei memorem, quasi quendam Dei nuntium atque etiam suauissimum odorem accipio. Sum etiam magnopere in spiritu recreatus vestris precibus atque orationibus, quas ad Deum cum assidua mei memoria adhibetis, quas scio, quemadmodum vos dicitis, non inanes & fructu vacuas à conspectu Altissimi abituras. Quare te toto corde rogo, ne in hoc pietatis officio fatiscas[?] atque orare desinas, vt hoc excellens certamen, ad quod me Dominus deduxit, ad ipsius gloriam & ecclesiae aedificationem obire possim, id quod eius gratia spero & cōfido. nam is quidem optimè scit, quàtopere ego desiderem vt nomē ipsius per me exiguum eius instrumentum glorificetur, si eo quidem tum ad vitam, tum ad mortem vti vult. Ego enim nihil aliud cupio atque appeto, nisi vt sanctissima eius voluntas de me perficiatur, non solùm vt in infimum obscurúmque aliquem carceris locum demittar: verumetiā vt pro ipsius nomine moriar, si illud mea morte potest vllo modo illustrari, persuasus eius verbo Christum mihi esse lucrum, tum ad vitam tum ad mortem.
units.tr: I, most dear and most loving sister, with my whole heart give you thanks for the remembrance and care that you have shown for me, both for my body and for my spirit. Indeed, I receive such love from you, so mindful of me, as though it were a messenger of God and a most sweet fragrance. I am also greatly refreshed in spirit by your prayers and supplications, which you offer to God with constant remembrance of me; I know, as you say, that they will not depart from the sight of the Most High empty and without fruit. Therefore I beg you with my whole heart not to grow weary in this duty of godliness, nor cease to pray that I may be able to undertake this excellent contest, to which the Lord has led me, to his own glory and the building up of the Church. I hope and trust this will be granted by his grace; for he indeed knows very well how earnestly I desire that his name be glorified through me, his poor instrument, whether he wishes to use me in life or in death. For I desire and seek nothing else than that his most holy will be accomplished in me; not only that I be thrust down into some lowest and darkest corner of the prison, but also that I die for his name, if by my death that name can in any way be made illustrious, being persuaded by his Word that for me Christ is gain, both in life and in death.

units.la: Ego verò, charissima soror, nōdum plane cōstituerā hanc cōfessionē meam ad te mittere, quoad scirem an isti ex me aliquid amplius vellent quaerere: sed quoniā hic tabellarius mihi significauit se ad biduum aut triduum domo profecturum aliquò, eam ob rem mittere coactus sum. Neque verò banc confessionem ad te mitto vt tu ea quasi excellenti quadam perfectâque sapientia erudiaris atque instruaris: sed vt consessione serui Dei minimi, qui noluerim defodere talentum quod à Domino mihi commissum acceperam, ut tu tantummodo intelligas me in simplicitate mea Dominum Jesum Christum coram hominibus non abnegasse, sed pro mensura fidei mihi ab eo tributae confessum esse. Qua in re confido Dominum hoc meo studio atque officio contentum esse, quum vitae non parcam meae ut eam conseruem, sed eam negligam & perdam, quoniam Dominus eam dignam existimat quae coram hominibus amittatur. Sic habeto, mea soror, cor meum, simulatque a satellitibus magno cum impetu & vi comprehensus fui, exclamasse, O Domine, ego paratus sum non modo in carcerem coniici, sed etiam mortem pro nomine tuo perpeti, si id in gloriam posset tuam redundare.
units.tr: Indeed, most dear sister, I had not yet fully decided to send this my confession to you, until I knew whether those men wanted to seek anything more from me. But since this messenger told me that he would be setting out from home for a day or three days to somewhere, I was compelled to send it on that account. Nor do I send this confession to you so that you may be taught and instructed by it as by some outstanding and perfect wisdom; but so that you may understand, from the confession of the least servant of God, who would not bury the talent that he had received from the Lord, that I have not, in my simplicity, denied the Lord Jesus Christ before men, but have confessed him according to the measure of faith given me by him. In this matter I trust that the Lord is pleased with this my zeal and duty, since I do not spare my life so as to preserve it, but disregard it and lose it, because the Lord judges it worthy to be lost before men. Know this, my sister: as soon as I was seized with great force and violence by the guards, my heart cried out, "O Lord, I am ready not only to be thrown into prison, but also to suffer death for your name, if it might redound to your glory."

units.la: Atque haec quidem erat voluntas mea, quae in confessione quoque mea fuit, & erit usque ad ultimam guttam mei sanguinis, postremumque os membrorum meorum, quae igne combusta in cinerem sunt redigenda. Equidem ipsius sum & ad vitam & ad mortem. faciat de me quod statuerit. ego enim sive vivendum sit, sive moriendum, mihi plane persuasi me ipsius semper fore, propterea quod filii eius sum Jesu Christi, a quo permagno pretio redemptus sum, ita ut iam haeres Dei, & cohaeres Jesu Christi sim. Itaque nunc quidem persuasum plane habeo mea esse omnia, sive vitam sive mortem, sive praesentia sive futura: omnia, inquam, mea esse: me autem Christi, Christum vero Dei esse: atque ita persuasus, ipsum Christum cùm ad vivendum tum etiam ad moriendum lucrum esse. Neque vero me pudet coram hominibus confiteri eum solum fuisse & nunc esse in quo omnem spem salutis meae vitaeque beatae reposuerim: quo cum me perpetuo victurum esse spero. Itaque quoniam nulla alia in re spes fiduciaque salutis posita mihi est, quam in eo sacrificio Jesu Christi, in quo semel crucifixus corpus suum Deo Patri pro meis peccatis obtulit: idcirco adduci nullo modo possum, ut iis assentiar quae ex me quaesiverunt, approbarique voluerunt, cum praesertim Spiritus Dei certissimus sit testis & comprobator huius animi mei atque iudicii, quod ea quae sentio & credo vera sunt, & quae ab adversariis mihi proponuntur, falsa, atque ab omni verbi Dei veritate abhorrentia. Illud etiam certo sciens, in me que experiens, corde credi ad iustitiam, ore vero confessionem fieri ad salutem. Itaque Dominus hoc exiguo volens uti instruuento Trumento, me dignum iudicauit vt vocarer ad hoc genus excellentis confessionis, & coram hominibus producerer, vt ex abundantia cordis ore ter interrogatus ipsum confiterer. Prima confessio à me edita fuit VIII.die Martij anni M.D.LI. circiter tertiam horam pomeridianam, cum Decanus Officialisque adessent, & praeterea Inquisitores duo cum notario qui scribebat. Priusquam in praecipuam & legitimam confessionis meae rationem ingrederer, multa sunt ex me quaesita & agitata, quae longa nimium essent ad scribendum. Neque vero ego omnia verba his literis committere, sed breuiter ac summatim tantum praecipua capita scribere constitui earum rerum quae ad fidem ac religionem pertinent.
units.tr: And this indeed was my purpose, which was also in my confession, and will remain until the last drop of my blood and the last bone of my limbs, which are to be burned by fire and reduced to ashes. Truly I am his, both in life and in death. Let him do with me what he has decided. For whether I must live or die, I am fully persuaded that I shall always be his, because I am a son of Jesus Christ, by whom I have been redeemed at a very great price, so that I am now an heir of God and a fellow heir with Jesus Christ. And so now I am fully persuaded that all things are mine, whether life or death, whether present or future things: all, I say, are mine; but I am Christ's, and Christ is God's. Being thus persuaded, I hold that Christ himself is gain both for living and for dying. Nor am I ashamed to confess before men that he alone was, and now is, the one in whom I have placed all hope of my salvation and of a blessed life, with whom I hope to live forever. Therefore, since no other hope or confidence of salvation is placed in me except in that sacrifice of Jesus Christ, in which he, once crucified, offered his body to God the Father for my sins, I cannot in any way be brought to assent to those things which they have asked of me, and wish me to approve, especially since the Spirit of God is the most certain witness and approver of this my mind and judgment, that the things which I feel and believe are true, and the things put forward to me by my adversaries are false and utterly opposed to all the truth of God's Word. I also know this for certain, and have experienced it in myself: "with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Therefore the Lord, willing to use this small instrument, has judged me worthy to be called to this kind of excellent confession, and to be brought before men, so that out of the abundance of the heart I might confess him with my mouth when I was questioned three times. My first confession was made by me on the eighth day of March in the year 1551, about the third hour after noon, when the Dean and the Official were present, and besides them two Inquisitors with a notary who wrote. Before I came to the principal and lawful account of my confession, many things were asked and debated from me, which would be too long to write down. Nor did I decide to commit all the words to this letter, but only briefly and summarily to write down the principal heads of those matters which pertain to faith and religion.

units.la: Ac primum vt ad rem ipsam veniamus, quaesiuerunt ex me, quanliu[?] iam non confessus fuissem. Ego ab illis primum postulaui, vt mihi nouum darent Testamentum, in quo responsa mea & fidem fundare constituereque plane possem. Id cum illi recusassent, atque instarent vt responderem ad id quod rogauerant, ego eis dixi, vt illud quidem mihi concederent. Quaesiuerunt, an no crederem sacerdote ab ecclesia Romana instituto, cum peccatorum confessio ad aures eius fieret, posse agnoscere peccata, atque absoluere per poenitentiam. respondi me nullam peccatorum veniam nec absolutione expectare, nisi a sola Dei misericordia, per gratia Filij eius Iesu Christi. Quaesiuerunt, an non crederem in ecclesiam Romanam cuius Papa esset caput & successor Petri, cui Christus claues dedisset: multaque alia quae ad illum impium dominatum confirmandum nefarie vsurpata omni vi tueri solent. Quibus ego deliberato animo respondi, me Ecclesiam sanctam credere per Spiritum sanctum institutam & fundatam, quae vnum Christum caput habere atque agnoscere: deinde successores eos, qui doctrinam Apostolorum ac Prophetarum sequerentur. ecclesiam vero Romanam me non habere pro vera ecclesia, quae potius esset synagoga quaedam Antichristi, in qua tantum abest vt omnes Iesu Christi foueatur & saluberrimo verbi Dei pastu nutriantur, vt potius ab immanissimis voracissimisque lupis devorentur, aut erroribus doctrinarum humanarum perniciosissimis pascantur. Siccine ais? inquit Decanus: scriptis haec mandentur. Deinde quaesierunt ex me quid de ipsa Missa sentirem, ego vero eos monui, vt de iis rebus, quæ in scriptura sancta continentur loquemur.nam me illud nomen Missæ nusquam nec in nouo nec in veteri Testamento reperire, quantum quidem legere aut meminisse poteram. Ita sane, inquiunt Decanus & cæteri murmurantes: ac iubebant id notarium scribere, quod Missam nusquam in Scriptura inuenirem.
units.tr: And first, to come to the matter itself, they asked me how long I had not confessed. I first asked them to give me a New Testament, on which I could firmly base and establish my answers and faith. When they refused this and pressed me to answer what they had asked, I told them that they should at least grant me that. They asked whether I did not believe that a priest instituted by the Roman Church, when confession of sins is made to his ears, can recognise sins and absolve them through penance. I answered that I expect no forgiveness of sins nor absolution except from the mercy of God alone, through the grace of his Son Jesus Christ. They asked whether I did not believe in the Roman Church, whose Pope is the head and successor of Peter, to whom Christ gave the keys; and many other things which the Papists are accustomed to defend with all their might, wickedly usurped to confirm that impious dominion. To these things I answered with a deliberate mind that I believe the holy Church is instituted and founded by the Holy Spirit, which acknowledges and holds Christ alone as its head; and then, that its successors are those who follow the doctrine of the Apostles and Prophets. But the Roman Church I do not regard as a true Church; rather it is a certain synagogue of Antichrist, in which far from all the faithful of Jesus Christ being cherished and nourished with the most wholesome pasture of God's Word, they are rather devoured by the most savage and ravenous wolves, or fed on the most pernicious errors of human doctrines. "So you say?" said the Dean; "let these things be written down." Then they asked me what I thought of the Mass itself. I, however, admonished them that we should speak of those things which are contained in Holy Scripture, for as far as I could read or remember, I cannot find that name "Mass" anywhere, either in the New or in the Old Testament. "Indeed so," said the Dean and the others, murmuring; and they ordered the notary to write down that I could not find the Mass anywhere in Scripture.

units.la: Tum illico ex me quæsuit, an transsubstantiationem panis in corpus Christi crederem: Cui ego respondi, me Missam eorum credere merum esse hominum inuentum & commentum cum maxima contumelia Iesu Christi ac dedecore coniunctum: propterea quod ipsum populum in eum impium perniciosumque errorem induxerunt, vt Christum credat in frusto panis inclusum, panemque ipsum adoret: non quærat Christum, veneretur, colatque in cœlis ad dexteram Dei Patris supra omnes creaturas elevatum & collocatum. Quod vero ad transsubstantiationem ipsorum attineret, dixi libere, mihi quidem eam videri impostu-ram quandam & ludificationem huiusmodi, quæ ad magos atque incantatores pertineret. Rogarunt me, crederémne septem esse Sacramenta. respondi, me duo tantummodo tenere. Quæ? inquiunt illi: Baptismum, inquam, & Cœnam, quæ vos Sacramenta appellatis. Tum quæsiuerunt ex me, quid sentirem de ipsa Cœna, cum eam Sacramentum appellarem. Ad id autem simpliciter ego respondi, sicut à Domino acceperam, ipsam Cœnam, cum ita administratur vt est instituta à Domino, conuiuium esse spirituale fideli animæ propositum sub specie panis & vini, ita vt qui fide eum panem vinumque sumit, is corpus quoque Christi sanguinemque eius sumat: non quod in eo pane corpus Christi fit, aut sanguis in vino aut cum vino: sed quod credam id omne me spiritualiter accipere ad salutarem refectionem animæ meæ & consolationem: ita vt edens eum panem vinumque bibens eo quo dixi modo, corporis Christi eiusque sanguinis vere sim particeps: neque oculos meos defigo solum in ea caduca elementa quæ corruptioni sunt obnoxia, sed longius oculos fidei meæ reicio in Iesum Christum semel pro peccatis meis crucifixum & oblatum: vulnus contemplor lateris, ex quo purissimus sanguis emanauit, vt ab omnibus vitiorum peccatorumque meorum maculis purgarer, ac eo liberarer debito quo me iudicium Dei obstrictum obligatumque tenebat. Quæsiuerunt ex me, an panis ita suam naturam retineret, vt maneret panis sine aliqua immutatione, eodémque[?] modo vinum? respondi, nihil plané in his elementis immutari: sed quemadmodum ea corpus alerent ac sustentarent, ita fide, quæ carnem & sanguinem Christi sumeret, animam ali, vegetari, confirmari: neque vero opus esse aut necesse dixi, ut Christus Dominus à dextera Patris in hæc inferiora descendat elementa, quò se nobis communicet atque impertiat: sed potius ut mentes ipsinostras & cordis cogitationes, ab huiusmodi rebus quæ sunt aspectabiles atque ad tempus propositæ, ad alia æterna & spiritualia quæ non cadunt sub sensum & aspectum, traducamus, animósque nostros revocemus & erigamus ad dexteram Dei Patris: unde nullum eius corporalem adductum expectamus ante illud tempus quo ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos venturus est: tum sane Christus Dominus venict[?] non occultus & obscurus, sed illustris & gloria sua ornatus.
units.tr: Then at once he asked me whether I believed in the transubstantiation of the bread into the body of Christ. To this I replied that I believed their Mass to be a purely human invention and fabrication, joined with the greatest insult and dishonour to Jesus Christ, because they have led the people into that impious and destructive error, that they believe Christ is enclosed in a morsel of bread and worship the bread itself, instead of seeking Christ, reverencing and honouring him as raised up and set in heaven at the right hand of God the Father, above all creatures. As for their transubstantiation, I said freely that to me it seemed a kind of trickery and delusion of that sort, belonging to magicians and enchanters. They asked me whether I believed there were seven sacraments. I replied that I held only two. Which two? they said. Baptism, I said, and the Supper, which you call sacraments. Then they asked me what I thought of the Supper itself, since I called it a sacrament. To this I answered plainly, as I had received from the Lord, that the Supper itself, when it is administered as the Lord instituted it, is a spiritual feast set before the faithful soul under the appearance of bread and wine, so that whoever receives that bread and wine in faith also receives the body and blood of Christ; not that the body of Christ is made in that bread, or the blood in the wine or with the wine, but that I believe I receive all of this spiritually, for the saving refreshment and consolation of my soul, so that, by eating that bread and drinking that wine in the way I have said, I truly partake of the body of Christ and of his blood. Nor do I fix my eyes only on those perishable elements, which are subject to corruption, but I lift the eyes of my faith further, to Jesus Christ, who was once crucified and offered for my sins; I contemplate the wound in his side, from which the most pure blood flowed, so that I might be cleansed from all the stains of my sins and vices, and freed from the debt by which the judgement of God held and bound me. They asked me whether the bread so retained its nature that it remained bread without any change, and likewise the wine. I replied that nothing at all is changed in these elements; but just as they nourish and sustain the body, so by faith, which receives the flesh and blood of Christ, the soul is fed, quickened and strengthened. Nor did I say that it is necessary or needful for Christ the Lord to come down from the right hand of the Father into these lower elements, in order to impart and communicate himself to us; but rather that we should turn our own minds and the thoughts of our heart away from such visible things, which are set before us only for a time, to other eternal and spiritual things that do not fall under sense and sight, and that we should recall and raise our souls to the right hand of God the Father, from whence we look for no bodily coming of his before that time when he will come to judge the living and the dead. Then indeed Christ the Lord will come, not hidden and obscure, but resplendent and adorned with his glory.

units.la: Cùm hæc ita utrinque tractarentur ac dicerentur, septima hora iam appropinquare videbatur. Itaque eam disquisitionem atque interrogationem, um[?] quidem progredi longius noluerunt. me vero in alium carcerem obscurum induxerunt: ubi ego sum adhuc, quoad optimo Deo meo placuerit. Ab eo igitur die Martij, quem supra scripsi, ab illis eo in loco fui relictus usque ad xv.diem eiusdem mensis: eo quidem die tanta molestia affectus, quantam verbis non possem satis explicare, non propter obscuritatem carceris, aut quod vererer in eorum conspectum venire: sed potius quòd me amplius rationem fidei meæ declarantem audire nollent. ego enim multo vehementius cupiebam fidem meam coram illis testificari ac plane confiteri, quàm ipsi me audire. Itaque Dominum orabam, ut mihi eam daret facultatem, qua simplicis ac purae confessionis meæ munere officióque perfungi possem, quà in re ipse pro singulari suâ benignitate, studio animi mei ac desiderio cumulatè satisfecit. Die igitur xv.Martij hora octava audiui vocem ianitoris mihi nuntiatis dominos iam aduenisse[?], & ut me præpararem admonentis. Illud nuntium, ut fuerat mihi optatum, ita periucundum accidit. tum dixi, Perfice, Domine, quod in me iam cœpisti, & quod promisisti mihi conserua ac præsta. nam hæc quidè tua causa est, in qua oportet Spiritum tuum mihi esse adiutore. Cùm in ea secunda interrogatione coram eis productus fuissem, quæsierunt ex me an essem baptizatus. dixi quamobrem id à me quærerent: an vero me Anabaptistam esse existimarent. Sed cùm illi instarent, respondi, me iam inde prima ab infantia, non alio tempore aut aliter baptizatum fuisse. Ac cùm quæsiuissent, an ego eum Baptismum approbarem atque amplecterer, dixi me eo quidem contentum esse. Postea quæsierunt, an ego Baptismum in Scriptura reperirem. hoc autem rogabant eo consilio, ut nomine Sacramenti à me expresso cauillatorie atque insidiose ad Sacramenta reliqua, & commenta ab ipsis introducta, comprobanda abuterentur. ego vero eis simpliciter respondeo, Circumcisionem patri nostro Abraham datam fuisse, ut ipse ac semen eius octauo die circumcideretur: eique postea Baptismum successisse, quo Christiani in ecclesia utuntur, baptizantes in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti. Deinde quæsierunt ex me, an ulla præterea eius approbatio esset in Scriptura. ego eos remisi ad x.cap.1. epistol. ad Cor. ubi ab Apostolo dicitur, Patres in mari rubro sub ipsa nube baptizatos fuisse. ea autem debere eis satisfacere. Tum vero cupidissimè arripuerunt, quod ego (nullas eorum insidias suspicans) de Sacramentis dixeram atque ita nominaueram: nóxque quæsierunt, ubi illud nomen Sacramenti invenirem. ego tum ita circumuentus, confiteri coactus sum quod verum erat, me illud Sacramenti nomen propterea usurpasse, quod inter ipsos ad maiorem intelligetiam magis esset usitatum: nolle autem posthac eo appellare nomine, sed Baptismum & Cœnam ut Scriptura nominaret. nam si illud nomen eis concessissem aut recepissem, magnopere eos armasset contra me ut peraccommodatum ad Missam, Purgatorium, & alia huiusmodi multa comprobanda, quæ ab ipsis introducta, nusquam in Scriptura nominantur. itaque dixi me in his nominandis nullo alio nomine usurum, quàm eo, quo Scriptura uteretur. Tum dixerunt, existimantes me cauillis suis implicare aut protelare, Tu quidè tam sæpe dicis te nihil plane velle credere aut respondere nisi id quod in Scriptura continetur: quid ais de coniugio? habésne pro Sacramento? Ego, inquam, sic statuo, coniugium sanctum Dei institutum, cubileque immaculatum, eámque coniunctionem ac societatem vitæ tantâ esse ut homo patrem ac matrem suam derelinquat, adhærescátque uxori suæ ut sint duo in carnem unam. Itaque hoc genus vitæ atque institutum tâ necessarium & honestum maximi facio: quod ipse Christus tantopere approbavit, cum in Cana Galilææ nuptias & præsentia & miraculo ibi primum edito honorare voluit. Tum quidam, qui satis versatus in Scriptura videbatur, Credisne, inquit, verbis ipsi[?] Apostoli? Absit, inquā, ut ei ullo modo cōtradicā. Tu, inquit, duo recipis solūm sacramenta: Apost. tamen ad Ephesios coniugium sacramentum appellat, dicens, Sacramentum hoc magnum est. Quid tu ais? inquit. Cui ego respondi, me nullo in verbo velle differentire[?] ab Apostolo, siquidem ille coniugium nominasset Sacramentum. Sanè in omnibus quæ mihi proposita quaesitāque fuerunt, nihil me magis conturbavit, nec maiore molestia affecit, quàm hoc unum, in quo nihil dicere contrà poteram nec audebam. Sed Dominus me in hac difficultate ac obturbatione non diu hærere voluit: mox enim Spiritus eius me commonuit rem nō ita se habere quemadmodum ab illis allegabatur. Itaque memoria mea eius loci ita diuinitus renovata, eis dixi non ita legendum esse in ea Pauli epist. sicut ab ipsis citaretur: sed pro sacramento Secretum esse legendum, iuxta postremam translationem, qua novum Testamentum ex Graeco in linguam Gallicam conversum est. Tum vero ira atque indignatione vehementer in me commoti fuerunt, cum propositum locum in libro novi Testamenti Lugduni impresso inspexissent, atque ut dicebam reperissent, multa tum dixerunt, quæ longum esset scribere. Ac quoniam duodecina jam hora appropinquabat, hæc omnis ea collocutio fuit intermissa. Postero autem die, qui dies fuit XVI. Martij, ab illis sum revocatus horam circiter octavam, & interrogatus an Sacramentum confirmationis crederem, quod episcopus hominibus in legitima eorū ætate administrare solet. Ego vero respondi, huiusmodi ceremoniis fidem meam non confirmari: sed tantummodo ea ratione virtuteque Spiritus, quæ aut in Baptismo me regeneraret ac novam creaturam efficeret, aut me in Cœna communione corporis Christi in fide aleret & confirmaret. Cum autem illi ex octavo capite Actum protulissent exemplum Apostolorum, qui baptizatis hominibus manus imponebant: dixi me id quidem quod à Petro atque Apostolis factum fuisset, approbare: eiusque impositionis authorem ac moderatorem fuisse Spiritum: sed eam ceremoniam postea finem habuisse. Rogarunt an Sacramentum extremæ unctionis credere. respondi me credere verbum Dei esse verum & sanctum oleum quod homini periculosè ægrotanti adhibendum esset, quód que omni credenti salute afferre posset. Illud vero oleum, quod ægrotis hominibus applicare solet, inutile plane esse, ut obnoxiū corruptioni. Tum illi, ut eam unctionem probarent, proposuerunt tritum illud ex epistola, qua Divus Iacobus scripsit. Quibus ego, Vos quidem, inquam, videtis quid ea de re sentiam & credam. Postea de festis diebus interrogatus, respondi, Dominum sex dierum laborem populo suo præcepisse, nec ullum alium die hebdomadis quàm septimum à negotiis vacuum ac liberum instituisse. Eodem modo de Quadragesima & quatuor ipsorum temporibus aliisque hominum comentis interrogatus, respondi, ea mandata hominum ad populum onerandum inventa, nusquam in Scriptura inveniri: sed aliam esse rationem & disciplinam mortificandæ carnis nostræ, totúmque hominis vitæ cursum perpetuum quoddam esse ieiunium: non ut comedamus semel in die, sed ut in tota nostra vita summam sobrietatem sine ulla intemperantia conseruemus. Item de abstinentia à carnibus & ouis in illo quadragenario tempore rogatus, dixime quidem ex quo Dominus e tenebris ad veram lucem & cognitionem veritatis transtulisset, nullum discrimen dierum ac temporum facere, atque sine ullo conscientiæ scrupulo posse bibere ac comedere quicquid à Domino creatum ad necessarium hominis victum tribuitur. Fides tantum adsit, qua his Dei beneficijs cum omni gratiarum actione pure ac pie perfruamur: sicut Apostolus in 1. sua ad Timotheum epistola præcipit. Tum illi, Ergo, inquiunt, tam facile carnes comederes die magnoVeneris qui Pascha præcedit, quàm ipso die Paschatis. Ego vero, inquam, hic quidem nullum discrimen dierum plane facio, ac sive Quadragesima esset sive aliud tempus, nihil aspernarer eorum quæ ad esum mihi essent appositæ: sed libere his vescerer in fide & cum gratiarum actione absque ullo animi scrupulo. Quod si quis infirmus, cum videret me vescentem, offenderetur, tum nollem mea libertate uti, ne hoc modo non tam ad ædificationem, quàm ad offensionem proximi mei ambularem: non enim regnum Dei in cibo est constitutum, neque ego sive comedam, sive non comedam, melior & sanctior sum. pie tamen ampliorem eam libertatem, quæ per verbum: um Dei benignissimè offertur, vt omnibus eius beneficijs cum gratiaum actione vti possim.
units.tr: When these matters had been debated and discussed from both sides, the seventh hour already seemed to be drawing near. So they did not want to carry that inquiry and questioning any further, and instead led me into another dark prison, where I am still, for as long as my most good God pleases. From that day in March which I described above, I was left in that place by them until the fifteenth day of the same month. On that day I was affected by a distress that I could not adequately express in words, not because of the darkness of the prison, nor because I feared coming into their presence, but because they were unwilling to hear me any longer declaring the grounds of my faith. For I was far more eager to bear witness to my faith before them and to confess it plainly than they were to hear me. So I prayed the Lord to grant me the opportunity to discharge the duty and office of a simple and pure confession, and in this he, by his singular kindness, abundantly satisfied the zeal and longing of my mind. Then, on the fifteenth day of March, at the eighth hour, I heard the voice of the doorkeeper telling me that the gentlemen had now arrived and urging me to prepare myself. That news came as welcome as I had wished, and I was overjoyed. Then I said, "Lord, complete what you have begun in me, and keep and perform what you have promised me. For this is your cause, in which your Spirit must be my helper." When I had been brought before them for this second questioning, they asked me whether I had been baptized. I said, "Why do you ask me that? Do you think I am an Anabaptist?" But when they pressed me, I replied that I had been baptized from my earliest infancy, at no other time and in no other way. Then, when they asked whether I approved of that baptism and embraced it, I said that I was content with it. Afterwards they asked whether I found Baptism in Scripture. They asked this with the intention of using the name "sacrament," which I had used, to lure me craftily and treacherously into approving the other sacraments and the inventions introduced by themselves. But I answered them plainly: that circumcision was given to our father Abraham, so that he and his seed should be circumcised on the eighth day; and that Baptism, which Christians use in the Church, baptizing in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, had succeeded to it. Then they asked me whether there was any other approval of it in Scripture. I referred them to the tenth chapter of the first epistle to the Corinthians, where the Apostle says that the Fathers were baptized in the Red Sea under the very cloud, and I said that this ought to satisfy them. Then they eagerly seized on what I had said about the sacraments, and had so named them, not suspecting any of their snares; and they asked me where I found that name "sacrament." Thus ensnared, I was compelled to confess what was true: that I had used the word "sacrament" because it was more customary among them, for the sake of greater understanding; but that from now on I would not use that name, and would call Baptism and the Supper as Scripture names them. For if I had granted or accepted that name, they would have armed themselves greatly against me, since it lends itself very readily to approving the Mass, Purgatory, and many other things of this kind, introduced by themselves, which are nowhere named in Scripture. So I said that in naming these things I would use no other name than the one Scripture uses. Then they said, supposing that I was entangling or delaying them with my quibbles, "You say so often that you want to believe and answer nothing except what is contained in Scripture. What do you say about marriage? Do you hold it to be a sacrament?" I answered, "This is my view: marriage is a holy institution of God, and a undefiled bed, and that union and partnership of life is so great that a man leaves father and mother and cleaves to his wife, so that they are two in one flesh. Therefore I hold in the highest regard this kind of life and institution, so necessary and honourable, which Christ himself approved so greatly when he chose to honour with his presence the marriage at Cana of Galilee, and there first performed his miracle." Then a certain man, who seemed well versed in Scripture, said, "Do you believe the words of the Apostle?" "Far be it from me," I said, "to contradict him in any way." "You," he said, "receive only two sacraments; yet the Apostle, in Ephesians, calls marriage a sacrament, saying, 'This sacrament is great.' What do you say to that?" To this I replied that I wished to differ from the Apostle in no word, since he had called marriage a sacrament. Indeed, of all the things that were put to me and asked, nothing troubled me more or distressed me more than this one point, on which I could say nothing against them and did not dare to. But the Lord did not want me to remain long in this difficulty and perplexity. For soon his Spirit reminded me that the matter did not stand as they alleged. So my memory of that passage was divinely renewed, and I told them that the passage in that epistle of Paul was not to be read as they cited it, but that in place of "sacrament" the word "secret" should be read, according to the latest translation in which the New Testament has been turned from Greek into French. Then they were greatly stirred to anger and indignation against me, when they had looked at the passage in the New Testament printed at Lyons and found, as I said, that it was so. They then said many things, which would be too long to write down. And since the twelfth hour was already approaching, the whole discussion was broken off. On the following day, which was the sixteenth of March, I was summoned by them at about the eighth hour and asked whether I believed in the sacrament of confirmation, which bishops are accustomed to administer to people of suitable age. I replied that my faith is not confirmed by such ceremonies, but only by that grace and power of the Spirit which either regenerates me in Baptism and makes me a new creature, or nourishes and strengthens me in faith in the Lord's Supper through communion with the body of Christ. Then they brought forward from the eighth chapter of Acts the example of the Apostles, who laid hands on baptized people. I said that I approved of what had been done by Peter and the Apostles, and that the Spirit had been the author and director of that laying on of hands; but that this ceremony had afterwards come to an end. They asked whether I believed in the sacrament of extreme unction. I replied that I believed the Word of God to be true, and that the holy oil which is to be applied to a man in dangerous sickness, and which can bring salvation to every believer, is real; but that the oil which they are accustomed to apply to sick people is clearly useless, being subject to corruption. Then they, in order to prove that anointing, put forward that well-worn passage from the epistle in which the blessed James wrote. To them I said, "You see, I think, what I hold and believe about this matter." Afterwards, when I was asked about feast days, I replied that the Lord commanded his people six days of labour, and instituted no day of the week, apart from the seventh, to be free and exempt from business. In the same way, when I was questioned about Lent and the four seasons of theirs and other inventions of men, I replied that those commandments of men, devised to burden the people, are nowhere found in Scripture; but that there is another method and discipline of mortifying our flesh, and that the whole course of a man's life should be a kind of perpetual fasting: not that we eat once a day, but that throughout our whole life we keep the highest sobriety without any intemperance. Likewise, when I was asked about abstaining from meat and eggs during that forty-day season, I said that since the Lord had brought us out of darkness into the true light and knowledge of the truth, he makes no distinction of days or seasons, and that without any scruple of conscience one may drink and eat whatever the Lord has created and bestowed for the necessary sustenance of man. Only faith should be present, so that we may purely and piously enjoy these benefits of God with all thanksgiving, as the Apostle directs in his first epistle to Timothy. Then they said, "So you would eat meat as easily on the great Friday that precedes Easter as on Easter Day itself?" I said, "Here indeed I make no distinction of days at all; and whether it were Lent or another time, I would reject nothing of what was set before me for food, but would eat it freely in faith and with thanksgiving, without any scruple of mind. But if some weak person, seeing me eat, were offended, then I would not wish to use my liberty, lest in this way I walk not so much for the building up as for the offence of my neighbour; for the kingdom of God does not consist in food, and I am neither better nor holier whether I eat or do not eat. Yet I piously embrace that greater liberty which is most graciously offered through the extreme unction ... through the Word of God, so that I may use all his benefits with thanksgiving.

units.la: Deinde quaesiuerunt, an preces ad virginem Mariam adhibendæ essent, vt ea pro nobis aduocata apud Filium intercederet. Ego autem id id respondi, me quidem credere eam apud Deum plenam gratiæ re[?]ertam fuisse, ac benedictam inter omnes mulieres: Dominumque ita humilitatem ancillæ suæ respexisse, vt Filius Altissimi saluator mundi in eius utero resideret, vt humanitatem nostram susciperet: quem postea sine vlla corruptione est enixa. Eandem etiam verbis Angeli à Deo missi fidem habuisse: & propterea beatam iudicatam fuisse. Verum vt honorem Filio Dei debitum in eam transferamus, absit à me, & ab iis omnibus qui Christi nomen verè profitentur. Nam ne ipsa quidem me docuit dare ei vllum titulum honoremque adorationis, aut inuocare & orare vt mihi apud Filium patrona sit & aduocata: sed potius me monuit loquens de Filio suo in nuptiis in Cana Galilææ, vt quæ ille præciperet ac iuberet facerem. Idem quoque quæsiuerunt de Sanctis, qui hac vita sunt defuncti, inuocandis & orandis, vt in curia cælesti suo nos patrocinio atque hoc aduocationis officio prosequantur. Respondi, me nullum alium aduocatum agnoscere aut habere, quàm Iesum Christum ipsum iustum, qui merito mortis suæ vt solus purus atque innocens, hoc officium honoremque adeptus est, in quo vno Pater sibi bene complacuit, in cuius ore nullus vnquam dolus est inuentus. Itaque me eum solum Mediatorem, Aduocatum, Intercessorémque agnoscere: quemadmodum I.Ioan.II.cap. scriptum est.
units.tr: Next they asked whether prayers should be addressed to the Virgin Mary, so that she might intercede for us with her Son as our advocate. I answered that I did believe she had been found full of grace before God and blessed among all women, and that the Lord had so regarded the humility of his handmaid that the Son of the Most High, the Saviour of the world, dwelt in her womb to take on our humanity, and that she afterwards bore him without any corruption. She likewise had faith in the words of the angel sent by God, and for that reason was judged blessed. But that we should transfer to her the honour owed to the Son of God, far be that from me and from all who truly profess the name of Christ. For she herself has never taught me to give her any title or the honour of adoration, or to invoke her and pray that she be my patron and advocate with her Son. Rather, when she spoke of her Son at the wedding in Cana of Galilee, she advised me to do whatever he should command and order. They also asked whether the saints who have died in this life should be invoked and prayed to, that from the heavenly court they might support us with this office of advocacy. I answered that I acknowledge and have no other advocate than Jesus Christ the righteous himself, who, by the merit of his death, as the only pure and innocent one, obtained this office and honour, and in whom alone the Father was well pleased, and in whose mouth no deceit was ever found. Therefore I acknowledge him alone as Mediator, Advocate and Intercessor, as it is written in 1 John 2.

units.la: Quæsitû etiam est de imaginibus, num liceret effigiê habere crucifixum repræsentantem. Respondi, quomodo id ex me quærerent, cum legerent Scripturam tum veteris tum noui Testamenti, in qua huiusmodi simulacra tam disertis verbis prohiberentur. Tu igitur, inquiunt, nullas vis imagines? Non, inquam: nam ex eius verbo didici cum in spiritu ac veritate adorare: & qui volunt à Deo exaudiri, oportet eos oculis fidei Patrem cælestem in cælo quærere.
units.tr: They also asked about images, whether it was lawful to have an effigy representing the crucified Christ. I answered that they should not ask me this, since they read the Scripture of both the Old and the New Testament, in which such likenesses are forbidden in such plain words. "So you want no images at all?" they said. "No," I said, "for I have learned from his word to worship in spirit and truth, and those who wish to be heard by God must seek the heavenly Father in heaven with the eyes of faith."

units.la: Postremò interrogatus ab iis, num crederem certum esse locum, in quem animæ ex hac vita decedentes concederent, vt ibi purgarentur: respondi tato animi studio ac gaudio, quanto esuriens cibum vnquam [?]umpsi, ita ut interiora viscera mea quadam voluptate perfundi viderentur, cum ita commode de honore, gratia & salute Domini mei Iesu Christi loquerer: respondi igitur me nullum aliud purgatorium agnoscere, quam sanguinem Iesu Christi salvatoris mei, a quo credebam aeternum sacrificium factum esse, facta omnium meorum peccatorum purgatione, cum praesertim eo perfuncto sacrificio, nunc ad dexteram Dei Patris vivat in perpetuum, atque pro nobis intercedat. Neque vero dubito quin Deus pro-sua misericordia homini peccatori plane ignoscat, tum cum ille relicta pristinae vitae ratione ad eius gratiam ita confugit, ut cum poenitentia melioris vitae propositu suscipiat. Neque enim Dominus aliqua ex parte peccata ignoscit: sed omnia plene perfecteque remittit. Atque haec quidem sunt, quae in hac postrema interrogatione ex me quaesiverunt: aliane praeterea sint quaesituri, plane ignoro. Unum pene oblitus sum, quod ut me fraudulenter circumvenirent, Purgatorium suum approbarent, ex me scire voluerunt quosnam libros sacrae Scripturae ego reciperem atque approbarem, quibus ego respondi, vetus ac novum Testamentum. Tum illi, Omniane, inquiunt, credis esse bona sanctaque? Maxime, inquam, exceptis iis libris, qui Apocryphi appellantur, quibus fundamentum fidei meae niti nolem, neque eorum authoritatem pro capitibus fidei aut firmamentis allegare: cum caeteros, qui fidei meae satisfaciunt, approbem. Cur, inquiunt, hos potius quam alios hoc iudicio fidei amplecteris? Quoniam, inquam, hi habent tam insignem authoritatis notam, ut Spiritum eorum authorem esse dubitare nullo modo possim: de caeteris vero, quorum certus non est author, idem affirmare non possum. Quamquam illos quidem propter multa bona exempla & praecepta quae in iis continentur, non omnino reiicerem, sed meam in iis fidem fundare nollem. Itaque hac mea responsione impediti, Purgatorium suum comprobare non poterant. Interea ipsi inter se Latine loquebantur, in quo quidem ut nihil a me metuerent, ex me quaesiverunt, an ego Latine scirem, id cum negassem, iusserunt a notario scribi. Haec, soror charissima, sunt & ab illis interrogata & responsa a me. Ex eo tempore ne-minem eorum vidi, nisi canonicum quendam, Quintinum Charlardum nominatum: quem ad me iam aliquoties miserunt, ut me in ipsorum fi-dem dē inducēret. Maxima fuit mihi cum eo disputatio quatuor horas habita.Itaq; maximopere doleo in eo genere vitæ atque errore eū adhuc versari, neque deduci ad hanc lucem admirabilem, quam aliquo modo aspicit. Studium enim quoddā Dei habet, sed non secundum scientiam: cùm illorum causam tueatur, nihil magis cupiens, quàm ut ego cum ipso consentiam, imprimisque in ea doctrina, qua ille in Sacramento corpus Christi in pane inclusum esse statuit. Affert ille quidē nescio quas rationes de descensu Domini ad nos: quas ego nullo modo approbare possum, propterea quòd & à natura veri corporis, quod Christus in cælū extulit, & à veritate verbi & fidei ratione cōfessioneque abhorrent. Itaque ei vsque ad hunc diē acerrimè restiti, speróque Dei gratia me restituturum adiuuantibus vestris precibus. Te autē, charissima soror, rogo, & eos omnes qui summo studio verbum Dei amplectuntur, ut simul pro me Dominū oretis, ut ipse me purū atque integrum in fide Filij sui conseruet, atque in ea constantia & perseuerantia confessionis quā ego hactenus edidi, mihi impertiens eam victoriam, quā aduersus omnes inimicos tum carnis tum verbi sui promisit. Quòd si hoc corpusculo vult uti, ut ad obsignandam Euangelij veritatem sanguis meus effundatur, atque in cinerem ossa mea redigantur: is me confirmet virtute Spiritus sui usq; in finem, ut fidei meæ testimonium sine vllo pudore, fidele illustréque ad ipsius gloriam atque electorum salutem extare possit. Si verò vult me adhuc retinere in ista vita, & ad gloriam suam, atque Ecclesiæ utilitatem reseruare, ipse furorem tyrannorū mitiget, ac me ex ore leonum eripiat. Equidem ad utrunque sum paratus, ut me in sacrificium Domino in omnibus offeram. Mea soror ac cæteri Euangelii amatores, gaudete mecum. nemo verò offendatur & perturbetur iis persecutionibus, quæ hisce diebus acciderunt: quemadmodum illi qui semen missum inter saxa receperunt. sed potiùs huiusmodi persecutiones ad confirmandam fidem vestram cum summa animi æquitate à vobis suscipiantur, & cum patientia perferantur, cùm in hoc quidem ad imaginem eius conformentur, qui dixit, Si me persecuti sunt, vos quoq; persequentur. Hæc enim est conditio propositá ijs omnibus, qui Christum verè profiteri volunt, in eóque piè viuere. Neque verò hoc donum Dei est vulgare cum multisque commune: sed iis tantum tributum ac datum, quos Deus vocavit non solum ut in Christum credant, sed etiam ut pro eius nomine patiantur & moriantur. Orate pro me, nec pro me solum, sed etiam pro iis qui vos persequuntur: ut si errore atque ignorantia eo sunt delapsi, misericordiam Dei consequantur, atque ad hanc viam salutis adducantur. Itaque benedicamus eis, & non maledicamus. Salutate eos qui me amat. Gratia Domini nostri vobis adsit. Frater vester Godef.
units.tr: Finally they asked me whether I believed there was a certain place into which souls departing from this life go to be purged. I answered with as much eagerness and joy of mind as a hungry man ever took food, so that my inward bowels seemed to be filled with a certain delight, since I was speaking so fittingly of the honour, grace and salvation of my Lord Jesus Christ. I answered, therefore, that I acknowledge no other purgatory than the blood of Jesus Christ my Saviour, by which I believed an eternal sacrifice had been made, and by which all my sins were purged; especially since, having completed that sacrifice, he now lives for ever at the right hand of God the Father and intercedes for us. Nor do I doubt that God, out of his mercy, fully pardons a sinful man when, having abandoned his former manner of life, he flees to his grace in such a way that he embraces it with repentance and a purpose of a better life. For the Lord does not forgive sins in part, but remits them all fully and completely. These, indeed, were the things they asked me in this last question; whether they will ask anything further, I altogether do not know. I had almost forgotten one thing: in order to trap me by deceit and to approve their purgatory, they wished to know from me which books of Holy Scripture I accepted and approved. I answered: the Old and New Testament. Then they said, "Do you believe all of them to be good and holy?" "Most certainly," I said, "except those books which are called Apocrypha, on which I would not wish the foundation of my faith to rest, nor cite their authority as articles of faith or as proofs; though I approve the rest, which satisfy my faith." "Why," they said, "do you embrace these rather than others with this judgement of faith?" "Because," I said, "these bear so remarkable a mark of authority that I can in no way doubt that the Spirit is their author; but of the others, whose author is not certain, I cannot affirm the same. Yet I would not altogether reject those apocryphal books on account of the many good examples and precepts contained in them, but I would not wish to found my faith on them." Thus hindered by this answer, they could not approve their purgatory. Meanwhile they spoke Latin among themselves, and, so that they would have nothing to fear from me, they asked me whether I knew Latin; when I denied it, they ordered a notary to write it down. These things, most dear sister, were both asked of me by them and answered by me. Since that time I have seen none of them except a certain canon named Quintinus Charlardus, whom they have sent to me several times already to bring me over to their faith. My disputation with him was very great, lasting four hours. And so I greatly grieve that he still lives in that kind of life and error, and is not led out into this wonderful light, which he somehow sees. For he has a certain zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; since he defends their cause, wanting nothing more than for me to agree with him, and especially in that doctrine by which he holds that the body of Christ is enclosed in the bread in the Sacrament. He indeed brings forward I know not what arguments about the descent of the Lord to us, which I can in no way approve, because they are at odds both with the nature of the true body which Christ carried up into heaven, and with the truth of the Word and the reasoning and confession of faith. Therefore I have most strongly resisted him up to this day, and I hope, by the grace of God and with the help of your prayers, to bring him back. As for you, most dear sister, I ask you, and all who embrace the Word of God with the greatest zeal, to pray to the Lord for me as well, that he himself may keep me pure and whole in the faith of his Son, and grant me, in that constancy and perseverance of confession which I have so far made, that victory which he has promised against all enemies, both of the flesh and of his Word. But if he wishes to use this little body so that my blood is poured out to seal the truth of the Gospel, and my bones are reduced to ash, may he strengthen me by the power of his Spirit to the end, so that the testimony of my faith may stand, without any shame, faithful and illustrious, to his glory and the salvation of the elect. If, however, he wishes me still to remain in this life, and to keep me for his glory and the profit of the Church, may he himself restrain the fury of tyrants and snatch me from the mouth of lions. Indeed I am prepared for either, so that I may offer myself to the Lord as a sacrifice in all things. My sister and the other lovers of the Gospel, rejoice with me. Let no one be offended or disturbed by those persecutions which have befallen in these days, like those who received the seed sown among the rocks. But rather let such persecutions be received by you for the strengthening of your faith with the greatest calm of mind, and let them be borne with patience, since in this you are being conformed to the image of him who said, "If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you." For this is the condition set before all those who wish to profess Christ truly and to live godly in him. Nor is this gift of God common and shared with many; it is given and bestowed only on those whom God has called, not only to believe in Christ, but also to suffer and die for his name. Pray for me, and not for me only, but also for those who persecute you, that if they have fallen into this by error and ignorance, they may obtain the mercy of God and be brought to this way of salvation. Therefore let us bless them, and not curse them. Greet those who love me. The grace of our Lord be with you. Your brother, Godef.

units.la: Idem Godefridus cum adhuc in carcere esset, alias epistolas scripsit, inter eas unam, quam misit ad eos qui eo tempore Tornaci iudicia exercebant. In qua quidem accuratissime se purgavit atque defendit adversus illud crimen, quo ab inquisitoribus fidei iniquissime gravatus fuit, & ut haereticus declaratus, in potestatem iudicum traditus. Itaque integritatem fidei suae eo modo atque ordine declaravit, quo tota fidei Christianae ratio in symbolo Apostolorum est comprehensa, atque a piis doctoribus explicata. Ea autem in confessione omnibus etiam iniquis alienisque hominibus satis ostendit se in religione talem non esse, qualem adversarii arguerent atq; damnarent: sed ea pietate atque fide, ad quam declarandam & testificandam non modo nullam interrogationem, sed nec tormentorum perpessionem defugeret.
units.tr: The same Godefridus, while still in prison, wrote other letters. Among them was one which he sent to those who at that time were administering justice at Tournai. In it he most carefully cleared and defended himself against the charge by which the inquisitors of the faith had most unjustly burdened him, and by which he had been declared a heretic and handed over to the power of the judges. He therefore set forth the soundness of his faith in the manner and order in which the whole account of the Christian faith is comprehended in the Apostles' Creed and explained by pious teachers. In that confession he showed sufficiently, even to unjust and foreign men, that he was not in religion the sort of man his adversaries charged and condemned him as being. Rather, he possessed such piety and faith that, in declaring and testifying to it, he shrank from no questioning and not even from the endurance of torments.

units.la: Sunt praeterea aliae eiusdem epistolae ad pios homines missae, summae consolationis plenissimae, quas ut prolixitate euitaremus, huic libro minime opportunam, omisimus. Reliquum est, ut felicissimum eius exitum ac genus mortis, testimoniis hominum certissimorum approbatum, demonstremus. Die igitur Sabbathi, qui dies fuit xxiii. Iulij, anni M.D.LII. sententia capitis pronuntiata, in qua ipse Godefridus haereticus est declaratus, his verbis tantum exclamasse dicitur, Heu, non haereticus, sed seruus Dei inutilis. Deinde positis in terram genibus, Dominum testem causae suae ac vindicem magna voce ita appellasse, Domine Deus, tu solus causam nostri, propter quam ego sum condemnatus. Cum autem venisset ad locum, in quo supplicium passurus erat, satis diu locutus est, populumque adhortatus ut in Christum Iesum crederet, totamque fiduciam salutis in eo uno poneret, cuius morte ac passione remissionem peccatorum per solam fidem in eius nomine consequuturus esset. Loquebatur autem ea constantia, ut omnes eius oratio grauissimè afficeret ac permoueret: adeò ut vulgus diceret se ignorare cur hominem huiusmodi morte multarent, qui de Christo Domino eum in modum loqueretur. Iam quum esset in theatro, se in genua abiecit, & capita fidei Apostolicæ in modum confessionis pronuntiauit, in qua cùm illud caput pronuntiaret: Credo Ecclesiam sanctam, catholicam: & supra dictus canonicus ciuitatis Tornacensis Charlardus eum monuisset ut ecclesiam Romanam diceret. Minimè vero, inquit Godefridus: sed ecclesiam credo solùm catholicam. Tu propius accessit ad patibulum, in quo erat alligandus: ac dum carnifex eū ad supplicium accingeret, catenisque ligaret, dixit, Pater cœlestis, exaudi gemitū serui tui. Et cùm Charlardus dixisset ei, ut se Virgini commendaret. Solus, inquit Godefridus, aduocatus meus apud Patrem pro me intercedens est Christus Jesus, cui me vni commendo. Hæc autem cùm dixisset, carnifex humanitate quadam adductus volens eum subleuare, cruciatúmque ignis minuere, se comparabat ut eum strangularet. Sed Godefridus hoc eius officium aspernatus, Sine, inquit, sine amice, ego sententiam, vt est pronuntiata, sequi ac perpeti volo. Deinde maxima voce exclamauit, Pater æterne, in manus tuas spiritum meum hodie suscipe. Igne verò accenso, cùm angorem mortis iam sentiret, iterum ad Deum clamauit, Pater cœlestis, recipe me in regnum tuum. Tum visus est obdormiscere medio in igne, non minus placidè quàm si quis somno naturali quiesceret: atque ita faciem habens in cœlum erectam expirauit.
units.tr: There are also other letters of the same man, sent to godly people, very full of the highest consolation. We have left them out, so as to avoid excessive length, since they are hardly suited to this book. It remains for us to show his most happy end and manner of death, as attested by the most trustworthy witnesses. On Saturday, which was the 23rd of July in the year 1552, the sentence of death was pronounced, in which Godefridus himself was declared a heretic. He is said to have cried out only these words: "Alas, not a heretic, but an unprofitable servant of God." Then, kneeling on the ground, he called upon the Lord, the witness and avenger of his cause, with a loud voice: "Lord God, you alone are the cause of us, on account of which I have been condemned." When he came to the place where he was to suffer punishment, he spoke at considerable length and exhorted the people to believe in Christ Jesus and to place all their hope of salvation in him alone, through whose death and passion he would obtain the forgiveness of sins through faith alone, in his name. He spoke with such constancy that his whole speech deeply moved and stirred all who heard it, so much so that the common people said they did not know why men were put to death in such a manner for speaking of Christ the Lord in such a way. When he was on the scaffold, he knelt down and recited the articles of the Apostolic faith in the form of a confession. When he came to the article "I believe the holy, catholic Church," the canon of the city of Tournai, Charlardus, who was mentioned above, admonished him to say "the Roman Church." "By no means," said Godefridus, "but I believe only the catholic Church." Then he drew nearer to the post to which he was to be bound. While the executioner was preparing him for punishment and fastening the chains, he said: "Heavenly Father, hear the groaning of your servant." When Charlardus told him to commend himself to the Virgin, Godefridus replied: "Christ Jesus is my only advocate, interceding for me with the Father, and to him alone I commend myself." When he had said this, the executioner, moved by a kind of humanity and wishing to relieve him and lessen the torment of the fire, prepared to strangle him. But Godefridus rejected this kindness, saying: "Let be, let be, friend. I wish to follow and undergo the sentence as it has been pronounced." Then he cried out with a very loud voice: "Eternal Father, receive my spirit into your hands today." When the fire was lit and he already felt the anguish of death, he again called upon God: "Heavenly Father, receive me into your kingdom." Then he seemed to fall asleep in the midst of the fire, no less peacefully than if he were resting in natural sleep, and so, with his face turned up toward heaven, he breathed his last.

units.la: GULIELMUS GARDINERUS Anglus,
units.tr: GULIELMUS GARDINERUS, Englishman,

units.la: Ulyssiponæ primaria Portugaliæ urbe, ob Euangelium immani supplicio affectus. Cuius constantissimi martyrii adeo apud Lusitanos recens etiamnum viget recordatio ut in hodiernum diem viua illius memoria tanquam fœlix semen fructum vberem ferat.
units.tr: Put to a monstrous death at Lisbon, the chief city of Portugal, on account of the Gospel. The memory of his most steadfast martyrdom still flourishes so freshly among the Portuguese that, to this very day, his living remembrance bears abundant fruit like a happy seed.

units.la: Apud Lusitanos rarum & memorabile martyrij hisce temporibus exemplum dedit Gulielmus Gardinerus ab extremis Angliæ finibus Bristoliæ urbe apud Anglos maritima & emporiali natus: juvenis, natura ad grauitatem compositus, statu corporis mediocri & æquabili, vultu aspectabilis elegánsque: sed nusquam elegantior, quàm interni animi decoris, & moribus quos semper ille à puero sine omni reprehensionis nævo inculpatos retinuerat. Augebat porrò hæc ornamenta doctrinæ ac literarum mediocris accessio. Adolescente iam ætate, qua solent iuvenes ad aliquod vitæ institutum animos appellere: evenit ut is mercaturæ operam exercendæ daret, sub auspicijs & ductu cuiusdam quem Bristoliensis Mag. Pagetum cognometo appellabant, professione mercatorem. A quo demum Guilielmus hic XXVI. ætatis suæ anno, aut non multo secus, in Hispaniam est missus. Quo tum Lisbonam primum, forte ut fit, appulsa navi, quæ urbs est Portugaliæ primaria: ea in urbe mercaturæ rei causa est commoratus, ubi demum percepta facile illorum lingua, moribusque consuefactus, utilem tum sibi, tum hero, aliisque operam navavit in negotijs ac mercimonijs, quæ ad eius artis disciplinam spectare videbantur. Quibus il-le rebus ita incumbebat, in exterorum commercijs frequens, ut nihilominus religionem patriam, qua esset in Anglia imbutus ab eorum superstitione semper integram illibatamque retineret. Nec desuerunt alij item Angli in ea urbe viri boni: codices non defuerunt sacri, ac utiles honestorum hominum congressus, apud quos crebro imbecillitatem suam est deplorare solitus: quippe qui nec peccatorum suorum odio, nec pietatis amore flagraret satis. Interea dum illic ageret, solennes intercedunt nuptiæ inter principes nescio quos, in ea urbe, ingenti cum apparatu cal. Sept. cocelebrandæ. Itaque adventante iam nuptiarum die, frequens fit ordinum, ac nobilitatis omnisque generis concursus. Nec desunt episcopi mitrati, quin nec Cardinales galerati aliquot sua præsentia regales nuptias honestaturi. Quid multis? magna cum pompa, maiori multitudine, maximaque omnium expectatione ad nuptias proceditur. Ingens per totam urbem celebritas, apparatus (ut in re tanta confucuit[?]) maximus, publica & festiva lætitia perstrepunt omnia. In hac igitur longe omnium maxima totius regni panegyri adest inter cæteros Guilielmus hic Gardinerus, qui licet spectacula huiusmodi non magni faceret, fama tamen & conspectu tatæ[?] celebritatis attractus, abesse unus inter omnes noluit. Venit ergo summo mane, quo locus esset spectandi, & facultas in templo commodior. venit hora. In templum solenni pompa ascenditur. Rex primum, reliqui deinde sequuntur ordines. Quo maior erat personarum dignitas, hoc minus decerat cæremonijs. Post hæc, ordinatus rite rebus, ad Missæ liturgiam pergitur(quoniam hæc vna omnibus seruit rebus) quæ plurima symphonia, voce, cantu, organis, adnuistrante[?] Cardinale peragitur. Stat multo silentio & religione venerabundus populus orans, spectas, adgeniculans, tundens, & oculis & animis totus hærens ac suspensus, vt mos est in extremo sacramento. Dici non potest, ea res quam miserè altéque pio iuueni perculsit animum, partim rerum miserandam absurditatem, partim vulgi ineptiam contemplanti: nec vulgi solum, sed quum ipsum maximè Regè, tum tot sapientissimorum hominum senatum, communi pariter idololatria cum plebe seduci cerneret. Parumque abfuit quin hoc ipso die insigne aliquid in conspectu Regis totiùsque theatri designasset, ni conferta multitudo, qua vndiq; claudebatur obstitisset quo minus ad aram penetrare potuisset. Quid hîc verbis explicem, quod vix quisquam æstimando consequi poterit? interim dum hæc contemplatur, quas intus in animo curas versat? quos ignes? quos aculeos sentit mens consilij inops? Quid enim faceret? abiret è templo? præ turba non licuit: ministrum prohiberet? multò minus potuit, & pudor & loci reuerentia vetabant. quid ergo, voce abominationem detestaretur? è vestigio gladius mūdi huius cervici imminebat. Taceret? at hic gladium metuebat Dei. Quid multis? finitis orgijs, redit domum mœsto animo prorsusque perturbato, vsque adeò vt commilitones suos in magnam sui admirationem omnes raperet. qui licet & ipsi nonnullam tristitiæ huius causam coniecturis concipiebant, attamen quàm pe-nitus pio animo hæc insideret perturbatio, non intelligebant: nec is cuiquam consilia communicabat. sed secessum captans & solitudinem coram Deo prostratus, multis lachrymis deplorata prætermisi officij negligentia, deliberat de populo Christiano ab ea impietate & superstitione reuocando: id quod & fecit. In ea igitur deliberatione mēs penitus obfirmata, nec diutius rem producendam putans, mundo se prorsus abdicat, rationes omnes, quid sibi, quid alijs deberetur, ad calculū subducit tam acuratè, vt nemo haberet quod de teruntio quiritari posset. Qua confecta re, totos deinde dies noctesque in assiduis precibus, invocando Dei præsidio, aciugi[?] meditatione cōsumit, vix semel interdiu cibi paululum, somni etiam minus noctu capiens, cui una, ad summū duæ noctis horæ quieti dabantur. cuius rei testis etiamnum vivit Pedigratius, lesti[?] eiusdem simul & hospitij socius.Redit dies iterum Dominicus, vel pari, aut non multo inferiori pompa celebrandus. Adest & Guilielmus summo mane, quam cultissime vestitus de industria, nimirum quo facilior sibi locus iuxta altarium sine repulsa permittteretur.Nec multo post Rex cum satrapali comitatu in templum ingreditur.ibi tum Gardinerus altari se adiungit quam proxime, in manibus ferens Euangelium Iesu Christi, in eius incumbens lectionem, precibusque ardentissime insistens quoad instaret tempus quo negotium aggredi constituisset.Fit igitur Missa, incipit sacerdos (qui tum & ipse quoque Cardinalis erat) sedet adhuc quietus noster.Procedit porro Missagogus, sacrificat, consecrat, sublime procul sublatis brachijs quantum potest tollit ac ostentat populo. denique ex sacramento idolum facit. ingens in plebe veneratio. Atque ne adhuc quidem mouet ille. Ventū est tandem ad cum Missæ locum, ubi sacrificus ceremoniosam hostiam altera manu acceptam, circa patera in circulos quosdam ac semicirculos crebro iactatu circumuersat[?]. Hic Guilielmus non ferens amplius, impigre ad Cardinale accurrit.Incredibile dictu: præsente ac spectâte Rege, in tot nobilium ac ciuium oculis, altera manu libum adoreum sacerdoti eripit, ac proterit pedibus: altera patera cucurtit[?]. Habuit primum ea res omnes attonitos: mox ingenti orto tumultu, exclamare populus: Cardinalis tantum non insanire, nobiles cū plebeiis concurrere, e quibus vnus educto pugione scapulam ei alteram ingenti perfodit vulnere, rursusque repetito ictu certam illi caedem parabat, & perfecisset, nisi Regis audita vox bis iussisset seruari hominem. sicq; à caede temperatum est.Sedata tandem rabie, Guilielmus ad Regem perducitur. à quo interrogatus de patria, quaque audacia maiestatem ipsius, ac sacramenta ecclesiae sacra afficere ea esset ausus contumelia? Illustriss. (inquit) Rex, patriae meae nihil pudet, qui & natione & religione Anglus sum, unde huc mercaturae faciendae causa aduceni[?]. quum autem tantam vidi in tam celebri concentu idololatriam fieri: pati non potuit nec debuit conscientia, quin hoc facerem quod maiestas tua hodie a me factu videt. Quum autem audissent Anglum esse, meminissent quae restaurata per Edouardum religionis facilem inde arripiebat suspicionem quasi nobilis isthic fuisset quispiā, atque per Anglos subornatus atus ad ludibrium suæ religionis, eò magis scire ab eo contendebant, uo tandem authore induceretur. quibus respondit ille, ac orat, Se nullius impulsu huc adactum esse, præterquam suæ duntaxat ipsius conscientiæ: alioqui nullum esse sub cælo mortalium, cuius gratia in tantum sese tamque manifestum discrimen conijceret. Verum Deo primum, tum saluti ipsorum hoc ipse obsequium debuisse. qua in re, si quid esset quod ipsis displiceret, nulli id magis imputandum quàm sibi ipsis qui sacratissima Christi cœna tam intemperanter ad tantam idololatriam abuterentur: idque non sine magna tum ecclesiæ ignominia, tum sacramentorum violatione, tum etiam saluti ipsorum ac animarum periculo, nisi resipiscat.
units.tr: Among the Portuguese, William Gardiner gave a rare and memorable example of martyrdom in these times. He was a native of Bristol, a maritime and trading town at the far end of England. As a young man he was naturally serious, of medium and even height, with a pleasant and elegant appearance. Yet he was never more elegant than in the beauty of his inner character and in his conduct, which from boyhood he had kept free of any blemish of reproach. These ornaments were enhanced by a modest measure of learning and letters. When he reached the age at which young men usually turn their minds to some course of life, he took up commerce and trained as a merchant under the direction of a certain Master Paget of Bristol. In the year 26 of his age, or not much otherwise, Paget sent him to Spain. He first landed at Lisbon, the chief city of Portugal, when his ship happened, as it does, to put in there. He stayed in that city for the sake of trade. Once he had quickly learned their language and adapted himself to their customs, he was useful to his master and to others in business and dealings that belonged to his trade. He applied himself to these affairs so diligently, and was so often among foreign merchants, that he nonetheless kept the religion of his homeland, in which he had been brought up in England, always whole and unstained by their superstition. Nor were there lacking other good Englishmen in that city. There were sacred books, and useful gatherings of honest men, where he often lamented his own weakness, since he did not burn enough with hatred of his sins or with love of godliness. Meanwhile, while he was there, a solemn wedding was arranged between certain princes, to be celebrated with great pomp in that city on the first of September. So when the day of the wedding drew near, a crowd of all ranks and all kinds of nobility gathered. Mitred bishops were present, and several cardinals in their galero came to honour the royal wedding with their presence. In short, with great pomp, a larger crowd, and the greatest expectation of all, they proceeded to the wedding. There was a huge gathering throughout the whole city, and the display was (as is customary on such an occasion) very great; everything resounded with public and festive joy. Among the others at this, by far the greatest public festival of the whole kingdom, was this William Gardiner. Although he did not think much of such spectacles, he was drawn by the reputation and the sight of so great a celebration, and he did not want to be the only one absent. So he came very early in the morning, so that he would have a place to see and a more convenient opportunity in the church. The hour came. They ascended into the church with solemn pomp. The king went first, and the other orders followed. The higher the dignity of the persons, the less the ceremonies were lacking. After this, with things duly arranged, they proceeded to the liturgy of the Mass (since this one thing serves all purposes), which was carried out with much symphony, voice, singing and organs, the cardinal officiating. The people stood in great silence and reverence, praying, watching, kneeling, beating their breasts, their eyes and minds wholly fixed and held in suspense, as is the custom at the most solemn sacrament. It cannot be told how grievously and deeply this sight struck the pious young man's mind: partly at the wretched absurdity of the affair, partly at the foolishness of the common people. He saw that they were led astray not only the common people, but also the king himself and so many senators of the wisest men, all alike in the same idolatry with the crowd. He came very close, on that very day, to doing something notable in the sight of the king and of that whole theatre, had not the dense crowd which enclosed him on every side prevented him from getting through to the altar.
