What can I explain in words here, which hardly anyone could grasp by guessing? Meanwhile, while he was contemplating these things, what cares did he turn over inwardly? What fires, what stings did his mind, without counsel, feel? What was he to do? Should he leave the church? The crowd did not allow it. Should he stop the minister? He could do that even less, since both shame and reverence for the place forbade it. What then, should he denounce the abomination with his voice? At once the sword of this world hung over his neck. Should he keep silent? But he feared the sword of God. In short, when the rites were finished, he went home with a sorrowful and thoroughly disturbed mind, so much so that he astonished all his fellow soldiers. Although they themselves guessed at some cause of his sadness, they did not understand how deeply this disturbance sat in his pious heart, and he did not share his plans with anyone. Instead, seeking seclusion and solitude, prostrate before God, he lamented with many tears his neglect of the duty he had let slip, and he deliberated about calling the Christian people back from that impiety and superstition. And this he did. In that deliberation his mind was wholly fixed, and thinking the matter should not be put off any longer, he renounced the world completely. He reckoned up all accounts, what was owed to himself and what to others, so exactly that no one could complain about a penny. When this was done, he spent whole days and nights in constant prayer, calling on God's protection and in anxious meditation, taking food only once a day, a little, and taking little sleep at night, only one or at most two hours being given to rest. Pedigrat, his fellow lodger and companion of the same lodging, is still alive as a witness to this. The Lord's day came round again, to be celebrated with equal or not much less pomp. William was present very early in the morning, dressed with the greatest care on purpose, so that a place near the altar might be granted to him without rebuff. Not long after, the king entered the church with his royal retinue. Then Gardiner joined himself as closely as he could to the altar, holding the Gospel of Jesus Christ in his hands, leaning over its reading and devoting himself most ardently to prayer until the time came when he had resolved to undertake the deed. So the Mass began. The priest (who was himself also a cardinal) began, and our man still sat quietly. The celebrant went on, sacrificed, consecrated, and raised up the host on high, with his arms stretched out as far as he could, and displayed it to the people. Finally he made an idol out of the sacrament, and there was great veneration among the people. And even then that man did not move. At last they came to that point in the Mass where the priest, taking the ceremonial host in one hand, turned it around the paten in certain circles and semicircles with repeated motions. Here William, no longer able to bear it, ran quickly up to the cardinal. It is incredible to say: in the presence and sight of the king, in the eyes of so many nobles and citizens, he snatched the wheaten cake from the priest with one hand and trampled it underfoot, and with the other hand he overturned the paten. At first this action stunned everyone. Then, a great tumult arising, the people cried out that the cardinal was almost mad, and nobles ran together with commoners. One of them drew a dagger and stabbed him deeply in the other shoulder with a great wound, and, repeating the blow, was preparing certain death for him. He would have finished it, had not the king's voice, heard twice, ordered the man to be spared. So the killing was held back. When at last the rage had subsided, William was brought before the king. Questioned by him about his country, and about what boldness had led him to dare to insult the majesty of the king and the sacred sacraments of the Church, he said: "Most illustrious King, I am not ashamed of my country: I am an Englishman both by nation and by religion, and I came here to trade. But when I saw such idolatry carried on in so famous an assembly, my conscience could not and ought not to endure it, so that I should not do what Your Majesty today sees me do." When they heard that he was English, they remembered that the religion restored under Edward had given an easy ground for suspicion, as if some nobleman there had been persuaded by the English to mock their religion. So they pressed him all the more to say who had finally led him into it. To this he answered, and pleaded, that he had been driven here by no one's urging except his own conscience. Otherwise, there was no mortal under heaven for whose sake he would expose himself to such a manifest danger. He had owed this service first to God, and then to their salvation. If anything in this displeased them, it should be imputed to no one more than to themselves, who so intemperately abused the most sacred supper of Christ for such great idolatry: and that not without great dishonour to the Church, without violation of the sacraments, and even without danger to their own salvation and souls, unless they repented.

units.la: Dum in hanc sententiam multa prose[?] & graviter & magno spiritu diceret, defluente ubertim è vulnere recenti sanguine, corpori penè iam deficienti adhibetur chirurgorum manus: quo nimirum curato(si fieri posset) vulnere, ad prolixiorem disquisitionem, graviorésque cruciatus servaretur. prorsus enim eis inhærebat persuasio, factu hoc suis æquaquam ducibus & impulsoribus caruisse. quæ causa fuit, cur & ceteri omnes eadem in urbe Angli in nonnullam eiusdem periculi partem levenirent, atque custodiæ mandaretur.
units.tr: While he was speaking at length, weightily and with great spirit on this point, the blood flowed copiously from the fresh wound and his body was almost failing. Surgeons' hands were applied to it, no doubt so that the wound might be healed, if that were possible, and he be kept for a longer examination and more severe torments. For they were firmly convinced that the deed had lacked any leaders or instigators. This is why all the others in that same English city were also subjected to some measure of the same danger and handed over to custody.

units.la: Inter quos erat Pendigratius, qui quòd lecti effet illi socius, in gravissimas quæstiones & tormenta vocatus est: qui vix demum post biennale custodiam domum inde redijt. reliqui Ducis cuiusdam intercessione, multò sunt prius soluti.
units.tr: Among them was Pendigratius, who, because he had been a bedfellow of the wounded man, was called to the most serious questioning and torments. He was hardly released from custody and returned home after two years. The rest, through the intercession of a certain Duke, were freed much earlier.

units.la: Quin nec iis hactenus cōtenta pertinax suspicio, venit porrò in cubiculum, si quid forte literarum reperiri posset exploratura, unde conjectare aliquid de incepti huius authore potuisset. quum neque hic quicquam inveniri quitu[?] est, ad sauciū iterū cum tormentis redeunt, primum ut de impulsore, si quē haberet, cognosceret: tū ut gravissimæ eum hæreseos reum faceret, quorū ille utrumq; quàpotuit dexteritate removebat.
units.tr: Their stubborn suspicion was not satisfied with these things. It went further, entering the bedchamber to search for any letters that might reveal something about the author of this undertaking. When nothing could be found there either, they returned to the wounded man with the torments: first, so that he would name the instigator, if he had one; then, so that they could make him guilty of the gravest heresy. He avoided both as skilfully as he could.

units.la: Nā licet satis dextrè Hispanicam teneret linguā, tamē certius & exactius sermone est Latino usus.
units.tr: For although he spoke Spanish quite well, he nevertheless used Latin, which is more precise and exact.

units.la: Verum quū verbis illi nō haberet fidē, ad tormenta demū itum est. quibus etiā ipsis fidem adhibuissent Portugaleses, etsi satis quidē acerbos, minus tamē crudeles se iudices declarassent.
units.tr: But since they put no faith in his words, they at last resorted to torture. Even the Portuguese judges would have trusted such methods, and though they would have shown themselves rather harsh, they would have appeared less cruel.

units.la: Quāquā nō erat res tā ambiguæ cōiectūræ, quin ratio ipsa & communis sensus facilè vel absque tormentis, verum videre potuisset.
units.tr: Yet the matter was not so ambiguous a conjecture that reason itself and common sense could not easily have seen the truth, even without torments.

units.la: Nam an quisquam tam demens est mortalium, qui alieno persuasu ac ductu, in re tanta caput atque fortunas tam certis periculis
units.tr: For is there any mortal so mad as to expose his head and fortunes to such certain dangers, at another's persuasion and urging, in a matter of such magnitude,

units.la: obijceret,idque in tali loco,vbi nulla elabendi non modò copia,sed ne minima etiam spes poterat superesse,ni res ipsa,ni religio ac conscientia hominem huc solicitasset? Nunc neque verbis ipsius, nec literarum indicio, nec sociorum testimonijs, nec ipsis denique tormentis contenti, aliud superaddunt cruciamenti genus inauditum, quoddque superat opinor Phalaridis tauros,ne quid iam restet amplius quo humana crudelitas altius possit ascendere. Curant consui linteum,fere in modum pilae orbicularem,illud per gulam vi traijciunt in imum stomachum,tenui alligatum chordulae quam ipsi manu tenent:traiectum rursus ad se trahunt,retrahuntque per occultas ciborum fistulas,sic natura excarnificantes,vt minori cruciatu rumpi ipsa possent ilia.
units.tr: and in such a place, where there could remain not only no means of escape but not even the smallest hope, unless the matter itself, unless religion and conscience had urged the man hither? Now, not content with his words, nor with the evidence of letters, nor with the testimony of his companions, nor finally with the torments themselves, they add a kind of cruelty unheard of, which surpasses, I think, the bull of Phalaris, so that nothing further remains by which human cruelty could rise higher. They take care to have a linen cloth sewn, roughly in the shape of a ball, which they force by violence through the throat into the lowest stomach, tied to a slender cord that they hold in their hands. Having passed it through, they pull it back towards themselves, drawing it back through the hidden passages for food, so tearing him apart within his very nature that his entrails might burst with less torment.

units.la: Ita demum fatigatis machinis omnibus ac tortoribus,quum nequicquam proficerent: cō descendunt denique, rogantes ecquid facti tam intempestiui,ac perturbationis eum poeniteret? De facto dicebat adeò se nihil poenitere, vt etiamsi factum non fuisset, debuisse tamen id à se fieri putaret. Caeterum de modo quidem actionis nonnihil dolere sibi, maximè quod praesente Rege, tantaque cum omnium perturbatione fieret. quanquā non tâ sibi id imputandum, qui id ea causa neque suscepit nec cogitarit, quàm ipsi potius regi ascribendum esse, qui tam foedam in ciuibus suis idololatriam, quum posset, non prohiberet. haec verò ille magna cum parrhesia. Illi autem consumptis tormentis omnibus, quum neque ab illo plura expectari, neque ille ex vulnere aliisque tormentis posse diutius viuere videretur, post triduum vltimo afficiendus supplicio ducebatur, primum quidem in summi templi sacrarium, vbi manus illi dextra amputatur: quam mox ille sinistra ad os sublatam deosculatur. Deinde productus in forum detruncatur & altera: qui & hanc similiter humi procumbens osculo prosequitur. Quibus rebus more & humanitate Hispanicis [?] confectis, religatis postea brachijs pedibusque sub equi ventrem, ad martyrij locum pertrahitur. erat eo in loco machina, vnde canabinus funis ex trabe trafuerfa per rotulam dimissus volubilem Christi martyrem medio corpore circunligatum, primo sublime arripit. infrà quam vehementissimè pyra accendebatur: in quam sensim dimittitur ille, non toto corpore, sed ita vt pedibus tantum ardores sentiret. Deinde sublatus, atque demersus terum in flammas, subinde trahitur ac retrahitur, velut per interualla redeunte cruciatu. In quo tamen ille magno ac libero spiritu perdurauit, quantóque ardet vehementius, tanto precatur ardentius. Tandem consumptis iam pedibus, & truncatis manibus, rogant incendiarij ecquid eum facti demum pœniteret? simúlque ad Mariam, diuósque inuocados hortatur. At ille, vt nihil admiserit, cuius cum valde pœniteret: ita minus esse quòd Mariæ diuorúmque præsidio indigeret, respondit. adderent illi quantum vellent externis tormentis, veritatem tamen semper cădem esse ac sui similem, quam vt vita prius confiteretur: ita nec morte nunc esset negaturus. proinde desistere ipsos ab huiusmodi ineptis rogat. Quādo autem desineret esse aduocatus Christus, Mariam tum demũ adhibiturum se aduocatricem. Aeterne, inquit, Deus, Pater misericordiarum, respice quæso seruum tuum, &c. Quúmque illi precantem hunc in modum & laudantem Deum, qui-buscunque possent modis & conuiciis impedirent: magna voce exclamans ille, Psalmum 43. recitauit, Iudica me Deus, & discerne causam meam de gente non sancta, &c. Nondum peruenit ad psalmi finem. dum illi nunc demersum in ignes, nunc rursus ad maiorem cruciatum subleuare niterentur, quum exusto rudente in mediam concideret pyram, vbi præbito in holocaustum corpore, temporarium dolorem æterna finiret requie
units.tr: So at last, when all their machines and torturers had worn themselves out to no avail, they finally came down to him, asking whether he regretted such an untimely and disruptive deed. About the deed itself he said he regretted nothing; even if it had not been done, he would still think it ought to have been done by him. But concerning the manner of the action he did grieve somewhat, chiefly because it was done in the presence of the King and with such disturbance to everyone. Yet this was not so much to be imputed to him, since he had neither undertaken it nor thought of it for that reason, but rather to the King himself, who, when he could, did not prohibit such foul idolatry among his subjects. He said these things with great frankness of speech. Then, when all the torments had been used up, and since nothing more could be expected from him, and he seemed unable to survive much longer from the wound and the other torments, after three days he was led to his final execution. First he was taken into the sacristy of the chief temple, where his right hand was cut off; he soon raised it to his mouth and kissed it. Then he was led out into the forum and his other hand was cut off too, and he likewise, lying prostrate, kissed this one. When these things had been done in the Spanish manner and custom, his arms and legs were bound beneath a horse's belly, and he was dragged to the place of martyrdom. In that place there was a machine from which a hempen rope, let down through a pulley from a crossbeam, first seized the rolling martyr of Christ around the middle of his body and lifted him up. Beneath him a fire was blazing most fiercely. He was lowered gradually into it, not with his whole body, but in such a way that he felt the heat only in his feet. Then he was raised up, plunged down again into the flames, and drawn up and down repeatedly, as the pain returned at intervals. Yet in this he endured with great and free spirit, and the more fiercely he burned, the more ardently he prayed. At last, when his feet were consumed and his hands cut off, the burners asked whether he now at last regretted his deed, and at the same time urged him to call upon Mary and the saints. But he answered that, since he had done nothing for which he should repent, he had no greater need of Mary's or the saints' protection. Let them inflict as many external torments as they wished; the truth would always remain the same and like itself, which he had confessed in life, and so he would not now deny it in death. Therefore he asked them to desist from such foolish things. When Christ should cease to be his advocate, then he would call upon Mary as advocate. "Eternal God, Father of mercies," he said, "look, we beg you, upon your servant, &c." While he prayed in this way and praised God, they tried to hinder him by whatever means and abuse they could. Exclaiming in a loud voice, he recited Psalm 43: "Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation," &c. He had not yet reached the end of the psalm when, while they were now plunging him into the fire and now trying to raise him again to greater torment, the burnt rope fell into the middle of the pyre. There, his body offered as a burnt sacrifice, he ended his temporary pain in eternal rest.

units.la: Hic fuit Gardinerij exitus, quo voluit Dominus Portugalenses ad synceriorem sui agnitionem expergefacere. Ipse verò Rex tertio aut quarto post mense ab huius Gulielmi martyrio, morte dicitur abreptus.
units.tr: This was the end of Gardiner's work, by which the Lord willed to awaken the Portuguese to a purer recognition of himself. The King himself is said to have been carried off by death three or four months after the martyrdom of this William.

units.la: Liber sextus Actionum
units.tr: Book Six of the Acts

units.la: MARTYRVM.
units.tr: OF THE MARTYRS.

units.la: MARTIALIS ALBA Montalbanus. PETRVS SCRIBA Boloniensis in Vasconia: BERNARDVS SEGVINVS Reolensis in Bazadoia. CAROLVS FABER Angolisinensis[?]. PETRVS NAVIHERVS Lemouix.
units.tr: Martial Alba of Montauban; Peter Scriba of Bologna in Gascony; Bernard Seguin of Réole in Bazadais; Charles Faber of Angolisinensis[?]; Peter Naviherus of Limoges.

units.la: QVINQVE SCHOLASTICI gymnasii Laufannensis.
units.tr: FIVE SCHOLARS OF THE ACADEMY OF LAUSANNE.

units.la: Qui pro nomine Dei confitendo mortem in igne propositam & oblatam, Lugduni constanter pertulerunt.
units.tr: Who, for confessing the name of God, constantly endured at Lyon the death of fire that was set before them and offered to them.

units.la: INGREDIMVR iam Annum quinquagesimum tertium, qui vt variarum rerum historia, ita multorum martyrio insignis fuit: eorum vero maximè qui Lugduni nobilissimo totius Galliae emporio mortem oppeticerunt. De quibus primi vt passi sunt, ita nobis in hac historia occurrunt quinque Scholastici vrbis atque vniuersitatis Laufannensis, Martialis Alba, natus Montalbani in Quercyo: Petrus Scriba, patria Bolonien- sis in Vasconia: Bernardus Seguinus ex vrbe Reola in Bazadoia: Carolus Faber, Blanzaci natus in regione Angolismensi: & Petrus Naubcrus [?] Lemouix: qui omnes simul Lugduni capti fuerunt, atque in carcerem coniecti primo die Maij, M.D.LII. Nos eorum confessiones, quas singuli ediderunt, ac res perpetua dignas memoria, suo quaeque loco ordineque retulimus, cum aliquot eorum epistolis selectis ex multis aliis, quas tum ipsi inter se alij ad alios in carcere scripserunt, tum etiam ad ecclesias atque amicos suos miserunt. Ratio autem institutae eorum professionis & captiuitatis huiusmodi fuit. Cum hi quinque Lausannae Studiorum causa egissent, alij diutius quàm alij, literisque tum Diuinis tum humanis studuissent, post festum Paschae constituerunt omnes simul, optimis Dei auspiciis in patriam se quisque suam conferre, alij versus Tholosam, alij Burdigalam, alij ad Santones, alij ad Lemouices, vnusquisque ad ea loca & oppida, in quibus patria natiuitatis suae habebat: eo quidem consilio & animo, vt gloriae Dei seruirent eamque gratiam, quam à Deo acceperant, cum parentibus suis communicarent atque impertirent, vt si possent, eos adducerent ad eam Christi cognitionem, qua à Deo illuminati fuerant. Neque verò solum hoc studium pietatis plenum in parentes ac propinquos suos susceperunt, sed etiam in alios, quos opera ipsorum, Deum ad agnitionem veritatis vocaturum sperabant. Hoc autem professionis ad suos suscipiendae consilium communicauerunt cum ecclesiae Laufannensis ministris ac scholae professoribus, qui illud vt pium ac sanctum magnopere probarunt, atque illud ad honorem Dei amplificandumque regnum Christi eius ilij pertineret. Atque ut eorum adductus maiorem haberet approbationem, ea ecclesia tribus illorum testimonium dedit fidei ac probitatis ius quæ ea in urbe perspecta fuisset, ut fideles homines, quos ita pie vivebant, eo testimonio quod afferebant adducti, eos libentius excirent, melíusque de illorum & vita & doctrina existimaret, cui quidem testimonio, Ioannes Caluinus à Petro Vireto rogatus, facilè suum con[?]junxit. Cæteri verò duo, aliquandiu in eadem urbe servierunt, alter nempe Petrus Nauherus apud ipsum Viretum, alter verò Bernardus Seguinus apud Theodorum Bezam, eáque in conditione ac vitæ ratione ita integrè versati fuerunt, ut fidem, officium & modestiam ecclesiæ suam probaverint. Paulo post Geneuæ aliquot dies comorati, iter susceperunt ut Lugdunum proficiscerentur. Atque in itinere quendam Lugdunensem nacti comitem, rogatíque ab eo ut ipsum quò Lugdunum pervenissent, invíserent, se id facturos promiserunt. Itaq; quoniam nullum aliud diversorium reperiebant, in quo ad unum aut alterum diem Lugduni commodè possent commorari, ad insigne triu pisçium diverterunt: ac postridie duabus aut tribus post prandium horis, omnes simul domum eius à quo in ipso itinere humaniter fuerant invitati accesserunt: quæ est ad Rhodanum, in ea urbis regione quæ à quibusdam Athenæus appellatur. Ubi cùm in horto aliquandiu deambulassent, invitati ab eo amico, adhibitáque nominis Dei invocatione inter pios priusquam cibus capiatur usitata, cœperunt accumbere, seque ijs reficere, quæ ipsis appósita fuerant. Cùm autem ita in mensa dominis piè fruerentur, lætarenturque in Domino, Latrunculator Lugdunensis urbis, Poulletus cognominatus, cum suo satellitio advenit, qui simulatque cubiculum in quo illi erant, ingressus fuisset, nomen & cognomen uniuscuiusque, patriam, rationemque vitæ ab eis quæsuit, aliáq; huiusmodi ad indaginem reorum usitata. Id cùm fecisset, quatuor corum vinciendos curavit binos ac binos, quintum verò medium inter satellites collocavit, nulla parte adversatrice expressa causæque informatione habita contra omne ius in carcerem Officialis ducti fuerunt, in locúq; profundu & obscuru coiecti, atque horá propè post singuli ordine coram Officiali accersiti, codéq; die interrogati de ijs religionis capitib° quæ illi magna constantione & vi tueri solet. ad quæ illi pro eximiis Dei donis,quibus praediti erant, constanter secundum verbum eius responderunt, & gloriam ei dederunt, confitentes eius nomen apud eos, qui etiam à mentione eius maximopere abhorrebant. Postero autem die, iterum interrogati fuerunt, & sequenti eam adepti facultatem ut confessionem suam ex scripto ederent, quam illi scripserunt: sed ita subito ut vix eius exemplum retinere potuerint. Sequenti etiam hebdomade quidam eorum ad examen revocati sunt: in quo quidem de religionis capitibus cum tribus monachorum generibus erat eis disputandum. Postremo cum eos adhuc ad se vocauissent, ut viderent an in priore sententia permanerent: cognita eorum hominum constantia, confessioneque ipsorum obsignata, eos in fossas carceris singulis separatim assignatas remiserunt. Postridie autem, qui erat dies Veneris 13.Maij, singulos eorum seorsim in auditorium Officialis produxerunt. à quo cum in maxima hominum frequentia haereseos condemnati essent, atque in manum Magistratus civilis traditi: quisque eorum, cum huiusmodi sententia contra se pronuntiatam audivisset, provocavit de eo quidem, quod ut haereticus condemnaretur, postulavitque ut ad parlamentum Parisiense duceretur. Id autem cum Officialis magnopere esset admiratus, tamen appellationem eorum admisit. In quo cum quidam qui Officiali assidebat, audivisset unum eorum ita appellantem, quaesuit ex eo, an de reliqua quoque sententia idem faceret. Ad id alter respondit, se quod intelligeret praecipuum sententiae caput in eo consistere, quod haeretici essent declarati, ea quidem in parte ut iniqua appellare, in reliqua vero se non intelligere quid vellent. Tum Officialis satis esse dixit, quod illi ita appellassent. Ita his tredecim diebus ab adversariis causa illorum fuit cognita, in iudicioque versata. Reliqua autem quae ab illis & dicta & facta sunt, ex ipsorum scriptis cognoscentur: ex quibus nos ea sermone Latino exponemus, quae & gravem aliquam consolationem, & illustrem Euangelij fideique confessionem continere videbantur. Martialis quidem Albae nullum extat scriptum, quod ad illud tempus causamque pertineat. Neque vero in scribendo ita fuit versatus ut caeteri: in orando meditandoq; magis occupatus: ad quae caeteri eius socij propter huiusmodi meditationes officium orandi inter ipsos deferebat. Petrus vero Scriba & Bernardus Seguinus nō studio solum olum pietatis, sed etiam ingenio doctrinaque excelluerunt, multasque pistolas in carcere scripserunt: quae ostendunt illos non modo in sacris literis diligenter versatos fuisse, verumetiam ad mortem pro causa Christi Evangelique suscipiendam toto animi studio paratos. Quod ut facilius perspici possit, nos primum confessionem a Petro Scriba in iudicio editam ac Latino sermone expositam hoc loco inseruimus.
units.tr: WE now come to the year 1553, which was remarkable, as the history of various events is, so also for the martyrdom of many, and especially of those who met their death at Lyon, the most noble trading centre of all Gaul. Of these, the first to suffer, as they came to our notice in this history, were five scholars of the city and university of Lausanne: Martial Alba, a native of Montauban in Quercy; Peter Scriba, from Bologne in Gascony; Bernard Seguin of the town of Réole in Bazadais; Charles Faber, born at Blanzac in the region of Angoulême; and Peter Nauherus [?] of Limoges. All of them were arrested together at Lyon and thrown into prison on the first day of May, 1552. We have set out in their proper place and order their confessions, which each of them published, and the matters worthy of perpetual memory, along with some selected letters of theirs out of many others, which they wrote to one another while in prison, and also sent to churches and to their friends. The reason for their profession and imprisonment was as follows. When these five had gone to Lausanne for the sake of study, some for a longer time than others, and had devoted themselves to both divine and human letters, after the feast of Easter they all agreed together, under God's best auspices, to go each to his own homeland: some toward Toulouse, some toward Bordeaux, some toward Saintes, some toward Limoges, each to those places and towns where his native family lived. They did this with the intention and purpose of serving the glory of God, and of sharing and imparting to their parents the grace they had received from God, so that, if they could, they might lead them to that knowledge of Christ by which they themselves had been enlightened. Nor did they undertake this zealous work of piety only toward their parents and kinsfolk, but also toward others whom they hoped God would call to the knowledge of the truth through their efforts. They communicated this plan of going to their own people to the ministers of the church of Lausanne and to the professors of the school, who greatly approved it as pious and holy, and as something that would pertain to the honour of God and the enlarging of the kingdom of Christ. And so that their undertaking might have greater approval, that church gave them a testimony of three things: their faith, their uprightness, and their conduct, as these had been observed in that city; so that the faithful men to whom they went, moved by the testimony they carried, might more willingly receive them, and might judge more favourably both their life and their teaching. John Calvin, asked by Peter Viret, readily added his name to this testimony. The other two stayed for some time in the same city: Peter Nauherus with Viret himself, and Bernard Seguin with Theodore Beza. In that position and manner of life they conducted themselves so blamelessly that they proved their faith, duty and modesty to the church. Shortly afterwards they stayed a few days at Geneva and then set out on their journey to Lyon. On the way they met a certain Lyonnais as a fellow traveller, and when he asked them to visit him when they arrived at Lyon, they promised they would. Since they could find no other inn where they might stay at Lyon comfortably for a day or two, they put up at the sign of the Three Fishes. On the following day, two or three hours after dinner, they all went together to the house of the man who had kindly invited them during the journey; it lies by the Rhone, in that part of the city which some call Athenaeus. When they had walked for a while in the garden there, and had been invited by their friend, and after the customary invocation of the name of God among the godly before taking food, they began to recline at table and refresh themselves with what had been set before them. While they were thus enjoying the Lord's gifts at table and rejoicing in the Lord, Poulletus, the cognomen of the thief-catcher of the city of Lyon, arrived with his band of officers. As soon as he had entered the room where they were, he asked each of them for his name and surname, his homeland and his way of life, and other such things customary in the questioning of accused persons. When he had done this, he had four of them bound two by two, and placed the fifth in the middle among the officers. Without any adversary appearing, and without any statement of the charge being taken, they were led against all right to the prison of the Official, and thrown into a deep and dark place. Nearly an hour later, each one was called in order before the Official, and that same day they were questioned about those heads of religion which he usually defends with great firmness and force. To these questions they answered constantly, according to the Word of God, by the outstanding gifts of God with which they were endowed, and they gave glory to him, confessing his name before those who most vehemently shrank even from mention of it. On the next day they were questioned again, and on the following day they were given the opportunity to publish their confession in writing, which they wrote; but so hastily that they could scarcely keep a copy of it. In the following week also, some of them were recalled for examination, in which they were to dispute about the heads of religion with three kinds of monks. Finally, when they had summoned them again to see whether they still held to their earlier opinion, and had recognised the constancy of these men and sealed their confession, they sent them back to the pits of the prison, each assigned separately. On the next day, which was Friday, 13 May, they led each of them separately into the hall of the Official. When they had been condemned there as heretics, before a great crowd, and handed over into the hands of the civil magistrate, each of them, having heard the sentence pronounced against him, appealed; he appealed, indeed, against the fact that he had been condemned as a heretic, and asked that he be taken to the Parlement of Paris. When the Official was greatly astonished at this, nevertheless he admitted their appeal. In this, when one of those sitting beside the Official heard one of them appealing in this way, he asked him whether he did the same with regard to the rest of the sentence. To this the man replied that, so far as he understood, the chief point of the sentence consisted in their having been declared heretics, and that he appealed against this part as unjust, but that as to the rest he did not know what they meant. Then the Official said it was enough that they had appealed in this way. Thus over these thirteen days their cause was examined by their adversaries and was brought before the court. The rest of what was said and done by them will be known from their own writings, from which we shall set out in Latin those things which seemed to contain both a weighty consolation and an illustrious confession of the Gospel and of the faith. Of Martial Alba indeed there is no extant writing that relates to that time and cause. He was not so practised in writing as the others, being more occupied with prayer and meditation; because of such meditation, his companions for their part assigned him the duty of praying. Peter Scriba and Bernard Seguin excelled not only in zeal for piety but also in talent and learning, and wrote many letters in prison, which show that they were not only diligently versed in the Holy Scriptures but were also prepared with their whole mind to undergo death for the cause of Christ and the Gospel. So that this may be more easily perceived, we first insert here the confession of Peter Scriba, published at his trial and set out in Latin.

units.la: Petrus Scriba pro verbo Dei captiuus, omnibus fidelibus Christianisque hominibus ratiam, pace, salutemque a Deo Patre, & Domino Iesu Christo etiam atq; etiā exoptat.
units.tr: Peter Scriba, a prisoner for the Word of God, wishes grace, peace and salvation from God the Father and from our Lord Jesus Christ, again and again, to all the faithful and Christian people.

units.la: CVM ego, fratres in Christo charissimi, animo mecum perpenderem cum fructum qui ad universam ecclesiam venturus esset, ea argumenta, quae de fide adversarij in carcere Lugduni mihi proposuerunt, & simul quae sunt à me responsa vobis exponerem: ob id confessionem meam ad vos scribere volui, tum ut omnes fideles consolarer, tum etiam ut regnum Iesu Christi amplificarē: in qua quidem etiam completar ea capita, quae tractaui ac posui in ea confessione, quam ego manu mea scripsi, atque adversarijs dedi, cum eam ex scripto recitassem. Cum igitur nos inclusi essemus in carcere Archiepiscopi Lugdunensis, separatique alij ab alijs, Deumque summo animi studio oraremus ut ad nomen ipsius cum omni fiducia & libertate confitendum nos Spiritu suo confirmaret: venit ad me ianitor carceris, qui duobus ostijs apertis eius infimi loci in quo erā[?], comitatus legato Prae-secti me ducit ad auditorium coram Officiali, aliisque hominibus qui maxima frequentia & authoritate aderant. Tum Officialis ex me quaerit, Quomodo appellaris? Petrus, inquam, Scriba. Qua, inquit, es vitae professione? Scholasticus, inquam. Unde, inquit, nunc venis? Ex Sabaudia, inquam, & ditione principum Bernatum. Qua ex urbe? Lausanna, inquam. Quid, inquit, ibi agebas? Verbo Dei, inquam, studebam. Quam, inquit, Lausannae doctrinam amplectuntur? Verbi Dei, inquam. Quomodo, inquit ille, scis tu verbum Dei esse, quod illi amplectuntur? Quoniam, inquam, iandiu in ea urbe studui, concionibusque interfui, quae ibi quotidie habentur, vidi & audiui eos aliud nihil quam purum Dei verbum praedicare, & ita credo, propterea quod Spiritus sanctus animo meo eius rei testimonium dat, atque ita affirmat, ut nullo modo dubitare possim aut debeam. Visne, inquit, amplecti eorum legem ac secundum eam viuere? Ego vero, inquam, volo: quoniam verum Dei verbum est. Num credis, inquit ille, corpus Iesu Christi in Sacramento altaris esse? Minimè, inquam: nam id quidem repugnat illi fidei nostræ capiti, in quo dicimus ac credimus eum sedere ad dexteram Dei Patris, nec inde ante venturum, quàm dies iudicij ille magnus & illustris venerit. Diuinitatem quidem eius per totum mundum diffusam esse fateor. Sed ne vos exi-stimetis me sanctum negare sacramentum, à Iesu Christo institutum: ego credo & confiteor, Sacramentum sacrosanctæ Cœnæ, in qua comedo corpus Iesu Christi, sanguinemque eius bibo, non eo modo ac ratione carnis absurda qua Capernaitæ & Papistæ arbitrabantur: sed ita statuo me capiendo eū panē ac bibendo vinū, vere corpus Christi edere ac sanguinem eius bibere: idque per fidem atque in spiritu. Tum Procurator fiscalis, homo doctus (quemadmodum ego intellexi) Clepierius nominatus, qui proximus Officiali assidebat, Tu, inquit, ais te cum panem ac vinum in Cœna sumis, simul corpus & sanguinem Christi sumere? Sanè inquam: sed spirituali quadam ratione, non carnali. nam quanuis Christus nunc in cælo sit, ubi eum fide quæro: virtute tamen Spiritus sui qui res longo interuallo remotas, separatasque coniungit, animas nostras alit, fouet, reficit admirabili quadam ratione: quæ ab humano ingenio minimè comprehendi potest: atque hoc modo efficit, ut nos corporis ipsius membra, os ex ipsius ossibus, carôque ex carne simus.
units.tr: Since I, dearest brothers in Christ, have pondered within myself the fruit that would come to the whole Church, both from the arguments which my opponents put to me on matters of faith in the prison at Lyon and from the answers I gave them, I have wished to write my confession to you, both to console all the faithful and to extend the kingdom of Jesus Christ. In it I shall also complete the heads which I treated and set out in the confession that I wrote with my own hand and gave to my opponents when I had read it aloud from the text. When we had been shut up in the prison of the Archbishop of Lyon, and kept apart from one another, and were praying to God with the utmost earnestness that he would strengthen us by his Spirit to confess his name with all confidence and freedom, the jailer came to me. Having opened two doors of that lowest place where I was kept, he led me, accompanied by the messenger of the Prefect, to the hall, before the Official and other men who were present in great numbers and authority. Then the Official asked me, "What are you called?" "Peter," I said, "Scriba." "What is your calling in life?" "I am a scholar," I said. "Where are you coming from now?" "From Savoy and the territory of the princes of Berne." "From what city?" "Lausanne," I said. "What were you doing there?" "I was studying the Word of God," I said. "What doctrine do they embrace at Lausanne?" "The doctrine of the Word of God," I said. "How do you know," he said, "that the word they embrace is the Word of God?" "Because," I said, "I have studied in that city for a long time and have been present at the sermons held there every day, and I have seen and heard them preach nothing but the pure Word of God. And I believe it, because the Holy Spirit gives testimony of this to my mind and so affirms it that I can and ought to have no doubt." "Do you wish," he said, "to embrace their law and to live according to it?" "I certainly do," I said, "since it is the true Word of God." "Do you believe," he said, "that the body of Jesus Christ is in the sacrament of the altar?" "Not at all," I said, "for that is contrary to that article of our faith in which we say and believe that he sits at the right hand of God the Father, and from there will not come until that great and illustrious day of judgment has come. I confess indeed that his divinity is diffused throughout the whole world. But lest you think I deny the holy sacrament instituted by Jesus Christ: I believe and confess that in the sacrament of the holy Supper, in which I eat the body of Jesus Christ and drink his blood, I do so not in the absurd manner of the flesh which the Capernaites and Papists supposed, but I hold that in taking that bread and drinking that wine I truly eat the body of Christ and drink his blood, and this through faith and in the Spirit." Then the fiscal procurator, a learned man (as I understood), named Clepierius, who sat next to the Official, said, "Do you say that when you take bread and wine in the Supper, you receive at the same time the body and blood of Christ?" "Certainly," I said, "but in a spiritual manner, not a carnal one. For although Christ is now in heaven, where I seek him by faith, yet by the power of his Spirit, who joins together things separated by a long distance, he nourishes, cherishes and refreshes our souls in a wonderful manner which human understanding cannot grasp; and in this way he makes us members of his body, bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh.

units.la: Credisne, inquit, Purgatorium esse, vbi animæ purgentur, pro quibus nos orare debeamus? Ego vero, inquam, credo sanguine Iesu Christi nos purgari, omniaque peccata nostra eluì[?]. nam eam ob causam effusus est: neque aliam credo, habeoque peccatorum purgationem. Scriptura enim duas nobis vias proponit: vnam fidei ad vitam æternam, alteram incredulitatis, per quam omnes infideles, qui non credunt in Christum, ad mortem æternam deducuntur. nã ita scriptum est, Qui in Filium Dei credit, vitam habet æternam: qui verò in Filium Dei non credit, is iam condemnatus est, iráque Dei super eum manet. Quare pro mortuis nullo modo orandum est. nam si in paradiso sunt, superuacanea est oratio, planéque inutilis iis qui iam fructum sentiunt
units.tr: "Do you believe," he said, "that there is a Purgatory, where souls are purged, and for whom we ought to pray?" "Indeed," I said, "I believe that we are cleansed by the blood of Jesus Christ, and that all our sins are washed away by it. For he was poured out for this reason, and I believe, and hold, that there is no other cleansing of sins. For Scripture sets before us two ways: one of faith to eternal life, and the other of unbelief, by which all unbelievers, who do not believe in Christ, are led to eternal death. For it is written: He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life; but he who does not believe in the Son of God is already condemned, and the wrath of God remains upon him. Therefore one must by no means pray for the dead. For if they are in paradise, prayer is superfluous, and plainly useless to those who already feel the fruit

units.la: mortis ac passionis Iesu Christi omniumque promissionum, quæ in Euangelio offeruntur. Sin damnati sunt, nil oratio potest illis prodesse, qui à Deo sunt maledicti in perpetuum. Num credis, inquit, sacerdoti esse confitendum? Ego vero, inquam, sentio uni Deo confitendum esse, sicut Dauid multis locis dicit, ac præcipuè Psalmo xxxii, Tum dixi, Confitebor aduersum me præuaricationes meas Domino & tu dimisisti iniquitatem peccati mei. Hæc vera est confessio, quam statim absolutio peccatorumque gratuita remissio sequitur. Ergo, inquit, tu non credis confitendum esse sacerdotibus? Minimè, inquam. nam id quidem planè pugnat cum verbo Dei, in quo docemur unum Deum esse apud quem peccatorum confessio facienda sit, quemadmodum Dauid ostendit Psalmo li, Tibi soli peccaui, & malum coram te feci. Quid tu, inquit, sentis de ecclesiæ cæremoniis, ut de campanis, aliisque rebus ab ea institutis? Quoniam, inquam, nos hac carne circundati non possumus comprehendere res Diuinas ac cælestes, sentio ad infirmitatem nostram subleuandam huiusmodi adiumentis atque adminiculis nos opus habere. itaque in Ecclesia Domini nostri certæ cæremoniæ sunt obseruandæ, conueniendúmque unum in locum, tum ad audiendum Dei verbu, tum ad sacramenta à Domino instituta administranda & celebranda: quas ego cæremonias approbo.
units.tr: mortis and passion of Jesus Christ, and of all the promises offered in the Gospel. But if they are damned, prayer can profit nothing to those who are cursed by God forever. "Do you believe," he said, "that confession must be made to a priest?" "Indeed," I said, "I think it must be made to God alone, as David says in many places, and especially in Psalm 32: 'I said, I will confess my transgressions to the Lord, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin.' This is the true confession, which is immediately followed by absolution and the free remission of sins." "So," he said, "you do not believe that confession must be made to priests?" "Not at all," I said. "For that plainly conflicts with the Word of God, in which we are taught that there is one God before whom the confession of sins is to be made, as David shows in Psalm 51: 'Against you only have I sinned, and done evil in your sight.'" "What do you think," he said, "of the ceremonies of the Church, such as the bells and other things the Church has instituted?" "Since we, surrounded by this flesh, cannot comprehend divine and heavenly things," I said, "I think we need such aids and supports to relieve our weakness. Therefore certain ceremonies are to be observed in the Church of our Lord, and we are to come together in one place, both to hear the Word of God and to administer and celebrate the sacraments instituted by the Lord. These ceremonies I approve.

units.la: Quæ verò à Papa in ecclesiam sunt introductæ, eas planè repudio, ut perniciosas alienasque à verbo Dei, quibus homines à vero Dei cultu pietateque abducuntur. Credis, inquit, virginem Mariam orandam esse, cæterosque item Sanctos qui sunt in cælo: eosque nobis esse aduocatos & patronos? Nullum, inquâ, credo alium esse aduocatum, qui pro nobis apud Deum Patrem intercedat, quàm Iesum Christum, in cuius nomine certissimam habemus promissionem, nos in nostris precibus à Deo Patre exaudiri. Is etiam solus est Mediator inter nos & Deum, quemadmodum dicit Apostolus: neque vllus est alius. Quòd verò ad Virginem attinet, credo eam inter omnes mulieres maximè beatam esse, propterea quòd ea credidit, atque Christum in utero suo tulit, virgo & antequam eum parëret & postquam peperisset: eiusdemque fidem ac consuetudinem vitæ imitandam: Deum verò solum eius exemplo inuocandum atque imitandum: quemadmodum in cantico suo nos monuit. Idem de Sanctis quoque sentio. quos quidem existimo esse beatos, eorumque exemplum imitandum, & laudandum Deum, quod tantis eos beneficiis affecerit atque ornauerit. Ut vero eos invocem adoremque, nulla ratione adduci possum. nam neipsi quidem huiusmodi honorem volunt. Cùm autem animaduertere notarium non scribere ea quae à me dicerentur, ac locos Scripturae qui à me citarentur, in scribendo praetermittere, ea de re Officiale admonui, abeoque papyrum atque atramentum petij, ut confessionem meam ederem, atque ex certis Scripturae testimonijs fidem meam declararem, demonstrarémque eam meam testificationem à veritate verbi Dei nulla in parte discrepare. Id cùm mihi ille assensisset, chartámque & atramentum se postridie mihi curaturum promisisset, iussit ut meam confessionem subsignarem: atque à janitore legatoque Praefecti in carcerem meum reducerer. Ubi gratias Deo meo per Jesum Christum eius Filium egi, quod me ita ad confitendum coram inimicis sanctum eius; nomen virtute Spiritus sui confirmasset, eúmque rogaui ut in eadem fidei confessione perseuerantiam usque in finem mihi praestaret. Post hanc precationem, quanuis in loco essem admodum obscuro & tetro, in quo vix respirare poteram: tamen Spiritus virtute magnopere fui recreatus & confirmatus, eáque consolatione ac laetitia affectus, quae omnem tristitiam, angorem, molestiámque superabat. Postero autem die, qui erat dies Lunae ac secundus mensis Maii, custos carceris hora octaua me alium in locum traduxit: in quo aliquanto plus lucis ad scribendum habere poteram, partémque folii dimidiam mihi dedit ad perscribendam confessionem meam. Id quod ego feci, invocans Dominum ut author moderatorque totius confessionis meae esse vellet. Postridie janitor saepius ad me venit, valde urgens ut scriptum quaprimum conficerem. cui ego respondi me non posse, propterea quod ad scribendum non multum lucis haberem. Porro duabus horis post meridiem legatus Praefecti venit, méque in amplam aulam adduxit, in qua erat Officialis, & judex Cortrerius, aliíque plurimi magnae authoritatis aduocati, ciues, mercatores, caterique alterius generis atque ordinis homines, multi praeterea monachi tum Dominicani tum Franciscani, aliíque pseudoprophetae qui insignia bestiae in capite atque in toto corpore impressa habent. Tum Officialis ex me quaesiuit, num vellem in suscepta sententia permanere, & quod essem confessus defendere. Ego vero, inquam, cum nihil aliud quam purum Dei verbum senserim ac dixerim, volo id omni ratione tueri, atque in eo quod sum confessus & viuere & immori. Scripsisti ne, inquit, confessionem tuam ac perfecisti? Partem, inquam, vnam tantum scripsi: sed vos rogo, vt concessu vestro absoluere mihi liceat, ad idque faciendum iussu quoque vestro iani-tor mihi chartam suppeditet. Lege, inquit, id quod scripsisti. Tum ego magna voce, quod a me erat scriptum legere coepi. quo lecto atque recitato, Officialis ex me quaesiuit, num id quod scripsissem tueri vellem ac defendere. Ego vero, inquam, etiam vsque ad mortem, cum id purum sit Dei verbum, tueri paratus sum. Et postea cum is iussisset vt confessionem meam obsignarem, id feci summo cum studio ac voluntate. Deinde ille, Hic adsunt, inquit, doctores, qui sententiam tuae opinioni confessionique contrariam tibi demonstrabunt. Incipiant igitur, inquam. nam ego eis respondere paratus sum.
units.tr: But those things which the Pope has introduced into the Church I plainly reject, as pernicious and alien to the Word of God, and by which men are drawn away from the true worship and piety of God. "Do you believe," he said, "that the Virgin Mary is to be prayed to, and likewise the other saints who are in heaven, and that they are our advocates and patrons?" "I believe," I said, "that there is no other advocate who intercedes for us before God the Father than Jesus Christ, in whose name we have the most certain promise that we are heard by God the Father in our prayers. He is also the only Mediator between us and God, as the Apostle says, and there is no other. As for the Virgin, I believe that she is the most blessed of all women, because she believed and bore Christ in her womb, a virgin both before she bore him and after she had borne him; and her faith and manner of life are to be imitated. But God alone is to be invoked and imitated after her example, as she herself admonished us in her song. I think the same of the saints. Whom indeed I consider blessed, and their example to be imitated, and God to be praised, who has endowed and adorned them with such great benefits. But that I should invoke and worship them, I can by no means be brought to, for they themselves do not want such honour. When, however, I noticed that the notary was not writing down what I said, and was omitting in his writing the passages of Scripture that I cited, I warned the Official about this, and asked for paper and ink, so that I might publish my confession and declare my faith from certain testimonies of Scripture, and show that my testimony does not differ in any part from the truth of the Word of God. When he agreed to this, and promised that he would see to paper and ink for me the next day, he ordered me to sign my confession, and I was led back to my cell by the jailer and the Prefect's messenger. There I gave thanks to my God through Jesus Christ his Son, that he had strengthened me by the power of his Spirit to confess his holy name before enemies, and I asked him to grant me perseverance in the same confession of faith to the end. After this prayer, although I was in a very dark and foul place, where I could scarcely breathe, I was greatly refreshed and strengthened by the power of the Spirit, and was filled with such consolation and joy that it overcame all sadness, anguish and distress. On the following day, which was Monday and the second of May, at the eighth hour the jailer moved me to another place, where I had somewhat more light for writing, and gave me half a sheet of paper on which to write out my confession. This I did, calling upon the Lord to be the author and guide of my whole confession. Afterwards the jailer came to me several times, urging me strongly to finish the writing as soon as possible. I replied that I could not, because I had little light for writing. Then two hours after noon the Prefect's messenger came and led me into a large hall, where the Official and the judge Cortrerius were, and many other advocates of great authority, citizens, merchants and men of other kinds and ranks, besides many monks, both Dominicans and Franciscans, and other pseudo-prophets who have the marks of the beast impressed on their heads and over their whole bodies. Then the Official asked me whether I wished to remain in the position I had taken and to defend what I had confessed. "Indeed," I said, "since I have thought and said nothing but the pure Word of God, I wish to defend it in every way, and to live and die in what I have confessed." "Have you written your confession and finished it?" he asked. "I have written only one part," I said, "but I beg you, with your leave, that I may be allowed to finish it, and that, by your order too, the jailer may supply me with paper for this." "Read what you have written," he said. Then I began to read aloud what I had written. When I had read and recited it, the Official asked me whether I wished to maintain and defend what I had written. "Indeed," I said, "I am ready to maintain it even unto death, since it is the pure Word of God." And afterwards, when he ordered me to sign my confession, I did so with the greatest zeal and goodwill. Then he said, "Here are teachers present who will show you a doctrine contrary to your opinion and confession." "Let them begin, then," I said, "for I am ready to answer them.

units.la: Tum vnus ex illis monachis, quem caeteri dominum Doctorem honorificentissimis verbis appellabant, coepit mecum ita loqui, Age, inquit, amice, tu in confessione tua dicis Papam non esse ecclesiae caput. at ego contrarium tibi probabo: Papa est successor sancti Petri, ergo ecclesiae caput est. Ego, inquam, primum nego antecedens, quod Papa diui Petri successor sit. Ego, inquit, tibi probo, Papa est in loco sancti Petri, ergo eius successor est. Ego vero, inquam, neutrum concedo. neque enim Papa annuntiat verbum Dei, quemadmodum fecit diuus Petrus. Porro oportet eum qui S. Petro vult succedere, illum quoque imitari, vt & annuntiet verbum Dei, & oues Domini nostri Iesu Christi pascat: id quod Papa nullo modo facit, sicut ego in confessione mea vobis ostendo.
units.tr: Then one of those monks, whom the others addressed with the most honourable titles as "Lord Doctor," began to speak with me like this: "Come now, friend, in your confession you say the Pope is not the head of the Church. But I will prove the opposite to you: the Pope is the successor of St Peter, therefore he is the head of the Church." I replied: "First, I deny your premise, that the Pope is the successor of the blessed Peter." "I prove it to you," he said, "the Pope is in the place of St Peter, therefore he is his successor." "But I concede neither," I said. "The Pope does not proclaim the Word of God, as the blessed Peter did. Moreover, whoever wishes to succeed St Peter must also imitate him, both by proclaiming the Word of God and by feeding the sheep of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Pope does nothing of the kind, as I show you in my confession."

units.la: Praeterea etiam si Papa, vt verus verbi Dei doctor pastorque Ecclesiae, exemplum Petri sequeretur, atque ei ita succederet: non tamen caput esset Ecclesiae Domini nostri Iesu Christi, sed membrum tantum, aut minister & Apostolus. Itaque nullum est aliud caput Ecclesiae : neque alterum ego agnosco, quam Dominum Iesum solum sine vicario ac successore. Nam diuus Paulus cum vnum constituit Angelorum caput & hominum. Tum monachus, Equidè, inquit, scio Paulum dicere Christum totius Ecclesiæ caput constitutum: verumtamen vicarius qui vices eius suppleat, est in terra constitutus. Minimè, inquam ego. nam cùm ille magnitudine ac virtute Diuinitatis suæ omnia impleat, atque Spiritu suo Ecclesiam suam regat, vbi ille ita præsens est, nullum vicarium esse oportet. Ego, inquit monachus, ostendo Christum, quàuis totius cœli ac terræ rex sit, plurimos tamen vicarios habere in hoc mundo, reges ac principes, quos vult populo suo præesse. Aliud est, inquam, in rebus ciuilibus, aliud in spiritualibus. nam in illa rectione rerumpublicarum atque rerum humanarum administratione reges vult esse ac principes qui ad societatem generis humani conseruandam dominentur: in ecclesia verò & regno Christi, quod est spirituale, non eadem est ratio regendi & gubernandi. Tum is mihi alias similitudines afferebat: quas ego vt leues & ineptas prætermitto.
units.tr: Moreover, even if the Pope, as a true teacher of God's Word and pastor of the Church, followed Peter's example and succeeded him in this way, he would still not be the head of the Church of our Lord Jesus Christ, but only a member, or a minister and apostle. So there is no other head of the Church. I acknowledge no other than the Lord Jesus alone, with no vicar or successor. For when the blessed Paul appointed one head of angels and of men, ... Then the monk said: "Indeed, I know that Paul says Christ has been appointed head of the whole Church. Nevertheless, a vicar who takes his place has been set up on earth." "Not at all," I said. "For since he fills all things by the greatness and power of his divinity, and rules his Church by his Spirit, where he is so present, there ought to be no vicar." "I show," said the monk, "that Christ, though he is king of all heaven and earth, nevertheless has many vicars in this world, kings and princes, whom he wills to rule over his people." "It is one thing," I said, "in civil affairs, and another in spiritual ones. For in the governing of commonwealths and the administration of human affairs he wills there to be kings and princes who rule to preserve the society of mankind; but in the Church and the kingdom of Christ, which is spiritual, the principle of ruling and governing is not the same." Then he brought forward other comparisons, which I pass over as weak and inept.

units.la: Cùm autem in hac mihi cum illo monacho institutâ disputatione cateteri eiusdem farinæ ac rasuræ homines viderent illum magnum doctorem ita victum: tum contrà vt me clamoribus suis consternarent, bini aut terni interdum vociferabantur. Ex illis vnus fuit Franciscanus, doctor Cumbanus appellatus, qui me hunc in modum aggressus est, Tu ais, inquit, sanctum Petrum ecclesiæ caput non fuisse. Maximè, inquam. Ego verò, inquit, contrarium probo, Dominus noster dicit Petro, Tu es Simon filius Ionæ, tu Cephas vocaberis. porrò Cephas, caput Latinè dicitur. Vnde, inquam, hanc tu interpretationem accepisti? Ioannes quidem in Euangelio suo aliter interpretatur, cùm in primo capite eius Euangelij ita scribit, Tu Cephas vocaberis, quod declaratur Petrus. Tum index Vilardus nouum Testamentum in manu suscepit, vt videret an ea interpretatio ita esset quemadmodum ego dicerem: quam à meis verbis discrepare nullo modo comperit. Itaque monachus demisso capite summoque affectus pudore conticuit, ac plane concidit. Tum Dominicanus interruptum suum sermonem hoc modo continuauit: Tu, inquit, tua confessione dicis hominem nullum habere liberum arbitrium: ego verò contrariam sententiam probo. nam ita scriptum est in Euangelio, hominem quendam cùm Hierosolymis in Iericho descenderet, in latrones incidisse, à quibus fuit spoliatus ac vulneratus, semimortuúsque relictus: Thomas autem Aquinas, eam parabolam à Domino propositam interpretatur de libero arbitrio, quod dicit in parte quidem laesum, sed non plane comminutum attritúmque fuisse ut nulla vis amplius hominis remanserit. Hanc ego interpretationem, inquam, nullo modo accipio. Quid, inquit ille, ésne doctior S. Thoma? Ego, inquam, non tantum mihi arrogo, ut me eo docti-orem esse dicam, sed hanc parabolam ita exponendam esse nego: sed potius eo proposito à Domino Iesu exemplo nobis eam charitatem commendari, quam nos erga proximum nostrum suscipere & habere debemus. De libero vero arbitrio, nos omnem eius facultatem ac vim amisimus, quemadmodum ego in mea confessione declaraui. Nos enim plane mortui sumus & non aliqua in parte, sicut ait Divus Paulus. Quod si bene agimus, id nobis non est attribuendum, sed Deo, qui per Spiritum suum in nobis agit: qui etiam, ut idem Apostolus testatur, facit ut nos & velimus & efficiamus. ita fit Deus huiusmodi voluntatis & facultatis largitor effectórque in nobis est, nullo iure eam possumus nobis arrogare. Tu, inquit, ais in confessione tua, nos sola fide iustificari. Maxime, inquā. at ego, inquit ille, probo nos operibus iustisicari: Nos operibus meremur, ergo nos per ea iusti fiumus. Ego nego, inquam, antecedens. Ego vero, inquit, illud probo: Divus Paulus ultimo capite epistolae ad Hebraeos ita dicit, Beneficentiae & communicationis ne obliuiscamini: talibus enim victimis promeretur Deus: Vides, inquit, promereri significare mereri. ergo nos operibus nostris meremur. Nego, inquam, in eo textu ita legi: siquidem veram translationem sequi velimus. Tum Officialis ac monachi caeteri, Dic tu ipse, inquiunt illi, quomodo eo in loco legendum sit. Si, inquam, proprium sermonis genus quo usus est Apostolus, eiúsque sensum sequamur, ita legendum est: Talibus victimis Deus delectatur, aut gratas acceptásque habet: huiusmodi hostiae ei placent. Itaque Iudex Vilardus in novo Testamento Francisçani mox inspexit, atque ita esse ut ego dixeram comperit. Tum vero Pseudoprophetae illi vehementer perturbati fuerunt, tantóque pudore affecti, ut loqui non possent nec auderent homines alioqui audaces atque impudentes. Ego autem, fratres, vobis vere affirmare possum, me quum disputarem cum miseris huiusmodi hominibus, ita liberum, alacrem, paratumque fuisse, ut ad omnia quae mihi ab iis proponerentur, placidè comitèrque responderem. Illi vero erant plane consternati & attoniti. Alii caput demittebant, alii frendebant dentibus, quemadmodum ego facile videre poteram, inprimisque Franciscani ea in disputatione cum maxima animi indignatione, molestia & confusione versabantur. Ex quibus unus quaesiuit ex me, quid de confessione sentirem. Cui ego cum respondissem uni Deo confitendum esse, eosque locos quos ad probandam auricularem confessionem afferret, ut Iacobi Apostoli, non debere de ea intelligi aut exponi, sed potius de fraterna reconciliatione: miseri homines obmutuerunt. Tum Officialis, Equidem, amice, inquit, video ea quae isti ad te admonendum afferunt: sed tu in tuo errore obstinatus semper permanes. Quare cogita, quemadmodum res tua causaque se habeat. Tu vero, inquâ, optimè perspicis eas demonstrationes, argumenta, rationes quas undique afferunt, non valere ut me de eo quod affirmo, redarguant atque convincant, neque vero eos, quae à me secundum verbum Dei dicuntur, posse refellere ac refutare. quare ego non sum pertinax, neque ullo in errore: neque aliud quidquam affero quàm purum Dei verbum, quod ego usque ad ultimum vitae spiritum tueri paratus sum. Tum iussit ut ego in carcerem meum reducerer, ubi ego fui usq; ad diem Martis sequentem, qui dies decimus erat mensis Maij, Dominum orans, ut me ad causam suam defendendam virtute Spiritus sui confirmaret.
units.tr: When, in this debate I was having with that monk, the other men of the same stamp and shaving saw their great doctor so defeated, they tried instead to dismay me with their shouting, two or three of them now and then bawling out. One of them was a Franciscan, called Doctor Cumbanus, who attacked me in this way: "You say, the blessed Peter was not the head of the Church." "Certainly," I said. "But I prove the contrary: our Lord says to Peter, 'You are Simon, son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas.' Now, Cephas in Latin is called 'head.'" "From where," I said, "did you get this interpretation? John, indeed, interprets it differently in his Gospel, where in the first chapter he writes: 'You shall be called Cephas, which is translated Peter.'" Then the judge Vilardus took up the New Testament in his hand, to see whether that interpretation was as I had said; he found that it did not differ at all from my words. So the monk, with head bowed and overcome with shame, fell silent and utterly collapsed. Then the Dominican continued his interrupted speech in this way: "You, in your confession, say that man has no free will; but I prove the opposite. For it is written in the Gospel that a certain man, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers, by whom he was stripped and wounded, and left half dead. Thomas Aquinas, however, interprets that parable, proposed by the Lord, as referring to free will, which he says was wounded in part, but not so completely crushed and broken that no power at all of man remained." "I do not accept this interpretation at all," I said. "What," he said, "are you more learned than St Thomas?" "I do not claim so much for myself," I said, "as to say that I am more learned than he; but I deny that this parable should be explained in that way. Rather, the Lord Jesus proposed this example to commend to us the love which we ought to show and have towards our neighbour. As for free will, we have lost all its capacity and power, as I have declared in my confession. For we are altogether dead, and not dead in some part only, as the blessed Paul says. If we do well, that is not to be attributed to us, but to God, who works in us through his Spirit; who also, as the same Apostle testifies, makes us both will and accomplish. Thus God is the giver and the author of such will and capacity in us; we can claim it for ourselves by no right." "You say in your confession," he said, "that we are justified by faith alone." "Certainly," I said. "But I," he said, "prove that we are justified by works. We merit by works, therefore we are made righteous through them." "I deny your premise," I said. "Indeed, I prove that," he said, "the blessed Paul, in the last chapter of his Epistle to the Hebrews, says: 'Do not forget beneficence and fellowship, for with such sacrifices God is merited.' You see," he said, "that 'merited' means 'deserved'; therefore we merit by our works." "I deny," I said, "that this text reads so, if we wish to follow a true translation." Then the Official and the other monks said: "You yourself tell us how that place ought to be read." "If," I said, "we follow the proper manner of speaking which the Apostle used, and his sense, it should be read thus: 'God is delighted with such sacrifices, or holds them pleasing and acceptable; such offerings please him.'" So the judge Vilardus promptly looked into the New Testament of the Franciscan, and found that it was as I had said. Then indeed those false prophets were greatly disturbed, and were so overcome with shame that they could not speak, nor dared to, although otherwise they were bold and shameless men. But I, brethren, can truly affirm to you that when I was disputing with such wretched men, I was so free, cheerful and ready that I answered all that was put to me by them calmly and courteously. But they were plainly dismayed and astonished. Some hung their heads, others gnashed their teeth, as I could easily see; and especially the Franciscans were in that debate in the greatest indignation, distress and confusion of mind. One of them asked me what I thought of confession. When I replied that confession is to be made to God alone, and that the passages which they brought forward to prove auricular confession, such as those of the Apostle James, ought not to be understood or explained of it, but rather of brotherly reconciliation, those wretched men fell silent. Then the Official said: "Indeed, friend, I see what these men bring forward to admonish you; but you remain always obstinate in your error. Therefore consider how your affair and cause stand." "But you, indeed," I said, "clearly see that the demonstrations, arguments and reasons which they bring from every side are not enough to refute and convince me of what I affirm, nor can they refute or overthrow what is said by me according to the Word of God. Therefore I am not stubborn, nor in any error; nor do I offer anything but the pure Word of God, which I am ready to defend to my last breath of life." Then he ordered that I be led back to my prison, where I remained until the following Tuesday, which was the tenth day of May, praying to the Lord that he would strengthen me by the power of his Spirit to defend his cause.

units.la: Et quoniam in postremis disputationibus de sacramento Coenae nihil obiectum mihi fuerat, praeparaui me ut responderem ad ea quae ab illis dici atq; obiici possent contra ea quae ego in confessione mea professus sum. Qua in re Deus benignissimus voto meo ac desiderio respondit & satisfecit.
units.tr: Since nothing had been objected to me about the sacrament of the Supper in the last disputations, I prepared myself to answer whatever might be said and objected against the things I professed in my confession. In this matter, most gracious God answered and satisfied my prayer and desire.

units.la: Decimo igitur die Maij, eodemque Martis, circiter horam septimam ianitor me accersit ut ad Officialem adduceret, quocum etiam erat Officialis Primatius, ut vocant, primus in inimicis Iesu Christi infestissimúsque hostis: praeterea Clepicrius procurator, cum quibusdam aliis Antichristi administris, eiúsq; impiae sectae & causae defe[?] foribus[?] oribus: in quibus erat Dominicanus doctor, qui nostris interfuerat disputationibus, sed mecum congressus non erat. Cùm igitur ad eos essem productus, Amice, inquit Officialis, visne permanere in ea sententia & confessione, quam tu antea nobis edidisti? Sanè, inquam. nam ea quidem à me facta est ex verbo Dei, pro quo ego tuendo & vivere & mori paratus sum. Tum Dominicanus, Num credis, inquit, corpus Christi certa corporis locíque ratione in Sacramento inclusum? Minimè, inquam. nam verbum Dei nos docet cum esse in cælo, ibíque tandiu futurum quoad iudicaturus vivos & mortuos veniat. Atque hoc quidem unum fidei nostræ caput est, in quo credimus eum in cælū ascendisse, ac sedere ad Dei omnipotentis dexteram. Quare si Christus est in cælo, quòd ad ipsius humanitatem attinet, atque ibi, quemadmodum dicit S. Petrus, usque ad restitutionem omnium futurus est, non oportet in Sacramento eum quærere, quasi quodam in loco inferioris terræ inclusum. Iesus Christus, inquit, sumens panem dixit, Hoc est corpus meum. In pane ergo corpus est. Non ita est, inquam. Neque enim Christus dicere volebat cum panem quem discipulis suis dabat, suum esse corpus: sed signum eius tantùmodo. neque enim EST substantiue accipitur in sua propria significatione, ut naturam rei existentis significet: sed significationem rei significantis notat, genere sermonis in Script. usitato, quo nomen pro nomine accipitur, & ita signū nomine rei significatæ appellatur, aut contrà nomen signi cum re quâ significat, communicatur: ut in Genesi Dominus Circuncisionem fœdus suum esse dicit: neque tamen Circuncisio fœdus erat, sed signum ac sigillum fœderis, quemadmodum eo in libro nominatur: & à Paulo sigillum insitiæ Abraham dicitur. De agno etiam in Exodo scriptum est, eum esse Pascha, id est transitum Domini. Neque tamen agnus erat transitus: sed significatione rei præteritæ habebat illius prædaræ memorabilisque redemptionis, qua Deus populum suum ex Ægypto eduxerat. Itaque verbum substantivum EST his duobus locis pro Significat accipitur, præsertim cum sermo de Sacramentis est institutus. Tum monachus, Maxima, inquit differentia est inter Sacramenta veteris Testamenti, & noui. Neque enim Sacramenta veteris Testamenti gratiam conferebant, sicut ea quæ in nouo sunt instituta. Nec veteris, inquam, nec noui Testamenti sacramenta gratiam conferunt: sed solum eam a Iesu Christo in nos conferri ostendunt. Nam minister quidem tantummodo sacramenta nobis administrat: sed Iesus Christus virtute Spiritus sui gratias dat, easque communicat quae promissa nobis in Sacramentis proponuntur & repraesentatur. Patres, inquit, veteris testamenti, nonne eiusdem gratiae promissionumque participes fuerunt, quibus nos hodie participamus? Maxime, inquam. Nam Paulus ad Corinthios scribit, Patres veteri testamenti eundem nobiscum cibum spiritualem comedisse, eundemque potum bibisse spiritualem. Ex quo efficitur eandem gratiam nobiscum & promissiones iustitiae ac vitae communes habuisse per fidem, qua Christum ipsis promissum ac mutis signis praemonstratum expectarunt. Iesus Christus, inquit, in Euangelio Ioannis VI. cap. ita loquitur, Patres vestri in deserto comederunt manna & sunt mortui. ergo eiusdem gratiae nobiscum participes non fuerunt. Iesus Christus, inquam, eo in loco de iis loquitur qui man per fidem non acceperunt, symbolum & sacramentum eius panis, quem ipse de caelo missum ac viuificum largitur: sed non de iis loquitur qui fide illum cibum acceperunt, quo in numero fuit Moyses, Aaron, Iosue, Caleb, & alij pij qui sub illis figuris umbrisque veteris testamenti Christum venturum, quasi eminus aspexerunt. Nam de A-braham ipse Dominus dicit in Euangelio Ioannis, vidisse suum diem laetatumque fuisse. Abraham autem vidit Iesum Christum, non corporis, sed fidei oculis. Itaque dominus doctor tum magnopere erat perturbatus, atque ita incertus, ut quid ageret, aut quo se verteret plane nesciret. Et simulatque ego aliquot eius argumentum dissoluera[?], quaerebat semper aliquid, quo posset effugere, ne victus a me esse plane videretur, saepe me his verbis interpellans, Audi, amice, ne tatopere incalescas, neque ita clames: expecta parum, expecta. Ego, inquit, probo homines veteris testamenti, eius gratiae, cuius nos sumus, participes non fuisse. Diuus Paulus ait, Lex irain operatur: & alio loco, Quicunque sunt sub Lege, sub maledictione sunt. Quod si sub ira sunt & maledictione, sequitur eos gratiae nobis communicatae participes non suisse. Diuus Paulus, inquam, ostendit his locis, Legem non posse nos iustificare, propterea quod eam nemo praestare potest: atque omnes qui volunt olunt per eam coram Deo iusti esse, in iram Dei maledictionemque incurrere: sed ad Christum esse confugiendum, qui eam omnibus partibus complevit, perque fidem in ipsum ea nobis iustitiam donari, quae iustitiae Dei respondeat ac iudicio Dei satisfaciat. Itaque Lex iram efficit, nosque omnes condemnat, non natura sua quae ad vitam salutemque data est, sed culpa nostra, qui non possumus eam implere.
units.tr: On the tenth day of May, which was also a Tuesday, at about the seventh hour, the doorkeeper came to fetch me to lead me before the Official. With him was the Official Primatius, as they call him, the first among the enemies of Jesus Christ and his most hostile foe; besides him were the procurator Clepicrius and certain other servants of Antichrist, of his impious sect and cause, at the doors. Among them was a Dominican teacher who had been present at our disputations but had not met me in debate. When I had been brought before them, the Official said, "Friend, do you wish to remain in the opinion and confession that you previously published to us?" "Certainly," I said, "for it was made by me from the Word of God, for defending which I am prepared both to live and to die." Then the Dominican said, "Do you believe that the body of Christ is enclosed in the Sacrament in a definite manner of body and place?" "By no means," I said. For the Word of God teaches us that he is in heaven and will remain there until he comes to judge the living and the dead. And this is indeed one article of our faith, in which we believe that he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God Almighty. Therefore, if Christ is in heaven as regards his humanity, and is to remain there until the restoration of all things, as St Peter says, one ought not to seek him in the Sacrament, as if he were enclosed in some place of the lower earth." "Jesus Christ," he said, "taking bread, said, 'This is my body.' Therefore the body is in the bread." "It is not so," I said. For Christ did not mean, when he gave the bread to his disciples, that it was his body, but only its sign. The word "is" is not taken substantively in its proper meaning, to signify the nature of an existing thing; it marks the signification of the thing signifying, by a manner of speaking common in Scripture, in which the name of one thing is applied to another, so that the sign is called by the name of the thing signified, or the name of the sign is shared with the thing it signifies. Thus in Genesis the Lord says that circumcision is his covenant, yet circumcision was not the covenant but the sign and seal of the covenant, as that book itself names it; and by Paul it is called the seal of Abraham's righteousness. Also of the lamb in Exodus it is written that it is the Passover, that is, the passing over of the Lord; yet the lamb was not the passing over, but by signifying a past thing it carried the memory of that remarkable and glorious redemption by which God had led his people out of Egypt. Therefore the substantive verb "is" in these two places is taken for "signifies", especially since the discussion is about Sacraments." Then the monk said, "The difference between the Sacraments of the Old Testament and those of the New is very great, for the Sacraments of the Old Testament did not confer grace, as those instituted in the New do." "Neither the Sacraments of the Old Testament nor those of the New confer grace," I said, "but they only show that it is conferred upon us by Jesus Christ. For the minister only administers the Sacraments to us, but Jesus Christ by the power of his Spirit gives grace and communicates those things which are promised and represented to us in the Sacraments." "The fathers of the Old Testament," he said, "were they not partakers of the same grace and promises in which we partake today?" "Most certainly," I said. For Paul writes to the Corinthians that the fathers of the Old Testament ate the same spiritual food as we do and drank the same spiritual drink. From this it follows that they had the same grace as we do, and the promises of righteousness and life in common with us, through the faith by which they looked for Christ, who was promised to them and foreshown by dumb signs. "Jesus Christ," he said, "in the sixth chapter of John's Gospel speaks thus: 'Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and are dead.' Therefore they were not partakers of the same grace with us." "Jesus Christ," I said, "in that place speaks of those who did not receive the manna by faith, the symbol and sacrament of that bread which he himself, sent from heaven, gives as life-giving. He does not speak of those who received that food by faith, among whom were Moses, Aaron, Joshua, Caleb and other godly men who, under those figures and shadows of the Old Testament, saw Christ who was to come, as it were from afar. For the Lord himself says in John's Gospel of Abraham that he saw his day and rejoiced. Abraham, moreover, saw Jesus Christ not with the eyes of the body but with the eyes of faith." So the lord teacher was then greatly disturbed and so uncertain that he plainly did not know what to do or where to turn. And as soon as I had dissolved some of his argument, he always sought something by which he might escape, lest he seem plainly to be defeated by me, often interrupting me with these words: "Listen, friend, do not grow so heated, nor shout so. Wait a little, wait. I maintain that the men of the Old Testament were not partakers of that grace of which we are partakers. The divine Paul says, 'The law works wrath'; and in another place, 'Whoever are under the law are under the curse.' But if they are under wrath and curse, it follows that they were not partakers of the grace communicated to us." "The divine Paul, I said, shows in these places that the Law cannot justify us, because no one can fulfil it; and all who wish to be righteous before God through it incur the wrath and curse of God, but must flee to Christ, who has fulfilled it in every part, and through faith in whom that righteousness is given to us which answers to the righteousness of God and satisfies the judgment of God. Therefore the Law produces wrath and condemns us all, not by its own nature, which was given for life and salvation, but by our fault, since we cannot fulfil it."

units.la: Patres autem veteris testamenti videmus iustitiam non in Lege quaesuisse, sed in Christo Iesu, qui ipsius Legis finis est, in quem ipsi crediderunt.
