The nature of a sign, however, shows that one thing is what signifies and another thing is what is signified by it: the sign is that which is visible and falls under the senses, while the thing itself is entirely different in nature and substance, although it has some similar relation to its sign. Therefore, just as the water in Baptism is not converted into the blood of Christ, by which we are washed, so the bread in the Supper cannot be converted into the flesh of Christ, since the reason of both sacraments is the same, and the nature of all signs and symbols of this kind is such that, by reason of their substance, they are distinguished from those things for which they are used to signify and represent. But that impious custom and sacrilegious audacity, by which they have diminished the Lord's Supper and deprived the laity of the one part, I can in no way approve. For it conflicts with the institution of the Lord, who willed that all should drink from the same cup, and with the testimony of Paul, who says that he had delivered to the Corinthians the manner of celebrating the Supper just as he had received it from the Lord. For the Lord willed that his whole communion be shown by both kinds of signs set before us. Therefore, that we may be partakers of the body and blood of Christ, it is not at all necessary that they be enclosed in these elements. For although the body of Christ is in heaven, yet by faith, which perceives and grasps absent things, and by the power of the Spirit, who joins together things that are separated by a long distance, we can truly partake of it. These words, "This is my body," are therefore to be understood figuratively, just as the Lamb is called "the Passover of the Lord," and the Rock is called "Christ," since they were only signs of those things, of which they either renewed the memory of things past, or by some notable signification foreshowed the hope of things to come. As for the Mass, which they say was instituted by Christ, and is a sacrifice profitable both for the living and the dead, I say that this is false and wholly contrary to the Word of God. For the very institution of Jesus Christ admonishes and commands something else, namely that we eat and drink, not that we offer him to God in sacrifice. Next, this office of offering pertains to no mortal man, but is the proper work of Christ alone, by which he is most holy, since, as the Apostle says, he offered himself once, and by one offering sanctified his own for ever; and once this sanctification is accomplished, no other offering remains. For it was for this reason that he was appointed priest according to the order of Melchisedec, so that he should have no companion or successor in this office and honour. Thus Christ Jesus is stripped of the supreme dignity of the priesthood, when the right of sacrificing is transferred to others, so that they may be permitted to repeat, renew, or confirm that sacrifice and apply it to others. Finally, as the Apostle says, no one ought to take this honour upon himself unless he is called by God. But we do not read that any other besides Christ was called to that dignity. Moreover, since the promise contained in these words, "This is my body which is given for you," is offered only to those who partake of the sacrament, its benefit and power cannot pertain to the dead, who no longer belong to that communion. Add also that the fruit of that Mass, which they want to reach the dead, consists in Purgatory, a most empty invention and fiction of men, contrary to every word of God, in which we read of no other purgation than the blood of Jesus Christ. These are my views and beliefs on those heads of faith and religion which are today in controversy; in which you can easily see that I bring forward nothing of my own wit or invention, but, by the grace which God has bestowed upon me, I approve all things by the authority of his Word. But if, neglecting and rejecting these things, you are working to prove me a heretic, as I was earlier declared by you, then consider how dangerous it is to proceed in this way against one who sets before you the pure Word of God. But I commend the whole cause of the truth to God, the author of my calling, and entrust it to his faith, praying him to grant me patience and constancy, with a mind not only calm but even willing to endure all that he has willed me to suffer for his name, to whom be honour and glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: Epistola eiusdem Bernardi Seguini, quam misit ad quendam amicum suum de memorabili admirabilisque conuersione latronis Ioannis Chamboni appellati qui cum in horrendis tum corporis tum animi tenebris inclusus, laetum Euangelii nuntium audiuisset, ad veram Dei cognitionem, poenitentiam, fidemque Iesu Christi opera Petri Bergerii, tum ob Euangelium captiui (vt postea suo loco dicetur) conuersus est.
units.tr: A letter of the same Bernard Seguin, which he sent to a certain friend of his concerning the memorable and wonderful conversion of the robber called John Chambon, who, shut up in the dreadful darkness both of body and of mind, heard the joyful message of the Gospel, and was converted to the true knowledge of God, to repentance, and to faith in Jesus Christ, through the work of Peter Berger, himself also a prisoner for the Gospel (as will be told in its place later).

units.la: Ex his literis, frater charissime, poteris intelligere cum cuius causa nos in his vinculis sumus, co nos sensu fauoris amorisque paterni afficere, vt cum omnia quae ad sublevandam corporis necessitatem pertinent, cumulate ab eo suppeditentur, nihil praeter consolationem atque confirmationem animi desideremus. Non quòd hac in parte eius ope destituamur, qui testem Deum adhibere possumus earum consolationum, quas ex eo tempore, quo ipse nobis os ad sanctum nomen suum confitendum aperuit, incredibiles accepimus: sed quòd oportet nos magis ac magis confirmari, armisque huiusmodi muniri, quibus gravissimos impetus eius hostis repellamus, cum quo nobis dimicandum est. Neque enim possumus unquam satis esse muniti & parati adversus inimicum, cum praesertim qui non potentia modo, sed etiam astutia omnique calliditate praeditus, ac mille nocendi artibus instructus nos oppugnat, ut summa nobis cautio sit adhibenda, ne imparati, atque armis Spiritus ac verbi destituti subito ab eo opprimamur.
units.tr: From these letters, dearest brother, you will be able to understand with what feeling of fatherly favour and love he regards us, for whose sake we are in these chains: since everything that pertains to relieving the needs of the body is supplied to us abundantly by him, we desire nothing but consolation and confirmation of mind. Not that we are deprived of his help in this respect, for we can call God to witness of those consolations which, from the time when he opened our mouths to confess his holy name, we have received beyond belief; but rather that we ought to be more and more strengthened and armed with such weapons as will enable us to repel the most grievous assaults of that enemy with whom we must contend. For we can never be sufficiently fortified and prepared against an adversary who attacks us, endowed not only with power but also with cunning and every craft, and equipped with a thousand arts of harming; so that we must exercise the greatest caution, lest we be suddenly overwhelmed by him, unprepared and destitute of the weapons of the Spirit and of the Word.

units.la: Itaque praecipuum nostrum officium est, ut dum inducias habemus nobis datas, nos etiam atque etiam magis confirmemus, ut cum hostilis impetus, cuius diem horamque nescimus, ingruerit, eum possimus magno ac forti animo excipere ac sustinere, atque etiam victoriam obtinere. Hoc autem assequemur, non virtute nostra freti, quae hoc in genere nulla est, sed ope illius adiuti ac planè moniti, qui gravissimum suum inimicum atque nostrum superavit, de eoque triumphavit: ut nos quoque cum eodem adversario dimicantes, in eius victoriae societatem veniremus.
units.tr: Therefore our chief duty, while the truce granted us lasts, is to strengthen ourselves more and more, so that when the hostile attack comes, on a day and at an hour we do not know, we may receive and withstand it with a great and brave spirit, and even win the victory. We shall achieve this not by trusting in our own strength, which in such a matter is nothing, but by being helped and plainly guided by him who overcame his and our most grievous enemy and triumphed over him, so that we too, fighting with the same adversary, may share in his victory.

units.la: Hac igitur praediti virtute armisque ducis ac regis nostri Iesu Christi instructi confidimus nos, ut Dauid confecit Goliath gigantem ingenti corporis magnitudine ac robore praeditum, ita gigantes istos devicturos, qui bellum audent suscipere ac gerere adversus eum, qui eos usque in profundum inferorum solo nutu verboque suo potest deicere: cum ipsius membra tanto surore persequantur. Qua in re de nobis quidem nihil promittere debemus: sed nostra considerantes imbecillitatem, cum timore ac tremore in hoc certamine versari. Tametsi hactenus steterimus, firmíque atque invicti adversus omnes inimici conatus impetusque fuerimus, tamen cum verbo Dei, tum exemplo multorum qui hac in causa indignè inimico cesserunt, admonemur ut nobis ipsis diffidentes, nos in eius fidem totos permittamus, qui nos ad testificandam & tuendam veritatem suam vocavit.
units.tr: Armed with this virtue and with the weapons of our leader and king, Jesus Christ, we are confident that, as David overcame the giant Goliath, who was endowed with great bodily size and strength, so we shall conquer those giants who dare to undertake and wage war against him who can cast them down into the depths of hell by a mere nod or word, since they pursue his members with such fury. In this matter we ought to promise nothing on our own account, but, considering our weakness, we should live in fear and trembling in this struggle. Although hitherto we have stood firm, and have been steadfast and invincible against all the enemy's attempts and assaults, nevertheless, both by the word of God and by the example of many who in this cause have shamefully given way to the enemy, we are admonished to distrust ourselves and to commit ourselves wholly to his faith, who has called us to bear witness to and defend his truth.

units.la: Si igitur infirmitatem nostram consideremus, nihil aliud quàm versari in metu possumus, ne vincamur ab eo qui hactenus nihil aduersus nos potuit. Si vero oculos nostros conuertamus in eum qui hanc veritatis suae causam nobis commisit, in eaque defendenda opem suam nobis ita promisit, ut non adiutor modo ac propugnator, sed etiam vindex & liberator futurus sit, confidamus nos constantiam usque in finem retenturos, & omnia incommoda, difficultates, periculaque superaturos. Nam cum is promiserit se affuturum iis omnibus qui calamitatum magnitudine oppressi ad eius misericordiam confugiet, eumque invocabunt freti gratia eius in quo uno optimus Pater sibi complacuit, cumque inprimis huiusmodi opem ac liberationem promiserit iis, qui propter nomen verbumque ipsius patientur, non est cur diffidamus, aut de optimo huius causae ac dimicationis nostrae exitu dubitemus ac desperemus. Idem enim est in nos futurus, qui semper fuit, aequitatis, iustitiae, ac veritatis studiosus, memorque eorum quae promisit. Eius quidem fidei, iustitiae, bonitatis illustre iam documentum dedit in iis omnibus qui eius virtute opeque confisi, constanter ipsius nomen sunt confessi: quos quidem etiam in gravissimis tormentis ea animi magnitudine ac robore sepsit & firmavit, ut adversus omnes inimicos victores reddiderit. Quare idem in nobis quoque effectum speramus, cum ipse nos ad hunc tantum honorem vocaverit, ut coram principibus ac sapientibus huius mundi, testes veritatis suae simus, eamque adversus omnem hominum iniuriam, mendacium, calumniamque defendamus. Haec Dei authoritas & optima voluntas, & ipsius causae aequitas ac summa dignitas, nobis maximam in his afflictionibus consolationem afferre debet. Cum autem multa & gravia sint verbi Dei testimonia, quae hac quidem in parte & causa certissimum eius auxilium nobis promittunt, tum vero non ita diu benignissimus ac fidelissimus Dominus, praeclarum & memorabile exemplum nobis proposuit, & quotidie proponit, in quo ipse nobis & gravissimum veritatis suae testimonium, & suavissimum in his vinculis aerumnisque solatium, & vero certissimum quoddam pignus suae perpetuae defensionis salutisque dare voluit. Res autem huiusmodi est. Quidam homo iuuenis, in eodem carcere cum fratre nostro Petro Bergiero induscus constrictusque habetur, accusatus quod duos aut tres abhinc annos latrocinia quaedam exercuerit, atque pannum holosericum ricū in itinere cuidam mercatori per vim eripuerit. Quam ob causam decem iam sunt menses, ex quo in carcere tum pedibus tum manibus cõstrictus fuit, vt se mouere nullo modo posset, aliáq; in calamitate ac fœditate pædoris iaceret, quæ honestè dici commemorarique nõ potest.
units.tr: If, then, we consider our weakness, we can do nothing but live in fear, lest we be overcome by him who has so far been unable to do anything against us. But if we turn our eyes to him who has entrusted us with this cause of his truth, and who has promised us his help in defending it, not only as helper and champion but also as avenger and deliverer, we may be confident that we shall hold to our constancy to the end and overcome all troubles, difficulties and dangers. For since he has promised to be present with all those who, oppressed by the greatness of their calamities, flee to his mercy and call upon him, trusting in the grace of him in whom alone the best Father is well pleased, and since he has especially promised such help and deliverance to those who suffer for his name and word, there is no reason for us to distrust him, or to doubt or despair of the best outcome of this cause and of our struggle. For he will be toward us what he has always been, a lover of equity, justice and truth, and mindful of what he has promised. He has already given a remarkable proof of his faithfulness, justice and goodness in all those who, trusting in his power and help, have constantly confessed his name; these he so fortified and strengthened, even in the most severe torments, with such greatness and firmness of spirit, that they were made victors over all their enemies. Therefore we hope that the same will be done in us also, since he has called us to such an honour that we should be witnesses of his truth before the princes and wise men of this world, and defend it against all the injury, lies and calumny of men. This authority and best will of God, and the justice and great worth of his cause, ought to bring us the greatest consolation in these afflictions. Now, although there are many weighty testimonies of God's word which in this matter and cause promise us his most certain help, yet the most kind and faithful Lord has not long ago set before us, and daily sets before us, a notable and memorable example, in which he wished to give us both a most weighty witness of his truth, a most sweet consolation in these chains and distresses, and, as it were, a most certain pledge of his perpetual defence and salvation. The matter is of this kind. A certain young man, who was locked up and bound in the same prison as our brother Peter Bergier, is accused of having carried out certain robberies two or three years ago, and of having violently seized a rich silk cloth from a merchant on the road. For this reason, it is now ten months since he was bound in the prison, both feet and hands, so that he cannot move at all, and he lies in a state of misery and filth that cannot decently be described or related.

units.la: Eo autem tepore, quo Petrus Bergierus in ea carceris parte fuit, pro opportunitate quam Deus ei dederat vt hominem consolaretur, illum miserum ærumnosúmque sæpius compellauit. cuius quidem fidei atq; opportuna opera Deus ita est vsus, vt infelix homo, qui omne vitæ suæ tempus ad Deum maleficijs suis dedecorandum cõtulerat, ob quæ etiam in tam arcta acerbáque captivitate tenebatur, ad agnitionem Iesu Christi saluatoris sui conuersus fuerit. cuius quidem cognita in miseros peccatores misericordia, eam animo consolationem accepit, vt pro eo quod antea & Deum & parentes à quibus esset natus, & diem horámque ortus sui execraretur, maiestatem Creatoris sui contumelijs lædens perpe-tuis propter grauissima tormenta in quibus versabatur: nunc perpetuas ei gratias agat quòd ipsum ad cognitionem peccatorum suorum, atque spem salutis vocauerit: toto autem animi sensu summa cũ humilitate sua peccata recognoscat, seipsum graviter accusans coram Deo, patienterq; perferens ea tormenta, in quibus adhuc grauibus est: tametsi Dominus ea illi nonnihil alleuarit. Itaq; vt primum de illius conuersione à fratre nostro Bergiero certiores facti fuimus, officium ei nostrum quantum possumus, præstamus, vt pro exigua gratia quâ Dominus nobis impertiuit, eum consolemur. Nam ipse vt hoc faceremus, à nobis per literas cõtédit, quas manu sua ad nos scripsit, quanuis manus cõstrictas habeat. Petiit etiã vt si aliquê librû habemus ad cõsolandũ accõmodatũ, ipsi eum mittamus. Et quoniã metuit ne breui supplicio affligatur, consilium quoq; à nobis petiit quê admodũ in ipso supplicio suscipiendo se gerere debeat: ne quid contra verbũ Dei faciat, cuius gratia singulari ad cognitionem eius vocatus sit. De eo nos, Deo adiuante nostrâ sententia ad eũ perscribemus, quid nobis pro intelligetia sacrae Scripturæ quâ habemus, videatur. Ego autem hac in re tibi narrãda diutius immoror eò quòd in ea extat summũ Dei miraculum ac exemplum memorandum, dignumq; quod ad omnem posteritatê perferatur. Nos quidem hoc eius exemplo, magnopere in gratia Dei nostri authorisque huius nostræ vocationis confirmamur. Nam si Deus ita benignè clementérque cum hoc misero latrone agit, quomodo cum ijs actúrus est quorum opera ad tuendam verbi sui veritatem vti vult? Te etiam atq; etiam vehementer rogo, vt si habes aliquem librum, qui idoneam & afflictis hominibus opportunam consolationem complectatur, eum ad nos mittas: vt eum huic captiuo consolando, atque in gratia Dei confirmando dare possimus. Illud postremò à te peto, vt tu nostri in precibus tuis memor sis, sicut nos in nostris eam memoriam benevolentiæ quam debemus, tibi præstamus. Is cuius sine voluntate & prouidentia nihil fit, qui se & mihi & tibi patefecit, nos in tutela & protectione sua perpetuò habeat & custodiat, quoad in regnum ipsius cæleste recipiamur. XI. Febr. anno M.D.LIII.
units.tr: At the time when Peter Bergier was in that part of the prison, he, using the opportunity which God had given him to console the man, often addressed the wretched and afflicted fellow. God so used the faithful and timely labour of Bergier that the unhappy man, who had devoted all the time of his life to dishonouring God by his crimes, for which he was also held in such narrow and bitter captivity, was converted to the knowledge of Jesus Christ his Saviour. Having recognised the mercy of God toward miserable sinners, he received such consolation of mind that, whereas before he had cursed both God and the parents from whom he was born, and the day and hour of his birth, offending the majesty of his Creator with constant insults amid the very great torments in which he was placed, he now gives perpetual thanks to God that he has called him to the knowledge of his sins and to the hope of salvation. With his whole heart and in great humility he acknowledges his sins, grievously accusing himself before God, and patiently bearing those torments in which he is still heavily afflicted, although the Lord has somewhat lightened them for him. So, as soon as we were informed by our brother Bergier of his conversion, we have performed our duty to him as far as we can, so that we may console him with the small measure of grace which the Lord has bestowed upon us. For he himself asked us, by letter, to do this, which he wrote to us with his own hand, although his hands are bound. He also asked that, if we have any book suited to consolation, we should send it to him. And since he fears that he may soon be afflicted with execution, he also asked us for advice on how he ought to conduct himself in undergoing that punishment, so that he may do nothing against the word of God, to whose knowledge he has been called by such singular grace. Concerning this, with God's help, we shall write to him our opinion, as far as the understanding of Holy Scripture that we have seems to allow. But I am lingering longer on this matter for you, because in it there is a supreme miracle of God and a memorable example, worthy to be handed down to all posterity. We ourselves are greatly strengthened by this example in the grace of our God and in the authority of this our calling. For if God deals so kindly and mercifully with this wretched thief, how will he deal with those whose work he wishes to use for defending the truth of his word? I also earnestly and urgently beg you, that if you have any book which contains a suitable and fitting consolation for afflicted men, you send it to us, so that we may give it to this captive, to console him and confirm him in the grace of God. Finally, I ask you this: that you be mindful of us in your prayers, as we, for our part, keep the same remembrance of you in ours, with the goodwill we owe you. May he, without whose will and providence nothing happens, who has revealed himself to me and to you, keep and guard us always in his protection and care, until we are received into his heavenly kingdom. 11 February 1553.

units.la: Epistola ad eum Chambonum consolandum, cùm is in grauissima corporis afflictione carceri inclusus esset, scripta à Petro Scriba: & nomine cæterorum sociorum eius ac captiuorum missa: quæ quidem ostendit eam curam & solicitudinem, quæ illi etiam in suis vinculis de eo misero peccatore ad Dominum conuerso susceptâ habebant.
units.tr: The letter, written by Peter Scriba, was sent in the name of his fellow prisoners and of the others who were captives with him, to console Chambon, who was shut up in prison in very grievous bodily affliction. It shows the care and concern that they, even in their own chains, felt for this wretched sinner who had been converted to the Lord.

units.la: Andiu nihil literarum ad te misimus, frater charissime, impeditì certis quibusdam rebus nostris, in quibus ratio fidei nostræ nobis coram aduersarijs declaranda fuit. Deinde quòd videbamus fratrem nostrum Petrum Bergerium, qui propter Euangelium captiuus est, eum in locum carceris missum fuisse ac seclusum, vt nihil tecum communicare posset, nec literas ad te sine maxima difficultate periculóque mittere. Sed tamen gratissimum iucundissimúmque nobis fuit, cùm ex Bergerio summam tuam constantiâ intelleximus, & consolationem quam Dominus virtute Spiritus sui in his grauissimis vinculis ærumnijsque tuis tibi impertit: quam etiam ex ea epistola, quam ad ipsum Bergerium scripsisti, cognouimus: cùm is eam nobis misisset tu consolationis nostræ causa, tum vt cognosceremus eam fidem atque spem quam in Deo habes, & summam afflictionem quam tu istis cõpedibus ac vinculis constrictus magna cum patientia perfers. Itaque hæ tuæ literæ, frater charissime, maximam nobis in his vinculis nostris consolationem attulerunt, in quibus admirabilem Dei, te ita consolantis confirmantisque gratiam perspeximus. Nec verò minorem molestiam dolorémque accepimus ex ista tua grauissima ærumna diuturnáque captiuitate, in qua ita constrictus atque afflictus teneris, tormentáque istorum vinculorū & compedum, vt eiusdē corporis mebra, in nobisipsis sensimus. Etsi nos à te disiuncti sumus, cū loci interuallo, quo maximè discludimur, tum etiam ratione causæ propter quam nos patimur, quæ cum tua maximam habet dissimilitudinem: vinculum tamen fidei & charitatis quo in Christo Iesu quasi membra eiusdem corporis coniuncti sumus, filiique vnius Dei patrisque habemur, facit vt istorum vinculorum quibus tu grauiter affligeris, participes sumus quasi nos eodem in loco inclusi acerrimé constricti tenerenur. Itaque congemiscimus & condolemus quodam ærumnarum tuarum sensu affecti. Deumque ac Patrem omnis misericordiæ oramus, vt te Spiritu suo confirmet, quo patienter atque humiliter istas pœnas salu-tares, castigationesque paternas perferre possis, te æquo ac mansueto animo ei submittens, à quo vt ab optimo parente castigaris. Cogita, frater, cogita hanc manum esse Patris cælestis, qua in hoc mundo corrigeris, ad eumque clementer reuocaris, ne in altero ab eo abiectus damnatúsque intereas. Cogita te nunc ab ipso diligi amore quodam singulari: etiam tum, vt ait Paulus, dilectum fuisse, cùm esses eius inimicus. neque enim Filio suo vnigenito pepercit: sed eum pro tuis nostrisque peccatis morti crucis ignominiosæ acerbæque exposuit. O admiranda bonitatem, misericordiam, charitatem, quam humanissimus Deus erga nos in morte Filij sui Iesu Christi declarauit & præstitit: in qua vna est certa consolatio & salus omnibus afflictis calamitosisque peccatoribus proposita, qui eam quidem vera fide amplecti volunt. Etenim Christus morte sua mortem ac diabolum eius authorem vicit, effecitque vt ea quæ terribilis ac formidabilis est ijs qui in Christum eiusque Euangelium non credunt, iam non formidada & pertimescenda sit: sed potius vt via ad vitam æternam & beatam expetenda atque amplectenda. Morte sua Iesus Christus omne maledictionem exitiosúmque terrorem à morte abstulit, atque omne gratiam, benedictionem cælestémque lætitiam in eam effudit: ita vt Filij Dei solatia gaudiáque amplissima reperiant in ea, & sentiant: neque vllo periculi metu territi vnquam à via proposita deflectant, scientes eam esse finem miseriarum omnium, atque ostiū & felicem introitum ad eam vitam sempiternam, quæ ipsis morte Filij Dei parta est. Et quanuis carceribus inclusi, ac vinculis, compedibus, catenisque ferreis constricti, multa gravia acerbaque patiantur, tamen mortis et crucis Christi participes, sentiunt ea suavissima beatissimae vitae solatia et gaudia, quibus Christus huiusmodi aerumnas expertus atque perpessus, omnes fidelium aegritudines, acerbitatesque aspergit: ita ut si magnae sint in eo afflictiones, maiores tamen atque uberiores in eodem consolationes reperiantur. Nam Filius Dei, Dominus gloriae, et caeli terraeque rex, omni iustitia, sanctitate, innocentia praeditus, in manus hominum impiorum traditus est, ligatus vinculisque, atque ita ut homo omnium sceleratissimus coram magistratibus, principibusque productus, irrisus, consputus, caesus colaphis et flagellatus, coronaque donatus spinea, omnia quae dici aut cogitari possunt acerbissima atque indignissima tormenta opprobriaque pertulit, primum ut filios Dei vinculis Diaboli, peccati ac mortis, quibus constricti tenebantur, solveret, carceribusque inferorum, ad quos propter ipsorum peccata in aeternum damnati erant, liberaret: deinde ut omnes carceres, opprobria, afflictiones, gratia, benedictione, gloriaque sua afficeret: in quibus quidem filij Dei, sive pro verbo eius confitendo tuendoque eas suscipiant, sive etiam pro suis peccatis perferant, vehementius laetantur et gloriantur, quam principes ac reges huius mundi in amplissimis diutes [?] opibus, honoribus, deliciis ac voluptatibus gaudere solent. Huiusmodi enim carceres, vincula et compedes sunt quaedam schola disciplinaque fidelium ac piorum hominum, in qua ipsi in vera Dei cognitione instituuntur, atque ipso usu vitae suae, gratiam et misericordiam eius experiuntur, eamque opem et consolationem quam Spiritus sanctus huius schola optimus magister eis affert. In hac schola filij Dei bonis ijs gaudijs perfruuntur, quae nullis verbis exprimi, ne cogitatione quidem comprehendi possunt, cum interim diutes ac potentes huius mundi homines, qui praeclaras magnificasque aedes sibi parauerunt, in lachrymis saepe et summis animi angoribus versentur, omnique consolatione destituatur propter ea conscientiae tormenta, quae sensus irae vindictaeque Diuinae ex cogitatione vitae anteactae ac timore mortis futurae susceptus eis affert. In hac schola fideles homines peccata in tota vita contra maiestatem Dei admissa serio recognoscunt, gemunt damántque ad misericordem Deum, ab eo veniam peccatorum petentes suorum. Dominus vero eorum gemitus questúsque intelligens, atque ærumnas & miserias perspiciens, ipsos exaudit, ac per Spiritum sanctum ad æternam consolationem omnibus fidelibus promissum, iis cælestibus gaudiis afficit atque perfundit, quorum magnitudo & suavitas omnem dolorum cruciatuumque acerbitatem non solum mitigat, sed etiam plane absorbet. Hoc autem nos, qui nomine verbi Dei captivi sumus, in nobisipsis experti fuimus, teque idem experiri intelligimus. Quanvis enim non eadem sit causa tua quæ nostra, quanvis tu inhumaniter ac crudeliter tractaris in carcere: tamen Pater tuus cælestis, qui prope te est, qui in corde tuo per Spiritum suum habitat, non permittit ut à magnitudine afflictionis opprimaris, gravíusque tenteris quàm ferre possis: sed te virtute sua confirmat, consolatur, animumque tuum ea explet tum gratiæ suæ salutisque fiducia, tum Spiritus sancti lætitia, quasensus istorum gravissimorum tormentorum minuitur ac mitigatur. Si tu nunc quidem à mundo prorsus es abiectus, atque omni humana tum ope tum consolatione destitutus, Deus tamen pater tuus te ut charissimum libentissimè humanissimèque suscipit, commendatum atque gratum ea fide & spe quam in Filio eius Iesu Christo salvatore nostro omnem fixisti ac locasti. Tua quidem causa, ut tu ipse confiteris, est iniqua & iniusta: sed iustitia Christi, atque summa obedientia qua Dei iudicio pro nobis passus ac moriens satisfecit, facit ut totius causæ tuæ iniquitas tibi condonetur, atque in cōspectu Dei planè deleatur. Quare confide gaudéque in Christo Domino, tibíque persuade, eius iustitiam, sanctitatem, innocentiam tuam esse: usque causa & gratia te nunc à Patre cælesti in numerum filiorum ipsiꝰ recipi. nulla igitur carceris afflictionisque diuturnitas atque acerbitas minu tuum infringat, mæroreque cōficiat, sed tu potius in istis acerbitatibus, gratia, ope, beneuolentia Dei fretꝰ & cōfisus, summa constantia patientiámq; adhibeas atque retineas, ante oculos semper tibi proponés eam vitam quæ morte Filij Dei parta, in cælo tibi asseruatur, in qua ppetuò cū Deo iucundissimè ac beatissimè vivitur es. Cōsidera afflictione in qua tu nunc versaris, breue esse & momentanea, consolationè vero ac leuitá tibi promissa nullum vnquam finem habitura. quòd si tu molestè fers te non diligentius sacris literis studuisse, in isque magis versatum esse, sic habeto, te tum denique perfectam omnium rerum cognitionem habituram, cùm Dominus te apud se in illam lucem cælestem, quæ nullis tenebris perfusa est, collegerit. Ne igitur ea res, aut vlla alia animum tuum affligat: voluntatem potius Dei cum omni patientia, atque æquitate animi expectā. Si enim Dominus voluerit te, vt ei seruias, in ista adhuc vita retinere, tibi persuade eum contra omne spem liberaturum: sin te vult ad se ex hoc malo & misero mundo euocare: gaude eius rei nomine, atque ei pro tanto beneficio maximas gratias age. Nam hoc quidem modo beatior futurus es quàm si in hac vita remaneres. Te igitur in omnem para euentum: sed in eum, qui te potius ad salutare ac felicem mortem vocet, quàm in hac vita retineat. Neque verò te pudeat in ipsa morte Christum Dominum confiteri, eiusque virtute munitus sathanâ atque omnes eius administros forti animo repellas. Cõfitere, inquam, Christum Iesum saluatorem ac redemptorē tuum esse, eumque pro tuis peccatis mortuum: quorū nulla magnitudo gratiam eius tam certam & illustrem in Euangelio promissam impedire nec debet nec potest. misericordia enim Dei per eum declarata, sua magnitudine illa longè superat. Si tibi aliqua in corpore tuo pœnarum tormenta sunt perferenda, ne ob ea perturberis: sed in cælum caput attolle, atque spiritum tuum Deo commenda, fidelissimo custodi, exemplo Christi ducis nostri qui ipse suum moriens in manus optimi Patris tradidit: neque dubites quin in hæreditatem regni sui sit recepturus.
units.tr: We have sent you no letter for some time, dearest brother, being hindered by certain matters of our own, in which we had to give an account of our faith before our adversaries. Then, too, we saw that our brother Peter Bergerius, who is a prisoner for the sake of the Gospel, had been sent to a place of confinement and shut away so that he could communicate nothing with you, and could not send letters to you without the greatest difficulty and danger. Yet it was most welcome and most pleasing to us when we learned from Bergerius of your great constancy, and of the consolation which the Lord, by the power of his Spirit, bestows on you in these most grievous chains and hardships. We learned this also from the letter you wrote to Bergerius himself, which he sent to us, partly for our comfort, and partly so that we might know the faith and hope you have in God, and the great affliction which you bear with much patience, bound with these fetters and chains. So this letter of yours, dearest brother, has brought us the greatest comfort in our own chains, in which we have seen the wonderful grace of God, who so consoles and strengthens you. Nor have we received less distress and sorrow from this your most grievous hardship and long captivity, in which you are held so bound and afflicted, and from the torments of these chains and fetters, which we have felt as the limbs of the same body. Although we are separated from you, both by the distance that keeps us apart and by the nature of the cause for which we suffer, which is very different from yours, yet the bond of faith and love, by which we are joined in Christ Jesus as members of the same body, and are counted sons of one God and Father, makes us sharers in these chains with which you are so heavily burdened, as though we too were shut up in the same place and held in the tightest bonds. And so we groan with you and grieve with you, affected by a certain feeling of your troubles. We pray to God the Father of all mercy that he may strengthen you by his Spirit, so that you may bear these saving punishments and fatherly chastisements patiently and humbly, submitting yourself to him with an even and gentle mind, since it is he who chastises you as the best of parents. Consider, brother, consider that this is the hand of the heavenly Father by which you are corrected in this world, and by which you are mercifully called back to him, so that you may not perish cast away and condemned by him in the next. Consider that you are now loved by him with a singular love, and that, as Paul says, you were loved even when you were his enemy. For he did not spare his only-begotten Son, but gave him up to a shameful and bitter death on the cross for your sins and ours. O wonderful goodness, mercy and love, which the most kind God has shown and bestowed upon us in the death of his Son Jesus Christ! In this alone is a sure comfort and salvation set before all who are afflicted and all sinners in distress, who are willing to embrace it with true faith. For Christ by his death has conquered death and the devil, its author, and has brought it about that death, which is terrible and fearful to those who do not believe in Christ and his Gospel, should no longer be feared and dreaded, but rather sought and embraced as the way to eternal and blessed life. By his death Jesus Christ has taken from death every curse and dreadful terror, and has poured into it every grace, blessing and heavenly joy, so that the children of God find and feel in it their greatest consolations and joys, and, never frightened by any fear of danger, they do not turn aside from the way set before them, knowing that it is the end of all miseries, and the gate and happy entrance into that eternal life which was won for them by the death of the Son of God. And although they are shut up in prisons, and bound with chains, fetters and iron bonds, and suffer many grievous and bitter things, yet, being partakers of the death and cross of Christ, they feel those most sweet consolations and joys of the most blessed life, with which Christ, who has himself experienced and suffered such hardships, sprinkles all the sorrows and bitternesses of the faithful; so that if their afflictions in him are great, still greater and richer consolations are found in the same. For the Son of God, the Lord of glory and king of heaven and earth, endowed with all righteousness, holiness and innocence, was delivered into the hands of wicked men, bound and fettered, and was led before magistrates and princes as the most wicked of all men, mocked, spat upon, struck with fists and scourged, and crowned with a crown of thorns; and he endured all the most bitter and undeserved torments and reproaches that can be said or thought. He did this first to loose the children of God from the bonds of the devil, of sin and of death, by which they were held fast, and to free them from the prisons of hell, to which they had been condemned for ever on account of their sins; and then to endow all their prisons, reproaches, afflictions, with his grace, blessing and glory. In these the children of God, whether they undergo them for confessing and defending his word, or bear them for their own sins, rejoice and glory more vehemently than the princes and kings of this world are wont to rejoice in the abundant riches, honours, delights and pleasures of their great wealth. For such prisons, bonds and fetters are a kind of school and discipline for the faithful and pious, in which they are taught the true knowledge of God, and by the very experience of their life they learn his grace and mercy, and that help and consolation which the Holy Spirit, the best master of this school, brings to them. In this school the children of God enjoy those good joys which cannot be expressed in any words, nor even grasped by thought; while meanwhile the rich and powerful men of this world, who have prepared for themselves splendid and magnificent houses, often live in tears and the greatest anguish of mind, and are deprived of all comfort because of those torments of conscience which the sense of divine anger and vengeance, arising from thought of their past life and fear of death to come, brings to them. In this school the faithful recognise seriously the sins committed against the majesty of God throughout their whole life, they groan and condemn themselves before the merciful God, asking from him forgiveness of their sins. But the Lord, understanding their groans and complaints, and seeing their troubles and miseries, hears them, and through the Holy Spirit, the eternal consolation promised to all the faithful, he fills and overwhelms them with those heavenly joys, whose greatness and sweetness not only soften but altogether swallow up the bitterness of all pains and torments. We who are captives for the name of the Word of God have found this to be true in ourselves, and we understand that you too experience the same. For although your cause is not the same as ours, and although you are treated inhumanly and cruelly in prison, yet your heavenly Father, who is near you, who dwells in your heart through his Spirit, does not allow you to be crushed by the greatness of your affliction, or tempted more severely than you can bear. Rather, he strengthens you by his power, comforts you, and fills your mind both with confidence in his grace and salvation and with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that the sense of these most grievous torments is lessened and softened. If you are now utterly cast out by the world, and deprived of all human help and comfort, God your Father nevertheless receives you most willingly and kindly as his dearest child, commended and dear to him, because of the faith and hope which you have fixed and placed in his Son Jesus Christ our Saviour. Your cause, as you yourself confess, is wicked and unjust; but the righteousness of Christ, and the perfect obedience with which he satisfied the judgment of God by suffering and dying for us, makes the wickedness of your whole cause forgiven you, and altogether blotted out in the sight of God. Wherefore trust in and rejoice in the Lord Christ, and be persuaded that his righteousness, holiness and innocence are yours, so that for his sake and by his grace you are now received by the heavenly Father into the number of his children. Let no length or bitterness of imprisonment and affliction therefore break your spirit or wear you down with sorrow; rather, in these bitternesses, relying and trusting on the grace, help and goodwill of God, hold fast and keep up the greatest constancy and patience, always setting before your eyes that life which was won by the death of the Son of God and is kept for you in heaven, where one lives with God for ever most happily and blessedly. Consider that the affliction in which you now are is brief and momentary, while the consolation and rest promised to you will never have an end. But if you take it badly that you have not studied the sacred letters more diligently, and have not been more practised in them, know this: you will then at last have a perfect knowledge of all things, when the Lord has gathered you to himself into that heavenly light which is free of all darkness. Let that matter, then, or any other, not trouble your mind; rather wait for the will of God with all patience and an even mind. For if the Lord wills to keep you still in this life, so that you may serve him, be persuaded that he will set you free beyond all hope; but if he wills to call you out of this evil and wretched world to himself, rejoice on account of this, and give him the greatest thanks for so great a benefit. For in this way you will be happier than if you remained in this life. Therefore prepare yourself for every outcome, but for that one which calls you rather to a saving and happy death than keeps you in this life. Nor should you be ashamed, even in death itself, to confess Christ the Lord, and, armed with his power, to repel Satan and all his servants with a brave spirit. Confess, I say, that Christ Jesus is your Saviour and Redeemer, and that he died for your sins; no greatness of your sins ought to, or can, hinder that grace of his, so certain and so clearly promised in the Gospel. For the mercy of God declared through him far surpasses them all in its greatness. If any torments of punishment in your body must be endured, do not be disturbed by them; rather lift up your head to heaven, and commend your spirit to God, the most faithful keeper, following the example of Christ our leader, who, dying, delivered his own spirit into the hands of the best Father; and do not doubt that you will be received into the inheritance of his kingdom.

units.la: Hæc sunt, charissime frater, quæ ad te hoc tempore voluimus scribere, Deum orantes vt summam tibi patientiam & perseuerantiam in fide Iesu Christi vsque in finem præstare velit. Omnes fratres, qui vnà mecum propter verbum captiui sunt, tibi in nomine Iesu Christi, plurimum salutis dicunt, perpetuò pro te orantes, sicut tu mutuò pro ipsis facis. Dominus tecum sit in perpetuum. Si vlla re tibi est opus, mitte ad nos, & te omnibus, quibus poterimus rebus iuuabimus.
units.tr: These things, most dear brother, are what we wished to write to you at this time, praying God that he may grant you complete patience and perseverance in the faith of Jesus Christ until the end. All the brothers who are imprisoned with me for the Word send you, in the name of Jesus Christ, very many greetings of salvation, always praying for you, just as you do in turn for them. The Lord be with you forever. If you have need of anything, send to us, and we will help you in every way we can.

units.la: Superioribus horum martyrum scriptis hanc etiam epistolam hoc loco subiungere volu-imus, qua ipse Ioannes Chambonus in loco carceris obscurissimo, etiam manicis vinctus constrictusque, totam conuersionis suæ rationem ad illos fratres scripsit: in qua singularis Dei gratia, & virtus admirabilis Spiritus sancti animum fidelem in summis ærūnis ac miseriis crigentis[?], consolantis, confirmantisque clarissimè perspicitur.
units.tr: Having added the writings of these martyrs above, we wish to append here also this letter, in which Jean Chambon himself, in the most obscure place of his prison, bound even with manacles and fetters, wrote to those brothers the whole account of his conversion: in it the singular grace of God and the admirable power of the Holy Spirit, sustaining, comforting and strengthening a faithful mind amid the greatest distresses and miseries, is most clearly seen.

units.la: FRatres charissimi, ac verè Christiani, primùm vobis omnibus salutem in Christo Iesu exopto ac dico: quod ego iandiu quidem cupiebam facere, sed usque ad hunc diem, nullam unquam scribendi facultatem habui: quanuis aliter facere cuperem, si ea optimi Patris nostri cælestis esset voluntas, ut ego vobiscum coràm communicarem. Sed tamen vos rogo, ut hoc quod nunc per literas facio, tâ vobis gratum sit, quàm si coràm facerem, ac me ita vobiscum consolarer. Illud quidem verè vobis significare possum, me à quarto die Augusti, quo de vestra captiuitate à Petro Bergiero fratre nostro cum magno animi mei dolore certior factus sum, nec vestri, nec illius in meis precibus, quas ad Deum interdiu noctúque adhibeo, oblitum unquam suisse: sed memoriam quam debeo, vobis praestare. Neque ullus est cruciatus morbúsque, qui hanc vestri memoriam benevolentiámque impediat: non magis quàm eam, quam fratri meo debeo & præsto, qui propter maleficium à me commissum & perpetratum est in carcere, cùm eo in crimine plane sit innocès, non minus quàm vos qui nihil huiusmodi unquam admisistis. Hæc autem iniuria ei facta, mihi plus doloris affert, quàm ullæ ærumnæ, tormentorúmque acerbitates quas in his vinculis perfero. Atque huius quidem rei totius Deus mihi testis esse potest. Sed gratias, fratres charissimi, vobis agere volo pro ea epistola, quam ad me consolatoriam & plane Christianam scripsistis, ac per fratrem nostrum misistis: cùm ego huiusmodi studia & officia, quæ mihi defertis, nunquam promeruerim. Qua ex epistola ego tantam consolationem & lætitiam accepi, quantam nullis verbis explicare possem. Itaque cùm hoc vestrum in me officium atque beneficium nullo sapientiæ studio aut alio beneficio compensare possim, & parem vobis gratiam referre: reliquum est, ut Deum benignissimúmque Patrem orem, ut Spiritu suo ita vos regat & gubernet, ut adversus inimicos veritatis, qui sunt nostri quoque, victores permaneatis, quemadmodum vos quidem desideratis, vel ut melius dicam, sicut voluntas Dei, quæ omnibus in rebus non potest non iusta bonáq; esse, constituit atq; decreuit. Si ego hæc vobis proponens & scribens, aliqua in re errem, vos rogo ut me admoneatis. Neque enim sum vobis sapientia illa cælesti coparandus, ut qui ab incunabulis in via sathanæ fuerim institu tus à cæcis hominibus, qui adhuc viuut, à recta salutis via semper deerrantes, quæ illis nunquam monstrata fuit. Neque enim illi impostores, ac potius de grege porcorum quam ordine sacerdotum homines, hūc pretiosum veritatis thesaurū soluūt: sed potius clausum in obscuritate abdunt, incurrentes in illam Christi execrationem qua væ iis denuntiat, qui claves scientiæ auferentes, ipsi nec introeunt, nec volentes ingredi permittunt. Ita fit ut miser populus nec prima, nec media, nec postrema salutis intelligat. O si ego essem apud eos, ipsam veritatem eis demonstrarem, nec ulla in re illis assentarer! Sed satis à me de huiusmodi rebus, quas vos quidem melius intelligitis quam ego, quem imperitum ac fatuum in iis existimare potestis. Nunc autem oportet ut ad vos etiam scribam de singulari gratia, quam Deus in me fratremque meum contulit, pro ea iniuria, quæ ei illata fuit. Is cæcus, id est, Dei veritatisque ipsius planè ignarus in carcerem Roanæ ingressus fuit. Sed opera, studio ac diligentia Petri Bergieri fratris nostri institutus, per admirabilem Dei misericordiam salutari veritatis luce illuminatus ex ipso carcere egredietur ac dimittetur. Quod quidem ego pluris facio, quam si ille totam copiam auri quod esset in mundo, adeptus esset. Qua quidem ex re ego maximam lætitiam atque voluptatem capio. Certè si Bergierus in his carceribus nihil aliud boni egisset, illud quidem quod in fratre meo egit, maximum est. Sed cum multis aliis salutaria huiusmodi officia præstitit, tum vero mihi ipsi, quem maximis molestiis afflictum subleuauit ac recreauit, cum literis vestris ad me missis, suauissimæ consolationis plenis, tum etiam suis, una cum libris ad consolationem meam accommodatis: adeo ut omnia officiorum genera mihi detulerit, facturumque quoad posset, promiserit: sicut vos quoque amanter humaniterque obtulistis. quorum nomine maximas vobis gratias ago, Deumque oro ut eorum gratiam cumulatissimè reddat. Sed in hac summa consolatione mea, maxima inest molestia, quam ex eo quod frater meus, qui una cum Bergerio cubare solebat, ab eo nunc disiunctus est, atque ita disclusus, ut alter alterum amplius videre non possit. Itaque frater meus ea re non mediocri dolore affectus est, quemadmodum suis mihi literis significavit: in quibus suam vestri memoriam, in suis precibus declararunt. Neque vero, fratres, silentio prætereire debco tum ea beneficia, quibus Deus me in carcere affecit, tum etiam grauissima & corporis & animi tormenta, in quibus sum versatus, priusquam voluntatem Dei cognoscerem, meque ei submitterem, ac libenter obtemperarem. Nam duobus primis mensibus, quibus in hanc fossam obscuram ac tetram sum demissus, huiusmodi vinculis ferreis compedibusque constrictus fui, ut nullam me in partem vertere, nec die nec nocte dimouere plane possem: adeo ut necessarianaturae in eodem loco, in quo ita detinebar, sub me ipso reddenda essent. Itaque in huiusmodi calamitate ac foeditate paedoris, maledictionibus omnibus atq; execrationibus eos prosequebar, à quibus ita tractabar: etiam patrem ac matrem, quorum beneficio hanc lucem vnquam aspexeram. Sed cum ego ita clamarem, Dominus me non exaudiebat, sed meos dolores duplicabat. Accedebat etiam alia poena, quae acerbitate cetera omnia cruciamenta opprobriaque superabat, quod tanta vis pediculorum in corpore extiterat, ut digitis duodenos in carne vestéque mea capere possem. Quam quidem poenam ego sane meritus fueram, etiam si nihil vnquam in vita commisissem praeter eas blasphemias, quas impie in parentes meos, atque ipsum Deum iaculabar. neque enim haec ratio probanda & adhibenda est, qua diaboli diabolo expellamus, aut incendium ita extinguamus, ut illud maius oleo copiose infuso accendamus. Sed Deus in his tantis meis miseriis misertus mei, me admonuit ac docuit non ita agendum esse. Nam cum viderem huiusmodi blasphemiis ac maledictis dolores cruciatuum meorum in dies maiores fieri & acerbiores, mutaui planctus quesfusque meos & ratione[?] moderationemque[?] Christiano homine digna adhibui, quae mihi attulit maximam omnium malorum leuationem, ut recolligerem meipsum atque recognoscerem, memoriamq; totius vitae meae praeteritae, in omni scelere impietateque traductae, repeterem; atque omnia mea peccata & maleficia mihi proponerem, quae magnitudine atq; atrocitate omnia, quibus grauissime affligebar, tormenta superabant. Itaq; ad Deum conuersus, mea miseria deplorare coepi, veniamq; ab eo peccatorum meorum petere, ac orare, ut aliquam mei misericordiam caperet. hac autem mea in conuersione atq; precatione Domini respexit me & exaudiuit, ita ut postea non mediocre & animi consolatione & dolorum leuationem senserim, eamque suscepi patientia quae me nunquam dereliquit. Præterea eodem ipso die compedibus, quibus arctissime vinctus tenebar, solutus fui & liberatus. Pediculi vero, quibus coopertus erã, a me omnes discesserunt, ut jam septem sint menses, ex quo ne unum quidem in corpore meo repererim aut senserim. Frigus quidè perexiguum sentio, quanvis nec lectum, nec integumentum ullum præter pallium meum habeam. Quinetiam in ipso victu quotidiano Dominus mei non est oblitus. nam antea quidem huiusmodi panem mihi præbebat, à quo, ut ministri caeteris[?] retulerunt, canes ipsi & equi abhorrebãt: nunc vero benignitate Dei, albus panis mihi tribuitur, portioque opsoniorum duplo maior quàm antea dare consueverant. Accedunt etiam nonnullæ eleemosynæ, quas Dominus pro sua gratia & beneficetia ad me mittit: ita ut nunc quidem hac in parte satis bene nutriar atque reficiar. Sed nimiũ longa esset hæc mea epistola, si singula solatia & beneficia commemorare vobis vellem, quibus Dominus me afficit, qui nihil horum sum meritus, sed supplicia tormentaque multo maiora quàm ferre possim. Itaque maximas ei gratias ago cum nomine istorum beneficiorum, tum etiam quòd me paterne & summa cum clementia lenitateque in hoc misero mundo castiget: ne in altero ab eo damnatupeream. Si pœnæ quas nunc luo, sunt graves atque acerbæ, peccata ad huc mea sunt huiusmodi, ut supplicia infinitis partibus graviora ei debeantur. Itaque has pœnas ego virgâsque optimi Patris non aspernor ut alienas: sed summa cum patientia atque æquitate animi amplector, Deiq; misericordiam potius admiror, quòd me tam benignè tractet. Quare ita animo paratus sum, ut patienter omnia sim suscepturus ac passurus, quæ ipse imponere mihi voluerit. Vos autem magnopere rogo ut ad me scribatis, quæ madmodum[?] in ipsa morte, si condemnatus fuero, me gerere debeam, ut ad eum diem paratus esse possim, eaque dicere quæ tum ad gloriam Dei, tum ad salutem meam pertineant: hoc magnū vestrū beneficium esse putabo. Ego me interea vestris precibus commendo, pro mutua benevolētia & charitate quam in meis etiã vobis præstto. Si ego graviter peccavi, sicut feci, illud quidem antè factum[?] est quàm Dominus cognitionem sui ullam mihi impertiisset. Ac ma-leficium illud propter quod in carcere nunc tenecor, iam tres ab hinc annos totidemque menses designatum à me est. Si vos aliquos habeti[?] bros, eorum consolatione velim me iuvetis. Eos simulatque legero, eddam nostro fratri Petro Bergerio. Nulla mihi re alia opus est hoc eodem tempore: Deo gratias. Hæc autem sunt quæ nunc ad vos scribere volui. Pater omnis misericordiæ, ac Deus omnis patientiæ & consolationis consoletur vos, firmámque patientiam in ista captiuitate vobis impertiat, virtute Spiritus sui vos confirmans, ut constanter omnia ferre tolerareque possitis quæ ipse vobis immittere voluerit, per Iesum Christum Filium suum, Dominum nostrum, vnicúmque Saluatorem: cui honos & gloria imperiúmque sempiternum, Amen, Amen. Si epistola mea incommodè, & cum molestia legitur, vos me ne eo excusatum habebitis. neque enim lucem habebam, nisi per exiguum[?] foramen, quo manus tantum transmitti posset: nec calamum, quo ad scribendum nihil valet, parare possum. Hæc autem maiore cum molestia, metu, difficultatéque scripsi, quàm vos possetis credere: propterea quòd occultè mihi scribendum est. Nam ne aliquid omnino scriberem, mihi interdixerunt, papyrúmque atque atramétum mihi ademerunt. Hæc autem maxima cum difficultate comparaui, neque est vllus præter vnum seruum conscius.
units.tr: Dearest brothers, truly Christian, first of all I wish and send greetings in Christ Jesus to you all. I have long wished to do this, but until today I have never had the chance to write. I would rather have done otherwise, speaking with you face to face, if that had been the will of our best heavenly Father. Still, I ask you to take this letter, which I now write, as kindly as if I were with you in person and could comfort you that way. I can truly tell you that since the fourth day of August, when our brother Pierre Bergier informed me, to my great sorrow, of your captivity, I have never forgotten either you or him in my prayers, which I offer to God day and night. I give you the remembrance that I owe you. No torment or sickness of body keeps me from remembering you and holding you in kindness, any more than it keeps me from my duty and care for my brother, who is held in prison for a crime committed and carried out by me. He is entirely innocent of that charge, just as you are, since you have never done anything of the kind. This wrong done to him causes me more pain than any hardship or the bitter tortures I suffer in these chains. God alone can bear witness to the whole of this. But, dearest brothers, I want to thank you for the letter you wrote to me, a letter of consolation and truly Christian, which you sent through our brother. I have never deserved these kindnesses and services you offer me. From that letter I received such comfort and joy that I could not express it in words. And since I cannot repay this kindness and benefit of yours with any scholarship or other favour, and cannot return the same grace to you, what remains is to pray to God, our most kind Father, that by his Spirit he may rule and guide you, so that you remain victorious over the enemies of the truth, who are ours as well, just as you yourselves desire. Or, to put it better, you should desire what the will of God has decided and determined in all things, which cannot but be just and good. If in setting out and writing these things I make any mistake, I ask you to correct me. For I am not to be matched with you in that heavenly wisdom. From infancy I was taught in the way of Satan by blind men, who are still alive, always straying from the right path of salvation, which was never shown to them. Those impostors, men of the herd of swine rather than of the order of priests, do not open this precious treasure of truth. Instead they hide it, shut away in darkness, and incur that curse of Christ by which he pronounces woe on those who take away the key of knowledge: they do not enter themselves, and they do not allow those who wish to enter. So it happens that the wretched people understand neither the first, nor the middle, nor the last of salvation. Oh, if I were among them, I would show them the truth itself, and I would not flatter them in anything! But enough from me on such matters, which you understand better than I do, though you may think me unskilled and foolish in them. Now I must also write to you about the singular grace that God has given to me and to my brother, in return for the wrong done to him. He, being blind, that is, entirely ignorant of God and of the truth itself, entered the prison at Rouen. But through the work, zeal and diligence of our brother Pierre Bergier, who has taught him, he will go out of that prison and be released, enlightened by the light of saving truth through the wonderful mercy of God. I value this far above what I would have gained had he obtained the whole supply of gold in the world. From this I take the greatest joy and delight. Certainly, if Bergier had done nothing else good in these prisons, what he has done for my brother would be great enough. But he has rendered such saving services to many others, and above all to me, whom he lifted up and refreshed when I was afflicted with the greatest troubles, both with your letters sent to me, full of the sweetest consolation, and with his own, together with books suited to my comfort. So he has offered me every kind of service and has promised to do all he can, just as you too have offered, lovingly and kindly. For this I give you the greatest thanks, and I pray God to repay their kindness to the full. But in this great consolation of mine there is a great distress: my brother, who used to lie beside Bergier, has now been separated from him and shut away so that the one can no longer see the other. My brother is therefore affected with no small grief, as he has told me in his letters, in which he declared his remembrance of you in his prayers. Nor, brothers, should I pass over in silence the benefits by which God has favoured me in prison, or the very grievous torments of body and mind through which I went before I came to know the will of God and submitted to him and gladly obeyed him. For during the first two months, when I was lowered into this dark and foul pit, I was bound with iron fetters and chains of this kind, so that I could not turn in any direction or move at all by day or night. So much so that the necessities of nature had to be performed under me on the very spot where I was held. In such misery and filth of excrement, I cursed and execrated with every kind of curse those who treated me so, even my father and mother, through whose kindness I had ever seen this light. But when I cried out like this, the Lord did not hear me, but multiplied my pains. Another punishment was added, which surpassed all the other tortures and reproaches in bitterness: so great a number of lice had got into my body that I could pick up twelve at a time with my fingers from my flesh and clothing. I truly deserved this punishment, even if I had never committed anything else in my life except those blasphemies which I impiously hurled against my parents and God himself. For this is not the method to be approved and used, by which we drive out one devil with another, or put out a fire by pouring in much oil so that it burns more fiercely. But God, having mercy on me in these great miseries, taught me that I must not act in that way. For when I saw that my pains grew greater and more bitter every day through such blasphemies and curses, I changed my laments and complaints, and adopted a manner of restraint and moderation worthy of a Christian man. This brought me the greatest relief from all my evils: I gathered myself together and came to know myself, and I recalled the whole memory of my past life, spent in every kind of wickedness and impiety. I set before myself all my sins and crimes, which by their greatness and atrocity surpassed all the torments by which I was most severely afflicted. And so, turning to God, I began to lament my misery, to ask pardon from him for my sins, and to pray that he might take some pity on me. In this conversion and prayer of mine the Lord looked upon me and heard me, so that afterwards I felt no small consolation of mind and relief from pain, and I received it with a patience that has never left me. Moreover, on that very day I was loosed and freed from the fetters with which I had been tightly bound. The lice with which I was covered all left me, so that now for seven months I have not found or felt even one on my body. I feel only a very slight cold, although I have no bed or covering except my cloak. Indeed, the Lord has not forgotten me even in my daily food. Before, they gave me a bread from which, as the servants reported to the others, even dogs and horses shrank. Now, by the kindness of God, I am given white bread, and a portion of relish twice as large as they used to give. Some alms are also added, which the Lord sends to me by his grace and generosity, so that now in this respect I am fed and refreshed well enough. But this letter of mine would be too long if I wanted to recount to you each comfort and benefit with which the Lord has favoured me, though I have deserved none of them, but rather far greater punishments and torments than I can bear. So I give him the greatest thanks, both for these benefits and because he chastises me in this wretched world as a father would, with the greatest mercy and gentleness, so that I may not perish in the next world, condemned by him. If the punishments I now suffer are heavy and bitter, my sins are still of such a kind that far greater punishments are due to me from him, by infinite measure. So I do not spurn these punishments and the rods of the best Father as if they were another's; rather I embrace them with great patience and equanimity of mind, and I admire the mercy of God, that he treats me so kindly. Therefore I am so prepared in my mind that I shall undergo and endure patiently all that he is pleased to lay upon me. But I ask you earnestly to write to me how I ought to conduct myself at the very moment of death, if I am condemned, so that I may be ready for that day and may say those things that pertain both to the glory of God and to my salvation. I shall count this a great kindness from you. Meanwhile I commend myself to your prayers, in return for the mutual goodwill and love which I also show toward you in my own prayers. If I have sinned gravely, as I have, that happened before the Lord had granted me any knowledge of himself. And the crime for which I am now held in prison was marked down by me three years ago and as many months. If you have any brothers, I would like you to help me with their consolation. As soon as I have read them, I will hand them over to our brother Pierre Bergier. I need nothing else at this time. Thanks be to God. These are the things I wished to write to you now. May the Father of all mercies, and the God of all patience and consolation, comfort you, and grant you steadfast patience in this captivity, strengthening you by the power of his Spirit, so that you may bear calmly and endure whatever he is pleased to send you, through Jesus Christ, his Son, our Lord and only Saviour, to whom be honour and glory and everlasting dominion, Amen, Amen. If my letter is read awkwardly and with difficulty, you will not hold it against me. For I had no light except through a small hole through which only a hand could pass, and I cannot get a pen, which is of no use for writing anyway. I have written these things with more trouble, fear and difficulty than you could believe, because I have had to write in secret. For they forbade me to write anything at all, and they took away my paper and ink. But I have got these with the greatest difficulty, and no one knows of it except one servant.

units.la: Vester humilis frater & amicus, Petrus Ioannes Chambonus, propter peccata sua captivus, vos vero propter veritatem.
units.tr: Your humble brother and friend, Peter John Chambon, a captive on account of his own sins, while you are captives on account of the truth.

units.la: PETRUS autem NAVIHERUS, quum fidei suae confessionem in- terrogatus coram iudicibus Lugdunensibus edidisset, eandem scriptam quoque hunc in modum proposuit, codem mense Maio, anni M. D. LIII.
units.tr: Peter Navihierus, having been questioned before the judges of Lyon and having made his confession of faith, also set it down in writing in this form, in the same month of May, 1553.

units.la: Vobis interrogat°[?] de mea fide, domini ac Iudices, existimavi me conveniens huic meae vocationi facturum, si interrogatis vestris responderem ac satisfacerem. Ac quoniâ plane sentio me in Scripturis sacris non ita esse versatù, ut possim hoc ita facere, sicut rei magnitudo dignitasque postulat, à vobis peto & oro, ut mihi ignoscatis, si in ea quidem vobis plane non satisfacio. Ego tamen puto me nihil dicturum, quod à verbo Dei discrepet, sicut omnes fideles homines intelligent, & vos quoque cognoscere poteritis. Primùm igitur credo in unum Deum immortalem, invisibilem, tribus distinctum personis, Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti: quorum una eadémque est substantia, & essentia æterna: ad cuius Dei cognitionem homo naturâ sua non potest peruenire, propterea quod in Divinis rebus caecus est, nec potest de iis judicare, sicut ait Divus Paulus i. Corinth. ii. cap. animalem hominem ea quae sunt Spiritus non percipere, nec ullo modo posse comprehendere atque intelligere, quoniam spiritualiter diiudicantur. Nam primum homo cum se a Deo suo auertisset atque abalienasset, ita in seruitute peccati est redactus, ut venundatus sub eo quasi mancipium quoddam teneatur. Ne tamen ullam ignorationis excusationem obtenderet, relictum fuit in animo eius testimonium quo Deum esse sentire posset. sed tantum abest ut ad veram eius cognitionem quae est per Jesum Christum veniat, ut eum tantumodo agnoscat justum judicem eorum qui illum offenderunt.Quare dico hominem uniuersam quandam notitiam intelligentiamque habere naturaliter in corde suo impressam, ut sit inexcusabilis. eam vero cognitionem quae est per Christum Jesum, qua possumus eum Patrem appellare, eum nullo modo habere: sed oportet ad eum vere cognoscendum, ut ipse nobis oculos aperiat, cor nostrum ita immutet, ut ex lapideo carneum efficiat, atque in eo verbum suum imprimat. Hoc autem omne bonum a solo Deo proficiscitur, & non ab homine, quemadmodum ait divus Augustinus:Nam postquam, inquit, homo peccato suo se a Deo auertit, unius jam gratiae Dei est eum convertere ad seque reducere: atque ita in obedientia ac reverentia nominis sui retinere. Praeterea credo hominem non posse nisi sola fide justificari: quae quidem donum Dei est, & sine qua quicquid homo facit nihil aliud est quam peccatum.Postquam autem donum fidei obtinuit: quicquid is agit Deo gratum est, & propter eam justus existimatur: quae in homine minime otiosa ac mortua, sed uiua & efficax fructus Spiritu Dei in eo inhabitante dignos producit. atque adeo si Deus hos eius fructus compenset, id certe facit sola sua gratia, nullo omnino nostro merito adductus. Nam nos quidem natura nostra ex nobisipsis nihil boni proferre unquam possemus. quum ergo Deus coronat bona opera, quae sunt in nobis, nihil nostri coronat, sed id solum quod ipse in nos per Spiritum suum contulit. Quod vero ait Jacobus de operibus ii. cap. vos scitis eum loqui de iisqui fidem se habere gloriabantur, quam nullis operibus ea dignis declarabant. Itaque qui fidem suam jactat bonorum operum inanem, is plane lanè illudit. neque enim fides potest esse magis sine bonis pisque operibus, quàm bona arbor sine bonis fructibus. Credo etiam cùm Deus sit spiritus immortalis & non aspectabilis, eum non posse nec debere illa re corruptibili, sed in spiritu & veritate adorari. Quare qui eum magínibus simulachrisque effingit, atque in illis colit, agit contra mandatum eius, quod de huiusmodi veneratione datum est: quemadmodum ex cap. xx. Exod. satis constat. Qui etiam coram simulachro aliquo abycit ac prosternit, ei honorem tribuens, is idolum colit. Neque enim, ut inquit Paulus 1.Cor.viii.cap. simulachrum in mundo aliquid est, &c. Ioannes in prima sua epistola, v. cap. diligenter nos monet, ut huiusmodi simulachra euitemus. Qua in re illa excusatio nihil plane valere debet, qua dicitur, id quod fit imaginibus non fieri earū causa, sed potius eorum qui per illas repræsentatur. nam quemadmodum ait Augustinus, Psalm. cxiii. ipsa effigies à cælo magis cor hominis ab-lucit, quàm in cælum erigit atque attollit: propterea quòd cùm eam videamus ita expressam, instarque nostri effictam, habentem oculos, os, aures, brachia & tibias, existimamus in ea aliquid Diuinitatis esse, eique magno cum errore adhaerescimus. Idem etiam scribens in primum cap. Epistola ad Romanos, dicit impium esse, in templis Christianorum simulachrum forma, figuraque humana fictum erigere, ne illud quidem fas esse quod Dei aliquam effigiem haberet. Alio autem loco in lib. de civitate Dei. 17. cap. 31, Omnia, inquit, simulachra sunt per Evangelium profligata, oblivionique mandata, quasi sepulta iacerent.
units.tr: Since you, my lords and judges, have asked me about my faith, I thought it fitting to my calling to answer your questions and give you satisfaction. Since I plainly feel that I am not so well versed in the holy Scriptures that I can do this as the weight and dignity of the matter demand, I ask and beg you to pardon me if in this I do not fully satisfy you. Yet I think I will say nothing that departs from the Word of God, as all faithful people will understand, and as you also will be able to recognise. First, then, I believe in one immortal, invisible God, distinguished in three persons, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, who have one and the same substance and eternal essence. Man by his nature cannot attain to the knowledge of this God, because he is blind in divine things and cannot judge of them, as the divine Paul says in 1 Corinthians 2, that the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit, nor can in any way grasp and understand them, since they are spiritually discerned. For when man first turned away from his God and estranged himself, he was reduced into such bondage to sin that he is held under it like a sold slave. Yet lest he should have any excuse of ignorance, a testimony was left in his mind by which he could perceive that God exists. But he is so far from coming to the true knowledge of God, which is through Jesus Christ, that he acknowledges Him only as the just judge of those who have offended Him. Therefore I say that man has by nature a general notion and understanding of God impressed upon his heart, so that he is without excuse; but the knowledge that is through Christ Jesus, by which we can call Him Father, he has in no way. To know Him truly, it is necessary that He Himself open our eyes, change our heart so that He makes it of flesh instead of stone, and imprint His Word upon it. All this good comes from God alone and not from man, as the divine Augustine says: for after man has turned himself away from God by his sin, it is the work of the grace of God alone to convert him, bring him back to Himself, and so keep him in obedience and reverence to His name. Moreover, I believe that man cannot be justified except by faith alone, which is the gift of God, and without which whatever man does is nothing but sin. But once he has obtained the gift of faith, whatever he does is pleasing to God, and on account of that faith he is counted righteous. This faith is in no way idle or dead in man, but living and effective, and by the Spirit of God dwelling in him it produces fruits worthy of it. And so, if God rewards these fruits, He certainly does so by His grace alone, moved by no merit of ours at all. For by our own nature we could never bring forth any good from ourselves. So when God crowns the good works that are in us, He crowns nothing of ours, but only what He Himself has bestowed upon us by His Spirit. As for what James says about works, Chapter 2, you know that he speaks of those who boasted that they had faith, which they did not show by any works worthy of it. Therefore whoever boasts of his faith without good works plainly mocks himself; for faith cannot be without good and pious works any more than a good tree can be without good fruit. I also believe that since God is an immortal and invisible Spirit, He cannot and should not be worshipped in any corruptible thing, but in spirit and truth. Therefore whoever fashions Him in images and statues and worships Him in them acts against His command given concerning such veneration, as is clear enough from Exodus 20. Whoever also casts himself down and prostrates himself before some image, giving it honour, worships an idol. For, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 8, an image is nothing in the world, etc. John in his first epistle, chapter 5, diligently warns us to avoid such images. In this matter that excuse ought to count for nothing at all, which is offered, that what is done to images is not done for their sake, but rather for the sake of those who are represented by them. For, as Augustine says on Psalm 113, the image itself does more to darken the heart of man than to raise and lift it up to heaven, because when we see it so formed, and fashioned like ourselves, with eyes, mouth, ears, arms and legs, we suppose that there is something of divinity in it, and we cling to it with great error. The same writer, commenting on the first chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, says it is impious to set up in Christian churches an image fashioned in human form and shape, and that it is not even right to have any likeness of God. In another place, in the book On the City of God, chapter 17 (31), he says: all images have been overthrown by the Gospel and consigned to oblivion, lying as if buried.

units.la: De veneratione autem Sanctorum post ipsorum mortem, nos nihil habemus in Scripturis sanctis: nec reperimus quicquam praeceptum nobis & mandatum, ut eorum auxilium ac patrocinium imploremus: sed tantum ad Deum accedamus per Iesum Christum, qui unus advocatus noster & patronus est. qui quidem non praecipit ut ad Petrum, ut ad Paulum confugiamus: sed Matth. xi. humanissimè omnes ad se invitat qui afflictionibus oppressi sunt, eisque malorum levationem quietémque promittit. Deinde Ioan. 14. 15. 16. pluribus verbis nobis promittit Patrem daturum quae in ipsius nomine petierimus, caeterarū. vero Sanctorum nominis aut patrocinij nulla vnquam mētio facta est. Diuus quidē August. 6. cap. Hebr. scribit solum Iesum Christum inter eos qui hac carne humana induerunt pro nobis intercedere. Et alibi in Psalmo cviii. scribens, ait oratione quae per solum Iesum Christum non est facta, non posse peccata delere: sed potius in peccatum redudare. Postremo cum in veteri Testamento pij homines petunt aliquid a Deo, proponentes ac memorantes nomen Abrahae, Isaac, & Iacob: illud quidem faciunt revocantes in memoriam promissiones factas a Deo Patriarchis, non eorum nomen invocantes. Quod ad mortuos attinet, Paulus 1. Thessalonicensium cap. 4. nobis praecipit ne nomine eorum moereamus, quemadmodum gentiles atque infideles homines, qui nullam spem habent eos aliquado resurrecturos. Apostolus non praecipit ut pro illis preces ullas adhibeamus: quod profecto non praetermisisset, si tam prodesse eis intellexisset quàm vulgò homines dicere solent & credere. Ad haec si ita esset ut precibus eorum salutem iuvare possemus: oporteret ut Christus Iesus mediam tantum partem redemptionis nostrae effecisset, nos reliquam perficeremus. At vero manifestum est & certum, eum plenè ac perfectè eam obligationem deleuisse, qua nos diabolo obstricti obligatique eramus. Divus enim Petrus ostendit nos non auro & argento, sed pretioso sanguine Agni immaculati Iesu Christi redemptos esse, neque in alio nomine salutem esse. Divus etiam Chrysostomus scribit in homilia 11. in Psalmum L. cum misericordia a Deo postulatur, id ob eam causam fieri, ne acerbius examinemur rigoreque iustitiae ab eo severius tractemur. Nam ubi est misericordia ibi amplius nec gehenna, nec examen, nec rigor aut ulla poena est, aut superesse potest. Quare qui semel misericordiam per Iesum Christum obtinuerunt, ij iam hac vita defuncti, nulla purgatione opus habent, nec ullam poenam cruciatumque expectant: sed omnibus malis liberati in vitam laetitiamque aeternam transferuntur. Quod autem de mortuis dictum est in Machabaeis: Vos scitis eum librum non esse Canonicum, quemadmodum Divus Hieronymus ostendit. Duo in Ecclesia habemus Sacramenta a Iesu Christo instituta, Baptismum & sacram Cœnam. Baptismus est Sacramentum poenitentiae, & quasi quiddam introitus in Ecclesiam Dei, ut in ipso corpore Iesu Christi inferamur. In eo autem nobis proponitur remissio peccatorum, tum praeteritorum, tum etiam futurorum: quâ una mors Iesu Christi nobis plenè ac per-
units.tr: Concerning the veneration of the saints after their death, we have nothing in the holy Scriptures, nor do we find any command or precept that we should implore their help and patronage. Rather, we should come to God alone through Jesus Christ, who is our only advocate and patron. He does not command us to flee to Peter or to Paul, but in Matthew 11 most kindly invites all who are oppressed by afflictions to himself, promising them relief from their evils and rest. Then in John 14, 15 and 16 he promises us at greater length that the Father will give whatever we ask in his name; but of the name or patronage of other saints there is never any mention at all. The divine Augustine, in his book on Hebrews, chapter 6, writes that Jesus Christ alone intercedes for us among those who have put on this human flesh. And elsewhere, writing on Psalm 108, he says that prayer which is not made through Jesus Christ alone cannot blot out sins, but rather adds to them.
