Finally, when the godly in the Old Testament ask anything of God, setting forth and calling to mind the name of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, they do so by recalling the promises God made to the patriarchs, not by invoking their names. As for the dead, Paul in 1 Thessalonians 4 instructs us not to grieve for them as the Gentiles and unbelievers do, who have no hope that they will rise again someday. The Apostle does not command us to offer any prayers for them; which he certainly would not have omitted if he had understood that they help them as much as men commonly say and believe. Moreover, if it were so that we could help their salvation by our prayers, it would follow that Christ Jesus had accomplished only half of our redemption, and we would complete the rest. But it is plain and certain that he has fully and perfectly cancelled that debt by which we were bound and obligated to the devil. For the divine Peter shows that we were redeemed not with gold and silver, but with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ, and that there is no salvation in any other name. The divine Chrysostom also writes, in homily 11 on Psalm 50, that when mercy is asked of God, this is done so that we may not be examined too harshly or treated more severely by the rigour of justice. For where mercy is, there is no longer any gehenna, any judgment, or any punishment, nor can any remain. Therefore those who have once obtained mercy through Jesus Christ, once they have departed this life, have no need of any purgation, nor do they expect any punishment or torment, but being freed from all evils they are carried over into eternal life and joy. As for what is said of the dead in the Maccabees, you know that this book is not canonical, as the divine Jerome has shown. We have two sacraments in the Church instituted by Jesus Christ, Baptism and the holy Supper. Baptism is the sacrament of repentance, and a kind of entrance into the Church of God, by which we are brought into the very body of Jesus Christ. In it is set forth to us the remission of sins, both past and future, which the one death of Jesus Christ has fully and perfectly obtained for us.

units.la: Perfecta fa lus à Chri- sto. 1.Pet.1. [?] esse[?] acquisiuit. Præterea significatur nobis in eodem & demonstraur mortificatio carnis nostræ, & renouatio vitæ in pietate instituē-le ac degēdæ: quarum vtramque aqua repræsentat super infante aspersa, in qua est signum notáque insignis Spiritus sancti, vitia animarum nostrarum abluentis ac purgantis. Atque ita admonemur, quòd quemadmodum magnus ille Pharao in mari rubro submersus est, ita nostrum veterem Adam, atque id omne quod habemus ab eo summerri oportet. Et quemadmodum aqua super infantem iacitur, non vt is summersus pereat, sed viuat: ita nos debere in nouitate vitæ ambulare, vt non nobis amplius, sed ipsi Christo Iesu, cum quo ita sumus conuncti, viuamus. Aliud vero nihil legimus in hoc Sacramento à Chri-sto Iesu institutum aut traditum, quàm aquam & formam in Ecclesia vsitatam, quæ in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti ad sacramentum adhibetur. Quòd autem ad chrisma & alias ceremonias attinet, nos nihil de iis in Scriptura sacra legimus. Nec vero illud præoccupare possumus, Baptismum externum per aquam factum atque administratum, esse ad salutem ita necessarium, vt qui eum non receperit, salutis planè expers sit: sed illud vt iniquum improbamus. Nam hoc quidem modo gratia Dei rebus externis alligaretur, quasi ea sine illarum adiumento salutem afferre non posset. In veteri quidem testamento legimus Circumcisione, quæ figura quædam erat baptismi, cùm octauo tantùmodò die illi tùm vterentur, nulla tamen aut ipsorum culpa, vt infantum periculo omissam sæpe fuisse. Idem etiam possumus de infantibus Christianorum & sentire & dicere. neque enim Sacramenta nouæ Legis maiorem vim in iis habuerunt, quàm veteris: quemadmodum Paulus satis ostendit, 1.Cor. x. cùm ait Patres eundem cibum comedisse spirituale nobiscum, eúdémque potum bibisse. Si aliqua in his Sacramentis erat differentia, ea in tempore erat non in re: quòd illa spem Christi redemptoris aliquando venturi ostendebant, hæc iam venisse demõstrant, sicut Augustinus in Ioan. ait, Conteptus Sacramenti tantūmodò absit, infantes fidelium in promissione illa comprehensi sunt, qua Dominus se tum parentū, tum etiam liberorum posterorúmque Deum futurum etiam vsque in millecsimā progeniē confirmat: sine vlla dubitatione participes sunt eius salutis, quæ à Deo, qui metiri non potest, promissa est. Nam sicut ait Ambrosius in epistola ad Corinthios, satis notum est Spiritum sanctum sine manuum impositione datum, atque eum qui non fuerat baptisatus, remissionem peccatorum obtinuisse. at qui donum Baptismi accepit, visibili signo est baptizatus. Et Augustinus diçit sanctificationem esse aliquando sine Sacramento visibili, ipsumque Sacramentum externum sine sanctificatione interiore. Quamobrem ego statuo & concludo externum Baptismum, qui aqua administratur, non esse necessarium ad salutem, neque aquæ adiumento hominem saluari: sed eo bonæ conscientiæ testimonio, quod aqua repræsentatur, de remissione peccatorum per mortem Iesu Christi nobis parta: cuius quidem nisi simus participes, nos plane perire necesse est. Restat vt dicamus de altero Sacramento, quod est sacrosanĉta Cœna, quam sicut quatuor Euangelistæ & Paul.1.Cor.11.testatur, Dominus nostu priusquam paterctur, instituit, panemque acceptum fregit, ac Discipulis suis præbuit, inquiens, Accipite, edite: hoc est corpus meum quod pro vobis traditur. Et quum gratias egisset, calicem quoque accepit, dicens, Hoc est nouum Testamentum in meo sanguine: omnes ex eo bibite. Hoc quotiescunque vos feceritis, mortem Domini, quoad veniat annuntiabitis. Hæc quidem est sacræ Cœnæ institutio, in qua primum vos videtis, quemadmodum mandatum bibendi de calice est violatum, cum laicis denegetur. Omnes quidem veteres Doĉtores disertis verbis præceperunt, vt omnes vtraque parte Sacramenti atque specie panis & vini vterentur, vt ita corporis & sanguinis Domini participes esse possent. Chrysostomus ait, in hoc Sacramento non ita habere, vt in veteri Lege, in qua sacerdotes portionem à populo separatam accipiebant: sed in Eucharistia omnia populo cum sacerdote sunt communia. nam idem corpus omnibus proponitur & idem calix. Gelasius etiam episcopus Romanus constituit vt quicunque abstinerent à calice, à Sacramento omnino repellerentur: quoniam, inquit, diuisio huius mysterij sine sacrilegio fieri non potest. Sed loquamur de iis, quæ in hoc Sacramento fieri solent. Vos dicitis in eo corpus ac sanguinem Iesu Christi recipi. Id quidem ego confiteor, sed videamus quomodo. Vos certè mihi non negabitis nos non posse vlla alia ratione participes fieri Iesu Christi, vt salutem adipiscar ​ mur, quàm per fidem: quæ cùm non sit res corporea, non oportet ut ad accipiendum Iesum Christum & edendum, dentes carnis afferamus: sed tantùm spiritum animámque cibi tam salutaris avidam: quod quidem fit per fidem, qua sola Iesum Christum ad salutem recipimus. eius autem officium est credere. itaque qui credit in Iesum Christum, cum in spiritu comedit. In quo plane consentio cum Augustino, admonente ne dentem ac ventrem praeparemus, sed credamus, atque ita manducemus. Neque ab eius sententia & authoritate discrepat Decretum de pœnitentia. Quare ita sentio atque statuo, Quicunque credit Iesum Christum descendisse de cælo, pro se passum & mortuum fuisse, per eiusque mortem, morte æterna liberatum, atque hæredem cæli factum: eundemque resuscitatum in cælum ascendisse, indeque ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos venturum esse: eum, inquam, dico plane participare Iesu Christo, atque eius carnem edere ac sanguinem bibere. Atque hoc quidem modo ut ait Augustinus, Christus habitat in nobis, & nos in eo. Hæc est enim vera communicatio, quam nos habemus cum eo, quæ per fidem fit. Nam illa quidem coniunctio & communio, qua Christus factus filius Adam cū toto genere humano se coniunxit, veramque humanitatem suscepit, nihil plane proderit, nisi alia spiritualis quæ fit per fidem, instituatur atque adhibeatur. Qua una nos regeneramur, & in numerum filiorum Dei adoptamur, & cuius tantummodo sunt participes, qui electi à Deo, in Christum credunt. Sentio igitur illam manducationem carnalem corporis & sanguinis naturalis Iesu Christi, in qua dicunt panem ac vinum converti, nullo modo fieri in Cœna: sed credo cum ad dexteram Dei Patris sui sedere: si caput illud communis fidei nostræ & historia Ascensionis eius non me fallit, quemadmodum fallere nullo modo potest. sed eo symbolo tantummodo admonemur, quòd sicut corpora nostra pane ac vino nutriuntur & sustentantur, ita animas nostras carne eius ac sanguine ali, foveri, confirmari, tum cum per fidem atque in spiritu ea sumimus. Sed ut hoc apertius demonstretur & confirmetur, veram interpretationem verborum Iesu Christi consideremus. Is ait, Hoc est corpus meum. Obsecro vos, ne aliquid de nostro afferamus, sed in nostras conscientias introcamus[?]. Tertullianus quidem haec verba ita exponit: Hoc est signum corporis mei & figura. Diuus autem Augustinus, Dominus, inquit, non dubitauit dicere, Hoc est corpus meum: quanuis nihil praeter figuram corporis dispertiret. Et deinde, Iesus Christus Iudam cum discipulis in conuiuium recepit, quibus signum & figuram corporis sui commendauit atque exhibuit. Omnes denique Doctores veteres idem sentiunt & dicunt. Diuus Irenaeus ait panem terrestrem, qui benedictionem Dei recipit, non iam amplius esse communem, sed Eucharistiam complectentem duo, quorum alterum terrenum est, alterum Diuinum.
units.tr: Perfect salvation from Christ. 1 Pet. 1. [...] has acquired. Moreover, it is signified to us in this sacrament and shown to us that our fleshly nature must be mortified and that we must be renewed to live and walk in piety. Water, poured over an infant, represents both of these, and in it is the sign and the distinguishing mark of the Holy Spirit, who washes and cleanses the vices of our souls. We are thus admonished that, just as that great Pharaoh was drowned in the Red Sea, so our old Adam and everything we have from him must be drowned. And just as the water is poured over the infant not so that he perishes submerged but so that he lives, so we ought to walk in newness of life, that we may live not to ourselves but to Christ Jesus himself, with whom we are so joined. Indeed, we read of nothing else instituted or handed down by Christ Jesus in this sacrament than the water and the form used in the Church, which is employed for the sacrament in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. As for the chrism and the other ceremonies, we read nothing about them in Holy Scripture. Nor, indeed, can we hold that external baptism performed and administered through water is so necessary to salvation that whoever has not received it is altogether without salvation; rather, we reject that view as unjust. For in this way the grace of God would be tied to external things, as if it could not bring salvation without their help. In the Old Testament we read of circumcision, which was a certain figure of baptism, though it was used only on the eighth day; yet it was often omitted, without fault on the part of the infants' parents, and at the risk of the infants. We can feel and say the same of the infants of Christians. For the sacraments of the New Law did not have greater power in them than those of the Old, as Paul sufficiently shows, 1 Cor. 10, when he says that our fathers ate the same spiritual food as we do and drank the same spiritual drink. If there was any difference between these sacraments, it lay in time and not in substance: those sacraments showed the hope of Christ the Redeemer who would one day come, while these show that he has already come. As Augustine says on John, provided only that contempt of the sacrament is absent, the infants of believers are comprised in that promise by which the Lord confirms that he will be the God of parents, and of children, and of their descendants, even to the thousandth generation. Without any doubt they share in that salvation which has been promised by God, who cannot be measured. For, as Ambrose says in his epistle to the Corinthians, it is well known that the Holy Spirit was given without the imposition of hands, and that one who had not been baptized obtained the forgiveness of sins; yet one who received the gift of baptism was baptized with a visible sign. And Augustine says that sanctification is sometimes without a visible sacrament, and that the external sacrament itself is sometimes without inward sanctification. Therefore I establish and conclude that external baptism, which is administered with water, is not necessary to salvation, nor is a man saved by the help of water, but by that testimony of a good conscience, which the water represents, concerning the forgiveness of sins won for us by the death of Jesus Christ; of which, indeed, unless we are partakers, we must certainly perish. It remains for us to speak of the other sacrament, which is the most holy Supper, which, as the four Evangelists and Paul, 1 Cor. 11, testify, our Lord instituted on the night before he suffered. He took bread, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: "Take, eat; this is my body, which is given for you." And when he had given thanks, he also took the cup, saying: "This is the new covenant in my blood; drink of it, all of you. As often as you do this, you shall proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." This is indeed the institution of the holy Supper, in which you can first see how the command to drink from the cup has been violated, since it is denied to the laity. Indeed all the ancient teachers have commanded in plain words that everyone should partake of both parts of the sacrament, both the bread and the wine, so that they might be partakers of the body and blood of the Lord. Chrysostom says that in this sacrament it is not as in the old Law, in which the priests received a portion separated from the people; rather, in the Eucharist all things are common to the people together with the priest, for the same body is set before all, and the same cup. Gelasius, the Roman bishop, also decreed that whoever abstained from the cup should be altogether cast out from the sacrament, since, he says, the division of this mystery cannot be made without sacrilege. But let us speak of those things which are usually done in this sacrament. You say that in it the body and blood of Jesus Christ are received. I indeed confess this, but let us see how. You will certainly not deny to me that we cannot become partakers of Jesus Christ in any other way, so as to obtain salvation, than through faith; and since faith is not a corporeal thing, it is not necessary, in order to receive and eat Jesus Christ, that we bring the teeth of the flesh, but only the spirit and soul, eager for such wholesome food. This indeed happens through faith, by which alone we receive Jesus Christ to salvation, and whose office is to believe. Therefore he who believes in Jesus Christ eats with the spirit. In this I plainly agree with Augustine, who warns us not to prepare our teeth and stomach, but to believe, and so to eat. Nor does the Decree on repentance differ from his opinion and authority. Therefore I think and determine thus: whoever believes that Jesus Christ came down from heaven, suffered and died for himself, was freed from eternal death through his death, and was made heir of heaven, and that he was raised again and ascended into heaven, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead, that man, I say, plainly partakes of Jesus Christ and eats his flesh and drinks his blood. And in this way, as Augustine says, Christ dwells in us, and we in him. For this is the true communion which we have with him, and it is made through faith. For that conjunction and communion by which Christ, made the son of Adam, joined himself to the whole human race and took on true humanity, will profit nothing at all unless another, spiritual communion, which is made through faith, is established and employed. Through this alone we are regenerated and adopted into the number of the sons of God, and only those who are elected by God and believe in Christ are its partakers. I therefore hold that that carnal eating of the body and blood of the natural Jesus Christ, in which they say the bread and wine are changed, is in no way done in the Supper; but I believe that he sits at the right hand of God his Father, if the article of our common faith and the history of his Ascension do not deceive me, as they cannot in any way deceive. And we are admonished only by that sign, that just as our bodies are nourished and sustained by bread and wine, so our souls are fed, warmed, and strengthened by his flesh and blood, when we take these through faith and in the spirit. But so that this may be more clearly shown and confirmed, let us consider the true interpretation of the words of Jesus Christ. He says, "This is my body." I beg you, let us not bring anything of our own, but let us enter into our consciences. Tertullian indeed explains these words thus: "This is the sign and figure of my body." But the divine Augustine says: "The Lord did not hesitate to say, 'This is my body,' although he distributed nothing but the figure of his body." And afterwards: "Jesus Christ received Judas with the disciples at the table, and to them he commended and gave the sign and figure of his body." In short, all the ancient teachers think and say the same. The divine Irenaeus says that the earthly bread, which receives the blessing of God, is no longer common bread, but embraces two things, one of which is earthly and the other divine.

units.la: Idem Augustinus loquens de eodem sacramento, in eo libro quem de doctrina Christiana scripsit: Quemadmodum, inquit, seruilis est infirmitas literam plane sectari, ipsaque signa pro rebus quae illis significantur accipere: ita signa inutiliter interpretari error est perniciosus. Si hoc vobis non satisfacit: videamus rem propius, vos confitemini sacram Coenam esse sacramentum.
units.tr: The same Augustine, speaking of this same sacrament in the book he wrote on Christian teaching, says: "Just as it is a slavish weakness to cling to the letter alone and to take the signs themselves for the things they signify, so it is a pernicious error to interpret signs uselessly." If this does not satisfy you, let us look at the matter more closely: you confess that the Holy Supper is a sacrament.

units.la: Videamus igitur simplicem sacramenti definitionem alibi positam ab Augustino, Sacramentum, inquit, est rei sacrae signum, aut symbolum visibile gratiae inuisibilis. id igitur illud ipsum esse quod significat non potest: nec enim iam amplius sacramenti nomen aut naturam habere posset. Coena autem est sacramentum ac signum huiusmodi, quod rem aliquam demonstret: sed ita, ut illud quod eo significatur ac repraesentatur, vere tribuatur atque impertiatur ei, qui id per fidem recipit: aliter non. Praeterea, vos scitis verbum substantiuum E S T saepe in sacris literis accipi pro verbo Significare, sicut octauo capite Genesis, Septem vaccae & septem spicae frumenti, sunt septem anni: Petra autem erat Christus: Ioannes erat Helias. Puto vos mihi non negaturos omnes huiusmodi locos debere declarari & exponi per verbum Significare. Quid autem impediet, quo minus idem faciendum sit in his verbis Iesu Christi? cum praesertim veteres Doctores ita interpretati fuerint. Postremo si dicunt hanc transsubstantiationem panis & vini in corpus & sanguinem Iesu Christi, miraculo quoda fieri: in eo quidem non magna ratio est. Nam quod miraculum ex omnibus Scripturis sanctis proferetis, quod non ita sub sensus omnes corporis ceciderit, ut omnes qui illud viderent aut audirent, in admiratione non conuerteret? cuius generis sunt ea, quae Moyses fes in AEgypto admiranda edidit. At vero in Cœna nō videmus panem ac vinum immutari, atque in alium colorem saporémque conuerti, ut ita fieri magnopere admirari debeamus. Itaque nullum in eo miraculum est. Vos dicitis illud totum fide comprehendi, quæ de verbis Iesu Christi non dubitat, cuius vi altissima mysteria comprehenduntur. equidem vobis in hoc assentior: sed illud etiam statuo ac dico, fidem non ita esse crassam, atque in hac carne inuolutam, ut in hoc sacramento, ac mysterio quidquam carnale terrestréque percipiat aut sapiat. etenim mysterium spirituale plane est & cæleste[?]. nihil igitur cogitare debemus in eo cum carne terráque coniunctum, nec quemadmodum fuit constitutum in concilio Niceno in primo canone, oculos solum nostros defigere in pane & in vino, quæ nobis in Cœna administrantur, sed oculos mentis ac fidei nostræ altius in cælum attollere, ut agnum pro nobis semel immolatum atque ad dextera Dei collocatum contemplemur. Vos rogo per nomen Dei, ut ipsi consideretis in res non ita se habeat, vos etiam scitis canonem de transsubstantiaione non alium ante authorem habuisse, quam Gregorium Romanum Pontificem[?] septimum. Nam hoc quòd idem sacramentum ab antiquis ac piis doctoribus Sacrificium appellatur, id fit propter commemoratio-nem illius summi atque æterni sacrificij, quod Christus Iesus pro peccatis nostris semel in cruce peregit. Nominatum est etiam Eucharistia, id est, gratiarum actio, quod unum nobis ut illud Deo offeramus sacrificium relictum est:quemadmodum in epistola ad Hebræos, Fructus labiorum, & à Davide Cor contritum & humiliatum appellatur. Cætera vero sacrificia omnia finem acceperunt in Christo Iesu, qui seipsum Deo Patri semel obtulit, neque alius eum offerre jam potest. In hac autem tota institutione sacrosanctæ Cœnæ, atque in universa Scriptura sancta nulla plane fit mentio Missæ eiusque institutionis, quæ hodie tanto opere celebratur. Quare nescio quam rationem ij habeat qui aunt Iacobum Hierosolymis eam primum celebrasse. alij dicunt Petrum fuisse, qui Antiochiæ celebrarit. alij Gregorium eius authorem referunt. quidam etiam Ambrosium. Hæc quidem parum sunt firma ad authoritatem eius rei declarandam, quam inter maxima & præcipua fidei Christianæ capita haberi volunt. Divus Paulus dicitse Corint.tradidisse quod acceperat a Domino. Nec dubiu est, quin caeteri omnes Apostoli idem fecerint. Certu autem est Christi nunqua Missam instituisse. sequitur igitur Iacobum & Petrum, si eam tradiderunt, fideles servos Iesu Christi, Apostolosque no fuisse, cum aliud tradiderint aut celebrarint, quam quod a Domino Magistroque praeceptum fuerat. quod quidem de illis minime est cogitandum. Caeterum vos non ignoratis Missam initium coepisse suum a veteris ecclesiae consuetudine, in qua aliqui Psalmi canebantur, aut aliquod Scripturae sanctae caput legebatur, dum populus introiret & conveniret. Ea autem quae nunc offeruntur ortum suum habuerunt ab illis collectis, quas diaconi pro pauperibus faciebant. Videte quaeso, quae postea mutatio eorum omnium facta fuerit. Ego vero nulla alia Sacramenta, praeter ea duo quae ante commemoraui, in Ecclesia a Iesu Christo institua, traditaque esse scio. Nam confirmatio quidem, atque impositio manuum, extremaque unctio, cur tantopere retineantur, nulla causa ratioque videtur esse: cum id propter quod huiusmodi ceremoniae fuerant institutae, donum miraculorum iam desierit. Neque enim vos confertis Spiritum sanctum, cum id unius Dei donum sit, ut ait divus Ambrosius in tertium caput primae ad Corinthios scribens. Unctione vero nullam aegrotis affertis sanationem, quemadmodum Apostoli: sed potius signum mortis aut morbi mortiferi, ac cum prorsus omnia sunt desperata.
units.tr: Let us then look at the simple definition of a sacrament that Augustine gives elsewhere: "A sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing, or a visible form of invisible grace." Therefore it cannot be the very thing it signifies, for otherwise it could no longer have the name or nature of a sacrament. The Supper, however, is a sacrament and sign of this kind, which points to something, but in such a way that what is signified and represented by it is truly given and bestowed on the one who receives it by faith, and not otherwise. Moreover, you know that the substantive verb "is" is often used in Holy Scripture in the sense of the verb "to signify", as in the eighth chapter of Genesis: "The seven cows and the seven ears of grain are seven years"; and "The rock was Christ"; and "John was Elijah". I think you will not deny that all such passages must be explained and expounded by the verb "to signify". What, then, would prevent the same being done in these words of Jesus Christ, especially since the ancient teachers have interpreted them in this way? Finally, if they say that this transubstantiation of bread and wine into the body and blood of Jesus Christ happens by some miracle, there is not much reason in that. For what miracle will you produce from all the holy Scriptures which did not fall so under the senses of all the body that it turned all who saw or heard it to wonder? Of this kind are the marvels that Moses performed in Egypt. But in the Supper we see no change in the bread and wine, nor any conversion into another colour and taste, so that we ought greatly to marvel that it happens. Therefore there is no miracle in it. You say that the whole of it is comprehended by faith, which does not doubt the words of Jesus Christ, by whose power the most lofty mysteries are comprehended. Indeed I agree with you on this point; but I also affirm and say that faith is not so gross, nor so wrapped up in this flesh, that it perceives or savours anything carnal and earthly in this sacrament and mystery. For the mystery is altogether spiritual and heavenly. We ought therefore to think nothing in it that is joined with flesh and earth, nor, as was laid down by the Council of Nicaea in its first canon, to fix our eyes only on the bread and wine that are administered to us in the Supper, but rather to lift the eyes of our mind and faith higher to heaven, so that we may contemplate the Lamb once sacrificed for us and placed at the right hand of God. I beg you in the name of God to consider for yourselves whether the matter is not as I say. You also know that the canon on transubstantiation had no other author before him than Gregory VII, Roman Pontiff. For the fact that this same sacrament is called a sacrifice by the ancient and pious teachers happens because of the remembrance of that supreme and eternal sacrifice which Christ Jesus once accomplished on the cross for our sins. It is also called the Eucharist, that is, thanksgiving, because one sacrifice has been left to us to offer to God, as in the Epistle to the Hebrews, "the fruit of the lips", and as David calls it "a heart contrite and humbled". All other sacrifices came to an end in Christ Jesus, who offered himself once to God the Father, and no one can offer him again. But in the whole institution of the holy Supper, and in all of holy Scripture, there is absolutely no mention of the Mass and of its institution, which is today celebrated with such great effort. Therefore I do not know what reason those have who say that James first celebrated it at Jerusalem. Others say it was Peter, who celebrated it at Antioch. Others refer its author to Gregory, and some even to Ambrose. These claims are indeed too weak to establish the authority of a matter which they wish to be held among the greatest and chief heads of the Christian faith. The divine Paul says in the first Epistle to the Corinthians that he handed on what he had received from the Lord. Nor is it doubtful that all the other apostles did the same. But it is certain that Christ never instituted the Mass. It follows that if James and Peter handed it down, they were not faithful servants of Jesus Christ nor apostles, since they handed down or celebrated something other than what had been commanded by the Lord and Master. Yet this is by no means to be thought of them. Moreover, you are not unaware that the Mass began from the custom of the ancient Church, in which some psalms were sung, or some chapter of holy Scripture was read, while the people came in and assembled. But the things that are now offered arose from those collections which the deacons made for the poor. Consider, I beg you, what change of all these things was made afterwards. As for myself, I know that no sacraments other than the two I mentioned before were instituted by Jesus Christ and handed down in the Church. For as to confirmation, and the laying on of hands, and extreme unction, there seems to be no cause or reason why they are so strongly retained, since the gift of miracles, for which such ceremonies were instituted, has now ceased. For you do not confer the Holy Spirit, since that is the gift of God alone, as the divine Ambrose says in writing on the third chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians. Nor do you bring any healing to the sick by anointing, as the Apostles did, but rather a sign of death or of a deadly sickness, when everything is utterly despaired of.

units.la: Credo etiam Ecclesiam nullum habere caput praeter Iesum Christum, cuius omnes fideles membra sunt: ex quibus nullus in alium praestantiam aut potestatem ullam habet, ut eum sibi subijciat, sed omnes in Domino ita sunt fratres, ut mutuam obedientiam atque observantiam inter se habeant ac praestet, alique aliis invicem pareant, quaeadmodum[?] in prisca Ecclesia observatum, ac monumentis literarum prodiditum, facile cognosci potest. S. Cypriani in epist. quae in concilio Carthaginensi scripta est, huiusmodi sunt verba, Nos quidem omnes conveniemus, ut opinionem nostram & sententiam exponamus. Quod si alius quispiam dissentiat & contradicat, illum ex conventu consessuque non eiiciemus. Neque enim in nobis est quispiam, qui se summum episcopum audeat dicere, ut alios in sententiam suam cogat. Vos videtis tum quidem nullum episcopum fuisse, qui in alios dominatum usurpa-ret, ret,nedum in reges ac principes, quemadmodum Papa se habere hodie iactat. Vos scitis diuum Gregorium hoc nomen repudiasse, cùm dicat, eum qui sibi illud assumeret atq; usurparet, praecursorem Antichristi esse. Idè dicit Amianus Diaconus de Ioan. episc. Constantinopolitano, qui illud nomen arroganter volebat usurpare. Neque verò ignoratis quod erat officium veterum episcoporum, & quae vita, morum ac doctrinae ratio à Paulo descripta: & quòd nomen canum mutorum à S. Gregorio est eis attributum, nisi officio fungantur suo. Neque etiam ignoratis officium sacerdotum ac presbyterorum, & quam vim illud nomen habeat. quo nomine solo homines hodie contenti sunt, vitam prorsus purámque doctrinam negligentes.
units.tr: I believe too that the Church has no head but Jesus Christ, of whom all the faithful are members; among these none has any pre-eminence or power over another so as to subject him to himself, but all are so brothers in the Lord that they have and show mutual obedience and observance among themselves, and some yield to others in turn, as can easily be recognised from what was observed in the early Church and handed down in written records. The words of St Cyprian in the letter written at the Council of Carthage are of this kind: "We shall all meet together, so that we may set forth our opinion and judgement. But if anyone else dissents and contradicts, we shall not expel him from the assembly and gathering. For there is no one among us who dares to call himself the chief bishop, so as to compel the others to his opinion." You see that at that time there was no bishop who usurped lordship over others, much less over kings and princes, as the Pope today boasts he has. You know that the divine Gregory repudiated this title, saying that whoever assumed and usurped it was the forerunner of Antichrist. Hence Amianus the Deacon says of John, bishop of Constantinople, who was arrogantly wishing to usurp that name. Nor indeed are you ignorant what the office of the ancient bishops was, and what manner of life, morals and teaching was described by Paul, and that the name of "dumb dogs" was given them by St Gregory, unless they discharge their office. Nor are you ignorant of the office of the priests and elders, and what force that name has, with which alone men today are content, neglecting entirely a pure life and sound teaching.

units.la: His omnibus addo & confiteor solius Verbi esse, peccata hominibus remittere, homine verò, sicut ait diuus Ambrosius, eius remissionis tantùm modò ministrum esse. Itaque si is condemnat, ea non est eius vis & potestas, sed Verbi quod ab eo annuntiatur. Hoc autem plane congruit cum quadam sententia diui Augustini in Decretis posita, ubi ait non fieri hominum meritis quòd peccata remittantur, sed virtute Spiritus sancti. Nam Dominus Apostolis suis dixerat, Accipite Spiritum sanctum: & deinde addidit, Si vos remittatis sua alicui peccata: non vos quidem sed Spiritus sanctus, quae accepistis: haec Augustinus. Cyprianus verò ait servum non posse remittere offensam adversus dominum suum commissam. quare nullam aliam ego confessionem novi, praeter eam quam Deo nos debemus, & fraternam reconciliationem & publicam coram Ecclesia confessione eorum qui aliquod scandalum admiserat, quemadmodum omnes veteres doctores docet.
units.tr: To all this I add, and I confess, that it belongs to the Word alone to forgive sins, and that a man, as the divine Ambrose says, is only the minister of that forgiveness. So if a man condemns, the power and authority is not his but that of the Word which he proclaims. This plainly agrees with a saying of the divine Augustine recorded in the Decretals, where he says that sins are forgiven not by the merits of men but by the power of the Holy Spirit. For the Lord had said to his Apostles, "Receive the Holy Spirit," and then added, "If you forgive anyone's sins, they are forgiven" (not by you, but by the Holy Spirit, whatever you have received). So Augustine. Cyprian also says that a servate cannot forgive an offence committed against his lord. Therefore I know of no other confession than that which we owe to God, and the brotherly reconciliation and public confession before the Church of those who have given some scandal, as all the ancient teachers teach.

units.la: Postremò ego ab omnibus fidelibus quaero auditoribus, qui in historiis Ecclesiasticis versati sunt, an non ea fuerit consuetudo veterum Patrum, ut haereticos persequerentur non ad mortem, sed per Scripturas, ut earum authoritate veritateq; convincerent, ac si possent, in rectam viam reducerent. Quòd si erat in suscepta opinione pertinaces, summa erat poena ut in exilium mitterentur, ne reliquum gregem contagione sua inficerent. Hoc verò tempore in ecclesia tanta saevitia adhibetur, ut homines nihil aliud planè velle ac studere videantur, quàm violentum tyrannicumq; dominatum in alios exercere. Neque verò hoc ego dico, quòd ullum crimen haereseos in mea confessione agnoscam[?] nam Deus primum testis est, nihil à me dictum esse, in quo vlla prava atque impia opinio perspiciatur. Deinde omnes verè Christiani si haec legant, idem de me iudicabunt: etiam vos ipsi, domini, si parumper in conscientias vestras intrare vultis, ac verè sine immoderato animi studio iudicare, cognoscetis. Gloria Deo sit.
units.tr: Finally, I ask all faithful hearers who have studied the ecclesiastical histories whether it was not the custom of the ancient Fathers to pursue heretics not unto death but through the Scriptures, so that by their authority and truth they might convict them and, if possible, bring them back to the right way. If anyone was obstinate in his chosen opinion, the highest penalty was exile, so that he would not infect the rest of the flock with his contagion. But in this age such savagery is practised in the Church that men seem to want and aim at nothing else than to exercise a violent and tyrannical lordship over others. Nor do I say this because any crime of heresy is to be acknowledged in my confession; for God is my first witness that nothing has been said by me in which any wicked or impious opinion can be seen. Then, if all truly Christian people read these things, they will judge the same of me. You yourselves also, my lords, if you are willing to enter your consciences for a moment, and to judge truly without immoderate zeal of mind, will come to know it. Glory be to God.

units.la: Epistola eiusdē Petri Nauiheri ad quendā amicū missa propter verbū Dei captiuum.
units.tr: The letter of the same Peter Nauiherus, sent to a certain friend while he was a prisoner on account of the Word of God.

units.la: Si[?] minus, charissime frater, officio inscribendo fungor, nec te per literas consolor, à te peto ac rogo ut mihi ignoscas. nam si mihi plus otii & commoditatis esset, nihil libentius facerem, meque una tecum consolarer. Nunc autem tu existimare debes, nobis esse cogitandum quomodo ei respondeamus, apud quem nos propediem prodituros, rationemque fidei nostrae reddituros arbitramur atque expectamus. Et quoniam ad defensionem nulla arma sunt meliora atque aptiora, quam gladius verbi Dei, non oportet nos torpere ac iacere, sed eum arripere, nosque munire, tametsi nunquam eam diligentiam adhibebimus quam magnitudo rei postulat: sed tamen confidimus, eum cuius causam nos tuemur nudos & inermes in hoc certamine non relicturum, sed verbo suo ita muniturum, ut eius honorem gloriamque defendamus, cuius testes ac procuratores coram hominibus constituit. Dominus autem se nobis adfuturum suo sacro ore promisit, cum nos admonuit, ne anxii ac solliciti simus, quid in synagogis aut apud magistratus potestatéque respondeamus aut loquamur. nam Spiritum sanctum doctorem nostrum futurum, ac demonstraturum quid & quomodo loquendum sit. Haec promissio nullo modo nos potest unquam fallere. itaque Dominus tantummodo orandus est, ut pro sua misericordia & fide nos opus manuum suarum respiciat, ut quoniam nos coram hominibus produxit, & confessione nominis sui ore nostro facta in lucem protulit, nos Spiritu suo confirmet, atque ea constantia muniat, ut quod hactenus professi & confessi sumus, id usque ad extremum vitae spiritum tueamur. Ego & tu propter eandem causam tenemur in vinculis. ea autem nostra non est, sed Dei. Itaque demonstremus nos non nostra, sed ipsius causa nomineque dimicare: simul etiam ei nostram infirmitatem, summamque fragilitatem proponamus, quae tanta est, ut ne puncto ac momento temporis coram inimicis nostris consistere possimus. Petamus igitur ab eo ut pro sua gratia virtutem suam in nobis, vasis fragilibus, often[?] dat, in nostraque infirmitate suam potentiam declaret, ut per crucem Iesu Christi, quae stultitia hominibus videtur, prudentia ipsorum & sapientia confundatur. Confidercenus[?], charissime frater, eam optimi Dei nostri esse voluntatem, ut ita conversemur inter infideles, ut consuetudo totius vitae nostrae relucet aliis, ut nostro exemplo aedificentur, aliis vero ut eiusdem vitae nostrae ac doctrinae testimonio convincantur, nullamque excusationem habeant. Cogitemus Deum olim, cùm populum suum affligeret, eumque in exilium mitteret, id fecisse, non solum ut eum castigaret, verumetiam ut in ea populi captivitate multos ad cognitionem sui vocaret. Quantum enim Danielis sociorumque eius exilium ad gloriam Dei illustrandam profuit? Nec enim dubium est, quin infideles homines cùm vident bona opera, sanctam vitam, honestaque studia eorum quos arbitrantur quasi monstra quaedam, cogantur confiteri, opinionem quam de nobis habent, esse falsam, Deoque gloriam tribuere. Itaque cum patientia & aequitate animi feramus quicquid ab eo profectum fuerit: optimam eius voluntatem expectemus, perseverantes in precibus, ut tela ignita inimici Sathanae repellamus, qui instar leonis rugientis nos circuit. Oremus, oremus optimum Deum, ut pro sua gratia brachium suum forte ac robustum exerat, quo nos humiles, inopesque servos suos tueatur, gloriaque per nos in omnibus consequatur.
units.tr: If, dearest brother, I am less than faithful in fulfilling the duty of writing, and do not console you by letter, I ask and beg you to pardon me. For if I had more leisure and opportunity, I would do nothing more gladly than console you and be consoled with you. But now you ought to consider that we must think how to answer him before whom we expect and believe we shall shortly appear and render an account of our faith. And since there are no weapons better or more fitting for our defence than the sword of the Word of God, we ought not to grow sluggish and lie idle, but to take it up and arm ourselves, although we shall never apply that diligence which the greatness of the matter requires. Yet we trust that he whose cause we defend will not leave us naked and unarmed in this struggle, but will so fortify us with his word that we may defend the honour and glory of him whose witnesses and advocates he has appointed before men. The Lord has promised with his holy mouth to be present with us, when he warned us not to be anxious or troubled about what we shall answer or say in the synagogues, before magistrates and powers. For the Holy Spirit will be our teacher and will show us what and how we must speak. This promise can never deceive us. Therefore we must only pray the Lord that, in his mercy and faithfulness, he will look upon us, the work of his hands, so that, since he has brought us forward before men and has brought to light the confession of his name made by our mouths, he will strengthen us with his Spirit and fortify us with such constancy that we may keep what we have hitherto professed and confessed, even to the last breath of life. You and I are held in chains for the same cause. Yet the cause is not ours but God's. Let us therefore show that we fight not for our own sake but for the sake and name of him; and at the same time let us set before him our weakness and our great frailty, which is so great that we cannot stand before our enemies for even a moment. Let us therefore ask him that, in his grace, he will show his power in us, frail vessels, and reveal his might in our weakness, so that through the cross of Jesus Christ, which seems foolishness to men, their prudence and wisdom may be confounded. We trust, dearest brother, that it is the will of our best God that we so conduct ourselves among unbelievers that the manner of our whole life shines out to others, so that they may be edified by our example, and convinced by the testimony of this same life and teaching, and have no excuse. Let us consider that God, when he afflicted his people of old and sent them into exile, did this not only to chastise them but also to call many to the knowledge of himself in that captivity of the people. For how much did the exile of Daniel and his companions contribute to the glory of God? Nor is there any doubt that unbelieving men, when they see the good works, holy life and honest pursuits of those whom they consider as if they were monsters, are compelled to confess that the opinion they hold of us is false, and to give glory to God. Therefore let us bear with patience and equanimity of mind whatever has come from him; let us await his best will, persevering in prayers, so that we may repel the fiery darts of Satan, the enemy, who goes about us like a roaring lion. Let us pray, let us pray to the best God, that by his grace he will stretch out his strong and mighty arm to defend us, his humble and poor servants, and that his glory may be obtained through us in all things.

units.la: Haec sunt praeclara acta eorum quinque Scholasticorum quos supra memorauimus, dictaque eorum & responsa & scripta quoad fuerunt in carcere: quibus duas nos epistolas summae eruditionis atque opportunae consolationis plenas adiunximus, quas fidelis Euangelii minister Ioannes Caluinus ad eos scripsit, accommodatas ad consolandos omnes pios, qui propter eandem causam Euangelii eadem vincula tormentaque patiuntur.
units.tr: These are the remarkable acts of those five scholars whom we mentioned above, and their sayings, answers and writings, as long as they were in prison. To these we have added two letters full of the highest learning and most opportune consolation, which the faithful minister of the Gospel, John Calvin, wrote to them, fitted to console all the godly who suffer the same chains and torments for the same cause of the Gospel.

units.la: EGO, fratres charissimi, hactenus nihil ad vos scribere volui veritus ne si literae meae in manus inciderent alienas, novam id causam durius vos affligendi inimicis afferret. Praeterea intelligebam Deum sua gratia ita agere in vobis, ut non magnopere literis meis opus haberetis. Interea neque ego neq; caeteri fratres qui sunt hic, vestri obliti fuimus, omnibusque in rebus quibus potuimus, officium studiumque nostrum vobis praestitimus. Nam simulatque vos captivi suistis, nos de eo certiores facti, cognovimus quemadmodum id acciderit: Statimque ac diligenter operam dedimus, ut auxilium vobis mittertur. Nunc responsum expectamus, ut intelligamus quid impetratum sit ab illis, à quibus opem vestra causa petimus. qui autem aliquid possunt apud eos principes, quorum in manum Deus vitam vestram tradidit, ea in re & causa vestra summam fidem, studium ac diligentiam adhibuerunt: sed quid effecerint atque impetrarint, nihil adhuc plane sciebamus. Interea quidem omnes filij Dei preces faciunt pro vobis, quae admodum debent: cum pro mutua humanitate ac misericordia, quae inter eiusdem corporis membra esse debet, tum etiam quod intelligunt atque optime sciunt vos sua causa laborare, cum causam salutis suae procuratis ac defenditis. Quomodocunque fit, nos quidem speramus & confidimus optimum ac benignissimum Deum felicem exitum captiuitatis vestrae daturum, ita ut inde habituri simus quamobrem magnopere laetari debeamus. Vos ipsi videtis quo ille vos vocet.
units.tr: I, dearest brothers, have until now been unwilling to write anything to you, fearing that if my letter fell into strangers' hands it would give the enemies a new cause for afflicting you more harshly. Besides, I understood that God works in you by his grace in such a way that you have no great need of my letters. Meanwhile neither I nor the other brothers who are here have forgotten you, and in all the matters in which we could, we have rendered you our duty and zeal. For as soon as you were taken captive, we were informed of it and learned how it happened; and at once we took care diligently that help should be sent to you. Now we await a reply, so that we may understand what has been obtained from those from whom we seek aid for your cause. Those who have some influence with those princes into whose hand God has delivered your life have shown the greatest faith, zeal and diligence in this matter and your cause; but what they have accomplished and obtained we have not yet known at all. Meanwhile all the children of God make prayers for you, as they ought to do, both out of mutual humanity and mercy, which ought to exist between the members of the same body, and also because they understand and know very well that you labour for their cause, since you are caring for and defending the cause of their salvation. However it happens, we hope and trust that the best and most kind God will give a happy outcome to your captivity, so that we shall have from it a reason to rejoice greatly. You yourselves see whither he calls you.

units.la: Ne igitur dubitetis, quin ea in re, in qua ipse opera vestra uti volet, vobis eam virtutem daturus sit, qua opus iam in vobis institutum inchoatumque perficiatur. hoc enim se facturum promisit, & nos multa praestatis fidei eius exempla documentaque habemus, quibus plane cognovimus Deum nunquam ulla in re ijs defuisse, qui se illius Spiritu duci ac gubernari passi sunt. Quin etiam id in vobis ipsis iam satis experti estis ac sensistis. nam in eo quidem suam operam ac virtutem declarauit, quod eam vobis constantiam dedit, ut primos inimicorum impetus forti animo sustineretis, eosque propulsaretis. Confidite igitur eum opus manuum suarum nunquam imperfectum relicturum. Vos scitis quid Scriptura nobis proponat, ut nos ad pugnam atq; dimicationem pro causa Filij Dei suscipiendam & sustinendam animet, omnique studio accendat, quae vos vidistis antea & audiuistis meditemini ut ea nunc in usum conferatis. Nam quidquid ego vobis possem dicere atque scribere, id vobis omne parum prodesset, nisi hoc ex fonte hauriretur. Et certe maiore firmioreque praesidio, quam hominum solatio atque adiumento opus est, ut nos inimicis tam potentibus, diabolo, morte, mundo superiores ac victores existamus. sed firmitas illa quae est in Christo Iesu, ad id assequendum satis magnam vim habet, & aduersus ea omnia pericula, quibus perturbari facile commoue-ríque rique possemus, nisi ipsius gratia ac virtute niteremur, & plane consideremus. Itaque cum vos sciatis cui crediderit, eam ei tribuite authoritatem quam meretur. Sed quoniam spero me posthac ad vos adhuc scripturum, hoc tempore hanc epistolam longiore non faciam. Tantum respondebo breuiter iis capitibus, de quibus frater Bernardus meam sententiam requisiuit. Ac primum de votis haec regula tenenda est: Homini non licere quicquam Deo vouere, nisi id quod ab eo approbetur. at vota monastica eo tantum spectant, ut purus Dei cultus plane corrumpatur. Secundo loco obseruandum, arrogantiam esse in homine plane diabolicam, vouere aliquid maius quam ratio vocationis patiatur. Scriptura autem nobis declarat, donum continentiae esse singulare, non vulgare aut cum multis commune, tum Matt.19.tum 1.Cor.7. Ex quo efficitur, eos qui huiusmodi vinculum sibi imponunt ac necessitatem ut tota vita a coniugio abhorreant, non posse in eo temeritatis crimine vllo modo excusari, atque ita Deum tentare. Res quidem haec plurib° posset explicari, si diceretur tria in ea quaestione consideranda esse. primum quis est is cui votum nuncupatur: deinde quid voueatur: postremo quis ille qui votum facit. Nam Deus quidem maior est Dominus quam ut cum eo iocandum esse videatur. homo autem quid possit considerare debet. Sacrificium vero offerre sine obedientia, mera pollutio est, summaque abominatio. Veruntamen haec ratio una pro omnibus sufficiet, si demonstretur, seipsum continere donum Dei esse singulare, atque ita singulare ut non perpetuum sit in plerisque, sed eis ad tempus concedatur. Itaque qui triginta annis eo continentiae dono praeditus fuerit, quemadmodum Isaac, illud in reliquo tempore vitae non habebit. Ex eo concludere poteritis, quod monachi, qui se eo obstringunt voto ne uxorem unquam ducant, sine vlla fide audent id Deo promittere. quod ipsis concessum non est & datum. Paupertas vero eorum pugnat omnino cum ea quam Dominus Iesus suis praecipit. Caeterum de corpore in altera vita gloria ornando: qualitates quidem eius immutabuntur, sed non omnes. oportet enim distinguere qualitates quae a corruptione peccati existunt, ab iis quae naturae ipsius corporis propriae sunt nec ab eo possunt separari. Diuus Paulus tertio Philipp. dicit hoc nostrū corpus abiectum aut infirmum, fore conforme glorioso corpori Iesu Christi. Eo autem nomine ταπεινώσεως aut humilitatis, Apolus notat eas qualitates, quas gestamus hodie in his corporibus, quæ tum quidem immutabuntur: hæ nimirum quæ fluxæ & caducæ in hoc mundo, & corruptioni obnoxiæ sunt. Atque in hanc sententiam diuus Augustinus in epistola ad Dardanum LVII. ait, Venturus est in eadem carnis forma atque substantia, cui profectò immortalitatem dedit, naturam non abstulit, secundum hanc formam non putandus est vbique diffusus. Hoc autem argumentum ille doctor prosequitur longius, demonstrans corpus Christi suis dimensionibus contineri. Et certè corpora nostra eam gloriam tum non habebunt, vt vbique diffundi versarique possint. Eam tamen habebunt similitudinem atque conformitatem, de qua Paulus loquitur. Quòd autem ad locum illum ex Apocalypsi pertinet, verba in eo ita habent v.cap. Audiui omnem creaturam, quæ in cælo est & super terram & sub terra, & quæ sunt in mari, omnes audiui dicentes, Sedenti in throno & Agno benedictio, honor & gloria. Vos quidem perspicitis, quàm puerilis, inepta, leuísque sit cauillatio, ea verba ad animas purgatorij accommodare. Nam Ioannes potius intelligit figura quadam, quæ prosopopœia appellatur, quòd ipsi etiam pisces Deu benediceret: de locisvero testimoniisq; Doctorum, remittite aduersarios vestros ad epistolam diui Augustini ad Bonifacium. xvii. vbi in fine ita scribit, Quòd Sacramenta similitudinem quandam habent earum rerum quas figurat. quo fit, vt secundum aliquem modum Sacramentum corporis Christi corpª Christi fit. Item lib. iii. de doctrina Christiana, vbi inter cætera cap. v. ita ait, Ea denùm miserabilis est animæ seruitus signa pro rebus accipere, & supra creaturam corporeã oculum metis ad hauriendum æternum lumen non leuare. Item capite nono, Agnoscat fidelis, quo referatur mysterium Baptismi & corporis ac sanguinis Domini celebratio, vt ea nö carnali seruitute, sed spirituali potiùs libertate veneretur. vt autè literæ sequi, & signa pro rebus accipere, seruilis infirmitatis est, ita inutiliter signa interpretari, malè vagatis erroris est. Alios ego locos plures nö colliga, quoniam hi vobis sufficere poterunt. Itaq; finè scribedi facies, Deũ oro vt eũ gratiæ suæ sensu in animis vestris efficiat, vt modis omnibꝰ cognoscatis, planéq; sentiatis, quantum valeat fi-delissima delissima ipsius pro suis suscepta protectio atque defensio: vosque sancto spiritu suo repleat, providentia virtutemque vobis impertiat, pacem, laetitiam, & αὐ πάρεσιν [?] afferat, quo nomen Domini nostri Jesu Christi per vos ipsos ad aedificationem Ecclesiae omni gloria celebretur.
units.tr: Do not doubt, therefore, that in the matter in which he wishes to use your labour, he will give you that strength by which the work already begun in you will be brought to completion. For he has promised to do this, and we have many examples and records of his faithfulness, from which we have clearly learned that God has never failed in any matter those who have allowed themselves to be led and governed by his Spirit. Indeed, you have already found and felt this in yourselves. For he has shown his power and effort in this, that he gave you such steadfastness that you could withstand the first attacks of your enemies with a brave spirit and drive them back. Trust, then, that he will never leave unfinished the work of his own hands. You know what Scripture sets before us, to stir us up and kindle in us every zeal to take up and sustain the battle for the cause of the Son of God. Meditate on what you saw and heard before, so that you may now put it to use. For whatever I could say or write to you would be of little benefit unless it were drawn from this source. Indeed, we need a stronger and firmer defence than any human comfort or help, so that we may stand superior to and victorious over such powerful enemies as the devil, death and the world. But that firmness which is in Christ Jesus is greatly powerful enough to achieve this, and against all those dangers by which we could easily be disturbed and shaken, unless we rested on his grace and power and fully considered it. Therefore, since you know in whom you have believed, give him the authority that he deserves. But since I hope to write to you again hereafter, I will not make this letter longer at this time. I will only briefly answer the points on which Brother Bernard asked my opinion. And first, concerning vows, this rule must be kept: it is not lawful for a man to vow anything to God except what is approved by him. But monastic vows aim only at this, that the pure worship of God is utterly corrupted. Secondly, it must be observed that arrogance is thoroughly devilish in a man, when he vows something greater than the calling of his station allows. Scripture, moreover, declares that the gift of continence is singular, not common or shared with many, as in Matthew 19 and 1 Corinthians 7. From this it follows that those who impose such a bond upon themselves, and the necessity of shunning marriage for their whole life, cannot in any way be excused from the guilt of rashness, and so tempt God. This matter could be explained at greater length if it were said that three things must be considered in this question: first, who it is to whom a vow is made; then, what is vowed; lastly, who it is that makes the vow. For God is indeed too great a Lord for it to seem fitting to joke with him, while man must consider what he is able to do. But to offer a sacrifice without obedience is mere pollution and the greatest abomination. Nevertheless, this one reason will suffice for all, if it is shown that to contain oneself is a singular gift of God, and so singular that it is not perpetual in most people, but is granted to them for a time. Therefore, whoever has been endowed with the gift of continence for thirty years, like Isaac, will not have it for the rest of his life. From this you may conclude that monks, who bind themselves by the vow never to take a wife, dare to promise this to God without any warrant of faith, since it has not been granted or given to them. Their poverty, moreover, utterly conflicts with that which the Lord Jesus prescribes to his people. As for the adorning of the body with glory in the other life: its qualities indeed will be changed, but not all of them. For one must distinguish between the qualities which arise from the corruption of sin and those which are proper to the nature of the body itself and cannot be separated from it. The divine Paul says in Philippians 3 that this our body, lowly or weak, will be made conformable to the glorious body of Jesus Christ. But by the name of humiliation [ταπεινώσεως], the Apostle denotes those qualities which we bear today in these bodies, which indeed will then be changed: namely, those which are fleeting and frail in this world and subject to corruption. And to this effect the divine Augustine, in his letter to Dardanus, number 57, says: he will come in the same form and substance of flesh, to which indeed he has given immortality but has not taken away its nature; according to this form he is not to be thought to be diffused everywhere. This argument that teacher pursues at greater length, demonstrating that the body of Christ is contained by its own dimensions. And certainly our bodies will not then have that glory, that they could be diffused and move everywhere. Yet they will have that likeness and conformity of which Paul speaks. As for the passage from the Apocalypse, the words there are in chapter 5: I heard every creature which is in heaven and upon the earth and under the earth, and which are in the sea, all of them saying: To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing, honour and glory. You see how childish, foolish and frivolous a quibble it is to apply those words to the souls of purgatory. For John rather understands, by a certain figure called prosopopoeia, that even the fishes bless God. As for the testimonies and passages of the Doctors, refer your adversaries to the letter of the divine Augustine to Boniface, number xvii, where at the end he writes thus: because the sacraments have a certain likeness to the things which they signify, therefore in a certain manner the sacrament of the body of Christ is the body of Christ. Likewise in book 3 of On Christian Doctrine, where among other things in chapter 5 he says: it is a wretched slavery of the soul to take signs for things, and not to lift the eye of the mind above corporeal creation to drink in the eternal light. Likewise in chapter nine: let the faithful acknowledge to what the mystery of Baptism and the celebration of the body and blood of the Lord refer, so that they may venerate it not with carnal servitude but rather with spiritual freedom. And just as to follow the letter and to take signs for things is a servile weakness, so to interpret signs uselessly is the fault of a wandering error. I will not gather many other passages, since these will be enough for you. And so, to make an end of writing, I pray God that he may bring it about, by the sense of his grace in your minds, that in every way you may know and truly feel how much the most faithful protection and defence which he has undertaken for his own is worth; and may he fill you with his Holy Spirit, grant you providence and strength, and bring peace, gladness and self-sufficiency [αὐ πάρεσιν], so that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be celebrated with all glory through you, to the edification of the Church.

units.la: Genevae x. die Junij, M. D. LII.
units.tr: Geneva, 10 June, 1552.

units.la: Alia eiusdem Caluini epistola ad eosdem captivos missa.
units.tr: Another letter of the same Calvin, sent to the same captives.

units.la: H[?]arissimi fratres, hoc tempore necessitas vos etiam atque etiam magis quam antea hortatur, ut omnes sensus vestros in caelo collocatis ac firmetis. Nondum quidem nos scimus quis causae vestrae & captivitatis exitus futurus sit: sed quoniam videtur Deus ad obsignandam veritatem suam sanguinem vestrum postulare, nihil melius est quam vos eam ad rem comparare, eúmque orare ut vos ad suam voluntatem ita conformet, ut nihil impediat, quo minus sanctam eius vocationem sequamini. Nam vos scitis, fratres, nos oportere ita mortificari, ut ei in sacrificium offeramur. Neque vero fieri potest, quin vos dura atque aspera certamina sustineatis, ut quod Petro dictum est, in vobis quoque compleatur, Vos eo quo nolletis trahemini. Sed vos intelligitis ac scitis, qua virtute vobis dimicandum sit. Cuius fiducia qui pugnabunt, nunquam se territos & consternatos, multo vero minus confusos sentient. Itaque, fratres, confidite vos, cum opus erit, Spiritu Domini nostri ita firmos constantesque futuros, ut nulli tentationum oneri, quantumuis sit magnum & grave, oppressi succumbatis, non magis quam ipse qui victoriam gloria insignem illustremque retulit. in qua quidem in summis nostris miseriis certissimum nostri triumphi pignus est constitutum. Quum autem opera vestra etiam usque ad mortem ut velit ad tuendam causam suam, manu forti vos tenebit: neque patietur ut ulla gutta sanguinis vestri fructu inanis effundatur. Quod si fructus non tam cito existat aut appareat, proferetur tamen maior & uberior aliquando, quam nosullis verbis nunc declarare possimus. Nam quoniam Deus vobis jam eam largitus est gratiam, ut fama vinculorum vestrorum longe lateque sit peruagata, oportebit etiam invito ipso Sathana, ut mors vestra maiore adhuc sonitu edat, & clarissimam voce veritatis Dei testem, in qua suavissimus odor, & ad vitam multorum salutaris, ad omnem posteritatem diffundatur. Equidem non dubito, quin Deus, si ei placet ad se vos evocare, usque ad hunc diem reservaverit ut diuturnior in hac vita retentio, praeparationem quandam haberet ad excitandos magis eos, quos ipse vestra morte aedificare confirmareque constituit. Ego autem vos neque consolor, neque exhortor: certò sciens optimum Deum Patremque cælestem eò gratiæ suæ sensu animos vestros affecisse, ut quantæ & quàm suaves sint ipsius consolationes percipiatis ac sentiatis, summáque diligentia ea meditemini quæ ab eo in verbo ipsius vobis proponuntur. Jam reipsa satis declarauit, quemadmodum virtus ipsius in vobis resideret, ut dubitare nullo modo debeamus, quin suam gratiam ad extremum usque tueatur. Vos quidem optimè scitis nostrum ex hac vita excessum, non fortuitum quendam atque incertum esse cursum: non modò propter certitudinem, quà persuasi estis vitam aliam esse cælestem: verumetiam quòd verissimo gratuitæ Dei adoptionis testimonio obsignati, ita ex hoc mundo deceditis, ut hæreditatem vestram adeatis. Quòd autem Deus vos Filii sui martyres testesq; constituit, singularis quædam & eximia honoris nota est, quæ ad communem illam omnium filiorum Dei adoptionem accessit.
units.tr: Most dear brethren, at this time necessity urges you, more than ever before, to fix all your thoughts on heaven and keep them there. We do not yet know what the outcome of your cause and captivity will be. But since God seems to demand your blood to seal his truth, nothing is better than for you to prepare yourselves for this, and to pray that he will so conform you to his will that nothing hinders you from following his holy calling. For you know, brethren, that we must be mortified so that we are offered to him as a sacrifice. Nor can it be that you will not endure hard and bitter conflicts, so that what was said to Peter may be fulfilled in you also: "You will be taken where you do not wish to go." But you understand and know with what courage you must fight. Those who fight in confidence of this will never feel themselves terrified and dismayed, and much less confused. So, brethren, trust that when the need arises, by the Spirit of our Lord you will be so firm and steadfast that you will not succumb, crushed by any burden of temptation, however great and heavy it may be, no less than he himself, who brought back a victory notable and renowned for its glory, in which, even in our greatest miseries, the most certain pledge of our triumph has been laid up. And since God wishes to defend his own cause, he will hold you with a strong hand, even unto death, and will not allow a single drop of your blood to be poured out in vain. If the fruit does not appear so quickly, it will nevertheless be brought forth at some time, greater and more abundant than we can now declare in words. For since God has already granted you such grace that the report of your chains has spread far and wide, it will be necessary, even though Satan is unwilling, that your death should sound out with still greater noise, and that you, a most clear witness to the voice of God's truth, should be spread abroad to all posterity, as a most sweet fragrance, salutary to life for many. Indeed I do not doubt that God, if it pleases him to call you to himself, has kept you alive until this day so that your longer retention in this life might be a kind of preparation for stirring up more those whom he has resolved to build up and confirm by your death. For my part, I neither console you nor exhort you, knowing for certain that our best God and heavenly Father has so affected your minds with the sense of his grace that you perceive and feel how great and how sweet his consolations are, and that you meditate with the greatest diligence on those things which he sets before you in his word. Already he has shown in fact how his power dwells in you, so that we ought in no way to doubt that he will keep his grace toward you to the very end. You know very well that our departure from this life is not a chance and uncertain course, not only because of the certainty by which you are persuaded that there is another, heavenly life, but also because, sealed by the most true testimony of God's free adoption, you depart from this world so as to enter upon your inheritance. But that God has appointed you martyrs and witnesses of his Son is a singular and outstanding mark of honour, which has been added to that common adoption of all the sons of God.

units.la: Restat ipsa dimicatio, ad quam hortatur nos Spiritus sanctus: non modò ut accedamus, sed etiam cum omni animi alacritate curramus. Molesta quidem & acerba est tentatio, videre tantam tamque immoderatam eorum qui veritatem hostiliter oppugnant, superbiam & audaciam quæ nulla vi cælesti reprimatur: videre sævitiam eorum & crudelitatem sine modo incitatam, cum Deus suorum nullam rationem habere, neque ita afflictos oppressosque subleuare videatur. Sed si nos memoria tenemus id quod est dictum, Vitam nostram nunc esse absconditam, nosque videri mortuis similes, atque etiam doctrinam non unius esse diei, sed temporum omnium: nobis alienum aut novum inusitatumque minimè videbitur, si ita afflictiones & calamitates continuentur. Cum enim Deo placeat tandiu habenas laxare inimicis, nostri est officii æquo animo has acerbitates ferre, atq; in patientia animas nostras possidere, quamvis tempus nostræ redemptionis retardetur. Postremò si is promisit se eorum judicem futurum, qui in servitutem populum suum redegerint: ne dubitemus quin horribilem vindictam habeat paratam iis, qui maiestatem ipsius cum tanta superbia audaciaque spreuerint, atq; atque cos qui purè & castè eum colunt, crudelissimè persecuti fuerint Experiamini igitur, fratres, eam Dauidis sententiam, quòd legis Dei minimè estis obliti, etiamsi vita vestra veluti in manibus sit, ut eam omni tempore linquatis. Cùm autem Deus vitam vestram impendat in re tam sancta & praeclara, cuiusmodi est Euangelij testimonium, ne dubitetis quin ea illi chara sit atque pretiosa. Tempus jam illud appropinquat, quo terra sanguinem effusum abditúmque deteget, atque in lucem proferet: & in quo nos cùm his corporibus caducis exuti suerim°, plenè ac perfectè restituemur. Interea dem° operam, ut nostro cum opprobrio nomen Filij Dei omni honore gloriáque afficiatur atque illustretur, eóque testimonio contenti sumus, quo certi sumus nos nullam aliam ob causam nec opprobria nec persecutiones pati, nisi quòd in Deo viuente sperámus. Eo autem uno conscientiae nostrae testimonio nos possumus totum mundum cum ipsius fastu cótemnere atque despicere, quoad in illud regnum recolligamur æternum, in quo plenè & cumulatè iis bonis & gaudijs perfruemur, quæ nunc quidem in spe duntaxat possidemus. Ego, fratres, cùmme vestris precibus summo animi studio commendo, tum etiam suppliciter Deum oro ut vos in sua tutela custodiáque perpetuò habeat, ac virtute sua magis magísque confirmet, planéque persuadeat de ea cura & solicitudine quam optimus Pater de vobis habet, vos omnibus Spiritus sui donis ita augeat, ut ea ad gloriam nominis ipsius amplificandam atque illustrandam usque in finem conferatur. Cæteros autem fratres nostros singulos non saluto, quòd existimo hanc epistolam eis vobiscum fore communem. Ego cum ignarus incertúsq; essem quo in statu essent res vestrae, usque ad hunc diem nolui ad vos scribere, ne sine causa molestus essem. Iterum Deũ[?] orabo, ut manum suam ad vos protegedos & cóferuãdos parata exertámq; habeat. Vester humilis frater Joa. Caluinus.
units.tr: There remains the struggle itself, to which the Holy Spirit urges us: not only that we approach it, but that we run to it with all eagerness of mind. Indeed the trial is grievous and bitter: to see such great and immoderate pride and audacity in those who hostilely attack the truth, pride that is restrained by no heavenly power; to see their savagery and cruelty incited beyond measure, while God seems to take no account of his own, and does not relieve them when they are so afflicted and oppressed. But if we keep in mind what has been said, that our life is now hidden, and that we seem like the dead, and that the doctrine is not for one day only but for all times, then it will by no means seem strange or new to us if afflictions and calamities continue in this way. For since it pleases God to give the reins to his enemies for so long, it is our duty to bear these bitternesses with an even mind and to possess our souls in patience, even though the time of our redemption is delayed. Lastly, if he has promised that he will be the judge of those who have reduced his people to slavery, let us not doubt that he has a dreadful vengeance ready for those who have despised his majesty with such pride and audacity, and for those who have most cruelly persecuted those who worship him purely and chastely. Therefore, brothers, make trial of that saying of David, that although you have not forgotten the law of God, even though your life is as it were in the hands of your enemies, you should leave it at every time. Since God is giving up your life in a cause so holy and excellent as the testimony of the gospel, do not doubt that it is dear and precious to him. That time is now drawing near in which the earth will uncover the blood that has been shed and hidden and will bring it into the light; and in which we, when we have been stripped of these fragile bodies, will be fully and perfectly restored. Meanwhile let us take care that the name of the Son of God is honoured and glorified with all honour, even at our own disgrace; and let us be content with this testimony, that we are sure we suffer neither reproaches nor persecutions for any other cause than that we hope in the living God. By this one testimony of our conscience we can despise and scorn the whole world with all its pride, until we are gathered into that eternal kingdom, in which we shall enjoy in full and abundant measure those goods and joys which we now possess only in hope. I, brothers, while I commend myself to your prayers with the greatest earnestness of mind, also humbly pray to God that he will keep you always under his protection and guard, and strengthen you more and more by his power, and make you fully sure of that care and concern which the best Father has for you; that he will so increase you with the gifts of his Spirit that they may be turned to amplifying and illustrating the glory of his name to the end. I do not greet each of our other brothers, because I think this letter will be common to them with you. Since I was ignorant and uncertain what state your affairs were in, I have until this day been unwilling to write to you, lest I should be a nuisance without cause. Again I will pray to God that he may keep his hand ready and stretched out to protect and preserve you. Your humble brother, Joh. Calvin.

units.la: Exitus quinque supra nominatorum Martyrum.
units.tr: The end of the five martyrs named above.

units.la: Um igitur illi quinque fideles Euangelij testes, quorum metio supra est facta, omnes impetus inimicorum veritatis summa cõstantia sustinuissent, ab eo die qui 1. erat Maij M.D.LII. quo in carcerem coniecti fuerant, semper eundem animum in confessione nominis Dei, studiúmque in optima causa retinuerunt, seipsos continuis ad Deum mutuisque precibus confirmantes, usque ad eum diem, qui anno exacto fuit eiusdem mensis Maij xvi. qui sane dies gratus faustusque venit liberationis eorum, ac coronae eius quae ipsis a Domino post insignem dimicationem proposita & parata fuerat. Itaque circiter horam nonam matutinam eius diei, cum in cancellorum area carceris Roanensis sententia recitata capitis damnati fuissent, cuius summa erat: ut ad locum Territorij nomine appellatum duceretur, ibiq; sepultura ignea absumerentur collocati fuerunt quodā in loco, in quo facinorosi ac damnati capitis supplicium expectare solent. Illi itaque eo in loco locati, ut primam aut secundam supplicio dictam horam pomeridianam expectarent, coeperunt Deum invocare & orare maximo cum ardore spiritus, atque eorum admiratione qui eos inspectabant: alij se in terram prosternentes, alij faciem in caelum attollentes: ea denique comprecatione facta, in Domino gaudere ac laetari, eiq; Psalmos canere coeperunt. Cum autem secunda iam hora appropinquaret, eo ex loco educti sunt vestitu subcinericio induti, ac vinctis funibus, sese invicem hortantes ad constantiam perseveranque studium, atque ad eum cursum vitaeque exitum, qui ad postem cui mox alligandi erant propositus erat, ubi Dominus insignia ornamentaque victoriae eis constituerat. Impositi igitur currui nonum canebant Psalmum, Celebrabo te Domine toto corde meo: & quanuis eis per adversarios non liceret canticum institutum absoluere, Deum tamen invocare nunquam desiterunt, multaque Scripturae sententias transeuntes pronunciare. Inter caeteras autem cum per forum transiret olitorium, ad exitum pontis qui Arari iunctus est, unus ex iis multitudinem alloquens, maxima voce precatus est in ea sententiam quae est in fine epistolae ad Hebr. Deus pacis, qui eduxit e mortuis magnum illum ouium Pastorem per sanguinem fœderis aeterni Dominum Iesum Christum, vos in omni opere bono confirmet, ut eius voluntatem faciatis. Deinde pronunciare coeperunt symbolum Apostolorum, per ea fidei capita, quibus distinctum est, ita ut cum unus eorum incepisset, alius quod sequebatur ordine excipere ac pronunciaret. Cui autem ille articulus obvenit, Conceptus de Spiritu sancto natus ex Maria virgine: sublata quam maxime potuit, voce pronunciavit, ut populus falsam iniquamque calumniam intelligeret, gerct[?],qua[?] inimici sparserant de ipsorum fide, quasi id caput negarent, ac de virgine Maria malè & sentirent & dicerent. Satellitibus vero, qui cos perturbabat, ac nisi tacerent, minabantur, manSuetè bis responderunt, Siccine vos agitis, vt nos impediatis, quominus in hoc breui & exiguo spatio quo in hac vita futuri sumus, Deum nostrum invocemus & laudemus? Cùm vero ad locum supplicio constitutum pervenissent, summa cum animi alacritate conscenderunt ingentem congeriem lignorum, quae circa postem erectum coniecta erant: duo eorum qui minimi natu erant primi ascenderunt: quos postquam carnifex vestibus exuisset, ad postem constitutum alligavit. Postremus ascendit Martialis Alba, natu omnium eorum maximus, qui diu genibus superstruem lignorum positis Deum orabat. Itaque carnifex, cum caeteros ad postem alligasset, venit ad eum adhuc in genua prolapsum, quem erectum per axillas volebat ad alios eius socios deducere. Tum Martialis Praefecto Regis in ea urbe Tignacio dixit, domine Praefecte largire mihi unum. Cui ille, quidnam illud est? Vt possim, inquit Martialis, antequam moriar, fratres meos deosculari. Hoc autem ei cum praefectus concessisset, ille ex summa lignorum strue in qua erat seipsum inclinans, fratres suos reuinctos atque alligatos osculatus est, eorum vnicuique amantissimè dicens, Vale mi frater. Eum autem caeteri quatuor sequuti sunt, atque alij alios osculati, retrorsum reflectentes collum, ac suum quisque ab alio digressum ex hac quidè vita verbis verè fraternis prosequentes dicebant, Vale mi frater. Ea amoris charitatisque significatione facta, Martialis, cùm fratres suos Deo commendasset, priusquam descenderet, vt ad postem ipse quoque alligaretur, admonuit tortorem ne eorum quae ei dixerat obliuisceretur. Deinde statim vt caeteri quatuor ligatus fuit, omnésque vna vincti catena quae circū postè ducebatur. Porrò carnifex cùm mandatū à Iudicibus haberet, vt mortem eorum acceleraret, singulorum collo funem alligauit, ita vt quinque illi funes recíderent in alium maiorem funem, qui trochleis volubilibus versabatur, vt hoc modo strangulando eos citius necaret. Itaque carnifex, cùm adipe vnxisset eorum facies, sulphurque atque stramen circumiecisset, putabat se eo versatili instrumento mortem eis celeriorem allaturum. sed funes vi ipsius ignis consumpti fuerunt ac quinque Martyres exauditi, aliquandiu se inuicem huiusmodi verbis cohortantes, Bono animo, fratres, bono animo. Quae fuerunt postremae ipsorum voces, in ipsa media flamma editae atq; exauditae, testes eius constantiae ac fidei Christianae, quam pro nomine Iesu Christi vsque ad extremum spiritum retinuerunt & conseruarunt.
units.tr: When those five faithful witnesses of the Gospel, whom I have mentioned above, had withstood with great constancy all the assaults of the enemies of the truth, they kept the same spirit and zeal for the best cause from the first day of May 1552, when they were thrown into prison, confessing the name of God. They strengthened themselves continually by prayer to God and to one another, until the sixteenth day of that same month of May, which came as a welcome and happy day of their deliverance and of the crown that the Lord had set before them and prepared for them after their remarkable struggle. So at about nine o'clock in the morning of that day, after the sentence of condemnation to death had been read out in the courtyard of the prison at Roanne, the substance of which was that they should be led to a place called Territorium and there be burned alive, they were placed in a certain spot where criminals and those condemned to death are usually kept to await their execution.
