Placed there, and waiting for the hour of execution, which was set for one or two in the afternoon, they began to call upon God and pray with the greatest fervour of spirit, to the amazement of those who watched them: some threw themselves prostrate on the ground, others lifted their faces to heaven. When that prayer was finished, they rejoiced and exulted in the Lord and began to sing psalms to him. When the second hour was drawing near, they were led out of that place, dressed in sackcloth, with cords tied on them, exhorting one another to constancy and perseverance, and to that course and end of life which was set before them at the post to which they were soon to be bound, where the Lord had appointed for them the marks and ornaments of victory. So they were placed on a cart, and they sang the ninth Psalm, "I will praise you, O Lord, with my whole heart." And although the adversaries did not allow them to finish the song they had begun, they never ceased to call upon God, and they recited many sentences of Scripture as they passed along. Among others, as they went through the vegetable market and came to the end of the bridge that joins the Arar, one of them addressed the crowd and prayed aloud with a great voice the words that close the Epistle to the Hebrews: "May the God of peace, who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus Christ, that great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant, make you perfect in every good work to do his will" [Heb. 13:20–21]. Then they began to recite the Apostles' Creed, article by article, so that when one of them had begun, another took up and recited the article that followed in order. When the article fell to one of them, "conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary," he pronounced it with his voice raised as loudly as he could, so that the people might understand the false and unjust calumny, which their enemies had spread about their faith, as if they denied this article and held and spoke ill of the Virgin Mary. But when the guards, who disturbed them and threatened them unless they kept silent, tried to stop them, they answered gently, twice: "Do you act like this to prevent us from calling upon and praising our God in this brief and small space of time that we have left in this life?" When they reached the place set for execution, they climbed with great cheerfulness onto the huge pile of wood that had been heaped around the upright post. The two youngest of them went up first; after the executioner had stripped them of their clothes, he bound them to the post. Last to climb up was Martial Alba, the oldest of them all, who knelt on the top of the pile of wood and prayed to God for a long time. Then the executioner, having bound the others to the post, came to him, still kneeling, and wanted to raise him up by the armpits and lead him to his other companions. Then Martial said to the king's prefect in that city, Tignacius: "Lord prefect, grant me one request." He replied: "What is it?" Martial said: "That before I die I may be allowed to kiss my brothers." When the prefect had granted this, he leaned over from the top of the pile of wood and kissed his brothers, who were bound and tied to the post, saying to each of them most lovingly, "Farewell, my brother." The other four followed him, and they kissed one another, turning their necks backwards, and each one, as he parted from the other, took leave of him with truly brotherly words, saying, "Farewell, my brother." When this sign of love and charity had been made, Martial, having commended his brothers to God, before he came down so that he himself might be tied to the post also, reminded the executioner not to forget what he had said to him. Then, as soon as the other four were tied up, all of them, bound together with one chain, were drawn round the post. Now the executioner had orders from the judges to hasten their deaths, so he tied a rope around the neck of each, so that the five ropes ran into one larger rope which turned on movable pulleys, so that by this means he might strangle them and kill them more quickly. Accordingly, the executioner, having smeared their faces with fat and heaped sulphur and straw around them, thought he would bring them a quicker death by this turning device. But the ropes were burned through by the very force of the fire, and the five martyrs were heard for some time encouraging one another with words such as these: "Be of good courage, brothers, be of good courage." These were their last words, uttered and heard in the middle of the flames, witnesses of their constancy and Christian faith, which they held and kept for the name of Jesus Christ until their last breath.

units.la: PETRVS BERGIERVS, vrbis Geneuensis incola.
units.tr: PETER BERGIER, an inhabitant of the city of Geneva.

units.la: ONIUNCTAM habet cum superioribus quinque martyribus causam atque historiam Petrus Bergierus, Barti natus oppido ad flumen Sequanam posito: mercator annonarius atq; œnopola professione. Is cum Geneuae habitaret, subinde Lugdunum vbi aliquandiu artocreaticam artem exercuerat, commeabat atque vxoris suae parentes inuisebat. Anno autem M.D.LII. cum esset Lugduni in domo eius cuius sororem in matrimonio habebat, captus est circiter quartum Maij diem quatriduo postquam illi quinque Scholastici capti fuissent. Is autem cum esset in carcere, purissimam doctrinae Filij Dei confessionem edidit, non solum coram Iudicibus ad quos productus suit: sed etiam vt erat ingenio alacri & vehementi, apud omnes qui ab eo rationem eius fidei disciplinaeque Christianae, quam profitebatur, quaesiuerunt. Quin etiam cum apud eos Iudices saepius eandem doctrinam declarasset, qua omnia fidei suae capita complectebatur, ad eam magis adhuc testificandam & confirmandam, manu sua subsignauit confessionem Bernardi Seguini, in superiore quinque Martyrum narratione positam, quandoquidem vnam cum illis eandemque Euangelij ac religionis causam confitendam & tuendam suscepisset. Itaque Lector eam historiam, quae omnia illorum acta complectitur, repetere poterit, imprimisque vt admirabile latronis Ioa. Chaboni conuersione cognoscat: quem diabolo mancipatum, & tatumnon[?] desperationis voragine absorptum Bergierus sanctissimis suis exhortationibus ac precibus Christo Domino in vinculis suis genuit. Atque vt praestantissimus pietatis fructus perspiciatur, quem ille Geneuae in ecclesia verbo Dei emendata, optimeque constituta ceperat, in qua vxorem & familiam habebat, nos vnam eius epistolam hoc loco posuimus, quam is horam martyrii sui iam expectans, ad coniugem suam non minus prudenter quam amanter ac fideliter misit, cum eam captiuus multis aliis literis ante consola tus fuisset.
units.tr: Peter Bergier is joined to the five martyrs above in cause and history. He was born at Bar-sur-Seine, a town on the river Seine, and worked as a grain merchant and wine seller. While he was living at Geneva he often travelled to Lyon, where he had for some time practised the baker's trade, and he visited his wife's parents there. In 1552, while he was at Lyon in the house of the man whose sister he had married, he was arrested about the fourth day of May, four days after those five scholars had been taken. In prison he made a most pure confession of the teaching of the Son of God, not only before the judges to whom he was brought, but also, being of a lively and vehement temperament, before all who asked him for an account of the faith and Christian discipline he professed. Indeed, after he had often declared before those judges the same doctrine, embracing all the articles of his faith, he signed with his own hand, to bear witness to and confirm it all the more, the confession of Bernard Seguin, which is set out in the narrative of the five martyrs above, since he had undertaken to confess and defend together with them the same cause of the Gospel and of religion. So the reader may go back to that history, which contains all their acts, and especially learn of the remarkable conversion of the thief John Chabon, whom the devil had made his own and who was wholly swallowed up in the abyss of despair. Bergier, by his most holy exhortations and prayers, begot him to Christ the Lord in his chains. And so that the most excellent fruit of piety which he had gained at Geneva, in the church purified by the Word of God and very well ordered, may be seen, where he had a wife and family, we have placed here one of his letters. He sent it to his wife while already awaiting the hour of his martyrdom, no less prudently than lovingly and faithfully, after he had been comforted in his captivity by many other letters earlier.

units.la: Gratia & pax tibi per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Grace and peace to you through our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Tui[?],charissima fidelissimáq; uxor, crebris iam literis ad te scriptis, quasi discedens ex ista vita te valere iussi, quemadmodum quidem Deus signa nobis dabat non obscura eius suae voluntatis, qua nos ad se evocare videbatur, imprimisque honorem ac timorem Dei, ut propria chariorem vita tibi diligenter atque studiose commendavi: tamen cum Dominus postea inimicorum consilia everterit, nobisque vitam praeter omnem nostram opinionem atque spem, ad aliquod tempus prorogaverit, & ad novum deinde vocaverit certamen, ut sanctam ipsius veritatem sanguine nostro ita obsignemus, ut nulla vis mundi nos impedire possit, minimè superuacaneum sum arbitratus, iisdem de rebus adhuc scribere, teque rogare ut gloriam Dei omnium maximè commendatam & charam habeas, maioresque in dies studeas in sancta eius cognitione progressus pietatis facere, quo eum integrè & caste colas sanctissimumque eius nomen optima ac modestissima vitae morumque ratione ornes atque illustres. Utere iis rationibus & adiumentis, quae tibi à Deo ad salutem, non ad condemnationem tribuuntur: in quibus intelligo imprimis verbum Dei, quod tu quotidie audire potes maxina cum efficacia & puritate annuntiatum. deinde tot praeclara exempla cum optimorum Deumque timentium hominum, tum vero tot lectissimarum atque honestissimarum foeminarum, quas Dominus tibi ante oculos, quasi praeclara quaedam lumina & sanctae vocationis suae doctrinaeque ornamenta constituit, eo in loco quem ipse omni bonorum ac solatiorum genere ornavit & cumulavit. Et quoniam Dominus vobis liberos dedit, cura ut in timore ipsius ac pietate instituantur, quo eius gloriae aliquando servire possint. Equidem cum Dominus me ad suum nomen sanguine meo testificandum velit pro singulari sua gratia adhibere, eo iam onere solutus sum ac liberatus. Nunc onus totius piae educationis atque institutionis tibi incumbit. Quare da operam, ut ea in re officio fungaris tuo. Nulla melior aut praestantior haereditas eis relinqui potest, quam si à te ita pie educentur atque instituantur, ut Deum unum imprimis metuant, venerentur & colant. Tu quidem in ea cura, quemadmodum debes, tuum officium studiumque præstabis. Quod autem tui solatij proprium est, cum Dominus me ad se vocauerit, te cosolaberis in eo, in quo vno firmum viduis pupillisque præsidium est constitutum. Quod si fientis in te à Deo tibi dari continentiæ donum, manebis in viduitate tua, sequesque illud consilium quod à Paulo piis viduis datum est. Nam hac quidem ratione maiorem commoditatem habebis ad meditandas res diuinas ac cœlestes, plane libera solutaque ijs curis quibus homines coniuges distrahuntur atque impediuntur, quominus plene ac perfecte Deo seruire possint. Atque hæc quidem vitæ ratio, si continentiam adiunctam habeat, eò minus tibi est aspernanda, quòd Dei benignitate ea adhuc bona habeas, quibus te cum liberis nostris facile tueri possis. Quòd si non possis teipsam continere, tibi consulo vt cum alio viro societate coniugij coeas, modò nihil suscipias & facias nisi de sententia atque authoritate parentum tuorum, aliorumque amicorum qui ea in re non minus tibi, quàm sibi vellent consulere: atque imprimis eam diligentiam curamque adhibeas, vt ei viro te coiungas, quicum in timore Domini pie ac sancte viuere possis. Vt autem liberi nostri perpetuam mei memoriam custodiant, te magnopere rogo, vt recuperes omnes epistolas tum eas quas ego ad vos scripsi, tum etiam illas quas alij ad me nuper miserunt, quarum in hac vrbe magnus est numerus apud fratrem tuum, quas omnes describendas atque vnum in librum referendas curabis. Deinde eas ita descriptas poteris cum cæteris hominibus fidelibus communicare atque impertire, vt aliquis consolationis fructus ex illis ad Ecclesiam perueniat. Ego verò hæc tibi eò vehementius commendo, quod tempus dissolutionis nostræ magis quàm vnquam appropinquare videtur. Na vt tu intelligas, quinque fratres nostri Bernatum principum Scholastici die Lunæ, qui dies fuit xv. Maij hora nona matutina, alij post alios, ad Iudices producti fuerunt, quos ego postremus sequutus sum. Hoc autem Iudices eo consilio fecerunt, vt viderent an nos apud ipsos respondere vellemus. Quibus nos omnes respondimus, eis iudicium in nos minimè competere, ipsos Iudices plane recusare, atq; ad eos appellare, ad quos iudicium pertineret. Tum Supprafectus (quem Locumtenentem vocant) dixit se mandatum à Rege habere, vt de causa nostra iudicaret, ac de nobis decerneret, atque etiam[?] multas literas ab eo missas: quas nobis ita ostendebat, ut tamen non legeret. Sed nos, ac præcipue quinq; Scholastici, ab ea impetratione atq; auctoritate literarum appellauimus, quasi eas falso intelligentiæ prætextu, ac fauore Cardinalis Turnonij impetrassent, qui paucis post diebus in hanc urbem venit, ut nos summo ignis supplicio afficiendos curet. Ne sim longior, Iudices multa & varia cum vnoquoq; nostrum loquuti sunt, ut quisque priuatim ac seorsim ad eos productus est. Sed nos omnes eam Dei gratiam atque opem percepimus ac sensimus, ut nemo fuerit, qui non se mirabiliter confirmatum senserit. Equidem vere non possim dicere me à Deo derelictum destitutumque fuisse, sed ea virtute Spiritus & constantia firmatum, quam summa temporis nostri necessitas postulabat ac flagitabat.
units.tr: My dearest and most faithful wife, I have already written to you many times, and I bade you farewell as one about to depart from this life. God gave us clear signs of his will, by which he seemed to be calling us to himself. Above all, I earnestly and diligently commended to you the honour and fear of God, which you should hold dearer than your own life. Yet afterwards the Lord overturned the plans of our enemies, and beyond all our expectation and hope he prolonged our life for a while, and then called us to a new contest, so that we might seal his holy truth with our blood, and no power of the world could hinder us. So I have thought it by no means superfluous to write to you again on the same matters, and to beg you to hold the glory of God, which is commended above all, as dear and precious, and to make greater progress from day to day in its holy knowledge, so that you may worship him wholly and purely, and adorn and illustrate his most holy name by the best and most modest way of life and conduct. Use those means and aids which are given to you by God for salvation, not for condemnation. Among these I understand first of all the Word of God, which you can hear every day, proclaimed with the greatest power and purity. Next, there are so many outstanding examples, both of the best men who fear God and of so many most select and honourable women, whom the Lord has set before your eyes as bright lights and as ornaments of his holy calling and doctrine, in the place which he has adorned and filled with every kind of good and comfort. And since the Lord has given you children, take care that they be brought up in his fear and piety, so that they may one day be able to serve his glory. For my part, since the Lord wishes to use me by his singular grace to bear witness to his name with my blood, I am now released and freed from that burden. Now the whole duty of their godly upbringing and instruction falls upon you. So take pains to perform your duty in this matter. No better or more excellent inheritance can be left to them than that they be brought up and taught by you so piously that they above all fear, reverence and worship the one God. In that care you will, as you ought, give your duty and zeal. As for what belongs to your own comfort: when the Lord has called me to himself, you will be consoled in that which alone is a firm defence for widows and orphans. But if God gives you the gift of continence, so that you remain in your widowhood, follow the counsel given by Paul to pious widows. For in this way you will have greater opportunity to meditate on divine and heavenly things, free and released from those cares by which married people are distracted and hindered, so that they cannot serve God fully and perfectly. And this way of life, if joined with continence, should be all the less despised by you, because by God's goodness you still have the means by which you can easily support yourself and our children. But if you cannot contain yourself, I advise you to enter into marriage with another man, provided you undertake nothing and do nothing except with the consent and authority of your parents and of other friends, who would be no less concerned for you in this matter than for themselves. And above all, take the greatest care and diligence to join yourself to a man with whom you can live piously and holily in the fear of the Lord. Now, so that our children may keep a perpetual memory of me, I earnestly ask you to recover all the letters, both those which I wrote to you and those which others have lately sent to me, of which there is a large number in this city with your brother. Take care that all of them are copied out and gathered into one book. Then, once they have been copied in this way, you may share and impart them to the other faithful, so that some fruit of consolation may come from them to the Church. I commend these things to you the more earnestly because the time of our departure seems to draw nearer than ever. For you should know that our five brothers, the scholars of Bernay, were brought before the judges one after another on Monday, which was the fifteenth day of May, at nine o'clock in the morning, and I followed them last. The judges did this so that they might see whether we were willing to answer before them. We all answered that judgement over us did not belong to them, that we plainly refused the judges themselves, and that we appealed to those to whom the judgement properly pertained. Then the sub-prefect (whom they call the lieutenant) said that he had a commission from the King to judge our cause and to decide about us, and he also showed us many letters sent by him, but in such a way that he did not read them. But we, and especially the five scholars, appealed from that grant and authority of the letters, on the ground that they had obtained them under a false pretext of misunderstanding and by the favour of Cardinal Turnon, who came to this city a few days later, to see that we were condemned to the supreme punishment of fire. To make a long story short, the judges spoke many and various things with each of us, as each was brought before them privately and separately. But all of us received and felt that grace and help of God, so that there was no one who did not feel himself wonderfully strengthened. Indeed, I could not truly say that I had been abandoned and forsaken by God, but that I was strengthened by that power of the Spirit and that constancy which the great necessity of our time demanded and required.

units.la: Frater quoque Dymonctus ad carceres Archiepiscopi ductus fuit, & palam hæreticus ab Ossiciali declaratus. Et quamuis ab ea sententia appellauerit ut iniquam tamen statim in hunc carcerem regium Roanam adductus est, ut eadem in causa & pœna nobiscum esset: quæ res satis indicat appellationem eius non valituram. Paulo post ad Iudices productus, quemadmodum nos fuimus, non magis quam cæteri os clausum habuit ut Deo gloriam daret: sed eam virtutem in verbo eius declarauit ac præstitit, ut non Officiales modò attonitos reddiderit, verumetiam summo pudore affecerit concionatorem quendam monachum ex eorum secta qui Infumati à colore vestis quam gerunt, appellantur, qui ac quadragesima in templo S. Crucis est concionatus, ea existimatione atque authoritate, ut imperiti homines eum probe adorent. Is tamen ita affectus planéque confusus ab eo Officiali[?] consessu discessit, ut nec cōclusiones quidé, quas aduersus Dymonetum fratrem nostrum ōfecerant[?], vnquam signare voluerit. De fratre nostro Dionysio Pelouino nihil plane scimus. Rumor est hac tota urbe sparsus, nos sequee[?] hebdomade vitam nostram supplicio ignis visitato finituros, eodem imul[?] die aut diuersis diebus. Sed mihi credas velim, nos eo sermone nul-lo[?] quoque huiusmodi terrore consternari, neque animo ita debilitari ut eum despondeamus: sed Deus nos sua virtute magis magisque atque in dies singulas confirmat, & admirabilem constantiam nobis dat, ámque animi fiduciam, qua ipsum in nobis opus institutum absoluturūsperamus & cōfidimus: ita vt ex eo Ecclesia maximū ædificationis & consolationis fructū sit perceptura. Nam is quidem pro gratia sua facit, vt nos iam animo cernamus eum fructum, quem mors nostra omnibus electis afferet: quæ nobis cogitatio non mediocrē consolationem in his vinculis nostris affert. Cæterum hac postrema epistola iubens te ac liberos nostros valere, Dominū oro vt vos in omni sanctæ voluntatis suæ obedientia retineat, & mihi vsq; ad extremū eam præstet voluntate, vt me ei in sacrificium voluntarium, maximéque odoratum offeram, vtque tandem nos recolligat in illud suum regnum cœleste, vbi nos alij alios inuitis veritatis inimicis, cum maximo gaudio visuri sumus. Cæteri omnes fratres idem & sentiunt & dicūt, simulque te rogamus, vt nostro omnium nomine plurimum salutis fidelibus istius Ecclesiæ ministris dicas, & præterea cæteris fratribus ac sororibus, qui propter coniunctam Euangelij causam in seipsis afflictiones nostras sentiunt, nunc quidem nos precibus ecclesiæ nō commēdamus, propterea quòd antequam has literas acceperis, speramus nos cum Domino futuros in illo cœtu sanctorum spirituum perbeato, vbi nullis opus erit pro nobis precibus, cum Dominus omnibus lachrymis abstersis nos summis ac suauissimis gaudijs explebit. Tātum hoc vnum te rogamus, vt cum Ministros nostros verbis salutaueris, eos nostro mandato rogatúque admoneas, vt simulatque intellexerint gratiam, quā speramus Dominum in nos vsurum, ipsi cum tota ecclesia maximas ei pro tanto benefício gratias agant. Quanquam sciebamus id illos per se saturos, etiamsi nihil ad tescripsissemus, id tamen tibi voluimus mandare, vt tanta gratia Dei atque ope omnibus cognita & prædicata, magis vniuersa ecclesia ædificetur, & qui sunt adhuc infirmi in fide ita confirmentur, vt totam in Deo vno salutis suæ fiduciam reponant, & sixam plane habeant. Eius gratia & pax sit tecum. Hoc die Lunæ X V. Maij. M.D.L I I I.
units.tr: Brother Dymonctus too was led to the Archbishop's prison and was openly declared a heretic by the Official. Although he appealed from that sentence as unjust, he was at once brought to this royal prison at Rouen, to share our cause and our punishment. That fact sufficiently shows that his appeal will not avail. Shortly afterwards he was brought before the judges, and like us he did not keep his mouth shut to avoid giving glory to God. Instead he showed and displayed such power in his words that he not only left the Officials astonished but also covered with great shame a certain monk, a preacher of their sect (the sect called Infumati from the colour of the clothes they wear), who preaches during Lent in the church of the Holy Cross and is held in such esteem and authority that ignorant people worship him greatly. Yet that monk, so affected and thoroughly confused, left the Official's assembly and would not even sign the conclusions they had drawn up against our brother Dymonetus. About our brother Dionysius Pelouinus we know absolutely nothing. A rumour has spread through this whole city that we are to end our lives by the punishment of fire within the next week, on the same day or on different days. But believe me, I would have you know that we are not dismayed by such talk or by any terror of this kind, nor so weakened in spirit that we despair. Rather, God strengthens us by his virtue more and more every day, and gives us an admirable constancy and a confidence of spirit, by which we hope and trust that he will bring to completion the work he has begun in us, so that the Church will reap from it the greatest fruit of edification and consolation. For by his grace he lets us now see with the eye of the mind the fruit which our death will bring to all the elect. This thought brings no small consolation in our chains. Moreover, in this last letter, bidding you and our children farewell, I pray the Lord to keep you in obedience to his holy will in everything, and to grant me, even to the end, the will to offer myself to him as a voluntary sacrifice, and a most fragrant one; and at last to gather us into that heavenly kingdom of his, where we shall see one another with the greatest joy, while the enemies of the truth are unwilling spectators. All the other brothers both feel and say the same, and we ask you together to convey our greetings, on behalf of all of us, to the faithful ministers of this Church, and also to the other brothers and sisters who feel our afflictions in themselves because of the cause of the Gospel that binds us together. We do not now commend ourselves to the prayers of the Church, because before you receive this letter we hope to be with the Lord in that most blessed assembly of holy spirits, where there will be no need of prayers for us, since the Lord, having wiped away every tear, will fill us with the highest and sweetest joys. We ask only this one thing: when you have greeted our ministers with words, admonish them, at our command and request, that as soon as they understand the grace which we hope the Lord will show us, they themselves, with the whole Church, give him the greatest thanks for so great a benefit. Although we know they will be satisfied of this by themselves, even if we had written nothing to you, we nonetheless wished to commission you with it, so that, with such great grace and help of God known and proclaimed to all, the whole Church may be built up more, and those who are still weak in the faith may be so strengthened that they place their whole confidence of salvation in the one God and hold it firm. May his grace and peace be with you. This Monday, 15 May 1553.

units.la: Alia epistola ad eundem Petrum Bergierum missa ab eo qui in carcerem coiectus, eandem causam tuebatur.
units.tr: Another letter, sent to the same Peter Bergier by the man who, cast into prison, was defending the same cause.

units.la: Frater charissime, inter Christum & Belial, inter communionem Christianorum & impiam Antichristi synagogam, pax esset proclamata, facilè crudelitas modum aliquem finémque accipe-ret, ret, tuque ac nos omnes qui in vinculis propter communem Euangelij causam sumus, soluti & liberi carcere dimitteremur. Sed ut partes adversariae huiusmodi dissidium habent, quod nullum opinionum voluntatumque consensum habere potest: ita non oportet nos expectare ullam moderationem eius inhumanitatis, sævitiæ & crudelitatis, quæ inimici sunt inflammati, sed patienter tolerare quoad Princeps ac Rex noster omnium potentissimus eorum immanitati finem imponat. quod quidē suo tempore, eáq; optima ratione quā novit, facilè efficiet. Nostrum igitur officium est, ut cum silentio cum exitum atq; eventum expectantes[?] cuius Dominus est moderator, oculos in caelum nostros attollamus, unde ope ac salute, non aliunde speremus[?]. Hoc autē propterea dico, charissime frater, quòd nisi virtus tibi Divinitus è cælo mitteretur, facile in tanto inimicorum conatu atq; impetu cederes atque succumberes, cùm horrendis minis quæ tibi quotidie intentantur, territus & consternatus: tu verò illectus iis magnificis promissis, quibus homines te à proposito fidei volùt abducere. Sed maximam Deo gratiam & habemus & agimus, qui te ac cæteros fratres nostros ita conservavit, ut inimici nostri victi, vos vero victores fueritis. Equidem non dubito, quin tu interdum sensu carnis, ut ea est infirma, ea percipias quæ animo magnum terrorem afferre solent: sed quemadmodum gubernator summa maris tempestate agitatus, maximopere reficitur ac recreatur simulac portum videre potest, etiāsi suum eo appulsum non ita exploratum habeat, ita oportet te atq; etiā multo magis in hoc certamine, quanvis difficili & aspero, animum erigere, consolari, sustinereq; ea una spe, quæ præmiū pulcherrimæ coronæ victoribus propositum, certius quàm ea quæ oculis cernuntur, spiritu intuetur: sicuti qui illud proposuit, ea est fide ac veritate ut fallere nullo modo pos-it. obsecro vos, conferte paulum vestram cum eorum conditione qui vos crudeliter persequuntur. Hi quidem optimè sibi sunt conscij eius iniquitatis atq; iniuriæ, qua vos in optima causa vestra afficiūt. Crudelitas ipsorum inaudita singulari vestra patientia superatur: sua ipsis conscientia non solùm est gravis quidā accusator, testisq; un° pro mille, veumetiam[?] iudex eos perpetuò condenans, atque etiā carnifex graviter nexans & crucians. Velint nolint, sentiant oportet Deum acerrimum ipsis esse aduersarium. Cum vero iniquissimâ causam suam vincere pro animi libidine non possunt, strident dentibus: & quanuis liberi in hac vita esse videantur, magis tamen quam vos, captiui sunt. Etenim certò quidem scitis, vos in hunc carcerem coniectos & conclusos esse summa eius prouidentia qui vobis est pater: pro causa illius cui omnis potestas est data in caelo & in terra: cuius sine voluntate, diaboli ne porcis quidem nocere possunt: tantum abest vt aliquid mali aut incommodi vobis absque eius permissu ac ductu afferant. Conscientia vero vestra vobis pacem affert & summam tranquillitatem pari cum laetitia coniunctam. Et quanuis in carcere inclusi sitis, in maxima tamen estis libertate. nam verbum Dei quod habitat in vobis, ligari nullo modo potest. Deniq; inimici vestri rebus omnibus sunt vobis inferiores, nisi furore & violentia, ad quae postrema sua praesidia armáque confugiunt, vt sua mendacia tueantur. L. Sanctandreanus.
units.tr: Dearest brother, if peace had been proclaimed between Christ and Belial, between the fellowship of Christians and the impious synagogue of Antichrist, cruelty would easily accept some measure and end, and you and all of us who are in chains for the common cause of the Gospel would be loosed and set free from prison. But since the adversaries' side holds a division of this kind, which can have no agreement of opinions or wills, so we ought not to expect any moderation from that inhumanity, savagery and cruelty with which our enemies are inflamed; rather we must patiently endure until our Prince and King, the most powerful of all, puts an end to their brutality. He will do this easily, in its own time and by the best method he knows. Our duty, therefore, is to wait in silence for the outcome and the event, of which the Lord is the governor, and to lift our eyes to heaven, whence we hope for help and salvation, and from nowhere else. I say this, dearest brother, because unless virtue were sent to you from heaven by God, you would easily have yielded and given way in such a great effort and attack of enemies, terrified and dismayed by the dreadful threats that are levelled at you every day, and tempted by those magnificent promises with which men want to draw you away from the purpose of your faith. But we both have and give the greatest thanks to God, who has so preserved you and the other brothers that our enemies are defeated and you have been the victors. Indeed I do not doubt that sometimes, in the feeling of the flesh, which is weak, you perceive things that are wont to bring great terror to the mind. But just as a steersman, tossed in the greatest storm at sea, is greatly restored and refreshed as soon as he can see the harbour, even though he does not yet have his ship safely landed there, so you ought, and much more in this struggle, however difficult and harsh, to raise up your spirit, to comfort it and sustain it by that one hope which the prize of the most beautiful crown, set before the victors, holds in the spirit more surely than what is seen by the eyes; since he who has set it before us is so faithful and true that he can in no way deceive. I beg you, compare for a little while your condition with the condition of those who cruelly persecute you. They are indeed well aware of the wickedness and injury with which they treat you in your most righteous cause. Their cruelty is overcome by your singular patience. Their own conscience is not only a heavy accuser, a witness worth a thousand, but also a judge condemning them continually, and even an executioner tormenting and racking them grievously. Whether they will or not, they must feel that God is most bitterly their adversary. And when they cannot win their most unjust cause as their lust desires, they gnash their teeth; and although they seem free in this life, they are nonetheless more captive than you. For you surely know that you have been thrown into this prison and shut up by the great providence of him who is your Father, for the sake of his cause, to whom all power is given in heaven and on earth; without whose will the devils cannot harm even pigs; so far is it from being the case that they can bring you any evil or inconvenience without his permission and guidance. Your conscience brings you peace and the greatest tranquillity, joined with equal joy. And although you are shut up in prison, you are nonetheless in the greatest liberty, for the word of God that dwells in you can in no way be bound. Finally, your enemies are inferior to you in all things, except in fury and violence, to which at last they flee for their weapons and defences, so as to protect their lies. L. Sanctandreanus.

units.la: Sequitur praeclarus & beatus exitus Petri Bergieri.
units.tr: Here follows the illustrious and blessed death of Peter Bergier.

units.la: PETRVS igitur Bergierus cum sententiam capitalem contra se pronunciatam accepisset, ducibus est è carcere, vultu tranquilliore ac laetiore quàm vnquam antea in eo visus fuisset, adeo vt multi qui eum ante cognouerant, eum ita compositum laetumque intuentes summa admiratione afficerentur. Prius autem quam currum conscenderet, à Iudice familiarem in modum petiit vt vnam sibi gratiam impetraret. Quem cum Iudex reiecisset, Tu quidem, domine, inquit Petrus, hoc vnum mihi concedes, vt mihi liceat dicere meum Pater & meum Credo, vtens huiusmodi verbis, quae in vsum quotidianum ac vulgarem recepta sunt. Cui ille, Dic si volueris, sed inter eundum. Ego, vero, inquit Petrus, maximas tibi domine gratias ago, acmeas pro te ad Deum preces promitto. Tum satellites, qui ibi aderant, cum irridentes, Sane, inquiunt, tuis precibus valde opus habet. Cum autem currui impositus fuisset, petebat ab omnibus vt sibi ignosceret, omnibusque ipse ignoscebat. Ac in ipsa via praeteriens vnumquemque iubebat valere ea vultus hilaritate & oris modestia, quàm paulò ante significauimus, ab omnibus postulans vt pro se Deum orarent. Porro inter caeteros ex turba fuit quidam senex sacerdos Iudaeus, qui eum praetereuntem, huiusmodi verbis est prosecutus: Hodie tua in inferno commoratio erit. Cui Petrus, Dominus, inquit, tibi ignoscat. Ad platcam vero illam, quae ad Rhodanum usque producta & complanata, vulgo Territorii appelatur, cum venit, magna voce exclamavit, O copiosam atque ingentem messem! bonos, Domine, operarios mitte. Deinde cum paratam ad supplicium Strum[?] lignorum ascendisset, & causam quam tuebatur declarasset, coniunctam cum fidei suae confessione, quasi exultans, summaque Spiritus laetitia seipsum efferens, magna cum exclamatione & clarissima voce dixit, Quam suave, ô Domine, atque amabile est nomen tuum! Postea cum carnifex alligaret eum, ac sicut caeteros martyres, sublimem attolleret, Petrus se totum in fide Dei permittens & tradens, Domine, inquit, ego tibi commendo animam meam: eademque verba repetivit saepius. Denique intuens in caelum intentis ac defixis oculis vultuque immobili, exclamavit, Ego hodie caelos apertos video. Id autem cum multi ex turba non intelligerent cum oculis fidei atque spiritus videre, convexum caelum suspiciebant. Postea statim vir pius placidissime moriens, spiritum Domino suum reddidit.
units.tr: Peter Bergier, when he had received the sentence of death pronounced against him, was led out of prison. His countenance was calmer and more cheerful than it had ever appeared before, so that many who had known him earlier were struck with great wonder at seeing him so composed and joyful. Before he climbed into the cart, he asked the judge, in a familiar manner, to grant him one favour. When the judge refused, Peter said, "You, sir, will at least grant me this one thing: that I may say my Pater noster and my Credo, using words that are received in everyday and common use." The judge replied, "Say it if you like, but as you go." "Indeed," said Peter, "I give you the greatest thanks, sir, and I promise my prayers to God for you." Then the guards who stood there mocked him: "Surely he has great need of your prayers." When he had been placed in the cart, he asked everyone to forgive him, and he forgave them all. Along the way, as he passed, he bade each person farewell with the cheerfulness of face and modesty of manner we have described above, asking everyone to pray to God for him. Among the crowd there was an old Jewish priest, who followed him as he passed with these words: "Today your dwelling will be in hell." Peter answered, "May the Lord forgive you." When he came to that open square which extends down to the Rhone and is levelled, commonly called the Territory, he cried out in a loud voice, "O what a plentiful and great harvest! Lord, send good labourers." Then, when he had climbed the prepared pile of wood and had declared the cause he defended, joined with the confession of his faith, he lifted himself up as if exulting, filled with the highest joy of the Spirit, and said with a great cry and a very clear voice, "How sweet and lovely is your name, O Lord!" Afterwards, when the executioner bound him and raised him up on high, as with the other martyrs, Peter, giving and committing himself wholly into the faith of God, said, "Lord, I commend my soul to you," and he repeated these same words many times. Finally, gazing into heaven with fixed and steady eyes and an unmoving countenance, he cried out, "Today I see the heavens opened." When many in the crowd did not understand this, since he saw with the eyes of faith and spirit, they looked up at the vaulted sky. Soon afterwards this godly man died most peacefully and gave back his spirit to the Lord.

units.la: DIONYSIVS PELOQVINVS.
units.tr: DIONYSIUS PELOQUINUS.

units.la: Amplissima Dei dona atque ornamenta, quibus miseros homines afficit: tantam virtutem & constantiam quam Dominus suis impertit, hunc honorem tribuens, ut ad tribunalia iudiciaque hominum eos producat, atque testes, procuratores ac defensores veritatis suae constituat, quis satis mirari possit? Hic est Dionysius Peloquinus, generis ac nominis familiae suae fœdus[?], in quem Deus hanc summam gratiam & dignitatem contulit. Nam aliquo ante tempore frater huius Stephanus Peloquinus eam crucis viam ingressus, qua Filius Dei ac Dominus gloriae in carne sua consecravit, fratremque in ea praecedens, eo usque progressus est, ut pro sanctissimo Filii Dei nomine crematus, lentoque igne constantissime consumptus, praeclara martyrii insignia adeptus fuerit. Hoc fraternum religionis studium illustreque exemplum Dionysius Peloquinus imitatus, cum Genevae in ecclesia pie modesteque vixisset, fuit captus Eleutheropoli, quae urbs sex milliaria Lugduno abest, xix, die Octob. anni M.D.LII. cui praeclara confessio sequitur, coniuncta cum iis actionibus, quae iudicialiter in eum tum Lugduni, tum Eleutheropoli, in qua tandem fuit combustus, constitutae fuerunt.
units.tr: Who can sufficiently marvel at the very great gifts and ornaments of God, with which he endows wretched men? He bestows such virtue and constancy on those whom he favours, granting them this honour: that he brings them before the tribunals and courts of men, and appoints them witnesses, advocates and defenders of his truth. Here is Dionysius Peloquinus, of the glory of his family's name and lineage, on whom God has bestowed this great grace and dignity. For some time before, his brother Stephen Peloquin had entered upon that way of the cross which the Son of God and Lord of glory hallowed in his own flesh, and going before his brother on it, he advanced so far that, burned for the most holy name of the Son of God and consumed most constantly by a slow fire, he obtained the glorious marks of martyrdom. Dionysius Peloquinus, imitating this brotherly zeal for religion and this illustrious example, after he had lived piously and modestly in the church at Geneva, was seized at Eleutheropolis, a town six miles from Lyons, on the 19th day of October in the year 1552. There follows his notable confession, joined with the proceedings which were conducted against him judicially, both at Lyons and at Eleutheropolis, where at last he was burned.

units.la: Epistola Peloquini ad quendam ipsius amicum missa.
units.tr: Letter of Peloquin sent to a certain friend of his.

units.la: CVM ego memoria repetito eam offensionem, quam tibi carcer & mors Stephani optimi fratris mei attulit, verens etiam ne similis casus meus, qui in eodem versor certamine atque discrimine, eodem modo animum perturbet tuum, existimavi non alienum ab officio meo fore, si causam tibi demonstrarem eam, propter quam & ille tam constanter morte oblatam suscepit ac pertulit, & ego summa patientia atque animi aequitate fero eas molestias atque aerumnas quibus Deus nunc me probat, expectans cum exitu atque eventum qui Deo authori vocationis meae videbitur. Hoc eo facio libentius, quod eam scribendi ad amicos commoditatem ac facultatem habeo, quae fratri meo defuit.
units.tr: Since I recall with pain the grief which the prison and death of my excellent brother Stephen have caused you, and since I fear that my own case, which lies in the same struggle and peril, may similarly disturb your mind, I have thought it not out of keeping with my duty to explain to you the cause for which he so constantly took up and endured death when it was offered. I too bear with the greatest patience and calmness of mind those troubles and hardships by which God now tests me, awaiting the outcome and event that will seem good to God, the author of my calling. I do this the more willingly because I have the opportunity and ability to write to friends, which my brother lacked.

units.la: Ac primum ut omne offendiculum tollatur, illud te scire oportet, nihil fieri in hac vita nostra, nec quicquam nobis evenire sine providentia Dei nostri & voluntate: neque vero homines ullam in nos habere potestatem, nisi eam quam Deus illis tribuit, ac tantum quidem quantum permittit & concedit. Is autem huiusmodi curam nostri habet, ut ne pilus quidem capitis nostri sine eius voluntate casurus sit. Praeterea nos nō patimur ut homines facinorosi ac malefici, ut homicidae, latrones, fures atque bonorum alienorum appetentes, sed ut Christiani, quemadmodum facile cognoscere poteris, cum ex iis quae adversarij ex me quaesiverunt, tum vero ex iis quae ego eis respondi.
units.tr: And first, so that every stumbling block may be removed, you ought to know that nothing happens in this life of ours, nor does anything befall us, without the providence and will of our God. Nor do men have any power over us except what God gives them, and only so much as he permits and allows. Moreover, he has such care of us that not even a hair of our head will fall without his will. Besides, we do not suffer as wicked and criminal men, as murderers, robbers, thieves and grabbers of other men's goods, but as Christians, as you can easily perceive, both from the questions my adversaries have put to me and from the answers I have given them.

units.la: Primum igitur ex me quaesiverunt, num crederem Missam esse bonā ac digna quae audiretur. Quibus ego respondi, me credere eam sacrificium esse ab hominibus inventum atque institutum cum maximo con-ceptu gloriae Dei, ad abolenda mortis Christi memoriam magnopere accommodatum, propterea quod id ei attribuitur quod ad sanguine Iesu Christi pertinet, pro satisfactione, purgatione ac remissione nostrorum peccatorum effusum. Itaque Missam statuo idololatriam esse detestandam, quam omnes Christiani evitare debent, nisi velint in summam Dei offensionem atque indignationem incurrere.
units.tr: First, then, they asked me whether I believed the Mass to be good and worthy to be heard. To this I answered that I believe it is a sacrifice devised and instituted by men, under the pretext of great glory to God, and very well suited to abolish the memory of Christ's death, because what belongs to the blood of Jesus Christ, shed for the satisfaction, cleansing and remission of our sins, is attributed to it. Therefore I judge the Mass to be idolatry, to be detested, and all Christians ought to avoid it, unless they wish to incur the great offence and indignation of God.

units.la: Interrogatus deinde ab iis, an sanctum altaris sacramentum crederem. Respondi, non eo quidem modo quo Papa illud instituit, sed Sacramentum sacrosanctæ Cœnæ Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ut est ab eo institutum, atque in Scriptura declaratum, præcipuéque ac luculenter. 1. Corinth ix.c. Quod nimirum in Cœna panem ac vinum accipientes de manu ipsius ministri, verè corporis ac sanguinis Domini participes efficimur. Neque verò minus quàm nostra corpora quotidiano victu aluntur & sustentantur, animæ nostræ eo salubèrrimo[?] pastu carnis & sanguinis Domini nostri nutriuntur, fovetur, confirmantur. atque ea verè manducamus, non quidem ore ac ventre, sed spiritu & fide, quæ nihil crassum, terrenum, caducúmq; in eo mysterio quærit aut percipit. Itaque nihil est opus ut ad eum cibum spiritualem capiendum, Christus de cælo in terram ad nos descendat, aut nostros oculos in pane & vino solùm defixos habeamus: sed potius ut mentes animósque nostros in cælum attollamus, & Christum ad dexteram Dei sedentem fide contemplemur, quemadmodū eum ibi esse, nec inde ante iudicium reversurum in symbolo fidei nostræ confitemur, cōfirmati testimonio Angelorum, Act.1.cap. Quare illam transsubstantiationem quam Papistæ excogitarunt, plane repudio, credóque panem ac vinum suam naturam retinere, absque ulla mutatione & conversione in corpus & sanguinem Domini. Quanquam de pane eo & vino quæ in Cœna adhibentur & consecrantur ita sentio, ut à communi cibo ac potu multum differre dicam, cùm ipso usu, tum etiam vi promissionum ad quas confirmandas atque ante oculos constituendas hæc symbola proponuntur.
units.tr: Then they asked me whether I believed in the holy sacrament of the altar. I answered that not indeed in the way the Pope has instituted it, but in the sacrament of the most holy Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, as it was instituted by him and declared in Scripture, most especially and clearly in 1 Cor. 9. That is, that by receiving bread and wine in the Supper from the hand of the minister itself, we truly become partakers of the body and blood of the Lord. And just as our bodies are nourished and sustained by daily food, no less so our souls are fed and strengthened, and are nourished by that most wholesome food of the flesh and blood of our Lord; and we truly eat these things, not indeed with mouth and belly, but with spirit and faith, which in that mystery seeks and perceives nothing gross, earthly or perishable. Therefore there is no need for Christ to descend from heaven to earth to us in order to receive that spiritual food, nor for us to keep our eyes fixed only on bread and wine; but rather we should lift up our minds and spirits to heaven, and by faith contemplate Christ sitting at the right hand of God, and, as we confess in the creed of our faith, that he is there and will return from there only at the judgement, confirmed by the testimony of the angels, Acts 1. Wherefore I plainly reject that transubstantiation which the Papists have devised, and I believe that bread and wine keep their own nature, without any change or conversion into the body and blood of the Lord. Yet concerning that bread and wine which are used and consecrated in the Supper, I think this, that they differ greatly from common food and drink, both in their use and also by the force of the promises, for the confirmation and setting before our eyes of which these signs are set forth.

units.la: Interrogatus etiam, num peccata ad aurem sacerdotis essent confitenda. negaui, eámque confessionem à Deo minimè traditam & præceptam esse dixi: quoniam huiusmodi peccatorum confessio fieret homini, qui nullam habet potestatem peccata remittendi: sed hoc ad unum Deum, quem offendimus pertinet. Tum mihi illum locum Diui Iacobi allegarunt, in quo fideles admonentur ut alij alijs peccata sua delicta que confiteantur. Quib° ego respondi, illud præceptum atq; admonitio Iacobi ad hanc auriculare confessionem non esse referendum, sed ad fraternam reconciliationem, qua mutuæ offensiones peccatis amater humanitérq; condonatis deponuntur: alioqui si ille locus de ista infusurratione in aurem facta intelligendus esset, oporteret sacerdotem, cùm muliere ei peccata confitentem audit, sua vicissim illi cofiteri. Præterea hæc confessiotyrannis quædam est diabolica, & teterrima animarum carnificina, propterea quod in ea requiritur peccatorum omnium enumeratio, quæ à nemine, ne à iustissimo quidem præstari potest, quemadmodum videmus Davidem, qui integritate vitæ erat quasi quidam Angelus, petere tamen à Deo, ut ab occultis peccatis ipsum purget. Quare ego statuo peccata non hominibus, sed vni Deo quem offendimus, confitenda esse, non diebus modo, sed etiam horis singulis, si fieri potest, sicut videmus à patriarchis & Prophetis cæterisq; hominibus piis factitatū.
units.tr: Being asked also whether sins were to be confessed into the ear of a priest, I said no, and that such confession was in no way handed down or commanded by God, since confession of this kind is made to a man who has no power to forgive sins; rather, it pertains to God alone, whom we have offended. Then they cited to me that passage of St James in which the faithful are urged to confess their sins to one another. To this I replied that the precept and admonition of James is not to be referred to this auricular confession, but to brotherly reconciliation, by which mutual offences are laid aside through the kindly and humane forgiveness of sins. Otherwise, if that passage were to be understood of such whispering into the ear, the priest, when he hears a woman confessing her sins to him, would have to confess his own sins to her in turn. Moreover, this confession is a kind of diabolical tyranny and the most foul butchery of souls, because it requires an enumeration of all sins, which no one can perform, not even the most righteous. We see that David, who in the integrity of his life was almost an angel, nevertheless asked God to cleanse him from his hidden sins. Therefore I hold that sins are to be confessed not to men but to God alone, whom we have offended, and not only on days but also, if it can be done, every single hour, as we see was done by the patriarchs, the Prophets and other godly men.

units.la: Illud etiam ex me quæsitum est, num crederem purgatorium esse, ubi animæ post excessum ex hac vita paterentur, & num pro iis esset orandum. Ad quod ego respondi, me nō credere aut statuere vllum aliud purgatorium esse quam Iesu Christi sanguinem, qui ut testatur Ioannes, omnia vitia nostra & peccata eluit. Præterea Scriptura sacra duplicem tantum animarum cursum, unum in paradisum, quo pij proficiscuntur, alterum in infernum, impijs hominibus ac reprobus comparatum statuit. Hoc autem facile intelligere possumus ex eo quod dictum est Ioannis III.cap. Qui credit in Filium Dei non condemnabitur: qui vero non credit, iam condemnatus est. Preces vero pro mortuis facere, Missasque celebrare & aquam aspergere lu-stralem: dixi eis in eo non solum operam perdi, verumetiam impiam Dei blasphemiam & contumeliam Christi constitui. propterea quod de eo nihil est præceptum verbo Dei, sed etiam contra omne verbum à fallacibus spiritibus inventum atq; introductum. Hic illi quidem, mihi aliqua nescio quæ nugamenta allegarunt, sed minime digna quæ à nobis commemorentur. Postea quæsierunt ex me quid de virgine Maria sentirem. quibus respondi me quidem eam credere matrem esse Iesu Christi secundum carnem, eúmque peperisse virginem, sicut nos in symbolo fidei nostræ confitemur. simul etiam omnium fœminarum esse beatis-simam, quemadmodum Spiritus sanctus de ea testatur. Sed adorare ea atq; in necessitatibus nostris invocare: regina cæli, advocatam ac patronam appellare, aliáq; huiusmodi ei tribuere, credo ac iudico his rebus eam non modo non honorari, sed potius vituperari, contumeliose atque indigne ab hominibus tractari. Nec enim illa vult aut volunt unquam eum honorem qui ad solum Iesum Christum pertinet, ei à Patre uni datus, rapere atque ad se transferre: sed contrà, nos ad illum mittit, ut nos ei obediamus, & ea faciamus quae nobis ipse mandaverit, Ioannis secundo capite. Quare ij contumeliosi in Deum sunt, eúmque magnopere offendunt, qui Mariam virginem adorant, venerantur, invocant, aut alios Sanctos & Sanctas, cùm nihil de eorum cultu in Scriptura sancta à Deo praeceptum sit: sed contrà, ut unum Deum adoremus & colamus, oremus atque invocemus per nomen unius Iesu Christi, qui à Deo Patre advocatus mediatórq; inter nos & Deũ est constitutus. Porrò vera ratio, qua virginem Mariam & caeteros Sanctos honorare possimus, haec est optima & praestantissima, ut piè ac sanctae vitae eorum exemplum nobis imitandum proponamus, in eo quidem, quòd Iesum Christum Dominum sequuti sunt, sicut Paulus monet 1.Cor.10. De imaginibus verò ac simulachris, quibus Deum Sanctósque effingunt, dixi in eo superstitionem esse detestabilem à Deo vehementissimè damnatam, quemadmodum in secúdo Legis praecepto satis constat. Scimus etiam Deum maledicere tum imaginem, tum eius effectorem atque artificem, sicut ex Psalmo cxv. satis notum est.
units.tr: They also asked me whether I believed there is a purgatory, where souls suffer after their departure from this life, and whether prayers should be offered for them. To this I replied that I neither believe nor hold that there is any other purgatory than the blood of Jesus Christ, which, as John testifies, cleanses all our vices and sins. Moreover, Holy Scripture establishes only a twofold course for souls: one into paradise, to which the godly go, and the other into hell, prepared for impious and reprobate men. We can easily understand this from what is said in John 3: "He who believes in the Son of God shall not be condemned; but he who does not believe is already condemned." As for making prayers for the dead, celebrating Masses and sprinkling lustral water, I told them that in this not only is effort wasted, but also an impious blasphemy against God and an insult to Christ is committed, because nothing about these things is commanded in the Word of God, but on the contrary they were invented and introduced by deceitful spirits, against every word of God. Here they indeed alleged to me certain trifles, I know not what, but they are in no way worth our mention. Afterwards they asked me what I thought of the Virgin Mary. To this I replied that I indeed believe her to be the mother of Jesus Christ according to the flesh, and that she bore him while still a virgin, as we confess in the creed of our faith; and at the same time that she is the most blessed of all women, as the Holy Spirit testifies of her. But to adore her and invoke her in our necessities, to call her Queen of heaven, advocate and patroness, and to ascribe to her other things of this kind, I believe and judge that by such acts she is not honoured at all, but rather disparaged, and treated with insult and indignity by men. For she neither wishes nor ever wished that honour which belongs to Jesus Christ alone, given to him alone by the Father, to be snatched away and transferred to herself; but on the contrary, she sends us to him, that we may obey him and do whatever he commands us, as in John chapter 2. Therefore those who adore, venerate or invoke the Virgin Mary, or other saints, men and women, are insolent toward God and greatly offend him, since nothing about the worship of them is commanded by God in Holy Scripture; but on the contrary, we are to adore and worship the one God, and pray and call upon him through the name of the one Jesus Christ, who was called by God the Father and appointed as mediator between us and God. Moreover, the true way in which we can honour the Virgin Mary and the other saints is this, the best and most excellent: to set before ourselves their pious and holy lives as an example to imitate, in that they followed the Lord Jesus Christ, as Paul admonishes, 1 Cor. 10. As for the images and likenesses with which they portray God and the saints, I said that in this there is a detestable superstition, most vehemently condemned by God, as is sufficiently clear from the second precept of the Law. We also know that God curses both the image and its maker and craftsman, as is well known from Psalm 115.

units.la: De Papa etiam quaesiverunt an non crederem illum caput esse Ec-clesiae, quibus respondi me longè secus de eo sentire, ac credere eum verum esse Antichristum qui adversus Deum se extollit, ac quodammodo & numen & nomen Dei sibi tribuit. Denique dixi me credere illum esse sceleratum ac filium perditum, de quo Paulus ad Thessalonicenses secundo capite loquitur. Postremò eam ecclesiam cuius Papa caput esset, verá non esse Ecclesiam, cùm verae Ecclesiae notae, ut praedicatio verbi Dei & legitima Sacramentorum administratio, nullae in ea, ne vestigia quidem Ecclesiae appareant.
units.tr: They also asked me about the Pope, whether I did not believe him to be the head of the Church. To this I replied that I think of him quite otherwise, and believe that he is the true Antichrist, who exalts himself against God and in a manner assumes to himself both the divinity and the name of God. Finally I said that I believe him to be the wicked man and son of perdition of whom Paul speaks to the Thessalonians in the second chapter. Lastly, I said that the church whose head is the Pope is not truly the Church, since the marks of the true Church, such as the preaching of the Word of God and the lawful administration of the sacraments, do not appear in it at all, not even traces of the Church.

units.la: Atque haec quidem sunt, quae illi ex me quaesiverunt Eleuthero-poli: & ego illis respondi. Postea autem cùm Lugdunum deductus essem, Inquisitor & Officialis aliique ea mihi legerunt, quaesiverúntque à me vellémne in iis erroribus, quemadmodum appellabant, permanere. Quibus ego respondi, me quidem id cupere, Deúmque quotidie orare, ut mihi eam constantiam ac perseverantiam impertiret, cum eam gratiam iam impertierit, ut ex Scriptura sancta cognouerim quid sit veritas, & in quo fides mea sit constituenda & fundanda. Tum inquisitor me rogauit quid Scripturam sanctam appellarem. Cui ego respondi, eam esse veritatem certam & perfectam, quae nullo modo potest fallere, quae in veteri ac nouo Testamento continetur, ad quam nefas est quicquam addere aut demere, in qua etiam nihil est plane praetermissum eorum omnium, quae ad salutem nostram pertinent. Itaque statuo eam unam religionis Christianae normam esse. Inquisitor autem eo responso valde conturbatus, magnáque molestia affectus, Quis, inquit, tibi dixit eam esse Scripturam sanctam: & quomodo id scire potes, nisi ecclesia te de eo certum reddiderit? Ego autem optime sciebam eum intelligere Papae ecclesiam. Itaque ei respondi, ecclesiam non esse, quae mihi id persuaderet, sed solum Spiritum sanctum, qui mihi verissimum ac certissimum in conscientia mea testimonium redderet, ita ut cupiam viuere & mori in eius obedientia. Quae quidem, inquam, authoritatem suam a veteri Ecclesia non accipit. Nam hoc quidem esset praeposterè atque peruerse ordinem inuertere: quum Ecclesia potius sit fundata in doctrina Prophetarum atque Apostolorum Domini nostri Iesu Christi, sicut Paulus secundo capite ad Ephesios testatur. Porro cum illi intellexissent me monachatum abominabilem aliquando professum esse, quaesiuerunt ex me, quid me commouerit ut illud vitae institutum reliquerim. Quibus ego respondi, gratiam Dei fuisse, camque fecisse ut illud genus vitae impium esse cognouerim ac deposuerim, ut a verbo eius maximopere alienum, ab hominibus tantum inuentum: quod qui profitentur, operibus nescio quibus, Legi quidem Dei plane repugnatibꝰ, paradisum mereri volunt. De votis interrogatus, num ea reddenda essent ac seruanda, respondi ea quidem quae Deo aut hominibus ex verbo Dei nuncupata sunt: ea vero quae sine verbo, aut etiam contra verbum facta & suscepta sunt, minime praestanda esse, neque hominem obstringere atque impedire, quo minus ea suscepta, pie & sancte possit omittere. Interrogatus autem cur uxorem duxissem, cum ego castitatem ante vouissem, respondi castitatem donum Dei esse singulare, sicut satis constat ex Matt. xix. cap. quod quidem omnibus monachis minimè concessum est, quemadmodum experientia & consuetudo impudicae ac flagitiosae vitae ipsorum nimium ostendit. Me autem, cum animadverterem ac sentirem huiusmodi gratia Dei ac virtute non esse praeditum, confugisse ad remedium, id est, ad coniugium, ut libidinem impudicam cuitarem, atque ita mandatum Dei sequutum esse, scientem quidem, quod nec adulteri, nec scortatores, nec cinaedi, impuriqué huiusmodi homines unquam in regnum coelorum ingredientur. Praeterea coniugium est perhonoratum, & cubile nulla macula aspersum & plane impollutum: scortatores vero & adulteros Deus iudicabit, ut Apostolus Hebr. xiii. admonet. Ac ipsius coniugii prohibitio certis factis hominibus, doctrina est diabolorum & spirituum fallacium, 1. Timoth. 4. Alia ex me nō sunt quaesita, digna quidem quae scribantur. Inquisitor quidem bellis quibusdam blanditiis mecum egit, ut me a proposito susceptáque sententia deduceret, cum multa magnifica mihi promittens, tum vero aetatem iuvenilem mihi proponens. cuius, inquit ille, maxima erit iactura, si igni consumatur: quod certe fiet, si tu in proposito tuo perseveraveris. Considera igitur & vide: nam in tua quidem est potestate, ut salvus evadas atque incolumis: atque anima, inquit, tua in tuis est manibus. Ei ego respondi, quod anima mea valde male custodiretur, atque in summo versaretur discrimine, nisi alius praeter me eius curam, tutelam, custodiamque suscepisset. Me vero alia in schola fuisse Domini nostri Iesu Christi, in qua quidem aliud ab eo Magistro didiceram: eum qui animam conservare suam voluerit, perdituum: qui vero perdiderit, conservaturum. Sed non contentus eo Inquisitor, misit ad me monachum suum, ut per eum id mihi persuaderet, quod ipse coram non poterat. Qui cum venisset, optimam Cardinalis Turnonij erga me voluntatem declaravit, ut me deposita mea opinione & sententia in pristinum vitae meae statum ac monachatum revocaret, cum huiusmodi promisisset, ut me nova veste optima donatum in aliquam domum suam monasticam mitteret. Ei ego respondi, me vestem nigram nimium diu tulisse, nunc autem optare albam ferre, non illa quidem obnoxiam corruptioni, sed his similem, quarum mentio sexto capite Apocal. ficeret. Haec autem causa est, charissimi fratres ac sorores, cur omnes filij Dei persecutionem patiuntur: imo vero Iesus Christus in illis, propterea quod non ea causa nostra est, sed ipsius propria quam tuemur. Nos etiam videmus eam iniuriam quae nobis infertur, cum ita accipere quasi in ipsum conferatur, quemadmodum Paulum Ecclesiam persequentem admonet. Neque vero Christum ille persequebatur ad dexteram Dei iam evectum, ab omnique iniuria ereptum, sed in membris suis, cum quibus eam habet spiritus coniunctionem, ut quod fit uni etiam ex minimis ipsius, sibi ipsi factum dicat. Cum igitur tantus sit amor Iesu Christi erga nos, ut opprobria quibus nos afficimur, in seipsum recipiat, quanta, obsecro, erit ingratitudo nostra post acceptum singulare beneficium, quod in hac declarata nobis veritate perspicitur, nisi eam edamus nominis eius confessionem quam summa eius dignitas amplitudoque requirit: praesertim post tot gravissimas minas iis propositas, quos nominis eius atq; Evangelij puduerit? Qui, inquit Christus, me coram hominibus negaverit, negabo eum ego quoque coram Patre meo: qui vero me confessus fuerit, cum etiam ego apud Patrem meum confitebor. Quid autem, obsecro, hoc est aliud a Christo Domino tum non agnosci, sed abnegari, quam mortis aeternae condemnari? Tyranni quidem atque inimici Dei, propositis minis ac poenis gravissimis interdicunt ne Christo testimonium quod ei debemus, tribuamus: sed ea aequitatis ratio semper est adhibeda et servanda, ut exemplo Apostolorum Deo potius quam hominibus ipsis pareamus. Neque vero metuendi sunt ii qui postquam corpus occiderint, nullam in animam habent potestatem. Omnino iniurias, persecutiones, et contumelias in hac quidem ratione vitae et Christiana professione propositas nobis scimus atque expectamus, sed illud etiam intelligimus planeque cognoscimus hanc unam esse viam in carne Filii Dei consecratam, qua per multas afflictiones in illam regni caelestis gloriam eundum sit. Paulus quidem 1. Philip. ait nobis datum esse, non modo ut in Christum credamus, verum etiam ut pro eodem patiamur. Alio etiam loco monuit eos omnes qui pie in Christo vivere volent, ut persecutionem expectent. Ad id enim sunt positi et vocati, ut pie in Christo Deum colentes atque invocantes, multa et tormenta et opprobria patiantur. Atque haec causa nobis coniuncta est cum Evangelio, et ho, & quaedam societas, qua oportet nos omnes συγκοινωνίαν[?], ut in eo & cum eo non consolationes modo, sed etiam afflictiones communes habeamus. Sed in his tantis miseriis & contumeliis Divus Petrus nos beatos esse dicit, cùm propter nomen Iesu Christi haec patimur atque vituperamur: nā hoc modo Spiritum Dei super nos requiescere. Nunc ergo post tot tamque grauia testimonia existimabimúsne vitam nostram perdere, cùm eam pro causa tam iusta & sancta in manus inimicorum trademus? An vero nos miseros esse dicemus, cùm Christus Dominus suo ore sacro nos beatos esse pronuntiat? aut putabimus nos mortem temerè oppetere ut amentes & insanos, cùm Christus amplissimum nobis in caelo praemium proponat? Quare charissimi fratres ac sorores, vos magnopere hortor & rogo ne vanam mundi opinionem & consuetudinem sequamini, qui ita est occaecatus, tantisque errorum omnium tenebris circumfusus, ac potius oppressus, ut vitam in morte, benedictionem in maledictione reperire non possit. Neque vero offendamur si seruos Dei videmus multa grauia & acerba perpeti, cùm sciamus eam viam esse viam & rationem, qua nos capiti nostro ac principi Iesu Christo conformes fiamus, si post eum impositam nobis crucem ferimus. neque enim seruus domino suo maior est. Exeamus igitur ad eum extra castra eiusque opprobrium feramus. neque enim ciuitatem hic habemus permanentem: sed futuram aliam quaerimus: ad quam nos Dominus pro sua misericordia omnes conducat, Amen.
units.tr: These are the questions they put to me at Eleutheropolis, and I answered them. Afterwards, when I had been taken to Lyons, the Inquisitor, the Official and others read these answers to me and asked whether I wished to persist in those errors, as they called them. I replied that I did wish it, and I pray to God every day that he would bestow on me that steadfastness and perseverance, since he has already granted me the grace to know from holy Scripture what the truth is and on what my faith should be founded and grounded. The Inquisitor then asked me what I meant by holy Scripture. I answered that it is the certain and perfect truth, which cannot in any way deceive, contained in the Old and New Testaments, to which it is wrong to add or from which to take away anything, and in which nothing at all has been omitted of all that pertains to our salvation. So I hold that it alone is the rule of the Christian religion. The Inquisitor, greatly disturbed by this answer and much troubled, said: "Who told you that this is holy Scripture, and how can you know it unless the Church has made you certain of it?" I knew well enough that by "the Church" he meant the Church of the Pope. So I answered him that it was not the Church that persuaded me of this, but only the Holy Spirit, who gives me in my conscience the most true and certain testimony, so that I desire to live and die in obedience to it. This authority, I said, does not come to it from the ancient Church. For that would be to invert the order absurdly and perversely, since the Church is rather founded on the doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, as Paul testifies in the second chapter of Ephesians. Then, since they had learned that I had once professed the hateful monastic life, they asked what had moved me to abandon that way of life. I answered that it was the grace of God, which made me recognise that this kind of life was impious, and cast it off, since it is utterly alien to his Word and invented only by men; and those who profess it, relying on some works, which plainly oppose the Law of God, want to earn paradise. Asked about vows, whether they ought to be kept and fulfilled, I answered that those which have been made to God or to men according to the Word of God are indeed to be kept, but those which have been undertaken and taken up without the Word, or even against the Word, are by no means to be performed, and do not bind a man so that he may not piously and holily set them aside. Then I was asked why I had taken a wife, since I had previously vowed chastity. I answered that chastity is a singular gift of God, as is sufficiently clear from Matthew 19, a gift which has by no means been granted to all monks, as the experience and custom of their shameless and disgraceful lives show only too well. When I perceived and felt that I was not endowed with this grace and power of God, I had recourse to the remedy, that is, to marriage, in order to avoid unchaste lust, and so I followed the command of God, knowing indeed that neither adulterers, nor fornicators, nor the effeminate, nor impure men of this sort, shall ever enter the kingdom of heaven. Moreover, marriage is most honourable, and the marriage bed is unstained and wholly undefiled; but God will judge fornicators and adulterers, as the Apostle warns in Hebrews 13. And the forbidding of marriage to certain kinds of men is the doctrine of devils and of deceiving spirits, 1 Timothy 4. Other questions were not put to me, and they are not worth writing down. The Inquisitor, indeed, tried with certain charming flatteries to draw me away from my purpose and the opinion I had embraced, promising me many splendid things and then holding up before me my youthful age. "Its loss," he said, "will be very great if it is consumed by fire, which will certainly happen if you persevere in your purpose. Consider therefore and see: for it is in your power to escape safe and sound, and your soul," he said, "is in your own hands." I answered him that my soul would be very badly guarded and would be in the greatest danger, unless someone other than me had taken up its care, protection and keeping. For I had been in another school, that of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which I had learned something different from that Master: whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it, and whoever loses it will save it. But the Inquisitor, not content with that, sent his monk to me, so that through him he might persuade me of what he himself could not do face to face. When this man came, he declared the excellent goodwill of Cardinal Tournon towards me: that, if I set aside my opinion and judgment, he would restore me to my former state of life and to the monastery, promising that I would be given a fine new garment and sent to some monastic house of his. I answered him that I had worn the black habit far too long, and now I desired to wear white, not indeed one liable to corruption, but like those whose mention is made in the sixth chapter of Revelation. This, dearest brothers and sisters, is why all the children of God suffer persecution; indeed Jesus Christ himself suffers in them, because the cause is not ours but his own, which we defend. We also see that the injury done to us is received as though it were done to him himself, as Paul admonishes him who persecuted the Church. Nor did he persecute Christ, who is already exalted at the right hand of God and snatched from every injury, but his members, with whom Christ has a spiritual union, so that he says that what is done to even the least of them is done to himself. Since, then, the love of Jesus Christ towards us is so great that he takes upon himself the reproaches with which we are loaded, how great, I beseech you, will our ingratitude be after receiving this singular benefit, which is seen in the truth now declared to us, unless we make that confession of his name which his supreme dignity and greatness require, especially after so many very grievous threats offered to those who were ashamed of his name and of the Gospel? "Whoever," says Christ, "shall deny me before men, I will deny him also before my Father; but whoever shall confess me, I also will confess before my Father." But what else, I beseech you, is it to be not acknowledged by Christ the Lord, but disowned, than to be condemned to eternal death? Tyrants and enemies of God, by proposing threats and most severe punishments, forbid us to give to Christ the testimony we owe him; but the rule of equity must always be applied and observed, so that, following the example of the Apostles, we obey God rather than men themselves. Nor indeed are we to fear those who, after they have killed the body, have no further power over the soul. We know and expect, of course, injuries, persecutions and insults in this way of life and Christian profession, but we also understand and clearly recognise that this is the one way, consecrated in the flesh of the Son of God, by which we must go through many afflictions into that glory of the heavenly kingdom. Paul indeed, in Philippians 1, says that it has been given to us not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him. In another place he also warned all who wish to live piously in Christ to expect persecution. For they are appointed and called to this, that, worshipping and invoking God piously in Christ, they should suffer many afflictions, torments and reproaches. And this cause is joined to us with the Gospel, and this is a certain fellowship [συγκοινωνίαν], by which we all ought to have in it and with it not only consolations but also common afflictions. But in these great miseries and reproaches the divine Peter calls us blessed, when we suffer and are reviled for the name of Jesus Christ, for in this way the Spirit of God rests upon us. Now, then, after so many and such grave testimonies, shall we think that we lose our life when we hand it over into the hands of enemies for so just and holy a cause? Or shall we say that we are wretched, when the Lord Christ with his holy mouth pronounces us blessed? Or shall we think that we rush headlong into death like madmen and fools, when Christ sets before us a most ample reward in heaven? Therefore, dearest brothers and sisters, I earnestly exhort and beg you not to follow the vain opinion and custom of the world, which is so blinded, and so enveloped and rather overwhelmed by the darkness of all errors, that it cannot find life in death or blessing in curse. Nor should we be offended if we see the servants of God endure many grievous and bitter things, since we know that this is the way and the manner by which we are made conformed to our head and prince, Jesus Christ, if we bear the cross laid upon us after him; for the servant is not greater than his lord. Let us go out therefore to him outside the camp, and bear his reproach; for here we have no abiding city, but we seek one to come. To this city may the Lord in his mercy lead us all, Amen.

units.la: Nos institutum ordinem sequentes, inseruimus hoc loco eam epistolam, quam Ioannes Calvinus ad Dionysium Peloquinum, atque ad Ludovicum Marsacum, cuius mentio fiet paulò post, misit: quæ quidem non mediocrem hominibus piis ac fidelibus consolationem afferre poterit.
units.tr: Following the order we have set, we insert here the letter that John Calvin sent to Denis Peloquin and to Louis Marsac, whom we shall mention shortly. It will surely bring no small consolation to godly and faithful people.

units.la: VT SI fratres charissimi, vos cùm ad me scriberetis, putabatis etiam ipsos inimicos in sacrificium vos oblaturos, ego tamen praetermittere nolui, quin has ad vos literas mittere, ut si voluntate Dei in manus vestras peruenirent, vos aliquid adhuc consolationis peràpe-re ex me possetis. Recte quidem & prudenter gratiam Dei reputatis, cùm animaduertitis eum adhuc in vobis promissiones suas confirmasse, impertita vobis ea constantia, quam vos non ita diu in postremis responsis vestris sensistis. Hoc autem profecto beneficium eius est, quòd vos ita firmi in sententia vestra permansistis, ut nulla vos res unquam ab ea deducere potuerit. Itaque mihi plane persuasi, illud figillum, quod veram atque insignem praefert Spiritus sancti notam, nullam rem unquam deleturam. Neque vero dubito, quin ipsi etiam inimici cogantur confiteri, aut certe in seipsis convincantur hanc tantam mutationem ab homine minime profectam esse. Quo magis oculos nostros aperire debemus ad contemplandam Dei manum, quam is mirandum in modum exeruit, ut miserum hominem ab ea horribili confusione, in quam prolapsus fuerat, erigeret, atque ad se revocaret. Quandiu iste sensum suum iudiciumque secutus est, arbitrabatur se multum consecuturum, si aliquam huius vitae caducae ac miserae usuram exiguam redimeret, cum interim seipsum in abyssos mortis aeternae praecipitaret. Hoc igitur opus est vere Diuinum, quod sua sponte in mortem ingressus fuerit, ut ad veram ac beatam vitam peruenire, a qua non solum longe seipsum remouerat: sed quantum in eo quidem fuit, plane excluserat. Nam hac quidem in parte praeclarius & admirabilius summa Dei bonitas est declarata atque exhibita, quod miserum hominem a se creatum, ex huiusmodi casu tam exitioso erexerit, ut ita erectus ac restitutus, in ea bonitate triumpharet, eiusque gloriam celebraret atque illustraret, quemadmodum iam coepit sphaero [?] perficiet. Eius autem confessionem vidi, in qua testimonium fidei suae reddidit: quae quidem est pura & libera, & plane homine Christiano digna. Sed tamen non incommodum mihi videtur, ut is in aliquot certis capitibus melius instruatur, ut aduersarij maiore pudore afficiantur cum is distinctius planiusque illis responderit. Non quod ea quae Michael dixit, vera non sint: sed quia iniqui homines semper & facile arripiunt etiam leuissimas occasiones, quibus calumnientur, & ea quae vera & recta sunt deprauent. Idcirco responsio quaedam apertior ac magis explicata & distincta mihi videtur adhibenda. Interrogatus num corpus Christi sub specie panis in Coena sit, negauit. Cum autem illi quaesuissent, Cur? is respondit, eam opinionem meram esse blasphemiam, quae mortem Iesu Christi plane aboleret.
