Sed oportebat eum duo diserte in Missa reprobare: unum, quod in ea idololatriam constituunt abominandam, dum frustum panis, ut idolum quoddam proponunt. illudque pro Deo ducunt & adorant: alterum, quod in eadem sacrificium Deo offerunt, quo homines ei reconcilient. At Iesus Christus, quemadmodum solus a Deo Patre sacerdos est constitutus, ita seipsum semel omnino obtulit: cuius quidem mors sacrificium pro nostra redemptione unicum, perpetuumque extitit. Quinetiam bonum fuisset fidem suam in eo testificari, quod crederet in Coena nos verè corporis ac sanguinis Iesu Christi participes fieri: sed per fidem, ut mentibus animisque nostris in coelum, ubi Christus est, ascendamus: non ut ipse ad nos descendat, seque in his caducis elementis includat. neque id tamen quicquam facit ad Missam eorum approbandam, quae Coenae Domini plane repugnat. Praeterea interrogatus num virgo Maria ac ceteri sancti hac vita defuncti, pro nobis apud Deum intercedant, respondit unum esse, qui intercedit, Christum Iesum aduocatum & patronum: & rectè atque verè. Neque enim ulli sunt homines aut Angeli, qui ad Deum accessum aditumque habeant, nisi gratia atque authoritate huius unius Mediatoris commendati. Sed non incommodum fuisset declarandi causa illud addere, officium intercedendi & orandi mortuis non esse datum, sicut Deus nobis praecepit ut nos in hac vita alij alios mutuis precibus adiuuemus. Caeterùm quoniam non possumus nec debemus Deum inuocare, nisi certa fide ac fiducia eius gratiae: caeteris omissis una nobis via restat, ut ad eum per nomen Iesu Christi accedamus atque inuocemus. Caeteri verò qui virginem Mariam aliosque Sanctos quaerunt, ut aduocatos ac patronos adhibeant, a recta via deerrantes cuagantur. Porrò de libero arbitrio interrogatus, ut demonstraret nullam in nobis esse facultatem qua aliquid boni possimus agere, adducit locum Pauli ad Romanos sept. cap. Non enim quod volo bonum facio. In quo quidem certum est Paulum de incredulis non loqui, qui omni gratia Dei sunt destituti, sed de seipso aliisque fidelibus quibus Deus iam gratiam impertierat, ut ad bonum aspirarent. In eo autem confitetur se sentire in natura sua eam repugnantiam, ut quod cupit secundum Legem Dei, id plenè ac perfectè praestare non possit. addedū igitur erat ad maiorē declarationē. Si homines fideles sentiunt totā naturam suam cum voluntate Dei plane pugnare, quid iudicandum est de iis qui in sua malitia ac rebellione Deo inimica sunt reliEst[?] quemadmodum viii. cap. eiusdem Epistolae ab eodem dictum est, Omnes cogitationes atque affectiones carnis esse inimicitias adversus Deum suscepras, & 2. Eph. idem Apostolus satis ostendit quae vis insit in homine. Item, 1. & 2. cap. primae ad Corinth. & 3. cap. Rom. Ex quo sequitur Deum esse qui efficit in nobis ut & velimus & perficiamus pro optima ipsius voluntate, quemadmodum 2. Philippensium dicitur. De votis vero interrogatus, respondit omnia nostra promissa nihil aliud esse quam mendacia. Quo in genere optimum fuisset notare ac demonstrare, cum aliqua eorum vota nullo modo praestari possint, eos plane cum impio conceptu Deo obsistere: ut cum monachi ac sacerdotes matrimonio renuntiant. Ac generatim quidem vota eorum vana esse inventa & commenta, quibus verus Dei cultus depravetur: neque vero nobis licere quicquam Deo promittere aut offerre, nisi id quod ipse in verbo suo approbavit. Equidem existimo ac persuasum plane habeo ei fratri nostro non ingratum fore, si his de rebus a nobis admonitus fuerit, ut hac ratione veritas Dei facilius & praeclarius victoriam obtineat. Reliquum est ut cogitetis, quod quemadmodum dum in hac vita sumus in ipsa morte versamur: ita nunc etiam cum in periculo mortis versamini, ab ipsa vita non abesse. quae res vobis magnam consolationem afferre debet.
units.tr: Dearest brothers, when you wrote to me you thought that your enemies themselves would offer you up as a sacrifice. Still, I did not want to hold back from sending you this letter, so that, if by God's will it reaches your hands, you may be able to draw some further consolation from me. You judge God's grace rightly and wisely when you notice that he has already confirmed his promises in you, granting you the steadfastness that you did not feel for very long in your last replies. This is indeed his gift: that you have remained so firm in your position that nothing could ever draw you away from it. So I am fully persuaded that the seal which bears the true and distinctive mark of the Holy Spirit will never be effaced. Nor do I doubt that your enemies themselves will be forced to confess, or at least will be convicted in their own minds, that so great a change was not brought about by man. All the more must we open our eyes to contemplate the hand of God, which he has stretched out in a wonderful way to raise up that wretched man from the dreadful confusion into which he had fallen, and to call him back to himself. As long as he followed his own feeling and judgment, he thought he would gain much if he bought for himself a little enjoyment of this brief and miserable life, while in fact he was throwing himself into the abysses of eternal death. This is therefore truly a divine work: that he entered upon death of his own accord, so that he might arrive at a true and blessed life, from which he had not only removed himself far away but, so far as lay in him, had quite shut himself out. For in this respect the supreme goodness of God has been declared and displayed more brightly and admirably: that he raised up from such a deadly fall a wretched man whom he had created, and that, once raised and restored, he should triumph in that goodness and celebrate and illustrate his glory, just as he has already begun to bring to completion sphaero [?]. I have seen his confession, in which he gave witness to his faith. It is pure and free, and wholly worthy of a Christian man. Yet it seems to me not unhelpful that he should be better instructed on certain specific heads, so that the adversaries may be put to greater shame when he answers them more distinctly and plainly. Not that what Michael said is untrue, but wicked men always and readily seize upon even the slightest occasions to slander, and they distort what is true and right. Therefore a somewhat fuller, clearer and more distinct answer seems to me to be needed. Asked whether the body of Christ is present in the Supper under the appearance of bread, he denied it. When they asked him why, he replied that this opinion was sheer blasphemy, since it utterly abolishes the death of Jesus Christ. But he ought to have plainly rejected two things in the Mass: first, that they set up in it an abominable idolatry, while they display a piece of bread as an idol, and regard it and worship it as God; second, that in it they offer a sacrifice to God, by which men may be reconciled to him. But Jesus Christ, just as he alone was appointed priest by God the Father, so he offered himself once for all, and his death is the one and perpetual sacrifice for our redemption. It would even have been good for him to testify his faith in this, that in the Supper we truly become partakers of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, but through faith, so that with our minds and souls we ascend into heaven, where Christ is, and not that he descends to us and encloses himself in these earthly elements. Nor does this in any way support their Mass, which is utterly contrary to the Lord's Supper. Furthermore, when asked whether the Virgin Mary and the other saints who have departed this life intercede for us with God, he replied that there is one intercessor, Christ Jesus, our advocate and patron; and rightly and truly so. For there are no men or angels who have access and entry to God except as commended by the grace and authority of this one Mediator. But it would not have been out of place, for the sake of clarity, to add that the office of interceding and praying has not been given to the dead, just as God has commanded us in this life to help one another by mutual prayers. Moreover, since we can neither ought to call upon God except with a sure faith and trust in his grace, with everything else set aside, one way alone remains for us: to approach and call upon him through the name of Jesus Christ. Those, however, who seek the Virgin Mary and other saints to use as advocates and patrons, wander from the right way and go astray. Next, asked about free will, in order to show that there is in us no ability by which we can do any good, he cites the passage of Paul in Romans chapter seven: "For the good that I would I do not." Here it is certain that Paul is not speaking of unbelievers, who are destitute of all grace of God, but of himself and of other faithful people to whom God had already granted grace, so that they might strive toward good. In that passage, however, he confesses that he feels in his nature such a resistance that he cannot fully and perfectly do what he desires according to the law of God. So something more should have been added for fuller explanation: if faithful people feel that their whole nature is utterly at odds with the will of God, what is to be judged of those who remain in their wickedness and rebellion, hostile to God? As the same author said in Romans chapter eight, "the affections and thoughts of the flesh are enmity against God," and in Ephesians chapter two the same apostle shows well enough what power is in man. Likewise, 1 Corinthians chapters one and two, and Romans chapter three. From this it follows that it is God who works in us both to will and to perform, according to his good pleasure, as is said in Philippians chapter two. Asked about vows, he replied that all our promises are nothing but lies. On this point it would have been best to note and demonstrate that when some of their vows cannot in any way be kept, those who make them plainly oppose God with an impious purpose, as when monks and priests renounce marriage. And in general their vows have been found to be vain inventions and fictions, by which the true worship of God is corrupted; and we are not permitted to promise or offer anything to God except what he himself has approved in his word. Indeed I think and am fully persuaded that it will not be unwelcome to our brother if he is reminded of these matters by us, so that the truth of God may by this means win the victory more easily and more brilliantly. It remains for you to consider that, just as while we are in this life we are in the midst of death, so now, even though you are in danger of death, you are not far from life itself. This should bring you great consolation.

units.la: Atque in hoc quidem facile videre possumus, ut Iesum Christum sequamur, nostros nobis sensus minime sequendos esse. Neque enim quicquam nobis alienius videtur, quam conijcere nos in opprobria & plane deprimere, atque usque ad mortem penitus abijcere, ut ad gloriam caelestem extollamur. Sed tamen reipsa tandem sentiemus, Filium Dei noluisse nos frustrari, cum promisit eum qui vitam suam in hoc mundo amiserit, eam recepturum, ut perpetuo perfruatur. quare fratres mei, si vos hactenus experti estis, quantum valeant consolationes quas optimus Dominus Iesus suis dat, ut omnia quae nomine ipsius patiuntur, dulcia atque amabilia esse sentiat, & quanta sit vis Spiritus eos adiuvantis & confirmantis ne in certamine deficiant, orate cum ut utrumque continuet in vobis: itaque vobis persuadete eum vestris optatis responsurum, planeque satisfacturum. Nos quidem vobis dum in hac dimicatione versabimur, eam memoriam & benevolentiam præstabimus quam debemus. Omnes fratres vobis multum salutis impertiunt. Deus benignissimus, & Pater omnis misericordiæ vos in sua tutela perpetuo habeat: qui si vult vos mortem pati ad testimonium Euangelij sui confirmandum, quemadmodum ea ipsius voluntas esse videtur, ostendet eam curam atque opem suam, ut vos nullo modo deseruerit: sed cum martyres suos constituerit, habitet in vobis semper atque regnet, ut in vobis ipsis triumphet, ad confusionem inimicorum, & ædificationem ac salutem electorum. Is nos Spiritu suo ducat & gubernet, quoad simul omnes in regnum suum recolligat. Benè valete. die vicesimo secundo Augusti, M. D. LIII. Velim me excusatum habeatis, si vobis citius non responderim. Nam heri vestras literas accepi, XII. die huius mensis scriptas. Humilis frater vester Ioannes Caluinus.
units.tr: In this we can easily see that we must follow Jesus Christ, and that our own feelings are by no means to be followed. For nothing seems more alien to us than to cast ourselves into reproach, to press ourselves down completely and cast ourselves away even to death, in order to be raised up to heavenly glory. Yet in the end we shall truly perceive that the Son of God did not wish to disappoint us, since he promised that whoever loses his life in this world will receive it again, to enjoy it forever. Therefore, my brothers, if you have so far experienced how great are the consolations which the most excellent Lord Jesus gives to his own, so that they feel all that they suffer in his name to be sweet and lovable, and how great is the power of the Spirit who helps and strengthens them lest they fail in the struggle, pray that he may continue both in you. So persuade yourselves that he will answer your desires and fully satisfy them. We, indeed, while we remain in this conflict with you, will show the remembrance and goodwill that we owe. All the brothers send you much greeting. May the most kind God, and Father of all mercy, keep you ever under his protection; who, if he wills that you suffer death to confirm the testimony of his Gospel, as that seems to be his will, will show you that care and help of his, so that he will in no way forsake you. But since he has appointed you as his martyrs, may he dwell in you always and reign, so that he triumphs in you, to the confusion of his enemies and the edification and salvation of the elect. May he lead and govern us by his Spirit, until he gathers us all together into his kingdom. Farewell. On the twenty-second day of August, 1553. I would like you to excuse me if I have not replied to you more quickly; for yesterday I received your letter, written on the twelfth day of this month. Your humble brother, John Calvin.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad Dionysium Peloquinum, eiusque præclaram mortem demonstremus. Is cum decem menses Lugduni in carcere fuisset, à XIX. die Octob. anni M.D.LII. ubi firmus inuictúsque semper permansit: inde fuit eductus die Dominica, quarto Septembris, M.D.LIII. hora tertia matutina, atque Eleutheropolim deductus. Postero die, qui dies fuit quintus eiusdem mensis, de gradu atque ordine Papistico deiectus fuit, deinde condemnatus ut vivus cremaretur. Sequutus est postea dies Lunæ XI. eius mensis præclaro eius martyrio insignis ac memorabilis, in quo quidem huiusmodi genus mortis est perpessus quod summam admirationem omnibus spectatoribus attulit. Nam cū inferiorem corporis partem iam vstulatam haberet, nunquam destitit manus in cælum tollere opémque Dei implorare. Atque ita grauissimo testimonio declarauit, veritatem Dei & gloriam Christi omnibus Christianis ac piis hominibus propria vita antiquiorem & chariorem esse debere.
units.tr: But let us return to Dionysius Peloquinus, and set forth his notable death. He had been in prison at Lyon for ten months, from the nineteenth day of October in the year 1552, where he always remained firm and unconquered. He was led out from there on Sunday, the fourth of September, 1553, at three in the morning, and was taken to Eleutheropolis. On the following day, which was the fifth of the same month, he was deprived of his rank and Papist order, and then condemned to be burned alive. Afterwards came Monday, the eleventh of that month, made remarkable and memorable by his excellent martyrdom, in which he endured a kind of death that brought the greatest admiration to all the spectators. For although the lower part of his body was already burned, he never ceased to raise his hands to heaven and implore the help of God. And so by this most weighty testimony he declared that the truth of God and the glory of Christ ought to be dearer to all Christians and pious men than their own life.

units.la: Cæterùm quanuis Matthæus Dymonetus hoc genere mortis ac martyrio ante fit perfunctus, quàm suprà memoratus Peloquinus, tamen quia in huius scriptis mentio Dymoneti ac cæterorum qui sequuntur facta est, non incommodum nobis est visum ut hunc Peloquinum cæteris præponeremus, cùm præsertim temporis ratio quo capti fuerunt, hunc ordinem postularet.
units.tr: Moreover, although Matthew Dymonetus underwent this kind of death and martyrdom before the aforesaid Peloquinus, nevertheless, because mention of Dymonetus and of the others who follow has been made in the writings of this man, it has seemed not unsuitable to us to place Peloquinus before the rest, especially since the order of time in which they were taken demanded this sequence.

units.la: LVDOVICVS MARSACVS, ET ipsius Cognatus, cum Stephano Lignifabro.
units.tr: LUDOVICUS MARSACUS AND HIS COUSIN, WITH STEPHEN LIGNIFABER.

units.la: SVPRA[?] cum ea quae à Dionysio Peloquino facta sunt, exponeremus, mentio Ludouici Marsaci facta est, pij hominis: qui Gallus natione & patria Borbonius, cum diu ratione militarem professus esset, ex equestri ordine eorum militum, qui ordinati regij, id est conscripti ac designati appellantur, ad meliorem disciplinam professionemque Christianam traductus, & praestantiora Christi summi regis atq; imperatoris stipendia amplexus, ita integrè ac fideliter se gessit, ut causam eius & gloriam summa animi magnitudine, constantiaque propugnarit ac defenderit. Extat praeclara eius confessio, quam ultimo die Julij. M.D.LIII, judicibus Lugduni scriptam praesentauit, eamque morte postea obsignauit, quam cum duobus vinculorum sociis, altero ipsius Consobrino, altero Stephano Lignifabro constantissimè perpessus est. Historia autem sic se habet.
units.tr: Above, when I set out what was done by Dionysius Peloquinus, mention was made of Louis Marsacus, a godly man. A Frenchman by nation and country, a native of Bourbon, he had long followed the military profession. He was drawn from the equestrian order of those soldiers who are called ordinary royal troops, that is, enrolled and designated, to a better discipline and the Christian profession, and embraced the far more excellent service of Christ, the supreme King and Emperor. He conducted himself so uprightly and faithfully that he championed and defended his cause and glory with the greatest greatness of spirit and constancy. His famous confession survives, which he presented in writing to the judges at Lyon on the last day of July 1553, and afterwards sealed with his death, which he endured most steadfastly together with two companions in chains, one his own cousin and the other Stephen Lignifaber. The history is as follows.

units.la: Interrogatus ab Officiali & iis qui cum eo aderant, num crederem in hominibus liberum arbitrium esse, nósque habere facultatem tam ad bene quàm ad male agendum: me quidem nullam agnoscere respondi, nec ullam ex meipso vim habere ad bene agendum nisi ea mihi à Deo concedatur: atque omnia dona à caelo proficisci à Patre luminum, meque posse cum Paulo vere dicere, quod volenti mihi facere bonum, adiunctum est malum, ut non quod volo bonum, sed quod nolo malum facio.
units.tr: Asked by the officer and those who were with him whether I believed that men have free will, and that we have the ability to act both well and badly, I answered that I acknowledged no such freedom, and that I had no power of my own to do good unless it were granted me by God. All gifts come from heaven, from the Father of lights, and I could say truly with Paul: "When I want to do good, evil is present with me; so I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want."

units.la: Item, num crederem Sanctorum veneration em, eósque tum pro nobis orare, tum à nobis invocados esse: denique an nostri non essent aduocati, ac patroni, imprimisque virgo Maria: Ego autem respondi, me nullum aduocatum alium cognoscere aut habere quàm unum Jesum Christum à Deo Patre mediatorem atque intercessorem constitutum. Tum illi mihi dixerunt Sanctos, quorum ego negare intercessionem, multa miracula edidisse, quae ex Scriptura probarent: Quibus respondi, nihil opus esse probatione, cùm id eis concederem. Sed alium miraculorum usum suisse quae ab Apostolis sunt edita, ut essent quaedam quasi sigilla eius doctrinae, quae ab illis annuntiabatur, ut virtute miraculorum ac magnitudine, populus ad audiendum atque amplectendum Dei verbum attentior esset: ut in Actis Apostolorum atque Evangelio Joannis videre lice licet. neque vero me aliud quicquã credere, aut præter eam verbi Dei doctrinam allegare. Qua in re illi nihil tum contra me dixerunt, nisi se adhibituros eum doctorem, qui me facilè revinceret.
units.tr: Likewise, they asked whether I believed in the veneration of the saints, and that they pray for us and are invoked by us; and finally whether the saints were not our advocates and patrons, especially the Virgin Mary. I replied that I knew and had no other advocate than the one Jesus Christ, appointed by God the Father as mediator and intercessor. Then they said that the saints, whose intercession I denied, had performed many miracles, which they proved from Scripture. To this I replied that there was no need of proof, since I granted it to them. But the miracles performed by the Apostles had another use: they were, as it were, seals of the doctrine which was proclaimed by them, so that by the power and greatness of the miracles the people would be more attentive to hearing and embracing the word of God, as can be seen in the Acts of the Apostles and the Gospel of John There was nothing else I believed or alleged beyond that doctrine of God's word. In this matter they said nothing then against me, except that they would bring in a teacher who could easily refute me.

units.la: Sum etiam ab ijs interrogatus, num crederem[?] me bonis operibus eorúmq; merito saluũ esse, ipsaque bona opera esse necessaria ad salutem. quibus ego respondi, me sola fide saluari, non vllis Legis operibus. nos tamen bona opera facere, quæ Deus in nobis qui sumus opus gratiæ eius, præparauit, vt in illis ambulemus. Meritum vero non alibi esse quærendum quàm in vno Christo Iesu, qui est salus nostra: neque est aliud sub cælo nomen hominibus datum in quo nos salui efse possimus. Deinde progressi ad Purgatorium, interrogatus num esse crederem. respondi me Purgatorium illud credere ac recipere, quosanguine[?] Filij Dei ab omni vitiorum meorum labe purgatus essem. Tum illi quæsiuerunt an non crederem ignem esse purgatorium, quo animæ ex his corporibus egressæ expurgarentur. quibus dixi me nullum aliud intelligere, præter illud quod in Christi purißimo sanguine pro peccatis nostris semel effuso, confiteret: mortuos autem in manu esse Dei, qui æquus omnium iudex est.
units.tr: They also asked me whether I believed that I was saved by my good works and their merit, and whether good works were necessary to salvation. To them I replied that I am saved by faith alone, not by any works of the Law. Nevertheless we do good works, which God has prepared in us, who are his workmanship of grace, so that we may walk in them. But merit is not to be sought anywhere but in Christ Jesus alone, who is our salvation; for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we can be saved. Then, passing on to Purgatory, they asked whether I believed there was one. I replied that I believed in and accepted that purgatory by which I was cleansed from every stain of my sins by the blood of the Son of God. Then they asked whether I did not believe that fire is a purgatory, in which the souls that have left these bodies are purged. I said that I understood no other purgatory than that which is confessed in the most pure blood of Christ, once poured out for our sins; but the dead are in the hand of God, who is the just judge of all.

units.la: Quæsiuerunt præterea, num confessio peccatorum in aurem sacerdotis esset deferëda, vt nos absolutionem ac pœnitentiam auferre possimus: Quā de re respondi, me cùm sensu peccatorum suum oppressus ad nullum alium confugere, peccataque mea deferre, quàm ad vnum Deum quem offendi, eúmque nobis pro sua gratia ignoscere, quam in Christo Iesu nobis declarauit & commendauit.
units.tr: They also asked whether the confession of sins was to be made into the ear of a priest, so that we could obtain absolution and penance. On this I replied that I, oppressed by the sense of my sins, had fled to no other, and carried my sins to no one but the one God whom I had offended, who forgives us by his grace, which he has declared and commended to us in Jesus Christ.

units.la: Tum mox quæsiuerunt, num sacerdotes parœciæ nostræ pro meis pastoribus haberem, eósque tum doctrina tum vita tales agnoscerem: Ego vero respondi eos vtroque in genere falsos pastores esse: maléque pasci, duci ac gubernari eos omnes qui eorum custodiæ commissi sunt. Tu, inquiunt, habes eos pro ignaris? Ego vero, inquam, pro pastoribus nullo modo habere volo nec debeo. Tum unº ex iis, Tu, inquit, nimium te sare[?] arbitraris: Ego vero inquam, me nihil aliud, quàm Iesum Christum eúmque pro me crucifixum scire arbitror. Ego etiam, inquit ille. Nos ergo, inquam, in eo quidem consentimus.
units.tr: Soon afterwards they asked whether I regarded the priests of our parish as my ministers, and acknowledged them as such in both teaching and life. I replied that they were false ministers in both respects, and that all who were committed to their keeping were fed, led and governed badly. "Do you," they said, "regard them as ignorant?" I said, "I certainly do not regard them, and must not regard them, as ministers in any way." Then one of them said, "You think yourself too wise." I said, "I think I know nothing but Jesus Christ, and him crucified for me." "I too know that," he said. "Then in that we agree," I said.

units.la: Post hæc homines sobrij ac temperantes de ieiunijs me interrogarunt, num ieiunandum esset. Quibus respondi me ea ieiunia probare, quae cum precibus coniuncta essent, ac tum quidem praecipue adhibenda, cum aliqua graui calamitate premimur & affligimur, aut etiam vt animum in hoc corpore languentem, ad orandum, per huiusmodi sobrietate atque abstinentia praeparemus. Tu, inquiunt, vis ieiunia pro tuo arbitrio praefinire, non praescripta ab ecclesia, certisque diebus constituta obseruare. Verum, inquam, ieiunium Christiano homini moderatione totius vitae, temperantia, sobrietateque perpetuum esse debet. Credisne, inquiunt symbolum Apostolorum? Sane, inquam.
units.tr: After this, sober and temperate men asked me about fasts, whether one ought to fast. I replied that I approved those fasts which are joined with prayer, and which are to be used especially when we are pressed and afflicted by some grave calamity, or also to prepare the spirit, languishing in this body, for prayer, through such sobriety and abstinence. "You want," they said, "to fix fasts at your own discretion, and not to observe those prescribed by the Church and appointed for certain days." Indeed, I said, a Christian's fasting ought to be perpetual, through moderation of the whole life, temperance and sobriety. "Do you believe the Apostles' Creed?" they asked. "Certainly," I said.

units.la: Deinde de Sacramento Cœnæ quæsiuerunt, eóque verbo usi sunt. Quibus ego respondi, me id quidem credere; ac cum recte puréq; administratur, sub specie panis ac vini carne & sanguine Iesu Christi vere participare. Sed credisne, inquiunt, corpus Iesu Christi vere in eo pane contineri? Minime, inquam: quin potius credo illud in caelum euectum atque receptum, Christumque Dominum ad dexteram Patris ita sedere, vt huiusmodi elementis inclusus nullo modo teneatur.
units.tr: Then they asked about the Sacrament of the Supper, using that very word. To them I replied that I did indeed believe in it, and that when it is rightly and purely administered we truly partake, under the appearance of bread and wine, of the flesh and blood of Jesus Christ. "But do you believe," they said, "that the body of Jesus Christ is truly contained in that bread?" "Not at all," I said. Rather I believe that he was carried up and received into heaven, and that Christ the Lord sits at the right hand of the Father in such a way that he is in no way held enclosed in such elements.

units.la: Tum vnus ex iis, me Iudæis Capernaitis similem esse dixit. neque enim, inquit, vis credere, nisi corporalem Christi praesentiam in ipso pane inclusam videas. Neque vero potes negare, quin Christus dixerit, Qui edet carnem meam, & sanguinem meum bibet. Tu vero, inquam, vide quemadmodum Christus dicat se panem esse viuum qui de caelo descendit, vt vitam omnibus in ipsum credentibus impertiat: carnem denique nihil prodesse, Spiritum autem viuificare. Adhæc illos etiam admonui, vt ea quae a Luca Euangelista narrantur, traduntúrque a Paulo, inspicerent & considerarent, cum ita dicitur, Accipite, edite, Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur: hoc quotiescunque feceritis, in mei memoriam facietis. nam ita mortem Domini, inquit Paulus, quoad is veniat, annuntiabitis. Tum ego eos diligenter monui vt eum locum annotarent. Neque vero memoriam rerum praesentium recoli ac celebrari, sed praeteritarum: nec memoriam Christi vsurpandam esse, si eum praesentē ante oculos nostros habemus. Sane inquiunt illi, sed annon vis tu amplecti quod a sacrosancto Concilio atque doctoribus est constitutum? Sane, inquam, id quidem duntaxat quod cum verbo Dei cõsentiat: præterea nihil. Nã si ego ipse, ait Paulus, aut Angelus de cælo veniat, qui aliud verbum vobis annuntiet quam quod ego annuntiavi, anathema sit. Tum illi ex me, ubi ista didicissem, quæsiuerunt. In sancto Euangelio, inquam, & verbo Dei. Est ne tuum, inquiunt, officium id legere, cum sis homo mechanicus, nulla scientia præditus? Quomodo vero scis tu id esse Euangelium, & quis te docuit? Deus inquam, me Spiritu suo docuit. Omnium autem Christianorum est illud legere, audire & cognoscere, sine quo via ad vitam & salutem nullo modo cognosci aut teneri potest. Postremo quæsiuerunt num Institutionem Caluini vidissem quæ Christiana inscribitur & appellatur. Quibus ego ingenuè confessus sum. Atque hæc quidem quæsita sunt ex me in prima interrogatione.
units.tr: Then one of them said that I was like the Capernaite Jews: "For you will not believe," he said, "unless you see the bodily presence of Christ enclosed in the bread itself. Nor can you deny that Christ said, 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood...'" I replied: "But see how Christ says that he is the living bread which came down from heaven, to impart life to all who believe in him; and finally that the flesh profits nothing, but the Spirit gives life." I also admonished them to look at and consider what the Evangelist Luke relates and Paul hands down: "Take, eat; this is my body, which is given for you; as often as you do this, do it in remembrance of me; for so, says Paul, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes." I urged them carefully to note that passage. The memory of present things is not recalled and celebrated, but of past ones; nor is the remembrance of Christ to be used if we have him present before our eyes. "Certainly," they said, "but do you not wish to embrace what has been established by the most holy Council and the teachers?" "Certainly," I said, "but only so far as it agrees with the word of God, and nothing beyond that. For even if I myself, says Paul, or an angel from heaven, should bring you a word other than the one I have proclaimed, let him be anathema." Then they asked me where I had learned these things. "In the holy Gospel," I said, "and the word of God." "Is it your office," they said, "to read that, since you are a mechanic, endowed with no learning? But how do you know that this is the Gospel, and who taught you?" "God," I said, "taught me by his Spirit. But it is the duty of all Christians to read it, hear it and know it, without which the way to life and salvation cannot be known or held in any way." Finally they asked whether I had seen the Institutes of Calvin, which is entitled and called Christian. To this I openly confessed. These were the questions put to me in the first interrogation.

units.la: Secunda autem interrogatio per magnum Vicarium facta est, qui pro sua summa insci-tia atque stoliditate, multa ex me levia friuolaque quæsiuit, minimè digna quæ hoc loco ac tempore commemorentur. Postea rogauit me, quam ratione vitæ professus essem. Cui ego respondi, militarem ex equestri ordine eorum qui delecti & conscripti, certas Regis turmas conficiunt: Lorgio autem duce stipendia meruisse. Tum quidam ex iis qui aderant, Ille quidem, inquit, qui præstantissimus eques extitit, te in hac doctrina disciplinaque minimè instituit. Non sanè, inquam: neque enim ego, quemadmodum paulo ante dixi, ab hominibus hæc didici: neque in bello inter pugnandum eddiscuntur. Interrogatus num crederem votum castitatis, quæsiui ex eo, quodnam illud esset. Vt homines, inquit, fiant religiosi, & alia quædam faciant, quæ ille nescio quæ nugamenta referebat. Tum ego ei respondi, me nullam castitate meliore existimare, quam vt cum nos aculeis carnis pungimur atque incitamur, ad Deum confugiamus, petamúsque ab eo vt prauas atq; immoderatas carnis nostræ libidines cõprimat & extinguat, nosque eas iis rationibus quæ à Deo nobis proponuntur, refrenemus. Religionem vero me nullam aliam intelligere, præter eam de qua diuus Iacobus loqueretur.
units.tr: The second examination was conducted by the great Vicar, who, through his great ignorance and stupidity, asked me many trivial and frivolous questions, not at all worth recording here and now. Afterwards he asked me what my way of life was. I answered that I was a soldier of the knightly order, among those chosen and enrolled who make up the King's companies of horse, and that I had served for pay under the captain Lorgio. Then one of those present said: "Surely the most distinguished cavalryman was the one who has trained you in this doctrine and discipline?" "Certainly not," I said. "As I said a little earlier, I did not learn these things from men, nor are they learned in battle amid the fighting." Asked whether I believed in the vow of chastity, I asked him what that vow was. "That men become religious," he said, "and do certain other things," and he went on to describe some trifling matters I cannot recall. I replied that I knew of no better chastity than this: when the goads of the flesh prick and stir us, we flee to God, and ask him to restrain and quench our depraved and immoderate lusts of the flesh, and to curb us by those means which God sets before us. As for religion, I said I understood no other than that of which the blessed James speaks.

units.la: Interrogatus num Sacramenta Ecclesiæ crederem, quæsiui ab eo quæ essent illa. Cum autem ille mihi ea numerasset, dixi duo tantùm à Deo in Ecclesia Christiana instituta & tradita, Baptismum & sacram Cœnam.
units.tr: Asked whether I believed in the sacraments of the Church, I asked him what they were. When he had listed them for me, I said that only two had been instituted and handed down by God in the Christian Church: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Interrogatus an eo tempore quo illum ordinem militare equestremque profiterer ac sequerer, ad Missam audiedam accederem, corasimulachris[?] atque imaginibus genua flecterem, ac peccata mea sacerdoti confiterer. Non negaui me quidem antea in mea summa ignoratione ac caecitate ea omnia fecisse: nunc vero summas Deo gratias agere, qui me ab illis tantis erroribus reuocarit, atque in viam salutis reduxerit. Tu quidem, inquiunt, ab ea longe abes: Imo vero, inquam, longius aliquando abfui. Putasne tu, inquit Vicarius, te in ea via salutis esse? Ego vero, inquam, non solum puto, sed etiam credo, persuasus iis promissis, quibus Christus de salute mea certissimum reddidit. Tum ille dixit se doctorem perhibiturum, qui mihi ostenderet quanto in errore ego versarer. Cui dixi me quidem ei crediturum, atque errorem meum agnituru, si cum ex Scriptura sancta mihi ostenderet. Ille quidem, inquit, cum ex Scriptura sacra, tum etiam ex constitutionibus Conciliorum facillime tibi ostendet. Ego vero, inquam, si eius demonstratio consentiat cum verbo Dei, fidem ei adhibebo: sin doctrinam diuersam a verbo Dei eique repugnantem afferat, eam, ut duus[?] Paulus ait, ut quoddam anathema detestabor. Illi semper authoritate Conciliorum doctorumque protulerunt: cui ego hunc Pauli locum fortiter oppossui, illudque etiam ostendi, fidem meam in authoritate verbi Dei, non hominum opinione aut consuetudine fundatam esse. Porro tribus diebus post, Vicarius sperans se praedam ingentem a me ablaturum, venit cum capitalium caesarum Iudice. Hi pecuniam quam habebam, mihi ademerunt, nisi quod quantum satis esset ad viuendum reliquerunt. Vicarius autem post multa inepta & absurda, quae tum mihi loquutus est, quaesuit num ego vellem me plane referre ad Concilium iudiciumque doctorum, ad quos Scripturae sacrae interpretatio atque explicatio pertineret, & num vellem magis quam Rex Gallae sapere ac non ea quae ille credere: Respondi ei nihil opus mihi esse eorum interpretatione, meque sine vllo huiusmodi interprete ac doctore facile aperteque ostensurum id quod dicerem verum esse: neque meam fidem in ipso Rege fundatam esse & constitutam, neque etiam hic esse ut de illius fide loquerer. Tum ille iterum se doctorem nuhi daturum dixit. Quid Quid tu, inquā, num præstare id ipse potes, cùm præsertim iuridiciale munus officiumq; sustineas? Tertius eorum ad me aduentus accessitque fuit, vbi Suppræfectus aderat. tu summus Vicarius ex me quæsiuit, num vellem in meis opinionibus atq; erroribus, vt vocant, permanere: Quæ ego rogaui, vt ea quæ dixeram, mihi legenda curaret. id quod ipse fecit, quærens semper ex me, num meam vellem sententiam deponere, misericordiam mihi promittês. Ego autè eis dixi, me causam veritatis tã iustã & æquam nullo modo velle deponere aut abijcere: neq; verò petere ab iis misericordiam: sed Deum orare, vt eam mihi impertiret. Interea dum interrogata & responsa mea mihi legerentur, me de Euangelio interrogantes, captiosè aggressi sunt, num meum esset officium illud legere, & quisnam me de eo erudisset ac docuisset: Quibus ego respondi, Deum Spiritu suo fecisse vt aliquâ eius cognitione adeptus fuerim, nec me sine gratia illius atque Spiritus illuminatione quicquam posse in Euangelio comprehendere atq; intelligere. Tum Suppræfectus Regis dixit, quòd ad quatuor Euangelistas attineret, duos tantùm esse, Matthæum & Ioannem, qui puri essent: Marcum verò & Lucam centones quosdam habere hinc illinc colle&os: quo in genere Paulum etiam ponebat. Illud præterea dixit, se epistolas Pauli, nisi doctores Ecclesiæ eis authoritatem dedissent, non pluris quàm Æsopi fabulas facturum. Ego ei dixi, Diuum quidem Paulum habere optimum certissimúmque vocationis suæ testimonium, quemadmodum in epistola ad Galatas 1.ca. scriptum est. Tum ille, Paulum sibiipsi testimonium dare dixit. Videtis fratres, quæ & quanta sit hæc blasphemia aduersus sacrosanctũ Dei verbũ impurissimè proiecta. Oremus igitur eum vt nobis eam gratiã impertiat, ne in huiusmodi impietatē delabamur: sed virtute Spiritus eius confirmati, in obseruantia obedientiáque verbi ipsius cum omni reuerentia permaneamus. Postea Suppræfectus iussit iterum recitari ea quæ ego de Cœna interrogat, responderā, ac quæsiuit num velle credere verum corpus Iesu Christi ibi in eo pane inclusū cõti-neri: Ego, inquā, id credo quod ante dixi. Tum ille, Ego, inquit, credo simulatque verba sacramenta ita[?] super panè sunt pronuntiata, corpº Christi in eo inludi[?] & contineri: Ego, inquam, illud nego, credóque Christum in cælum ascendisse, atque ad dexteram Dei patris sui sedere. Mea hæc quidem, inquit, fides est, in qua volo viuere & mori. Et ego quoque, inquam, volo & viuere & mori in ea, quam sum confessus & professus.
units.tr: Asked whether, at the time when I professed and followed that military and knightly way of life, I went to hear Mass, bowed my knees before images and statues, and confessed my sins to a priest, I did not deny that I had indeed done all these things before, in my great ignorance and blindness; but now I give the greatest thanks to God, who has called me back from those great errors and restored me to the way of salvation. "You are certainly far from that," they said. "Not at all," I said, "I was once far off, and further than now." "Do you think, then," said the Vicar, "that you are on that way of salvation?" "I not only think so," I said, "but I also believe it, persuaded by those promises through which Christ has made my salvation most certain." Then he said he would bring a doctor who would show me how far I was living in error. I replied that I would indeed believe him and acknowledge my error, if he showed it to me from holy Scripture. "Indeed," he said, "he will very easily show you from Scripture, and also from the decrees of the Councils." "For my part," I said, "if his demonstration agrees with the Word of God, I will give him credence; but if he brings a doctrine different from and opposed to the Word of God, I will detest it as, in the words of the blessed Paul, an anathema." They always put forward the authority of the Councils and the teachers; to this I strongly opposed that passage of Paul, and I also showed that my faith rests on the authority of the Word of God, not on the opinion or custom of men. Three days later, the Vicar, hoping to carry off a great prize from me, came with the judge of the capital cases. They took from me the money I had, leaving me only enough to live on. Then the Vicar, after much silly and absurd talk, asked me whether I would be willing to refer myself wholly to the Council and to the judgment of the teachers, to whom the interpretation and explanation of Holy Scripture belongs, and whether I would be willing to be wiser than the King of France and not believe what he believed. I answered him that I had no need of their interpretation, and that without any such interpreter or teacher I would easily and plainly show that what I said was true; and that my faith is not founded and established on the King himself, nor am I here to speak about his faith. Then he again said he would provide a doctor. "And what," I asked, "can you yourself do this, especially since you hold a judicial office?" A third visit came to me from them, at which the sub-prefect was present. The chief Vicar asked me whether I wished to persist in my opinions and errors, as they call them. I asked that what I had said be read back to me, which he himself arranged, always asking me whether I wished to give up my opinion, and promising me mercy. But I told them that I by no means wished to abandon or cast off a cause so just and right, nor did I ask mercy from them, but prayed to God to grant it to me. Meanwhile, while my questions and answers were being read to me, they came at me craftily, asking about the Gospel: whether it was my business to read it, and who had instructed and taught me in it. To them I replied that God by his Spirit had brought it about that I had gained some knowledge of it, and that without the grace and illumination of his Spirit I could comprehend and understand nothing in the Gospel. Then the sub-prefect of the King said that as for the four Evangelists, only two were pure, Matthew and John; Mark and Luke, he said, were patched-together cloaks gathered from here and there; he even put Paul in that class. He also said that unless the teachers of the Church had given authority to Paul's epistles, he would value them no more than Aesop's fables. I told him that the blessed Paul had the best and most certain testimony of his calling, as is written in the epistle to the Galatians, chapter 1. Then he said that Paul gave testimony to himself. See, brethren, what and how great a blasphemy this is, impiously uttered against the most holy Word of God! Let us therefore pray that he grant us the grace not to fall into such impiety, but, strengthened by the power of his Spirit, to remain in obedience to and in observance of his Word with all reverence. Afterwards the sub-prefect ordered read again what I had answered when questioned about the Supper, and asked whether I was willing to believe that the true body of Jesus Christ is contained in that bread. "I believe," I said, "what I said before." Then he said: "I believe that as soon as the words of the sacrament have been pronounced over the bread, the body of Christ is included and contained in it." "I deny that," I said, "and I believe that Christ ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God his Father." "This," he said, "is my faith, in which I want to live and die." "And I too," I said, "want to live and die in that which I have confessed and professed.

units.la: Atque hic quidem finis fuit sermonum nostrorum: in quibus non potui commodè ordinem, quo fui interrogatus, conseruare. Ego autem malui aliquid omittere, quàm aliquid quod quæsitum ex me non suisset, addere. Neque verò hanc confessionem meam propterea scripsi vt ea in lucem emittatur: sed vt Deus hoc meo testimonio aliquam gloriam consequatur, quemadmodum ipse me honorauit, suamque virtutem in mea summa infirmitate exhibuit, ita vt inimici nostri victi & consusi nihil plane habeant quod dicant, nisi quod nos rationem fidei nostræ ad iudicium arbitriumque doctorum suorum referre nolumꝰ, quasi sapientiores quàm illi sint, esse velimus. Interea tamen ita premuntur, vt quod dicant nihil plane habeant, nisi quod pudore impediuntur quo minus Scripturam sacram plane repudient. Ego autem Deum optimum atque omnis misericordiæ Patrem etiam atque etiam oro vt sua in nos dona augeat & confirmet, quo nos tum in vita tum in morte sanctiffimum[?] eius nomen omni gloria illustrare possimus, ita vt & regnum eius amplificetur, & Ecclesia plane vastata & desolata ædificetur, atque in optimum statum restituatur, nostraque salus procuretur: hocq; ab eo peto in nomine & summa gratia charissimi eius Filij Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui regnat cum Patre & Spiritu sancto, Amen.
units.tr: And this was the end of our conversations, in which I could not well keep the order in which I was questioned. I preferred to leave something out rather than add anything that had not been asked of me. Nor have I written this confession of mine so that it may be published; rather, I have written it so that God may gain some glory from this my testimony, just as he himself has honoured me and shown his power in my great weakness, so that our enemies, defeated and confounded, have nothing at all to say, except that we are unwilling to refer the reasons for our faith to the judgment and opinion of their teachers, as if we wished to be wiser than they are. Yet in the meantime they are so hard pressed that they have nothing at all to say, except that shame keeps them from utterly rejecting holy Scripture. As for me, I pray again and again to God, the best and Father of all mercy, that he increase and confirm his gifts in us, so that we may glorify his most holy name with all honour, both in life and in death; that his kingdom may be enlarged, and the Church, now utterly laid waste and desolate, may be built up and restored to its best condition, and our salvation may be secured. This I ask of him in the name and by the great grace of his most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, Amen.

units.la: Sequitur epistola Ioannis Caluini missa ad Peloquinum, & Marsacum, aliósque, qui eodem tempore Lugduni in carcere captiui propter Euangelium tenebantur.
units.tr: There follows the letter of John Calvin, sent to Peloquin and Marsac and others who at the same time were held captive in prison at Lyons on account of the Gospel.

units.la: GO, fratres charissimi, credo vos intellexisse, me tum cum nuntium captiuitatis vestræ huc est allatum, ab hac vrbe abfuisse, quo octo post discessum meum diebus reuersus sum. Itaq; minimè necessarium esse puto, vt me vobis excusem quòd ad hunc vsque diem scribere ad vos distulerim. Quanuis autem illud nuntium, secundum quidem carne nobis tristè & acerbum acciderit, etiam pro eo amore & benevolentia quam in Spiritu ac Deo erga vos habemus, quemadmodum par est: nos tamen oportet ad voluntatem optimi Patris ac summi Domini conformari, neque solùm iudicare iustù & æquum quod is de nobis statuit, sed etiam vt bonum amoríque plenum & ad salutem nostram accómodatum optimo gratissimóque animo accipere, patienter expectantes vt reipsa ita esse ostendat. Caeterum in summa nostra tristitia ingens inest consolatio ac laetitia, quod Deus tanta virtute & potentia vobis affuerit. Etenim maximopere fuit necessarium, vt ipse Spiritu suo vos confirmaret ac roboraret, quo sacrosanctam eius veritatem vestra vita pretiosiorem charioremque haberetis. Nos quidem omnes etiam nimium scimus, quam difficile hominibus sit sui oblivisci. Itaque tum demum Deus robustissimum ac potentissimum brachium suum exerit, cum pro nomine eius illustrando nullum aut tormentum aut opprobrium aut etiam genus mortis pertimescimus. Cum autem is vos sua virtute hactenus muniverit, summoque robore sepserit, vt primum impetum sustineretis: reliquum est, vt cum oremus vt vos magis magisque confirmet pro magnitudine ac difficultate certaminis eius quod vobis est subeundum. Ac quum ipse nobis summam totius dimicationis victoriam promiserit, ne dubitetis quin cum vos iam singulari eius gratia aliquam virtutis eius partem in vobis senseritis, in posterum maius re ipsa atque experientia testimonium sitis habituri: ex quo plane intelligere poteritis, eum opus quod semel incepit, nunquam imperfectum relinquere, quemadmodū est in Psal. cxxxviii. Imprimis vero cum suis hunc tribuit honorem, vt eos ad veritatem verbi sui propugnandam tutandamque adhibeat, atque ad martyrium quasi manu sua ducat, nunquam inermes eos relinquet, sed omnibus, quae sunt necessaria, armis instruet. Tantummodo eam suscipite cogitatione atque opera date, vt in caelesti Iesu Christi regnum oculos vestros attollatis, atque animis vestris perpendatis pro qua causa hāc dimicationem suscipitis ac sustinetis. Nam hic quidem aspectus, non solum vincet omnes tentationes, quibus ab infirmitate carnis attentari posse tis, sed etiā invictos vos faciet adversus omnes Sathanae fallacias, eaque omnia quae infestissimus hostis ad obscurandam veritatem machinari poterit. Nam certo scio, animos vestros singulari Dei gratia ita fundatos & constitutos esse, vt non casu ac temere in hoc certamen incideritis, sed certissimo Spiritus iudicio, & (vt paulo ante dixi) quasi manu Dei ducti veneritis: ita vt cum egregio illo Iesu Christi milite possetis vere dicere, Ego scio cui crediderim. Atque ea causa est, quo minus ad vos mitta ea fidei confessione qua optimo frater noster Peloquinus à me petijt. Nam Deus faciet, ut ea confessio qua vos pro ea mensura Spiritus que vobis dedit, ediderit, maiore aedificationis fructu asserat, quàm cætera omnia quæ aliunde suppeditari vobis possunt. Quinetiam rogatus à piis fratribus, qui non ita diu sanguine suum pro gloria Dei tuenda profuderunt, ut eorum confessione videre & corrigerem, non solum in ea nihil immutare volui, sed ex ea huiusmodi cōsolatione cepi, qua me in fide magnopere confirmatum sensi. nullu autem verbu addereaut demere plane volui, existimas quātum in ea mutaretur, tātu de au-thoritate ac virtute detraheretur ea qua meretur summa sapientia & co-stantia, qua videmo ab Spiritu Dei profecta esse. Ita igitur statuatis, vobisq; plane persuadeatis, optimu Deu, qui se, cum opo est, ostedit, suam in vestra infirmitate virtutē præstaturu, neque vos unqua relicturum, quin præclarè ac magnificè positis ei nomē celebrare atq; illustrare. Tātum summa moderatione & reuerentia adhibete, certo sciētes Deo sacrificiu, quod ei pro portione Spiritus & facultate, qua ab eo accepistis, offeretis, nō minus gratu futurum quàm si omnes Angelorum reuelationes comprehenderitis, eundemq; facturum ut id quod ori vestro inseruerit, tum ad confirmandos suos, tum ad aduersarios omni pudore afficiendos valeat. Nam quemadmodum vos satis intelligitis, nobis constanter resistendum esse omnibus impijs Papistarum abominationibus, nisi velimus Christum abnegare, à quo percare redempti ipsiqué acquisiti sumus: ita debetis eam gloriam cælestem atque immortalem meditari, ad quam vocamur atque inuitamur, certi nos ad ea per crucē, ignominiam, ipsamq; morte peruenturos. Omnino huma-no ingenio alienum magnopere videtur filios Dei ita angoribus satiari, cum interea impij homines in suis deliciis ac voluptatibus exultet: imò vero teterrima fathanæ macipia nos pede gutturi impositio ita premere atq; affligere, ut suos de nobis triumphos agat. sed tamen in his tatis ærumnis atq; miseriis vehementer nos debemus consolari, quòd possimus felicissimū exitu, qui nobis est promissus, expectare, & quòd Deo non modo ex his omnibus malis per Angelos suos eripiet, sed etiā lachrymas per ipsos Angelos ex oculis nostris abstergêt: atq; ita rectè despicere poterimus superbia istorum hominum miserorum planèque occæcatorum qui suum in exitium omne vim furoris sui in caelum conferunt. Interea quidem, etsi, nos non sumus eadem conditione qua nunc vos estis, non tamen desistimus precibus, misericordia, solicitudinibus laborare, ac vobis συμπαθὴν[?] ut membra vestra, quandoquidem placuit Patri caelesti p sua bonitate nos unire in unū corpꝰ sub Filio suo, nostro capite. Itaque supplex cum orabo cam vobis gratiam impertiat, ut freti ipsius fauore, eiusque ope nixi, nulla in parte vacilletis, sed potius virtutis incrementum suscipiatis: idēq; vos in sua tutela & fidelissima custodia tueatur, cū ea certitudine atque animorum vestrorum persuasione, ut quicquid est in mundo contemnere possitis. Fratres mei & alij complures vobis plurimum salutis dicūt Geneuae. quoniā autem spero hanc epistolam vobis duobus fore communem, addam illud tātum, maiorem exhortationem mihi apud vos minime adhibēdam esse. Satis enim est me à Deo petere ut id magis ac magis imprimat in cordibꝰ vestris quod ex literis vestris intellexi vos optime gustasse. Quāquam molestū est tādiu in carcere lāguere, tamē si nullꝰ alius extaret fruct mus. Nam post eam declarationem nos omnes ad carcerem regiũ, Romanam appellatum, traducti fuimus, praeter Dionysium fratre nostrũ, quem, ut a quibusdam intelleximus, Eleutheropolim ducturi sunt, ut in ea urbe, in qua fuit captus, quasi quaedam victima caedatur: atque ita variis diversisque in locis nomen Dei nostri morte filiorum suorum illustretur. Nos quidem expectabamus eam sententiam, qua postridie eius diei quam haereticis sumus declarati, capitis damnaremur. Sed benignissimus Deus ad hunc usque diem nos conservavit, ut magis magisque semper corroboremur, quemadmodum sentimus, virtute quidem eius atq; operita ut ii qui maxime imbecilles ac debiles esse putabantur, nunc omnium sunt fortissimi atque constantissimi. Itaque ipsi adversarii nostri maxima molestia sunt affecti propter Consobrinum meum, quem iudicabant non constanter in proposito fidei permansurum, quasi nos aliquam opinionem in eius cerebro commovissemus. Sed benignitate Dei ea opinio illos multum fefellit. Vident enim in eo summam constantiam, quam Deus ad tuendam fidei declaratae confessionem ei dedit. Proximo die Mercurij, nos à regio Suppraefecto interrogati fuimus. Is perseverans semper in suis blasphemijs usitatis, multa & varia à nobis quaesivit, imprimisque à me qui primus coram eo productus fui. Quasi autem me nunquam vidisset, ita me interrogavit. Optimus Deus mihi eam vim Spiritus ad respondendum praestitit, quemadmodum & caeteris fratribus, ut ille miser nihil quod diceret haberet, nisi me ignarum atque imperitum esse sine ulla scientia: neque meum esse sacram scire Scripturam, quam tot homines summis ingenijs praestantes qui viginti quinque aut triginta annos in eius studio consumpsissent, intelligere non potuissent. Cui ego respondi, id quidem maiori illis esse dedecori ac turpitudini, idemque Scribis ac Pharisaeis, priscisque Legis doctoribus evenisse: Deum autem piscatoribus, mulieribus, claudis, caecis, leprosis, paralyticis, aliisque huiusmodi hominibus revelasse, ut illud quod Christus Dominus gratias Deo Patri agens dixit, in hoc hominum genere atque omni tempore conservaretur, quod Deus ab intelligentia sapientium doctorumque removit atque abdidit, & parvulis simplicibusque revelavit. Tum vero illi ridere coeperunt, ac me irridere: cum interea egregius vir Suppraefectus loquens cum regio Procuratore, per suam fidem iurauit. itaque eum ego reprehendi ac monui, eum qui me docuisset non esse iurandum, eundem me docuisse, id quod confitebar ac tuebar, purum eius verbum esse. Tum ille pudore aliquo affectus fuit, ac dixit, se in eo quidem falsum & lapsum esse potuisse. Porro regius Procurator mihi dixit, me negare non posse quin divus Ioannes Ephesi Missam celebrasset. à quo quaesiui vbinam illud scriptum reperisset, num id in Euangelio extaret. Is tum conticuit sine vllo responso, nisi quod me ignarum bestiamque appellabat. Ego ei dixi, me quidem facile id pati, ut essem talis qualem ipse existimaret, sed me tamen Christum Iesum cognouisse, qui ei esset incognitus. Itaque nos facile videre summam eorum ignorantiam atque stoliditatem plane belluinam possumus. Caeterum nos, quod ad homines quidem attinet, arbitramur nos cras huc processuros, ut in sacrificium Deo offeramur, eámque adipiscamur coronam gloriae aeternae atque haereditatem, quae nobis antequam mundus constitueretur parata est. In quo quidem magnopere gaudemus & laetamur, orantes benignissimum Deum ut hoc nostrum sacrificium ei sit gratum atque odoratum, quemadmodum quidem fore speramus & confidimus. Nam nos opem eius ac virtutem in nobis experimur ac sentimus, eo quidem nunc maiorem, quo finis dierum nostrorum magis appropinquare videtur: finis, inquam, huius vitae caducae atq; miseriarum plenae: in qua quid aliud videre possumus, quam summam desolationem: aut habere quam materiam plurimarum lachrymarum, maximarumq; acerbitatum propter tot tamq; horredas blasphemias, quae contra Dei nostri maiestatem scelerate proiiciuntur? Vna enim ex parte videmus hostes Ecclesiae manifestos, qui aperto marte Ecclesiam acerrime oppugnant, ac filios Dei persequentes, atque innocentium sanguinem fundentes, nihil aliud conantur nisi ut Christi haereditatem vastent & plane deleant. Altera ex parte, inimicos alios non minus perniciosos, qui in ipsa Ecclesia versantur, homines inordinatos atque dissolutos, qui se aduersum verbi Dei ministros fidelissimosq; eius servos extollentes, nihil aliud student quam omnem ecclesiasticam disciplinam dissipare, atque e vita omnem religionem ac timorem Dei tollere. His accedunt alij, qui in occultis conuenticulis suis seminant zizaniam doctrinásque impias, quibus simplices & imperitos homines corrumpant. Heu miseri, qui ita stupidi sumus, ut haec tanta mala non sentiamus, quae causam gemendi ac flendi multo maiorem atque acerbiorem nobis afferre debeant, quam omnes acerbitates quas homines in nos exercent, quae blasphemiis illis nominis Dei comparatae, leuissimæ sunt iudicandae. Itaq; fratres, illud quidem debuerat maximopere nos humiliare, cognoscentes ea nobis ab optimo Deo immitti, ut admoneamur, paterneque ab eo castigemur atque emendemur, atque etiam probemur, ut in patientia exerceamur. Nam ficut dicit Divus Iacobus, summam debemus laetitiam existimare, cum in varias tentationes incidimus, scientes probationem fidei nostrae patientia fieri. Sed oportet patientiam habere etiam opus perfectum, ut simus perfecti atque integri, nullaque in re deficiamus. Et certe nos in regnum Dei intrare non possumus, nisi ea una via quae a Christo Iesu nobis praemonstrata est. Ea autem est angusta & aspera, qua per multas magnasque difficultates & calamitates pervenire dum est. Ac tu quidem cum ea nobis accidunt, possumus plane nobis persuadere nos habere arrhas adoptionis nostrae, filiosque Dei esse, in librum vitae jam adscriptos. neque vero aequum esset & consentaneum ut servus bene tractaretur, cum dominus eius irridetur, conspuitur, colaphis caeditur, omníque opprobriorum genere afficitur. Oportet igitur nos, si volumus cum Christo vivere, ut cum eodem quoque patiamur, amareque ploremus, dum mundus insolentissime exultat. Sed tota ratio & conditio vitae ita commutabitur, ut impius istorum risus in questu fletúmq; perpetuú, aut dentium stridore converteatur: nos vero omnibus molestiis atque aerumnis liberati, sempiternis solatiis & gaudiis perfruamur. Gratulare igitur nobis, ac laetare charissime frater, quod benignissimus Deus animos nostros ita confirmaverit, ut illum diem tam felicem atque optabilem summa cum laetitia expectemus: in quo quidem speramus & confidimus nos morte nostra gloriam Deo daturos quam debemus: eúmq; etiam nobis eam constantiam praestaturum, qua quáusq; ad ultimam sanguinis nostri guttam, puram fidei nostrae confessionem tueamur, ita ut & regnum Domini nostri Iesu Christi augeatur, & sathanae eiusque vicarii Antichristi diminuatur atque evertatur: Ecclesiaque quam ita confusam ac desolatam cernimus, in meliorem statum restituatur. Harum quidem rerum initia jam videmus in ipsis nostris adversariis, qui cum nullo furore suo possunt nobis silentium imponere, ad eas confugiunt blasphemias, ut sanctissimam Domini nostri Jesu Christi doctrinam detestentur. Quemadmodum miserrimus iste homo regius Suppraefectus, qui heri cum interrogaret quandam mulierculam, domini Copi famulam, non est veritus hanc blasphemiam proferre,Detestandus sit Deus istius Legis. Ego Deum clementisimum[?] oro ut eius misereatur, eumque Spiritu suo illuminet, ut miserrimus homo ad veram peccati sui cognitionem adducatur. Quoniam autem tempus dissolutionis meae jam appropinquat, vos quasi ex hac vita decedens valere ac saluere iubeo, Deumque oro ut vos in purissimo nominis sui cultu perpetuo retineat atque conferuet. Fratres mei se vestris ac totius ecclesiae precibus etiam atque etiam commendant: siquidem erunt in hac adhuc vita, cum haec literae ad vos perlatae fuerint. Gratia Domini nostri Jesu Christi vobiscum sit. Hoc die Veneris xxv. Augusti. Vester amantissimus frater Ludovicus a Marsaco.
units.tr: Dearest brothers, I believe you understood that I was away from this city when the news of your imprisonment came here. I returned eight days after my departure, so I think it is quite unnecessary for me to apologise for having put off writing to you until today. Although that news was sad and bitter for us according to the flesh, and so it should be given the love and goodwill we bear you in the Spirit and before God, we must still conform ourselves to the will of our best Father and highest Lord. We should not only judge what he has decided about us to be just and fair, but also receive it with the most grateful and good heart, as something full of goodness and suited to our salvation, patiently waiting for him to show that it is so in fact. In the midst of our sadness, however, there is great consolation and joy, because God has stood by you with such great strength and power. It was altogether necessary that he should himself confirm and strengthen you by his Spirit, so that you would hold his most holy truth dearer and more precious than your life. We all know only too well how hard it is for people to forget themselves. So God stretches out his most mighty and powerful arm only when we fear no torment, no reproach, and not even any kind of death for the sake of making his name known. Since he has so far fortified you by his power and surrounded you with great strength, so that you could withstand the first assault, what remains is that we pray he will strengthen you more and more, in proportion to the greatness and difficulty of the struggle you must undergo. Since he himself has promised us the full victory of the whole conflict, do not doubt that, now that you have already felt some part of his power in yourselves through his singular grace, you will in future have a greater testimony in fact and experience. From this you will be able to understand plainly that he never leaves unfinished the work he has once begun, as is said in Psalm 138. Above all, he grants this honour to his own, that he uses them to defend and protect the truth of his word, and leads them to martyrdom as if by his own hand; he will never leave them unarmed, but will equip them with all the arms they need. Only take this up in thought and deed, so that you lift your eyes to the heavenly kingdom of Jesus Christ, and weigh in your minds for what cause you undertake and endure this struggle. For this view will not only overcome all the temptations by which the weakness of the flesh can be assailed, but will also make you invincible against all the deceits of Satan and all that the most hostile enemy can devise to obscure the truth. For I am certain that your hearts have been so founded and established by the singular grace of God that you did not enter this contest by chance or rashly, but came to it by the most certain judgement of the Spirit and, as I said a little while ago, led as if by the hand of God, so that with that excellent soldier of Jesus Christ you can truly say, "I know whom I have believed." That is also why I have not sent to you the confession of faith which our excellent brother Peloquinus asked of me. For God will cause that confession which you have made, according to the measure of the Spirit given to you, to yield a greater fruit of edification than all the other things that can be supplied to you from elsewhere. Moreover, when I was asked by pious brothers, who not long ago shed their blood to defend the glory of God, to look over and correct their confession, I not only wished to change nothing in it, but I took from it such comfort that I felt myself greatly strengthened in the faith. Indeed, I did not wish to add or take away a single word, for you can see how much would be changed in it, and how much authority and power would be taken from it, which is deserved by the highest wisdom and constancy that we see proceeded from the Spirit of God. So then, be assured and fully persuaded that our best God, who shows himself when there is need, will display his power in your weakness, and will never leave you, so that you may celebrate and make illustrious his name in an excellent and splendid way. Only use the greatest moderation and reverence, knowing for certain that the sacrifice you offer to God, according to the measure of the Spirit and the ability you have received from him, will be no less acceptable to him than if you had grasped all the revelations of the angels. He will also make it so that what he has put into your mouth may serve both to strengthen his own and to put all the godless to shame. For as you well understand, we must steadfastly resist all the impious abominations of the Papists, unless we wish to deny Christ, by whom we have been redeemed at a price and acquired. So you ought to meditate on that heavenly and immortal glory to which we are called and invited, certain that we shall attain it through the cross, dishonour, and even death. It seems altogether strange to human understanding that the sons of God should be sated with such anguish, while in the meantime impious men exult in their pleasures and delights. Indeed, the most loathsome slaves of Satan press and afflict us with their feet set on our throats, so that they may celebrate their triumphs over us. Yet in these troubles and miseries we ought to console ourselves greatly, because we can look for the most happy end that has been promised us, and because God will not only rescue us from all these evils through his angels, but will also wipe away the tears from our eyes through those same angels. And so we may rightly despise the pride of those wretched and utterly blinded men, who bring all the violence of their fury upon their own destruction. Meanwhile, although we are not in the same condition as you are now, we do not cease to labour in prayers, in compassion, and in anxious care, and we feel for you as members of one body, since it has pleased our heavenly Father, by his goodness, to unite us under his Son, our head, into one body. So I pray earnestly that he grant you his grace, so that, relying on his favour and leaning on his help, you may waver in no part, but rather gain an increase of strength; and may he keep you in his protection and most faithful custody, with such certainty and such persuasion of your hearts that you can despise whatever is in the world. My brothers and many others send you many greetings from Geneva. Since I hope this letter will be shared by you both, I will add only this: I ought by no means to give you any further exhortation. It is enough for me to ask God that he impress more and more on your hearts what I have understood from your letter, that you have tasted it very well. Although it is grievous to languish so long in prison, yet if there were no other fruit, we would still have it. For after that declaration we were all taken to the royal prison, called the Roman one, except our brother Dionysius, whom, as we have learned from some people, they are going to lead to Eleutheropolis, so that he may be cut down there like a sacrifice in the city where he was captured; and so the name of our God may be made illustrious in various and diverse places by the deaths of his sons. We indeed were expecting that sentence by which we would be condemned to death the day after we were declared heretics. But the most gracious God has preserved us until this day, so that we are continually strengthened more and more, as we feel, indeed by his power and working, so that those who were thought the weakest and most feeble are now the bravest and most constant of all. So our adversaries themselves have been greatly troubled on account of my cousin, whom they judged would not remain constant in his profession of faith, as if we had stirred up some notion in his brain. But by the goodness of God that opinion has greatly deceived them. For they see in him the highest constancy which God has given him to defend the confession of the faith he has professed. On the next Wednesday we were questioned by the royal sub-prefect. He, still persisting in his customary blasphemies, asked us many and various questions, and above all me, who was the first brought before him. But as if he had never seen me, he questioned me in this way. The best God gave me such power of the Spirit to answer, as he did also to my other brothers, that the wretch had nothing to say except that I was ignorant and inexperienced, without any knowledge; and that it was not for me to know the holy Scripture, which so many men, outstanding in their great abilities, who had spent twenty-five or thirty years in its study, could not understand. To him I replied that this indeed was a greater disgrace and shame to them, and that the same had happened to the Scribes and Pharisees and the ancient teachers of the Law; but that God had revealed it to fishermen, women, the lame, the blind, lepers, paralytics, and other men of that kind, so that what Christ our Lord said, giving thanks to God the Father, might be preserved in this kind of men and at all times: that God has removed and hidden from the understanding of the wise and learned, and revealed to the little ones and the simple. Then indeed they began to laugh and mock me, while in the meantime the excellent sub-prefect, speaking with the royal procurator, swore by his faith. So I rebuked him and warned him that he should not swear by one who had taught me, since the same one had taught me what I confessed and defended, that his word is pure. Then he was somewhat affected with shame, and said that he might indeed have been false and mistaken in that. Further, the royal procurator told me that I could not deny that the blessed John had celebrated Mass at Ephesus. I asked him where he had found that written, and whether it was in the Gospel. He then fell silent without any answer, except that he called me ignorant and a beast. I told him that I was indeed willing to suffer this, that I should be such as he judged me to be, but that I had nevertheless known Christ Jesus, who was unknown to him. And so we can easily see how great their ignorance and utterly brutish stupidity is. For the rest, as far as men are concerned, we expect that tomorrow we shall be brought here to be offered to God as a sacrifice, and so obtain the crown of eternal glory and the inheritance which has been prepared for us before the foundation of the world. In this we greatly rejoice and exult, praying that most gracious God will find our sacrifice pleasing and fragrant to him, as indeed we hope and trust it will be. For we experience and feel his help and power in us, and now the more so, since the end of our days seems to draw nearer: the end, I say, of this frail life, full of miseries. What else can we see in it but utter desolation, or find in it matter for so many tears and such great bitterness, on account of so many and such horrible blasphemies which are wickedly hurled against the majesty of our God? For on the one side we see the manifest enemies of the Church, who attack the Church most fiercely in open war, persecuting the sons of God and shedding the blood of the innocent, and who aim at nothing else than to lay waste and utterly destroy the inheritance of Christ. On the other side are other enemies no less destructive, who live within the Church itself, disorderly and dissolute men, who, setting themselves up against the faithful ministers of the Word and his most faithful servants, aim at nothing else than to scatter all ecclesiastical discipline and to remove from life all religion and the fear of God. To these are added others, who sow tares in their secret conventicles and impious doctrines, by which they corrupt simple and unlearned people. Alas, wretched are we, who are so dull that we do not feel these great evils, which ought to give us far greater and more bitter cause for groaning and weeping than all the bitterness that men inflict upon us, which, when compared with those blasphemies against the name of God, must be judged very slight. So, brothers, this should especially have humbled us, recognising that these evils are sent to us by our best God, so that we may be admonished, fatherly chastised and amended by him, and also tested, so that we may be exercised in patience. For as the blessed James says, we ought to count it the greatest joy when we fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of our faith produces patience. But patience must also have its perfect work, so that we may be perfect and whole, lacking in nothing. And indeed we cannot enter the kingdom of God except by that one way which Christ Jesus has shown us beforehand. That way is narrow and rough, and it must be travelled through many great difficulties and calamities. Now when these things happen to us, we can quite persuade ourselves that we have the earnest of our adoption, and that we are sons of God, already enrolled in the book of life. Nor would it be fair or fitting that a servant should be well treated when his master is mocked, spat upon, struck with blows, and subjected to every kind of reproach. So we must, if we wish to live with Christ, also suffer with him, and weep and mourn while the world exults most insolently. But the whole reason and condition of life will be changed, so that the laughter of those impious men is turned into lamentation and perpetual weeping, or into gnashing of teeth; while we, freed from all troubles and distresses, shall enjoy everlasting comforts and joys. Therefore rejoice and be glad with us, dearest brother, because our most gracious God has so strengthened our hearts that we await that day, so happy and so much to be desired, with great gladness; on which we hope and trust that by our death we shall give to God the glory we owe him, and that he will also give us that constancy by which, even to the last drop of our blood, we shall maintain the pure confession of our faith; so that the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ may be increased, and Satan and his vicar Antichrist may be diminished and overthrown, and the Church, which we see so confused and desolate, may be restored to a better state. Indeed we already see the beginnings of these things in our adversaries themselves, who, since with all their fury they cannot impose silence on us, take refuge in those blasphemies by which they abhor the most holy doctrine of our Lord Jesus Christ. Just as that most wretched man, the royal sub-prefect, did yesterday, when, questioning a certain little woman, the servant of Master Copus, he did not hesitate to utter this blasphemy: "God of that Law should be detested." I pray that most merciful God to have mercy on him, and to enlighten him by his Spirit, so that this most wretched man may be brought to a true knowledge of his sin. Since the time of my departure is now at hand, I bid you farewell as one departing from this life, and I pray God to keep and preserve you in the purest worship of his name for ever. My brothers commend themselves again and again to your prayers and to those of the whole Church; for they will still be in this life when this letter is brought to you. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Written on this Friday, 25th August. Your most loving brother, Louis de Marsac.

units.la: Sequitur mors Ludovici Marsaci eiusque Consobrini, atque Stephani Lignifabri, te- stata commemoratione eorum, qui [illegible, ~7 letters] fuerunt, ac rem, quemadmodum est ge- sta, totam viderunt.
units.tr: The death of Ludovicus Marsacus and his cousin, and of Stephen the carpenter, with a faithful account by eyewitnesses who [illegible] and saw the whole matter as it was done.

units.la: PAVCIS post diebus, ipse Marsacus eiusque socii, Consobrinus, & Stephanus Lignifaber, qui natus fuit Genabi ad Ligerim, homo cum ardentissimo studio, tum etiam in verbo Dei optime institutus. hi tres Lugduni eadem sententia, pro tribunali pronuntiata, capitis damnati fuerunt ut vivi igne cremarentur. Judices autem postquam eam sententiam pronuntiarunt, vehementer fuerunt perturbati atque attonti, cum viderent eos tres martyres, non solum mortem propinquam no perhorrescere, verum etiam Deum omni gratiarum actione atq; laude celebrare, quòd digni ab eo habiti essent, ut pro sanctissimo ipsius nomine paterentur, adeò ut ex audientia judiciaria egredientes, Psalmum quendam canere coeperint. Neque vero Suppraefectus hoc diutius dissimulare potuit, eorumq; sanctam in Deo laetitiam atque hilaritatem ferre: sed maxima indignatione commotus, iussit eis silentium imponi, egrediensque inde, dixit, Itáne abiecti isti homines, adversus tantam Monarchiam regni se extollet? Tum Marsacus in exiguū eius loci, in quo erant, angulum secessit, ibique Deum orare cœpit, quæ cum unus ex satellitibus impedire vellet, Num, inquit Stephanus, est æquum hoc tempore nos impediri quò minus Deum nostrum invocemus & orémus? His illius verbis territus satelles conticuit, seque illico recepit. Porrò antequam educerentur è carcere, ut ad ultimum supplicium ducerentur, cæteris duobus, Consobrino ipsius Marsaci & Stephano funem singulorum collo apposuerunt. Ludovicus autē Marsacus, cum idem insigne atque ornamentum expectasset, neque videret id sibi deferri, quòd Iudices rationem quandam haberent eius qui ex equestri eorum ordine fuisset, qui Ordinati regij nominantur: coram Suppræfecto ac cæteris magistratibus maxima voce quæsiuit, num causa fratrum sociorumque suorum alia esset atque sua.
