Petrus: in quibus nulla erat authoritas, virt° neque dignitas antequam à Christo vocati essent. nam miseri piscatores erant, nullius existimationis homines, ut pote idiotae & literarum imperiti. Postquam Deo visum est eos vocare ut pro Apostolis haberet, tum in magnam dignitatem & potentiam Euangelij sui virtute euexit, constituens eos legatos & praecones ad publicandum nomen suum per universum orbem terrarum, cum mandatis istis, Ite & praedicate Euangelium omni creaturae: qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit, & qui non crediderit damnabitur. Videtis igitur ad quem dignitatis gradum pervenerint Apostoli per Euangelium. nam in hoc Spiritum sanctum Dominus semel sub visibili specie linguarum igneārum dissectarum, iis contulit, ut per omnes populos dispergerent quod ipsis traditum fuerat, atque in beatam unitatem homines huc illuc palatos revocarent. Nec vero aliud ipsos per orbem docere voluit Christus, quàm Euangelium quod est verbum Dei Patris sui: dicens, Sicut misit me Pater, ita & ego mitto vos. Apud Esa. certum extat de Christo misso testimonium ubi sic loquens introducitur, Spiritus Domini super me, & me misit ut euangelizem pauperibus. eadem ratione de Apostolis aperte habemus Christi mandatum, Ite & publicate Euangelium omni creaturae. Atq; ex Euangelij doctrina constat penes solum Deum esse, remittere peccata: qui sic per os Prophetae sui Esaiae de se ipse loquitur, Ego sum qui deleo iniquitates propter me, nec est ullus alius. itē S. Ioan. non recitat Scribas & Pharisaeos unquā eo arrogantiae venisse, ut dicerent se remittere peccata: quin potius cum indignatione ita exclamasse: Quisnam peccata condonat, nisi solus Deus? non est igitur in homine situm remittere alteri delicta. nam quod Christus ait discipulis suis: Quicquid solveritis solvetur, quodque ligaveritis ligatum manebit, id potentiae verbi divini ipsis commissi attribuēdu[?] est, in quo verbo salus & vita consistit. Neque enim legimus Petrum aut discipulorum aliquem antequam ad munus Apostolicum vocati essent, miracula aut signa edidisse, sed tum demum cum à Domino authoritas ipsis data est praedicandi Euangelij ubique gentium. idque publicè & aperté, vel (ut est apud Matth.) super tecta: non vero tecte aut in aurem, quomodo sacrificis confessio insusurratur. Euangelium enim ad communem omnium salutem datum est. proinde libere & palám illud profiteri debemus, ubicunque terrarum degamus. Veritas autem verbi Dei facilè perspicitur ex sermone quae habuit Petrus ad claudum illum ab utero matris suae, In nomine Iesu Christi Nazareni surge & ambula: atque ita protinus factũ est. deinde Petrus videns populum attonitum, negavit claudum propria ipsorum potentia vel pietate ambulare, sed in fide nominis Iesu Christi (quae illi crucifixerant) stabilitas homini plantas. Idem de omni opere divino quod Deus per ipsos passim fecit, semper testificati sunt Apostoli nihil sibi arrogantes, omnem virtutem atque honorem Euangelicae praedicationi deferentes. Quantū autem ab hac simplicitate absint ii qui se tamen istorum successores iactitant, satis omnibus notum est. nam quod illi dicunt, Non crederem Euangelio nisi ecclesia Euangelium recepisset: haec verba profectò abundè declarant eos sibi plus potentiae ascribere quàm verbo Dei. imò hac oratione profitentur se id abolere posse, non secus quàm si dicerent, Nos sumus Ecclesia, quod si nos Euangelium reiceremus, iam Euangelium esse definiret. Quod plane repugnat confessioni Apostolorum qui nihil à se, utpote miseris hominibus profectum aicebant, sed nomini Iesu & virtuti doctrinae sibi commissae omnem laude atque honorem rei gestae tribuebant. Ea quidē integritas fuit confessionis Apostolorum, qui merito primitiva Ecclesia censentur: quorum coetu, accepto iam Spiritu sancto, nullus unquã fuit sanctior nec Perfectior. Illi autem nihil noui aut de suo protulerunt, sed tantum Evangelij doctrinam populis proposuerunt. erant enim praecones Spiritus sancti, quo duce agebant omnia, quoque dirigente linguas ipsorum, loquebantur: quemadmodum Luc. in Actis ipsos dixisse refert, Visum est Spiritui sancto, ac nobis. Particula autem haec, Nobis, nequaquam arrogantiam ipsorum notat: sed contra egregia humilitate significat, quasi dicerent: Visum est Spiritui sancto, & nobis: qui nos totos voluntati eius accommodamus, eiusdemque instinctu loquimur. Nam si virtute propria locuti fuissent, non congrueret verbum illud Christi de ipsis pronuntiantis, Non estis vos qui loquimini, sed Spiritus Patris mei qui per vos loquitur. Recte ergo sequitur eos omnem auctoritatem verbo Dei quod ipsis per Christum traditum erat, attribuere. nec sane proiiciunt eiusmodi ampullas, Nisi nos qui ecclesia sumus, Evangelium recepissemus, Evangelium nullum esset. attamen sacer ille Apostolorum coetus omnium extitit perfectissimus, a quibus nihil unquam dictum aut scriptum est quam verbum vitae atque Evangelium salutis. Quod quidem vere dici non posset de iis qui tam prophanè de Evangelio garriunt, etiamsi multum absint ab auctoritate qua pollebant Apostoli. Si quid est in Ecclesia Iesu Christi potentiae, id verbo Dei acceptum referri debet, quae unica clavis claudit ac recludit regnum caeleste iis qui illud aut recipiunt aut repudiant. Nullum etiam Ecclesia telum habet quo se defendat quam idem verbum Dei: ideoque Paulus Corinthiis scribit, arma nostra non carnis sed spiritus esse: atque in epistola ad Ephesios, militiae Christianae gladio salutis accingi iubet, quod est verbum Dei. Cuius rei ratio redditur in epist. ad Heb. nēpe quod verbum istud sacrosanctum aciem habeat exactiore quātumuis[?] acuta bipenni. idē est culter quem Deus Hieremiae tradidit, ardēs velut igneus carbo: quemque Esa. in ore g.[?] sit utrinq; incidētem. Os nimirum illud & sapientia qua Christus Apostolus suos muniuit ad superandos omnes aduersarios, qui ipsis neutiquam potuerunt resistere, ut conflat exemplo Stephani ἀντιστῆναι[?] idemque ratum & firmum manebit in omnibus iis qui hac doctrina Evangelij instructi nomen Iesu Christi confiteri, causamque eius susceptam defendere volent. Verbum enim Dei sceptrum est quo Dominus Ecclesiam suam gubernat: pabulum quo oves suas pascit: idque nunc facit opera fidelium ministrorum qui tantum hanc sapientiam Dei praedicant. Quocirca Divus Paulus ad Ephesios secundo capite, dicit fundamentum Ecclesiae esse doctrinam Prophetarum & Apostolorum. Antichristi vero & administrorum eius ecclesia mendaciis scatet, calliditatum & fallaciarum omnis generis plena: quae cum destituta sit verbo Dei regimine, nihil sani habere potest. neque enim usquam salus restat quam in verbo Dei. Unde tanta in ecclesiis malignorum crudelitatis, superbiae atque inhumanitatis exempla, ut sunt in veteri testamento, Cain parricida: Iezabel prophetarum caede gaudens: sanguinis pii profusor Manasses: & superbus Israelis persecutor Pharao? In nouo testamento, Scribae & Pharisaei qui principem vitae interemerunt, eiusque discipulos qui salutem ipsis annunciabat, odio sunt prosecuti? unde inquam? nisi quod spreto verbo Dei & excusso pietatis iugo, mendacio potius se addixerunt & patri eius Sathanae turpiter servire maluerunt. quod ita esse sacra nos Biblia passim docet, ac praesertim caput illud Ieremiae xxiii. Quamobrem solo Dei verbo vivifico adhaereamus: qui praecepta eius observat, eum ipse pro fideli servo habebit. In hac ego doctrina permaneo & mori in eadem sententia non recuso, sciens quod Deus me non deseret. idque propter nomen suum, & honorem charitatemque Filii sui dilecti, quae nobis dedit Salvatorem ac redemptorem animarum nostrarum. cui gloria & honor in secula, Amen.
units.tr: That saying of Augustine, namely that he would not believe the Gospel unless the Church had received it as the Gospel, was put to him among other questions, so that his opponents might learn what he thought of it. He answered the matter in this way: the Gospel has such virtue and dignity that it can easily do without the help of all the creatures, both in heaven and on earth, and this is because of the wonderful power with which it is filled. For in it are laid up the treasures and riches of God, such as the promises of the forgiveness of sins and of eternal rest made to us through his mercy. But if we embrace this holy Gospel with a sincere faith as the Gospel of salvation, as it really is, we shall find no other gospel elsewhere that saves souls. This is the power of this Gospel, as Saint James, Saint Paul and Saint Peter bore witness, men who had no authority, virtue or dignity before they were called by Christ. For they were wretched fishermen, men of no standing, being unlearned and without letters. After it pleased God to call them to be his apostles, he raised them by the power of his Gospel to great dignity and power, appointing them as ambassadors and heralds to proclaim his name throughout the whole world, with this commission: "Go and preach the Gospel to every creature; he who believes and is baptized will be saved, and he who does not believe will be condemned." You see, therefore, to what height of dignity the apostles were raised through the Gospel. For in this the Lord once gave them the Holy Spirit under the visible appearance of divided tongues of fire, so that they might spread among all peoples what had been handed on to them, and call back men who had been scattered here and there into the blessed unity. Nor did Christ wish them to teach anything else throughout the world than the Gospel, which is the word of God his Father, saying: "As the Father has sent me, so I send you." In Isaiah there is a clear testimony concerning Christ as sent, where he is introduced speaking thus: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, and he has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor." In the same way we have the clear command of Christ concerning the apostles: "Go and proclaim the Gospel to every creature." And from the teaching of the Gospel it is established that the power to forgive sins belongs to God alone, who speaks of himself through his prophet Isaiah in this way: "I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and there is no other." Likewise Saint John does not record that the scribes and Pharisees ever came to such arrogance as to claim that they forgave sins; rather, they cried out indignantly: "Who forgives sins but God alone?" It is not therefore in man to remit the offences of another. For what Christ said to his disciples, "Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed, and whatever you bind shall remain bound," is to be ascribed to the power of the divine word committed to them, in which word salvation and life consist. Nor do we read that Peter or any of the disciples performed miracles or signs before they were called to the apostolic office, but only when the Lord gave them authority to preach the Gospel throughout the nations. And this they did publicly and openly, or (as it is in Matthew) "upon the housetops," not secretly or in the ear, as confession is whispered to priests. For the Gospel was given for the common salvation of all. Therefore we ought to profess it freely and openly, wherever in the world we live. The truth of the word of God is easily seen from the speech which Peter addressed to the lame man who had been lame from his mother's womb: "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk," and immediately it was done. Then Peter, seeing the people astonished, denied that the lame man walked by their own power or piety, but said that the man's feet were made strong by faith in the name of Jesus Christ, whom they had crucified. The apostles always bore witness to the same concerning every divine work that God did through them from time to time, claiming nothing for themselves, but ascribing all virtue and honour to the preaching of the Gospel. But how far from this simplicity are those who nevertheless boast that they are the successors of these men is well enough known to everyone. For when they say, "I would not believe the Gospel unless the Church had received the Gospel," these words clearly declare that they ascribe more power to themselves than to the word of God. Indeed, by this speech they profess that they are able to abolish it, no differently than if they said, "We are the Church; if we rejected the Gospel, it would then cease to be the Gospel." This plainly contradicts the confession of the apostles, who said that nothing came from themselves, since they were wretched men, but who ascribed all praise and honour for the deeds done to the name of Jesus and the power of the teaching committed to them. Such was the integrity of the apostles' confession, and rightly the primitive Church is regarded as theirs; among their company, once the Holy Spirit had been received, there was never anyone more holy or more perfect. They, however, brought forward nothing new or of their own, but only set before the peoples the teaching of the Gospel. For they were heralds of the Holy Spirit, by whose leading they did all things, and by whose directing they spoke with their tongues, just as Luke reports in the Acts that they said: "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us." Yet this particle "to us" by no means marks their arrogance; on the contrary, it signifies with remarkable humility, as if they said: "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us, who devote ourselves wholly to his will and speak at his prompting." For if they had spoken by their own power, that word of Christ, pronounced about them, would not fit: "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks through you." It follows rightly, therefore, that they ascribe all authority to the word of God, which was handed down to them through Christ. Nor indeed do they cast aside such empty boasts as, "Unless we who are the Church had received the Gospel, there would be no Gospel." Yet that holy company of the apostles was the most perfect of all, and from them nothing was ever said or written except the word of life and the Gospel of salvation. This could truly not be said of those who so profanely chatter about the Gospel, even though they are far from the authority which the apostles possessed. If there is any power in the Church of Jesus Christ, it must be referred to the word of God, which alone is the key that shuts and opens the kingdom of heaven to those who either receive or reject it. The Church also has no weapon with which to defend itself except this same word of God; therefore Paul writes to the Corinthians that our weapons are not of the flesh but of the Spirit, and in his letter to the Ephesians he bids us be girded with the sword of salvation for Christian warfare, which is the word of God. The reason for this is given in the Epistle to the Hebrews, namely that this holy word has an edge more exact than any two-edged sword, however sharp. It is the knife which God gave to Jeremiah, burning like a fiery coal, and which Isaiah describes as cutting on both sides from the mouth. That mouth, and the wisdom with which Christ the Apostle armed his people to overcome all adversaries, who could in no way resist them (as the example of Stephen shows, "they were not able to withstand [ἀντιστῆναι] the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke"), will remain equally sure and firm in all those who, instructed in this doctrine of the Gospel, wish to confess the name of Jesus Christ and defend the cause they have taken up. For the word of God is the sceptre by which the Lord governs his Church, the food with which he feeds his sheep; and he does this now through the work of the faithful ministers who preach only this wisdom of God. Therefore the divine Paul, in the second chapter of Ephesians, says that the foundation of the Church is the doctrine of the prophets and apostles. But the Church of the Antichrist and of his servants is full of lies, teeming with every kind of cunning and deceit; since it is deprived of the rule of the word of God, it can have nothing sound. For nowhere is salvation left except in the word of God. Hence the many examples of cruelty, pride and inhumanity among the wicked in the churches, such as are found in the Old Testament: Cain the murderer of his brother, Jezebel rejoicing in the slaughter of the prophets, Manasseh the shedder of pious blood, and Pharaoh the proud persecutor of Israel. In the New Testament, the scribes and Pharisees, who put to death the Prince of life and pursued with hatred his disciples who announced salvation to them: whence, I ask, does this come? Only because, having despised the word of God and thrown off the yoke of piety, they preferred to devote themselves to lying and shamefully to serve their father, Satan. That this is so the holy Bible teaches everywhere, and especially that chapter of Jeremiah, chapter 23. Therefore let us cling to the life-giving word of God alone; he who keeps its precepts, God himself will hold as a faithful servant. In this doctrine I remain, and I do not refuse to die in the same opinion, knowing that God will not forsake me, for the sake of his name, and out of the honour and love of his beloved Son, who has given us the Saviour and Redeemer of our souls. To him be glory and honour for ever, Amen.

units.la: Ad quaestionem de jejunio & certorum ciborum abstinentia sic dixit Neelus, Jejunium quidem bonum & sanctum esse, non illud quod certorum dierum spatio ab Antichristo circunscriptum esset, sed de quo Christi mandatum habemus, Cum jejunaveritis, &c. quod ad domandam carnis ferociam adhibetur, quo melius in servitutem redacta carne, spiritus Deo obediat. Neque vero consistit modo in cibi & potionis abstinentia, neque opsoniorum delectu: sed ut recte istud colatur, requiritur vitae integritas, sobrietas non unius tantum diei, sed perpetua castitas, dilectio & charitas erga proximum. de quo bene Isaias, Frange panem esurienti, atque eos qui teEscis[?] carent in domū tuā recipe: ac tum sanctè ieiunabis, ieiuniumq; tuū Deo gratū erit. Abstinentia in ieiunio nō improbamus, dummodo absit superstitio & abusus, quibus vitiis laborant ij, qui dum se ad ieiunia parant, cibis delicatioribus se ingurgitant, vina quaerunt meliora, quae nō abstinetia sed vitae ratio Epicuri de grege porcis, (ut ait ille) digna est: quíq;[?] inter cibos multum discriminis ponunt, quasi plus sanctitatis huic cibo quàm alteri insit. Nec enim, ut inquit Paulus ad Romanos, Regnū cælorum in esca aut potu sitū est. vesci licet cum gratiarum actione omnibus quae Deus ad nutriendū nos largitur. præsertim cum in Euangelio dicatur, Quod per os intrat, nō inquinare animam. Omni itaque errore remoto, viva atque efficaa[?] fide credere oportet, victu ad sustentandū corpus necessariū à Deo nobis datum, ab eodem quoque benedictum esse, nec vetitum esse quenquam cibum Christianis. Interea tamen, monente Paulo, cauendum est, ne is qui edit, præ se[?] contemnat eum qui non edit, aut contrà. nam firmum imbecilli rationem habere necesse est ne ullam illi in victus usu offensionem afferat: sciens quòd multò fuisset satius nunquã carnem gustasse quàm eum perdere pro quo Iesus est mortuus. Vitæ itaque suæ quisque eum habere modum debet, ut omnia ad ædificationem proximi spectent: id quod tum demum efficiemus, si regula in veteri ac novo Testamento nobis à Deo & Salvatore nostro præscriptam summo studio sequamur, quoniam fundamentum Ecclesiæ non est aliud quàm doctrina Prophetarum & Apostolorum. De Papa ipsiúsque authoritate rogatus, respondit solum Deum esse magistrum ac præceptorem, qui nec ignorare quicquam, nec in ullo falli posset. proinde nulli aut ignorantiæ aut errori obnoxiū. Opera, inquit, eius à nemine reprehendi possunt, dum fecit cælum & terram, & quæ in eis sunt: ac postremò hominem formauit ad imaginē suā ut præesset cæteris creaturis. cui etiam in paradiso iam lex à Domino data est, quum præciperet ei, ut omne fructum paradisi libere comederet, fructum vero vitæ minimè: nā quocunque die comederet morte mulctatum iri. Hac lege primùm Dominus hominem in obedientia maiestatis suæ continere voluit. at homo sua conditione non contentus, Deo similis esse voluit, actus spiritu ambitionis quô illum impulerat ingluuies. Ex hoc solo Adæ peccaco tanta in totum genus humanum ingruit calamitas & maledictio, vt Iesum Christum, qui est Filius dilectus Dei Patris carnem nostram assumere atque reatum pro nobis subire necesse fuerit. nam alioqui omnes nos exitio deuoti eramus. Atque ea quidem ille nostra causa volens ac libens præstitit: adeò vt maledictio illa crucis quam tulit, nobis in benedictionem cedat sempiternam apud Deum: & cuius antea eramus hostes nunc ab eo in gratiam recepti sumus, quoniam Filius eius dilectus mortuus & resuscitatus est pro nobis, quos prosponsa & grege suo habet. Attamen priusquam cælos conscenderet, nobis verbum suum reliquit, Euangelium scilicet. & post mortem Apostolorum constituit episcopos, pastores, doctores qui nos in doctrina Prophetarum & Apostolorum eruditerent, & vitæ integritate viam rectam præmonstrarent. Nec verò me quis hic loqui putet de cornutis aut personatis illis belluis: equidem episcopos intelligo ijs virtutibus ornatos quas in ipsis requirit Paulus 1. Timoth. 11. Non nego tamè quòd Christus de Scribis & Pharisæis loquens iubeat fieri quæ illi dixerint, sed ea conditione vt sedeant super cathedram Mosis. Cathedra autem Mosis est Lex: quam remotis alijs doctrinis tantùm concionari debebant. nam in hoc omnis populus conueniebat vt ex lectione Legis sciret quid sibi faciendum esset: quod humanæ præceptiones docere non possunt, quia in ijs Deus voluntatem suam non declarauit. Atque ideo sancti Prophetæ vt se vere Dei seruos esse, nec quicquâ ex suo ingenio exhibere populo profiterentur, eiusmodi fere vsi sunt loquendi formulis aut dasulis, Audite verbũ Domini: Hæc est vox Domini: Loquutus est Dominus: Sic dicit Dominus. Quos in hoc imitati sunt Apostoli, nec ipsi vnquam aliquid de suo prædicantes, sed doctrinam tantùm Spiritus sancti proferentes: quod de ipsis testatur Iesu Christi elogium, Non vos ipsi loquimini, sed per vos Spiritus Dei Patris mei. Vnde sequitur, successores Apostolorum, nisi doctrinæ eorũ quoque acquiescat, aut si præter Euangelij ac verbũ Dei, aliud quippiâ pronũciare audent, maledictos esse. Ac quisquis ille fuerit qui hoc pacto Christi & Apostolorum vestigiis non insiStet[?], pseudopropheta & Antichristus iure vocabitur: etiamsi fuerit ipse Papa, non tamen Prophetis aut Apostolis maior aut sanctior censeri debet. Sed quicunque pios istos viros imitatur tam in doctrinae synceritate quam vitae sanctimonia, is demum verus Ecclesiae pastor erit: alioqui dissipator potius & velut lupus inter oves.
units.tr: In answer to the question about fasting and abstaining from certain foods, Neelus spoke thus: fasting is indeed good and holy, not the fasting that Antichrist has bound to set spans of days, but the fasting of which we have Christ's command, "When you fast," and so on. It is used to tame the fierceness of the flesh, so that, with the flesh the better brought into subjection, the spirit may obey God. Nor does it consist merely in abstaining from food and drink, or in choosing delicacies. To practise it rightly requires integrity of life: sobriety not for one day only but perpetual chastity, and love and charity towards one's neighbour. Isaiah speaks well of this: "Break your bread to the hungry, and bring into your house those who lack..., then you shall fast well, and your fasting will be pleasing to God." We do not disapprove of abstinence in fasting, provided that superstition and abuse are absent. Those who are afflicted with these vices, while they prepare themselves for fasts, stuff themselves with richer foods and seek out better wines. That is fitting not for abstinence but for the way of life of Epicurus' herd of swine, as he puts it. They also make much distinction among foods, as if one food had more holiness in it than another. For, as Paul says to the Romans, the kingdom of heaven does not consist in food or drink. It is lawful to eat, with thanksgiving, all the things that God gives us in abundance for our nourishment, especially since the Gospel says that what enters through the mouth does not defile the soul. Therefore, with all error set aside, we must believe with a living and effective faith that the food necessary for sustaining the body is given to us by God, and is blessed by him, and that no food is forbidden to Christians. Meanwhile, however, as Paul warns, care must be taken that he who eats does not despise him who does not eat, or the reverse. For the strong must take account of the weak, so that they cause him no offence in the use of food, knowing that it would have been far better never to have tasted meat than to destroy the one for whom Jesus died. Each person should therefore keep a measure in his life, so that all things look to the edification of his neighbour. We shall achieve this only if we follow with the utmost zeal the rule prescribed to us by God and our Saviour in the Old and New Testaments, since the foundation of the Church is nothing other than the doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles. Asked about the Pope and his authority, he replied that God alone is the master and teacher, who can neither be ignorant of anything nor be deceived in anything, and so is subject to neither ignorance nor error. His works, he said, can be blamed by no one: he made heaven and earth and all that is in them, and finally formed man in his own image, to rule over the other creatures. Even in paradise a law was given to man by the Lord, when he commanded him to eat freely of every fruit of paradise, but not at all of the fruit of life, for on whatever day he ate of it he would be punished with death. By this law the Lord first wished to hold man in obedience to his majesty. But man, not content with his condition, wished to be like God, driven by the spirit of ambition to which gluttony had impelled him. From this sin of Adam alone such great calamity and curse fell upon the whole human race that it was necessary for Jesus Christ, the beloved Son of God the Father, to assume our flesh and bear our guilt on our behalf; otherwise we were all doomed to destruction. He did this willingly and gladly for our sake, so that the curse of the cross which he bore turns to our everlasting blessing with God. Those who were once his enemies are now received by him into favour, because his beloved Son died and rose again for us, whom he holds as his bride and flock. Yet before he ascended to heaven, he left us his word, namely the Gospel. After the death of the Apostles he appointed bishops, pastors and teachers, who would instruct us in the doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles and show us the right way by the integrity of their lives. Nor let anyone think that I am speaking here of those horned or masked beasts. I mean by bishops men adorned with the virtues that Paul requires of them in 1 Timothy 3. I do not deny, however, that when Christ speaks of the Scribes and Pharisees he bids that what they say be done, but on this condition, that they sit on the chair of Moses. The chair of Moses is the Law, and they ought to preach only that, with other doctrines set aside. For in this the whole people gathered, so that from the reading of the Law they might know what they must do, which human precepts cannot teach, because in them God has not declared his will. And so the holy Prophets, to profess that they were truly servants of God and brought nothing of their own invention to the people, almost always used formulas of speech such as: "Hear the word of the Lord," "This is the voice of the Lord," "The Lord has spoken," "Thus says the Lord." The Apostles imitated them in this, never preaching anything of their own but only setting forth the doctrine of the Holy Spirit. The saying of Jesus Christ bears witness to this of them: "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who speaks through you." Whence it follows that the successors of the Apostles, unless they too acquiesce in that doctrine, or if they dare to pronounce anything beyond the Gospel and the Word of God, are accursed. Whoever he may be who does not hold to the footsteps of Christ and the Apostles in this way will rightly be called a pseudo-prophet and Antichrist, even if he should be the Pope himself. Yet he ought not to be counted greater or holier than the Prophets or Apostles. But whoever imitates those pious men, both in the purity of his doctrine and in the holiness of his life, will be the true pastor of the Church. Otherwise he is rather a destroyer, a wolf among sheep.

units.la: Haud quidem inficior quin sit penes Christi ministros qui pure verbum Dei annuntiant, populo imponere ieiunia, iniũgere preces & eleemosynas ad obuiandum irae Diuinae quae terris imminet tempore belli, pestis, famis atq; aliarum plagarum Dei. Caeterum leges sancire perpetuas iis nusquam concessum legimus, idque nō fieret sine superstitione & abusu atq; adeo idololatria nō careret. De traditionibus vero humanis sic locutus est, Angeli, inquit, ipsi qui Dei throno astant ut ad nutum illi seruiant, quiq; virtus Dei in Scriptura vocatur, creaturae eius omnium excellentissimae, in hoc toti ut voluntati Dei obsequatur, missi ad praesidium eorum quos Deus ad hereditatem beatae immortalitatis praedestinauit, ut est in epist. ad Hebr. nunquam de suo quicquam hominibus proposuerunt: Prophetae deinde excellentia post illos secundi, os Domini appellati, nihil unquam ex se comenti sunt. Christus etiam ipse qui hos secutus est, hoc pacto loquitur: Doctrina mea non est mea, sed eius qui misit me Patris. atq; id variis locis iterauit ipse qui exemplum sanctitatis erat, Filius nempe Dei viuentis. Apostoli quoq; nihil praeter doctrinam Euangelij sibi commissam praedicarunt: cuius ea est potentia & virtus ut salute afferat omni credenti. At Papa cum suis Praelatis voluit sibi plus dignitatis vel authoritatis attribuere, qui maximis Dei contumeliis afficiunt, quo suas traditiones tueantur: adeo ut non modo nulla poena in Papatu afficiatur qui stuprum aut adulterium commiserit, sed etiam ab omnibus laudetur: verum si quis forte buccellam porcinae carnis comederit die Veneris, aut crassos abusus eorum reprehenderit, continuo ad supplicium petrahetur miser. Sed Dominus patiens ac lenis, qui nunc tacere videtur, aliquando eos coram arguet. Nec tunc quidem erit locus excusandi sese quod Patres suos secuti fuerint: maximam & praestantissimam mundi partem semper pro se habuerint: se nunquam induci potuisse ut crederent Deum velle tanta hominum multitudinē in errorē versari. hoc autem praetextu deficere a verbo Dei valde periculosum est. nam si in maiori numero populi cōsisteret falsus, Scriptura mendax esset, quae semper paucis hominibus aut vni aliquando familiae, populi Dei verum attribuit titulum: considera quaeso, fericm omnium exemplorum veteris ac noui Testamenti, & reperies profecto a paucis usque abiectis hominibus culta suisse pietatem: confer Abrahamum & Lotum cum Gomorrhaeis ac Sodomitis: Aegyptiorum copias cum populo Israelis: Prophetas cum cultoribus Baal tempore Iesabelis: constabit pios semper fuisse exiguo numero si cum aduersariis ipsorum comparentur. Veniamus ad initia & progressus Ecclesiae sub nouo Testamento, quid Christus & Apostoli eius cum Scribis & Pharisaeis, atque infinitis aduersariis gentibus collati, erunt? Denique Filius Dei viuentis hanc perpetuam Ecclesiae suae consolationem esse voluit: quod multi sint vocati, pauci electi, quos hac sententia insuper hortatus est ne ob exiguum numerum animis caderent. Ne metuas pusille grex, quoniam Patri meo placuit te donare haereditate regni coelestis. ac contra XI. Matth. Deo Patri suo gratias agit, quod salutis documenta sapientibus & magnis huius saeculi non aperuerit, sed humilibꝰ ac parvulis. praeterea, quid aliud significat eiusdem concio de seminate ubi quarta demum seminis pars in bonam terram cadit quae ad frugem perueniat, nisi paucissimos salvos fore? Quapropter ne temere multitudini fidamus: quin potius ad exiguum gregem Christi nos recipiamus, quem is morte sua reatu liberauit.
units.tr: I do not indeed deny that it belongs to the ministers of Christ who purely proclaim the Word of God to impose fasts on the people, and to enjoin prayers and alms to avert the anger of God which hangs over the lands in time of war, plague, famine and other scourges of God. But we nowhere read that perpetual laws were granted to them, and this could not be done without superstition and abuse, and would not be free from idolatry. Concerning human traditions he spoke thus: "The angels themselves, who stand around God's throne to serve at his nod, and whom Scripture calls the power of God, his most excellent creatures, sent wholly to obey the will of God for the protection of those whom God has predestined to the inheritance of blessed immortality, as is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews, never put forward anything of their own to men. The Prophets, next in excellence after them, called the mouth of the Lord, never invented anything from themselves. Christ too, who followed them, speaks in this way: 'My doctrine is not mine, but that of the Father who sent me,' and he who was the example of holiness, the Son of the living God, repeated this in various places. The Apostles also preached nothing beyond the doctrine of the Gospel committed to them, whose power and virtue is such that it brings salvation to every believer. But the Pope with his Prelates has wished to attribute more dignity and authority to himself, and they inflict the greatest insults on God in order to defend their traditions. So much so that in Popery not only is no punishment inflicted on the man who has committed fornication or adultery, but he is even praised by all; yet if anyone perhaps eats a morsel of pork on a Friday, or rebukes their gross abuses, the wretch is at once dragged off to punishment. But the Lord, patient and gentle, who now seems to be silent, will someday convict them before everyone. Nor will there then be any place for excusing themselves on the ground that they followed their Fathers, that they always held the greatest and most excellent part of the world on their side, and that they could never be brought to believe that God wishes so great a number of men to wander in error. But to desert the Word of God under this pretext is very dangerous. For if the true religion consisted in the greater number of people, Scripture would be a liar, for it always assigns the title of the true people of God to a few men, or sometimes to a single family. Consider, I beg you, the whole range of examples in the Old and New Testaments, and you will surely find that piety was cultivated by a few, often by abject men. Compare Abraham and Lot with the Gomorrhites and Sodomites; the forces of the Egyptians with the people of Israel; the Prophets with the worshippers of Baal in the time of Jezebel. It will be clear that the godly have always been few in number when compared with their adversaries. Let us come to the beginnings and progress of the Church under the New Testament: what will Christ and his Apostles be, when set against the Scribes and Pharisees and the countless adversaries among the nations? Finally, the Son of the living God wished this to be the perpetual consolation of his Church: that many are called, but few chosen. With this saying he further exhorted them not to lose heart because of their small number: "Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased my Father to give you the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom." And in Matthew 11 he gives thanks to God the Father that he has not revealed the teachings of salvation to the wise and great of this age, but to the humble and little ones. Moreover, what else does his parable of the sower mean, in which only a fourth part of the seed at last falls on good ground and comes to fruit, except that very few will be saved? Therefore let us not rashly put our trust in the multitude; rather let us withdraw to the little flock of Christ, whom he has freed from guilt by his death.

units.la: De templis quid sentiret rogatus, dixit Deum esse spiritum qui corpus ex carne & ossibus coagmentatum non habeat. proinde spirituali ratione colendum, teste Propheta Esaia, vbi sic vltimo capite Deus ipse loquitur: Quam domum aedificabitis mihi? nonne caelum sedes mea, & terra scabellum pedum meorum? Nullum sane Deo commodum parari poterit aedificium, nisi ipsemet sibi struat: idque efficit quando cor hominis virtute Spiritus sui purum ac mundum reddit, vt illud subeat atque in eo habitet: ac propterea Diuus Paulus fideles templa Dei viuentis vocat, Si, inquit, aliquis templum Dei sanctum, quod vos estis, vastarit, Deus perdet eum. nam in eo uoluptatem capit, dicens, uersabor inter eos, & ero Deus eorum & ipsi erunt populus meus. Itaq; ne quis pro modulo ingenij sui maiestatem diuinam metiatur, sed rogemus Dominum ut corda nostra purget, in usque habitet, quod quidē pro suo arbitratu facit is qui inestimabili potentia cælum ac terram replet. Templorum uero materialium usus erit legitimus, si in eo habeatur pij cœtus ad uerbi Dei auditionem, sacramentorum Baptismi & sacræ Cœnæ perceptionem: ut dum ita concorditer in unum locum conuenimus per prædicationem Evangelij, quæ eius est uis, in mutua dilectione confirmetur fidelium animi.
units.tr: Asked what he thought of temples, he said that God is a spirit, who has no body knit together from flesh and bones. Therefore he must be worshipped in a spiritual manner, as the prophet Isaiah testifies, where God himself speaks in the last chapter: "What house will you build for me? Is not heaven my seat, and the earth the footstool of my feet?" Indeed, no building can be prepared that is pleasing to God, unless he builds it himself, and he does so when by the power of his Spirit he makes the heart of man pure and clean, so that he may enter it and dwell in it. For this reason the divine Paul also calls the faithful "the temples of the living God." "If anyone," he says, "destroys the holy temple of God, which you are, God will destroy him." For he takes pleasure in it, saying, "I will walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." Therefore let no one measure the divine majesty by the measure of his own wit, but let us pray the Lord to cleanse our hearts and to dwell in them, which he who fills heaven and earth with his inestimable power does as he pleases. The use of material temples will be lawful if in them the godly assemble to hear the Word of God and to receive the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper, so that, as we come together in one place in harmony through the preaching of the Gospel, which is its power, the hearts of the faithful may be strengthened in mutual love.

units.la: Confessionem illam auricularem prorsus reiecit: reconciliationem autem fraternam de qua Divus Jacobus loquitur, omnino dixit inter Christianos necessariam. nam nisi peccata (inquit) alij aliis ignoscamus, non exaudiet nos Dominus, quemadmodum testatur quotidiana nostra oratio Dominica. atqui exemplo Dauidis soli Deo delicta cōfiteamur implorantes syncero corde eius misericordiam omnibus diebus vitæ nostræ, ut in æternum cum eo viuamus, Amen. Ad percontationem de Missa in hunc modum respondit: Habemus in Scriptura omnia quæ ad salutem obtinendam obseruatu sunt necessaria. Vetus testamentum plenam nobis Dei voluntatem duobus his præceptis comprehendit, primò ut Deum amemus ex toto corde, anima, totisque viribus. deinde, proximum ut nosmetipsos: omnem insuper detestans idolomaniam. Christus in nouo Testamento suis mandat ut sese mutuò ament, diligant inimicos, precentur pro persecutoribus suis & iis benefaciant, esurientibus cibum, sitientibus potum præbeant. præterea iubet nos simplices esse velut columbas, prudentes ut serpentes: monet ut mansuetudinem atque humilitatem suam imitentur: discamus esse misericordes exemplo Patris cœlestis: thesauros in cœlis colligamus, pauperes scilicet & re & consolatione omnis generis juvando, loculos nobis comparemus qui vetustate non corrumpantur: multaque eiusmodi & varia in Evangelio nobis à Filio Dei mandata proponuntur. Sed nusquam in sacris literis vel minima fit mentio Missæ. Proinde & ego illam repudiandam atque abiiciendam censeo, contentus monitionibus alis & præceptis ad vitam æternam comparandam necessariis. Atque interea Deum orabo ut Legem suam mentibus nostris insculpat, ne forte aliquid faciamus quod ei displicere queat. Hoc pacto in gratia Dei vivemus, quae anteponenda est tali mysterio abominationis, cuius Sathan inventor ac fabricator extitit, eamque tradidit filio perditionis ad communem generis humani perniciem.
units.tr: He utterly rejected auricular confession; but he said that the fraternal reconciliation of which the divine James speaks is altogether necessary among Christians. For, he said, unless we forgive one another's sins, the Lord will not hear us, as our daily Lord's Prayer attests. Yet, following the example of David, let us confess our sins to God alone, imploring his mercy with a sincere heart all the days of our life, so that we may live with him for ever. Amen. To the question about the Mass he answered in this manner: "We have in Scripture everything that is necessary to be observed for obtaining salvation. The Old Testament comprehends the full will of God for us in these two precepts: first, that we love God with our whole heart, soul and all our strength; then, that we love our neighbour as ourselves; and besides, that we utterly detest all idolatry. In the New Testament Christ commands his followers to love one another, to love their enemies, to pray for their persecutors and to do good to them, to give food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty. Moreover he bids us be simple as doves and wise as serpents; he urges us to imitate his meekness and humility; we are to learn to be merciful after the example of our heavenly Father; we are to gather treasures in heaven, that is, to help the poor with money and every kind of comfort, and to provide for ourselves purses that do not wear out with age; and many such and various things are set before us in the Gospel as commanded by the Son of God. But nowhere in the sacred writings is there the least mention of the Mass. Therefore I too judge that it should be rejected and cast away, being content with the other admonitions and precepts necessary for obtaining eternal life. Meanwhile I will pray God to engrave his Law upon our minds, lest by chance we do anything that might displease him. In this way we shall live in the grace of God, which is to be preferred to such a mystery of abomination, whose inventor and fabricator was Satan, and which he handed over to the son of perdition for the common ruin of the human race."

units.la: Sententiam suam de votis sic explicuit: Ingenium hominis pronum inclinatumque ad idololatriam magis esse quam ad veram pietatem. propterea quicquid inde proficiscitur, vanum & impium esse: neque vero nobis licere quicquam Deo promittere aut offerre, nisi id quod ipse in verbo suo approbavit. Votum, inquit, quod omnes recte nuncupare possimus, esset orare Deum ut nos in obedientia voluntatis suae retineat, renuntiantes nostrae quae ad malum semper est proclivior. Idque Divus Paulus multis locis declarat, dicens quod nos, optanus ac volumus bonum, praestare haudquaquam posse. Optima autem ratio & modus abnegandi nostri, ac deprimendae voluntatis propriae, foret sincero corde, ut edocti sumus a Christo Domino nostro, dicere Deo, Fiat voluntas tua: & cum vera animi testificatione nos ei soli velle obsequi. nam quicunque suam mentem sequi volet, ridebit Deum quotiescunque hunc articulum recitabit. Nos igitur nostráque Deo commitamus. ab eo enim procedit omne bonum, is efficit ut & velimus & efficiamus pro bona voluntate. Pareamus ei praecepto quod apud Mosen Deuteronomij quinto capite scriptum est: Custodite & facite quae praecepit Dominus Deus vobis: nō declinabitis neque ad dexteram neq; ad sinistram. sed per viam &c.
units.tr: He set forth his opinion on vows in this way: "The nature of man is more prone and inclined to idolatry than to true piety. Therefore whatever proceeds from that is vain and impious; nor are we permitted to promise or offer anything to God, unless it is what he himself has approved in his Word. The vow, he said, which we could all rightly make, would be to pray God that he would keep us in obedience to his will, renouncing our own will, which is always more inclined to evil. And the divine Paul declares this in many places, saying that we, though we desire and wish for the good, are by no means able to perform it. But the best reason and method of denying ourselves and of subduing our own will is, as we have been taught by Christ our Lord, to say to God with a sincere heart, 'Thy will be done,' and with a true witness of the soul to wish to obey him alone. For whoever wishes to follow his own mind will mock God every time he recites this article. Therefore let us commit ourselves and ours to God; for every good thing comes from him, and he brings it about that we both will and do what is good. Let us obey the precept written by Moses in the fifth chapter of Deuteronomy: 'Keep and do what the Lord your God has commanded you; you shall not turn aside either to the right hand or to the left, but walk in the way,' etc."

units.la: Ad interrogationē de Peregrinationibus papisticis, dixit peregrinationem Christiano salutare esse, vitae in hoc mundo sanctimonia, patientiam, dilectione, castitatem & charitate. quia dū in hac terra peregrini-fumus nemo exploratum habet quo die, quaue hora Dominus venturus sit. Quod si temere huc illuc concursando in orbe cuius ipse possessor est, tepus inutiliter consumpserimus, opus Domini negligentes: rationem profecto eius ocij exiget, nō secus quam princeps aliquis aut Rex in scurram vagum ac perditum hominem per agros suos palantem animaduerteret. Quare recta ad Deum accedamus, ut ab eo solo per fidem in Iesum Christum remissionem peccatorum & viam æternam obtineamus: orantes eum ut in extremo die nos in remum suum recipiat. Interrogatus quænam ipsius esset de sacerdotio sententia, confessus est simpliciter omnes Christianos esse sacerdotes. Idque probavit hoc Pauli ad Romanos testimonio, Quòd Deus nobis dat Filium suum, omnia simul cum eo bona dedit. Unde, inquit, liquet si hunc habeamus pro nobis, nihil deesse. neque enim Filius est unquam absque Patre & Spiritu sancto, quandoquidem hæ tres personæ unum tantummodo constituunt Deum, unam voluntatem, unam essentiam, unam potentiam, unam quietem ac vitam æternam. Ipse cum sit Deus, Rex & sacerdos, nos secum deos fecit & reges constituit ad fruitionem regni cælestis in perpetuum. assumpsit etiam nos in sacerdotes ut grata faciamus sacrificia, offerendo corpora nostra, animas, & corda summissa & abiecta Deo Patri: quemadmodum epist.ad Rom. & Hebr. & Psalmi, istius modi sacrificij meminerunt. Non loquor equidem de sacerdotio Romano, nec confundo hic administrationem Verbi & Sacramentorum, ut dicam id omnibus commune officium, quod Pastoribus tantum Ecclesiæ commissum est: sed de interiori quodam effectu & dignitate spirituali veri sacerdotij ago, quod adepti sumus omnes per Christum, ut mactemus Deo Patri gratas victimas: nosipsos scilicet, vitulos labiorum & cor contritum. Atque hæc dignitas animos nobis addere debet, ut cum fiducia impetrandæ veniæ peccatorum ad Deum accedamus: certò etiam persuasi quòd vitæ æternæ hæreditate donabimur per Christum Salvatorem nostrum, qui nos omnium bonorum cælestium participes fecit, ut cum ipso in æternum viuamus: cui honor & gloria sit in sæcula.
units.tr: Asked about papistical pilgrimages, he said that pilgrimage is salutary for a Christian, consisting in holiness of life in this world, patience, love, chastity and charity. For while we are pilgrims on this earth, no one knows the day or the hour when the Lord will come. If we were to waste our time in vain by running hither and thither around the world, of which he himself is the possessor, neglecting the work of the Lord, he would certainly call us to account for that idleness, just as a prince or king would take note of some wandering and lost fellow straying through his fields as a jester. Therefore let us come straight to God, so that we may obtain from him alone, through faith in Jesus Christ, forgiveness of sins and the way to eternal life, praying him that on the last day he will receive us into his kingdom. Being asked what his opinion was of the priesthood, he simply confessed that all Christians are priests. He proved this by the testimony of Paul to the Romans: "Because God has given us his Son, he has given us all good things together with him. From this, he says, it is clear that if we have him on our side, nothing will be lacking to us." For the Son is never without the Father and the Holy Spirit, since these three persons constitute only one God, one will, one essence, one power, one rest and eternal life. Since he himself is God, King and priest, he has made us gods with him and constituted us kings, for the enjoyment of the heavenly kingdom for ever. He has also taken us up as priests, so that we may offer acceptable sacrifices, presenting our bodies, souls and humble and abject hearts to God the Father, as the Epistles to the Romans and the Hebrews and the Psalms speak of this kind of sacrifice. I do not speak indeed of the Roman priesthood, nor do I here confuse the administration of the Word and the Sacraments, which is a common office, and which has been committed to the ministers of the Church alone; but I am speaking of a certain inward effect and spiritual dignity of the true priesthood, which we all have obtained through Christ, so that we may offer to God the Father acceptable victims: namely, ourselves, the calves of our lips and a contrite heart. And this dignity ought to add courage to our minds, so that we may approach God with confidence of obtaining pardon for sins, being also firmly persuaded that we shall be given the inheritance of eternal life through Christ our Saviour, who has made us partakers of all heavenly blessings, so that we may live with him for ever, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever.

units.la: Postquam hanc fidei suæ confessionem manu sua subsignatam exhibuisset, administri Episcopi Aurincensis toti in hoc erat ut hos articulos & responsiones hæreseos (ut loquuntur) condenarent. Neelus quòd in carcere Episcopi asperius tractaretur, postulauit à Suppræfecto causarum capitalium (qui sæpius ipsum invisebat consolandi gratia cum quodam aduocato, vir sanè timens Deum) ut ipsum ad custodiam Curiæ secularis, ut vocant traducendum curaret. Quo audito administri Episcopales mortis & exaugurationis sententia contra Neelum perferretur. At Neelus suasu amicorum, sententiam eorum ut abfuam[?] reiecit, atque ad superiorem iudicem appellauit. Rationes autem appellationis ut ipse scriptas reliquit, erant eiusmodi, quod vocatus in cubiculum Episcopi Aurincensis die Mercurij feriarum Paschæ M.D.LIII. dixit aperte Decani inquisitionem nihil omnino valere: testimonia aduersariorum non esse legitima. Illinc deductus in prætorium Curiæ ecclesiasticæ, ut vocant, Episcopus iussit Neelum in genua procidere, ubi tum reus dixit confessionem suam quam obtulerat parui non esse ponderis: vitam hominis multo pluris faciendam quam pulli gallinacei. attamen Episcopus nullam dictorum ipsius rationem habens, sed valde irascens illi, Quoniam, inquit, in tua opinione obstinatus atque obfirmatus permanes sententiam adversus te pronuntiabo. Sed antequam verbum ullum protulisset Episcopus, ipse reus dixit se non admittere ipsum iudicem propter certas & idoneas recusationis causas, quod si nihilominus procederet, fore ipsius sententiam nullam & irritam, quia iniqua & abusiva esset: proinde se appellare ad maiorem iudicem. Officialis autem his dictis nihil commotus perrexit sententiam pronunciare. Tum Neelus ad Episcopum, Memineris, inquit, quod te ut iudicem non idoneum iustis de caussis repudiauerim, tu vero non auscultaueris: proinde ego appellaui, atq; etiamnum appello iudicem æquiorem. Atque adeo has recusationum causas (inquit) pono. Primam, quod Episcopus me afferentem causas idoneas reiiciendi ipsum iudicem antequam tulisset sententiam, audire noluit. Alteram, quod appellatio mea ob iniquitatem & abusum, nihil apud eum valuit, quo minus ulterius ad condemnationem mei procederet. Tertiam, quod in lite quam mihi intentauit ipsius Decanus, delatio nominis mei habetur, ac si dixissem Episcopum Aurincensem hominem esse sceleratum: siquidem asinos in sacerdotium assumeret. quare equidem bono iure ipsius iudicium accipere nolui, metuens ne invidia ac privatæ vindictæ cupiditate ductus ultricem ferret de me sententiam: quod factum ab eo constat ex sententia exaugurationis, qua me de gradu sacerdotali demouendum censuit. Quartam, quod Decanus ille (ut liquet ex scriptis nostræ litis) suggessit hæc verba cuidam e testibus, Fer mihi opem ut facinorosum hunc hominem e medio tollamus, cultum mehercule Deo præstiteris. atque idem Decanus anus omnibus me spoliarat rebus & pecuniis. Quintam, quòd me vt Sacramentarium Episcopus cum suis iudicarit, quum ipsi contrà errét toto cœlo, & sacramentum negent, terrenis his elementis plus æquo tribuentes, & ad pastum huius corporis, velut brutæ pecudes, tantumodò abiecti: quemadmodum supra plenius dictum est in confessione nostra. His sic coram Episcopo pro tribunali recitatis rationibus, convertit se Neelus ad causæ suæ patronum, eúmque his verbis compellavit, domine, rogo te propter nomen Iesu Christi vt meâ causam tueris[?] aut potius ipsius Episcopi. Equidem mihi probè conscius sum nihil dixisse me quod ad Dei gloriam & proximi ædificationem non pertineret: nemini convicium feci, sed hæc verba semper in ore habui, Nullius ego sum iudex, nec fidem alterius confiteor. Sed loquor velut is qui in lecto æger est morti vicinus, conscientiam meam ipse examinans, & fidei quam habeo dans testimonium.
units.tr: After he had handed over this confession of his faith, signed with his own hand, the officials of the Bishop of Aurincum were wholly intent on condemning these articles and answers as heresy, as they put it. Because Neelus was treated more harshly in the Bishop's prison, he asked the sub-prefect of capital causes (who often visited him to comfort him, together with a certain advocate, a man truly fearing God) to arrange for him to be transferred to the custody of the secular court, as they call it. When the episcopal officials heard this, a sentence of death and degradation was brought against Neelus. But Neelus, on the advice of his friends, rejected their sentence as void, and appealed to a higher judge. The grounds of his appeal, as he himself left them written down, were of this kind: that, when he was summoned to the chamber of the Bishop of Aurincum on the Wednesday of Easter week, in the year 1553, he plainly said that the Dean's inquiry was worth nothing at all, and that the testimonies of his adversaries were not lawful. Led from there to the hall of the ecclesiastical court, as they call it, the Bishop ordered Neelus to kneel down; whereupon the accused said that the confession he had offered was of little weight, and that a man's life should be valued far more highly than a cockerel's. Yet the Bishop, taking no account of what he said, and being very angry with him, said: "Since you persist obstinate and hardened in your opinion, I will pronounce sentence against you." But before the Bishop had uttered any word, the accused himself said that he did not accept the judge himself, on account of certain sound and proper grounds of challenge; and that if he nevertheless proceeded, his sentence would be null and void, because it would be unjust and abusive; therefore he appealed to a greater judge. The official, however, unmoved by these words, went on to pronounce sentence. Then Neelus said to the Bishop: "Remember that I rejected you as an unsuitable judge for just causes, but you did not listen; therefore I have appealed, and I still appeal, to a fairer judge." And so, he said, I set forth these grounds of challenge. The first: that the Bishop, when I alleged proper causes for rejecting him as judge, refused to hear them before he had pronounced sentence. The second: that my appeal, because of its injustice and abuse, had no effect with him, so that he proceeded further to my condemnation. The third: that in the suit which his Dean brought against me, the naming of my name is held as though I had said the Bishop of Aurincum was a wicked man, since he takes asses into the priesthood. Wherefore I rightly refused to accept his judgment, fearing lest, led by hatred and a desire for private revenge, he would pass a vindictive sentence against me; which is shown to have been done by him from the sentence of degradation, by which he decided that I should be removed from my priestly rank. The fourth: that this Dean (as appears from the written records of our suit) said these words to one of the witnesses: "Help me to remove this criminal man from the midst, and by heaven you will have rendered worship to God." And the same Dean had stripped me of all my goods and money. The fifth: that the Bishop, with his men, judged me a Sacramentarian, when they themselves are wholly in error, and deny the sacrament, attributing to these earthly elements more than is right, and being cast down like brute beasts only to the feeding of this body; as was said more fully above in our confession. When these grounds had thus been recited before the Bishop seated on the tribunal, Neelus turned to the advocate of his cause and addressed him in these words: "Sir, I beg you, for the name of Jesus Christ, to defend my cause, or rather that of the Bishop himself. Indeed I am well aware in my own conscience that I have said nothing that does not pertain to the glory of God and the edification of my neighbour; I have insulted no one, but I have always had these words on my lips: 'I am the judge of no one, nor do I confess the faith of another.' But I speak like one who lies sick in bed, near to death, examining my own conscience and bearing witness to the faith I hold."

units.la: Neelus itaque conquestus de iniuria quandoquidem eosdem haberet iudices, testes & aduersarios: sacrificos nempe quos benevolè admonverat, quãdo illos poculis & genio indulgentes cum summa Dei contumelia, reperisset: die Martis (quem pinguem appellitant Papistæ) è carcere egreditur, vt Rothomagū duceretur. In ipso carceris egressu oculos in populum coniiciens, qui ibi in eum multa & grauia convicia ingerebat: vir pius misericordia ductus eum monebat, eúsque inscitiam deplorabat. Sed cùm videret nullam sibi fieri audientiam, & satellites ipsum ad progrediendum impellerent: orsus est canere Psalmum XL. Expectans expectaui Dominum. In itinere autem non destitit vnquam se in Domino oblectare, & obuium quemque salutare. Rothomagum ingressus, mox ad Curiam parlamenti deducitur, vbi illum certi eiusdem Curiæ consiliarij benignè admodum de fide sunt percontati adeò vt spes esset demonstratum iri, Neelum rectè ac bono iure appellasse, alterum verò male iudicasse. Idque certis de causis, inter quas erat hæc: Quòd Officiales Aurincenses persecuti fuissent condemnationis sententiam, hebdomade quam ipsi sanctam nominant. Verum Neelus zelum suum erga veritatem nec occultare, nec dissimulare volens, in eius confessionem prorupit, totus in asserenda Filij Dei doctrina: contráque Missæ abominationem omnibus suis coloribus depingendo. Quamobrem Aurincum remissus fuit, ut de gradu sacerdotali demoueretur. Ministri vero & affedae [?] Aurincensis Episcopi non distulerunt diutius pronunciationem sententiae, sed mox theatrum extrui curauerunt ante magnum templum, ut degradatio actualis, quam vocant, executioni mandaretur. In ipso autem theatro erant, Episcopus cum suis, Poenitentiarius ille, quem initio nominauimus, qui quod iactasset [?] se publice refutaturu Neeli opiniones, notas ac digitis designas reum, sic loqui coepit ad populum: Puer qui liberaliter & blande educatus a matre non solum ei non obsequitur, sed insidias & exitium molitur, &c. tandemque hanc suo proœmio subiecit clausulam: Qualis est iste homo maledictus, qui olim religiosus ordinis Augustinensium, nunc persequitur Deum, eiusque ecclesiam pro matre non agnoscit, &c. Ad haec verba, firma voce exclamauit Neelus, Poenitentiarium non vera loqui, se namque in Deum credere, atq; de Ecclesia sancta bene sentire. Poenitentiarius autem sperans hic egregiam se nactum ansam ipsum confutandi, multis verborum ambagibus se implicauit, ut diceret Neelum quidem credere ecclesiam quandam invisibilem: deinde ut sua placeret oratio, multa attulit ad imminuendam authoritatem verae Ecclesiae quam profitebatur Neelus: Papae vero ecclesiam dixit fundatam esse in doctrina veterum episcoporum qui Apostolos sunt secuti: longaque serie & catalogo Episcoporum recitato, eiusmodi addidit epilogum: Haec nostrae ecclesiae sunt fundamenta. Ad extremum conuertens sermonem ad reum, velut per contemptum affatus est, Magister Gulielme, inquit, quodnam est tuae ecclesiae fundamentum? quos enarrare potes tu veteres episcopos? Cui Neelus, Christus, inquit, cum suis Apostolis nostrae sunt authores Ecclesiae. nec verbum amplius ullu protulit. Non multo post haec degradationis mysteria capitis damnatus fuit ut vivus igne absumeretur, pila in os inserta ne populo loqui posset. Homo autem pius constantissime omnes cruciatus passus est. ac quum iam in summo flamae ardore existeti decidisset ex ore pila, vox eius adhuc divina ope implorantis audita est. Carnifex deinde fustem capiti impinges, penitus eu prostrauit. quo viso populus totra vociferatus est detestas crudelitatem carnificis: cernensque hominis patientia, ipsum pro martyre habuit, quae antea haereticum execrandum exstimarat.
units.tr: Neel therefore complained of the injustice done to him, since the same men were his judges, witnesses and adversaries: the priests whom he had kindly admonished when he found them indulging in drink and lust, to the great dishonour of God. On Tuesday (which the Papists call Fat Tuesday) he came out of prison to be taken to Rouen. As he left the prison, he looked at the crowd, which heaped many grave insults upon him there. Moved by pity, the pious man admonished them and lamented their ignorance. But when he saw that no one would listen, and the guards pushed him to move on, he began to sing Psalm 40: "I waited patiently for the Lord." On the journey he never ceased to delight himself in the Lord, and he greeted everyone he met. Once he had entered Rouen he was at once taken before the Court of Parliament, where certain councillors of that court questioned him very kindly about his faith, so much so that there was hope it would be shown that Neel had rightly and lawfully appealed, and that the other side had judged wrongly. This was for certain reasons, among which was this: the officials of Avranches had pursued the sentence of condemnation during the week they call holy. But Neel, unwilling either to hide or to disguise his zeal for the truth, burst forth into a confession of his faith, wholly devoted to asserting the doctrine of the Son of God, and painting in all its colours the abomination of the Mass. For this reason he was sent back to Avranches, to be deprived of his priestly rank. The ministers and assessors of the bishop of Avranches did not delay the pronouncement of sentence for long, but soon had a platform built in front of the great church, so that the actual degradation, as they call it, could be carried out. On the platform itself were the bishop with his men, and that penitentiary whom we named at the beginning, who, having boasted that he would publicly refute Neel's opinions, pointed at the accused with his finger and began to speak to the people: "A boy who has been liberally and kindly brought up by his mother not only does not obey her, but plots snares and ruin against her," and so on. Finally he appended to his preamble this conclusion: "What manner of man is this accursed fellow, who was once a religious of the Augustinian order, and now persecutes God and does not acknowledge His Church as his mother," and so on. At these words Neel cried out in a firm voice that the penitentiary was not speaking the truth, for he himself believed in God and thought rightly of the holy Church. The penitentiary, hoping that he had found a splendid opportunity to confute him, entangled himself in many verbal circumlocutions: he said that Neel did indeed believe in some invisible church; then, to make his speech pleasing, he brought forward much to diminish the authority of the true Church, which Neel professed. He said that the Church of the Pope was founded on the teaching of the ancient bishops who had followed the Apostles; and after reciting a long series and catalogue of bishops, he added this summary: "These are the foundations of our Church." At last, turning his speech to the accused, he addressed him with contempt: "Master William," he said, "what is the foundation of your Church? Which ancient bishops can you name?" Neel replied: "Christ, with His Apostles, is the author of our Church," and he uttered not another word. Not long after this mystery of degradation, the condemned man was sentenced to be burned alive, with a pike thrust into his mouth so that he could not speak to the people. The pious man, however, endured all the torments most steadfastly, and when, already in the full heat of the flames, the pike had fallen from his mouth, his voice was heard still calling upon God's help. Then the executioner, striking him on the head with a club, completely prostrated him. Seeing this, the people cried out loudly against the cruelty of the executioner, and seeing the man's patience, they regarded as a martyr the one whom before they had judged a heretic to be execrated.

units.la: Stephanus Regius natus in quodam pago Belsiæ, Calsurnis nimirum, qui pagus distat ab urbe Carnutensi duobus prope nullis haribus: ut primum veritatis lux ei affulsit, relicto natali solo Argentinam se contulit, tum ut ibi in ecclesia Gallicana maiores in vera religione fructus faceret ex auditione verbi Dei, tum ut sine metu Sacramentis frui posset. Postquam vero in ea ecclesia ad tempus commoratus fuisset, recepit se in patriam, vixitque in paroecia Sancti Georgii non procul a Calsurnorum pago: ibique Notarii fungebatur officio, habebatque secum quendam a manibus famulum Petrum Denocheum, qui olim quin Geneuæ aliquadiu egerat, magnos in doctrina Evangelii progressus fecerat: adeo ut talentum sibi commissum deinceps in pios usus impederit, docendo scilicet ignorates, ac reprehendendo blasphemos.
units.tr: Stephen Regius was born in a village of the Beauce, Chalou to be precise, which lies about two leagues from the city of Chartres. As soon as the light of truth shone upon him, he left his native soil and betook himself to Strasbourg, partly so that in the French church there he might make greater progress in true religion by hearing the Word of God, and partly so that he might partake of the sacraments without fear. But after he had stayed for a time in that church, he returned to his homeland and lived in the parish of Saint George, not far from the village of Chalou. There he held the office of notary, and he had with him a certain manual servant, Peter Denocheus, who had formerly spent some time at Geneva and had made great progress in the doctrine of the Gospel, so that he afterwards applied the talent entrusted to him to pious uses, namely by teaching the ignorant and rebuking blasphemers.

units.la: Isti autem non diu una vixerant, quin Lutheranismi nomine suspecti accusarentur. Mense itaque Decemb. M. D. LII. ambo per Latrunculatores capti Carnutũ abducuntur, atque in carcere Episcopi eius urbis conjecti fuerunt. In eodẽ carcere per annũ detenti, atque de fidei suæ confessione interrogati, amplissimum veritati uterque dedit testimonium.
units.tr: These men had not lived together long before they were accused of being suspected of Lutheranism. Therefore, in December 1552, both were seized by constables and led away to Chartres, and they were thrown into the prison of the bishop of that city. Held in the same prison for a year, and questioned about their confession of faith, each of them gave a magnificent testimony to the truth.

units.la: Stephanus autem carmina quædam in carcere composuit spiritualia, ut vocant, in quibus fidem suam & spem quam in Domino posuerat, decantabat: statum quoque suum & conditionem, dignitatisque gradu ad quem Deus eum euexerat ut coram hominibus fidelis ei testis & Christi martyr esset, divinis laudibus efferebat. Iis cantionibus vir ille pius diuturni carceris tædia solabatur, prædicans semper mirifica opera Dei in quo se plane oblectabat. Postquam viderent adversarii se nihil proficere, nullisque rebus constantiam eorum concuti, ut nec longi ac diri carceris horror, nec blandæ pollicitationes futuræ liberationis, nec plures illecebræ quibus ipsemet episcopus eos ad revocationem & palinodia solicitabat, unquam efficere potuerint quo minus in sententia pe-starent. Tandem capitis damnati, appellarunt summum Senatum Curiæ Parisiensis, idque non eo faciebant, ut morte evaderet, sed quo pleniore apud magnos & sapientes huius mundi confessionem doctrinæ Filij Dei ederet. Curia autem Parisiensis eos remisit, addito arresto confirmate priore sententia. Reversi Carnutũ, diro ignis supplicio affecti fuerunt.
units.tr: Stephen, moreover, composed in prison certain spiritual songs, as they are called, in which he sang of his faith and of the hope he had placed in the Lord; he also extolled with divine praises his state and condition, and the rank to which God had raised him, so that he might be a faithful witness before men and a martyr of Christ. With these songs the pious man consoled himself in the weariness of his long imprisonment, always proclaiming the wonderful works of God, in which he took true delight. When the adversaries saw that they were achieving nothing, and that their constancy could not be shaken by any means, neither by the horror of a long and harsh imprisonment, nor by smooth promises of future release, nor by the many enticements with which the bishop himself urged them to recant and retract, they resolved to stand firm in their opinion. At last, having been condemned to death, they appealed to the supreme Senate, the Parlement of Paris, and they did this not in order to escape death, but so that they might give a fuller confession of the doctrine of the Son of God before great and wise men of this world. The Parlement of Paris, however, sent them back, adding a decree confirming the earlier sentence. Returning to Chartres, they were subjected to the dreadful punishment of fire.

units.la: PETRUS SERRA.
units.tr: PETER SERRA.

units.la: PETRUS Serra, natus in quodam loco qui Læsa appellatur in prouincia Cozerana, non procul ab urbe Tolosa, cum sacerdos antea fuisset, se Genevam in ecclesiam Dei contulit, ubi, artē sutoriam didicit. Postea singulari studio charitatis, amoréque permotus, ut fratrem suum, qui uxorem habebat, e Papatu atq; idolorum cultu educeret, iter ad eam rem suscepit hyberno tempore, anno M.D.LIII.
units.tr: Peter Serra was born in a place called Læsa, in the province of Couserans, not far from the city of Toulouse. He had been a priest before, but he went to Geneva into the Church of God, where he learned the trade of shoemaking. Later, moved by a singular zeal and love, so that he might lead his brother, who had a wife, out of the Papacy and the worship of idols, he undertook the journey for that purpose in winter, in the year 1553.

units.la: Cùm autem in patriā venissét, cum fratre suo locutus est atque illius uxore, quæ à consolatione verbi, quam Petrus ei afferebat, atque ab ea discessione ac migratione vehementer abhorrebat. Itaque eius aduentum illa cuidam mulieri vicinæ statim annuntiauit, quæ quod audierat ita secretum tacitúmque habuit, ut ad Officialem eius diocesis illico detulerit. Qui metuens ne ille sibi elaberetur, sine ulla informatione eum comprehendendum curauit. Neq; vero ea opus magnopere fuit, in tā prompta & parata Sarræ confessione: in qua ubi ageret, & qua religione teneret declarauit. porrò Officialis eiusq; socij metuētes, ne alia appellatio ipsis morā tarditatēq; afferret, consilio capto egerunt, ut Serra in manus Inquisitoris fidei Tolosæ constituti traderetur. apud quem Petrus amplissimā fidei suæ confessionem edidit, adeò ut inquisitore ad sensum conscientiæ interiorem reuocauerit, eúmq; monuerit, ut purā Dei veritatē quā ipse cōfitebatur, animaduerteret atq; cognosceret, quā ei facile demonstrabat & probabat, locos ei annotans & capita: tā fideli ac recenti memoria præditus erat. Id tamen nihil impediuit, quo minus ab inquisitore vicarioq; Episcopi Cozerani condenarctur, ut de gradu sacerdotali dimoueretur, atq; in manu potestatis ciuilis traderetur. Itaque ad eā degradationē faciendā, ductus fuit ad oppidulū Muretū appellatū, prope Tolosā: indeq; traditus iudici, qui appellationū nominatur in iurisdictione Tolosana, ad quē etiā crimina hæresis referūtur. Iudex tū à Petro quæsiuit, quo esset artificio. ac cum ex eo audiuisset aliquanto ante artē sutoriā didicisse: intelligere ex eo voluit, quod artificiū antè pfessus esset. Tū Petrus, Heu, inquit, me pudet dicere. nā illud vitæ institutū fuerā amplexus quod in mundo est omnium teterrimū ac miserrimū. Complures iis verbis in eā opinionem adducebantur ut eū latronē quēdā & ficariū, aut falsæ monetæ effectorē esse exīstimāret. Quare horut sine pudore ac timore ullo libere diceret. Sed is ita erat affectus atque impeditus, ut dolor animi ex recordatione pristinæ vitæ susceptus, obstruere ei os videretur. Tandem importunitate eorum qui instabat coactus, maximis cum suspiriis se Sacerdotem fuisse dixit, rationémque cur illud genus vitæ ita fœdum ac miserum existimaret, attulit. Quamobrem commotus Iudex, ea pœna eum condemnauit, ut primùm ea afficeretur ignominia, quam emendationem honorariam appellant: in qua veniam à Deo, & à Rege, iustitiáque peteret: deinde lingua ei præcisa vivus cremaretur. Qua quidé à sententia cùm ille appellasset, ad Camerà criminosam parlamenti Tolosani adductus est: ibíque constanter in sua confessione permansit. Interrogatus autè cur appellasset, dixit se quidem eò no fecisse, quòd sententiam capitis recusaret, mortémque defugeret: nec enim suam sibi vitā ita esse charā, ut eā honori Dei ac testimonio veritatis anteponeret: se etiā scire eos ad quos appellasset, vitā sibi minimè cōseruaturos: sed appellationis causā eā fuisse, quòd fuisset cōdēnatus ut veniā à Rege peteret, quē nunquā offenderat. Nā quod ad Deum quidem attineret, se obstrictum ac paratum esse, ut sibi ab eo ignosci postularet. Causa etiā cur appellaret ab ea sententia, hæc fuit, quòd eam linguæ præcisionem proponebat, quā Dominus ut illū laudaret ei dederat. Itaque iniquū ei atque indignū videbatur, si facultas eius rei in extrema vitæ suæ parte ei eriperetur. Ea tamen sententia decreto Camerę criminosæ cōfirmata est. Sed cùm primo Præsidi mādatū esset, ut eas causas & cōtroversias, quæ ad fidē pertinerēt, curaret disceptandas iudicādásque in ea camera, quæ idonea ei videretur: & quia superiore anno summā Cameram delegerat, ipse Præses demonstrabat iudicium eius causæ apud illos criminum iudices fieri non potuisse. quare qui ex utraq; erat curia Iudices, post prandiū cōuenerūt: ad quos Petrus iterū productus est. Eò autè cum venisset, diu ibi fuit, nihil plane respōdens, dicénsq; sibi nihil cū ullo homine nisi cū Deo quicquā esse negotij, cū ea sententia sibi pronūtiata esset, in qua periculū vitæ suæ propositū intelligeret. postea tandē respōdit, atq; in cōfessione fidei suæ perstitit: à qua quidē nullis rebus, quibus tū attētatus atq; oppugnatus fuit, deduci unquā potuit. Cōstitutū est igitur, ut prius decretū in ea pœna cōstituēda vim suam haberet, sublata emendatione honoraria, ac præcisione linguæ, modò contra ipsorum religionem nihil plane diceret. Porrò cùm ad supplicium duceretur, gymnasiumque sancti Martialis præteriret, Iudex quoddam simulachrum ei ostendit virginis Mariæ, eíque dixit, vt veniam ab ea peteret. Cui Petrus respondit, se id quidem minimè facturum esse: nec enim se illam offendisse, neque eam effigiem esse virginem Mariā, sed idolum lapideū. Id cùm dixisset, Iudex iußit statim linguam exhibere ac exerere, quod ille sine vlla mora fecit, & placidè linguam sibi amputari passus est. Deinde alligatus ad postem, vt viuus cremaretur, vsque ad mortem ita oculos in cælum erectos intentósque habuit, vt nullo ignis ardore & vi commoveretur, non magis quàm si omni sensu caruisset. Quæ res populo magnam admirationem attulit, atque à quodam parlamenti Consiliario dictum fuit, eo modo Lutheranos non amplius esse multandos pœnaque afficiendos, cùm ea res plus obesset religioni quàm prodesset.
units.tr: When he came into his homeland, he spoke with his brother and his brother's wife. She greatly shrank from the comfort of the Word that Peter offered her, and from leaving and migrating from there. So she at once announced his arrival to a certain neighbouring woman, who kept what she had heard so secret and quiet that she promptly reported it to the Official of his diocese. He, fearing that Serra might slip away from him, had him arrested without any inquiry. Indeed there was hardly any need for one, given Serra's prompt and ready confession, in which he declared where he was and what religion he held. Moreover the Official and his companions, fearing that an appeal would bring them delay and postponement, took counsel and arranged for Serra to be handed over to the Inquisitor of the faith appointed at Toulouse. Before him Peter made a very full confession of his faith, so much so that he called the Inquisitor back to the inner sense of conscience and urged him to notice and recognise the pure truth of God, which Peter confessed. He easily demonstrated and proved this to him, citing passages and chapters, so faithful and ready was his memory. Nevertheless this did not prevent him from being condemned by the Inquisitor and the vicar of the Bishop of Couserans, to be stripped of his priestly rank and handed over to the civil power. For that degradation to be carried out, he was taken to the little town called Muret, near Toulouse, and from there handed over to the judge called the judge of appeals in the jurisdiction of Toulouse, to whom cases of heresy are also referred. The judge asked Peter what his trade was. When he heard that Peter had learned shoemaking some time before, he wished to know from him what occupation he had followed before that. Then Peter said: "Alas, I am ashamed to say it. For I had embraced that way of life which is the most foul and wretched of all in the world." By these words many were led to think that he was some robber and cutthroat, or a maker of counterfeit coin. So the judge urged him to speak freely, without shame or fear. But Peter was so affected and impeded that the grief he felt at remembering his former life seemed to block his mouth. At length, compelled by the importunity of those pressing him, he said with great sighs that he had been a priest, and he gave the reason why he judged that kind of life so foul and wretched. Moved by this, the judge condemned him to this penalty: first he was to undergo that disgrace which they call honorary amends, in which he would ask pardon of God, of the King and of justice; then his tongue was to be cut out and he was to be burned alive. When he appealed from this sentence, he was brought before the criminal chamber of the Parliament of Toulouse, and there he steadfastly persisted in his confession.
