Asked why he had appealed, he said that he had not done so because he refused the sentence of death or sought to escape death. For he did not hold his life so dear that he would set it above the honour of God and the witness of the truth; he also knew that those to whom he appealed would not spare his life. The reason for the appeal was that he had been condemned to ask pardon of the King, whom he had never offended. As for God, he said, he was bound and ready to ask Him for pardon. Another reason he appealed from that sentence was that it proposed the cutting out of the tongue which the Lord had given him to praise Him; it seemed unjust and unworthy to him if the opportunity for that were snatched from him in the last part of his life. Nevertheless that sentence was confirmed by a decree of the criminal chamber. But since the First President had been ordered to see that cases and controversies concerning faith were disputed and judged in whichever chamber seemed suitable to him, and since in the previous year he had chosen the Grand Chamber, the President himself showed that judgment of this cause could not be made before those criminal judges. Therefore the judges of both courts met after lunch, and Peter was brought before them again. When he came there, he remained a long time, answering nothing at all, saying that he had no business with any man but God, since a sentence had been pronounced on him in which he understood that the peril of his life was set forth. Afterwards he at last gave an answer and persisted in the confession of his faith, from which he could never be drawn by any of the arguments with which he was assailed and attacked. It was therefore decided that the earlier decree should keep its force in fixing the penalty, the honorary amends and the cutting of the tongue being removed, provided he said nothing at all against their religion. When he was being led to execution and passed the college of St Martial, the judge showed him an image of the Virgin Mary and told him to ask pardon from her. Peter replied that he would by no means do so: he had not offended her, nor was that image the Virgin Mary, but a stone idol. When he had said this, the judge at once ordered him to show and put out his tongue, which he did without delay, and he calmly allowed his tongue to be cut off. Then, tied to a post to be burned alive, he kept his eyes raised and fixed on heaven until death, so that he was moved by neither the heat nor the force of the fire, no more than if he had lacked all feeling. This brought great wonder to the people, and a certain councillor of the parliament said that in this way Lutherans should no longer be fined or punished, since such a thing did more harm to their religion than good.

units.la: NICOLAVS NAILVS.
units.tr: NICOLAS NAIL.

units.la: NICOLAVS Nailus patria Cenomanus sutorio artificio deserviens cùm Lutetiæ aliquot librorum sacrorum sarcinas detulisset, captus fuit die Martis mensis Februarij X I I I I. Qui cùm puram doctrinæ Euangelij confessionem edidisset, grauissimis in carcere tormentis fuit cruciatus, vt eos quos sciret doctrinæ suæ cõscios ac socios, non minaret. Sed quanuis ea tormenta etiam vsque ad membrorum ci° dissolutionem sæpius fuerint repetita, tamè singulari fide, constantia, virtuteque munitus, neminem vnquam prodidit aut nominauit. Postea condemnatus vt viuus igni cremaretur, antequam è carcere educeretur ad plateam Malberti, qui locus supplicio eius erat constitutus, ori eius ligneum epistomium inseruerunt, à posteriore capitis parte sunibus ita constrictu, vt acerrima eorum vi compressum os, sanguine vndique emitteret, faciesque horrenda deformitate demonstraret. Quæ quidem in re primus fuit Lutetiæ, in quo hoc genus crudelitatis editum est. Sed tamen egregius martyr & fortis vir, quauis haberet os ita obstructum, nunquam destitit, signis aspectuque in cælum perpetuo erecto declarare ea spe, constantia atq; animi magnitudine quâ habebat: adeo vt cum ad xenodochium venisset, quod domicilium Dei vulgò appellatur, cogeretúrq; prætepræteriens quoddam simulachrū nostræ Dominæ, vt vocant, adorare, nunquam vt id faceret adduci potuit. Sed exiguis viribus, qui ei adhuc supererat, suffultus atque excitatus, se à tortore, qui eum suis comprehensum manibus tenebat, auertit, dorsumque idolo ostendit. Tum vero populus, qui ea in vrbe natura maximè est mobilis, ad superstitionemque procliuis{?} cum id spectasset, ita commotus fuit, vt in eum quanuis iam ad mortem accederet, impetum facere voluerit. Ad locum vero supplicio assignatū, cum venisset, crudelissimè tractatus est. Nam antequam ille alligaretur, vt sublimis tolleretur in aerem, corpus eius adipe perunctum est, puluisque sulphuris corpori eius inspersus, ita vt ignis subiectus vix arsisset, cum flamma straminum subito accensa, summam cutem corporis eius inuaderet atque ustularet, sed ad interiores partes nullo modo penetraret. Sed in hoc grauissimo cruciatu Dominus summam ei consolationem opemque attulit, eique gratiam impertiuit, vt eo in tormento sanctissimum eius nomen maxima & clarissima voce inuocaret, quæ media ex flamma audita fuit. Nam funes quibus epistomium illud astrictum tenebatur combusti fuerunt aliquanto ante, quam sanctissimus martyr expiraret.
units.tr: Nicolas Nail, a native of Le Mans, who earned his living as a shoemaker, was arrested at Paris on Tuesday, 14 February, after he had carried bundles of holy books there. When he had made a plain confession of the pure doctrine of the Gospel, he was tortured with the most severe torments in prison, in the hope that he would name those he knew to share his beliefs and to be his companions. But although these torments were repeated often, even to the dislocation of all his limbs, he was armed with singular faith, constancy and courage, and he never betrayed or named anyone. Afterwards he was condemned to be burned alive. Before he was led out of the prison to the Place Maubert, where his execution had been appointed, they put a wooden gag in his mouth, tied at the back of his head with cords so tightly that, under their violent pressure, the mouth bled on every side and his face showed a dreadful disfigurement. This was the first time that this kind of cruelty was practised at Paris. Yet the outstanding martyr and brave man, although his mouth was so blocked, never ceased, by signs and by a gaze fixed constantly on heaven, to declare the hope, constancy and greatness of mind that he possessed. So when he came to the hospital, which is commonly called God's house, and was forced to pass by an image of what they call Our Lady in order to adore it, he could never be brought to do so. Instead, supported and roused by what little strength he still had, he turned away from the torturer who held him fast in his hands, and showed his back to the idol. Then indeed the people, who in that city are very fickle by nature and prone to superstition, when they saw this were so stirred that they wanted to attack him, even though he was already approaching death. When he arrived at the place assigned for his execution, he was treated most cruelly. For before he was tied up to be lifted high into the air, his body was smeared with fat and powdered sulphur was sprinkled over it, so that when the fire was put under him it had scarcely caught when the flame of the straw, suddenly kindled, attacked the outer skin of his body and scorched it, but in no way penetrated to the inner parts. But in this most grievous torment the Lord brought him the greatest consolation and help, and granted him the grace that in that torment he called upon his most holy name with a great and clear voice, which was heard from the midst of the flame. For the cords by which the gag was held tight had been burned away a little before the most holy martyr breathed his last.

units.la: SIMON LALOE.
units.tr: SIMON LALOE.

units.la: SIMON Laloéus patria Suessionensis, eáque arte qua perspecilla conficiuntur, Geneua, vbi sua cū familia degebat, pfectᵗ[?] vt in Galliam quorundam negotiorum causa iret, Diuione à Præfecto eius vrbis captus est, die Martis 17. Sep. M.D.LIII. Is autē initiò statim fuit à Præfecto Diuionensi tribus de rebus interrogatus. Nam primum quo in loco ageret quæsitum est, deinde quam fidem de religione haberet, postremò quos socios & conscios haberet eius doctrinæ quam ipse profiteretur. Ac de loco quidē commorationis suæ respondit, se Geneuæ sedem ac domicilium omnium rerum suarum constituisse, familiámque ea in vrbe habere, vt liberè frueretur iis beneficiis & solatiis, quæ Deus ibi tot ac tanta posuisset, ecclesiámque verbo Dei emendatam constituisset. Quid autem de religione sentiret, purè declarauit, plura confessus & professus quàm aduersarij audire vellent. Quod verò illi audire maximopere cupiebant, ad id dixit se nihil habere quod responderet: neque scire quid factum esset iis qui comites itineris fuissent. Quos vero ipse cognosceret, Geneuae esse atque habitare. Itaque quum aduersarii suis interrogationibus, quaestionibusque acerrimis nihil ab eo elicere aut extorquere potuissent, omni studio & contentione ad eum capitis damnandum progressi sunt. ac die Martis, qui fuit dies xxi. Nouembris, M.D.Liii. quum sententiam pro tribunali capitalem pronunciassent, eum e carcere ad ultimum supplicium duxerunt. Tum vero egregius martyr Jesu Christi orans pro suis inimicis, summa constantia & animi magnitudine mortem propositā suscepit ac pertulit, eo ipso die xxi. Nouemb. anni M.D.Liii. Quo quidem tortor Jacobus Syluester nominatus, vehementer in fide ac timore Dei fuit confirmatus, atque in eam sententiam adductus, ut illud genus vitae deponeret, neque amplius sanguinem innocentem funderet. Haec autem dicta multaque alia verae poenitentiae signa, quemadmodum cetera omnia sunt testata authoritate hominum fidelium, ac testium locupletium, qui non solum in morte eius martyris affuerunt, verum etiam quae sunt commemorata, ex eo ipso tortore Jacobo Syluestro audiuerunt. quem magnopere dolentem propter effusum innocentum sanguinem, ac de venia tantorum peccatorum consequenda diffidentem & plane desperatem, suauissimis Euangelii verbis confirmarunt, atque in eam gratiae, misericordiaeque Dei fiduciam, & animi sententiam adduxerunt, ut is statim se cum familia sua Geneuam in ecclesiam Dei contulerit, sedemq; rerum suarū ea in urbe collocarit.
units.tr: Simon Laloe, a native of Soissons, who practised the craft by which spectacles are made and lived with his family at Geneva, set out for France on some business. He was arrested at Dijon by the governor of that city on Tuesday, 17 September 1553. At the outset the governor of Dijon questioned him on three matters. First he was asked where he was living; then what he believed about religion; and lastly what companions and sharers of the doctrine he professed he had. As to his place of residence, he replied that he had made Geneva the seat and home of all his affairs, and had his family in that city, so that he might freely enjoy the blessings and comforts that God had there bestowed in such abundance, and the Church there had been reformed by the Word of God. As to what he thought about religion, he declared plainly, confessing and professing more than his adversaries wished to hear. But as to what they most eagerly wanted to hear, he said he had nothing to answer, and did not know what had become of those who had been his travelling companions; those he knew personally, he said, were living and dwelling at Geneva. Since his adversaries, with their questions and most searching interrogations, could extract or draw nothing more from him, they proceeded with all zeal and effort to have him condemned to death. And on Tuesday, which was 21 November 1553, when they had pronounced the capital sentence from the judgement seat, they led him from prison to the final punishment. Then indeed this outstanding martyr of Jesus Christ, praying for his enemies, underwent and endured the death set before him with the greatest constancy and greatness of mind, on that same day, 21 November 1553. The executioner, named Jacques Sylvestre, was strongly confirmed in the faith and in the fear of God by this, and was led to the resolve to give up that way of life and to shed innocent blood no more. These words, and many other signs of true repentance, are attested, as all the rest are, by the authority of faithful men and of weighty witnesses, who not only were present at this martyr's death but also heard what is recounted from the executioner Jacques Sylvestre himself. He, greatly grieved at the innocent blood he had shed and despairing of obtaining pardon for such great sins, was strengthened by the sweetest words of the Gospel and brought to such trust in the grace and mercy of God, and to such a resolve of mind, that he at once went with his family to Geneva, into the Church of God, and there in that city set up the seat of his affairs.

units.la: JOANNA GRAIA.
units.tr: JOANNA GRAIA.

units.la: Historia de D Joanna Graia, filia Ducis Soffolcensis: quae quum à Senatu Regina esset designata, constans in fide Euangelii à Maria capite plexa est.
units.tr: The story of Lady Joanna Grey, daughter of the Duke of Suffolk. Although the Senate had named her queen, she was beheaded by Mary, remaining steadfast in the faith of the Gospel.

units.la: Egrotante primum rege Edouardo, Northumbriae dux (penes quem summa tum erat & arbitraria rerum gerendarum potestas) consilia agitat cum Duce Suffolcensi, filiam ut suam filio ipsius in matrimonium daret. Non hîc excutio nuptiarum harum mysteria: nec morbum Regis, occultasque Ducis petitiones exquiro, nec ea coniecturis in praesentia tanquam vestigiis venor, quae facilius deplorari à nobis, quàm nunc emendari possunt. Verum ita res habuit: Dum illi tam alieno tempore in publico omnium luctu suas agitat nuptias, Edouardus Rex aegrè decumbens, suam propemodum agit animam: quali indole, pietate ac literis Principem vix scio an Anglia post cum fit habitura. Ne longum faciam: finitis demum nuptiis, ac ingravescente magis magisque Regis morbo, quum tam de salute illius omnia viderentur desperata: perfectum interea est instinctu quidem paucorum, at non sine suffragiis tamen ordinum & iureconsultorum omnium, ut Rex testamentaria voluntate sua, haereditariam regni successionem in Ioannam hanc, quam dixi, Ducis Suffolciae filiam, Henrico octavo ex sorore proneptim devoluerit[?]: praeterita interim utraque sorore, Maria & Elisabetha. Solus e iureconsultis D. Halesius evangelicus, & iudex quo nullus in tota Anglia tu fuit incorruptior, Mariae suffragatus non subscripsit, cuius viri exitus horrendus suisse dicitur. Hisque ita constitutis, ac subscriptione omnium confirmatis, paucis post diebus Edouardus Angliae rex tantae spei adolescens, decimo sexto suae aetatis anno, magnitudine morbi adhuc nō-satis comperti, moritur: simulque cum illo Anglorum fortuna fere universa moritur & dignitas. Hic in misero sane statu res erant Anglorum relictae. Tum cum multo etiam miseriorem reddidit patriciorum & plebeiorum intestina inter se & capitalis simultas. Mortuo igitur Edouardo, suffecta est in eius honoris titulum, ex consensu quidem nobilium, sed ipsius admodum refragante voluntate, Ioanna haec: quae Londini mox publico praeconio perque celebriores quasdam civitates Regina recipitur & salutatur. Erat huius adolescentulae aetas, regis Edouardi annis haud multum impar: quem tamen illa eruditione, literis ac linguis non solum aequaret, sed superaret etiam, sub doctissimo viro Ioanne AElmero instituta. Quae si tam felicem fortita fortunam esset, quam cum felici ingenio non infelicem coniunxit educationem, non modo cum Aspasiis, Sempronijs, Gracchorum matre, & literaria laude commendatissimis quibusque feminis, sed viris, Academicis etiam titulis lauroque onustis, pari certare commendatione potuisset. Interea temporis dum haec Londini geruntur, Maria, fratris audita morte, latebris ac fuga sibi procul Londino cauit, popularis potissimum fauore freta, quanquam nec occultis interim ex nobilitate forsan consiliis destituta. Northumbriensis ubi eius videt obstinationem, nec omnia satis ei ex sententia succederent, comparato quantum potest exercitu, ac conscriptis copijs, ad persequendam Mariam mouet: perfacile, vt videbatur, hoc negotium confecturus, si suo frui impetu licuisset. Verùm quia in recenti regno nihil sibi adhuc permittere priuata authoritate audebat, ex publico senatus consulto rem omnem gubernare cogebatur. Quo factum est, vt itinerum metæ, ac dierum spacia, quid, quantùmque quoquo die consiceret, ex formula illi mandaretur, quam prætergredi nec licitum erat ei nec tutum. Inter hæc Maria huc illuc varijs iactata itineribus, ac tuta sequens, tandem in Northfolciæ, Suffolciæque fines contendit: vbi Ducis nomen quàm maximè inuisum, ob rusticorum stragem recens editam, intelligebat. Vbi demum vndecunque corrogatis populi præsidijs, in castello Fremynghamensi aliquandiu se continuit.
units.tr: While King Edward was first ill, the Duke of Northumberland, who then held the chief and arbitrary power over the conduct of affairs, plotted with the Duke of Suffolk to give his daughter in marriage to his son. I will not here investigate the secrets of these marriages, nor inquire into the king's sickness or the duke's hidden requests, nor do I hunt after these things by conjecture, following their tracks, things which can more easily be lamented by us than now corrected. But the matter went thus. While those men, at so unseasonable a time and amid the public grief of all, were arranging their marriage, King Edward, lying gravely ill, was all but at the point of death. I scarcely know whether England will ever again have a prince of such character, piety and learning. To be brief: when the marriages were at last concluded, and the king's illness grew ever worse, and all hope of his recovery seemed lost, it was determined, at the urging of a few but not without the votes of all the orders and of all the jurists, that the king should by his testamentary will pass the hereditary succession of the kingdom to this Joanna, the daughter of the Duke of Suffolk whom I mentioned, a granddaughter of Henry the Eighth through his sister, with both sisters, Mary and Elizabeth, passed over meanwhile. Of the jurists, Judge Hales alone, an evangelical man and a judge than whom none in all England was more incorruptible, supported Mary and would not sign; the end of this man is said to have been dreadful. With these arrangements made and confirmed by everyone's signature, a few days later Edward, King of England, a youth of such great promise, died in the sixteenth year of his age, from the severity of an illness not yet fully understood; and together with him almost the whole fortune and dignity of the English died. The affairs of the English were left in a truly wretched state, made far more miserable by the internal quarrels between nobles and commons and their deadly enmity. So, Edward being dead, this Joanna was placed in the title of that honour, by the consent indeed of the nobles, but against the very strong will of the king himself. Soon she was received and hailed as queen at London by public proclamation, and through certain more famous cities. This young woman's age was not much unequal to King Edward's, and she not only equalled him but even surpassed him in learning, letters and languages, having been trained under the most learned man John Aylmer. If she had obtained a fortune as happy as the education she joined to her happy talent, she could have competed, with equal praise, not only with Aspasia, Sempronia, the mother of the Gracchi and all the women most commended for literary fame, but also with men laden with academic titles and laurels. Meanwhile, while these things were going on at London, Mary, on hearing of her brother's death, took care for her safety by hiding and flight far from London, relying chiefly on the favour of the people, though perhaps not without secret support from some of the nobility. When Northumberland saw her obstinacy, and not everything went according to his wishes, he gathered as large an army and as many forces as he could and moved to pursue Mary, a task which he thought would be very easily finished had he been allowed to follow his impulse. But since in the new reign he did not dare to permit himself anything on his own private authority, he was forced to manage the whole affair by a public decree of the senate. As a result, the limits of his marches, the spans of his days, and what and how much he should accomplish each day were prescribed to him by a formula, which it was neither lawful nor safe for him to exceed. Meanwhile Mary, tossed hither and thither on various journeys, following safe routes, at last made for the borders of Norfolk and Suffolk, where she understood the name of the duke to be most hateful on account of the recent slaughter of the countrymen. There at last, having gathered a force of the people from wherever she could, she kept herself for some time in the castle of Framlingham.

units.la: Ad quam primi omnium aduolarunt Suffolcenses, quorum semper accerrimum fuit in propagando Euangelio studium, opem operámque suam ea quidem lege ac pastione pollicentes, modò nequid vnquam moueret contra eum religionis statum quem frater reliquisset Edouardus. Quid multis? Accepit illa conditionem, fidémque vt quisquam posset credere, suam interposuit: quam si postea tam constanter seruasset illa, quam ipsi lubenter corporibus & armis salutem tegebant illius, rem fecisset, mea opinione, & ipsius dignam nobilitate, simúlque imperium forsan sibi ipsi firmius maiori cum tranquillitate & diuturnitate peperisset. Nam quantunuis[?] per te potentia polleas, dissicilis tamen diuturnitatis custos perfidia est, difficilior metus: omnium vero difficillima, crudelitas. Hunc itaque in modum euangelicorum maximè septa præsidijs Maria, caeteros quosque cum ipso Duce ad deditionem compulit. Quæ quum ita sint, indigna profecto videtur mihi vox Maria illa qua Suffolcensibus postea fidem sibi datam, per supplicationem appellatibus, respondit: Quoniam, inquit, membra quum sitis, regere vultis caput vestrum: intelligetis tandem, capiti subesse membra, non præesse oportere. Quo tempore porrò, eadémque de causa, ingenerosum quendam D. Dobum, qui non procul ab oppido windamo habitarat, animaduersum est: qui propterea in medium forum ter productus[?], publicam subire ignominiam cogebatur. Sed ita fit communi hominum more, vt semper ferè sumus, quum officijs egemus aliorum,ad quærendam gratiam, quàm postea acceptis beneficijs, ad referendam paratiores. At enim hoc bene habet, quod unum miseris mortalibus firmo esse solatio queat, quod æquitas & fides quantumlibet exclusa à terris, apud homines non reperiatur, certò tamen in cælis reperietur apud Deum. Sed quoniam historiam scribimus, non de officijs: Suffolcenses istos mittamus paululum. Qui quantum sua promptitudine & sedulitate apud Reginam promeruerint, non hîc disquiro: quid autem illa præstiterit, res ipsa aperta voce, totáque persecutionis huiusce historia testatur. Habetis nunc ergo Mariam ex fugitiua reginam factam. Habetis è summis periculis & metu eô emergentem, ut ipsa metuenda fit cæteris. Habetis denique positum eius in manu potestatis gladium, quem quo modo postea exercuerit hoc nunc libro audiamus. Postquam itaque, ut dixi, per euangelicos sic amplificata, subactisque hostibus cuncta iam tuta videt, è castris Londinum, multorum magno plausu, sed plurium maiori metu, omnium verò maxima assentatione producitur. Ubi primùm regni sui auspicia à sanguine Ioannæ huius adolescentulæ exorditur, quam in ipso mox aduentu custodiæ haberi mandat, cùmque marito securi non multis post diebus multat. Deinde Northumbriensem, nec multò post Suffolcensem, Duces capite plectit. Cæteri verò nobiles sanguine tantùm pecuniario suam luunt rebellionem: quemadmodum fusius à nobis alio in loco, in vita Cantuariensis explicatum est. Cæterùm quod ad Ioannam attinet, quatriduum antequam ad supplicium educeretur, venit ad eam Feknamus (qui postea in abbatem westmonasteriensem allectus fuit) de Reginæ voluntate eò missus, ut sententiam eius de iis quæ ad religionem & fidem attinent, exploraturus: si quid à Pontificia disciplina aberraret, denuò in viam (quam ipsi iudicant) reduceret. Eius verò colloquij summam eo compendio, quo ab ipsa excepta est & euulgata, nos hic subijciendam, tibique, Lector, æstimandam censuimus.
units.tr: To her the men of Suffolk first of all flocked, whose zeal for spreading the Gospel had always been most eager. They promised their help and labour, on this one condition and pledge: that she should never move against the religious state which her brother Edward had left. What more is there to say? She accepted the condition and gave her pledge, so that anyone could believe it. If she had afterwards kept it as faithfully as they gladly protected her safety with their bodies and arms, she would have done a deed, in my opinion, worthy of her nobility, and perhaps would have secured her rule more firmly, with greater tranquillity and durability. For however powerful you are, faithlessness is a poor guardian of lasting power, and fear is a poorer one; but the most difficult of all is cruelty. In this manner Mary, chiefly protected by the evangelicals, compelled the rest, together with the duke himself, to surrender. These things being so, that saying of Mary's seems to me truly unworthy, by which she answered the men of Suffolk, who afterwards appealed to her by supplication about the faith pledged to them: "Since you are members, you wish to rule your head; you will understand at last that members ought to be subject to the head, not to rule over it." At that same time, and for the same cause, an ungenerous man, Master Dobbe, who had lived not far from the town of Wingham, was singled out; for this reason he was led three times into the middle of the market-place and forced to undergo public disgrace. But it happens, by the common custom of men, as it almost always does, that when we need the services of others, we are eager to seek favour, but once the benefits are received, we are more ready to repay them. Yet this much is well: one thing can be a firm comfort to wretched mortals, that although justice and good faith, however banished from the earth, are not found among men, they will certainly be found in heaven with God. But since we are writing history, not about services, let us set those men of Suffolk aside for a little. How much they deserved with the queen by their readiness and diligence I do not inquire here; but what she gave in return the thing itself declares in plain words, and the whole history of this persecution bears witness. You now have Mary made queen from a fugitive. You have her rising out of the greatest dangers and fear, so that she herself becomes feared by others. You have, finally, the sword of power placed in her hand; how she afterwards wielded it, let us hear in this book. Therefore, as I said, having been so magnified by the evangelicals, and having subdued her enemies, and seeing all things now safe, she is brought from the camp to London, with the great applause of many, but the greater fear of most, and the utmost flattery of all. There, first of all, she begins the auspices of her reign with the blood of this young woman Joanna, whom she orders to be held in custody at the very moment of her arrival, and a few days later punishes with the axe, together with her husband. Then she beheads the Duke of Northumberland, and not long after the Duke of Suffolk. The other nobles, however, paid for their rebellion only with money and blood-money, as has been explained at greater length by us elsewhere, in the life of the Archbishop of Canterbury. But as far as Joanna is concerned, four days before she was to be led to execution, Feknamus (who was afterwards appointed abbot of Westminster) came to her, sent there at the queen's wish, to explore her opinion about matters pertaining to religion and faith, and, if she strayed at all from Papist discipline, to lead her back again into the way which they judge to be the right one. We have thought it right to set down here the substance of that conversation, in the abbreviated form in which it was taken down and published by her, and for you, reader, to weigh.

units.la: Colloquium inter Feknamum & D.Ioannam, Ducis Suffolcensis filiam, quatriduum antequam capite plecterctur.
units.tr: Conversation between Feknamus and Lady Joanna, daughter of the Duke of Suffolk, four days before she was beheaded.

units.la: FEknamus: Domina, indolesco tristi & ærumnosæ fortunæ tuæ, sed nihil addubito quin acerbitatem hanc satis constanti & mafculo animo sustineas. Ioan. Gratus est accessus tuus, modò Christianæ exhortationis causa aduenias. Quod ad calamitatem attinet (est Christo laus) adeò mihi molesta non est, vt eximij potius fauoris Dei sacramentum esse ducam, quantò nunquam alias maiori me complexus est. Quapropter nihil est quod ea res, quæ mihi tam salutaris sit, tibi aut iis qui vere mihi fauent dolorem pariat. Fek. Missus à Regina, eiusque Senatu venio, vt te in orthodoxa veritate instituam: etiamsi ea mihi de te spes sit, vt nihil esse opus sentiam. Ioan. Equidem gratias habeo reginæ sublimitati, quæ meî submissæ ipsius famulæ velit non obliuisci, simulque confido, te munere hoc tibi credito pie syncereq; perfunctur ū. Fek. Quid ergo exigitur in Christiano? Ioa. Vt in Deū credat Patre, Filium, & Spiritum sanctū: vnū Deū, & tres personas. Fek. Quid, nihilne aliud in Christiano præter solā fidem in Deum requiritur? Ioa. Maxime vero. nam & credere in eum, & diligere eundē oportet, toto pectore, tota anima, totisque viribus: simul & proximos tanquam nos ipsos. Fek. Recte fides ergo per se sola non iustificat, aut seruat. Ioan. Imò fides, vt inquit Paulus, sola iustificat. Fek. At idem Paulus confirmat, quòd si fidem omnem habuero, charitatem non habeam, nihil sum. Ioan. Verißimum quod dicis, inquit. quo pacto enim eum diligam, in quem non credam? aut qua ratione illi fidam, cuius nulla dilectione afficior? Fides & charitas coniunctim se comitantur, at charitas tamen fide comprehenditur. Fek. Quonam pacto diligendus est proximus? Ioan. Dilectio proximi in iis consistit, vt famefcētem cibo, nudum vestibus, sitientem potu subleuemus. breuiter, vt eadem illi faciamus, quæ nobis ipsis fieri velimus. Fek. Proinde necessario adiungendum est pie agendi studium, alioqui sine operibus fides satis momenti non habet. Ioan. Illud falsum, affirmóque fidem solam adferre salutem: attamē Christianos, ne discipuli degeneres sui præceptoris videantur, piis operibus studere decet, quæ tamen ad salutem ipsa non conferunt. Nam quum omnia egerimus, serui sumus inutiles: solàque in sanguinem Christi fides seruat. Fek. Sacramenta quot sunt? Ioan. Duo, Baptismi, & Cœnæ Dominicæ. Fek. Quid ais, an non septem sunt? Ioan. Quibus Scripturæ argumentis id me doccebis? Fek. De hac re alius erit agendi locus. Dic tandem quid his duobus tuis Sacramentis significatur? Ioan. In Ba-ptismi sacramento aqua foris emundor, intus spiritu renascor & renovor. estque lavacrum hoc ceu sigilli vice, quo sciam me in nu-merum filiorum Dei insertam esse. Rursus Cænæ sacramentum tanquam certum fœdus ac symbolum accipio, me sanguinis illius precio, quem in cruce largiter pro nobis effudit, participem vitæ æternæ fieri. Fek. Quid? annon verum Christi corpus & sanguinem in synaxi percipis? Ioan. Equidem ita credo: in Cœna nec carnem nec sanguinem Christi carnali aliquo modo, sed spirituali magis ratione simul cum pane & vino percipi. qui panis quum frangitur, & vinum quum hauritur, me rite admonent corporis Domini pro me fracti, & sanguinis in cruce profusi. Cum pane itaque & vino, simul beneficia illius & corporis attriti, & sanguinis in cruce exhausti pro peccatis nostris percipio. Fek. Atqui annon Christus expresse hæc habet verba: Accipite, edite, hoc est corpus meum? Quæ lux clarior hac voce esse potest? annon significanter corpus hoc suum appellat? Ioan. Christum ita dixisse, negari non potest: at si tantopere externam faciem verborum spectare ac urgere velimus, dicit & idem alibi, Ego sum vitis, Ego sum ostium. annon Paulus quoque eum vocare quæ non sunt, tanquam ea quæ sunt, affirmat? absit à me tantum facimus, ut unquam verum Christi & naturale corpus carnali ratione esitem[?]: ita enim aut meam auferrem redemptionem, aut duo corpora, duosque Christos, aut duodecim etiam corpora illius statuerem. Siquidem unum corpus in cruce fixum est: tum si alterum illi exedissent, necessario efficeretur, ut aut bina illi corpora suisse, aut si unicum fuerit, hoc ipsum aut in cruce minimè subactum fractumque, aut certè à discipulis non præmansum esse, fateamur oportet. Fek. Perinde est Christo facile pro sua omnipotentia corpus in Cœna præbere ad vescendum & bibendum: ac difficile non erat illi, citra viri commercium de matre nasci virgine, aut pedibus aquis inambulare, siue aliud id genus quoduis miraculum nutu solo potentiæ suæ edere. Ioan. Fateor, si miraculum tum illi in Cœna exhibere libuisset. Sed nihil eiusmodi id temporis decreuit facere: tantummodo id voluit, corporis & sanguinis in cruce pro peccatis atterendi communionem impendere. Caeterum hoc unum mihi respondeas velim, ubinam Christus tum erat, quum haec diceret: Accipite, edite, hoc est corpus meum. annon mensae unà cum suis accubuit unus? necdum enim mortem ante alteram lucem oppetierat. Age, quid accepit ergo aliud nisi panem? quid fregit, nisi panem? quid porrò dedit, nisi panem? Quod itaque accepit, id fregit: quod fregit, dedit: quod dedit, id illi manducabant. Atqui interim toto hoc tempore unà cum illis mensae interfuit, praesensque à discipulis cernebatur, aut ipsi egregiè profecto fallebantur. Fek. Fidem tu quidem collocas in eos authores, quorum levis & instabilis doctrina nunc huc nunc illuc fluctuat. ex eodem ore, quod aiunt, simul & calidum & frigidum spirans: non autem in ecclesiam, cui soli fidere conueniebat. Joan. Fides mea solidissimis divinae Scripturae firmamentis, nequa-quā ecclesiae innititur. Ea enim si vera & genuina fit Ecclesia, sesuáque omnia ad certissimos verbi divini gnomones exigit: non autem contrà, ad huius placita verbum Dei accommodandum est, nec fides mea. An ideo ecclesiae fidem solùm antiquitatis causa? Aut illîne ego ecclesiae fidem sim habitura, quae me bona magnáque cœnae Dominicae parte defraudauit, nec quenquam hominum ad utramque Sacramenti speciem praeter sacrificos admittit? Quod quùm nobis negant, partem nobis salutis negant. Eam igitur non veram esse ecclesiam, nec germanam Christi sponsam, sed sponsam diaboli, liquidò dixerim: quae sic cœnam Domini partim auferendo, partim addendo polluit. Dico huic ecclesiae Deum additurum plagas, partésque eius à libro vitae delituru m. Hóccine didicerunt à Paulo, qui Corinthiis suis utramque Sacramenti partem tradidit? An huic ecclesiae me credere postulatis? absit. Fek. Non sine graui causa id ab ecclesia factum est ad vitandam haeresin, quae tum emergere inceperat. Joan. Quid audio? an ecclesia audebit Christi legem ac instituta antiquare, ob causae quemcunque praetextum? quamobrem igitur Dominus in regem Saulum tantopere offensus dicitur? His aliisque id genus argumentis persuadere nitebatur, ut ecclesiae decretis acquiescerem, sed frustra. multa inter nos alii agitabantur: haec autem praecipua erant capita.
units.tr: Feckenham: Madam, I grieve at your sad and wretched fortune, but I have no doubt that you will bear this bitterness with a steadfast and manly spirit. Joan: Your visit is welcome, provided you come for the sake of Christian exhortation. As for my calamity (thanks be to Christ), it is not so grievous to me that I do not regard it rather as a sign of God's special favour, which has embraced me more closely than at any other time. Therefore there is nothing in this matter, which is so healthful to me, to cause pain to you or to those who truly wish me well. Feckenham: I come sent by the Queen and her Council, to instruct you in the orthodox truth, although I have such hope of you that I feel there is little need. Joan: I indeed thank the Queen's majesty, who is willing not to forget her humble servant, and at the same time I trust that you will discharge this task entrusted to you faithfully and sincerely. Feckenham: What, then, is required of a Christian? Joan: That he believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one God and three persons. Feckenham: What, is nothing else required of a Christian beyond faith alone in God? Joan: Very much more. For one must both believe in him and love him with the whole heart, the whole soul, and all one's strength, and at the same time love one's neighbours as ourselves. Feckenham: Rightly, then, faith by itself alone does not justify or save. Joan: Nay, faith alone justifies, as Paul says. Feckenham: But the same Paul affirms that if I have all faith and have not charity, I am nothing. Joan: What you say is most true; for how could I love him in whom I do not believe? Or on what ground could I trust him by whom I am moved by no love? Faith and charity accompany each other together, yet charity is nonetheless comprehended by faith. Feckenham: In what way is our neighbour to be loved? Joan: Love of neighbour consists in this: that we relieve the hungry with food, the naked with clothing, the thirsty with drink; briefly, that we do to them the very things we would wish done to ourselves. Feckenham: Therefore the zeal for doing good must necessarily be added, otherwise faith without works has little value. Joan: That is false, and I affirm that faith alone brings salvation; yet Christians ought to apply themselves to good works, lest they seem degenerate disciples of their teacher, although these works do not themselves contribute to salvation. For when we have done all things, we are unprofitable servants, and faith alone in the blood of Christ saves. Feckenham: How many sacraments are there? Joan: Two, of Baptism and of the Lord's Supper. Feckenham: What do you say? Are there not seven? Joan: By what arguments of Scripture will you teach me that? Feckenham: That matter will be a place for another discussion. Tell me at last what is signified by these two sacraments of yours? Joan: In the sacrament of Baptism I am cleansed outwardly by water, and inwardly I am born again and renewed by the Spirit; and this washing is like a seal, by which I know that I have been inserted among the number of the sons of God. Again, I receive the sacrament of the Supper as a sure covenant and token, that by the price of that blood which he poured out abundantly for us on the cross, I may be made a partaker of eternal life. Feckenham: What? Do you not receive the true body and blood of Christ in the synaxis? Joan: I indeed believe so: in the Supper the body and blood of Christ are received together with the bread and wine, not in any carnal manner, but rather in a spiritual way. When the bread is broken and the wine is drunk, they duly remind me of the body of the Lord broken for me, and of the blood poured out on the cross. Therefore, with the bread and wine, I receive at the same time the benefits of that body bruised and that blood drained on the cross for our sins. Feckenham: But does not Christ expressly have these words: "Take, eat, this is my body"? What light can be clearer than this voice? Does he not call it his body with meaning? Joan: It cannot be denied that Christ spoke thus; but if we want to insist so strongly on the outward face of the words, he also says elsewhere, "I am the vine," "I am the door." Does not Paul also affirm that God calls those things which are not as though they were? Far be it from me that I should ever imagine the true and natural body of Christ eaten in a carnal manner; for then I would take away my own redemption, or I would posit two bodies and two Christs, or even twelve bodies of his. For one body was fixed on the cross; and if they had then eaten another, it would necessarily follow that either he had two bodies, or, if there was only one, that this very body was either not subdued and broken on the cross, or was certainly not chewed by the disciples, which we must admit. Feckenham: It is just as easy for Christ, by his omnipotence, to offer a body in the Supper to be eaten and drunk, as it was not difficult for him, without the intercourse of a man, to be born of a virgin mother, or to walk on water with his feet, or to perform any other miracle of that kind by the mere nod of his power. Joan: I grant it, if he had then been pleased to exhibit a miracle in the Supper. But he decided to do nothing of that sort at that time; he only wished to offer the communion of his body and blood to be broken for sins. Moreover, I would like you to answer me this one thing: where was Christ then, when he said, "Take, eat, this is my body"? Did he not recline at the table with his own, one of them? For he had not yet suffered death before the next day. Come, what did he take then but bread? What did he break but bread? What, moreover, did he give but bread? So what he took, he broke; what he broke, he gave; what he gave, they ate. And yet all this time he was present at the table with them, and was plainly seen by the disciples, or they were most egregiously deceived. Feckenham: You place your faith in those authors whose light and unstable teaching now wavers this way, now that, breathing out, as they say, both hot and cold from the same mouth; and not in the Church, to which alone it was fitting to trust. Joan: My faith rests on the most solid supports of divine Scripture, by no means on the Church. For if the Church is true and genuine, and conforms all things to the most certain rules of the divine Word, then it is not the other way round: the Word of God is not to be adapted to its decrees, nor is my faith. Or should I trust the Church's faith only because of its antiquity? Or should I then have faith in that Church which has defrauded me of a large and important part of the Lord's Supper, and admits no one to both kinds of the sacrament except the priests? When they deny us this, they deny us a part of salvation. I would therefore plainly say that this is not the true Church, nor the genuine spouse of Christ, but the spouse of the devil, which thus pollutes the Lord's Supper, partly by taking away, partly by adding. I say that God will add plagues to this Church, and will blot out its parts from the book of life. Did they learn this from Paul, who handed down both parts of the sacrament to his Corinthians? Do you ask me to believe in this Church? Far be it from me. Feckenham: The Church did this not without grave cause, to avoid the heresy which had then begun to emerge. Joan: What do I hear? Will the Church dare to abrogate the law and institutions of Christ, on whatever pretext of cause? Why, then, is the Lord said to have been so greatly offended with King Saul? They strove to persuade me by these and similar arguments to acquiesce in the decrees of the Church, but in vain. Many other matters were debated between us; these, however, were the principal heads.

units.la: Finitis his colloquiis, Feknamus[?] quum valere me iussisset disce-dens, dens,dolere se aiebat,addens se certum scire, nos deinceps nunquam conuicturos. Tum ego, Verum: inquam, nunquam nos conuicturos certissimum est, nisi Dominus cor tuum conuertat, scio causam tuam esse perditissimam: itaque rogo Dominum in visceribus misericordiae Iesu Christi ut tibi sanctum Spiritum suum impertiat: video enim illum donasse te magna dicendi facultate. Atque ita tandem discessum est.
units.tr: When these conversations were over, Feknamus[?] took his leave of me as he departed, bidding me farewell, saying that he was sorry, and adding that he knew for certain we would never convert him. Then I said: "It is most certain that we will never convert you unless the Lord converts your heart. I know your cause is utterly lost. So I ask the Lord, in the bowels of the mercy of Jesus Christ, to bestow his Holy Spirit upon you, for I see that he has given you great gifts of speech." And so at last we parted.

units.la: Epistola paraenetica Illustrissimae Heroinae D. Ioannae, quam in calce Testamenti noui inscriptam, sorori Katharinae misit, pridiana nocte ante decollationis suae diem.
units.tr: Exhortatory letter of the most illustrious heroine Lady Joan, which she sent to her sister Katharine, inscribed on the flyleaf of the New Testament, on the night before the day of her beheading.

units.la: MITTO ad te Katharina soror librum, etsi foris quidem nullo auro bracteatum, intus tamen quouis auro & Margaritis infinitis modis superiorem. Codicillus est Diuinae legis, & noui simi testamenti foedus, quod nobiscum miserrimis peccatoribus pepigit Deus. Cuius ductu, si te sequacem praebueris lectricem, perducēris non ad huius mundi omnibus momentis nutantia bona: sed ad verae felicitatis, atque aeternae vitae immortalem possessionem. Docebit te & pie viuendi & bene moriendi rationem. Denique plus hinc tibi lucri accessurum est, quam alioqui ex infelicis & captiui parentis tui, terris & latifundijs omnibus. Quemadmodum enim, si integrae illi res manssissent, & incolumis status, ad te, quae iam proxima es, hereditaria illius omnia bona obuenissent: ita si nunc gnauiter & studiose felicissimum huius testamenti aruum coleueris, eam reperies margaritam, eas tibi opes parabis, quas nec rapaces auaritiae manus eripient, nec fures deprædabuntur, nec corrumpent tineae. Id vnice sit tibi studio (chara soror) vt cum Dauide proficias & meditēris in lege Domini Dei tui. Sic viue vt quotidie discas mori: quo per mortem ad vitam contendas, nunquam deinde perituram. Nec te fallat tenera aetatis tuae flos, & iuuenta fiducia: quasi hoc nomine longiorem tibi vitam pollicens. Aeque enim cito (si euocarit Deus) iuuenes & virgunculae tenerae, atque decrepiti abripiuntur senes. Assidue igitur in hoc incumbe, vt mori assuescas. Hoc quidquid est mundi, abiice: Diabolo obsiste, carnis respue cupiditates, teipsam totam exue, in Domino vnice te oblecta. Sic deplores admissa tua, ne quid desperes tamen. Ita in fide fis alacris, ne interim immodica ruas confidentia. Semperque cum beato Paulo dissolui expete, vt sus[?] cum Christo: in quo quisquis est, etiā si mortuus fuerit, non poterit tamen non viuere. Sic te compara, ac vitam institue, vt cum fideli seruo omnibus horis aduigiles, etiam nocte media: nequum[?] mors ingruerit, tanquam fur nocturnus, te imparatam, ac cum seruis Sathanae stertetem[?], aut cum fatuis virginibus oleo destitutam, aut inter eos quibus vestis deest nuptialis, reperiat: atque ita e nuptijs excludaris. Te in Christo exhilara, quod etiamnum facere te confido. Quoniamque professione & titulo censeris inter Christianos, huius ergo incede vestigijs, cuius gestas nomen, crucemque tolle tuam:peccata tua in eius impone humeros, atque eum perpetuò amplectere. Quódque ad mortem meam attinet, hortor te (adamata soror) mecum pariter laetari velis: quando à corruptione ad incorruptionem me mors ista transfert. Perfuasissimum enim hoc habeo, momentaneæ huius vitæ iacturam, mihi cessuram in vitæ nunquam defuturæ lucrum. quam tibi etiam, germana soror, opto mecum aliquando in Domino contingere. Interim custodiat te pietas illius, vt viuens in timore ipsius, ita moriaris vt integram fidem Christianam ad finem vsque tuearis[?]. A qua nunquam te abduci patiaris neque spe vitæ, nec mortis minis. Nam si veritatem illius abnegabis vllis vitæ huius præmijs, ille te vicissim abnegabit, & vitæ dies contrahet. Sin illi adhærebis, vitam tuam in longum producet in consolationem animæ tuæ, & gloriam ipsius. Ad quam gloriam omnipotens Dominus me modò, te posthac, quum illi videbitur, perducat. Vale, germana soror, ac fiduciam omnem in Domino constitue, in quo solo vniuersum auxilium tuum situm est, Amen. Tua germana soror Ioanna.
units.tr: I send you, sister Katharine, a book which, though it has no gold leaf on the outside, is inwardly far better than any gold and countless pearls. It is a little codicil of the divine law and the covenant of the New Testament, which God has made with us most wretched sinners. If you will follow it as a diligent reader, it will lead you not to the goods of this world, which totter at every moment, but to the immortal possession of true happiness and eternal life. It will teach you both the way of living piously and of dying well. In short, more gain will come to you from it than from all the lands and estates of your unhappy and captive father. For just as, if his affairs had remained whole and his condition unharmed, all his inheritance would have come to you, who are now his nearest heir, so if you now diligently and eagerly cultivate the most fortunate field of this testament, you will find that pearl, and you will acquire riches which no grasping hands of greed can snatch away, which no thieves will plunder, and which no moths will consume. Let this above all be your concern, dear sister: that you may advance with David and meditate on the law of the Lord your God. Live so that you learn to die every day, so that through death you may strive towards life, which will never perish afterwards. Do not let the tender bloom of your age and the confidence of youth deceive you, as if they promised you a longer life. For young men and tender maidens are snatched away just as quickly (if God calls them) as worn-out old men. Therefore apply yourself constantly to this, that you may grow accustomed to dying. Cast off whatever belongs to this world, resist the Devil, reject the lusts of the flesh, strip yourself wholly of yourself, and find your delight in the Lord alone. Thus you will mourn your sins, yet not despair of mercy. Be eager in faith, yet do not rush into immoderate self-confidence. And always, with the blessed Paul, long to be dissolved and to be with Christ, in whom whoever lives, even if he has died, cannot fail to live. Prepare yourself and order your life so that, like a faithful servant, you keep watch at all hours, even at midnight, lest death come upon you like a thief in the night and find you unprepared, snoring with the servants of Satan, or like the foolish virgins without oil, or among those who lack the wedding garment, and so you be shut out from the marriage feast. Rejoice in Christ, as I trust you still do. And since you are reckoned among Christians by your profession and name, walk in the footsteps of him whose name you bear, and take up your cross; lay your sins upon his shoulders and embrace him for ever. As for my death, I beg you, beloved sister, to rejoice with me, since that death transfers me from corruption to incorruption. For I am thoroughly persuaded that the loss of this momentary life will turn to my gain in a life that will never fail. I pray that you too, dear sister, may one day attain this with me in the Lord. Meanwhile may his goodness keep you, so that, living in his fear, you may die holding the Christian faith whole to the end. Never allow yourself to be drawn away from it, either by hope of life or by threats of death. For if you deny his truth for any rewards of this life, he in turn will deny you, and the days of your life will be shortened. But if you cling to him, he will lengthen your life to the comfort of your soul and to his glory. May the almighty Lord bring me to that glory now, and you hereafter, when it pleases him. Farewell, dear sister, and place all your trust in the Lord, in whom alone all your help lies. Amen. Your sister, Joan.

units.la: Verba D.Ioannis quum ad supplicium produceretur.
units.tr: Words of Lady Joan when she was led out to execution.

units.la: Uri fratres Christiani. Sub lege atque per legem sum morti adiudicata, non equidem ob sceleus aliquod aduersus Reginæ maiestatem perpetratum, cuius nullius conscia sum, vt meam in hac re innocentiam apud vos profitear: verùm ob id quia consenseram illi rei ad quam inuita cogebar voluntate. Fateor tamen contra Dominum deliquisse me, tum quia carnis, tum quia mundi huius illecebris & cupiditatibus nimium indulserim, nec vitam ad præscriptum sanctissimæ voluntatis ipsius, eámque normâ quam è verbo eius edoctâ sum, accommodarim. qua de causa, Dominus hoc mortis genere me nunc castigauit, idque maximo merito meo. Quanquam ago gratias beneficentiæ ipsius ex intimo pectore, quod spacium mihi ad deploranda peccata in hoc mundo concesserit. Quamobrem etiam atque etiam vos rogo, Christiani commilitones, dum adhuc vitam spiro, vt iunctis simul precibus mecum, & pro me comprecemini, vt peccata mihi condonet diuina clementia. simulque testes mihi adsitis precor, me fidem Christianam constanter hic ad mortem tueri, fiduciam omnem salutis collocantem non alia in re, nisi in sanguine duntaxat Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Itaque nunc vos rogo omnes, pro me & mecum precemini. Conuersaque ad Feknamum[?]: Dicámne, inquit, pace vestra Psalmum hunc? Age, inquit ille, si libet. Tum illa explicato libro Psalmū LI. Miserere mei à principio ad finē ingenti cordis affectu recitat. Rursusque eo finito erecta vbi in pedes esset, chirothecas & sudarium D. Tylneae ancillae suae, librum D. Brugio fratri illius qui turri praeficiebatur commendauit, mox-que vestes exutura, pallam primum enodare aggreditur. Ibi tum lictor opem ei laturus accurrit. Quem illa esse vt sineret paulisper rogat: atque ad duas vertens ancillas generosas, quae famulatum ei praestabant, illis se exuendam praebuit. Exutae denique mundo, tiara, ac peplo, sudarium illae velandis oculis in manus praebet. Secundum haec lictor flexis genibus supplex ab ea veniam stipulatur: cui illa toto condonauit pectore, rogatque ille vt cōcedat paululum eò vbi stramina ponerentur. Quod vbi fecisset illa, per eum locum truncum in quo auferendum erat ei caput, conspicit.
units.tr: Good Christian brethren, I have been condemned to death by the law and under the law, not indeed for any crime committed against the majesty of the Queen, of which I am conscious of none, so that I may profess my innocence in this matter before you; but because I consented to that deed to which I was forced against my will. Nevertheless I confess that I have sinned against the Lord, both because I indulged too much in the allurements and desires of the flesh and of this world, and because I did not shape my life according to the rule of his most holy will, and of that norm which I have been taught from his Word. For this reason the Lord now chastises me with this kind of death, and I deserve it greatly. Yet I give thanks from the depth of my heart for his goodness, in that he has granted me space in this world to lament my sins. Wherefore I ask you again and again, Christian comrades, while I still breathe, to join your prayers with mine and pray for me, that the divine mercy may pardon my sins. And I ask you to bear witness for me that I here steadfastly hold to the Christian faith unto death, placing all my hope of salvation in nothing else but the blood alone of our Lord Jesus Christ. So now I ask you all to pray for me and with me. Then, turning to Feknamus[?], she said: "With your leave, may I say this psalm?" "Go on," he said, "if you wish." Then, having opened the book, she recited Psalm 51, "Have mercy upon me," from beginning to end with great feeling of heart. When she had finished, she rose and, standing where she was to stand, she entrusted her gloves and handkerchief to Tylney, her maid, and her book to Brugis, brother of the man who was in charge of the tower. Then, about to take off her clothes, she began to unfasten her cloak first. At this the executioner ran up to help her. She asked him to let her be for a little while, and turning to the two noblewomen who were attending her, she offered herself to be undressed by them. Finally, stripped of the world's trappings, of her headdress and her robe, they gave her a handkerchief to bind her eyes. After this the executioner knelt humbly and begged her pardon. She forgave him with her whole heart, and he asked her to step aside a little, to where the straw was laid. When she had done so, she caught sight of the block on which her head was to be cut off.

units.la: Tum illa ad lictorē: Quaeso, inquit, celeri manu rē velis cōficere. Quibus rebus ita praeparatis, procumbit tum in genua adolescentula, rogans hoc modo lictorem, an caput ei prius praecideret, quàm se super truncum reponeret. Non ait ille, ô Domina. Tum illa linteo velamine obductis oculis, ac obtecta facie, Quid, inquit, nunc agam, quid nunc faciam, vbinam illud est? Ibi tum ex astantibus quispiam, caudex vbi esset manu praemonstrauit. Tumque illa humiliter reclinato capite, stratoque ac exporrecto in longum corpore: Domine, inquit, in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum. ad quam vocem imminens cervici lictor, reducto confestim ense, capite plexam humi prostrauit, Anno Domini M.D.LIIII. Februarij XII.
units.tr: Then she said to the executioner: "I beg you, please finish quickly." With these preparations made, the young woman knelt down and asked the executioner in this way whether he would cut off her head before she laid herself down on the block. He said, "No, my lady." Then, with a linen cloth bound over her eyes and her face covered, she said: "What shall I do now? What shall I do? Where is it?" Then one of the bystanders showed her with his hand where the block was. She laid her head humbly down, stretched out her body at full length, and said: "Lord, into your hands I commend my spirit." At this word the executioner, standing over her neck, at once drew back his sword and struck her head off, and she lay prostrate on the ground. In the year of the Lord 1554, on the twelfth of February.

units.la: Erat Ioanna haec quam nos & Ianam populari cognomento diximus, tum quum hoc modo moreretur, annorum XVII. adolescentula, non amplius. Cuius mors hoc mihi indignior fuisse videtur, non solùm ob cultissimi ingenij illius singulares dotes: quippe quae cum Latinis, cumque Hebraicis, sic & Graeca coiunxit vt declamare etiam in ea lingua, eáque in aetate, idque extempore potuisset: verùm & ob hoc ipsum multò magis quòd nulla culpa, nullo merito suo, hoc ei supplicium inflictum fuit: tantùm quòd infelia fato parentes ipsam cum ea copulassent familia.
units.tr: This Joanna, whom we have also called Jane by her popular nickname, was a young girl of seventeen years, no more, when she met her death in this manner. Her death seems to me the more undeserved, not only because of that most refined mind's singular gifts, since she had joined Latin, Hebrew and Greek so well that she could speak even in that last language, and at that age and extempore; but still much more because no fault or desert of her own brought this punishment upon her, only that her parents, through an unhappy fate, had joined her to that family.

units.la: Rogata à D.Ioanne Brugio turris Londinensis toparcho, vt libro ipsius aliquid sua manu inscriberet, quod tanquam gratum sui mnemosynon seruare possetʼ: hanc illi paucis lineis delineauit gnomographiam. Quoniam ita a me, D. praefecte, postulas, vt nonnullum in tam nobili libro tuo calami mei relinquam monumentum: obsequens igitur voluntati tuae, primum te hortor, proque Christiano etiam officio moneo, velis inuocare Dominum, quo cor tuum in Legis ipsius obseruantiam inclinet, teque in viis adiuuet, vegetetque ipsius: ne quando verbum veritatis auferat ab ore tuo. Viue, quasi quotidie moriturus. sicque morere, vt viuas perpetuo, moriturus nunquam. Ne te fallat vitae incertae vitrea fiducia. Mathusalem, sicut te sacrae docent literae quanlibet in longissimos vitae numeros excessit, decessit tamen, habuitque & ipse suum exitum. Et vero, vt sapiens ille concionatur Ecclesiastes, Tempus est nascendi, tempus moriendi: meliorque est dies mortis die natiuitatis. Sua manu Ioanna, in Domino tua.
units.tr: At the request of Sir John Bruges, lieutenant of the Tower of London, that she write something in his book with her own hand, to keep as a token of remembrance, she sketched for him this short motto in a few lines: "Since you ask me thus, Sir Governor, that I leave some memorial of my pen in your so noble book, I therefore, complying with your wish, first urge you and, as a Christian duty, advise you to call upon the Lord, that he may incline your heart to keep his law, help you in your ways and strengthen you, so that he never takes the word of truth from your mouth. Live as if you were to die each day, and so die that you live forever, never to die. Let not the glassy confidence in uncertain life deceive you. Methuselah, as the sacred letters teach you, though he reached the longest span of life, yet died, and he too had his own end. Indeed, as the wise Ecclesiastes preaches, there is a time to be born and a time to die, and the day of death is better than the day of birth. Joanna, yours in the Lord, in her own hand."

units.la: ANTONIVS MAGNEVS.
units.tr: ANTONIUS MAGNEUS.

units.la: Ntonius Magneus Orleaci natus in montibus Aruerniae, nuti captiuitatis Lugdunensium qui supra memorati sunt, ecclesiae Geneuensi attulit. aliorum etiam qui eodem tempore Lutetiae nomine Euangelij comprehensi fuerunt, vt vnumquenque eorum precibus ecclesiae commendaret. Aliquanto post quum propter quaedam sua negotia in Galliam reuerteretur, Biturigibus captus est, proditus a quibusdam sacerdotibus, qui eum in manus Officialis tradiderunt, tribus horis postquam in eam Biturigensium vrbem venissetʼ, xviii. Martij, M.D.LIIII. Post aliquot dies e iurisdictione ac potestate Officialis a iudicibus regijs ereptus fuit, Lutetiamque postea deductus, vbi capitis damnatus est, postea aquam fidei suae confessionem edidisset, atque in carcere omnia opprobria & tormenta summa virtute & constantia pertulisset. Is igitur lingua ei primum praecisa, viuus in platea Malberti crematus est, xiii. Iunij, anno eo qui supra notatus est.
units.tr: Antonius Magneus, born at Orleans in the mountains of Auvergne, brought to the Genevan church news of the captivity of the Lyonnais mentioned above, and also of others who at the same time were seized at Paris for the Gospel, so that the church might commend each of them to its prayers. Some time later, when on account of certain business of his own he was returning to France, he was taken at Bourges, betrayed by some priests who handed him over to the official, three hours after he had come into that city of the Bituriges, on 18 March 1554. A few days later he was snatched from the jurisdiction and power of the official by the royal judges, and afterwards was led to Paris, where he was condemned to death. After he had published a confession of his faith, and had endured in prison all insults and the greatest torments with great courage and constancy, his tongue was first cut out, and then he was burned alive in the Place Maubert, on 13 June of the year noted above.

units.la: GVILIELMVS D'ALENÇON.
units.tr: GUILLAUME D'ALENÇON.

units.la: D doctrinam Euangelij nostris temporibus promulgandam atque illustrandam, insignis extat opera eorum, qui libros eos quibus sacra Scriptura pure piéque est explicata, in Papatum deportarunt, atque ita illos qui in tam miseranda dispersione omni pietatis doctrina & consolatione sunt priuati, adiuuerunt. In eorum numero egregia fides & opera Ecclesiæ Christi maximè opportuna extitit Gulielmi Alençonij, patria Monsalbani, cuius memoria nobis perdigna est visa quæ literis mandaretur. Nam quum is sæpe in varias regni Galliæ prouincias profectus esset, tandem Monspessuli in Gallia Narbonensi captus est, à falsis fratribus proditus, atque coniectus in carcerem ab iis qui in ea vrbe iurisdictionem habet. Qui quum eum de fide ac religione quam profiteretur, interrogassent, viderentque in pura Euangelij confessione firmum & constantem esse, die Sabbathi, qui fuit vii.dies Ianuarij, M.D.LIIII. capitis eum damnauerunt.
units.tr: For the teaching of the Gospel, to be spread and made clear in our times, there stands out the work of those who carried into the Papacy those books in which Holy Scripture has been purely and piously explained, and so helped those who in such a pitiful dispersion were deprived of all the teaching and consolation of piety. Among these the excellent faith and work most useful to the Church of Christ were those of Guillaume d'Alençon, a native of Montauban, whose memory seemed to us worthy to be committed to writing. For although he had often travelled into various provinces of the kingdom of France, at last he was taken at Montpellier in Languedoc, betrayed by false brethren, and thrown into prison by those who hold jurisdiction in that city. When they had questioned him about the faith and religion he professed, and saw that he was firm and steadfast in his pure confession of the Gospel, they condemned him to death on Saturday, the seventh day of January 1554.

units.la: Fuit autem alius arte sua panni tonsor pro eadem veritatis causa captus atque in carcerem inclusus, quem infirmitate carnis debilitatum, atque à vera Filij Dei confessione auocatum, iudices ea condemnarunt pœna, vt honorariam, quam vocant, emendationem subiret, atque in morte Alençonij spectator adesset. Sed eo ipso die, qui ad eas pœnas irrogandas erat constitutus, Deus eam Alençonio gratiam largitus est, vt eum ita territum ac fractum, quum verbo Dei, tum suo exemplo vehementer confirmauerit, atque ad constantiam verè Christianam reuocauerit. Itaque quum nouam animi virtutem recepisset, à iudicibus postulauit, vt aut reduceretur in carcerem, aut vna cum ipso Alençonio cremaretur: dixitque se nullam erroris emendationem aliam facturum, quam eam confessionem, qua moriens tandem Euangelij doctrinam, quam Alençonius confiteretur, confirmaret. Hac fidei firmitate & constantia duo præstantes Iesu Christi martyres, Monspessuli combusti fuerunt. Librarius Alençonius die vii.Ianuarij: alter verò die Martis sequenti, qui fuit dies decima eiusdem mensis, anno M.D.LIIII.
units.tr: There was also another, a cloth-shearer by trade, who was taken for the same cause of truth and shut up in prison; the judges, finding him weakened in the flesh and turned away from the true confession of the Son of God, condemned him to the penalty of making what they call an honorary recantation, and to be present as a spectator at Alençon's death. But on that very day which had been appointed for inflicting these penalties, God granted Alençon such grace that, having found him so terrified and broken, he strongly confirmed him both by the word of God and by his own example, and called him back to truly Christian constancy. So when he had received a new strength of spirit, he asked the judges either to be taken back to prison or to be burned together with Alençon himself; and he said that he would make no other amendment of his error than that confession by which, dying at last, he would confirm the doctrine of the Gospel which Alençon professed. By this firmness and constancy the two excellent martyrs of Jesus Christ were burned at Montpellier: the bookseller Alençon on 7 January, and the other on the following Tuesday, which was the tenth day of the same month, in the year 1554.

units.la: PETRVS DV VAL.
units.tr: PETER DU VAL.

units.la: Odem anno M.D.LIIII. Petrus Vallensis ex oppido Pantillaco, quinque ab vrbe Tolosa milliaribus, artem profitēs sutoriam, Nemausi in Gallia Narbonensi, nomine Euangelij comprehensus est. Is quum purissimam religionis Christianæ doctrinam constantissimè confessus esset: vt conscios eiusdem doctrinæ homines fideles indicaret, grauissima tormenta & cruciamenta corporis perpessus est. quibus tamen mutilatus, fractus, oppressusque, neminem unquam nominavit. Postremo in ea urbe vivus poenam ignis usitatam sensit, ac maximo fortissimoque animo sustinuit, anno M. D. L IIII.
units.tr: In the same year, 1554, Peter Vallensis (Peter du Val) of the town of Pantillac, five miles from the city of Toulouse, a shoemaker by trade, was seized at Nîmes in Narbonese Gaul on account of the Gospel. Although he confessed the purest doctrine of the Christian religion most steadfastly, he was made to suffer the most severe torments and bodily tortures so that he might point out the fellow-believers who shared that doctrine. Yet although he was maimed, broken and crushed by these, he never named anyone. Finally, in that city, he was burned alive, the usual punishment by fire, and he endured it with the greatest and bravest spirit, in the year 1554.

units.la: RICHARDUS LE FEURE.
units.tr: RICHARD LE FEVRE.

units.la: MAXIMA ac justissima est causa, cur Deum omni gloria celebrare debeamus, quod non ita pridem Richardum Feurum prosessione aurifabrum, patriaque Rothomagensem pro nomine Filij sui Jesu Christi confitendo ac tuendo in extremum certamen produxerit. Nam is antea eadem ob causam Lugduni comprehensus, in carcere diu fuerat, anno M.D.LI. ubi veritatem Evangelij ita constanter defendit, ut capitis a judicibus eius urbis damnatus fuerit. A qua tamen sententia Lutetiam ad Curiam supremam quorundam hominum impulsu appellaut. Cum autem jam esset in itinere ut Lutetiam duceretur, ereptus fuit e manibus eorum, qui cum ad illud parlamentum deducebant. ac quanvis multa sint scripta & dicta praeclare in eius prima captivitate ac confessione, monumetis literarum digna: quia tamen mors, quae jure optimo est gravissimum quoddam sigillum eorum omnium dictorum atque scriptorum, eo tempore non est consequuta, nos in hac historia ea praetermisimus, ac pro omnibus quae tum acta sunt, unam tantum epistolam inservimus, quam Joannes Calvinus ei rescripsit, respondens ad ea quae Richardus per literas ab illo quaesuerat, ut quemadmodum scribebat, his sublevatus, instructus ac munitus, melius sustinere posset ea quae inimici, tum aspectabiles, tum etiam spirituales ei obiycerent. Itaque, cum ea epistola summam tum eruditionem, tum consolationem complectatur, nos eam hoc loco adscripsimus, quemadmodum caeteras omnes eius viri literas ad afflictos consolandos missas, ut temporis atque ordinis ratio postulabat, quo aliquis consolationis fructus ad homines fideles pervenī-re posset.
units.tr: It is a great and most just reason why we ought to celebrate God with all glory, that not long ago he brought Richard Feure, a goldsmith by profession and a native of Rouen, to the final contest, for confessing and defending the name of his Son Jesus Christ. He had previously been arrested for the same cause at Lyon, and had been held in prison for a long time, in the year 1551, where he defended the truth of the Gospel so steadfastly that the judges of that city condemned him to death. Some men, however, urged him to appeal this sentence to the Supreme Court at Paris. When he was already on the road to be taken to Paris, he was snatched from the hands of those who were leading him to that parliament. And although many things were written and said admirably in his first imprisonment and confession, worthy of being preserved in writing, nevertheless, because the death which is the most excellent seal of all such sayings and writings did not follow at that time, we have passed over those things in this history. Instead of all that was done then, we have inserted only one letter, which John Calvin wrote back to him, answering what Richard had asked of him in writing, so that, as he wrote, he might be supported, instructed and fortified by it, and might better endure those things which his enemies, both visible and spiritual, were throwing at him. Therefore, since that letter contains both great learning and great consolation, we have added it here, as we have done with all the other letters of this man sent to comfort the afflicted, in the order and manner which the course of time required, so that some fruit of consolation might reach the faithful.

units.la: Epistola Joannis Calvini Geneva ad Richardum Feurum: milia[?], gravissimique tum consilii, tum solatii plenissima.
units.tr: Letter of John Calvin from Geneva to Richard Feure: [?] and most full of both weighty counsel and comfort.

units.la: Quemadmodum, frater charissime, Deus te vocavit, ut Evangelio suo testimonium dares, ita minimè debes dubitare, quin virtute Spiritus sui te confirmet, ac quod iam in te instituit perficiat, séque in te victorem aduersus omnes inimicos suos ostendat. Quanquam tri-umphi quidem Iesu Christi, iudicio mundi contemnantur. Cum nos quidem in summo versemur opprobrio, impii vero superbia sua gloriáque extollantur. id tamen non impedit, quo minus & illi confundantur potentia veritatis eius, quam Deus nobis in ore posuit: & nos in cordibus nostris sustentemur, atque ita confirmemur, ut aduersus Sathanam omnesque eius ministros gloriari vere possimus, expectantes illum diem illustrem, in quo gloria Dei cum impiorum atque incredulorum confusione plenissime reuelabitur. Quod tu ad hunc vsque diem de singulari eius bonitate es expertus, id in optimam spem debet te inducere, atque in ea fiducia confirmare, eum in posterum tibi nunquam defuturum. Interea cum ora ut ipsius gratia magis ac magis intelligas & sentias quantus thesaurus sit eius doctrinæ, pro qua tu hanc dimicationem suscepisti: cui quidem vita tua comparata, tibi minime chara aut pretiosa esse debet. Tuos etiam attolle oculos in cælum ad optimum ac fidelissimum Dominum Iesum, qui tuus certissimus vindex futurus est, cum tu nullā aliam ob causam, quam propter sanctissimum eius nomen vincula ista patiaris. Cogitatione complectere eam immortalem gloriam, quam ipse nobis acquisiuit, quo maiore animi æquitate & patientia afflictiones, in quibus hoc tempore versaris, ferre possis. Optimum ac benignissimum Deum sine vlla intermissione ora, ut pro ea examinis ratione ad quod fidem tuam adduxit, eam quoque gratiam tibi impertiat, ut vsu virtutem promissionum suarum sentire possis: ac cum ipse omnis lucis sit Pater, ita mentem tuam illuminet, ut omnes fumi, quos impii homines tibi offundere poterunt, oculos tuos non obfuscent & obscurent, neque fallaciæ captionesque eorum mentem tuam perstringant atque impediant, quo minus tu semper clarissimum illum ac salutarē solem Iesum Christum, verum Dei Filium contueri possis.
units.tr: Just as God, dear brother, has called you to give testimony to his Gospel, so you must not doubt in the least that he will strengthen you by the power of his Spirit, and bring to completion what he has begun in you, and show himself victorious in you against all his enemies. Indeed, the triumphs of Jesus Christ are despised in the judgment of the world. While we stand in the greatest disgrace, the ungodly are lifted up in their pride and boasting. Yet this does not prevent them from being confounded by the power of his truth, which God has put in our mouths, and from our being sustained in our hearts, and so confirmed that we may truly glory against Satan and all his ministers, looking for that bright day on which the glory of God will be fully revealed, to the confusion of the impious and unbelieving. What you have so far experienced of his singular goodness should lead you into the best hope and confirm you in that trust, that he will never fail you in the future. Meanwhile, I pray that you may understand and feel more and more, by his grace, how great a treasure is that doctrine for which you have undertaken this struggle, to which your life ought to be counted as of little value and no price to you. Lift up your eyes also to heaven, to the best and most faithful Lord Jesus, who will surely be your avenger, since you suffer these chains for no other cause than his most holy name. Keep before your mind that immortal glory which he himself has acquired for us, so that you may bear with greater equanimity and patience the afflictions in which you now stand. Pray without ceasing to the best and most kind God, that according to the measure of examination by which he has brought your faith to this point, he may also grant you this grace, that you may by experience feel the power of his promises. And since he is the Father of all light, may he so illuminate your mind that all the smoke which wicked men can cast before you does not dim or darken your eyes, nor do their deceits and snares bind and hinder your mind, so that you may always be able to behold that most clear and saving sun, Jesus Christ, the true Son of God.

units.la: De ratione vero ac moderatione, qua aduersariorum argumentis respondendum est, tu quidem prudenter facis cum simplicitate & modestia illis respondens pro modo fidei tuæ, quemadmodum scriptum est, Credidi, idcirco loquar. Quanquam omnia quidem eorum acuta argumenta, quæ ad oppugnandam veritatem afferunt, nihil aliud sunt quam stolida & ridicula hominum commenta: tu tamen acquiescas in ea cognitione, quam Deus tibi impertuit, eáque contentus, testimonium eius veritati sine vlla simulatione da. Nam quanuis illi irrideant quod abs te dicetur, illud tamen ad eos perturbandos & confundendos vim cuiusdam fulminis habebit, quum in Deo eiusque verbo fundatum atque constitutum erit. Neque vero tu ignoras eum qui promisit se os suis & huiusmodi sapientiam largiturum, cui omnes aduersarij resistere non poterunt. pete igitur ab eo vt te ita regat & gubernet, sicut opus esse cognoscet. Quanquam id quidem eos minime impediet, quo minus, qua sunt audacia & temeritate, te haereseos condemnent: tamen id æquiore animo ferendum est, quod non est nouum atque inusitatum: sed ita semper cum Apostolis, Prophetis, Martyribusque faćtitatum[?]. Actuarius quidem, quæ ei videbuntur, tantum in acta referet: sed id non impediet quo minus confessio tua coram Deo eiusque Angelis perscripta extet, eámque vim ei dabit, quam communis Ecclesiæ ædificatio postulare videbitur.
units.tr: As for the manner and moderation with which the arguments of your opponents must be answered, you act wisely in answering them with simplicity and modesty, according to the measure of your faith, as it is written: "I believed, therefore I spoke." Although all their subtle arguments, which they bring forward to attack the truth, are nothing but the foolish and ridiculous inventions of men, you should nevertheless rest content in the knowledge which God has given you, and, being satisfied with it, bear witness to the truth without any pretence. For although they mock what you say, it will have the force of a thunderbolt to disturb and confound them, once it is grounded and established in God and his word. Nor do you forget that he who promised to give his own mouth and such wisdom will give it, and that none of the adversaries will be able to resist it. Therefore ask him to rule and guide you as he knows to be needful. Yet this will not prevent them, with all their boldness and rashness, from condemning you as a heretic. Still, this must be borne with a more even mind, since it is not new or unusual; it has always been so with the Apostles, Prophets and Martyrs. The clerk will indeed record in the acts whatever seems fit to him, but this will not prevent your confession, written down before God and his angels, from standing, and it will give it the force which the common edification of the Church shall seem to require.

units.la: Ego paucis aliquot capita attingam, in quibus conati sunt te conturbare, molestiáque afficere. Vt demonstrarent tibi nos non sola Dei gratia iustificari, allegarunt Zachariam aliosque multos in Scriptura Iustos fuisse appellatos. In eo autem considerare conuenit, quemadmodum eos Deus tales acceperit, iustósque habuerit. Quod si reperiatur id gratuita eius bonitate fieri, ea ipsis ignoscentis quæ in eis requiruntur, nec eis vitia peccataque attribuentis, omne iam meritum exclusum est.
