Etenim quum dicitur nos sola fide per Christum iustificari, primum intelligimus nos plane esse maledictos, neque quicquam aliud in nobis quam peccatum esse, neque posse quicquam boni facere, nisi quatenus Spiritu Dei sancto, vt membra Filij eius regimur ac gubernamur. Præterea, quanuis Deus eam nobis gratiam impertiat, vt in timore ipsius ambulemus, longissimè tamen ab eo absumus, vt officio nostro satisfaciamus, præstemúsque eam iustitiam, quam is in sua Lege à nobis requirit. Est autem scriptum, eum esse maledictum, qui non omnia quæ scripta sunt præstiterit. Itaque nullum aliud iustitiæ salutisque perfugium habemus, quam ad purissimum Iesu Christi sanguinem, cuius sacrificio, quod in eius morte ad sanctificationem nostram factum est, omnia vitia nostra & peccata eluuntur.
units.tr: I will touch briefly on a few points on which they have tried to disturb and trouble you. To show you that we are not justified by the grace of God alone, they have cited Zechariah and many others who are called righteous in Scripture. But in this matter we ought to consider how God accepted them as such, and held them righteous. If it is found that this was done by his free goodness, forgiving them the things which are required in them, and not imputing to them their faults and sins, then all merit is already excluded. For when it is said that we are justified by faith alone through Christ, we first understand that we are plainly accursed, that there is nothing in us but sin, and that we can do no good at all, except insofar as we are ruled and governed by the Holy Spirit of God, as members of his Son. Moreover, although God grants us that grace that we may walk in his fear, we are nevertheless very far from him in satisfying our duty and performing that righteousness which he requires of us in his Law. And it is written that he is accursed who does not perform all the things which are written. Therefore we have no other refuge for righteousness and salvation than the most pure blood of Jesus Christ, by whose sacrifice, which was made in his death for our sanctification, all our faults and sins are washed away.

units.la: Hoc eodem modo Deus opera quae nos ipsius virtute facimus, grata & accepta habet: quanuis ea semper aliquibus vitiorum maculis affecta sint. Ita qui voluerit niti suis meritis, is quasi in aere suspensus erit: itaque de sua salute incertus, ut quasi omni vento agitari videatur. Denique qui aliquid se mereri arbitrantur, ij Deum sibi deinctum atque obligatum huiusmodi opinione faciunt, cum nos omnia eius bonitati plane debeamus. Nos quidem meritis diuites & abiudátes [?] erimus, si in Iesu Christo sumus ac viuimus. Eius vero gratia priuati, statuamus ne guttā quidē boni nos habituros. Neque vero debes coturbari si inimici nomen Mercedis tibi allegant. nam Deus mercedem reddit suis, non quod illi ea digni sunt, sed quod ea opera quae in ipsis posuit, pro sua gratia accipit, cum ea in sanguine Filij sui consecrauit, ut inde omnem aestimationem dignitatemque accipiant. Itaque merces, quam Deus suis fidelibus promittit, habet antea constitutam remissionem peccatorum, eamque gratiam, qua eos ut filios suos in ipsorum infirmitatibus prosequitur ac tuetur, non acerbe omnia exigens, sed clementer multa ignoscens. Et certe hoc iustitiae nomen eam vim habet, ut cum Deus nos pro iustis accepit, gratos quoque & charos habeat: id quod sola fide in Christo, in quo vno causa salutis nostrae est constituta, consequimur.
units.tr: In the same way God accepts and approves the works that we do by his power, although they are always stained with some spots of faults. Thus whoever wishes to rest on his own merits will be like one hanging in the air, uncertain of his salvation, so that he seems to be tossed about by every wind. Finally, those who think they deserve anything make God indebted and bound to them by such an opinion, whereas we owe everything entirely to his goodness. We indeed shall be rich in merits if we are in Jesus Christ and live in him; but if we are deprived of his grace, we must reckon that we shall have not a drop of good. Nor should you be troubled if your enemies throw the name of reward at you. For God gives reward to his own, not because they are worthy of it, but because he accepts the works which he has placed in them by his grace, after he has consecrated them in the blood of his Son, so that they receive from that all their value and worth. Thus the reward which God promises to his faithful has as its prior condition the forgiveness of sins, and that grace by which he cherishes and protects them as his sons in their weaknesses, not exacting everything harshly but kindly pardoning many things. And indeed this name of righteousness has such force that when God accepts us as righteous, he also holds us as pleasing and dear to him; and this we obtain by faith alone in Christ, in whom alone the cause of our salvation has been established.

units.la: Diuus quidem Iacobus id nomen alia significatione accipit, cum ait operibus ipsam fidem adiuuari, ut nos iustificemur. Intelligit enim tum approbari, ac re ipsa declarari nos iustos esse, cum in bonis operibus illustria extant testimonia. Neque vero Iacobus disputat in quo salus nostra est fundata, & quo nostra fiducia niti debeat: sed tantummodo quemadmodum vera fides cognoscatur & cernatur, ut nullus ea abutatur, solo eius nomine leuiter se efferens. Si illi ad te redeant, ut importune tibi negotium facessant, spero Deum os tibi daturum, quo possis eos vincere.
units.tr: Holy James, to be sure, uses the word in a different sense when he says that faith is helped by works, so that we are justified. He means that we are shown and declared to be righteous when clear evidence of good works is present. James is not arguing here where our salvation is grounded or where our trust should rest. He is only showing how true faith is recognised and seen, so that no one abuses it by boasting of its name alone. If they come back to you and trouble you with their importunity, I trust God will give you the words with which you can overcome them.

units.la: De intercessione virginis Mariae, eorumque Sanctorum, qui iam vita defuncti sunt, redeundum semper est ad hoc principium, non esse nostrum aduocatos constituere in paradiso: sed eam authoritatem ad Deum pertinere, qui Iesum Christum vnum pro omnibus aduocatum patronúmque constituit. Item preces nostras debere fieri in fide, atque ex verbo Dei institui & adhiberi, sicut x. Rom. Paulus monet. At in toto Dei verbo nulla reperitur syllaba eius quam perhibet aduocationis. omnes igitur eorum orationes sunt profanæ, ac Deo ingratæ. Quod si obijciant nobis non esse interdictum, quo minus illud Sanctorum patrocinium imploremus atque adhibeamus, facilis responsio est, nihil nobis tentandum aut instituendum esse ex ingenio nostro ac sensu proprio, ne in re quidem minori: minimè uero in oratione, quæ multo est maior ac sanctior, quàm ut in ea instituenda atque adhibenda leuitatem opinionis nostræ sequi debeamus. Quin & iam negare nullo modo possunt, quod perfugium suum in aduocatione Sanctorum constitutum habeant, id ex mera diffidentia existere, quasi unus Iesus Christus ipsis non sufficiat. Quod uero excipiunt, charitatem Sanctorum non esse diminutam, facile est respondere, charitatem conformare se atque accommodare ad eam Dei uoluntatem, qua certa ac definita unicuique officia præscribuntur. Is autem uult, ut qui remanent in hac uita se in iis precibus exerceat, quibus alij alios Deo commendent: mortuorum uero nulla unquam mentio facta est. Atque in his quidem rebus nihil ex nostro ingenio cogitare debemus: sed in eo solum acquiescere, quod in Scriptura propositum est atq; præscriptum.
units.tr: On the intercession of the Virgin Mary and of those saints who have already departed this life, we must always return to this principle: it is not for us to appoint advocates in paradise. That authority belongs to God, who appointed Jesus Christ alone as the one advocate and patron for all. Likewise, our prayers ought to be made in faith and framed and offered according to the Word of God, as Paul admonishes in Romans 10. But not one syllable of the intercession they claim can be found in the whole Word of God. All their prayers, therefore, are profane and displeasing to God. If they object that we are not forbidden to implore and use the patronage of the saints, the answer is easy: we must attempt or undertake nothing from our own wit and private opinion, not even in a minor matter, and least of all in prayer, which is far greater and holier, so that in framing and using it we should follow the lightness of our own opinion. Indeed, they cannot deny that they have set up their refuge in the intercession of the saints, and that this arises from sheer distrust, as if Jesus Christ alone were not enough for them. As to their objection that the saints' love has not been diminished, it is easy to reply that love must conform and accommodate itself to the will of God, by which definite duties are prescribed to each. He wills that those who remain in this life exercise themselves in those prayers by which some commend others to God; but of the dead no mention has ever been made. In these matters we ought to think nothing from our own wit, but to rest only in what is set forth and prescribed in Scripture.

units.la: Quod autem afferunt ex Genesi, nomen Abrahæ & Isaac inuocandum esse post ipsorum mortem, textus quidem ita habet: sed periculum est eum locum ad hoc propositum adducere. Id autem scriptum est XLVIII. Genes. vbi memoratur, Iacobum quum Ephraim & Manasse filios Iosephi benediceret, Deum orasse ut nomen patrum suorum Abraham & Isaac, & suum ipsius super eos duos Iosephi filios inuocaretur, uelut super duo capita earum tribuum quæ ex ipso orientur. Hoc autem perinde est acsi diceret, ut illi censeantur atque ita habeantur in numero duodecim tribuum, ut duo capita efficiant, quasi primo gradu filij ipsius essent. Præterea, quum illi nati essent in AEgypto, eos sua precatione ad eam progeniem adiungit, quam Deus benedixerat ac sanctificauerat: quoniam eo quidem tempore externa quadam specie ab illo sancto semine ac genere quasi segregati esse uidebantur. Ita hæc loquendi forma nihil aliud significat, quam nomine Abrahæ appellari, atque ex illius progenie censeri, quemadmodum 4. Esaiæ etiam dictum est, nomen viri super mulierem coniugem invocari, propterea quod ea est ὑπήκοος[?], atque in potestate gubernationeque mariti constituta. De sancto Ignatio, quem tibi proferunt, non necesse est multis eis verbis respondere. Extat in eius libro huiusmodi sententia, in qua dicit Iesum Christum unum sibi esse pro omni antiquitate. Hoc igitur te uno verbo arma, ut eos ad puram Evangelij doctrinam revoces. Quoniam autem ego ea sententia contra Papistas usus sum, inde illi colorem quendam accipiunt, ut dicant me approbare eum librum ac magnificare. Ne vero id te conturbet, ego tibi affirmo eo in libro huiusmodi acervum nugamentorum esse adeo absurdorum, ut monachi hodie ineptiora ac magis nugatoria scribere non possent. Sed quoniam tu nullam habes linguae Latinae cognitionem, multo etiam minus Graecae, in qua sanctus Ignatius scripsit (siquidem ea illius sunt quae nomine ipsius inscribuntur) nihil opus est te in huiusmodi disputatione ingredi. Satis quidem sit tibi ita illis respondere, ut sequendo Iesum Christum mundi lucem, errare nullo modo possis. Quod ad veteres Doctores attinet, ii qui in huiusmodi rebus magis sunt exercitati, ea poterunt dicere, quibus os illorum obstruatur. Tu vero tantum fidem tuam in verbo Iesu Christi, qui fallere aut mentiri non potest, fundatā & plane constitutam habeas. Nam illud unum est, quo veteres Doctores referunt omnia, adversariosque remittunt cum huiusmodi testificatione quod eatenus fidem sibi volunt haberi, quatenus ipsorum ratio cum iis consentire videbitur quae Deus nos docuit, atque in eius verbo continentur. Porro in quaestione de sacramento Cœnæ, quū de sua transubstantiatione tibi loquentur, respondere apte potes, omnes eas sententias quas adducunt, etiamsi ita essent intelligendae ut ipsi arbitrantur, eas tamen non posse ad Missam accōmodari. Nam sicut est dictum, Hoc est corpus meum, & sanguis meus, ita statim adiunctum est, Accipite, edite, bibiteque omnes de hoc calice. At inter eos unus tantummodo est qui comedit: populo vero dimidia pars sacramenti impertitur, idque in festo Paschae. Quinetiam in hoc ipsorum abusu maius inest malum, quod pro eo quod Iesus Christus dicat, Accipite: illi hac opinione adducūtur, quasi Deo sacrificium unicum perpetuumque offerant. Itaque ut his sacramenti verbis iuuarentur, oporteret cos habere verum Cœnæ usum, quem non habent. Cæterum tu debes semper testificari te nullo modo negare quin Iesus Christus nobis suum corpus det, modo illud in cælo quæram[?]. In omnibus autem argutis cauillationibus quibus tecum possunt agere, tibi quidem nihil præter id quod vidisti, declarandum est, cum optime scias persuasumque habeas, Deum esse a quo id acceperis ac didiceris. Nam fides quidem nostra valde esset tenuis ac ieiuna, si in hominum doctrina atque opinione fundata esset. nihil igitur melius est, quam perpetuo meditari eam doctrinam, in qua tota vis nostræ fidei religionisque Christianæ consistit, ut in tempore & loco demonstrare possis, te non temere credidisse. Ac quemadmodum initio dixi, si inimici veritatis pro honore suo ambitiose pugnant, tui est officij ac muneris in hac dimicatione ita modeste versari, ut contra omnes ipsorum calumnias captionesque Deo gloriam tribuas: neque vero aliud requiras, quam clypeum veræ ac syncerę confessionis, qua id quod Deus in animo tuo impressit, ingenuæ testari possis. Multo vero minus debet id te perturbare atque angere, si me aut alios impudenter criminantur & calumniantur, cum eam iam licentiam sunt adepti, ut sine ulla ratione maledicant. Feramus patienter omnia probra & crimina, quæ illi in nos conijcient, nec enim meliores sumus diuo Paulo, qui dicebat, nobis per huiusmodi infamias & contumelias eundum esse. Agamus id modo quod rectum est: cum de nobis maledicetur, id erit huiusmodi, ut in eo conscientiam nostram sublcuare sustentaréque possimus. Atque etiam cum illi in nos huiusmodi calumnias conferunt, nos magnam habemus causam, cur Deo gratias agamus, cum ita coram eo atque hominibus conscientiam nostram puram habemus, longéque ab omni prauitatis suspicione absumus: Deinde quanuis sumus peccatores miseri, multorumque malorum ita pleni, ut ea gemere perpetuo debeamus: orandus tamen Deus est, ne permittat impios homines maledicere de nobis, nisi mentiendo, ut ipsi hoc modo suo ore condemnentur, quod de nobis ea impudenter confingant, quæ vere in seipsis deprehendere poterant, nisi amentia ac furore occæcati impedirentur. Lætemur igitur ac gloriemur cum omni humilitate in gratia Dei nostri, cum huiusmodi miseros homines videmus, quasi quosdam temulétos in sua turpitudine gloriari. Si tibi molestum est, cùm audis eos de nobis calùniosè detrahere: multò certè molestius esse debet, cùm audis eos de ipso Domino gloriæ ac saluatore Christo contumeliosè indignéque loquentes. Nam nos quidem tota cum nostra innocentia digni sumus vt omni confusione opprimamur. Interea autem consolare te in optimo Deo nostro, qui pro sua gratia ita nos cum Filio suo coniunxit, vt omnes inferorū diaboli, atque omnes mundi iniqui & impij, ab eius coniunctione atq; amore nos nunquam diuellere possint. Lætare porrò in eo, quòd optima conscientia causam illius tueris, sperésque eum virtutem tibi daturum qua id quod ipse te ferre voluerit, fortiter & constanter ferre possis. Nos quidem in precibus nostris eam memoriam & charitatem tibi præstamus, quam debemus. Denique supplices oramus, vt qui pro sua gratia ad veritatem suam tuendā te delegit, istúmque in locum deduxit, idem tibi omnia Spiritus sui dona adiumentáque impertiat, quæ in hoc officio tam honorifico ac testimonio requiruntur, summámque præstet perseuerantiā, eámque prudentiam spiritualē, vt incrementum regni eius ac nominis tantummodò propositum habeas, illúdque vitæ tuæ anteponas: idémque se tuum defensorē, protectorémque ita ostendat, vt id & tu ad consolationē tuā sentire possis, & cæteri etiā animaduertere, consolationémque accipere. Omnes fratres, qui hic sunt, tibi in Domino plurimum salutis dicunt, gaudéntque quòd ipse tantam in te potēctiam exhibuerit: eámque misericordiam ex istis tuis vinculis capiunt, quam fraternus amor postulat: à Deóque optimo petunt, vt te summa bonitate sua & misericordia complectatur & tueatur. Genevæ, xix. Ianuarij. Tuus frater in Domino Ioan. Caluinus.
units.tr: As for what they bring from Genesis, that the name of Abraham and Isaac is to be invoked after their death, the text indeed reads so, but it is dangerous to bring that passage to this purpose. It is written in Genesis 48, where we are told that Jacob, when he blessed Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, prayed that the name of his fathers Abraham and Isaac, and his own name, might be invoked over those two sons of Joseph, as over the two heads of the tribes that would spring from him. But this is just as if he had said that they should be counted and reckoned among the twelve tribes, so as to make two heads, as though they were, in the first degree, his own sons. Moreover, since they had been born in Egypt, he joins them by his prayer to that offspring which God had blessed and sanctified, because at that time they seemed in an outward way to have been set apart from that holy seed and race. Thus this manner of speaking means nothing other than to be called by the name of Abraham and to be reckoned in his posterity, just as it is said in Isaiah 4 that the name of a man is invoked over a woman who is his wife, because she is [ὑπήκοος] subject, and placed under the power and government of her husband. As for Saint Ignatius, whom they put forward to you, it is not necessary to answer their many words. In his book there is such a sentence, in which he says that Jesus Christ is for him the one antiquity. Therefore arm yourself with this one word, so that you may call them back to the pure doctrine of the Gospel. Since I used that sentence against the Papists, they take from it a certain colour, saying that I approve and magnify that book. So that this may not trouble you, I assure you that the book contains such a heap of trifles, so absurd, that the monks of today could not write anything more foolish or more trifling. But since you have no knowledge of the Latin tongue, and much less of Greek, in which Saint Ignatius wrote (if indeed those are his writings which go under his name), there is no need for you to enter into such a dispute. It will be enough for you to answer them thus: that by following Jesus Christ, the light of the world, you can in no way go astray. As for the ancient teachers, those who are more practised in such matters can say what will stop their mouths. You, however, should have your faith simply founded and settled in the word of Jesus Christ, who cannot deceive or lie. For this is the one thing to which the ancient teachers refer everything, and they send their adversaries back with this declaration: that they wish to be believed only so far as their reasoning seems to agree with what God has taught us and what is contained in his Word. Further, in the question concerning the sacrament of the Supper, when they speak to you of their transubstantiation, you can aptly reply that all the sayings they bring forward, even if they were to be understood as they themselves think, still cannot be applied to the Mass. For as it was said, "This is my body and my blood," so it was immediately added, "Take, eat, and drink all of you of this cup." But among them only one person eats; to the people only half of the sacrament is given, and that at the Feast of Passover. Moreover, in their abuse there is a greater evil: whereas Jesus Christ says, "Take," they are led by this opinion to think that they offer to God a single and perpetual sacrifice. Therefore, to be helped by these words of the sacrament, they would need to have the true use of the Supper, which they do not have. For the rest, you must always testify that you by no means deny that Jesus Christ gives us his body, provided I seek it in heaven. In all their subtle quibbles, with which they may deal with you, you need to explain nothing to them except what you have seen, since you know well and are persuaded that God is the one from whom you have received and learned it. For our faith would indeed be very slight and bare if it were founded on the teaching and opinion of men. It is therefore best to meditate constantly on that doctrine in which the whole force of our faith and of the Christian religion consists, so that in time and place you can show that you have not believed rashly. And as I said at the beginning, if the enemies of the truth fight ambitiously for their own honour, it is your duty and office in this contest to conduct yourself so modestly that, against all their calumnies and snares, you give glory to God; and you need seek nothing more than the shield of a true and sincere confession, by which you can frankly bear witness to what God has impressed on your mind. Far less should it disturb or trouble you if they shamelessly accuse and slander me or others, since they have now gained such licence that they speak evil without any reason. Let us bear patiently all the reproaches and charges which they heap upon us, for we are no better than blessed Paul, who said that we must go through such infamies and insults. Let us only do what is right; when evil is spoken of us, it will be of such a kind that in it we can relieve and sustain our conscience. And even when they bring such calumnies against us, we have great cause to thank God, since we have a clear conscience before him and before men and are far from any suspicion of wickedness. Then, although we are wretched sinners, full of so many evils that we must groan over them continually, yet we must pray God not to allow impious men to speak evil of us except by lying, so that they may thus be condemned by their own mouths, since they shamelessly invent about us those things which they could really discover in themselves, were they not blinded by madness and frenzy. Let us therefore rejoice and glory, with all humility, in the grace of our God, when we see such wretched men boasting of their own baseness, like certain drunkards in their shame. If it grieves you when you hear them slandering us, it ought to grieve you much more when you hear them speaking insultingly and unworthily of the Lord of glory himself, Christ the Saviour. For we, with all our innocence, deserve to be overwhelmed with every confusion. Meanwhile, console yourself in our best God, who by his grace has so joined us to his Son that neither all the powers of hell and the devil, nor all the wicked and impious of the world, can ever tear us from his fellowship and love. Rejoice further that you defend his cause with a most good conscience, and hope that he will give you the strength to bear, bravely and steadfastly, whatever he has willed you to bear. For our part, in our prayers we show you the remembrance and affection that we owe you. Finally, we pray earnestly that he who, by his grace, has chosen you to defend his truth and has led you into this place, may himself grant you all the gifts and helps of his Spirit that are required in this so honourable office and testimony, and give you the highest perseverance, and such spiritual prudence that you may have in view only the increase of his kingdom and name, and set it above your life; and may he so show himself your defender and protector that you may feel this for your own consolation, and others too may notice it and receive consolation. All the brothers who are here send you many greetings in the Lord, and rejoice that he has shown such strength in you; and they take from these your bonds that mercy which brotherly love demands, and ask of our best God that he embrace and protect you with his supreme goodness and mercy. Geneva, 19 January. Your brother in the Lord, John Calvin.

units.la: Epistola Richardi Feuri, in qua exponit totam rationem quemadmodum captus fuit Gratianopoli, simul què ab aduersariis sunt proposita quęsitáque, & ab ipso responsa.
units.tr: Letter of Richard Feure, in which he sets out the whole account of how he was captured at Grenoble, together with the questions put to him by the adversaries and the answers he gave.

units.la: Ivos charissimi fratres, me videtis in hanc captiuitatem revocatum, minimè vobis mirum videri debet, si paulùm consideretis Dominum Iesum nihil adhuc quietis in hoc mundo mihi constituisse, quod maximè expertus sum ex eo tempore, quo me è periculo mortis liberauit, è manibusque inimicorum, quos cognoscitis, eripuit, atque hanc vitæ meæ conditionem ea experientia cognoui, in qua sæpe ac varie aggressus est, vt ego inde nihil aliud quàm noua certamina expectare potuerim. Neque verò Iesus Christus in hac quidem vita, multam nobis pacem promittit, aut certè longas inducias, tametsi ego magnopere eas optarem. Quinetiam per me non stetit, quo minus quæsiuerim omnes rationes, quibus quiete ac tranquille viuere possem. Sed quemadmodum ait Dauid, cum eas optarem ac quaererem, bellum mihi obijciebatur. atque etiam in his tentationibus ita fui excussus, ut sæpius in terram deiectus fuerim, & ita attonitus & consternatus, ut quo me verterem plane nescirem. Quibus in periculis, si Dominus mei misertus non fuisset, plane oppressus perijssem. Ego autem spero Dominum, si hæc consideraueritis, præsertim cum eo Spiritus iudicio, quod vobis dedit, non permissurum, ut in vanas speculationes & cogitationes incidatis, quibus perturbati omnem eius prouidentiam ignoretis, eiusque consilium æternum, quo uno tota hæc mea causa usque ad hunc diem fuit gubernata. Qua quidem in re spero eum exitum futurum, qui ad gloriam nominis eius & ecclesiæ ædificationem atque ad meam consolationem redundabit. Quemadmodum quidem iam initium huiusmodi fuit, ut complures qui in eo examine adfuerunt, tum ex magistratibus, tum etiam ex cæteris hominibus, qui vel in carcere sunt vel expertes huius miseriæ Deum tamen reuerentur, magnopere ædificati & confirmati in fide fuerint, qui omnes testes esse poterunt eorum quæ in hac controuersia agitata & acta fuerunt. Ego autem, quoniam esset prolixum omnia commemorare quæ tum acta sunt, perscribam quæ vos velle scire arbitror, existimans vos ea non tam curiositate quadam, quam ad ædificationem ecclesiæ requirere.
units.tr: You see me, dearest brothers, recalled into this captivity. It should not seem at all strange to you if you consider a little that the Lord Jesus has not yet appointed any quiet for me in this world. I have learned this most clearly since the time when he freed me from the danger of death and snatched me from the hands of the enemies you know. Through that experience I have come to understand the condition of my life: he has attacked me often and in various ways, so that I could expect nothing from it but fresh conflicts. Indeed, Jesus Christ does not promise us much peace in this life, or at least long truces, although I would greatly wish for them. Nor has it been my fault that I have not sought every means by which I might live in quiet and tranquillity. But as David says, when I desired and sought peace, war was thrown in my way. Moreover, I have been so shaken in these temptations that I was often cast down to the ground, and so stunned and dismayed that I did not know at all where to turn. In these dangers, had the Lord not taken pity on me, I would have been utterly overwhelmed and perished. But I hope, if you consider these things, especially with that judgment of the Spirit which he has given you, that he will not allow you to fall into empty speculations and thoughts, by which, being disturbed, you would lose sight of his providence and his eternal counsel, by which alone this whole cause of mine has been governed up to this day. In this matter I hope that the outcome will be one that redounds to the glory of his name, to the building up of the Church, and to my consolation. Indeed, the beginning has already been of this kind: many who were present at that examination, both from among the magistrates and from among the other men, who are either in prison or free of this misery but still fear God, have been greatly edified and strengthened in faith. All of them can be witnesses to what was discussed and done in this controversy. But since it would be lengthy to recount everything that was then done, I will set down what I think you wish to know, supposing that you seek it not so much out of curiosity as for the building up of the Church.

units.la: Non ignoratis, fratres charissimi, nos sæpe incidere in huiusmodi & tempus & locum, ut ea videamus, atque audiamus, quibus honos Dei contumeliose læd360ditur ac violatur, quæ fuit causa, ut me ipsum excitarim ad veritatem Dei defendendam pro ea facultate quam Deus mihi dederat, eoque magis, quod omnibus modis eo me inducere volebant ut consentirem cum eorum superstitionibus, quibus me a vera religione & fide Christiana ad impios cultus suos traducerent, cum optime scirent me Geneuæ in ecclesia commoratum suisse. Itaque illi Latrunculatorem in Delphinatu constituti instigarunt, ut ad me cum essem in diuersorio, prehendendum veniret. Is autem circiter horam nonas decimam aut undecimam eo venit, meque comprehensum, ac funibus vinctum (quoniam nox erat) duxit in cubiculum cuiusdam comitis fui aut satellitis Branchæ appellati, ut postridie in carcerem includeret. id quod factum fuit. Eo autem die productus fui ad iudicem Latrunculatorem, qui statim me in infima & obscura carceris loco deducedum [?] curauit, ubi duodecim prope dies sum commoratus cum duobus latronibus, qui vesperi eum in locum demisi, improbissimis verbis mihi plurimum molestiæ exhibebant. Qua quidem re multi honesti ac probi viri, qui captiui erant, cum meam afflictionem intelligerent, egerunt cum Præfecto carceris, ut audientia mihi concederetur, quo postea aliqua aeris commoditate frui possem. Itaque Præfectus carceris qui porta Troena appellatur, cum iudice Latrunculatore diligenter egit, ut me audiret. Sed quum is atque Episcopus totum hoc negotium recusarent, ad Suppræfectum remissus fui, atque ita primo die captiuitatis meae, per vrbem circumductus, atque de carcere in carcerem traductus fui. Tandem Suppraef. misit ad me in carcerem Portam Troenam, vnum ex aduocatis consiliariisque suis cum actuario, vt me examinaret, vbi coram multis fratribus interrogatus sum, cum de nomine meo, tum de loco natali, & unde venirem, quonam irem, quid in urbe quaererem, simul etiam quae causa esset cur captus fuissem, & quos libros, quosque sermones in diuersorio habuissem. Cùm autem ad ea multis verbis respondissem. Num, inquit aduocatus, tu credis ecclesiam Romanam? Minimè, inquam, sed credo Ecclesiam catholicam & vniuersam. Quaenam, inquit, est, catholica Ecclesia? Congregatio, inquam, Christianorum & communio. Quae, inquit, ista congregatio est & quomodo existit? Ea, inquam, constat numero eorum quos Deus elegit, vt sint membra Filij sui Iesu Christi, qui etiam illorum caput est. Vbinam, inquit, illa est & quomodo cognoscitur? Ea, inquam, per universum mundum est diffusa in diuersis locis ac regionibus: cognoscitur verò ea rectione spirituali, qua cum verbo Dei gubernatur, tum etiam iis sacramentis, quae Dominus Iesus Christus à se institutas ei tradidit: sicut videmus multas ciuitates ac nationes hoc modo atque ordine gubernari. Num, inquit, credis ea, quae Geneuae, Lausannae, Bernae, in caeterisque huiusmodi ciuitatibus habetur, magis esse veram Dei ecclesiam, quàm sanctam ecclesiam Romanam? Sanè inquam: quoniam illae certas verae ecclesiae notas habent. Quid, inquit, interest inter ecclesiam Romanam, & eas quas modò memoramus? Permultum, inquam: quod Romana traditionibus humanis regitur: aliae verò, solo Dei verbo ac mandato gubernantur. Vbinam, inquit, primùm istam doctrinam didicisti? In Anglia, inquam, Londini, atque ab ineunte aetate mea in sanctis Scripturis fui institutus. Quandiu, inquit, Geneuae es commoratus? Decem, inquam, aut certè nouem annos. Credisne, inquit, virginem Mariam peccatorum esse aduocatam & patronam? Ego, vero, inquam, credo id quod verbo Dei nobis testatum est, Iesum Christum vnum esse Mediatorem & peccatorum aduocatum: virginem autem Mariam, esse illam quidem perbeatam, sed huiusmodi aduocationis officium non vsurpare. Quid, inquit, Sancti qui sunt in paradiso, nullamne habent pro nobis orandi potestatem? Non, inquam: sed credo illos beatos esse, contentósque ea gratia & gloria, qua summo Dei beneficio perfruuntur, vt sint membra eius Filij Iesu Christi, quo quidem nunc cum gratiarum actione ita fruuntur, vt hoc tam sanctum officium ac patrocinium, quod Deus vni Filio suo charissimo commisit, nullo modo occupent.. Ecquid, inquit, tu de iis sentis, qui religionem ecclesiae Romanae amplectuntur, num eos Christianos iudicas? Minimè, inquam, sed infideles. Cur ita? inquit ille. Quoniam, inquam, vt antea dixi, ea ecclesia non gubernatur verbo Dei: sed potius hostiliter cum eo belligeratur. An, inquit, credis eos omnes, qui recedunt ab ecclesia Romana Christianos esse? Ego, inquam, non debeo respondere, nisi de mea fide, de eóque quod mihi impositum est. Itaque mihi quidem satis est, si pro meipso ac non pro alijs respondeam. Suum enim quisque, quemadmodum monet Paulus, onus feret. Tum aduocatus me iterum folicitans, ac vehementer vrgens, minatus est mihi, nisi ipsi responderem, se me ad responsionem coacturum. Non igitur, inquam, hoc quidem modo fiet cum iustitia atque aequitate. Caterum quod quaesitum est ex me de iis, qui Geneuae, Laufannae, Bernae, caeterisque in locis veram religionem amplectuntur, respondi, eos me credere Christianos esse. Ex his vero qui a Romana ecclesia discesserunt, permultos esse spurios, omnis religionis expertes, Anabaptistas, aliosque Epicureos ac voluptarios homines, qui etsi e Babylone exierunt, non propterea tamen in vera Iesu Christi Ecclesia sunt, quemadmodum ij qui in solo Christi verbo acquiescunt, seque eo placide ac modeste gubernari sinunt. Tum aduocatus, cum illud genus hominum memorassem, dixit me eos optime cognoscere. Ego vero inquam, illos quidem Dei benignitate cognosco, non ut cum illis aliquam rationem habeam & communionem, sed potius ut ab eis me maxime disiungam & caveam. Mihi enim propositum est ac constitutum in vera Ecclesia Iesu Christi doctrina permanere. Imo vero, inquit ille, Antichristi. Deinde quaesiuit, num vellem in hac doctrina ita reprobata & damnata permanere. Ego vero, inquam, statuo eam quam profiteor, non esse huiusmodi, sed plane Christianam & sanctam. Itaque quoad Deus mihi eam gratiam concesserit, qua in hac vita possim eum invocare, nihil aliud cupio, quam usque ad ultimum vitae meae diem extremumque spiritum in hac una doctrina acquiescere constanterque perseverare. Tu quidem, inquit ille, magnopere in tua opinione es obfirmatus. Ac quum videret tempus prandendi appropinquare, iussit reliqua in tempus pomeridianum reseruari, eaque mihi recitari quae & ab ipso interrogata essent & a me responsa: quae notarius ad verbum singula excepserat. Ea autem cum ego ipsorum mandato signassem, postulatum est ab advocato, ut aliquam aeris perfruitionem mihi concederet, quod ille fecit. Multique qui in carcere erant, maximopere ea re laetati sunt. Ego autem a Praefecto carceris cum huiusmodi fratribus sum relictus, qui me omni cosolatione refecerunt ac recrearunt. Hora prima post meridiem, Supprafectus me in auditorium accersiit, quo cum venissem, a Praefecto carceris deductus, coram Supprafecto multisque aliis advocatis, cum quibus erat quidam Franciscanus, productus fui. Ibi iterum interrogatus sum, quae in diuersorio meo fueram locutus, praecipueque de eo, quod hospitem & hospitam reprehenderam, quia liberi eorum in ea precatione, quae in mensa adhibetur, melius non essent instituti: me autem quod in Ecclesia Dei piorumque virorum consuetudine & viderām & audiueram, maxime mouerat ut eos admonerem, docerémque quid & quomodo in huiusmodi refectione capienda orandum esset. Itaque hac re illi offensi me calumniose detulerunt, multaque secus quam dicta erant in me contulerunt. Quae quidem causa fuit, ut ego ea nec agnoscere, nec accipere volucrim, eo quidem modo, quo Supprafectus a me dicta esse demonstrabat: sed ei exposui quibus de causis ac rationibus ego eos admonuissem, nimirū mirum Christianos omnes debere ex corde atque in Spiritu orare, & ea lingua quæ ab omnibus intelligatur, quemadmodum apertè verbo Dei admonemur: idque eò fieri, vt proximus aliquem ædificationis fructum percipiat. Præterea huiusmodi consuetudinem, qua lingua incognita oratur, profectam esse à superstitione atque introductam, quæ adhuc in mundo maximam vim cum summa ignoratione obtineret. Tum Franciscanus, cùm ea quæ à me dicerentur audiuisset, potestatem loquendi postulauit, & pluribus mihi verbis demonstrauit suum ipsorum Benedicite, Agimus tibi gratias, Laus Deo, pax viuis requies defunctis: & alias nescio quas precationes, atque adeò omnes linguas Deù intelligere, ecclesiamque Romanam hanc orandi formam retinuisse, traditam à vetere ecclesia antiquisque Doctoribus, qui ea Latinè vsi fuissent. illud praeterea incommodum consequi fi ita fit, vt non liceret nisi sermone Gallico orare: multáque alia dixit, quæ commemorare longum esset. Ego autem cùm ea audiuissem, audiri postulaui, atque ea quæ à me dicerentur scribi. Quod cùm mihi concessum effet: respondi me non ita dicere quasi nefas esset lingua Latina, Hebraica, Græca, aut alia orare: sed in consuetudine vitæ, conuictu ac societate eam precationem esse adhibendam, quæ cognita ab omnibus & intellecta fructum pietatis omnibus afferat, sicut Paulus ecclesiam Corinth. instituens præcipit. Tum Franciscanus commotus, cœpit de huiusmodi re concionem integram habere, afferens nescio quas subtiles acutáque ex philosophia rationes de ordine precum faciendarum & laudum, accommodans ea quæ Euangelistæ memorant dicta esse ab iis qui in introitu Iesu Christi in urbem Hierosolymitanam acclamarunt, Osianna Filio Dauid, affirmans eos qui huiusmodi laudibus Iesum Christum afficiebant, genus sermonis non intellexisse, quemadmodum Diu9 Hieronymus interpretaretur. Cui ego respondi, Hieronymum quidem potuisse scribere, eos qui huiusmodi laudes Iesu Christo in ipsius introitu tribuissent, significationem ac vim earum & laudum & precum non intellexisse: cùm præsertim ea esset Dauidis prophetia, in qua aduentus Domini atque introitus ab eo Psalm. CXVIII. prædictus fuerat. Euangelistas verò qui illud vaticinium à Christo Iesu completum fuisse demonstrarint, nullam mētionē fecisse an illi sermonis genus intellexerint. Sed Paulus certa precum regulam communémque doctrinam omnib9 Christianis dedit, cùm ait eas debere adhiberi ea lingua quæ ab omnibus intelligatur, & ad omnium ædificationē institui: quod apud me quidem tantum valet vt subtiles ac philosophicas disputationes non magnopere requiram. Tum Franciscanus dixit, me minimè esse idoneum ad sanctas Scripturas interpretandas, cùm præsertim linguæ Latinæ ignarus essem. Nam cùm is Latinè mihi multa narraret, postulaui ab eo, ne alia mecum, quàm mea lingua vteretur: nec enim opus esse Latinam eum adhibere, cùm Gallicam communem haberemus. Iterum ille mihi aliam concionem instituit, authoritates Conciliorum & Doctorum proferens, atque alia quædam hominum testimonia, quæ apud Suppræfectum plurimum valere videbantur. Itaque quum ille iudex constituisset prosequi quæstionem eorum criminum quæ accusatores in me conflauerant, quæ ad Regis infamiam & seditionem, contemptumque virginis Mariæ & Sanctorum, atque ad rebellionem contra Principes Regesque susceptam: ego de omnibus huiusmodi rebus interrogatus, respondi, eaque singula quemadmodum dixeram, exposui, & quomodo aduersarij conati essent me adducere in opinionem earum superstitionum ac traditionum humanarum, quibus nullo modo assentiri poteram. Postea Suppræfectus quæsiuit ex me, num crederem sacrosanctam hostiam, quam sacerdos in Missa consecrat. Ego vero, inquam, nec eam hostiam credo, nec ullam huiusmodi consecrationem. Cur, inquit ille, non credis sanctum altare sacramentum quod à Iesu Christo est institutum? Ego vero, inquam, credo sanctissima Sacramenta, quæ Christus Dominus instituit, eaque vsque ad mortem constanter tueri constitui. Num, inquit, Missam vnquam fide tua es complexus? Nunquam, inquam, in ea superstitione fui institutus, neque quid sit Missa atque huiusmodi consecratio, scio. De Sacramento vero Cœnæ Domini nostri credo, quum eo quidem ita vtimur, quemadmodum Paulus præscribit, 1. Cor. xi. nos alii ac refici spiritualiter corpore ac sanguine Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui verus pastus spiritualis animarum nostrarum & potus est. Ille est verum altare, in quo vno conquiesco, quemadmodum ait Apostolus Hebr. xiii. neque aliud altare Sacramentumque agnosco. Tum Franciscanus allegauit mihi xi. cap. 1. Corinth. adducensque ea quæ vi. Ioannis sunt scripta, vbi dicitur, Caro mea verus est cibus, &c. dixit veteres ecclesiæ Doctores de iis in Conciliis decidisse, Missamque mortis & passionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi memoriam esse sanctam. Cui ego respondi, me ita credere atque statuere, sacramentum Cœnæ ad memoriam mortis Christi celebrandam piamque gratiarum actionem institutum, quemadmodum Paulus docet eo allegato capite. neque aliam probationem dignitatemque requiri, quàm vt vnusquisque videat, num ipsum peccatorum suorum pœniteat, verámque is fidem & certam fiduciam in misericordia Dei habeat, fretus merito illius, qui seipsum morti pro peccatis nostris exposuit, & certissimæ salutis nostræ illustre reliquit monumentum in Cœna constitutum, & quasi quoddam pignus earum promissionum quæ in Euangelio continentur. Hoc vero ita esse mihi plane persuasi, quod à Christo institutum ac traditum, & ab Apostolis memoratum & celebratum est, vt in hoc Sacramento nihil ipsi offeramus: sed beneficia à Deo nobis in Christo Iesu liberalissimè oblata cum omni pietate atque animi gratitudine accipiamus. Ea autem omnia vt à Notario scriberentur, postulaui cum meis responsis, quæ Suppræfectus me obsignare iussit. Et quoniam iam valde aduesperascebat, à carceris Præfecto ad portam Troenam remissus fui.
units.tr: You are not unaware, most beloved brethren, that we often fall into such times and places where we see and hear things by which the honour of God is shamefully wounded and violated. This was the cause that stirred me up to defend the truth of God with whatever ability God had given me, all the more because they tried every way to bring me to consent to their superstitions, by which they would lead me away from the true religion and the Christian faith to their impious worship, since they knew very well that I had lived at Geneva in the church. So they stirred up a brigand stationed in Dauphiné to seize me while I was at my lodging. He came there about the tenth or eleventh hour and, since it was night, seized me, bound me with ropes, and led me into the chamber of a certain companion of mine, or of a guard called Branche, to shut me up in prison the next day, which was done. On that day I was brought before the judge, the provost, who at once saw to it that I was taken to the lowest and darkest part of the prison, where I stayed for nearly twelve days with two robbers, who came down into the place in the evening and gave me a great deal of trouble with the most wicked words. Many honest and upright men who were also prisoners, when they learned of my affliction, approached the warden of the prison so that I might be granted a hearing, after which I might enjoy some comfort of air. So the warden of the prison, who is called of the Troena Gate, pressed the judge, the provost, diligently that I should be heard. But when he and the bishop refused the whole business, I was sent back to the deputy governor, and so on the first day of my captivity I was led through the city and taken from prison to prison. At last the deputy governor sent to me in the Troena Gate prison one of his advocates and counsellors, together with the clerk, to examine me. There, before many brethren, I was questioned about my name, my birthplace, where I came from and where I was going, what I was seeking in the city, and also what was the cause of my arrest, and what books and sermons I had had at my lodging. When I had answered these questions at length, the advocate said: "Do you believe in the Roman Church?" "Not at all," I said, "but I believe in the catholic and universal Church." "What is this catholic Church?" he said. "The assembly and communion of Christians," I said. "What assembly is this, and how does it exist?" he said. "It consists," I said, "of the number of those whom God has chosen to be members of his Son Jesus Christ, who is also their head." "Where is it, and how is it recognised?" he said. "It is spread throughout the whole world in various places and regions. It is recognised by the spiritual government by which it is ruled by the Word of God, and also by those sacraments which the Lord Jesus Christ instituted and delivered to it, just as we see many cities and nations governed in this way and by this order." "Do you believe," he said, "that what is found at Geneva, Lausanne, Berne, and other such cities is more truly the Church of God than the holy Roman Church?" "Certainly," I said, "since those churches have the certain marks of the true Church." "What difference," he said, "is there between the Roman Church and those we have just mentioned?" "A great deal," I said, "because the Roman Church is ruled by human traditions, but the others are governed by the Word and command of God alone." "Where did you first learn this doctrine?" he said. "In England, at London," I said, "and from my early youth I was instructed in the holy Scriptures." "How long did you stay at Geneva?" "Ten," I said, "or at least nine years." "Do you believe," he said, "that the Virgin Mary is the advocate and patroness of sinners?" "I believe," I said, "what has been witnessed to us by the Word of God: that Jesus Christ is the one Mediator and advocate of sinners; the Virgin Mary is indeed most blessed, but she does not assume the office of such advocacy." "What," he said, "do the saints who are in paradise have no power to pray for us?" "No," I said, "but I believe they are blessed and content with that grace and glory which they enjoy by the highest benefit of God, that they are members of his Son Jesus Christ; and now they enjoy this so thankfully that they in no way usurp this holy office and patronage, which God committed to his most beloved Son alone." "What," he said, "do you think of those who embrace the religion of the Roman Church? Do you judge them to be Christians?" "Not at all," I said, "but unbelievers." "Why so?" he said. "Because," I said, "as I said before, that church is not governed by the Word of God, but rather wages war against it in hostility." "Do you believe," he said, "that all who withdraw from the Roman Church are Christians?" "I," I said, "am not obliged to answer except about my own faith, and about what has been laid upon me. So it is enough for me if I answer for myself and not for others, for each one, as Paul admonishes, will bear his own burden." Then the advocate, pressing me again and urging me vehemently, threatened that unless I answered him, he would compel me to answer. "This will not be done," I said, "in this way, with justice and fairness. But as to what was asked of me about those who embrace the true religion at Geneva, Lausanne, Berne, and other places, I answered that I believe them to be Christians. But of those who have departed from the Roman Church, I said that there are many who are spurious, without any religion, Anabaptists, and others who are Epicureans and lovers of pleasure, who, although they have come out of Babylon, are nevertheless not therefore in the true Church of Jesus Christ, unlike those who rest in the Word of Christ alone and allow themselves to be governed by it calmly and modestly." Then the advocate, when I had mentioned that kind of people, said that I knew them very well. "Indeed," I said, "I know them by the goodness of God, not so that I may have any relation or communion with them, but rather so that I may separate myself from them as far as possible and beware of them. For it is my purpose and resolve to remain in the true doctrine of the Church of Jesus Christ." "Nay indeed," said he, "of Antichrist." Then he asked whether I wished to remain in this doctrine, so condemned and damned. "Indeed," I said, "I hold that the doctrine which I profess is not of that kind, but is plainly Christian and holy. Therefore, as long as God grants me that grace by which I may call upon him in this life, I desire nothing else than to rest in this one doctrine and to persevere constantly until the last day of my life and my last breath." "You are indeed," said he, "very firmly fixed in your opinion." And when he saw that the time for dinner was approaching, he ordered the rest to be reserved for the afternoon, and that those things be read to me which both he had asked and my answers, which the clerk had taken down word for word. When I had signed these at their command, the advocate was asked to grant me some enjoyment of air, which he did. And many who were in prison rejoiced greatly at this. But I was left by the warden of the prison with brethren of this sort, who refreshed and restored me with every consolation. At the first hour after noon, the deputy governor summoned me to the hall, and when I had come there, I was brought by the warden of the prison and presented before the deputy governor, with many other advocates, among whom was a certain Franciscan. There I was questioned again about what I had said at my lodging, and especially about the fact that I had reproved the host and hostess because their children were not better taught in the prayer which is used at table. I had been moved most of all, from what I had seen and heard in the Church of God and in the custom of pious men, to admonish them and to teach what and how one ought to pray in taking such a meal. So they, offended at this, accused me falsely and attributed to me many things otherwise than what had been said. This was the reason I was unwilling either to acknowledge or to accept these things in the way the deputy governor showed I had said them. But I explained to him the reasons and grounds on which I had admonished them, namely: that all Christians ought to pray from the heart and in the Spirit, and in a language that is understood by all, as we are plainly admonished by the Word of God, and that this is done so that the neighbour may receive some fruit of edification. Moreover, that this custom of praying in an unknown tongue came from superstition and was introduced, and that it still holds the greatest power in the world together with the greatest ignorance. Then the Franciscan, when he had heard what I was saying, asked for leave to speak, and at length showed me their own "Benedicite," "Agimus tibi gratias," "Laus Deo," "Pax vivis, requies defunctis," and other prayers I know not what, and said that God understands all tongues, and that the Roman Church has kept this form of prayer, handed down from the ancient Church and the ancient Doctors, who used Latin for it. He added that another inconvenience would follow if it were so that one could pray only in the French language; and he said many other things which would be tedious to recount. But when I had heard these things, I asked to be heard, and that what I said be written down. When this was granted, I replied that I did not say it as if it were wrong to pray in the Latin, Hebrew, Greek, or any other language, but that in the custom of life, in fellowship and in society, that prayer ought to be used which, being known and understood by all, brings the fruit of piety to all, just as Paul, in instructing the Church of Corinth, directs. Then the Franciscan, moved, began to deliver a whole sermon on this matter, alleging I know not what subtle and sharp arguments from philosophy about the order of prayers and praises to be made, applying to them what the Evangelists record was said by those who cried out at the entry of Jesus Christ into the city of Jerusalem, "Hosanna to the Son of David," and affirming that those who honoured Jesus Christ with such praises did not understand the kind of speech, as Saint Jerome explains it. To him I replied that Jerome could indeed have written that those who gave such praises to Jesus Christ at his entry did not understand the meaning and force of those praises and prayers, especially since this was the prophecy of David, in which the coming and entry of the Lord was foretold by him in Psalm 118. But the Evangelists, who showed that this prophecy was fulfilled by Jesus Christ, made no mention of whether they understood that kind of speech. But Paul gave to all Christians a certain rule of prayer and a common doctrine when he said that prayers ought to be made in a language understood by all and instituted for the edification of all; this, in my judgement, counts for so much that I do not greatly require subtle and philosophical disputations. Then the Franciscan said that I was in no way fit to interpret the holy Scriptures, especially since I was ignorant of the Latin tongue. For when he was telling me many things in Latin, I asked him not to use any language with me except my own, for there was no need for him to use Latin, since we had French in common. Again he delivered another sermon to me, citing the authorities of Councils and Doctors and certain other human testimonies, which seemed to carry great weight with the deputy governor. Then, since that judge had decided to pursue the inquiry into the crimes which the accusers had heaped upon me, namely those touching the infamy of the King, sedition, contempt of the Virgin Mary and the saints, and rebellion against princes and kings, I was questioned about all such matters; I answered and set out each of them just as I had said them before, and how my adversaries had tried to bring me into the opinion of those superstitions and human traditions to which I could in no way assent. Afterwards the deputy governor asked me whether I believed the most holy host which the priest consecrates in the Mass. "Indeed," I said, "I believe neither that host nor any such consecration." "Why," he said, "do you not believe the holy sacrament which was instituted by Jesus Christ?" "Indeed," I said, "I believe the most holy sacraments which Christ our Lord instituted, and I am resolved to defend them constantly even to death." "Have you ever embraced the Mass with your faith?" he said. "Never," I said, "for I was not instructed in that superstition, and I do not know what the Mass is or such a consecration. But concerning the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper, I believe that when we use it just as Paul prescribes, 1 Cor. 11, we are spiritually nourished and refreshed by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true spiritual food and drink of our souls. He is the true altar, in which alone I rest, as the Apostle says, Heb. 13, and I acknowledge no other altar or sacrament." Then the Franciscan cited to me 1 Cor. 11, and bringing forward what is written in John 6, where it is said, "My flesh is true food," etc., he said that the ancient Doctors of the Church had decided those matters in Councils, and that the Mass is a holy memorial of the death and passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. To him I replied that I so believe and hold: the Sacrament of the Supper was instituted to celebrate the memory of Christ's death and a pious thanksgiving, just as Paul teaches in the chapter cited. Nor is any further proof or dignity required than that each one should see whether he repents of his sins, and whether he has true faith and sure trust in the mercy of God, relying on the merit of him who exposed himself to death for our sins, and who left an illustrious memorial of our most certain salvation, established in the Supper, and as it were a pledge of those promises which are contained in the Gospel. And indeed I am fully persuaded that it is so, because it was instituted and handed down by Christ, and recorded and celebrated by the Apostles, that in this Sacrament we offer nothing ourselves, but receive with all piety and thankfulness of heart the benefits offered to us by God most liberally in Jesus Christ. I then asked that all these things be written down by the notary with my answers, which the deputy governor ordered me to sign. And since it was already growing very late, I was sent back by the warden of the prison to the Troena Gate.

units.la: Diebus octo post Suppræfectus me in ædes accersuit, vbi certi homines conuenerant cum aliis monachis Dominicanis, & illo Franciscano, cuius supræ mentio facta est. Eo in conuentu confessíque Supprafectus institutum examen repetens, denuo me interrogare coepit, num purgatorium crederem. Ego vero, inquam, credo Iesum Christum sanguine suo purgationem peccatorum nostrorum perfecisse. An, inquit, non credis vllam aliam purgandi rationem, & post hac vitam locum alium, in quo animæ commorentur tandiu, quoad pro peccatis commissis satisfiant? Minimè, inquam, sed credo vnam, quæ pro omnibus sufficit, eam satisfactionem, quæ in sacrificio à Iesu Christo oblato, eiusque sanguine effuso peracta est, in quo quidem vno ablutio peccatorum nostrorum & purgatio. Tum vnus ex iis monachis, qui ibi aderant Latinis verbis mihi protulit eam similitudinem, quæ extat apud Matthæum decimo octauo capite, de eo qui debitum noluit socio suo remittere. Sed Supprafectus eum monuit, ne vllo modo mecum Latinè loqueretur, quoniam ita loquenti ego responsurus non essem. Franciscanus autem tum mihi similitudinem exposuit multaque alia dixit, in quibus hoc demonstrabat, Iesum Christum aliquando huiusmodi similitudinibus vsum fuisse, in quibus certa rei significatio continueretur. Cuius generis eâ dicebat esse, in qua dictum est, Eum inde nunquam discessurum, quoad extremum quadrantem persolueret: atque intelligi certum quendam ac medium esse locum, in quo satisfactio pro peccatis relinquatur.
units.tr: Eight days later the sub-prefect summoned me to his house, where certain men had gathered with other Dominican monks and that Franciscan, of whom mention was made above. At this meeting the sub-prefect resumed the examination he had begun and started again to question me whether I believed in purgatory. I said: "I believe that Jesus Christ by his blood has accomplished the purging of our sins." "Do you not, then," he said, "believe in any other means of purging, and after this life another place where souls remain for as long as they must, until they make satisfaction for the sins committed?" "Certainly not," I said, "but I believe in one satisfaction, which suffices for all: the satisfaction accomplished in the sacrifice offered by Jesus Christ and in the blood he poured out. In that one alone is the washing away and purging of our sins." Then one of the monks present there put to me in Latin the comparison found in Matthew, chapter eighteen, about the man who would not forgive his fellow servant his debt. But the sub-prefect warned him not to speak Latin with me in any way, since I would not be able to answer him if he spoke it. The Franciscan then explained the comparison to me and said many other things, by which he showed that Jesus Christ had sometimes used such comparisons, in which a certain meaning of the matter is conveyed. Of this kind, he said, was the saying that the man would never leave there until he had paid the last penny, from which one understands that there is a certain intermediate place where satisfaction for sins is left to be made.

units.la: Ad id autem respondi, me quidem amplecti vnam, quæ maximam vim habeat satisfactionem, eam in qua Christus morte suâ peccata nostra expiauit, eâsque promissiones Euangelij, quibus plenam nobis quietè offerunt: quemadmodum vbi nos suauissimè ad se inuitat: Venite, inquit, ad me omnes qui laboratis, & ego reficiam vos, & requiem animarum vestrarum inuenietis. Et Ioan. x. Ego sum ostium: qui intrat per me, saluus erit. Item, xiii. Ioan. Ego sum via, veritas, & vita. Idem etiam Ioannes de mortuis dicit, Apoc. xiii. beatos illos esse, qui in Domino moriuntur, eôsque tum denique à laboribus suis requiescere. Latroni verò qui prope Dominum Iesum fuit crucifixus, promissum est regnum cœleste in paradiso, sine vlla alia ratione, eo ipso die quo è vita excessurus erat. Quòd verò ad simile quod tu adduxisti attinet, illud quidem nullam aliam habet demonstrationem, quàm communionem nostri officij, vt si velimus nobis à Deo ignosci, proximis quoque nostris ignoscamus: nisi hanc præstemus humanitatem & misericordiam, nullam nobis veniam à Deo esse sperandam. Porrò cùm Franciscanus nullum mihi loquendi locum dare vellet, ac me impediret, Supprafectus eum monuit vt me respondere paterer, & ea quæ vellem dicere: se enim plane auditurum. Tum Dominicanus ait, si mea responsa essent vera, nullum fore purgatorium aut limbum. Id autem cum fide Christiana plane pugnare, ac symbolo Apostolorum, vbi Christus dicitur descendisse ad inferos. Tum Supprafectus, Credisne, inquit limbum esse? Ego sanè inquam nescio quidnam id sit, neque Scriptura sancta vllam limbi mentionem facit: ita ne ego quidè eum credo. Dominicanus sermonem excipiens, Vbinam, inquit, erat veteres Patres ante mortem Iesu Christi? In vita, inquam, æterna, quam propter semen Adæ, Abrahæ, Patriarchisque promissum expectarunt. Deinde progressi sunt ad quæstionem de Papa: in qua Suppræfectus, Credisne, inquit, Papam vllam habere potestatem? Maximè, inquam. An vero, inquit, credis cum, vt vicarium Iesu Christi posse absoluere? Minimè, inquam. Quomodo igitur, inquit, intelligis eã Papæ potestate? Eam, inquam, intelligo, quam diuus Paulus declarat, 2. ad Thessal. epistola, vt quoniam mundus vt seruaretur, studium & amorem veritatis non est amplexus, Deum dedisse Sathanæ eiusque administris efficaciam illusionum ac errorum, vt homines mendacio crederent, haberentque eos pastores ac doctores quos merebantur. Tum Franciscanus mihi ostendit quomodo Iesus-Christus potestatem ligandi soluendique diuo Petro dederit, Papamque illius esse successorem atque Iesu Christi vicarium, ecclesiamque hoc modo fuisse semper gubernatam, vt caput haberet vnum in hoc mundo, quemadmodum in cælo habet. Quòd si pastores vitam suam non degerent ex verbo Dei quod annuntiat, non tamen propterea doctrinam esse repudiandam, sicut Christus docet in Euangelio Matthæi, XXIII, capite: multáque alia in eandem sententiam locutus est. Ego ei respondi, Si Papa & ii [?] qui cum eo sunt coniuncti, purè ac fideliter verbum Dei annuntiarent, vt nulla humana inuenta affingerent, legésque pro arbitrio suo introduceret, me amplexurum esse puram Iesu Christi pastorumque ecclesiæ doctrinam, etiamsi vita eorum ab ea discreparet: quemadmodum Christus monet Matth. XXIII. Scribas & Pharisæos sedere in cathedra Moysis, hortatúrque vt doctrinam eorum, non ipsam vitam sequamur. Sed multum interest sedeántne ii [?] qui Ecclesiam tenent, in cathedra Moysis, quæ est sedes veritatis, an in cathedra mendacij ac sede abominationis, omnisque iniquitatis: quemadmodum Daniel prædixit, atque etiam Paulus, futurum vt homo perditus ac sceleratus sederet in templo Dei, seque aduersus omne numen insolenter extolleret. Quod autem Christus Petro ius ligandi & soluendi dedit, in eo certam etiam officij rationem ei præscripsit, cum eum ac cæteros discipulos monuit vt Euangelium annuntiarent, eósque ad suum exemplum & ministerium verbi reuocauit. quod quidem Petrus eiusque socij optimè intellexerunt, cum ii [?] vt pastores Ecclesiæ nullam proponunt aliam doctrinam quam purum Dei verbum, in quo vno est tota vis potestásque ligandi ac soluendi, clauésque illæ, quibus regnum cælorum & aperitur & clauditur. Leges verò nouas constituere, eásque imponere hominum conscientijs, cum eo ministerio pugnat & voluntate Dei, qui nihil vult ad verbum suum addi, aut de eo detrahi, quemadmodum Papa fecit, qui pro sua libidine puram religionem verbo Dei præscriptam atque in Ecclesia constitutam depranauit & corrupit, planéque peruertit. Neque verò Ecclesia vllam aliam doctrinam, quam verbi Dei amplectitur ac profitetur, neque authoritate hominum ac dignitate eorum vitæ nititur: sed vt ait Paul. in æterno Dei consilio eiusque verbo fundata est, in doctri-na na Prophetarum atque Apostolorum aedificata, cuius aedificij totius Christus est lapis ἀκρογωνιαῖος in quo ipsa exaedificatio nititur, quemadmodum idem Apostolus secundo Ephes. ostendit.
units.tr: To this I answered that I embraced the one satisfaction that has the greatest power, the one in which Christ expiated our sins by his death, and those promises of the Gospel by which they offer us full rest. So, where he most sweetly invites us to himself: "Come to me, all you who labour, and I will refresh you, and you will find rest for your souls" (Matt. 11). And John 10: "I am the door; whoever enters through me will be saved." Likewise, John 14: "I am the way, the truth, and the life." John also says the same about the dead, Rev. 14: that those who die in the Lord are blessed, and that they then at last rest from their labours. To the thief who was crucified near the Lord Jesus, the kingdom of heaven in paradise was promised without any other condition, on the very day he was to depart from this life. As for the comparison you have brought forward, it has no other proof than the fellowship of our duty: if we wish to be forgiven by God, we too must forgive our neighbours; unless we show this kindness and mercy, we cannot hope for any pardon from God. Moreover, since the Franciscan would not give me any chance to speak and kept hindering me, the sub-prefect warned him to let me answer and say what I wished, for he would plainly hear me out. Then the Dominican said that if my answers were true, there would be no purgatory or limbo. But this, he said, plainly clashes with the Christian faith and with the Apostles' Creed, where Christ is said to have descended into hell. Then the sub-prefect said: "Do you believe there is a limbo?" "Indeed," I said, "I do not know what it is, and holy Scripture makes no mention of any limbo; so I do not believe in it either." Taking up the discussion, the Dominican said: "Where, then, were the ancient Fathers before the death of Jesus Christ?" "In eternal life," I said, "which they awaited on account of the promise made to the seed of Adam, to Abraham and to the Patriarchs." Then they went on to the question about the Pope. On this point the sub-prefect asked: "Do you believe that the Pope has any power?" "Very much so," I said. "But do you believe," he said, "that he can absolve as the vicar of Jesus Christ?" "Certainly not," I said. "How, then," he said, "do you understand that power of the Pope?" "I understand it," I said, "in the sense that the blessed Paul sets out in his second Epistle to the Thessalonians: since the world did not embrace the zeal and love of the truth, so that it might be saved, God gave to Satan and his ministers the power of delusions and errors, so that men would believe a lie and have as ministers and teachers those they deserved." Then the Franciscan showed me how Jesus Christ gave the power of binding and loosing to the blessed Peter, and that the Pope is his successor and the vicar of Jesus Christ, and that the Church has always been governed in such a way that it has one head in this world, just as it has one in heaven. He added that, even if the ministers did not lead their lives according to the Word of God, which they proclaim, the teaching should not for that reason be rejected, as Christ teaches in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-three; and he said many other things to the same effect. I answered him: "If the Pope and those who are joined with him preached the Word of God purely and faithfully, adding no human inventions and not introducing laws at their own pleasure, I would embrace the pure doctrine of Jesus Christ and of the ministers of the Church, even if their lives departed from it; as Christ warns in Matt. 23, that the scribes and Pharisees sit in the seat of Moses, and urges us to follow their teaching, not their way of life. But it makes a great difference whether those who hold the Church sit in the seat of Moses, which is the seat of truth, or in the seat of lies and the seat of abomination and of all iniquity; as Daniel foretold, and Paul too, that a man of perdition and of wickedness would sit in the temple of God and would insolently exalt himself against every divinity. Moreover, when Christ gave Peter the right of binding and loosing, in that same grant he also prescribed for him a definite rule of his office, when he warned him and the other disciples to proclaim the Gospel and recalled them to his own example and to the ministry of the Word. Peter and his fellows understood this very well, since those who, as ministers of the Church, put forward no other teaching than the pure Word of God, in which alone lies the whole force and power of binding and loosing, and those keys by which the kingdom of heaven is both opened and shut. But to make new laws and impose them on men's consciences is at odds with that ministry and with the will of God, who wills nothing to be added to his Word or taken from it; as the Pope has done, who, for his own lust, has corrupted and utterly perverted the pure religion prescribed by the Word of God and established in the Church. Nor does the Church rest on any doctrine other than the one of God's Word that it embraces and professes, nor on the authority of men or the dignity of their lives; but, as Paul says, it is founded on the eternal counsel of God and his Word, built upon the doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles, of which whole building Christ is the cornerstone [ἀκρογωνιαῖος], on which the whole structure rests, as the same Apostle shows in Ephesians 2.

units.la: Ecclesia etiam duo capita non habet, unum in caelo, & alterum in terra: sed unum tantummodo Iesum Christum, & in caelo & in terra summa authoritate ac potestate praeditum: sicut Paulus multis locis epistolarum suarum docet.
units.tr: Nor does the Church have two heads, one in heaven and another on earth; but only one, Jesus Christ, endowed with supreme authority and power both in heaven and on earth, as Paul teaches in many passages of his Epistles.

units.la: Ad ea Franciscanus me admonuit ac docuit quemadmodum Paulus exponendus esset, me eum non intelligere: se vero Rome vidisse Papam concionantem, meque quodam animi studio incitatum haec in eum dicere: veteres vero Doctores Scripturas sanctas & sacra Concilia interpretatos esse, pluribus verbis mihi demonstrauit.
units.tr: To this the Franciscan admonished and taught me how Paul ought to be expounded, saying that I did not understand him; he himself, he said, had seen the Pope preaching at Rome, and I, driven by a certain zeal of mind, was saying these things against him. He then set out for me at considerable length how the ancient Doctors interpreted the holy Scriptures and the sacred Councils.

units.la: Sed Suppraefectus, cum id quod propositum erat persequi vellet, monuit me, ne ita effem in mea sententia[?] pertinax, cui ego dixi, me aliter non posse respondere. Cum autem ex me quaesiuisset, num alias Lugduni captus fuissem: respondi, fuisse. atque interrogatus, quemadmodum & quam ob causam captus fuissem, de tota ratione atque informatione causae, quae sententia pronuntiata fuisset, & quomodo ego dimissus, & per quos liberatus essem, & quanam res eos ad liberationem meam induxisset: respondi, me eam ob causam comprehensum fuisse, quod ad inuidendum quendam, qui nomine Evangelij captiuus erat, ad carcerem accessisem: & ea quæ tum mihi obiecta fuerunt propter fidem quam ego ex Evangelio susceptam habeo, in me collata fuisse. Cum autem à Iudicibus Lugdunensibus appellassem, decem diebus post eam appellationem certis hominibus fui traditus, ut Lutetiam ad supremam Curiam deducerer: in ipsoque itinere, cum fluvium Ligerim traiceremus, ereptum fuisse per quosdam homines personatos & incognitos, qui cum me in sylvas proximas deduxissent, in viaque mea constituissent, me gratia Dei ita commendarunt, incolumemque dimiserunt, ut sua ipsorum nomina mihi nunquam indicarint. Tum autem Suppraesectus mecum diligenter ac saepe egit, ut eos homines illi indicarem. In quo cum constanter negarem me eos cognoscere, ille nihil eorum credens, quaesivit ex me, num ego vellem me referre ad ea quae Lugduni in ea prima causa acta fuerant. Cui ego respondi, me id quidem non recusare, sed libenter velle.
units.tr: But the sub-prefect, wishing to pursue the matter he had set out to pursue, warned me not to be so stubborn in my opinion[?]. I told him that I could not answer otherwise. When he then asked whether I had ever been arrested at Lyon before, I said that I had. Asked how and why I had been arrested, he wanted the whole account of the case: the proceedings and the examination, what sentence had been pronounced, how I was released and by whom, and what had led them to secure my freedom. I replied that I had been seized because I had gone to the prison to visit a certain man who was held captive for the name of the Gospel, and that the charges then brought against me were aimed at me on account of the faith I hold, which I have received from the Gospel. After I had appealed to the judges at Lyon, ten days after that appeal I was handed over to certain men to be taken to Paris, to the supreme court. On the journey itself, as we were crossing the river Loire, I was snatched away by some masked and unknown men. They led me into the nearby woods, set me back on my way, and, commending me to the grace of God, let me go unharmed, without ever telling me their names. The sub-prefect then pressed me carefully and often to point out those men. When I firmly denied that I knew them, he did not believe any of it and asked whether I was willing to refer to what had been done at Lyon in that first case. I replied that I did not refuse, but was glad to do so.

units.la: Postea quaesierunt de confessione auriculari, num crederem sacerdoti confitendum esse. De quo respondi, me aliam confessionem non intelligere, nisi eam quam quotidie debemus ad Deum adhibere, & reconciliationem fraternam, quam Iesus Christus eiusque Apostoli magnopere nobis commendarunt. Tum Franciscanus ex me quaesiuit, an non legissem id quod Christus docet in Evangelio de confessione apud sacerdotem deponenda, cum infit[?] Leprosum qui ab ipso sanatus fuerat, ut se sacerdoti ostenderet. Illud autem Doctores veteres Conciliaque de auriculari confessione intellexisse atque exposuisse. Ego autem cum eius longam ea de re institutam orationem audivissem, dixi Ecclesiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi nunquam huiusmodi genus confessionis observasse, ut homines peccata sua deferrent ad aurem sacerdotis, atque summissa voce insusurrarent. Quod si ecclesia Romana eam confitendi rationem introduxit & obseruauit, non tamen propterea rectam esse & vtilem, nec enim Ecclesiam Iesu Christi in ea vnquam fuisse institutam. De Leproso vero quem Dominus sanauit, ei nō mandatum fuisse vt peccata sua in aurem sacerdotis exponeret: sed seipsum illi ostenderet, testimoniumque daret sanitatis per summum Sacerdotem recuperatae ac restitutae. Caeterum quomodo peccata nostra vni Deo sint confitenda, Dauid satis suo & exemplo & testimonio nos monuit, Psalmo xxxii, & li, & cvi, vbi ostendit quemadmodum Deo peccata sua confessus, veniam ab eo impetrarit, Deumque dolorem animi ex sensu peccatorum susceptum, ita accipere, vt eum omnibus sacrificijs anteponat.
units.tr: Afterwards they asked me about auricular confession, whether I believed that confession must be made to a priest. I replied that I understood no confession other than the one we ought to make to God every day, and the fraternal reconciliation which Jesus Christ and his apostles commended to us so earnestly. Then the Franciscan asked whether I had not read what Christ teaches in the Gospel about confession to be made before a priest, when he bade the leper he had healed show himself to the priest. The ancient teachers and councils, he said, had understood and expounded that passage as referring to auricular confession. When I had heard his long speech on the subject, I said that the Church of our Lord Jesus Christ never observed this kind of confession, in which men disclose their sins into a priest's ear and whisper them in a lowered voice. Even if the Roman church introduced and observed that way of confessing, it is not on that account right or useful, for the Church of Jesus Christ was never founded upon it. As for the leper whom the Lord healed, he was not commanded to lay out his sins in the priest's ear, but to show himself and bear witness to the health recovered and restored through the chief Priest. As for how our sins are to be confessed to God alone, David has sufficiently taught us by both his example and his testimony, in Psalms 32, 51 and 106, where he shows how, having confessed his sins to God, he obtained pardon from him, and how God accepts the grief of mind arising from a sense of sin and prefers it above all sacrifices.

units.la: Suppræfectus autem, cum videret tempus vespertinum iam adesse, remisit me per eum qui Portæ Troenæ præfectus erat. quo in loco satis diu cum fratribus sum commoratus: qui vt requiescerem cum ipsis, ab eius carceris custode petierunt, vt me cum aliquo ipsorum cubare nocte pateretur. id quod ille interposita eorum fide & cautione mihi concessit. Sed quoniam complures homines ex vrbe, atque ex eo carcere cupiebant audire eam doctrinam, quæ ibi annuntiabatur: ea res ad parlamentum, quod ea in vrbe est, perlata, Suppræfecto mandatum est, vt ego ab illis segregarer, atque alium in locum traducerer. itaque ille me in domum Episcopi transtulit: qui quidem cum ab eo parlamento & ab eo Suppræfecto mandatum haberet, me in carcerem inclusit, tametsi me nullo modo domi suæ habere vellet. quæ fuit causa, vt aliquanto post iterum a Suppræfecto eiusque consilio fuerim accersitus, quo Franciscanus & Dominicanus, quorum supra meminimus, multique alij ordinis sacerdotalis homines conuenerant. Ibi tum mecum summo studio egerunt, & magnopere a me contenderunt, vt ad Papalem redirem religionem, omnemque mihi misericordiam obtulerunt. Sed ego respondi eis, me nullam misericordiam expectare nisi a Deo meo & Domino Iesu Christo, in cuius gratia omnem spem meam reposui. Franciscanus igitur longa oratione demonstrauit quantum interesset inter ecclesiam Romanam, atque eam quæ Geneuæ est constituta. Ille autem ad eam comparationem eo adductus est, non licere Papæ absque vllo Dei verbo leges conscientijs imponere. Itaque adduxit mihi illud quod Ioan. cap. vlt. scriptum est, multa esse alia, quæ in eo libro non extarent perscripta. Item ea quæ Christus dicit in eodem Euangelio, xv, & xvi, capite, vbi Dominus discipulos suos admonet vt consolatorem expectent, Spiritum sanctum, qui eos in omnem veritatem induceret. Doctores autem Eccl. sia Conciliaque omnia constituisse ac decidisse. diffe. Præterea Geneuæ certas leges esse constitutas, sine certa verbi Dei præscriptione ac declaratione: idque probabat ex libro quodam Psalmorum, quem apud me habebam: atque ex eo ordine, quo preces publicæ die Mercurij junt institutæ, quasi ille dies a cæteris sanctitate differret.
