Itaque postulaui a Suppræfecto, vt mihi potestatem respondendi faceret, tum ad eam calumniam refellendam, quam in Ecclesiam Geneuensem conferebat, tum etiam ad cætera, quæ ab eo prauè dicta fuerant: aut vt ipsi inter se loquentes ac dispututantes, me quietum esse paterentur. Eam autem cùm mihi concessisset, ego commonitionem inspexi, quæ in eo Psalmorum libro, quem Franciscanus in manu tenebat, posita erat, eique ostendi die Mercurij in ea ecclesia fuisse constitutum, ut ordinis causa & commoditatis alicuius ad audiendum Dei verbum, precesque solennes & communes adhibendas homines convenirent, sine aliqua conscientiæ obligatione, aut superstitiosa observatione, quæ mutari nullo modo possit. Reges etiam veteres Deúmque timentes, huiusmodi ordinem, ac rationem civile semper cóseruasse, ut populum in cognitione & reuerentia Dei, veráque religione retinerent, conscientiáque hoc modo subleuarent potius, quàm ulla necessitate obligarent. De ÿs verò quæ ille diccret à doctoribus ecclesiæ conciliique decisa, & constituta sine expressa verbi Dei authoritate, dixi non ita esse: sed verbo Dei omnia præscripta & tradita, quæ ad gubernationem Ecclesiæ atque hominum salutem sunt necessaria: ut nulla postea decisione vel præscriptione opus sit. Paulus quidem ait se nihil audere dicere quod Christus per ipsum non fecerit, ut gentes ad obedientiam Euangelij tum verbo tum opere adduceret. Ioannes etiam in secunda sua Canonica loquens de doctrina Iesu Christi, monet non esse excipiendum si quis veniat neque eam doctrinam afferat. Paulus vero Gal.gravissime admonet, ut si Angelus etiam veniret, aliam doctrinam quàm Euangelij à se prædicati annuntiás, ut eum quasi anathema quoddam habeant. Christus etiam in Euangelio Ioannis, ostendit se verum ac bonum esse pastorem, suisque oves vocem alienorum non audire: sed qui ex Deo est audire verbum Dei: seque ad vitam æternam ostium esse. Item, se sicut missus fuerat à Patre, Apostolos quoque suos mittere: qui quidem nunquam aliam doctrinam tradiderunt, nisi eam quam ab eo acceperant, in qua una postea à Spiritu sancto illuminati, instituti, confirmatique fuerunt. Et divus Petrus in prima sua Canonica cap.iii. pastores Ecclesiæ monet, eisque illud officium præscribit, ut verbum Dei tantummodo proponant sine ullo dominatu, quo gregem Christi opprimant. Ab hac autè moderatione longissime abesse eos pastores, qui in Papatu sunt: quorù tyrânis satis ostédit quam ecclesiæ rectione habeat.
units.tr: The sub-prefect, seeing that evening was already come, sent me back by the man who was prefect of the Troyes gate. There I stayed for quite some time with the brothers, who asked the keeper of that prison to let me sleep the night with one of them, so that I might rest with them. He granted this on the pledge and security of their faith. But since many people from the city and from that prison wished to hear the doctrine proclaimed there, the matter was reported to the parlement which sits in that city, and the sub-prefect was ordered to separate me from them and move me to another place. So he transferred me to the bishop's house. The bishop, though he had a mandate from that parlement and that sub-prefect, shut me in prison, although he did not at all want me in his house. This is why, some time later, I was summoned again by the sub-prefect and his council, where the Franciscan and the Dominican mentioned above, and many other men of the priestly order, had gathered. There they dealt with me with the greatest zeal and strongly urged me to return to the Papal religion, offering me every mercy. But I answered that I expected no mercy except from my God and Lord Jesus Christ, in whose grace I have placed all my hope. The Franciscan then, in a long speech, showed how great a difference there is between the Roman church and the one established at Geneva. In drawing that comparison he argued that the Pope may not impose laws on consciences without some word of God. So he cited to me what is written at the end of John, that there are many other things not set down in that book; likewise what Christ says in the same Gospel, chapters 15 and 16, where the Lord bids his disciples await the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, who would lead them into all truth. The teachers of the Church and all the councils, however, had established and settled these matters, and [diffe.] they differ. Moreover, he said that at Geneva certain laws had been laid down without any definite prescription or declaration of God's word, and he proved this from a certain book of Psalms that I had with me, and from the order in which public prayers are appointed on Wednesday, as if that day differed in sanctity from the others. So I asked the sub-prefect to give me leave to answer, both to refute the slander he had brought against the church at Geneva and to reply to the rest of what had been said wrongly; or else to let them talk and debate among themselves while I remained quiet. When he granted this, I looked at the notice placed in the Psalm book that the Franciscan held in his hand, and showed him that the meeting on Wednesday in that church had been appointed so that people might gather, for the sake of order and some convenience, to hear God's word and to offer solemn and common prayers, without any obligation of conscience or superstitious observance that could never be changed. Ancient kings also, who feared God, always maintained this kind of order and arrangement in civil life, so as to keep the people in the knowledge and reverence of God and in true religion, and to relieve consciences in this way rather than bind them by any necessity. As for the things he said were decided and established by the teachers of the Church and the councils without express authority of God's word, I said that this was not so. Rather, everything necessary for the governance of the Church and the salvation of men has been prescribed and handed down in God's word, so that no later decision or prescription is needed. Paul indeed says that he dares to say nothing that Christ has not accomplished through him, to bring the Gentiles to obedience to the Gospel, by word and by deed. John too, in his second Epistle, speaking of the doctrine of Jesus Christ, warns that if anyone comes and does not bring that doctrine, he is not to be received. Paul, in Gal., most gravely warns that even if an angel should come announcing a doctrine other than the Gospel he preached, they should hold him as a kind of anathema. Christ also, in the Gospel of John, shows that he is the true and good shepherd, that his sheep do not hear the voice of strangers, but that whoever is of God hears the word of God, and that he is the door to eternal life. Likewise, as he was sent by the Father, so he sends his apostles, who never handed down any doctrine except what they had received from him, and in that alone were afterwards enlightened, instructed and confirmed by the Holy Spirit. And divine Peter, in his first Epistle, chapter 3, admonishes the ministers of the Church and prescribes this duty for them: that they set forth only the word of God, without any lordship by which they oppress Christ's flock. But the ministers who are in the Papacy are very far from this moderation; their tyranny sufficiently shows what kind of government of the Church they have.

units.la: Tum Franciscanus excipiens, mihi demonstrauit in vetere ecclesia presbyteros ac Ecclesiæ ministros solitos fuisse convenire, ut de ÿs rebus, quæ ad eâ constituendam pertinerent communi consilio deciderent, quorum nihil in ecclesia Geneuensi fuisse factum se ostensurum esse dixit ex eo libro meo, Testamenti nomine inscripto, quem in manibus tenebat, ut apertius ego veram ecclesiæ formam cognoscerem. Ego autem me id quidem maximè velle dixi, ab eóque petiu, ut eam rationem qua Apostoli in ecclesia constituenda fuissent usi, consideraret, neque existimaret reformationem Geneuensis ecclesiæ temere susceptam factámque fuisse sine consilio Magistratuum, ac senum, ministrorumque ecclesiæ, eáque diligentia, ordine & cura quam Apostoli Paulus & Silas in ecclesia Thessalonicæ ac Berrhœæ instituenda atque ordinanda adhibuissent. In qua quidem nihil nisi ex authoritate verbi Dei est institutum, sicut ex XVII. Act. facile cognosci potest. Quòd si ministri magnæ ecclesiæ Romanæ ad eam institutionem non sunt vocati, eiusque sponsus Papæ: non tamen propterea existimandum est ordinem cæteris ecclesiis ordinandis prætermissum fuisse. Ac ex eo quidem Concilio quod Hierosolymis ad confirmandam ecclesiam Antiochenam coactum est, satis constat Act. XV, Apostolos nullam legem aut doctrinam nisi verbi Dei in Ecclesiam introduxisse, quemadmodum Petrus aperté ostendit, obiurgans eos, qui conabatur Ecclesiæ huiusmodi iugum imponere, quod nec ipsis, nec patribus eorum fuerat tolerabile. Quinetiam rescripserunt fidelibus, qui Antiochiæ erant, vt ab idolis abstinerent, aliisque huiusmodi pollutionibus atque abominationibus, quæ in Papatu magnam vim habent. Tum Franciscanus mihi obiecit, me in ecclesia Papæ baptizatü fuisse. quod ego quidé nō negaui: sed id non impedire gratiam Dei, quò minus me in numero suorum, quemadmodum iniquitas hominum & pravitas eius misericordiam non impedit, quam declarat in iis quos per Spiritum suum ad vitam regenerat, sanguine Filij sui eorum animas asperges, sicut Paul. VI Roma.de Baptismo loquens docet. Postea alius, qui ibi aderat, méque de Missa parum honorificè loquentem audiuerat, impetrata loquendi potestate, dixit me de sacrificio Missæ cum contemptu & contumelia locutum esse: longáque oratione distinxit vetera sacrificia ab eo quod in Missa offerretur. Ad id autem probandum & confirmandum tandem adduxit Psal. Dauidis C X. Tu es sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedec: eum versum ad perpetuum Missæ sacrificium accommodans, méque admonens, ne diuinis Scripturis contradicerem: ac quaerenti quid ego super ea re vellem, dixi Apost. ad Hebræos satis pro me respondere, totámque ecclesiam monere, ne vlla alia sacrificia aut expectet, aut adhibeat. nam illum Psalmi versum ab Spiritu sancto de nullo alio sacrificio editum fuisse quàm de vno & æterno Iesu Christi qui semel se Deo pro omnibus obtulit: quemadmodum ex iis quæ ab Apostolo accuratè disputantur facilè potest intelligi. Alia quædam sunt piorum sacrificia Deo non ingrata, contritio cordis & pœnitentia, de qua in Psalmo L I. & sacrificium laudis, quod Apostolus ad Hebr. XIII, fructum labiorum esse dicit. cæterum cum illi multa mihi demonstrassent, quamobrem ego ad ecclesiam Romanam reuocari deberem, Suppræfectus quæsiuit, num ego vellem me ad ea referre quæ Lugduni in prima mea causa & confessione acta fuissent. Cui cùm ego me velle & libenter quidem respondissem: mihi partem quandam eorum actorum, quæ à me signata fuerant, ostenderunt: simul etiam sententiam in membrana perscriptam, quæ pœnam meam complectebatur, vt in crate positus traherer ad eum locum, quem Territorium appellant, ibique ad postem alligatus, postquam Strangulatus essem, igne cremarer. Ea autem cùm mihi lecta fuissent, Suppræfectúsque quæsiuisset, num hæc scripta consentirent cum iis quæ Lugduni demonstrata mihi pronunciátáque fuissent. respondi ea quidem acta, quæ à me signata essent, partem quandam illius causæ meæ continere: sententiam verò nunquam mihi fuisse pronuntiatam: neque tamen eam me defugere, sed accipere libenter cum appellatione qua usus fuerat, paratum semper meo sanguine obsignare ea religionis ac fidei meæ capita, quæ tum Lugduni, tum Gratianopoli atramento subsignassem. Postea aliud scriptum mihi fuit propositum & lectum, in quo regius Procurator concludebat, ut quoniam nolebam eos indicare per quos ad Ligerim ereptus fueram, in summam darer quæstionem: ac propter iniuriam, & contumeliam, quam Regem ecclesiamque Romanam dicebar affecisse, simul etiam propter hæresim quæ mihi imponitur, ad plateam Franciscanorum ducerer, ibique lingua primùm præcisa, exiguo ac lento igni vstularer, &c. Quæ quidem cùm mihi essent recitata, & Suppræfectus quæsiuisset, quid ad ea vellem dicere: respondi me nunquam potuisse cognoscere nomina eorum, à quibus liberatus fuissem, quoniam nunquam qui essent, aut quæ res ipsos ad eam opem mihi ferendam adduxisset, declarare voluerunt, nisi solo studio doctrinæ eius ac religionis quam ego amplecterer, quam illi ex me Lugduni audiuissent. Is de causis me non posse eos nominare. neque verò de Rege quicquam contumeliosè dixisse, neque hæreticum esse, sed Christianum. Quæ omnia, ut à me responsa perscriberentur in conclusionibus Procuratoris regij postulaui. Tum Suppræfectus me in custodiam remisit, vsque ad illud tempus, quo denuò coram eo sum productus, atque testibus duobus comparatus, qui calumniosè & iniquè in me conferebant ea quæ suprà fuerunt memorata. Sed cùm illi adessent, Suppræsecto demonstraui eas omnes causas, quibus illi ad falsum testimonium in me dicendum adducti essent. Itaque Deus, qui est pater pupillorum, peregrinorum que protector ac defensor, sua providentia eò rem deduxit, ut accusatores ac testes, tum apertè iniqua & improba accusandi ratione, tum etiam propria confessione, studium suum & voluntatem inimicam declararint. Cùm autem Suppræfectus mecum egisset ut responderem ad ea quæ Procurator regius de me statuerat, dixi me amplecti eam sententiam, quæ Lugduni de me antè pronuntiata fuerat: cùi qua appellatio mea erat coniuncta. Postea causa inter ipsos multum & sæpe disceptata, Suppræfectus me adse, cæterósq; omnes qui ibi iurisdictionem habent accersiuit. me cùmque diligenter egit, consuluit, suasit ut ad ipsorum ecclesiam me referrem. Sed ego ei respondi, mihi planè constitutum esse in Ecclesia Iesu Christi, eiúsque verbo permanere, neque aliam religionem quàm eam agnoscere. Quòd si alia melior ex verbo Dei mihi ostendatur, me non esse ita pertinacem ut id non sequar, quod Deus suo mihi verbo declararit. Tum quidam ex consiliariis me monuit, ne ita prudentiæ meæ atque opinioni adhærerem, cùm præsertim ecclesiæ, quæ essent in Germania, aliæ ab aliis dissentirent ac discreparent: ac nisi iudicium meum authoritati conciliorum submitterem, futurum hoc modo, ut nouus quotidie Christianismus exoriatur. Huic ego respondi, me quidem meam opinionem sequi nolle, neque niti velle alia sapientia, quæ summa in Christo Iesu esset, tametsi eam mundus stultitiam existimet. Quod vero diceret ecclesias Germanorum alias ab aliis in religione disiunctas esse, ostendi eas quidem quæ Euangelium essent amplexæ, maxime inter se coniunctas esse sine ulla differentione, quod ad fundamentum fidei Christianæ ac religionis attineret. Neque vero verendum esse vt novus quotidie existat Christianismus, nisi authoritati Conciliorum pareatur. nam dictum esse à Dauide Psalm. xxxiii. aliisque Scripturæ locis, Concilia Gentium ac populorum à Domino dissipari atque everti. Quare consilium Dei eiusque verbum sequendum esse, atque eius authoritatem omnibus Conciliis atque iudiciis præferendam, meque ita malle in paruo Christianismo, quàm in maximo & copiosissimo Papatu permanere. Post hæc autem Suppræsectus me in carcerem Episcopi remisit. vbi cum intellexissem me Lugdunum reiectum esse, quoniam quidem nullam aliam causam quare plecterer, nisi eam religionem & fidem quam in confessione mea declarassem, reperiebant:[?] magnopere cupiebam loqui cum Suppræfecto: idque sæpe per lictorē[?] Episcopi quæsiui. ac cum id mihi recusaretur, ad Iudices Gratianopolitanos multas literas scripsi, in quibus una est hæc epistola quæ sequitur.
units.tr: Then the Franciscan, taking up the argument, showed me that in the early Church the elders and ministers of the Church used to meet together to decide by common counsel those matters which pertained to the constitution of the Church. He said that none of these things had been done in the Church of Geneva, and that he would show this from my book entitled Testament, which he held in his hands, so that I might more clearly recognise the true form of the Church. I said that this was indeed what I most wanted, and I asked him to consider the method the Apostles had used in constituting the Church. He should not suppose that the reformation of the Church of Geneva was undertaken rashly and carried out without the counsel of the magistrates, the elders and the ministers of the Church, and with the same care, order and diligence that the Apostles Paul and Silas applied in founding and organising the churches of Thessalonica and Berea. Indeed, nothing was instituted there except by the authority of God's Word, as can easily be seen from Acts 17. But if the ministers of the great Roman Church were not called to that institution, and its champion is the Pope, it should not therefore be thought that order was neglected in ordering the other churches. Moreover, from that council which was gathered at Jerusalem to confirm the church of Antioch, it is quite clear from Acts 15 that the Apostles introduced no law or doctrine into the Church except the Word of God. Peter plainly showed this when he rebuked those who tried to impose such a yoke on the Church, a yoke which was intolerable neither to themselves nor to their fathers. Indeed, they also wrote back to the faithful at Antioch that they should abstain from idols and other such pollutions and abominations, which hold great sway in the Papacy. Then the Franciscan objected to me that I had been baptised in the Church of the Pope. I did not deny this, but I said that it does not hinder the grace of God from numbering me among his own, just as the wickedness and perversity of men does not hinder his mercy, which he displays in those whom he regenerates to life by his Spirit, sprinkling their souls with the blood of his Son, as Paul teaches in Romans 6, speaking of baptism. Afterwards another man who was present there, who had heard me speak somewhat disrespectfully of the Mass, obtained permission to speak and said that I had spoken of the sacrifice of the Mass with contempt and abuse. He went on at length, distinguishing the ancient sacrifices from that which is offered in the Mass. To prove and confirm this he finally cited Psalm 110: "You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek," applying that verse to the perpetual sacrifice of the Mass, and warning me not to contradict the divine Scriptures. When he asked what I had to say on this matter, I replied that the Apostle in Hebrews gives a sufficient answer on my behalf, and warns the whole Church that it should neither expect nor employ any other sacrifices. For that verse of the Psalm was uttered by the Holy Spirit not about any other sacrifice but about the one and eternal sacrifice of Jesus Christ, who once offered himself to God for all, as can easily be understood from what the Apostle carefully argues. There are certain other sacrifices of the godly which are not unpleasing to God: a contrite heart and repentance, of which Psalm 51 speaks, and the sacrifice of praise, which the Apostle in Hebrews 13 calls the fruit of lips. But when they had shown me many things as to why I ought to be called back to the Roman Church, the deputy prefect asked whether I was willing to stand by what had been recorded at Lyons in my first trial and confession. When I answered that I was willing, and indeed gladly so, they showed me part of those records which had been signed by me, and at the same time a sentence written on parchment, which laid down my punishment: that I was to be dragged on a hurdle to the place called the Territory, and there, tied to a post, after being strangled, I was to be burned with fire. When these things had been read to me, the deputy prefect asked whether this writing agreed with what had been shown and pronounced to me at Lyons. I replied that the records signed by me did indeed contain a part of that trial of mine, but that the sentence had never been pronounced to me; nevertheless I did not shrink from it, but gladly accepted it, with the appeal which I had made, being always ready to seal with my blood those articles of my religion and faith which I had signed with ink, both at Lyons and at Grenoble. Afterwards another writing was put before me and read, in which the royal procurator concluded that, since I was unwilling to name those by whose help I had been snatched away to the Loire, I should be put to the question, and that, on account of the injury and insult which I was said to have done to the King and the Roman Church, and also on account of the heresy imputed to me, I should be led to the Franciscans' square, and there, after my tongue had first been cut out, be burned slowly over a small and gentle fire, and so on. When these things had been read to me, and the deputy prefect asked what I had to say to them, I replied that I had never been able to learn the names of those by whom I had been set free, since they never wished to declare who they were, or what had moved them to bring me this help, except the sole zeal for the doctrine and religion which I embraced, and which they had heard from me at Lyons. For these reasons I could not name them. Nor had I said anything insulting about the King, and I was not a heretic but a Christian. I asked that all these answers of mine be written down in the conclusions of the royal procurator. Then the deputy prefect sent me back into custody, until the time when I was again brought before him and confronted with two witnesses, who maliciously and unjustly brought against me the things mentioned above. But when they were present, I showed the deputy prefect all the reasons which had moved them to bear false witness against me. Thus God, who is the father of the fatherless and the protector and defender of strangers, by his providence brought the matter to this point, that the accusers and witnesses revealed their hostile purpose, both by the openly unjust and wicked manner of their accusation and by their own confession. When the deputy prefect then urged me to answer the decision which the royal procurator had made about me, I said that I embraced the sentence which had earlier been pronounced about me at Lyons, to which my appeal was joined. Afterwards the case was argued often and at length between them. The deputy prefect summoned me to his presence, together with all the others who hold jurisdiction there. He dealt with me diligently, consulted me, and urged me to return to their Church. But I answered him that I had firmly resolved to remain in the Church of Jesus Christ and in his Word, and to acknowledge no other religion; if a better one were shown me from the Word of God, I was not so obstinate that I would not follow what God had declared to me by his word. Then one of the councillors warned me not to cling so tightly to my own prudence and opinion, especially since the churches in Germany differ and disagree among themselves; and unless I submitted my judgment to the authority of the councils, Christianity would in this way be renewed every day. To this I replied that I was indeed unwilling to follow my own opinion, and did not wish to rely on any other wisdom than the supreme wisdom which is in Christ Jesus, even though the world considers it foolishness. As for his saying that the churches of the Germans are separated from one another in religion, I showed that those churches which had embraced the Gospel are very closely united with one another, without any difference as far as the foundation of the Christian faith and religion is concerned. Nor need one fear that a new Christianity should arise every day, unless obedience is given to the authority of the councils; for it is said by David in Psalm 33, and in other passages of Scripture, that the councils of the nations and peoples are scattered and overthrown by the Lord. Therefore the counsel of God and his Word must be followed, and his authority must be preferred to all councils and judgments; and I said that I preferred to remain in a small Christianity than in the greatest and most copious Papacy. After this the deputy prefect sent me back to the bishop's prison. There, when I had learned that I had been sent back to Lyons, since they found no other reason why I should be punished except the religion and faith which I had declared in my confession, I greatly desired to speak with the deputy prefect, and I often sought this through the bishop's officer. When this was refused me, I wrote many letters to the judges of Grenoble, of which the following letter is one.

units.la: D. Suppræfecto Grisuodano, eiusque consilio Richardus Feurus captiuus.
units.tr: To Sir Suppraefect of Grenoble and his council, Richard Feurus, prisoner.

units.la: Gosæpe, domine, interrogatus sum coram te de ea religione ac fide, quam in Deo ac Domino nostro Iesu Christo, eiusque Euangelio fundatam plane & constitutam habeo. Atque apud te ipsum tumque consilium, vbi multi affuerunt qui communem tecum habent religionem, edidi eam fidei meæ confessionem, quæ cum veritate verbi Dei, Euangelio Iesu Christi & doctrina Apostolorum, ac denique tota cum vera Ecclesia plane consentit, pro ea mediocri cognitione quam Deus mihi impertiuit. quæ tamen satis magnam vim habet ad sapientiam humanam refutandam & confundendā. Neque vero quenquam in Curia vestra reperi, qui causam meam vnquam suscipere ac defendere voluerit: tantumque abest vt quisquam mihi aliquid studij auxiliúque ferat, vt potius omnes sitis mihi & iudices & aduersarij constituti: quod quidem satis ostendit vaticinium Dauidis de Iesu Christo eiusque membris editum in oculis vestris verè præstari, quemadmodum Psal.2.extat scriptum, Cur fremuerunt gentes, & populi meditati sunt inania? &c. Itaq; mihi quidē pro iustissima causa, mortis pœna crudeliter feréda est. sed ego spero per eam me ad Deū & Dominum meum Iesum Christum iturum, ad summum iudicem in illo regno æterno & curia suprema, vbi nos omnes aliquando sisti oportet ad tribunal maiestatis eius, vt ius causæ, quæ non solum mea, sed etiam illius est, obtineatur: quam vos nunc vehementissimè oppugnatis. in qua quidem Dominus nibil referret ad summa Concilia, maximamque multitudinem mundi, neque ad eius fallacem speciem ac opinionem: sed ad suum tantum verbum, sicut ait David, eum iudicaturum mundum in veritate, ac populos in iustitia: & Divus Ioannes in Apocalypsi dicit, omnem oculum visurum, eosque qui illum vulnerarunt. Neque verò ea ignorationis integumenta, quæ obtenditis, vobis aliquid proderunt, non magis quam illa aqua, qua Pilatus suam innocentiā in sanguine Iesu Christi effundendo testatā esse volebat: Christus enim de omnibus suis membris, fidelibusque dicit, se in eorum despicietia & iniuria despici ac violari, in seipsumque conferri quicquid officij ac beneficij in aliquē eorum minimum collatum est. Itaque Dominum oro vt Spiritu suo vos illuminet, atque in vestris rebus gubernet, vobis gratias agens pro ea humanitate, qua in me vsi fuistis, vosque orans per nomen Dei, vt quoniam declarare quæ cupiebam vobis non potui, pro vestra humanitate me certiorem de eo faciatis, quod de me & causa mea constituistis. Valete. Ex carcere Episcopi Gratianopolitani, quarto die Ianuarij M.D.LIIII. Vester captiuus Richardus Feurus.
units.tr: Often, sir, have I been questioned before you about the religion and faith that I hold firmly and securely founded in God and our Lord Jesus Christ and his Gospel. Before you yourself and your council, where many were present who share your religion in common, I set out that confession of my faith, which agrees entirely with the truth of God's Word, the Gospel of Jesus Christ and the teaching of the Apostles, and in short with the whole true Church, so far as the modest knowledge God has given me allows. That knowledge nonetheless has considerable power to refute and confound human wisdom. Yet I have found no one in your court who has been willing to take up and defend my cause. Far from anyone offering me any support or help, you have all been appointed as my judges and my adversaries. This certainly shows that David's prophecy about Jesus Christ and his members is truly fulfilled before your eyes, as it is written in Psalm 2: "Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?" and so on. So for me, though my cause is most just, the penalty of death is to be cruelly endured. But I hope that through it I shall go to God and my Lord Jesus Christ, to the supreme judge, in that eternal kingdom and supreme court, where we must all one day appear before the tribunal of his majesty, so that the right of a cause which is not only mine but also his may be upheld, the cause you now oppose most vehemently. In that cause the Lord will take no account of great councils, the greatest multitude of the world, or its deceptive appearance and opinion, but only of his own Word. As David says, he will judge the world in truth and the peoples in righteousness; and the divine John in the Apocalypse says that every eye shall see him, and those who pierced him. Nor will those veils of ignorance that you put forward profit you anything, no more than the water with which Pilate wished to show his innocence while shedding the blood of Jesus Christ. For Christ says of all his members and faithful people that whatever service or kindness is done to the least of them, he takes as done to himself, and whatever contempt or injury is done to them, he takes as done to himself. So I pray the Lord to enlighten you by his Spirit and to guide your affairs, thanking you for the kindness you have shown me; and I beg you by the name of God that, since I have not been able to make known to you what I wished, you will in your kindness inform me of what you have decided concerning me and my cause. Farewell. From the prison of the Bishop of Grenoble, 4 January 1554. Your prisoner, Richard Feurus.

units.la: Quemadmodum Richardus Feurus Gratianopoli Lugdunum reiectus fuerit.
units.tr: How Richard Feurus was sent back from Grenoble to Lyons.

units.la: Cum autem ego cum Suppræfecto nullo modo loqui possem, circiter decimam horam aut undecimam quum essem in carcere, Latrunculator cum suo satellitio & notario criminum ad me venit, nubique significauit mandato Suppræfecti Lugdunum eundum esse. Itaque me statim in cubiculum suum duxit catenis ferreis constrictum, vt ibi tandiu essem donec illuceseceret: deinde tribus horis post media nocte celeriter discessimus, ego equo impositus catenisque ferreis vinctus. Itinere autem quo Lugdunum itur relicto, Viennam defleximus metu insidiarum, quas Latrunculator ex rumore quodam suspicabatur. Lugdunum quum venissemus, ille me ad carcerem Roanæ deduxit, ac custodi commendauit: deinde Præfecto Lugdunensi meum aduentum nuntiauit. Duodecim diebus post is Præfectus quum ad me venisset, me interrogauit, ac quæsiuit quisnam essem, à quo ductus fuisse, quo nomine appellarer, etiam de illa mea liberatione, atque de quibusdam capitibus religionis. Ad quae omnia respondi pro ea gratia ac facultate, quam Dominus mihi impertiuit. Ignarus plane quid illi de me constituerint, expecto felicem illum diem liberationis meae, Deumque oro ut mihi cum patientia eam ferat opem, quam intelligit esse necessariam: fidemque in me ita augeat atque confirmet, ut ea toto hoc mundo superato, supra caelos penetret ad illam vitam beatam regnumque caeleste, in quo cum optimo Deo nostro & Patre misericordiae, ac Saluatore Iesu Christo perpetuo victurus sum.
units.tr: Since I could in no way speak with the Suppraefect, about the tenth or eleventh hour, while I was in prison, the Latrunculator came to me with his guard and the notary of the charges, and told me that by the Suppraefect's order I was to go to Lyons. He at once led me into his chamber, bound with iron chains, so that I should remain there until daybreak. Then, three hours after midnight, we left quickly, I mounted on a horse and bound with iron chains. But leaving the road by which one goes to Lyons, we turned aside to Vienne, for fear of an ambush which the Latrunculator suspected from some rumour. When we had come to Lyons, he took me to the prison of Roanne and committed me to the jailer; then he announced my arrival to the Lyons provost. Twelve days later, this provost came to me and questioned me, asking who I was, by whom I had been brought, what name I was called by, and also about that liberation of mine, and about certain articles of religion. To all these things I replied with the grace and ability the Lord has given me. Quite ignorant of what they have decided about me, I await that happy day of my deliverance, and I pray God to give me the help he knows I need, so that I may bear it with patience; and may he so increase and strengthen my faith that, having overcome this whole world, it may reach above the heavens to that blessed life and heavenly kingdom, where I shall live forever with our best God and Father of mercies, and with our Saviour Jesus Christ.

units.la: Postea Richardus saepius interrogatus est a iudice Tignaco, atque doctore Sorbonensi, quem Fumosum appellant, de iis religionis ac fidei Christianae capitibus, de quibus Gratianopoli responderat, ut de Ecclesiae authoritate, ac potestate Papae, de sacramento Coenae, de confessione, de verbo Dei eiusque doctrina & intelligentia, caeterisque huiusmodi articulis, in quibus acriter illis restitit, veritatemque semper defendit, nec vllis vnquam eorum argumentis ac rationibus, nec minis aut promissis adduci potuit, ut sententiam fidei susceptam deponeret, ipsamque veritatem proderet. Diligenter etiam ab eodem est quaesitum de iis, per quos in itenere quum Lutetiam duceretur, ereptus fuerat ac liberatus. Sed is neminem vnquam nominauit: quum se eos plane ignorare semper diceret. Itaque inuictus in optima causa & confessione Euangelij permansit, aduersarios suos appellans vocansque ad eum diem, in quo Dominus summa aequitate & iustitia totius mundi iudicium facturus est. Is igitur post sententiam iudicialem, in qua capitis fuit condemnatus, ad supplicium ductus est, in quo lingua primum ei fuit amputata: deinde corpus viuo vstulatum, die Sabbathi vii. Iulij, anno supra notato, M.D.LIIII.
units.tr: Afterwards Richard was questioned repeatedly by the judge Tignac and by a doctor of the Sorbonne, whom they call Fumosus, about those articles of the Christian religion and faith on which he had answered at Grenoble: about the authority of the Church, the power of the Pope, the sacrament of the Supper, confession, the Word of God and its teaching and understanding, and other articles of this kind. On these he resisted them sharply and always defended the truth, and by none of their arguments or reasons, nor by threats or promises, could he be brought to abandon the faith he had embraced or betray the truth itself. The same man also made diligent inquiry about those by whom he had been snatched away and freed on the journey when he was being taken to Paris. But he never named anyone, always saying that he knew them not at all. Thus he remained unconquered in his good cause and in his confession of the Gospel, calling his adversaries to that day on which the Lord will pass judgment on the whole world with the utmost equity and justice. After the sentence, by which he was condemned to death, he was therefore led to execution. There his tongue was first cut out, and then his body was burned alive, on Saturday, 7 July, in the year noted above, 1554.

units.la: PARIS PANIER.
units.tr: PARIS PANIER.

units.la: Paris Panerius è Salinis oppido in Burgundiae comitatu IurisconPfultus, ut puram & homine Christiano dignam Euangelij confesfionem tueretur, mortem constanter pertulit, cui caput Dolae est amputatum die Sabbathi vii. mensis Aprilis, anno M.D.LIIII.
units.tr: Paris Panerius, a jurist from Salins, a town in the county of Burgundy, endured death steadfastly in order to defend the pure confession of the Gospel, which is worthy of a Christian man. His head was cut off at Dole on Saturday, 7 April 1554.

units.la: FRANCISCVS GAMBA Italus.
units.tr: FRANCISCUS GAMBA Italian.

units.la: FRancifcus Gamba Italus, ex ea vrbe Longobardiæ quæ Brixia appellatur, cognitione Euangelij adeptus, Geneuā venit vt cōsilium de quibusdā rebus necessarijs à viris piis ac prudētibus qui ea in ecclesia sunt peteret. Eo autē tēpore in ea vrbe fuit, quo Cœna in festo Pēteco stes celebratur, ibiq; cū fidelib° cōmunicauit. Postea in reditu cum lacu Comēse traiiceret, captꝰ est, atq; ad oppidū Comū deductꝰ. vbi cū veritatē Dei constātisfima confessione tutatus esset, damnatus est, vt igni cremaretur. xii.die Iulij, M.D.LIIII. quemadmodum constat ex ijs literis, quas quidam nobilis Comensis amicus Gambæ, ad quendam fratrem eius scripsit, quibus tum singularem illius in religionem animum studiumque exponit, tum etiam felicem exitum, in quo pro causa Euangelij ea in vrbe combustus fuit. Earum literarum nos hîc exemplum subscripsimus:
units.tr: Francis Gamba, an Italian from the city of Brescia in Lombardy, came to the knowledge of the Gospel and went to Geneva to seek advice on certain matters from godly and prudent men who serve in that church. He was in that city at the time when the Lord's Supper was celebrated at the feast of Pentecost, and there he communed with the faithful. Afterwards, on his return journey, he was crossing Lake Como when he was seized and taken to the town of Como. There, after he had defended the truth of God with a most steadfast confession, he was condemned to be burned at the stake on 12 July 1554. This is clear from a letter which a certain noble friend of Gamba at Como wrote to a brother of his. In it he sets out both his remarkable zeal for religion and his happy end, since he was burned in that city for the cause of the Gospel. We have appended a copy of that letter here:

units.la: Mantissime ac charissime frater, Deus quidem mihi testis esse potest eius mœroris, quo nunc animus meus vehementer premitur, cum de beata morte fratris tui ac mei, mihi ad te est scribendum: neque dubito, quin consobrinus tuus, qui hic fuit, tibi iam ea omnia narrauerit, quæ ex me in hac vrbe audiuerat. sed quoniam hinc redire ad vos cogebatur, quemadmodum ei consulebam, non potui tum quidem omnia ei accurate ac diligenter declarare, quemadmodum cupiebam, & fratri tuo me facturum receperam, vt tu, res quemadmodum gesta esset & frater tuus vsque ad mortem se gessisset, cognoscere, causamque potius Dei laudandi, quam dolendi habere posses. Itaque nactus istam summam scribendi opportunitatem, prætermittere nolui quin ad te de tota re, sicut hic gesta est, scriberem: tum vt materiam lætitiæ potius, quam molestiæ in Domino tibi darem: qui pro sua gratia & misericordia fratrem tuum delegit, ac dignum iudicauit, qui veritatem ipsius sanguine suo consignaret: tum etiam, vt id præstarem, quod me facturum ei promiseram, eiusque mandato ad te de re tota scriberem. Quod quidem facio non ita copiose, vt res ipsa meretur: sed tamen breuiter exponam ea præcipua, quæ ego ipse & vidi & audiui. Hoc modo igitur res habet.
units.tr: Most beloved and dearest brother, God himself can bear witness to the grief which now weighs heavily on my spirit, since I must write to you of the blessed death of your brother and of mine. I do not doubt that your cousin, who was here, has already told you everything he heard from me in this city. But since he was obliged to return to you, and as I advised him, I could not then set out for him fully and carefully all that I wished, as I had promised your brother I would do, so that you might know how the matter was carried out, and how your brother conducted himself to the end, and so that you might have cause to praise God rather than to grieve. Therefore, having found this opportunity to write, I did not want to let it pass without writing to you about the whole affair as it took place here, so that I might give you matter for joy in the Lord rather than distress: he, by his grace and mercy, chose your brother and judged him worthy to seal his truth with his blood. I also wish to do what I had promised him, and to write to you about the whole matter at his command. I do this not as fully as the matter deserves, but I will briefly set out the chief points which I myself saw and heard. The matter stands thus.

units.la: Ex eo tempore quo frater tuus in carcerem coniectus est, quandiu in eo fuit,non credibile est quot homines huius vrbis ex omni genere atque ordine,in primisque Doctores, ac nobiles cum vehementer rogauerint,ne pertinaciter huiusmodi vanas opiniones,vt illi arbitrantur,tueretur: ad quas ita putabant eum adductum esse,vt mente ac ratione omni alienatum esse existimarent. Itaque magnopere eum hortabantur,vt aliquam rei suae salutisque cogitationem & curam suscipéret,atque omnia huiusmodi delirla abiiceret,quibus illum affici ac teneri arbitrabantur.Sed vir pius constanter semper eis respondit, id quod ipse protulisset constantérque defenderet,non esse inanes aliquas speculationes aut vanas opiniones: neque se mente perturbatum esse,vlloque humore fantastico correptum,vt insaniret: sed puram Dei veritatem,sanctumque Domini nostri Iesu Christi verbū & doctrinam salutare.de qua quidem quum singula capita proponeret,simul etiá statim grauissima Scripturae testimonia afferebat,quibus orationem suam probabat & confirmabat,testificans inuicta quadam constantia se multo malle morte subire, quàm Iesum Christū unū Saluatorem nostrum atque Redemptorem mundi,cuius causam & doctrinam tueretur,quàm denique perfidia sua veritatem Euangely prodere, & causam eam quam Deus ipsi commiserat, & commendarat vt eam vsque ad mortem tutaretur . Postremo quum is diu cum Doctoribus huius vrbis,monachis ac sacerdotibus disputasset, caterifque multis qui ad eum accedebant: alij vt illum ab ea sententia deducerent: alij vero misericordia quadam permoti, quod eum hominem plane bonum atque integrum cognouerant,omnes summo consensu simul eum adierunt: quem quum rogassent vt eam opinionem deponeret,ciuitatem etiam ei promiserunt ac detulerunt cum huiusmodi commodorum prouisione quam ille posset expetere. Sed quum viderent se nihil posse ab eo obtinere,paulo post aliud nuntium miserunt,eum nisi fuscepram opinionem & sententiam deponeret,poena mortis perpeffurum. Ad quod nuntium ille laetissimo animo respondit,id quidem vnum esse quod omnium maxime expeteret,neque aliud eo iucundius nuntium afferri posse. Interea dum haec aguntur, literae veniunt a senatu Mediolanensi, cum huiusmodi mandato, vt Franciscus Gamba morcretur,igneq; viuus cremaretur. Sed quu ludices iam in eo essent vt ut conficeret illud mandatum, eáque pœna Francifcũ afficerent, aliæ literæ Genua sunt allatæ commendatitiæ, quas Legatus Imperatoris multique nobiles Mediolanenses scripserant. Itaque constitutio executióque supplicij in aliquot dies dilata est. Quo quidem toto tempore optimus frater tuus, in proposito suo firmus permansit. Neque diu post aliæ literæ mortis eius nuntiæ, allatæ fuerunt. Itaque, ex ea arce, in qua, ut tu scis, captivus tenebatur, eductus est, productúsq; ad eum Magistratum quē Potentatum vocant: qui in ea urbe est Iudex causarum tum civilium tum capitalium: ibique huiusmodi sententia lata est, eum nisi ad se rediret, opinionémque deponeret, iam condemnatum esse, ut summo supplicio afficeretur. Tum ille ostendens se magnopere lætum, & mirifica quadam consolatione affectum, modestissimè gratias egit Potentatui, pro eo nuntio quod ei allatum fuerat. Is tamen Magistratus, tum mea causa, tum etiam quòd à quibusdam aliis nobilibus rogatus esset, Franciscum in carcere incolumem ea adhuc hebdomade conseruauit. Quo quidè tempore is summa libertate & audacia cum omnibus disputabat; permultas afferens sem[?] per rationes atque authoritates ex Scriptura sancta, quibus quod tuebatur confirmaret. ita ut animus eius magis ac magis augeretur, eiusque constantia eo maior in dies perspiceretur, quo longior ei vita concedebatur. Postremò Iudex cum accersiuit, eique dixit ipsum postridie aut certè perendie mori oportere, ex eo mandato, quod à senatu Mediolanensi acceperat. Ille verò idem quod antea respondit, sibi quidem id nuntium gratissimum ac iucundissimum accidere. At cum Iudex illum iterum rogasset, pluribúsque monuisset, si ea quæ dixerat retractare vellet, id quidem certè quod de Sacramento Missæ dicere ausus fuerat, id quod ei esset delatum ac promissum plane futurum: ille huiusmodi promissa nihil curabat, nec pluris ea quàm leuissimum venti flatum faciebat. sæpe etiam dicebat ea commoda, quæ sibi ab iis proponerentur, nullo modo esse comparanda cum iis bonis, quæ certus erat à Domino se accepturū, cuiusmodi est corona immortalitatis vitáque æterna, omnibus piè Deum colentibus promissa & constituta. Neque verò animi magnitudine suscepta unquam abiecit aut infregit, tametsi ab hostibus veritatis ad eum labefactandum ac plane debilitandum multa ei grauia proponerentur: quin potius cernere quisque poterat constantiam illius ac virtutem in horas singulas maiorem fieri, eaque ab illo dici, quae omnes qui audiebant magnopere admirarentur. Itaque magistratus quum videret eum ita assectum & confirmatum, constituit ut postridie moreretur. Quod ille quum intellexisset, finemque vitae suae iam appropinquare cognouisset, me ad se accersiuit, ut ipse mecum loqueretur. Inter multa alia magno studio rogauit me, ut de tota sua re & causa, quis exitus eius fuisset, ad te scriberem, teque rogarem tum honoris Dei causa, tum etiam eius amoris ac beneuoletiae quam erga se haberes, ut nullam molestiam dolorémque ex morte sua caperes, quum eam quidem propter Iesum Christum perlubenter pateretur, incredibilem quandam in animo suo sentiens consolationem & laetitiam, recognoscénsque tantam Dei gratiam, qua ab eo electus fuisset & vocatus ad opprobria mundi, crudelémque mortem perferendam, ut causam Filij eius Iesu Christi tueretur, qui vitae propriae non pepercit, ut salutem omnibus fidelibus afferret. Postremò se tibi sorores suas & tuas, nepotes, neptesque commendare, ac Deum orare ut vos in optima pace amicitiaque conseruet, eámque gratiam impertiat, ut totam vitam vestram ad ipsius cultum consecrare ac conferre possitis. Postero die mane carnisex, qui natione erat Germanus, ad eum accessit, ut eum admoneret de supplicio, quod ipse eo die erat executurus, utque sibi ob eam rem ignoscere[?]. Cui frater tuus respondit, ne vereretur audacter facere quod ipsi iniunctum erat. Se quidem non solum ei ex animo ignoscere, verumetiam Deum orare ut pro sua gratia ipsum illuminaret, atque ad cognitionem salutis suae adduceret. Addidit etiam, se si pecuniam habuisset, illi daturum fuisse. Deinde ad Potentatum adductus est, ab eoque iterum rogatus ut quae dixerat retractaret atque opinionem deponeret. sed ille non plus quam antea quicquam eorum voluit facere. Itaque iudex quum eum orasset, ne id quod faceret, alienum ei videretur, declarauit ei se summa necessitate atque authoritate dominorum adduci, ut eum morte multaret. Tum Franciscus modestissimis verbis ei gratias egit, ac dixit se animo magnopere dolere quod illi quid facerent plane nescirent, Deumque orare ut sua eis mifericordiam impertiret. Simulatque campana significationem supplicii futuri dedit, duo patria monachorum prodierunt, ex eorum genere ac ordine qui Capucini appellantur. Venicbant autem eo animo ut eius confessionem audirent: ac prima fronte eum monuerunt ne molestiam aliquam mæroremque animo acciperet. Sed eis ille plane respondit, sibi eorum comitatum nullo modo esse necessarium, monuitque ut se reciperent. Caterum fraterculi, ut mos ipsorum est, habebant crucem in manu, eamque ostendebant ut memoriam crucis Christi illi renovarent. Sed Franciscus aiebat Iesum Christum optime in corde suo esse impressum, eiusque mortis memoriam plane infixam, cuius virtutem sentiebat. Quumque illi iterum dixissent, eum nisi ad crucem respiceret in desperationem delapsurum quum tormenta ignis sentiret: respondit cor suum ea consolatione ac lætitia perfusum esse, ut iam gaudio quodam, quod omnem sensum intellectumque humanum superaret, frueretur. Quod vero ad cruciatum attinet, quem in corpore suo sensurus esset, eum subito transiturum: animam vero suam participem suturam beatitudinis cælestis, in illa societate beatorum spirituum atque Angelorum, cum quibus perfrueretur in perpetuum iis bonis quæ Deus filiis suis comparavit, quæ neque oculi hominum unquam viderunt, nec aures eorum audierunt. Postea quum hæc & alia huiusmodi, singularis consolationis plenissima dixisset, ut ei adimeretur omnis loquendi facultas, neque amplius ab iis qui aderant intelligeretur, lingua ei est perforata. Ipse deinde ductus ad locum supplicio constitutum: ibi positis in terram genibus, oculisque in cælum sublatis, Deum orabat tanto animi ardore ut omnes admirarentur. Deinde quum surrexisset, ita se ad supplicium composuit atque accinxit, ut carnifex postulabat: statimque laqueo vitam finiuit. Nam quanuis condemnatus esset ut vivus cobureretur, ei tamen ea gratia impertita fuit, ut sine magno languore doloreque moreretur. Nemo quidem eorum qui ibi affuerunt, cuiusque constantiam summamque animi æquitatem spectarunt, fuit, qui non ita admiraretur, ut attonitus plane incertusque quid ageret, existeret. neque aliud dicere poterant, quam optimum innocentissimumque hominem, ac verum Iesu Christi martyrem ac testem ab illis neccatum esse. Atque ille quidem pius vir multa alia sanctissime est debilitandum multa ei grauia proponerentur: quin potius cernere quisque poterat constantiam illius ac virtutem in horas singulas maiorem fieri, eaque ab illo dici, quae omnes qui audiebant magnopere admirarentur. Itaque magistratus quum videret eum ita affectum & confirmatum, constituit ut postridie moreretur. Quod ille quum intellexisset, finemque vitae suae iam appropinquare cognovisset, me ad se accersivit, ut ipse mecum loqueretur. Inter multa alia magno studio rogavit me, ut de tota sua re & causa, quis exitus eius fuisset, ad te scriberem, teque rogarem tum honoris Dei causa, tum etiam eius amoris ac benevolentiae quam erga se haberes, ut nullam molestiam dolorémque ex morte sua caperes, quum eam quidem propter Iesum Christum perlubenter pateretur, incredibilem quandam in animo suo sentiens consolationem & laetitiam, recognoscénsque tantam Dei gratiam, qua ab eo electus fuisset & vocatus ad opprobria mundi, crudelémque mortem perferendam, ut causam Filii eius Iesu Christi tueretur, qui vitae propriae non pepercit, ut salutem omnibus fidelibus afferret. Postremo se tibi sorores suas & tuas, nepotes, neptesque commendare, ac Deum orare ut vos in optima pace amicitiaque conservet, eamque gratiam impertiat, ut totam vitam vestram ad ipsius cultum consecrare ac conferre possitis. Postero die mane carnisex, qui natione erat Germanus, ad eum accessit, ut eum admoneret de supplicio, quod ipse eo die erat executurus, utque sibi ob eam rem ignosceret. Cui frater tuus respondit, ne vereretur audacter facere quod ipsi iniunctum erat. Se quidem non solum ei ex animo ignoscere, verumetiam Deum orare ut pro sua gratia ipsum illuminaret, atque ad cognitionem salutis suae adduceret. Addidit etiam, se si pecuniam habuisset, illi daturum fuisse. Deinde ad Potentatum adductus est, ab eoque iterum rogatus ut quae dixerat retractaret atque opinionem deponeret. Sed ille non plus quam antea quicquam eorum voluit facere. Itaque iudex quum eum orasset, ne id quod faceret, alienum ei videretur, declaravit ei se summa necessitate atque authoritate dominorum adduci, ut eum morte multaret. Tum Franciscus modestissimis verbis ei gratias egit, ac dixit se animo magnopere dolere quod illi quid facerent plane nescirent, Deumque orare ut sua eis mifericordiam impertiret. Simulatque campana significationem supplicij futuri dedit, duo patria monachorum prodierunt, ex eorum genere ac ordine qui Capucini appellantur. Venicbant autem eo animo vt eius confessionem audirent: ac prima fronte eum monuerunt ne molcstiam aliquâ mœroremque animo acciperet. Sed eis ille plane respondit, sibi eorum comitatum nullo modo esse necessarium, monuitque vt se reciperent. Caterùm fraterculi, vt mos ipsorum est, habebant crucem in manu, eámque ostendebant vt memoriam crucis Christi illi renouarent. Sed Franciscus aiebat Iesum Christum optimè in corde suo esse impressum, eiúsque mortis memoriam plane infixam, cuius virtutem sentiebat. Quúmque illi iterum dixissent, eum nisi ad crucem respiceret in desperationem delapsurum quum tormenta ignis sentiret: respondit cor suum ea consolatione ac laetitia perfusum esse, vt iam gaudio quodam, quod omnem sensum intellectúmque humanum superaret, frueretur. Quod verò ad cruciatum attinet, què in corpore suo sensurus esset, eú subitò transiturum: animâ verò suam participem suturam beatitudinis cœlestis, in illa societate beatorû spirituum atque Angelorum, cum quibus perfrueretur in perpetuũ ijs bonis quæ Deus filijs suis comparauit, quæ neque oculi hominum vnquam viderunt, nec aures eorum audierunt. Postea quum hæc & alia huiusmodi, singularis consolationis plenissima dixisset, vt ei adimeretur omnis loquendi facultas, neque amplius ab ijs qui aderant intelligeretur, lingua ei est perforata. Ipse deinde ductus ad locũ supplicio constitutũ: ibi positis in terram genibus, oculisque in cælum sublatis, Deum orabat tanto animi ardore vt omnes admirarentur. Deinde quum surrexisset, ita se ad supplicium composuit atque accinxit, vt carnifex postulabat: Statimque laqueo vitam finiuit. Nam quanuis condemnatus esset vt viuus coburetur, ei tamen ea gratia impertita fuit, vt sine magno languore doloréque moreretur. Nemo quidem eorum qui ibi affuerunt, cuiusque constantiam summámque animi æquitatem spectarunt, fuit, qui non ita admiraretur, vt attonitus plane incertúsque quid ageret, existeret. neque aliud dicere poterant, quàm optimum innocentissimumque hominem, ac verum Iesu Christi martyrem ac testem ab illis necatum esse. Atque ille quidem pius vir multa alia sanctissimè est loquutus cum eo toto tempore quo fuit in carcere, tum etiam quum jam ei moriendum esset. quae quidem digna sunt, quae ad omnium cognitionem peruenirent: sed ego ea non possum ad te hoc tempore scribere: ac vereor ne paulo longior fuerim. Hoc solum addam, quod ille fecit quum jam spiritum redditurus esset. nam quū ego seorsum essem post multitudinem quatuor millium hominum, oculos satis procul in me coniecit, manuque dextra quae non erat ligata signum dedit, quo ego admonitus ad te scriberem, & ea quae promiseram praestarem. Et mox caput inclinans, Deo spiritum reddidit, die xxi. mensis Iulii, M.D. LIIII. Scriptum Comi, XXIX. Iulii, M.D.LIIII.
units.tr: From the time when your brother was thrown into prison, for as long as he remained there, it is incredible how many people of this city, of every kind and rank, and especially teachers and nobles, earnestly begged him not to cling so stubbornly to these empty opinions, as they called them, into which they thought he had been led, so that they judged his mind and reason to be deranged. So they urged him strongly to take some thought and care for his own welfare and salvation, and to cast off all those delusions by which they believed he was affected and held. But the godly man always answered them steadily that what he had put forward he would firmly defend: it was not idle speculations or vain opinions, nor was his mind disturbed or seized by any fantastic humour so as to be mad, but the pure truth of God, the holy word of our Lord Jesus Christ and his saving doctrine. When he set out the individual articles of this, he immediately cited the weightiest testimonies of Scripture, by which he proved and confirmed his statement, declaring with unconquered constancy that he would much rather undergo death than betray, through perfidy, Jesus Christ the one Saviour and Redeemer of the world, whose cause and doctrine he was defending, and betray the truth of the gospel, and the cause which God had committed and entrusted to him, to be defended even unto death. At last, after he had disputed for a long time with the teachers of this city, monks and priests, and with many others who came to him, some wishing to turn him from that view, others moved by a certain pity because they had found him to be a truly good and upright man, they all came to him together with one accord. When they had asked him to give up that opinion, they promised and offered him citizenship together with whatever provision of advantages he might desire. But when they saw that they could obtain nothing from him, shortly afterwards they sent another message: unless he renounced the opinion and view he had taken up, he would suffer the penalty of death. To this message he replied with the gladdest mind that this was the one thing he most wished for, and that no more welcome news could be brought to him. Meanwhile, while these things were going on, a letter came from the senate of Milan with an order that Francis Gamba should be put to death and burned alive. But when the judges were already about to carry out that order and inflict that punishment on Francis, other letters arrived from Genoa, letters of recommendation which the Imperial Legate and many Milanese nobles had written. So the decision and the execution of the sentence were postponed for some days. Throughout this whole time your excellent brother remained firm in his purpose. Soon after, other letters announcing his death were brought. So he was led out of the citadel in which, as you know, he was held captive, and brought before the magistrate they call the Potentate, who in that city is judge of both civil and capital causes. There a sentence was pronounced that, unless he returned to them and abandoned his opinion, he was already condemned to be subjected to the supreme punishment. Then he, showing that he was greatly glad and affected with a wonderful consolation, most modestly thanked the Potentate for the news that had been brought to him. Nevertheless that magistrate, both on my account and because he had been asked by certain other nobles, kept Francis safe and unharmed in prison for another week. During this time he disputed with everyone with the greatest freedom and boldness, bringing forward very many arguments and authorities from holy Scripture by which to confirm what he defended, so that his spirit was increasingly raised, and his constancy was seen to grow greater by the day the longer his life was granted to him. Finally the judge summoned him and told him that he must die the next day, or certainly the day after, under the order he had received from the senate of Milan. He replied as before that this news was most welcome and most pleasing to him. But when the judge asked him again and warned him many times that, if he wished to retract what he had said, and especially what he had dared to say about the Sacrament of the Mass, the promised reward which had been offered to him would certainly be his, he took no account of such promises and valued them no more than the lightest breath of wind. He often said too that the advantages offered to him by them could in no way be compared with the good things which he was certain to receive from the Lord, such as the crown of immortality and eternal life, promised and laid up for all who devoutly worship God. Nor did he ever abandon or weaken the greatness of his spirit, although the enemies of the truth set many grave things before him to shake and utterly weaken him. Indeed, anyone could see that his constancy and virtue grew greater hour by hour, and that the things he said were such that all who heard him were greatly astonished. So when the magistrate saw him so disposed and confirmed, he decided that he should die the next day. When he learned this, and perceived that the end of his life was now near, he summoned me to speak with him in person. Among many other things he asked me with great earnestness to write to you about his whole case and cause, and how it had ended, and to beg you, both for the honour of God and for the love and goodwill which you bore towards him, not to take any trouble or grief from his death, since he was suffering it most gladly for the sake of Jesus Christ, feeling in his mind an incredible consolation and joy, and recognising the great grace of God by which he had been chosen and called to the reproaches of the world and to endure a cruel death, so that he might defend the cause of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who did not spare his own life so that he might bring salvation to all the faithful. Lastly, he commended to you his sisters and yours, and your nephews and nieces, and asked that God would keep you in the best peace and friendship, and grant you that grace, that you might consecrate and devote your whole lives to his worship. The next morning the executioner, who was a German by birth, came to him to warn him about the punishment which he was to carry out that day, and to ask his forgiveness for it. Your brother replied that he should not hesitate to do boldly what had been enjoined on him. For his part he not only forgave him from his heart, but also prayed to God that by his grace he would enlighten him and lead him to the knowledge of his own salvation. He added also that, had he had money, he would have given it to him. Then he was brought before the Potentate, who again asked him to retract what he had said and to give up his opinion. But he would do none of those things any more than before. So when the judge asked him not to think ill of what he was doing, he declared to him that he was being brought to put him to death by the utmost necessity and by the authority of his masters. Then Francis thanked him in the most modest words, and said that he grieved deeply that they did not truly know what they were doing, and prayed to God that he would grant them his mercy. As soon as the bell gave the signal of the coming punishment, two little Capuchin friars came out, of that kind and order which are called Capuchins. They came with the intention of hearing his confession, and at first they warned him not to take any trouble or sorrow to heart. But he plainly answered them that he had no need at all of their company, and urged them to withdraw. Meanwhile the little brothers, as is their custom, held a cross in their hand and showed it, so that they might renew in him the memory of Christ's cross. But Francis said that Jesus Christ was most fully impressed in his heart, and that the memory of his death was fixed there, whose power he felt. When they said again that, unless he looked to the cross, he would fall into despair when he felt the torments of the fire, he replied that his heart was so filled with consolation and joy that he now enjoyed a certain delight which surpassed all human sense and understanding. As for the torment which he was about to feel in his body, it would pass quickly; but his soul would share in heavenly blessedness, in that fellowship of blessed spirits and angels, with whom he would enjoy for ever those good things which God has prepared for his children, which neither the eyes of men have ever seen nor their ears heard. After he had said these things and others of the same kind, most full of singular consolation, his power of speech was taken away, and he could no longer be understood by those present; his tongue was pierced. Then he was led to the place set for the punishment, and there, kneeling on the ground with his eyes raised to heaven, he prayed to God with such fervour of spirit that everyone marvelled. Then, when he had risen, he prepared and girded himself for the punishment as the executioner required, and at once ended his life with the noose. For although he had been condemned to be burned alive, this favour was granted to him, that he should die without great pain and anguish. Indeed none of those who were present there, and who saw his constancy and the highest equanimity of his spirit, failed to be so astonished that they stood there utterly amazed and uncertain what to do. Nor could they say anything else than that an excellent and most innocent man, a true martyr and witness of Jesus Christ, had been put to death by them. Indeed that godly man spoke most holily of many other things with him during the whole time he was in prison, and even when he was now to die. These things are certainly worthy to reach the knowledge of all, but I cannot write them to you at this time, and I fear I have already been rather long. I will add only this, which he did when he was about to give up his spirit. For when I stood apart, after a crowd of some four thousand people, he cast his eyes upon me from a fair distance, and with his right hand, which was not bound, he gave a sign, by which I was reminded to write to you and to perform what I had promised. And presently, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit to God, on the 21st day of July, 1554. Written at Como, 29 July 1554.

units.la: OTTHO CATELINA.
units.tr: Otho Catelina.

units.la: Ttho Catelina, natus Gandaui, Flandriae metropoli, eximius artifex caelando vario opere vel etiam inaurando superficiem armorum & cultrorum, à prima aetate in Angliam se contulerat, ut in ea regione sub magistro opificium suum exerceret. Anno autem M.D. L. regnante Edouardo VI. quum Flandri eius regionis incolae permissu Regis ecclesiam Londini instituissent ex verbo Dei emendatiorem: hic noster Ottho sedulo conciones frequentabat, ut doctrinam Euangelii audiret. Sed quia imbuta ac praepedita Papistarum superstitionibus mens eius non satis initio capiebat scientiam illam salutis: Catelina se totum lectioni sacrae Scripturae dedit, in qua breui tempore tantos fecerat progressus, ut Ecclesiae Christi perutilis operae ipsius accideret. Postquā quatuor annis aut eo amplius in piorum coetu non sine magno fructu vixisset, decreuit ob quaedam negotia Gandauum reuerti. Amici ipsius antequam se itineri commisisset, monuerunt benevolè hominem, ut siquando inter lupos versaretur, considerate omnia ac modeste ageret, ne sponte in discrimen capitis se conijceret: quibus ille respondit, nihil se quidem temere aut inconsiderate acturū: sed si, inquit, incidero in eos qui suis blasphemiis Deum eiusque Filium Jesum Christum contumelia afficiunt: absit ut tale quid audiens, ulla ratione taceam. neque enim lampas vasi supponenda est. In traiectu ipsius maris quod Angliam seiungit à Flandria, non sine magno periculo cum multis aliis nauigans, comites suos ex verbo Dei consolabatur. quúmq; jā[?] salvi portū ingressi essent, hortatus est omnes ad agendum Deo gratias, atque in timore eius permanendum: fieri enim posse, ut qui illos maris periculo liberasset, is fidē illorū postmodò per ignem probaret atque ita ex hac vita criperet. quod quidem verè est de se locutus. nā feruor ac zelus quo veritatis studiū amplexus erat, haud passus est ipsum diu in his mūdi miseriis viuere: qui hoc pietatis amore flagrās, omni plane metu remoto, nō destitit etiā publicè idololatriā detestari.Res autem sic se habet: Gandauū qui peruenisset, certior factus est ea in urbe Dominicanū quendā, cui Pistorius cognomen erat, veritatis habere cognitionem, verámq; doctrinam populo annuntiare, ac propterea ingentē hominū frequentiā ad eius cōciones audiēdas cōcurrere. Hoc rumore incitatus Catelina die Iouis ante festum Paschæ ingressus est tēplū S. Michaelis (in quo ferè semper monachꝰ ille cōcionari solitus erat) sibiq; locū delegit è regione suggesti, quò melius quæ dicerentur audire posset. Sed ecce monachus conscēso suggesto pro thesauro carbones affert, loco salubris pabuli dira venena proponit populo. Etenim multis verbis in ea cōcione transsubstantiationē suā cōfirmabat, magnopere cupiēs persuadere populo, virtute verborum Sacramentalium (ut aiunt) panē conuerti in substantiā corporis Christi. Hæc verba adeò Catelinam pupugerunt, quum tam aperte populo illudi cerneret, ut vultus eius præ animi perturbatione planè immutaretur: atque ægrè admodum se continuit dum finem concioni imposuisset monachus, quem ex suggesto descendentem, Ottho nudato capite his verbis excepit: Heus, amice, tota oratio tua manifestè pugnat cum Sacris literis, per quas (si quidē mihi fiat audientia) clarè demōstrabo falsam te populo annuntiasse doctrinā. Cucullatus vero animo perturbatus, hunc auscultare noluit, sed ei fecit indicium ut recederet. Ottho cōtrà propiùs ipsum accessit magnóq; Spiritus ardore flagrās, O Pseudoprophēta, inquit, qui falsò persuades populo panē verè esse corpus Christi, quū Sacramentū tantùmmodo sit Christi pro nobis passi ac mortui! Dum hæc fiūt, ingēs populi tumultus oritur, multiq; utriusque sexus homines ad illum, Heu, inquiunt, amice, quid agis? Quibus ille respondit, Pseudoprophetæ sunt isti, qui vos specie veri decipiunt: ne credite. His dictis, impetu turbæ è templo egredientis unà quoque ipse abreptus egredi coactus fuit, ac quanuis plurimi cū hortarentur, ut se in pedes conijceret: negauit tamen facturum se, quin potius eos monebat, ut quæ palàm & publicè dixisset apud se quisq; diligenter expenderet: ac tum moderato incessu abiēs, quum vixdum ad Portam quæ fere in meditullio urbis non procul a prædicto templo Michaelis sita est, peruenisset, interceptus fuit a Procuratore fisci Iacobo Hesselio, qui hominem iussit deduci ad vetus Comitis castrum circiter horam decimam antemeridianam xi. Apr. M.D.LIII. Pomeridianis horis Procurator ille cum Pistorio ciusque collega Ioanne Bunderio, aliisque eiusdem farinæ hominibus ad carcerem se contulit, qui cum Otthone tribus ad minimum horis disputarunt de præcipuis religionis papisticæ capitibus, quæ illi cauillis & multis logomachijs, tueri & asserere conabantur: transubstantiationem videlicet, invocationem Sanctorum, Purgatorium, ac cæteras ciusmodi nugas, quæ tantum ὡς τὰ ἀλφίτα[?] faciunt: Ottho ea omnia verbi Diuini trutina examinari, atque ex doctrina Filij Dei, velut Lydio lapide probari cupiebat. Illi verò metuentes ne causa caderent, ab eo examine abhorrebant: tandemque constitutum est inter ipsos ut sententiam suā scripto declararet Catelina, cui Procurator papyrum & alia ad scriptionem necessaria tradi curauit. Nos autem hic adjiciemus quandā veluti summam disquisitionis.
units.tr: Otho Catelina, born at Ghent, the metropolis of Flanders, was an outstanding craftsman in engraving various designs and even in gilding the surfaces of weapons and knives. From his earliest years he had gone to England to practise his trade there under a master. In the year 1550, in the reign of Edward VI, when the Flemish inhabitants of that country had set up in London, with the King's permission, a church reformed more purely according to the Word of God, our Otho attended the sermons diligently so that he might hear the doctrine of the Gospel. But because his mind, steeped in and hampered by the superstitions of the Papists, did not at first grasp that knowledge of salvation well enough, Catelina gave himself wholly to reading Holy Scripture. In a short time he made such progress in it that he became very useful to the Church of Christ. After he had lived for four years or more among the godly, not without great profit, he decided to return to Ghent on certain business. Before he set out on the journey, his friends kindly warned him that if he should ever be among wolves, he should consider everything carefully and act with moderation, so as not to put his life in peril needlessly. He replied that he would indeed do nothing rashly or inconsiderately; but, he said, if he should fall in with those who insult God and his Son Jesus Christ with their blasphemies, far be it from him, on hearing such things, to keep silent by any means, for a lamp is not to be put under a bushel. On the crossing of the sea that separates England from Flanders, he sailed with many others, not without great danger, and comforted his companions from the Word of God. When they had now entered the harbour safe, he urged them all to give thanks to God and to remain in his fear, for it could happen that he who had freed them from the perils of the sea would afterwards test their faith by fire and so take them out of this life. He truly spoke of himself in this. For the fervour and zeal with which he embraced the pursuit of truth did not allow him to live long in these miseries of the world. Burning with this love of godliness, and wholly free of fear, he did not cease even to denounce idolatry publicly. Matters stood thus. When he reached Ghent, he was told that in that city a certain Dominican, whose surname was Pistorius, had knowledge of the truth and preached sound doctrine to the people, and that therefore a great crowd gathered to hear his sermons. Stirred by this report, Catelina entered the church of St Michael on the Thursday before Easter (where that monk was almost always accustomed to preach), and chose for himself a place opposite the pulpit, where he could hear better what was said. But behold, the monk, having climbed the pulpit, brings coals in place of treasure and sets deadly poisons before the people instead of wholesome food. For in that sermon he confirmed his transubstantiation at length, very eager to persuade the people that by the power of the sacramental words (as they say) bread is turned into the substance of the body of Christ. These words so stung Catelina, when he saw the people being so openly deceived, that his countenance was plainly changed by his agitation of mind, and he could hardly restrain himself until the monk had finished his sermon. As the monk came down from the pulpit, Otho met him with bared head and these words: "Hey, friend, your whole discourse plainly contradicts the Holy Scriptures, by which (if I am given a hearing) I will clearly show that you have announced a false doctrine to the people." But the hooded man, disturbed in mind, would not listen to him and signalled him to withdraw. Otho, on the contrary, came closer to him, and burning with a great ardour of the Spirit, said: "O false prophet, who falsely persuade the people that bread is truly the body of Christ, when the sacrament is only a sign of Christ who suffered and died for us!" While these things were happening, a great tumult of the people arose, and many men and women said to him, "Alas, friend, what are you doing?" He answered them: "They are false prophets who deceive you under the appearance of truth; do not believe them." With these words, he was carried out of the church by the rush of the crowd leaving, and he too, swept along, was forced to go out. Although very many urged him to throw himself at their feet for safety, he refused to do so, but rather advised them to weigh carefully in their own minds what he had said openly and publicly. Then, walking away at a measured pace, he had scarcely reached the gate that lies almost in the middle of the city, not far from the said church of St Michael, when he was intercepted by the fiscal prosecutor Jacob Hesselius, who ordered the man to be taken to the old castle of the Count at about ten o'clock in the morning of 11 April 1553. In the afternoon that prosecutor went to the prison with Pistorius, his colleague John Bunderius, and other men of the same stamp, and for at least three hours they disputed with Otho about the principal heads of the papistical religion, which they tried to defend and assert with jests and many wordy quarrels: namely transubstantiation, the invocation of saints, purgatory, and other such trifles, which amount to nothing more than barley-meal [ὡς τὰ ἀλφίτα]. Otho wished all these things to be weighed in the balance of the divine Word and proved by the doctrine of the Son of God, as by a touchstone. But they, fearing that their cause would fall, shrank from that examination. At last it was agreed between them that Catelina should state his opinion in writing, and the prosecutor had paper and the other things needed for writing handed to him. Here we shall add a kind of summary of the discussion.

units.la: Ac primum de cœna Domini, dicebat subesse tropum verbis Christi, Hoc est corpus meum: neque enim id crasse intelligendum esse ac si panis fit ipsa substantia naturalis corporis Christi, quod variis exemplis ac testimoniis Scripturæ ostendebat sic nec posse nec debere intelligi. Aduersarii interrupto eius sermone venerunt ad quæstionem de invocatione Sanctorum. respondit ille, unum tantummodo Deum adorandum esse in Spiritu & veritate. nam quū is, inquit, ad se vocet omnes qui sub onere gemunt, ut iis alleuationem afferat: quū hortetur ut pulsemus, quæramus ac petamus, addita promissione nequaquam frustratum in ipsa sua quenquam: denique, cum certò sciamus Deus summè bonus, haud dubiè daturus quidquid in nomine Christi petierimus, summa profecto ipsiꝰ maiestate iniuria afficimus, si in precibus nostris ad Deum, alium mediatorem vel aduocatum adhibeamus quàm Christum: quocirca impudenter ac scelerate tè illos facere dicebat qui Christū iure suo priuantes persuadent plebi Sanctos nobis apud Deū patrocinari ac pro peccatoribus intercedere: quod officiū vni Christo commissum est, qui in cruce pependit & nostrū reatum subijt. neque enim ad quenquam maiori cum fiducia ac spe salutis obtinendae accedere possumus quàm ad eū qui communis omnium nostrū frater est, Filius æternus Dei viuentis: qui solus & vult & potest bene facere generi humano. Ad quæstionem illam friuolam de igne Purgatorij, duas se tantum nosse vias aiebat, alteram quæ ducit ad cælum vbi quietis beatorum sedes est, alteram quæ ducit ad inferos, reproborum omnium triste domicilium. Hæ viæ nobis proponuntur Scripturæ exemplis de malè Diuite ac Lazaro, atque Latrone altero cui Christus in cruce dixit, Hodie eris mecum in paradiso: nō autem, Hodie coijcieris in igne Purgatorij vt ibi pro peccatis tuis poenitentiam agas. Rogatus etiam à monachis an Papam agnosceret, quippe qui caput sit sanctæ & Apostolicæ Ecclesiæ: respondit, Christo Redemptori cum tantùmodò honorem tribuendum, vt summū sit & vnicum Ecclesiæ caput: Papam verò se habere pro Præsule ecclesiæ Antichristi, eundémque detestari vt filium perditionis sedentem in loco sancto. Deinde rediens ad sermonē de cœna, quē interruperant Cucullati, negauit plane, Christum in ea corporaliter, ac realiter, vt loquuntur, contineri, manibúsque sacrificorum attrectari: dictúmque suum aut potius Christi, confirmabat Scripturæ locis tam cōmodis atque dilucidis, vt patroni dignitatis papisticæ & transsubstantiationis defensores prorsus obmutescerent, suámque infantiam cum summa impietate ac nequitia coniunctam in cavillis & tergiversationibus friuolis facilè auditoribus proderet. Præses autē Flandriæ Helwegh quum videret hominem coram se & nonnullis consiliariis, tam præsenti animo, magna ingenii dexteritate, sermonisque mirabili suauitate interrogatis respondere: Ottho nē affatus, Nō licet, inquit, mihi per edictū Principis disputare de fide cū haeretico cuiuscunq; sectæ, sed mittā ad te monachū aut si mauis sacerdote laicum (vt vocant) qui coeptā disputationem persequatur. Ottho autem respodit se paratū esse fidei suæ ratione reddere nō solum illis, sed etiā ex plebe infima abiectissimo cuiq;. Præsidi verò & consiliariis qui aderat bene precabatur, optabátque ut diu officio suo fungi possent ad gloriam Dei atq; animarum suarum salute. Scripsit autem post ad uxorem suam Christina quam reliquerat Emedæ, consolans illam atq; exhortans ut omne curam vitæ huius caducæ Domino commendaret, qui viduas & pupillos in tutela sua recipit, ut ipse in Scripturis testatur: monebat præterea ea ut quæ coniugi pignora habebat Samuelem scilicet & Saram diligeter in Christiana institueret fide, quam quidem quinque annis simul coluerat, ꝑ qua breui morte subiturũ se significabat: postremò iubebat ut ductu Spiritus sancti, certũ aliquod vitæ genus ampleƈteretur. Die Sabbathi qui 27. erat Ap. anni supra nominati, Ottho, natus annos circiter triginta, capitis danatus, secunda pomeridiana in forũ ductus est, ubi fasces ad eũ exuredũ dispositi erant.
