Quum autem populũ qui tam tristis supplicii spectator aderat, hortari vellet Catelina, interpellatus fuit ab Hesselio, qui carnifice sæpius monebat, ut expediret suum negotium. Quo viso, reus ægerrimè tulit sibi nullam fieri potestatem loquendi ad populum. proinde Hesselium compellans, Video, inquit, te sollicitum esse & anxie laborare ad effundendū sanguinē innoxiū, sed precor Deū ut tibi ignoscat. Ad quæ verba Procurator ille respodit, Amen, amen. Deinde Ottho se convertes ad plebem, multa, inquit, decreuerā vobis declarare, sed imperatur mihi filetiū, quæ res admodum me male habet. Tum carnifex, ut moris est in iis locis, procubes in genua ante ipsum, rogauit ut sibi ignosceret quod per eum plectendus esset: Ottho autem tortore osculatus, Ego, vero, inquit, tibi condono ac lubēs: peccata tibi tua condonet Dominus opto. Ac protinus se in genua prosternes, in hanc ratione precatus est, Pater cælestis qui secundum ꝑmissiones tuas misisti Filium tuum unigenitum ut se offerret in sacrificium ꝑ peccatorum nostrorum reatu: supplico tibi unus e seruis tuis etiā minimus, ut me quoque gratiæ tuæ ac misericordiæ participe facias. Vos autem fratres charissimi, obsecro & obtestor ut concorditer omnes Deum pro me precemini, ut quemadmodum pollicitus est suis, in extrema hac vitæ meæ hora mihi adsit, nec deserat unquam. Hic rursus Procurator, ad carnificem ut supplicium maturaret clamauit. ac tu placidè velut ouis se Catelina ad palū deligari passus est. dumq; catenis circumcirca vinciretur, ad populū hæc verba habuit, Cauete a pseudoprophetis, qui dicut Ecce, hic est, aut illic Christus: ne erretis, quoniam in caelis est ad dexteram Dei Patris. Ad extremum sublata voce, Pater, inquit, caelestis in manus tuas commendo Spiritum meum, teque oro vt pro gratia tua, puerulos meos in timore nominis tui coferues. His dictis primum laqueo suffocatus, flammisque adustus, deinde in patibulo extra vrbem suspensus inter fures & latrones fuit: sed haud dubie anima ipsius in caelum sublata est, propter Saluatorem nostrum Iesum Christum, qui corpus etiam eiusdem in vltimo die excitabit, vt beata immortalitate cum omnibus Sanctis fruatur.
units.tr: And first, concerning the Lord's Supper, he said that there is a trope in Christ's words, "This is my body." They are not to be understood crudely, as if the very substance of Christ's natural body became the bread. He showed by various examples and testimonies of Scripture that they could neither be nor ought to be understood in that way. When his opponents broke into his discourse, they moved on to the question of the invocation of the saints. He replied that only one God is to be adored, in Spirit and in truth. For, he said, when God calls to himself all who groan under a burden, to give them relief; when he urges us to knock, seek and ask, with the promise that no one who does so will be disappointed in his expectation; and finally, since we know for certain that God is supremely good and will undoubtedly give whatever we ask in Christ's name, we do the greatest injury to his majesty if in our prayers to God we employ any mediator or advocate other than Christ. Therefore, he said, those who deprive Christ of his right, and persuade the people that the saints intercede for us with God and plead for sinners, act impudently and wickedly. This office was committed to Christ alone, who hung on the cross and bore our guilt. For we can approach no one with greater confidence and hope of obtaining salvation than him who is the common brother of us all, the eternal Son of the living God, who alone both wills and is able to do good to the human race. As for that trifling question about the fire of Purgatory, he said that he knew only two ways: one leads to heaven, where the blessed have their seat of rest; the other leads to hell, the sad dwelling of all the reprobate. These two ways are set before us by Scripture, in the examples of the rich man and Lazarus, and of the other thief to whom Christ said on the cross, "Today you will be with me in paradise," not "Today you will be cast into the fire of Purgatory to do penance there for your sins." Being asked also by the monks whether he acknowledged the Pope, who is supposedly the head of the holy and apostolic Church, he replied that honour is to be given to Christ the Redeemer alone, as the sole and supreme head of the Church. He regarded the Pope as the prelate of the church of Antichrist, and he detested him as the son of perdition sitting in the holy place. Then, returning to the discourse on the Supper, which the cowled men had interrupted, he flatly denied that Christ is contained in it corporally and really, as they say, and handled by the hands of the priests. He confirmed his statement, or rather Christ's, with passages of Scripture so apt and clear that the defenders of papistical dignity and the champions of transubstantiation were struck completely dumb, and his hearers could easily see how their infancy, joined with great impiety and wickedness, was exposed in their frivolous quibbles and evasions. When the governor of Flanders, Helwegh, saw that the man answered questions put to him in his presence and before several counsellors with such presence of mind, great quickness of wit and wonderful smoothness of speech, Ottho was told: "It is not permitted to me, by the prince's edict, to dispute about the faith with a heretic of any sect. But I will send you a monk, or, if you prefer, a layman (as they call him), who may continue the disputation that has begun." Ottho replied that he was ready to give an account of his faith not only to them, but also to the most abject person of the lowest rank. He then gave good wishes to the governor and the counsellors who were present, and wished that they might long discharge their office to the glory of God and the salvation of their souls. Afterwards he wrote to his wife Christina, whom he had left at Emden, consoling and exhorting her to commit all care of this fleeting life to the Lord, who takes widows and orphans under his protection, as he himself testifies in the Scriptures. He further advised her to bring up diligently in the Christian faith the pledges she had from her husband, namely Samuel and Sara, whom she had cherished together with him for five years, and he signified that he would soon undergo death for that faith. Finally he bade her, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, to embrace some definite way of life. On Saturday, the 27th of April of the year mentioned above, Ottho, about thirty years old, condemned to death, was led at two o'clock in the afternoon into the square where the faggots had been arranged to burn him. When Catelina wished to address the people who were present as spectators of so sad a punishment, he was interrupted by Hesselius, who kept urging the executioner to get on with his business. Seeing this, the prisoner took it very badly that he was given no opportunity of speaking to the people. So, addressing Hesselius, he said, "I see that you are anxious and labour eagerly to shed innocent blood, but I pray God to forgive you." To these words the procurator replied, "Amen, amen." Then Ottho turned to the people: "I had decided to declare many things to you," he said, "but silence is ordered me, which grieves me greatly." Then the executioner, as is customary in such places, knelt before him and asked him to forgive him for having to put him to death. Ottho, embracing the executioner, said, "Indeed I forgive you gladly; I pray the Lord to forgive you your sins." And at once he prostrated himself on his knees and prayed in this manner: "Heavenly Father, who according to your promises sent your only-begotten Son to offer himself as a sacrifice for the guilt of our sins, I, one of your servants, even the least of them, beseech you that you would make me also a partaker of your grace and mercy. And you, most beloved brothers, I beg and entreat you that you all together pray God for me, that, as he has promised to his own, he may be with me in this last hour of my life, and never forsake me." Here again the procurator shouted to the executioner to hasten the punishment. And Catelina, gentle as a sheep, allowed himself to be tied to the stake. While he was being bound with chains all around, he addressed the people with these words: "Beware of false prophets, who say, 'Behold, here is Christ, or there': do not err, for he is in heaven at the right hand of God the Father." At last, raising his voice, he said, "Heavenly Father, into your hands I commend my spirit, and I pray you that, for the sake of your grace, you preserve my little children in the fear of your name." With these words he was first strangled with a noose and burned with flames, and then hanged on a gibbet outside the city between thieves and robbers. But without doubt his soul was carried up to heaven, for the sake of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who will also raise up his body on the last day, so that it may enjoy blessed immortality with all the saints.

units.la: IOAN. FILIEVL, & IVLIANVS LEVEILLE.
units.tr: JOHN FILIOLUS AND JULIAN LEVEILLE.

units.la: Horum duorum exemplo intelligere licet, cum quatenus in optima causa fidendum sit vel suspectis ac perditis hominibus: tum vero etiam, quata vis sit diuini numinis, cuius afflatu consequamur vt neque casu aliquo graviore perturbemur: O, vel capti membris omnibus, sublime suspirantes tamen corporis officio perinde fungamur.
units.tr: From the example of these two we may learn both how far one should trust in a good cause, even among suspect and wicked men, and what power the divine majesty has. By its inspiration we are kept from being thrown into confusion by any heavier misfortune, so that even when captive in every limb, sighing upward, we still perform the duties of the body just the same.

units.la: A[?]NNO Domini M.D.LIII. I.XVII. Cal. Maij. Ioannes Filiolus faber lignarius, & Iulianus Leue[?]lhæus ligularius, Sanserræ Burgundionum oppido natus, comprehensi fuerunt à Gillio Perfio Latrunculatore prouinciæ Borbonensis, auspicio D. Sanctandreani, Tribuni celerum: idque, duobus circiter à Niuerno milliaribus quà Desiram itur. Comprehensurus autem eos Gillius, Sat scio, inquit, o fratres, quo pergatis. cedite anabo[?], nobisque vos aperire ne dubitate. nos enim ij profectò sumus[?], o fratres, qui quidem vos vniuersos omni sceleratorum hominum contumelia, nedum iniuria, prohibere maxime velimus. His blanditiis eos paulatim allicere veterator ille nitebatur, assimulatæ veritatis specie, falsaque animi erga illos sui praedicatione tectus, ac fidem etiam suam, si egerent, vltro pollicitus. Quin vt callidi° exciperet incautos, praemisit sagittarios suos his verbis, Ite prae, inquit, ite, equosque admittite: nihil enim hic ad vos locus. Postmodum autem insequens vndique, Eia, inquit, fratres, quonam pergitis, inquam? Perginus[?], inquiunt, Desiram. Nec longius? Sanè quidem. Num, inquit, Geneuam? eodemque & infantulum hunc & filiam deducitis? Illi ingenuè fateri. Et vxores, inquit, vestræ illic nesunt? Illi fateri rursum. Mox ad os admoto pugno sibilans Gillius aduocat sagittarios, atque vt Niuernum in custodiam adducantur iubet: id quod actutum est factum. Illo deducti, pluribus ab code verbis super eo quod paulo ante confessi fuissent, interrogantur: eo se nimirum consilio profici Geneua, vt in rem diuina, quam passim in Gallia tum blasphemijs, idololatria, pseudoprophetia, tum abusu Sacramentorum inexpiabili contaminari quotidie cerneret, incumbere rectius possent: Geneuam autem esse ciuitatem, in quam re diuina iam Euangelicae disciplinae veritas quasi postliminij iure quodam reuersa esse videretur. Quoniam autem Sacramenta nonnihil attigerat, rogabat primum quem Sacramentorum vsum optimum esse arbitrarentur: quam item Euangelicam doctrinam, quam quidem auspicatae maxime ciuitatum omnium Geneuae consedisse dicerent. Ac primum quidem, num Christum ipsum hostia sacerdotali sic inclusum crederent, vt & panem & vinum pronuntiatis nonnullis a sacrificulo verbis id quod sunt protinus esse desinere, ac repente verum Christi corpus & sanguinem effici conflarique iudicarent. Illi tum Iesum Christum (vt scriptum est) in caelum ascendisse, se credere, ad dexteram sedere Dei Patris, indeque venturum iudicatum viuos ac mortuos: eoque modo & panem & vinum naturae suae proprietatem vtique retinere. Nec vero panem ipsum & vinum aliud esse quicquam in hoc genere putandum, nisi signum ac indicium veri corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi: quoniam sicut pane cor humanum vegetaretur, vino delectaretur, sic animus pretioso Iesu Christi corpore quasi sustentaretur, sanguine relaxaretur: per illum enim receptum habuisse nos ad Patrem. Haec se omnia sine controuersia verissima & fateri esse, & vitae periculo profiteri cupere. Interrogati deinde quid de Communicatione statuerent, aiebant administrari pane & vinu in commemorationem mortis passionisque Iesu Christi: ac tu quidem non accipi tantum panem & vinum, sed plane etiam fidei beneficio verum ipsum corpus & sanguinem eiusdem Christi, qui animum interposito fidei velut instrumento purgaret atq; reficeret. Quod ad Missam, de qua quoque interrogarentur, pertineret, meram superstitionem & idololatriam aiebant esse, merum hominum inuentum, meram condemnationem. Quod autem diuum Petrum Papam, Missaeque potissimum authorem existimaret, opinione longe falsum illud. nihil enim de Missa ne cogitasse quidem diuum Petrum vnquam, tantum Euangelio nuntiando interpretandoq; praefectum, atque eo nomine vocatum & selectum fuisse. Itaque si quam salutis partem in illa Missa poneremus, inanem ac ieiunam Domini nostri Iesu Christi passionem esse oportere: quòd nemo mortalium, Christianorum praesertim hominum,non modò non vsurpare sermone,sed ne cogitatione quidem vlla comprehendere velle debeat. atque hinc effici quidem id quod est,nihili plane rem esse Missam istam:meram,inquam,idololatriam esse Missam istam,quae (nefandam sane re ac morte piandam)passionem Domini nostri Iesu Christi post hominum memoriam improbiffimè flagitiosissiméque conuellens & obliterans,seipsam ingerat impudentiffimè:feque aliquid esse ac plane iam etiam mordicus oportere retineri tranfucrfis quibusdam,sed alienis & exoticis hominibus indignißimè persuadeat.Interrogati praeterea num sacrificus panem in corpus Christi reuera conuertendi facultatem haberet,Deum ipsum neque subditum hominibus,neque eorum linguis & exorcismis obnoxium aiunt esse. quin contrà Deo subiecta & obsequiosa dicunt omnia:delirúmque & errorem insanum effe quendam,attribuere virtutem aliquam eis verbis,quae sacris in rebus hominum inuentione & artificio proferuntur. Vtrum autem ea quae posuimus,aliquid ad manes è Purgatorio detrahendos conducere putarent: num Purgatorium etiam ipsum constituerent.respondet, tantum abesse vt conducerent vt etiam condemnationem illis accerserent,Deíque indignationem aduersum fe prouocarent.Porrò Purgatorium nec esse vllum praeterquam sanguinem Domini nostri Iesu Christi,vt scriptum est,neque purgari cuiufquam posse peccata nisi per effusionem illius sanguinis.Interpellationem igitur Sanctorum eiurantes,ait latrunculator,nullo nec honore,nec veneratione prosequendos censetis. Honorē depeculari Sanctorum, inquiunt, minimè volumus:at debitā vni Deo gloriam auferre & Sanctis ascribere, id quidem fit vel ipsorum voluntati Sanctorum intemperanter obsistere.Scitum enim scriptúmque est,ad Deum honorem & gloriam vnum referri semper oportere. Quòd vt adesse Sancti nobis & opitulari possint: tamen honorem qui foli Deo debetur,vndéque vis omnis ac potestas proficiscitur,impudenter ad fe rapere profecto nolint.Quòd ad postulationis aduocationisque fpeciaret[?] natura,hanc solius Christi propriam agnoscere & fateri sese,qui Christus petitione nulla extrinsec adhibita, tantùm motu quodā proprio suo ac officio nobis adsit praestóq; fit apud Patrē. Apud quē igitur exomolegesin facere oportet, quis ille tandē esset qui peccata condonaret, an non sacerdoti confitendū, an ab eodē nō expectanda remissio peccatorū, interrogati: Aiunt, conscientiae causam non ad sacerdotē, quē in eadē offensa nobiscum esse videamus: sed ad Deum vnicū humanarū offensionū expiatorem, solum iustum, vt scriptum est, tantùm esse deferenda. Potestatem igitur ligandi & soluendi nō habebunt? Mandatum, inquiunt, illis est, Euangelium vere profiteri, veritatémque qua huiusce modi ligatio solutióque tam hic apud nos, quā superius in caelo conficitur, enuntiare.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1553, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, John Filiolus, a carpenter, and Julian Leveilhe, a maker of laces, both natives of the town of Sanserre in Burgundy, were arrested by Gilles Perfy, provost of the province of Bourbonnais, under the authority of Sanctandreanus, tribune of the celeres. This happened about two miles from Nevers, on the road to Dezize. Gillius, who meant to arrest them, said: "I know well, brothers, where you are going. Come over to us and do not hesitate to open yourselves to us, for we are indeed men who wish above all to protect you from every insult, let alone injury, of wicked men." With such flattery that old fox tried to win them over little by little, hiding behind a show of truth and a pretended friendliness toward them, and even promising them his own faith if they would yield. Moreover, to catch them off guard, he sent his archers ahead with these words: "Go on, go on, and let the horses through; this place has nothing to do with you." Then, following them from every side, he said, "Hey, brothers, where are you going, I ask?" "To Dezize," they replied. "Not any further?" "Certainly not." "Surely to Geneva? And you are leading this little boy and this girl there too?" They frankly admitted it. "And your wives," he said, "are they not there?" They admitted that as well. Then, hissing and bringing his fist up to their face, Gillius called his archers and ordered that they be led to Nevers and put in custody. This was done at once. Brought there, they were questioned at length about what they had admitted a little earlier: that they were setting out for Geneva with the purpose of devoting themselves more fittingly to the divine work which, as they saw it, was everywhere in France being defiled daily by blasphemies, idolatry and false prophecy, and by an unspeakable abuse of the sacraments. Geneva, they said, was a city into which the truth of the gospel seemed to have returned, as if by a kind of right of postliminy. Since he had touched on the sacraments, he first asked which use of the sacraments they considered best, and likewise what gospel doctrine they said had settled in Geneva, a city which they claimed had begun most auspiciously of all the cities. And first, he asked whether they believed Christ himself to be so enclosed in the priestly host that, when the priest pronounced certain words, the bread and wine immediately ceased to be what they are, and the true body and blood of Christ were at once made and formed. They answered that they believed Jesus Christ had ascended into heaven (as it is written), sits at the right hand of God the Father, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead; and that in this way both the bread and the wine indeed retain the property of their nature. Nor should the bread and wine themselves be thought to be anything else in this matter than the sign and token of the true body and blood of Jesus Christ: just as the human heart is nourished by bread and cheered by wine, so the soul is, as it were, sustained by the precious body of Jesus Christ and refreshed by his blood, for through him we have been received into the Father's favour. They said they acknowledged all these things to be most true without any dispute, and were willing to profess them even at the risk of their lives. Then, when asked what they thought about the Communion, they said that bread and wine are administered in remembrance of the death and passion of Jesus Christ; and that not only bread and wine are received, but also, by the benefit of faith, the true body and blood of that same Christ, who, as an instrument of faith placed between, cleanses and refreshes the soul. As for the Mass, about which they were also questioned, they said it was pure superstition and idolatry, a mere invention of men and a pure condemnation. As for the claim that the blessed Peter was Pope and above all the author of the Mass, they said that this was far from the truth: blessed Peter never thought at all about the Mass, but was appointed and chosen under that name only to preach and interpret the gospel. Therefore, if we put any part of salvation in that Mass, the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ must be empty and bare, something which no mortal, Christians especially, should not only refuse to use in speech, but should not wish to grasp even in thought. From this it follows, indeed, that the Mass is a thing of no worth at all: I say it is pure idolatry, which, by most shamefully and disgracefully overturning and obliterating (a thing to be expiated only by a dreadful death) the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, after human memory, thrusts itself in most shamelessly, and most unworthily persuades certain strangers and outlandish people that it is something and must be held on to tooth and nail. Then they were asked whether the priest truly had the power to change the bread into the body of Christ. They said that God himself is subject neither to men nor to their tongues and exorcisms. On the contrary, they said that all things are subject and obedient to God, and that it is a kind of madness and insane error to attribute any power to those words which are uttered in sacred matters by human invention and trickery. Whether they thought that the things we had mentioned contributed in any way to releasing souls from Purgatory, and whether they held that Purgatory itself existed: they answered that these things were so far from helping that they actually drew condemnation upon those who did them, and provoked the anger of God against themselves. Purgatory, moreover, was nothing other than the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, as it is written, and the sins of no one can be cleansed except through the shedding of that blood. Then the provost said: "So you reject the intercession of the saints; you think they should be honoured and venerated in no way?" "We by no means wish to rob the saints of honour," they said, "but to take the glory due to God alone and ascribe it to the saints is in fact to resist the will of the saints themselves to excess. For it is known and written that the honour and glory are always to be referred to God alone. Although the saints may be present and may help us, they certainly would not wish to rashly claim for themselves the honour that is due to God alone, from whom all power and authority proceeds." As to the nature of the request and advocacy, they acknowledged and confessed that this belongs to Christ alone, who, without any external petition, by his own proper motion and office, is present with us and intercedes with the Father. Then they were asked before whom, therefore, one ought to make confession, and who then could forgive sins, and whether confession should not be made to a priest, nor forgiveness of sins expected from him. They said that the matter of conscience is not to be referred to a priest whom we see to be in the same offence with us, but to God alone, the only expiator of human offences, who alone is just, as it is written. "So they will not have the power of binding and loosing?" "They have been commanded," they said, "to profess the gospel truly, and to proclaim the truth by which such binding and loosing is accomplished here among us as well as above in heaven."

units.la: Ad extremum autem interrogati an res omnes quas asseruissent, sibi constarent, veraeque essent. verissimas dixerunt esse, in eisque sita fidem atque persuasionē suam. Itaque chirographum eis suum apposuerunt: testificatíq; sunt se valde sibi fortunatos videri, quos Deus dignos censuisset, qui in hanc causam deducerentur. Paulò post ad Sampetrū monasterianū à Latrunculatore ducuntur: oppidíque suppraefecto cum elogijs & interrogationibus superioribus traduntur. quo in loco eisdem de rebus interrogati, sibi consenserunt. Quocirca re ad forenses homines delata, inque deliberatione cum quibusdā acaitis Patronis deducta, tanta varietate sententiarum, vt cui potissimū adiudicari supplicio deberent, exputare nullo modo possent: frequentes in eam ibant sententiam, vt adnotatis illorum bonis ipsi proscriberetur. Cui sententiae cum à Ioan.Bergeronio quaesitore suppraefecto reclamaretur, ipse decreuit vt tædiferorū habitu per ora vulgi traducti, nudi Missae operā darēt primum, deinde comburerētur. Pronocatur ad curiā Parisiensem: quo in loco quanto rogantur diligētius, tantò se gerunt constantius. quanquā enim & amicorū gratia valerent, & diplomatibus quibus series ipsa tota causae de integro inspici iubebatur, vti possent: tamen in sententia permanserunt. Dum Lutetiae sunt, Latrunculator fanaticus & insanus moritur. cuius viri morte perculsi quidam, animus consternantur: alij verò iustissimum Dei iudicium admirati, sibi inuicem gratulantur. Tandem autem reiecti martyres Sampetrum monasterianum Lutetia reuersi xviii.Calendas Febr. In Concilium venire iubentur, vt quid animi tum demùm habeant, ostendant. Perseueraturos ad extremū se dicunt esse: prævaricatores se rati fore, si quod verissimum esse cognouerint, abiurent. Tum actuarius Parisiensis curiæ decretum recitat: quo decreto continebatur, vinos ambos exuri oportere, siquidem sibi perpetuò consentientes pervicaciam istiusmodi non abiicerent: profert item decretum alterum memoria tantum hominum, non scripto consignatum: quo constabat præcidi quoque eis linguas oportere, si pergerent: sin veterem istam opinionem excuti sibi paterentur, sane fore ut & laquei præfocatione flammam antecuerterent, & linguæ sectione liberati iucundius vitam cum morte commutarent. Velletis ipsi quidem, inquiunt, ut reiecta veritatis optima causa Deum nostrum abiuraremus: at frustra vos vniuersi conficitis. Vix absoluerant, quum decreti capita tria recitari desierunt: quorum primum illud erat, perperam ac peruerse ambos de sancto sacramento loquutos. Imò verò, inquiunt, optime verissimeque. Secundum, falsò Baptismum eosdem abiurasse. Imò constanter asseruisse, sed informasse, inquiunt. Tertium, Deum ac diuos ipsos immortales acerbitate contumeliosa verborum insectatos fuisse. Quin contrà, inquiunt, & Dei causam strenuè suscepisse, & diuos in honore semper habuisse. Mox se ipsi contuentes ambo, inuicem hortari se, paratósque esse dicere non tantum vnius alterius-ue membri facere iacturam, verum etiam totius corporis naufragium, dum ea sustineant quæ cum ad salutem suam, tum verò Dei opt.max. decus & ornamentum pertinere arbitrentur. Genus enim hoc totum supplicium & animaduersionum momentaneum, vel potius etiam optabile & suaue[?], si cum tanti boni quantum ipsi iam spe atque animo consecuti sint, præstatia[?] & diuturnitate comparetur. Suppræfectus grauissima post homines natos illis genera tormentorum indicere, nisi dicta revocarent: illi contrà (pergeret audacter) eis enim se tormentis perterrefieri nullo modo, quibus hæreditatem adituri essent, quam amplissimam & expeditissimam sibi propositam esse minimè dubitarent. Exuuntur, vinciuntur, idque à meridie ad tertiam. Nihilominus oratione perpetua Dei bonitate ac misericordia dilaudātes, præclarissimè secū agi testantur, quos in causam suam demisisset, quos honore tato dignatus esset. Itaq; supplicij genus acerbissimum expectātes, vnà canunt Psal.6, Domine ne in, &c. & deinceps cant. Symeonis, Nunc dimittis seruum tuum Domine. Mox suppræfectus insania & furore præceps, Dominicanum præmittit ad illos quendam, captiosum hominem in disputatione, & in comprimenda veritate veteratorem eximium ac prope singularem. qui cum multiplicem ac variam cum martyribus disputationem instituisset, exceptus ille quidem initio fuit: postea vero fractus atque fusus. Abite, inquit, in malam crucem o intemperiæ, o agitatæ furiæ. Succedit Suppræfectus: ligneam crucem in utriusque colligatas manus imponit: arripitur dentibus crux, usque summa projicitur, gerendam enim aliam ambobus cruce longe pretiosiorem & excellentiorem esse. Hoc facto concitatus Suppræfectus linguas edere ambobus iubet: faciunt incredibili constantia. quódque maiorem in re noua mirationem facit, exectæ iam eædem illæ linguæ postridie in ipsa Concilij publici classe reperiuntur. Itaque horum martyrum exemplo duorum liquidò ostendit Dominus se loquendi facultatem non alligasse linguæ. præcisa enim ea concessit utrique bonus ac misericors Deus ut loquerentur. nam ad supplicij locum progressi, Nos, inquit, aliquando tandem & peccato & carni & mundo & diabolo postremum vale dicimus: nunquam cum illis commune quicquam habituri sumus. Alia præterea quædam à summis illis sane viris intelligenter excipiebantur. Quin etiam litore[?] eos sulphureo & tormentario puluere conspergente & succuffante: Age, inquit Filiolius, falle, falle serió putridas & cariosas hasce carnes. Mox prorupta in faciem flamma, immoto corpore consistentes, feliciter spiritum ediderunt.
units.tr: At the end they were asked whether all the things they had asserted were consistent with each other and true. They said that they were most true, and that their faith and conviction rested on them. So they signed their confession, and they testified that they seemed very fortunate, since God had thought them worthy to be drawn into this cause. Shortly afterwards the Latrunculator led them to the monastery of Saint Peter, and they were handed over to the sub-prefect of the town together with the reports and the earlier questions. There, when questioned on the same matters, they stood by what they had said. The case was then referred to lay men and, when it was debated with some advocates, opinions differed so widely that they could in no way agree on the punishment to which the prisoners should be assigned. Most leaned towards the view that their goods should be noted and that they themselves should be outlawed. But when Jean Bergeron, the questor and sub-prefect, objected to this opinion, he decided that they should be led through the crowd of the common people, dressed in the garb of torch-bearers, naked, that they should first assist at the Mass, and then be burned. They appealed to the Parliament of Paris. Here, the more carefully they were questioned, the more steadfastly they behaved. For although they had the favour of friends, and could make use of the documents by which the whole course of the cause was ordered to be examined afresh, they nevertheless remained firm in their judgment. While they were at Paris, the Latrunculator, a fanatic and a madman, died. Some were struck with dismay and their spirits were troubled by his death; others, marvelling at the most just judgment of God, congratulated one another. At last the martyrs, having been sent back from Paris, returned to the monastery of Saint Peter on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February. They were ordered to come into the Council, so that they might show what their mind was at that point. They said that they would persevere to the end; they would be prevaricators, they thought, if they abjured what they knew to be most true. Then the clerk of the Parisian court read out the decree, by which it was laid down that both of them ought to be burned, unless they gave up such stubbornness as they consistently maintained. He also produced another decree, not written down but recited from the memory of men, by which it was established that their tongues too ought to be cut out if they persisted; but if they allowed that old opinion to be shaken off, then the strangling would surely precede the flame, and, freed by the cutting of the tongue, they would exchange life for death more pleasantly. "You would indeed wish us," they said, "to abjure our God and reject the best cause; but you labour in vain." They had scarcely finished when the reading of the decree's three heads ceased. The first was that both had spoken perversely and wrongly about the holy sacrament. "On the contrary," they said, "very well and most truly." The second was that they had falsely abjured baptism. "Rather," they said, "they had constantly affirmed it, but had been misinformed." The third was that they had attacked God and the immortal saints with bitter, insulting words. "On the contrary," they said, "they had both vigorously taken up God's cause and always held the saints in honour." Then, looking at each other, they urged one another, and said that they were ready to bear not merely the loss of one limb or another, but the shipwreck of the whole body, as long as they endured those things which they believed pertained both to their own salvation and to the honour and ornament of the best and greatest God. For all this kind of punishment is momentary, or rather even desirable and sweet, if it is compared with the greatness and duration of the good which they had already attained in hope and mind. The sub-prefect threatened them with the most severe tortures ever devised for men, unless they recanted their words. They replied, boldly, that they were in no way terrified by the torments, through which they would enter upon an inheritance which they did not doubt was set before them as most ample and most readily obtained. They were stripped and bound, from noon until three. Nevertheless, praising God's goodness and mercy in unceasing prayer, they testified that they had been most nobly dealt with, since he had admitted them to his cause and had deigned to honour them so greatly. And so, awaiting the most bitter kind of punishment, they sang together Psalm 6, "Lord, rebuke me not," and so on, and then the canticle of Simeon, "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart." Then the sub-prefect, rushing headlong in insanity and fury, sent to them a Dominican, a crafty man in disputation and an outstanding, almost unique, deceiver in suppressing the truth. He conducted a long and varied debate with the martyrs. At first he was indeed received, but afterwards he was broken and routed. "Go to the devil, you intemperate creatures, you driven furies!" Then the sub-prefect came in. He placed a wooden cross in the hands of both, bound together; the cross was seized in their teeth and thrown down to the ground, since they were to carry another cross, far more precious and excellent than this one. At this the sub-prefect, roused, ordered both of them to put out their tongues. They did so with incredible constancy, and what made the matter even more remarkable was that those same tongues, now cut out, were found the next day in the very chamber of the public Council. Thus by the example of these two martyrs the Lord clearly showed that he had not tied the power of speech to the tongue; for, though it was cut away, the good and merciful God granted that they should still speak. When they came to the place of execution, they said: "At last, once and for all, we bid farewell to sin, to the flesh, to the world and to the devil; we shall never again have anything in common with them." Other words were also gathered up intelligently by these most excellent men. Indeed, when the executioner sprinkled them with sulphur and gunpowder and shook them, Filiolius said: "Come on, deceive, deceive, in earnest, these rotten and decaying flesh." Immediately the flame burst out in their faces, and standing with unmoved bodies, they happily gave up the ghost.

units.la: DIONYSIUS VAYRUS.
units.tr: DIONYSIUS VAYRUS.

units.la: D Ionysius Vayrus, Fontenij ortus, diœcesis Baiocensis, in inferiori Northmaniæ parte, valeiuso[?] presbyteratu Papali, Genevam est profectus, ubi artem librariam didicit, atque inde libros sæpenumero in Galliam asportavit. Tandem in insulis Gerzæis & Guernezæis domicilium delegit: in quibus, quod Anglorum essent ditionis, haud ita pridem iussu ac voluntate Illustrissimi ac Christianissimi Edovardi sexti Regis syncere Evangelium prædicari coperat. Ibi Dionysius artem suam exercuit: & aliquandiu verbi Dei minister constitutus, Christum annunciauit in quodam Guernezæ viculo. Sed quoniam anno M.D.LIIII. defuncto Edouardo, successerant Mariana tempora, quæ impios cultus ac Papisticas superstitiones in totū regnum inuexerunt, adeò vt in illis insulis impia religio pristina receperit ornamenta: Vayrus comitatus quibusdam, per Northmaniam iter fecit eo animo vt se Genevā reciperet: atque in vicum qui appellatur Fullium peruenit, adferens multos sacræ Scripturæ libros. Et quum abijsset rhedam[?] rebus suis vehendis conducturus, Gulielmus Anglus vicecomitis suppræfectus, cum fratre suo Ioanne Anglo procuratore regio aduenit, ac libros sibi ac reliquam suppellectilem exhiberi præcipit: cui obtemperatum est, atque omnia interdicto retenta sunt, ipse etiā qui ea asseruabat. Dum hæc geruntur, interuenit Vayrus, qui licet omnia intellexisset quæ euenerant, ipsosque satellites ob oculos haberet, tamen repente absque vlla dissimulatione rationem causamque interdicti ac retentionis ex ipsis quæsiuit. cui responsum est, libros esse hæresi refertos: ipse contra, nihil nisi vera in eis contineri: suósque esse, non eius quem ceperunt. Proinde qui eos asseruauerat mox dimissus fuit: ipse vero Vayrus in custodia Periesum adductus, vbi per duos menses & dimidium arctissimis vinculis constrictus mansit. Interea à iudicibus eius loci multis de rebus fuit interrogatus, qui crimen proditionis ei obijciebant, quòd apud Anglos capitales Gallorum hostes esset commoratus. Ad quæ respondit, se illuc venisse non studio prodendi quenquam, sed vt liberum sibi esset rite Deum inuocare, & ex eius præscripto vitam degere. Porrò quum iudices Periesi, Vayri causam protrastinarent, mandato Cognitoris regij apud Rothomagum, adductus est Baiocum, & decem dies ita constrictus in carcere Episcopi remansit, vt omnis aditus ad eū fuerit interclusus. Inde Rothomagum ductus est, vbi senatus consulto sancitum est, vt viuus comburerctur[?], ac ter è rogo extraheretur. Hac sententia pronuntiata, omnes ei instare vt suæ sectæ fautores patefaceret, alioqui omnia eius membra in quæstione comminuta irí: quibus ille respondit, omnes veros Christianos à se stare, ex quorū numero esset saniorpars Galliæ, imò verò è Senatorum numero plerósq;: neque vllo cruciatus genere quidquam aliud à se eos extorsuros, nec coniecturū quenquam in capitis aut fortunarum discrimen. Quòd si me tormentis enecauerit is crudeles vestros ignes non sentiam. Hæc cum audissent, tanta animi constantia perspecta in quæstionem eum non coniecerunt: sed ad supplicium protinus agi iusserunt. Cum è carcere exiret, magna aderat hominum frequentia, quam Vayrus præsenti animo & singulari vultus alacritate hortari cœpit, vt doctrinam Christi amplecterentur, licet quidam monachus Carmelitanus qui cum eo in plaustro erat, cum interturbaret. Ibi vnus ex lictoribus acclamauit ad carnifice, Resecà, resecà ei linguam: quod sine vlla mora factum est. Tunc monachus crucem quandam lignam ei obtulit, ac manibus quæ arctissime erant alligatæ, inseri iussit. at pius ille vir quantum in se erat recusabat, vultum à monacho auertens: hic verò beluino boatu exclamás, Videte iam, videte execrandum hominem qui respuit crucem. Adductus est postea ante vastam ædem Rothomagensem, quam vocant Diuæ Mariæ, vt significationem aliquam daret populo venerationis eorum idolorum (quos Sanctos vocant) qui pro templi foribus locantur, atque ita honorariam quam dicunt emendationem admisisse videretur. At ipse manibus, oculis, vultu, toto denique corporis gestu satis præ se ferebat, solum Deum esse adorandum: tergum obuertens eorum idolis, & aperte declarans ea despicere ac detestari. Cum ad supplicij locum ventum est, protinus in ignem coniectus est, è quo, vt aresto [?] pronuntiatum erat, ter erat educendus, quod tamen ad effectum non fuit perductum. nam vbi primum ignis fuit accensus, adeò flamma inaluit vt hastæ altitudine supra corpus Vayri se extulerit: & ambo carnifices quantumuis adniterentur, eum in altum erigere nequiuerunt. Interea satellites baculis turbam quæ circumstabat adigere conabantur vt subsidio esset carnificibus, nec tamen effecerunt vt vel vnus quidem manum admoueret. Sanctus igitur Dei martyr ad hunc modum expirauit nono die Augusti anno, M.D.LIIII. cuius rei laus, honor & gloria, soli Deo viuenti in perpetuum, Amen.
units.tr: Dionysius Vayrus, born at Fontenay in the diocese of Bayeux, in the lower part of Normandy, after leaving the Papal priesthood, went to Geneva, where he learned the bookseller's trade, and from there often carried books into France. At last he chose as his home the islands of Guernsey and Jersey, which, being under English rule, had not long before begun, by the command and will of the most illustrious and most Christian King Edward VI, to have the Gospel sincerely preached. There Vayrus practised his trade, and having for some time been appointed minister of the Word, he proclaimed Christ in a village of Guernsey. But when Edward died in 1554, the Marian times followed, which brought impious worship and Papistical superstitions into the whole kingdom, so that in those islands the old impious religion regained its trappings. Vayrus, accompanied by some companions, travelled through Normandy intending to return to Geneva, and came to the village called Fullium, carrying many books of Holy Scripture. When he had gone off to hire a cart for carrying his goods, William English, deputy of the viscount, arrived with his brother John English, the royal procurator, and ordered the books and the rest of his baggage to be handed over to them. This was obeyed, and everything was held under the interdict, including the man who was keeping them. While this was going on, Vayrus came up. Although he had understood everything that had happened and had the officers before his eyes, he at once and without any pretence asked them for the reason and cause of the interdict and the seizure. He was told that the books were full of heresy; he replied that they contained nothing but truth, and that they were his, not the property of the man they had seized. Accordingly the man who had been keeping them was soon released, but Vayrus himself was taken into custody at Périers, where he remained for two and a half months, bound in very tight chains. Meanwhile the judges of that place questioned him on many matters, charging him with treason because he had stayed among the English, the mortal enemies of the French. To this he replied that he had come there not with any purpose of betraying anyone, but so that he might be free to call upon God duly and to live his life according to God's prescription. Moreover, while the judges of Périers were delaying Vayrus's case, by order of the royal commissioner at Rouen he was brought to Bayeux, and for ten days he remained in the bishop's prison, so closely confined that all access to him was cut off. From there he was taken to Rouen, where a decree of the senate ordered that he be burned alive and drawn out of the fire three times. When this sentence was pronounced, everyone urged him to reveal the supporters of his sect, otherwise all his limbs would be crushed under torture. He replied that all true Christians were on his side, among whom was the saner part of France, indeed many of the senators themselves; and that by no kind of torture would they extort anything else from him, nor would he bring anyone into danger to life or property. "But if you destroy me with torments, I shall not feel your cruel fires." When they had heard this and seen such constancy of spirit, they did not put him to the question, but ordered him to be led at once to execution. As he came out of the prison a large crowd was present, and Vayrus, with presence of mind and a remarkable cheerfulness of countenance, began to exhort them to embrace the teaching of Christ, although a certain Carmelite monk who was with him in the cart kept interrupting. Then one of the lictors shouted to the executioner, "Cut out his tongue!", and this was done without delay. Next the monk offered him a wooden cross and ordered it to be placed in his hands, which were tightly bound; but that godly man, as far as he could, refused it, turning his face away from the monk. The monk, bellowing like a beast, cried out, "See now, see the accursed man who spurns the cross!" Afterwards he was led in front of the vast church at Rouen which they call Our Lady's, so that he might give the people some sign of reverence for those idols (whom they call Saints) which are set up at the doors of the church, and so seem to have admitted the so-called honorary correction. But he, by his hands, eyes, face and indeed his whole bodily gesture, made it plain enough that God alone is to be worshipped: turning his back on their idols and openly declaring that he despised and abhorred them. When they reached the place of execution he was at once thrown into the fire, out of which, as had been pronounced, he was to be drawn three times; but this was not carried out. For as soon as the fire was lit the flame blazed up so high that it rose above Vayrus's body to the height of a spear, and though both executioners strained, they could not raise him up. Meanwhile the officers tried with their staves to drive back the crowd standing round, to give help to the executioners, yet they did not manage to make even one man lay a hand to it. So the holy martyr of God breathed his last in this way on the ninth day of August, 1554. To God alone, living for ever, be the praise, honour and glory for this matter. Amen.

units.la: BERTRANDVS BLASVS Tornacensis.
units.tr: BERTRANDVS BLASVS Tornacensis.

units.la: Bertrandus Blafus Tornaci Neruiorum natus, sericatorum e la-na cõfectorum opifex, quum a Deo veritatis cognitionem accepisset, demigrauit wesaliam ( quod oppidum ad imperium ac iurisdictionem ducis Cleuesis, Iuliacensisque pertinet) co[?] animo, ut receptus ibi in ecclesiam Gallicam, excipienda concione divini Verbi, ritúque Sacramentorum usurpando, Deum pie religiosèque coleret: & si res facultatem habitura videretur, eódem uxorem suam atque familiam adduceret. Quo consilio quum wesalia jam ter Tornacum profectus esset, nihil tamen cum uxore conficere, neque ut sequi se quam remanere Tornaci mallet, impetrare ab ea potuit. Postremum autem quum wesalia decedens in iter jam esset ingressus, comitatus officij gratia fuisse fertur a multis, nominatim autem N. Ludovico ecclesiae Gallicae ministro: ab eodemque monitus ut idololatriam fugeret, & quam olim veri inuestigandi rationem iniisset, in ea fortiter in posterum constanterque perseueraret. cui Bertrandus, Vero se quodam ac tacito divini Spiritus affectu sensúque commoueri: sperare denique nihil commissurum se, quod quidem aut indignum eo ordine quem duxisset, aut alienum a fidei quam haberet, praeiudicio videretur. Porro simulac Tornacum attigit, quum uxori persuadere non posset ut oppidum superstitiosum idololatriaeque deditum relinqueret, in eodē est ipse dies aliquot ante Natale silentio commoratus. Quo ipso die Natalis, anni M.D.LV. domo progrediens, ab uxore fratréque postulauit uti precibus a Deo peterent, ut consilium institutúmque suum (cuius ipse rationem inclusam animo contineret) ad felicem exitum adduci vellet. Itaque profectus in aedē divae Mariae vulgò nostrae Dominae (quod templum caeterorum omnium quae Tornaci numeratur, maximum amplissimúmque est) confectis tribus circa chori spatiis, magnū altare commodissimum duxit esse, in quo molitione sua quam optimè defungi posset. Quod quum ei non succederet, essétque sacellum ibi parœciæ, corripuit intrò sese: quo in loco stetit tecto capite tantisper, dum flamen curialis deum illum suum panaceū soleniter attollens, eodem vestigio sibi ereptum sensit a Bertrādo: his verbis populū qui aderat, inclamate, Ut circunscripti estis universi? quid? adeone caecutitis, ac dementi ruina sese inflectunt mentes vestrae, ut istud crustulū, Iesum Christum verum Deum ac seruatorem esse vobis persuadeatis? Ecce, & habitis aliis nonnullis ad admonitionem pertinentibus verbis, arreptam (quam vocant) hostiam comminuit: comminutam percutit atque conculcauit. Ad quod inuisum eatenus inauditumque spectaculum circumfusa multitudo, die praesertim tam festo ac religioso, animo constitit adeo pauido atque consternato, ut Bertrando ipsi nihilo fuerit difficilius futurum expedire salutem suam, indeque se proripere[?], atque e medio de caelo tactorum hominum conspectu. Sed illum Dominus ad facinoris sui tam praeclari probandam rationem exponendamque reseruasse eo videtur, quod comprehensum & captiuum in arcem Tornaci munitissimam duci permiserit. Haec dum Tornaci geruntur, curator oppidi prouinciaeque Neruiorum, Humorum praefectus, Biesi tum quidem agens, domi sedebat articularius: qui ad huius facti mentionem attonitus, & exclamans, Dij vestram, inquit, fidem! Sicine tu tandem, o bone Deus, hominis impurissimi pedibus opprimi te coculcarique sinuisti? quin tantam impietatem, tantum scelus acriter, ut erat vindicari multò dignissimum, ultus ipse es atque persecutus? Miserum me! Tantúmne te patientiae praestare potuisse? Istáne tandem esse perpessum? Polliceor tibi, in meque recipio, o Deus, ea seueritate tantum facinoris crimen accepturum esse me, eiusmodi proditurum exemplum, ut defixum ad memoriam omnium hominum sempiternă indicium esse possit. Mox ira furiosè percitus, tantum acerbitatis virus euomuit, verba quaedam tam impotenter effudit, ut ab omnibus qui aderant hominibus, exijsse plane de potestate, necnon impetu quodam animi vesano ferri raptarique iudicaretur. Haud ita post multò quum utcunque morbus animi resedisset, deportari se in castrum Tornaci iussit: quo in loco decerni Bertrādo quaestionem natalitijs feriatis diebus, ut indicia profiteri cogeretur, postulauit. Nec enim curiosius facti confessionem exprimi oportere censebat, quum hoc toto de genere omnes antea longe plura iam ab illo quam aut optarent, aut opinarentur, intellexissent. Etenim interrogatus primum, nu qua facti sui poenitentia duceretur: ac integrum ei si fit, vtrum co progredi vellet, singulari quadam animi constantia grauitateque[?] responderat, Id ipsum centies, si liceat, velle se facere: mori denique centies, si totidem sibi vitæ suppeterent: siquidem id ad Iesu Christi seruatoris amplitudinem & gloriam pertinere existimaret. Tum carnifices quum iudice ex ille possent exprimere nemine, de integro quæstionem interminabatur: quibus ille, proptum ac paratum se ad nouam perpessione: indicaturum autem esse nemine. Quo facto fuit ut ter ei quæstio repeteretur, quam idem tamen inuicta animi magnitudine superarit. Postridie porro feriarum, qui dies erat iiii.Cal.Ian. quum ad condemnationem ventum esset, accidit ut mortis ei sententia in hanc rationem pronunciaretur.
units.tr: Bertrandus Blasus, born at Tournai in the land of the Nervii, a weaver of woollen silk fabrics, after he had received from God the knowledge of the truth, moved to Wesel (a town under the rule and jurisdiction of the Duke of Cleves and Jülich), with the intention that, once received there into the French church, he might hear the sermon of the divine Word, take part in the rite of the Sacraments, and worship God devoutly and religiously; and if his means seemed likely to allow it, he would bring his wife and household there as well. With this plan he had already gone from Wesel to Tournai three times, but he could not prevail on his wife either to follow him or to be willing to leave Tournai rather than stay. Finally, when he had set out on the journey from Wesel, he is said to have been accompanied, as a courtesy of duty, by many people, and especially by N. Ludovicus, minister of the French church, who admonished him to flee idolatry and to persevere bravely and steadfastly in the way of seeking the truth which he had once entered upon. To this Bertrandus replied that he was moved by a certain quiet and inward influence of the divine Spirit; and in short he hoped he would commit nothing that seemed either unworthy of the calling he had chosen or foreign to the faith he held. But as soon as he reached Tournai, since he could not persuade his wife to leave the superstitious town given over to idolatry, he remained in silence for some days before Christmas in the same house. On Christmas Day itself, in the year 1555, going out of the house, he asked his wife and brother to pray to God that he would bring his plan and purpose (the reasons for which he kept shut within his mind) to a happy outcome. So he went to the church of Saint Mary, commonly called Our Lady (the largest and most spacious of all the churches counted in Tournai). Having made three circuits of the space around the choir, he judged the great altar the most convenient place in which to carry out his undertaking as well as he could. When this did not succeed, and there was a parish chapel there, he rushed inside. There he stood with his head covered for as long as the parish priest, solemnly lifting up that god of his, which was his panacea, felt it snatched from him at the same moment by Bertrand. With these words he called out to the people who were present: "Are you all bewitched? Has your mind sunk into such mad ruin that you can persuade yourselves this little wafer is Jesus Christ, the true God and Saviour?" Then, after saying some other words to the purpose of admonition, he broke the so-called host that had been seized, and having broken it he trampled and crushed it underfoot. At this hateful and hitherto unheard-of spectacle the crowd that stood around, especially on so festive and holy a day, was so terrified and dismayed that it would have been no harder for Bertrand himself to save his own life, slip away and vanish from the sight of men who had touched heaven. But the Lord seems to have reserved him, in order to be called to account and to explain so notable a deed, when he allowed him to be seized and taken as a prisoner to the most strongly fortified citadel of Tournai. While these things were happening at Tournai, the governor of the town and province of the Nervii, the prefect of the Hainaut, who was then staying at Bièvres, was sitting at home, gouty. Startled at the mention of this deed, and crying out, "Good heavens, what faith! Did you really, good God, suffer yourself to be trampled and crushed under the feet of so vile a man? Why did you not yourself avenge and pursue so great an impiety and so great a crime, as it deserved to be most sharply punished? Woe is me! Could you really show so much patience? Did you really endure that? I promise you, O God, and take it upon myself, that I will exact punishment for such a crime with such severity, and make an example of such a kind, that it may stand fixed as an everlasting sign to the memory of all men." Then, furiously stirred up in his anger, he poured out such a venom of bitterness and uttered such words so intemperately, that everyone present judged he had clearly gone out of his mind and was being carried away by some frenzied impulse of spirit. Not long afterwards, when the sickness of his mind had somehow subsided, he ordered himself to be carried into the castle of Tournai; and there he asked that Bertrand be examined on the feast days of the Nativity, so that he might be compelled to declare what he knew. For he thought the confession of the deed ought not to be extracted with too much care, since they had all by now learned from him in this whole matter far more than they had hoped or expected. For when he was first asked whether he repented of his deed, and whether, if it were still open to him, he would wish to do it again, he answered with remarkable firmness and seriousness of spirit: "I would wish to do this a hundred times over, if it were allowed; indeed I would die a hundred times, if I had as many lives, since I judge it pertains to the honour and glory of Jesus Christ our Saviour." Then, since the executioners could draw nothing else from him, the examination was threatened again from the beginning; to which he replied that he was ready and prepared to suffer a new torment, but that he would name no one. So it came about that the question was repeated three times, and he overcame it each time with unconquered greatness of spirit. The next day, which was a holiday, the fourth day before the Kalends of January, when they came to sentencing, it happened that the sentence of death was pronounced against him in the following form. (not translated)

units.la: Ifo[?] processu criminali facto coram nobis aduersus te Bertrandum le Blas, per quem processum simul & per tuas confessiones libere facti sufficienter constat, quod in die Natalis Domini nuper elapso, hora magnæ Missæ coparueris in ecclesia parochiali in templo cathedrali nostræ Dominæ Tornacensis: & ibi malo, perverso & felonia turgenti animo, proposito deliberato propius accessisti ad Curatum celebrante prædictam magnam Missam parochialem, ac tenentem sanctissimam ac sacratissimam hostiam & sanctum sacramentum altaris inter suos digitos, paratum ad eleuandum & ostendendum populo: quam quidem hostiam tu ab illius digitis violenter manu tua dextra arreptam maxima irreuerentia & contemptu proiectam in terram, ac desuper tuo pede dextro conculcatam verbis probrosis prosequutus es, dicens, Hoc facio ad ostendendum gloriam illius Dei, & quod nullam potentiam habeat. Et tum in promptu per eos qui circumstabant quum fuisses apprehensus ut captiuus constitueris, multa verba hæretica pronunciasti, ut eos induceres in tuam damnabilem intentionem: imo in tuis interrogationibus respondisti de sacro sacramento Baptismatis prorsus hæreticè & contra sanctam Scripturam. Item contrauenien[?]do ordinationibus Imperatoris nostri domini tu fuisti pluries Wefaliæ, ibidem conuersando commorando per aliquod tempus cum iis qui illam urbem inhabitant. Pro quibus omnibus casibus supradictis ex consilio & resolutione domini Baillui Tornacensis & Tornesii ac ipsius Locutenentis: simul & consiliariorum Imperatoris nostri domini in eodem Balliagio, magna & matura deliberatione habita, nos te condemnauimus & condemnamus ut super cratem traharis a loco pronunciationis sententiæ usque ad magnum forum istius urbis, ut ibi super facto theatro manus dextera tibi forcipibus igne rubentibus vi euellatur, similiter & pes dexter, ac deinde lingua præcidatur: ac corpus tuum viuum per medium ligatum ad summum trochleæ paulatim lento igne flammificetur: in eo denique igne sæpius demittatur & attollatur ac finaliter in cineres consumatur. Atque insuper declaramus omnia tua bona confiscata ad utilitatem Imperatoris domini nostri: aut eius aut eorum ad quos pertinebit per nostram sententiam diffinitiuam criminale & pro iure. Actum & pronunciatum ianuis apertis per excelsum & potentem dominum Senescallum Hannoniæ, &c.
units.tr: After a criminal process had been conducted before us against you, Bertrand le Blas, by which process, together with your own free confessions, it is sufficiently established that on the day of the Lord's Nativity just past, at the hour of the High Mass, you appeared in the parish church of the cathedral of Our Lady of Tournai. There, with an evil, perverse and felonious mind swollen with malice, and with deliberate purpose, you drew near to the curate who was celebrating the aforesaid parish High Mass and was holding the most holy and sacred host, the holy sacrament of the altar, between his fingers, ready to raise it and show it to the people. You violently seized that host from his fingers with your right hand, threw it to the ground with the greatest irreverence and contempt, and trampled on it with your right foot, pouring out abusive words and saying: "I do this to show the glory of that God, and that he has no power." Then, when you had been seized by those standing around and taken captive, you uttered many heretical words, so as to draw them into your damnable intention. Indeed, in your interrogations you answered about the sacred sacrament of baptism in a wholly heretical manner and contrary to holy Scripture. Likewise, acting contrary to the ordinances of our lord the Emperor, you were several times in Wesalia, living and staying for some time there among those who inhabit that city. For all these cases above, by the counsel and resolution of the lord Bailiff of Tournai and Tournésis and of his lieutenant, together with the councillors of our lord the Emperor in the same bailiwick, after great and mature deliberation, we have condemned you and do condemn you: you are to be dragged on a hurdle from the place where this sentence is pronounced to the great market of this city; there, on a scaffold erected for the purpose, your right hand is to be torn away with pincers glowing red from the fire, likewise your right foot; then your tongue is to be cut out; and your living body, bound through the middle and hoisted to the top of a pulley, is to be slowly burned with a low fire; finally you are to be repeatedly lowered into that fire and raised again, and at last consumed into ashes. Moreover, we declare all your goods confiscated to the use of our lord the Emperor, or of those to whom they shall belong, by our definitive sentence, criminal and according to law. Done and pronounced with the doors open by the lofty and powerful lord Seneschal of Hainaut, etc.

units.la: Die Sabbati xxix. Decembris, anni M. D. LV, præsentibus viris consiliariis ad hoc ordinatis & deputatis.
units.tr: On Saturday, the 29th of December, in the year 1555, in the presence of the councillors appointed and deputed for this purpose.

units.la: ILLO igitur ipso die dum sententiæ executione obeunt, miserum, super cratem assidentem, à Tornaci castello ad forum usque nun-dinarium trahunt. ibi contabulationem extruunt: productum atque vinctum cedere manum qua sacrificulo hostiam extorserat, cogunt: quam cauteriis ictis duobus, ignitisque ferreis cuspidibus arreptam eoúsque comprimunt, dum in totum manus ipsius species & forma detraheretur. Alia præterea ferramenta superioribus simillima proponuntur ignis ardore & inflammatione coruscatia: in quæ ipse sponte pedem, quo pesundasset[?] hostiam, inferens, mirabile proposuit exemplum animi grauitatis atque constantiæ suæ. His confectis rebus dissolvitur. infra descedere, globulumque, ferreuque castro progrediens eatenus ore tenuerat, edere, & lingua abscindenda proferre iubetur: paret. Inseritur in os rursum ei globulus, quòd ne tum quidem perpetuis clamoribus, eisque quibus universa multitudo vehementer sane commoueretur, Dominum appellare desineret. Mox contabulationem alteram depressiore aliquanto ea, in qua candentibus forcipibus manu & pede fuerat inustus, eadem alacritate con-scendit, eodem animo, quo si neque captus aliquo membro, neque ullo proposito vitæ periculo concitatus esset, planè facturus esse videretur. Ibi manibus atque pe-dibus à tergo circumducta per medium corpus ferrea catena reuinctus incumbebat rogo: sursum ac deorsum adductus & inclinatus miserabile populo spectaculum præbebat: Hannoniæ Præfecto interim martyrem ipsum nunc attolli, nunc deprimi iubente, & oculos immanitatis suæ pascente tantisper ac satiante, dum viri sanctissimi corpus illius in cinerem conversum, in profluentem iniicitur. Hoc confecto negotio tā præclaro, ut & sacellum in quo res inauspicato perpetrata suisset, occluderetur, & lignum quo sacrificus ante ara posito supergressus esset, exureretur, & marmoreus lapis quo pariter incessisset, confringeretur, imperavit: interdixitque, quoniam Bertrandus ipse quicquid eruditionis ac veræ religionis habuisset, ecclesiæ wesaliesi[?] totum referre se acceptū dixisset: ne quis aut commercii, aut cuiusquam alterius negotii nomine illo proficisceretur: alioqui fore ut in multam Imperatoris (quam illi Placardum appellant) incurreret.
units.tr: On that very day, while they carry out the execution of the sentence, they drag the wretched man, seated on a hurdle, from the castle of Tournai to the market square. There they build a scaffold, and, when he has been brought forward and bound, they force him to surrender the hand with which he had wrested the host from the priest. They grip it with two hot irons and with glowing iron points, and press until the whole shape and form of the hand is burned away. Other instruments, very like the former, glittering with the heat and glow of fire, are then set out; and he himself, of his own accord, puts his foot, with which he had trampled the host, into them, displaying a wonderful example of his seriousness and constancy of spirit. When these things are done, he is ordered to come down from the scaffold, and to put out the tongue with which, up to that point, he had held the little ball of iron in his mouth, and to bring it forward to be cut off. He obeys. The little ball is put back into his mouth, so that not even then did he cease to call upon the Lord with continual cries, cries by which the whole crowd was greatly stirred. Soon he climbs up onto another scaffold, somewhat lower than the one on which his hand and foot had been burned with the red-hot pincers, with the same eagerness and the same spirit, as though he had been neither maimed in any limb nor brought into any danger of his life, and as though he were about to do it of his own accord. There, with his hands and feet bound behind his back and an iron chain fastened round his middle, he was laid upon the pyre; raised up and lowered and tilted, he presented a pitiful spectacle to the people, while the Governor of Hainaut ordered the martyr now to be lifted up, now to be lowered, feeding and satisfying for a time his eyes of savagery, until the body of that most holy man, turned to ash, was thrown into the flowing stream. When this so notable business was finished, he ordered that the little chapel in which the unlucky deed had been committed be shut up, that the wood on which the priest had stood before the altar be burned, and that the marble stone on which he had likewise stepped be broken. He also forbade anyone to set out from that place on account of trade or any other business, since Bertrand himself had said that whatever learning and true religion he had, he owed entirely to the church of Wesel; otherwise, he warned, whoever did so would incur the fine of the Emperor, which they call the Placard.

units.la: Liber octauus Actionum MARTYRVM.
units.tr: Book Eight of the Acts of the MARTYRS.

units.la: Historia de actis quinque Martyrum, qui exusti sunt Cameriaci, vbi suprema est Curia Sabaudiae, nempe
units.tr: History of the acts of five martyrs who were burned at Chambéry, where the supreme court of Savoy sits, namely

units.la: IOANNIS VERNVTII, Pictauiensis, ANTONII LABORIERII, Cahortensis in Quercyo, IOANNIS TRIGALETI, Nemausensis, GVYRAVDII TAVRANI, Cahortensis, BERTRANDI BATALLII, Vasconis.
units.tr: JOHN VERNUTIUS of Poitou, ANTHONY LABORIERIUS of Cahors in Quercy, JOHN TRIGALETUS of Nîmes, GUYRAUDUS TAURANUS of Cahors, BERTRAND BATALLIUS, a Basque.

units.la: X[?] eo tempore quo Dominus pro singulari bonitate sua Euangelium Geneuae publicari voluit, quum suos circiter viginti annos in ea tutatus ef-set, tandem velut ex septis suis & arena permultos emisit athletas fortissimos, qui veritate suam sincere hominibus patefacerent. Ac non ita pridem quinque eximios testes doctrinae suae produxit, qui hanc coram senatu Cameriacensi constanter assererent: quorum tres nempe Ioannes Vernutius Pictauus, Antonius Laborierius Cahorti Quercianorum natus, ac legum peritus, quique iudicij regij officio illic defunctus erat: & Ioannes Trigaletus Nemausensis, iuris etiam peritus, ecclesiae Geneuensis consensu delecti ad promulgandum Christi Euangelium, munus hoc libenter & summis animis susceperunt, vt qui iam antea se Dei mandato & vocationi consecrauerant.
units.tr: At the time when the Lord, in his singular goodness, willed the Gospel to be published at Geneva, after he had kept that city safe for about twenty years, he at last sent out, as from his fold and arena, a great number of most valiant athletes to declare his truth sincerely to men. Not long ago he brought forward five outstanding witnesses of his doctrine, who steadfastly affirmed it before the senate of Chambéry. Of these, three were John Vernutius of Poitou, Anthony Laborierius, born at Cahors in Quercy and learned in the law, who had held the office of royal judge there, and John Trigaletus of Nîmes, also learned in the law, chosen with the consent of the church of Geneva to proclaim the Gospel of Christ. They undertook this office gladly and with the greatest zeal, as men who had already dedicated themselves to God's command and calling.

units.la: Etsi autem non ita stupidi nec hebetes erant, quin facile perspicerent quae suis capitibus imminebant pericula, & ignes quasi iam accensos praeuiderent: Studium tamen illud pium quo seruire Dei gloriae cupiebant pro sua vocatione sanctissima, illos sic perpulit, vt omnem hostium veritatis truculentiam plusquam barbaram contemnerent: atque etiam licet quidam vir pius illos praemonuisset quum viam ingressi sunt, periculum esse ne comprehenderentur in itinere, nullo tamen metu nec terrore percelli aut abstrahi potuerunt quin pergerent quo erant vocati. Duo item alij, Guyraudus scilicet Tauranus Cahorti Quercianorum natus, ac mercator: & Bertrandus Batallius natione Vasco & schoo-
units.tr: Although they were not so dull or stupid as not to see clearly the dangers that hung over their heads, and to foresee the fires as if already kindled, nevertheless that pious zeal by which they longed to serve the glory of God in their most holy calling so moved them that they despised all the savagery of the enemies of the truth, more than barbarous. Indeed, although a certain godly man had warned them as they set out that there was a danger of being seized on the journey, they could not be struck down or turned aside by any fear or terror, so as not to press on to where they had been called. Two others likewise joined the three as companions of the journey: Guyraudus Tauranus, born at Cahors in Quercy, a merchant, and Bertrand Batallius, a Basque by nation and a scholar. (Continued in the next paragraph.)

units.la: lasticus itineris comites se illis tribus adiunxerunt, acsi ægre tulissent eos ad coronam martyrij accipiendā ita properare, vt interim pedem non monerent ipsi: nam Batallius quum statuisset illos tantum comitari paulò vltra pótem Aruæ torrentis, qui Geneuæ est vicinus, quò subleuaret Laborierum, rogatus vt etiā vlterius pergeret, tam prompto & alacri animo consensit, vt quanuis ad iter minimè esset paratus, ad vltimum tamen vsque spiritum comes fuerit indiuiduus. Quinque igitur illi Dei serui cum alijs octo comitibus iter susceptum, lætis animis prosequuntur. canunt enim Deo laudes, & gratias agunt vera fiducia instructi, paratíque ad profundendas animas pro tuenda eius gloria, cui operam suam impendebat, sicuti postea satis comprobarunt. Quum ita proficiscerentur, vbi tandem simul omnes peruenirent ad eum locum, cui vulgare nomen est Collum Tamisii montis apud Fossimianos Sabaudiæ populos: occurrit illis præfectus quidam rerū capitalium qui paulò ante venerat Geneuā, vbi astutè simulās se religioni faucre: quia nonnihil de ea profectione subolfecerat, eos illic expectabat, vt incautos velut ex insidijs deprehenderet. Vt autem ostenderet se palàm mancipatum esse furiosæ istorū libidini, qui odio plusquam belluino contra Euangelium rapiuntur, eos in vincula coniecit. Atque vbi multa percontatus esset, & quas secum ferebant literas & libros extorsisset, colligatos omnes rectà Cameriacū duxit: idque fecit vt illis gratus esset, qui velut leones famelici huic prædæ inhiabant. Vt tamen quamuis sæuierint truculentæ belluæ, singularis omnium Christi mansuetudo ac tolerantia, tantam rabiem aliquatenus mitigauit, effecítque vt non ita crudeliter tractati sint, atque solet aliquì qui eandem causam tuentur. Sed longè satius fuerit ex ipsorum literis intelligere quid contra eos actū sit, qua prudentia respoderint superbis iudicū interrogationibus, & quàm modestè se gesserint in tota actione. quanta porrò constantia pertulerint mortem hominum opinione turpem & ignominiæ plenam, cui tandem adiudicati sunt, relatum fuit ab his hominibus, quorum ea est fides vt abrogari nullo modo possit, quemadmodum postea suo loco dicetur. Ac primò quidem ea proposuimus scripta, quibus acta iudiciaria & causæ progressus continentur, sicuti etiam ipsi conscripserunt.
units.tr: a scholar, who joined them as companions on the journey, as though they were sorry that these men were hastening so eagerly to receive the crown of martyrdom that they did not warn their own feet. For when Batallius had decided to accompany them only a little beyond the bridge over the Arve torrent, which lies near Geneva, in order to relieve Laborierius, he was asked to go further, and he consented with such a ready and eager mind that, although he was not at all prepared for the journey, he remained their inseparable companion to the last breath. So those five servants of God, together with eight other companions, went on their way with joyful hearts. For they sang praises to God and gave thanks, armed with true confidence and ready to pour out their souls for the defence of that glory to which they devoted their labour, as they afterwards amply proved. As they travelled in this way, they at last all reached the place commonly called the Col de Tamisy, near the people of Faucigny in Savoy. There a certain officer of capital crimes met them, who had lately come from Geneva, where he had pretended to favour religion. Because he had got some scent of this journey, he was waiting for them there, so as to catch them unawares, as from an ambush. In order to show that he had openly given himself up to the savage lust of those who are carried away against the Gospel with a hatred more than beastly, he threw them into chains. After he had questioned them at length and wrested from them the letters and books they carried with them, he led them all bound straight to Chambéry, and he did this in order to please those who, like hungry lions, were gaping after this prey. Yet, although these savage beasts raged, the singular gentleness and endurance of all of them, as Christians, somewhat softened such a frenzy, so that they were not treated as cruelly as is usual with some who defend the same cause. But it will be far better to learn from their own letters what was done against them, with what prudence they answered the haughty questions of the judges, and how modestly they conducted themselves throughout the whole proceeding. How much constancy they showed in enduring the death, which men regard as base and full of disgrace, to which they were at last condemned, has been reported by those men whose faithfulness is such that it can in no way be discredited, as will be said later in its place. First, then, we have set out those writings in which the judicial acts and the course of the case are contained, as the men themselves also wrote them down.

units.la: Ea[?] fuit Dei optimi maximi bonitas & amor erga nos, tantúmque honoris indulgentissimus Pater nobis detulit, fratres unicè dilecti, ut catenis vincti sigillatim ex carcere deducti simus in auditorium, quod vocant, ubi iam sedebant: qui locum Prætoris tenebat, Præfectus rerum capitalium, Causidicus regius, Officialis huius urbis, & ditionis Tarentesiæ fidei inquisitor, Furbitus episcopum referens, aliquot etiam monachi & alij nonnulli coram aderant.
units.tr: Such was the goodness and love of God, the best and greatest, towards us, and so great an honour did the most indulgent Father bestow on us, dearly beloved brethren, that we, bound in chains, were led one by one from the prison into the hall which they call the auditorium, where they were already sitting. The one holding the place of the praetor was the prefect of capital cases, the royal advocate, the official of this city and district, and the inquisitor of the faith for Tarentaise, Furbitus representing the bishop; several monks and some others were also present.

units.la: Illic rursus quæsitum est vellemusne nostras quas odiosè nominant hæreses pertinaciter tueri. nos vero Spiritus sancti præsidio freti exposuimus quòd iniectæ sunt in nos manus, nihil aliud quàm viâ placidè ingressos trasiisse[?]: cæterum quod ad fidei nostræ spectat, eandem esse quàm Geneuensis, Bernensis, aliæque omnes ecclesiæ Euangelij lucem & veram prædicationem amplexæ, profitentur: sicuti etiam edita iam à nobis fuerat aliqua confessio. nos autem iure non posse ab ipsis cogi ad eam deferendam, ut quæ in Papatu obtinet, vllo modo amplectamur, quia præsertim nemo ob fidem suam vexari debeat, modò ne statu publicum perturbet aut convellat: atque si constaret eorum fidem esse veram, ad illam cogi non debere, quemadmodum Hilarius & Athanasius contra Arrianos perspicuè tradunt.
units.tr: There they were asked again whether we would stubbornly maintain those heresies of ours, which they hatefully call such. We, relying on the protection of the Holy Spirit, explained that hands had been laid on us though we had done nothing except pass along the road peacefully. As for what concerns our faith, we profess that it is the same as that embraced by Geneva, Berne and all the other churches that have embraced the light of the Gospel and its true preaching; as indeed some confession had already been published by us. We maintained that we could not rightly be compelled by them to accept, in any way, what prevails in Papacy, especially since no one ought to be harassed on account of his faith, provided he does not disturb or overthrow the public state; and that if their faith were shown to be true, they ought not to be compelled to it, as Hilary and Athanasius clearly teach against the Arians.

units.la: Deinde quanuis, Dei gratia, de nostra fide certi essemus, si tamen ex Scriptura doceamur nos errore labi, vel aliquod dogma falsum tueri, paratos esse ad præstandū Deo nostro obsequium, ut qui studium hoc sanctum, quo ad eius cultum ferimur, animis nostris iam à longo tempore indiderit, etiam quum in tenebris adhuc cæcutientes illum temerè ac pro arbitrio nostro colere mus: atque ita nos ab eo impulsos fuisse ad inuestigandum paulò diligentius ab utra parte staret eius veritas, præsertim hoc tempore quo turbulenta de religione dissidia & contentiones ubique feruent: & tandem iudicio ecclesiæ Genevensis nos assensisse, ut quæ veram pietate tueatur: non aliud postulare, nisi ut sacra Biblia in medium proserantur, ex quibus tota controversia dirimatur. & quoniam liber institutionis Christianæ qui nobis abreptus fuerat, illic erat in promptu, nos quidquid obiiciant, solutiones certissimas in eo monstraturos: & quas uis libram illum reprobatū esse conclamarent, & in concilio Tridetino cautum fuisse ne ullo modo legatur, Doctoribus tamen id licere, præfertim verò quum agitur de reuocadis in viam miseris hæreticis, quo elogio nos insigniebant. Quòd autem damnatum esse pronuntiant, ac singulis quibusque hæreticis opus fore nouo Concilio: excepimus, si hæc ratio ad nos flectendos plus momenti haberet quàm omnes contrariæ rationes in eo libro expositæ ad nos in fide nostra confirmandos & retinendos, fieri non posse quin larvati & hypocritæ censeamur, & quidem digni quos Deus & omnes creaturæ odio prosequantur: etiamsi lingua fateretur verum esse quod affirmant, conscientiam nihilominus conuictam, adeóq; rationibus illis coacta reluctari, nec sinere ut ita impudenter metiamur.
