On the following day we were called out one after another, all of us except Brother Vernutius, who was not summoned, and thus we were led forward to our judges, who had gathered in the place where capital cases are heard in the palace. There the Propraetor sat first, and there were also present those who represent the king's interests, and the councillors, and about twenty advocates. Besides these, the Inquisitor of the faith with the officials (as they are called) of this city and of the district of Tarentaise, and finally four or five monks, partly Franciscans and partly Dominicans. And since it was the Lord's day, many others were also present, who, having nothing else to do, had gathered there. Then, by order of the Propraetor, a decree of the Senate was read to us, in which he and his colleagues were expressly instructed to bring our case to an end within three days, otherwise they would be removed from their office for a full year. By the same decree the Propraetor ordered that we should listen to, and also answer, the admonitions which the Inquisitor was about to set before us, unless we were willing to be regarded as convicted heretics, seditious and factious men, obstinate and perverse, and so be condemned at once by the votes of all. Here, having first invoked the name of God, we replied that we had already answered those admonitions more than enough, and that we did not wish to take anything away from the privileges of our lords of Berne and Geneva. Once again we were urged by the same order. So we answered (after we had clearly quoted what is said in Isaiah 38, "Lord, I am oppressed; answer for me") that we would comply on the condition that nothing be diminished or taken away from the privilege and liberty of those lords of ours, and that nothing should prevent them from complaining to the Senate itself, and to the King, and pursuing the wrong done to them, especially since we were being violently forced to this. Then the clerk at once read out to all what had been our answer, both before the Propraetor and to the others, from the written text. When he had finished reading, after an oath had been taken, we were asked whether we wished to persist in our answers. We replied that, since they rest on the pure Word of God, and since from that single fount of truth nothing has yet been brought against them or proved against us, we could in no way declare otherwise. And so that it might clearly be established that we are by no means heretics or obstinate, we declared that if we slip through ignorance or err in any point, and are taught from the Word of God, we shall at once change our opinion. For we have no other counsel or purpose than to believe and follow Jesus Christ, and him crucified, in that way which he himself has pointed out in his word. Therefore, if it is shown that we have strayed from it, we ask them to direct us to it and reveal to us the truth which we should follow, and we promise to obey gladly and from the heart. Here the Inquisitor of the faith began a polished speech, as he had often done before, and so wove it together that he spoke only of the Pope and made no mention of Christ at all. And since by his exhortation he asserted that certain articles in our answers were plainly heretical, we asked him to point them out to us. Now we shall not report each one to you, but only the chief ones. That Inquisitor objected that we receive only two sacraments, while we reject the other five, which had always held a place in the Church. We replied that if he would plainly show from the Word of God that there are others, we would readily assent and promise so. Then he cited the fifth chapter to the Ephesians: "What? Does it not say of marriage, 'This is a great sacrament'?" We answered: "Do you then understand the Scriptures so well, master, that you twist this to refer to marriage? Yet Paul himself declares that he is speaking of Christ and the Church. So you utterly overturn the genuine meaning of the Apostle. But if he were speaking even of marriage, were you only tinged with Greek, you would at once perceive that the word was wrongly rendered. Indeed," he said, "I know something of that language. Tell us then, if you please, what is written in Greek." Then he, astonished, fell silent. We therefore added, "Lord, we see that you are overcome with shame and do not dare to pronounce that word. We shall therefore tell you what it is: the Greek word has the same force as 'secret' or 'mystery', and not 'sacrament'." Then the Inquisitor said, "We have argued enough already, because you are heretics. What do you think of extreme unction?" We answered, "But, Sir, let us first dispute about marriage and proceed in order, or at least confess that you are beaten." Here suddenly all of them, both officials and monks and advocates, cried out that more than enough words had already been poured out, and that there should be no further disputing. Then they sternly ordered us to answer. We, however, marvelling at such haste on their part, said that they were being carried too headlong towards condemning five innocent men and adjudging them to death, since they were unwilling to weigh their cause more closely or to see what sort of calumny their opponents were. So we added these few points, and you understand well enough that these men who oppose us cannot in any way prove what they say; and because this is troublesome to you, you pour out your bile upon us. But if you refuse to hear us here, as your duty requires, we have God as the supreme Judge of all judges, who will hear us calmly and render justice to us all, and before whose sight you will at last have to render account, even against your will, for the wrong which you do not hesitate to inflict upon Christ, his only Son, while you treat us, who are his members, so wretchedly. Nevertheless they ordered us to answer about that extreme unction. They say that James commanded it, and you cannot evade or escape this. We replied that we certainly acknowledge that, since at the beginning the Gospel was published by the Apostles, and since it was necessary that the teaching be confirmed by miracles performed, there were then signs, or sacraments, which referred to those miracles, whose truth followed them. Of this kind was the laying on of hands, which signified the gift of the Holy Spirit, and at the same time the truth itself followed, as is sufficiently clear from the history of the Acts. So too that anointing with oil was so salutary that health wonderfully followed it. But when the publication of the Gospel was received by the world, then the visible gift of the Holy Spirit, and also the miracles, ceased; and therefore those signs, which without the truth are altogether empty. Then: "What agreement has that anointing with your own, which you boast of? Is it not plain that whatever is done by you is full of blasphemies? What health follows from it? You never bring it forward except when all hope is lost." They asked again whether that anointing did not confer the forgiveness of sins. We answered that in our account the forgiveness of sins is by no means attributed to the anointing, but plainly to prayers offered in faith, since the forgiveness of our sins is found nowhere else than in the blood of Christ. They objected that all these things had been utterly condemned by the Councils, and so we were heretics. But how great the disorder in all this discussion was, and how confused the uproar, cannot be told. For always seven or eight shouted at once; and meanwhile we pointed out their folly and absurdities as we went along, so that those present were compelled even to laugh at such madness in them. Besides this, we were asked whether we were not willing to have faith in the Councils. We answered that we always accept Councils and decrees only so far as they agree with the Word of God and rest upon it; otherwise we do not admit them at all. Rather we detest them as human traditions, and as plainly diabolical inventions, which oppose the truth of God, just as Paul in Galatians commanded them to do, even if an angel from heaven should bring us a teaching other than that which is contained in the Gospel.

units.la: Hic exorta est magna quaestio, qua nobis proposuerunt, nempe qui fàiremus[?] vetus ac novum Testamentum esse Dei verbū, nisi quatenus Concilia & ecclesia Romana ita censent[?], nosque certiores reddunt? Quibus responsum fuit, quanuis Deus opera Iudaeorum & Papistarum usus sit in conseruandis sacrosanctis Libris, quibus voluntate erga nos sua patefecit, non ideo tamen nos ab illis testimonia petere, nec probationes, quibus cõstet esse verbū Dei: sed certū ac ratum testimonium habere in conscietijs nostris per Spiritū adoptionis, qui operatur in cordibus nostris certóq; nobis persuadet, ac sancit Dei promissiones, & impellit ut clamemus, Abba, Pater, queadmodum ait Paulus 8, ad Rom. cap. atq; etiam subiunximus[?], quisquis ab eode illo Spiritu non ita persuasus est, eū non posse Dei filium ceferi[?]: hoc caput prolixe agitatum fuit, ac copiosius tractatū & pspicue[?] simul illis ostensum, Dei gratia, quam impio scelere sese obstringerent & horrendam blasphemiam vomerent, dum volunt aeternum Dei verbum authoritati hominū carnalium, adeoque diabolorum lorũ subiicere. certũ enim esse, neminẽ qui Dei Spiritu regatur, & aliqua ratione sit præditus, tantam impietatem somniaturum. Sed vobis nunc perscribi sigillatim quidquid dictum fuit, nullo modo potest. Vnum tamen non est omittendum, fuisse quosdam in eo consessu, qui palàm dicerent, esse diaboli, non Dei Spiritum, qui certiores de his rebus nos redderet. Istos igitur rogauimus, quonam Spiritu iussus fuerit Abraham filium suum Isaac immolare. Spiritu Dei responderunt. nos statim excepimus, si Abraham patrare non dubitauit parricidium, quod erat contra legem naturæ, certè perpulsum fuisse oportet interno quodam & longè alio quàm carnis suæ motu, quæ quidem potuit illum eò adducere, vt putaret diabolum quendam esse potius quàm Dei Spiritum. atqui erat idem ille Spiritus, à quo certiores reddimur, qui impellebat eum vt crederet Dei esse voluntatem. Sed mirum non est, si hoc prorsus ignoretis. nam animalis homo de rebus spiritualibus iudicare non potest. Ac multa alia de hoc capite illis exposita fuerunt. Postea rogati sumus de Cœna, de Missa, de Purgatorio, de confessione auriculari, & alijs ipsorum sacramentis. Atque de singulis capitibus ita copiosè vltro citróque disceptatum fuit, vt perinde ac de reliquis constitutum fuerit. Nimis longum esset ac tædiosum, referre quidquid hoc loco tractatum est. Id autem vnum sufficiat, respondisse quemque nostrum pro mensura suæ fidei, & quæ Dei est gratia, hostes ita repressos ac cohibitos omni ex parte, vt confusi iacuerint. Tandem postulauimus, vt de Papa nonnihil diceretur, & quidem ea lege, vt si probare possent ex Scriptura Papam esse caput Ecclesiæ Christi, nos omnia eius decreta admissuros. verùm ad hoc caput nunquam attendere, neque de eo disceptare vllo modo voluerunt. Tunc igitur diximus quia probare nolebant Papam esse caput Ecclesiæ, nos ex contextu sacrosanctæ Scripturæ palam facturos, & quasi digito monstraturos Papam esse Antichristum: Biblia tantùm nobis proferrent, vt sæpius hoc ab illis petieramus: quod tamen semper denegarunt. Cœpimus itaque locum ex 2. capite posterioris ad Thess. tractare: sed audire placidè non sustinuerunt: quin potius instar luporum vlulare & vociferari, nos magis hæreticos esse quàm wicleuum, Hussium, Lutherum, & quosuis alios: neque contra nos disputandum: monere nihilominus vt in viam rediremus. Quum haec peracta essent, in carcerem remisi sumus, sed alij ab alijs separati ad horam quintam serotinam. Postridie vero Tauranum fratrem qui vix Geneuae tres menses commoratus fuerat atque adeo antea nunquam de Deo quidquam noverat, accersi iusserunt. hunc sub noctem a nobis segregatum atque abstractum conabantur modis omnibus in suam nassam pellicere. Sed Dei optimi gratia & beneficio illis ita respondit, & eorum petulantiam sic retudit, ut istorum turpitudinem ac dedecora omnia detexerit, idque multo melius quam nos antea fecisse videremur. Quod quidem graviter & iniquis animis tulerunt, & eum ad nos remiserunt cum hac exprobratione. En etiam de isto ut de aliis iam actum est. Postea deductus fuit ad nos: unde magnam consolationem coepimus, & gratias Deo nostro optimo simul egimus ob eam animi magnitudinem & constantiam, quam nobis omnibus pro sua bonitate contulerat. Caeterum, die Mercurij (qui xxi, erat Augusti) hora quinta pomeridiana, iudex noster, qui Proprætoris partes sustinet, in cubiculum, quo vincti concludimur, venit sententiam contra nos scriptam pronuntiaturus: qua quidem nos tres nempe Vernutius, Laborierius, & Trigaletus in totam vitam mancipamur illi miserrimae servituti, in quam addicuntur qui remos cogunt. Batallius autem & Tauranus ad decennium duntaxat: & ea quidem lege, ut vetent diserte ac minaciter, ne quis unquam stationem illam deserat, alioqui fore si reperiamur, ut ignis supplicio luamus: ac ne etiam illinc duo illi fratres ante praescriptum tempus abeant. Haec pronuntiata sententia rogavit iudex anne provocaremus. Tum vero Laborierius omnium nomine, Nequaquam, inquit, sed nos libenter accipere quidquid Deo optimo & Patri nostro visum est nobis dare, ac illi gratias immortales agere, eumque ex animo laudare, quod nos censuerit dignos, qui pro nomine suo patiamur. Procurator vero regius, qui in Curia eorum est scopulus, a Senatu perpulsus provocauerat ab ea quam dixi sententia. Statim igitur eadem hora Vernutius frater accersitus est in Senatum, & eo ipso die, atque etiam postridie causam dixit cum a nobis separatus esset. Proximo die Veneris Laborierius frater vocatus & deductus, mane & a meridie satis prolixè dixit, ut ex eorum ad vos literis perspicere licet: ac sepatus quoque à nobis fuit. Eodē ipso die ego in Senatum etiā ductus sub horā quartam, illic ad sextam vsque constiti. Totius autem actionis cōtra me progressus eiusmodi fuit, primū omnium iussus sum in genua procūbere. quod quū libenter fecissem, mihi propositā est tabella quaedā lignea, in qua crucifixi (quē vocāt) imago viridi colore depicta erat. Tū Valentierus Praeses summus, vniuersi senatus nomine iussit vt manū tabellae imponerē: quod protinus recusare non dubitaui, ob eā quae expressa erat, imagine: & testatus sum palā me per Deū viuū iurare erectus in caelū manib° & oculis: deinde verā me dicturū quidquid de fide mea rogarer. Tū à Senatu petijt, an quod conceperā iusiurādū illi satisfaceret. Ita esse respōdit, nec posse me per vllū maiorē iurare. Postquā igitur ex meo respōso intellexerūt, quodnā esset nomen meū, quae patria, qui ortus, & cur vinculis constringerer: pronūtiauit ille, ex meis corā Praefecto rerum capitalium editis de fide mea responsis plus satis constare, hominem haereticum me esse, atque talē iudicatum cēfura & supremis Inquisitoris, & Doctorum theologicorū calculis. Hīc ego acriter retorsi, eos ipsos re vera esse haereticos, quū à Christo Iesu Domino nostro tā perfidē defecerint, & ab eius doctrina turpiter defecuerint: acsese Antichristo coniunxerint, & impia eius dogmata sint sequuti. itaque ab illis me haereticum iudicari non posse: quin potius mihi facillimū esse ex Dei verbo coprobare, si me aequis animis dicentē audirent, eos esse impios, & plane haereticos. Tum summus Praeses excēpit, me praesertim duobus confessionis meae capitibus aperte convinci haereseos, nēpe dū affirmo Missae sacrificiū esse detestandū & execrādū sacrilegū, quo sanguis Iesu Christi pedibus calcatur, & quo etiam sacrificiū morte eius peractum abrogatur, & in nihilū prorsus redigitur: deinde, quū Missa censeatur esse memoria cēnae Domini (sicuti re vera est) id vero diabolicū esse figmentū à patre mendacij excogitatū, & confirmatū, ad eos in aeternū exitū praecipitandos, qui fide illi habent, & mordicadhaerent. Quū autē ingenuē respōdissē haec esse verissima, adiunxi vnicū esse sacrificiū aeternū, idq; iā peractū à sacerdote aeterno secundū ordinem Melchisedech, nēpe Christo. quod quidem ipse in ara crucis obtulit sanguine suo in remissionē peccatorū nostrorū fuso: qui ingressus est sancta sanctorū, hoc est, in caelū ad Patrē suum, quō etiam accessum habemus per eum, qui solus est Mediator noster & Aduocatus apud Patrem, quae ex 9. ad Hebræos cap.confirmabam. Quod autem ad Christianorum sacrificium attinet, constare laudibus & gratiarum actione, adeóque totam piorum vitam, quam in iustitia & sanctitate peragunt (quae viua est & rationalis hostia) sacrificium esse quod offerre Deo ipsi debeant, se ipsos totos consecrantes, & plane addicentes in eius obsequium: in quo essent velut socij & participes sacerdotij Christi, cuius nomine acceptos habeat Pater, & quicquid secum ferunt, vtcunque mutilum sit & imperfectum. Tum ille Missam & Coenam rem vnam & eandem esse pronuntiat, & nominibus tantum differre, non autem substantia vel re ipsa: ad hoc, differre quidem agendi modo, quod ad externas ceremonias spectat. Imo vero Coenam & Missam pugnare ex diametro (vt loquuntur) ingenuè re-spondi, & non minus inter se distare quam caelum a terra: ac tum denum Latino sermone differimus quid nobis in Coena quaerendum & accipiendum sit: itémque signa panis & vini quo nos ducant: quid sacrificus in Missa sua offerat & Deo proponat: discrimen quoque expositum inter eum qui confert donum, & eum cui confertur. Nobis enim in Coena Christum dari in cibum, & perfectum integrúmque animarum nostrarum alimentum in vitam aeternam, quum scilicet accipimus panem & edimus, ac bibimus vinum, quae vera sunt & integra corporum nostrorum alimenta ad tuendam hanc vitam: haec signa nobis esse adminicula, quibus fidem nostram & spem vitae aeternae confirmemus, quae in Christo nobis datur, vt scribit Ioānes 6. capite, Qui videt Filium, & credit in eum, habet vitam aeternam: & eum vltimo die a mortuis excitabo. Palàm testatus sum me participem fieri corporis & sanguinis Christi per fidem, qua in caelum conscendo, vt illic ad dextram Patris quaerà Christum salute meam & vitam: non autem in pane & vino, sicuti sacrificus & Papistae faciunt. Hic ergo conatus est probare corporis Christi praesentiam in pane, & sanguinis in vino: & verba Domini nostri expendit, quum ait in Coena, Hoc est corpus meum. Ego vero respondi, particulam E S T, pro significat accipi, vt alijs quibusdam locis, veluti quum dicitur, Petra erat Christus: de columba etiā, & Spiritu sancto: de agno, & paschate: ac tropū esse tritum Scripturis, quem Metonymiam vel Synecdochen appellant, quum scilicet rei significatæ nomen signo tribuitur. atque citauit locum illum Ioannis 6, Ego sum panis vitæ. & , Qui manducat carnem meam, & bibit meum sanguinem: vbi de Cœna non agi, sed de fide in Christum excepi: quod ex verbis Domini probare promptum fuit, quum inquit, Verba mea spiritus & vita sunt: & ex xi.cap.prioris ad Corinth.vb: vocabula Panis & Calicis (quæ à Paulo quater repetuntur) diligenter perpendere oportuit. Hic multi sermones vltrò citròque sunt habiti, quos referre nimis longum foret: atque vt videtis, chartæ penuria laboramus. De Papa quoque, quem Antichristum esse cõfirmabam, disputatum fuit de eius authoritate, & decretis vel Statutis, quæ Christi legibus plane sunt contraria. citaui 2.cap.2.ad Thessal. & 4.prioris ad Timoth. In summa, quicquid rationum suarum tandem protulerint, Deus tamen Spiritu oris sui Antichristum occidit. Tunc autè longo sermone vsi sunt, quo me velut illecebris inescarent, pollicentes, si vellem in catholicæ & sanctæ matris suæ ecclesiæ sinum redire, statim fore vt me loco fratris haberent: atque ita mei ipsius miseritũ posse me magnos fructus posthac edere & quamplurimis prodesse. Tentarũt denique illecebris omne genus animum meum cõcutere & de gradu exturbare, si posset fieri. sed virtute Spiritus sancti suffultus, constanter inuictóque animo perstiti, vt nunquam vlla responsione permotus, Dei gratia, vacillauerim. Quod quum satis intelligerent, ad vltimum perfugium recurrunt, acminantur se pronuntiaturos cõtra me ex Regis legibus & ediclis. Tandem vero paucis respondi, sedere in cælo iudicem, ad cuius tribunal aliquando se sistere cogerentur, quum scilicet illud conscendet, singulos conuocaturus ad reddendam factorum dictorúmque omnium rationem: & tum denique libros & acta resignatum & patefactum iri, quibus explicatis causam suorum vt iustissimam tuebitur, ipsorum vero conatus & audaciam reprimet ac damnabit. Me igitur tunc amandarunt in carcerem, sed nonnulli eorũ quiritabantur, & prorumpebant in hanc vocem, Quanta est istæc proteruia, & quàm intolerabilis factus? alij autem subsannabant, ac perperam in nos torquebant illud Psalmi, Oculos habent, &c. Itaque hanc sententiam in cos reieci, nec enim verius quicquam in ipsos dici posse affirmari: nos autem iam Dei gratia, oculos fidei apertos habere, ut veritatem ipsam cernere possimus: idque solis datum esse iis quibus lumen illud Evangelij admirabile affulserit. Atque ea tum sic gesta fuere. Subsequeti die Sabbathi, Batallius & Tauranus coram ipsis constituti, pro constantia qua à Deo praemuniti erant, proque fidei mensura quam ab eodem acceperunt, fortiter inimicis restiterunt, aptéque interrogatis responderunt. Die Lunae proximo ad Senatores & Iudices nostros accersiti fuimus unà omnes, qui admonitione blanda, longaque verborum circuitione nos in suam sententiam perducere conabantur, sed, laus Deo, nos haudquaquam commouerunt illa verborum lenocinia. Nam Vernutius frater noster in eo consessu multis vicissim nostrae, vel potius Filij Dei, causae aequitate demonstrauit, nos deinde orationi adsensimus omnes, unoq; ore acclamauimus Amen. Ac repente velut homines in opinione obfirmati atque obstinati in carcerem nostrum reducimur. Postea etiam in nos quinque illorum decreto ignis supplicium constitutum fuit, cuius nos sententiae pronuntiationem heri expectabamus: actum Dei bonitate misericordiaq; praefulti, supplicium illud libere quidē & lubenti animo subire ac sustinere parati eramus, sed ipse mera sua benignitate spatium adhuc aliquod concessit respirandi. Qui autē has ad vos perfert literas famulus est Secretarij M. qui ut est vir bonus, tata[?] in nos contulit beneficia, ut plura, si vellet, in sua ipse causa facere non queat. Orate Dominum, ut illi pro tot officijs ac meritis in nos referat gratiam, remuneretur etiam suae liberalitatis praemijs eum qui in aula est, & reliquos qui hic sunt fratres. Scriptum die Dominico ipsis Calend.Septeb. anni M.D. LV. Commendat autem se quisque nostrum vobis omnibus: cupimusq; ut in precibus vestris nostri quoque memores sitis. Vester humilis filius, seruus & frater in Domino, Ioan. Trigaletus.
units.tr: Here a great question arose, which they put to us: how could we know that the Old and New Testament are the Word of God, unless insofar as the Councils and the Roman Church judge so and make us certain? To this it was answered that although God used the work of Jews and Papists in preserving the sacred Books, by which he has revealed his goodwill toward us, we do not for that reason seek from them testimonies or proofs that they are the Word of God. Rather, we have a certain and firm testimony in our consciences through the Spirit of adoption, who works in our hearts, certainly persuades us, seals God's promises, and impels us to cry, Abba, Father, as Paul says in Romans 8. We also added that whoever is not persuaded by that same Spirit cannot be a son of God. This point was discussed at length and treated more fully, and it was clearly shown to them, by the grace of God, that they were binding themselves with impious wickedness and spewing forth a horrible blasphemy, while they wished to subject the eternal Word of God to the authority of carnal men, and so to the lordship of devils. For it is certain that no one who is ruled by the Spirit of God and has any sense would dream up such impiety. But it is impossible to write out to you item by item everything that was said. One thing, however, must not be omitted: there were some in that assembly who openly said that it was the Spirit of the devil, not of God, that makes us certain of these things. So we asked them by what Spirit Abraham was commanded to sacrifice his son Isaac. They answered: by the Spirit of God. We at once replied: if Abraham did not hesitate to commit a parricide, which was against the law of nature, he must certainly have been moved by some inner impulse, quite different from the motion of his flesh, which could have led him to think that it was some devil rather than the Spirit of God. Yet it was that same Spirit, by whom we are made certain, who impelled him to believe that it was God's will. But it is no wonder if you are altogether ignorant of this, for the natural man cannot judge the things of the Spirit. Many other things were set out to them on this point. Afterwards we were asked about the Supper, the Mass, Purgatory, auricular confession, and their other sacraments. On each of these heads there was discussed back and forth at such length that it was settled as if concerning the rest. It would be too long and tedious to report everything that was treated here. This one thing will suffice: each of us answered according to the measure of his faith, and by the grace of God our enemies were so checked and restrained on every side that they lay confounded. At last we demanded that something be said about the Pope, and indeed on this condition: that if they could prove from Scripture that the Pope is the head of the Church of Christ, we would admit all his decrees. But they never would attend to this point, nor would they in any way discuss it. Then we said that since they were unwilling to prove that the Pope is the head of the Church, we would from the context of holy Scripture make plain, and as it were point with the finger, that the Pope is Antichrist; they should only bring forward the Bibles, as we had often asked them to do, which they nevertheless always refused. So we began to treat the passage from the second chapter of the latter Epistle to the Thessalonians, but they would not calmly listen. Rather, like wolves, they howled and shouted that we were more heretical than Wycliffe, Hus, Luther, and any others, and that there should be no disputing with us, though they warned us to return to the right path. When this was done, we were sent back to prison, but each separately from the others, until five in the evening. Next day they ordered Tauranus, a brother who had scarcely stayed three months in Geneva and so had never before known anything of God, to be summoned. Towards nightfall they tried by every means to lure him, separated and drawn away from us, into their net. But by the good grace and kindness of God he answered them in such a way and so repulsed their insolence that he laid bare all their baseness and disgrace, and did so far better than we seemed to have done before. This they took very ill, and with hostile minds they sent him back to us with this reproach. Behold, of this man too, as of the others, the matter has now been dealt with. Afterwards he was brought to us, whereupon we began to feel great consolation, and together we gave thanks to our most good God for that greatness of spirit and constancy which he had bestowed on us all by his goodness. Moreover, on Wednesday (which was the 21st of August), at five in the afternoon, our judge, who holds the office of Propraetor, came into the chamber where we prisoners are shut up, to pronounce a sentence written against us. By it Vernutius, Laborierius, and Trigaletus are condemned for their whole lives to that most wretched servitude into which those are sold who row the galleys; Batallius and Tauranus only for ten years, and indeed on this condition: that they are plainly and threateningly forbidden ever to desert that post, otherwise, if they are found, they will pay with the punishment of fire; and that those two brothers may not depart from there before the prescribed time. When this sentence was pronounced, the judge asked whether we would appeal. Then Laborierius, on behalf of all, said: "By no means, but we gladly accept whatever our most good God and Father has thought fit to give us, and we give him immortal thanks, and praise him from our hearts, because he has judged us worthy to suffer for his name." The royal prosecutor, who is the stumbling-block of their court, driven on by the Senate, had appealed from the sentence I have mentioned. Immediately at that same hour brother Vernutius was summoned before the Senate, and on that day and also the next he pleaded his case, having been separated from us. On the following Friday brother Laborierius was called and taken away; in the morning and from noon he spoke at considerable length, as may be seen from their letters to you, and he too was separated from us. On that same day I too was led before the Senate about the fourth hour, and stood there until the sixth. The whole course of the proceedings against me was as follows. First of all I was ordered to kneel down. When I had gladly done so, a wooden tablet was put before me, on which an image of the crucified one (as they call him) was painted in green. Then Valentierus, the chief President, in the name of the whole Senate, ordered me to lay my hand on the tablet. I did not hesitate at once to refuse, because of the image that was displayed there, and I openly testified that I swear by the living God, lifting my hands and eyes to heaven; and that I would speak the truth about whatever I was asked concerning my faith. Then he asked the Senate whether the oath I had made satisfied them. They replied that it did, and that I could not swear by any greater. After they had learned from my answer what my name was, what my country, what my birth, and why I was held in chains, he pronounced that from my answers given before the Prefect of capital cases concerning my faith, enough was plainly established: that I am a heretical man, and so judged by the censure and the verdict of the supreme Inquisitor and the doctors of theology. Here I retorted sharply that they themselves were in truth heretics, since they had so faithlessly fallen away from Christ Jesus our Lord, had shamefully departed from his doctrine, had joined themselves to Antichrist, and followed his impious dogmas. So I could not be judged heretical by them; rather, it would be very easy for me to prove from the Word of God, if they would hear me with fair minds, that they are impious and plainly heretics. Then the chief President took it up, saying that I was especially convicted of heresy by two heads of my confession: namely, when I affirm that the sacrifice of the Mass is a detestable and accursed sacrilege, by which the blood of Jesus Christ is trodden underfoot, and by which the sacrifice accomplished by his death is abrogated and reduced to nothing; and then, since the Mass is held to be a memorial of the Lord's Supper (as indeed it is), that this is a diabolical fiction, invented and confirmed by the father of lies, to plunge into eternal ruin those who trust in it and cling to it stubbornly. When I had frankly answered that these things were most true, I added that there is one eternal sacrifice, already accomplished by the eternal priest according to the order of Melchisedec, namely Christ, who offered it himself on the altar of the cross, his blood poured out for the remission of our sins; who entered into the holy of holies, that is, into heaven, to his Father, and through whom we too have access, through him who alone is our Mediator and Advocate with the Father, as I confirmed from Hebrews 9. As for the Christian sacrifice, I said, it consists in praises and thanksgiving; indeed the whole life of the godly, which they lead in righteousness and holiness (which is a living and reasonable sacrifice), is the sacrifice they ought to offer to God, consecrating and wholly devoting themselves to his service, in which they are, as it were, partners and sharers in the priesthood of Christ, in whose name the Father accepts whatever they bring, however mutilated and imperfect it may be. Then he declared that the Mass and the Supper are one and the same thing, differing only in name and not in substance or reality, and differing indeed in the mode of acting so far as the external ceremonies are concerned. Nay rather, I answered frankly that the Supper and the Mass are in direct opposition (as they say), and are no less distant from each other than heaven from earth. Then at last we discussed, in the Latin tongue, what we ought to seek and receive in the Supper, and likewise the signs of bread and wine by which they lead us; what the priest offers in his Mass and presents to God; and also the distinction set out between the one who bestows the gift and the one to whom it is bestowed. For in the Supper Christ is given to us as food, and as the complete and whole nourishment of our souls unto eternal life, when we take the bread, eat it, and drink the wine, which are the true and whole nourishment of our bodies for sustaining this life; these signs are aids to us by which we confirm our faith and our hope of eternal life, which is given to us in Christ, as John writes in chapter 6: "He who sees the Son and believes in him has eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day." I openly testified that I become a partaker of the body and blood of Christ through faith, by which I ascend into heaven, there to seek Christ at the right hand of the Father as my salvation and life, and not in the bread and wine, as the priest and the Papists do. Here he tried to prove the presence of Christ's body in the bread and of his blood in the wine, and weighed the words of our Lord when he says in the Supper, "This is my body." But I answered that the particle IS is taken for SIGNIFIES, as in certain other places: for instance, "The rock was Christ"; likewise of the dove and the Holy Spirit, and of the lamb and the Passover. This trope is common in Scripture, and they call it metonymy or synecdoche, when the name of the thing signified is given to the sign. I also cited that passage of John 6: "I am the bread of life," and "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood," where I pointed out that it is not about the Supper but about faith in Christ. This was easy to prove from the words of the Lord, when he says, "My words are spirit and life"; and from the eleventh chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, the words Bread and Cup (which Paul repeats four times) had to be weighed carefully. Here many speeches were made back and forth, which would be too long to report; and, as you see, we are short of paper. The Pope too, whom I affirmed to be Antichrist, was disputed about, concerning his authority and his decrees or statutes, which are plainly contrary to the laws of Christ. I cited 2 Thessalonians 2 and 1 Timothy 4. In sum, whatever reasons they finally put forward, God nevertheless kills Antichrist with the Spirit of his mouth. Then they used a long speech, by which they tried to entice me as with baits, promising that if I would return to the bosom of their Catholic and holy mother the Church, they would at once treat me as a brother; and that I might take pity on myself, since I could henceforth produce great fruits and profit very many. Finally they tried with enticements of every kind to shake my mind and drive it from its place, if that were possible. But supported by the power of the Holy Spirit, I persevered constant and undaunted, so that by the grace of God I never wavered under any answer. When they understood this well enough, they resorted to their last refuge and threatened that they would pronounce against me according to the laws and edicts of the King. At last I answered briefly that there is a judge sitting in heaven, before whose tribunal they will one day be forced to present themselves, when he shall ascend it to summon each one to render an account of all their deeds and words; and then at last the books and records will be unsealed and laid open, and by them he will defend the cause of his own as most just, and will restrain and condemn the attempts and audacity of these men. So they sent me back to prison; but some of them grumbled and burst out in this voice: "How great is this insolence, and how intolerable has he become?" Others, however, mocked us and wrongly turned against us that verse of the Psalm, "They have eyes," and so on. So I threw that sentence back at them, for nothing truer could be said of them; but we, now by the grace of God, have the eyes of faith open, so that we can see the truth itself, and this is given only to those on whom that admirable light of the Gospel has shone. These things were so done then. On the following Sabbath day, Batallius and Tauranus, standing before them, relying on the steadfastness with which they were fortified by God and on the measure of faith which they had received from him, bravely resisted their enemies and answered the questions put to them aptly. On the next Monday we were all summoned together before our Senators and judges, who by gentle admonition and a long circuit of words tried to bring us to their opinion; but, praise be to God, those verbal enticements did not move us in the least. For our brother Vernutius, in that assembly, in turn demonstrated with many arguments the fairness of our cause, or rather of the Son of God. Then we all assented to his speech and with one voice cried out, Amen. And suddenly, like men fixed and obstinate in their opinion, we were led back to our prison. Afterwards the punishment of fire was also decreed against us by the decision of those five, whose pronouncement of this sentence we had been awaiting the day before. But we, fortified by the goodness and mercy of God, were prepared to undergo that punishment freely and with a willing mind; yet he, by his sheer kindness, has granted us some further space to breathe. The one who brings these letters to you is the servant of the Secretary M., who, being a good man, has conferred so many benefits on us that, were he willing, he could not do more in his own cause. Pray the Lord that he may repay him for so many services and merits toward us, and reward with the prizes of his own liberality both him who is at court and the other brethren who are here. Written on the Lord's Day, on the Kalends of September, in the year 1555. Each of us commends himself to you all, and we wish that you too would remember us in your prayers. Your humble son, servant, and brother in the Lord, John Trigaletus.

units.la: Ertiores, opinor, facti estis de rerum nostrarum statu, qualemq; causae nostrae exitu fore sperauerimus, nempe ut lata capitis sententia postridie frequenti in ea urbe mercatu, publice de nobis velut victimis fieret holocaustu. Fasces enim & catenae iam apparati erat: pali tantum restabant in terram defigendi, struendúsq; rogus, cui corpora nostra imponerentur. Sed Deus pro bonitate ac misericordia sua exaudiuit orationem eorum qui pro nobis eius opem implorabant: unde effectus subsequutus est ciusmodi: Quod scilicet die Veneris proximo hora secunda pomeridiana Iudices couenerint ad imponedum finem causae nostrae. ac duodecim quum essent, magna inter eos fuit sententiarum varietas: sex enim in nos supplicium exigui & lenti ignis constituendum, alij vero ad remigium relegandos, aut in exilium pellendos censebant. Quae causa fuit ut eo die nihil certi Statutum fuerit.
units.tr: You will have heard, I suppose, how our affairs stand, and what outcome of our cause we had hoped for: namely, that after sentence of death was pronounced, we would be publicly sacrificed like victims as a burnt offering on the next day, at the crowded market in that city. The fasces and chains were already prepared; only the stakes remained to be driven into the ground, and the pyre built on which our bodies were to be laid. But God, in his goodness and mercy, heard the prayers of those who implored his help for us. The result followed in this way: on Friday next, at two in the afternoon, the judges assembled to bring our case to an end. There were twelve of them, and there was great disagreement among them. Six thought that we should be punished by a slow and gentle fire, while the others judged that we should be sent to the galleys or driven into exile. For this reason nothing certain was decided that day.

units.la: Postero die alijs nonnullis in iudicium conuocatis, constitutum fuit quod in nobis qui membra Christi sumus, ipse non combureretur velut haereticus, ne forte ea res populo offensionem aliquam afferret: sed tanquam fur aut latro ad remiges condemnaretur. diuersa tamen ratione quo ad temporis spatium. nam Batallium & Tauranum ad decem annos tantum, me vero cum duobus socijs, omnibus diebus vitae nostrae remigio destinarunt.
units.tr: On the following day, after some others had been summoned to the court, it was decided that we who are members of Christ should not be burned as heretics, lest that business perhaps give some offence to the people; rather, we should be condemned to the galleys like thieves or robbers. Yet the length of the term differed. For they assigned Batallius and Tauranus to the galleys for ten years only, but me, with my two companions, for the rest of our lives.

units.la: Multum se nostra causa fecisse existimant, quod nos morte perbeata liberarint, ut vitam degamus mille mortibus acerbiorem. attamen speramus Dominum, qui nobis nunquam defuit in terra quandiu in manibus aduersariorum & vinculis Cameriaci detenti sumus, eundē etiam in mari sua inexhausta benignitate affore inter manus eorum qui remigum praefecti sunt: nec etiam diffidimus quin nostra in triremibus mansio aeque utilis sutura sit, atque haec Cameriaci in carcere magnae consolationi & aedificationi fuit iis qui nobis affuerunt, aliisque qui nos quandoque inuiserunt. Memini porro eorum quae mihi aliquando narrata sunt de Maioris: sed causa nostra, Dei beneficio, melior est. Nam quod ad nos attinet, nulla sunt mali alicuius aut revocationis indicia: sed misericordia quadam tali ac συμπαθεία [?] erga quinque miseros homines ducti, metuentes iram Dei ob tantam humani sanguinis effusionem, hoc pacto nobiscum egerunt. Haec nobis acciderunt post longam expectationem voluntatis Domini, qui causam nostram suscepit ac defendit, & vocem nostram tempore opportuno exaudiuit. Hic noster tabellarius vir est bonus, qui in carcere nos inuisit: audiuit etiam totam rationem iudicij nostri, opinorque ipsum deferre secum eius exemplum. ex eo [?] rem totam a principio cognoscere poteritis. Precibus vestris ac totius ecclesiae, parentū, amicorumq; omnium & vicinorum nos: ex animo commendamus: quibus, si unquam, nunc nunc maxime indigemus, quum ad vitae genus abripiamur cui vel mille mortes, si totidem obire liceret, merito quidem praeferri possint. Dominus Deus & Pater omnis misericordiae ac Deus omnis consolationis nostri misereatur, nosque magis ac magis confirmet, sicuti etiam magis opus nunc habemus. Scribit prolixe ad uxorem suam Laborierius frater ac socius noster: eius literas si legeris, cognosces quid respondere statuerimus, quum nobis iudicum sententia pronuntiabitur: quod hodie fiet, ut iam accepimus. Fratres mei te salutant, & se precibus etiam ecclesiae, ac vestris privatim commendatos cupiunt.
units.tr: They think they have done a great deal for our cause in releasing us from a most blessed death so that we might live a life more bitter than a thousand deaths. Yet we trust in the Lord, who never failed us on land, while we were held in the hands of our adversaries and in chains at Cambrai, and who, in his inexhaustible kindness, will be with us also at sea, among the men set over the galley slaves. Nor do we doubt that our stay in the galleys will be as useful as our time in the prison at Cambrai was a great comfort and building up to those who attended us and to others who at times visited us. I recall, moreover, what was once told me about Maioris, but our cause, by God's favour, is better. For as far as we are concerned, there are no signs of any wrongdoing or of any recantation; rather, moved by a certain pity and sympathy [?] for five wretched men, and fearing the wrath of God on account of so great an effusion of human blood, they have dealt with us in this way. These things have happened to us after a long waiting upon the will of the Lord, who has taken up and defended our cause and heard our voice at the right time. Our messenger here is a good man, who visited us in prison. He also heard the whole account of our trial, and I think he will bring a copy of it with him; from it you will be able to learn the whole matter from the beginning. We commend ourselves heartily to your prayers, and to those of the whole Church, our parents, friends and neighbours; we need them now most of all, if ever, since we are being carried off to a manner of life for which a thousand deaths, if we could die that many times, would rightly be preferred. May the Lord God and Father of all mercy, and the God of all consolation, have mercy on us and strengthen us more and more, as we now especially need. Our brother and fellow-prisoner Laborierius is writing at length to his wife; if you read his letter, you will learn what we have resolved to answer when the judges' sentence is pronounced, which, as we have heard, will be today. My brethren greet you, and they wish to be commended to the prayers of the Church and to your own private prayers.

units.la: Quae deinceps sequentur literae singulares, ab illis quinque vinctis conscriptae fuerunt in piorum omnium consolationem. Antonius Laborierius omnibus in Christo fratribus suis, qui communicarunt vinculis, quibus ob Dei veritatem constringitur, S.
units.tr: The letters that follow were written individually by those five prisoners, for the consolation of all the godly. Antonius Laborierius to all his brethren in Christ who share the bonds with which he is bound for the truth of God: greetings.

units.la: Harissimi fratres, gratias ago Deo nostro, qui pro sua indulgentia voluit, ut re ipsa experirer quam verax sit in suis promissis, & quanta humanitate suorum infirmitates ferat. Vult suos omnes cruci subiectos esse: sed unumquenque pro mensura sua, ut vi-sum est, ne supra vires quas ipse nobis contulit onere grauati succumbamus. Quod quidem (Deo optimo gratia) ita in me completum sentio, ut nunquam in alio magis fuisse credam. Quid enim obstitit quominus excitauerint fratres meos & sanguine mihi coniunctos qui me persequerentur, sicuti Cainum excitauit Abeli, Ismaelem Isaaco, Esau Iacobo, & Iosepho omnes suos fratres? Annon etiam poterat me per filium meum discruciare, ut scimus Noah à suo exagitatum fuisse, & Davidem ipsum ab Absalone filio? annon poterat per uxorem meam negotium mihi facessere, quemadmodum pius ille Iob suam sibi infestissimam sensit? annon poterat efficere ut ab omnibus amicis intimis & cognatis deserer[?], sicuti Moses, David & omnes Prophetae reiecti sunt: atque adeo Christus ipse & omnes Apostoli qui tot iniurias à suis popularibus acceperunt? Denique, annon poterat me in manus tyrannorum conijcere, qui in profundum carcerem, obscurum & foetoris plenum detrusissent? ac me detinuissent illic catenis vinctum, compedibus constrictum, & privatum omni ratione, qua mihi laetari commodè non licuisset: quod certè Patriarchis, & Prophetis, vt Isaiæ, & Ieremiæ, adeóque ipsi Christo & Apostolis contigisse satis constat. Quemadmodum nostro quoq; seculo intelleximus complures pios & sanctos viros crudelius in vinculis fuisse tractatos quàm brutæ pecudes vel à leonibus, vel canibus, vel lupis, & aliis rapacibus belluis tractari soleant. Certum quidem est, si omnibus eiusmodi afflictionibus me voluisset probare, id iure, ac merito facturum fuisse, sed interim carnè meâ non parum cruciassent & exagitassent multæ duræque tentationes. Dominus ergo pro immensa sua bonitate, dum effecit vt serio misericordiæ suæ gustu tangerer, ac percipere fructum verae illius fiduciæ, qua promissiones ipsius amplexus sum, ita se ad captum meæ ruditatis, & miserae tenuitatis accommodauit, vt non modò me integrum & intactum à tot insultibus & horrendis cruciatibus servauerit (licet his omnibus obnoxij sint pij eius cultores) sed etiâ magnum inde solatium mihi attulerit, animi quoque tranquillitatem, & robur suppeditauerit. Nam quod ad utrumque parentem meum, fratres meos ac sorores spectat, certo scio (quae Dei est gratia) si de cruce mea certiores facti sunt, participes eius esse adeóque gravius ferre quàm ipse feram, & ipsis vehementer dolere, quòd mihi succurrere aliqua ratione non possint. Filiola verò mea tantum abest vt quidquam molestiae facessat, vt potius ad me consolandum multo melius, Dei beneficio valeat, ex quo in carcerem sum coniectus, sicuti ex tuis literis intellexi: ac si hoc modo ad agnoscendas Dei gratias me impelleret. Quod autem attinet ad uxorem meam, licet rudior sit, nec satis vt decebat pietatis doctrinam teneat (quod certè dico, vt me accusem, ac dedecus meum retegam) an quaeso posset à me explicari quantum solatij acceperim partim ex eius literis, quibus me hortatur vt serio gustè Dei beneficia, & me præparare ad mortem adeò felicè: partim verò ex inuicta eius constantia, qua præditam esse mihi renuntiatum est, vt sponte & ex animo cruci meæ communicet, seque totam Deo in obsequium addicat? Si de amicis agitur, miror sanè & me etiam pudet, dum tantum eorum numerum animo complector, quos mihi Dominus conciliauit, vt tam singulari benevolentia me prosequantur. Nam me miserū ac nihili prorsus hominē, qui toto vitæ cursu Deum meum ad irâ provocare non desiti, quique sicuti res habet, nulla non dico doctrina vel gratia excello, sed ne gutta quidem rectæ voluntatis præditus sum, quæ vel minimum obsequium cuiquam possim præstare: ego tamen video mœrore affici ob mea vincula quosdam ex clarissimis Dei servis, & qui hodie excellentissimis eius donis pollent, atque in ecclesia præcipuum munus exercent & docendi officio funguntur: à quibus certè summa beneficia, & exhortationes plane divinas accepimus. Deinde Principes omnium felicissimi nostris quoque vinculis communicare non dubitarunt, quum nobis tanquam filijs suis opem & solatium tulerunt. Quid totū ecclesiæ corpus commemorem? non dubium est quin illa profuderint lachrymas, ingemuerit, Deum precata sit pro nobis, ac multa suspiria ediderit, ut admirabiles inde fructus percepimus. Neque id solum, sed in medio etiam nostri, & qui aliqua Dei notitia imbuti erant, adeoque omni cognitione vacui, operam suam nobis impenderunt, tum ut nos consolarentur, tum ut quæ nobis erat necessaria suppeditarent. Quum autem mecum expendo, fratres mihi unice dilecti, innumera quæ à vobis seorsum accepi beneficia, qui nihil omnino eorum quæ ad me iuuandum spectabant, prætermisistis (nam præter amplissimas & sanctissimas consolationes vestras, quibus me sæpiò[?] animastis, viscera quoq; vestra aperuistis, ut abundè mihi ex vestris divitiis elargiremini, ut ne vitæ quidem vestræ quum opus fuit parceretis) quum hæc, inquam, reputo, nescio sane unde incipiam, ut animi mei gratitudinem apud vos tester. Verum, nouit Dominus quantopere id ex animo desiderem, ista quidem omnia fieri constat ob eam quam tueor causam: sed interim efficit Deus, ut incredibilem inde fructum percipiam. Quod ad carcerem attinet, neque verbis neque scripto explicare possem quanta lætitiæ ac dulcedinis voluptate in eo perfusus sim. mihi tamen licet vere & merito prositeri, me nunquam felicius egisse nec melius habuisse tum corpore tum animo, quàm habuerim & habeam ex quo captiuus tencor[?]. Hoc quidem neque ex carceris pulchritudine, neque ex loci natura pendet: sed quemadmodum iam dixi, ex eo quòd Dominus omnia in bonum conuertit ijs quos diligit. Vobis hæc omnia scribere, fratres charissimi libuit, ut lætitiæ meæ participes sitis, sicuti afflictionis meæ partem sensistis: & ut mecum reputetis, serio quàm verax & fidelis sit Deus, ut simul eundē Deū Patrem opt. precemur, quò nos intus afficiat, & ad se agendum impellat. Nam quòd ad me spectat, ingenuè fateor, mihi si cuiquam alteri, eo stimulo opus esse, quum me ita stupidum sentiam, ut Dei nostri bonitates animo concipere non possim, licet in earum velut abyssò demersus iaceam. In quo quidem certè agnosco, ac liberè fateor me ter miserum esse, & infinitis corruptelis obnoxium. Utinam fratres mei, Deus mihi concederet, ut cor meum aperire liceret, quo dolorem inde conceptum vobis patefacerem? Sed unde fit ut non possim?
units.tr: Most dear brethren, I give thanks to our God, who by his indulgence has willed that I should learn by experience how true he is in his promises, and how great a humanity he shows in bearing with the weaknesses of his people. He wills all his people to be subject to the cross, but each in proportion to his strength, as seems good to him, so that we do not succumb under a burden heavier than the powers which he himself has given us. This I feel to have been fulfilled in me (by the goodness of God) in such a way that I believe it was never fulfilled more fully in anyone else. For what prevented my brethren and those related to me by blood from rising up to persecute me, just as Cain rose against Abel, Ishmael against Isaac, Esau against Jacob, and all Joseph's brothers against him? Could he not also have tormented me through my son, as we know Noah was harassed by his own, and David by his son Absalom? Could he not have caused me trouble through my wife, as that devout Job felt his own wife to be most hostile to him? Could he not have brought it about that I was deserted by all my closest friends and kinsfolk, as Moses, David and all the prophets were rejected, and indeed Christ himself and all the apostles, who received so many injuries from their own countrymen? Finally, could he not have thrown me into the hands of tyrants, who would have thrust me into a deep, dark prison full of stench, and kept me there bound in chains and fettered, and deprived of every means by which I might rejoice in a decent way? Surely it is well established that this happened to the patriarchs and prophets, such as Isaiah and Jeremiah, and indeed to Christ himself and the apostles. Likewise in our own age we have learned that many godly and holy men have been treated in chains more cruelly than brute beasts are commonly treated by lions, dogs, wolves and other ravening beasts. It is certain that if he had wished to test me by all such afflictions, he would have done so justly and rightly; yet meanwhile many hard temptations have not a little tormented and harassed my flesh. Therefore the Lord, in his immense goodness, while he has brought it about that I have been touched by a real taste of his mercy, and that I might perceive the fruit of that true trust by which I have embraced his promises, has so accommodated himself to the measure of my roughness and wretched slightness that he has not only kept me whole and untouched from so many assaults and dreadful torments (though all his pious worshippers are exposed to them), but has also brought me great consolation from them, and has supplied me with tranquillity of mind and strength. As for my parents, my brothers and my sisters, I know for certain (by the grace of God) that if they have been informed of my cross they share in it, and bear it even more heavily than I do, and grieve greatly that they cannot help me in any way. My little daughter, however, is so far from causing any trouble that, by God's favour, she is rather very well, and so much the better for comforting me, ever since I was thrown into prison, as I have learned from your letters; as if she would thereby urge me to acknowledge the favours of God. As for my wife, though she is rather unlearned and does not hold the teaching of piety as well as she ought (which I say truly, so that I may accuse myself and expose my own shame), can I, I ask, possibly explain how much consolation I have received, partly from her letters, in which she urges me to taste the benefits of God seriously and to prepare myself so happily for death, and partly from her unconquered constancy, with which, I have been told, she is endowed, so that she shares my cross willingly and from the heart and dedicates herself wholly to the service of God? If we speak of friends, I am truly astonished, and I am even ashamed, when I embrace in my mind the great number of those whom the Lord has won over to follow me with such singular goodwill. For I, a wretched man and utterly worthless, who in the whole course of my life have not ceased to provoke my God to anger, and who, as things stand, excel in no learning or grace (I will not say), nor am I endowed with even a drop of right will, so as to be able to render the least service to anyone: yet I see that some of the most distinguished servants of God, who today excel in his most excellent gifts and exercise the chief office in the Church and discharge the duty of teaching, are grieved on account of my chains; from whom I have certainly received the greatest kindnesses and entirely divine exhortations. Then the most blessed princes have not hesitated to share in our chains too, when they brought help and comfort to us as their own sons. Why should I mention the whole body of the Church? There is no doubt that she has poured out tears, groaned, prayed to God for us, and uttered many sighs, from which we have received wonderful fruits. And not only that, but also in the midst of us, those who had some knowledge of God, and yet were empty of all understanding, have devoted their labour to us, both to console us and to supply what we needed. Moreover, when I weigh within myself, my dearest brethren, the countless benefits which I received from you individually, you who have omitted nothing at all of those things which pertained to helping me (for besides your most ample and holy consolations, with which you have often encouraged me, you have also opened your hearts, so that you have generously poured out to me from your riches, and when there was need you did not spare even your own lives), when I consider these things, I truly do not know where to begin, so that I may bear witness before you to the gratitude of my mind. Yet the Lord knows how much I desire this from my heart. It is certain that all these things have happened on account of the cause which I uphold; but meanwhile God brings it about that I receive from them an incredible fruit. As for the prison, I could not explain in words or in writing how much I have been steeped in the delight and sweetness of joy in it. Nevertheless I may truly and rightly profess that I have never fared more happily, nor been in better health, both in body and in mind, than I have been, and am, since I have been held captive. This certainly does not depend on the beauty of the prison nor on the nature of the place, but, as I have already said, on the fact that the Lord turns all things to good for those whom he loves. I have wished to write all this to you, most dear brethren, so that you may share my joy, as you have felt a part of my affliction; and so that you may consider with me how seriously true and faithful God is, and that together we may pray to the same God, the best of Fathers, that he may move me inwardly and drive me to act. For as far as I am concerned, I frankly confess that I need this spur more than anyone else, since I feel myself so dull that I cannot conceive in my mind the goodnesses of our God, even though I lie plunged, as it were, into an abyss of them. In this I certainly recognise, and freely confess, that I am thrice wretched and exposed to infinite corruptions. Would that, my brethren, God would grant me that I might open my heart, so that I could lay bare to you the grief conceived from it! But how is it that I cannot?

units.la: Quanquam facultas qua id exprimam, mihi deest, verè tamen affirmauerim in co præcipuè culpam esse, quòd nimium à familiaritate Scripturarum me subduxerim. Sed Deo gratias ago, qui ingrati animi mei rationem non habuit: quin potius in sanctam hanc schölam me deduxit, ut ita quis sim agnoscam. Neque enim satis scio quò prolapsus fuissem, nisi me Dominus quasi porrecta manu visitasset. Quum ad pium illum qui Geneuæ est, cœtum accessi, consilium erat omnino me studiis quàm maximè possem addicere: quemadmodum etiā Deus illuc suos in eū finē emittit, dum nos è medio mundo auocat, ut ad omne opus pium præparet, & ad regale sacerdotium: quò scilicet nobis ipsis renuntiantes, eius gloriæ nos totos consecremus. At ò me miserum! quàm longè ab ossicio meo abfui! quàm malè partibus meis sum defunctus! Vos ipsi nouistis, ego verò nimium experior. Satis quidem otij mihi suppetebat, sed potius ad res nihili animum adijciebam, nescio qua diffidentia, & præposttero metu pculsus, quàm ad iudicia Dei ac statuta diu & noctu meditanda, atque diligenter expendenda. Vos igitur obsecro Dei nomine ut dispendio meo discatis non esse vobis dormiendum. Nam certò scio, ac proinde etiam doleo vehementer complures inter vos esse, qui eodem hoc morbo laborent. Atque utinam in multis non vigeret amplius: sed vestram ipsi quæso conscientiam excutite, ac sedulò dispicite quo ardore & zelo verbum Dei excipiatis: atque re ipsa comperietis verius esse quàm vellem: plurimos esse nimium frigidos. Concionibus quidē publicis frequētes adestis, sed toto reliquo tēpore quo pacto[?] revocatis in memoriam quæ audiuistis? id verò fit ut plurimum defunctorie. Cæterùm, hæc dico, quia saluti vestræ consultū cupio & vos singulari benevolentia prosequor. An ignoratis olim sub Lege animal quod non ruminabat immundum ac pollutum fuisse, ita ut carnibus eius vesci populo Dei fas non esset? Ergo Dei verbum postquam audieritis ruminate: atque ita publicis concionibus adesse, et Scripturarum lectioni date operam, ut non immundi sed puri sitis, ut Domino in sacrificium grati odoris offeramini, et afflictionis tempore invicto animo perstetis.
units.tr: Although I lack the ability to express this, I can truthfully say that the chief fault lies in this, that I have withdrawn myself too far from familiarity with the Scriptures. But I give thanks to God, who did not take account of my ungrateful mind; rather, he led me into this holy school, so that I might recognise what sort of person I am. For I do not know well enough where I would have slipped, had the Lord not visited me, as it were with an outstretched hand. When I came to that godly congregation at Geneva, my intention was altogether to devote myself to my studies as far as I possibly could, just as God sends his people there for this very purpose, while he calls us out of the midst of the world, to prepare us for every good work and for the royal priesthood: namely, that, renouncing ourselves, we might wholly consecrate ourselves to his glory. But alas, how far I was from my duty! How badly I have discharged my responsibilities! You yourselves know it; I experience it all too much. Certainly I had enough leisure, but instead I applied my mind to trifles, struck by I know not what distrust and a misplaced fear, rather than to meditating day and night on the judgments and statutes of God, and weighing them diligently. I therefore beg you, in the name of God, to learn from my loss that you must not sleep. For I know for certain, and therefore also grieve greatly, that there are many among you who suffer from this same malady. And I wish it did not flourish among many! But I ask you yourselves to examine your own consciences, and to look carefully at what ardour and zeal you receive the Word of God with; and in fact you will find it truer than I would wish, that very many are far too cold. You are present in large numbers at the public sermons, but during the rest of the time, in what way do you call to mind what you have heard? For the most part it is done in a perfunctory manner. But I say these things because I desire to care for your salvation, and I embrace you with a singular goodwill. Or do you not know that under the Law the animal that did not chew the cud was unclean and polluted, so that it was not lawful for the people of God to eat its flesh? Therefore, after you have heard the Word of God, ruminate upon it; and so attend the public sermons and give yourselves to the reading of the Scriptures, that you may be not unclean but pure, that you may be offered to the Lord as a sacrifice of sweet savour, and that in the time of affliction you may stand firm with an unconquered mind.

units.la: Reputate quanto pretiosior sit Dei sapientia auro, argento, et lapidibus pretiosis. Ergo subijciamini Spiritui Dei, ut illa ductu eius impleamini, quo possitis de operibus Domini iudicare. nam homo spiritualis omnia iudicat, et a nullo iudicatur. An non in loco totius orbis ad discendum aptissimo degitis? in quo scilicet velut Dei theatro, vel potius sacrosancto eius Tabernaculo versamini. Deinde an pastorum fidelissimorum opera, et sedulitas ullo modo vobis deest? Minime vero: atque id confirmare et testari merito possumus, Dei beneficio, si qui unquam affirmare potuerunt. Quid igitur praetexere vobis licebit nisi serio profeceritis, dum vobis inducias concedit Dominus, ac tempus largitur quo vos ipsos exerceatis? Pudendum certe, ac probrosum erit, si tanquam tyrones deprehendamini, cum vobis manus erunt conserendae. neque etiam talis ingratitudo impune cedet. Spero autem, fratres, eiusmodi iudicium in capita vestra minime redundaturum. nam certo persuasus sum vos esse Dei filios. Vigilate nihilominus et orate quia non dormit hostis noster. Date operam, ut oleum vobis suppetat, dum adventum suum differt Dominus, ut quo die venerit vos reperiat instructos his omnibus quae ad expectandum diem adventus et ipsum excipiendum necessaria sunt. Atque ita quietem conscientiis vestris obtinebitis, neque afflictionum tempestates vos exagitabunt. Oro autem Deum et Patrem omnis consolationis, qui nos opportune solatus est, ut quod in vobis coepit ipse perficiat, quo vos in opere suo perfectos reddat in gloriam nominis sui et aedificationem Ecclesiæ suæ, Amen.
units.tr: Consider how much more precious the wisdom of God is than gold, silver and precious stones. Therefore submit yourselves to the Spirit of God, that you may be filled with it and guided by it, so that you may be able to judge the works of the Lord; for the spiritual man judges all things, and is judged by no one. Do you not live in a place most suitable for learning in all the world? In it, as in a theatre of God, or rather in his most holy Tabernacle, you are conversant. Then, does the work and diligence of the most faithful ministers fail you in any way? By no means; and we may rightly confirm and testify this, by the blessing of God, if ever anyone could. What excuse, then, will be open to you, unless you make progress in earnest, while the Lord grants you a truce and gives you the time in which to exercise yourselves? It will certainly be shameful and disgraceful if you are caught like raw recruits when you must engage in battle. Nor will such ingratitude go unpunished. But I hope, brothers, that such a judgment will by no means fall upon your heads; for I am firmly persuaded that you are the sons of God. Nevertheless, watch and pray, because our enemy does not sleep. Take care that you have oil at hand, while the Lord delays his coming, so that on whatever day he comes he may find you equipped with all those things that are necessary for awaiting the day of his coming and for receiving him. And thus you will obtain quiet for your consciences, and the storms of afflictions will not harass you. And I pray God, the Father of all consolation, who has comforted us in due time, that he himself may bring to completion what he has begun in you, and make you perfect in his work, to the glory of his name and the edification of his Church. Amen.

units.la: Epistola Ioannis Vernutii ad Cognatum suum.D.L.P.
units.tr: Epistle of John Vernutius to his cousin, D.L.P.

units.la: I tantum sperare, mi Cognate et amice integerrime, hoc turbulento tempore ausus non es, ut literas nobiscum posses communicare, sicuti scribus[?]: multo certe minus idem nobis licebat. Dominus enim ad sepulchrum usque et mortis umbram nos deduxerat, ita ut ultimo die Augusti certo persuasi essemus nos mortem obituros. Et Deus optimus maximus pro sua singulari gratia ad id probè nos instruxerat, animósque nostros composuerat ut ad rem longè præstantissimam, & qua nobis optatior contingere non poterat: utcunque caro nostra obstreperet, tumultuaretur, ac sese nimiû efferret, Spiritus tamen prævalebat. Ecce vero præter omnem nostram & omnium hominum expectationem Dominus, qui è sepulchro nos eripuit, atque cöpleuit quod scribitur Psalmo cxxix, dum funes è iugo impiorum abscidit. Et quanuis hæc mora & quidem breuissima esset (ut nos ad hoc paratos esse oportet, ac tutius etiâ erit quicquid accidat) in eo nihilominus & tanto beneficio, quemadmodum quod nunc quoque tibi scribimus, satis superq; cõfirmatur nobis omnibus hæc Pauli sententia, Deum multò plura nobis elargiri, quàm sperare possimus. Quum præter verbum eius qui est ipsa veritas, ore pronuntiatum, accedit experientia quæ oculis cernitur in fratribus nostris, qui & ante nos vixerunt, & qui nunc adhuc sunt superstites, ac ne longius petantur exempla, quæ in nobis ipsis palàm constant: ad manum proculdubiò habemus inuictum clypeum contra quascunque tentationes, & arcem inexpugnabilem aduersus portas inferorum, nempe quia Deus stat à parte nostra. Jam si ille est pro nobis, quis contra nos erit? Itaque inimicis omnibus, & Sathanæ eorum capiti intrepidè insultamus, & quicquid conentur parui facimus, exemplo Dauidis qui priorum omnium insigne speculum merito censetur, Psalm.xviii.xxxii.xxvii.cxviii, & multis aliis. Sed quò in fide & vero Dei timore proficiamus, ita certè nobis agendum est, ut diligenter notemus eiusmodi exempla, & eorum circunstantias, ut tenacius memoriæ inhæreant: deinde coniungamus ea, & referamus ad Dei verbum, quò fides nostra illius naturam resipiat: ut quemadmodum illud Dei verbum fixum atque æternũ manet, sic etiam perpetuò certam fiduciam habeamus in Deo optimo, qui postquam mera sua gratia & bonitate singularibus suis promissionibus se obstrinxit nobis (qui sumus cadauera tantùm putrida, & creaturæ naturâ execrabiles) variis ac mirís modis illas complere non desinit. Cor igitur nostrum velut findatur, ut Domino viva fide gloriam demus: os nostrum aperiatur, ut laudes eius ubique resonent. nam eius misericordia super nos aucta est, & eiusdem veritas manet in æternum. Infelix & misera caro nostra omnino crucifigatur, mortificetur ac sepeliatur unà cum Domino nostro Jesu Christo, quum eò peruicaciæ prorumpat post tot promissiones tot experimentis etiam comprobatas, ut dubitationes de verbo Dei nostri optimi & fidelissimi subinde in animis nostris audeat excitare. Nullum unquam argentum ita exploratum fuit, ut est sacrosanctum hoc verbum: nos eius rei testes sumus locupletissimi: & interim caro isthæc nimium imprudens contrà insurgere audebit! O Domine, quoúsque tandem eris? adauge nobis fidem. Caterùm, amice integerrime, nos omnes habemus tibi gratiam ob pias & sanctas admonitiones tuis literis perscriptas: deinde ob labores quos suscipis, & impensas quas nostro nomine facis. Certè quòd hæc apud nos reputamus, iam à mundo cupimus abesse, ne scilicet tot viris bonis oneri simus, qui magis (tanta est eorum erga nos benevolentia) quàm nos ipsi de nobis sunt soliciti, ac magis constricti, & corde vincti tenentur quàm nos qui corpore sumus captivi. Vobis Deus optimus rependat, & opes vestras sic augeat ut re ipsa sentiatis vos in eius gratiam diuitias vestras exponere: & quemadmodum inquit Ecclesiastes, vos panem vestrum in profluentes aquas proicere. Interim quia nihil aliud in praesentia praestare possumus, illum pro vobis & vestris omnibus precabimur, nosque omnes precibus vestris ex animo commendabimus.
units.tr: I did not dare, my dear cousin and most upright friend, in these turbulent times, to hope that you could exchange letters with us, as you write. Certainly it was much less possible for us to do the same. The Lord had brought us down even to the grave and the shadow of death, so that on the last day of August we were fully persuaded that we would die. God, the best and greatest, by his singular grace had prepared us well for this and had composed our minds for a thing far the most excellent, which could not have been more desirable to us. However much our flesh resisted, stirred up itself, and rose up excessively, the Spirit nevertheless prevailed. But now, beyond all our expectation and that of all men, the Lord, who has snatched us from the grave, has fulfilled what is written in Psalm 129, when he cut the cords of the wicked. And although this delay was very brief (as we ought to be prepared for it, and whatever happens will be safer for us), nevertheless in this and in so great a benefit, just as in what we now write to you, this saying of Paul is more than sufficiently confirmed for all of us: that God grants us far more than we can hope. For besides the word of him who is truth itself, spoken by mouth, there is added the experience that is seen with the eyes in our brethren, who lived before us and who are still alive, and, that we need not seek examples further afield, that which is plainly established in ourselves. Surely we have at hand an invincible shield against all temptations and an impregnable fortress against the gates of hell, namely because God stands on our side. If he is for us, who can be against us? Therefore we boldly insult all enemies and Satan, their head, and we make light of whatever they attempt, following the example of David, who is rightly reckoned the outstanding mirror of all who went before, Psalms 18, 32, 27, 118, and many others. But if we are to make progress in faith and in the true fear of God, we must certainly act in this way: we must carefully note such examples and their circumstances, so that they cling more tenaciously to the memory; then we must join them together and refer them to the word of God, so that our faith may take on its nature. Just as that word of God remains fixed and eternal, so also we should always have firm confidence in God, the best, who, after binding himself to us by his mere grace and goodness through his singular promises (we who are only rotting corpses, and by nature hateful creatures), does not cease to fulfil them in various and marvellous ways. Let our heart therefore be, as it were, broken open, so that we may give glory to the Lord by living faith; let our mouth be opened, so that his praises resound everywhere. For his mercy has been increased over us, and his truth remains for ever. Our wretched and unhappy flesh must be utterly crucified, mortified and buried together with our Lord Jesus Christ, since it breaks out into such obstinacy, after so many promises confirmed also by so many experiences, that it dares from time to time to stir up doubts about the word of our God, who is best and most faithful. No silver was ever so tested as this most holy word; we are most abundant witnesses of this matter; and yet this very imprudent flesh dares to rise up against it! O Lord, how long will you be? Increase our faith. But, my most upright friend, we all owe you thanks for your pious and holy admonitions written in your letters, and then for the labours you undertake and the expenses you incur in our name. Certainly, since we reckon these things among us, we now desire to depart from the world, lest we be a burden to so many good men, who (so great is their goodwill toward us) are more anxious about us than we are about ourselves, and who are held more tightly and bound in heart than we who are captives in body. May God, the best, repay you, and so increase your resources that you may actually feel that you are expending your riches for his grace, and, as Ecclesiastes says, that you are casting your bread upon flowing waters. Meanwhile, since we can offer nothing else at present, we will pray to him for you and all yours, and we commend ourselves to your prayers from our heart.

units.la: Alia eiusdem Vernutii epistola ad D. D.
units.tr: Another letter of the same Vernutius to D.D.

units.la: Iteras tuas, observande domine & chariss. frater, accepimus, quibus nos de tua valetudine adversa certiores facis, & simul petis ut aliquid ad te scribamus, quo tuum animum consolemur. Laudetur Deus & Pater Domini Iesu Christi, Pater misericordiae, & Deus omnis consolationis, qui nos in omni afflictione nostra solatur, ut eos qui afflictatur quocunque modo consolari possimus, solatio quo Deus ipse nos consolatur. Nam ut Christi afflictiones abundant in nobis, ita per Christum quoque consolatio nostra abundat. Et certè admirabilis est haec Dei gratia quàm in suos omnes filios confert, quòd quum egeant, cruciantur & iam iam illis mors infert, ita eos locupletat, consolatur & viuificat, ut quod aliis largiantur, suppetat. Haec procul dubio non proficiscuntur ex imaginaria vel fanatica philosophia, quae nunquam re-vera fuit: sed vsitata est ac trita piis omnibus ϑεόξες, quâ ut in nobis, Dei beneficio, perspicis (ita etiam in te cernimus, sicuti literae tuae satis ostendunt, quibus ingenuè profiteris morbum quo tu laboras, & vxor etiâ tua, soror nobis chariss.) non aliunde tibi quàm ex paterna Dei optimi manu profecta esse. Hoc verò nosse, sapientia est incredibilis, quae omne humanum sensum longè superat, & qua Deus filios suos donat per Spiritum veritatis quae illis promisit. Hoc idem gustare consolatio est eximia, quae piis omnibus maximè conuenit. Vulgò fertur, si cui negotium fuerit cum viro probo & integrae fidei, illu securè quiescere, ac multò magis si eu singulari benevolentia completatur. atqui negotium est cum iusti ss. optimo & omnipotente, qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed nostro nomine in mortem adeò crudele & probrosam tradidit, & in eo foedus nobiscum sanxit perpetuum, se nunquam nos deserturum, vtcunque miseriis ac sordibus omni ex parte simus referti. Quid maius, quaeso, expetimus? quid iam impediet quominus in eo plena fiducia coquiescamus? obstabunt ne peccata nostra? at vbi abundauit peccatum, illic gratia magis abundauit: & vbi plura remittuntur peccata, maior est etiam dilectio erga Deum opt.max. tàtum abest vt ex eius bonitate belli cum ipso gerendi occasio nobis offertur. Quid? an miseriæ nostræ ab illo nos abstrahent? quin potius quàto sunt graviores & magis asperæ, tàto maior ac luculentior eius misericordia sese erga nos proferet. an denique nostra infirmitas auocabit? Atqui in hac ipsa virtus eius elucet ac perficitur: & quo magis desunt nobis vires, tanto fortiores in illo sumus. Quod certè facit, ne quis in se ipso glorietur, ac multò minº singularibus donis, quæ ex eius manu accepit: sed potius vt illis velut eiusdẽ manu ducatur, quò in ipso solo glorietur, atq; ita eò referantur omnia vnde proficiscuntur. Quemadmodum autem hoc est valde consentaneum rationi, ita etiam nobis maximè vtile esse constat, ne scilicet puteos fodiamus qui aquas continere non possint, vt fontes aquæ viuæ & scaturiginem vitæ deseramus, nempe illum in cuius manu est omnis felicitas, ad quam humaniter nos inuitat, & ea quidem liberalitate, vt nobis dare magis cupiat ipse, quàm nos accipere. Quum igitur, frater charissime, persuasum habeas negotium tibi esse cum eo Patre, qui tantam tui ac tuorum curam gerit, petimus abs te vt diligentiùs cogites quàm feliciter tecū agatur, & qualis futurus sit exitus huius afflictionis qua nunc laboras. Satius verò esse credimus si tibi relinquamus hoc reputandum, quàm si copiosiùs à nobis tractetur.
