Interim vnum tibi in memoriam reuoco, vnde magnum solatium accipias: nimirum adoptione tua fretus, & gratuita iustificatione (qua quidem tum persona tua, tum piæ cogitationes, affectus, & opera tua vel potius Spiritus sancti qui in te habitat, indulgentissimo Patri tuo grata sunt, idque Christi nomine ) Iam dicere potes Ezechiæ exemplo, ac profusis lachrymis in eius sinum familiariter cor tuum velut explicare hoc modo: Quæso, Domine, meminerisste mihi pro tua liberalitate largitum fuisse hunc animum & exercitium, vt miseros & afflictos consolcr. neque verò imbecillitas & sordes, quas corrupta caro permiscuit operi tuo, impediant quominus hoc opus vt sigillum perpetui erga me amoris tui excipiam. Etenim si dona communia, quæ omnibus creaturis confers, atque adeò illa quæ extra me sunt ad hoc ipsum mihi conducunt, mihi, inquam, filio tuo: quanto magis quæ filiorum tuorum sunt propria, & quæ intus ac per me largiris? Deinde non obstabunt quominus certò sim persuasus de tuis promisfis abs te operi tuo in me factis, quum præsertim omnes tuæ promissiones non sint Etiam & Amen, nisi in solo Christo, quem tuo beneficio accepi in pignus, redemptionem, iustitiā & sanctificationem, quum meo nomine factus fuerit peccatū, vt iustitia Dei in illo efficerer. Atqui ex promissionibus tuis hæc vna est quam Dauidi seruo tuo fecifti, eum scilicet beatum fore, qui prudenter de paupere & calamitoso iudicabit, quèque rationem eius habebit: atque illum in sua calamitate abs te subleuatum iri. propterea nobis remensum iri eadem mensura, qua proximis nostris mensi fuerimus. Mihi certè conscientia mea testatur me ex animo id conatū fuisse. Et vero nimium ingratus essem, si quod est tuum turpiter tacere, quasi ex meo aliquid esse videatur. Itaque, Deus mi, fretus Christo tuo non minus securo quam summisso animo abs te petā, vt fiat mihi secundū verbum tuum. Hanc sane precatione concipere no possunt filij Agar ancillæ, qui merita, satisfactiones & liberum arbitrium fabricant: sed solis filijs promissionis & gratiæ, filijs Saræ liberæ ita precari datum est. Quum sis ex horum numero & ordine, non est quòd bona conscientia dubites has preces fundere, etiam inuito Sathana calumniarū parente, inuito peccato, morte & omnibus inferi portis obstrepentibus. Viuat & regnet Dominus Iesus Christus, qui de his omnibus pro te iam triumphum egit. Illi ergo confidas: & te qui volet aggrediatur: satis in eo virtutis est, qua te protegat & tueatur: non minus etiam amoris plusquam paterni reperietur: cuius quidem rei habes multa testimonia tum ex sacro eius verbo, tum etiam opere illustrissimo. Vnum hoc superest, vt supplicitèr ab eo petas quod est maximè optandum, nempe vt ipsa sentias quàm vera hæc sint & certa, sicuti facturum ipsum certò scimus, etiamsi nullum aliud signum extaret, præter id quod in tuū solatium referimus, te scilicet in omnibus nostris precibus quas singulari Dei beneficio concipimus, nobis ante oculos semper versari, in animis nostris & linguis esse: vt corda nostra magis inflammetur, ex quo de tua necessitate certiores facti sumus. Quum hic ardor proficiscatur à Spiritu sancto, qui in cordibus nostris ingemiscit & clamat, hoc certè indicio est iam nos tuo nomine à Deo esse exauditos, ut qui per Isaiam pollicetur nos antequam clamemus exauditum iri.
units.tr: We have received your letter, esteemed lord and most beloved brother, in which you inform us that your health is poor, and at the same time ask that we write something to you by which your spirit may be comforted. Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are afflicted in whatever way, with the comfort with which God himself comforts us. For as the afflictions of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds. And truly this grace of God is admirable, which he bestows upon all his sons: that, when they are in want, tormented, and already death is brought upon them, he so enriches, comforts and quickens them that they have enough to give to others. These things surely do not arise from an imaginary or fanatical philosophy, which has never existed in reality, but from a teaching common and well-worn among all the godly, by which, as we see in ourselves by God's benefit (so also we perceive in you, as your letter sufficiently shows, in which you frankly confess the illness you suffer from, and your wife too, our most beloved sister), you have received it from nothing other than the fatherly hand of God, the best. Truly, to know this is an incredible wisdom, which far surpasses all human understanding, and by which God gives his sons, through the Spirit of truth, what he has promised them. To taste this same thing is an outstanding consolation, which is especially suited to all the godly. It is commonly said that if anyone has business with an upright man of sound faith, he may rest securely, and much more so if he is embraced with singular goodwill. But our business is with the Judge, the best and almighty, who did not spare his own Son, but for our sake delivered him to so cruel and shameful a death, and in him made an everlasting covenant with us, that he would never forsake us, however much we are filled on every side with miseries and filth. What greater thing, I ask, do we seek? What now will hinder us from resting in him with full trust? Will our sins be an obstacle? But where sin abounded, there grace abounded all the more; and where more sins are forgiven, the love toward God the best and greatest is also greater. So far is it from the case that an occasion of war with him is offered to us by his goodness. What then? Will our miseries draw us away from him? Rather, the heavier and harsher they are, the greater and clearer his mercy will show itself toward us. Will our weakness at last call us away? Yet in this very weakness his power shines out and is made perfect, and the less strength we have, the stronger we are in him. Surely he does this so that no one may glory in himself, and still less in the singular gifts he has received from his hand, but rather that, being led by them as by his hand, we may glory in him alone, and so all things may be referred to the source from which they come. Just as this is most consonant with reason, so it is also plainly most useful for us: namely, not to dig cisterns that cannot hold water, nor to forsake the fountain of living water and its spring of life, that is, him in whose hand is all happiness, to which he kindly invites us, and with such generosity that he himself desires to give more than we desire to receive. Since therefore, dearest brother, you are persuaded that your business is with that Father, who takes such care of you and yours, we ask you to consider more carefully how happily things are going for you, and what the outcome of this affliction you now suffer will be. Indeed we believe it is better to leave this for you to consider than for us to treat it at greater length. Meanwhile I recall one thing to your memory, from which you may receive great consolation: namely, relying on your adoption and on gratuitous justification (by which indeed, both your person and your pious thoughts, affections, and works, or rather the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, are pleasing to your most indulgent Father, and this for the sake of Christ). Now you may say, after the example of Hezekiah, and with a flood of tears, pouring out your heart familiarly into his bosom, something like this: "I beseech you, Lord, remember that by your liberality this spirit and this exercise were granted to me, to comfort the wretched and afflicted. Nor let the weakness and filth which corrupt flesh has mingled with your work hinder me from receiving this work as a seal of your everlasting love toward me. For if the common gifts which you bestow on all creatures, and indeed those things which are outside me, serve this very purpose for me, your son, I say, how much more those which are proper to your sons, and which you bestow within and through me?" Then the fact that you have promised such things to your work in me shall not stand in the way of my being firmly persuaded of your promises, since all your promises are not "Yea and Amen" except in Christ alone, whom by your benefit I have received as pledge, redemption, righteousness and sanctification, since he was made sin in my name, so that in him I might become the righteousness of God. Indeed, of your promises this is one which you made to your servant David: that he will be blessed who judges wisely concerning the poor and the afflicted, and takes account of him; and that he will be raised up by you in his calamity. Therefore the same measure will be measured back to us with which we have measured to our neighbours. My conscience certainly testifies to me that I have tried this from my heart. And indeed I would be exceedingly ungrateful if I were to keep shamefully silent about what is yours, as if something of mine were involved. So, my God, trusting in your Christ with a mind no less secure than humble, I ask of you that it be done to me according to your word. Indeed the sons of Hagar the maidservant cannot conceive this prayer, those who fabricate merits, satisfactions and free will; but to the sons of promise and of grace alone is it given to pray thus, as the sons of free Sarah. Since you are of their number and order, there is no reason why you, with a good conscience, should doubt pouring out these prayers, even though Satan, the parent of calumnies, is unwilling, though sin, death and all the gates of hell make an uproar. Let the Lord Jesus Christ live and reign, who has already celebrated a triumph over all these things on your behalf. Trust therefore in him; and let whoever wishes attack you: there is enough strength in him to protect and defend you, and no less love, more than paternal, will be found in him, of which you have many testimonies, both from his holy word and from his most illustrious work. One thing remains: that you earnestly ask of him what is most to be desired, namely that you may yourself feel how true and certain these things are, just as we know for certain that he will do it, even if no other sign existed except this one which we report for your consolation: that you are always before our eyes in all our prayers, which we offer by singular benefit of God, and are in our minds and on our lips, so that our hearts may be kindled more, now that we have been informed of your need. Since this ardour proceeds from the Holy Spirit, who groans and cries out in our hearts, this is certainly a sign that we are already heard by God on your behalf, since he promised through Isaiah that he would hear us before we call.

units.la: Alia eiusdem Vernutii epistola ad ministros ecclesiae Geneuensis.
units.tr: Another letter of the same Vernutius to the ministers of the church of Geneva.

units.la: Ibi vehementer dolet, fratres plurimum obseruandi, quòd ego & socij mei de rebus nostris certiores vos facere nondum potuerimus, neque vobis perscribere quo animo varios inimicorum nostrorum insultus sustinere datum sit, ex quo postremas nostras literas accepistis.
units.tr: There he is deeply grieved, most esteemed brothers, that my companions and I have not yet been able to inform you of our situation, or to write to you about how it has been granted to us to endure the various assaults of our enemies, since you received our last letter.

units.la: Nam scimus quàm gratum hoc vobis fuisset, atque etiam cessisset in communem omnium aedificationem & vsum: quia in nobis multò luculentius Dei optimi erga vos & pios omnes bonitatis & fidei testimonium habuissetis, in quo placidius quiescere, & ardentius quàm vnquam, illi gloriâ tribuere vobis licuisset, tum in rebus aduersis tum etiâ prosperis, tam in vita quàm in morte. Sed Satha infestissimus hostis gloriae Dei & communis omnium salutis, quicquid potuit molitus est vt hoc opus impediret: quia minimè dubitat interitum regni sui inde sequuturum. Itaque suorum opera fecit, vt satis diu libris, atramento & charta nudati simus. Quid si Pater caelestis virtute Spiritus sui nobis non succurrisset, quum nos deficerent inferiora haec infirmitatis nostrae adminicula? certè tristitia & moerore confecti suissemus, quia animis nostris suum alimentum ereptum erat: Nos, inquam, dolore obruti tacuissemus, qui, Dei beneficio, summam voluptatem antea capiebamus ex quotidiana auditione & lectione sacrosancti huius verbi, & ex Sacramentorum perceptione. Nos procul dubiò similes eramus auiculis in caueam inclusis, quibus nihil apponitur quo se nutriant. Etsi enim corpori sustentando satis esset cibi, quia tamen à spirituali cibo separatus erat, nihil aliud quàm nos stupidos reddere, adeóque interficere poterat, non id quidem ex sua natura, sed potius ex nostra corruptione, nisi Deus (vt iam dixi) pro sua bonitate remedium adhibuisset. laudetur ergo nomen eius perpetuò.
units.tr: For we know how welcome this would have been to you, and how it would have served the common edification and benefit of all. In us you would have had a much clearer testimony of the goodness and faithfulness of the best God toward you and all the godly, in which you might have rested more calmly, and given glory to him more ardently than ever, both in adversity and in prosperity, in life and in death. But Satan, the most hostile enemy of God's glory and of the common salvation of all, has tried whatever he could to hinder this work, because he has no doubt that the ruin of his kingdom would follow from it. And so, through the work of his servants, he has brought it about that we have been stripped of books, ink and paper for quite a long time. What if the heavenly Father had not come to our aid by the power of his Spirit, when these lower supports of our weakness failed us? Certainly we would have been worn down with sadness and grief, since the food of our souls had been snatched from us. We, I say, overwhelmed with pain, would have fallen silent, we who, by God's kindness, had previously taken the greatest delight in the daily hearing and reading of this most sacred word, and in receiving the sacraments. We were without doubt like little birds shut up in a cage, to which nothing is given to feed on. For although there was enough food to sustain the body, yet since it was cut off from spiritual food, it could do nothing but make us dull and even kill us, not by its own nature but rather by our corruption, unless God (as I have already said) had applied a remedy in his goodness. Let his name therefore be praised forever.

units.la: Iam verò deflendum est hoc vnum, quod etiam nos grauiter & acerbè cruciauit, nempe Sathanam, ita grassari, vt qui profitentur se esse pios, eorum quoque opera vtatur ad vulnerandas miseras nostras animas, quantum in ipsis est, ac simul etiam corpora nostra: vt munera quibus funguntur, opes, quietem & delicias carnis suae praeferant gloriæ Filij Dei, vitæ æternæ, ac vitæ tum animi tum corporis proximorum suorum: alij palàm, alij occultè, nonnulli aperte ac directè, ut loquuntur, alij autem obliquis artibus, & vulpinis fraudibus manus suas commaculent, ac polluant innoxiorum hominum sanguine: quid innoxios dico? quin potius filiorum Dei, & Iesu Christi membrorum innoxio sanguine. Ut tinam ea prudentia & humanitate præditi essent, qua multi increduli, qui in extremo iudicio consurgent adversus eiusmodi Christianos prorsus degeneres, qui sibi fabricant sericium[?] quendam Christum, vel eum pro sua libidine confingunt, & Euangelium ab omni cruce & molestia separatum, quique pacis aut induciarum tempore plenis buccis iactabunt se esse Christi. Sed quum ad examen vocantur, & quum opus est maxime, coram hominibus turpissimè deficient: nec aliud quaeret vel captabunt quam cursum reflectere, adeoque pietati renuntiare, ut veri sint Christi carnifices, etiam ubi a mortuis excitatus de morte triumphum egit, quum scilicet tanta crudelitate in eius membra saeviunt. Haec autem querimonia nunc utor nō solum, ut quasi in sinum vestrum quidquid fert animus libere coniciam, quum praesertim in omnibus vos mihi vel iam ad extrema redacto fidos & integros esse amicos testati re ipsa fuistis: sed etiam ut fiat quidam velut ingressus ad ea vobis exponenda, quae Deus mirabiliter & pro solita sua bonitate nobiscum egit, ex quo postremas nostras literas ad vos dedimus, unde non immerito me conqueri iudicabitis. Neque vero singula referam: nam & temporis angustia, & chartae penuria impedior: neque etiam narrabo quae gesta sunt a fratribus mecum hic vinctis. Quum enim eo toto tempore quo nos iudices interrogarunt, alij distracti fuerimus ab alijs, longè facilius & commodius singuli referemus quid seorsum quisque gesserit. Cum igitur duodecimo Calendas Septembris, ea iudicum sententia qua damnati eramus ad remos, nobis pronuntiata esset a Propratore, sub horam quartam a meridie in Curiam eductus sum ad Senatores, quorum impulsu & instigatione Procurator regius pro uocauerat, tanquam a nimia, ut ipsi loquuntur. Summus Praeses iusserit proferri librum, ut manu admota velut sanctis Euangelijs, iuraturum me vera dicturum: sed quum animadvertisem illic depictum esse crucifixum, quem vocant, statim professus sum quid crederem, ac fidem meam plane contrariam esse eorum opinioni,quod ad imagines spectat.Hic Crassus causæ nostræ inspector citauit uersiculum illum ineptum ac ridiculum, Nam Deus est quod imago docet,sed non Deus ipsa.Ego vero palàm rogaui, essetne materia imaginis, an forma quæ mihi Deum referret, ecquid inter vtrũque esset simile? quid etiam consentaneum vel affine habeat verus Deus cum eo vetulo triplici corona exornato, qualem ipsi pingunt in pulchra illa sua imagine Trinitatis? Excipiunt Deũ induisse hominis personam, vel factum fuisse hominem.atque ita repente sermonem hunc abrumpunt,& dicendi facultatem mihi præcidunt.Idem ille Præses quum me accuratius interrogasset de meo nomine,de ætate,de patria,& natali solo,vbi,& qua de causa captus essem,quúmque intelexisset me vera respondisse ad rogata sua, blandè quidem & humaniter,sed in speciem loqui cœpit, ac primùm Dei gloriam mihi proponere: deinde totius Curiæ fauorem,& singularem erga me beneuolentiam commemorare: magnum me posse proximis meis afferre adiumentum: se & reliquos ad negocium hoc tractandum minimè conuenisse, nisi ductu & auspiciis Spiritus sancti,& eo prius inuocato: fas non esse tantum mihi arrogare, vt putem me vnum plus sapere quàm tot hominum millia, atque regi potius à Spiritu sancto quàm alios mortales: denique hortari & consulere, vt in sinum matris ecclesiæ redeam.
units.tr: Now indeed this one thing must be lamented, which also grievously and bitterly tormented us: namely, that Satan rages in such a way that he uses the work even of those who profess themselves godly to wound our wretched souls, as far as in them lies, and at the same time our bodies as well. They prefer the offices they hold, their wealth, their ease and the delights of their flesh to the glory of the Son of God, to eternal life, and to the life of the soul and body of their neighbours. Some do this openly, some secretly, some plainly and directly, as they say; others, by crooked arts and foxlike frauds, stain and pollute their hands with the blood of innocent men. Why do I say innocent men? Rather, with the innocent blood of the sons of God and the members of Jesus Christ. Would that they had that prudence and humanity which many unbelievers have, who will rise up at the last judgment against such utterly degenerate Christians, who fashion for themselves a kind of silken Christ, or invent him according to their lust, and make the gospel separate from all cross and trouble, and who, in time of peace or truce, boast with full mouths that they are Christ's. But when they are called to account, and when it is most needed, they shamefully fail before men. Nor will they seek or grasp at anything except to turn their course back and so renounce piety, so that they become true executioners of Christ, even though he, raised from the dead, has triumphed over death, since they rage with such cruelty against his members. I make this complaint now not only so that I may freely pour into your bosom whatever my mind bears, especially since you have shown yourselves to me, now reduced to the last extremity, faithful and sincere friends in all things, by your deeds; but also so that there may be a kind of entrance to setting out for you those things which God, in his accustomed goodness, has wondrously done with us since we sent you our last letter, for which you will judge that I do not complain without reason. Yet I will not relate the individual things, for I am hindered both by the shortness of time and by the scarcity of paper; nor will I narrate what has been done by the brothers imprisoned here with me. For since, during that whole time in which the judges questioned us, we were separated from one another, each of us will more easily and conveniently relate what each one did apart. So when, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, the sentence of the judges by which we were condemned to the galleys was pronounced to us by the Propraetor, at about the fourth hour after noon I was led into the Court before the Senators, at whose urging and instigation the royal Procurator had summoned me, as they put it, on account of excessive [zeal]. The chief Praeses ordered a book to be brought, so that, with my hand laid on it as on the holy Gospels, I would swear to tell the truth; but when I noticed that the crucified one, as they call him, was depicted there, I at once declared what I believed, and that my faith was plainly contrary to their opinion as regards images. Here Crassus, the inspector of our case, quoted that silly and ridiculous little verse: "For it is the image that teaches, but not God himself." But I openly asked whether the matter of the image, or the form, which was to represent God to me, had anything similar between them. What also does the true God have in common, or in affinity, with that little old man adorned with a triple crown, such as they paint in their beautiful image of the Trinity? They claim that God put on the person of a man, or was made man. And so they suddenly break off this speech and cut off my power of speaking. The same president, when he had questioned me more carefully about my name, age, country and native place, and where and why I had been arrested, and had understood that I had answered his questions truthfully, began to speak in a kindly and humane manner, but in appearance only. First he set before me the glory of God; then he recalled the favour of the whole court and their singular goodwill toward me; that I could bring great help to my neighbours; that he and the others had not come together to handle this matter except under the guidance and auspices of the Holy Spirit, and after first invoking him; that it was not right for me to claim so much for myself as to think I alone am wiser than many thousands of men, and that I ought to be ruled by the Holy Spirit rather than by other mortals; and finally he urged and advised me to return to the bosom of mother Church.

units.la: Quærebat insuper Præses,vnde mihi tanta isthæc audacia, vt ita in Papam debaccharer, Antichristum eum nominans: vt in Missam sic inuehrer,idololatriam esse affirmans,& idololatras,omnes qui eam sequuntur: quum satis constet, quod attinet ad Papam, quanuis sit peccator, eius tamen munus à Deo esse: Lutherum & similes non debere ita illi conuitiari, sed potius ingemiscere,non autem sectas eiusmodi inuehere, nec turbas excitare:quòd si recte & proprie velimus aptare locos epistolæ ad Thessalonicenses,& Apocalypseos, vbi de antichristo agitur, ad Mahometum referendos esse: non autem ita contumeliosè cum Christianis miseris fratribus nostris agendum. Quod ad Missam spectat, tantùm esse sacrificium gratiarum actionis, & illic esse corpus Christi, quum id possit aut velit: iuxta illud, Hoc est corpus meum: de modo & ratione qua id fiat, inquirere vel scrutari nostrum non esse. ac proinde stultum & temerarium videri quod ita nos ipsi ea de re cruciemus vel tumultuemur. sibi compertum esse dissidium inter Lutherum, Zuinglium, & OEcolampadium se legisse doctorum nostrorum libros: sed mihi potius accedendum esse ac subscribendum antiquis doctoribus & sanctis Concilijs: nos porro nimium audaces in asseuerando & iudicando de rebus altioribus, & quae captum humanum superant. Haec summa est quaedam sermonum qui eo die habiti sunt (ut ego certe memini) non ordine quidem, & eadem serie, sed quatenus respondere mihi licebat per summi illius Præsidis decretum, & libidinem. Ea enim astutia & vafritie utebatur, ut me dicentem interturbaret, ac sermonem abrumperet, simulatque vel rimulam unam deprehendisse sibi videbatur, qua se putabat elabi posse, & argumenta argumentis connectebat: ut tandem coactus fuerim testari palam, mihi opus esse memoria plane Diuina, vel Angelica, si ad omnia respondere vellem. Caeterum si per otium illi placeret me audire vel mihi tempus concedere, quo responderem ex scripto, me non modo ad singula copiose & aperte responsurum, sed illi suppeditaturum alia contra nos argumenta, quae nisi perspicue diluerem, me paratum esse ad subeundum quoduis genus mortis, cui me addiceret pro suo arbitrio. Hoc tamen mihi denegarunt, ac simul adiecerunt se nunquam tantum fauoris cuiquam alteri concessisse, ut ea humanitate illum in eiusmodi crimine audierint. Itaque coactus sum breuiter, ut referam, obiectiones sic soluere. Principio me non inficiari, quin confessus illorum esset honore quidem dignus, sed si iudicium fiat ab externa specie, tot urbes, tot populos, tot regna, tot denique eximios esse homines, qui singularibus tum corporis, tum animi dotibus excellunt, & qui hodie eandem quam ego doctrinam tuentur, iure etiam promereri, ut eodem quo ipsi loco & numero à me censeantur: idque ne molestum, vel graue esset me orare. Sed interea mihi longe aliud fundamentum fidei meae constitutum esse, quod planum ac perspicuum facerem, si per tempus liceret. Citauit illud tritum, Multa habeo dicere quae non potestis, &c: deinde Concilium Hierosolymae habitu. Rogauit unde, & quo modo persuasus efsem de Scriptura: addidit in rebus externis connivendum esse & licere Christianis se omnibus accommodare. quibus ut abunde responderem obtinere non potui. Quod ad Papam spectat, dixi vitam eius documento esse quaenam sit ipsius doctrina, si ad examen verbi exigatur: non quod ipse doceat. neque enim quadraret sacrae eius maiestati, docere sive recte, sive perperam: verum illi satis esse, modò se flammis, & gladio tueatur: eius tamen doctrinam prorsus contrariā esse Christi verbo, atque adeo evertere ac delere ipsum & eius gratiam: quod illis statim probavi, impietate Purgatorij, & Satisfactionum in medium proposita: quibus capitibus instiliti, quoad de ipsis palàm constaret, quia iam hominis vafritiem & astum detexeram, quo prosilire ab equis ad asinos (ut aiunt) solebat. Exprobrabat ille nos in hac controversia, & aliis ferè omnibus, ex composito & perperam ludisicari, vel ut ipse suis verbis dicebat, nos aequivocare in facto: ac persuadere mundo velle ab ipsis dici quae minimè dicunt: Idem ille Crassus, quem nominavi, locum illum Pauli ad Corinth. Quasi per ignem, &c. citans, ita se ridendum propinauit, ut coram suis collegis erubuerit. Quod ad Lutherum attinet, ostendi, quàm sanctè ac syncerè cum Papa se gessisset: ac doctrinae examē pertinere ad unumquemque piorum. itaque multò magis ad plures populos, regna, &c. Optabam mirum in modum acrius impetere eorum Missam, sed mihi non fuit permissum: unde coactꝰ illos remisi ad Missae anatomē à fidelissimo Christi ministro, & vigilantissimo ecclesiae pastore Petro Vireto conscriptā. Tandē me hortati sunt, ne opinioni meae pertinacius adhaerere.
units.tr: The President further asked where I got such great audacity to rage so against the Pope, calling him Antichrist; and to rail against the Mass in this way, affirming it to be idolatry and all who follow it idolaters. Since it is quite agreed that, as far as the Pope is concerned, although he is a sinner, his office is nevertheless from God; Luther and similar men ought not to revile him thus, but rather to lament, and not to bring forward sects of this kind nor stir up disturbances; and if we wished to apply rightly and properly the passages of the Epistle to the Thessalonians and the Apocalypse, where Antichrist is treated, they must be referred to Mahomet, and not so insultingly dealt with against our wretched Christian brothers. As for the Mass, it is only a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and there the body of Christ is present, as he is able and willing: according to that saying, This is my body: it is not for us to inquire into or investigate the manner and way in which this happens. And therefore it seemed foolish and rash that we tormented and stirred ourselves up over this matter. He had found that there was disagreement among Luther, Zwingli and Oecolampadius, as he had read the books of our teachers; but I ought rather to agree with and subscribe to the ancient teachers and holy Councils; we are too bold in asserting and judging concerning higher matters, which surpass human understanding. This is a certain summary of the speeches that were given that day (as I certainly remember), not indeed in order and sequence, but as far as I was permitted to answer by the decree and pleasure of that supreme President. For he used such cunning and craftiness that he would confuse me while I was speaking and break off my speech as soon as he seemed to have caught even a small crack through which he thought I might slip away; and he linked argument to argument, so that at last I was forced to declare openly that I would need a memory altogether divine or angelic if I wished to answer everything. Otherwise, if he were pleased to hear me at leisure or to grant me time to reply in writing, I would not only answer each point fully and openly, but would supply him with other arguments against us, which, unless I refuted them clearly, I was ready to undergo any kind of death to which he might condemn me at his discretion. Yet they denied me this, and at the same time added that they had never granted such favour to anyone else as to hear him with such courtesy in a matter of this kind. So I was forced to answer the objections briefly, as I now relate. First, I do not deny that he was worthy of honour, as far as his confession goes; but if judgement is made from outward appearance, then so many cities, so many peoples, so many kingdoms, and finally so many outstanding men, who excel in singular gifts both of body and mind, and who today uphold the same doctrine as I do, also deserve to be counted by me in the same place and rank as they themselves; and that would not be troublesome or burdensome to me to beg. But meanwhile a quite different foundation of my faith has been laid down, which I would make plain and clear if time allowed. He cited the trite saying, "I have many things to say which you cannot bear," etc.; then the Council held at Jerusalem. He asked whence and in what way I was persuaded about Scripture; he added that in external matters one must connive and that Christians are permitted to accommodate themselves to all. To these points I could not obtain leave to answer fully. As for the Pope, I said that his life is evidence of what his doctrine is, if it is brought to the test of God's Word: not that he himself teaches; for it would not befit his sacred majesty to teach, whether rightly or wrongly; but it is enough for him, provided he defends himself with flames and sword. Yet his doctrine is wholly contrary to Christ's word, and indeed overthrows and destroys him and his grace; this I immediately proved to them, by setting forth the impiety of Purgatory and of satisfactions, on which points they were pricked, since it was now clear about them, because I had already uncovered the man's craftiness and cunning, by which he used to leap from horses to asses (as they say). That man reproached us in this controversy, and nearly all others, for mocking deliberately and wrongly, or, as he himself put it in his words, for equivocating about the fact, and for persuading the world that we want them to say what they by no means say. That same Crassus, whom I named, quoting that passage of Paul to the Corinthians, "as through fire," etc., so drank to his own ridicule that he blushed before his colleagues. As for Luther, I showed how holily and sincerely he had conducted himself with the Pope; and that the examination of doctrine pertains to every one of the godly; and therefore much more to many peoples, kingdoms, etc. I wished wonderfully to attack their Mass more sharply, but it was not permitted to me; so I sent them back, compelled, to the anatomy of the Mass written by the most faithful minister of Christ and most watchful minister of the Church, Peter Viret. Finally they urged me not to cling more stubbornly to my opinion.

units.la: Ego verò excepi, à Deo optimo me non ita desertū esse, cuius verbo libenter omnes sensus meos subiicere paratus eram, atque rem gratissimam mihi facturos quoties per otium certò probarent me ab illo vel tantillum deflectere, & hinc etiā postridie initium dicendi feci, ac de iisdem prope rebus disputatum est. Die autem Lunae qui proximè sequutus est, nos omnes simul convocati sumus in Senatum, ubi Dominus pro sua bonitate mihi dedit, ut aperte ludicum iniquitatem coarguere non dubitaverim, quod minus audientiae facerent in causa tanti momenti, quàm soleant in qualibet privata: deinde etiam, quod nobis saltem non concederent illud ipsum quod olim & adhuc hodie in ecclesiis repurgatis facilè datur iis qui palàm sunt hæretici: nempe ut ad manum habeant arma, quibus instructi sunt Christiani, hoc est, sacra Biblia, & veterum quoque Doctorum, adeóque suorum aduersariorum scripta possint euoluere. Atque hic conscientias eorum appellans, quæsiui annon ita nos rogassent, ut inter respondendum nunquam nobis licuerit vel vnicam rationem copiosius explicare, ac multò minus concessum fuerit tempus quo plures alias in medium proponeremus: quæ quidem nos impedunt, ne monitis illorum pareamus, nisi velimus esse perfidi hypocritæ. Cæterum à vobis precamur, obseruandi domini, vt nos excusetis.
units.tr: I, however, replied that by the best God I had not been so deserted, to whose word I was ready to submit all my own feelings willingly, and that they would be doing me a most welcome favour whenever they could show with certainty at leisure that I had deviated from him even slightly; and so the next day I also began speaking, and nearly the same matters were discussed. On the Monday following, we were all summoned together into the Senate, where the Lord, in his goodness, gave me that I did not hesitate to openly convict the judges of iniquity, in that they gave less hearing to a cause of such importance than they usually do to any private one; then also, in that they did not grant us at least that very thing which is still easily given today, in the reformed churches, to those who are openly heretics: namely that they may have at hand the weapons with which Christians are equipped, that is, the holy Bible, and the writings of the ancient Doctors, and also those of their adversaries, so that they can unroll them. And here, appealing to their consciences, I asked whether they had not so dealt with us that, while answering, we were never allowed to explain even a single reason more fully, and much less was time granted by which we might put forward several others; which things indeed hinder us from obeying their admonitions, unless we wish to be faithless hypocrites. Moreover we beg you, most observant lords, to excuse us.

units.la: Alia eorundem captiuorum epistola ad ministros ecclesiæ Geneuensis missa.
units.tr: Another letter of the same prisoners, sent to the ministers of the Geneva church.

units.la: Ioannes Vernutius, Antonius Laborierius, Ioannes Trigaletus, Bertrandus Batallius, Guyraud Tauranus, vincti Iesu Christi Domini nostri, obseruadis Ministris Geneuensibus, & omnibus fratribus nostri in Domino vnicè dilectis, Gratia & pax à Deo Patre nostro, & Iesu Christo Domino nostro, in virtute Spiritus sancti, Amen.
units.tr: John Vernutius, Antony Laborierius, John Trigaletus, Bertrand Batallius, Guyraud Tauranus, prisoners of Jesus Christ our Lord, to the observant ministers of Geneva and to all our brothers, uniquely beloved in the Lord: grace and peace from God our Father and from Jesus Christ our Lord, in the power of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

units.la: QVum Deus optimus maximus pro immensa sua misericordia nos retraxerit ex mundo hoc corrupto, ac infinitis offendiculis referto, nosque sibi in vasa honoris consecrauerit, vt ipsius gloria in nobis elucescat, & ad illum, & in eius Ecclesiam proximos nostros adducamus: æquum est certè vt sedulò summaque diligentia caueamus non solùm ab omni scandalo, sed etiam ab omni specie mali: contrà verò tàgamur serio, & eo zelo domus Dei nostri feramur, vt omnino ardeamus & absumamur, idque exemplo Dauidis, qui speculum est omnium piorum: vel potius capitis nostri & ducis Iesu Christi, quem ille nobis adumbrauit. Omnibus tamen seculis, atque etiam hodie Sathan ita grassatus est in mundo, & sic vbique fere dominatur, vt quàtunuis studeant pij Dei cultores, & solicitè dent operam ne quemquam offendant, sed potius vt omnes ædificent: hoc tamen cõsequi non possunt vt decet, & vellent etiam per Spiritum regenerationis, qui habitat & regnat in ipsis: quemadmodum videmus in Abraham patre credétium, in Loth, Dauide, Rahab & aliis fidelibus, qui eò fere proruperunt tum Sathanæ malitia & eius mancipiis, tum etiam propriæ carnis infirmitate, vt aliquando obliquis rationibus vsi sint, & imperu quodam abrepti, quo scilicet ad aliquem rectum finem peruenirent. Hoc modo certè Dominus illos erudire voluit & nos eorum exemplo instituere ad humilitatem, & timorem: tantum abest, ut miserae carni nostrae pulvinar aliquod supponere voluerit, cui suaviter indormiat: vel ullam occasionem praebere, qua exultemus in his rebus quae non licent, ut potius coram eius bonitate contremiscamus, quūm pro singulari foedere (quod dignatus est pacisci nobiscum, qui sumus cadavera putida, & miseri homunciones) tāta humanitate & indulgentia nos tractet. Ista quidē à nobis dicuntur, fratres observandi & unicè chari, nō ut facilè nos excusetis, vel nostrae ignorationi, & debilitati indulgeatis, quae proculdubiō manant à nimia incredulitate, ac diffidentia immensae sapientiae & providentiae plusquam paternae Dei nostri optimi, sapientissimi, & potentissimi, qui novit absque ullis mediis operari, atque etiā contra omnia media: sed ut misericordia commoti Deum ꝓ nobis precemini, literisq; vestris nos consolemini, & nostro dispendio discatis vos exercere in perpetua meditatione huius tam sanctae & admirabilis Dei providentiae: ac detestemini sceleratos istos nebulones, qui conantur evertere caput fidei nostrae adeo utile, necessarium & quod nos experti sumus ipsi fortissimum esse propugnaculum & invictissimum contra omnes hostium impetus: sed nō semper tamen aequali mensura fidei: quae quidē causa fuit, ut quadam obliqua ratione alicubi coacti fuerimus, ut, quae admodum copiosius narrare possent hic frater qui vobis has literas reddet: & nos etiam breviter aliquid attingemus: nempe quum rogati fuimus, an non unus ex nobis concionatus esset Barbottae, Fenestellae, & in aliis urbibus, ac praesertim die Paschatis in prato quodam: annō etiam cognoscerenus Barbam Paulū, & alios multos quos nominarunt ex literis quas Praeses Gratianopolitanus ad illos scripserat de hoc negotio, & omnibus coeptis vel saltem maiori parte eorum quae boni illi viri, & fratres nostri susceperant: nos plane & uno verbo negasse factum, & nihil horum omnium novisse. Id autem non fecimus nisi a fratribus perpulsi, idque cum gemitu & precibus ad Deum optimum effusis, quas simul cum fratribus illis concepimus ac supplices obtulimus: atque velut in trutina accuratē expendimus (quantum scilicet iudicij nostri tenuitas ferebat, vtrum ex duobus malis minus & levius foret, vel palam mentiri) vel gladio interimendos tradere, ac ignibus exponere tot bonos viros iam senes, tot mulieres & pueros: adeo ut Pastores ipsi quodammodo carnifices essent ovium suarum, pro quibus ne vitæ quidem parcere deberent. Quàm grauis & acerbus hic erat dolor! Certè fratres nobis charissimi, quū de obijciendis ad mortem coporibus nostris tantùm agebatur pro fidei confessione & pietate tuenda, Deus unà cum tanto honore hanc quoque gratiam addebat, ut in ipso lætaremur & Psalmos concineremus: hostes verò nostri ægerrimè ferrent, & in rabiem agerentur. Sed quum nobis renunciatum est de his capitibus nos interrogatum iri, quia id vrgebat ille, quem dixi, summus Præses, qui in medium proponebat quæ iudices nostri libenter tacebant, tametsi nõ deesset illis occasio inquirendi propter eas quas ferebamus literas, fatemur tum demùm nos valde attonitos fuisse. neque enim occurrebat quid cogitaremus, nec quid facto vel dicto opus esset. Nam si tātum subeunda nobis fuissent tormenta omne genus, caro quidem fremuisset, ac suo more fuisset tumultuata, sed spiritus eam vicisset: iudicio tamen nostro hostes minimè cessaturos prospiciebamus: & quā-tumuis diros cruciatus perpeti statuissemus, nostros in vitæ discrimen venturos, quia si palàm affirmare nõ dubitassemus quod rogabamur, Gratianopolim tracti fuissemus, & illic tormentis excruciati, testes nobis obiecti, adeóque in locum ipsum deducti. In hac tam graui anxietate, decreuimus omnes quidquid peteretur pernegare, recumbentes nihilominus in Dei providentiam, & confisi eius auspiciis & ductu, qui rationibus nobis incognitis uti potest. Iam totum hoc negocium ita moderatus est, ut hæc tempestas aliqua ex parte sedata fuerit, ut amici quoque dicerent omnia fœliciter cessura: & nihil superesse præter sententiam qua Iudices nos damnent ad remos, sicuti etiam hic frater vobis narrabit. Interim Deo optimo gratias agimus pro sua in nos bonitate, atque adeo in nostra viscera, hoc est, miserum nostrum gregem: & precamur ex animo, ut eam prosequi dignetur, ac in dies augere pro sua promissione & qua solet uti ratione erga suos omnes. Quod autem attinet ad id quod ex nostra corruptela permixtum fuit eius providentiæ & operi, ne in iudicium contra nos descendat: sed nobis hoc, & alia tot scelera remittat, nomine Filij sui Iesu Christi: ac nos Spiritu suo ita refingat, ut quietis animis ardentius ipsum colamus, & reijciamus quidquid est ex nostro ingenio: ac placidè sinamus nos regi eius arbitrio & voluntate. Si vero nos castigare tanquam filios visum fuerit, potius remis perpetuis addictos & ludicum sententia mancipatos vitam transfigere permittat, aut alio quovis modo cursum nostrum conficere: tantum nos percutiat & domum patrum nostrorum, & huic populo parcatur, nos potius in profundam abyssum detrudat. Sed Domine, fiat voluntas tua: miserere nostri, & ovium pascuorum tuorum, quas curae nostrae commisisti: non aliter quam propriam animam nobis dedisti. Quod Petro dicebas, auribus nostris & cordibus semper insonet, Petre amas me? Pasce oves meas. Mosis charitas, Pauli, atque etiam Iesu Christi perpetuo nobis ob oculos versetur. quod nobis ipsi petimus, vobis quoque idem precamur fratres unice dilecti, ac praesertim vobis optimi patres in Christo, & charissimi maximeque observandi Pastores ecclesiae ipsius: obsecrates vos ut pro nobis vicissim praecemini, quemadmodum nos ex animo vobis commendatos esse cupimus. Postremis autem literis quas ad nos scripsistis in praesentia non respondemus, quia paulo post quam nobis redditae fuerunt, eas abstulerunt amici, ne ab illis inveniretur qui omnia excutere debebant ut magna tunc erat suspicio. Huc etiam accedit, quod discessum ita maturare cogebat qui nostras vobis perfert, ut coacti quoque fuerimus scribendi finem prius facere quam optabamus. Gratia & dilectio Dei Patris nostri optimi, per Dominum & Salvatorem nostrum Iesum Christum eius Filium, in communicatione Spiritus sancti sit perpetuo cum omnibus vobis, Amē. ex carcere Cameriaci 18. Cal. Augusti. Vestri observantissimi fratres iam antea nominati.
units.tr: Since almighty God, in his immense mercy, has drawn us out of this corrupt world, which is full of endless stumbling-blocks, and has consecrated us to himself as vessels of honour, so that his glory may shine forth in us and that we may bring our neighbours to him and into his Church, it is surely right that we take careful and utmost pains to avoid not only every scandal but also every appearance of evil. On the contrary, we ought to be seriously touched and carried away with that zeal for the house of our God, so that we burn and are consumed entirely, following the example of David, who is the mirror of all the godly, or rather of our head and leader Jesus Christ, whom David foreshadowed for us. Yet in every age, and today too, Satan so rages in the world and so nearly everywhere holds sway that, however earnestly the godly worshippers of God strive and diligently take pains not to offend anyone but rather to edify all, they cannot achieve this as they ought, though they would wish to, through the Spirit of regeneration which dwells and reigns in them. We see this in Abraham, the father of believers, in Lot, David, Rahab and other faithful people, who were driven to such lengths, partly by the malice of Satan and his servants, and partly by the weakness of their own flesh, that at times they used crooked methods and, carried away by a certain impetus, aimed at some right end. In this way the Lord surely wished to instruct them, and through their example to teach us humility and fear. He was far from wishing to place some cushion under our wretched flesh on which it might sleep soundly, or to offer any occasion for us to exult in things that are not lawful. Rather, we should tremble before his goodness, since he deals with us, who are rotting corpses and wretched little men, with such kindness and indulgence under a singular covenant which he has deigned to make with us. We say these things, brothers to be observed and uniquely dear, not so that you will readily excuse us or grant indulgence to our ignorance and weakness, which without doubt flow from excessive unbelief and distrust of the immense wisdom and more than paternal providence of our God, who is best, wisest and most powerful, and who knows how to work without any means, and even against all means. Rather, we say them so that, moved by compassion, you will pray to God for us and comfort us with your letters, and learn from our loss to exercise yourselves in the constant meditation on this so holy and admirable providence of God, and to detest those wicked scoundrels who strive to overthrow the foundation of our faith, which is so useful and necessary, and which we ourselves have found to be the strongest bulwark and most invincible against all the assaults of the enemy. Yet it has not always been held with an equal measure of faith. This is the reason why, in some way, we were at one point compelled to adopt a crooked course; this brother who brings you this letter will be able to tell you much more fully, but we too shall touch on it briefly. Namely, when we were asked whether one of us had not preached at Barbotte, at Fenestrelle, in other towns, and especially on Easter Day in a certain meadow; and when they also named Barbe Paulus and many others, from the letters which the governor of Grenoble had written to them about this business, and about all the undertakings, or at least most of what those good men and our brothers had taken up, we flatly and in a word denied that it had happened and said we knew nothing of all these things. We did not do this except having been driven by the brothers, and that with groaning and with prayers poured out to God, which we conceived together with those brothers and offered as suppliants. And we weighed the matter carefully, as if on a balance (as far as the slightness of our judgement allowed), whether it was the lesser and lighter of two evils to lie openly, or to hand over to the sword and expose to the fires so many good men, now old, so many women and children. So much so that the ministers themselves were, in a certain sense, the butchers of their own sheep, for whom they ought not to spare even their lives. How grievous and bitter this pain was! Truly, dearest brothers, when it was only a matter of exposing our bodies to death for the confession of faith and the defence of piety, God, along with such honour, added this grace too, that we rejoiced in it and sang psalms. Our enemies, however, took it very badly and were driven into a rage. But when we were told that we would be questioned on these heads, because that chief governor I have mentioned insisted on it, and he put forward in public what our judges were gladly keeping silent about, although there was no lack of opportunity for them to inquire, on account of the letters we were carrying, we confess that we were then utterly astonished. For nothing came to mind as to what we should think, or what needed doing or saying. For if only torments of every kind had been set before us, the flesh would indeed have shuddered and stirred in its usual way, but the spirit would have overcome it. Yet we foresaw that our enemies would by no means relent in their judgement, and however dire the torments we resolved to endure, our friends would be put in peril of their lives. For if we had not hesitated to affirm openly what we were asked, we would have been dragged to Grenoble, and there tortured, and witnesses would have been set against us, and so we would have been led to that very place. In this so grave anxiety, we decided to deny everything that was asked, nonetheless resting in God's providence, and trusting in his auspices and guidance, who can use reasons unknown to us. Now he has so governed this whole affair that this storm has been in some measure calmed, so that even our friends say that all will turn out happily, and that nothing remains except the sentence by which the judges condemn us to the galleys, as this brother will also tell you. Meanwhile we give thanks to the best God for his goodness towards us, and indeed towards our very bowels, that is, our wretched flock. And we pray from the heart that he may deign to continue to care for them, and to increase them daily, according to his promise and the manner he is accustomed to use towards all his own. As for what was mixed into his providence and work through our corruption, may he not enter into judgement against us on this account, but forgive us this and our many other sins, in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and so reform us by his Spirit that with quiet minds we may worship him more ardently, and cast off whatever belongs to our own nature, and calmly allow ourselves to be ruled by his will and pleasure. But if it seems good to him to chastise us as sons, may he allow us rather to spend our lives condemned to the galleys in perpetuity and handed over to the sentence of judges, or to finish our course in some other way. Only let him strike us, and spare the house of our fathers and this people; let him rather cast us down into the deepest abyss. But, Lord, let your will be done. Have mercy on us, and on the sheep of your pastures, whom you have committed to our care, since you gave us our own soul no differently. What you said to Peter, Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep, let it always ring in our ears and hearts. Let the charity of Moses, of Paul, and indeed of Jesus Christ, always be before our eyes. What we ask for ourselves, we also ask of you, brothers uniquely beloved, and especially of you, best fathers in Christ and most dear and most to be observed ministers of the Church itself, begging you to pray for us in turn, just as we long to be commended to you from our hearts. As for your last letters, which you wrote to us, we do not answer them at present, because shortly after they were delivered to us, our friends carried them off, lest they should be found by those who ought to search everything, as there was great suspicion at that time. Moreover, the departure was hurried by the one who carries our letters to you, so that we were also forced to make an end of writing sooner than we wished. May the grace and love of God our best Father, through our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ his Son, in the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, be with you all for ever. Amen. From the prison of Cambrai, 18 days before the Kalends of August. Your most observant brothers, already named above.

units.la: Gratia, misericordia & pax à Deo Patre nostro, & Domino Iesu Christo, virtute Spiritus sancti vobis multiplicetur.
units.tr: May grace, mercy and peace be multiplied to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, by the power of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: L[?]iteras tuas, observande domine & pater in Christo Iesu Domino nostro, Nonis Sept. accepimus, quae nobis maximū solatium attulerunt. Nam vestrum, & fratrum omnium singularem erga nos amorem testantur, quod ita malo nostro secundum carnem condoleatis, ut interim nostro bono secundum spiritum lætari non desinatis, cum lachrymantibus scilicet lachrymas fundentes, & cum ridentibus etiam ridentes: unde magnas vobis gratias agimus. Quod ad nos attinet, quanvis ex animo lætemur, quia Dominus pro sua bonitate nobis largitur unde sanctam lætitiam cap:atis[?], licet abiecti, despicabiles ac miseri homunciones sumus, nobis tamen dolet quod nostro nomine tot molestias & labores vos, & tot illustres viri, adeoque tota ecclesia, feratis. Quanquam multæ ingemiscendi occasiones nobis quotidie offeruntur: illa tamen postrema non est, ita ut optemus, & precemur à Deo optimo, ut vos breui liberet ab ea anxietate, qua distringimini assiduè propter vincula quibus constringimur, quacunque ratione ipsi visum fuerit. Si per mortem id efficiat, commodo nostro cedet. Tantum ab eo petimus, ut hunc in nobis affectum magis augeat, quem ipse pro sua liberalitate dedit. nam hoc modo eripiemur ex multis carceribus ac vinculis longè etiam gravioribus, quàm sit hæc turris qua nunc concludimur. Si vero alia ratione nos velit ereptos, ut votis eorum satisfaciat, qui nostram fortem multò acerbius ferunt, quàm si mus promeriti, id certè fieri ita cupimus, ut illorum expectationi & vestræ respondeamus, nempe ut magis quàm unquam nos addicamus celebrando eius sancto nomini & impendamus ædificandæ ipsius Ecclesiæ. Sæpius igitur cum Dauide exclamamus, Domine Deus exercituum, ne pudefiant in me qui in te sperant ac recumbunt, & qui te quærunt, ne pudore suffundantur in me, Deus Israël. Nunquam huius vitæ umbra fruamur, nisi ea lege, quû pro sua bonitate eò nos adduxerit, ut nobis exire liceat è medio huius generationis peruersæ & adulteræ, in qua tot blasphemiis proscinditur, ut horrorem sola cogitatio incutiat: ut felicet pergamus ad canendas illi perpetuas laudes in beatorum cœtu: atque vehementer a vobis petimus ut vestris precibus apud Deum nos iuuetis, quò simus huius voti compotes, & quum ad ecclesias quæ sunt Lausannæ, & Neocomi scribetis, ut ad idem præstandum incitetis, & gratias etiam agatis ob singulare erga nos beneuolentiam, de qua quidem, & vestra minimè dubitamus, sed nobis dolet, quòd illi respondere non possimus: & tamen ad id enitimur, & supplices Deum optimum oramus, ut vobis remetiatur & cumulet tot beneficia tum corporis tum animi, quæ in nos tanquam veri parentes & nutritij nostri, conferre non definitis. In quo certè satis experimur suauem illam Filij Dei promissionem, qua pollicitus est, quicunque deseruerit domos, vel fratres, vel sorores, vel patrem vel matrem, vel liberos, vel agros ipsius & Euangelij nomine, accepturum in hoc seculo centuplam, & cum afflictionibus domos, & fratres, sorores matres, liberos & possessiones: atque in futuro seculo vitam æternam consecuturum. Quum hic & alibi sæpius illum esse veracem, & sibi constare in suis promissis experti simus, an non plusquam ingrati essemus, & omni probro digni, nisi fixum & persuasum nobis esset quod scribitur in clausula Psalmi xlviii, Hic Deus, Deus noster in seculû & vsque: ipse deducet nos vsque ad mortè. Ex his quæ perstrinximus iudicare potestis quo simus animo, quæ Dei optimi summa est gratia, & liberalitas.
units.tr: We received your letter, honoured lord and father in Christ Jesus our Lord, on the Nones of September, and it brought us the greatest comfort. For it bears witness to your singular love for us and for all the brethren, in that you so grieve for our trouble according to the flesh, and yet do not cease to rejoice in our good according to the Spirit, weeping with those who weep and rejoicing with those who rejoice. For this we give you great thanks. As for ourselves, although we rejoice from the heart, because the Lord in his goodness grants us that holy joy, and although we are cast down, despised and wretched little men, it grieves us that you and so many illustrious men, and indeed the whole Church, bear so many troubles and labours on our account. Yet many occasions for sighing are offered to us every day, and this is not the least of them. So we wish and pray to the best God that he may soon free you from that anxiety by which you are constantly distressed on account of the chains with which we are bound, by whatever means it shall please him. If he brings this about by death, it will be to our advantage. We ask only that he increase in us that affection which in his generosity he has given. For in this way we shall be delivered from many prisons and chains, far heavier than this tower in which we are now shut up. But if he wishes to set us free in some other way, so as to satisfy the desires of those who bear our lot far more bitterly than we have deserved, we desire indeed that this be done, so that we may answer their expectation and yours, namely that we may devote ourselves more than ever to celebrating his holy name and to spending ourselves in building up his Church. Therefore we often cry out with David: Lord God of hosts, let not those who hope in you be put to shame through me, and let not those who seek you be confounded through me, O God of Israel. May we never enjoy the shade of this life, except on this condition: that, in his goodness, he should bring us to the point of being allowed to depart from the midst of this perverse and adulterous generation, in which he is so reviled by blasphemies that the very thought of them strikes horror; and so that we may go on to sing his perpetual praises in the company of the blessed. And we earnestly ask you, by your prayers, to help us before God, that we may obtain this wish; and when you write to the churches at Lausanne and Neuchâtel, urge them to do the same, and give thanks for their singular goodwill towards us. Of this goodwill we ourselves have no doubt, yet it grieves us that we cannot make any return to it. Nevertheless we strive towards this, and we pray the best God in supplication that he may repay you and multiply the many benefits, both of body and of soul, which you do not cease to bestow upon us as true parents and nurturers. In this we surely experience that sweet promise of the Son of God, by which he promised that whoever has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or fields for his own sake and for the sake of the Gospel, shall receive a hundredfold in this age, with afflictions, houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children and possessions, and in the age to come shall obtain eternal life. Since we have often here and elsewhere found him to be true and consistent in his promises, should we not be more than ungrateful, and worthy of every reproach, if we were not fixed and persuaded of what is written at the close of Psalm 48: This God is our God for ever and ever; he will lead us even unto death. From what we have touched upon you may judge with what spirit we are disposed, which is the supreme grace and generosity of the best God.

units.la: Dominus Deus noster faxit, ut reipsa sentias, non abs re ipsum vocari Patrem misericordiæ, & Deum omnis consolationis, nomine Domini nostri ac Redemptoris Christi.
units.tr: May our Lord God grant that you may truly know that he is rightly called the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort, in the name of our Lord and Redeemer Christ.

units.la: QVum satis constet, Soror charissime, nos coronam consequi non posse nisi rite certaverimus: operæpretium est nos sæpe ac diligenter moneri quibus cum hostibus nobis sit negotium ac certamen, & quæ sint eorum artes & astutiæ ad nos impetendos. Et vero magna pars est victoriæ, hostem novisse, cum quo manus conferendæ sunt. Omnes quidem tenent nomen inimicorum communium generis humani: sed perpauci student multiplicem eorum malitiam cognoscere, ut serio illis resistant. nemo certe penitus æstimare potest animo complecti, ac multo minus verbis explicare. nam si solus est Deus, qui profundâ carnis malitiâ scrutari possit, & corruptæ & perversæ cordis humani naturæ, & sensuum hominum: eius quis tot astus & fraudes huius mundi superet, quem pronuntiat Ioānnes positum esse in malo, & Sathanæ, quem Paulus vocat cum tota eius cohorte nempe omnibus malignis spiritibus,Potestates, Principatus, Rectores mundi, tenebrarum huius sæculi, Malitias spirituales, quæ sunt in cælestibus, numirum in aere? Quod ad nos spectat, licet hæc scientia captum nostrum excedat, vult tamen Deus, ut quotidie in ea nos exerceamus, quo scilicet in nobis humiliati, & destituti omnibus nostris viribus quas in nobis esse imaginamur, adipsum erecti in potente eius manu tuto recubamus. Iam inter diaboli innumeras astutias, & aliorum hostium, quibus tanquam organis utitur, hæc maxime notanda est & Dominus ad eam meditandam magis quam unquam te adigit, propositis pœnis quas tibi infligere in dies pergit, nempe quacunque ratione Pater ille optimus filios suos tractet, ut ad se propius adducat: callidum hunc & vafrum serpentem eniti, ut ipsos quam longissime abducat. Si Deus bona nobis largiatur, quibus testatur paternum suum erga nos amorem, ut corda nostra quæ obduruerunt frangat vel emolliat, Sathan utetur propria carne nostra, sicuti Dalilæ opera usus est adversus Sampsonem, & Bethsabæ contra Davidem, ut nos hic sopitos & torpentes detineat & fascinet, quo deseramus Deum qui cotulit ut beneficiis illius fruamur, adeoque bellum cum ipso geramus. Si Deus flagella sua in nos explicet, vel potius adhibeat remedia sanandis animorum nostrorum morbis apta: Satha hic psuadere conabitur, huc optimum Patrem nobis infestum esse hostem, atque ita nos impellere, ut illi obstrepamus & fremamus contra eum ac si crudelis esset tyrannus. Itaque si fides hosti nostro, qui mendaciorum est pater, habeatur, nunquam Deus nos amore prosequitur utcunque nos tractet, & quocunque modo nobiscum agat. Quum ex verbo Dei, quod est ipsamet veritas, sciamus vaferrimum hunc hostem ita mentiri, quum etiam, vbi patri nostro Adamo fore ipsum æqualem, vel similem Deo promisit: è contrario sibi reddidit similem, dum in idem secum exitium pertraxit: sedulo nobis cauendum est, ne illi fidem adhibeamus, sed infinitis illis miseriis, quas in nobis ipsis sentimus, & in aliis quoq; ceruinus mendacio istius perditi hostis, cautiores simus in posterum, & nostro dispendio sapiamus, vt autem id facere possimus, assiduis precibus petimus a Domino, vt carnis nostræ iudicio nos exuat, & nobis det aliud, nempe spirituale per Iesum Christum qui illud cum omni donorum genere accepit, vt nobis communicet. Deinde ipsum audiamus loquentem in sacris suis scripturis, quas velut literas è cælo misit, vt à mendacijs & præstigijs diaboli nos abstraheret, ac deduceret ad omnem veritatem. Illic autè clarè docet, quicquid nobis accidat, vt primum ad se oculos semper erigamus: ac præsertim quod ad res aduersas spectat, quæ videtur parum congruere eius naturæ, certò simus persuasi ab ipso manare & proficisci: non quòd inde oblectetur, vel capiat vllam voluptatem: sed vt gustum aliquem hominibus præbeat eorum, quæ palàm editurus est vltimo die, nimirum se iustum esse mundi iudicem, cui iustitia serò sit cordi, & iniustitia summo odio: idque non modò vt magis inexcusabiles reddat incredulos, sed etiam vt piis omnibus in maius bonum cedat. Nam testatur se pœnas his infligere, non odio aliquo, sed potius quia ipsos summo amore prosequitur: cuius quidem rei locupletissimus est testis vnigenitus eius Filius, quem demersit in abyssum omnium miseriarum, quibus erant obnoxij, imò fere obruti, vt eos inde extraheret. Rebus etiam aduersis, quæ sunt peccati fructus, vult suos ad odium peccati adducere, atque ita excitare, vt ardentius confugiant ad gratiam Iesu Christi: quò scilicet ipse ab eius tyrannide vindicet, & in libertate afferat. Vult quoque dum in afflictione experiuntur qualis sit ira Dei, etiamsi minimum ex ea sentiant præ impijs, qui perpetuò diris cruciatibus obruetur, vt tanto alacriori animo gratias agant optimo illi Saluatori, qui eos à tam tetro & horredo gurgite liberauit, liberavit: quum exhausit illorum nomine calicem irae Divinae: & qui etiam ita sanctificavit ac benedixit eorum miserias in cruce sua, ut fespiritualissimus correpti: adeo vt dum nos fide in Christum iustificatos sentimus, ipsi gloriemur ob illos quos dixi fructus, & innumeros alios quos inde percipimus. Atque vt melius expendamus, & æstimemus felicem nostrum in afflictionibus statum, videamus e contrario quam misera sit omnium incredulorum conditio, quibus noxiæ sunt res aduersæ, quia tanto grauius illis exitiū afferent, quòd moniti non resipuerint, sicuti Deus ipsos cô inuitabat. Ad manum percutientis, inquit Isaias, non respexerunt. Duplex est præterea discrimen inter nostras & eorum calamitates nempe quòd nostræ temperantur pro mensura fidei nostræ, & fortitudinis, quam contulit nobis Deus ad eas constanter ferendas: illorum vero miseriæ carent mensura. Nam vt sunt contra Deum peruicaces, & peruerse cum eo agunt: ita Deus mercedem illis rependit sua peruicacia & obstinatione dignam: & quemadmodum in horrendam scelerum omnium licentiam sine modo sese proiiciunt: ita modum non tenet in exigendis pœnis de illorum sceleribus: vt induciæ etiam ipse, quas per res prosperas concedit, in grauius exitium illis cedant. Deinde, quòd miseriæ nostræ temporales sunt, eorum autem perpetuæ. Quid maius nunc expetimus? Deus nos maximo nostro bono affligit: Deus non castigat durius quàm simus ferendo: Deus finem malis omnibus nostris imponet, & lætum exitum dabit. Plura huius rei confirmandæ testimonia tibi proferrem: sed quia præter expectationem meam cogor scribendi finem facere, tantum hoc vnum addam, quo facile poteris incredibile piorum felicitate cognoscere. Omnium miseriarū, quibus obnoxij sunt homines, grauissima est mors, & acerbissima. Dominus tamē pronūtiat mortem suorū esse sibi pretiosam. Quod ita miserrimus ille Pseudopropheta Balaā perspexit, vt morte iustorū interire optauerit, & vltimū suū exitū illis esse simile. Nos igitur qui filij Dei sumus, quidnā metuemus: annon perbeati sumus, etiā quum mundus ipse, & caro nostra infelicissimos nos esse iudicant? Nos itaque Soror charissima, in Deo optimo lætemur, in ipso gloriemur, siue nobis penuriam, morbos, carceres & vincula, vel quascunq; alias calamitates immittat, siue beneficia in nos cŏferat. Inuito Sathana, conuertamus hoc totum in nostram vtilitatē, vt scilicet tanto magis eius obsequio simus addicti. Quū nobis omnia fluunt ex voto in timore, & solicitudine ambulemus, ne frænum insanæ libidini nostræ laxemus. contrà verò in rebus aduersis ita nos coram ipso cum vera resipiscentia deijciamus, ut interea syncer-is precibus ad eum confugere non dubitemus, certò persuasi nos exauditum iri, & eum nobiscum esse dum affligimur, & audacter insultemus omnibus nostris hostibus, qui suadere nobis conantur nos ab ipso desertos esse. Si Dominus dederit ut de hac re tibi scribam, vel etiam ut coram præsens dicam plura, id certè libenter & ex animo faciam. sancta eius voluntas fiat. Et quemadmodum virtutem suam sic in me exeruit ut quodammodo ipsi respondeam, ita dignetur opus suum ad finem usque prosequi: & verò mihi non est dubium, quin hoc efficiat. Quum dignatus quoque suerit se totum mihi dare in persona Filij sui, ego me prorsus illi addictum iure profiteor, sive nunc viva sive moriar. Me hoc toto tempore quo vim Etus[?] hic ago, leui morbo corripuit, nempe continuo sanguinis fluxu, qui nondum sisti potuit. Qualiscunque tandem sit exitus, mihi maximo usui futurum spero. Est enim Pater meus optimus, & pro immensa bonitate sua tot signis id obsignauit, ut merito filium illi obsequentem & moriturum præbere me debeam, & vehementer mihi doleat quod melius erga ipsum non defungar. huic morbo dignetur mederi.
units.tr: Since it is well established, dearest sister, that we cannot win the crown unless we have fought lawfully, it is worth our while to be warned often and carefully about what enemies we have to contend with, and what their arts and wiles are for attacking us. Indeed, a large part of victory is knowing the enemy with whom we must engage. Everyone knows the name of the common enemies of mankind, but very few take pains to learn their manifold malice so that they can resist them earnestly. Certainly no one can fully grasp this in mind, much less explain it in words. For if God alone can search out the deep wickedness of the flesh, and the corrupt and perverse nature of the human heart and senses, who can overcome the many tricks and frauds of this world, which John says lies in evil, and of Satan, whom Paul calls, with his whole band, namely all the evil spirits: "principalities, powers, the rulers of the darkness of this world, spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places," that is, in the air? As far as we are concerned, although this knowledge exceeds our grasp, God nevertheless wills that we exercise ourselves in it every day, so that, humbled in ourselves and stripped of all the strength we imagine we have, we may be lifted up by his mighty hand and rest there safely. Now among the countless tricks of the devil, and of the other enemies whom he uses as his instruments, this one above all must be noted, and the Lord now urges you to consider it more than ever: by the punishments which he keeps inflicting on you day after day, whatever way that most excellent Father deals with his sons, He does so to bring them closer to himself, while that crafty and sly serpent strives to lead them as far away as possible. If God bestows good things on us, by which he shows his fatherly love toward us, so that he may break or soften our hardened hearts, Satan will use our own flesh, just as he used the work of Delilah against Samson and of Bathsheba against David, to hold us here drowsy, numb and enchanted, so that we abandon God, who has given us his benefits to enjoy, and so wage war against him. If God unfolds his scourges upon us, or rather applies remedies suited to healing the diseases of our souls, Satan will try here to persuade us that the best of Fathers is an enemy to us, and so drive us to rail against him and rage at him as if he were a cruel tyrant. Therefore, if credit is given to our enemy, who is the father of lies, God never shows us love, however he treats us and however he deals with us. Since we know from the word of God, which is truth itself, that this most crafty enemy lies in this way, and since, when he promised our father Adam that he would be equal to him, or like God, he on the contrary made him like himself, by drawing him into the same ruin, we must take careful heed not to give him credence. Rather, let the endless miseries which we feel in ourselves, and which we also see in others, be a warning that we should be wiser in the future and learn by our own loss not to be taken in by the lie of that lost enemy. In order to do this, we ask the Lord with constant prayers that he strip us of the judgment of our flesh and give us another, namely a spiritual one, through Jesus Christ, who received it together with every kind of gift so that he might share it with us. Next, let us hear him speaking in his holy Scriptures, which he sent down from heaven as letters to draw us away from the lies and deceits of the devil and lead us into all truth. There he teaches clearly that, whatever happens to us, we should always first lift our eyes to him; and especially as regards adversity, which seems to agree poorly with his nature, we should be firmly persuaded that it comes and proceeds from him. Not that he takes delight in it or derives any pleasure from it, but so that he may give men a taste of what he will openly make known on the last day: namely, that he is the just judge of the world, to whom justice is always dear and injustice most hateful. And he does this not only to make unbelievers more inexcusable, but also so that it may turn to the greater good of all the godly. For he testifies that he inflicts these punishments not out of any hatred, but rather because he loves them most dearly. Of this the richest witness is his only-begotten Son, whom he plunged into the abyss of all the miseries to which they were liable, indeed almost overwhelmed, in order to draw them out of it. Also, by adversities, which are the fruit of sin, he wills to lead his people to hatred of sin, and so to stir them up to flee the more ardently to the grace of Jesus Christ, so that he may free them from its tyranny and bring them into liberty. He also wills that, while they undergo affliction, they should learn what the wrath of God is, even if they feel only a little of it compared with the wicked, who will be overwhelmed forever by dreadful torments; so that they may give thanks with all the more eager spirit to that best of Saviours, who has freed them from so foul and horrible a whirlpool, since he drained for them the cup of divine wrath. And he has so sanctified and blessed their miseries in his cross that they are most spiritually seized, so that, while we feel ourselves justified by faith in Christ, we ourselves glory in those fruits I have mentioned and in the countless others which we gain from them. And so that we may weigh more carefully and value our happy state amid afflictions, let us look on the other side, at how wretched is the condition of all unbelievers, for whom adversities are harmful, because they bring them a destruction all the more grievous, in that, though warned, they do not repent, just as God was inviting them to. "They did not look to the hand of the one who struck them," says Isaiah. Moreover, there is a twofold difference between our calamities and theirs: namely, that ours are tempered according to the measure of our faith and of the strength which God has given us to bear them steadfastly, whereas their miseries have no measure. For just as they are stubborn against God and act perversely toward him, so God repays them with a reward worthy of their stubbornness and obstinacy; and just as they throw themselves without limit into the dreadful licence of all sins, so God observes no limit in exacting punishments for their crimes, so that even the respite which he grants them through prosperous circumstances turns to their greater destruction. Further, our temporal miseries are temporary, but theirs are everlasting. What greater thing could we ask? God afflicts us for our greatest good; God does not chastise us more harshly than we are able to bear; God will set an end to all our evils and give a happy outcome. I would bring forward more testimonies to confirm this, but since, contrary to my expectation, I am forced to bring my letter to a close, I will add only this one thing, by which you can easily recognise the incredible happiness of the godly. Of all the miseries to which men are liable, death is the most grievous and bitter. Yet the Lord declares that the death of his own is precious in his sight. The most wretched false prophet Balaam saw this so clearly that he wished to die the death of the righteous, and that his last end might be like theirs. Therefore we, who are sons of God, what shall we fear? Are we not supremely blessed, even when the world itself and our flesh judge us most unhappy? So let us, dearest sister, rejoice in the best God, and glory in him, whether he sends us want, sickness, prisons and chains, or any other calamities, or whether he confers benefits upon us. Though Satan is unwilling, let us turn all of this to our advantage, so that we may be all the more devoted to his service. When all things flow to us according to our wish, let us walk in fear and anxiety, lest we give free rein to our mad lust. On the other hand, in adversities let us so cast ourselves down before him in true repentance that, in the meantime, we do not hesitate to flee to him with sincere prayers, firmly persuaded that we shall be heard, and that he is with us while we are afflicted; and let us boldly mock all our enemies, who try to persuade us that we have been forsaken by him. If the Lord grants that I write to you about this matter, or even that I speak more fully in person, I will certainly do so gladly and from my heart. May his holy will be done. And just as he has displayed his power in me in such a way that I can in some measure answer him, so may he deign to carry his work through to the end; and indeed I have no doubt that he will accomplish this. Since he has also deigned to give himself wholly to me in the person of his Son, I profess myself wholly bound to him by right, whether now I live or die. During all this time in which I am struggling here with this [?] violence, a slight illness has seized me, namely a continual flow of blood, which has not yet been stopped. Whatever the outcome may be, I hope it will be of the greatest use to me. For my Father is most good, and in his immense goodness he has sealed this with so many signs that I ought rightly to offer him a son who is obedient and ready to die, and it grieves me deeply that I do not die in a better way for his sake. May he deign to heal this disease.

units.la: Epistolæ quædam Antonij Laborierij summa pietate & doctrina refertæ, ex his decerptæ quas ad uxorem suam scripsit.
units.tr: Letters of Antonius Laborierius, full of the greatest piety and learning, selected from those which he wrote to his wife.

units.la: Dilectio Dei nostri & Patris optimi, gratia Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & virtus Spiritus sancti tecum sit perpetuò, Amen.
units.tr: May the love of our good God and Father, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the power of the Holy Spirit be with you always. Amen.

units.la: PRoximo die Dominico, soror unicè dilecta, ad te scripsi copiose, ut Deus pro sua bonitate res nostras regat & moderetur: sed suspicor literas meas tibi redditas non fuisse. Hic bonus frater qui tibi meas perferet, mihi pollicitus est se inquisiturum an illæ sint adhuc in urbe, & daturum operam, ut eas tibi reddendas curet. Itaque nunc minimè repetā quæ illic colligor. huc accedit quòd ex eo melius intelliges quicquid hactenus factum fuit, quàm ego possum scribere. Sathā ꝑ suo ingenio conari non desinit, ut Dei opus impediat, dum nos acrius quàm unquam impetit. Sed Deus eò fortiores nos reddit, ut illi strenuè reluctemur: non quòd desint multæ infirmitates quibus cincti obsidemur, & horrenda carnis nostræ corruptela experimur, dum plusquam vellemus Dominum Deum nostrum offendimus. Verum misericordia & bonitas Dei nostri malitiam nostram superat, ut virtute Spiritus sui in nobis operari non desinat: & semper magis ac magis animos nostros inflamet ad mortem pro sacrosancto suo nomine tuendo libenter oppetendam.
