God the best has done this so that we may be seriously touched by them, so that we may groan, grieve, be ashamed of them, and from the heart be displeased with them; and on the contrary, that we may devote ourselves wholly to virtue, justice and holiness: let us crucify our old man and subdue our flesh, lest perverse desires rule any longer in us, but rise again into a new life, so that we may render obedience to our best God and bring forth fruits of justice and integrity that he may find pleasing, so that it may plainly be evident that we are members of Christ his Son, and truly regenerated and renewed by the Holy Spirit, to his glory and the building up of our neighbours. These are the benefits and fruits which we receive, among others, from the death and resurrection of that great Saviour and Redeemer Jesus Christ. To this the Holy Spirit urges us through the mouth of the Apostles, namely Paul in Romans chapters 6, 7 and 8, and in the epistles to the Ephesians and Colossians, and Peter in his two epistles; in whose constant reading you should exercise yourself, and by frequent meditation and reading of all the Psalms. Do not grow weary, but always keep them as a catechism: that is, when you have read through once, return to the beginning; and so, God helping, you will gather a singular fruit from them. Finally, the fourth and last prison pertains to us now in a particular way, and that by the benefit of our best God, who has given us, bound and captive for his Son Jesus Christ, into this castle of Cambrai, in which, in his greater goodness, he has poured out upon us a greater abundance of gifts and blessings, both of mind and of body, than in any other place where we have ever been. And this is the first advantage that comes back to us from it. Moreover, if we weigh the life which all men so naturally desire so greatly, do we not by a happy death enter into true life? Or [do we enter into] joy and delight[?]

units.la: { } Note: the printed marginal reference "1.Cor.15." is set in the left margin beside the line "annon felici morte". Statione, quam ita cupimus cernere & ea frui, perfectè unquam & in solidum fruimur, nisi hac morte suavi & optanda? Testimonio satis amplo nobis esse possunt Psalmi 90.103, & 104. Denique voces commutare non immerito licet, & vitam hanc breve tot miseriis & calamitatibus refertam nominare mortem ipsam: contra vero mortem naturalem, quae est corporis & animae dissolutio & abitus ex alieno hoc domicilio in patriam nostram, vocare vitam beatam possumus, & quidem iure, modo eam meditemur ac perpendamus in Christo Iesu Domino nostro tanquam ipsius membra: non autem alia ratione. Illa ergo ut nobis charissima libenter amplectamur, neq; ampliꝰ ut hosti infestu exhorreamus. Per eam alacriter & sponte transeamus, quum nos minime vincat & superet, ut ignominiae & contemptui subiciat, sed nobis potius ianua sit ad gloriam & ingressus. Comprehendamus illam quum nunc telum manu non gestet, ad nos lethali vulnere feriendos, aut aeternae morti addicendos: sed est veluti quaedam clavis, qua caeli ostium nobis aperiatur, ut illic Iesum Christum aeternam nostram vitam conspiciamus. Quid plura? nos sine eius opera in hoc mundo semper morimur, neque ulla unquam laetitiae voluptate fruimur: nunquam praesentia fidissimi & integerrimi sponsi nostri potimur, cum quo & per quem diuites ex paupertate euadimus, sani & incolumes ex morbo, vivi ex morte, felices ex miseriis, denique ex probro & ignominia participes immortalis gloriae, ut erepti ex faucibus hostium nostrorum, adeoque illis deuictis, & perfecto de isdem triumpho coronam hanc aeternae gloriae consequamur, & perpetuo triumphum aganus sub nostro Imperatore summo, victore & duce praestantissimo Iesu Christo Domino nostro, qui in unitate Patris & Spiritus sancti in aeternum vuus[?], nobis vitam suppeditabit, ac efficiet ut in se, & secum & cum Patre & Spiritu sancto subsistamus, postquam unum cum ipsis erimus, Amen.
units.tr: (Marginal reference: 1 Cor. 15.) [the] state which we so desire to behold and enjoy, do we ever fully and wholly enjoy it, except by this sweet and desirable death? The Psalms 90, 103 and 104 can be ample testimony for us. Finally, it is not wrong to change the words, and to call this brief life, full of so many miseries and calamities, death itself; on the contrary, we may rightly call natural death, which is the dissolution of body and soul and the departure from this alien dwelling into our homeland, a blessed life, provided we meditate on it and weigh it in Christ Jesus our Lord as his members, and not otherwise. Let us therefore embrace it gladly as most dear to us, and no longer shrink from it as an enemy. Let us pass through it eagerly and willingly, since it cannot conquer and overcome us so as to subject us to shame and contempt, but is rather a gate and entrance to glory for us. Let us take hold of it, since it now does not bear a weapon in its hand to strike us with a deadly wound or to doom us to eternal death; but it is like a certain key by which the door of heaven is opened to us, so that there we may behold Jesus Christ, our eternal life. What more? Without his work we always die in this world, and never enjoy any pleasure of joy; we never possess the presence of our most faithful and upright Bridegroom, with whom and through whom we pass from poverty to riches, from sickness to health and soundness, from death to life, from miseries to happiness, and finally from disgrace and shame to share in immortal glory; so that, snatched from the jaws of our enemies, and they having been conquered and complete triumph won over them, we may obtain this crown of eternal glory, and may celebrate a perpetual triumph under our supreme Commander, Victor and most excellent Leader Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives in the unity of the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever, will supply us with life, and will bring it about that we subsist in him, and with him and with the Father and the Holy Spirit, since we shall be one with them, Amen.

units.la: Antequam felix horum quinque Martyrum exitus describatur, hic quod mox sequitur inseruimus, ex quibusdam I.C. ad illos literis, quae eximiam consolationem continent.
units.tr: Before the happy end of these five martyrs is described, we have inserted here what follows, taken from certain letters of I.C. to them, which contain remarkable consolation.

units.la: Charitas Dei Patris nostri, & gratia Domini nostri Iesu Christi, per communicationem Spiritus sancti semper sit vobiscum.
units.tr: May the love of God our Father, and the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, through the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, always be with you.

units.la: Cum primum vos esse captos, fratres unice dilectos, & in carcerem coniectos intelleximus, statim illuc nuntium misi, qui rem totam certius nobis referret, atque diligentius exquireret si quid opis & auxilii adferre vobis possemus. Proximo die Jovis ingressus est iter, sub horam tertiam pomeridianam: heri demum huc rediit quum nox iam immineret. Nunc rursum proficiscitur ut vobis literas nostras reddat, & dispiciat vobiscum quanam ratione fieri possit, ut malis vestris, & afflictioni levationem aliquam afferamus. Minime autem necesse est copiosius explicare quantopere de vobis simus solliciti, & quanta anxietate vincula vestra nos constringant. Mihi ergo dubium non est, quum tot pij Dei cultores pro vobis assidue vota & preces concipiant, quin Deus noster opt.max. eorum desideria & gemitus exaudiat. Ac literis vestris iam video ut in vobis operari coeperit. nam si carnis infirmitas admixta se prodit, ita ut gravia molestaque certamina vobis sustinenda sint, mihi certe mirum non est, sed Deum laudo & extollo, quod supra illa vos erigat. Quod ad fratres Laborierium & Trigaletum attinet, habent quo se consolentur, quia illorum amici & arctiore quidem vinculo coniuncti, placide submittunt[?] se Dei voluntati: quam libenter amplectitur. Sed iam eos progressus in Christi schola fecistis, ut minime sit opꝰ[?] literis prolixioribus ad vos cohortandos. Tantùm quæ didicistis antehac ad usum vestrum accómodare vos oportet: & quoniâ Domino visum est vos ad hoc obsequiû vocare, & huic operi dicare, in eo quod cœpistis conficiendo pergite infrasti: Etsi autem vobis aditus nunc præcluditur, quominus coràm præsentes doceatis illos, quibus labore vestrum consecraueratis: quod tamen edetis palàm testimonii eosdem enimus confirmare nõ desinet: Deus enim virtute illi inspirabit, ut lõgius resonet, ac progrediatur ulterius, quàm possit vox humana pertingere. Quod vero spestat [?] ad rationes, seu media, quæ ex mundo apparet, utinam quidè eiusmodi nobis suppeterent ad vos eripiedos, ut illis minimè cõsisi, vobis prodessent: neque conatus nostri ad id efficiendum unquam deerunt: verùm Deus nos impellit, ut altius oculos erigamus. Et certè hoc primum est ac maximum, sensus omnes vestros colligere, ut in paternam eius bonitatem recumbatis, certò persuasi & corpora vestra & animas in eius esse fide ac tutela: & si pretiosus est illi filiorû suorum sanguis, eû palàm re ipsa monstraturum in vobis, quandoquidè vos in testes suos delegit. Si autem vita vestra ad veritatem suam afferendam & sanctiendam [?] ut velit, præterquàm quòd scitis esse sacrificium illi gratissimum, vobis hoc sit summæ consolationi, nihil scilicet vobis deperiturum, siquidè vos totos & vestra omnia in eius manum & obsequium addicatis. Namsi dum hanc vitam miseram viuimus, in fidem suam nos recipere dignatur, multò magis postquam ex hoc mundo reuocauerit, sefidum animarum nostrarum custodem probabit. Quantum attinet ad consilium quod petitis, vereor ne tempus opportunum effluxerit: iam enim amplissimæ fidei vestræ consessione edidisse vos intelligo. Quùm Deus optimus eô vos adduxerit, vobis retrocedere fas non est, sed potius omnia in Dei nostri prouidentiam reijcienda sunt. Interim date operam, ut inter respondendum prudentiam vestram à Dei Spiritu profestam esse omnes agnoscant: non autem ex mundi astu & calliditate. Si mihi ulla spes esset libellum vestrũ supplicem ad Regè peruenturum, minimè obstarem: sed illum, qui vobis id pollicitus est, credo nihil aliud captasse, nisi ut vos lacet [?] vana expectatione. ne tamen per vos stare videcatur, ego prorsus non refragor, quin perseueretis in eo quod à vobis illi propositum est. Et quoniâ in formula quam ad me ad me misistis, nihil reperiebā quod emendare necesse sit, nisi forte comparationem Achab, & rerum similium, quas lenire, vel emollire operæpretium esset: exemplar illud apud me retinui. Ego quidem formulā diversa libellum supplicem conscribere potuissem: sed malo, si quis offerendus est, nihil aliud extare, nisi quod Dominus vobis dictaverit: hac spe fretus, quòd uberiorem inde fructū proferet. Quòd si mundo grata non fuerit tam æquæ & sanctæ fidei vestræ professio, saltem Deo probabitur, eius Angelis, Prophetis & Apostolis, ac toti Ecclesiæ: adeoque pij omnes qui eam viderint, habebunt unde illum laudet, quòd Spiritu suo vobis illam dictaverit. Copiosius ad vos non scribam: hoc etiam accedit, quòd frater noster G. Farellus adest hic opportunè, ut vobis scribat. Finem ergo scribendi facturus, charissimi fratres, Deum nostrum optimum supplex rogabo, ut vos protegat, & subsidio suo tueatur, Spiritu suo gubernet, virtute & constantia instruat, quo scilicet ita certare positis, ut in vobis ipse triumphum agat sive mortem subeatis, sive proroget vobis vitam, & efficiat ut serio sentiatis quidnam sit & valeat in eo solo prorsus acquiescere. Quoniam autem comunes sunt hæ literæ fratrum meorum nomine seorsum vos non salutavi. Sed vobis minimè dubium esse credo, quin non illi modo, sed magnus etiam piorum numerus, atque adeò totum ecclesiæ nostræ corpus de salute vestra sic cogitent, ut officij ratio postulat & obstringit. Frater vester, quem optimè nostis, & vestri amantissimus.
units.tr: As soon as we learned that you, most dearly beloved brothers, had been taken and thrown into prison, I at once sent a messenger there to report the whole matter to us more accurately and to inquire carefully whether we could bring you any help or aid. He set out on the day before Thursday, at about three in the afternoon, and yesterday at last he returned here, when night was already at hand. Now he is setting out again to deliver our letter to you and to consider with you by what means we might bring some relief to your troubles and affliction. It is hardly necessary to explain at length how anxious we are about you, and how greatly your chains weigh on us. I have no doubt, then, that since so many godly worshippers of God offer vows and prayers for you without ceasing, our good and greatest God will hear their desires and groans. And from your letter I already see that he has begun to work in you. If the weakness of the flesh shows itself mingled in, so that you must endure grievous and troublesome struggles, this does not surprise me at all; rather I praise and extol God, who lifts you up above them. As for the brothers Laborierius and Trigaletus, they have something to console them, since their friends, joined to them by an even closer bond, calmly submit themselves to the will of God, which they gladly embrace. But you have already made such progress in the school of Christ that there is little need for lengthy letters to exhort you. You ought only to apply what you have learned hitherto to your use. Since the Lord has seen fit to call you to this service and to dedicate you to this work, press on in completing what you have begun. Although access is now closed to you, so that you cannot teach in person those to whom you had devoted your labour, you will publish a testimony which will continue to confirm them, for God will inspire that voice with power so that it resounds further and reaches beyond what human voice can attain. As for the reasons or means that appear from the world, would that such were available to us to snatch you away, so that they might profit you without our trusting in them. Our efforts to bring this about will never be lacking, but God urges us to lift our eyes higher. And certainly this is the first and greatest thing: to gather all your thoughts so that you rest upon his fatherly goodness, firmly persuaded that both your bodies and your souls are in his faith and keeping. If the blood of his sons is precious to him, he will show this in fact in you, since he has chosen you as his witnesses. If it pleases him that your life be given to assert and sanctify his truth, then, besides knowing that this is a most acceptable sacrifice to him, let this be your highest consolation: nothing will be lost to you, provided you devote yourselves wholly, and all that you have, to his hand and service. For if, while we live this wretched life, he deigns to receive us into his faith, much more after he has called us out of this world will he prove himself the faithful guardian of our souls. As for the counsel you ask for, I fear the opportune time has slipped away, for I understand that you have already made your most ample confession of faith. Since good God has brought you to this point, it is not right for you to turn back; rather, all things must be committed to the providence of our God. Meanwhile, take care that in your answers everyone recognises your prudence as coming from the Spirit of God, and not from worldly cunning and craftiness. If I had any hope that your supplicatory petition would reach the King, I would not object at all; but I believe the one who promised you this sought nothing else than to hold you with vain expectation. Yet, lest it seem that the fault lies with you, I by no means oppose your persevering in what you have proposed to him. And since in the form you sent to me I found nothing that needed correcting, except perhaps the comparison with Ahab and similar things, which it would be worth softening or moderating, I have kept that copy with me. I could indeed have written a supplicatory petition in a different form, but I prefer, if anything is to be offered, that nothing appear except what the Lord has dictated to you, relying on this hope: that it will bring forth more abundant fruit. But if the profession of so just and holy a faith is not pleasing to the world, it will at least be approved by God, his angels, prophets and apostles, and the whole Church; and all the godly who see it will have cause to praise him, because he dictated it to you by his Spirit. I will not write to you at greater length, and moreover our brother G. Farellus is here at hand, opportunely, to write to you. Therefore, making an end of writing, most dear brothers, I will humbly beseech our best God to protect you and keep you under his help, to govern you by his Spirit, and to furnish you with virtue and constancy, so that you may so contend that he himself triumphs in you, whether you undergo death or he prolongs your life, and so that you may truly feel what it is to rest in him alone. Since this letter is written in the name of my brothers as well, I have not greeted you separately. But I believe you have no doubt that not only they, but a great number of the godly, and indeed the whole body of our Church, think of your welfare as the duty of their office requires and obliges them to. Your brother, whom you know well and who loves you dearly.

units.la: Epistola Guyraudi Taurani ad quendam amicum.
units.tr: Letter of Guyraud Tauran to a certain friend.

units.la: Gratia Dei Patris nostri per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum virtute Spiritus sancti perpetuo tecum sit, Amen.
units.tr: May the grace of God our Father, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be with you always by the power of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

units.la: Q[?]uae vnquam literae fratres integerrimi, solatiū mihi attulerunt, procul dubio fuerunt vestrae, quo nomine vobis gratiā habeo, ex quibus etiam intelligere licuit, vos graui tristitia & anxietate constringi, nempe insci & ancipites, quam mihi Deus optimus opem tule-rit, & ferat quotidie (cui maximas ob id gratias ago) quia scilicet in mentem vobis veniebat ecquid in me situm esset: quod quidem non moleste nec graviter fero. erat enim unde mœror contraberetur. Verum habita illius ratione, cuius nomine certabam, nihil erat periculi, quoniam instructus est omni genere armorū, quae necessaria sunt: & quum fuit opus ea mihi suppeditauit. Nam vel hoc vno possum iudicare ac certo statuere, ab illo me non fuisse ereptum ex miserrimo atque horrendo Papatus gurgite, sub quo in densissimas tenebras eram demersus, vt semel in lucem pretractus, eo rursum detrudar. Et quanuis culpa mea non leui par non essem qui responderem tot capitibus quae mihi sunt proposita, quaeque magnum Theologum desiderabant: Deus tamen os mihi dedit quo pudefierent veritatis hostes. Conscius etiam meae infirmitatis, & magno in periculo me versari videns, ego totus in Dei optimi gratiam & paternam eius indulgentiam omnino recubui, quam ita exeruit erga me miserum peccatorem, vt re ipsa expertus sim promissionem illam quam Dòminus fecit Apostolis suis, sicuti scribitur Matth.x, non solum ad eos spectasse quum illis diceret, Quando ad Reges & Principes tracti fueritis, ne sitis soliciti quomodo vel quid respondeatis. tunc enim dabitur vobis quid loquamini. Iam quum ego videam hanc tam paternam Dei optimi bonitatem qua me complectitur, vobis cogitandum relinquo, an vlli erunt ignes, vel gladij, vel cruciatus quanlibet graues & acerbi, quibus possim abstrahi aut auerti, quominus quum me vocabit, libenter sequar. Certum est nunquam fieri posse: sed vobis hoc confirmo, quaecunque tormenta ad me cruciandum excogitent homines, me illa excepturum vt auxilia quaedam & subsidia, quibus ad Deum optimum accedam. Si me vocet per ignem, mihi summa est consolatio quod certo sciam illos tres pueros ex fornace ignis ardentis extractos suisse, & virtutem eius imminutam non esse: si vero per aquam, ipse quoque Israelitas per mare rubrum traduxit absque vllo discrimine. Denique sicuti visum illi fuerit, voluntas eius fiat. hanc placidè expectato[?], paratus ad emigrandum, quoties me vocabit. Atque hic finem scribendi faciam, quia non possem vel prolixissimis[?] literis exprimere quas in me gratias Deus optimus contulit: ille, inquam, qui non est imperitus artifex, sed qui opus quod in me coepit, absoluet omnibus numeris. Id autem vt faciat eum quotidie precor ex animo: ac vos etiam rogo & quotquot isthic sunt fratres, vt idem meo nomine praestetis.
units.tr: What letters from you, most upright brothers, have ever brought me comfort? They were surely yours, and for them I give you thanks. From them I could also understand that you are held down by a heavy sadness and anxiety, namely that you are uncertain and fearful about how God, most good, has helped me and daily continues to help me (for which I give him the greatest thanks), and whether, as a result, anything was happening to me. I do not bear this unhappily or grievously, for there was indeed cause for sorrow. But, taking into account the one in whose name I am contending, there was no danger, since he is equipped with every kind of weapon that is needed, and when there is need he supplies them to me. For by this alone I can judge and firmly determine that I have not been snatched by him from the most wretched and dreadful whirlpool of Papacy, under which I was plunged into the thickest darkness, only to be dragged back down again once I had been brought into the light. Although, through my own fault, I was not at all equal to answering the many charges laid against me, charges that called for a great theologian, God nonetheless gave me a mouth by which the enemies of the truth were put to shame. Aware also of my own weakness, and seeing that I was in great danger, I have wholly rested in the favour and fatherly indulgence of the best of Gods, which he has shown towards me, a wretched sinner, so that I have in fact experienced that promise which the Lord made to his apostles, as it is written in Matthew 10: that it applied not only to them when he said to them, "When you are brought before kings and governors, do not be anxious how or what you shall answer; for it will be given you in that hour what you shall say." Now, since I see this so fatherly goodness of God by which he embraces me, I leave it to you to consider whether there will be any fires, or swords, or torments, however grievous and bitter, by which I could be drawn away or turned aside from following him gladly when he calls me. It is certain that this can never happen. But I assure you of this: whatever tortures men devise to torment me, I shall receive them as certain aids and supports by which I draw near to God most good. If he calls me through fire, my greatest consolation is that I know for certain that those three boys were brought out of the blazing furnace and that its power was not diminished; if through water, he himself also led the Israelites through the Red Sea without any peril. Finally, let his will be done as it seems good to him. I await this calmly, ready to depart whenever he calls me. And here I will make an end of writing, because I could not express in the longest letter the thanks that God most good has bestowed upon me, he who is not an unskilled craftsman, but who will bring to completion in every respect the work he has begun in me. I pray to him daily from my heart that he will do this; and I ask you too, and all the brothers there, to do the same in my name.

units.la: Nunc sequitur descriptio felicis ac pretiosæ mortis quinque Martyrum, de quibus iam actum est,
units.tr: Now follows a description of the happy and precious death of the five martyrs of whom we have already spoken.

units.la: QVO die ad supplicium pertracti sunt, quidam vir bonus quum in eorū gratiâ fecisset quidquid potuerat, illos adiit ut colloqueretur. Et quum renuntiasset moriendum ipsis esse, pro modulo suo, & gratia sibi à Deo collata eos consolatus est: & hortatus etiam, ut inuicta constantia pergerent, quandoquidem Deus opt. eorum opera in asserenda veritate sua uti statuerat. & quemadmodum ille opus feliciter in eis auspicatus fuerat, ita perstarent infracti, & palam intrepidum animum in reliquo certamine sustinendo commostrarent [?]. Hic omnes uno ore, & eadem voce Deo gratias egerunt, quod tantum honorem ipsis detulisset. Unus illorum nempe Ioannes Vernutius [?], hoc nuncio accepto, initio quidem attonitus & metu perculsus est, ut nulla totius corporis esset particula, quæ non contremisceret, atque cohorresceret: ac proinde in hanc vocem erupit, Sentio in me gravius certamen, quam possit ab homine mortali sustineri: spiritus tamen vincet miseram hanc carnem: & confido me non desertum iri à Deo optimo max. ac vos rogo, integerrimi fratres, ne mea causa offendamini: nō deficiā omnino. Deus enim promisit se nobis adfuturum in nostris afflictionibus: sed Dominus habet varias rationes, quibus suos exerceat. Atque tantus hic pauor nos monere debet nostræ infirmitatis, & excitare ut toti ex Dei virtute pendeamus, qui virtutem suam perficit in eorum infirmitate, quos sibi delegit in peculium, ut omnis gloria illi soli tribuatur.
units.tr: On the day they were led away to punishment, a certain good man, after doing all he could on their behalf, went to them to speak with them. When he had told them that they must die, he comforted them according to his ability and the grace given him by God, and he also urged them to press on with unconquered constancy, since God the best and greatest had determined to use their work in asserting his truth; and just as he had begun the work happily in them, so they should stand firm, unbroken, and openly display a fearless spirit in bearing the rest of the struggle. Here all of them, with one voice and one accord, gave thanks to God that he had conferred such honour upon them. One of them, John Vernutius, on hearing this news, was at first astonished and struck with fear, so that there was no part of his body that did not tremble and shudder; and so he burst out in these words: "I feel a harder struggle in me than any mortal man can sustain. Yet the spirit will overcome this wretched flesh, and I trust that I shall not be forsaken by God most good and greatest. And I ask you, most upright brothers, not to be offended on my account; I will not fail altogether. For God has promised to be with us in our afflictions, but the Lord has various ways by which he trains his own. And this great dread ought to warn us of our weakness, and to stir us to depend wholly on the power of God, who perfects his power in the weakness of those whom he has chosen as his own possession, so that all glory may be given to him alone."

units.la: Quum autem ad locum supplicio destinatum venissent, idem ille Ioannes Vernutius quod sibi pollicitus fuerat de bonitate Dei & virtute, consecutus est, constantiam videlicet invictam & fortitudinem vere Christiano dignam. Primus omnium à carnifice tractus est: verum antequam mactaretur, preces ad Deum fudit: ita exorsus, Domine Deus & Pater omnipotens ego certè corā sacrosancta maiestate tua ex animo & sincerè agnosco me peccatorem esse miserrimum: & cætera quæ in precationum formula recitantur statim initio: deinde fidem suam audiente universo populo clarè professus est, quum verò spiritum suum Deo commendasset, mortis acerbitate perpessus, hostes suos devicit.
units.tr: When they had come to the place appointed for execution, that same John Vernutius obtained what he had promised concerning the goodness and power of God, namely an unconquered constancy and a fortitude truly worthy of a Christian. He was the first of all to be dragged forward by the executioner; yet before he was put to death he poured out prayers to God, beginning thus: "Lord God and almighty Father, I truly and sincerely acknowledge in your most holy majesty that I am a most wretched sinner," and the rest that are recited at the very beginning of the set form of prayer. Then, with the whole people listening, he professed his faith clearly. And when he had commended his spirit to God, having endured the bitterness of death, he overcame his enemies.

units.la: Antonius Laborierius imperterrito animo & læto vultu, perinde ac si ad nuptias (quod aiunt) invitatus, sese ad mortem intrepidè obtulit. Ac priusquam obiret, carnifex ab eo veniā petiit, præfatus se illum nō esse qui morti ipsum addiceret, sed eos demū qui iuri dicundo præficerentur. Tunc autem Laboricrius, Amice, inquit, me profsus nō offendis: quin potius opera tua ex miro carcere eripior. Id cùm dixisset, carnificem osculatus est. Ex plebe multi miseritordia commoti lachrymas fundebant. Deinde eadem quas antea Vernutius, preces concepit, & diserte fidei suæ confessionem edidit, atque ita spiritu ultimum summa constantia emisit.
units.tr: Antonius Laborierius, with an undaunted spirit and a cheerful face, offered himself fearlessly to death, just as if he had been invited to a wedding, as they say. And before he died, the executioner asked his pardon, saying beforehand that he was not the one who was condemning him to death, but those who were appointed to pronounce judgment. Then Laborierius said, "Friend, you do not offend me at all; rather, through your work I am being released from a wonderful prison." Having said this, he kissed the executioner. Many of the common people, moved with pity, shed tears. Then he offered the same prayers as Vernutius had before, and set forth a clear confession of his faith, and so with the greatest constancy he breathed out his last.

units.la: Ioannes Trigaletus infracto quoque animo ad mortem progressus est: ac pro inimicis suis orauit, quosdam esse clamans, qui nescirèt quid facerent ipsi: alios etiam esse qui certò scirent, fascinatos tamen à Sathana, & mundi honoribus ebrios, nolle palam nec ingenuè profiteri. O, mi Deus, inquiebat, oro te vt eos liberes! Tandem subiunxit, Deus mi, iam te spiritu cerno sursum in tuo folio sedentem, & cælos apertos video, sicuti Stephano seruo tuo dedisti vt moriturus intueretur. Sic fidem suam professus, feliciter expirauit.
units.tr: John Trigaletus also went to his death with an unbroken spirit. He prayed for his enemies, crying out that some of them did not know what they were doing, and that others knew for certain, yet, bewitched by Satan and drunk with the honours of the world, were unwilling to profess it openly and frankly. "O my God," he said, "I beg you to set them free!" At last he added, "My God, now I see you sitting upon your throne on high in spirit, and I see the heavens opened, as you granted your servant Stephen to behold when he was about to die." Having professed his faith in this way, he happily breathed his last.

units.la: Bertrandus Batallius coram omnibus audacter hæc verba protulit, Nos hic nō sumus vel ob latrocinium, vel homicidium, aut aliud scelus: sed quia iustissimam Dei causam tuemur. Et quum precatus esset Deum, supplicio mortis affectus fuit.
units.tr: Bertrand Batallius boldly spoke these words before them all: "We are not here for theft, or murder, or any other crime, but because we are defending the most just cause of God." And when he had prayed to God, he was condemned to the death penalty.

units.la: Postremus Guyraudus Tauranus, Psalmum vnum ita cecinit, vt ab omnibus audiretur: & quanquam erat adhuc iuuenis non minore tamen constantia quàm reliqui excelluit: Deum magno ardore & voce firma orauit: deinde mortem obiit.
units.tr: Last of all, Guyraud Tauran sang one Psalm so that all could hear it. Although he was still young, he excelled no less in constancy than the others. He prayed to God with great fervour and a firm voice; then he met his death.

units.la: Simplex hæc narratio satis indicat, nihil fucatū fuisse, sed rem totam vt gesta est expositam: quæ posset etiam ex proprio illorum ore extorqueri, qui morti eos adiudicarunt, modò conscientijs suis non iniicerent frænum, sed plenam dicendi facultatem concederent. Impij ac scelerati homines oculos non habent aptos perspicuedis[?] insignibus Dei miraculis: erit tamen aliquando tempus, quo subijcientur formidabili Christi iudicio, quem in suis membris tam superbè & crudeliter configunt. Faxit autem Deus opt.max. virtute sua, vt nobis hæc exempla sic prosint & animos addant, ne vllus impiorum furor impediat vel remoretur, quò minus constanter reddamus testimonium eius veritati, quoties visum fuerit nos ad certamen euocare, Amen.
units.tr: This simple narrative sufficiently shows that nothing was embellished, but that the whole matter is set out as it actually happened. It could even be extracted from the very mouths of those who condemned them to death, provided they did not put a bridle on their consciences but granted them full freedom to speak. Impious and wicked men do not have eyes fit to perceive the notable miracles of God; yet there will come a time when they will be subjected to the dreadful judgment of Christ, whom they crucify so proudly and cruelly in his members. May God almighty, by his power, grant that these examples so benefit us and add courage to our hearts that no fury of the ungodly may hinder or delay us from bearing witness constantly to his truth, whenever it shall seem good to him to call us to the contest. Amen.

units.la: IOANNES CRISPINVS CHRISTIANIS LECTORIBVS.
units.tr: JOHN CRISPIN TO THE CHRISTIAN READERS.

units.la: VOLVMEN istud Actionum Martyrum,quum ad iustam magnitudinem excreuisse videremus, Christiani Lectores, octauo demum libro claudendum duximus, ne vos diutius huius operis expectatione suspensos teneremus, neue rerum praeclarissimarum à ἀνθρώποις[?] cuiuscunque generis, ordinis, aetatisque hominibus gestarū fructu vtilitateque priuaremus: deinde vt maiori tum otio tum commoditate ad ea colligenda pergeremus, quae iam breui in Gallia Cardinalis ille Lotharingus piorum sanguine rubens dispersit ac dissipauit: inter quos egregiè cordatus Dei Martyr Annas à Burgo supremae Parisiēsis Curiae senator, XXII.die mensis Decemb. anni M.D.LIX. admirabilem martyrij coronam accepit. Hispaniae quoque (cui nunc etiam sol iustitiae ac veritatis lux affulsit) Martyrū his temporibus actiones eadem editione Deo fauente, daturos nos speramus. Interea omnes hortari ac per sacrosanctum Christi martyrum ducis ac principis nomen obtestari non desinam vt in hoc opus tam vtile ac necessarium diligentiam omnem & operam conferatis.
units.tr: Christian readers, when we saw that this volume of the Acts of the Martyrs had grown to a fitting size, we decided to close it with the eighth book. We did not want to keep you waiting longer for this work, nor deprive you of the fruit and usefulness of these most distinguished deeds, which were done by people of every kind, rank and age. Moreover, we wanted to gather with greater leisure and convenience the accounts of those whom that Cardinal of Lorraine, reddened with the blood of the pious, has lately scattered and destroyed in France. Among them the Martyr of God, Annas du Bourg, a senator of the supreme court of Paris, a man of outstanding wisdom, received the admirable crown of martyrdom on the 22nd day of December in the year 1559. We also hope, by God's favour, to publish in the same edition the acts of the martyrs of this time in Spain, where the sun of righteousness and the light of truth have now also risen. Meanwhile I shall not cease to urge all of you, and to beseech you by the holy name of Christ, the leader and prince of the martyrs, to bring every care and effort to this work, which is so useful and so necessary.
